If perhaps he lived and married there, and, according to tradition, Sarai and Yiska are identical, so that Sarai was the daughter of Haran, and Lot and Sara came from Ur-Kasdim, the words: ויצאו אתם become understandable. Sarai and Lot went with Terach and Abram out of the land of their birth.

The story of the wandering forth of the Terach family gives the impression of being quite similar to what happened further in Aram which had such far-reaching consequences for the future, both for those that left and those that remained. Nobody knew that it was God Who said to Abram in Charan לך לך. “Unpleasant family affairs caused the people to go away”. However we see that Terach and the other members of the family gave up the idea of treking to Canaan when they were half way there. Only Abram, leaving the paternal home, followed the call of God to which the following chapter refers.

V. 1. לך לך. If all that this wanted to says was: Go from Aram to Canaan it would not say: לך לך but לך, or perhaps צא. But then the departure from the fatherland would include that from the birthplace and the father’s home, ממולדתך ומבית אביך would be quite superfluous, and in any way, in the wrong order. The departure occurs first from the father’s house, then from the birthplace and then from the land. Moreover the separating accent of the cantillation on מבית אביך makes לך לך into a self-contained closed order by itself. The addition of a pronoun to הלך, as in וילך לו לא ארצו ,אלכה לי אל הגדולים etc. and equally so in קומי לך רעיתי etc. always gives the action a particular, individualising or isolating tendency.

הלך related to חלק, to be divided, i.e. that two things are no longer connected, and חלק smooth i.e. to have a surface to which nothing adheres any longer: hence also עלג the divided speech, words not hanging together, stammering. So that already in the word itself הלך has the idea of separating oneself from the place where one happens to be. This going away can be a means, for the purpose of going to another place, or it can be a purpose in itself, simply to get away from where one is. By the addition of a pronoun this second idea is more precisely stressed לך לך: “go for yourself, to yourself, isolate yourself”. Thus by Jethro: וילך לו he renounced the advantages which his connection with Israel had brought him. Thus also Joshua to the sons of Gad and Reuben: ועתה פנו ולכו לכם לאהליכם (Jos. 22,4) now you have done your duty to the community, and now you can go “for yourselves”. So here לך לך means: go for yourself, leaving your land etc., detaching yourself from all your previous connections, go your own isolating way. The first departure from Ur-Kasdim was perhaps for safety’s sake. This demand makes going away its own purpose.

מולדת ,ארץ and בית together form the soil out of which the personality of people grows. ארץ, the country, the nationality, with all the special bodily, mental and moral characteristics which it gives, (ארץ, as our country, is ארס, to which our whole being is “married”; ערש, the cradle in which we grow to life; ערס: the kneading-trough in which we are moulded, ערץ the mighty power from which nobody can escape. ארץ as the earth is our “cradle” and over it is שמים, our שם, “there”, our future) — So that ארץ gives our personality the stamp of the national characteristics and participation in the power and worthiness of a nation — מולדת, birthplace gives us civic position and independence — בית, the home, finally, is the narrower sphere in which we grow up individually, and find individual care and development: בית, is phonetically related to בגד and בגד .פקד is the garment, the protective casing which closely envelops people. בית also is nothing other than an extension of the garment as the enveloping limit which protects the developing and working person. Man has three casings, בשר, the body (בסר the peel or husk of fruit), the garment and the house. פקד too, is nothing other than to clothe, to invest, for פקד in its original meaning is to give something its external fitting surroundings. Thus primarily of the Divine dispositions. God gives every individual the external conditions which are befitting to him, they form his garment, his external appearance. Then it means, to place something in one’s mind in the sphere to which it belongs, i.e. to think of it. Then in its social meaning: to establish somebody in an office, to appoint an officer. In contrast to the German conception the office invests, “clothes” the man, the mission which the office involves forms the sphere in which he has to move. Hence also הפקיד to give something into somebody’s care, really to make its home with him.

We have mentioned these thoughts innate in the Hebrew language to realise how deeply and intimately even our very language feels and values the worth of one’s fatherland and birth-place. It is certainly not meant to be any belittleing of this factor if the planting of the first Jewish germ demanded forsaking fatherland, birth-place and the paternal home. It is rather just the appreciation of these factors wherein lies the greatness of the isolation demanded here. This demand itself placed Abraham in the completest contrast to the ruling tendency of his age. Not individualism, not recognition of the worth and importance of the individual, but centralisation which makes men lose their personal value, and lowers them to mere subordinate workers, mere bricks for the building of the fame of a supposed representation of the community, that was the tendency of the age, which, under the slogan of נעשה לנו שם began building the tower of the glory of Man. This tendency begot the erroneous conception of a majority which has sway in every direction and in every case. So that finally everything that is considered the highest by the majority, ipso facto becomes considered and honoured as the highest by everybody. It is true of course that the majority of every community should be the representative of all that which is truly the highest and holiest, and it is in the presumption that such is the case, that Judaism, too, values attachment to the community as being supremely important. Nevertheless at the head of Judaism the words לך לך “go for yourself” stand as being higher still; nobody may say: I am as good, as honest, as everybody else is, as is the fashion here today. Everybody is responsible to God for himself. If necessary, alone — with God, — when the principle worshipped by the majority is not the true godly one. This is what was demanded from Abraham as the starting point for his and his future people’s mission. Our very language teaches, as we have seen, in the word ארץ and בית how strong are the bonds that attach a person to both; yet stronger than the bond that attaches us to fatherland and family should the bond be that attaches us to God.
How could we have existed, how continue to exist, if we had not, from the very beginning received from Abraham the courage to be a minority!

“Up to date Judaism!” The loudest protest against it is the first Jewish word לך לך. Was Abraham’s first stand in accordance with the spirit of his times? In the midst of Chaldea, Babylon, Assyria, Phonecia, Egypt! Idolizing sensuality and power was the contemporary sermon there, worshipping the life of the senses in Asia, worshipping human power and killing freedom in Egypt, only slight traces of the thought “God” remaining — and there an Abraham is to arise. While everybody in the whole world was making every effort to establish themselves, to settle securely, he is to give up his homeland and his rights as a citizen, of his own freewill to make himself a refugee, to throw a protest in the face of the gods worshipped by all the nations. This demands courage and the conviction of the truth of the inner feeling, and consciousness of God, this demands the Jewish conception of God and Jewish confidence and boldness — and that was the first thing that Abraham had to do to justify his appointment.

Thus we can well understand how our נביאים, those watchers of the times, appointed by God, צופים, introduced the five final letters into the alphabet of their people as signs of all past and future special periods in the history of the salvation of Israel קצים (“endings of periods”). They epitomize the whole of Jewish history in the doubled ך, doubled מ, doubled נ, doubled פ and doubled צ of the לך לך of Abraham, the עצמת ממנו of Isaac, the הצילני נא of Jacob, the פקוד יפקוד of the redemption from Egypt, the צמח שמו ותחתיו יצמח, of the future גאולה; they could see in the לך לך of Abraham the first starting point of the גאולה. With the call to isolation which Abraham obeyed, the salvation of the world through Judaism was decided.

V. 2. ואעשך לגוי גדול. Even looked at quite superficially, it is already evident that Abraham was to receive back from God everything that he had given up, and indeed in a considerably enhanced measure. By renouncing מארצו he gave up his nationality. But instead of having to attach himself to another one, God says that he himself is to be the founder of a new one. By giving up his birthplace, מולדתו, he is not to miss the civic rights which are the natural source of prosperity for ואברכך, in God will he gain the right to prosper on earth. And inasmuch as he forsakes his family, and thereby gives up the respect and honour given to well-known old families אגדלה שמך, in him, a new name is to grow to great renown.

Our sages in ב״ר ל״ט remind us that it does not say אשימך לגוי גדול that God will be the protector of and look after the national development of his descendants similarly to the way He directs and guides the growth of nations in general, but אעשך, I will make you, create you to a great nation. All external natural conditions shall speak against it, and here it shall be strikingly apparent that God is the creator of this nation as such. Already the age and the barrenness of the pair who were chosen to be the roots of the future nation denied the presumption of the promised future according to all natural assumption. God alone could make Abraham to a great nation. So already beforehand, the very existence of this people was to be a revelation of God.

But numerous descendants do not yet constitute a nation. That any mass of people should become a גוי, a nation, there must be some uniting bond. Everywhere else this is a common land, living together under the same influences and conditions. But the descendants of Abraham are also to become a nation, but not through a common land, but again only through God. Abraham’s spirit is to repeat itself in his descendants: what their country is to other nations, that, you yourself are to be to your descendants. With their descent from you they are also to inherit the uniting element that forms a nation. By the fact that, still today, we call our God אלקי אברהם, God as Abraham knew him, as He revealed Himself to him, showed Himself in the guidance of his life — and we need this designation, not as a God Who shows us any particular favour, but, on the contrary, just to keep the Abrahamitic and most comprehensive conception of God as קונה שמים וארץ, clear from any tendency of particularization — by this common heritage that we have received from Abraham we are a people still to-day long after we have lost the bond of a common country. And in the fact that not only Abraham, but that also his son and his grandson became such personalities in whose lives God’s direction was so manifest that they too remained models for the whole Jewish nation and we speak not only of אלקי אברהם, but also of אלקי יצחק and אלקי יעקב, in that our sages see primarily the blessing and the greatness that Abraham attained. And just in אלקי יעקב the ואגדלה שמך becomes realised. In Jacob’s fate and position in the world above all is the example given that the Jewish calling is independent of outward greatness and outward show. The less a man has the greater does his personality appear. The greatness, the blessing that a person without means spreads can only be attributed to his personality. If a יעקב is great, if a nation becomes outstanding, which for centuries has won no fame by battles etc. then this prominence can only be due to their spiritual personality, just יעקב is מגדל שמך.

Considered more closely, the whole sum of Jewish history is given to Abraham in a nutshell in these three sentences. In ’לך לך מארצך וגו Abraham appears merely as an individual “dare to be alone, to stand by yourself”. In ’ואעשך לגוי וגו, the nation already appears, but still by itself and without external contact or relation to the rest of the world. In ’ואברכה וגו the Jewish nation is shown in connection with other nations, the blessing of Abraham is already dependent on others blessing him, yea others can already venture to curse him. Abraham’s task was to isolate himself, to live alone with God. Then a second stage, to create a people out of this Abraham. If it is to come to pass that the existence of this people is to be a second creation of God’s in history then this people can only come to be a nation by way of homelessness, of גלות and גרות. If it were already established it would be no אצבע אלקים no ’ואעשך לגוי גדול ,מעשה ה, from יצחק to יציאת מצרים ,ואברכך, then will I plant you in an ואגדלה שמך ;ארץ זבת חלב ודבש, not אגדל שמך. God can bless people and nations, but that they shall attain such spiritual greatness to become called a model man, a model nation, that God can only wish, that depends on the faithful loyalty which is given to the laws of God. In the same way it does not say והײת ברכה or ותהיה ברכה but והיה ברכה “become a blessing”. In these two words the whole moral task is summarised the accomplishment of which is the condition for the fulfilment of God’s wish. “O that your name should become great, that you become a blessing”. I would make you into a nation to which other nations have only to look to become conscious of what their task is, and this task, which you are to accomplish, in contrast to the efforts of all other nations, is “to become a blessing”!

All others strive, not להיות ברכה to be a blessing, but להיות ברוכים, to be blessed. And this is especially the case with nations. The honesty, humanity and love which one still demands from individuals is regarded as folly in the relation of nation to nation, have no meaning in diplomacy and politics. Deception and murder which in individuals lead to prison and gallows, if exercised on a grand scale in the “interests of the state” are crowned with laurel and medals. The Abrahamitic nation is to know nothing of these national institutions, is to have no national politics and no political economy. The One Who would be the bearer of their national prosperity need give no subsidies, has not to reckon on any coalitions or treaties. At His command rain and sunshine, strength and life, power and victory stand. אם בחוקותי תלכו is the one condition, then everything else goes by itself. In the midst of a world of men who stamp נעשה לנו שם as the motto on all their endeavours, and self-aggrandizement and ruthless extension of their own well-being the deciding goal for all their efforts, the People of Abraham, are, in private and public life to follow the one calling: היה ברכה to become a blessing. To dedicate themselves with all devotion to the Divine purpose of bringing happiness to the world and mankind, thereby as models, to re-establish Man to its original pure calling of אדם, then God will grant His blessing to fresh activity of life and to the awakening and education of the nations to similar efforts and make the name of the People of Abraham shine forth far afield: ואברכך ואגדלה שמך. This second stage was to have become a reality in ארץ ישראל, there Israel was to have become in its isolation not only the blessed nation, but in the first place, the spreader of blessing, a source of blessing, a well from which the world would draw its blessing — וישכן ישראל בטח בדד עין יעקב. Had we lived up to our mission, then all that, which only beckons to us באחרית הימים, in the distant future, would have been realised thousands of years ago, and the history of the world would have worn a very different aspect.

But this first promise to Abraham seems to point to a third stage. We have already remarked that the optative ואגדלָה makes the realisation of the second stage, not a definite promise, but only a conditional wish that the promise could be fulfilled. Now the third clause seems to indicate a stage in which the blessing or the reverse of the Abrahamic people would be dependent on men, where men would have the power to bless them, men the power to curse them. This would be the stage of גלות which would await this people if they would forget their mission, and instead of striving להיות ברכה would give themselves up, like the other nations להיות ברוכים. And here for this Galut, where it is scattered amongst the nations and dependent on them and apparently abandoned to them for their blessings and curses, God pronounces this weighty Word:- ואברכה מברכיך, “those that bless thee, will I bless”, those that bless you, help you, who recognise and appreciate your principles, and submit to your moral sensibility and your honouring God, those will I bless. Here too the optative is again used, may Israel behave in the dispersion in such a manner that furthering their well-being may mean furthering the well-being and happiness of the nations in general.

ומקללך אאור, not אוררך אאור but מקללך. There are two conceptions of the reverse of ברכה viz. קללה and קלל .מארה (from which we get קל light in weight) and קללה, material reduction, decreasing the material means of a person or thing, making it “light”. ארר (related to חרר, to dry up, to scorch, parch, and ערר the root of ערירי, childless and ערער lonely) not only curtailing material means but also the inner forms and energies. That which קלל is externally and extensively, ארר is internally and intensively, to rob somebody of the abilities for their inner life, to make them ערער and ערירי. In contrast ברכה, to bless, is to give strength to both internal and external forces of development. — So that what it says here is:- I will accompany you also in life out amongst the nations, in accordance with the respect a nation pays to the Jewish spirit will I bless that nation. But a nation — not that takes away from you the ability for your inner life, for that no nation has the power to do — but that restricts and embitters your existence, that does not allow you to find the means for your development, that nation — not אקלל — but I will deprive of the internal ability for its own continued development.

Accordingly, as it says that only those nations will flourish who not only do not stunt the development of your principles but who acknowledge and further them, that says by itself that the משפחות האדמה will be blessed through you, the more they acknowledge you the more ברכה will they receive. But God asserts that finally כל משפחות האדמה all the peoples of the world (whose relations to one another will then be that of families I.L.) will participate in this blessing inasmuch as they will all found their lives on the same foundation on which you are to found yours. — So it seems to be.

קלל ist verwandt mit גלל und גלל ילל: rollen, Kreis, Rad. Dasjenige kann am leichtesten gerollt werden, das am wenigsten Seiten hat, die ihm einen Stütz- und Ruhepunkt gewähren, am meisten also das, was gar keine der Unterlage parallele Flächen bietet, die vollendete Kugel. Dies geistig übertragen, bezeichnet einen Schicksalszustand, wo die äußeren Verhältnisse gar keine Unterlage, keinen Stütz- und Ruhepunkt gewähren, wo sich der Mensch völlig halt- und ruhelos findet, von allen äußeren Verhältnissen zurückgestoßen, geistig נע ונד. Sein Ausdruck wird יללה: die wehevollste Klage. Was nun nicht durch die äußere Form, sondern durch inneren Mangel an Stoff und Wesenheit, keinen Ruhepunkt findet, ruhelos fortbewegt wird, leicht ist, heißt: קל, das Leichte. Andererseits wird dasjenige, was keines Zusammenhanges mit allem außerhalb mehr bedarf, weil es bereits sämtliches zu ihm Gehörige in sich trägt, das in sich Geschlossene, der Kreis und das Ganze, Vollendete, durch כלל ausgedrückt. כלכל heißt, in jemandes Kreis alles, dessen er bedarf, hineintragen: versorgen; geistig ומי יכלכל את יום באו, alles in den Begriff eines Wesens hineintragen, was in ihn gehört, gänzlich ermessen.

V. 4. It is probably not without reason that it uses דבר here and not אמר .אמר would refer to the whole promise so full of benevolence with which the order לך לך was accompanied; and which well may have been qualified to make Abraham’s feelings ready to yield to this demand. But Abraham did not obey the promise but the order of God. He went because God had told him to. Abraham was 75 years old when God chose him. Moses and Aaron too, had already a whole life behind them when God elected them to be His instruments.

V. 5. רכושם, root is רכש from which we get רתם המרכבה לרכש ,רֶכֶשׁ (Micah I.13), רכש seems to be the draught-horse whereas סוס is the horse in general and especially next to רכש designates the riding horse. רכוש is the mobile possession, מטלטלין which can be acquired by משיכה, not immobile property קרקעות, also not מקנה the herd which accompanies men by itself, but lifeless movable property which men can take away with them.

ואת הנפש אשר עשו: where עשה occurs as acquiring, that conception lies not in the word עשה but in the object which is added to it, כבוד ,חיל etc., but here, with נפש it can only mean, formed, fresh-created. That these fresh-formed persons were probably the inmates of their household, and that these had also spiritually attached themselves to them, we can see from Eliezar who shows himself a true גר צדק. The significance of the lasting educational influence of such attachment in his case shows off the contrast to the one of Lot on whom Abraham had surely worked and tried to influence most of all, and whom he was nevertheless unable to attach to himself permanently.

They went forth to go to ארץ כנען. God had said to Abraham לך לך, separate yourself from your homeland, and had added אל הארץ אשר אראך. One usually takes this to mean, to which I shall “direct” you. But אראך never means this, it always means only “let you see”. Further, one can not say to somebody: “Go to the place to which I shall direct you”, he would then have to wait until he is at least told in which direction to go. Abraham would not have known, so to speak “by which gate to leave Haran”. Therefore the positive command could only have been, go away, never mind where, and wander about until you come to a place where I shall let you see by some visible sign, that there you are to remain. Abraham chose the way to Canaan by his own decision. If we realise the significance of that land, it becomes clear to us, why Abraham, and even earlier, Terach, could have had the intention to go to Canaan.

Although Canaan was in the possession of the most degenerate race of the descendants of Noah, we still find מלכי צדק מלך שלם (according to tradition Shem) living there, just those remaining there in whom the recognition of God had been retained in its purest form. A further tradition teaches us that on Moriah where Abraham brought the עקדה, where later the Altar, the Temple was erected, Noah and Abel also brought their offerings. Our sages even picture the earth out of which the first man was created being taken from this spot which later became the home of כפרה, the constant spiritual and moral rebirth of mankind. Taking all this together we could say: when Abraham had to flee from Chaldea because he stood alone with his convictions and was in danger from the kings and priests of Chaldea, it was quite natural that he should wander in the direction towards where remembrance told of a time in which men stood in closer and nearer relationship to God.

ארצה כנען. Just as a ה added to the concept of a place takes the place of a prefixed ל and means a movement towards that place, so does the added ה to the future tenses or imperative mood indicate a mental movement towards the future or imperative concept. אדבר I will speak: אדברה, my mind has “made a movement” towards my speaking i.e. I wish to speak, I would speak. דבר speak, דברה, move yourself to speak, desire to speak, etc. Also the feminine ה, expressing female nature could be taken as an inclination towards, a desire towards the masculine eg. אשה ,איש, the אשה is לאיש, the מלכה is למלך, etc.

V. 6.—7. ויעבר. Abraham “passed by everywhere”, considered none of the places that he “came across” as the one where he should remain, because he was waiting for the promised sign which would show him the place where he was to stay. The Canaanites were then already in the land. For at the time when this was written down the Canaanites were still in the land. The land had not originally been destined for the descendants of Ham, nevertheless in Abraham’s time it had already passed into Hamite hands. But Abraham journeyed on and on until God would show him that he was to stop. — וירא: then God made Himself visible to Abraham and said etc. The whole stress lies on this visibility. The altar, too, was built to לה׳ הנראה אליו. For this was the visible sign that this was the land for the future of Abraham and his people. Far from wishing to give even the very slightest idea of how God spoke to Abraham and to those chosen men to whom He revealed Himself, we still have to note what is actually told us here. The expression used says that not only was the Voice of God heard but וַיֵרָא, and not הֵרָאֶה מ־ seen by, but הֵרָאֶה אֶל, made visible to Abraham, for Abraham. In the first case the action would emanate from the one who sees, the fact of being seen would depend on his ability and desire: But הראה אל designates the opposite procedure: emerging from invisibility to visibility for somebody, the act emanates from the one who “reveals himself”. This is of far-reaching importance, and for an age which tends to level everything out, and by putting a different interpretation on words makes them delusive, is by no means superfluous. All our revelations of God emanate from God to man. God speaks to the prophet, not in him. The Hand of God comes on to the prophet not out of him: ’היתה עלי יד ה. In all the Hebrew expressions for the revelation of God, Man is, in every case, only the receiver, never the active producer. And all these expressions are the most definite denial of all those views which deny actual revelations but nevertheless try to gloss over their denials by classing them together as products of human imagination and ecstasy. How God spoke to us human beings can remain an eternal mystery — after all the speech of man to man, the communion of mind with mind by means of the influence proceeding from bodily matter to bodily matter is scarcely a lesser mystery — it suffices for us that He did speak and made Himself visible in some way to them.

Inasmuch as here God appeared to Abraham after he had already lived, worked, and suffered for Him for 75 years, and had already heard the Voice of God in his homeland, but only now appeared to him, נראה, in this land, he was thereby told that this was the land where the שכינה בתחתונים was first to come back which was, and is, altogether the goal and purpose of human history. There, where Man first wandered, where, or in whose proximity the Garden of Eden had been, the land which, according to tradition, escaped the disturbance of the Flood and whose soil accordingly remained most virginal, that was the land which God chose to be the one in which the return of God-dwelling-on-earth was to begin. Now the place where, after 2000 years, God again revealed Himself on earth is described firstly as שכם .מקום שכם was not exactly the locality in the much-praised land which had gained for itself the most glorious reputation. It had the unsavoury repute of being שכיחי רוצחים a district which was the haunt of hot-blooded men to whom murder and violence were nothing unusual, as appears in fixing the location of the cities of refuge, and to which the prophet refers in Hosea VI.9. דרך ירצחו שכמה, just as the parallel-lying city of Gileah in Transjordania for similar reasons is called עקבה מדם (Makkoth 9). Secondly it is described as אלון מורה. This is the same place where, from one and the self-same soil, two peaks Ebal and Gerisim rise in the most striking contrast to each other. The one, green and smiling like a garden from base to summit, the picture of most complete blessing and prosperity, the other, bleak and bare from top to bottom, the picture of the reverse. And then it says further, והכנעני אז בארץ, that already then, when here the return of the Schechina began with this revelation to Abraham, the Canaanites were there. And we know to what degree of degeneration this race had sunk in this land, so that a merciful and loving God decreed their expulsion or destruction. So we note the following: Here, with Abraham, the regeneration of mankind, the return of godliness is to be replanted. A soil most suitable for this purpose is sought and selected, it is one on which certainly, men who live their lives in accordance with the Will of God can attain the fullest and highest degree of spiritual and moral consecration of their lives, but on which at that time, and later too, men degenerated more and more until all they merited was extermination. In the same way, the תורה was given in the wilderness to teach that it was not on any particular age or land to which the elevation of the human race is attached. It was on the very place on which the degeneration of mankind appeared in the highest degree that God allowed the return of His שכינה to occur. This can well tell us that although the nature of a country is indeed not without influence on the tendencies and disposition of its inhabitants, the achievement of “nearness to God” is equally within the reach of the Lapp in Lapland as to that of the Greek in Greece. There where an Abraham lived, רצחנים, murderers, can also live, and the same soil can bear a נביא next to a רוצח. It was just that land which is so seductive that on it its inhabitants became so debauched in voluptuous luxury that the very land itself “spued them out”, just that land God chose to plant therein His People — who themselves are not the most tractable, whose fundamental character is that of קשה עורף, obstinacy, — so that if the Divine Fire of Torah, the אשרת, would succeed — as it did succeed — in winning over this people on this land to itself, then there can be no race of mankind in no land whatsoever who can not be won to this אש דת through this אש דת. The victory of godliness was to begin with the stubbornest race (עז שבאומות) on the stubbornest soil (הארצות האל our sages take to mean קשות Yebamoth 21a and ב״ר ס״ד I.L.). Now it is quite possible that this alternative of the land, either the height of morality and spirituality or the depth of depravity and degeneration, and correspondingly, either the blessing or the curse, were represented by the blossoming Gerisim and the stark Ebal standing next to each other. It would then be deeply significant that the first national altar erected at the first entry into this land was not on Gerisim but just on the bleak Ebal. The blessing is not the condition for, but the result of, building up earthly life in a godly manner. Such building up of life is not to require any stipulations. The altar of God’s Torah can be erected on the most desolate soil. Finally, it does not seem impossible that אלון מורה — whether אלון means tree, grove, or, according to אונקלס, plain — that the grove or valley round about Gerisim and Ebal was designated מורה “teaching”, because the sight of these two mounts brought to everybody who approached them the significant sermon: “Here you have the blessing, there the curse, the choice is yours”.

V. 8. עתק. If we compare the various meanings of this root, the underlying conception in all cases is the forcible (or unexpected, unnatural, against the ordinary order of things etc.) transposition of something to a place, time, moral or social position, to which it did not belong originally. Hence צור יעתק displacing rocks; עתיק, reaching over to another period, ancient. Hence also the real expression for tradition: העתקה, carrying facts and truths from one age to another: עתק .אשר העתיקו אנשי הזקיה impropriety, abuse, and עתוק (Job. XXI.7) the position of the wealthy who overstep the bounds of what is fit and proper. ויעתק in the sense used here only occurs elsewhere in Ch. XXVI.22, where Isaac who had reckoned on remaining there, on account of the frequent quarrels, after having to dig fresh wells three times, reluctantly decided to move away. So we are justified here too, not to take it as an ordinary moving on, but as being of such a nature where some unwillingness, resistance, something or the other had first to be overcome. So that we are directed to think not on the removal of his tent, for that would entail no unusual difficulty, but the object of the verb ויעתק is, rather, the unexpressed because self-understood words “his people”. Abraham had to exercise his energy to bring his people to move away to the mountains. He was still seeking isolation. The Land has been promised לזרעך not לך. His people may have felt more comfortable in the fruitful pleasant valley, he follows his duty which points to the lonely and isolating mountains and prevailed on his people to follow him there. Our sages significantly describe the relation of our three Patriarchs to each other: אברהם קראו הר, יצחק שדה, יעקב בית Abraham called the place of the revelation of God to him, there where man can best find God: הר, the mountains. He standing alone in the midst of mankind could no longer find God in the social sphere of men. To find the traces of God’s rule and management and elevate himself up to God, he had to go to free Nature in the mountains where the traces of human management and rule did not reach. The more the history of the patriarchs progressed the more they could find the Finger of God revealed in their own history. Isaac named it שדה, fields, no longer the wild open mountains, but already Nature directed towards nourishment for men. Isaac saw in this condition of Nature closely affecting the existence of mankind — even though still only externally — the revelation of God’s management for Man. (ויזרע וגו׳ וימצא וגו׳ מאה שערים). Jacob no longer had to leave his house to see God. He found Him there, where He always wants to be found by us, not in the mountains, not out on fields and meadows, in his home he saw God, his family life was the place of the revelation of God. קראו בית, the stone on which a man lays down his weary head was to him “the House of God”. הר, root is הרר related to ערר ,ארר ,חרר, all roots of the concept of isolation perhaps a mountain is called הר because it breaks the continuity of the surface of the world, and rises as an isolated and isolating piece of the world.

It is highly significant that it says אהלה, written with the feminine ה, as opposed to ויעתק. Whereas there, where it affected the whole household Abraham had to exert his authority, ויעתק, possibly even to persuade Sarah, here in the home, his house was really Sarah’s house. For external matters the man, internal ones the woman; as leader, guiding star, to submit the whole household in every way to the Will of God, the man is in authority, in every other matter of managing and directing the home, the woman has precedence. Such is the principle of intimate happy Jewish family life, the origin of which has its roots in Abraham’s tent. There too, in the highlands, he could have moved to a city, but he avoided the towns and remained between Bethel and Ai. Bethel was the place which was first really taken into possession by Jacob. Ai, the first piece of land that Abraham’s descendants took into actual possession (but they left it to remain in ruins — as already in Abraham’s time the whole district seems to have been rich in ruins as is indicated by the distinguishing adjective העי). He by-passed the ruins but did not proceed to רמב״ן .בית אל already refers to the fact that this first move as well as the later ones of Abraham are analogous to the later history of his people.
’ויקרא בשם ה, in contrast to a world whose whole lives were directed נעשה לנו שם.

V. 9. Abraham journeyed on, always to the south. We have already seen that Abraham did not seek the vicinity of cities. He wanted first to build a firm foundation for himself and his household in isolation. The south of Palestine was by no means the most flourishing part, the whole district from Jerusalem southwards is called in Zacharia ערבה, wilderness. Corresponding to the whole planting of the Jewish People — the תורה in the wilderness, the Altar on Ebal, Israel the עם קשה ערף (an intractable obstinate people I.L.) — the spiritual metropolis of the people was set, not in the north, the most flourishing, but in the south the unfruitful part. The success of the Torah, and through the Torah, presupposes nothing material at all, “out of the rock”, saith God, “do I satisfy you with honey” Abraham’s לך לך drew him ever further in the inhospitable south.

נגב (verwandt mit נקף ,נגף ,נקב): etwas perpendikulär auf den Kopf treffen, daher der Süden, wo die Strahlen der Sonne senkrecht treffen. Sodann gesteigert bis zum Durchbohren: נקב, und Stoßen, plötzlich stoßen, d. i plötzlicher Tod durch Gott: מגפה ,נגף. Nun wäre noch zu erklären, wie נקב zugleich auch bestimmen heißt: נקבה שכרך, es heißt vielleicht: etwas mit Worten so "auf den Kopf treffen" etwas mit Worten so umgrenzen, daß der Gegenstand dadurch entschieden fixiert wird.

V. 10.—13. ויהי רעב בארץ etc. With these words we come to a story, which at first glance, seems not a little striking. That Abraham should forsake the land to which he had been directed and not trust to God Who knows how to provide in hunger and desert! That he — as it seems on the surface — should expose the moral well-being of his wife to such danger just to save himself! Were we not in a position to do away with all this that seems so strange, we too would have to say with חטא אברהם ,רמב״ן אבינו חטא גדול בשגגה וכוי “here Abraham committed a great sin in his behaviour towards his wife and even his deserting the land to which he had been directed was already an עון אשר חטא a wrong in which he sinned”, and that need not have misled us, or worried us. The Torah never presents our great men as being perfect, it deifies no man, says of none “here you have the ideal, in this man the Divine became human”. Altogether it puts the life of no man before us as the pattern out of which we are to learn what is right and good, what we have to do, what refrain from doing. Where the Word of God would set a pattern before us for us to imitate, it places no man born of dust, there God says “Look at Me, imitate Me, wander in My Ways”. We are never to say: This must be right for did not so-and-so do it! The Torah is no “collection of examples of saints”. It relates what occurred, not because it was exemplary but because it did occur.

The Torah never hides from us the faults, errors and weaknesses of our great men. Just by that it gives the stamp of veracity to what it relates. But in truth, by the knowledge which is given us of their faults and weaknesses, our great men are in no wise made lesser but actually greater and more instructive. If they stood before us as the purest models of perfection we should attribute them as having a different nature, which has been denied to us. Were they without passion without internal struggles, their virtues would seem to us the outcome of some higher nature, hardly a merit and certainly no model that we could hope to emulate. Take, for instance Moses’s ענוה. Did we not know that he could also fly into a passion, his meekness and modesty would seem to us to be his inborn natural disposition, and lost to us as an example. Just his שמעו נא המורים gives his ענוה its true greatness, shows it to us as the result of a great work of self-control and self-ennoblement which we all should copy because we all could copy. The Torah also shows us no faults without at the same time letting us see the greater or lesser evil consequences. From our great teachers of the Torah, and truly רמב״ן can be reckoned amongst the very greatest, we would accordingly learn that it may never be our task to whitewash the spiritual and moral heroes of our past, to appear as apologists for them. They do not require our apologies, nor do such attempts become them. Truth is the seal of our Torah, and truthfulness is the principle of all its true and great commentators and teachers. All this, if we would have to say with רמב״ן: חטא אברהם אבינו חטא גדול בשגגה.
But before we come to this decision, let us consider more closely the facts which are told us of this event.

Abraham left Canaan after the advent of famine. He did not wait to see whether God would feed him in some miraculous manner in the midst of the universal dearth, but went to Egypt to seek food. There an equally threatened danger brought him to a denial of the true relationship between Sarah and himself through which Sarah’s moral condition became very nearly damaged. First of all, let us remind ourselves, with regards to this second point, that the danger must have been of such a threatening nature, so unavoidable, so unable to be circumvented, that it was repeated later in exactly a similar manner in the land of the Philistines. Had it been possible to avoid it in any other way, surely Abraham, after this first experience, would not have resorted to the same attempt a second time. More, we see his son Isaac, in a similar plight, taking refuge in exactly the same means of evasion. Now, of course, it is easy for רמב״ן or for us, who have such an abundance of experiences in our history, to say: Abraham should have stayed in Canaan, in Egypt he should simply have left everything to the management of God, the same One Who said to you: “this is the Land” can also feed you miraculously there, הפלא ה׳ חסיד לו, God has fed with manna even in deserts, and ’מלאכיו יצוה לך וגו. But that God surrounds with special protection those that are fulfilling His commands that שלוחי מצוה אינן ניזקין was an experience that Abraham and his descendants had still to have, no Abraham had preceded Abraham, and even having this experience does not preclude the duty of doing everything that is legally within ones own powers first, and having confidence in God only for that which lies beyond. Abraham could well say to himself אין סומכין על הנס.

And now for his behaviour in Egypt. Did Abraham really fear only for himself, and for that, to save himself, risk the honour of his wife? Let us listen to his words: ’הנה נא ידעתי וגו, see “after all I know that you are a beautiful woman, etc.” This word הנה “after all’ implies a preceding conversation. After all that occurred in Egypt and in the land of the Philistines we can conclude that — to which European countries in our modern times may be not without analogy — virgins, unmarried women were more protected against the prevailing immorality than married women. And add to that, a stranger! In both cases, married or unmarried, Sarah’s honour was in danger. But as a married woman the danger would be imminently threatening. One simply kills the objecting husband and rapes the wife. In the case of an unmarried girl accompanied by her brother one hopes to get her through the favour of that brother. In any case this way takes longer, postpones the matter, and in the meantime God can help. This alternative Abraham put to himself before they came to Egypt. And for Sarah’s sake he decided for it. As a married woman she would certainly be lost, as unmarried there was still a possible chance. Sarah, with her modesty, did not believe at all in the danger, she did not think she was beautiful. Hence the “See, after all I know that you are a beautiful woman, the Egyptians have only to see you, and they will do away with me as your husband and you — with euphemistic delicacy he puts what will happen to her — you, they will keep alive”. Were they to kill you too, it would not be the worst, but they will let you live for something worse! So rather say you are my sister, then they will show themselves friendly towards me hoping to get you through my good offices”. (as a rule בעבור expresses the purpose, and בגלל the cause) — and to overcome the last scruples which Sarah’s reluctance might have to this procedure, he added with apparent egoism “and so I will have to thank you for my life”. — if you will not do it for your own sake, do it for mine. (נא, as already remarked always comes as an interruption of, or hindering to, the direction of the thoughts or will of another. Hence also הניא to refuse, to deny, not to allow to happen, and נא concretely, half-cooked where the process of cooking is interrupted). Let us see whether the continuation of the story justifies our way of taking it.

V. 14—19. The Egyptians saw the woman “that she was very beautiful”. People turned to look at her, but nothing more than that. It seems that Sarah could have remained quite untouched — but Abraham had not thought of kings. Had anyone out of the people become enamoured of Sarah he would have taken the way through the brother. But the King reversed the order. ותקח, meanwhile she was taken to the palace, but nevertheless he dared not touch her, he hoped to gain his end in a respectable manner. He showered favours on Abraham, who soon received צאן ובקר etc. Had Sarah not been protected by being considered as Abraham’s sister Pharaoh would at once have taken her, then no time would have been wasted in sending presents to Abraham, God would have had to intervene immediately to protect Sarah. Possibly also the על דבר שרי (similarly to the ‘על דבר הצפרדעים וגו (Ex. VIII.8) does not mean “on account of” but on the “word” of, because Sarah had at last confessed that she was Abraham’s wife. Now through this, she was really in danger, now any prospect of Pharaoh taking a respectable course was cut off, now God’s Divine ordinance had to intervene to protect her. Further, how could the things be reconciled. A few pages further on, Abraham most disinterestedly refuses, with the memorable הרימתי ידי etc., even the most honourable offers, and here the same man should be low enough to barter away his wife’s honour to obtain צאן בקר וחמרים עבדים ושפחות אתונות וגמלים. Even the order in which the enumeration of the gifts is given is significant. If the riches which Abraham acquired here were to be described the order would be different. When Eliezer describes his master’s riches he reckons, sheep and cattle (silver and gold), man servants and maid servants, camels and asses. Similarly Jacob’s riches are described as masses of sheep, man servants, camels and asses (Gen. XXX.43) That is an understandable grouping. Sheep and cattle are productive, real property, (of which the surplus in Abraham’s case is changed into gold and silver). This property requires care and attention so there is necessity for servants. Camels and asses are not productive property but have to be had as beasts of burden etc. bearers of the riches and so come last. Thus for an ordered household. But here everything is mixed up. Not only do asses come before servants and maids but even asses and she-asses are placed far apart from each other. This disordered confusion is certainly quite intentional to tell us that Pharaoh tried every means to win Abraham’s favour and sent him one day a nice ox, another an ass, then a slave etc. etc. and Abraham, of course, dared not refuse acceptance otherwise he would have shattered Pharoh’s hopes, and would have invited force for Sarah. All this receives further confirmation by what Pharaoh subsequently said to Abraham. He does not reproach him for in general having given Sarah out as his sister, but “why did you not tell me that she is your wife”. Pharaoh found it quite natural that he should tell the people that Sarah was his sister but “from me, surely you had nothing to fear! and you did not even tell me then when I wanted to take her as my wife: To that Abraham had naturally no answer. He could not tell him that he had considered him no better than his people.

גור: to stay somewhere as a stranger, also: to fear. Further גור a young animal, particularly used for a young lion. מגורה, barn, granary. It seems originally to mean “to be landless”, not to have roots in the ground, to feel that one has no support in the land beneath one’s feet. Hence: stranger, to be an alien. Further to lose one’s hold on the earth i.e. to fear. Then again, that place in which grain separated from the earth has its (temporary?) stay. Finally also the young animal which, taken away from its mother’s breast, — its hold hitherto — and not yet standing independent in its own strength.

צאן presumably related to שאן the root שאונן, quiet, undisturbed. The צ sound gives the conception of artificial, and צאן would be artificially undisturbed. That part of the herd which is artificially protected from disturbance, is provided with pens, sheep-folds.
בקר, in contrast, related to פקר ,בכר ,בגר, the free, independent.
חמור and אתון the specific term for beasts of burden. חמר related to חמר ,עמר, a heap, accordingly burden, and אתן related to אדן, the foot of a pillar, hence: bearer.
גמל, perhaps the camel, because it is גומל, because it goes a long time without drinking.

V. 20. ויצו עליו. According to the opinion of Eben Ezra this was a friendly gesture towards Abraham. The decree had been published that nobody was to interfere with him and his household. But nevertheless צוה על is usually a negative command, a limitation, but then the על always refers to the person or thing that is to be restricted. So here too, Pharoh placed the restriction on Abraham that he was to leave the country and appointed men over him to see that his command was carried out, — in exactly the same manner as occurred so often in later times to Israel, as altogether the whole event offers remarkable analogy to the later history.

V. 1.—2. Driven by the famine, he had temporarily left his isolation and had moved into populous Egypt where matters had not been exactly pleasant for him. Now he moved back again to the place where the meaning of this country for his future, and the necessity for isolation for the present, had first become clear to him through the visible revelation of God. There he lived and took up again his old profession, to summon men in the name of God. מקנה: (in contrast to רכוש moveable but lifeless property hence “carted”) is living property, which already by itself follows its master, is conscious of belonging to its owner, ידע קונהו, and so is a person’s real “belongings”.
V. 3. And here again it says אהלה, probably to indicate that, unaffected by the occurrence with Pharaoh, Abraham’s relations to Sarah were the same as they had always been.

V. 5. On the word אברם there is an אתנח (a semi-colon I.L.) “Lot also had” — before the object to the verb is mentioned, it makes us pause a moment to think what we should have expected from a relative who not only lived עם but את אברם intimately with Abraham. Intimately sharing life with Abraham who, in his isolation still by his hospitality drew strangers, who only came into contact with him en passant, into a knowledge of Him Who makes people hospitable and benevolent, and raises them from selfish greed to the aspiration to be like unto Him and to be a source of blessing להיות ברכה rather than to obtain blessing. Now here it says: Lot, too, who had lived so closely with Abraham had had something from it, had obtained something from Abraham — but what? Sheep and cattle and tents! Not a word of the spiritual calling. He accompanied because he profited materially by it. “And tents” ואהָלִים — the complete form, not אֳהָלִים, — he ceased being a member of Abraham’s household, had his own independent circle in which he was master of the house. Whereas Abraham’s was the tent of Sarah אהלה, the management of the house was given over to her and Abraham considered it his business ’לקרא בשם ה, Lot had very different ideas. He considered his business to be the acquirement of sheep and cattle and had no feeling for Abraham’s spiritual mission. This is the meaning of the accent and stress laid on the word “Abraham” in this verse, and this explains all what follows.

V. 6. The land was not able to bear them remaining together, Why? Because they had too many herds and flocks and there was not enough pasturage there for them? Not so. Were the whole one herd, one concern, it would have been sufficient. It was insufficient, we are told כי היה רכושם רב because their other property כסף וזהב etc. was too great, because if one is not united, if one does not trust the other, then אהלים are necessary, chests and safes, and everything separate. “Because their property, their fortune, was too great, they no longer fitted together, could no longer dwell together”, therefore they could also no longer remain on the same soil. Because in Lot’s affairs one cared only and solely for profit, but in Abraham’s other higher interests also came into consideration, because the use to which that which had been acquired was put was different — it is just in this, in the use which is made of one’s fortune that, above all, one man differs from another — that was why they could not remain together, that was why the land was not large enough to contain the two of them. Lot had to have his own separate pasturages so that not one tiny lamb from the one flock should lose itself in the other, etc.

V. 7. Above it says in general, וכנעני אז בארץ. Here פרזי is added, and it says ישב כארץ. Abraham and Lot as strangers could, of course, only use ownerless land for pasturage, but that was already limited. More that one nation had settled in the land. Had there been only one, they would only have taken into possession and fenced in what was sufficient for their immediate requirements, they could always take more if and when required. But as soon as several tribes lived in the land, each tried to take beforehand as much as he could so that the other should not forestall him. The amount of land available for Lot and Abraham was accordingly limited.

V. 8. Not בינינו but ביני ובינך. This repetition of בין is used preferably when the separation or union is mutual. Thus of ביני ובין :שבת בני ישראל, a double sign of recognition. As long as Israel keeps the Sabbath, it recognizes, acknowledges thereby that it belongs to God, and God acknowledges it as being His. Desecration of the Sabbath tears the bond asunder in both directions. So here too: our quarred is mutual: I do not like several things of yours and you, too, do not like certain things which I do, through this, strife occurs also between our people. But where there is no union, separation brings peace. — אנשים אחים, not simply אחים. Even if we separate as men, no longer live the same kind of lives, we are still relations.

V. 9. מעלי, from being next to me. Completely separating from one another. Abraham had to demand this to protect his people from the bad example of Lot’s menage. See, for me the choice is limited, I can not move everywhere where there happens to be a surplus of pasturage. I have to seek isolation. But you, since you have given up my way of looking at life, have no need to be so particular in your choice, for you the whole land lies open. Whether you go to the right or to the left I stay here in my isolation.

V. 10.—11. Lot found this argument quite rational, he seems to have been waiting only for some such opportunity. Wandering in inhospitable regions could not have appealed to a man like him. What he wanted was a rich luxurious district, protected against famine and scarcity, and that he found. וישא לוט את עיניו, he let himself be guided, undeterred by any consideration which would affect an Abraham, simply by what appealed to his sensuous eyes.

ככר, wohl nicht Kreis, sondern wie ת"א: Ebene. Wurzel wahrscheinlich: כרה, graben (vergl. יין von בבל ,ינה von בלל), verwandt mit כרע: knien, sich niedrig machen, ירה: werfen, גרה wovon גרון Kehle, Schlund: allmählich in die Tiefe ziehen. ככר: Talebene, das Flussgebiet, die durch Flüsse gegrabene Niederung. Für die Bedeutung Kaufen, Aneignen, bietet נהל eine sprechende Analogie, das auch Flusstal und Erbe bedeutet. Die Talebene des Jordans war ganz "Getränk", oder vielmehr, wenn partic. Hiphil, ganz d. h. überall tränkend, führte überall das gehörige Nass den Feldern und Pflanzungen zu. — כלָה femin. משקֶה mascul. Insofern der Boden das Nass empfängt, ist er femin,; insofern er es aber weiterspendet, mascul.

כגן ה׳ .(ב״ר) כגן ה׳ לאילנות, כארץ מצרים לזרעים “like a garden of God” for trees and plants, “like the land of Egypt” for grain and produce. It is not unlikely that the beauty of the garden would refer to Sodom and the riches of produce to Gomorroh. The names of the destroyed cities all really seem to refer to all the bounties that nature offers.

סדום reminds one of שדה, the מ is reproduced in עמורה .שַׁדמות ,שַׁדמה designates עומר the sheaf: corn. אדמה rich in minerals. צבוים, plural of צבי, fauna. The lords of Sodom could also go a-hunting. There were riches in all directions.

V. 12.—18. It does not say ויאהל ,ויאמר ה׳ ,וישב אברם but לוט ישב ויאהל אברם ויבא ,וה׳ אמר ,אברם ישב. In all such cases where the story continues, not in עתיד מהופך but interrupts and uses the עבר and only then resumes the ordinary historic tense, עבר is to be taken not as the perfect tense but as the pluperfect. Here it may want to indicate the contrast between Abraham and Lot. While Lot quickly and happily went away from Abraham’s isolated and isolating way of living, and had settled just in the most luxurious cities — he lived in the cities and kept his herds right up to Sodom — although these cities were sunk in a state of depravity that must have been apparent to the most short-sighted person at the first glance, Abraham had kept all the more to the isolated state in which he and his household kept away from contact with the Canaanite cities, and only remained in such proximity to human society to be able to ’קורא בשם ה. For had he not just had the painful experience of finding that he had not succeeded in winning and keeping even his nearest relation to himself and his mission. Only after God had encouraged him to look beyond his isolation and to move into the life of the whole land without fear for himself or his principles, only then did Abraham really go into the country and settled in Hebron.

V. 13. The אנשי סדום were, in their social life, man towards man, רעים וחטאים, evil and inconsiderate on principle. Everybody is probably חוטא occasionally, but חַטָא (like גַנָב) is one whose whole character is such, an indifferent person. So, in social life they were רעים, practising only evil, maliciously wicked to each other, and חטאים, their actions lacked all moral principles; but ’לה towards God, where the social welfare did not seem to be affected, מאוד “to the fullest possible extent”, their wickedness was beyond all limits. In social matters the evil is kept within some bounds by the fear of one to the other, by the self-interested fear of the consequences. Even amongst thieves there is a certain amount of honesty to each other. But where, to the unenlightened eye, the welfare of society in general is not entailed, where it does not directly affect anybody else, where everybody says to himself “it is only my own self, my own happiness, my own health which may be undermined” for which he would be responsible only to God, in the מצות בין אדם למקום in such circles the licentiousness and depravity knows no bounds.

חטא related to עטה, to wrap oneself up, and also, as in ויעט העם אל השלל (Sam. I. XIV.32) to rush forward greedily onto something without considering whether it is right or wrong. So also עטף which peculiarly means both to wrap up, to hide and also to be weak, faint. It lies to hand to say that just as עטף means to wrap up, hide and also to be physically weak so עטה could mean to wrap up and also to become morally weak. The application of this concept could lie in the not infrequent use of the phrase ותתעטף רוחי; — “my spirit has wrapped itself up” i.e. has retreated, so that the spirit no longer shines through the wrapping, the body is no longer ruled and borne by the spirit, as it is in living, healthy people. In such conditions the body then follows the force of gravity of material, it sinks, becomes faint unconscious weak and that condition is עטף where the body is solely a covering, a wrapping, in which the mind is not apparent. It seems that, similarly by עטה moral weakness is designated as a condition in which the spirit retires behind the wrapper. The wrapper, i.e. the body with its senses overpowers the spirit to such a degree that the mind only obeys the dictates of the material bodily impressions and urges of the bodily senses. If this is true, then חטא too would be such activity in which the moral power of the will has retreated to the background, and the deed is done without thought and consideration, only mastered by the senses and without that moral mental power which is meant to direct every manifestation of life. This way of taking it would be confirmed by the use of ערמה “nakedness” to designate such activity where the mind is in full control: cleverness, deliberation, craftiness etc. A similar trend of thought leads to a relationship of חטא to חתה which concretely means a fire-brand taken away from the fire, לחתות אש מיקוד (Is. XXX.14) and מחתה the vessel for that purpose. According to that חטא would be the state of being removed from the spiritual moral fire within oneself and חטאת the sin-offering which gives the חלב וכליות (back) to the godly fire, would then in a literal sense be the symbolic expression for the restitution of what had been lacking in the חטא, (see the whole idea of חטאת in Levit. I.L.).
V. 14.—15. הפרד מעמו not merely מעליו; a spiritual personal separation, not just going somewhere else.

After Abraham had had the bitter experience of seeing the son of his brother, the second generation that would live on after him, on whom he could have hoped to place his expectations for the continuance of his spiritual mission, depart from him, and on account of external material attractions prefer the company of the people of Sodom and Gemorrah, God said to him: — “Not to a man like Lot, but just to you whose first thoughts and efforts are not towards material gain is this land with all its abundance to come, I give it to you and to your descendants who come after you. You are not to go abroad, and as a missionary get other poeple for your mission. What is to belong to you must be sown by you, begotten and brought up by your pure spirit. Jews are to be born, not only brought up as such. לך אתננה ולזרעך עד עולם, By this it is not proclaimed that it will always be in their possession. It will always belong to them, they and the land will always be destined for each other, just as here it was given to Abraham without his ever receiving possession of it.
עולם is undeveloped time: either the time in which the present had not yet developed i.e. the past, or that which is not yet developed in the present, i.e. the future. Hence מן העולם עד העולם.

V. 16. מעפר הארץ. One may doubt whether here it means exactly a literal “countless”, uncountable number. Israel has actually repeatedly been counted, and altogether has never been prominent on account of its numbers, לא מרובכם כי אתם המעט. So that it does not refer to the number of Abraham’s descendants living at any particular time, but to the unlimited generations of an immortal nation which will continue throughout the centuries. But still, even so the analogy does not fit. For dust is something contemporary. But it is possible that the People of Abraham are distinguished by the fact that other nations hardly come from one single derivation whereas here such a comparatively numerous nation whose numbers form one single family, descend from one man. The Jews are perhaps the largest “family” on earth.

But if we compare the other meanings of the root ומניתי אתכם :מנה לחרב (Is. LXV.12), לילות עמל מנו לי (Job. VII.3) and also its relationship to מנע which, when construed with -מ means withdrawing from, to deny or refuse, then מנה would indeed not be quite identical with ספר .ספר to count, i.e. to find the sum of things which, belonging to a common conception, are present, are existing. מנה to allot (to) i.e. to reckon the sum of things that should be there for some common conception. Hence in Chron. I. XXI at the census ordered by David, in verse 2 the order is couched as: ספרו את ישראל, whereas in v.1 and 17 where this counting is regarded from its sinful and therefore pernicious aspect it uses the verb מנה for the order, to give it the accessory idea of limitation. According to this, the meaning here could also perhaps be: — as little as anybody could count the dust of the earth (מנה) i.e. reckon how much of this basic material is to be allotted to all the structures of the earth in general or to any one of them in particular, just as this is solely at the disposition of God, the Creator and Master, so no human power shall be able to fix the quantitative existence of thy descendants. עפר is the fundamental material of all earthly formations, it is a constituent of all earthly forms and ultimately all revert to it — הכל היה מן העפר והכל שב אל עפר — and in all its transformations no single atom of its power and no single grain of it gets lost — like this the seed of Abraham too! Our sages too do not see in this comparison merely a numerical similarity, but the analogy of the formative processes and importance of the dust of the earth to that of Israel.

V. 17. I give it to you, you will not become assimilated, absorbed by it — as no דבר חשוב and דבר המעמיד, nothing which has its own character and nothing which is really formative does become בטל — but rather the other way round, you will wander through it as its future victor and master. As long as Lot wandered with him as ערב רב, entering into the midst of the nations was dangerous, but now, the pure house of Abraham, as in future his people, can and should live amongst other people and still remain “Jews”. — Everywhere where his mission became clearer to him Abraham built an altar, so here too.

V. 1. Here we have the oldest account of kings and wars which history has to relate. Let us consider the conditions in the world which the Torah here may wish to make clear to us for our better understanding of the mission of Abraham and his people.

Here we see the system introduced to world-history by Nimrod quickly spreading and bearing most sumptuous fruit. For the דור הפלגה (when the people scattered Ch. XI.8 I.L.) fell in Abraham’s youth. At that time Nimrod made himself a King. It is true that he is not actually called King but his activity was to form a kingdom, ראשית ממלכתו (X.10). His system was to misuse the joint powers of the nation for his own purposes, under the cloak of patriotism, at the cost of the happiness of the individual. We see this tendency here quickly blossoming luxuriously. We see already not the history of People but of Kings. And in the small space of the valley of the Jordan no fewer than five kings. Here we have the beginning of the system of Kingship. A King to every town. Later on in Joshua’s time in the same small country we are told of thirty-one kings! the others, mentioned in V.1 were already kings over countries and empires as Shinar=Babylon and Elam=Media and also Goyim, a name which indicates several nations. Remembering the position of the better known lands, Babylon and Media, both distant from Palestine and yet for a time Palestinian Kings being subject to Chedorlomer, we find already an emperor or king over other kings.

We have already considered the root מלך in its relation to מלק and the Chaldean נמלך as being the conception of being the head, the brains for others, and also the Jewish conception of Kingship (Ch. X.10). Let us see how this actually worked out here. Each one of these luxurious cities had to have its King. The superabundance and the luxury could be responsible for this. If kings are there to spare the people the trouble of thinking, this would occur preferably where the individuals themselves have a great deal of personal matters to think about. The more comfortable, the more sensuous, the more luxurious, the less the people have to worry about the conditions of things in general, the readier they are to sacrifice rights and money only not to have to think about public matters in general. Further, no king would so easily wish to be, or be able to be, king over a poor people. He who has nothing to lose and little to gain can not easily be frightened or tempted. So we can understand how, in these most luxurious, voluptuous, lands even the smallest communities had their king to relieve them from having to bother about general public affairs, and how these kings again subordinated themselves to some foreign powerful monarch — just עבדי עבדים, as the ancestor already saw the Hamitic race — readily paid some yearly tribute with which to buy security to rule and enjoy royal status in their own lands.

From another point, too, this event is significant. Our sages already draw our attention to the fact here, on the first page of political world-history ד׳ מלכיות four victorious kingly powers appear, analogous to the general course of universal history which also will come to its end in ד׳ מלכיות, in four world-empires over which finally the sceptre of the conquering power of God will fall. At least two of these names which are unmistakable occur here: Babylon (Shinar) and Media (Elam). So that already in the very earliest times these two powers made military expeditions to Palestine and the surrounding countries, and we see here already Palestine succumbing to a foreign power.

The ancestor of the future Jewish people experienced here the universal fact: luxuriousness makes nations internally and externally into slaves, and for every nation it does not say חָרות but חֵרות על הלוחות, there is no internal or external freedom except by submission to law. But there was another fact which touched him, the ancestor of the Jewish nation, even more closely. The land where he was now had been promised to him for the future of his people, and the first experience he made there was: famine, and the second: war. Neither material abundance nor political independence was inherent in the land itself. In both it stood in the most complete contrast to Egypt. Just as its fertility was entirely dependent on rain, it had to look above to the heavens for its harvests, so was its political position such that it could offer no natural resistance to invaders. Left to itself the land of Israel lay open to famine and political dependence. Situated in the cockpit of the world, where Europe, Asia and Africa meet, hardly any world-war has occurred into the bitter suffering of which it has not been drawn. And just because of this was it chosen. If, in spite of this, in this land a national life would blossom against which no conqueror would dare attack, even if three times each year its borders were left open and all military defence withdrawn — if all the מלכיות of the world would clash together there and make war on each other, but no sword would dare enter this blooming and yet defenceless land — וחרב לא יעבר בארצכם — then the eternal fact would have been brought to the eyes of the nations “here God lives”! Here God is the Power, His Help and Protection stands in place of wall and bulwark אלקים בארמנתיה נודע למשגב (Ps. XLVIII.4 et seq.), ישועה ישית חומות וחל (Is. XXVI.1). Then that which now only beckons to us in the distant future would have been fulfilled thousands of years ago, Zion would have shone forth as a beacon to the nations and the nations would have said: “We would go with you, for we perceive that God is with you!”

For the People of God who lived about the site of the ruins of Sodom and Gomorrah the whole event was to be a warning to show how luxury and abundance in the natural course of events — if nothing works against them — are enemies of freedom; a warning that they will only be allowed to enjoy freedom and independence in this land as long as they nurture with all devotion the one factor by which luxurious “milk and honey” abundance which normally begets weaklings becomes transformed into something salutary and blessed. This factor is Law, the תורה, which, as it demands submission and self-control, is a guarantee for freedom and independence. Every field in the Jewish land is to bear the seal of belonging to the law (כלאים), and that is why the vineyards, just the vine-culture, the plant that represents most the idea of luxury has to be stamped with this seal with special sharpness (איסור הנאה, כלאי כרם). Everywhere and always throughout the life in the land the great warning: Israel will only prosper on the basis of the Law, and goes to ruin, physically and morally, if it withdraws itself from submission to the mastery of the Torah.

But for Abraham this event was a great one, probably his greatest adventure. The voluptuous lords of the land had been conquered, had become subject to Chedorlaomer, had finally rebelled against him — and they must have been powerful, as Chedorlaomer, the great King, called his allies to join him in subduing them — and had been beaten in this rebellion. And now he, a single man with his household, succeeds, with God as his ally, in overcoming this earthly king of kings! Here Abraham stands literally as the reconqueror of the Land. He pursues Chedorlaomer right through the land, from Hebron till Damascus, drives him out and frees the land! He lives to see לך אתננה literally carried out.

So our prophets, too, see the מלכיות conquering everything, everything falling into their hands, Eretz Israel also oppressed by them — but Israel overcomes them all, and with God’s assistance and support, becomes the conqueror of the whole world.

V. 2. עשו, “had made”, this seems to refer to the previous war in which Chedorlaomer had made the kings of the valley of the Jordan subject to him. מלחמה, root, לחם, related to דברי נרגן כמתלהמים) להם) (Prov. XVIII. 8, XXVI.22) and לאם the state. לחם strife, לֶחֶם bread, that obtained in the struggle for existence, the means of existence, and מלחמה לָחֶם real battle. Both sides fight for the continuance of the extension of the national existence. לאום, whereas גוי means the united body of a nation as presented externally, עם, the social life of the members of a nation, one with (עִם) the other, the nation regarded internally, לאום is the state, the representation for protecting the rights of a nation and keeping it to its laws, אין לאום אלא מלכות, the government.
V. 3. חבר never means, as קרב sometimes does, an inimical coming together, but always a peaceful union. So here too, the union of the allies.

אל עמק not בעמק, this was no chance meeting, but the field of battle which had been chosen after due consultation and deliberation. The nature of the terrain was accordingly known to both sides, or if one takes the כל אלה to refer only to the Jordanian allies just mentioned in verse 2, at least to these who knew the territory and must have promised themselves the advantage of it. They had chosen the ground, and the foreign kings also gathered there because these were waiting there to oppose them.

עמק, a deep-lying basin. Here a deep valley crossed by many fields. To which must be added, as v.10 tells us, the loam wells (בארות wells, not בורות pits) out of which loam and mud welled up out of the bottomless depths, with which the district was filled. It was a considerably intersected ground happily chosen by the city-kings, where a small body of men well acquainted with terrain could successfully oppose a force much superior in numbers and military powers and tactics, and in any case have the advantage of knowing the ground. Had the Kings of Sodom and Gemorrah and their people been as able and brave as they were wanton and luxurious the terrain would certainly have been well chosen. But, as we are soon told, they gave the enemy so little opposition and fled in such haste that they themselves fell into the loam wells which ordinarily were so well known to them.
V. 4. A nation that would free itself from a foreign yoke must begin by making itself free i.e. making itself moral. That, in their wantonness, they had overlooked.

מרד: sich empören, עניים מרורים: elend, מרט: haarausraufen und polieren; also eigentlich Unebenheiten nicht scheuen, dem Rauhen das Rauhe oder die Gewalt entgegensetzen. Was מרט mechanisch ist, das ist מרד geistig und sittlich: einer rauhen Seite sich nicht mehr fügen, einer rauhen Seite Stacheln entgegensetzen. מרודים: die Armen, die Gerupften, bei denen man keinen Widerstand duldet, die ganze Welt zeigt ihnen rauhe, unfreundliche Seiten. Jeder will auch noch etwas an ihnen zu polieren haben. So klagt Zion: ימי עניי ומרודי.

V. 5.—7. These verses show us in a quick review the might and bravery of these Kings. They first marched through the entire east of Palestine, southwards till Edom, conquering everything en passant, then they turned back northwards to their real goal and halted in the proximity of their real enemy.

V. 8.—10. But these did not wait for their approach, but went out to meet them, attacked them — and were quickly beaten and put to flight. The Kings were the first to flee! They fled to the mountains. This range was to the west of the battle-field, accordingly towards the district where Abraham lived.

V. 11. רכוש really means lifeless moveable possessions. But nevertheless, as we learn farther on, human beings were also dragged away, here, these, as unwilling captives led away perforce, are, significantly enough, included in the term אכלם .רכוש probably not just war-provender but the luxurious provisions stored up in the rich cities. “They took everything and went away”. This, too, is typical and repeats itself again and again in our history. Martial hordes come, conquer, not to inhabit the land, but drag everything away that can be taken away, including the inhabitants. Thus Shulmaneser, thus Nebuchadnezzar; sometimes they set other inhabitants in the land, otherwise left it bare and desolate.

V. 12. Both these facts are already known, that he was the son of Abraham’s brother, and that he dwelt in Sodom. They are surely not stressed here without reason. Lot was really not one of the Sodomites, he was known as the son of Abraham’s brother when he arrived, and had he remained as such, even in the midst of the happenings of war he could have hoped, as a stranger to be spared from the revenge of Chedorlaomer. But he had become an inhabitant of Sodom, had the civic rights of a citizen of that town and had to pay the forfeit for it with the others. Herein lies a warning hint for the members of the Abrahamitic family which has proved itself during the centuries of Jewish history. If one remains faithful to the Jewish calling one certainly has to do without a good deal, but one also saves oneself from a good deal, one seems to be borne by the כנפי השכינה. The isolating ghettos were not only against the Jews, they existed also for them. Within them they remained protected from many evils which, in the middle-ages, befell the people outside.
