They were certainly considered too inferior to become officials, magistrates or beadles, too inferior to be troopers in the train of knights, were not allowed to appear at tournaments, took no part in great local or world enterprises, but for that they also had no part in the torturing, murdering strangling and burning which the people habitually indulged in in that epoch — they were indeed often enough the victims but never the victimisers, their hands were unstained with human blood. Moreover when the emperors and their armies were overtaken by their fate, the Jews were protected in their ghettos. They can be pleased that when the time for them to be called on again to play a part on the stage of the world that the times are disposed to become more gentle, humane and just. — But sensual men will not learn. Lot should have learnt from this experience to avoid Sodom, but we find him nevertheless at the final catastrophe still living in Sodom.

V. 13. הפליט, referring to v.10 where we have already been told that those that escaped fled westwards to the hills, towards the district where Abraham lived. So that it is not necessary to take this word to refer to a special person who had escaped, but in general to the escapees. What is stressed here regarding Abraham is the complete contrast to what is told of Lot in the preceding verse. העברי, Abraham had remained the Ivri, whether that means the stranger who had come from the other side of the river, or, as Rab. Joshua takes it, the one who stands on the other side, who stands in opposition to the whole world, the first “Protestant”. In any case it tells us that he remained isolated in his own distinctive character, and was known and recognised as such — והוא שכן. Of Lot it says והוא ישב בסדום, but ישב (related to יצב to stand firmly upright) to rest, to find your stand, your support in the ground means, accordingly, to belong completely to the place where you are. As above והכנעני והפריזי אז יושב בארץ so here Lot יושב בסדום. But Abraham was ’שכן .שוכן באלני וגו is also resting quietly in a place, but does not refer to the relation to the ground, but the social relationship to the inhabitants, the peaceful living as neighbours next to one another but without being entirely mixed up and absorbed by each other. This is also the reason, as already remarked above, (Ch. IX.28) why it is the usual expression for the proximity of God to man on earth. Abraham was not shy to keep to his own special characteristics in the midst of the Amorites even if it meant his remaining a tolerated stranger; he was Abraham from “the other side”, and שוכן, “living next to” the Amorites, he lived in friendly neighbourly relations with them, neither disturbing the other. And although he was an alien and only tolerated, still Mamre, the lord of the region, and his relations were בעלי ברית אברם, not אנשי בריתו.

בעל everywhere (בעל דברים ,בעל אשה ,בעל כנפים etc.) expresses the person in his relation to things which are in some way subordinate to him. ברית can be thought of in two ways. (I) two parties are equal partners in a covenant, an alliance; (II) one party accepts the other in a bond of friendship, allows him to join himself to his party, then, in the relationship, one is above, the other below. This latter was the case here. Not, Abraham took them in his sphere of fellowship, but Aner, Eshcol and Mamre took him into theirs. They were the בעלים of the ברית, he was the stranger, they were at home. So not only Mamre in whose territory Abraham lived, but his relation too, found Abraham such an imposing personality that they accepted him into their fellowship.

This whole behaviour of Abraham could serve as a model to זרע אברהם for all time as long as they find themselves as זרע אברהם in a strange land, בארץ לא להם. The Jew remains a Jew, in no ways disturbing the peaceful strange conditions he finds; he is to develop and arrange his own Jewish conditions of life in such a way that the others want to draw him into their circle of friends, not the reverse. Every pure human being finds in true complete Judaism the most perfect conception of human beings, not the reverse, for the concept Jew goes further than the concept Man. He need only be a Jew, a complete perfect Jew then although only a שכן he will nevertheless be respected and participate in the ברית of the nations. Abraham did not purchase this alliance relationship by stripping himself of his calling.

V. 14. Before the separation Abraham had said “we are אנשים אחים men who should be brothers”. But when he heard of Lot’s misfortune, the unfortunate Lot is at once אחיו, his brother. וירק את חניכיו. Because הריק certainly does occur also referring to weapons for drawing the sword, אריק חרבי, one has given the word here the meaning: “armed”, provided with “weapons”, and then accordingly taken חניכיו to be “his trained, exercised” men. But when הריק occurs referring to weapons, the object of the verb is always the weapon not the bearer of it, הריק חנית ,הריק חרב, and moreover the word חנך never occurs referring to anything so dull and empty as military exercises. הריק certainly does mean to empty out, and, like מלא, refers equally to the container as to the contents, הריק שק and הריק חרב. When it refers to the contents it means: to take the contents completely out so that the container which up till now had hidden them, becomes empty. If, then, here, the object of וירק is חניכיו it can mean nothing other than he “emptied all his חניכו out” led them all out of the sphere which had hitherto enclosed them, led them out of the retirement in which they had hitherto remained. We find the same words used metaphorically in the same sense referring to Moab, in Jer. XLVIII.11. Moab had been undisturbed from its youth and rested on its fleshpots ולא הורק מכלי אל כלי and has not been emptied from one vessel to another. חנך is only used in the meaning of the initiation and habituating (of a home or a young person) in its pure human holy calling, and here, used of men can mean nothing else than: those who had been introduced by Abraham to their pure human calling i.e. those whose characters had been formed and trained by him, his pupils.

Placing this in connection with וירק may let us in to the secret why Abraham had avoided so much any intimate contact with others. Abraham and Sarah had probably nothing to fear for themselves, but he had 318 חניכים, three hundred and eighteen human souls, whom he had educated up to the pure human calling, and had to keep them for it in the midst of general degeneration. They had to be protected. For them primarily he sought isolation. They were, we are told, ילידי ביתו “born in his household”, and only because they were that, could they become חניכיו. That, he could not achieve with Lot because he was already a formed character when he came to him. Education must begin with birth, all the more so when, as in Abraham’s case, the person has to be born to be an עברי who must regard the whole of the rest of the world in opposition to his ideas. Up till now Abraham, just for the sake of his חניכיו, had kept his household back from contact with the outer world, up till now they had been contained within his own house. But now, when it was a question of saving human beings, he thought no longer of danger, he וירק את חניכיו, he “emptied them out”, “out with all of them”, and this family of Abraham, who hitherto had certainly been scorned and laughed at, as “stay-at-homes” by Lot and the people of Sodom and Gemorrah, hurried out and became their saviours.

These חניכיו ילידי ביתו are called עבדיו in the next verse, and this may well give us an illuminating insight into the meaning of “slavery” in the People of Abraham. It was a way to win human souls over from pagan degeneracy to Abrahamitic clarity of thought and truth. Jewish slaves became Jews, their children were born belonging to the “house of Abraham” and brought up as such. A Jewish slave became a בן ברית, a son of the covenant, and this relationship formed a striking contrast to the slavery of quite modern times (see slave laws in America as late as the middle of the nineteenth century I.L.) where a man would risk his life if he gave slaves spiritual or moral education.

Auf ein Haus übertragen ist חנוכה ebenfalls eine verneinende, und eben dadurch eine um so intensivere Aktivität gewährende Begrenzung. Vor dem חינוך war das Gebäude für alle möglichen Bestimmungen, und darum für keine ausschließlich da. Mit dem חינוך erhält es seine ausschließliche und ausschließende Bestimmung, d.i. Weihe. Wie die Weihe unserer Jugend nicht im Predigen, Moralisieren und Konfirmieren, sondern im חינוך, in der praktischen Einführung und Eingewöhnung in die Erfüllung der Lebenspflichten besteht, so macht auch nicht das Einweihungsprogramm, sondern der einfachste erste darin gehaltene Gottesdienst unsere Gotteshäuser zu Gotteshäusern.

Diese חניכיו ילידי ביתו werden im nächsten Vers עבריו genannt, und dürfte dies wohl geeignet sein, uns über die Bedeutung des "Sklaventums" im Volke Abrahams eine Aufklärung zu gewähren. Es war ein Weg, Menschenseelen aus der heidnischen Entartung für die abrahamitische Klarheit und Wahrheit zu gewinnen. Der jüdische Sklave ward Jude, seine Kinder wurden dem "Hause Abrahams" zugeboren, und zuerzogen. Der jüdische Sklave ward ein בן ברית, ein Sohn des Bundes, und bildet dieses Verhältnis einen schneidenden Kontrast zu dem Sklaventum der allermodernsten Zeit, die den Sklaven geistige und sittliche Bildung bei Todesstrafe verbot. —

V. 15. It does not say ויחלק עליהם את עבדיו, he divided his servants against them, nor simply ויחלק עליהם, but ויחלק עליהם הוא ועבדיו, by this addition we are shown the whole equal part and equal enthusiasm which “his slaves” shared with him in this enterprise showing such complete trust in God.

V. 16. Everything which had been carried off, see above on v.11. The second sentence is in explanation of the first. Everything, Lot and his possessions as well as the women and the rest of the captives. The order in which they are related shows the degree of urgency which had worried Abraham. First Lot, his nephew, then the women as being the weakest and most exposed to mishandling, and then the men.

V. 17.—18. These two verses show a striking contrast. The King of Sodom, who must have felt very humiliated, and still more deeply indebted towards Abraham, not only had allowed him to undertake the pursuit alone with his little band without joining him, but after the victory had been won, comes out to meet him entirely as a King, thinks it is already a sufficient honour for Abraham to be met on equal terms as King to King “in the valley שוה״. And still he comes to beg. To ask for favours, to “demand”, is what a King of Sodom understands, but to refresh the worn-out famished victors with a piece of bread, with a drink of wine, does not enter the head, forms no part of the code of manners of His Majesty of Sodom! On the other hand, Melchizedek, King of Salem, who really had nothing at all to do with the affair, had bread and wine brought out, but then he was also a priest to the Highest God. So that even amongst the polytheistic nations the conception of an All-highest God, אלקא דאלהא, a God of gods had not become entirely lost.

But still it seems that this All-highest God was to them only “an All-highest God”, that He too had his limited sphere, that He, too, like all the subordinate gods, had His place where He had to be honoured. But even so, here at once, two points become evident. (a) where this God does hold sway the place became שלם, a home of peace and salvation, (b) is conditional on צדק, on justice, righteousness, on the just, moral behaviour of men. Still in Joshua’s time the King of Salem was called אדני צדק as this one was מלכי צדק (Josh. X). So that we find the concepts צדק and שלם constantly paired. But these two ideas together comprise the whole content of that which Judaism is to bring to the world. But all this was a speciality. The God which Judaism has to teach as the One and Only One was there only the highest of the gods. The meaning and importance which Judaism maintains is the due of the whole world, was there limited to the speciality of one particular place, and the mission of life which Judaism proclaims as the common one of all men had here become the priestly rule of a local order of priesthood and its precincts. Just as there was a god of licentiousness who was served by debauchery, a god of war by slaughter, a god of revenge by revenge, so there was a God of Justice, Who was indeed the highest to Whom tribute was paid by a righteous life, and Whose domain meant Peace. One could almost say that in the unnatural self-interested attitude of the King of Sodom next to the considerate attentive behaviour of Melchizedek this particularism shows itself in the highest degree. What Melchizedek did, did not affect the Lord of Sodom in the least, he was only acting as the priest of the God of humaneness and benevolence. Sodom paid tribute to the god of the opposite traits, whose adherents could unblushingly serve him by the highest self-interest stripped of all vestige of humane feelings. Humanity, benevolence is a form of godliness, so, too, is inhumanity, egotism. They are just particular forces to whose mastery people can pay tribute according to their choice or circumstances.

So, that consciousness which one day will become the universal treasure of the whole of mankind, and “to which one day the whole social order of mankind will revert — כי עד צדק ישוב משפט — “to find peace” had, at that time, taken refuge in שלם. For a long time to come ירו-שלם was to remain the city of refuge, the shelter from the dark night, for the צדק which everywhere is banned on earth — צדק ילין בה. — In this name, Salem and in that of its King, Melchizedek, a tradition seems to have been kept in the bosom of the nation, of the ultimate salvation of mankind through צדק to שלום. In Psalm CX.4, God says to David the King of Salem: Thou shalt return to mankind as the old true Melchizedek “the King of Righteousness awaited for by mankind”, but not of the false sham man-made righteousness: על דברתי מלכי צדק, but the King who rules according to the righteousness revealed by My Word.

כהן from root כון like נהר from רהב ,נור from רוב, like בהן from בהן) בון, the thumb is the איש הבינים and מבין of the hand; it is the agent, the means, without it all the fingers are lame, can not grip, only by its coming to them do the fingers become tools, the mind of the hand lives in it, through it the fingers enter the service of the human brain, in short, it is the understanding quick-working agent which makes the hand active in the service of the brain. That is why the drop of oil on the thumb consecrates the whole hand whose representative it is). כון from which we get כן, thus, the expression of the special nature of a thing, הכין to get a thing ready for a special purpose. נכון that which is suitable i.e. which is filed for a certain purpose. כהן, that one who (by teaching, example and symbolic procedure) influences people that they become כן, that they correspond to the Will of God, are ready and fixed for godliness. The Jewish priest has not to make God and godliness satisfy human requirements, as the modern expression runs “to satisfy the religious requirements of man” but to shape men and human matters to satisfy God’s requirements, to be active for God’s satisfaction with human beings and human affairs.

V. 19. Not -ברוך מ but -ברוך ל, not blessed by the Highest, but for the Highest God. This expression ’ברוך לה we always meet in תנ״ך when recognition is paid to somebody for a good or great deed enacted. Thus Saul said to the inhabitants of Ziph who promised him that they would deliver David to him: ’ברוכים אתם לה (Sam. XXIII.21). Thus David to the men of Jebeth-Gilead who brought Saul to his grave (Sam. II.5). Thus Noami of Boas who had treated Ruth so well (Ruth II.20), thus Boas again to Ruth who accepted him as a husband in spite of his years (ibid III.10). The idea is that the blessing which God sends to good people comes back to Him, inasmuch as good people use all that they receive to bless God, i.e. for the realisation of His Will on earth. This thought applied to a man says the highest that can be said of him. It says that he is such a man whose being blessed is a blessing for God himself. And thus here too.

Melchizedek was conscious of the fact that his א׳ עליון was no עליון, no god enthroned in blessed repose in the highest heavens above the turmoil of the world, who, as the eternal immutable one, holds the central point of the forces of nature and the reins of the powers of fate in his hands, and then still allows everything to go as it goes; no אלקא דאלהא “who strolls above the heavens”, who — perhaps — did once upon a time give earth its existence, but since then leaves it as the playground of his great and little under-gods — not so, his א׳ עליון is קונה .קונה שמים וארץ looks on property from its moral side; קנה is the legal concept of property, not the idea of possession resulting from force or strength, but of legal right as the basis of property. The קונה of an object is the owner, even if the object is, at the moment, not in his possession. Wherever the object may be, it is לו, it appertains solely to him, awaits him. That is why that property is primarily called מקנה where the ownership relation is so lively that it itself recognizes its owner (’ידע שור וגו I.L.). So that there is no purer conception of the relationship of שמים and ארץ to א׳ עליון than קונה. The owner is not visible but there is no speck of dust that does not recognize the one Master. He has not only got everything in His power, but everything follows Him, carries out His Will; consciously and unconsciously everything is stamped with the pull of this belonging so that with all the energies and forces of its existence it follows and obeys His Will.

Accordingly ascribing קונה שמים וארץ to א׳ עליון declares a fact and an assumption. The fact: — that everything in heaven and earth which has no free will obeys Him, is guided and ruled by Him. The assumption: — that the homage which the whole of the universe pays Him perforce Man is to give of his own free will i.e. of his own free will to live solely in His service. So that Melchizedek was very conscious that the realm of his א׳ עליון was not confined to the city of Salem but that His Kingdom was all mankind between heaven and earth and by making the צדק demanded by Him a reality on earth they were to become שׁלֵם and find שלום.

Until Abraham appeared, Melchizedek with such pretentious ideas was surely, like Abraham, laughed at by his contemporary world, and found himself with his “cult of the Highest God” banished to his corner in Salem. Then Abraham appeared, and by his practical life became a proclaimer of א׳ עליון קונה שמים וארץ not only teaching the theory of all heaven and earth being in the service, not only of the Highest but of the Only God, He being the קונה, but also giving up his “heaven and earth” i.e. himself with all his spiritual and material powers exclusively to the service of this One God. He showed practically that צדק, which in the temple of Salem was taught as the demand of this צדק יקראהו לרגלו — א׳ עליון —. He had understood from God his mission to be, not to be blessed but to be a blesing היה ברכה. And in the recent event, in the courage which this God had inspired in Abraham and his adherents whom he had won over to this One God, and in the victory which He gave to this tiny troop over the vainglorious kings drunk with victories, such a striking demonstration was given, visible even to a blind man, that this א׳ עליון, demanding צדק from man, was not enthroned only in Salem but was יתן לפניו גוים ומלכים ירד — קונה שמים וארץ — and that heaven and earth lie at the feet of men who work in His service. Then Melchizedek came forth, brought out bread and wine and said to this Abraham “Thou art a man blessed for the God of heaven and earth”. Out of the blessing which you have had, and will have had, and will have, the Kingdom of א׳ עליון קונה שמים וארץ will grow; in it, and through you His Kingdom will be apparent to mankind, and by that His Kingdom will be furthered and blessed in you and through you: ברוך אברם לא׳ עליון קונה שמים וארץ. The following ’וברוך א׳ עליון וגו is the reasoned deduction from ברוך אברם לאי. By the fact that the Highest God has shown Himself, by giving you this marvellous victory, so near in His Almightiness to men who serve Him, He Himself, His Kingdom becomes blessed, people are awakened and won over to His service.
V. 20. מִגֵן, the same meaning as in Hosea XI.8 איך אמגנך ישראל “How can I completely abandon you O Israel”.

מעשר. To give a tithe, which we meet here for the first time, is a procedure by which the one, in whose name the receiver of the tithe stands, is recognized as the giver of that which is tithed. By giving the tithe to Melchizedek Abraham acknowledges the “Most High God” in whose name Melchizedek stands, as the One Who had given him the victory.

The form מעשר only occurs referring to this dedicating relationship. Otherwise the term for a tenth is עשר .עשירית related to פזר ,אזר ,עצר ,אצר ,אסר, all roots having the underlying meaning of holding together, binding together. עשר, ten, because with ten a sum is closed off, becomes a closed-off unit. Ten is the first group which forms a whole. We count all material in tens. When we have ten we have one complete set and start counting the next ten till twenty. The representation of our nation, the smallest number representative of the whole also consists of ten. Now, were it to say עשירית הכל then one tenth would have no special significance. It could just as well have been a third or any other fraction. But as the form מעשר occurs exclusively in the sense of dedicating a tenth to God we should look for the speciality of this meaning of that particular form of the word. The form מַעשֵׂר, like מַשׂעֵן ,מִפְתֵּחַ etc. is an active one and designates accordingly not so much the tenth itself as the closing-off act which makes a sum into ten, into a whole unit. That it does not mean merely a tenth part we can see from the term מעשר בהמה where the sheep that presents itself by itself as “the tenth” becomes קדש, is מעשר, i.e. that wherewith one has one whole complete set. This, it is true, is only possible with living creatures. But, nevertheless, from the sentence המרבה במעשרות מעשרותיו מקולקלין it seems to be clear that for lifeless things also one should not measure the whole quantity, and then take off a tenth for מעשר, but there too, each tenth measure is to be made קדש, holy, although this is not absolutely necessary. So that מעשר does not mean so much a tenth part, as every tenth one, the tenth. To make us keep in mind that God is the real giver and master of our property even after it has become ours, we have, accordingly, to dedicate it in two directions (a) the first, ראשית as תרומה ,ביכורים ,בכור, and (b) the last, the completing one. The first penny that we get finds us still with our feelings tender, still with the fresh recollection of the preceding state of bareness, still with the livly feeling “God has given us this”. This first comes from God, but the tenth, hundredth, thousandth, etc., seem already as the natural product of the preceding nine, ninety-nine etc. That the tenth, hundredth, thousandth are just as much a direct gift of the השגחה פרטית (individual personal provident care of God I.L.) as much as the first, that is the Truth that we are to keep in mind by מעשר.

V. 22.—24. To the א׳ עליון of Melchizedek Abraham adds the name ’ה, the most characteristic name of God which places the א׳ עליון קונה שמים וארץ in special relationship to mankind. Abraham’s victory only convinced Melchizedek that the “highest God” also was in relationship to men’s efforts and men’s doings. But Abraham expresses his conviction of a much higher degree of God’s relationship to man. The ’א׳ ע of Melchizedek differed from the other gods only in degree, only quantitatively. He was the highest power in the sphere of powers. Outside the Jewish teaching of God, apart from what has already become common property taken from Judaism, the conception of the greatness of God, was, and is, only the idea of a highest power, which in its relation to the cosmos, to the universe in general, is in no closer relationship to mankind than to the other created things. The highest god of heathenism was a god of nature, history was, above all, a product of man. The God of Abraham, was not only the God of nature but, above all, the God of history. After creation was completed in nature, creation in history began, since then God is מעלה ומוריד guides and leads — His greatest work lies in the future, not in the past, He is the four-lettered God, ’ה, the Creator of the future! This Name Abraham puts first; “the God whom your priest just mentioned is a God in Whose service, consciously or unconsciously, you and I, all of us stand, and He is the God Who sends me —”.

הרימתי. It is very doubtful what this really means. נשא ’ד certainly does occur with the meaning of taking an oath but only in God’s Mouth. But הרים יד never occurs as swearing except perhaps here. נשא and הרים are different. In נשא it is only the relation to the height to which an object is to be raised which is stressed without any relation to any lower place from which it is to be raised. But this is just what is stressed in הרים. It is not merely a raising but “raising out of”. Hence the word תרומה. It could therefore here very well mean: “When I went away I dedicated my hand to God, no self-interested motives directed me, but rather I withdrew my hand from all other purposes that are lower than God, and dedicated it solely to God, so that from all my victory I may take nothing for any other purpose, nothing for myself”. But the אֶל ה׳ is against this way of taking it, in the sense of תרומה is should say ’לה. Perhaps this “up to God” which ’אל ה expresses was called for to stress the contrast to Sodom, it was to express very definitely not only dedicating the hand to God, but just thereby the denial of any other selfish use.

Still, it is more probable that after all here, too, it is an expression of swearing which also seems indicated by the אם which follows. נשא יד is only used by promissary oaths. By raising one’s hand in an oath to God one pledges all one’s power (יד I.L.) to fulfil what one has promised. Used by God it makes the promise independent of circumstances or anything else, brings heaven and earth in service of what is promised. What other expression than הרימותי could Abraham have used towards a heathen when he wishes to swear in the name of God? With this word he raises his hand away from all the gods up to the Highest, who, for him is the Only One. Had he sworn by one of their gods נשאתי would have sufficed.

מחוט עד שרוך נעל. In the Jewish way of looking at things, if one wishes to designate something as all-embracing, one does not take something great and small, or something near and far, and say: from this smallest to the greatest, from this nearest point to that farthest one, but one looks at the world as a circle, takes two objects close to each other and says: from this one right round the world to this other next to it. Thus when it speaks of a whole nation — which is not looked on as a pyramid but as a circle (the beggar goes as much in front of the King as behind him if it is a circle) — it says from the hewer of wood to the drawer of water. So here too, from a thread to a boot-lace. So do our sages say מהודו ועד כוש (Esther I) שמלך בכיפה, going round the world, starting from הודו and arriving in כוש.

V. 1. דבר ה׳ אל אברם במחזה. God has spoken to Abraham before, but we do not find the expression דבר ה׳ אל אברם used. Our sages find here a special kind of נבואה. They reckon ten ways in which the word of God has been revealed to man, and teach that it has not come to every prophet in the same way, nor to the same prophet in the same way on every occasion. God Himself describes the relationship of Moses to the other prophets in this direction as something quite special. They lay stress on the fact that the Divine came to Abraham in מראה and מחזה, in אמירה and דבור, further that חזות and דבור designate a נבואה קשה, a fateful content (חזות קשה הוגד לי Is. XXL.2) and here both are combined. For that which is here to be revealed to Abraham is indeed, in its further ramifications, a ’דבר ה and חזות, for it is an introduction to the גלות, the hard history of suffering which his descendants would have to endure. Accordingly it forms a chapter on its own and therefore begins with אחר הדברים האלה.

This term אחר הדברים האלה occurs in the history of Abraham only once again, as introduction to the עקדה (Ch. XXII). It means, after all the preceding, all that we have heard up till now of Abraham, is only an introduction to what follows. The life of Abraham falls into three periods: — (1) from לך לך till here, the ברית בין הבתרים, (2) from there till the עקדה, (3) then till his death. אחר means both, after, and the other, the other presupposes something preceding, the other is the reverse, the first is the פנים. So that the periods introduced by אחר are, as it were, the reverse of what went before. Until now the way of Abraham’s life was a continuously upward one. From a single isolated man to a victorious conqueror, and, in truth, to a spiritual conqueror of the whole of his age. But that what he is still to become can only be achieved by the reverse side of fortune, by the hard schooling of suffering.

Far from presuming to wish to penetrate into the methods of any prophetic revelation, we still think that we may go into some consideration of that which is told us of them in the words of the Scriptures themselves. There is surely a difference whether it says A spoke to B or A’s words came to B. In the first case A is opposite B, is present with him. In the second case the hearer only receives the words, the speaker need not necessarily be present himself, he appears to be in a more distant, less intimate relationship to the hearer.

Equally so, חזה .מחזה is seeing in the distance, or seeing that which is not visible to the ordinary physical eye. Hence חזה the breast, the seat of the heart, with which, according to the Hebrew feeling for the use of language, one sees the invisible. חזה would be, to penetrate with one’s spiritual eye, into that which is hidden to other people. But it is nevertheless always an actual seeing, not merely mental. It is, in any way, something that is incomprehensible to, and beyond our ordinary experience. Human words can only be heard. God’s words are heard and seen at the same time, thus also רואים ושומעים את הקולות, they saw what they heard and heard what they saw. This is the highest state that the human mind and spirit can reach, that it at once sees realised that which it comprehends, and what it hears with its actual ears also absorbs at once with its “mental ear”.

We have only still to remember the different meaning of דבר and אמר; The one an absolute declaration without consideration of the hearer’s acceptance, or of his understanding and feelings regarding it, the other having the object of its being understood, taken to heart and transmitted further. ’דבר ה is a declaration from God, an absolute order which is to be carried out whether we understand it, like it, or not; but it comes to us לאמר, to take root, blossom, and bear fruit in us, to appeal to us, to be taken to our hearts and to be passed on to our children. Such a Word of God came to Abraham לאמר for him to understand and take to heart and transmit to his children, and this Word begins with: “Fear not Abraham!” So that it must have found him in an apprehensive, frightened mood.

Much thought has been given to find the reason for this mood, and different thoughts have been suggested over what it was — which is not told us — concerning which God had to reassure and calm Abraham. It could be, and has been suggested, that Abraham was worried with the thought: “Waging war; killing people, were there no innocent men amongst them?” Others suggest: Abraham left his homeland with the promise that he bore within him the salvation of the future of the whole world, and now, after his extraordinary success and good fortune he was afraid just because of this good fortune! Great though he had become, this was still far from the real goal in which his great mission was to mature. He was apprehensive that perhaps God no longer considered him worthy for the old mission to rescue mankind from their aberrations through his descendants (he was still childless, I.L.) and that he was already overpaid, had used up all such זכות that he might have, by this great good fortune — and several other suggestions. All this is possible. But still possible and probable too, that there is no necessity to go beyond which is expressly told us in the text itself and to find therein the answer to our question.

We find an analogy in the אל תירא said to Jacob in Ch. XLVI.3; Jacob is journeying to Egypt in the most joyous mood to find the reward for his whole life, to meet again his most beloved son, whom he had thought dead, as the ruler of the land. And yet God appears to him and says: “Fear not to go down to Egypt!” The fear concerning which he is to be reassured was itself only brought about by the address of God. ויסע ישראל It was as “Israel”, as the God-conquering happy joyful man (no longer “Jacob” I.L.) that he had journeyed forth and had just offered happy offerings to God (זבחים = שלמים I.L.). Then God spoke “unto Israel in the visions of the night: Jacob, Jacob! And he said: I am ready. Then God said: I am the God of thy father, fear not to go down to Egypt; for I will there make of thee a great nation etc. etc.” The manner of the vision itself, and Galut-name “Jacob” addressed to the joyous Israel, reminded him, in the midst of his most happy mood, that the future into which he was just journeying was the beginning of the Galut prophesied long ago, Not as Israel, as Jacob was he going down to Egypt. And when Jacob replied to this call with הנני, “I am ready for that too”, God reassured him as to the ultimate purpose and goal.

That אל תירא to Jacob throws a light on our realisation of what came to Abraham here as a proclamation of God’s decisions, and which was similarly introduced by a אל תירא after a similar serious foreboding mood had been induced by the manner of the revelation. Not as otherwise, “God appeared, or became visible, to Abraham” ( וירא I.L.) or “God said to Abraham” (ויאמר I.L.) but “the Word of God came to Abraham and it was in a vision, perspective (במחזה I.L.). This whole manner of God’s approach to him shook Abraham and prepared him for some serious, stern communication, awoke the apprehension that he was now, to use the words of our introduction, אחר הדברים האלה, at the beginning of the “reverse” of the preceding cheerful upward path of the prosperous past, hence:

אל תירא, fear not, what I have to tell you is not a change from your own personal past. I remain your shield, and the happiness which blossoms from your devotion and self-sacrifice has no bounds. שכר related to סגר ,סכר to stop up, close, fill up holes, make good. Similarly שכר, to fill out a space i.e. compensate (cf. VII.2; II.21). If שכר is reward, compensation, to fill up a “hole” (caused in your time, strength or energy) then one can only expect שכר from God if it has been preceded by some sacrifice לפום צערא אגרא. He who loves himself and his possessions too much to give anything to God can not expect any שכר. So what is said here is: That which will be demanded from you will certainly entail sacrifice — hence the mood I have awakened in you — but שכרך, the compensation for it will be without limits.

In תנ״ך there is altogether very little said of reward, it hardly occurs again in this manner. The good that God wants us to practice is itself the truest reward. שכר, compensation is only demanded by one who believes he has sacrificed something. But to the true Jew, fulfilling a duty, doing a Mitzva, is no sacrifice but in itself a gain; שכר מצוה מצוה. The promised blessings are everywhere merely the results, עקב תשמעון something that follows behind, not the goal in front which one strives to reach. Here too God did not speak to Abraham of reward. God considered Abraham’s unexampled devotion as a sacrifice to which He referred the resulting boundless happiness as boundless compensation. In the same way Boaz speaks to Ruth of her reward as תהי משכרתך שלמה in as much as he considers it having been a great sacrifice for her to have attached herself to an impoverished, unfortunate family to enter and remain תחת כנפי השכינה.

V. 2. אדנ׳ ידוד. An appellation of God which altogether does not often occur and which we meet here for the first time. In the תורה we only find it three times more, once again in the mouth of Abraham in Ch. XV.18 במה אדע כי אירשנה and twice used by Moses, אתה החלות להראות (Deut. III.24) and אל תשחת עמך ונחלתך (Deut. IX.26).

The שם אדנות. Abraham was the first to call God אדון. It is a name that is constantly in the mouth of an ’עבד ה, a נביא. The man who regards himself as one of God’s tools, in His service, calls his God אדון, (Master, I.L.) and indeed not אדני but א-ני, not merely “a Master of mine”, one amongst others but “my Masters”, he has and knows no influences, considerations, relationship, forces that rule and order him other than God, Whom accordingly he calls his ”Masters”.

ידוד is the most profound combination, even according to the simple understanding of the names of God, which is the common heritage of our consciousness of being a nation. It is written as מדת הרחמים and pronounced as מדת הדין. It teaches, accordingly, that when God appears on the surface in His severity and His strict justice, this severity and strictness is itself in reality, a manifestation of His Love and is to be regarded as such. ברגז רחם תזכור His severity is only an instrument of love by which the foundations of a blissful future are built up. It is the same שם הויה, only it is read as שם אלקים. So that when Abraham replies to the vision of God which had awakened in him a sense of foreboding of a severe troubled future, and at the same time assured him of His lasting protecting Grace, with these words ידור, he expresses thereby: “Thou, my Master, in Whose service I stand, Who art Severity and yet Love, I need not understand Thee, I require no explanation, Thou art ’ה also when Thou appeareth to be אלקים״. Thereby he had expressed the whole of his inner completely unconditional devotion. This Abraham states first and then adds: “מה תתן לי what blessing wouldst Thou give me further; for myself I have no further wishes, ah! if I had a child who could benefit by it, then yes, but I go about childless”. Abraham understood the assurance of the continuance of God’s Love to refer primarily to himself personally, as indeed at the end of this reassurance there was a purely personal reference אתה תבא אל אבותיך בשלום.

משק root שקק, like מכם from שקק .כסם is a strong form of שוק, to long for something, to be hungry, lusting for something, the basic meaning: powerful longing movement towards something, שוק market where everything streams together, שוק, thigh, the strong muscles of movement, hence משק: longing. בן משק ביתי as much as to say בן תשוקת ביתי, the calculating heir, the one who is expectantly waiting for my house is not Eliezer, he does not wait for Abraham’s death, he himself is already an old man; the heirs who are casting longing eyes at my heritage are the relations of Eliezer, Eliezer’s Damascus. These relations Abraham had just recently come to know, he had pursued the defeated Kings up to Damascus. — Therefore give me nothing, what Thou wouldst give me, Thou wouldst only be giving to Eliezer’s Damascus relations”.

V. 3. לי comes significantly before the verb, and נתתָּה stresses the person addressed. Wouldst Thou really give me something, see, riches I do not desire, but even if I were a beggar, the most simple man to whom God had granted intelligence, power, or material means, wishes to see himself and his endeavours live on in his children. I have, it is true, ילידי בית but they are not ילידי, not זרעי, brought up by me but not begotten by me, bought by me but not given to me by You. Abraham does not ask for an alteration of this condition, he only refers to it: הנה ,הן, see, look at it whether it is right. If it is right in Your Eyes, then it must be right, You are Love even if I can not understand it. Possibly, more, it seems probable that ויאמר repeated here does not mean that Abraham actually said this to God as in the preceding verse but he said it to himself in his mind, that would be why the next verse does not say ויאמר אליו God answered him, but ’והנה וגו a sudden interruption to his thoughts.

V. 4. ממעיך, not חלציך or ירכך the usual terms. Whereas both these latter designate purely physical parts of the body, just מעים is used as a designation for that sphere of the human body which is the seat of feelings, especially pity and sympathy, just those qualities which are the most characteristic delicately sensitive traits of Jewish people which are the heritage of זרע אברהם. Minds can be improved, learning imparted, but what is difficult to accomplish is an ennobling change to refinement of character, that, above all has its roots in מעי אבות. It is not so much intelligence as fine feelings that give character to a human being. Children have to thank their parents for nothing more than for that which they have inherited זרע כנען .ממעיהם can also have mind and intelligence, can be brought up and educated to a sense of duty. But the true Jewish humane feelings can not be inculcated by education, they must be inherited ממעי אברהם. It was just on this innate receptivity for all refinement and nobility and readiness to sacrifice joyfully that God built the foundation of His future nation.

מעים rad. מעה, verwandt mit מהה und מהה .מחה, wovon מה das stofflich Unbestimmte, Formlose, nicht zu Fassende. Sowie מי nach dem persönlich Unbestimmten fragt, so ist מַה die Frage nach dem stofflich nicht Definierten, sich nicht in bestimmter Form Darstellenden. Verstärkt: מחה, das gänzliche Auflösen. In der Mitte dürfte מעה stehen und zur Bezeichnung der ganzen inneren Maschinerie im Menschen dienen, die alles von der Außenwelt von dem Menschen Aufzunehmende auflöst und durch diese Auflösung zur Aufnahme fähig macht. Alles, was ein lebendiger Organismus in sich aufnimmt, sind an und für sich differenzierte, d. h. einem besonderen Dasein angehörige Stoffe. Als solche können sie nicht in einen anderen Organismus übergehen. Die מֵעַים schaffen alles Eingehende zuerst zu einem מֵעים, d. i. zu einem indifferenten Stoffe um. Dieses indifferenzierende System ist ein dualistisches, מֵעים, ein vegetabilisches und ein animalisches: Verdauungs- und Atmungssystem. Wie dieses Gesamtsystem das Eingehen der stofflichen Außenwelt in das Individuum vermittelt, so auch die Eindrücke der moralischen Außenwelt. Es ist Sitz der Empfindung. Wie aber im normalen, gesunden Zustand das Individuum kein Bewusstsein von seinen "Eingeweiden" hat, es vielmehr nur dann fühlt, daß es ein Herz, einen Magen, einen Darm usw. hat, wenn die Maschine oder ein Teil derselben stockt, wenn den מעים etwas gegeben ist, was sie nicht zu verarbeiten, nicht zu "indifferenzieren" vermögen, ebenso finden wir empfindende Gefühlstätigkeit durch מעים nur in schmerzlicher Beziehung ausgedrückt; מעים המו, dieses Innere kommt in Störung, המרמרו, in heftige Gärung durch Eindrücke der Mitleidenschaft mit dem Leiden anderer.

V. 5. “Raise, now, thine eyes, away from the earth up to the heaven, to the stars: thus will thy seed be!” כה is not so much a numerical particle to describe the quantitative size but rather one of kind and manner. And anyway, if what was meant to be said to Abraham was only “as countless as the stars” it would hardly have been necessary to take him out in the open to realise this thought. Surely Abraham knew how numerous the stars were, how countless for the human eye. Wherever in the תנ״ך some external object is brought before the eyes of the hearer in addition to the speech, where signs, happenings, symbols are given together with the word of God, then these speeches are meant thereby to be given a deeper, more comprehensive, more lasting way of being taken. So that here the sight of the stars was meant to illustrate to Abraham a thought which was to remain deeply impressed on his soul, and in which the core of the whole speech must lie. When, before, he had been told “I will make thy seed like the dust of the earth”, he was not first shown dust.

Let us consider the sentence more closely: נא .הבט נא as remarked already, always comes to oppose some existing mood, opinion, tendency of thought or will. So that here, at this moment there must have been something present in the mind of Abraham which was to be met by this speech of God. The tendency of Abraham’s thought is clear from the context. He had given up all hopes of getting a child, and in the natural course of events he could no longer look forward to the joys of fatherhood. It was in this feeling that he said “see, everything that You might still give me, would be of no value to me as I shall depart from this world childless”. Thereupon God led him out into the open. “Just take a look, I pray thee at the heaven”, up there you see quite a different state of existence to that on earth. On earth one no longer sees any direct creation of God. Everything that we see on earth is a product of something else already created, does not come directly from the Hand of God, but follows the natural laws of production. Within these earthly conditions where every effect comes from its given cause, Abraham is quite right, all premises are lacking to give rise for hopes of the blessing of children. Then God directs his sight up to the heavens. There things are different, what one sees there are bodies, creations which have been called into existence directly by God, in their pristine state just as they were when placed there by God at the Creation (if we could see the earth as a whole, as a heavenly body it would present us with a similar sight). So that if somebody is to be made to visualise an existence brought about by the immediate direct power of God’s Almightiness, he can only be shown the stars. His sight must be raised above to the heavens, to the double שָׁם from where a world called forth directly from God shines down on him — and “can’st thou indeed count them?” These, these creations direct from the Creator are more numerous than those produced indirectly on the limited space of earth, — therefore צא מאצטגנינות שלך — leave your natural earthly calculations and let your mind sink into the conception of this world of stars “thus shall thy people be!” So directly from God, so without all natural premises, yea, against all natural combinations and sequences, a second Creation, a יש מאין, so shall they be. Thirty years longer must Abraham and Sara wander about without children, and the very last earthly prospect of parental joy must have disappeared; by all earthly reckoning any such hope must first become completely “ludicrous”, Abraham, Sarah must involuntarily laugh at the idea, כל השומע יצחק לי, the whole world must laugh, before the first child of the God-promised nation is to come into existence.

This looking at the stars to illustrate the existence of Israel depending directly on the Mouth of God is also sung in Ps. CXLVII. “He Who now buildeth Jerusalem, God, He also gathereth together again the outcasts of Israel, He Who healeth broken hearts hath also healing for their pains. He Who counts the number of the stars, calleth them all by name. Great is our Lord and great is His Power, His Discernment is beyond all calculation, etc.”. However wretched and improbable the נדחי ישראל have become, they still depend directly and individually, like each star, on the word of God. Each individual Jew, however wretched his conditions may be, as long as he remains a Jew, he is under the personal השגחה פרטית “Who calleth him by name”, for חֵרות על הלוחות, treading in the paths dedicated to God raises one above the might of all nature-bound powers, makes one free, places one directly under God.

It does not say ’ויאמן בה as it says of Israel, ’וירא ישראל וגו׳ ויאמינו בה that Abraham had gained אמונה by what had just occurred, but ’והאמין בה Abraham’s whole previous life was אמונה. Already in the name יקוק with which he had answered God, he had shown his complete אמונה, and this last revelation of his own future and the future of his people only gave him fresh food for אמונה and fresh opportunity to exercise it.

אמונה is not belief, by which word one robs this central idea of Jewish consciousness of its real conception. Belief is an act of the mind, is often only an opinion, is always only believing something to be true by reason of judgment and the assurance of somebody else. In making religion into a belief, and then making the cardinal point of religion believing in the truth of theses quite untenable to the intelligence, religion has been banned from everyday life and made into a catechism of words of belief which will be demanded as a passport for entry into the next world. But to believe the words of another is never expressed by -האמין ב, at most -והם לא יאמינו לי — האמין ל (Ex. IV.1) — but -האמין ב is not a mere submitting our theoretical mind to the insight of another, ’האמין בה is placing full confidence, setting our whole theoretical and practical hold, our guidance, our strength and firmness in God. Already the verbal concept אמן is mainly practical. מעשי ידי אמן (Cant. VII.2) from which we get in rabbinic Hebrew אומן: “sculptor, former, אומן, one who shapes living people, tutor, nurse, educator, education אָמְנָה, So that אמן means not simply being firm, but actively making firm, to give a firm shape and definite form and direction to the indefinite material being of another. ’האמין בה is accordingly the whole formation of your life, culture, education, direction of all your being and efforts in God; leaving yourself entirely to Him, giving yourself up as plastic material to be moulded by God, in short; to refer yourself and all you have entirely to God. To respond to a spoken sentence with אמן does not only mean to declare it to be true, but to give yourself up to the truth expressed in the sentence, to make it your own, and to vow to allow yourself to be guided by it. For אמן does not refer to the contents of the pronouncement but to the person who hears and adopts it. המתברך יתברך באלדי אמן Isaiah LXV.16. says: “that he who blesseth himself in the world, shall bless himself in the God of אמן״ in the God of these people and that nation who give themselves up entirely to the guidance of God. Even אמת itself is not only truth in theory it is also truth in practice, in deed: loyalty, faithfulness.

Now here it says of Abraham: ’והאמין בה. He had given himself over completely and unconditionally to the direct guidance of God. God had raised him above the sphere of conditions on earth, where things are bound by the cause-and-effect laws of Nature, to look at a concrete existence directly proceeding from the Will of God, and had said to him: Thus shall thy seed be, similarly directly from Me and through Me, without all natural premises, yea, against all natural calculations. ’והאמין בה, and, as his seed are to allow themselves to be borne solely by God alone, so did Abraham enlightingly lead the way with this ויחשבה לו ,צדקה .אמונה. It is questionable whether it is God or Abraham who is the subject in this sentence. It depends on the meaning in which צדקה is taken.

For צדקה occurs in two apparently basically different meanings. In verses like וענתה בי צדקתי (Gen. 30,30)or וצדקת צדיקים יסורו ממנו (Is. X) it undeniably means simply: doing right, righteousness. If Jacob served Laban faithfully it was no more than what his duty demanded. If the bribed judge gives the guilty party right, and has no consideration for the צדקה of the other party, it is the righteousness of the latter which is “done away with” — יסורו ממנו by the bribery. On the other hand צדקה is not exactly right, justice, not משפט, it is always mentioned next to משפט as something different; it is only משפט וצדקה together which make the sum of an active life lived in accordance with duty, and used in reference to God it is just an act of benevolence. משפט does nothing to enrich or expand. משפט only ensures that you hold what you have got, or get it restored if unjustly lost. When I restore to someone that which he has forfeited through me or for me by expending his forces or fortune, I have performed משפט.

צדקה is something else. The root is צדק .צדק, as already remarked (on Ch. VI.9 and VII.1) is related to שדך (phonetically) to soothe, satisfy, care for, to give that which the other lacks, which conduces to his well-being. צדק is that happy conformation of circumstances in which, according to God’s plan of human welfare, the world as a whole and every individual in it should participate, and which with certainty will ultimately be reached. It is the goal of God’s management and direction of the world. It is, speaking from the human point of view, the ideal. Every act of God or Man which brings the individual or the whole nearer to this ideal is: צדקה .צדקה is presupposed by צדק and leads towards it. Used referring to God it is always a deed of benevolence; referring to man, it is benevolence towards the receiver, duty toward God. For God placed every man, with every grain of his spiritual and material powers, in the service of צדק. He is only given them to use them to further the צדק-well-being of the world about him. Every such contribution is צדקה, so that צדקה is the total sum of a life lived faithfully to duty of which משפט is but the negative side, not doing wrong, whereas צדקה is the positive realisation of what is good.

ויחשבה לו צדקה. So this could mean here: Abraham placed all his confidence in God, and reckoned it to Him, God, as benevolence. He was convinced that the childless state of which he complained — although he could not understand it — must be a benevolent act of God which would somehow further the salvation of the world which was to be founded by him. The similarity of the subject in both the sentences, והאמין and ויחשבה would seem to favour this way of taking it. But nevertheless it is probable that God is the subject and לו refers to Abraham: God reckoned the אמונה which Abraham proved as צדקה, as the most complete dutiful accomplishing his life’s task. Thus it says of Phinehas: “Then Phinehas stood up and executed judgment and the ‘plague was stayed, and it was reckoned unto him as “Zedoka” unto generation after generation for evermore’” (Ps. CVI.30, 31). In this one act Phinehas reached the summit of the accomplishment of his life’s task, this act was the highest contribution he made towards furthering the work of God, and as such was it reckoned to him, and thereby he won eternal priesthood. So also with Abraham. אמונה, this boundless confidence in God for a future for which he could not see the very first beginning and all human reckoning spoke against its realisation, in this אמונה the task of Abraham’s life reached its highest point, it was his highest contribution towards the building of this very future. Whereas his descendants would have to say to themselves: וצדקה תהיה לנו, our Zedoka, our faithfulness to duty will be accomplished if we carefully carry out the whole of this Law before God as we have been commanded, כי נשמור לעשות את כל המצוה הזאת לפני ה׳ אלקינו כאשר צונו, Abraham had not been given the תרי״ג מצות to keep. His task consisted in first planting the whole of his being in God in אמונה, the complete confidence in, and devotion to, His guidance and education. And this task — for Abraham in his isolation and without the preceding experience of the miraculous providence of God, so much an infinitely heavier one — Abraham had fully accomplished by his whole life, and thereby laid the foundation for the future which now was to be revealed to him.

V. 7. If we see here how God introduced the important revelation of the future of His people with a reference to Abraham’s departure out of Ur-Kasdim, then this departure must have been no ordinary going-away. It must have been an event demonstrating God’s miraculous assistance, must have been a deliverance like the יציאת מצרים was for his descendants. Only a reference to some extraordinary deliverance from some extraordinary danger — such as the tradition we have of Nimrod’s outrageous attempt on Abraham’s life — could make this “exodus from Ur-Kasdim” into an experience out of which the Patriarch and his people could draw the strength and hope to enable them to endure bravely the four-hundred years of Galut suffering until the “exodus from Egypt”. Now if this deliverance was a deliverance from death by burning — and possibly אור, glowing fire, refers to this, and the passage might mean: “I Who brought you out of the glowing fire of Chaldea — this might also make it likely that the תנור עשן ולפיד אש in the sequel makes the danger in Egypt appear as a smoking and flaming furnace of fire which his descendants would have to withstand in the political fiery furnace of Egypt. יציאת אור כשדים would be a prototype of יציאת מצרים.

V. 8. במה אדע כי אירשנה: It is impossible that this can mean: “by what shall I know that I shall take possession of it”. The man who has just been praised for having ’אמונה בה as the highest content of his life, the completest, most unreserved devotion and confidence in God’s guidance can not possibly want any further assurance, ask for some definite sign that what God had repeatedly promised would actually come to pass. Neither do the words bear the explanation of meaning באיזה זכות אירשנה for then it would have to have said אדע במה אירשנה. But this promise here had a word added that did not appear in the previous ones. The first promise ran: לזרעך אתן את הארץ הזאת Ch.. XII.7. Similarly in XIII.15, לך אתננה ולזרעך עד עולם “To thee and to thy descendants will I give this land”, a wording of this promise, which refers to no co-operating action on the part of Abraham or his descendants. But here it says: לתת לך את הארץ הזאת לרשתה “to give you this land to take it into possession” לרשתה, a word which has the idea of “self-action” so strongly that it is used with the meaning of conquering, capturing, and is so used, in this sense, in the actual conquest of the land, ’ראה נתן לפניך ה׳ א׳ את הארץ עלה רש וגו (Deut. I.21). And equally so in I.8; IX.23; II.31. So that Abraham was told here that God had brought him out of Ur-Kasdim to give him this land for him to take it into his possession as a conqueror. Abraham had just fought and won a glorious victory over four world-conquering kings. He had not even undertaken that battle following a special expressed promise from God, but from his general feeling of duty. He could very well have concluded from that, he (or, if you will, his descendants) upheld by the assistance of God was to conquer the promised land in a similar fashion, so that he asked: “by what shall I know that the right time has arrived for me to conquer the land?” Far from being a lack of confidence, this question expresses the highest degree of confidence in God. Just as he was given the victory over the four kings so is he ready to undertake the conquest of the whole land. It suffices that God had promised him possession for him to be certain of the result. God is אדניו his Lord and Master in Whose service he lives and strives, He is ידוד, to Whose orders he is according ready to place himself in all danger and battles with all worries and labours.

V. 9.—21. במה אדע was Abraham’s question, ידע תדע (V.13) runs the answer. To know by what he was to recognise the right time in which, in accordance with God’s advice he was to take possession of the land, was Abraham’s request. “Know well” came the answer given to this wish “thou thyself will not take possession of the land, nor will thy descendants do so immediately, nor by the way of ever-prospering good fortune. As aliens, slaves, maltreated, without homeland, freedom or power of resistance will three generations first have to go through life, and it will only be the fourth generation which will return here to take possession of the land. The moral degeneration which imposes the death sentence of the present inhabitants of the land will not have reached its utmost depth until then. The present inhabitants will first ripen in luxurious wantonness towards their condemned degeneration, the future inhabitants mature in poverty, slavery and wretchedness for their future possession. But as far as thou thyself art concerned, it is only the covenant which is made with thee, thou wilt go in peace to thy fathers”.

This announcement, which was given to the Patriarch in answer to his question, and which, just because it was announced beforehand, was to be, for his descendants, a source of endurance and courage and the ground for confidence and persevering hope during the testing and educating centuries of unspeakable wretchedness, was not only given to the Patriarch in words but deeply impressed on him by symbolic signs and acts and occurrences. The ancestor had to experience figuratively the endless night and dread and the exulting awakening therefrom so that it could be grasped more surely and more deeply and be handed down with all the certainty of something that had already been lived through. The ידע תדע is nothing but the explanation of what had already been said symbolically, is nothing but the verbal translation of the symbolic performance which preceded it. All that remains for us to do is to find the meaning of the symbols i.e. to find the connection of the happenings to the explanation of them that followed.

As שַׁלֵשׁ means to do something three times, חוט המשולש (Eccl. IV.12) a threefold cord, the משלשת and משלש here can also mean nothing but three times, three calves, three goats, three rams. But it does not say עגלות שלש עזים שלש ,ואילים שלשה, three calves, three goats and three rams, but three times a calf, three times a goat, and three times a ram, to designate each of these three animals as being a group belonging together, as well as taking these animals separately three times to designate something repeated three times. If one connects the symbolism of the act with the spoken part of this revelation that followed, it at once springs to one’s mind that cutting these living creatures into pieces on whose carcases the greedy birds of prey want to swoop down, represents the condition and the danger which hangs over the coming generations. These animals represent, accordingly, the coming generations, and when it is said that only the fourth generation will rise again to salvation, three generations accordingly having to suffer the predicted wretchedness, it is equally clear that giving up these three animals three times to God (ויקח לו...... קחה לי I.L.) means nothing else but: three times your descendants, i.e. three of your coming generations will have to give themselves up to Me with what they are as עז ,עגלה and איל and with what they have to give up as עז ,עגלה and ויבתר וגוי .איל, three of your coming generations will I allow to be forcibly killed in what they represent as עז ,עגלה, and איל and only remain alive as תור and גוזל. As dead bodies of עז ,עגלה and איל they lie on the ground, the birds of prey see in them a welcome spoil, and only you, with your זכות, prevented them from becoming a feast for them. It is quite clear that the subject of ויבתר is God, and not Abraham, as it is only in וישב אותם אברם that Abraham is brought as the subject.
It remains to find out what תור וגוזל ,איל ,עז ,עגלה mean when used referring to the personalities of men or nations.

That they do have definite meaning used figuratively for human personalities is clearly proved by even a superficial glance at the laws of the offerings, where just these animals are exclusively permitted to be used, and only certain kinds and sexes are definitely prescribed for different persons, and then again for different circumstances even for those same persons.

Cattle, שור ,בקר, are animals of work, actively working in the service of their master (whereas חמור represents the beast of burden). Thus we find לא תחסום שור בדישו (Deut. XXV.7); רב תבואות בכח השור (Prov. XIV.4) לא תעבוד בבכור שורך (Deut. XV.19). Hence the young ox always appears as the animal to be educated for work: כעגל לא לומד (Jer. XXXI.18); אפרים עגלה מלומדה (Hosea X.11); כעגלה דשה (Jer. L.11); hence also פרה סוררה (Hosea IV.7). Hence cattle represent the power of action and active usefulness. The fully developed animal of the species is the פר, and פר in offerings always represents a personality called on to work in the public service of God and the community and to be in the fore with his work. Thus we have פר העלם דבר של צבור ,פר כה׳׳ג ביה״כ ,פר כהן משיח etc. So that עגלה designates the approaching power of action, power of action in development.

צאן, sheep and goats, the flock, are the real pastoral animals, hence the so-frequently used metaphor for the most general relationship to God. People and nations are the sheep, the flock, God is the Shepherd. ואתן צאני צאן מרעיתי אדם אתם ,צאן מרעיתו ,ה׳ רועי לא אחסר (Ez. XXXIV.31) etc. Hence שה is the most general expression to represent the general people of Israel in offerings, thus in קרבן פסח, in the תמידים etc., and so also private individuals in חטאת יחיד represent themselves in צאן, a כבשה or שעירה. But in the flock, the species of צאן has two animals specially characterised viz., עז the goats and איל the ram.

עז, as already its name indicates (from עז, hard, firm, strong) is an animal that is only tame and tractable towards its master but which obstinately shows its horns to any stranger. It is accordingly the purest characterisation of resistance, especially of that virile independence which, firm against, and deaf to all external and internal enticements, remains immovable and faithfully follows the commands of its master. Hence it is chosen for the חטאת which is to preach against careless easy-going, in the שעיר חטאת of the נשיא, the שעיר העם בי״כ the שעיר ושעירת ע״ז, the שעירי רגלים ור״ח etc. So that עז represents the power of resistance.

איל is the mature sheep, the old ram that, on account of its strength goes in front of the flock and is its leader. Hence the common designation of the opulent, the great men of a nation אילי הארץ ,אילי מואב etc. איל is the characterisation of the “man of property”. It is therefore the most characteristic animal in offerings where expiation is to be sought for sins which are related to property or to a superior position in the world, as in אשם שפחה חרופה ,אשם גזלה ,אשם מעילה or in the ordination of an office which authorises great privileges, as in the מלואים etc. So that איל represents an outstanding personality through property and rights.

צפור, the pure (in the sense of our being allowed to eat it I.L.) bird (— the “feathered” bird (see above VII.14) where feathers are the predominant feature in contrast to birds of prey who have claws as tools and weapons —) is that living creature without strength or powers of resistance, but which nevertheless is the one which escapes from Man’s realm of power and violence more than any other by means of its power of upward flight. Hence the picture of a shy, fugitive, free existence which is threatened by snares from which however it escapes by its soaring flight. כצפור מיד יקוש, כצפור לנוד ,כצפור נודדת (Prov. VI.5) מי יתן לי אבר כיונה (Ps. LV.7). Hence a picture of the existence of Israel, without might or armour and yet free and happy and protected: כנפי יונה נכפה בכסף (Ps. LXVIII.14) יונתי בחגוי הסלע (Song of Songs II.14). In offerings birds appear to represent a person stripped of all power or position, just enjoying a bare existence, in the קרבן עולה ויורד etc. and on the other hand, representing fresh free life regained and escaped from the bonds of illness and weakness, in קיני זב זבה, ויולדת וציפורי מצורע. Now amongst the birds תור, the turtle dove, is the migrating bird, whose return heralds the Spring (Song of Songs II.12) which, accordingly, borne by its power of flight, designates a free existence even more pithily. Hence in offerings, in contrast to בני יונה, only the older, fully mature birds are allowed. — גוזל is the quite young bird, still requiring the care and protection of its mother, על גוזליו ירחף (Deut. XXXII.11) — So that צפור represents a life, without power or weapons which lives and saves itself by its power of soaring upwards, and moreover, תור וגוזל, the older generation saving and protecting the younger at the same time by its upward flight.

Now translating the meaning of the symbolic procedure into words, the קחה לי עגלה משלשת ועז משלשת ואיל משלש ותור וגוזל would mean: — “Place at My disposal, yourself (or as Patriarch, your descendants in you) three times with your powers of action, three times with your powers of resistance, three times with your powers of property and rights, and with your power of upward flight keeping the older and younger generations alive. ויקח לו את כל אלה he placed all these at His disposal, ויבתר אותם בתוך, and He cut them into pieces through the centre, i.e. in three Abrahamitic generations He broke all their powers of using their energy, all resistance and all rights ואת הצפור לא בתר and only the naked internal power of soaring above the wretchedness did He leave unbroken. But this, at once is clearly nothing other than: “Know well, that thy descendants will be strangers in a land which does not belong to them”, accordingly, people without rights, this is the איל cut into pieces; they will be made into slaves, accordingly their free power of working will be broken, this is the עגלה cut into pieces; they will be maltreated, accordingly they will have to endure without resistance, the עז broken up; but nevertheless they will not sink below the possibility of being redeemed. גרות ,עבדות and ענוי is to be the fate of the Abrahamides, the calf cut up is slavery, the goat broken is mishandling, the ram cut up is the condition of stateless aliens without rights.

The only question which could be asked is why the order in which these three fates are placed differs in the verbal expression from that of the symbolic one. In the verbal explanation they follow the chronological order in which they occurred, ענוי ,עבדות ,גרות. They were aliens, through that they became slaves, and as a result mishandled. But the answer given in symbolic terms came directly to the question posed, and that, of course, assumed an independent ability victoriously to conquer the promised land. This was answered by showing ענוי ,עבדות, and גרות as the fate of the descendants. Not only would they not be able to develop conquering force, but would have to give up even the free disposition of their own activity for ordinary private life, would not only not conquer others, but themselves would have to endure ill-treatment without being able to offer resistance, and so for centuries would be homeless strangers without rights.

ויתן איש בתרו לקראת רעהו, the divided parts were laid down each part opposite its corresponding part so that it was apparent they were waiting to be joined together again, that is why ואת הצפר לא בתר is added there. Just the power to soar upwards remaining unbroken was what was necessary for the hoped-for reunion of these broken powers.

“And then, when the sun had gone down, ana complete darkness had set, lo, it was a smoking furnace and a torch of fire — it had been a refining and an enlightening — which had temporarily kept these pieces apart” (עבר not עובר) — the purification was completed, the enlightening had worked, the broken parts were joined again.

דן אנכי not אדון I will judge, but: I judge it now. The nation that I have appointed for a refining glowing furnace, a melting-pot for your descendants receives herewith the declaration of the fate that will overtake it when its mission ends, in the punishment it so richly deserves.

עלט ,עלטה vielleicht identisch mit לעט, hastig hinunterschlucken. So wie בלע verschlingen und zugleich, כבַלַע את הקדש, dem Auge entziehen heißt, so dürste עלטה den Moment bezeichnen, in welchem die Gegenstände völlig "verschluckt", d. h. völlig unsichtbar geworden sind. Lautverwandt mit חלט, das auch ein unwiederbringliches Entziehen bezeichnet. ויחלטו Kön. I. 20, 33, sie ergriffen rasch das Wort, damit es nicht zurückgenommen werden konnte. So תרגום ,לחלוטין von לצמיתות: was für immer in den Besitz eines andern übergegangen ist.

V. 1.—2. By the plaintive cry: מה תתן לי “What is the use of Your giving me anything. I have no child, etc.” we can see how deeply Abraham felt his childlessness. But we can well understand how this condition must have hurt Sarah most deeply. For was she not, as this verse seems specially to stress, אשת אברם, Abraham’s true wife in every way, taking part in every phase of his life, following him and joining him in the whole trend and mission of his life. If it was a great act on Abraham’s part to tear himself away from his home and relations, it was a no lesser one for Sarah. Abraham did it for God’s sake, Sarah for Abraham’s and together they achieved the high accomplishment עשו) את הנפש אשר עשו, in the plural I.L.) בחרן. But the one thing which he could have expected from his wife — which every husband expects but which with Abraham was doubly important on account of his mission to the world — to have children, that was denied to him. Now she had a slave-girl who was primarily her slave — she was not שפחת אברם but שפחת שרי — and she said to Abraham: ’הנה נא עצרני וגו We have already discussed the finer implications of the word נא in talks between Abraham and Sarah (see on Ch. XII.13 I.L.). “See, in spite of what you always say to the contrary, I know quite well that if we have had no children, the fault lies solely with me — ( אזר ,אסר ,אצר ,עצר, עצרני, holding one’s forces together, restraining, binding etc. Not מנע refusing a wish but: God has kept me back in achieving the purpose for which He has given every woman forces) — ’בא נא וגו even if she herself could not place a baby in Abraham’s lap, she still wanted to give him a child in whom Abraham could have every, and she the greatest possible, share. Abraham was against it. This is evident from the נא. Sarah was only thinking of him, but knew that he would not do it for his own sake, so she says אולי אבנה, perhaps through that I will become “built on”. If he would not be willing to do it for his own sake, perhaps he would do it for hers, because she so ardently wished it.

בנה ,אבנה, in space, is to add stone to stone to create a place in which a person develops his life. בית phonetically related to בית .בגד is an extended garment. Now just as בית is that sphere in space in which human beings consummate their activities, live their lives, so, in Jewish thought expressed in language, there is also a “house” in time, throughout the ages. In this “house” a human being, or a nation or any contemporary generation brings its utility into play. Every generation goes on with the building of this “time-בית״ adding stone to stone on it. Every child is a a stone, a brick, בֵן, brought to it by its parents, by which it adds, by its own individual existence and accomplishments, its own contribution to the continuous building of the edifice. בית אברהם is such a “house in time” which comprises all the succeeding generations, in which all the characteristic special qualities of the Patriarch are deeply impressed and continued in ever richer, more widely spread and fuller diversity. בית ישראל comprises all the generations in which the total complex of the ideal of Israel taken over from its ancestor Israel comes to its realisation. The whole of human history is the continuous work on a great building of which the master-builder is God, and the individual and team-workers — who at the same time are the bricks — are the human beings and generations from age to age. “In His own image, God created Man and from him He has prepared for Himself a building reaching into eternity — והתקין לו ממנו בנין עדי עד״, so runs the deep consecrating speech of our marriage service. Childless parents fall out of the building, one addition goes no further, nothing more is built on it. “Perhaps I shall become built on through her” says Sarah, perhaps through this God will grant me a child. In giving you my own maid, I shall have the right to bring the child up, and even though I can not claim to be the actual physical orginator of the child, I shall still be the nearest possible thing to it, the cause of its existence and the means of its spiritual development. I shall thus fit myself in and become a part of the building of the “house in time”, and in the child and its children I will live on.

וישמע אברם לקול שרי not לקול אשתו, not in so far as she was his wife, not with the intention that Sarah had in eye, for not from a Hagar did he expect the child for his future. He acquiesced in her wish as he saw therein satisfying her personal desire. He did it for her sake, as she did it for his, a relationship that we find repeatedly between Abraham and Sarah, and which are universally to be found where man and woman are true husband and wife together.

V. 3. After ten years waiting in the land of Canaan, accordingly not thoughtlessly and not without sufficient reason לאברם אישָׁהּ, the relations between Abraham and Sarah were not altered in the slightest thereby. Sarah could feel that by making this sacrifice she was more than ever Abraham’s wife. לו לאשה to be his proper wife, the relationship was to be a perfectly pure one. Of course Hagar was still to remain her slave, so that she, Sarah, would alone be in a position to bring the child up in her way. This was the fundamental condition on which the whole purpose of Sarah’s plan depended.
V. 4. וַתֵּקַל most probably the Kal of קלה, of which the Hiphil מקלה means: to make light of, to disregard or slight, so that the Kal would be: to lose value.

V. 5. חמס ,חמסי (related to חמץ) continuous small wrongs (פחות משוה פרוטה which can not be reclaimed in court) (— e.g. if one helps oneself to a single pea out of a sack, the value is too small to make you liable in court, but if continuously done by everyone the owner can be ruined I.L.), small petty needle pricks which disturb one’s life, put one into a “ferment”, continuously disturbing the quiet peaceful atmosphere till it becomes “sour” (חמץ), needle-pricks which do not kill but make one ill. עליך, it rests on you, it must be your fault if Hagar now considers herself superior to me now that she has hopes to become a mother; for it was just for that purpose that I, אנכי, I, myself placed her in your arms. She knows quite well that it was I who brought about the whole matter, and brought it about just with the intention of her becoming a mother. So it must be in your behaviour and conduct that I have lost value in her eyes.
