Just as God made Mila the foundation-stone of His People, just as later in His Torah חק nearly always comes before משפט, first הקים and then משפטים, first those laws that plant and keep the whole of our bodily life of the senses within the limits of purity and holiness, and then those laws which regulate our life with our fellow men, so here, too, it says ושמרו דרך ה׳ לעשות צדקה ומשפט, a pure moral life before God is the preliminary condition and source for a truly just life of righteousness with our fellow-men. Only a generation conceived, born, brought up in the lap of the הקים and continuing therein is made apt and capable to live a life of צדקה ומשפט in the sense which God’s Torah demands. The keeping of the מצות שבין אדם למקום is the preliminary condition and the root of the מצות שבין אדם לחבירו. A generation that is degenerating morally has also no social future.

צדקה ומשפט. We have already recognised that, whereas משפט designates something that a person has the right to demand from another, צדקה — used referring from man to man — designates something which in itself no man has the right to demand from another but which God has given everybody the right, not indeed to demand but to be justified in expecting it. משפט is simply:— justice, צדקה, benevolence but regarded as duty. But whereas, as a rule, משפט is placed before משפט וצדקה ,צדקה, here, characteristically enough, צדקה is in the foreground. First משפט then צדקה, so runs the rule. צדקה can never make good, can never atone for משפט which has been transgressed. To rob or act dishonestly with one hand and to give charity from what had been dishonestly acquired with the other is an abomination to Jewish ideas. Against an offering brought from the product of robbery, God hurls His אני ה׳ אוהב משפט שונא גזל בעולה (Is. LXI.8) “I am God, I love justice, hate robbery in offerings”. One may approach nearer to God only with clean hands. Hence משפט first, then צדקה.

But here צדקה is placed first, for here it is a question of the Jewish protest against the principles of life and the rules of the state in Sodom. Not צדקה ,משפט is the word, the world-redeeming word, which the House of Abraham is to carry in the world and through the world. How far even justice — man-made justice — is from the justice that God teaches is sung by the Jewish singer: “even משפטים, even justice בל ידעום״, (Ps. CXLVII.20), the non-Jewish world has hardly any idea of it. משפט, yes a kind of משפט, rules in Sodom too; yea, Sodom shows us how a pleasure-seeking world, sunk in sensual pleasure, which finally only values a person for the pleasure he can give, and at the end twists the idea of strict justice to a double-edged sophism, and with the maxim שלי שלי שלך שלך, “I keep what is mine, you keep what is yours” stamps being necessitous as a crime, and relieving it as folly and a crime against the public welfare. Under the regime of Sodomite justice, where only achievement but not necessity, is considered as a ground for a claim, poverty and wretchedeness are despised; at most, strangers who are prospective profit-bringing rich men, like Lot, may be admitted, but “begging is prohibited”, and improvident hungry unfortunates are treated as criminals and can only expect “jail and being moved on”. Justice without Zedaka becomes perverted into uncharitableness and harshness. In contrast to this, the “testament” of Abraham to his children stresses צדקה before משפט, more, in certain cases the legal code of the Children of Abraham recognises צדקה as משפט and declares: זה נהנה וזה לא חסר כופין על מדת סדום. And it is the Jewish conception of Zedaka which Abraham is to recommend to his children, not that “charity” which makes the giver proud and humbles the recipient, nor that care for the “lower classes”, which, for the protection of the rich, does not wish to allow the poor to reach the stage of despair and desperation, but that “act of duty” to which every necessitous person is given the right by God to claim, to which the poor can stand upright before the rich, and which makes the rich consider themselves merely as administrators of a treasury which belongs to the poor.

And it is not just absolute צדקה and משפט which will rescue and free the world from crime and misery, but only both in the Jewish sense of being fruit matured on the tree of “living before God”, ושמרו דרך ה׳ לעשות צדקה ומשפט. The whole person must live before God, his whole life must be spent in the idea of duty before God, then his whole behaviour between man and man will only be making the dictates of duty a reality.

But not only by external means, not by enforcement of rules and laws, nor by world upheavals which send the red peril against the palaces and manors of the rich, but only from within, by an inner revolution of mind and feelings, by the production and education of a generation to a sense of duty, can such “men of duty” be gained, who will hand this God-dictated testament of the ancestor to the last descendant as a guiding last will: — ושמרו דרך ה׳ לעשות צדקה ומשפט. The generation must be born and brought up not to a “belief in God”, but to “fulfilling His commands”, otherwise wisdom could well lead to respect for law, and fear to charity, but in the midst of all theoretical “belief in God”, people could degenerate to ’רעים וחטאים לה, and under the pretext of what is right and proper צדקה ומשפט can be so worked that one could well say: “Woe to him that falls into the hands of one who administers charity or who is יושב על המשפט״.

That is why we can understand how, at the time when the foundation stone of the Jewish People was laid with Mila and brotherly love of mankind — the People who were to be educated to לשמר דרך ה׳ לעשות צדקה ומשפט — Abraham, the instrument for such a training of a nation, was told of the judgment of God which, at that same time, was to be exercised on a province of cities, proud in their strength and success, in which the ’דרך ה had been lost in moral degeneracy and צדקה ומשפט transformed to their very opposite.

By this insight into the ways of God’s rule given to the ancestor, the bleak borders of the once luxuriant, blooming acres of Sodom and Gemorrah become reminding memorials for all the descendants of Abraham who are to be trained in דרך ה׳ לעשות צדקה ומשפט which, more than anything else, demonstrate visibly the results of forsaking it.

V. 20. By its context as well as by its construction V.20 is introductory to V.21 and says: Even if that which exists in Sodom and Gomorrah is actually already great and very onerous, still I will go down etc. Here again the same two factors are mentioned. זעקתם, the cry against their inhuman harshness, their sins between man and man, their scorn of all צדקה רעים :ומשפט; and חטאתם, their moral degeneracy, their forsaking דרך: ה׳ הטאים. The cry against their social sins was רבה, widespread, or, according to ר׳ הנינא, ever increasing רבה והולכת, regarding this they were already condemned by mankind. Concerning sexual excesses there is generally no just outcry, it is thought to be no matter for the civil authorities, they can very well simply be due to the general prevailing laxity of morals, at most, a sin against God, they can even become the mode and fashion, are, in any case, excusable, over that there is no great outcry. But before God, כבדה מאוד, they weigh very heavily on the land and its future. Nature itself rises against Sodomite viciousness, and, as the Torah puts it “the ground itself spues forth its degenerate inhabitants”.

So now it says here: Although Nature and mankind already condemn Sodom and Gemorrah, I will nevertheless first examine ’הכצעקתה וגו. According to its being construed with ה and not with אם, as well as according to the accent which would make כלה belong to עשו as its object (— for it is to be questioned whether the פסוק after the Munach in a case like this separates the sense sufficient for it to be considered as a separate sentence, cf. for instance Ch. XIX.14)—) it could be understood as:- whether כצעקתה, they had already achieved destruction i.e. whether their degeneracy had already reached its summit, so that they had thereby prepared themselves for complete destruction. As עשה כלה elsewhere always means achieving destruction it would be highly significant that here the destruction is expressed as the work of the sinners themselves, who are, of course, in fact the actual generators of it. But it is generally taken, guided by the פסיק, that כלה must be taken as an elliptic separate sentence and the ה as conditional, “if” (for which however we can find no analogy), and it would read: “if they have done כצעקתה, destruction (shall come to them). In any case כצעקתה requires explanation. The suffix ה can hardly refer to Sodom and Gemorrah, as the subject of the sentence is immediately put in the plural עשו. It rather seems to refer back to the preceding חטאת or rather צעקה .זעקה is a stronger form of זעקה. That, about which people make an outcry is often only the smallest part of what does cry out to God. The cry which did go to God was still greater than the outcry which people made. According to this urgent cry which went up to God they had already reached the stage of — destruction, but God will still give them a final examination to see if this height of inhumanity had been reached by the whole population and if this is not the case “I will gladly (the optative ה in אדעה I.L.) recognise the individual cases”, will punish the guilty and exempt the others. In the דור המבול also השחתת דרך went hand in hand with חמס. Moral degeneration everywhere begets social degeneration, and there too, just as here, finally it was social sins, צעקה = חמס, that condemned the generation, קץ כל בשר בא לפני כי מלאה הארץ חמס מפניהם.

V. 22. ’עודנו עומד לפני ה, for with all his activity in exercising hospitality Abraham had not gone away from the ’עמידה לפני ה to which he had been called by the “appearance” of God recorded in the first verse.

V. 23.—26. ספה .תספה occurs in similar cases of people, who on their own account would have escaped the misfortune, being caught up in a general calamity which befalls others. Thus David (Sam. I. XXVI.10) reckons up three ways in which Saul could die. (a) God could let him die suddenly; (b) his appointed span of life could be reached; (c) or he goes to war ונספה, there he falls amongst those killed, without already יבוא יומו and without direct, apparent ה׳ יגפנו. Equally so in Numb. XVI.26, סורו וגו׳ פן תספו בכל חטאתם.

Two alternatives were announced to Abraham for the threatened fate of Sodom, כלה: complete destruction, or ידיעה: punishment of the guilty but allowing the whole to continue. As God found him worthy of being given this insight into His verdict, he feels and thinks deeply of the execution of this verdict, and tries to get clear concerning a thought which worries him. Not that he has the slightest doubt that, even if the degree of degeneracy did demand the destruction of the whole district, any innocent person, were it but one in a million, would be saved, and no innocent individual would be punished together with the guilty, even the thought of such a thing, he says in V.25, would be a defamation of God. But he puts himself in the place of such an innocent person to be saved in the midst of the general terrible catastrophe. He feels what he would feel in such a position. He feels how, had he lived in Sodom he would never have failed unceasingly to try to better his fellow-citizens and countrymen, how he would never have given up hope, and how at the fall of every single soul at whose salvation he had worked, and whom he had so hoped to save, he would suffer as at his own death. And now he ventures to express the thought: — whether perhaps the pain which the righteous would have to endure at seeing the terrible destruction of their fellow-citizens all around them might not be worthy of consideration, whether otherwise would it not be a ספות הצדיק עם רשע, making the righteous suffer with the death of the wicked, whether this consideration could not be strong enough that, just למען הצדיקים for the sake of the righteous, to spare them the great mental suffering, God could not grant remission to the whole guilty community?
Everything speaks in favour of this way of taking it. The meaning of תספה and then the להמית and והיה כצדיק כרשע of V.25 which he himself rejects as impossible.

Equally so, the expression למען הצדיקים which makes the righteous not the cause but the purpose of forgiving the whole town. For, while בגלל always expresses the cause, בעבור, mostly the purpose but also sometimes also the cause, למען always the purpose (not on account of but for the sake of I.L.) Abraham thinks of the salvation of all, as a reward for the righteous ones, who, through their compassion for the others would participate in their suffering.

Finally, equally so, both in Abraham’s request and in God’s reply is the marked stress on בתוך העיר. Abraham does not say אולי יש המשים צדיקים בעיר but בתוך העיר, the answer even runs בסדום בתוך העיר. This בתוד העיר seems to be quite in the same sense as בתוך עמי אנכי יושבת (Kings II. IV.13). The idea of a righteous man in the midst of Sodomite depravity which Abraham visualises, for whose sake the city might be saved, is not one who keeps to his own four walls, in haughty pride of his own superiority gives up the masses and just looks on at their ruinous moral lapses, who thinks he has done quite enough if he saves himself and at most his own household. Yea, such a one Abraham would not class as righteous, he would not consider that he had at all fulfilled the duty which lies on every good man in bad surroundings. The ruin of the masses whom he had long given up, would leave such a man cold, he might even possibly feel a certain smug satisfaction in it.

That is not Abraham’s “righteous man” out of consideration of whom the salvation of the city should be effected. His righteous man is to be found בתוך העיר “in the midst of the city” and in lively connection with everything and everybody. He never leaves off admonishing, teaching, warning, bettering wherever and however he can. He takes everybody and everything to heart, he never despairs, is never tired of trying, however distant the hopes of success may be. Those are the righteous ones whom he presumes must be בתוך העיר who would feel grief and pain at the death of each individual of these thousands, as a gardener for the plant for whose survival he had toiled early and late. For fifty of these he dared to hope the whole might be spared.

At the downfall of Jerusalem — so our sages teach — it was just the “righteous ones” who had kept the Torah from א till ת who were first doomed, just because they had not been בתוך העיר and had not occupied themselves with bettering their fellow-citizens (Sabbath 59a. on Ezekiel IX).

ולא תשא למקום, we find מקום used for a whole district, yea for a whole country. Thus ’נוסעים אנחנו אל המקום אשר אמר ה (Numb. X.29). Thus also for a whole country in Numb. XIV.40, and of a district והנה המקום מקום מקנה (Ibid XXXII.1).

V. 26. God answered: If there are still, in a state like Sodom, fifty righteous men who not only publicly live a moral and just life, but who even can stand up for morality, justice and humaneness, then, not only למענם, not only out of consideration of, for the sake of, these righteous ones, but בעבורם through them, because these righteous ones exist and are tolerated, the whole city deserves forgiveness. (in the same sense as בעבור דוד (Ps. CXXXII.10, בעבור טמאה, Micha II.10). Their existence and being tolerated would itself be a proof that the degeneration had not yet reached the lowest depth.

We find it described similarly in ת״כ on בחקתי, that the progressive development of depravity has not yet reached its lowest depth where the God-fearing righteous ones and goodness is only derided. As long as they are tolerated, publicly tolerated, even though mocked at and scoffed, as long as fearing God and goodness are only regarded as folly but no crime evil has not yet reached its worst. The worst has arrived only when one no longer laughs but grinds one’s teeth at the righteous, and practising goodness is forbidden as a crime against the system of public welfare and stopped and punished accordingly, — אינו מניח אחרים לעשות. Thus the sum of the sins of the Amorites was not yet “full’ as long as an Abraham and his household could publicly and unhindered erect there an altar to Truth and Goodness. And Sodom too, only went to ruin when this ultimate depth of depravity had been reached in the valley.

V. 28. et. seq. לא אשחית “I shall not destroy”, not merely the city but altogether, I will not destroy. The gradually increasing demand in Abraham’s requests are difficult to understand, and the change in the terms used in the replies לא אעשה ,לא אשחית ,לא אשחית, also seems strange. Perhaps the following suggestions may throw some light. If our assumption of the nature of the incident is correct, then God’s reply looks on the saving of the town, if fifty righteous men can be found, from a different point of view to that of Abraham’s supposition. Not out of consideration for them and their feelings but on the ground of their existence, of their being there at all. From the former point of view, of course the consideration for the righteous would become less and less the fewer their number happened to be, but that could not be the case from the latter point of view. The fact that a party of righteous men is allowed to exist in a goodless state loses its value as a proof of liberal tolerance with a maximum and minimum size of the party, and only has real meaning at a medium size. If the number of its members is imposing, it is tolerated out of fear. If it is small enough to be neglible, it is tolerated because it is overlooked. Only when it consists of a medium number, where it is neither feared nor overlooked, does its existence, its being tolerated, have its full significance. Above this number and below it its significance lessens. Perhaps Abraham was seeking clarity concerning this condition, and perhaps the change in the expression that we noticed might correspond to it. לא אשחית, I will not destroy, will not bring כלה, but will perhaps interpose My authority otherwise to effect betterment: לא אעשה .אדעה, I will do nothing at all, there are sufficient moral elements amongst the masses so that a betterment from within is still not impossible. Hence with forty-five, twenty and ten, לא אשחית, and only with forty-five and thirty לא אעשה. Perhaps.

It is also possible that the reverse is the case; that לא אעשה בעבור only means that for the sake of the forty or thirty I shall differentiate and act accordingly: אדעה. I will not forgive entirely but will take into consideration the זכות (merit I.L.) which some of the people have gained and those will be saved. Then לא אעשה would be less than לא אשחית, and this would assume a point of view that there would be more merit in allowing the two extremes in numbers to exist and less in the middle numbers.

In any case this insight into His rule which God granted Abraham to obtain has vividly brought to the consciousness of his children the mission, meaning, and importance of such a minority. His children, whose fate it has been to wander for thousands of years in midst of the nations as a minority, and even in their own midst the righteous have been, and are, only too often to be found in a minority.

Had there been in the purlieus of Sodom and Gemorrah, ten righteous men to be found, God would not have despaired of a better future for all, and would have let them all live for this better future. But where God shows us no reason for despair, we too must courageously preserve and play our part, and unremittingly and confident of ultimate success stand up for what is right even if it means being in opposition to the whole of our erring contemporaries, and even if this ultimate victory will only dawn long after we are in our grave.

V. 32.—33. Finally, this dialogue — so to call it — between Abraham and the Judge of the World, in which a creature of dust dares to step before the Presence of God with his feelings of justice and finds agreement and approval is a guarantee of the godliness of that voice within [illegible]] which pleads for the right and for the duty of fidelity of a king.

V. 1 ישב בשער העיר. The gate of a city was not the place where private people sat. Only of kings do we find it said they “sat in the gate” (Sam. II. XIX.9; Jer. XXXVII.7); or of Boas (Ruth IV.1) for the undertaking of a public official procedure. Nor can it mean “he lived in the gate’ for then it would say בחומה as at Rahab (Josh. II.15). It designates, accordingly, as our sages remark, a prominent public position which Lot occupied in the commune.
שער is the Jewish forum. Whereas פתח also designates the smallest opening, שער is always a public entry for many.

(Ähnlich verhält sich שהר zu בקש und דרש. Während בקש ein Objekt suchen, דרש ein Objekt suchen oder einen Zustand erforschen, also beide etwas Unbekanntes, oder etwas suchen bedeuten, von dem man nicht weiß, ob und wo es zu finden ist, heißt שחר aufsuchen eines Gegenstandes, dessen Ort uns sehr wohl bekannt ist, der aber nicht zu uns kommt, sondern den wir an seinem Orte aufsuchen. Daher auch שחר schwarz, die Farbe, die uns die Gegenstände in den Hintergrund treten lässt, so daß wir sie aufsuchen müssen. Der Moment, in welchem wir dies bereits können, aber noch müssen, heißt: שחר; der noch fortgeschrittenere, in welchem die Gegenstände schon von selbst in ihren Umrissen hervortreten: בקר, so wie im Gegensatz ערב die Zeit, in welcher die Gegenstände sich zu mischen beginnen, לול) ליל) in welcher sie bereits in einander geschlungen sind, und endlich אפל (verwandt mit אול) die Finsternis, die alles zweifelhaft lässt und in welcher nichts mehr zu erkennen ist —).

חסר ,ישב, as our sages remark, he had only attained that position just on that day. It must certainly have been something quite extraordinary that in Sodom, where no stranger was tolerated, here a stranger was raised to a superior position. Lot could have felt proud to be in a position today for the first time to be able to oppose the first paragraph of the laws of Sodom not to allow the practice of הכנסת אורחים. Up till now he, as a “clever” man, must have kept quiet, so that he had even been made a judge. Anyway here we see him, as Abraham had pictured a צדיק in Sodom, daring to set an example of something better in the midst of the people.

V. 2. סורו אל: “turn aside from the direction in which you were going, to the house of your servant”. The speech begins with הנה נא אדני, words which we do not find at Abraham’s address to strangers, and which here are characteristicly stressed by the unusual ∵ and הנֶה נא ,דגש expresses the unexpectedness of the invitation. He, whose way lay through Sodom, knew well enough he could find no hospitality there, and had to be quite prepared to spend the night in the street. Lot must have assumed that they had this supposition, and now approaches them with the unexpected. “See, gentlemen, after all there is a nephew of Abraham still here.” For, as such we see him showing himself. Not for nothing had he been taught at Abraham’s home, much, as we have seen, as he had allowed his tendency to be swayed rather too much by material considerations to lead him away from Abraham’s views of life. לון to spend the night, and in the Niphal הלון to grumble. The underlying idea is probably, protection from discomfort, to seek remedies against inconveniences. Hence הלון על to demand redress from somebody for grievances supposedly caused by him, to try to get redress from grievances by blaming somebody else.

V. 3. פצר, to force a way into something to gain something from it, hence פצירה, a file; related to בצר, the grape-harvest. He prepares the meal, he bakes the cakes — how sadly this bleak isolation strikes us in comparison with the cheerful bustle in Abraham’s household when it is a matter of practising the Mitzva of entertaining guests. Here, no wife, no child takes part in the mitzva of the father and husband. Even in his own house he stands alone with that which he had learnt from Abraham.

V. 4. With great circumspection we are told who the people were who gathered about Lot’s house. It was not just a rabble of curious people, they were אנשי העיר, the towns-people, and moreover אנשי סדום, citizens, representative of the state, who came to oppose this “unheard-of attack on the old established laws, customs and privileges of our town”.

Further, it was the young and old, and finally, it was the whole population מקצה, from the extreme ends i.e. the lowest and the highest classes, the common folk and the upper-classes. So that in this flocking together all ages and all classes were represented, and this is significant when we consider their intention and what it meant. The people of Sodom were accused of being רעים וחטאים to the highest degree. This intention of theirs offers the final proof; הוציאם ונדעה אותם Practising hospitality was such a grave crime, that an example was to be made on the strangers who had been invited in, to make it impossible for the recurrence of such an attempt to be made. That showed the inhumanity. And this mishandling was to take the form of the most bestial debauchery. That showed the immorality. Now the susceptibility to these extremes of evil is different according to age and class. Youth, which generally is susceptible to sexual excess, as a rule has a humane, feeling heart which revolts against cruel mishandling of people. The so-called lower classes may well be inclined to low, coarse gross sexual immorality, but, being themselves oppressed, generally are on the side of other persecuted people and revolt against the mishandling of helpless unfortunates. The reverse is the case with the aged. They certainly have become hardened by the toll of the experiences of their lives, but, having “sown their wild oats” will not tolerate in the youth excesses which possibly they themselves indulged in in their own youth. And again, in the so-called higher classes, though indeed, by their position, they may become hard and without feelings for the suffering and mishandling of the “lower classes”, if not out of regards for morality, still out of feelings for decency and respecatbility, they would put a stop to public coarse scandals of immorality. So that had not evil been so all-prevalent in every way throughout Sodom, the carrying out of such a project in the midst of the population representing all ages and all classes would have remained an impossibility. Against the inhumanity the youth would have combined with the “common people”, and for upholding public decency the older people would have joined the upper classes. But here old and young, high and low were all unanimously joined to practice inhumanity and immorality, and that clinched the sentence of death over the “men of Sodom”.

נער, Grundbegriff Abschütteln, נוער כפיו מתמוך בשוחד (Jes. 33, 15). Dann: die Jugend, an welcher die Eindrücke noch nicht lange haften bleiben, die alles leicht noch abschüttelt. Dagegen זקן, vielleicht verwandt mit סכן, dessen Bedeutungen: סכן pflegen, סכנה Gefahr, מסכנות Dürftigkeit, auf die Grundbedeutung: für äußere Eindrücke empfindlich und empfänglich sein, hinweisen, daher sehr bezeichnend für: Krankenpflege, auf die schädlichen Einflüsse achten, die den Kranken treffen könnten, sie für den Kranken gleichsam auffangen und dadurch von ihm abwehren. Daher auch הַסכן etwas mit anhaltender hingebender Achtsamkeit tun. Daher denn זקן: der viel Erfahrene. Verwandt vielleicht auch mit זין: der Gerüstete.
דלת, Wurzel דלה schöpfen, die Türe schöpft ein und aus (s. Kap. 6, V. 10).

V. 8. צל, shadow, from צלל. The basic conception is to be inaccessible to external impressions, hence צל, shade, where entry of the rays of light is hindered. צלל deafness, where the vibrations of sound do not penetrate the ear; from which we also get צלצלים deafening instruments. צלל to sink into the depths where neither sound nor light penetrates; finally also צללו שערים the gate being shut by which entry is barred.

קרתי from קרה to hit upon, to meet by chance, related to קרא to call, (וקרהו אסון Gen. XLII.38; את אשר יקרא אתכם, ibid XLIX.1., et. alia). To call, means to cause somebody to set himself, mentally or actually, towards us. That which calls to us, brings us out of the direction in which, left to ourselves, we are taking, into the direction which emanates from the call. That which occurs and we call chance is something we did not reckon on, did not lie in what we thought was our direction, and as it did happen it “calls” to us, it alters the direction which we had hitherto decided on. What we call chance is only “by chance” to us, seems accidental to us because we had not reckoned on it. But that does not exclude the possibility of its being the result of the very highest calculation, perhaps the more so the less it lay in our reckoning. Jewish thought as expressed in its language, accordingly does not speak of chance occurring to us, but of us occuring to it, it “calls” us to it קרא ,קרה. Therefrom, finally, concretely too, קרה the rafters of a house, the roof that brings and keeps the perpendicular boards of the walls in their respective upright position, “calls” זו לקראת זו, and prevents them from going in their natural direction and falling down.
כי על כן באו וגו׳, for I am asking this (not as an act of benevolence on your part) but only therefore because once I have asked them in they are under my protection. Do it for my sake.

V. 9. גש הלאה. “Push up closer!” (lit. approach beyond I.L.), they said to each other. עתה, now that you even defend your action, you are more punishable than they are, a greater danger to us than they are. באיש בלוט. Lot resisted them with all his manly strength. They pushed strongly against him, he opposed them like a man.
V. 11. סנורים, perhaps composed from סנה thorn and אור light.

V. 12. עוד מי לך פה: what others have you still got here, besides the members of your household here whom we already know? — חתן. Just as in our language, the way and manner in which husband and wife, father and mother, son and daughter, brother and sister, are expressed, tell us the conception and meaning of these near family relationships, so is it extremely precise in the designation of the family bonds brought about by marriage. Nothing could confirm the fact that the words of our language are based on underlying ideas, more than the conception of parents-in-law being given quite different words when it refers to a son-in-law or a daughter-in-law. Referring to a son-in-law they are called חותן ,חותנת, and he, חָתָן but a daughter-in-law is called כלה and the parents-in-law חמיה ,וחמותה. A daughter-in-law is a much more intimate member of their household than a son-in-law. With her husband she enters into and becomes one of the members of her husband’s parents’ household, they become her “encircling walls”, and she becomes the “completion”, the “crown”, the “wreath”, the latest ornament which the home obtains. The son-in-law, who, as a son, only extends the home of his parents, is only joined to his parents-in-law by, what is of course the dearest bond, their daughter. This connection is not the merging of the one with the other, but is the mutual bond joining them together which affects the son-in-law and parents-in-law equally. They are accordingly joined together in the same relationships which חתן expresses, they become חותן ,חתן and חוחנת to one another, a word which altogether expresses the connection of families by marriage, the “in-laws”. A connection which, if we consider the root חתן in its phonetic relationship to עטן, fine threads, and to עדן, delight, perhaps even delightful connection — התקשר מעדנות כימה (Job. XXXVIII.31) — would express such a connection which refers to the highest mutual satisfaction and presupposes the most intimate harmony between the families in their attitude to life and their aims in life.

But it is deeply significant that our language has no special word for the relationship of a bride and bridegroom to each other. It only knows husband and wife. While, on the one hand, the relation of a bride and bridegroom to each other is recognised as being the most intimate and lofty — one need only think of phrases like ומשוש חתן על כלה etc. (Is. LXII.5), on the other hand it still has no other description for the relationship than again חתן and כלה, son-in-law, daughter-in-law. Thereby it seems to see the deep basis for this most intimate and passionate affection having its roots not so much in what they are at the time to each other as in what they are and remain to their mutual parents. The Jewish bridegroom loves his bride the “כלה״ so dearly first of all, because in her he is bringing his parental home a worthy beloved daughter, the “crown” of the parental home. The Jewish bride loves her bridegroom, the חתן, so dearly first of all because she finds in him the spirit of her parental home, and knows the satisfaction which her parents have with his outlook on life and his aims. So that it is on the parents, on the harmonious agreement between the two families, on which the rock-like foundation of the union of their children rests, and which is their guarantee that they will find their own loving life repeated in that of their children. Now we shall see what this relationship was in the house of Lot in a city like Sodom. The angels mention sons-in-law, sons and daughters, as those — apart from the immediate household — “still in the city” belonging to Lot. They accordingly reckon daughters-in-law included as daughters.

V. 13. It is significant that in this whole story God is called by the name ה׳, — God in His care for the future of mankind — as the One Who is bringing destruction to Sodom. To such depth of depravity, complete annihilation itself is an act of merciful love.

V. 14. Then the poor old man goes out in the night to his sons-in-law, to the men to whom he has entrusted his daughters, implores them to save them and themselves — and they just laugh at him as a joker. Not for nothing does it add לקחי בנותיו as an amendment to חתניו. They had married his daughters, but his “sons-in-law”, in the pure sense of the word “חתניו״ they had not become. For were they not men of Sodom, and in their outlook on life and aims, there could be no “mutual bond” between them and Abraham’s nephew. For him there could be no real חתן to be found in Sodom, and for his daughters, had he understood how to bring his children up for himself and his outlook on life, no husbands in Sodom. But, as already indicated in V.3, although he himself subscribed to better tendencies, and even had the courage to stand up against the whole community for the right, at great personal risk, nevertheless, in his own household, and towards his own children, he was evidently weak, and in consequence, lonely and isolated. An Abraham would never have satisfied himself with getting לקחי בנותיו who could not become חתניו; Abraham’s daughters would never have married men who could not have harmonised with the spirit of their parental home. Here we see a shortcoming which, still, thousands of years later, repeats itself in a similar way in similar circumstances, and takes its revenge in a similar manner — when he came to his sons-in-law and spoke to them of God, they simply laughed at him. And apparently he expected more consideration and attention from his sons-in-law than he did from his own sons. For he made the attempt to convince them at his sons-in-law first, and when he found that they only laughed at him and would pay no attention to his warning, he gave it all up and did not even make an attempt to get his sons to listen to him. To all this, unfortunately, our present days offer a sad commentary.
V. 15. קח, be satisfied with the members of your family whom you have here in your house; if you linger making further attempts, the oncoming catastrophe might overcome you also.

V. 16.—17. ויתמהמה, from the root מהה from which מה is derived, “what” the undecided. התמהמה, really to tarry in indecision. It is after all not so easy to abandon children and grandchildren to destruction.

חמל ,בחמלת ה׳, related to אמל ,עמל, a painful emotion, designates as a rule, undeserved mercy, or at any rate such mercy which only arises out of compassion. Lot, too, hardly deserved being saved. Even if he had been born in Sodom he ought to have gone away from there long ago, but, as it was, the material advantages and luxury of the place so attracted and held him, that of his own free will, he risked corruption. He got his punishment too. All the wealth he had brought with him, and all the comfort and luxury that had attracted him to settle there, he had to leave behind him. He had not simply to go away, but to flee form the precincts of the town, danger and death was hard behind him. He was not to look back, that which he was leaving he should never have had; and it was not just now that he was losing his children, he had consigned them to destruction at the moment when “to ensure their well-being” he had married his daughters to men of Sodom, and let his sons grow up as citizens of Sodom, and allowed his relation to his children to become of such a nature that in the hour of danger, he dared not even speak to them without being laughed at and ridiculed.

V. 19. I do not deserve even to be saved at all, and that you save my life is already a great favour on your part, but if it is only to be achieved by unbroken flight right into the mountains, the journey itself will kill me.

V. 20. He repeatedly dwells on the fact that the city is מצער. The word, by its form, is not an adjective but a noun. Not: “it is small”, but, “it is a petty thing”,tiny, of little importance, offering no wealth or comfort. By the prohibition to look back Lot recognised that the loss of all his possessions had been deliberately imposed upon him, it was intended that he should escape with his bare life and leave everything behind him. But he thinks that this city offers so little, is such a mean little place, that if I am allowed to stay there, after the luxury of Sodom, it can still be considered that my life, and my life only, has been saved.

V. 24. מאת ה׳ מן השמים. After it has said וה׳ המטיר וגו׳ this seems completely superfluous. But this repeated addition is of the greatest significance. People who visit the region of the Dead Sea and see the sulphur wells and the whole volcanic nature of the district, explain the destruction of these cities as a completely natural occurrence. The volcanic nature of the district explains the foundation of the Dead Sea. The causes are quite natural and earthly and need not be referred specially to God and heaven. Against this erroneous view the Word of God proclaims מאת ה׳ מן השמים “It was from God, from the heaven” that it came. You are confusing cause and effect. What you take to be cause is in reality effect. The present geological nature by which you explain the catastrophe is only the effect of the catastrophe which was not brought about by terrestial conditions but by God from heaven. Probably in quite a similar manner the geological theories err as to the creation of the world. The facts of what they see and on which they base their theories are true enough but the deductions which they make from them are false. They quite similarly, confuse cause and effect. What they view as the causes of the evolution and revolutions of the world are only the results of revolutions which God brought about for the formation of the world.
V. 26. As she stood still she was overtaken by the form of death which was following close behind them.

V. 29. Whereas in the whole story God is called ה׳ here His name is given as Judge. Looked at towards Lot the salvation was an act of mercy, while towards Abraham the salvation was as much an act of justice as the destruction of Sodom, as Abraham had just looked on it, which saves the guilty for the sake of the righteous who are near to them, to save the righteous from suffering on account of the punishment meted out to the guilty.

V. 31. et seq. In this story ונחיה מאבינו זרע is repeatedly stressed as the motive of the procedure and in passing judgment on it may not be left out of consideration. The daughters erroneously supposed they were the only human beings left alive on earth. With the death of their father — which must occur in the not-too-distant future — they saw themselves alone in the world; this fear, and the thought of the only one possibility of the continuance of the human race, drove them to committing the crime. Their motive was a moral one, and they thought that, not only were they doing no wrong, but actually to be doing right. Our sages (Horioth X.2) take the dot over ובקומה to be meant to indicate that he, Lot, was not quite so innocent and blameless in the matter, and ב״ר on this verse finds therein a reason for the later law: עמוני, ולא עמונית, מואבי, ולא מואבית.

V. 37.—38. These are the ancestors of the present-day Moabites and Ammonites. It is not the case of the inhabitants of the land changing and taking on the names of the previous inhabitants as has occurred in so many cases, but the present-day Moabites and Ammonites are the descendants of these sons of Lot.

V. 1. The reason for both these moves must be found. We have seen how Abraham considered it his duty at first to isolate himself and his household away from intercourse with towns, and therefore had chosen the inhospitable region of the south as his earliest place of settlement. Only gradually did he enter into the region of cities, and finally had lived for a long time in a most friendly and most highly respected position under his congenial allies Aner, Eshcol and Mamre. Now, in his declining years, we see him moving again to the south. He settled between Kadesh and Shur, in the loneliest part of the least frequented region, near to the desert of Shur, known as the most desolated waste, and at the same time sought to have connection with city life, and tarried temporarily in Gerar, the capital and residential place of the King of the Philistines.

Unless we are totally mistaken we would venture to say that it was the approaching expectation of the birth of a son which caused Abraham and Sarah to make this peculiar alteration in their place of residence. An Isaac should grow up again in isolation, away from every pernicious influence. But complete isolation where the youth never comes into contact with other people, other thoughts, people living different lives and aims, is an equally dangerous fault in education. A young man who has never seen any other way of life than that of his parents, who has never learnt to value, respect, and hold fast to that life by its moral contrast to others, surely falls readily under these strange influences as soon as he meets them, just as the anxious shutting out of all fresh air is the surest way of catching cold the first time one goes out. The son of Abraham, the future continuer of the heritage of Abraham is, from time to time, to go into the non-Abrahamitic world, there to learn to estimate what is in opposition to it, and to steel himself by practice, in the midst of a world opposed to the spirit and way of life of Abraham, to keep himself faithful and true to his mission. For that purpose Abraham chose the residential city of a Philistine prince. In the land of the Philistines the degeneration seems not to have reached the depth of their Amorite neighbours, and therefore they had not been included in the destruction.

V. 2. As here we see Abraham, in spite of his previous experience, and, later on his son Isaac too, deciding to resort to the same device, we must take it that the manners of the time made it imperative. As we have already remarked above, unmarried virgins must have been much safer amongst the people than married women (a state of affairs which unfortunately is not unknown in our so-called cultured society, where men think twice before seducing an innocent virgin, but have no such compunction for married women I.L.). It seems to have been only princes that just unmarried strangers had reason to fear. And actually it was again only a king that dared to take her, and who later on has no scruples in admitting it.

V. 3. חלום: its relationship, on the one hand, with אלם ,הלם ,עלם, giving the idea of something undeveloped, forced, bound, and the same word being חלמות, yolks of eggs and חלם the process of healing, has given us the Jewish conception of dreams. It is the condition which is described in Job. XXIII.15 “in dreams, in visions of the night, when men fall into a state of unconsciousness, asleep on their couches, then He opens mens’ ears, and impresses His seal upon their fettered state, removes activity from men, and deprives men of their bodies”. Freedom of will is bound, fettered, body and mind obey unusual laws; as in the yolk, all the germs for the future of the organism are there and swim about in unformed confusion because the נפש, that spark of independent individuality is missing, thoughts and the germs of ideas weave together in confusion, they join one to the other by the laws of affinity and chance contact because the conscious human intellegence does not hold the guiding reins. Every חלום is a הלמות a return of the psyche, the mind to the embryonic state. This state in which thoughts and ideas come, not so much from the mind as to the minds, is used occasionally by God as a means of communication, information and advice to men “uncovers the ears of men and impress His seal on their fettered state”. In a dream sent by Him, God is the forming intelligence.

הנך מת: thou wilt die; one has no right to take anything that is not one’s own, least of all a woman. Not even if you are a King, and even if it is the accepted custom, that does not make it moral, and, added to that, she is בעלת בעל, another has already the right to her.

בעל, related to בהל and פעל, the underlying conception: overwhelming, overpowering, overcoming, נבהל, overcome mentally, to be taken aback etc., פעל the highest degree of ascendency of one over another, to make, to produce. Whereas אדון, from אדן, the base, the foot of a pillar, expresses the relation of a lord as being the bearer, the protection and representative of the other; איש ואשה the relation of parity (which is why our sages already point with pride to the moral nobility of our language, which is the only one which has man and woman in their complete equality of birth and rank), בעל designates the relation of lordship as being of overwhelming power. Hence the characteristic verse in Hosea II.18 תקראי אישי ולא תקראי לי עוד בעלי, in thy relation to God thou art not to feel thyself thrown down, but raised up to be godlike like unto Him.

V. 4. הגוי גם צדיק תהרג, wouldst thou then also destroy a righteous nation? Of course Thou hast just passed sentence of death over Sodom (in ב״ר too, the fear of Abimelech and his court expressed in V.8, is referred to the fate of Sodom, “they still saw the smoke going up from the ruins of Sodom and feared a similar fate”) there too, the treatment of strangers and sexual sins were the immediate cause. But in Sodom it was atrocious inhumanity and bestiality in sexual life. Compared to this, Philistia, where Abraham and Sarah found undisturbed residence, and where that which Abimelech intended doing to Sarah may perhaps even have been considered as a marriage, could, in truth be called a גוי צדיק.

V. 5. בתם לבבי with the complete agreement of my mind did I do what I did, I did not have, and there was no occasion for me to have, the slightest scruples about it. לבב the centre point of the organism where all the threads and lives of the physical, spiritual, mental and moral life join, and from where they develop. לבב designates the entire inner self; לב, the more definite will, decision etc. Here בתם לבבי etc. says: I found nothing at all wrong in what I did, I could take the step I did with the full concurrence of my conscience, without any part of my inner self registering the slightest protest. From this one can deduce that, according to the accepted customs of the time, the King was free to take any unmarried girl or woman he pleased. Of course he added בנקיון כפי, but although God conceded him the תום לבב in V.6 the נקי כפים is missing there.
We have two expressions for the hand, יד and כף and similarly two for purity: טהר and נקי.

יד is the open active hand. כף from כפף: the closed hand holding what it has seized. טהר, related to זהר .צהר (צהרים in Chaldean טיהרא) inner purity, really the transparent, allowing the rays of light to enter, i.e. receptive to the godly and pure. נקי (from נקה related to נכה ,נגח ,נגע, all meaning an external touching); designates external purity, cleanliness, used referring to morals, having no external faults, no illegal possessions, no wrongful deed. Hence the legal concept נקי. In Jewish Law no attention is paid to antecedents or general character, the only thing to be considered are the actual facts of the case before the court. The accused may be נקי therein although in general a rascal, and the reverse holds good too.

At יד, deeds, mere external legality of an act is not sufficient, the intention, the motive, must also be honest, hence טהור ידים not נקי ידים. But with כף, at what you hold, what you possess, the external legality is more to the fore, hence not טהור כפים but נקי כפים.

Abimelech thinks — and so many people think with him — that because he acted בתום לבבו he was also נקי כפים, as if the real value of a deed depended entirely on the good intention in which it was done. But that is not the truth in the Jewish idea. There is a standard by which to measure the moral worth of our action quite apart from the intention, and that is: — to what extent does the deed itself, looked on quite objectively, comply with the Will of God. הגיד לך אדם מה טוב, this compliance with His revealed Will is the first consideration. A bad deed, i.e. one which is displeasing to God, does not become a good one just because the intention was innocent. More, the supposedly innocent intention at a bad deed, the תום לבב can even be a sin in itself. אומר מותר (thinking an act is allowed I.L.) can just as well be קרוב למזיד, for היה לו ללמוד ולא למד everybody has the duty of getting instructed in the demands God has made on the moral nature of our actions. If it is true that לא עם הארץ הסיד, that one uninstructed in the Divine teachings of morality can hardly become a morally perfected man, then to be, and remain, an עם הארץ in these matters is itself a sin — as our sages work out this theme (Makkoth 9a) just on Abimelech’s behaviour. Abimelech too seeks to find his complete justification in היא אמרה לי ,הוא אמר לי, in that which Abraham and Sarah had told him, but forgets to enquire what, even in those circumstances, God would say to it. For even if she had been his unmarried sister, must then every unmarried woman who puts her foot into the territory of a foreign prince, without any further ado stand at the disposition of the lust of that prince? And if custom does authorise such immorality, is it not up to just the princes, who are to set the example, to raise the customs to be such that are only intrinsically moral?

חשך, verwandt mit אזק, עזק, חזק, festhalten, umzäunen, fesseln, ebenso חשק, eigentlich umreifen. מחטו לי nicht mit א. Wir finden einigemal den Begriff חטא in der ל"ה-Form. So Kohelet 8, 12 u. 9, 18. Jesaias 65, 20: אחוטֶא. Ebenso Bereschit 31, 39 אְַחַטֶנָה. Wir haben einige Wurzeln, bei denen ל"א und ל"ה in einander spielen, und zwar erscheint da ל"ה in stärkerer Bedeutung. 3. B. מצא finden, מצה ganz in sich aufnehmen. קרא zu sich rufen, קרה etwas durch Balken mit einander verbinden. Möglich daher, daß hier das א zur Verstärkung des Ausdrucks ausgelassen ist, gerade weil Abimelech die Sache so leicht genommen. Du hast es mir zu verdanken, daß es beim bloßen Leichtsinn geblieben und nicht zu einem ernsten Verbrechen geworden, denn es wäre mir, לי, eine schwere Sünde gewesen. Du nennst dich und dein Volk גוי צדיק, so lange solche Vorgänge bei euch durch Sitte geheiligt sind, seid ihr weit entfernt צדיקים zu sein. — לנגע אליה, nicht nur nicht לנגע בה, sondern nicht einmal אליה.

V. 7. The train of thought in this verse is difficult: Give the wife of the man back for he is a prophet. How would it be if he had been a beggar? Surely this is not meant to be the reason for the duty of restoring the wife to her husband. Hence our sages in Baba kama 93a:—ת״ר כל אלו שאמרו דמי בשתו אבל דמי צערו אפילו הביא כל אילי נביות שבעולם אין נמחל לו עד שיבקש ממנו שנא׳ השב אשת האיש כי נביא הוא ויתפלל בעדך. דאשת נביא בעי אהדורי אשת אחר לא בעי אהדורי. אמר ר׳ שמואל נחמני אמר ר׳ יונתן השב אשת האיש מכל מקום ודקאמרת הגוי גם צדיק תהרוג הלא הוא אמר לי אחותי היא והיא אמרה אחי הוא נביא הוא וכבר למד (במכות ט׳ גרס ממך למד) אכסנאי שבא לעיר על עסקי אבילה ושתיה שואלים אותו או על עסקי אשתו שואלים אותו אשתך היא אחותך היא. מכאן לבן נח שנהרג שהיה לו ללמוד ולא למד.

If we understand this passage correctly, our sages see in the השב אשת איש the duty of doing something more than simply letting the woman go; and actually, as it does not say הוציא את האשה or השב את האשה but השב אשת האיש, the demand is implied to make good the wrong done to Abraham, and indeed conciliate him to such an extent that he will pray for you. But this assumes that Abimelech alone and not Abraham was in the wrong, and Abimelech’s protest against Abraham’s and Sarah’s assertion was completely valueless. He is a נביא, and accordingly judges conditions and the behaviour of people not in accordance with the views which arise from the customs and opinions of any particular age or country but in accordance with the eternal unchangeable Law of Morality. It may be that custom here has authorised immorality so that a foreign woman has to give herself up in any case, if married to the people, if unmarried to the pleasure of the prince, and instead of hospitably enquiring about the requirements of a stranger, your first question is; is she your wife, is she your sister? But he not only knows of a different “right of strangers”, but has already taught it by his well-known hospitality. He was forced (according to the version in Makkoth ממך למד) by the ruling immoral custom prevailing here with you, to disown his wife in order to ensure protection for her and for himself from assault at least from the people.

נביא from נבא (related to נבע, to spring, flow forth or well forth), the source from which the word of God issues, the organ through which the spirit of God speaks to men. The form of the word is accordingly also passive. The word itself by which our language designates prophets is, accordingly, already in itself the most definite protest against all which in general is attributed to prophets and prophecy. נביא is not pro-phet, prediction, not one who foretells, but essentially the organ of God. In circles where they play a deceptive game with the concepts of prophecy and revelation, poets and rapture are elevated to prophets and prophecy so as then to relegate prophets and phophecy to poetry and rapture, and to allow נבואה to be nothing more than a product of the human mind. Our prophet is a נביא, a vessel and an organ through which the spirit of God and the word of God reaches mankind, not from within himself, but to him does God speak, וידבר ה׳ אל משה לאמר for him to convey His Word further: לאמר.

But this word of God to Abimelech is of the highest importance for all future times. It is the first time that God brought the meaning and importance of Abraham directly to the consciousness of the strangers amongst whom he stayed. For Abimelech and his people formed the circle in whose midst Isaac was to be born and spend the greater part of his life, and indeed they were to be the permanent direct neighbours of the future People of Abraham. This occurrence was the warning cry to them: תגעו במשיחי ובנביאי אל תרעו אל!

ויתפלל בעדך, from פלל to judge, related to בלל. As we had recognised at the event of the division of languages, בלל does not mean confusion, mixing together and mixing up materials which are there in order, but bringing a fresh element into a mass, incorporating it in all parts of the mass and so forming a new material of the mass. But, according to the Jewish conception that is the business of a judge. Lies and wrong create opposing quarrels, they cause disunion. The judge brings justice and right, the Divine Truth of matters into the matter, makes it go into, and penetrate all phases of the dispute and by true justice brings about a harmonious unity into that which without it was clamouring dissention. Doing this to oneself is called התפלל .התפלל means: To take the element of God’s Truth, make it penetrate all phases and conditions of our being and our life, and thereby gain for ourselves the harmonious even tenor of our whole existence in God. Jewish תפלה is, accordingly, the most complete contrast to what is generally called “prayer”. It is not an outflowing from within, an expression of that with which the heart is already filled, for that we have other expressions, שיח ,תחינה etc. but it is a renewed intake and penetration of truth which come from outside. If our prayers were not תפלה, if our praying were not התפלל, working on our inner self to bring it on the heights of recognition of the Truth, and to resolutions for serving God, there would be no sense in having fixed times and prescribed forms for them. For this assumes that periodically at fixed times the masses of a community are always filled with one and the same state of feelings, one and the same trend of thoughts. Yea, such prayers would be rather superfluous. Feelings and thoughts which are already lively within us have no need first to be expressed, and least of all in set phrases placed in our hands. When the heart is full it can always find its own way to express itself, or it can be so full, that words, mere words, mean nothing, and inarticulate silence is the only expression of such depths of feeling. Hence our prescribed prayers are not facts, truths, which they assume we are already fully conscious of, but are such that they wish to awaken, reanimate and keep ever afresh in us. One can truly say that the less we feel inclined to prayers, the greater is the necessity for saying them, the greater the importance, the greater the effect on us, of the work which we have to accomplish on ourselves by תפלה. The lack of the inclination for it is itself the clearest sign of the clouding over and darkening of that spirit and that recognition of the great Truth which תפלה does not assume us to have, but which it is rather to create, animate and set right in us.

Here we see the efficacy of praying for other people vouched for by God Himself. This efficacy seems rooted in the same idea which we encountered already in Abraham’s prayer for Sodom. If the one who prays is a צדיק or better still, a community, who, in the lovely expression משתתף בצערו של חברו, identify themselves with the troubles of others, make their troubles their own worry, then God promises the possibility that, for their sake, to save them from pain, the trouble can be removed from one, who otherwise is perhaps unworthy of being relieved. And especially here גם ענוש לצדיק לא טוב. It hurts good people, it hurts an Abraham bitterly, if, however much they deserve it, other people get punished on their account.
V. 9.—10. At first Abimelech forgets himself and instead of excuses makes reproaches, but with V.10 he comes round and asks for an explanation.

V. 11. You had done nothing bad to me. I had had no special bad experience here which led to my behaviour. There is nothing missing here, you have the same laws and rules and order as everywhere else. Only, I could not assume that here, more than everywhere else, the fear of God prevails, the fear of God which forbids me voluntarily to expose my wife to dishonour, and which should forbid you to touch the wife of a stranger, or to kill him, should he dare to offer resistance to your immoral customs. This רק is only to be taken as having reference to the universal lack of the fear of God so that no special reproach is to be taken as being made in Abimelech’s country, but not that such a lack of the fear of God in itself could be considered by Abraham’s words as something trifling and insignificant.

V. 12. She was my foster-sister before she became my wife. In spirit she is my sister, the daughter of a brother who died early and she grew up with me under the same paternal roof and because we thus became in mind and feelings so sympathetic to each other, she was like a sister to me, and we married. For, according to our sages Sarah was identical with Iscah (the sister of Lot I.L.) the daughter of Haran who died early, and whose children, according to Ch. 11,31, seem to have lived with their grandfather Terah.

V. 13. According to another way of taking it, more in accordance with the plural used and with the term התעו: when then the gods, i.e. the universal idolatry banished me from my father’s home to wander about in the world, which perhaps means, as I had to wander forth from my paternal home as an apostate to the creed of the people; I was not tolerated, being a תועה מדרכי אלילים. Perhaps also, through his known opposition to heathenism it was more dangerous for him than for anybody else not to acquiesce in any objectionable custom sanctified by heathenism and this made it more imperative for him to impose this rule.
The known ritual of the cult of the Phoenician Astarte taken to gether with the demands of the men of Sodom make such an assumption not too monstrous.

תעה identical with טעה (related to תהה from which we get תהו, that which offers no clear presentation; in rabbinic Hebrew תהה to be astonished, similarly an unclearness of idea; and used for feelings, to regret, to be uneasy in your feeling about something). Phonetically related to דחה to push, to “push off”, to wander off haphazardly, from a safe, firm position.

V. 16. That I, the King who only attempted to get near to you, atoned so publicly for the attempt, and exerted myself so magnificently for reconciliation, that will cause such blinkers to be placed over the eyes of all my people that no one will dare to give an improper glance at you. So that henceforth there will be no necessity for you to deny your true relationship to Abraham and you can hold your head up before everybody just as his wife.

V. 1. פקד, as already mentioned, related to בגד, is mentally to clothe an object with its attributes; its conditions and relationship. Hence also, actually, to set somebody in some particular relationship, to place somebody in a new position, to invest him, as we say similarly in English, with an office, with full authority etc. Spoken of God’s providential care, as here, it designates His special intervention for the appropriate arrangement of conditions for a person or a nation. כאשר אמר, see on Ch. 1,22. The special promise for Sarah is what was said above in Ch. 17,15 et. seq. (refer to it). With the אמירה the פקידה was already achieved and Sarah “invested” with the ability for motherhood. Now, by the birth of Isaac, God fulfilled אשר דבר that which He had pronounced as something to be realised at a future date.

V. 2. בן לזקניו. Inasmuch as Sarah repeated כי ילדתי בן לזקניו in the words with which she expressed the enthusiastic feelings of a happy mother and the whole depth of the significance of this joy (V.7), the term can hardly be taken merely in the sense that Abraham had a son born to him in his old age. There is a similar expression in Ch. 37,3, referring to Joseph: וישראל אהב את יוסף מכל בניו כי בן זקנים הוא לו, and there too, it can not very well be taken in that sense. Joseph was hardly seven years younger than Reuben, and not more than about one or two years than the sons who had preceded him. In ב״ר both places are explained as meaning: מלמד שהיה זיו איקונין שלו דומה לו literally: the radiance of the child’s face was the same as that of his father. At Joseph another way of taking it is given as: שכל הלכות שמסרו שם ועבר מסרן לו all the traditions which Jacob had received he handed on to him. זקנים are the years in which thoughts of the no longer distant day of departure from this world come to a man. He therefore yearns for that younger branch to whom he can bequeath all the spiritual acquisitions of his life, who can take his place, and in whom he can spiritually go on living. The child who shows promise of becoming such a spiritual replica of the old man drawing near to his death, whom the father could bring up for such a purpose, is called בן לזקניו. Such a child was Isaac according to all he was destined for, and that he showed promise of becoming so, the words of our sages seem to think, shone already in the baby countenance of the little creature in whom the delighted mother saw a tiny reproduction of Abraham.

V. 3. הנולד לו אשר ילדה לו שרה, referring to both facts:— that to him, at the advanced age of a hundred years, still a son was born, and that Sarah at ninety years, still, and only then, became a mother, and especially having regard to all that was dependent on it, the birth of this child was צחק, something, according to ordinary natural conditions, rather laughable (see above on Ch. 17,17). So, when Abraham called his son יצחק these facts were vividly in his mind.

V. 6. יׅצַחַק, sounds like a combination of the Kal and Piel. צׅחק Kal, is the natural, involuntary laughter which we can hardly keep back at the sight of some absurdity. צַחֵק in the Piel is the intentional mocking laughter which jeers at the incongruity between the intention and the act, between the desire and the accomplishment. It is quite possible that already here this ironic phase of laughter is included. For the world knew the “pretension” with which these two individuals dared to swim against the tide of the times, yea, the hopes they were bold enough to entertain of ultimately stemming this mighty stream and turning it into another direction. And now to graft this pretentious idea, in itself so absurd, on a late-born tender sapling, how utterly absurd! one push and the whole hope is for ever buried, at its very inception. Can we take it amiss if the contemporary people at the cradle of the Jewish nation could not refrain from a mocking smile, when, to those who do not ponder on and realise the effect which Judaism has had on the world in the course of the ages the world-historic pretensions of the world-historic Jewish nation are still to day, a mockery. This condition and position in the world is pointed out to us from the very beginning — the first Jewish “son of Abraham” was called יצחק, and so will be continued to be called until the hopes founded on God’s promise and on His Management of the world will become a reality, and then אז ימלא שחוק פינו, then the laugh will be on our mouth — does not the word יצחק itself mean: he will laugh — and this laughter will be no צחוק but it will be the gentle smile of happiness — שחוק.

V. 7. מלל, a word that does not occur often. It really means, to pluck off, וקטפת מלילות. Whereas דבר (being related to תפר ,טור ,תור ,דור, all of which refer to a joining together of several components to form one unit) expresses a complete idea, hence also a thing, חשב is a single leaf plucked from the tree of thought, a word, that need not even express a complete concept, and מַלֵל means only: to say fractions of thoughts, to express something in a way that only gets near the real matter. Hence מילים in Job is used mostly in a rather disparaging sense for words which do not completely, or do not at all, speak out. Hence also מי ימלל גבורות ה׳, who can express even approximately the deeds of the Almight of God. And the same here: Many will have laughed, but who amongst all the laughter will have said a word to Abraham which even comes near to expressing what I press to my breast in this son! In him I feed the whole future of a nation, in him I am the mother of all the descendants of Abraham, for he will carry on all that Abraham has achieved. It is not just a baby that Sarah is suckling, when she gives her motherly care to this one child, she is feeding and bringing us sons, היניקה בנים שרה (not merely בן I.L.) for ילדתי בן לזקניו!

V. 8. גמל, of trees, that they have nourished their fruit with their sap till they are completely ripe and no longer require them ויצץ ציץ ויגמל שקדים (Numb. 17,23); in the same way referring to a mother regarding the child, hence: weaning. Perhaps the camel is also called גמל because it can go such a long time without drinking. Looking at all happenings as fruit matured on the tree of time, גמל in general would mean: bringing these fruits of time to maturity i.e. to guide the fate of men, thus, אשירה לה׳ כי גמל עלי. “Fain would I sing unto God, for what has happened to me is that which He brought to maturity for me” (Ps. 13,6); כל תגמולהי עלי “What return can I make unto God, when all the ripe fruit of His Care have come unto me” (Ps. CXVI, XII); and in particular: to bring the fruits of somebody’s actions to maturity, i.e. to compensate, recompense. When a tree permanently denies its sap to its fruit it is called קמל (Is. 33,9 & XIX,6 I.L.).

V. 9. Ishmael is characterised here according to the two natures combined in him: He was the son of a Hamitic mother and was to have been born to an Abraham. Sarah, who was the contriver of that birth had hoped that by the influence of education the Hamitic nature would be entirely overcome by the Abrahamitic spirit. She had hoped that, as the mistress of Hagar, she would be able to succeed in completely paralysing the latter’s influence. We have already been told how mistaken she was in this idea. (Ch. XV). There we tried to show how this double nature proved itself in the descendants of Ishmael. Sarah saw this contrast already in Ishmael himself coming to the fore. He took in just as much of the great ideas of Abraham to make him ironically disdain them, and over that which the world in general greeted merely with צחוק, in which (V.6) derision was only lightly mixed, Ishmael was completely מְצַחֵק, and was therefore completely unfit to join with Isaac in the heritage of Abraham.

V. 10. גרש is not simply at a distance, but a dismissing, a discarding, by which all connection with the home ceases. Thus, אשה גרושה מאישה. (גרש, related to ירש to force out of possession, hence also תירש, the juice pressed out of the fruit; קרש, the boards of the wall preventing access).

This sounds harsh but is entirely due to the conditions. If the house of Abraham and his son Isaac are not to have to fear the influence of Hagar and Ishmael, after the death of the parents, and, after all, Ishmael was the elder son, then both of them must be sent away in such a way that it is clear what their real relation to that house actually was, viz: as a slave and son of a slave, according, also a slave. Afterwards Abraham could, as indeed actually happened, provide generously for them in accordance with his prosperous position and the dictates of his heart. Not for nothing does Sarah repeatedly use the term: האמה הזאת, this maidservant. Not that altogether in principle no son of a slave should carry on as a co-bearer of the tradition of the house. For she herself had quite expressly had the intention, quite on her own initiative, of forming such an arrangement. But she had found this handmaid totally unfit for such a relationship hence: גרש בן האמה הזאת ,לא יירש בן האמה הזאת וגו׳ I had hoped אבנה ממנה, that Hagar’s son would become my son, that I would be able to bring him up for you. But Hagar’s nature spoilt that.

V. 11. The whole affair seemed to Abraham to be extremely bad, harsh, רע .רע (root רעע), it made an end to his plans to what he had pictured of his future, and indeed not only with regards to Ishmael but also regarding to his mother, as God says to him later על הנער ועל אמתך. Regarding both it seemed to him anything but good or right, but not from personal feelings of attraction for Hagar but solely על אודות בנו out of consideration for his son, out of motives regarding his son (אודות the plural of אוד, handle, lever). What Sarah had noticed has surely not escaped the notice of Abraham. But Abraham might have been thinking: — If here, at home, Ishmael has already become lost to all seriousness and has become מצחק and Hagar’s influence, although certainly partly countered by that of Abraham, has already become so powerful, what will become of the boy when they are both far away from here, and Ishmael is given over completely to Hagar’s influence!

V. 12. שמע בקול, real true obedience is expressed by שמע בקול not by בדבר, listen to the voice of another, not to his words, obey him because he says it, never bother about what he says. Listen to the voice of Sarah, obey her, even if you can not agree with her words, depend on her judgment, she goes deeper than you do, as altogether women have a deeper insight into character. Your seed will be called after Isaac, יקרא לך, in him, you will be called; Ishmael (V.13) זרעך הוא, he is your seed, he comes from you, he will have a good deal of the material and something of the spiritual from you. But to be called “the son of Abraham”, for that he is not worthy, your spiritual heir he can not be.

ביצחק not יצחק, as our sages remark, not Isaac but in Isaac will descendants mature for you. Do not let it be too hard and painful to separate from one son; from Isaac too, not all will remain your spiritual heirs, on the best of trees not every fruit ripens, and to keep right seed pure for the People of God some will have to be separated out as unfit.
V. 13. Ishmael is your seed, he has some germs of your spirit in him, and those will I allow to develop in the life of a nation.

V. 14. ואת הילד belongs to ויתן אל הגר, the שם על שכמה is in parenthesis, that is why it does not say וישם על שכמה, and is expressly stressed because it wants to show the manner in which she was sent away. As a slave, and not as the wife of Abraham and the mother of his son she had to be dismissed. The conditions and the purpose of this whole dismissal inexorably demanded this — ילד, Joseph, too, was seventeen years old and was still called ילד (Gen. 37,30). In comparison to the average length of life in those days to the present time, in proportion of 120 to 70, a seventeen year old person of that time would represent one of ten to eleven years of today.

V. 15.—16. Hagar’s whole behaviour is extremely characteristic and reveals the demerit, the imperfection of the Hamitic character. A Jewish mother would not have forsaken her child, even if all she could do would be to try to pacify him, even if it were only to soothe him for the millionth part of a second.

To go away, just because “one can not bear to see the misery” is not sympathetic feeling for another but is the cruel egoism of a human nature which is still crude. In truly humane people the feelings of duty master the strongest emotions, make one forget one’s own painful feelings and give helpful assistance even if one can do no more than give the comfort of one’s participating presence. Hence, so deeply significant, although Hagar wept too, it was not קול הגר but את קול הנער which God heard (V.17) for, doing nothing out of egoism, but sitting and crying does not penetrate to Him.

Further, ותשלך, threw the child away, תחת אחד השיחים “behind something that was growing there” (שיח is the most general name for growths related to שגה, to shoot up in the air, and hence, transferred to the inner working of the mind) quite indifferent where he falls, perhaps even amongst thorns where he could be scratched, and, through the carelessness of the mother unnecessary pain added to the tormenting thirst. All this shows how Hagar completely lost her head when overcome with her worry and behaved towards her child in a manner no Jewish mother would be guilty of.

כמטחוי קשת is usually translated by bowshot, the distance of a bow shot. This word does not occur elsewhere so its meaning can only be taken from the context. This expression certainly seems peculiar to be used here, one might be inclined to think it is used having in mind the future mode of Ishmael’s life. But if we examine the grammatical form of the word מטחוי it would definitely rule out the translation “shot”; it is an active participle of the Piel, and would seem to mean the shooter rather than the shot. Now of course	the bow is not shot but is the means for shooting, but we find a term quite analogous: רומי קשת shooters of the bow instead of shooters of arrows. So we believe we can take it to mean here “she retired to a distance as archers do, i.e. just as archers walk backwards from the target to the extreme point from which they can still see it, so did Hagar walk backwards from Ishmael as far as possible to avoid seeing his distress but still only so far that she could still keep an eye on the place. This would be quite in accordance with the feelings which were struggling within her, whereby the love for her child is only given as much consideration as the consideration for herself, sparing herself pain, allow.

V. 17. God has already heard your child, there where he lies struggling. Had you put your trust in God, had you not thrown your child there but laid him gently down, had you not left him but had you remained by him as becomes a mother, then you would already have seen the well, there just where he is.

V. 18. First get up and take the lad again as a strong never-despairing mother, for only as such are you worthy of God’s help; then give him to drink. החזיקי ידך בו, not החזיקי בידו which would be “hold him tight, support him with your hand”, but: “Let your hand keep a firm hold on him”. Be a strong and firm support and guide to him, for I have destined him for a great future.

V. 20. רבה קשת. We have already explained on פרו ורבו (Ch. 1,28) that in רבה lies the idea of spiritual education as parents can only reproduce themselves in their children if they make them spiritual replicas of themselves. Hence רבה meaning actual educating and תרבות discipline education, and רבי, not master, literally one who ranks above, but one who reproduces himself in his pupils. רֹבֶה קשת, a trainer of archers, and not רֹבֵה a master of archers, who could have some other occupation also, whose principle occupation may have been something else but, רֹבֶה, one whose constant occupation was this.

V. 21. Already above at the end of Ch. XVI we pointed out, how, and how strongly, the imprint of participation in the spirit of Abraham — although it is true, one sided only — is stamped on the Arab descendants of Ishmael. Now if we consider how, already at seventeen years of age Ishmael was withdrawn from Abraham’s influence, and the maternal Hamitic influence must thenceforth have been strengthened through his wife, the ancestress of Arab people, these Abrahamite traces so strongly marked in the Arab nation must transport us with wonder at the enduring, indestructable force which is innate in a true Abrahamic education.

V. 22. It was just at this time when Abraham had sent his eldest son away from him, and the whole future of his house rested on the recently-weaned little Isaac, that Abimelech, the King of the land, with the highest officer of his country, came to Abraham.
