They asked him to swear not to act falsely against him nor against his second and third generation; more, that he would remember and reciprocate all the friendly attitudes shown to him by himself and his country. Obviously Abimelech here is not addressing Abraham as a private individual whose importance comes to an end with his life, and who, as such, is never in the position of being able to do good or evil to a country. Obviously he has some idea of Abraham’s posterity, which as a nation, could stand as friends or as enemies to his people. In short, one can not take all this otherwise than to presume that Abimelech knew of the Abrahamitic promises and expectations, and for that future wished to ensure for himself and his land the friendship of that future nation on the grounds of the obligation which the ancestor had towards him.

Looked at in his way, בעת ההיא, just after sending Ishmael away, this approach of the king of the land, taken in conjunction with that which follows, the crowning story of Abraham’s life, assumes quite a special importance. Ishmael has gone, Abraham an old man who can be called away at any moment, the whole future rests on the child scarcely weaned, the future nation is still being rocked in the cradle, and already Abraham sees the promise bearing fruit. To Isaac’s cradle had the lord of the land come, to ask, in expectation of the future great nation, for a covenant for the future times — and then God comes down to Abraham and says: קח נא את בנך וגו׳ “offer up this only son to Me”, and with him the whole future.

In addition, we are shown again what great confidence was placed in the educational power of Abraham in that it could be taken for granted that his children and grandchildren could be relied on to honour his word. It is characteristic that while Abimelech demands that Abraham shall swear on behalf of his descendants he does not dare to make it reciprocal. He makes no oaths. For him, the gracious permission he gave Abraham to live in his land — a favour which apparently was rare in those days — was sufficient to justify his demand for the following generations. It seems that Abraham, too, did not think it worth while to ask for such a reciprocal oath binding Abimelech’s descendants. For he would know how little such political agreements were worth outside the Abrahamitic world. Abraham’s descendants, even as a state and nation never played about with their pledged agreements and covenants, and still at the time of the second Temple, when we were still a state amongst other states, Israel was renowned for keeping faith with their given word.

V. 23. — השבע אם. The characteristic fact that, in our language, the sentence in connection with השבע, if construed with אם denotes a negative oath, and if with אם לא a positive one can be understood if we realise the fundamental meaning of השבע. For the word seems to be formed from שבע, seven and in its reflexive form would mean literally “to give oneself up to the seven”. As the creation of the visible concrete world was completed in six days and the seventh became the memorial and reminder of the Invisible One being and remaining in connection with the visible world as its Creator and Master, so the number 7 remains altogether as the symbol indicating and referring to this invisible Master. Now taking an oath means: submitting yourself and all your visible material world to the Invisible One, i.e. to His punishing judgment, if etc. So that when the formula is used: השבעה לי בה׳ אם it means “give yourself and all you possess up to the punishment of God if you do this to me” i.e. you swear not to do it, and the reverse by swearing אם לא which would mean that you swear to do it. The word אלה for an oath is analogous being quite simply formed from the Name of God. At an assertive promissory statement, as here, the term השבע sets God as the guarantor against and the avenger for any broken promise.

The implication of the word הנה here is obscure. With עד it is an adverb of time, “till now”. Without עד, as here, an adverb of place, hither, here ישובו הנה. “Swear unto me here”, on this spot. This is just as obscure as the השבעה לי כיום “swear unto me as today” in Ch. 25,33. It almost seems that by these expressions an oath — which is an invocation to an Invisible Being, Whose intervention is to prove itself in a time which is not yet present — is supplemented by referring to some visible object or to a time which is there now. This would express the idea: the existence of this invisible Power is as certain to me as this visible spot on which I am standing (הנה) or this future is as certain to me as this present moment (כיום). The underlying idea of these expressions may be similar to the נקיטת חפץ (taking the Sefer Torah or Tephilin in the hand I.L.) at the later שבועה דאוריתא, but there at the same time the concrete object is to refer to the revelation of the Law of this Invisible One.

תִּשְׁקֹר, elsewhere always in the Piel, here is in the Kal: that you do not become false, a lie. (שקר related to שכר ,שיר ,שגר, all four are productions of things which were not in existance, only with very different modifications. שגר, physically, animal birth, bringing something forth into reality, שיר, spiritually, bringing to your mind the invisible which lies at the base of all visible, hence used in תנ״ך preferably in singing of the deeds of God which have been experienced; שכר, unintentionally seeing things which are not there, intoxication; שקר, intentionally saying things which are not in accordance with reality). There are two kinds of untruth, logical lies and moral ones. The first when the word is not in accordance with the truth; the second when the behaviour is not in accordance with what it truly should be. He who behaves as he should do is called an איש אמת. Here: “Swear that you will behave towards me and my descendants in accordance with what our behaviour towards you has deserved” — נין see notes on תנינים (Ch 1,21); נכד (related to נגד to be away from the other but still to be directed towards it) the generation which is farther off and still physically and spiritually belongs to the grandfather: כחסד אשר עשיתי etc. Here Abimelech undoubtedly has in mind a future time when his descendants will be in a similar position towards the Abrahamites as Abraham was to him.

V. 25. והוכח, not ויכח. It seems that Abraham had already before made representations to Abimelech about a well that had been taken from him, without specifying (out of discretion) who the robbers were, not telling him that they were his own servitors. Abimelech had taken no notice of the complaint. Now Abraham reminds him of it and tells him who had done it. Abimelech excuses himself by saying that the reason he had done nothing in the matter was because he did not know who had done it.

V. 27. It seems peculiar that here, at the conclusion of the agreement, which as a rule is based on mutual relationship, Abraham alone made gifts. This giving at the conclusion of a contract seems altogether to correspond to the idea of the later קנין סודר, and if, in accordance with the accepted Halacha, the symbol of the קנין has to be given by the receiver, it seems that Abimelech should have given Abraham a token as assurance for at least himself and for his own lifetime. Perhaps Abimelech thought this was not required as Abraham was actually receiving his part of the agreement there and then. Or on Abimelech’s side there was no gift called for, as he was to receive nothing concrete at all from Abraham, only an assurance by oath for the future of his descendants.

V. 28. et. seq. Out of the total mass of the symbols of the agreement, Abraham separated out seven ewe lambs and set them aside as special ratification for his legal right of possession of the well. Neither the sex nor the kind of animal, nor the number may have been just haphazard. The significance of the number seven at an oath we have indicated on V.23. (In verse 31 we also see the interplay of both seven and oath in the word and name given to the well). It was all about a well, the most fundamental condition for possessing herds and flocks. But ewes, כבשות, not כבשים, are the animals on which the whole future of the flock depends. Hence they are very suited to represent the wealth of possession of flocks in general. Now if השבע means nothing else but, to place himself with his whole “six” i.e. his whole material possessions, under the invisible Power that rules over all visible, which will not tolerate anything dishonest, and so stamping his possessions with the number “7”, then, “placing ewes to the number of seven” would express nothing else than: submitting his whole wealth of flocks to the Power of God punishing dishonesty if the well out of which they drink is not honestly his own. This would be an oath of innocence for the honesty of his property, נשבע ונפטר, and by accepting the seven ewes from Abraham’s hand Abimelech recognises his honest legal right to the possession of the well. His acceptance of these sheep becomes an עדה, a witness and memorial for the legality of this posession.

עדה from עוד to endure (related to עות from which we get עת, time, לעות את יעף (Is. 50,4) although the plural עתת and בעתו seem to come from העיד .(עתת to make something endure, to give permanence to something which otherwise would escape being recognised. But this is the business of a witness. Hence also memorial. העיד ב- is also to warn, i.e. to bring to the mind of somebody the duty and the consequence of transgressing it which had escaped his mind.

V. 31. שניהם, the future and the present rulers shake hands. And this event — the first recognition of, the first desire for allegiance with, the future Abrahamitic nation — was important enough for its memory to be perpetuated by the name of the place for the descendants, especially as thereby at the same time they would be reminded of the duty which the oath of their ancestor imposed on them.

V. 33. אשל only occurs elsewhere of Saul (I. Sam. 22,6), “Saul sat on a hillock (or in Gibea) under an אשל in the heights, and his spear was in his hand”, so it undoubtedly means a tree, as the Rabbinic Hebrew uses אשלי רברבי for the large trees. (Phonetically related to אצל, to lay by the side. So that perhaps אשל is so called as spreading its branches on all sides and so offering fruit in all directions). Our sages take this אשל to have been either an orchard or a caravanserai, which, according to the letters of the word אשל offered everything: אכילה ,שתיה ,לינה. Perhaps both come to the same thing, and אשל would designate a tree which, by its fruit gives אכילה and שתיה, and by its rich leafage, shade and shelter לינה. Anyway it is not far-fetched to assume, as our sages explain, that by practising ready friendly hospitality Abraham used the opportunity to lead them from thanking him to thanking God, yea to teach them in a practical way to recognise in this practice of brotherly love the happy and happiness-bringing effect of the worship of One Unique God.

Überlegt müsste nur noch werden, was Abraham bewogen haben dürfte, eben in באר שבע, vielleicht an den Brunnen einen solchen אשל zu pflanzen und bei ihm "die Menschen im Namen Gottes, des א׳ עולם, zusammenzurufen", während er bei seinen bisherigen Gottesverkündungen einen מזבח baute und auch dieser Gottesname hier im Munde Abrahams zuerst, und sonst nie wieder in תנ"ך vorkommt — nur einmal heißt es (Jesaias 40, 28) אלקי עולם ד׳ וגו׳. —

We still have to consider what might have moved Abraham to plant such an אשל just in באר שבע, perhaps at the well itself, and at it to call people together in the name of God, the א׳ עולם, whereas hitherto he had always built a מזבח at his proclamation of the Name of God. Also why this name of God occurs here for the first time in Abraham’s mouth and never again in the whole of תנ״ך — except once Is. 40,28 אלקי עולם ה׳. Up till now Abraham had taught of God, as being א׳ עליון קונה שמים וארץ as the living God of the present, Who not only brought the world into existence thousands of years ago, but Who “never sleeps and never slumbers.” Not, Who — as was blasphemously thought and said — since thousands of years is resting from the “hard” work of creation, but קוֹנֶה is still now the Bearer and Owner and Master of heaven and earth, Whom nothing escapes, Who is the most Living, most Present God of every present being and object in heaven and earth. Now here, all of a sudden, at this אשל, Abraham teaches a Name which apparently points beyond the visible horizon of the present, and to God, as the God Who proclaims the time that is hidden from human eyes. For that is what עולם means, from עלם, to be hidden, related אלם, to be mechanically or organically bound. In תנ״ך the word עולם never means the world but the hidden time, accordingly, as a rule, the whole future, and includes all the distant past which equally lies beyond our ken.

Abraham seems to have been prompted to this by the event he had just experienced which gave the place the name of באר שבע. The most important personage of the country, the King of the land, had come to him, the most isolated householder, a man without any real claim to rights, because he had a two-year old baby lying in a cradle of whom the King knew, or had a premonition, that a mighty nation was to grow. As a cautious politician he wanted to form an alliance with the father of that baby so that the descendants of the boy should still know how he and his country had behaved towards their ancestor and gratefully repay that behaviour. In this Abraham saw the beginning of the future which had been promised to him being actually realised. Without Divine direction the King and his general would surely never have sought to make such an alliance with a hundred-year-old greyhead and his two-year-old son, whose political hopes must have appeared simply “laughable”. At באר שבע the place at which is immortalised this whole God-directed contrast: באר, the well the insignificance of the present state, of a man without rights, so dependent, that the peaceful possession of a well he himself had dug has to be acknowledged as a “royal gracious kindness”, and שבע, the oath concluding an alliance with the king who could only have some idea of the promised future great nation that was to be evolved, — at that place Abraham planted a tree which was to grow into a rich blessing bringing happiness to people, and there he proclaimed, not the א׳ קונה שמים וארץ, Who reveals Himself in the laws of Nature, but א׳ עולם, the One Who sows the future with invisible seeds in the present.

It was the first trace of God’s constructive work in directing human history that Abraham had to greet, and he celebrated the occasion by perpetuating it by planting a tree in which — perhaps — he laid down his idea of this future. Out of simple unpretentious beginnings, like a tree, and, like it, spreading blessing far around when matured, does the future to which he belongs germinate; and it is God א׳ עולם Who thus plants and nurtures the tree of blessing of the development of the future. Just as here, a God-sent presentiment drove Abimelech to Abraham, and thereby the first respect was planted in Philistine minds which later on grew to the “fear and dread” which kept the “inhabitants of Philistaea in fear and trembling” when God led the people of Abraham to their promised heritage, so, frequently, — long before the events, — such ideas fall from heaven, catch the mind, affect actions, and later on people find it quite “natural” that events happen as they do.

א׳ עולם. But the sages of our people have brought the Name of God paired with עולם — which, as remarked above occurs only twice in תנ״ך — more than any other to constant use in our mouths, after the word עולם came to have for them the meaning also of “the world,” i.e. the most concrete actual present, and with its two meanings — the hidden future and the actual present — they have given us invaluable precious thoughts.

Everywhere else, when in trouble one directs one’s thoughts to the future, and looking to the future one tries to find consolation for an inconsolable present. Our sages lead us to the reverse idea. Just at the time when our present had become a laughing-stock for the world, they taught us to look on every present moment as being already a part of the future. At all times, when thunder rolls, lightning flashes, trees blossom, flowers smell, food nourishes, events mature, etc. etc. they teach us to take the fact to heart that the present is already a part of the future and to think of God as מלך העולם as the Ruler and Director of the hidden future which is slowly maturing to perfection in the course of time. For every second truly lived is in the very centre of that eternity in which we all not only will participate but in which we are participating if we are what we should be.

Yea, perhaps here an even deeper wisdom lies. In תנ״ך, the word עולם seems not only to mean the hidden past and future, but altogether that which is hidden from our eyes, invisible to us. It is indeed presumptuous to declare that only the past and the future are hidden from us. The most actual present in truth at the bottom is an עולם. Fundamentally, at rock bottom everything concrete has its roots in the נעלם which really is that which has the highest degree of permanent reality. Shapes, forms, change, the force, the נעלם, the abstract that lies invisibly at the base of everything that is concrete, is permanent, yea, is the one real thing on which one can depend. Thus it says in Ecclesiastes 3,11 את הכל עשה יפה בעתו גם את העלם נתן בלבם מבלי אשר לא ימצא האדם את המעשה אשר עשה האלקים מראש ועד סוף. “God made everything beautifully in connection with all that is contemporaneous with it, but He has also laid in the heart of mankind presentiment of the transcendental, without which they would never come to the slightest understanding of the nature of things”. Perhaps this way of looking at it is reproduced in the idea of עולם being “the world”, for the real world is actually the עולם, and it wants to accustom us to look at every occurrence beyond the actual visible to the invisible force that lies behind it, and up to God, the Ruler and Director of that force, the מלך העולם, to Whose Kingdom everything belongs which surrounds us in this “world of riddles”. Who is also אלקינו to Whom we too belong with all the forces of our lives as regards to existence and calling, and to Whom also we — ברוך — are to give ourselves up with all our forces to fulfil His Will and to increase the realm of giving Him satisfaction.

V. 1. אחר הדברים. Similarly to above, Ch. 15,1 (to which refer) these words introduce a crisis, a reversal of all that went before. Abraham had already proclaimed God as א׳ עולם, Isaac had been born, the elder son sent away for his sake, ביצחק, in Isaac the seed of the future is to be carried on, and this future had already been recognised in the present, the King of the land had already concluded a treaty embracing not only Isaac himself but with his further descendants, so that Isaac’s promised future had already struck roots in the contemporary present — and now comes the behest to break up all that has happened hitherto! הָאלקים, the God, the same God Who had revealed Himself to Abraham and had made Isaac the combination of the whole aim of Abraham’s life. — נסה, related to נסע, moving on, נסח, flinging away, נשא to raise up, all three having the concept of bringing something to a further or higher position. In the same way נסה regarding physical or moral forces: to test, i.e. to give it such tasks to do which, up till now, it has not proved its ability to accomplish. Hence every test is a step forward, is a strengthening of powers which exist already but which have not yet been proved in this further or higher task. A rope which has already stood the strain of fifty pounds is put to the test as soon as it is given fifty one pounds to bear, but moral and spiritual forces are thereby strengthened and raised.
Quite significantly the mark of cantillation on אברהם is a טפחא showing the immediate readiness of Abraham, as God calls to him he says הנני.

V. 2. נא, please take, do take, I know full well what I am asking of you, I know how your whole inner self must struggle against it; את בנך וגו׳ it is your son I am demanding, your only one, and one to whom your whole soul clings, it is Isaac to whom the whole meaning of your life is attached. —

הב ,אהב, give, with the prefixed א, hence, equally giving oneself up, devoting oneself to the other, and seeking to bring the other as near as possible to oneself, accordingly, to strive for the most intimate connection with somebody. It is the opposite of שנא related to סנה, really to be a thorn, to fend off, to keep the other as far away from oneself. For אהבה the existence of the other is a necessity, for שנאה, his absence, even his complete removal, death, is desirable.
לך לך, with such a task, calling him to isolation, attaching himself only to God, did Abraham’s life begin, with the same, but with greatly added intensity does it reach its culmination.

המוריה. If it is true, as our sages teach, that this name designates the place from which the תורה goes forth — (the teaching or the law, does not really convey the concept of the word תורה, it comes from הרה to receive the seed of life, hence in Hiphil, a spiritual begetting) — from where seed is to be strewn from which mankind is to be spiritually reborn; if further, this was the place on which the first offerings, the rejected and the accepted ones of Cain and Abel, shine out warningly and instructively to the world, if on this same place Noah brought his offering on the re-presented earth, in anticipatory feelings of the ניחוח of the ultimate future unified devotion of the whole of mankind; if all this is true, then Abraham was told already by the information of the place, that this action was not to have importance for him alone, but that it was to demonstrate right to the most distant future, by the most instructive example, what the fulfilment of a “הנני״ said to God really means. What “the Law of God”, “Divine Service”, “Temple” “Offerings” mean, how all these do not designate “ceremonies”, but contain the most earnest seriousness; how saying הנני, saying “we would serve God” implies completely giving up all one’s own ideas and one’s own Will, and without any further ado placing all one’s powers at the disposal of God’s insight and will. The name מוריה could tell Abraham that what was demanded of him was to be הוראה for his people, was to belong to all mankind, and — if his God-soaked soul still required support — the consciousness of this could help him to carry out what was demanded of him.

והעלהו שם לעולה. To the Jewish way of thinking, the concept עלה is taken in two ways. To human beings the material, earthly matter appears as being “below”, “low”. That which is to be separated from earth, to break away from the material is designated in all languages as “raising”, elevating. When matter receives life it rises up, עָלָה, the life-giving and life-keeping (giving suck) mother-animal, a hindered development becomes חלה illness. From this עלה לה׳, a complete sublimation, a complete breaking away from all holding to material, up to God, complete elevation, giving oneself up to God, and that is what the עולה-offering really is.

But taken in its actuality עולה is also used for simply going up away from earthly existence, as in Ps. 102,25 אל תעלני בחצי ימי without devoting oneself to any higher calling. Here, where the indication of this higher calling certainly should not have been missing, but nevertheless is missing, and it does not say והעלהו לי שם לעולה — which, also if it had meant an actual human sacrifice and not a symbolic one, would have been merely blasphemous nonsense as actual sacrifice of human life is the very diametric opposite of the Torah conception of an offering — but simply והעלהו שם לעולה is what it says, thereby it was just a removal from earthly existence that was demanded, a purposeless killing, purposeless in so far as the purpose was not revealed.

V. 3. “He took his two lads with him, and Isaac his son”. The order is not without significance. He told Isaac as late as possible. This ויקח את שני נעריו אתו does not yet refer to the journey. Starting on the journey only follows: ויקם וילך. But before he woke Isaac up, he got his people ready and saddled the ass. He wanted to spare Isaac having to make his resolution for as long as possible and wanted to avoid being alone with him. Isaac was no longer a child, he was an independent man of 37 years of age. So that the greatness of his soul in this whole affair ranks equally with that of Abraham. Isaac had not received the behest himself, he only knew it through the mouth of his father as תשב״פ. Similarly, in the case of Adam and Eve, where Eve was included in the punishment for transgressing a prohibition which she only knew through the mouth of Adam, so here the first Jewish son is ready to sacrifice himself for a tradition which he only knew through his father. Here the seed was sown for the devotion of the later generations to the traditions of their forbears. Thus our sages ask (Sanhedrin 89b) how could Isaac believe in such a הוראת שעה (a decision in law for a special occasion I.L.), how dared he do so? And the answer they give is: היכא דמוחזק שאני, not on the strength of some convincing miracle, but on his firm conviction of the proven character of his father. Our devotion to the traditions of our forbears also rests on their characters. They were as little hierarchs as Abraham was. No tradition came from them for which they themselves, in the first place, had not made sacrifices. There are no passages in the whole Midrash which are more touching than those which place in the mouth of the son all the doubts which could well be reckoned to have made Abraham and Isaac waver on the hard road they were traversing. In those three days not much seems to have been said, but what an infinite amount must have been felt and thought. Our verse seems to indicate that Abraham first woke his people up and kept them with him, to barricade himself against being overcome by his feelings, and to have avoided being alone with Isaac.

V. 4. Not ויהי ביום השלישי וישא וגו׳, but, on the third that he lifted up his eyes he saw the place. נשא עין is always an intentional looking up and looking around. The whole time he had been looking around but had seen nothing to indicate that here was the place of which God had spoken. He had always dreaded to see it, until finally on the third day he did see it.

V. 5. שבו לכם: stay here for yourselves, that which is about to follow is not for you. For they would not have allowed it without interfering, would not have understood it. Here at the foot of Moriah is the parting between זרע אברהם and בן נח. Only a breast in which the תורה awakens an immediate הנני, like Abraham, is able to give itself up to the Will of God, angel-like, with complete renunciation of its own comprehension of it, is able, angel-like, בשתים יכסה פניו וגו׳ to cover up eye and foot, not to see whither it leads, not to see where one is going, only cheerfully and courageously to use one’s powers to soar upward to fulfil the Will of God. This stage — soaring above the angels, — נדולים צדיקים יותר ממלאכי השרת, of one’s own free-will doing that which the angels, impelled by their one-sided natures, do without a struggle, fighting down all the objections raised by one’s senses, of one’s own free-will covering eyes and feet with one’s wings, of one’s own will using all one’s power of upward soaring in the service of God — this stage beckons only to those who follow the ways Father Abraham had illuminated for them. Up till Moriah they could go together, בני נח are also children of God, but only to the foot of the Mount of God, not up to the heights.

And with what complete lack of pomposity, and in what simple words does Abraham announce the great deed he intends doing! “We shall just go a little up there, prostrate ourselves and come back to you.”

But it is significant that, for that which he has in mind to do, he uses the term השתחויה, His attendants must have known that he intended to make a sacrifice as he had brought wood and fire with him. So that Abraham calling offering השתחויה, and that word alone in Abraham’s mouth would demolish — even if without it every page of the Jewish Word of God did not emphatically give the lie to it — all that people, entrapped by their ignorance, ascribe to “the bloodthirsty cult of offerings”, dragging the Jewish Temple and the Jewish conception of God in the dust, and babble about “the narrow-mindedness of our forefathers, who imagined that God finds joy in the smoking blood of an expiring animal, and try to obtain atonement by that”, and talk of “the progress that the חרבן בית מקדשנו has brought us inasmuch as it has freed us for all time from such bloodthirsty offerings and still more bloodthirsty ideas”. נשתחוה is what Abraham says his intention is in bringing his offering. Not the animal, he himself does he offer, his life, his forces, his eye, his breast, his hand, his foot, his whole living self does he lay symbolically by the animal on the Altar of God, ישתחוה, himself does he throw completely down before God, by his offerings. Only a Bileam lets a Baalak stand upright — התיצב על עולתך — next to his offering, for his offering is no representation of an ideal perfection which the bringer vows to try and reach, but is a slaughtered meal offered to the deity which is to have the effect of magically forcing it to favour the request of the bringer. The Jew is סומך שתי ידיו על הקרבן, lays himself with all his strength on his offering; for it is he himself which, in an offering, he gives over to the אש דת with the resolution, henceforth to let his whole being be fuel to keep the fires of godliness burning on earth.

V. 6 וילכו שניהם יחדיו. This refrain occurs twice again. Abraham and Isaac, the father and the son, the one to bring the offering, the other to be the offering wending the hard way upward together in complete, unswerving, harmonious unity, such is the picture of the example that is to point the way for all fathers and sons, for every old and young generation of the House of Abraham, the path they are to tread together.

V. 7. Up till then the father and son had not spoken to one another, that is why it says twice ויאמר here; and from the silent solemnity of those three days, Isaac could well have made a shrewd guess at the truth. Perhaps that is why it adds the word אל אברהם אביו, here. Till now in his silent solemn demeanour in the presence of attendants he had seemed to be only “Abraham”, and did not appear to Isaac to be in his usual manner “his father”.

V. 8. “All we have to do is to bring the wood, the fire and the knife, we have only to be ready for any offering; what He will choose, what will happen will only happen because it is the Will of God: the answer to your question we will leave to God”. And with that Abraham had told him everything which he had to know, which he needed to know. “We have to build the altar and leave it to God’s Insight to choose the offering which in His Insight is the right one”, — and they went on together. —

V. 9. It is by no means usual for the offering to be killed on the altar. It seems that Abraham wanted to sacrifice his son in such a way that, once he had performed the great act, he would not have anything further to do, and so wished to sacrifice his son directly on the stack of wood so that the flames would at once consume the body of his child. — עקד the strong form of אגד to bind together.

V. 11. Unlike the הנני above in V. 1, where it followed immediately at the first call, here he had to be called twice, for he was completely absorbed in carrying out the dread command of his God, and had ear for nothing else. It seems to be significant that here God sends an angel to deliver the message whereas elsewhere in Abraham’s life God Himself speaks to him. To tell him to stop an angel was quite sufficient. Herein, too, we are shown the depth of the struggle which Abraham had to overcome. Had an angel brought him the message to kill his son, he would simply not have believed it. It was so much out of any connection with, so directly contrary to, everything which he knew of God in general, and in particular to what God had revealed to him concerning Isaac. But to tell him not to sacrifice his son, a message through an angel sufficed; for, for that, and to explain the whole demand as a test, which had been proved by the readiness to accept it, for that there was no necessity for an extraordinary revelation, that fitted in harmoniously with everything else that Abraham learnt to know of God.

But we stress this quite specially because one who calls himself “a pathfinder of the science of Judaism” (Abraham Geiger I.L.), in raving madness has dared to raise his lying pen also against this, the very loftiest summit of spirituality reached, not only in Jewish, but in all events which show human greatness. He turns this, as he does so many others, into its very opposite, and says that Abraham’s greatness lay not in his being ready to obey the voice of His God, and sacrifice his son but his obeying the voice of the angel telling him not to do so, and his real greatness lay in his coming to his senses in time, and realising that God finds no pleasure in human sacrifices. Just by this did Abraham become the greatest reformer of his time, and he was the first to abolish human sacrifices and substitude animal offerings for them. And then we naturally have surpassed the spirit of Abraham and proved ourselves to be on a still higher level inasmuch as we have abolished sacrifices altogether! Only a twisted mind could possibly work this out of the story recorded here. “Where is the lamb for the offering?” asks Isaac on the way, so that he was already quite used to the fact that his father was no pagan who offered human sacrifices to his fetich, and absolutely clear and impossible to explain away are the words עתה ידעתי כי ירא אלקים אתה ולא חשכת את בנך את יחידך ממני. So we have God’s word for it that He recognised Abraham’s greatness that he was ready to sacrifice even his only son for Him, but not that he desisted in time! And just on that, on the “Akeida Yitchack”, Jewish Judaism looks enthusiastically still today, as the exemplary highest peak of the fear of God. Of course then that same “pathfinder of the science of Judaism”, with his twisted mind, finds no better name for this fear of God which uses the freedom of will and intelligence of human beings in submitting them to the insight and will of the Highest intelligence and Love than — doglike obedience.

V. 13. וישא. On that he looked around. He felt the urge to dedicate the sacrifice, this עקוד and העקד, this free-willed surrender of one’s whole being with hand and foot on the altar, which he had been ready to do in actuality, now, by a symbolic offering, to be the tenor of the whole future life of his son and the descendants of his son.

Just as Isaac had been ready to sacrifice himself on the altar of God, and had risen up to life from the altar of God, so is this same feeling and the same cheerful readiness for sacrifice to be the vow expressed in offerings by him and his children, and fulfilled in life. Isaac’s life and the life of his children are to form an eternal Akeida.

The identification of the person in his offering is established for all time with the greatest pithiness by this איל תחת בנו. In תנא דבי אלי׳ it says: — אותו יום שהעלה אבינו אברהם את יצחק בנו על גבי המזבח תיקן הקב״ה שני כבשים אחד בשחרית ואחד בין הערבים שנ׳ את הכבש אחד וגו׳ וכל כך למה שבשעה שישראל מקריבין תמידים על המזבח וקוראין את המקרא הזה צפונה לפני ה׳ הקב״ה זוכר עקידת יצחק מעיד אני עלי שמים וארץ בין גוי בין ישראל בין איש בין אשה בין עבד בין שפחה קורא את המקרא הזה צפונה לפני ה׳ הקב״ה זוכר עקידת יצחק בן אברהם.

There too the daily offering in the Temple is taken to be just a national continuation of the Akeida of the forefather, and especially the command צפונה לפני ה׳, that the holiest offerings had to be brought before God on the “midnight side” of the altar is taken in connection with it. In the “midnight of life”, with the sun far beneath us, around us all darkness, and still to say: Even if we can not see, ה׳ יראה God does see, — to stand צפונה, in midnights of life, לפני ה׳, before God, — to say: “God has insight, He can see for us, no need for insight into the insight of God, neither His Law nor His manner of ruling need to justify thesmelves before the tribune of our understanding, whatever the conditions may be here below: ה׳ יראה.” Such is the institution of the eternal offering on Moriah.

That was why Abraham looked for an animal, for words were insufficient, and see, there stands a ram, and אחר, afterwards, after Abraham had first seen it, it became caught by its horns in a bush. Then Abraham took it and brought it as “an offering in place of his son.” These words which we have stressed are a striking refutation of that narrow-minded or malicious misconception which disputes the symbolic meaning of our offerings, so as to be able to launch into a proud disparagement of the “bloody ritual of offerings”.

If offerings had no symbolic meanings, if the offering of this ram did not express a much higher and much more meaningful giving oneself up to God, what a blasphemy, yea, what an absurdity would it be to say תחת בנו; instead of the dearest, most precious thing, for which one would sooner have suffered death oneself ten times over, to substitute an animal that just happens to be running wild in the forest, so that it has not even the value of one’s own possessions! Somebody has generously given me a million pounds, and I pick up a pin and say, well at least take this for it!

V. 14. By the name ה׳ יראה Abraham bequeathed the הוראה which Moriah is to bring to his descendants by the remembrance of this event, ה׳ יראה (somewhat reminiscent of ה׳ יראה לו וגו׳) God sees. Even when we, and where we, do not see, God sees, freely and willingly have we to subordinate our own judgment to His. “God sees” thus Abraham expresses the general meaning of Moriah. But today, after this general conviction of God has manifested itself for us in a special act of revelation, and God has given us His insight into what is good and right for us in His Torah—for which a Sanctuary is to be erected on this Mount — so that we are to live the whole of our lives in accordance with it, today this great Truth is not expressed by the general term “God sees”, but that each one of us “is seen by God”, and has to present himself repeatedly on this Mount “to be seen” to be testingly inspected. Thrice yearly יֵרָאֶה, every son of Abraham and Isaac must be seen on this mount, and not ריקם, with mere inner, passing devotion, but with the sacrificing dedication of the whole of his being as expressed in עולת ראיה. Everybody who henceforth appears on Moriah with his עולת ראיה attaches himself to the עולה which Abraham brought תחת בנו, and vows to do his part of the Akeida task which his ancestor undertook for his son and his descendants on that spot, and in accomplishing it himself had pilgrimed up to the heights of Moriah as an example for all time.

V. 15. שנית. It was only after Abraham had sacrificed the ram in the place of Isaac, and had given the place its name that this announcement of the far-reaching blessing that would accrue to him as a result of his act, was made to him. For with both he had made this culminating act of his life into the loftiest goal of the whole of his descendants. In connection with it, this blessing is given to those descendants.

V. 16. That which before had been given merely as a ברית, accordingly as something completely independent of any external conditions but still dependent on mutual fulfilment, is now expressed here by a שבועה, to be henceforth completely unconditional. By the עקדה Abraham had already fulfilled, on his side, the highest demand and at the same time, thereby had ensured the final faithful fulfilment on the part of his descendants. That is the זכות of this Akeida. By it, the spirit of the highest moral perfection was sunk so deeply into Isaac, and shines forth so brightly as an example, that by both, by the inherited natural disposition, and by the glorious example, the descendants of Isaac can never be entirely lost, but even through by-paths of the deepest aberrations will finally work their way up to the loftiest heights of their calling. Therefore, יען אשר עשית, because it corresponds to it, is the corresponding effect of your deed (יען from ענה) can I promise with absolute certainty the most blessed and most blessing-spreading future for your descendants.

V. 17. וירש זרעך את שער אויביו. If here it is indicated that his descendants will also have enemies, this is just in connection with the aberrations which, as remarked on V.16, are envisaged in the בי נשבעתי. Israel will have fights, but finally the gates of his enemies will fall to his heritage. This can hardly refer to a military conquest. Military victories were never Israel’s calling. But it seems to have to be taken in the same sense as that in which the highest perfection of mental conditions is repeatedly expressed in תהלים as צדיקים יירשו ארץ, that the ultimate development of the world will fall as the heritage of the righteous, all other powers and influences will have disappeared and only what is morally right will prevail. So that what is said here would be: ultimately, the שער, the forum, i.e. the social and political formation of even those nations who have fought against the principles of Israel, will come to be a heritage for Israel, in Israel and through Israel they will obtain the blessing and happiness for which they have striven in vain in all other directions.

V. 18. שכר .עקב, in the meaning we have attached to it, reward for the good deeds of the righteous, hardly ever occurs in תנ״ך. A righteous man has no loss in service of God, even the biggest sacrifice that he might make, would be to him in itself the biggest gain; hence שכר (related to סגר and סכר, to close up blanks, to fill up holes, empty spaces), compensation does not exist for him, as he recognises no loss. Were he to hope for compensation he would not be the צדיק. The blessing that does accrue from his deeds comes to him עקב, literally “on the heel” of his deeds. It is not that which he had “in view” when he did the deed, it comes to him “unsought for”. He only wants to do his duty. (Hence עקב also means: to deceive, literally “at his heel”, behind his back, to entrap him). Here the עקב refers either to all what has just been said: all this blessing comes to you, your descendants and the nations of the whole world, as a result of the obedience you have proved to Me, or only to the last: now, you are just alone in obedience to Me, but as the final result of that, at present so unique, blind obedience, the whole of mankind will ultimately attach itself to the blessing-bringing ways of your descendants.

V. 19. וילכו יחדיו, all together, Abraham, Isaac and the attendants. This is the third time we read of this יחדיו in the Akeida, and it is the final stroke of the pen, the last move in the great story. Whereas יחד for the most part, means just an external being together in time or in person, יחדיו indicates rather a more internal and intimate being together (of course the suffix ו still remains obscure). Above, when Abraham and Isaac left the attendants at the foot of Moriah and he and his son set out for their great ordeal, it says “שבו לכם פה עם החמור״, for up to such heights only an Abraham and Isaac can wander, and, of them it repeatedly says that they went on that hard path יחדיו, harmoniously with one accord, together. Exceedingly characteristic and significant for the whole spirit of the frame of mind — which was to begin with Abraham and Isaac, does it now say here — after they had achieved the great, yea, the greatest loftiest height that a human being can reach — they returned to their attendants, and all of them — Abraham, Isaac and the men — went together, יחדיו, to Beer Sheba. In all other circles of humanity, after such a soaring into the proximity of God, after such elevation above everything earthly, an Abraham and an Isaac would have been so full of “I, myself”, or of the “Divine”, that they would have been lost for ordinary earthly life, and for “ordinary” human beings. Elsewhere such “standing near to God” — even if only presumed or imaginary — begets such pride that one proudly looks down on other people as “common mortals”, and avoids contact with them. Totally different from that is the spirit that should be inherited from the example of Abraham and Isaac. Just after they had achieved the very loftiest deed that could be made on earth, they return to the attendants they had left at the foot of Moriah, and go יחדיו with them, feel themselves no whit higher than anybody else. To the true son of Abraham everybody is equally respected in their vocation, he finds no difference between himself and the lowest hewer of wood or servant. The higher he stands spiritually, intellectually or morally, the less superior does he feel, the less is he conscious of his own greatness. Rightly indeed do our sages ז״ל waver as to whom to award the palm of superiority, whether to חסידות or to ענוה .ענוה is, after all, the only virtue of which a man can only be unconscious of possessing. He who knows he is an ענו is already no ענו; is filled with the worst kind of pride and conceit. He is always saying to himself of himself, that he has every right to be proud and is still so little proud! Abraham and Isaac, returned from the summit of Moriah as if they had done nothing special at all וישב אברהם אל נעריו ויקמו וילכו יחדיו.

V. 20. The word הנה here, indicates that these news were a reply to an enquiry: Yes Milka too, the sister of Sarah, has had children” (and so you can easily find a suitable match for Isaac, if you wish to find a wife for him). It seems that Abraham took the לך לך ,ומבית אביך וגו׳ so seriously that he had meticulously kept himself so much away from his relations, that he only came to know of their increase and extension when he looked around for a daughter-in-law.

V. 1. This is the only place in תנ״ך where the age of a woman is recorded. (The reason most probably being because the lives of the women are in general farther away from public life and a record of their age is not necessary to fix the chronological order of events of history). Apart from that it is peculiar that it says here ויהיו חיי שרה and not שני חיי שרה, and this must be so peculiar that — which is another peculiarity — the text finds it necessary to repeat the information by saying again at the end of the verse clearly שני חיי שרה. That our sages point out thereon that here the life of Sarah is presented in three age-groups is well known. Let us take it then, as is clearly presented to us, and thus we are told, not that Sarah lived one hundred and twenty seven years, but a hundred years, twenty years and seven years. These three numbers represent to us the three periods in the development of a human life: the age of childhood, mature youth, completed old age. A spiritually and morally perfected life could not be better expressed than: as an old man, he was old, as a man, a man, as a child, a child. More, our sages remark: one who lives truly takes the crowning speciality of each age into the next period. Hence the expression בא בימים “he comes home with his days”, his days are not spent and done with, he takes all the spiritual and moral acquisitions of his past days over with him into the coming days, and does not allow himself to be robbed by his years of anything that had been truly “his”. Sarah took the beauty of childhood with her into her womanhood, and the innocence of the twenty-years-old girl with her into the grave. How far and surely not to our advantage, does this point of view of our rabbis, contrast with that of our days! They look for beauty, not in the twenty year old but in the child, and innocence not in the child but in mature adolescence. We are accustomed to speak of “childish innocence”. It would be sad if childhood were to be enviable because of its innocence. Innocence assumes the possibility of guilt, to be not guilty implies to have had a struggle against the pull of one’s senses and passions and to have conquered, and only the girl matured to womanhood and the boy matured to manhood can crown their head with the wreath of innocence.

All these years are called חיי שרה, she lived in all of them, the whole of her hundred and twenty seven years existence was a life, a lively, cheerful, important, good life, no moment of it that she would have had to wish not to have been there, and still, the report concludes, this חיי שרה was only שני חיי שרה, years out of the life of Sarah, only one period, only one part of her life; for life is not measured by the span of time which is given to us to live here, צדיקים במיתתן קרויים חיים the righteous ones live on down here after their death, they go מחיל אל חיל to an ever progressing development. יודע ה׳ ימי תמימים “God”, it says in Ps. 37,18, “knows the days of those that live completely for Him”, there is no day, no moment, that is not recorded in God’s book, such a hundred and twenty seven years of life down here contains no day that is unimportant, but נחלתם their real heritage, לעולם תהיה, lies in the completely unlimited future; for, as our sages simply remark on this verse, it says שני חיי שרה (ב״ר) “these are but years of the life of Sarah”

V. 2. ויבא אברהם. This is usually taken to say: So Abraham came etc. so that he was not present at her death. And this is then explained that when he returned from the Akeida he found that his wife was no longer living. So little is the reward which was promised to the Patriarch to be measured by the joy and happiness he was allowed to enjoy here below. But this explanation has then to be supplemented by the supposition that, before he left Beer-Sheba to go to Moriah, Abraham had sent Sarah to Hebron to prevent her suddenly getting the painful tragic news of what he thought had to happen. But this whole supposition can be made unnecessary if one considers the real original meaning of בוא. The original meaning of בוא is, to betake oneself out of the open into the house, out of a public place into privacy. Thus, of Gideon (Judges Vi.19) וגדעון בא ויעש וגו׳; Is. 26,20, לך עמי בא בחדריך, Ez. 3,23 בא הסגר בתוך ביתך, “retire and shut yourself up in your house”. Thus also בא השמש the sun goes in, sets, in contrast to צאת השמש, comes out, rises So that here the meaning may simply be: — Abraham withdrew, shut himself in to mourn for his Sarah and to weep for her. He does not wear his heart upon his sleeve, makes no parade of his grief. Whether this is not indicated also by the small כ in לבכתה, we state as a possibility. We know what his Sarah had been to Abraham, how infinitely deep his grief must have been. He mourns, he weeps but he bears the pain in his heart, in the privacy of his home.

ספד, perhaps related to זבד, to apportion, to apportion to somebody that which he has accomplished in his life, to express his value. A similar conception to תנו לה מפרי ידיה (Prov. 31,31) בכה (related to בקע, to break out, to gush forth, also found referring to a spring issuing from the depths, בקעת מעין ונחל) (Ps. LII. 4,15) to weep, in tears one’s feelings stream out.

V. 3. ויקם ויאמר, he only left his dead in order to make arrangements for it; hence our sages lay down the law that as long as the dead be unburied, the relative is to think of nothing else than attending to the business of seeing that the dead receives its due. Until the burial is duly carried out, this, and nothing else at all, is to receive all his attention.

V. 4. גור ,גר, to be landless, not to be on one’s own land. גר ותושב: I have no right to your land, but I have lived amongst you for a long time. אחוזה: If this word is usually taken to designate property, because “the object is grasped” (from אחז) the explanation hardly fits the case. For אחוזה occurs exclusively referring to landed property which is just what can not be grasped. It is never used in connection with mobile property. Further when אחז is used for taking into possession, it is always expressed in the Niphal, והאחזו בה (Gen. 34,10), ויאחזו בה (ibid XLVI,27), ונאחזו בתוככם (Numb. 32,30). So that the object is not gripped by the owner, but the owner is gripped and held fast by the object, and that in fact is the case with the possession of land. Land holds its owner, he is chained to it, which is also why land can be a guarantee for its owner, and also probably why אין נשבעין על הקרקעות. By an oath a person sets himself and all that he possesses, all that can be considered as part and parcel of himself, under the punishing jurisdiction of God, if what he says is not true, or if he does not do what he swears to do. But only mobile possessions are really held by him, are at his disposal to be destroyed. Immobile possessions outlive their owner, he is considered as being held by them rather than the reverse. Hence he can not pledge the existence of the soil for the truth of his word.

So that the underlying idea of אחוזה is being settled, the act of permanent settling. Abraham does not ask for permission just to bury his wife. He wants his wife to rest in her permanent everlasting possession of her resting-place, that is why he first asks for the right to acquire a piece of land as freehold property for the purpose of a sepulchre. He had tarried for many years as an alien in the country and had never tried to acquire a single foot of land in it. For wandering was his calling. The necessity for burying his wife was the first cause that brought him the need to acquire the possession of land in the country. His wife’s grave was to be the first bond that attaches him to the land, the place that draws him to it and holds him: אחוזה.

V. 5.—6. The בני-חת consider the matter and let Abraham have their reply:- Although an alien, by his God-directed and godly activities amongst them for so many years he had gained such a high reputation as a נשיא אלקים in their midst, that, in truth he need not buy a piece of land to find a permanent grave for his wife. Let him pick out the very best grave in the land. Everyone would consider it such an honour, such a זכיה, to know that a Sarah, the wife of Abraham, was lying buried in his property, that not only would he not refuse to allow Sarah to be buried there, but that this grave would also remain untouched for all time. This seems to be implied in the לא יִכְלָא .לא יִכְלֶה would mean, nobody would close his graves to you, would not refuse to allow you to bury your dead there, but כלה means, to yearn for, so that it probably means to say: there is not one of us who would not long to have you bury your Sarah in his graveyard.

V. 7. לעם הארץ is probably used here in the same sense as in ואם העלם יעלימו עם הארץ (Levit. XX.4), where it does not refer to the people of the land or peasantry, but to the council, the representatives of the people who are empowered and in duty bound to punish crimes. In the same way here, to the representatives of the country who are entitled to grant aliens the right to acquire possession of land. Then לבני חת would also mean: for the Hittites, the council which acted for the sons of Heth.

בקצה שדהו. The cave was at the extreme end of the field, so that separating off the cave would in no way interfere with the use of the field. בכסף מלא etc. it seems that nevertheless, Abraham offered to pay the full value of the whole field for the cave, as the use to which he proposed to make of the cave might still possibly reduce the value of the field. As an alien, he did not dare to ask for permission to buy the field itself.

V. 11. Ephron had not understood Abraham, or pretended not to have understood him so as to make him declare his offer clearly and definitely. The actual meaning of his fine speech was probably: My intention is, that you should buy the field, but the cave, of that, I here and now publicly make you a present, so first bury your dead, and then afterwards we can come to terms about the rest. Abraham had only offered to buy the cave. But Ephron lets him know that he would only part with the cave to the buyer of the field.

V. 13. Abraham answers that he has already indicated that he was ready to pay the value of the whole field for the cave, he had the money all ready for that payment, there it was, he no longer considered it as his own, let Ephron pick it up, and the matter would be finished.
V. 14. It seems that the price of 400 shekels was such an enormous one that Ephron was ashamed to say it straight out personally and preferred to make it through a third party (לאמר לו I.L.).

V. 19. אל מערת המכפלה, not, as would be expected במערת וגו׳ this construction occurs only in one other instance: קברו אותי אל אבתי. Therein lies the thought that the particular place where it was wished that the burial was to be made had special value for the one who was to be buried there, or for those that belonged to him. It says that he is not just to be buried, but to be buried there. Now tradition says that Sarah was not the first to be buried in that cave. Adam and Eve already rested there. The parents of mankind were the first and they are to be joined by the parents of the Jewish people, those spiritual parents of mankind, that was why Abraham chose just this cave.

The place from which the cave had its name was called מכפלה and this name, from כפל double, points to some formation in pairs. It seems to have consisted of rows of double caves and so, by its natural formation to offer by itself a home for married couples who were united in death as they were in life, as indeed Adam and Eve, Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebecca, Jacob and Leah all found their last resting place on earth there. The first possession which the Jewish race received of their land was a row of pairs of graves which the first Jew bought to be used for his wife and then for himself and for his son and his grandson and their respective wives. The thought of the value of the family tie which attaches the heart of husband to wife, and children to parents was henceforth inseparably connected with the Jewish land, formed henceforth the fundamental trait of the character of the Jews, and enabled them to become what they became. Perhaps the name Hebron which henceforth was added to the place also came from this. For חברון means: the intimate union, the most appropriate name for the close intimacy which makes Jewish men and women grow together in unison as husband and wife, as father and mother. Centuries later, when their descendants had flourished into a great nation, no daily offering was allowed to rise from the height of Moriah in Jerusalem before the priestly herald at the turret of the Temple could see the rays of morn shining on the graves of the Patriarch and Matriarch at Hebron — כבוד אב ואם is for Jews the preliminary condition for, and the root of כבוד המקום. —

ואחרי כן, only after the place and its purlieus had become his permanent possession did Abraham bury his Sarah. Jews create no idolatry and make no parade of their feelings. They build no churches and mausoleums on their graves, nor do they deck them out as gardens. On the other hand they know no “time-limit”. The place where their dead rest remains holy to them for ever. The idea is strange to them which allows children to honour the graves of their parents with marble and everlasting flowers, and later generations to dig them all up, and, without thought or feeling, throw out the bones to nameless heaps.

Two remarks may still find room to be inserted here. Jews are reproached with nothing more than their propensity to “do business”, to buy and sell, to bargain. Then it is really remarkable that when the compilers of our laws look through the scriptures to illustrate the legal form for sale and purchase, they can only find two examples, one the purchase of a grave here — שדה עפרון — and the other the purchase of a field which Jeremiah was commanded to buy (and have the deeds of possession and the title to it legally endorsed and witnessed I.L.) at the time when the Babylonian armies had already overrun the country and were at the gates of Jerusalem, and the downfall of the state was imminent, all in order to fortify confidence in the future. So that the examples of “business” are only those before the beginning, and at the end of our national existence.

The legal form of Jewish marriage is also connected with this act of the acquisition of the field of Ephron. “The Jew buys his bride” is the reproach made by thoughtless tongues. Yes indeed, he buys his bride, but for that, she remains his “own”, and he honours in her, his highest, most precious possession. And well indeed would it be with us, if all our marriages were contracted having the memory of this sale in mind, and would remain penetrated with the spirit of a marriage as is represented by that of Abraham and Sarah which made its final impression by this “purchase of the cave of Machpelah”.

V. 1. This introductory sentence contains the summary of the life of Abraham. He was בא בימים ,זקן and God had blessed him בכל. His life’s work was finished, he had nothing more to strive for and to achieve, his one worry would be concerning his son and the household he would leave behind him.

זקן, probably related to סכן meaning to care for, סכנה danger, מסכנות, poverty indicate a basic meaning of being sensitive to, and appreciative of, external impressions, and hence very significant for sick-nursing, to watch for that which might be injurious to the patient, remedy them and keep them away. Hence also הסכן to do something with continuous devoted care. Then זקן would mean, one with much experience. Perhaps also related to זין, one who is armed, and זקן would be one who is armed with experience. It would be the opposite of נער youth, (the underlying concept of which is “shaking off, נוער כפיו מתמוך בשוחד, Is. 33,15) which easily “shakes off” impressions, has not yet learnt things from life, but still has the urge to develop everything by himself.

זקן, thus meaning mature experience is differentiated from the other term for age, ישן (from which שנה, sleep), designating worn-out energies, becoming sleepy and dull, hence also אישון, darkness. But זקן designates what has been gained in the achievement of life’s work, the maturity of the personality. Hence the words of our, sages: זקן זה שקנה חכמה or the more comprehensive saying: זה שקנה שני עולמים, who has conquered both worlds. Jewish wisdom always recognises to the full the value of life in this world as well as in the next, and declares that יפה שעה אחת בתשובה ומעשים טובים בעולם הזה מכל חיי העולם הבא, “one hour of moral spiritual progress and doing good deeds in this world surpasses the whole of the future life in Paradise”, although it adds that יפה שעה אחת של קורת רוח בעולם הבא מכל חיי העולם הזה “one hour of the quiet spiritual satisfaction of the next life is worth more than the whole of this life”. To it (Jewish Wisdom) זקן denotes one who, with his life down here, has acquired both these worlds, this one for the next, by the stamp of godliness which he has impressed on earthly life צדיקים ישכינו שכינה בארץ “the righteous ones prepare the world to be the home of the Divine”.

Thus, according to the same point of view, בא בימים means בא בדופלין he had gone through both, the earthly and the godly, material and spiritual; בא בפילון מפולש לחיי עוה״ב all the days of his life were for him פילון מפולש, a straight open road leading to the next world. He was not overcome by his years, he strode through the days, each one was a milestone marking progress on his path through life towards his final home.

ברך את אברהם בכל, our sages add to this the words of Isaac ואוכל מכל (Ch. 27,33) and those of Jacob יש לי כל (Ch. XXXII.11), and recognise in these three terms, בכל ,מכל ,כל, the quintessence of the lives of these three men: they say of them, שלשה הטעימן הקב״ה מעין עה״ב and these are they, אברהם יצחק ויעקב דכתיב בהו בכל ,מכל ,כל these three Patriarchs, different though their outward position in life, Abraham, the course of whose life took a continuous upward direction and culminated in his being regarded as a נשיא אלקים among the nations — in contrast, his grandson Jacob, who with but his staff in his hand had to wander away from his homeland to slave away at a tricky uncle — and between the two, his son Isaac, in whose life we see the beginning of the downward setting of the sun of good fortune and of the good will of his contemporaries: — To all three of them God nevertheless allowed a taste of the eternal beatitude of the next world, for all three were blessed down here with בכל ,מכל ,כל.

If we understand these words rightly, they mean to say that Abraham’s happiness was due to the fact that God blessed him בכל in and with everything. A man can be blessed with all prosperity, can be given everything, and still he, in himself can remain unhappy. Everything that he has prospered, but he himself is not שמח, does not “grow” (related to צמח I.L.) does not blossom internally. But Abraham did feel himself blessed, and “blossomed” through all his blessings.

The expression used by Isaac would be weaker, ואוכל מכל. It would correspond to the עוברים בעמק הבכא מעין ישיתיהו, “the righteous know how to change a vale of tears to a source of blessing”, שומר מצוה לא ידע דבר רע “he who looks on his whole life from the point of view of מצוה, of doing his duty, to him nothing is bad”. From the greatest trouble he extracts the duty which it entails, and fulfilling the duty, carrying out the task which misfortune brings makes him happy; — אוכל מכל, he “eats”, draws sustenance from everything.

The highest blessing, and at the same time one that can be obtained in every station of life, is Jacob’s יש לי כל, he has everything because he wants nothing more than what he has. Because altogether what he wants is “to do”, not “to have”. Thus, even in most depressing times as Jacob lived through (throughout his life he had troubles, Esau, Laban, loss of Rachel, loss of Joseph, loss of Simeon, and finally the worry of Benjamin I.L.) is content and finds happy satisfaction with life.

In Babe Bathra 16b. three more explanations are given to וה׳ ברך את אברהם בכל, which certainly require consideration. R. Meir: the blessing consisted in Abraham’s having no daughter. R. Jehuda the blessing consisted in Abraham having also a daughter. Others are of the opinion that he had a daughter whose name was בכל. Rabbi Eliezer Hammodai adds to this, that the fame of Abraham’s knowledge of astrology was so great that all the Kings of the east and west came to consult him daily. R. Simon ben Yochai: Abraham was ornamented with a precious gem, so that simply looking at him cured all illnesses. Now surely nobody could wish to say that the highest blessing can be to have no daughter at all. Apart from the fact that these same sages say that no marriage can be considered to have fulfilled its purpose until a son and a daughter have resulted from it (Yebamoth 61 I.L.), there could be no place more unsuited for making such a statement than just the very chapter the contents of which, Sarah and Rebecca — serve to glorify Woman more than any other. But all these sayings would say that בכל, that God had blessed Abraham “in all things”, showed itself just in that, i.e. in everything, even in such matters that without God’s special care would be likely to disturb the happiness of his life. Now just at this point where we see Abraham’s great worry to find a suitable wife for his only son — a worry to settle which he must have believed that he would have to trust to the quite special dispensation of God — the thought must come to one’s mind, what a worry, what a terrible, almost insolvable problem would have been presented to Abraham if he had had a daughter and would have had to look for a husband for her from out of the Canaanite or Aramaic men. A son of Abraham would be able finally to win even a daughter of Canaan or Aram over to himself to the spirit of an Abrahamitic home. But for the same reason an Abrahamitic daughter would be lost to the spirit and house of Abraham through a Canaanite or Aramaic husband. For a son carries on the paternal house, but a daughter goes over to the household of her father-in-law, who encompasses her as a protective wall (חמיה). Abraham would have to see his grandchildren born to idol worship if he had had a daughter. It was from this grief that R. Meir thinks God’s blessing in giving him no daughter, saved him.

R. Jehuda carries on with the same trend of thought, but thinks, on the contrary, that even in this point Abraham was blessed, not by the denial of, but by the granting of, a daughter. God did give Abraham a daughter, and he was blessed by her remaining “his” even in her marriage, and thereby formed a bridge between the isolated house of Abraham and the rest of the world. Abraham was thereby granted a blessing that would have remained unobtainable in his isolation, viz. to plant the Abrahamitic spirit in the non-Abrahamitic world.

But for that, other opinions say, there was no need of an actual concrete daughter. He had a daughter whose name was בכל. The fact that he was so visibly blessed in every direction, by which the eyes of the world were turned on him, and feelings of respect aroused and notice of his way of life was a still stronger means of establishing a bond with the non-Abrahamitic world, than even a daughter would have been.

This is then how R. Eliezer and R. Simon look at it. If Abraham had been poor, or even if had just possessed modest means, he himself would surely have been no less happy and contented, but he would have been unnoticed by the world in general. And if people had believed that his extraordinary good fortune was the result of his high morality, they would have gaped in admiration at him, but would have let him just go on in his own isolated way. For people do not come running to learn how to become moral. But his contemporaries believed that Abraham, like all men who had extraordinary success, owed his success to some secret knowledge and magic, and that drew the great ones from all corners of the world to come to him to consult him and get to know “the philosopher’s stone” from the successful recluse.

Finally, remarks R. Simeon, not only his material success, but his very personality was so strikingly impressive and so extraordinarily benevolent, that it alone was sufficient to draw suffering people to him.
In any case, by these sayings, our sages have given us an idea of the views about Abraham which must have been spread amongst his contemporaries.

V. 2. עבדו: he was subservient to him, was legally bound faithfully and exactly to carry out the wishes of his master. זקן ביתו: just as Abraham had become זקן, mature, by following the guidance of God faithfully in His service, so had Eliezer matured by his life in the house of Abraham and become completely absorbed in that life, and therefore was מושל etc., in the full meaning of the word (see Ch. 4,7) he appointed everybody and everything in the household to the position and task that it was to fulfil in accordance with the will of Abraham and in his spirit.

“Place, I pray thee, thy hand beneath my thigh” only occurs here, and once again when Jacob made his demand to Joseph (Ch. 47,29). It does not seem to have any reference to the Milah (to which it is usually taken to refer I.L.). The place is not the right one for that, it says תחת ירכי. Why does it not occur elsewhere as a sign of assurance? But ירך is that part of the body, which, on sitting down or lying down, first comes into contact with the ground (and in so far is the opposite of שכם, the shoulder, which, in rising from the recumbent position, is the first to be raised, from which we get the term השכים, to rise up in the morning), it is phonetically related to ירק and designates the end which is “thrown” to the back or underneath, the opposite to פנים, hence ירכתים, the back of a building. In the two instances in which it occurs it is a dying man, or one whose end is approaching, who exacts a promise from one who will outlive him, to carry something out, without which he feels he can not die in peace. So should not this שים נא ידך תחת ירכי be taken literally “Let me rest on your hand”? i.e. give me all the strength and power which lies in this hand, as a basis on which I can rest quietly depending on it. This way of taking it seems to be confirmed by the fact that the procedure of placing the hand under the thigh is not a part of the oath, but precedes it.

V. 3. ה׳, in Whose Hands the future rests. אלקי השמים ואלקי הארץ not אלקי השמים והארץ which might place God only indirectly in relation to the earth, the God of heaven Who is also the God of the earth, the earth being dependent on heaven, but the God Who is as directly the God of the earth as He is the God of heaven.

מבנות הכנעני, between a בת כנעני and a בן אברהם the spiritual and moral gulf is so great that they can never and in no wise be suitable for each other. Moreover the influence of a Canaanite wife on my son would be all the greater as “I dwell in the midst of the Canaanite people”. Not only the wife but her whole family and circle of friends and relations would have to be contended against. That this last sentence of Abraham does refer to the influence of the family is also evident by Eliezer later on, with great delicacy, changing the בקרבו to בארצו i.e. “in whose land I dwell, so that I know their ways and morals”. בקרבו would have been offensive: I come to you, because you live far away, if you lived near, we would not have you either!

V. 4. לבני ליצחק, two considerations are to guide Eliezer. In the first place לבני, that she is worthy to be the wife of my son, that one can feel justified in the hope that she will become my daughter even as he is my son. This would be the general consideration of her character. But two people can be of the most excellent character, and still not be suitable for each other. Hence, further, ליצחק, that she also fits in with Isaac’s personality. When Abraham rejected the daughters of Canaan, and wished for a girl from Aram for his son, we must remember that in Aram too, the people were idolators. So that his reason must have been, not the idolatory of Canaan but only the general moral degeneracy of the land. Idolatory is primarily an error of the mind, an intellectual error, which can be corrected and cured. But moral degeneration gets a grip on the whole nature of a person, on the whole depth of his feelings and thoughts, and there, even an Abraham could not hope to find a modest, morally pure, innocent girl for his son, who would bring with her the nobility of fine feelings and morals, as a pearl for his home.

Perhaps the לבני ליצחק might correspond to ארצי .לארצי ולמולדתי gives, as already remarked above on Ch. 12,1, the general tendencies, and מולדתי, the birthplace, the narrower, more special stamp of the family.

V. 5. אולי and אול, related to אפל ,אבל, all three having the concept of darkness. אפל, actual, physical darkness; אול, spiritual darkness, folly; אבל, darkness of mental clarity and cheerfulness, doubt and grief, mourning.

אבה, not to wish for something where the wish comes from oneself, that is called חפץ etc., but אבה means rather to conform to the wishes of somebody else, hence אניות אבה ships which are easy to manage, which respond quickly to the wheel (Job. 9,26). Hence also אביון, not so much one who is full of wishes, but one who has to conform to everybody else’s wishes, who has no independence.

V. 6. שמר .השמר לך פן, original meaning: to fend off. שמיר, the protecting thorn, which wards off. The שומר is to be a wall around that which is entrusted to him. השמר places the person under his own guard, guard yourself against something. But as, generally it refers to a care which has to be kept against oneself; although it is not to protect oneself against danger but to protect something else against danger arising through oneself, as the danger to the other thing, is, in the first place really endangering oneself, this deeper nuance is, as a rule, stressed by the addition of פן — .לכם ,לך (from פנה to turn): a direction, a possibility, literally, the way something might turn; hence “take care of yourself against the possibility that you might allow my son to return thither”. Guard yourself against such a possibility.

V. 7. Above in 5,3, at the oath, it says ואלקי הארץ also, for the one who is to swear, in accordance with the concept הִשָׁבֵעַ, places himself with all he possesses, under the punishing Arm of God if he should break his word, so that there the expression of the direct presence of God on earth is essentially pertinent. But when, as here, the expression of a complete confidence in God is made, expressing the true Jewish expectation of the direct special השגחה פרטית which leads a man to the right wife appointed for him, then Abraham refers to all that God had done specially for him and to him, in words which proclaim this השגחה פרטית as something far beyond that which would be expressed by the comparatively general term אלקי הארץ “The God of Heaven, Who none the less — not הוציאני, but לקחני — took me for His special purposes and Who דבר לי — not אמר לי which would have been a promise but דבר, made statements about me, such as ושמרו דרך ה׳ וגו׳ ,והיה ברכה — and Who נשבע לי gave me His Promise that my seed would have this land (true, He had neither directly forbidden me to give my son a wife from the present inhabitants of the land, nor to allow my son to return to my homeland, but both of which I recognise as the natural consequence of His promise and His mission), He — you can quietly depend on it — will send His angel — not אתך, with you but — לפניך, before you, you will have nothing to do, He Who knew how to find me out of my father’s house, will also see that you find the right girl for my son out of my relation’s house” — ולקחת in the same way as לקחני.

V. 8. But if, nevertheless, — for God forces nobody to act against their free will — the girl to whom you have been led is not willing to go with you, then you are freed from this, my oath, only do you nothing contrary to the Will of God. It is more important not to do wrong (and everything that we recognise as being against His will, is wrong) than to try and force right to be done through us. God sees to the means for right to be accomplished, only let us be careful not to do any wrong. This is implied in the ואם לא וגו׳, then you are free, you can do nothing more. Only do not think that then you are bound to do anything at all, and then perhaps something which would be even the reverse of God’s Will. Only do not take my son back there. A return of Isaac to the family in Aram would be giving up the whole of the Abrahamitic mission, which could only be accomplished in isolation. When Jacob returned there, the family home was still established in isolation in Canaan, and he returned to it at once after his children were born.
