נכה ,נקה ,נקית, Grundbedeutung schlagen, stoßen; נקה: alles Fremdartige völlig abgestoßen haben. טהר mehr die Durchsichtigkeit, die innere Reinheit, נקי die äußere, (siehe zu Kap. 20, 5): Dann bist du rein von diesem Eide, dann berührt er dich nicht mehr.

V. 10. As the departure on the journey is told, ויקם וילך, only in the second half of the verse, the וילך in the first half can not mean that he actually went away, but must belong to the preparations for it. The camels were not laden, they were meant for the bride and her attendants. They were riding camels, recognisable as such by their saddles and trappings. וילך but he went afoot and carried the presents. From Ecclesiastes 10,7 it seems that slaves never rode, one could recognise them as such by their always going on foot. On the return journey, too, he only walked and led Rebecca’s camel. Our ladies seem to have been no experienced riders but had to have their animals led, we find the same thing recorded of the Shunamite (II Kings, IV,24). So Eliezer travelled, not as a rich merchant with ten laden camels but completely as a servant, as a laden servant who had to take riding camels somewhere. For only so would the test which he had in mind to make of the character of the girl be a real one. The behaviour towards a tired over-laden slave that would show real humane feelings might have proved something entirely different if shown to a rich cavalier.
That the most valuable jewellery could be carried in quite a small box is, of course, quite evident.

According to our sages, Abraham’s camels were recognisable by the muzzles they wore to prevent them from eating from strangers’ fields. What they wanted to preach by this was, that Jewish greatness was not to be shown by indifference to other people’s property, but, on the contrary, by their greater consideration for it.

V. 11. ויברך from בֶרֶך the knee joint, in which the power and forces for moving forward are accomodated; analogous to ברך to bless and ברכה, a gathering of water or an aqueduct. אל באר, towards a well, not next to it. בַאֵר ,באר to make clear, in Kal, accordingly to become clear, to come to light out of the darkness.

V. 12. ה׳, Thou, Who art not only the old old Creator, Who laid the foundations of the world thousands of years ago, but Who art still מחיה every approaching moment, makes it come into existence, Whom I have quite specially learnt to know as such in the experiences of the life of my master, the further continuation of whose life is the matter here concerned with at the present moment:

הקרה נא. We have already indicated, not only the connection between the roots קרה and קרא, but that they are really identical. Nothing is farther from the Jewish concept of “מקרה״ than the idea “chance”, with which it is usually taken to be associated. When somebody speaks of כל הקורות or קוראות אותו, he refers indeed to moments of his life that he himself did not direct but which directed him; they were only events which were not expected, not reckoned on, not intended, but which, all the more, could be the most intentional messages sent by the One Who directs and brings about all things. נקריתי בהר הגלבע. “I happened to be on Mount Gilboa” (II Sam. 1,6) means: “I had been called there, it was not my special will or intention to be there, but some higher force led me there”.

This appears most distinctly when we are commanded to arrange a מקרה. In Numb. 35,11, speaking of the cities of refuge it says, והקריתם לכם, we are to appoint these cities in such positions in the country that they are easily accessible to the unintentional homicide, as is quite expressly said by תכין לך הדרך in Deut. 19,3 (see Makkoth 9b). The unfortunate one had certainly had no intention of committing his manslaughter just in the vicinity of a highway leading to a city of refuge, the whole fatal accident was indeed unintentional, that he did find himself near such a highway must certainly have seemed to him a lucky accident. But provision had been made beforehand that at certain fixed distances highways led to an עיר מקלט. So that Koheleth is perfectly right when he says that the wise ones and the fools מקרה אחד יקרה את כלם that the wise too, can not escape the מקרה; that the wisest, if you will, the cleverest, man has events in his life — perhaps even the greatest part of them are such — which he neither expected nor foresaw, and least of all that he intentionally brought about.

So that if here Eliezer prays: הקרה לפני, he is asking that God may take in hand the matter which had brought him hither, he, by himself could not bring it to its desired end. The addition of the word לפני expresses the wish that the direction for which he prays may be such that will further him along the path he has now reached, i.e. further the mission he had undertaken.

V. 14. Our sages (Tanith 4a) by no means recommend Eliezer’s procedure as an exemplary method for choosing a wife. Only an Eliezer, sent on such a mission by the confidence of an Abraham that God would send His angel already beforehand to lead him to the right girl, may act with such confidence. That his behaviour, which the Gemora (Chulin 95b) gives as an example of the formula for prohibited ניחוש, does not really come under that heading, is already explained by the ניחוש .ר״ן is making a decision, depending on happenings which have no rational connection with the matter concerned (e.g. deciding to undertake something because a black cat met you etc. etc. I.L.). But the sign by which Eliezer wanted to know the girl who was the destined wife for Isaac was one which belongs to the special traits of character, which, still today, are the most characteristic signs of the descendants of Isaac and Rebecca, and which we summarise under the heading of גמילות חסד. Of this love of fellowman, regardless of class distinction, everywhere and always ready to jump to help — which only slowly broke its way into the non-Jewish world through the direct and indirect influence and spreading of the teaching of the tenets of the Abrahamides — Eliezer had learnt in the house of Abraham, it was the most characteristic feature of his tent, and Eliezer felt that it must be prominently present in the right wife for Isaac and that such a tendency might be found in the family of Abraham, and it was on that, that he founded his procedure. But it must nevertheless have been rare, otherwise he could not have used it as a sure sign. — לעבדן ליצחק, with great delicacy he refers to Isaac as לעבדך not as לאדוני or לבן אדוני. Just the fact that Isaac himself, for whom he is seeking a wife, is עבד ה׳ makes him choose such a sign, and to hope that God will lead him to the right one. For it is for one who is dedicated to God’s service that he is seeking a wife, and the furthering of God’s Own purposes is dependent on the right choice.

V. 15. Abraham’s wish could hardly have been granted more fully. Bethuel was doubly related to him. Bethuel’s father was Abraham’s brother, his mother was Abraham’s niece and also a sister of Sarah. In this report it is really Milcah who is stressed, as also in Rebecca’s reply, Rebecca’s mother is not mentioned. She, the mother seems not to have come from Abraham’s family at all nor to have become imbibed with any of the Abrahamitic spirit. It seems that Rebecca took after her grandmother, while her brother followed the footsteps of his mother. The continuation of the story shows us that the two, mother and son, ran the household, but that Bethuel — more on the Abrahamitic side — probably looked on as an old good-hearted “Jew”, not keen enough on his own interests and money, was pushed in a corner.

V. 16. Possibly טובת מראה and יפת מראה have different meanings. The first denoting “a pleasing appearance”, more a spiritual beauty of the face, an impression of grace, indicating character, while the latter would be actual beauty. We would be certain that this assumption is correct were it not that it also says of Vashti that כי טובת מראה היא although this does not exclude the possibility that Vashti’s appearance too was pleasing and graceful rather than actually beautiful. Her refusal itself could well speak for spirit, and feelings of respectability.

והנערָ. With one single exception, the feminine ה is missing in the word נער in the Pentateuch, and it then includes קטנה a girl who has not yet reached puberty. The only place where it is written נערה is at מוציא שם רע (Deut. 22,19). Just to state that this law only applies to a grownup girl, i.e. one who is sexually mature, (see Ketuvoth 40b).

בתל ,בתולה, phonetically related to פתל and בדל which also mean to be sealed, closed up, to be separated — ואיש לא ידעה can not merely refer to her virginity, as this is already said by בתולה. Also it does not say לא ידעה איש as it does everywhere else, but ואיש לא ידעה which occurs nowhere else. So it means, not only was she בתולה which is identical with the usual לא ידעה איש but she was so extraordinary modest and retiring that איש לא ידעה that no man had dared to become intimately friendly with her. The truly modest Jewish girl has such a high innate morality and dignity that quite unconsciously she makes such an impression that the wildest boy does not dare to make nasty jokes in her presence and certainly not to approach her even with improper looks. This was certainly remarkable, especially in Aram.

V. 17.—20. וירץ העבד, not Eliezer, “the servant,” in the demeanour of a slave he hurried to meet her. He begs for just “a little water” to “gulp down”. She answers: “Drink”, and adds “my lord”, although he stands as a slave before her. And then, promptly step by step disclosed the woman who was worthy, with her Abrahamitic feelings, to take the place of Sarah. At first, not a word about the camels, as Eliezer had hoped. Only when she had completely quenched his thirst did she say: “For your camels, too, will I drew water until they will have completely drunk their fill”: Had Rebecca said this at once, a certain trait which characterises the true גומל חסד, and the true Jewish Woman, would have been missing. She would have been a conceited gossip who likes to make a big talk about her good deeds. And then she does not offer merely to give the camels also “a drink”. That, by itself, would already be quite a tiresome task, just to give each camel a jug-full would entail ten journeys down to the well and ten drawings up of the bucket. But no, she will draw and draw and fill the whole trough up until all the camels have drunk their fill! A camel drinks enough at a time to enable it to go for 3 days without water, perhaps it gets its name גמל from that fact. (A camel’s stomach is provided with pouches in which fluid is retained I.L.) And with it all, how nimble and quick she is, ותרץ ,ותמהר, she does not think long about it, and is not slow or dilatory when it is a matter of doing humane work. What Eliezer had left in the pitcher, she carefully empties into the trough. She could have left it in or thrown it out. But the Jewish nature is as economical with its forces and means as it is extravagant with them. Just because to it, even the tiniest means for doing a מצוה is fulfilling a duty, everything is holy to it. It will not waste uselessly the smallest expenditure of energy nor the tiniest drop of water. But, on the other hand, for a good purpose it knows no limit to what it will spend of its forces and means.

V. 21. שאה ,משתאה fundamental meaning: bleak, dull, desert, from that, unclearness of mind, השתאה ל-, to stop in wonder, to gape in astonishment. The immediate fulfilment of his prayer surpassed all his expectations. He wanted to say more, but restrained himself until he had finally ascertained whether the girl who had so marvellously fitted in with all previous ideas would also conform to Abraham’s conditions as to her parentage. משתאה, stat. const, “he was a gazer in astonishment”, he just gaped at her in wonder.

הצליח, from צלח related to שלח, to set something in motion towards a goal. The צ sound introduces the nuance of overcoming difficulties so that צלח means to attain a goal by overcoming all the opposing difficulties. Thus of the progress of fire which nothing can stop: פן יצלח כאש בית יוסף (Amos V.6) הצליח to make something successfully achieve its purpose. Perhaps סלח is also related. A sinful man deserves to be frustrated in the progress of his life. To allow him, nevertheless to progress to a new future, to grant him this progress again, is called סלח.

V. 22. ויקח. It does not say that he gave them to her yet. In his story in V.47, he also says that he only gave her the jewellery after she had told him who her family was. But he thought it just as well to bring it out already, to let her see some of the riches which he had with him. He now wanted to ask for lodging in her home. Eliezer knew the world, anyway the Aramitic world, otherwise he would not have found גמילות חסד something special, or showing special character. For the readiness to take in ten camels and the men attendant on them, it was necessary to find, not merely an Abrahamitic daughter but a whole Abrahamitic house. The girl was certainly a pearl in humaneness but who could tell in what metal the jewel was set. In any case Eliezer thought, that before he asked about her home, and the possibility of being received there, it was just as well to allow some gold to be seen. Who can say, also, whether Rebecca — as an understanding girl who knew full well the character of her brother, who ran the home, and who would scarcely have offered a friendly welcome to a number of mere servants and camels — would have given Eliezer her name at all if she had not seen something shining in his hand, which, certainly not for herself, but for the ruling spirit of her home, would have a somewhat greater attraction than just an opportunity of exercising humane hospitality. That Eliezer omitted this little incident when recounting the story in her parents’ house, and only mentioned the appearance of the presents as coming after the information given concerning her family and home, is again an example of the fine feelings and delicacy which characterised Eliezer’s behaviour and speech throughout the whole story.
V. 23. הגידי נא. He hardly expected that the girl would just tell this to a strange man, so he repeats his question more pressingly.
V. 24. She mentions Milcah and Nahor, being brother and sister of Abraham, as names likely to be known.

V. 25. Here again her delightful nature shows itself. Her first thought is for animals whom she has just relieved of their thirst and how refreshed they are, “well they have drunk, let them now have something to eat”. (It has been ascertained that 5 camels in two drinks a few hours apart, drank 140 gallons of water. Ten camels in the first drink would accordingly store away at least 140 gals, probably much more. The loving task which our Rebecca so happily undertook, going down to the well, lowering and raising the bucket, going to and fro and filling the trough with more than 1120 pints of water, was indeed no light one. I.L.). Her feeling for the poor thirsty animals was still pulsating through her. יודע צדיק נפש בהמתו “A righteous man understands the feelings of his animal”. (Prov. 12,10), hence in Judaism no society for the prevention of cruelty to animals is necessary, our ancestress Rebecca looked after that.

V. 26. קידה is bowing the head down to the ground without bending the knees, making as deep a bow as possible and means to submit your head, your mind completely to the one to whom you bow. השתחויה, prostrating the whole means placing the whole body, the whole of yourself at the disposal of the one before whom you prostrate yourself. Thus the people received the command to hand down to their children the meaning of the Pesach, with קידה and השתחויה (Ex. 12,27). Thereby they undertook to devote mind and body to this educational task as the positive duty of a Mitzva. Similarly Moses when the deepest revelation of God’s mode of management was vouchsafed to him (ibid. XXXIV,7). Here, too, Eliezer first bows his mind before the management and guidance of the Divine Providence which had so clearly been demonstrated to him, and then gives himself up entirely to it. He bows his own mind before the All highest Mind that had looked into his heart and that had sent Its angel ahead of him.

V. 27. חסד ואמת. What אהבה is in feelings, חסד is in deeds, love translated into action. אמת is, to a certain extent, a restricting, or at least a limiting addition. חסד ואמת is an act of love where the love does not run too close to overlooking the truth (not allowing one’s heart to run away with one’s head I.L.) Human love is blind. It is inclined to accede to the wishes of the beloved one without considering the true worth of these wishes. God’s Love is חסד ואמת, it only grants such wishes in which the truth is conserved, which truly do lead to happiness. Thus with Jacob (Ch. 47,29) the care for his burial in general is an act of חסד, the limitation, the observing the condition “but not in Egypt”, is the אמת. So, too, what the spies were to do for Rehab was a חסד ואמת, a conditional act of kindness (Jos. 2,14).

So perhaps here too. To see their children married is the dearest wish of parents. If they try to accomplish it at all costs, without consideration of the true essentials (if it is not with a girl with an Abrahamitic disposition, well then we will take one from ענד אשכל וממרא or from ארם) then they are endeavouring to do חסד without אמת. But Abraham wanted only חסד together with אמת and both were granted to him by God.

אנכי בדרך וגו׳. Had he not so conscientiously completely entered into the spirit of Abraham’s views and wishes, Eliezer’s task would have been quite an easy one. The country and family of Abraham were well-known, and it was unthinkable that the match-maker for the son of Abraham, such a renowned rich man, would receive a refusal anywhere. But Eliezer was זקן ביתו ,עבד אברהם, he was looking for a wife for לעבד ה׳ ,יצחק, and so the danger of finding a wife who was not the right one was greater, the more he could expect to be welcomed with open arms by all parents with marriageable daughters. Hence he felt that he would have to leave himself entirely to the guidance of God. And how that was granted to him! He was still on the way — had not yet arrived — and found himself already at his journey’s end! That was why he vowed with ברוך ה׳ to leave himself further in this matter entirely to the guidance of God.

V. 29. ושמו לבן. A cutting remark of our sages hereon says: there was nothing לבן about him except his name! אל האיש, Eliezer no longer appears as עבד until he declares himself as such later on (in V.33).

V. 30. This is a peculiar verse. It has already said that he had run out to the well, and now it says: when he saw the nose-ring etc. and heard the words etc. then ויבא, then he came etc. So that the whole seems to be one continuous story, and this verse seems to be the antecedent clause to the concluding sentence which follows (V.31). The whole household saw the jewellery, but while they were busy looking at it, (it does not say כראותו) to Laban the sight of gold at once exercised its magic: “Ha, there will be more where this comes from, if this is what he pays for a drop of water, what will it be for board and lodging!” So the speculative brother takes his sister aside and hears the whole story in detail again, and then hurries out that nobody should get ahead of him, expecting to find him just outside. He is not a little surprised to have to run to the well, and there (הנה I.L.) is quite confounded to find a man, who, according to all he has heard and seen, must be a gold-scattering Croesus, still modestly and patiently waiting with his camels at the well. That is why he does not bow, does not speak politely, — as Abraham and Lot did, when inviting strangers — he had already lost respect for him, and says somewhat abruptly: Come on, come in, what are you shy about, you are, after all, a ברוך ה׳ i.e. a rich man, blessed with wealth. This is also apparent in verses 32 and 33.

V. 32.—33. Eliezer had to look after the camels himself — perhaps also for himself and his men — the subject is doubtful — ויישם (from ישם, like טוב and יטב) and יושם, the way it is written and the way it is to be read shows that the food was just placed before him with distinct uncertainty to what extent Laban assisted thereat. All this proves how Laban felt, through Eliezer’s modest behaviour, that it was not a rich man himself that he was dealing with, and shows the character which we recognise again later in his more advanced age.

It seems remarkable to find the name ה׳ in the mouth of Laban, especially as later he calls only on אלהי נחור (XXXI,53). It is possible that Rebecca heard Eliezer saying ברוך ה׳ אלקי אדוני וגו׳, and had repeated it in her report to Laban, so that the latter already knew to which “religious sect” Eliezer belonged. That the name of God, or of any god, seems fluent in the mouth of a Laban need not surprise us, it is quite in keeping with his character: The more irreligious at heart, the more the speech is decorated with “pious phrases” — ויאמר דבר Laban always leads the conversation, either by himself or anyway before his father or mother.
V. 34. Your feelings are perfectly correct. I am not the master only the servant.

V. 35.—48. It is interesting to note the account of the story as recounted by Eliezer, and compare it with the preceding report of what actually happened. The reason for all the little differences can at once be seen to be based, either on considerations of politeness, to which we have already referred above, or to make it more plausible to his hearers whom Eliezer seems to have perfectly understood. The הקרה נא and all his worry about the success of the enterprise, which might have seemed to his hearers to be somewhat far-fetched and exaggerated, and have made them mistrustful, he left out. With a certain class of people it is dangerous to appear too full of feelings, they call it “romantic”, “exaggerated”, and are apt to have doubts of the solid practicability of the project into which they are invited to enter. So Eliezer satisfied himself with just sharply stressing the striking evident dispensation of Divine Providence in this matter, against which even a Laban, from his point of view, would be loath to offer opposition.
V. 49. חסד :חסד ואמת that you will give him your daughter for his son; אמת that you agree to his condition that, neither now, nor in the future, Isaac is to come to you to the homeland of his father.
V. 52. Here, for the only time in the whole chapter, he is given the title עבד אברהם. Now he has really accomplished his mission as Abraham’s עבד and feels himself completely and truly as such.

V. 53. מגדנות. One is not justified in taking this here to refer to anything other than delicious fruit etc. and not to precious valuable gifts. מגד from which the word clearly comes, only occurs in this sense, and מגדנות where it is mentioned with other gifts, as in Chron. II. 21,3, and Ezra 1,6, always comes last in the list, and so is certainly not the most valuable. He gave precious gifts to the young bride, confectionery, polite attentions, to the mother and brother, to the father — nothing! This is worth noting. What a lot of rubbish has not been read into, and attributed to our Jewish past. Travellers reports, and tales of the present-day customs and habits of the oriental — according to the axiom “nothing changes in the East” — have been laid down as the pattern according to which one understands Jewish life in the past to have been. The מהר ומתן, which is sometimes referred to, is at once taken to be the buying price which is paid to the parents with which to buy the bride. Here we have an “oriental” marriage in question, but Eliezer, gives the father nothing, and the other members of the family only get little marks of attention of small value. (Incidentally can be mentioned how hurt Rachel and Leah felt that Laban allowed himself to be paid for them, and after twenty years had not forgotten כי מכרנו).

V. 59. אחתם. Bethuel still keeps significantly in the background, Laban, the brother, rules the house, so that it is not so much a daughter as a sister who is leaving. What a contrast to the home of Abraham, where Isaac, a son forty years old leaves the most sacred occasion, on which the future of his whole life depends, entirely to his father’s arrangements and keeps himself in the background.

מנקתה her wet-nurse. Here, too, we see a closer relationship. Really it was the mother’s pride to nurse her baby herself as we know of Sarah. Where this was not the case the baby was not suckled merely for payment, but the woman who had fed her at her breast remained for her whole life attached to her.

V. 60. These words in the mouth of people of the type of Laban and his mother are only understandable, if we take it that they knew of the destiny foretold of Rebecca, that she would become the ancestress of a great nation, and also of the destiny of that nation. That this expected future of the house of Abraham was well-known, we have already seen in the visit of Abimelech after the birth of Isaac (see above XXI,22).
V. 61. ויקה העבד. Rebecca and her attendants rode, but Eliezer led Rebecca’s camel and went on foot.

V. 62. בא מבא does not occur in the whole of תנ״ך, “come from coming”. בא really means “to come there”, there where one belongs, where one feels at home, is attracted thither. So that he must have been at some place to which he felt drawn, מבא, and then, he must have come to some other place to which he now felt drawn, now felt at home. And to where had he gone? To באר לחי ראי! Now we know that well which had received its name from a colleague of Eliezer, who, driven from Abraham’s house by her urge for freedom had so named it. For there she had recognised, that, when and where everything on earth seems dead to us, “a Living One still sees us”. And it was there, that concerning the elder brother of Isaac, the providence and management of God had been revealed to a servant of Abraham. Is it then not extremely likely that, while Eliezer — also a servant in the house of Abraham — had gone away, in the hopes of God’s watching and guiding Providence, to undertake a step which, more than anything else, would be a fateful decision for the whole of Isaac’s future, — accordingly, although in quite different circumstances, still quite parallel to the position of Hagar and Ishmael — that Isaac, the one who was most concerned in the matter, should feel drawn to the place that could strengthen his confidence that God would act for him, would make His proximity apparent to Eliezer, just as He had done to Hagar for his elder brother. But, thereupon, he again longed to go back home, to the place where his family life was to blossom. For the well lay at the edge of the desert. והוא יושב בארץ הנגב. It seems that Isaac was already living on his own, and indeed in the Negev. Whereas Abraham had already lived for many years amongst the other nations, he found it good for Isaac, who was again at the beginning of life, to do as he had done at first, and live quietly in isolation (see on Ch. 20,1).

V. 63. שיח (from which we get שיחים, trees, plants), denotes the inner growth of spirit and feelings, gathering thoughts and feelings (cf. צמח = שמח ,צוץ = שוש). Like התפלל steeping one’s inner self with thoughts and feelings of purity and integrity (= התבלל). Our sages explain it here as being actual praying, like באים — שפוך שיח coming to his home.

V. 64. Undoubtedly Eliezer had taken the opportunity of talking to her of Isaac all through the journey, that would be only natural, so that she recognised him at once, so there is no necessity to think of any “intuitive presentiment”. She could also have recognised the field from its description, and from the manner in which Isaac just came to meet them there, have concluded that here was the owner.

ותפל, an intentional quick dismounting from the camel, as we find it said of Naamon ויפל מעל המרכבה לקראתו (II Kings 5,21) out of respect for Elisha, yea, for his servant. In the same way here too we can understand the feeling that Rebecca did not wish to meet Isaac, mounted. A proud lady would certainly have found something in it, to come riding stately to meet him at the head of a troop of followers and allow herself to be gallantly lifted down by her future husband. Especially as Isaac was not riding but on foot she did not find it seemly for her to ride towards him. Moreover riding seems to have been a sign of quality and Rebecca did not want to meet Isaac as an aristocratic lady. All this, however, was not a matter that she had thought out beforehand (in which case such modesty might not be so far off from pride) but ותפל, it happened quite spontaneously, without previous consideration, was just the instantaneous result of a correct feeling.

V. 65. ותתכס. Only then did she veil herself. Another piece of “orientalism” gone! And this is again a proof of how much we have to be on our guard to note everything which is so incontrovertibly and positively told us about these matters.
צעיף root is צעף probably related to שאף, to withdraw into oneself, similar to בלע to swallow up, and to withdraw from sight by covering up.

V. 67. Again a principle which, thank God, has not disappeared from the descendants of Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebecca. The more she became his wife the more he loved her! Like this marriage of the first Jewish son, Jewish marriages, most Jewish marriages, are contracted, not by passion but by reason and judgment. Parents, relations and friends consider which young people are really suited to each other, bring them together and then love grows more and more, the more they get to know each other. But most non-Jewish marriages are made by what they call “love”, and one has only to glance at the novels depicting life to notice what a gulf there usually yawns between the “love” before marriage and after, how rapid and insipid everything then seems, how different from all the glamour one had imagined etc. etc. Such “love” is blind, every step into the future brings disappointment. But of Jewish marriage it says: ויקה את רבקה ותהי לו לאשה ויאהבה. There the wedding is not the culmination but the seed, the root of love!

And then four more words, which, since God led Eve to Adam, until the end of time, nothing more glorious has been said וינחם יצחק אחרי אמו. A man, forty years old who is inconsolable for the death of his old mother, does find himself consoled again by his wife. And to what wretched drivel does all the talk about oriental sensuality and harem life which people like to impose on Jewish married life too, shrink. With Sarah’s death the whole spirit of a home, the whole feminine sweetness and feelings disappeared from the house. Isaac found his mother again in his wife (hence also “to him it was as if his mother was again in the tent, when he introduced Rebecca therein”). This is the highest tribute that has ever been paid to the nobility, to the worth of Woman — and it is on a page of the most ancient Jewish history that it is written.

V. 1. That Abraham married again is not so surprising when we remember that he lived thirty-five years longer after Sarah’s death, more than the average length of married life nowdays. Apart from that, our sages teach that a man is not “whole” without a wife, the task of a human being is at all times too great to be able to be fully accomplished by one person alone. According to Reb Yehuda (ב״ר) Ketura is only another name for Hagar, the same wife whom Sarah had led to him. Thereby one can not overlook how pure and human our sages regarded a relationship which later on is regarded as sad and depressing. Isaac, they say, went to the well in the desert to bring Hagar to Abraham to be what we call his “step-mother”. And still he had loved his mother so much. And when he went there he was still inconsolable for the loss of his mother! Now whether one takes this as an actual historical happening or whether the story was meant to be merely a means of teaching, in any case it shows — and in the latter case, even more forcibly — the point of view which was prevalent in the time of our sages. How much lower does even our present day aspect sink in which the relation of a second wife to grown-up children of the father tends to be strained if not actually hostile. According to Reb. Yehuda the ויוסף ויקח means “he took again”, and על פי דבור, following the same Divine command which previously had ordered him to obey Sarah who had demanded that Hagar be sent away. Hagar had lived since then as קטורה (קטר, Chaldean for knotted, tied up) closed up and lonely, without connection with any other man (her name Hagar, related to הגר ,אגר has a similar meaning) otherwise probably Abraham would not have been allowed to take her back.

V. 3. אשורם etc. seem to be, as Onkelos takes it too, not proper names, but the names of tribes, expressing their national characters, אשר, walking straight forward from which אשורים would come, those who walk straight ahead, living in the plains. לטושים from לטש to sharpen, perhaps living individually armed, able to look after themselves.

V. 6. Even as מלא דמלא, as in all our codices, this word פילגשים can only refer to the sons of Ketura. Otherwise nothing would be told us of the provision made just for these. The word אשר refers to בני and not to פלגשים. “To the pelagshim-sons of Abraham, etc. — they only had the rights of children of pelagshim, for Ketura was only a pelegath. Comparison with the four-lettered words, רטפש ,פרעוש ,עכביש ,חרמש ,חלמיש shows us that ש is added to the root as a formative letter. Thus חלם: strong, חלמיש, granite; עכב to hold fast, עכביש, a spider, חרם to destroy חרמש, a sickle; פרע, free; פרעש, a flea; רטף damp, רטפש, foul. So also פלג to be half, פלגש a wife who has not complete legal rights. פלגש is a condition — whether established by קידושים or ייחוד (the law is undecided) — in which the moral, personal bond between husband and wife is established, but there is no כתובה i.e. she has no legal claim to his fortune or possessions, etc.

That, in the lives of an Abraham and Isaac, we find only a few, chosen children were fit to receive not only מתנות, but also נחלה, the whole spiritual heritage, כל אשר לו, from the father, that, whereas in later times it is demanded and expected, that all children should follow the spiritual footsteps of their parents, that even an Abraham did not succeed in educating all of them in this, may not be surprising when we consider that Abraham and Isaac were in conflict with the whole of their contemporary world. Outside Abraham and Isaac’s tent there was not a single inch of the world for the spirit and morals of the covenant of Abraham so that the education of the home had to paralyse the weight and example of the whole of the contemporary world. How difficult even in the present day, are our parents finding it to bring up all their children in their own Jewish ways compared to a hundred years ago, and still our children can find other houses beyond their own four walls in which the atmosphere and spirit is equal to their own homes. And in any case this sending away of Ketura’s children was also in accordance with God’s stipulation כי ביצחק יקרא לך זרע. According to the way our sages take it the מתנות include spiritual gifts which they took out with them into the world from Abraham’s house, but which later on became misused and muddled and lost their original purity.

קדמה. He sent them eastwards, to the land of the east. The land promised for the Abrahamitic future is the extreme western point of the land of the east, on the border line of the orient and the occident. To the west lie the European countries, on which they were first of all to plant that of which Isaac’s descendants were to be the bearers. Everything spiritual and moral, enlightening and ennobling which mankind has obtained has come from this border. שם and יפת, Judea and Greece the two lands from which the culture and religion of the nations have emanated lie here, close together “in the navel of the world”. From there the path of culture and enlightenment and civilisation went westwards. Ketura’s children were sent eastwards. Only later would they enter this spiritual moral future.

V. 7. ימי שני חיי etc., see above Ch. 23,1. Abraham, too, lived days and years, every day full of importance and all together one individual whole and every period of life completely fulfilling its own significance. And yet all this were only days and years of the real life of Abraham which extended beyond the span of his earthly stay. It is peculiar that in Hebrew, large numbers of things are put in the singular, small ones in the plural. With years it is the same as with all large numbers. He who has a million pounds does not count single ones, who only has a little, every penny. So it is with years. When one has not lived up to ten, can not yet group the years into a decade, one looks on them in the plural, שנים, but when they can be grouped together they appear also as a unit שנה.

V. 8. (ויגוע וימת see on Ch. 7,21 I.L.) זקן ושבע, mature and satiated, he had reached all that was humanly possible to attain spiritually and morally and in his external life, the fulfilment of his wishes. Our sages take this word to describe death in terms that think of death more deeply and more beautifully than have ever been expressed as a human thought: — “When a צדיק dies, God allows him to get a glimpse of the bliss that is awaiting him, and this feeling of beatitude is so overpowering that the righteous one becomes שבע “filled to satiety” with its plentitude, falls asleep and dies”.

האסף אל עמיו ,ויאסף, with this term, which has become so general, a thought is expressed in our vernacular to which we can point with pride against those people who have the arrogance to declare that “in the Old Testament the dogma of immortality is not taught, that is a prerogative of the New”. Certainly it was not taught in the Old Testament but that is because there was no necessity to teach it. The people who speak of their dead as נאסף אל עמיו, where individuals speak of themselves: הנה אני נאסף אל עמי, to them the thought of immortality was so common, the denial of it lay so much out of their whole trend of thought, that it would have been quite absurd to want to make “the belief in immortality” something that had first to be taught to them. So that these people are on an incomparably higher level than those to whom this truth had to be taught as a “dogma”, and bolstered up in the minds of the people with so-called “proofs”. Also, “And the dust returns to the earth as it was: and the spirit returns unto God Who gave it” is not quotation from the New Testament but from the old, Ecclesiastes (Ch. 12,8), and there, too, it is not given as a sermon, but this description of human dissolution is inserted as a well-known fact. It was only when sects who were affected with un-Jewish ideas commenced to deny the immortality of the soul that the doctrine of immortality began to be preached and taught. Yea, the existence of God Himself is not taught in the תורה but is simply taken for granted: בראשית ברא אלקים! Further, it must not be forgotten that the idea of immortality is not peculiar to either Judaism or Christianity. No nation has yet existed in the world, — philosophers have wriggled out of this fact, as they have done out of many others — there has not yet been any race which has not believed in life in some form existing after death. The Jewish People spoke of the dead being נאסף אל עמיו long before the funeral, the קבורה always only came afterwards, the real person himself had already departed long before and gone to join “his people” who had preceded him, when one buried his earthly body in the earth.

Moreover the word אסף designates receiving a strayling into sheltering protection, and of an expelled one back into his original home — ואספתו אל תוך ביתך, (Deut. 22,2); עד האסף מרים (Numb. 12,15). According to that “האסף״ regards the next world as the real home to which mankind belongs, and this world, the testing years of wandering abroad, out of which at the end of the wandering, the soul returns home and is received in the waiting cricle of those to whom it belongs.

Now it is characteristic that it never says האסף אל אבותיו but always האסף אל עמיו with the single exception in Judges 2,10 referring to the contemporary generation of Joshuah. Otherwise it always says שכוב עם אבותיו and האסף אל עמו. One is buried to parents, there the child comes to its father and mother. Up above, there are no “children”, there, all are one family, there, there is no “father and mother”. That relationship remains behind. Up above the soul finds only similar souls who had been breathed into outer casings down here by the One Father, and they, as soon as these casings fall off become “gathered up” to their related souls. In contrast to this we find הכרת הנפש מעמיה. Only such souls are accepted in that circle who, down here, have not been unfaithful to the mission they shared with the company of souls to which they belonged. Perhaps it is not unintentional that it says in Judges II. 10 that וגם כל הדור ההוא נאספו אל אבותיו to contrast it to the following generation, of which it says in V.12 ויעזבו את אלקי אבותם. The generation which was buried with Joshuah remained faithful to the traditions of its fathers, they could be gathered up above to the עמים who, on earth, had been אבותם. But not so the following generation who were unfaithful to the mission handed down to them by their fathers.
V. 9. אל מערת See above on XXIII,19.

V. 10. The title of acquisition is repeated again and again, because this was the only human guarantee the children had that their fathers recognized this land as their land, and therefore had bought their permanent resting-place there.
V. 11. Up till then the blessing which Isaac enjoyed was only a part of the blessing granted to Abraham. Now God blesses him on his own account.

V. 12. We only find the word תולדות written מלא דמלא, completely “full”, with the ו of the root as well as the ו of the plural, twice, viz. אלה תולדות שמים וארץ (Gen. 2,4) and אלה תולדות פרץ (Ruth 4,18); at Esau the radical is missing, everywhere else the ו of the plural, here, at Ishmael both are missing. This certainly is not without meaning. Perhaps the missing ו of the root indicates some deficiency in the begetting, something lacking internally, that of the plural in the extension, the expansion, the increase in number and spreading. The products of heaven and earth resulting from the Divine laws of nature are complete and perfect both intensively and extensively. Equally, the descendants of Perez on whom the Jewish hopes of the salvation of mankind are placed. The numerous descendants of Esau are great extensively, but their inner, spiritual, moral selves are still deficient. The word occurs once in reference to Jacob’s offspring also with the ו of the root missing (Ch. 37,2), but that is just where, by their sin against Joseph, the fact that the sons of Jacob were still lacking in moral perfection, becomes apparent, and the process of remedying the deficiency (by their immersion in the melting-pot of the slavery in Egypt I.L.) had its beginning. The descendants of Ishmael had neither the extensive greatness of Edom nor the intensive greatness of Isaac, hence תלדת.

V. 13. This repetition of ואלה שמות and then once again נשמתם etc. is striking. From V. 16 we see that those who are named here were נשיאים, princes. According to that, these names were known as the names of the tribes of the Ishmaelites, and what it says here is, that these well-known names of the Beduin tribes were originally the names of the sons of Ishmael.

V. 16. בחצריהם ובטירתם. We have already remarked on the tenacity with which the two characters of the father and mother have clung to the descendants of Ishmael (see on Ch. 16,14 I.L.). In their spirit and intelligence they are sons of Abraham, in morals and the urge for freedom, sons of Hagar, they do not submit to the constraint of towns nor to the power of absolute rulers. They lived in חצרים in contrast to walled towns. חצר, related to עזר; the חצר of the Tabernacle became the עזרה (the assistant, auxilliary room I.L.) of the Temple. חצר seems to mean an accessory place, that surround of the residence which is at the disposition of its inhabitants for their homely requirements and work. The more that people were wedged in cities, the more they were cut off from Nature, the greater becomes the contrast between town and country (see above at Cain Ch. 6,17). חצרות, where everybody has the piece of land which he requires around his house. He has everything he needs, in his tent and in the surrounding subsidiary grounds, he is self-contained and independent. Later on, the style of building homes around חצרים — open spaces for auxillary uses — was introduced to the cities in the orient, where, then, as a rule, several houses were built to a common טיר — .חצר a strong form of דיר the sheep-pen, hence, enclosed by strong walls and bulwarks.

נשיאים. At the people of Ishmael and Israel, princes are called נשיאים, at those of Edom אלופים. In general the word נשיאים means clouds (Ps. 135,7, Jer. 51,16 et alia) and that gives us the purest conception of princes. All that a cloud is, has been obtained from the earth, and all that it has received from earth, it receives only to use it for the benefit of the earth, to return it to the earth in the blessing of rain. Such is the true Jewish prince, whom Koheleth describes (Eccl. 2,12) as one את אשר עשוהו, whom the people have made, i.e. who had already been prominent out of the company of the noblest and best of the people. It is a piece of luck for a nation when its prince is “a cloud”, a נשיא. A נשיא in this sense is a necessity, without it no nation, no community, can flourish. Through him the combined forces of the people are concentrated to a purpose, but this purpose, with a נשיא is not the welfare and prosperity of the prince, but the weal of the people. Just as a cloud returns all it has received back to the earth, so does the true prince return beneficially all the power and abundance which has been transferred to him from the people, back to the people.

In contrast to that is the אלוף, the prince who absorbs all the strength of the nation for the increase of his own power, a chief, a master, through whom the individuals do not become stronger, but weaker. In Hebrew the word אלף has bad cousins, it is related to עלף, weak, to faint, עלב in Rabbinic Hebrew, to put to shame, to hurt, mortify, even חלף, to be entirely absorbed by someone else, to disappear. Accordingly, such leaders, towards whom the followers lose all independence and personal meaning. Such אלופים are not wanted in Jewish circles. Not for nothing does our Jewish National hymn proudly sing. “Our אלופים are the heaviest burdened” — אלופינו מסובלים — the greatest national burden rests on them. They really pay the heaviest tax! And the אלופי יהודה (they only appear under such a denomination in Zach. 12,5 & 6) feel themselves strong only by the spiritual support and assistance of their people, they say: אמצה לי יושבי ירושלים בה׳ צבאות אלקיהם.

V. 18. וישכנו, a lower degree than וישבו, designates a rather temporary settling down, more corresponding to the normal life of the Ishmaelities. — על פני כל אחיו וגו׳ see Ch. 16,12. נפל, to alight somewhere where one does not belong, whither, through the ordinary course of events, one would not have reckoned to come. Thus, of the נפילים, as if they had dropped from the skies. So here from groups of people, who live wherever it happens to please them “as if they had dropped there”.

V. 19. When we consider how exactly the descent, relationship and origin of Rebecca is repeated in the next verse, the repetition of the short notice: אברהם הוליד את יצחק need not surprise us. This difference in the lineage of the two parents can account for, be the deep-lying cause of, all that follows.

V. 20. Not for nothing are we told that Isaac was already forty years old when he married Rebecca. Much as it was Abraham’s dearest wish and anxious worry that Isaac should get the right wife, he still waited till he was forty years old, although, at his advanced age, he could not know how much longer he would live. But just this delay would have arisen from the same cause. Isaac’s character was first to reach full virile independence and maturity, so that he could be, not only materially, but also spiritually the whole support of his wife. Hence also the extremely young age which tradition ascribes to Rebecca (which would also be indicated above by the spelling of נַעַרָ (חסר), although indeed as אילונית she could still have been older) so that, under the powerful influence of the Abrahamitic spirit, she would, all the more, be likely to become a second Sarah. We have already seen the striking difference between Rebecca and her surroundings. Neverthless the text reminds us again of her Aramic descent and family. Even if Isaac was Abraham’s son, and though Abraham, and Abraham alone, had influenced him, and although he had matured to a real son of Abraham, Rebecca was still, in spite of her undeniable good qualities, the daughter of an Aramite, born and brought up in Aram, and the sister of the most pronounced Aramite, Laban. If, according to the experience of our sages, most boys take after their maternal uncles — רב בנים הולכים אחר אחי האם — what children could be expected to come from this marriage, if most of them would become replicas of their uncle Laban! Thus we are prepared beforehand for the discord which arose later on, we can not be surprised that an Esau also appears, can only wonder at finding Jacob next to him.

V. 21. עתר .ויעתר יצחק related to התר to bore into, מחתרת, breaking-in. Also the forcible pushing forward of a ship against wind and billows, התר (Jonah I.13). Hence עתר a penetrating prayer and request. The pillar of smoke rising straight up is also called עתר ענן הקטורת ,עתר (Ez. 8,11) נעתרות נשיקות שונא (Prov. 27,6). When an enemy kisses us the kisses “are forced out of him”, they do not come from his heart. Pharaoh says: העתירו בעדי in the Hiphil, “Let your prayer force its way” up to God, make it a mighty influential advocate for me. He knew not that one can come to God more easily than to the under-secretary of the secretary of an official.

לנכח אשתו. Twenty long years had Isaac struggled in prayer before God for the fulfilment of the wish to have children from Rebecca. The promise כי ביצחק יקרא לך זרע was known to him, so he knew that, in any case, he could hope to have children. But whether the Covenant of Abraham would be carried on by one born from a sister of Laban, in spite of her own excellency, on that, especially after waiting so long, he could well begin to have doubts. So that his prayer was לנכח אשתו, specially referring to Rebecca. — We see here how, not only the first stone, but the further building up of the House of Israel had to come only as a direct gift from the Almightiness of God. Like Sarah, Rebecca too was עקרה, barren.

V. 22. ויתרצצו, from רוץ to run, hasten, in the Hiphil ויריצוהו מן הבור, they urged him to haste, so התרוצץ to urge oneself, or here where there are two, to urge each other to hasten. Each would not allow the other to rest — ותאמר אם כן by the notation these three words belong together, so it means “She said, when it was so”, when this occurred “why am I thus?” i.e. why do I have such an unusual experience? — ותלך, according to the explanation of our sages, to Shem and Eber — those who had preserved the traditions Noah had received — to ask for an explanation from God through them.

V. 23. שני גוים וגו׳ ושני לאמים וגו׳. We consider the explanation, parallel expressions, כפל ענין וכו׳, certainly a convenient, but even of a serious human speech, and most certainly of a Divine message, an unworthy crutch on which to lean. Children, or at most drunken men, may lisp without special meaning כפל ענין במלות שונות (repeat what they have to say using different expressions I.L.). לאם is the government of a nation אין לאום אלא מלכות. Different nations need not have different forms of government. Europe contains a number of nations but they are mostly under a form of government which basically and in principle is the same (this was the case in Hirsch’s time when practically all the countries of Europe had a form of monarchy I.L.) Rebecca was informed that she carried two nations in her womb who would represent two different forms of social government. The one state would build up its greatness on spirit and morals, on the humane in humans, the other would seek its greatness in cunning and strength. Spirit and strength, morality and violence oppose each other, and indeed, from birth onwards will they be in opposition to each other. One form of government will always be more powerful than the other. The scales will constantly sway from one to the other, between לאום ולאום. The whole of history is nothing else than a struggle as to whether spirit or sword, or, as our sages put it, whether Caesaria or Jerusalem is to have the upper hand.

רב never means the elder, but always: great in number and power. In the end it will be seen that the one who had seemed to be the mightier, who had fought only for lower purposes, the material, had in reality been working for the other, had really prepared the victory for him, and will finally submit to him. The representative of the spiritual and moral comes out of this struggle as the ultimate victor, and the representative of might and force is not destroyed, but at the end finds his own purpose served in submitting and devoting himself to the principles of the other.

V. 24. הנה .והנה תומם always introduces something unexpected. As Rebecca had already been fully informed that she had two boys in her womb, now that this fact is established it could not have been unexpected so that the והנה can not refer to that. The opposite seems to be the case. After she had been told of the contrasting difference between the expected children, one would have thought that they would be non-identical twins, and look not at all alike. The surprising thing was that they were really identical twins. The only difference was in their constitution, that the one — as we are immediately told — was much more developed, stronger, than the other. Perhaps also the way the word is speiled תומם :חסר דחסר for תאומים (like ויחדו יהי תמים על ראשו Ex. 26,24) points to the exterior complete apparent similarity. This complete exterior similarity taken together with the complete dissimilarity which had been predicted would develop in the future, could well have been designed to draw attention to the fact that the germ of this future dissimilarity lay deep below the surface, and so be the means of bringing about that this deep inner difference in the two boys be specially studied quite early.

V. 25. אדמוני, the same is said of David I. Sam. 16,12, red-cheeked, ruddy, a sign of radiant health. He was also hairy. Hair at newborn babies is a sign that there is sufficient strength and life-force to spare for the development of hair, which usually only gets developed properly later. And in this case, not merely on the head, but the whole body was covered with down. That is why they called him, i.e. all those who were present at the birth, עשו (from עשה) an already finished, completely “made” man. He brought “life” (red cheeks I.L.) and “protective strength” (hair I.L.) in full measure already with him into the world.

V. 26. ויקרא, then he, Isaac, called him Jacob. The others present paid no attention to this fact, but Isaac did indeed do so. The child looked almost exactly like Esau, but what specialised each baby was a contrast. Esau’s speciality was his outward appearance, his personality, Jacob’s lay in what he was doing, or in the position he adopted. Isaac called him יעקב, he will come behind. He allows Esau the precedence, but follows at his heels, he is just that צעיר, the lesser one, the weaker one, who unexpectedly will finally be the first (עקב means, unexpectedly to follow). Hence עקב, the unexpected result, the reward that one had not worked for. Hence also עקב to do unexpected harm to someone, to outwit him (See on Ch. 22,18).

V. 27. ויגדלו וגו׳. Our sages, who never objected to draw attention to the small and great mistakes and weaknesses in the history of our great forefathers, and thereby make them just the more instructive for us (see remarks on Ch. 12,10), here, too, on ויגדלו make a remark which is indeed a “signpost” for all of us. They point out that the striking contrast in the grandchildren of Abraham may have been due, not so much to a difference in their temperaments as to mistakes in the way they were brought up. As long as they were little, no attention was paid to the slumbering differences in their natures (see on V.24), both had exactly the same teaching and educational treatment, and the great law of education חנוך לנער על פי דרכו וגו׳ “bring up each child in accordance with its own way” was forgotten: — That each child must be treated differently, with an eye to the slumbering tendencies of his nature, and out of them, be educated to develop his special characteristics for the one pure human and Jewish life. The great Jewish task in life is basically simple, one and the same for all, but in its realisation is as complicated and varied as human natures and tendencies are varied, and the manifold varieties of life that result from them.

When Father Jacob visualised the tribes of our nation in the sons standing around his death-bed, he saw, not only future priests and teachers, he saw around him the tribe of Levites, the tribes of royalty, of merchants, of farmers, of soldiers, before his mental eye he saw the nation in all its most manifold characteristics and diverse paths of life, and he blessed all of them, and איש כברכתו ברך אותם each according to his speciality, with and in his different path in life, did he bless them. For the covenant which God established with Abraham wants to win a whole national life, a whole fresh, complete life of a nation with its manifold classes and occupations, all for the one and same great task of life: לשמר דרך ה׳ לעשות צדקה ומשפט. There, strength and courage, no less than brain and lofty thought and fine feelings are to have their representatives before God, and all, in the most varied ways of their callings are to achieve the one great common task of life.

But just because of that, must each one be brought up “על פי דרכו״ according to the presumed path of life to which his tendencies lead, each one differently to the one great goal. To try to bring up a Jacob and an Esau in the same college, make them have the same habits and hobbies, want to teach and educate them in the same way for some studious, sedate, meditative life is the surest way to court disaster. A Jacob will, with ever increasing zeal and zest, imbibe knowledge from the well of wisdom and truth, while an Esau can hardly wait for the time when he can throw the old books, but at the same time, a whole purpose of life, behind his back, a life of which he has only learnt to know from one angle, and in a manner for which he can find no disposition in his whole nature.

Had Isaac and Rebecca studied Esau’s nature and character early enough, and asked themselves how can even an Esau, how can all the strength and energy, agility and courage that lies slumbering in this child, be won over to be used in the service of God, and the future גבר be trained to become, not a גבר ציד, but in truth a גבר לפני ה׳, then Jacob and Esau, with their totally different natures could still have remained twin-brothers in spirit and life; quite early in life Esau’s “sword” and Jacob’s “spirit” could have worked hand in hand, and who can say what a different aspect the whole history of the ages might have presented. But, as it was, ויגדלו הנערים, only when the boys had grown into men, one was surprised to see that, out of one and the selfsame womb, having had exactly the same care, training and schooling, two such contrasting persons emerge.

Just as, with Jacob the איש תם denotes the nature of his character, and יושב אהלים the nature of his vocation, so with Esau too, the איש יודע ציד would be the nature of his character, and איש שדה, the vocation.

At Nimrod, whose spiriutal heir Esau seems to have been, we have already considered the concept צוד in its relation to סוד. In the same way as סוד implies keeping to oneself a secret plan until the time arrives for it to be carried out, so צוד has the same meaning with the additional nuance of overcoming difficulties in the carrying out of the plan. The צַיָד must understand the art of stalking, externally to appear quite innocent and still have the thought of killing quietly in his heart. It is the complete exercise of trickery, insidiousness; used in a different sphere: diplomacy. Esau understood hunting, the art of self-control in lurking self-interest. The whole way in which he had been brought up, so much against the grain of his temperament, which his real nature repressed in patience until the time he could become more his own master, could only have nurtured such a tendency. This temperament of his led him to become an איש שדה Just because he had earlier been fused to his seat in the schoolroom, now out of aversion to having been kept indoors, he was completely an איש שדה an outdoor man. In contrast to that Jacob was an איש תם, a man who only knows one direction, and gives himself up entirely to that, is single-minded. He gave himself up, as Abraham’s grandson, Isaac’s son, to fulfil his mission, and thereby he became a יושב אהלים, a man who recognised and taught that the highest mission of life lies in achieving the knowledge and practice to be obtained in the sphere of אהלים, the homes of mankind. In the same way, as a man, later in life, he recognised and taught the highest revelation of the Rule of God to be primarily there, in the sphere of mankind — יעקב קראו בית.

V. 28. A second factor, which could only have a pernicious effect was the difference of the feelings of the parents towards the children Unity and complete agreement of parents in the education, and the same feelings and love to all their children — even to those who are not so good, yea, just those require most of all, even more than those who are physically weak or ill, loving care and consideration and sacrifice — that is the first fundamental condition and the corner stone of every education — That Isaac’s sympathies were more inclined toward’s Esau, Rebecca’s to Jacob can moreover easily be explained by the attraction of opposites. We see Isaac, risen up again from death on the altar, preferring to withdraw from the bustle of the world and to live quietly in the proximity of the desert, living at the well of the “Live-One-Who seeth me” away from the busy traffic of men. That Esau’s lusty active nature appealed to him, and that he perhaps saw in him a force which he had lost could be a support to the home, would be quite possible. Rebecca, on the other hand saw in Jacob’s whole being a picture of a life unfolding of which in her father’s house she had never had the remotest idea — the sympathies are explainable, but parents should not allow such hidden feelings to influence them in making any difference in their love towards their children.

ציד בפיו. Either: “he went a-hunting with his mouth”, he knew how to enthral his father with tales of his adventures and deeds of derring-do at his hunting, or — which seems more probably — “he was also a hunter with his mouth”, he practiced his art of stalking, with his mouth too, was able to entrap his father by his speech. But Rebecca’s love for Jacob came by itself, was not “caught”, just he himself won her love, simply: אהבת את יעקב.

V. 29. ויזד: the Hiphil of זוד (the basic root of סוד and צוד) to prepare something for some time and let it become quite ripe. Hence also the expression for intentional premeditated acts, in contrast to unintentional ones. נזיד: like מול and זול ,נמל and זור ,נזל and זוד ,נזר and נזיד would belong together, and נזיד would mean boiled until it was soft.

V. 30. לעט ,הלעיטני (related to להט to glow) greedily to gulp down. It is not so much the dish itself as its colour that attracts him. It reminds him of the blood of a gasping dying animal that delights his eye when his arrow has found its mark. “Quickly give me some of that lovely red stuff!” And he still boasted later on of this characteristic phrase and called himself: Edom (the red one).
V. 31. כיום see on Ch. 21,23.

V. 34. ויעקב נתן, not ויתן יעקב, had already given it to him at once, did not take advantage of his hunger to force him to sell. Also the real meaning of מכר is not necessarily to sell, but has also the meaning of relinquishing, giving over, abandoning צורם מכרם (Deut. 32,30) ימכר ה׳ את סיסרא (Judges 4,9).

Moreover, out of this whole “sale” agreement we do not find that Jacob derived the slightest preference or advantage. On the contrary Esau became great as a rich prince while Jacob was still slaving as shepherd for Laban’s sheep. So that the בכורה gave him no material advantage at all. The question could only have been, to whom was the spiritual leadership of the house to be entrusted. To which must be added, that both of them were still just boys — according to Baba Bathra 16b, 15 years old. So that in any case the בכורה could only have been sold in boyish play. בר קפרא, too, in ב״ר, calls them משחקים, so that there can be no question of a real bargain, or a serious business deal. Esau comes home hungry in the evening, Jacob is just cooking a pottage for himself, “Quick, give me some of that delicious red stuff, my mouth is watering for it”, says Esau. Jacob gives him some and says: “Just as you are craving for this red pottage so do I crave for the בכורה. You run about the whole day in the woods, and it just strikes me, what would it be like if one day Father were to die, and the house of Abraham would be turned into a hunter’s lodge — that is why I crave for the בכורה just as eagerly as you crave for the pottage”. If we add to this, what the tradition quoted above records, that this day was the day of the death of Abraham, so that the thought must have occurred to Jacob, how would it be if, instead of my father Isaac, Ishmael would have succeeded Abraham; and he could well have been thinking, the Grandfather dies and the grandson, who is ultimately to take his place and carry on his spiritual mission, spends the whole day running about the fields a-hunting — then the whole procedure of the two boys is as understandable as it is characteristic. And as they then stood opposite each other, so have Jacob and Esau stood opposite each other throughout the centuries Jacob gladly gives up his material possessions to Esau who hankers greedily after them, if the latter will only allow him to attend to the spiritual mission of his life.

V. 1. Since the land had been promised to Abraham for his ultimate possession, we see it repeatedly visited by famine, just the land which was destined to overflow with milk and honey. For the blossoming of this land is not to be dependent merely on the work of man and the favour of nature, but, in the first place, on the morality and integrity of its inhabitants. “It spues its inhabitants out, as soon as they become morally degenerate”. Just as the nation who were to possess it were by nature, a “hard” obstinate intractable people, who through the power of the Torah became the People of God, so was their land, in itself, hard and unfruitful, subject to famine, and just through the power of that selfsame Torah was to become a land of abundance and blessing. Gerizin and Ebal, that is the picture of the alternative, between which the people were placed beforehand, bleak and desolate the one, luxurious and verdant the other. And it was on Ebal, the bleak mount, that the altar of the Torah was built. For, completely without prior conditions for it, is an Ebal to become a Gerizin through the Torah. Land and People belong intimately together, neither really blossom without the other.

V. 2. From V.3 it is apparent that Isaac had the intention of going to Egypt the usual place of refuge from famine. He first went to Abimelech who had made a treaty with his father, to see, so it seems, if it was possible to find help there. But there was famine there too. There, God appeared to him, and directed him not to seek help from human hands. His field was to be cultivating obedience to God. שכון, dwelling quietly, is more than גור and less than ישב. It repeatedly says הארצות האל just these lands, which you so repeatedly see affected by drought and famine, do I give you and your descendants, so that, by following My Laws, such a rich abundance shall flourish there, that all the nations of the world shall feel themselves impelled to find out from you and your example what are the causes that enable people so to be the creators of their own blessings.

V. 5. עקב, see V,6 of previous chapter. — שמד ,וישמר משמרתי is the most general term used for that which is expected from us regarding the Law, the Torah which is transmitted to us from God. It is a treasure entrusted to us towards which we are to be שומרים, which we are to guard and use according to the Will of the Owner, but which we have no right to dispose of as we ourselves wish.

The duty of שמר of guarding something entrusted to our care, involves two duties; (1) constant care, we must keep it constantly in our mind, hence the ordinary explanation ושמרתם זו משנה (ת״כ in many places) to guard the Torah means “learning”, for just by “learning”, the revealed Will of God is kept constantly in our minds in all its relations. (2) protection, to surround it with such protective measures that it remains unbroken and uninjured, hence those national laws of precaution which are made for the purpose of guarding oneself against transgression, תקנות and גזרות. That conscientiousness which guards itself not only against doing wrong but against anything that borders on wrong and easily leads to its being committed, which Abraham practised.

צוה ,מצותי, related, as already remarked on Ch. 2,1, to צבא to appoint to a post whereby the will of the one who gives orders is carried out in the widest circle by his representatives, and so his ideas attain the widest circumference (צבה). By צוה he makes a צבה for himself. Hence מצות, in a narrower sense, primarily refer to those orders by which the Divine purposes of justice and benevolence, משפט ,וצדקה which God wishes are to be carried out in His world. Accordingly the duties of justice, mercifulness, benevolence and love of fellowman which are to be kept.
חקותי (from חקק), the rules which limit the exercise of the freewill of the senses, the laws of the morality and sanctity of the life of the body.

תורתי, which we believe does not come from ירה, but from הרה, like הוליך from הרה ;הלך, to receive a seed within oneself, in the Hiphil הורה to plant a seed in someone else, hence to implant the seeds of truth and goodness, of spirituality and morality in others: to teach. So that תורתי are the teachings which God has revealed to us of truth and goodness which we are to accept in our minds and feelings, to beget in us the knowledge of truth and the decision to goodness. מצוה is the task to be accomplished, חוק makes people fit for the accomplishment, תורה gives the understanding thereto.

The fulfilment of his mission which is here testified concerning Abraham could be parallel to the description of that mission given him in Ch. 18,19. מצותי corresponding to חקותי ,עשות צדקה ומשפט to שמר דרך ה׳ לעשות וגו׳, the way to such fulfilment, and תורתי, the צוה בניו ואת ביתו, the teaching and education for such life.

V. 6.—11. See Ch. 12,10 et. seq. and Ch. XX. That Isaac’s precaution was not without cause is proved by the fact that, once the true relation between Rebecca and Isaac became known, Abimelech found it necessary to protect them by a decree of the death penalty for any assault. כי ארכו לו שם הימים, after a long time he became less careful. — אחד העם: he probably thought of himself.

V. 12. In that land and in that year, the country itself and the year in particular were unfavourable and still he found a hundred שערים. It is true that in Rabbinic Hebrew שער does mean measure, (and so it has been taken to mean here a hundred measures or a hundredfold I.L.) but in the whole of תנ״ך it only occurs with the meaning of gate or market place (as in II Kings 7,1). Hence also the verb שעור, to sit in the market, to haggle, to offer for sale, from which we get Prov. 23,6.7 אל תלחם את לחם רע עין וגו׳ כי כמו שער בנפשו כן הוא וגו׳. If a stingy man invites you to his table he is “as if he was bargaining at the market with his soul, “as if he was offering a bit of his life cheaply for sale”. תאנים שערים (Jer. 24,17) are fruit from a stall in the market, rotten fruit that are not saleable. שערוריה and שערורה in Jeremiah and Hosea mean vendible, cheap. Accordingly מאה שערים here would mean: a hundred markets. His produce was not only sufficient for his own requirements but he brought a hundredfold, compared to ordinary produce, to the market.

ויברכהו ה׳. Thus he became the “blessed of God”. Inasmuch as he did not usuriously hoard up the blessing but brought it out generously to the markets, in that year of famine used his blessing to the general good, he becomes recognised as the man blessed by God.

V. 13. ויגדל האיש, not ויגדל, also not ויגדל יצחק but quite from the point of view of the Philistines. The man became too great for them, and thereby excited not only their envy but their jealousy. In the same way as is later recorded of the feelings of Laban’s sons towards Jacob: ויפרץ האיש (Ch. 30,43)

V. 14. ויקנאו אתו, not ויקנאו בו as is usual. קנה to acquire something and possess it as one’s property, from which we get מקנָה sale, and מקנֵה property, possession. — קַנֵא to justify one’s property, to demand something as belonging to oneself. Hence to claim something from somebody else as really belonging to oneself, to be jealous of somebody having something that should be yours. קנא את to demand the person, to enforce his right to the person, thus וקנא את אשתו, he warns his wife against infidelity. So here too: ויקנאו אתו, not they envied him on account of his riches, at a time like that his being blessed was at bottom a blessing for them all, but they felt themselves injured by the position and respect which he received through his riches, the קנאה was directed more to the man than to his riches.

V. 15. This jealousy directed towards the alien Abrahamites as such had manifested itself already, immediately after the death of Abraham even before Isaac lived amongst them. It had shown itself in the malicious delight in destruction of the wells, which, wherever they were to be found were a public benefit for everybody.

With this קנאה a whole series of events are introduced, which show a new status of life starting with Isaac. Abraham, with all his riches, and equally an alien in the midst of the nations, had achieved by his whole personality, such respect, that, without exciting envy or jealousy, he wandered as נשיא אלקים amongst them. On one occasion only, a similar tendency to enmity did show itself, but was immediately disfavoured by the king of the country (above XXI,26). With Isaac the Galut began, the prophesy גר יהיה זרעך began to be fulfilled. The completely undistrubed status of Abraham was broken already with Isaac by plaguing jealousy, and Jacob had already to endure a state of complete servitude. Thereby a threefold position of the Abrahamites as strangers in the midst of the nations is demonstrated:— as slave, subservient, as tolerated but envied, and as honoured and respected. In all three positions and conditions of fate, the bond of God has been preserved, and has occordingly manifested itself not only as a ברית with, עם אברהם ,עם יצחק ,ועם יעקב but as a ,ברית אברהם ברית יצחק ,ברית יעקב in which expression the Patriarchs appear not so much as persons, but as types through which the different manifestations of the power of the Divine Covenant become apparent.

If finally the Galut of their sons is to lead to ultimate unlosable independence it must develop in a most contrasting upward line, and in each stage must preserve the ברית. It is first of all the ברית יעקב the testing centuries of the bond of God preserving us in slavery and wretchedness. This stage lies — perhaps — already behind us. As “Jacob” we have proved ourselves brilliantly, יאי עניותא לישראל. It is now a question of the solution of ברית יצחק, emancipated, free, and independent, to carry on the heritage of Abraham in the midst of the nations, not to shun being different from them not to fear their envy, and to look to the ברית יצחק, to the bond of God, to protect us against envy and jealousy. This is the Galut-test we still have to pass. Then, and only then, can we look forward to the last stage of Galut, to win the recognition and respect of the nations, not although we are Jews, but because we are Jews, and Abraham-like, wander amongst them as נשיא אלקים, the ברית אברהם. Then the nations themselves will plant us again in our old heritage. והביאו את כל אחיכם מכל הגוים מנחה לה׳ (“and they will bring all your brethren home from out of all the nations as an allegiance act of homage unto God” I.L.) Is. 66,20. Then, at last, world history will have accomplished that which is described in the old verse in Levit. 26,42, which thousands of years ago gave as the programme for our Galut and for our deliverance from it: וזכרתי את בריתי יעקב ואף את בריתי יצחק ואף את בריתי אברהם אזכר והארץ אזכר.

V. 16. לך מעמנו כי עצמת ממנו מאד. There may be profound truth in the ם-stage of the ways which further the קץ הימין, the ultimate goal of the ages, which our prophets have told us are laid down in the five final letters of our alphabet, and which stage they refer to our verse here (see final paragraph on לך לך Ch. 12,1). What they seem to want to tell us is: — how unfriendly קנאה, how the envy and jealousy of the nations who find the Jews well-to-do in the Isaac-stage of the Galuth, and say to them לך ממגו כי עצמת וגו׳ — send them out of their countries — may form not the least of God’s method for our salvation. Who can tell how easily Isaac, in the hustle and bustle of managing his great wealth, and in the prominent civic position he won through it, might not have given himself up to it more than would be seemly for the son of Abraham and the bearer of his spiritual heritage, had not the jealousy of the Philistines driven him again into isolation, and their repulsing קנאה saved him from it. Certain it is that his more modern emancipated sons, working themselves up to his wealthy status have always been thrown back on themselves by the haughty scorn of all the repulsing קנאה. Thereby this קנאה may have been no unimportant medicine added to their good fortune to work against its tempting attractions, and to admonish them again and again as to their real Jewish calling.

V. 20.
