That digging a well was something permitted, and the ground and well in common land, became the property of the one who had dug it, we can take for granted from a son of Abraham; moreover we find confirmation of this, above in Ch. 21,30, for there Abraham only demanded official recognition that he had dug the well. Moreover it was a well of “live” i.e. spring-water which they found, coming up from the depth, so that no one could claim it was drained off their land. Nevertheless they quibbled — in the exact style which down the centuries has been used against the Jews in Galut — “yes, you dug the well, the hole belongs to you, but the water is ours”. — עשִׂקֻ occurs in תנ״ך only in this single instance. In Rabbinic Hebrew עסק is quite common. מתעסק ,עסוק, to busy oneself with something. עיסקא, a business, and עסיקין, quite in the sense of our word here, litigation about the title to property. The root seems related to עשׁק, חזק, עזק, אזק, all of which have a meaning of a strong grasping and holding fast. Hence עשק means to grasp something forcibly with your mind, to try and obtain something by sophistry. But עסק is used quite generally in Rabbinic Hebrew to designate giving one’s whole mind up to obtaining ones purpose or to obtaining an object, to occupy oneself with something.
V. 22 ויעתק, see above Ch. 12,8.

V. 23 & 24 ויעל. Up till then the hostility of the Philistines had forced him into the isolation, which perhaps, as the son of Abraham, he ought to have sought of his own freewill. Similar to the isolation of the ghettos into which hatred and jealousy of the Jews forced his descendants for centuries. Until then God had not appeared to him again had not assured him again of His Protection, had allowed the jealousy and hostility against him to be unhindered, and to work its effect on him. Perhaps it might even have been salutary to have forcibly driven the son of Abraham out of the possibility of sinking into the business activity of acquiring riches and high standing amongst men. Only now when he (V. 22) could believe he could remain in the country and be able to thrive further there, and now, of his own freewill moves up to the old isolation where once his cradle had stood, where he had spent his childhood with his father, and where his father had lived and achieved his great spiritual mission (Ch. XXI. 33) — only then did God appear to him, assure him of His protection and blessing, tell him that He is still the old God of his father Abraham, Who will protect and bless him in the same way, and all this for the sake of his father, whom He — as never again anywhere else — calls “עבדי״, and with this name, the son is told everything that is expected from him too. And as he at once built an altar there and raised up the spiritual standard of the “profession” of Abraham, and pitched his tent there without first examining the nature of the soil or making sure that water was there in sufficient quantity, everything came to him by itself. His men found water at their first attempt, and the king who had sent him away, seeks him out in his retirement with every show of respect and honour — all things for which hitherto he had struggled under annoyances in, vain.

V. 25. כרה and חפר are not the same. From בור כרה ויחפרהו (Ps. 7,17), and as חפר also means generally to seek out, to spy out, accordingly, to raise out of the dark unknown depths into the light, כרה, which indeed altogether is used for preparing, would be the beginning of digging and חפר the completion, digging so deep till water gushes forth. Before, with the Philistines, Isaac had to look for water, and when he had found it, had to contend for it. Now, at the place where God had appeared to him, and where, caring about nothing else, he had set up his tent, he did not have to look for it, at the first spade-full his servants turned, there was the water. The visit of Abimelech and this digging came together.

V. 26 This visit of Abimelech is very characteristic. Although he himself had broken faith with the son of Abraham and had been unfaithful to the covenant made with the father, he still placed value on obtaining a covenant confirmed by an oath from the son. In the later and last periods of Jewish National life too, it was just the Jewish nation which always, and in all circumstances kept faith with all treaties duly confirmed by oath in accordance with international laws and customs. Equally characteristic is the ונשלחך בשלום “that they sent them away unplundered” they reckon as highly benevolent.

מרעהו, whereas רע from רעה designates a relationship of intimate friendship in which each one finds his “pasturage”, the satisfaction of his wants, in the other, מֵרֵעַ designates more boon companions, as by Samson. The מ seems to indicate more acquaintanceship than acquaintants. — אחוזה seems to mean, all that he possessed of friends. אחז does occur quite frequently of persons, ותאחזני ימינך etc. — פיכול as the field-marshal in Abraham’s time was also called פיכול, it must have been the same man, or פיכול is an official title, as אבימלך for the Kings, so פי כל “the mouth of everybody”, the commander, for the field-marshals.

V. 33 Abraham had called למקום, the place, the district, באר שבע, Isaac called the well שבעה — either to commemorate the oath that had been taken there, or because there God had been apparent as being in connection with concrete earthly material affairs (the Invisible Seventh with the visible six). This was the zenith of his material life. From both, the city which was built there later on, received its name.

V. 34 With this marriage with two Hittite girls Esau set the seal on his complete unfitness to be the one who was to carry on the mission of Abraham. In a home where even two daughters of Heth ruled, the Abrahamitic principle was just buried. We have just seen how Isaac and Rebecca recognized the necessity of isolating themselves, and then, just think: Isaac builds an altar and ויקרא בשם ה׳, proclaims the great Name ה׳, even as his great father had done, and his eldest son brings ע״ז into the home. Small wonder that it says then that they were מורת רוח etc.

V. 35 מרה ,מורת רוח has the basic meaning “to counter, to act in opposition”, hence מורה, a razor which has to run against the hair at the right angle (Similarly מול over against, opposite and also to cut off, to clip). Used for feelings and behaviour it accordingly has the meaning, to want to do something, or not to do something just because the other does not want it. Both of them, Isaac and Rebecca, were arrogantly, defiantly opposed, although in general, they were not of one mind in their sympathies towards their two children, and significantly Isaac even first. That daughters-in-law do not always see eye to eye with their mother-in-law is nothing so unusual, especially when the latter is not too favourable inclined to the son. But here it puts ליצחק in the first place, for here it was nothing that was contrary in immaterial matters. They were in complete opposition to the spirit that dominated Isaac and Rebecca.
These two verses are a highly significant introduction to the story that now follows.

V. 1 As repeatedly remarked, we follow the opinion of our sages, and do not consider it our task to be apologists for our great men and women, just as the Word of God, the Torah itself never refrains from informing us of their errors and weaknesses. If Rebecca brought it about that Jacob deceived his father, it says quite unequivocally בא אחיך במרמה. Reb. Chanina expresses himself about the events recorded in this chapter, as follows:- (ב״ר 67) כל מי שאומד הב״ה ותרן הרא “anybody who says that God is not so particular with His “pious ones”, that “frum” people need not be so particular in certain directions, יותרון מעיו, “deserves to have his inwards torn out” אלא מאריך רוחיה וגבי דיליה, זעקה אחת הזעיק יעקב אבינו לעשו אימתי נפרע לו בשושן הבירה ויזעק זעקה גדולה ומרה (Esther IV.1 and Gen. XXVII. 34), the forbearance of God grants long credit but the debt has to be paid in the end; one cry Jacob caused Esau to make, and that was repaid in Shushan when Esau’s descendant caused Jacob’s descendant “to cry with a loud and bitter cry” ג׳ דמעות “three tears” it says in Tanchuma הוריד עשו אחת מימינו ואחת משמאלו ואחת נסתלקה בתוך עינו והיא האכילתם לחם דמעה ותשקמו בדמעות שליש “three tears did Esau shed, one dropped out of his right eye, one from his left, and the third he kept back, and that one, the bitterest that he did not drop, salted our bread of exile with tears and made us taste tears in full threefold measure”. But if quiet thoughtful considerations of this event force one to conclusions that would remove a great deal of its bitterness, we do not think that we should refrain from giving them in order to avoid our appearing as apologists. Enough will still remain which can not be approved of, especially when measured with the yard-stick of character of a nation whose name of honour is ישורן, which is only to achieve its purposes in the “straight” (ישר) way, and is to oppose any crooked means for any purpose.

Let us then try and get some understanding of the manner in which the three principle actors in this homely drama behaved. Jacob’s behaviour is completely clear and transparent. Right from the beginning his mother appealed for his blind obedience to her orders. (V. 8) She did not expect that he would do it to get an advantage for himself, and quite expected that his whole character as איש תם would revolt against it. She therefore cuts all objections short by exercising her maternal authority, and appealing to his duty to obey the orders of his mother. She takes full responsibility for anything that seems wrong, and for all possible consequences of her plan. All he is to do is to obey. So that what Jacob did, was only out of obedience to his mother, and his behaviour can only be blamed inasmuch as the duty of obedience of children, too, is limited by the laws of morality, when one may not practise any deceit even out of obedience to one’s mother.

But what did Rebecca want? The worst antisemite or antibibliologicalist will want to find some reasoning, some sense, or if you prefer it, some cunning in her action. Yea the worse, the more artful, such a person would like to make the Jewish Ancestress appear the less would that attribute to her the most complete imbecility, the most childish stupidity. And even if her intention had been nothing more than, by her trickery, to manage to turn the paternal blessing on to the head of her beloved Jacob, what possible thinkable result could she have expected from that! Whatever one thinks her idea of the effect of a father’s blessing might have been, in any case she must have known that in this case it must infallibly have resulted in the very opposite of her expectations. Does she think the father’s blessing is to call down happiness and success and prosperity on the head of the one who received it, then, how can she imagine — even she succeeds in deceiving the old blind father — that God, the All-seeing One, could conceivably be taken in by such a pitiful mummery, or believe that the blessing of Abraham, which God had made conditional on צדקה ומשפט being practised, could be obtained from that same God by way of such trickery and deception. And if what she was thinking of, was some material benefit attached to this blessing, some legal preference in the ultimate heritage dependent on being thus recognized as the first-born, how could such an advantage fail to become utterly void as a מקח טעות (a transaction obtained under false impression I.L.). The discovery of the deception was unavoidable. Even if the carrying out of the masquerade were to be successful, with Esau’s return, everything was inevitably bound to be disclosed — Rebecca must have known this full well. And altogether, how crude was the whole comedy, a couple of goat-skins, what but the most absolute naivety could be taken in by that! What could her intention have been by playing such a comedy? What else but just the comedy itself! Only thus, if just the inevitable discovery was what was beforehand reckoned on, only then does the whole story make sense, and, from Rebecca’s point of view, become understandable, and — even if not completely approved of — in the circumstances, quite excusable.

As an introduction to this procedure, we were given the information how Esau, of his own accord, gave the great Abrahamitic mission a double knock-out blow by marrying two Hittite women. If anything could have opened Isaac’s eyes to the complete unworthiness of his elder son, surely this would have done it. Nevertheless we see Isaac calling his elder son to be blessed by him, i.e. to make him the future guide and leader of the House of Abraham. What a “hunter with his mouth” must Esau have been, how he must have known how to dissemble and feign, in spite of his completely unabrahamitic life, to ensnare the heart of his father and deceive him.

In the little word הנה נא זקנתי — נא — “see, after all, I am already old”, it is made clear that he had already long had the intention to bestow such a blessing, but had been dissuaded, had yielded to remonstration. Rebecca had probably constantly argued with him, trying to convince him of the truth, and had then persuaded him “anyway leave it for a time, you are not so old yet, there is still plenty of time etc., and had hoped, in the meantime, that he would be undeceived. But she had not succeeded. And now what was she to do? What could she have wanted with this plan? Nothing but to bring home to him, to convince him, ad hominem, that, and how easily, he could be deceived. If a Jacob, an איש תם can so easily masquerade as a גבור ציד, how much more easily can an Esau masquerade as an איש תם to him! And in this — Isaac’s undeception through Jacob’s deception — Rebecca succeeded perfectly. As soon as Isaac realised the trick that had been played upon him, ויחרד חרדה גדולה עד מאד (V. 35), he received a terrific shock, he saw — as our sages put it — Gehennam yawning at his feet, saw, how all his life he had allowed himself to be deceived. Immediately the scales fell from his eyes, and he immediately added deliberately his confirmatory and now fully conciously expressed blessing גם ברוך יהיה (ibid) “And indeed he shall be blessed”.

This also seems to be the way that ר׳ יהושע בן לוי takes this episode (ב״ר). לא ממה שהיתה רבקה אוהבת את יעקב יתיר מעשו עשתה את הדבר הזה אלא אמרה לא יעול ויטעי בההוא סבא. “Not just because Rebecca loved Jacob more than Esau did she do this, but so that the latter should no longer come and deceive his old father.”

A closer consideration of the blessing that Isaac wished to confer on Esau, could make his behaviour much clearer. Esau himself had not expected that his father wished to give him the whole of the blessing. He at once asked his father הלא אצלת לי ברכה, “Have you then not kept one blessing back for me,” i.e. if you had blessed me, you would certainly still have had a blessing left to give to Jacob, well, give me at least that blessing. Isaac readily admitted this, but in describing the blessing he had given to Jacob, he showed him how this blessing was intended and suitable for Esau, but the blessing he had reserved in his mind for Jacob would be quite unsuitable for Esau.

Two elements were represented in his house by his two sons, in Esau material power, in Jacob, spiritual. Isaac knew quite well that both these factors were necessary for the prosperity of the Nation. Further, Isaac probably knew of the prophecy (XXV. 23): ורב יעבד צעיר that the one who was materially stronger would ultimately serve the materially weaker one. But Isaac could have believed that the Abrahamitic calling was to be carried on by an Esau and an Isaac in brotherly unison, each one complementing the other; and therefore intended giving Esau a blessing of material content, but for Jacob a spiritual one, in petto. But this blessing which he had reserved for Jacob would have no meaning for Esau, whose temperament and feelings were not inclined to this part of the House of Abraham. But Rebecca knew from Laban and her own home, the impossibility and the failure of such a division. She knew from experience how the material too could blossom to blessing and true happiness only in a home in which the spirit of Abraham hovers, only by a hand guided by the spirit. She knew what was right, she recognised the curse that arises out of materialism which is devoid of spirit, and could only see blessing blossoming undivided on one single head. Such reflections could make the behaviour of both parents understandable. Let us now look at the text in detail.

Vv. 2, 3 & 4 What could have been Isaac’s motive in saying to his son whom he wishes to bless, “first cook a nice dish for me!” One has tried to find a parallel case with Elisha and his request for stringed music (II K. III. 15); as if a good piece of roast meat had some power to inspire lofty feelings! But then it must have been overlooked that here it says, not בעבור אברכך but בעבור תברכך נפשי. That is not to be found at any similar blessing. The person himself gives the blessing, but never some special part of himself as נפש. The only similar expression can be found in Job: אם לא ברכוני חלציו (Ch. XXXI. 20). There the meaning of the expression is clear. The loins, the warmed body of the poor naked man, feel the benevolence of his benefactor and bless him for it. Similarly from Man to God: ברכי נפשי which expresses the demand that not only is God to be “blessed” (i.e. recognised and given satisfaction I.L.) generally, but that the person is to be inspired to feel through and through all that God has done for him, so that every fibre of his being “blesses” i.e. serves Him.

Consequently here too the meaning may be clear. Isaac wanted to bless Esau in the sense of his future calling. As he hoped that his natural tendencies would come to be employed for useful moral purposes, he wanted him to show that he was turning in that direction at the time he received the blessing. Let him for once employ his wild sport for a true humane purpose. For it certainly seems that this hunting of Esau’s was not usually pursued for the purpose of providing his old weak father with a strengthening meal. What he enjoyed was the hunt for its own sake, the sight of the steaming blood gushing out after pitting his wits against the brute strength and evasive cunning of the animals. But to hunt for providing refreshment for somebody who was weak and ill, would not enter Esau’s mind, it was not in his character to do so. “Now for once gather up the weapons of your daily occupation, stalk some game, and, you yourself, prepare a dainty dish for me”; you are now for once to use your love of hunting for a benevolent purpose, for the refreshment of an old man, are to feel, for once, how good it feels to use one’s strength and skill to give someone else pleasure. That is also why, in the blessing he gave to the supposed Esau (V. 27), he led him from the joy of hunting over to that of agriculture, to “the field blessed by God”, with an eye to the prosperity of the future Jewish National Life. This becoming refreshed, and this receiving the blessing by having brought about the refreshment lies in the בעבור תברכך נפשי. That is also why it says in V. 5.: Then Esau went out on the hunt for once for the purpose להביא, “to bring it home”.
V. 7 The לפני ה׳ is a paraphrase of the נפשי, I wish to bless you as working לפני ה׳, i.e. doing good with your occupation.
V. 11 Here and in the following verses it repeatedly says אמו, driving home the fact that it was as the mother that she demanded, and as a son that he obeyed.

V. 12 כמתעתע, as a cheat, as one who would deceive somebody. This כ explains everything. Jacob was no cheat, did not want to deceive, but he is afraid he would not be given time to explain to his father that he was only blindly obeying his mother, Isaac would at once curse him for trying to deceive him. But thereby he also told her, indirectly and in the most respectful manner, how objectionable the whole affair seemed to him, as a deception meriting being cursed.
V. 15 אשר אתה בבית, incidentaly, a characteristic peep into Esau’s married life. His best treasures he seems to have left in his mother’s keeping, did not entirely trust them to his wives.
V. 17 בנה, see note on V. 11.

V. 23. The voice, and probably also the manner of speaking — ה׳ אלקיך — as our sages remark, Isaac recognised the voice and style of Jacob and still let himself be deceived by something so extremely external as the hand being hairy, so may it well have been in his whole life.

V. 27.—28. We know already what predilection Isaac had for agriculture under God’s blessing. Hence, “see”, says he, “my son already exhales the fragrance, not of the wild, not of the forests, but of the cutivated fields that God has blessed; so may God then give thee all the blessings of productivity and abundance”.

V. 29 States and nations do not bow before spiritual greatness, they only bow before material greatness. But it was Esau that Isaac thought he had before him. God had promised Abraham that his people would become a blessing for the whole world. In this mission, Isaac imagined Esau’s role was to be to gain the respect of the nations by the material well-being of the Abrahamitic nation. הֶוֵה is imperative, the task, not “be blessed”, but “become a blessing”. By the material prosperity which God will grant you, nations and states will bow down before you, but seek to compete with your brother Jacob to obtain the spiritual greatness also, so that not only strangers but also the sons of your mother bow down before you that you stand before them too as a “man”, then, if you achieve this, then אורריך ארור ומברכיך ברוך.

V. 37 That which Isaac only dared to express as a demand when he thought is was Esau that he had before him, viz. הוה גביר לאחיך he now says with certainty of Jacob. That he, Jacob, would have the spiritual leadership is self-understood, and — after the scales had fallen from his eyes — he had adjudged the material foundation to him, with full consciousness, by the גם ברוך היה. For now it had become clear to him, how in the Abrahamitic nation, everything and everybody, soldiers, merchants etc. too, have to be filled with the Abrahamitic spirit. So that he no longer saw any position in the House of Abraham for Esau.
V. 38 Is there then no blessing at all outside the House of Abraham?

V. 39.—40. Not ויתן לך האלקים, not under special Management and Guidance of God, but as far as it lies in “heaven and earth” in the ordinary course of things in accordance with the laws of nature, will you attain material plenty. Your sword will be the means by which you will carve your history in the world. You will be the stronger, will conquer the world — to lay the conquered world at the feet of Jacob. “Rome”, the power of the sword, conquers the world, only ultimately, after finding out all its errors, to lay it at the feet of the ideals of Jacob-Israel. As long as you persist in ruling, looking on and using every material conquest only as the step for further conquests, for so long you are in reality working for your brother (only proving to the world, and ultimately to yourself, the futility and lack of security which the power of the sword really acquires I. L.). As long as you are רב, for so long will רב יעבד צעיר, only כאשר תריד when you come down, by your own free-will, voluntarily acknowledge and submit yourself to the ideals of your brother, will you emancipate yourself and stand on an equal footing to your brother. — ריד and רוד, related to ירד (cf. היום רד מאד Judges XIX. 11) to be humbled, to humble oneself. אריד בשיחי (Ps.LV. 3) I sink down in woefulness in prayer”. ויהודה עוד רד עם ה׳ (Hos. XII. 1) “Even in humiliation, Judah is still with God”. יורד בבכי (Is. XV. 3) offers a parrallel to אריד בשיחי.

V. 41 שטם .וישטם related to שתם (Lament. III. 8) and סתם, closed in, stopped up, designates a hate which is kept back, a similar conception to נטר which in general, means: guarded, kept, and in particular: to keep, them, retain, hate. “On account of the blessing which his father had given him”. One can take either of the blessing which his father had given Jacob, or which he had given him, Esau. For in this latter it is only distinctly said how his whole future position would be subordinate to that of the future House of Jacob. For he had been told that his importance in the world was only for the benefit of Jacob, and if he wanted to be his equal he would have to subordinate himself to him — ואהרגה, did not my father say על חרבך תחיה, well that shall be the first use to which I shall put my sword.

V. 42 יעקב בנה הקטון ,עשו בנה הגדול, is certainly not stressed without reason, just as, at the end of the whole story: אחי רבקה אם יעקב ועשו. After all these happenings Esau remained the elder, Jacob the younger, and Rebecca Esau’s mother as much as Jacob’s. All this expresses fully the pure feelings of Rebecca and Jacob, and confirms the way we have taken the meaning of the story. When people of baser natures have done wrong to, and harmed somebody else, they then become even worse disposed towards that person, try to find pretexes and reasons to make their action justified. Ignoble characters become even less scrupulous after the injury has been done than before they committed it. How about Rebecca and Jacob? That Esau felt rather more than indignant after what had happened, Rebecca found perfectly natural. For Esau could never understand her reasons, much less forgive them. And did Jacob make the slightest use of the ברכה and the בכורה? Not in the least. Rather we find Jacob very definitely at a disadvantage. After all they were twin brothers. And yet Esau was already married at forty years of age, brings two, then three daughters-in-law into the home, takes part in the father’s housekeeping and household, while Jacob has to go away empty without a penny, to hire himself out as a servant and by hard toil acquire a household of his own, ויעבד באשה, ובאשה שמד. Many people have found it striking that Isaac, who, both by inheritance from Abraham and by his own successful good fortune, was more than an ordinary rich man, should have allowed his son to wander forth without anything at all, just with his wanderer’s staff in his hand. But the reason for this condition had its roots deep in the motives which lay behind all these happenings. If Jacob, induced by Rebecca, had obtained the ברכה and the בכורה, it was to be made perfectly clear that no trace of any material advantage ensued thereby. After Jacob’s departure Esau was not to be able to find a pin missing. This is the greatest testimonial of Rebecca and Isaac’s nobility of soul. These words אם יעקב ועשו are, at the same time, the epitaph of Rebecca. Henceforth we hear nothing more of her. In everything and until her end, she was the mother of Jacob and Esau, always behaved as a mother to both.

ותשלח, she had to send for him, he was not with her, was no “mummy’s boy” tied to his mother’s apron-strings. אחיך, who is and remains your brother, and towards whom you may never forget that he is your brother.
V. 43 ברח לך, flee, go as a fugitive.
V. 44 חמה, is a higher degree of אף .אף is the anger that shows itself in an angry face, it need not necessarily be so bad down in the heart. But חמה is the real glow of burning anger.

V. 45 עד שוב אף. It is not sufficient for the burning anger to cool down. I will wait until you can meet him without having to expect any unfriendliness. It is evident that Rebecca had the best opinion of Esau’s feelings, that he would be able to entirely forget even the wrong which he had endured. “Shall I then lose you both on one and the same day”, just as I bare you both on one day? The murdered one she would no longer have, and the murderer would no longer be her son. But inasmuch as she feared to lose them both, they are both hers, her heart still clings to both of them, and Esau is no less her son than Jacob. These are all traits which must not be overlooked.

שכל, to be bereft of children — and אשכל grapes! Perhaps אשכל does not designate so much the grapes as the bunch, the very short stalks on which the grapes hang. As long as the grapes are hanging there the stem is not seen. It is only visible when the grapes are plucked off. אשתך כגפן פוריה, The mother rich in children is like a vine full of grapes. Should her children die, there she stands like a naked stem of grapes from which the grapes themselves have been plucked of.

V. 46 Had Rebecca been an ordinary woman how she would have loved to disclose Esau’s murderous thoughts to show him how right she had been all along. Esau contemplating becoming a second Cain, etc. etc. But this “I told you so”, she does not say, prefers to make the reason for Jacob’s journey to Paddan-aram to be quite a natural and reasonable one — כאלה as we have unfortunately already got to know the two daughters-in-law. מבנות הארץ of whom God had said לא שלם עון האמורי עד הנה.
V. 1. ויברך אתו, now of his own free-will and with full consciousness. Rebecca’s medicine had completely opened his eyes.
V. 2 There, where a woman like your mother was born, and, in spite of a Laban brought up to be what she is, there it is quite possible that you, too, could find the right wife.

V. 3 You need take nothing with you but God, He will bless you, i.e. give you the means to found a household, and then give you the strength to beget children, and to bring them up in your own spirit, that you repeat and multiply yourself in them, and you will have, what I did not succeed in having, עמים, children of different kinds, roots of the future divers tribes, but they will still be a קהל, form one united body, there will be no פסול amongst them.

V. 4 אתך, not אחריך, the future kernel for a united nation will not develop only out of your later generations. None of your children will be estranged from you, all of them will inherit with you the blessing that had been promised to Abraham.

When we compare the contents of this blessing which was given with full consciousness to Jacob, to the one apportioned above to Esau, in which no trace of the Abrahamitic mission was contained, then the way we have taken the meaning of that latter seems fully justified. But the final seal of the whole is that which is recounted in V. 6. When Esau saw etc. and that his father blessed Jacob etc. etc., only after he had seen all this, he got some faint idea that his Canaanite wives must not seem quite right to his father. Of all the heartache and worry which the wives he had hitherto married had brought to his parents Esau seems to have had no conception: Only now when some glimmering of it dawns on him — what does he do? Divorce his Canaanite wives? Not a bit of it! He just took another wife in addition to his wives, על נשיו לו לאשה. So little did Esau have any feeling or understanding for what really was necessary for the building up and continuing the House of Abraham. And just by that was Rebecca’s judgment of his complete unfitness for the future guidance of that House fully and completely justified.
V. 10 Although it has already said above: פדנה ארם, nevertheless it still begins again with Jacob’s leaving the parental home, because that introduces the independent life of Jacob.

If Abraham is the root of the Jewish People, Isaac the growth towards the trunk. Jacob is the real trunk itself. That is also why Isaac said to him ויתן לך ברכת אברהם וגו׳. For Jacob is the one who was to give the heritage of name and history to the future nation. We are not called the People of Abraham but Israel. So we see Jacob carrying out a second לך לך like Abraham, we see him, our nearest ancestor, for the same history which had been worked up from Abraham to Isaac, also going away in isolation, but nevertheless in quite a different manner to that of Abraham. True, Abraham went away from his homeland into isolation, but he went with his household, with wife and entourage, relations and fortune, But we see Jacob, driven by circumstances, going away without anything at all to take with him. He preferred to leave everything behind him to his brother so that he could see that in the matter of the בכורה there was to be no question at all of material advantage.

Jacob went away to found a Jewish HOUSE, a Jewish home, and for that he takes nothing with him but himself, that which lies in his own personality — that is the fact that is introduced here, for everything which follows is concerned with the establishment of that house. For Jacob was the first to say that God was to be sought above all in the home, the first to have thought the great conception: בית אלקים .בית א׳, the House of God, which just means nothing else than: that the sphere in which human souls are planted and blossom, to which people take everything they accomplish, and in which all their activity in building up their lives takes place, that is the greatest and nearest place for finding the revelation of God.

That which Noah saw prophetically at the laying of the fresh foundation of human history, namely, that though it is given to Japhetic culture to win people to a sense of beauty and thereby to influence them to higher and nobler ideas, it will still be Shem’s mission “to build homes in which God lives”, that was first of all made apparent through Jacob. If Jewish wisdom has taught the great idea that transforms the whole point of view regarding the universe viz. that עיקר שכינה בתחתונים the principle and real place of Schechina is on earth; or: when people piously turn their eyes upwards to heaven and imagine they have to seek God up above, the angels laugh at them and call them “bags of wind” (ס״ח 18); or if someone is walking out of doors, studying, and interrupts his study to say “how beautiful is this tree, how beautiful that field”—who finds God more wonderful in the beauties of Nature than in the pious development of the human soul—has almost committed a capital crime (Ethics III. 9), for all these and similar sayings and teachings of Jewish wisdom we have to thank the spirit of Jacob. Under the influence of Japhetic culture one takes refuge out of “profane”, “common” life into the realm of the “poetry” of the beauties of nature. Jacob’s heirs find God and the sublime, first of all, and nearest of all, in the home. That is the contrast between Jewish and non-Jewish characters.

Thus Jacob went from Beer-Sheba towards Haran. באר שבע, which had been so pregnant with meaning for Isaac; where it had been brought home to him that — although not גרות — עבדות had begun. But where, when he had gone into isolation of his own free will, he had found not only quiet and peace, but recognition. This Beer-Sheba of rest and honour, Jacob gave up and wandered forth to Haran.

V. 11 ויפגע במקום, this can not simply mean he chanced to come to a place. Firstly because then it would have to say בְּמקום not בַּמקום further, פגע ב- never means just a meeting, but always such a meeting where the one makes an important impression on the other. Hence it is also used for the intentional going to meet with weapons, or to make a request, to attack, or to urge. So that here, too, it must have been a place to which he had been meaningfully attracted and held.

He goes out into the wide world without any means; added to that it is a Laban to whom he is going, whose character may well have been known to him, he is on his way to Haran to get himself a wife, so that his thoughts are all in Haran, the goal of his journey. Then “he struck this place”, it held him. “He spent the night there, for the sun had set”. The impression that the place had made upon him was still not strong enough by itself to have kept him back had not the sun already set. Then he took some of the stones of the place, arranged them round his head so that no man or beast tread on him. This protection of stones was the first house he built for himself. And although he had been quite excited by the place — it was at the border of the land of his future — he still lay down and slept at this place.

V. 12 סלם, a ladder was shown him, (סלם from סלל to go up) so there was a means of communication upwards from the earth, and it is מֻצב, placed there, did not come there by itself, nor just by chance, it had been placed there by a Higher power, and indeed ארצה, to the earth, the power and the will that set it was not to be looked for on earth, but above, it is set from the height above down to the earth, וראשו מגיע השמימה, nevertheless its purpose is primarily not only from heaven to earth, but to go up from earth to heaven. Such was the first trend of thought which was shown to him so that, first of all, in general, that the whole life on earth, including accordingly, human life, his own life also, has its goal, not in the plains — not from Beer-Sheba to Haran — but in the heights, and set from the heights; that everything earthly is invited from above to work itself upwards to a heavenly high goal; that this goal and this striving upwards to it is no fairy tale invented by Man, no erroneous theory originating on earth, but is a most substantial reality established from heaven itself. (Cf. the verses in ב״ר: סיני סולם זה — סולם זה כבש, מוצב ארצה זה מזבח — and חולין 91b. רחבו של סולם שמנה אלפים פרסאות wide beyond the whole world does the ladder reach, and its lowest rung can be mounted everywhere on earth).

והנה, a second set of ideas. He sees מלאכי אלקים angels of God, God’s messengers, beings on earth who are called, by God’s command to be active in the life on earth, sees them going up, coming down, going up to get the directions for their work, and coming down against him (which is the way one authority takes the meaning of the word literally to be, which opinion seems to us to be justified by the following explanation). He sees that the fate of men is not made on earth by the material world. He sees messengers of God, and notices that these messengers of God go up the ladder to get a picture of the ideal humanity, how human beings really should be, and then come down and compare what they find here below, with that picture to decide, according to that standard, whether to behave in a friendly assisting manner towards any particular member of mankind, or in very much the reverse way. And so — to quote the words of our sages in Chulin 91b — עולין ומסתכלין בדיוקנו של מעלה ומסתכלין בדיוקנו של מטה בעו לסכיניה they ascended and saw the picture depicted of him up above, and came down and considered the picture he actually made here below, as this is further worked out in ב״ר: ישראל אשר בד אתפאר את הוא שאיקוגיך חקוק למעלה ,עולין למעלה ומוצאין איקנין שלו ויורדין למטה ומוצאין אותו ישן. “up above they found his picture engraved as Israel glorifying God, they came down and found him fast asleep”, — sleeping at the very place which should have awakened in his mind the thoughts of his glorious mission, which thoughts would surely have kept him excitedly awake — so that on that account “they intended to endanger his life”, מיד, but at once, והנה ה׳ נצב עליו.

V. 13 והנה, a third trend of thought: ה׳ נצב עליו, this is usually taken to mean: stood on it, on the ladder, and that gives a lovely dramatic picture, the sleeping Jacob at the foot of the ladder, the ascending and descending angels, and the Glory of God high up above the ladder. But נצב על- designates almost everywhere in תנ״ך not the actual place on which somebody stands, but the one on which his mind, his attention is fixed. נצב על עין (Gen. XXIV.13), הנצבים עליו (ibid XLV.1), נצב עליך (Ex. XVIII. 14), נצב על עלתו (Numbs. XXIII. 6) נצב עליהם (I. Sam. XIX. 20), et alia, all designate standing next to something giving all one’s attention to it. The word נצב itself is not simply standing, but standing somewhere with forces alert and ready for action, hence מצב: post. Further, the Name ה׳ here seems to be in contrast to מלאכי אלקים. The angels are the messengers of God, that He has created and keeps for the laws of nature of the world in which everything is measured and weighed in accordance with what is right and correct. To them everything and everybody is only what it represents at that moment (cf. Ex. 23,21 לא ישא לפשעכם כי שמי בקרבו). But it is ה׳ Who stands by him, ה׳ that God of Love, Who does not have only the past and the present before His Eyes, but Who also sees and arranges the future, and Who recognises in every present person, the future person, and if He sees any seedling, any spark of purity, keeps and fans and develops that seed.

Or, if the בו is not to be taken as adversely “against him”, but on it, on the ladder, it would mean: he sees all forces that wish to seek God, ascending to find Him, but he need not seek God in heaven, he finds God next to him. There that which the sages teach from these words, that האבות הם הם המרכבה, that pure human beings like the Patriarchs are the true bearers of the Glory of God, which wants to have its home primarily on earth עיקר שכינה בתחתונים, then became clear to Jacob. For the meaning of this whole revelation is summarised in the fact that ה׳ נצב עליו (God was there, right next to him I. L.).

It appears here with great significance that it says אברהם אביך and then יצחק without that appellation. It does not seem to occur anywhere else that the grandfather is called the father and the father is mentioned at the same time just as if he was no relation. It obviously can not possibly refer to the physical derivation. But by this mode of address Jacob was told everything. Jacob was the son, the successor of Abraham, Isaac, only the intermediate member. Spiritually, Abraham was Jacob’s father. “Thou art the son of him to whom I spoke: התהלך לפני והיה תמים, be thou his son and heir!”. Also, with Jacob, the first to build a complete Jewish household, the Abrahamitic future had the first beginning of realisation.

V. 14 בך — ובזרעך (just as before לך ולזרעך) “through thee all the families of the world shall be blessed, and through thy seed”. Quite definitely the blessing that is to emanate from him, appears here to be a double one. Altogether, one man and one nation can be the source of blessing for the whole human race only by spiritual influence, and the example of the development of a model exemplary mode of life, until the time comes when the phophecy will be fulfilled that בימים ההמה אשר יחזיקו עשרה אנשים מכל לשונות הגוים והחזיקו בכנף איש יהודי לאמר נלכה עמכם כי שמענו אלקים עמכם “in those days, that, when ten men from every language of the nations will seek security, they will catch hold of the garment of a Jewish man and say: we would go with you, for we have heard that God is with you” (Zacc. 8,23). That is the blessing that Jacob, as a pater familias, and his seed as a nation, are to be to the world. Jacob demonstrates the first Jewish house, and teaches how, without נחלת אבותיו, without any inherited fortune, simply by the blessing and dignity of מלאכה, of work, one can build up, and live through a family life with all its drudgery, worries and griefs, and still have ה׳ נצב עליו, still not miss God in one’s life. Accordingly, it is family and national life, borne purely and entirely by the grace of God, and lived in accordance with the Divine Will, which mankind is to learn from you and from your seed.

V. 15 והנה אנכי עמך. I (the God of Love to mankind) am with you, and although you take nothing with you but your staff, you have Me. To the grandson of Abraham it is not promised, as it was to Abraham ואברכך ואגדלה שמך, he is going into Galut. What is promised to him is שמירה, protection, and ultimate return. In exactly the same way as in the future, when his people will leave the same land and wander out in exile. — לא אעזבך, I will work on you for so long, so long will I occupy Myself with your fate until you will have become what you should become, and then, through you, all families of the world will be blessed.

V. 16 יקץ ,ויקץ and קוץ both mean to awake, the latter in the Hiphil. The fundamental meaning of קוץ is disgust, to become sick of that which hitherto one had greedily enjoyed. The summer is called קיץ as being the time when the fruit, which up till then had greedily sucked up the sap from the earth, now disdains it, and has achieved complete independence. In the same way קוץ and יקץ designate the moment when man has satiated himself with sleep on the regenerating bosom of nature, and tearing himself free from it, rises again to an independent existence.

ויאמֶר, is not so separated as וירא ויאמַר which follows, what he says does not begin a fresh activity but is rather what he said as he woke up, the first impression that what he had lived through in sleep made on his conscious state: So God is here! He modestly ascribes the proximity of God, not to himself, but to the place. So there is no necessity to go to heaven to look for God, but where a guiltless man lays down his head, God is there! That was his first thought. And his second: And up till now I did not know this! Did not know that the Glory of God seeks its bearers amongst human beings!

V. 17 ויירא. What made him afraid? Probably nothing else, but the consciousness of this new idea and the new demands that it brings with it, that man, frail man, is to be, should be, the bearer of the Glory of God on earth, could have brought this overwhelming feeling of fear in him: how awesome is this place. What has been shown me here is nothing other than “the house of God”, and that, at the same time, is “the gate to Heaven”. The House of God, a house into which God moves, that a human life can be, and should be, such, that when the ascending angels seek God in heaven, they have to come down to find Him amongst mankind. And every such house, in which such a life is lived is the “gate of Heaven”, a gate through which we come to God, accordingly, the most consummate union of the earthly with the heavenly.

V. 18 מצבה consists of a single stone, מזבח is an elevation built up by many stones; מצבה is presented by nature, מזבח is made by man. Before מתן תורה God’s rule was manifest primarily only in the ways of nature and in Man’s fate, accordingly in what Man gets from the Hand of God. A מצבה corresponds to that, a stone taken from God’s creation as a memorial for something which He has done. But with מתן תורה God wishes to be revealed, not so much in what Man receives from Him, as in what Man does with what he gets from Him; not with God’s gifts but with Man’s deeds is God to be glorified. That indeed is the purpose of the Lawgiving, since then מצבה is rejected.

שמן על ראשה — either as consecration of the stone, as the vessels of the Sanctuary were anointed with oil by which — as oil does not mix with other liquids — the anointed object is set apart from, and raised above the others. Or, in the sense of a libation. Just as later on, wine was poured out to express the acknowledgment that all joy in life comes from God and remains dedicated to Him, (יין משמח אלקים ואנשים). Or in the highest national libation water was poured out on the Altar to express that, not only exceptional gifts, but that every drop of water is a gift from God, and with every drop of water we feel allied to God: so here oil — at later offerings the expression for health and well-being (להצהיל פנים משמן) — that he awaits his continued existence and well being from God’s Hand and would use it always regarding it as a continuous gift of God.

V. 19. Whereas God found this spot to be the most important centre on earth, to which the salvation of the whole of mankind would be attached, up till now nothing unusual had been noticed there, the city had been simply named after a hazel-nut tree, Hazelnut City.

V. 20. נדר (related to נתר to spring not vertically upwards, but horizontally from one place to another, quickly placing yourself in another place by springing over the intervening space: also to נטר which has not only the meaning of “keeping”, “hiding”, but also in מטרה has the meaning of target, goal, accordingly the point which one is נטר at which one looks with one’s mind, from a distance. לא תטר את בני עמך, “thou shalt not keep a son of thy people in the heart as a target to be hit”. Now just as נתר in space is getting somewhere by springing over the intervening space, and נטר in your mind is placing yourself in thought at a goal which is still far-off, the same idea applies to נדר. Cf. the Rabbinic expressions קפץ ונשבע קפץ ונדר). Everyone who makes a vow places himself now, already, in a point of time which is not present, and decides what is to happen at that distant time.

And it is just in that, in anticipating the future which you can not possibly know, that the sinfulness of a נדר lies. It requires quite a great deal really to see exactly what any present moment truly means, to value it correctly and to use it faithfully. What is good and right and our duty in any coming moment we will have to do in any case without any preliminary special vowing, what is bad and wrong at that time we may not do in spite of having previously vowed to do. So that for what is good or bad vows are completely superfluous. Only indifferent matters remain, but it is indeed more than folly to elevate indifferent matters to a solemn duty, and added to that, for it to be done in our unknown future.

Only in extraordinary cases, בשעת צרה, where, as here, it is not the future which is anticipated, but, on the contrary, it is the present moment which is so significant that it is to be a foundation for the life that lies before one, and is to be transposed into that coming life, only in such cases are vows permitted, and can even be a מצוה to make them.

The word עמדי is puzzling. Whereas עם (from עמם) means just being with, keeping parallel to somebody or something, עמדי, from עמד seems to indicate a more intimate participation where the one receives and keeps his standing from the other. What is striking, is that this preposition only occurs with the suffix of the first person singular.

ושמרני וגו׳. As here — in contrast to the יברכך וישמרך :ברכת כהנים — the prayer for protection precedes that for blessing of food and clothes etc., the protection prayed for here can not refer to these external possessions — of which indeed he did not possess any — but for the guarding of the spiritual and moral possessions which he bore in himself. And these were the more easily endangered “on the path which he was treading, בדרך הזה״ the poorer he was in external possessions. Ever since the gates of Paradise had closed, gaining one’s daily bread, keeping one’s own home, the ונתן לי is such a difficult task, is interlocked with so many artificial conditions and external requirements that it does really need God’s support not to give up the whole of one’s better self to gain that piece of bread. Who can count the number of men who, before they had “to tread the path of earning their daily bread” were morally pure and honest, and to gain their livelihood and attain a position in civic life, denied God, gave up morality, had no consideration for their neighbour’s honour, or even respect for his marriage etc. etc. Not for nought do our sages say, that path is beset with לה״ר ,ש״ד ,ג״ע ,ע״ז, scandal and lies, murder, immorality and worshipping false gods. Jacob, who hitherto had been יושב אהלים, and now wanders forth to win a wife, and bread for wife and family, is so deeply conscious of this danger that he first prays to God for protection for his own character, that he be given strength not to forfeit any of his spiritual and moral integrity.

Integrity is therefore the first thing that the first Jew, on the way to found a home, wishes for; and then לי לחם וגו׳, to me, i.e. an independent living, and בגד to be able to appear respectably clad in society, i.e. livelihood and position in civic life; thirdly, that which does live, and should live in every Jewish breast: שלום, the desire for peace; and finally בית אב, the indestructable attachment to family.

If God grants me this: והיה ה׳ לי לאלקים (then the God of Love will be for me a God of Justice, Who judges me. I.L.) This, too, is a thought, that is henceforth to be continuously vivid with us, and to which the very last גאולה refers. If, in this struggle for existence, God protects and blesses people, then God reveals Himself as ה׳, in His מדת הרחמים, and every one in the world wishes and prays for that relationship of God towards himself. But it is only the Jewish conception which says והיה ה׳ לי לאלקים, then God Who showers all His Love on me shall be, to me, in my mind, a God Who not only gives, but Who demands, Who wants to know that with all that He gives His Will is furthered. To do homage to God, not merely as a Giver, but as a Lawgiver, to make every breath that you take, every penny that you spend, in accordance with His directions, that is the meaning of ה׳ לי לאלקים. Thus God says to the redeemed descendants of Jacob: “I have redeemed you להיות לכם לאלקים: so that ye shall regulate and live the human and social lives ye have regained in accordance with My Will.

V. 22. “And so this stone, which I now set up as a memorial of this moment when I, as a poor man on a bleak moor stand forth looking forward to such a future richly blessed by God, this stone shall be built up to a house in which such a life shall be lived that God will enter therein. Thereby, and thereby only, by making ה׳ into אלקים to ourselves can a place on earth become a house of God. Not to realise this, is the mistake which ages which pride themselves more than anything else in building beautiful cathedrals and “houses of God” so often make. They build, as the Prophet (Ezekiel 43,8) puts it ספם את ספי “their doorsteps next to My Doorstep”. They visit God in His House but forbid His entry into theirs — where His presence with His demands might certainly be inconvenient.

That was not the thought with which the first foundation-stone was laid for the first “House of God”. The sanctity of the homes is the necessary condition for the sanctity of the House of God, which is not called מקדש because it is the place to which קדושה is relegated, but, because from there holiness is to flow out and penetrate all human conditions and places, it is to be their centre point. ועשו לי מקדש, let them make a Sanctuary unto Me” it says later on to the descendants of Jacob who are to build out the foundation of this stone into a system of private and national life, ושכנתי “that I may dwell”, not בתוכו, not in it, but בתוכם “amongst them” ה׳ אלקיך מתהלך בקרב מחנך .והתהלכתי בתוככם it says, even of the military camp in war, and the goal of the development beginning with this stone is כל סיר בירושלים וביהודה קדש לה׳ צבאות “every saucepan in Jerusalem and Judah shall be holy unto God (Zacc. 14,21).

To this stone Jacob still looked on his death-bed, as the beginning and foundation-stone of Israel, and says of God: משם רועה אבן ישראל “that from there from this stone He will protectingly shepherd Israel to its goal”. It is to this stone that perhaps Zaccariah refers to in Ch. III. על אבן אחת שבעה עינים that over this stone seven eyes, i.e. the whole complex of the Divine Providence watches. It was the אבן הראשה, the first corner-stone which was again to be laid afresh with the building of the second Temple, but which תשואות חן חן לה, by which the ultimate consummation of the final edifice was ensured. So that it says pertinently of this stone in פרקי דר״א. “God added this stone as a perpetual appendage to the formation of the world”. עשה אותה סניף לארץ for on the building of human homes to God which was started with this stone, the whole future destiny of the world rests. It is the אבן שתיה. See שרשים ,רד״ק Rad. שות.
עשר אעשרנו לך. See above on Ch. 14,20.

V. 1. Now he was quite a different person to what he was before, of whom it said ויצא וגו׳. Now it says “he lifted up his feet”. With such thoughts of the future, awakened in his mind by God, Jacob, even with only his staff in his hand, steps out fresh and gaily to meet his future.
בני קדם. See above on Ch. 25,6. The east-lying lands were very different in culture and manners from those of the west. That Jacob found out very quickly.

V. 2. Generally the cover of a well designed for general public use, is made to be removed as easily as possible to facilitate its use for everybody. But here — this introduces us to the character of the Arameans — no one trusted the other and nobody meant anybody else to have the slightest advantage. One person might take a drink more than the other. Hence they made the cover so heavy that no person alone but only by their combined effort could the well be used.

V. 7. האסף המקנה, not הצאן, he called the flocks מקנה, property and reminded them by that term of their duty towards the owner of the sheep, the sheep should not be allowed to lie about idle, but should be taken to the pastures.
V. 10. ויגל, Hiphil, “let it roll away”, the Hiphil does not occur elsewhere with this root. It designates the ease with which he pushed the great stone aside.

Now we get to know what Jacob really did take with him for building his future. Money he did not possess. What is striking, is his strength. What the others could only do by a combined effort he did alone, and without exertion, a strength which we should not have at all expected to find in Jacob. This strong healthy muscular body was at the moment his sole material wealth. A treasure that can not be sufficiently valued, which is an important asset for the whole future and can only be acquired by a purely lived past: It is the grounding for the עושר וכבוד the material benefits which the תורה offers with its left hand. The second, is his imperturbable sense of right and justice. Just like Moses, who also found his future at a well, he can not stand the least dereliction of duty which strikes him, a trait which he himself kept so brilliantly in the most difficult conditions of service which were imposed on him. Thirdly, a ready cheerful deftness in work and action which jumps to it and makes itself useful even where he is in no wise called upon to intervene, again which we should hardly have expected in the איש תם יושב אהלים. In all he appears a true prototype of the people whose ancestor he was to become who were to represent the most varied material and spiritual activities of life as being of equal value and estimation. The Ancestor possessed such versatility that each one of his sons could say that his own particular trend and ability was inherited from his father.

It is repeated three times in this verse that Laban was the brother of Jacob’s mother. For in everything that Jacob did here, he was moved by the thought of his mother who appeared living before him in the person of her nearest relative. We are told at once that Jacob kissed Rachel. Without this marked repeated reference to being reminded of his mother, Jacob’s whole behaviour might have been taken as a piece of gallantry towards a pretty shepherdess. In the same way when Moses behaved in a similar manner towards the daughters of Jethro this idea is averted by the striking change in the gender, indicating that he was not moved by any feelings of their sex, but entirely by his keen feelings of what was right ויבאו הרעים ויגרשום, the rude shepherds came and pushed them away (them with a masculine suffix I.L.) without regard to their being of the weaker sex. ויקם משה ויושען Moses rescued them (them with the feminine suffix I.L.) because they were the weaker sex, but וישק את צאנם he then went on helping them with their sheep (their, masculine again I.L.) regardless of their sex. So here, too. Although Rachel was beautiful, he only saw a relative in her. That is shown by his tears. Who knows how long Jacob had been wandering away from home without seeing one familiar face, and then suddenly he sees in Rachel the daughter of his mother’s brother, and the picture of his mother affects him to tears. These tears show how the kiss was an absolutely chaste one. Rachel must have thought him quite mad when he fell round her neck kissing and weeping. That is why he disengaged himself and explained the cause of his emotion.

V. 13. את כל הדברים האלה. All these matters of which we know, especially that, although he came from the rich home of his sister, he had still brought nothing with him but the staff in his hand. This explains the “אך״ in Laban’s reply. Nevertheless, although poor, you are welcome as a relative.

V. 15. Again a characteristic trait of Jacob. He had worked for him for the whole month gratuitously. Jacob did not like to accept charity. And his work must indeed have been valuable if even a Laban, who undoubtedly had reckoned out what the cost of “board and lodging for such a hefty fellow” had been for a month, still could not help calling it working for nothing, and preferred to try and tie him down by a wage rather than risk losing such a capable worker.
V. 17. Instead of saying Leah was not so beautiful, it very delicately just praises her good points. Her eyes were soft and tender whereas Rachel was altogether beautiful.

V. 21. הבה אשתי, not תנה and not הבה .בתך is the demand for a new decision, of which hitherto there has been no question. At the passing of the last minute of the agreed term of service, she has already become Jacob’s wife, the קידושין are already completed, she was already his and he now demands his own.

V. 24. He was very careful to give her, not to Jacob, but expressly to Leah as her own personal property. This is also not unimportant for later on. For if, later on, Jacob married her too, this could only occur on the initiative of Leah the mistress to whom she belonged.

V. 25.—26. You do not know the customs here. If here, with us, someone asks for the hand of a younger sister, he automatically includes an unmarried elder one, as here with us, it is not considered correct to marry a younger sister before an elder one. So that he can only get the younger through marrying the elder, and gets the elder one first and then the younger. It is all perfectly in order. After Leah’s marriage, comes Rachel’s. We shall “give her” to you then. In the “we” he tries to make it sound as if his lying trick was the accepted local legal procedure. “Of course then you will have to serve me for another seven years!”

רמה Grundbedeutung: schleudern. Was man schleudern will, muss man erst in die Hand bekommen und auf der Hand ruhen lassen; sobald es aber dort ruht, schleudert man es weg. Ebenso der Betrüger. Er kann nur den betrügen, der sich ihm zuvor in die Hand gegeben, der ihm zuvor getraut. Nur das Vertrauen ist Mittel zu seinem Verderben.
V. 28. The repetition of לו לאשה is striking. Possibly perhaps it indicates a greater degree of intimacy to her than to Leah?

V. 30. ויאהב גם את רחל, so he loved Leah too, and did not make her pay for her father’s behaviour and for the way she had become his wife. We can deduce from this that Leah too was taken in by her father by some story of a legal arrangement he had made with Jacob as to agreed customs and that she was not a party to any wilful deception. “He also loved Rachel, (and indeed) more than Leah.”

V. 31. Not כי לאה שנואה, that Leah was hated, but כי שנואה לאה, that the hated one of the two, i.e. the less beloved, was Leah. Similarly האחת אהובה והאחת שנואה (Deut. 31,15). It is deeply significant that the real pith of the Jewish nation has not the one for its mother whom Jacob — as far as the text itself relates — chose primarily more for the impression her beauty made on his senses, and that it was just the one who felt herself placed somewhat in the background whom God appointed to be the principal ancestress of His people. For the names which this less-loved wife gave to her sons shows us how, just in the feeling of being at first set back she was all the more deeply in love with her husband, and how she succeeded in working herself up to the highest pitch of mutual happiness with her husband by the happy and happiness-giving valuation of the vocations of motherhood and wifehood, and how for both, she clung to her trust in the All-seeing and All-hearing Presence of God in married life. The love of her husband was what she was aiming at, and with every child she bore to him she hoped to possess one brick more to this edifice of love she was building, and she succeeded in having her hopes fulfilled. That which was denied to the bride and wife was fully given to the mother of his children. And so the tribes of the Jewish nation were conceived and born, cared for and brought up in the sunny rays of a home of the warmest and purest happiness of married life and love, and in their names are immortalised all the cheerful and serious factors on which the happiness of Jewish marriages and Jewish homes depend. And it was just to Leah, the sad one that it was decreed to experience and immortalise the cheerful and brightest aspects of marriage and home, while to Rachel, the happy one was allocated the more serious ones.

V. 32.—35. The successive names show, how, with the blessing of each fresh child for which Jacob had to thank Leah, his attitude to her became increasingly more and more loving. At first ראה ה׳ בעניי. So that up to then Jacob’s preference for Rachel was visible. With the birth of Reuben that disappeared, but, to Leah’s ear, it could still be detected. Just in the tone of his voice to Rachel, Leah could feel that she still did not possess the full measure of her husband’s love, so she called her second son: Simeon.

With the birth of her third son, however, she felt the difference had quite disappeared, yea she felt she could now express with full confidence, that now the purest, truest loving relationship between husband and wife was established, which is exactly the conception of לויה. For הלוה ,לוה, is that attachment of two persons where each one of them feels themselves the לוה, the debtor of the other, feels that they owe their happiness and whole life to the other. It is accordingly highly significant that at Levi, it is not she, but he who expresses this in giving the baby its name. Had she done so, it might only have been supposition, or even wishful thinking on her part, but, coming from his mouth, it was the sweetest acknowledgment, על כן קרא שמו לוי. So that, when the fourth son was born, Judah, she no longer had primarily to welcome it as a means of progress in her husband’s love towards her, which she now fully possessed, but could simply enjoy her baby purely for its own sake. She accordingly pronounced the words of a happy mother “This time I can thank God, just for His gift itself” and called the child Judah.

V. 1. הבה לי בנים. She probably thought that, as he was getting children anyway from Leah he did not very much mind her being barren, and consequently was not sufficiently ardent in beseeching God for her. His mother, too, had only had children in response to his father’s prayers.
V. 2. התחת א׳ אנכי. It is not through lack of prayers on my part, but God has denied you the joy of motherhood.
V. 3. See on Ch. 16,2.

V. 6. דון means both, to carry out justice on someone as: וגם הגוי וגו׳ דן אנכי, as well as to see that someone gets his rights as כי ידין ה׳ עמו. It is doubtful in which way it is meant here. The וגם שמע וגו׳ would favour the first: God had dealt very strictly with me and has denied me the ability to have children myself, but He has nevertheless now heard my prayer; inasmuch as He has granted me a child to whom I can be at least a spiritual mother; and although I did not actually bear it, I can look after it and bring it up as my contribution to the House of Jacob.

V. 8. נפתולי אלקים, a sacred “wrestling competition” did I wage with my sister, not a match that struggles for something low or common, of which one would be ashamed, but for a sacred end did I compete against my sister, to do my part, too, for the spiritual building up of our house. I have given proof of that by even giving my slave to be a wife for my husband, to become, as nearly as possible, the giver of a child to our house to whom I can then fulfil all the duties of a mother as if it were really my own.

V. 11. גל from גדד to drive in quickly, suddenly, to cut separatingly into something. Hence גדוד, a raiding troop, a troop of armed men who quickly and suddenly invade another province, and גוד to form such a troop, or to make such a raid. The idea of some fate suddenly occurring in life is also expressed by גד. Isaiah speaks of עורכים לגד שלחן (LXV,11) “they prepare a table to “chance”, to “luck”. And so probably here too ב(א) גד means: an unexpected piece of luck has come. This son was one which, in ordinary circumstances, she could not have reckoned on. For she had come to the idea of getting him only through the example of her sister.

V. 13. אשר is related on the one hand to אצר ,חשר ,עשׂר ,אסר ,עשׁר, all of which have the meaning of a collecting, a heaping up, of forces, with more or less intensity; and on the other hand we find אשור with the meaning of “step” and, indeed, especially with spiritual reference, so that the fundamental conception of אשר could be essentially “progress” i.e. a constant step towards greater riches of power, forces or qualities. From that we get אֶשֶׁר and ﭏשֶׁר: thriving progress, and אשרי would mean literally: he is making all progress towards goodness and happiness who…etc.. אשרה is a tree which is thriving under the supposedly special blessing of a god to which it is dedicated. — באשרי, says Leah, just as through my own births, so do the births of my ex-slave show that I am still in my old state of progress to happiness; for, in fact, women in general have praised my progress in life in my having been blessed with children.

V. 14. This business of the mandrakes has again and again been taken by commentators in a serious vein. But it is quite unthinkable that Leah, whose whole life was devoted to gain the complete love of her husband could possibly have uttered the words “You have got my man and now you want my bunch of flowers also” in any serious sense. As if the possession of a few flowers could come into the very slightest consideration in connection with, or in comparison with, the possession of a beloved husband. Rather, the whole matter appears as an instance to show a state of the two sisters living together in the most confidential intimacy. While Jacob is out in the fields the two wives sit together. His evenings he spends alternatively with each one of them. Reuben, who was still a little boy, brings some wild flowers home to his mother. “Give me some of them” says Rachel “What sauce to ask for my precious flowers, etc.” says Leah jokingly, but of course she gives her some (that is evident from Rachel’s לכן). “Now” says Rachel, “because you have been so kind, he shall come to you this evening”. The קחתך את אישי can also, quite likely, refer just to that day. “Last evening you have had my husband etc.”

V. 20. זבד, related to ויצבט קלי ,צבט (Ruth II) to measure something out for somebody, to apportion. Also to הצבתים ,צבת (ibid), the bundles of sheaves gathered together. Also to צבת the tool with which one picks out something from a mass, tongs. Hence זבד the apportioned part. As the repeated אותי stresses the person, it could also mean: God hath made me into a good portion — to my husband. My husband has found in me the fulfillment of his wishes. Similarly יזבלני. When we consider that זבול occurs primarily only as a characteristic of the בית המקדש as being befitted for God: בנה בניתי בית זבול לך (I Kings 8,13) and מזבול קדשך ותפארתך (Is. 63,15), then זבל does not seem to designate just a simple dwelling-place, but such a home that completely corresponds to all the purposes, wishes and demands of the one for whom it is designed, an appropriate, desirable dwelling. Thus also in Habakuk 3,11. שמש ירח עמד זבולה, the sun, the moon keep to the place to which they always hurry home. And again in Ps. XLIX.15 וצורם לבלות שאול מזבול לו, they, the righteous, are destined to last beyond the grave, so that it, the grave is not to remain their real, final home. Accordingly הפעם יזבלני אישי means: now my husband will recognize me as his real home (cf. מעון אתה), will feel at home with me more than anywhere else.

V. 25. אל מקומי ולארצי. Jethro says (Numb. 18,30) אל ארצי אל מולדתי אלך, and actually, in terms of distance that is the right order, one can not get to one’s birthplace without first going to one’s country. But with Jacob, the case was different. He did have a “place”, a home, but he had no country to which he belonged. His country was only a promised land, the land of the future. That is also probably why he does not say ואל ארצי but ולארצי. The land in its actual present state does not draw him to it, and when he does return there he is actually no nearer “his own land” than he is in Aram. But, by the independence that he is to establish in the place where his home was, he will be living more for the land of his future. He wishes to let his family grow up, there, where their descendants are in the future to find their homeland.

V. 26. אתה ידעת את עבדתי אשר עבדתיך. Perhaps no man has ever served such fourteen years. For fourteen years Jacob had worked, not for his wife and children, but for getting his wife and children. With fourteen years of hard labour he had wooed two undowered girls. These fourteen years of service, in which the whole future national and family life of the House of Jacob had its roots, form the noblest and most illuminating portal to that most precious jewel of human acquirements — Jewish family life. They show what his wife means to a Jewish man, and silence all that nonsense that people dare to imagine of oriental depreciation or degradation of Jewish women. After fourteen years Jacob stood exactly where he was at the beginning, he had only worked up more and greater worries for himself, for he had now four wives and twelve children to to provide for. And for their future, he had still nothing more than he had fourteen years previously at the memorial stone on the moor, nothing but the treasure he bore in his heart and his head and the lusty power of work in his muscles.

תנה את נשי וגו׳ כי אתה ידעת וגו׳. You deceived me once, deceive me not a second time. Let me take my wives and children away. I have honestly earned them, for you know well how I have served you for them.

V. 27. Laban would like to retain his services, and preferably for his mere keep. So he speaks like a real cunning sanctimonious “pious” rascal. He does not say that he would like to keep him for his able services, he feels that such actual things have to be paid for, and if one has even praised them, well paid for. So he speaks uncommonly “piously”. — (and just as today those who have given up all true piety, become highly superstitious, and imagine ניחוש, believing in superstition is being “pious”). — I do not like to let you go, no real reason for it, but I have a נחוש about you, have a superstitious idea that “ה׳״, the God Whom you serve, has brought me luck, blessed me because you are such a pious man. That is why I do not like to let such a pious man go away from me”.

He hoped the “pious” man would feel flattered at this, and declare himself ready to stay on. But as Jacob was silent, he saw the necessity to come out with something a little more material. “You fix a wage, I will gladly pay it”. To which Jacob says: You know quite well and clearly, have no need to refer to some vague idea you have, what I have done for you, and hoy much of “your blessing” is due to my work; you have no need to “imagine” that God has blessed you בגללי, as you put it, for my sake, but you know full well that he did it לרגלי, in accordance with the way I went, how capably I moved day and night in your service. Not on account of my piety but on account of my diligence did God bless you — and now — when shall I begin to do something for myself and my household with this industrious power of work of mine?

נקבה. Der gemeinsame Grundbegriff, nach welchem נקב zugleich: ein Loch machen, und: bestimmen bedeutet, ist mir noch nicht klar. Analog heißt רצה wollen und רצע bohren, רצח morden; ערג sich nach etwas sehnen und הרג totschlagen. Vielleicht, wie in ויקב חר בדלתו, buchstäblich: er löcherte eine Öffnung in die Tür, somit נקב aus einem Ganzen ein entsprechendes Teil trennend herausheben heißt, liegt auch dem נקב בשם ,נקב שֵם ,נקב שכר dieselbe Anschauung, nur in abstrakter Bedeutung übertragen zu Grunde. Ehe der Lohn ausgesprochen, ist der Begriff "Lohn" etwas ganz allgemeines und umfasst alle möglichen Werte und Größen. Wie ein bestimmter Lohn in einer bestimmten Größe angegeben wird, wird dieser Wert in dieser Größe, aus allen den möglichen Werten und Größen, die der unbestimmte Begriff Lohn enthält, getrennt und herausgehoben, so daß alle anderen Möglichkeiten nicht weiter in Betracht kommen. Der Begriff Lohn bleibt fortan auf den Umfang dieses aus dem allgemeinen gleichsam "Herausgebohrten" beschränkt. Ebenso אנשים אשר נקבו בשמות: Männer, die durch die Angebung ihrer Namen aus der Summe aller sonst in dem allgemeinen Begriff "Männer" Enthaltenen ausgesondert und herausgehoben worden sind. Ganz ähnlich bildet sich für unseren Sprachgedanken der Begriff נכר, der Fremdsein und in הכיר, eigentlich fremdmachen, erkennen bedeutet. Denn jedes Erkennen besteht in Vergegenwärtigung derjenigen Merkmale, wodurch ein Gegenstand aus der Summe seiner Gattung oder Art sich ausscheidet, also aus seiner Gesamtheit ausgesondert und herausgehoben, somit "fremd" gemacht wird. Bemerkenswert ist, daß das mit נכר lautverwandte נקר ebenfalls "herausbohren" heißt.
V. 30. לרגלי does not mean after I came, but after my ways and steps. Thus לרגל המלאכה וגו׳ (Ch. 33,13) “in accordance with the steps of flocks and children”.

V. 31. You are not to give me anything. Jacob had had experience how Laban understood how to twist and deceive in paying after the work had been done. You are to pay me. An arrangement must be made whereby that which is to be Jacob’s wages becomes his property as soon as it is born; for once anything has become Laban’s property it is not so easily obtained from him, however justified the demand might be.

V. 32. נקד וטלוא. From the meaning נקודה a point, and נעלים מטלאות, patched shoes (Josh. IX), as well as טלאי the term for patching in Rabbinic Hebrew, the meaning of נקד וטלוא as spotted and speckled seems sure — חום does not occur elsewhere as a colour. In any case it means dark; whether because dark colours keep warmer, or because white turns dark through heat, is undecided. Small spots or large patches are to be reckoned both at sheep and goats; חום dark, probably black, only at sheep. The normal colour of wool is white: כצמר יהיו (Is. 1,18). In Song of Songs IV. 1, 2, the flowing black tresses are compared to a herd of goats hurrying down the mountain, and the teeth to a flock of sheep coming up from bathing. From that we can deduce (in opposition to רמב״ן) that the normal colour of sheep is white and of goats black.
V. 33. וענתה בי צדקתי. The loyalty which is to be expected from me shall testify against me should I not be faithful to it.
V. 34. Laban joyfully agrees to these terms — immediately to make them illusory.

V. 35. Jacob had stipulated for the removal only of the lambs that were spotted or mottled.
