Laban immediately took out all the rams and ewes also, of whom there was a likelihood of their casting any speckled lambs, and even those that had just a mark on the leg or foot, and from the goats every one that had the slightest mark of white on it, so that he was left with flocks of completely white sheep and completely black goats, and no likelihood of Jacob getting any more lambs or kids. Indeed only by a miracle would any fresh lambs or kids be born with any markings whatsoever.

V. 37. After that, what Jacob attempted with the sticks would have been a fully justified means of self-aid even if it could be considered as a proven expedient which experiments which have been made show hardly to be the case. But we know from what is told us later, that Laban altered the terms of the contract ten times, changing the form and position required for the spots and stripes again and again. Such nice exactitude would, in any case, be impossible to achieve by general effect of the sight of the striped stricks, that this time it is to product speckled, the next mottled, then marked on the feet etc., so that the result must be considered purely as the special Divine intervention, as indeed Jacob himself so describes it. The attempt with the sticks can only have been an extremely weak rejoinder on Jacob’s part to Laban’s illegal removal of all the breeding animals, which nevertheless Jacob would not refrain from making in accordance with the Jewish principle אין סומכין על הנס, one has to do at least as much as one can to help oneself, and only then can leave the rest to God.

V. 38. ויחמנה, a form made up of the masculine and feminine, presumably to designate the intended effect on both sexes, just as Laban had so wrongfully removed not only the female breeding animals but the males as well, if they were not perfectly one-coloured.

V. 41.—42. ובהעטיף ,המקשרות. There is hardly any analogy to be found for the usual explanation of מקשרות, early-casting, strong, and העטיף late-casting, weak. That way of taking the meaning of מקשרית is entirely without any support, and for העטיף the analogy of עני כי יעטף is hardly sufficient, as this always designates a weak condition which has occurred in time, but never a constitutional weakness. Added to which מקשרות quite definitely refers, not to a physical condition, but to something which has been done to the animals. On Sabbath 52b we read in the Mishna: רחלות יוצאות שחוזות, כבולות, וכבונות on which the Gemora gives the explanation: מאי שחוזות שאוהזין באליה שלהן למעלה כדי שיעלו עליהן הזכרים. According to that it does not seem far-fetched to take מקושרות as those that were tied up, and ובהעטיף, as “but when one left the animals covered” as they are in a natural condition. So that when the animals were artificially encouraged to breed — which naturally one would do with the best ones from whom one wished to have young — he placed the sticks before them, but when they were just left to breed naturally, he did not.
V. 43. ויפרץ האיש, see above on Ch. 26,13..

V. 1. Why does it speak here first of the sons and then of the father? It is possible that Laban’s former behaviour towards his father was revenged by the way his sons treated him, and it was the sons who had all to say in the household just as he used to have in Bethuel’s house.
V. 5. In the way your father now looks at me I can see how God has helped me, and it is only His help that I have to thank that it has not gone even worse with me.

V. 7. התל, root תלל from which we get תל a heap of ruins, hence probably ותוללנו שמחה the destroyer of our joy. Related to תלל are .דלל ,טלל ,טל that which falls down, dew which first rises up to the heights and then falls down. דל, one who has come down in the world, who previously had been rich. התל first to raise strong expectations in someone and then to let him down in ruin, to deceive, not to keep promises.

V. 9. הציל, either, God saved the possessions of your father from being in hands where they did not rightfully belong, and gave them to me; or what God has given me from your father’s goods, was something saved, was nothing that was not due to me, but was really my property which, in your father’s hands ran the danger of being witheld from me. And moreover it belonged to me, because I had worked and earned it, not anything that I could have expected from the father of my wives as the customary dowry. Hence אביכם not אביכן.

V. 10.—13. Although Laban had taken away all the males that were not pure white, look, I, God, so arrange matters that all the lambs get born exactly in accordance with the changes that Laban constantly makes in the conditions for your wages, I have indeed noted how Laban treats you. So that it is not because you can not depend on My protection to make your living here but because I am הא׳ בית אל, the God Who wants to have a house built to Him on earth, Who wants to find His Home in the family life of human beings, as you discovered at the memorial stone where you vowed to make it a reality. That vow is awaiting its fulfilment. I have now carried out what I promised you, now it is up to you to do your part, to keep yours — צא מן הארץ הזאת, in this land, in Aram, the family life which God wants to see can not develop; here, it was sufficient that Jacob remained in material and spiritual affairs unchanged in spite of living with Laban and had stood firm in his honesty against the hard test of living with, and working for such a rascal.
V. 14. Our sages with their fine feelings of delicacy reckon it heavily against Rachel that she took it on herself to answer before her elder sister, and quote this as a reason for her earlier death.

V. 15. חלק ונחלה, not now nor in the future. Our father has treated us as if we were strangers. He had no paternal feelings for our happiness when he married us off. He just used us to drive a hard bargain. Other fathers give their daughters dowries with which to increase the means of their sons-in-law, to assist their children having a better life. Not so our father. He demanded fourteen years free service from you for us, and then it would have been cheap enough for him to have given at least what he earned with us for our dowry. But that did not enter his head, what we earned for him, he kept for himself.

V. 18. מקנה when used together with רכוש, is preferably living property, herds and flocks, רכוש, other, moveable goods (see Ch. 12,5). It is expressly stressed that the other moveable property that he had was such that he himself had bought out of his own possessions, which, of course, directly consisted only of livestock.

V. 19.—20. The word “stolen” is mentioned twice. So that opportunities for stealing were there, but were solely used by Rachel stealing her father’s idols, and Jacob “stealing” the heart of Laban the Aramean. Our sages remark that Rachel stole these gods because she could not bear the thought of going away and leaving her father to idolatory without any further incentive to betterment. She accordingly stole his penates, the household gods supposed to be the protectors of the house. Their impotency would be brought home to Laban, if they can be stolen, can not even protect themselves, how much less can one put any trust in them to protect the home! The etymology of the word תרפים is obscure. From שאל בתרפים (Ezekiel 21,26), התרפים דברו און (Zacc. 10,2) and the juxtaposition אפוד ותרפים, it appears that they were idols who were also used as oracles. And Jacob too stole…the Aramean’s heart, just because he was an Aramean, because he dared not tell him, dared not even let him have an idea that he wished to go, which he had every right to do, because he would have to run away if he was to go at all.

גניבת לב, undeservedly to obtain the good opinion of somebody by false appearance of friendship, kindness, being obliging, etc. is an insincerity which our sages, under the name of גניבת דעת, disparage to the utmost degree, and insist on our avoiding even the slightest appearance of it. Jacob’s גניבת דעת here consisted in his not allowing Laban to notice either by his looks or word or deed that had observed the alteration in Laban’s feelings towards him. But he had to have recourse to such self-control, perhaps even to dissimulation, “because he did not tell him”, could not tell him, because “only as a fugitive could he get away”. Had he told him that he — as he was fully entitled to — was leaving his service, he would have had to expect as he told him openly later on — that he would throw him out, naked and alone, as he had arrived.

V. 23. The fact that he took his companions with him shows that he had the intention of using force. Laban’s lower nature did not recognise, as is perfectly clear in the following verses, in the whole of Jacob’s possessions anything which he had honestly acquired by the work of his hands — the power of labour is no visible capital — but only goods which he held by the good will of the overlord, and which were still at the latter’s disposal, and could only be taken away with his consent.

V. 24. The epithet Aramean is constantly tacked on to Laban. It was not from Laban, but from the Aramean-Laban, the personification of egoism which he represented, that Jacob had fled, and from whom evil threatened. מטוב עד רע whether good or bad Laban’s good was always cunning, and good or bad means, neither with guile nor force.

V. 25. The whole mountainous region later on was called Gilead, but particularly the mount on which the monument was erected. Jacob had pitched his tent on one of the mountains there and Laban arranged his people in rank and file on the same mountain which had the special name Gilead.

V. 26.—27. ותגנב אותי ,ותגנב את לבבי, the first: you have stolen my heart, have denied it the satisfaction which, as father and grandfather, is due to it, or, as above, you have deceived me as to your intentions. The second: you have stolen from me, all that you have taken without asking my permission, is stolen property. See above on V.23.

V. 28. הסכלת עשו. In Hebrew we have comparatively more words to designate folly than we have for wisdom. Perhaps because wisdom is simple but folly in fact appears in numerous motley shades. סכלות is sticking to one’s own subjective point of view, and סכל is the conceited fool, or rather the fool out of conceit. “הסכלת עשו״, says Laban, “you thought yourself wonderfully clever in the way you behaved, now see what a fool you have been”. Had you gone away openly, I would have sent you off in a paternal manner (perhaps would even have given you a parting gift!) but, now that you crept away not only like a thief, but actually as a thief, see you, I have both the power and the right to take everything away from you — had not God desired it otherwise.

V. 29. עמכם, I have enough people with me to deal with all of you — יש לאל ידי just as the relation of the blood to the soul, the directing mind, is preferably not expressed that the soul is in the blood, but on the contrary, that the blood is in the soul, is directed and contained by the soul (see Ch. 9,4), in the same way in Hebrew we do not say: the hand has power, but power has the hand. The soul, the mind has lost none of its ability or power, even if its instrument, the body, is partially or entirely stunted. The power may sometimes have no hand, but the hand by itself never has any power. Hence the expressions יש or אין לאל ידי etc. But אל could also simply be סמיכות, “it lies within the power of my hand”. — אמש, from מוש to decline with the individualising א, the one half of the day which has already gone, the first half of the day which has passed i.e. the past night.
V. 30. כסף to long for something, hence probably כֶסֶף: that, whereby one attains one’s longings.
V. 31. Your daughters and naturally everything else.

V. 32. How wonderfully Jacob must have understood how to impress his own spirit on every member, great and small, of his large entourage, that he could so confidently reckon that not even a small child would dare to take away even a pin to which he had no right — Jacob, of course, did not know of Rachel’s deed, and would not have condoned it in spite of her good motive.

V. 38. זה לי עשרים שנה בביתך — זה עשרים שנה אנכי עמך. Twenty years, and this is what I get for it. אילי צאנך. It seems to have been the custom for the old leading rams of the flock to be the perquisite of the shepherd when they have become too old for the task.

V. 39. טרפה, although I, as a “paid guardian” am not legally responsible for unpreventable accidents (אנוסין) I used always to do so voluntarily, and if I failed once to do so, or had I omitted doing so, you would demand it as if I owed it to you; and how much more then, that I had to replace anything stolen by day or night.

V. 42. פחד יצחק is not a name for God, but refers to that dread moment of the Akeda, when Isaac felt the knife already drawn at his throat. It is the zenith of the moral perfection which Isaac achieved. “Had not the God of Abraham and Isaac’s infinite merit stood by me,” etc. The observation our sages make on this sentence is significant: חביבה מלאכה מזכות אבות, שזכות אבות הצילה ממון ומלאכה הצילה נפשות, Deeds, active work (יגיע כפי I.L.) is worth more than the merit of one’s forefathers, for that only saved material values, while the former saves lives.

V. 43. It is doubtful in which sense this reply of Laban is to be taken. It seems that, after all, Laban’s humane feelings came to the fore. “Although I have the means and the right to do so, and even if God had not forbidden it, I still could not have done you any harm, as everything I see here round about me, even the very animals, originate from me and mine.

V. 44. והיה, as the word ברית is usually construed in the feminine, והיה can only refer to God, to Whom Jacob had referred and Who had already intervened between them, “Let Him”, says Laban, “continue to be a witness between us”.

V. 45. As soon as Laban spoke of a ברית and mentioned God, Jacob took a stone and put it up as a memorial. Laban erected no memorial, he could confidently rely on Jacob’s word. But Jacob seems to have placed more reliance on a concrete memorial than on words from Laban’s mouth. He accordingly makes Laban’s people erect a cairn also. Hence יריתי in V.51.
V. 46. לאחיו to Laban’s companions whom he had brought with him. Before one makes a covenant for the future, one must first make friends in the present. So they all had a meal together there.

V. 47. It seems that the cairn that Laban’s companions erected was called Gal-ed and Jacob’s memorial Mizpa. The former was to the east, on Laban’s side, the latter to the west on Jacob’s side. If Laban goes to Canaan he has first to come to the Gal-ed.
But Jacob did not have to come to the Gal-ed, were he to come to Aram, but would be reminded of what he had promised us soon as he passed the Mazeba which he himself had erected (see v.52).
V. 54. Now Jacob prepared a meal on his mountain. The אחיו again can only refer to Laban’s companions.

V. 2. Twenty years earlier when Jacob left his father’s house ויפגע במקום “he met the Divine”. Now, on his homecoming “angels met him”. Twenty years ago it was an “event”, that the Divine appeared to him and made it clear to him that the Schechina wished to return to earth in such a manner that when angels sought His Glory up in the heaven, it would be found on earth amongst mankind, and that he and every member of his future nation were to work for this return of the Glory of God to earth. Now, in the moment when, freed from all other conditions, he can first breathe as a free independent family, his appearance was an “event” for the angels, it was an experience for them to meet for the first time such a family on earth. While he, all unconscious of the importance and meaning for humanity of his godliness and of that of his household, quietly went on his way, ויפגעו בו, for them, for the angels it was an event.

V. 3. מחנה never means a permanent settlement, but only a temporary resting place for a company of people on their way to a goal. Such a מחנה was formed by Jacob with his wives, children, menservants, maidservants and flocks. They were on a journey to seek a homeland of which God had promised that He would be with them there. Accordingly, they were a מחנה seeking God in a homeland. And such a מחנה were the angels also, seeking human beings, earthly, human circles for the entry of God to the earth. These two מחנות met and Jacob called the place Machanaim, מחנה ישראל and חנה .מחנה אלקים, a “peripathetic” resting place, from the phonetic relationship to אנה, whither, to remove something some-where, אני the ego in action or motion (whereas אנכי from אנך, related to אנג, the ego at rest) הנה, the ego placing itself, or something else, at the disposition of another. חנה, resting, thought of as being in motion towards a goal.

V. 5.—6. We saw above the reasons for Jacob leaving his father’s house without taking a penny with him. Now that he returned as a rich man, and especially as Esau was also no longer at home, the necessity lay to hand for Jacob to inform Esau that, and how, he had acquired everything. In three words he tells Esau the whole bitter and trying time he had gone through, עם לבן גרתי. To be a stranger without any rights is a hard trial in any circumstances, but to have to live one’s life as an alien with Laban is indeed a bitter lot. ואחר עד עתה and not because I was so comfortable there, but I was forced to stop there so long. I would gladly have come back earlier. But, until six years ago, I had only wives and children but had not yet acquired the first penny of my own. On that hard, little to be envied, road of twenty years trouble and toil did I come to have all that I now possess. I considered it right to let you know this, that you may take that long period of duress as atonement for the past, and that my present state of prosperity itself may be an intercessor for me with you.

V. 8. We can easily put ourselves in Jacob’s place, and we must especially do so, as the meeting was so important that, as a consequence of it, a revelation was made to Jacob, an eternal reminder of which, the Torah has interwoven in the daily food of the People of Jacob.

As Jacob and Esau opposed each other here, so, right up to the present day do Jacob and Esau stand one against the other. Jacob: a pater familias blessed with children, serving, working, filled with care, Esau a “finished made man”. What Jacob had achieved after struggling for it for twenty toilsome years, in spite of the blessing he had received and the first-born right he had obtained, and which now he brought home as the great prize he had won, viz. to be able to be an independent father of a household, that, others have as their natural expectation from the cradle, that, Esau “the finished made” man, had already had in full measure when Jacob left home; and while Jacob by the labour of his hands had succeeded in obtaining the happiness of being a father of a family, Esau had become in the meantime, a political personality, a leader of an army, an אלוף with large troops. Thus, the external contrast between the “holder-on to the heels” and the “made” man.

There are two principles of life which meet in Jacob and Esau and the fight and victory between them is what the history of the world consists in. Family life which is happy and dispenses happiness in Jacob, and the glitter of political power and greatness in Esau. For thousands of years the battle has raged; whether it suffices just to be human beings, and all social, political power and organisation have only importance as means for ensuring this goal of all human endeavours to be reached, of whether all that is humane in mankind, all family and home life, has only importance as trophies of politics etc. to serve as a background.

And how different is Jacob’s attitude to Esau to what it was to Laban. We can recognise what strength the consciousness of innocence gives, and what an oppressive feeling even an appearance of guilt awakens Twenty years endurance of a fight against wrong which you innocently have to bear do not have such a depressing effect as one minute’s feeling towards somebody whom we know feels hurt by us, and who may not see the motive which, though it may not justify our action, can at least excuse it.

Jacob was afraid, although he had been guided by the protection which God had promised him. מכאן, our sages teach, שאין הבטחה לצדיקים בעה״ז, that there can be no unconditional assurance to the righteous in this life. Every such assurance is implicitly conditional on continued blamelessness, it can be forfeited at any minute by a false step. שמא יגרום החטא, that is the worry that never leaves the breast of the most select righteous ones — ויצר לו by the form of the word, it comes from יצר, not from צרר or צור, the usual expression for difficulty and trouble. יצר (a strong form of יסר to bind) means to fashion, to form. All forming is a compression of material into the desired shape. These concepts are so related to each other that we find forming also expressed by ויצר אותו בחרט :צור (Ex. 32,4) and צורה means the form. Perhaps there is a difference whether trouble is expressed by צור or צר .יצר is the external limitation to our sphere, so that we can not move freely. It leaves us untouched internally, the reverse is מרחב, giving us space. But יצר is such a narrowing of circumstances that we feel that we have no power to oppose its restrictions. It obtains such power over us that it can do what it likes with us. That is the condition which Jacob felt towards Esau, and that is the condition in which we have found ourselves through the centuries towards the Esaunations. It is that condition which, in the prophesy of the Galut, is called חמת קרי (Levit. 26,28) “the fury of chance”; that our happiness, our lives, our progress is never the definite intention, but has to submit to the purposes of everything else, and, without rights, has to be satisfied with such crumbs that, “by chance”, fall from the table of happiness of other nations. Accordingly ויצר לו would say Jacob felt that he was entirely at the mercy of an armed force headed by Esau, coming against him, but still, to save something he split up his camp. The same thing has been the means of our salvation and continued existence throughout the Galut. Nowhere, and at no time, has the sword of Esau been able to reach all of us at one swoop. When we bled on the Rhine, our brethren in the Slavonic lands were safe, and vice versa. צדקה עשה הקב״ה לישראל שפזרן לבין האומות (Peshachim 87b) Jacob did the same when pressed by necessity.

V. 9. Here, there is one little word, that shows the whole delicacy of feeling, which otherwise would be missed. מחנה, as a rule, is masculine, and here, too, appears as such in הנשאר, and in והכהו. But when Jacob thinks of its being destroyed he calls it feminine: אם יבא עשו אל המחנה האחת; in this אחת we can hear the deep sigh that is forced out of Jacob’s breast: if Esau comes to the one “poor weak” camp.
V. 10. “In me is the heritage of that which Abraham and Isaac had become through Thee, and Thou hast approached me also, if I am now coming home, I am obeying Thy instructions.

V. 11. I am not praying and begging anything for myself, I have already received so much from Thee that I can not possible have paid the debt of gratitude that I already owe Thee. By the abundance of what Thou hast already done for me, I feel quite small and too humble to approach Thee. For the greatness of a man is not measured by the actual amount of what he accomplishes or gives but by the relative proportion to what he has received. We all run the danger of being too small, the greater our possessions are: —

V. 12.—13. Nevertheless, I pray Thee, save me from my brother, who perhaps has some claim against me, from Esau, who, in accordance with his character, perhaps plans revenge, which perhaps, after all, I do not deserve, save me for the sake of my children, on whom Thou hast promised to build such a great future.
To this cry of anguish Jacob is given no reply, that is given to him by an experience which he is about to undergo.

V. 14. Just as later during the centuries of Galut, the People of Jacob had to seek their salvation from Esau by דורן ותפלה, in addition to praying to God for help, trying to appease their oppressors by gifts, so, in a similar manner their ancestor when in a similar plight had resource to similar means.

V. 19. et. seq. Jacob lays special stress on each leader of a drove leading Esau to expect to meet Jacob immediately, and then, instead of meeting Jacob, he comes to a fresh gift. So that repeatedly Esau may work himself up to an outburst, and then instead of the opportunity for such an outburst, he comes to a fresh appeasement, and hopes that — certainly with deep psychological insight — thus he can hope to expect a gradual cooling down and assuagement.

V. 21. אכפרה פניו. As פנים, from פנה to turn, to take one’s direction towards somewhere, really means in general, the trend, the direction, that somebody is about to take towards an object, and only from that the conception of פנים as the face originates, as being that part of the body in whose position, movement and glance that trend is expressed, so פנים is used to express both friendly and unfriendly mood. We find equally באור פני מלך חיים (Prov. XVI. 15) and פני ה׳ בעושי רע (Ps. 34,17). So that אכפרה פניו really means: I would pacify the mood he is in towards me (כפר, see on Ch. 6,14).

אולי ישא פני. In accordance with the various meanings of the root נשא, the expression נשא פנים also appears with various meanings. Especially the two, “to raise up” and “to take upon yourself”, are those which come into consideration here. Here it would mean: Perhaps he will raise up my face, which now is נופל, cast down, which I dare not raise up to him, i.e. by forgiving and forgetting, let me look in the face again. לא תשא פני דל, altogether referring to law-courts, נשא פנים במשפט, has the meaning, taking upon oneself, from which we get to take up in oneself, to take recognition of, and hence כי תשא את ראש, to count, which is to take cognizance of the number of individuals who come under some common conception. Equally so, נשא פנים במשפט, to recognize the individuality, the personality of the party as one of the factors to influence a verdict in court.
V. 23. ויקם. He first had the intention to stay overnight on that side of the Jabbok. But then his uneasiness gave him no rest.

V. 25. As he had already passed all his people and all his possessions to the other side of the stream, his being left alone can only be explained by, as the sages teach נשתייר על פכים קטנים, that after he had brought everything across, he returned to look round and see that no small things had been forgotten. And to this they attached the significant saying: ומכאן לצדיקים שחביב עליהם ממונם יותר מגופן כל כך למה לפי שאין פושטין ידיהם בגזל (Chulin 91a) that the righteous ones see even in the smallest value of honestly acquired fortune, something holy, which they may neither squander nor allow to be uselessly wasted, and for the rightful use of which they will be called to account. A million has, for them, only the value of a pin, if it is a question of spending it for God-pleasing purposes, and a pin has the value of a million if it is a question of wasting it uselessly. The smallest possession that he has, who does not פושט ידו בגזל who does not take anything by force, but only calls his own what he has acquired by his honest toil, is considered by him as a token of God’s Providence and Goodness, his very smallest possession, a produce of honest sweat and God’s Blessing and hence of invaluable worth.

Jacob measured the little help he could reckon on from his people against the large force of 400 men which Esau was bringing against him, and the result of that consideration drew from him a cry of anguish to God, the answer to which was to be given to him later on. This cry of anguish “הצילני נא״ is indicated by the Prophets as the third sign of the Geula, as the Geula which will come in the most complete helpless state of being without any power in the Galut. The experience which was to bring Jacob such an answer so pregnant with meaning came to him accordingly at a moment when he did not have even the little assistance he could call to his help, when he stood there all alone and was thrown back solely on what was innate in his own person.

האבק עם only occurs here, at this event. אבק is dust. עפר is also translated as dust, but עפר is not what we call dust, but the humus, the vegetable mould, the fruitful loose outer covering of the earth, related to עבר the external side, עור the skin. But אבק is exactly that which we call “dust”, i.e. such particles of earthly matter which, detached, have lost nearly all weight, and which at the slightest cause blow upwards. האבק עם would be: the mutual effort to make the other lose his stand on the earth, to bring him to the state of אבק. Related to it is חבק, the effort to draw somebody close to oneself, to embrace.

The dust that floated about from these “two wrestlers”, so runs a saying of our sages, “was a dust that rose to the Throne of God” מלמד שהעלו אבק רגליהם עד כסא הכבוד (Chulin 91a) for this fight is a prototype of the fight which lasts through the whole of history, yea, it is the meaning of what the whole of world-history really is.

שחר from שחר, to seek, the time when one can seek for things, but still has to seek for them, the beginning of dawn, the time which precedes the בקר the time of distant recognition and differentations.

As long as night reigns on earth, as long as the consciousness, the minds of men are confused, and things are not recognised clearly and distinctly for what they really are, for so long — thus the meaning of this experience at night is expressed as the answer to Jacob’s cry of distress — for so long will he have to reckon on struggle and opposition. And it is with the spirit of Esau, duly equipped with the orb of empire, the sceptre and sword, the שרו של עשו, as our sages term it — Jacob too clearly recognised his opponent as a higher being (V.31) and immortalised that recognition in the name he gave to the place — that Jacob will have to contend, until Night wanes from the earth. ויאבק איש עמו, not Jacob, his opponent is the aggressor. Jacob only fights in self-defence.

V. 26. נגע ב- is always an improper touching: נוגע בטומאה בקדש etc. Frequently also a violent inimical gripping, thus in Job 1,19 ויגע בארבע פנות הבית of the storm which caught the house on all four sides and pulled it down.

ותקע, from יקע, to become loose, hence הוקע, to make something loose, to hang. הירך is the strong fleshy muscle which controls the hipbone on which the firm standing and walk on the ground is conditional. His opponent wanted to lift Jacob up off the ground and throw him down completely. In this, he saw he would not succeed. Then he gripped him on his hip-joint, and as Jacob resisted him, the muscle was torn from its ligaments, so that it could no longer control the leg, so that Jacob was rendered limping. Accordingly: Throughout the whole of the struggle at night, Jacob’s opponent tries to take the ground from under his feet, to give him no standing at all, to have no claim to exist at all on earth. That, he will not succeed in doing, but what he will be able to do, will be to lame him, to weaken his material means and to hinder him in using his natural abilities and strength for making steady progress on earth.

V. 27. לא א֫שלחך כי אם-, literally: I shall not let you go, for (I will let you go) if you bless me. Everywhere where the form is לא כי אם-, the כי is elliptical: “for I will do it if” i.e. I will only do it if etc. So Jacob’s opponent can only fight as long as it is night on earth, and moreover, as long as it is night on earth, he seems to be, although indeed not the victor, still to be the stronger, to have the upper hand. But as soon as the day begins to dawn, the reverse takes place, and it is Jacob who imposes the conditions for the end of the fight. And the condition which Jacob sets for the fight to end, accordingly the purpose of the whole affair is: the recognition that Jacob deserves blessing and furthering instead of enmity and obstruction, the recognition that in such blessing the nations are only blessing themselves, for so will the promise be fulfilled: ונברכו בך כל משפחות האדמה ובזרעך. So Jacob says: “throughout the whole long night, you have attacked me, have looked on me as an obstruction, the removal of which was to be striven for in endless continuous attack. Now that daylight has come, you give up the fight, but I will not do so, until you have paid me my due by acknowledging me by blessing me. The purpose of history will not be accomplished by Jacob being forced to be absorbed by the masses of the nations, but by the reverse, that the nations will at last see, get the insight that it is just in the principles which had been represented and held aloft by Jacob in the midst of his struggle for existence, that their happiness and security lies too.

V. 29. לא יאמר, not לא יקרא: thy name shall no longer have the meaning, be explained as “the one who is destined to hold on to the heel”. Not, it shall no longer be called (he only received the name Israel later on, from God, Ch. 35,10), but the name Jacob itself shall be understood as Israel. ישראל: (from שרה, one of the aspects of ruling, that of being superior, greater) means literally, God is the All-conquering One. Who is superior to everything else in Power and Greatness, and here the angel (the genius of Esau I.L.) declares that that in truth is to be what the meaning of the condition which is expressed by יעקב. Only when a יעקב, one who, to all outward appearances is under the heel of all others, obtains the victory over the most vicious attacks of enemies fully equipped with all material means, does this victory show the existence of a spiritual power which outweighs all material might and power. It shows the existence of an Almighty God, Who reveals Himself just in the victorious endurance of this outwardly weak opponent, so that יעקב is just therein to be regarded and understood as ישראל.

ותוכל, as you have been able. You have obtained what you wished for, not I. All you wanted was not to be thrown down, and in that you succeeded. That, too, is the relative position of Jacob and Esau for all time. In politics and religion Esau says: apart from me there is no salvation. He feels himself affected as long as a Jacob exists apart from him, as long as there exists any element which considers itself to have the right to belong to the world and not acknowledge him. Jacob concedes all pure human beings the right to be left untouched. More, he declares all pure human beings to have the highest meaning and destiny if they accept the basic principles of human life which he brings to them. “Blessing acknowledgement” is all that Jacob fights Esau for.

The עם אלקים ועם אנשים seems to say the same as בעיני אלקים ואדם (Prov. 3,4). When Hosea refers to this event in Ch. 12,4: מבטן עקב את אחיו ובאונו שרה את אלקים וישר אל מלאך ויוכל בכה ויתחנן לו וגו׳, there the conception שר is taken in both its derivations. שרה from שרה and וישר from שור. It means: “In the womb he held on to the heels of his brother, and in his full vigour he became the superior with God (like קניתי איש את ה׳); to an angel he became the one who sets the pace (שרה I.L.) so that weepingly he (the angel I.L.) implored grace from him etc. See above Ch. 17,15.

V. 30. Why do you ask my name? When the sun does rise on earth, then all names will fade before the One Name (the four-lettered Name of the God of Love, I.L.) of Whom it says יהיה ה׳ אחד ושמו אחד, and the only one on earth who will then have a name will be the one who did not want to make himself a name, who did not join the rest of mankind when they said: נעשה לנו שם, and of whom God therefore said: ואגדלה שמך. “He blessed him there”. There, certainly limits it to that place. It was just there that Jacob received the acknowledgement that he was to be blessed. There, at the border, where Jacob was journeying to return the development of the Jewish spirit and the Abrahamitic mission in the Jewish Land. Thus recognition and blessing does not beckon to his descendants by going with the stream of the world, but just שם, by most complete entry into the apparently isolating destiny which the Jewish soil bears for all times.

V. 31. Jacob recognised in this opponent, something divine, something justified, appointed by God. “Art thou then a thief” our sages make Jacob ask “that thou art afraid of daylight?” “Nay” he answered,” מלאך אני I am also a messenger of God, but since I was created, the time had not arrived for me to join in the angels’ chorus singing the hymn glorifying God until now, מיום שנבראתי לא הגיע זמני לומר שירה עד עכשיו״ Esau’s spirit is also a מלאך sent by God, but his mission on earth is not accomplished until רב יעבד צעיר, until he acknowledgingly recognises the godliness of Jacob’s mission, only then is he called upon to join the hymn of the ages glorifying God, only then does he take his place, in harmonious agreement with the symphony of history glorifying God.

Our sages remark that, twenty years previously, when he was leaving the land, the sun set for him at the border (Ch. 27,11), the whole interim had been a period of dark conditions for him and now at his return, the sun rose again for him ויזרח לו השמש, he was not beaten, not broken, but limping.

V. 33. עד היום הזה does not refer to the time of the writer, but to that of the reader, as long as this will be read, accordingly, for ever. Thus of the grave of Moses: ולא ידע איש את קבורתו עד היום הזה. (Deut. 34,6).

נשה, the root of נשים women and of נשה, creditor, seems to have the underlying meaning of having given oneself, or something of one’s own, into the power of another, to have fallen into the power of another. Hence נשה ב-, being in somebody else’s power regarding a part of one’s possessions, to have to demand something from him. Transposed to the loss of some mental possession, נשה does not mean so much forgetting, as giving up. The root of אשה, woman, in the singular is not נשה but כי מאיש לקחה ,איש, for in the singular her relation to man is that of wife to husband, she is not something given over to the power of another, she is a co-worker, the complement of a man, placed completely equal to him, (אשה a feminine man I.L.). But in the plural, as a sex, the public relation of the feminine sex, her rights are represented together with those of her husband. Only in public life, in the plural as a sex, do women appear as powerless, weak, but they are נשים the “creditors” of the opposite sex.

גיד הנשה would accordingly be the sinew of submission, of lack of resistence, accordingly not the anatomic but the historical description of the tendon. By tearing it, Jacob’s opponent had taken away the power of the muscle of the hip attached to the bone to control the leg. This loss of control Jacob had suffered from his opponent, in that respect he had been powerless, had lacked resistence. The tendon is there, the muscle is there, the leg is there, but its use is hampered. But not for ever. נשה is only temporary giving up, not a permanent loss. Jacob is a נשה, a creditor who ultimately has a large account to settle with שרו של עשו.

But if the memory of this event is to be commemorated for all time for the descendants of Jacob by the prohibition of eating that sinew, the intention can surely not be that all his descendants should remember that, as a result of a wrestling contest, their ancestor limped, just as little as the prohibition of Chametz is to make us au fait for all time of the kind of bread which our forefathers ate at their exodus from Egypt. Both these facts, in themselves, are of extremely little importance. So that their being immortalised by a special Law of God, is only understandable if, as actually is the case, lessons which deeply affect our common mission in life, are connected with them; lessons, which just by such prohibitions of eating are to be constantly impressed on us, and kept vividly fresh in our minds.

Our sages too, have taken this prohibition to have such importance and meaning inasmuch as they have taken the verse in Is. 9,7 et seq: דבר שלח ה׳ ביעקב ונפל בישראל וידעו העם כלו אפרים ויושבי שמרון בגאוה ובגדול לבב לאמר לבנים נפלו וגזית נבנה שקמים גדעו וארזים נחליף וישגב ה׳ וגו׳ והעם לא שב עד המכהו ואת ה׳ צבאות לא דרשו. “God sent a word unto Jacob and it found its place in Israel, all the people shall learn to know it, Ephraim and the inhabitants of Samaria, who, in pride and haughtiness say: bricks have fallen, but we will build with hewn stone, sycamores are cut down but we will change them into cedars. And though God hath set the adversaries of Rezin against him etc., the people still do not return to Him Who is the One who really is smiting, neither have they sought God Zeboath in all this”, to mean: דבר שלח ה׳ ביעקב זה גיד הנשה ונפל בישראל שפשט איסורו בכל ישראל (Chulin 91a). “The word that God sent unto Jacob”, to which the prophet refers here, is the prohibition of the sinew (which was literally a word sent to Jacob) “it found its place in Israel”, that the prohibition is kept in all Israel.

After all this the meaning of the prohibition can not be doubted. The spirit of Esau will not be able to conquer Jacob nor to throw him down throughout the whole fight against him during the long ages of darkness on earth, but will be able to hamstring him, to prevent him standing firmly on both feet; without a firm stand and walk, does Jacob go through history. And this lack of stability is a necessary factor ultimately to open Esau’s eyes. Did Jacob stand, like Esau, at the head of his four hundred warriors, the fact that he can not be conquered would never show the Finger of God in history. Therefore the descendants of Jacob, too, (who just through their material weakness and in it are to be “Israel” the sign of the sole conquering power, God), “are not to eat this tendon of submission and material weakness”. Whenever they sit down to table, the admonition from the story of the wanderings of their life shall come to them, that they are cheerfully to renounce this tendon, this submission of their strength to Esau, realise that their existence, and the continuation of their existence is not dependent on it, that they are not to feel that without it, they are less protected, and less certain of enduring through the ages because they are not armed with the sword like Esau, yea, can not even take a firm step on earth. Strength for Jacob-Israel lies in other, higher factors which can not be weakened by Esau. If Jacob does fall it falls not because it is not equal to Esau in material power, but because it had not understood how to retain the protection of its God for itself. If Israel stands, it stands not because of its strong material power, but because its God bears it aloft on the eagle wings of His Almightiness. That is the word which was sent to Jacob, and which is to find its home in the hearts of Israel. That is the word, the full weight of whose meaning is to reach the consciousness of the nation, which when it finds itself beaten, seeks the cause of its calamity, not in God, but in its lack of providing sufficiently strong material military protection; and, instead of a return to God to ensure its future, says, in empty vain self-confidence: yes, the walls we built of bricks fell down, we will build with hewn stones, sycamores they could pull down, cedars they will not be able to!

The book of בראשית contains four divine institutions, שבת, and מילה ,קשת and גיד הנשה. What the first two mean for mankind in general, the last two do for the narrower circle of the Jewish people. שבת ensures the spiritual moral calling of mankind, מילה that of the Jews. קשת, is the sign for the history of mankind, גיד הנשה for that of the Jews. But the moral behaviour and actions of Man, and the fate meted out to Man by God together form the sum total of all individual and national life on earth.

V. 1. He saw Esau, not disarmed by the gifts, he had not disbanded his troops, so he divided etc. As our sages take this whole story as being the programme for our behaviour towards our Esaus, so we learn from here, that though we are filled with confidence in God and His promises, we still have to do all we possibly can do ourselves, אין סומכין על הנס.

V. 2. It is possible that his feelings and greater affection directed this order, but it is by no means necessary to assume that this was the reason for it. In verses 6 and 7 we shall find other and more probable reasons indicated.

V. 4. That here purely humane feelings overcame Esau is warranted for by the little word ויבכו, they wept. A kiss can be false but not tears that flow at such moments. (בכה, related to פקה ,בקע, to burst out), tears are drops from one’s innermost soul. This kiss, and these tears show us that Esau was also a descendant of Abraham. In Esau there must have been something more than just the wild hunter. Otherwise how could he have had the ability to domineer the whole development of mankind (which the Romans actually did I.L.). The sword alone, simply raw force, is not able to do that. But Esau also, gradually more and more lays the sword aside, turns gradually more and more towards humaneness, and it is just Jacob on whom Esau has most opportunity to show, that, and how, the principle of humaneness begins to affect him. When the strong respect the rights of the strong it may well be wisdom. It is only when the strong, as here Esau, fall round the necks of the weak and cast the sword of violence far away, only then does it show that right and humaneness have made a conquest.

V. 5. In his reply Jacob speaks only of the children, and, as this reply is also to the question about the women, he indicates with great delicacy how, next to the grace of God; he has to thank his wives for the bodily and spiritual richness he possesses in these children. The women are the mothers of his children.

V. 6.—7. ותגשן וגו׳ ותשתחוין ותגש וגו׳ וישתחוו ואחר וגו׳ וישתחוו. The general rule that when the predicate is governed by a masculine and feminine subject it takes the masculine form does not apply here. In the very first verse the predicate is in the feminine form. On more exact observation, it seems to disclose interesting noble traits, especially the whole noble courageous self-control of Jewish women, who, even in the most extreme danger hold themselves erect and remain outwardly composed, where the sex that calls itself the stronger loses its head. How much must the women and children have been hearing during the last days of the bad uncle, and how much must it have been impressed upon them to behave before the dreaded one with an outward appearance of due humility. Now, the שפחות stepped forth, they and their children, and bowed low. The otherwise quite superfluous הנה specially stresses this, hence ותשתחוין, the mothers included and placed first. Through their whole origin and past they were accustomed to bow before much less feared persons. Then Lea stepped forth, the noble, proud, self-conscious wife, the real mother and keeper of the household, a Leah does not bow down before an Esau, the children do it: וישתחוו! Then Rachel and her child should have come to the fore, but Joseph protectingly steps in front of his mother as her knight, and Rachel, afraid that Esau would take offence, quickly bows to disarm him, so that Joseph should also bow, וישתחוו, and so both of them bow. Therein the motive for arranging the order of their approach may also lie. Jacob let the maidservants go first because he could quietly reckon on their behaving with due humility. Rachel and Joseph last because he expected the least from them.

V. 10.—11. Jacob avers. At this moment I must recognise you as the moral and higher one of us, you have won a great victory over yourself and I bow before that nobility. בכורה and ברכה were the two points which had kept them apart. Jacob expresses himself about both. Regarding the בכורה, the spiritual moral factor, he gives his brother, in the מנחה, his homage, acknowledging the nobility of his mind. Regarding the ברכה he points out that he has drawn absolutely no material advantage; the riches which he has, have been granted to him by God Who had blessed the work of his hands, and for more than that he has no desire. So he has atoned for both.

V. 13. עלות עלי. As עלה, ascending, rising, in contrast to dead material which sinks to the ground and remains there, is used to express the development the progress which is demanded from all living and life-giving forces, and hence רפאות תעלה ,עלה ארכה, healing starting, and עלה means a leaf, so עלה seems to mean: that which is regarded as developing, or also the feeding animal which continuously produces life-giving organic material for the development of another living being. Here it seems to say: the animals which I have with me are required neither for work nor for slaughter, but for breeding, to increase my property, as such I have to look after them and treat them with consideration for their prosperous development.

V. 16. וישב לדרכו שעירה. This לדרכו is not quite clear. Perhaps it is significant of the trend of life to which Esau reverted. For this is the last time that we see Jacob and Esau together, henceforth their ways of life diverge completely. Just as the whole Gid-hanosheh incident awaits its realisation only in the distant future, so this meeting of the brothers in brotherly affection was only a sign and indication of how the relationship of Esau and Jacob will ultimately become in the distant future. For that time and for a long time yet, the words still ring: “On that very day Esau returned to his way to Seir”, to his usual way. Perhaps?
V. 17. This was the first real house that Jacob built for himself, and this indicates that he stayed there some time. The place is on the other side of the Jordan, outside Canaan.

V. 18. שלם, in full, harmonious, undiminished completeness, not only in material matters, but also, above all in moral and spiritual matter especially considering the moral dangers that beset a man who has to make the most strenuous efforts to secure material independence (See on Ch. 28,20). שלם is the expression of the most complete harmony, especially the complete agreement of external matters with internal ones. All true peace, worthy of the name שלום, even of civil life is not one made according to stereotyped external patterns, but must come out from inside, from the nature and ideal of the harmonious order of the matters of life.

V. 20. ויצב שם מזבח ויקרא לו וגו׳, two unusual terms. Erecting an altar is called elsewhere עשה ,בנה, but never הציב. Further, otherwise we read of the Patriarchs, after the building of an altar: ויקרא בשם ה׳ but here ויקרא לו א׳ א׳ י׳. We have already indicated, above on Ch. XXVIII.10, the relation of מצבה, (to which ויצב refers) to מצבה .מזבח, the rock or single stone offered by nature, corresponds to the idea of a memorial of what God has done for us, and was, therefore, אהובה לאבות, who had to recognise and teach God above all first in His Management and Ruling in nature and human affairs. What men did, their actions, was more a revelation of Man than of God, Who had not yet given the תרי״ג Mitzvoth to reveal Him in all the actions of human lives lived and regulated in accordance with His revealed Will. So that with the אבות a מצבה had its fully justified place next to the מזבח, the man-made erection, expressing the devotion of human activity to God. Corresponding to these ideas the מצבה was preferably meant for נסכים, for acknowledging the gifts of blessing as coming from God, but מזבח for קרבנות for dedicating the whole of life to Him. With מתן תורה, the מזבח not only came to the foreground, but מצבה was completely absorbed into it. Paying homage to, acknowledging our fate, what we receive, as coming from God, separated from devoting the whole activity of our internal and external lives to fulfilling His expressed Will, became actually sinful and was prohibited. For, from that time, God no longer wished to be regarded and revealed in what we get and become from Him, but in what He gets from us, and becomes to us. No longer is what we do to be the product of our fate, but our fate, our weal and woe itself, a product of what we do and what we refrain from doing, our actions to be dependent on Him, to be dictated by Him. מצבה disappears and מזבח alone becomes the one common place for עולה ומנחה for זבח ונסכים, the Altar which by its construction and symbolic meaning proclaims the mission: — by Man’s active life, through the Torah, to raise the earth to a הראל, to a Mount of God, on which the Divine Fire of the Law, the all-consuming אש דת, as אריאל is meant to master everything on earth, and to be the far-reaching illuminating revelation of God on earth. With Jacob’s entry into the future land of this Torah, Jacob preparatorily indicates this turning-point in ויצב שם מצבה, in erecting there a מזבח as a מצבה, as a memorial, expressing thereby, that here, on this soil, that which “men have to build” is to be the monument of the revelation of God, that God is to be shown by and in men’s actions. That here it is not only a question of submitting to, or thanking for, that which one receives from the Hand of God, but to change everything earthly and material to something higher giving satisfaction to God by fulfilling His Will.

Therefore also ויקרא לו, he proclaimed this conception of making מצבה into מזבח to himself and his people. The Patriarchs קראו בשם ה׳, proclaimed to the world the Name of God, proclaimed to the people that God is not merely the One Who created the world thousands of years ago, but is He Who still bears heaven and earth and from Whom still, every present and coming moment emanates directly. But what Jacob wanted to proclaim by erecting this מזבח as a מצבה was not yet for mankind in general, that he had primarily first to proclaim for himself and his own, that אל that the Almighty Director from Whom everything in heaven and earth originated, is to be, and wishes to be אלקי ישראל, Israel’s Law-giver, Judge, and God, recognisable not only in Israel’s fate and history, but, above all, in Israel’s deeds.

And this thought remains to the present day the primary heritage of the Family of Jacob, and still has to accomplish its full effect and be fully realised by us. “Belief and hope”, “comfort and strength”, these מצבה-thoughts are what, outside Judaism, “religion” expects from the relation of Man to God, and these are preferably where its success lies in helping people when their lives are wrecked, and in times of trouble. But the complete subordination of the whole of one’s life in full vigour to the Will of God, keeping His Law as the one “tree of life” for the individual and the nation, making every phase of life ruled by the revealed norm of His Will, in short, complete free-willed, cheerful obedience to the Divine Torah, this forming the whole of human life to a מצבה to the revelation of God, that is, up till now, a treasure which has only been cherished by the House of Jacob, and only in the far-distant future will the nations say: יורנו מדרכיו ונלכה בארחותיו.

According to the opinion of ר׳ יהודה that גיד הנשה was not only נכתב במקומו but that, already immediately after the event, was נוהג בבני נח, observed by Jacob’s descendants, all what we have written above would be even more pertinent, for then with גיד הנשה the beginning would have been made of thinking of God, no longer only by the dead מצבה-stone, but by the living, happiness-giving, acts of מצוה. And all the more pregnant with meaning would be the ויצב שם מזבח וגו׳.

V. 1. “The daughter of Leah”, equally the child of Leah as are the greater portion of all future Jewish people; and “she was born unto Jacob”, Jacob’s spirit lived equally in her. And even if she was mishandled, and, added to that, perhaps she herself gave the opportunity for it by her “going out”, out of the family circle into the midst of strangers she was nevertheless, through and through, a daughter of Jacob. She went out to look around at the girls of the country, to get to know the foreign girls. She was a young girl and curious.

V. 2. Schechem, the son, seems to have been the prince of the land, the city was named after him. He was “the lord of the manor”, the inhabitants were entirely dependent on him, otherwise their later compliance would be completely ununderstandable.
V. 3. After, driven by passion having first forcibly violated the daughter of Jacob, he was so held by her natural attractiveness that he wanted his relations with her to be on a permanent basis.

V. 4. קח לי. My lord Schechem speaks somewhat dictatorily. That she is to become his wife seems to him to be a matter purely dependent on his wish. After all he is the lord of the manor and she — a foreign Jew-girl.

V. 5. Jacob’s silence shows up the whole situation. Jacob was an old man, perhaps already ninety-seven years old. Had there been a question here of getting anything done by reason, by resort to rights or anything of that nature, Jacob would certainly not have remained silent. If the old grey-haired father goes to the lord and demands his dishonoured daughter back — if there was any hope at all of the voice of justice and rights to be listened to — the impression made would certainly be greater than achieved by the younger sons and brothers. Jacob’s silence shows that already beforehand he knew only too well how hopeless any appeal to justice or human rights would be, and the only way would be some resort to force which would be a matter for younger hands.

V. 7. The men’s feelings were affected in two ways. By עצב, the painful feeling of forcible renunciation, of having to give something up, loss. Their pure, innocent Dinah was no longer there, that they had lost even if they would succeed in getting her back out of the hands of Schechem. That was one way they felt, their personal feeling towards their lost sister. Then the wicked deed יחו להם מאד filled them with fiery indignation, for Schechem had disgraced — נבלה עשה — Israel in violating a daughter of Jacob. (נפל ,נבל ,נול — נבלה, all designate the same conception in various spheres, נפל ,נול, ruin, rubbish, נבל withering of leaves, weakening of forces, death of animal life, death of moral forces, in general, a previously healthy strong being going to ruin. — Hence נבלה, an act showing complete moral degeneration, a disgraceful act. Also an act which presupposes the complete unworthiness of that on which it is exercised, thus of himself in Job. 42,8. Thus also נבל to treat something as unworthy, or worth nothing).

Jacob, the weak defenceless family — that it found out at this first clash with the other nations — can only be safe by recognition of its moral, spiritual nobility, which is what, just in its material weakness, makes godliness victorious, and makes Jacob, Israel. But here, this quality was disregarded, killed, otherwise this would not have happened, Schechem would not have dared to treat the daughter of a citizen in such a manner, infringing the rights of a respectable community, only because she was a “Jew-girl”, a בת יעקב could it have happened. That affected them deeply. That they had to go through the world forfeiting the strong “ligament of firm stepping” had been just impressed on them. But they were immediately to find out that cases could arise, as here, where it was a question of saving purity and morality, where one could wish to take the sword out of Esau’s hands into one’s own, that was what ויחד להם מאד.

V. 8.—12. That is also why Chamor goes to the sons the younger ones and not to the father. The two fathers play a peculiar role here. One would have expected Jacob to stand up for Dinah. He is silent, for he knows that he “the old man” would only be laughed at. But Chamor also feels, he would get nowhere with his proposal with Jacob: No compensation would be acceptable to a father for his daughter’s honour. Moreover he feared that his proposed material advantages of a mutual union with the influential lord of the manor would be seen through by Jacob as mere idle talk. That is why he directed himself to the younger members of the party whom he thought he might win over by such a prospect. But Schechem himself addresses the father and brothers together: Place the מהר ומתן as high as you like; the מהר, the marriage agreement for the bride, and מתן, presents for the family. All this sounds very nice and fair, and would indeed be so had the gracious lord had the grace to first return the girl to her family, and then, when she was free, sue for her hand. But as it was, to deal with the father and brothers while keeping the girl in durance vile, meant no more than an attempt pro forma to give a legal appearance to an act of bare-faced rape and violence.

V. 13. Jacob’s sons spoke before their old father because what they wanted to say was not quite in accordance with Jewish honour and honesty. If there was any stain on it, let it fall solely on them. For themselves they had no hesitation, for the man they were dealing with was the one אשר טמא את דינה and to get her out of his clutches they felt everything was justified. His illusive suggestions did not even come into consideration at all.

V. 15. נאות. Just as אוד a lever, is a material means with which something is set in motion, so אות is a mental means by which recognition (a mental motion I.L.) is effected. Hence האות in the Niphal means to make oneself into the means by which somebody else achieves something.

They could see no other alternative. Either, they would not agree, and this was most probable, or their ruse would succeed, and then, in the weakened condition of the place they would be able to free their sister. They could give no reasonable objection to refuse the proffered offer of intermarriage proposed by the prince of the land. In all this there was not yet much that was blameworthy, for to rescue a sister from such a shameful situation, any lawful means are permissable.

V. 19.—24. It seems a most extraordinary thing that a whole city of free citizens should be ready to agree to be circumcised so that he could get Dinah. But perhaps an unusual epithet applied to these inhabitants, which we only find here, and find here markedly repeated, may throw some light on the matter. In V.4 they are repeatedly designated as יוצאי שער עירו. The inhabitants of a city are elsewhere called באי שער העיר. Thus in Ch. 23,11 and 48 in connection with the civic authorities having to decide a legal case. The expression יוצאי שער עירו seems almost to indicate that the inhabitants of the city of Schechem (עירו, his city I.L.) were, for the greater part, peasants, workers on the land, whose work took them daily out of the city. According to that Chamor and Schechem would be the owners of the whole district, and the people all dependent on them, perhaps owned by them as vassals, and used to harsh measures.

V. 25. et seq. Now the blameworthy part begins, which we need in no wise excuse. Had they killed Schechem and Chamor there would be scarcely anything to say against it. But they did not spare the unarmed men who were at their mercy, yea, and went further and looted, altogether made the inhabitants pay for the crime of the landowner. For that there was no justification. For that Jacob too reproached them: You have “clouded” me, our reputation, our name, our honour, which was clear as crystal you have besmirched, “have brought me in evil odour” even with the Canaanites and the Perizzites. And just as you have dealt unjusty so have you dealt unwisely, we are so few in number etc.

Their one answer הכזונה וגו׳ gives their whole motive. The lord would never have allowed himself to act as he did were it not a question of a foreign, friendless forsaken Jew-girl. That was the thought that brought home to the minds of Simeon and Levi that there are times when the Family of Jacob too must grasp the sword to protect the purity and honour of their women. They had no desire to act prudently. They wanted to make themselves feared so that nobody would attempt anything similar. The daughters of Jacob were not to be considered as being at anybody’s disposal. But nevertheless they went too far, to take revenge on innocent people for that which powerful ones had done.

In a peculiar manner this story follows immediately on the preceding one. There we saw a transitory קול יעקב, a humane emotion flaring up in Esau’s feelings, and we recognised in that, the germ of humaneness that ultimately was to grow to complete development in Esau too, and here we see, all at once the sword of Esau transitorily in the hands of Jacob, and learn from that the fact that brightens Jewish history, namely that, though we have ultimately become the nation to whose hands the least spilt blood sticks, if we have become the mildest most soft-hearted of nations, this is not due to any inherent weakness on our part, to any form of cowardice — the last days of our existence as a state showed our courage and military spirit in such a terrific manner that the very bravest and chosen legions of Esau-Rome had to be called against us. We can wield the sword of Esau, we can also become bloodthirsty. Our humaneness and mildness are the fruits of the education which God has given us through our history and through His Toarh.

It is only the means which they took and their going much too far in their use of them that is blameworthy. The motive that moved Simeon and Levi, the purpose they were striving for was a holy and most justified one. The spirit with which they were filled is an indispensable one for a family that had to wander about amongst the nations of the world, had to allow the bitterest fate to pass over them, to endure the deepest degradation, and yet was to remain upstanding with all elasticity of spirit and all nobleness of mind for their world-historic revival to an everlasting path through history which is unparalleled. Still on his death-bed we shall see the old father expressing his curse on the means and the excessive passion, but his blessing and recognition of the motive and the spirit which lay behind them. He indicates that Simeon and Levi should be allotted such a position in the future Jacob-Israel nation, that political and military powers of decision should never lie in their hands (see Ch. 49,5 & 6 I.L.), but, on the other hand, that their strong spirit, always conscious of their own worth and Israel’s lofty destiny, should come into contact with every sphere of the whole nation, actively imparting and teaching its life-giving, sustaining and saving effect. That same sword which Levi used here against an external foe to rescue the honour of his sister, we see him wielding internally against his own brethren when it was a question of ruthlessly — את אחיו לא הכיר ואת בניו לא ידע — saving his brethren up out of their degeneration.

Traits, finally, which we shall meet also in further events in this first family of Jacob, which may give us an idea of the necessity which there may have been to tame down, to purify and to steel this race of men in the “iron melting-pot” of trouble for the high mental ability and nobility of fellow-feelings which was to enable them thereafter to be chosen for showing the model life which was to serve for the salvation of mankind. Not because we are the most pliant of nations, but just because we are the most unyielding, the most obstinate — עז שבאומות as our sages term it — did God chose us to be His tool, to forge us to be His toughest, most lasting steel, and by winning us over to His Will, demonstrate the wonderful might of His Rule and the wonderful power of His Torah.

V. 1. The previous event had shown what a danger living together with the Canaanite inhabitants of the land was to the family of Jacob. Jacob should probably not have settled in such proximity to them, should have, before all, gone to the place where, when he went away from the paternal home, he laid the foundation stone for his future thereby making a vow for his way of life. And then he should have gone to the homeland which his parents and grandparents had found suited for the quiet development of Abrahamitic family life, and where their respected memories might also serve as a protection for him and his family. Here he is induced to do both. He goes first to Bethel and then to Mamre-Kiryaharba-Hebron.

ושב שם, remain there, settle quietly there for a while, probably to get yourself and your family impregnated with the spirit which the meaning of this place and the memories which are associated with it are so suited to awaken.

ועשה שם מזבח. He had erected a מצבה there to commemorate what he had received there from God, but had vowed to use the independence he hoped to get from God to change that memorial stone to a “house of God”, i.e. to a place of human endeavours and achievements which had the purpose of being worthy of the Presence of God on earth. The fulfilment of this vow is what is meant by building a מזבח where up till now only a מצבה stood. And ושב שם ועשה שם מזבח לאל הנראה אליך means: build your house at the place where God was revealed to you, and thereby erect an altar, the altar beside the house (cf. XXXVIII,17 et seq. & XXXVIII,20).

נכר. As this form of the word never occurs by itself to have the meaning of נכרי, but always in connection with a stat. constr. as ,בן הנכר אלהי נכר etc. it seems not to be adjectival, strange gods, but an abstract noun, gods of “strangeness”, and to mean equally foreign lands in contrast to the Jewish land, and the non-Jewish world and non-Jewish character in contrast to Jewry and Judaism. Once only it says (Nehem. 13,30) וטהרתים מכל נכר and there it seems to refer to non-Jewish wives. But there too it could mean: from everything foreign, of a non-Jewish character.

והטהרו והחליפו שמלתיכם similar to ויקדש העם ויכבסו שמלתם in Ex. 19,14. Going up to the place of the revelation to the father in Bethel was, for the family of Jacob the same as what going to the assembly on Sinai was to their descendants.

V. 4. The connection between rings and idolatory is obscure. That the golden calf as well as the ephod made by Gideon were made from such jewellery throws little light on the matter. Possibly the rings looted from Schechem may have had images of idols engraved on them. It is worth noting that the Chaldean word for נזמים is קדשיא.

V. 7. Previously he had called the place Bethel because there the fact had been revealed to him that God wished to have a house built for Him by Man on earth in which He would have His place to bless it and guide it. Now that he comes back to the place with such a “house”, he joins another thought to its name, viz. that the Almighty Ruling of God is also revealed in the spiritual and material powers granted for the building of such a “house of God”, that, therefore, the purest and highest acts of man become, at rock bottom, acts of God, and every true “house of God” built is not only a house of God by its purpose when built, but also by its very origin. He now accordingly calls the place, “God of the House of God”. David, later on expressed the same thought in I. Chron. 29,14, ממך הכל ומידך נתנו לך (Everything comes from Thee, so what we give Thee really comes from Thee I.L.).

כי שם נגלו וגו׳, for there, when he was a fleeing wanderer, completely without means, God’s support for such a future had once been promised him, and now that promise was so fully and completely fulfilled. The use of the plural in attributes and predicates referring to אלהים is by no means usual. If we compare the cases where it is used viz. אשר לו א׳ קרובים אליו (Deut. 4,7), ואם רע בעיניכם לעבוד את ה׳ וגו׳ לא תוכלו לעבוד את ה׳ כי א׳ קדושים הוא (Jos. 24,15,19) ומי כעמך כישראל וגו׳ אשר הלכו א׳ לפדות לו וגו׳ (II. Sam. 7,23) even א׳ חיים (I. Sam. 17,26 & 36, Jer. 10,11 & XXIII, 35) in all these cases the plural seems to come from the idea of the plurality of the godhead of the non-Jewish world to which all these places refer, and wish to stress, in contrast, the reality of the living existence of the One Unique God of Israel, His Proximity, His Holiness and Power and nature, Who in being sole and alone, is in reality all that the polytheistic world dreams of in their conceptions of plurality of gods. Thus, here too, possibly the plural form comes from the contrast to the אלהי נכר the emblems of which he had just removed from his people and from those who had joined them — the women and children of Schechem were with them, as it seems from V.29 of the previous chapter. To these he made it clear at this place how, that, which the rest of the world seeks in vain from their gods, he in truth, had found in אל בית אל, Who had been revealed to him here.

V. 8. How this old lady, who in any case must have been very advanced in years, found herself in Jacob’s company, is not told. Whether she, as some suppose, had been sent by Rebecca with a message, or had gone with him from Laban’s house in order to see her former nurseling, as רמב״ן suggests, are only suggestions. The name which he gave to the tree overshadowing her grave shows, in any case, Jacob’s filial piety to his mother, whom he honoured to such an extent, even in her aged wet-nurse that he wept bitterly at her loss.

V. 11.—12. גוי וקהל גוים. The nation that is to descend from him is to be, in its external relations גוי, one single unit, and internally a קהל גוים, a united congregation of many kinds of people and professions. Each tribe is to represent a special type of person. The People of Jacob, who, as “Israel” are to reveal to the world the directive power of God penetrating and conquering everything that is earthly in human beings is therefore not to show itself as being in any way one-sided, but as a model nation shall present in a nutshell the most varied appearance of all different characteristics. In its tribes, martial nations as well as merchant ones, agricultural nations as well as scientific and scholarly ones etc. are all to be represented. Thus the fact is to be made clear to the world that the devotion and sanctification of human life in the bond with God, through His Law, is not dependent on or conditional to, any special calling in life, or national characteristic, but that the whole of mankind, with all its diversity is called on to accept the one common conception of God, as taught by Israel, and so form all the different individual and national characteristics of mankind into one united Kingdom of God. Then the ולזרעך אחריך אתן את הארץ might have the meaning which Sforno gives it: “and to thy seed that follow after you will I ultimately give the world”. As Isaiah (II,3) prophesies וצדיקים יירשו ארץ, to them and to those that truly follow in your footsteps, the whole world will fall as their spiritual heritage.

V. 13. במקום אשר דבר אתו. According to the whole sequence, the place where God revealed Himself to Jacob here was not the same which he had previously called Bethel. If, nevertheless, we learn in V.15, that Jacob also called this place Bethel, the reason may have been that he wanted to express very significantly that the Presence of God was not attached to any particular place. Everywhere where a man dwells near unto God, there the place becomes dedicated to a place of the revelation of God, becomes a “Bethel”. And this is meant to be stressed by the addition of במקום אשר דבר אתו “God rose away from him at the place He had spoken unto him”. He, and not the place, was the cause and the condition for the special Presence of God which had become apparent to him there. האבות הן הן המרכבה runs an explanatory saying of the sages on this verse.

V. 14. נסך consisted either of wine, to express that it was God Whom one had to thank for one’s greatest joy, or of water, to express that every ordinary moment of one’s life comes directly from God. — יצק שמן על would mean, dedicating the stone permanently for the future, as above in Ch. 28,18. Cf. ויצק שמן על ראשו I. Sam. IX.6.

V. 16. כברת, the כ seems to be a conjunction, and ברת, related to פרט ,פרד ,ברד ,פרת, to mean separate, divide, share, as we believe this root to be found also in ברת הארץ .ברית, according to that, would be a piece of land, a stretch.

V. 18. בן אוני. The basic conception of און seems to be the physical or moral ability for acquisition or possession, hence also to mean the claim to a possession. In this sense in Rabbinic Hebrew און means exactly to have a legal title to something: כותבין עליו אונו (Baba Kama פ׳ ב׳). It is the preliminary condition for, and the beginning of, הון. The misuse of this power of acquisition or possession is called און, just as the misuse of עול being set above or over a person is עָוֶל. But then also און as the first feelings of pain and grief at a bitter loss. It is the feeling of having a right to the possession of somebody of whom you have been robbed, which is felt most keenly at the first moments when somebody has been taken away from you. Hence used primarily for the fresh feelings of pain when the body of the departed one is still lying unburied. ויהי העם כמתאוננים, the people were as if mourning over themselves, they saw themselves as already dead. So that בן אוני here means “son of my grief”, son of my departure which will so soon be mourned. But the father called him בן ימין “son of the right hand” i.e. son of the strength, the power, stressing the brighter meaning of און. For the change of name יעקב to ישראל in verses 20 and 21 see on Ch. 45,28.

V. 21.—22. We have repeatedly (Ch. 9,21; XII,8; XIII,3) found the spelling אהלה as designating the tent occupied by husband and wife, in which the wife is placed in the foreground as being the real mistress and ruler of the household. It is accordingly possible, that here too אחלה designates the tent which Jacob hitherto usually shared with Rachel, and that the meaning here would be: he pitched his tent that he could no longer share with Rachel, far away from the penns and sheds, round about which the family, accordingly Leah and the other wives too were encamped. As long as Rachel was alive, Jacob lived also with Leah and the other wives. With the death of Rachel, he separated himself from them too. Then it is possible that Reuben, to bring his father back to his mother and his other wives, slept in Bilhah’s tent so that his father should be brought to realise how his separating himself from his family struck his sons. But he did not succeed in his purpose. Jacob remained apart, one result of which was that the number of sons remained at the twelwe who were already there: ויהיו בני יעקב י״ב.

V. 29. עשו ויעקב בניו. As above in Ch. 25,9, at the funeral of Abraham, it says: יצחק וישמעאל בניו, although there, too, Ishmael was the older, but here Esau is put first, we think we can find in this, too, a confirmation of the fact that Jacob derived no outward material preference, either from the בכורה nor from the ברכה, but that, after Isaac’s death, without any ado, Esau was accorded the rank of the elder brother.
