Wenn in diesem Geschlechtsregister Namensverschiedenheiten in Vergleich mit anderswo Genannten vorkommen und solche Namensdifferenzen auch noch in andern historischen Teilen der Schrift sich finden, so wollen wir nur daran erinnern, wie wir ja schon bei den wenigen Gliedern des abrahamitischen Hauses eine verhältnismäßig sehr große Zahl von Doppelnamen finden: Abram, Abraham, Sarai, Sara; Esau, Edom; Jakob, Jisrael; Benjamin, Benoni; es kann daher auch nicht so sehr auffallen, wenn etwa Ada und Basmat identische Namen der Tochter Elons, Ahalibama und Jehudit etc. identisch wären.

V. 6.—7. מפני מקניהם — מפני יעקב אחיו. Two reasons are given here for Esau’s moving away. מפני יעקב אחיו, in any case gives getting away from Jacob as one incentive. As nevertheless, the word אחיו is added, the reason for this desire to get away can not be on account of unbrotherly relations. The past had been completely wiped out. But the spiritual and moral gulf between them was too great for Esau not to feel freer and less restrained at a distance from Jacob. Still he would not have done it if external conditions had permitted them to live together. But מפני מקניהם on account of their property this really was not possible. In the land of Canaan, they could not remain together. Between them they required so much grazing ground that they could not expect to be allowed to occupy in a land where they were only tolerated as גרים. So that, as in any case, מפני מקניהם, they would have to separate. Esau preferred rather to go to אל ארץ, to quite a different country, מפני יעקב אחיו, to get right away from the restraining spiritual and moral influence of his brother. It probably says intentionally, not אל ארץ אדום but אל ארץ “to some land” any land, just to make the reason clear, that his going away was to get far away from Jacob.

V. 8. וישב. Presumably with the meaning: he settled there. We find Esau already here in Seir before Jacob’s return. (Ch. 32,4) But he does not seem to have taken up his permanent residence there yet. His family and possessions were still in Canaan. Only after Jacob’s return did he move completely to Seir. Possibly this might also explain the לדרכו in Ch. 33,16. He did not yet live in Seir but was on the way to move there, and Jacob made the proposal to visit him there before his — Esau’s — return to Canaan.

V. 31 לפני מלך וגו׳. Esau’s destiny developed rapidly in accordance with the natural effects of the “power of the sword”. While Jacob’s descendants were still languishing in slavery in Egypt, and had not yet had their very first leader, Moses, Edom had already blossomed out into a state with a whole row of royal dynasties. A contrast to which Joshuah refers in Ch. 24,4: ואתן לעשו את הר שעיר לרשת אותו ויעקב ובניו ירדו מצרים!

V. 1.—2. ישב and גור are to a certain extent terms in contrast to each other. ישב is related to יצב .יצב is to stand firm and upright, and, indeed, in accordance with the צ sound, energetically overcoming obstacles. ישב in accordance with the ש sound, a natural, quiet, unobstructed staying: to sit. גור, in contrast, is staying at a place where one does not belong, has no land of one’s own. (Hence, also transcribed to conditions of the mind: to lose one’s hold, to be dismayed, to be afraid, terrified). Jacob row hoped to be able to settle down quietly, after all his long wanderings, there where his father had only found temporary sojourning; for was it not really the land that had been promised for the quiet development of his lite and family. But God did not consider the time ripe yet for that. But rather, only now do we stand at the תלדות יצקב. Until now when he is settling down as an independent pater familias, he himself belonged to תלדות יצחק, the development had been more passive, brought about by the family-history of Isaac. Only now does the further development of Jewish history through him and his household begin.

בן שבע עשרה שנה. We are all the children of the years we have lived through. They are, whether we are conscious of it, or not, the mother and educator which forms us. בצאן is not the object of a nominative רעה, but is the name of the place. היה רעה, “He was a shepherd, and as such, was with his brothers, with the sheep”. Only at the day’s work, at his occupation, was he together with his brothers, the sons of Leah. But as נער, his life as a “youth”, his youthful activities, he spent with the sons of the שפחות, who are called here, not his “brothers”, but the sons of “the wives of his father”. So the picture presented to us is of a motherless and brotherless youth. All the others grew up in company with brothers and under the wing and influence of mother-love. Joseph stood alone. He had lost his mother early in life, and Benjamin was still a child and no companion for the youth. With his step-brothers he did not feel entirely at home, and felt more drawn towards the sons of the שפחות, to whom also — perhaps — his vanity took him. We have already seen, at going to meet the dreaded uncle, the difference between the גבירות and the שפחות. At least we thought we could take it that these latter, risen in station though they were as Jacob’s wives, nevertheless never completely lost their feeling of inferiority. And this may well have been transmitted to their children. In Joseph was the making of a future ruler. He was a little vain and a little arrogant. Naturally then he preferred to be with the sons of the שפחות, who, possibly submitted a little to him, perhaps flattered him somewhat.

Of course all such differences should not exist in a Jewish home. The feelings of a common duty, and the common submission of life to God-set aims, and the combined working all together to carry out this mission should level out all differences. But the ideal Jewish household is a product of Divine Law and of the Jewish fate. If that nation, whose proclivity was עז שבאומות, by no means the most pliant of people, in whose natural tendencies נוקם ונוטר could very well lie, and in the early days of which, we even see crimes arising out of קנאה and שנאה; if that nation became so elevated by the education it received by its fate and teachings, that gross crimes like ש״ד and ג״ע were unknown amongst them centuries later; if it became the most humane, the most neighbour-loving nation; if Providence could risk throwing it into the arms of being mishandled by laws which throughout centuries were calculated to sow the strongest divisions, the most hopeless קנאה and שנאה in the heart of Jewish family life, Jew-laws which could make children long for the death of fathers, younger brothers for that of the older ones, as children could not come to anything at all as long as the father lived, younger brothers as long as the older ones lived, and so could turn the natural bond and union of families into hate and jealousy, and if nevertheless Jewish family life with its parental, children and family love could emerge from such terrible tests, pure as pearls and shining like diamonds; if the Jewish עזות can be transfigured into rock-like firmness and constancy against all trials and temptations — it is indeed a triumph for the תורה, a triumph for the Divine Law which did not come from us, but to us, and was to celebrate its first glorious victory in its conquest of us.

דבה .רבתם, from דובב, related to טפף, the toddling tottering gait of a little child, in a stronger form תפף, the single disjointed beats of a kettledrum. Transferred to words, it is a contrast to coherent, intelligent speech which תפר ,תור ,טור ,דור) ,דבר) and חמר ,עמר) אמר) express. So that it means tittle-tattle, idle rumours. Hence also דובב שפתי ישנים, the mutterings of the lips of one just awakening from sleep. In a narrower sense it then comes to mean: talking scandal. It is doubtful how the דבתם here is to be taken. Either about them, he brought tales of what he saw of them to his father, and moreover רעה, not excusing them, not דן לכף זכות but in a nasty way; or the suffix תם refers to the immediately preceding sons of Bilhah and Zilpah. The tittle-tattle about the other brothers he brought back in an unfriendly way to the father.

V. 3. In spite of the afore-mentioned weaknesses there was the making of a quite exceptional man in Joseph. Not Jacob, “Israel” saw in him the most excellent of his sons. בן זקנים הוא לו, he saw himself living on in him, saw, in him, all the spiritual acquisitions he had made (see on XXI. 7) — פסים, from פסס, to cease, to end, seems to be the trimming of the edges of a garment, which used to be made on all cloaks to mark the importance of the personality of the wearer. In any case it was a distinction which made him appear as one picked out for a special calling—That all this was not judicious or wise, that Jacob should not have listened to his tattle, that altogether to show favouritism to one child had only evil effects in the history of our forefathers, as indeed it has in any home, is stressed bitterly enough in the pernicious results which are shown in this story. They are weaknesses which occur only too frequently in people’s lives, but are none the less weaknesses.

V. 4. The construction of the verse stresses the אתו. Just him, the one who did not belong to them, who was in no friendly relations with them, who drew the reproaches of the father on them, just him they saw their father preferred. — הב(ה) ,אהב prefixed with the individualising א to give oneself completely up to another, and to wish to have the other one in the closest proximity. The opposite is סנה) שנא), to be a thorn, to reject, to keep as far away as possible. The extremes mutually produce each other. The love of the father begot the hate of the brothers — ולא יכלו וגו׳ “they could not speak to him in peace” i.e. in a way that would lead to peace, or it might mean “they could not bear his speaking for peace” when he wanted to speak peacefully to them. They took nothing from him in a friendly spirit, turned everything he said to a bad way, and most of all misunderstood any friendly advances.

Vv. 5 & 6. He had a dream and started telling it to his brothers. But as soon as he started trustingly telling it, they would have none of it. But he persisted: This dream you really must hear (V. 6). For the etymology of חלם see Ch. XX. 3. Whether dreams have any meaning, our sages leave as an open question. See Berachot 55a. But that Providence uses this half-conscious state to introduce thoughts in people’s minds, and thereby to contrive whole series of events to happen, that God uses people’s belief in dreams to this end, we see repeatedly from Jacob’s and Joseph’s history.

V. 7. There are three moments in the dream which are stressed by repeated בתוך השדה — .והנה is not just “on the field” that would be called בשדה. Also אלמים and אלמות are probably not the same. In Pea VI. 10 a difference is made between אגודים and אגודות, and there according to one opinion אלומה is a small bundle כריכות קטנות ועושין מג׳ או מד׳ עומר א׳. It seems that fields were first completely cut, then small bundles were tied up אלומות, which were then gathered together to make big sheaves, אלומים, in the centre of the denuded field. According to that what he described was: — in my dream we were not at all so divided, were united in our work and wanted to make big heaps in the middle of the field out of the smaller bundles. I, too, was about to carry my small sheaf to the big common heap, but my sheaf would not come but stood itself up and remained erect, would not allow itself to be carried to the general heap in the centre. And then all your sheaves came around my sheaf and bowed down to my sheaf! This presented a picture of the complete impression of one isolated reigning over the others before whom they took up a submissive attitude, and indeed against the will of the one; he was quite prepared to make his small contribution to the whole, and thereby to be just a part with the others of what was accomplished.

Further it is remarkable that he should have dreamt of binding sheaves. That was something with which ordinarily they had no connection, they were shepherds. To become an agricultural people lay for them still as their destiny in the distant future. If agriculture was so much in his mind that he even dreamt of it, the brothers were justified in thinking that could only be due to the teaching and information given to him by his father Israel over the expected national destiny of his house. All the more then could the brothers believe themselves justified in saying: Will you indeed in the future be a king over us, or perhaps even now already rule over us? Such a thought should not occur even in a dream! Accordingly they hated him even more, both on account of the contents of his dream and for his impudence — as they took it to be — in insisting on telling them of it.

V. 10. At first the brothers did not take this dream as referring to them at all. But when they heard the explanation their father gave to it, they, too, began to believe it and to be jealous of the future which lay before him.

V. 11.—12. Following the precedent of Sforno, one of the most thoughtful of our commentators, we think it our duty to look, if not for a justification, still for an explanation for the event which now follows. After all we have not to do with a band of robbers and murderers who would lightly commit murder for the sake of a coat. Sforno rightly points out how, later on, when in their direst need their consciences smote them (Ch. XLII. 21), they reproached themselves in no wise over a crime committed against Joseph, but only for their hard-heartedness in being able to withstand his pleading and begging. So that they must have considered the act in itself to have been harsh but not wrong. We must then, accordingly, keep our eyes alert for even the smallest indication which may make all this psychologically explainable.

We are told that the bad relationship started with קנאה, then שנאה came to it. They hated him because they believed that they could recognise his thoughts and plans out of his dreams. But they did not fear him, because they did not believe they would ever be realised. But when they now heard his last dream — which promised him the highest majesty on earth, and not just the ruling rank in the family circle — and saw how their father took it, not as a mere dream, but was pondering over it and thinking of the possibility of its coming true, then קנאה became keen again in their קנא ב—) שנאה means literally: to believe your justified demands to be endangered by someone), and immediately following thereon: וילכו אחיו, significantly separated from לרעות וגו׳ by an ethnachto, just “they went away”. It had been deeply impressed in their minds that the harmony of their rights was threatened by Joseph, and that was why they went away. And moreover, they went far away. שכם is about eighty kilometres away from חברון. According to מדרש רבה the את in לרעות את צאן is dotted to indicate that it was only ostentatiously for the sheep, but in reality to “shepherd themselves” to preserve their independence which they believed to be diminished by Jacob’s opinion over the future position of Joseph. It is significant that they went just to Schechem. For שכם was the place where the feeling of their all belonging together was first brought so energetically to the family. There Simon and Levi had spoken the memorable words הכזונה יעשה את אחתנו. If then the whole family stand unitedly together as one man when a single member is threatened from outside, how much more must they stick together when the honour and independence of the whole is threatened from within by one member — so could they have thought. And therefore have gone to שכם, there, at the place of the great deed of fraternity, they would get encouragement and incentive for, what seemed to them, the necessity for some similar decision. And their future would really have been threatened if Joseph’s future position was to be what they imagined and feared. For, after all, it was not so very long ago since Nimrod had introduced the idea of Kingship into the world. Their cousins were already enslaved under Alufim and Kings in Seir-Edom. Is was just in contrast to such dictatorship, where the inhabitants were considered as mere bricks for building up the fame and ambition of a single dynasty lowering the status of the individual, that the family of Abraham were to be the realisation of the establishment of human society on the basis of freedom and equality, where the value and nobility of every human being is recognised; where the common mission לשמר דרך ה׳ לעשות צדקה ומשפט as the expressed Will of God is alone to have the dictating rule equally over everybody. What would become of their future, and the future of the whole world, if they, too, were to allow themselves to be enchained by the ambition of one single individual. — It is a remarkable fact that, years later, after the death of Solomon, when the people first wanted to impose conditions on Rehoboam and keep their independence by making him come to terms with them, they again gathered in Schechem, there, to raise opposition to the misuse of power of royalty by the feelings of union and equality in all belonging to God. The occurrence here seems, on a small scale, to be something similar.

V. 13. Jacob feels the breach between Joseph and his brethren, and does not want to allow it to grow, and at the same time wants to test Joseph’s feelings towards his brothers, so at first he gives him no special errand, but simply says: I think it would be better to send you out to the flocks, to be with the others. Joseph is at once ready to go. His conscience is quite clear. He has no idea of wishing to be king or dictator.

V. 17. Whether Dothan was associated with some memory which would be still more in accordance with their mood and intentions than Schechem, whether Schechem, on the other hand, might awake fraternal feelings too strongly while דתן — as the name דת leads one to imagine—excites more the feeling of justice — we do not know.

V. 18. ויתנכלו אתו להמיתו. Sforno rightly reminds us that to forge a plan against somebody could not be written ויתנכלו אתו but would have to be ויתנכלו בו. The hispael construed with את as here changes the reflexive verb to the object which comes after. Thus והתנחלתם אותם (not you shall inherit yourselves with them, but) you shall inherit them for or to (dat.) yourselves. Similarly וכל בגד וכל כלי עור וגו׳ תתחטאו (not, you shall clear yourselves of sin but) every garment and every vessel you shall purify for or to (dat.) yourselves. So that ויתנכלו אתו is as much as וינבלו אותו להם. The piel גַדֵל ,צַדֵק etc. means just as much to consider and declare somebody to be righteous, great etc. as to make them so. Hence וינכלו אותו להם can very well mean, they considered him as a נוכל towards them, they imagined him as נוכל. From בנכליהם אשר נכלו לכם (Numb. XXV. 18) it is apparent that נכל describes a proceeding by which the moral life of our people is brought into a state of the greatest depravity. Equally so ארור נוכל (Mal. 1. 14). Woe unto him who, under the pretence of achieving the holiest, jeeringly violates just this holiest to the highest degree. He has perfectly fit animals and intentionally dedicates a בעל מום to God. נכל accordingly means: to injure the highest interests of others, in a secret and hidden manner. When Joseph came up to them, they imagined him to be a person most highly dangerous to all their highest and noblest interests, להמיתו, that one would be allowed to kill him, that, in self-protection it seemed to them right to kill him.

V. 19. בעל החלומות, like בעל מומות ,בעל כנפים, one who has wings ready for his movements at his disposal, one who has plans ready for his purposes, at his disposal. So בעל החלומות who has dreams at his disposal for his purposes, a master of dreams.

V. 21. Reuben’s relation to the other brothers, as he appears in this incident, is obscure. He seems to have been with them just by chance as he must very soon have gone away from them again and was not present at the actual development of the drama. Whether, as בכור, he did not have to take part in the ordinary daily work, or whether in general he differed from their ideas about Joseph, and therefore took no part in the plans and discussions which sent them to Schechem, is doubtful. We shall come back to this question again on V. 30. — לא נכנו נפש is quite positive. A thought like that, which has just come to you, we shall NOT put into practice. I, as the eldest brother, will not tolerate that. As what he says is freshly introduced again in V. 22 (it repeats ויאמר I.L.) there seems to have been a discussion over the matter, on which, to pacify them, he came out with the other proposal.

V. 23. The ויקחהו is said after the removal of the coat. He seems, accordingly, to have offered no resistance. Only by begging and entreating did he attempt to soften them, as we know from Ch. XLII. 21.

V. 25. נשא עינים is never just a casual looking round, but always an intentional one. They, too, when they sat down to eat, felt uneasy all the time. They kept on looking towards the pit. The Ishmaelites were a related tribe, and as they were no “merchants” who trafficked in all kinds of materials, including human beings, the brothers when they sold him to Ishmaelites could expect that he would remain with them, and after they had sold their spices in Egypt, would return to their homeland, Arabia. This explains why, later on, the brothers had no idea that Joseph could be in Egypt. This would be still more confirmed if, as is always possible, and as some people take it, the brothers sold him to the Ishmaelites, from whom, as we have said, they could expect him to be taken back with them to Arabia, had not, in between, Midianite merchants passed by, who bought him from the Ishmaelites as a speculation, and they sold him in Egypt. That would be in accord with the information given in V. 36 that the Medanites presumably the same as the Midianites, sold him in Egypt. If then it says in XXXIX. 1 that Potiphar bought him from the hands of the Ishmaelites who had brought him there, that can only be understood as indirectly, through the Midianites to whom these had sold him. And then the reason that the Ishmaelites there are referred to as the first hand through which Joseph was brought to Egypt, was because it was just due to that fact that the brothers did not expect to see him at all in Egypt, a supposition that is not unimportant in the pursuance of this story. But as, in any case, either V.36 or XXXIX,1 must not be taken literally, but that מיד ישמעאלים can be taken to mean indirectly much less easily than מכרו אתו אל מצרים, where the אל could well be taken to mean “towards Egypt”, not במצרים “in Egypt”, and as further the text of V.28 says that it was not the brothers, but these Midianite merchants who drew Joseph up out of the pit and sold him to the Ishmaelites, this way of taking it has much more to recommend it. The brothers wanted to sell him to the Ishmaelites meanwhile the merchants came along, fetched Joseph up and they sold him to the Ishmaelites. The brothers always believed that he was in their hands and had gone back with them to their homeland, they had no idea tha these had nevertheless sold him in Egypt. In any case the brothers had the responsibility for the sale, as it was what was in their mind, and they gladly allowed it to proceed without hindering it in any way which they could easily have done.
V. 26. מה בצע, how would the death of our brother profit our purpose more than sending him far away from us!

V. 30. אנה אני בא not אלד, not whither shall I go to be alone with my trouble. There would be no point or reason for that. For he was not alone in his trouble, he had the whole family implicated in it. Moreover בא really means to come home, to come to where one belongs (it is related to פא (Job. 38,11) the ordinary פה, here: the place where something belongs, also פה, mouth, the opening which opens to take in that which belongs inside it). So that these words rather express a feeling of shame or regret, the feeling of being deservedly or undeservedly reproached. “I can find no place where I can rest quietly, where I can hold my head up, everywhere everybody will avoid me”. Why should just he have felt like that? Possibly quite simply because he felt himself to blame for not having more energetically acted to oppose and prevent what had happened. He had started the מצוה and had then left it. But what was behind this lack of energy, he was, after all, the eldest brother? Perhaps because he was not really completely free from fault himself, and his conscience now smote and depressed him. The consciousness that in his innermost heart he had really had slight leanings in agreement with his brothers, he felt had prevented his standing up more strongly and energetically against their plans.

There could have also been another reason for this. The fear that had driven the brothers to commit the crime was the fear that their independence would be overpowered by Joseph. This fear would in the ordinary way have been taken to affect nobody more than Reuben. There were, after all, two firstborns in Jacob’s house, Reuben and Joseph, and Joseph was, moreover, the one from the wife he had really intended to marry. So that suspicion for the motive that lay behind the deed must primarily fall on Reuben. That is why he had kept himself right out of it, but that was why he feared that now the first stone would be thrown at him. And indeed what actually happened in the end would have justified these considerations. The “firstbornship” was really taken away from Reuben and transferred to Joseph.
V. 32. They did not send the cloak direct from them, but had it sent from elsewhere, and then came to their father.

V. 33. אכלתהו brought home his loss to him, טרוף טורף the horror of the happening — he sees his son, his beloved child, the blooming youth, in the snarling teeth of a beast of prey. “Torn to pieces, into pieces has Joseph been”! (But see note on Ex. 22,30).

V. 34. ויקרע שמלותיו only occurs on very rare occasions — as we find it again with Joshuah at Ai (Ch. 7,6) and with the brothers (Gen. 44,13). Otherwise as a rule it is בגד .קרע בגד is the garment which presents people in their outward appearance (hence בגוד to become completely nothing but the outward pretence of covering something real, a בֹגֵד, is nothing but the בגד of a man, we think we have a real man and have only the outward appearance of one), pain, grief, shame are expressed by a rent in the בגד, a rent has been made in the outward relations of people, their honour, their happiness has suffered a rent. Hence it is also an expression of אבל — .אבלות and its related roots all express a darkness, a lack of clarity (אפל, the darkness of night. אול, the root of אויל, a fool, and אולי, perhaps. There are two kinds of fools in the world. The one, who changes his opinion every minute, who has no opinion of his own, nothing is clear and definite to him, who says “yes” one minute, and “no”, the next. This is the unclear, undecided fool, אויל. The second, his counter-part, is the narrow-minded man, who, once he has formed an opinion, sticks to it, and can not be convinced he is in the wrong, the obstinate fool, כסיל). The preposition אבל always comes to oppose and limit something which had been considered true and decided. If, now, something has happened by which all joy, every bright ray, all cheerfulness, every firm step on earth is opposed by an אבל, a “but” then אבלות is there, grief, mourning. This grief is expressed by קריעה, tearing, the opposite of שלום, the condition of complete, unbroken well-being, literally, “being whole”. Now שמלה is preferably the garment worn next to the skin, in contact with the naked body, שמלתו לעורו (— hence probably why washing to clean, for cleanliness is called more כבס שמלות while טבילה from טומאה is called כבוס בגדים) Jacob tore his clothes right to his naked body, and in place of a soft soothing garment, put on a hair-shirt (שק is the name of the material, goat-hair, out of which sacks are made) something which touches a man uncomfortably at every movement, so that if, for a moment he would be happy, constantly reminds him he has no right to be so. Hence, also, ויתאבל, “he kept himself” in his grief, on every occasion thought “אבל״ “but — Joseph is no longer there!”

V. 35. He refused נחם .להתנחם, see Gen. 6,6. One can not actually console anybody, one can only offer them reasons for consolation, which they themselves must take to heart to effect a change in their mood. But he refused even to try to bring about such a change in himself. כי ארד אל בני אבל שאלה, not that he would die of grief, but he thought that he would have to mourn his son all his life, his departed beloved son, may never see himself in a cheerful mood. Jacob might also have reproached himself. After such a terrible occurrence one criticises oneself very sharply, and does not forgive oneself for the slightest slip. ויבך אתו אביו, not עליו but בכה .אתו related to פקח ,פקע ,בקע, all expressing a breaking forth, a becoming free from inside. בכה, the effect of a feeling breaking out. בכה על over some external cause. בכה את, to go on weeping over the thing itself, to go on keeping it constantly in one’s heart, and the effect of what one is carrying in one’s heart showing itself by a tear stealing out of the eye from time to time. Even when not weeping he still bears it in his heart. (יצא] יזע = [בקע] בכה]), tears are the sweat of the working soul, sweat is the tears of the working body). Significantly, the tears are mentioned here last. Jacob did not moan and did not cry out. The ויבך at the end refers to later times. When the others were merry, a furtive tear stole into the eye of the father. (See page 688 for additional commentary).

This paragraph was inadvertently omitted to be inserted here: All his sons and all his daughters — probably the daughters-in-law arose, יקמו, not went, ילכו, or יבאו, came, but “stood up” to comfort him. To stand up to do something always implies having to make an effort, to pull yourself together. So it seems that they themselves were also sunk in grief. After all, no one was likely to have felt worse than just the ones who had to try to bring consolation. To see their old father inconsolable, in a state where any cheerful thought is felt to be sinful (אבל), would make the most hardened sinner so full of remorse that instead of bringing consolation he really requires being consoled himself. But why then did nobody pour soothing oil on the smarting wound and tell the truth “he lives”? Because that would have inflicted the worst wound of all. However terribly a child may have been killed it is never lost to the parents mind but a depraved child is more than lost. If the pain was not to be increased a thousandfold, silence must be kept until Joseph would reappear and then the joy of finding him again, and the fact of his return would soften even the thought of the horrible crime committed. Had they told the truth they would only have added at one blow ten more sons to the one he had lost.

V. 36. סריס designates, on the one hand, indubitably, a bodily mutilation which does away with the ability for reproduction, and on the other, equally indubitably, simply, a servitor. Just this Potiphar was married, and אסנת was presumably his daughter. From cognate roots שרש ,זרז etc. סריס in general would mean agent, and in particular, an agent of the court, a court official, some official who is in the immediate proximity of the king and has to see to the prompt attention to the requirements of the king. There is analogy for the other meaning of the word: castrated, just as שָׁרשׁ, to root also means the opposite: to uproot, עֵקֶר, root and עקר, without children, without the power to be the root of a future human existence, so סריס, one who can not attend to the demands of the continuance of the human race. So Potiphar was an official of Pharaoh’s court, and indeed שר הטבחים Lord High Purveyor to His Majesty. Here we are introduced to the most important state of ancient times, which became so important for the culture of the ancient people, and it is characteristic to find at once a Lord High Purveyor, Lord High Baker and Lord High Butler. We are able to say that even in the most degenerate times of Jewish History, at least we do not find such dignitaries. He who proffered the cup, the plate etc. to the Jewish king was, and remained quite an ordinary man. Only in states, as in ancient Egypt, where the king was surrounded by a halo of divinity, where we can still find pictures of Egyptian kings kneeling before the divinity of their own majesty, do those who come into contact with the sacred person receive some resplendent reflection of that halo. If the king is a god, then his butler becomes the ministrant to a god, and the cook the Lord High Steward of the Kitchen. If this is the more cheerful aspect of the office, there is also a horrible combination attached, the Lord High Butcher was at the same time the Lord High Executioner. Thus we find Field Marshal Nebusaradon was also the Lord High Executioner (II Kings 25,9).

V. 1. In this separation of Judah away from his brothers, we may see a sign of tension and disunion between the brothers which would then have arisen as a result of the deed committed against Joseph, which was directed principally against Judah, as being the one through whose proposal and guidance — he seems to have had the most influence amongst them — the sad event had occurred. Moreover we see the wrong paid for heavily in Judah’s own family circle. He lost his wife and his sons, and what is still more bitter, the sons died because they were bad in the Eyes of God.

Moreover, though, on the one hand, Judah’s misbehaviour with Tamar was one of those things which were kept for the moral influence of the future Torah of God to prevent, nevertheless we see him practising monogamy, and only coming to this lapse after the death of his wife, and finally we see here, already before the Law giving, an institution authorised by custom in the House of Jacob, which seems to be based through and through on the most moral conception of the sanctity of marriage and family life.

That the moral character of marriage is only to be found in its final purpose, the begetting children and bringing them up, (פרו ורבו), that a marriage that has not accomplished this purpose appears disturbed and incomplete in its moral aspect; further, that the conception of a family circle, i.e. a father’s house together with the branch families that come from it, form a specific item with its own particular individuality on the tree of humanity, so that if, through the death of the husband, a marriage has been left without establishing this final purpose of continuing the human race in the particular tendencies of that particular family, this loss can be made good, and is to be made good, by the marriage of the childless widow to one of the nearest members of that family. This thought, expressing the highest moral character of marriage, and the highest spiritual conception of “the family” seems to be what lies at the base of the great institution of Yibbum (the marriage of the childless widow to the brother-in-law I.L.). Although a widow of the deceased, Tamar appears as being still engaged to the remaining members of the family (זיקה), indeed, to such a degree, that her supposed unfaithfulness (V.24) is considered to be adulterous. She is considered so much already married that the marriage to one of the nearest members of the family originally required no special ceremony to sanctify it, but could be just automatically continued הבא על יבמתו בין בשוגג וכו׳ קנה (Yebamoth 43b); a relationship we may not leave unconsidered in valuing Tamar justly.

V. 1. It is repeatedly stressed, referring to Potiphar, that he was an איש מצרי an Egyptian, a speciality which would be self-understood in an official of the Egyptian court. But we know the contrast that existed between the Egyptians and the rest of the world, especially the pride and contempt with which they looked down on the nomad races. A still greater contrast existed between the morals and mode of life of the Egyptians, and that of the “Hebrew youth”, as he was called. The word מצרי here stresses this contrast and brings home to us the temptations which the youth must have had to overcome to remain pure in an Egyptian household run under Egyptian rule, so that God found him worthy for Him to be near to him. This word also shows us the amount of spirit, and ability and efficiency which must have been needed for a youthful slave bought from Asiatic nomads to have found such favour with a Potiphar, an official of the court, who was in addition a מצרי, an outright Egyptian.

V. 2.—4. It says three times ויהי. Our sages remark: For the other brothers, grown-up men, at home and in company with father and family, no special care of God was required, but for Joseph, isolated, expelled and thrown out into such surroundings, the special care and protection of God was necessary. That was why God was always near and with him, and there he developed into the striking personality, the makings of which he had always had within him. They only needed just such happenings to bring them out fully awakened, and cleansed from all the little human weaknesses which had stuck to him in happier circumstances. If “God was with Joseph”, that could only have been because Joseph was with God. If the purposes which a man strives to achieve coincide with God’s purposes, then He arranges circumstances to be favourable and helpful for their achievement.

צלח (related to שלח, perhaps also שלח .סלח: to send, to move something towards a goal. סלח: perhaps, to let go; an unforgiven sin is an obstruction in the path of life of a man, he is held back, סליחה cuts the knot, and allows procedure to be unhindered), צלח is: a progress towards the goal, overcoming obstacles. Joseph was a man who brought everything he undertook to a happy conclusion. Then the Mitzri overcame his prejudice against the Ivri, even took him into his house, and occupied him near his awn person. And then, V.3, when his master saw that there, too, “God was with him” and made everything he undertook succeed — this was the first revelation of God in any Egyptian circle, in a circle where goodness and morality did not count, a youth appeared who was poor and in the most degraded class, and who, nevertheless succeeded in everything just because it was he who did it, suddenly demonstrated the blessed power of a pure and moral will — then finally Joseph found חן in his eyes, so that he promoted him to be his personal attendant, and then made him overseer over his whole household. For מצא חן see on Ch. 6,8.

V. 5. פקד (related to בגד) to present something to ones’ mind with all the relationships and individual circumstances with which it is invested. Hence, one who is charged with the care of something, who is appointed to watch over and keep all its relationships: פקיד; and to hand over to somebody the opportunities to watch over and take care of something: יש — הפקיד: (related to קשה and גשש) the hard, firm, concrete, real —. בגלל from גלל, related to גלל .כלל ,קלל, to turn about an axis, to contain the centre of gravity, to be able to move on the surface without any point of friction. Hence on the one hand קל light, which is held down nowhere, is not prevented from progressing anywhere, and on the other כלל, all embracing. Everything which brings things about, causes, is thought of figuratively as the movement of a revolving circle. — תואר from תור a row, the harmonious equality of limbs. — יפח ,יפה to breathe, יפע to radiate. The idea of beauty is designated in Hebrew not objectively, from the point of view of the actual beauty of the object, but of the impression it gives to the beholder, beauty is considered as an intaking of breath, as something radiating, the effect of beauty. It is deeply significant that the remark on Joseph’s beauty, which we should have expected to be mentioned at the beginning of the story, as after all it is the first thing which strikes one, the first recommendation which an unknown person brings, comes right at the end. This is perhaps of special importance for what follows. For it must have been a much greater temptation for a Joseph if it was not just an ordinary common woman who tried to lead him astray. So we are told that it was not primarily his good looks, but the wonderful result of his spiritual superiority which had raised him from the low slave to be almost the master of his master which had made such an impression on his mistress. His beauty was just the last straw to this impression אחר הדברים האלה is how the next verse starts. All the foregoing led up to it.
V. 8. לא ידע וגו׳, he has unbounded confidence in my capabilities, וכל אשר יש לו וגו׳, unbounded confidence in my honesty.

V. 9. וחטאתי לאלקים, apart from the wrong I should be doing against your husband, it would also be — as all immorality is — a sin against God. — חטא. It is important to get to the bottom of the conception of sin, in accordance with the Hebrew expression of thoughts in the words it uses, as thereby we can, at the same time, get the conception of the contrast which arises from a life of morality. In most languages sin (anglosaxon synn, Dutch zande, German sünde, Danish Swedish and Icelandic synd I.L.) has the idea of something that requires atonement (Sühne), a conception which does not lie basically in the word חטא. We venture to stress its relation to חתה .חתה, to take something out of the sphere to which it belongs, but specially to take burning coals out of the fire. Now it is by no means impossible that חטא similarly means: to take any of our relations or bearings out of that fire, the glowing rays of that element which should really hold, awake, keep alive, radiate through our whole being. The glowing coals I take out of the fire become extinguished, lifeless. As long as any of our forces are mastered by that Divine fire, it is alive and will achieve what it is meant for. But as soon as we do not leave any phase of our life to that fire, it becomes “sin”. We are justified in thinking of that element that is meant to master the whole of our being as “fire”. For the Divine Word itself calls it אש דת ,אש אוכלת. To that we are to render ourselves completely, and as long as we do that we are without clinkers, the Divine fire burns brightly on and on in us and through us, we are לחם אשה ה׳: food, fuel, for godliness on earth. But as soon as anything falls out of this fire, it becomes dull, dark, evil. If the life of our senses, our sensuality is not קדוש holy it becomes beastly: קָדֵשׁ. That which withdraws itself from being penetrated by the glow of the godly, runs into the glow of passion. But if חטא means taking something away from the hearth of the Divine fire, by which it becomes dull, not lit up, not penetrated by the glow of fire which it should serve to illuminate, then we can understand how the whole מעשה קרבנות, the whole procedure of the offerings is literally the symbolic restoration of the conditions which have been disturbed by חטא. If the חטא which we have committed is nothing else but that we have not left our חלב וכליות (our material wealth and the urge of our senses I.L.) to be fuel for keeping the fire of godliness alive on earth, then the re-establishment is equally nothing else but giving them up again to the Divine Fire (the אש דת I.L.). The whole of our being, our נפש (our life I.L.) belongs to God, and as a result therefrom all the members of our body, our אברים belong to His Fire. נתינת אברים על גבי אש is the immediate result of נתינת דם על המזבח (see also Ch. 13,13).

V. 11. The היום הזה and כהיום הזה usually refer to the present time of the relator or reader, neither of which could apply here. If one refers it to the time of the narrative it could perhaps mean: “on one of such of these days”, and it would refer to the preceding יום יום. She had already on these days tried her arts of seduction on Joseph, and nevertheless “on one of these days” Joseph ventured into the house although no other man was in it. Then these words would contain a reproach for Joseph which he paid for dearly enough. No man should depend too much on his moral firmness and powers of resistance.

V. 12. Sforno already has pointed out how considerate and thoughtful Joseph was even towards such a woman at such a time. וינס ויצא החוצה, he fled, he rushed away from her, but he did not rush out into the street, did not make a scene, but ויצא, just went out into the street. Of course when she gives her version of the event to the household (who perhaps saw him go out I.L.) she also says וינס ,ויצא החוצה (note separating cantillation I.L.). “He rushed away and slunk out”, for she wants to make him out as a criminal. (But to her husband she says: וינס החוצה I.L.).

V. 20. ויתנהו אל בית הסהר וגו׳, ויהי שם בבית הסהר. If the first sentence tells us he put him in prison, the second seems completely superfluous. But Potiphar was also the Governor of the State prison (see next Ch., v.3). Thither אֶל בית הסהר, thither he now placed him, transferred him to the prison to make himself useful there as he had been in his house, and so he became an inmate there. This would presuppose that in his heart he was really convinced of Joseph’s innocence, and only for the sake of his honour did he have to take the action that he did, אסיר is a noun, אסור a verb, the former, a prisoner, a permanent character, the latter, as verb, imprisoned, just temporarily. By the Keri and Kethib, both are indicated here. This was a prison to which both those condemned and those committed for trial were brought. The sequel, too, bears this out. Through that Joseph could come into contact with men who were only temporarily interned, and who, when acquitted returned to important position. As in fact the Lord High Baker and His Highness the Butler also seem to have been in the prison only awaiting trial.

V. 21. ויט אליו חסד. Not men’s kindness, His, God’s benevolence did He incline towards him. Joseph had reached the lowest level to which he was to sink. From now on God turned His חסד towards him — שר ב׳ ה׳. Another שר, the Lord High Gaoler! The more enslaved a nation is, the more “princes” does it have. Whoever stands just a little higher becomes at once a “prince”.
V. 22. “Everything which they did there, was his doing”, or “he did”. Either it was doings that he had seen to it to have done, or what previously a number had to do, he did alone.

V. 1.—2. In the first verse they are simply called butler and baker, in the second, the “Prince” of the butlers, and the “Prince” of the bakers. Therein lies the whole mockery and the pitifulness of these princelings. To those beneath him, to the people, he is a שר, but to those above him he is a lower slave than the crossing-sweeper. Just because his whole princely status rests solely on the fact that he has the honour of handing the king his goblet or reaching him the dish of cakes, solely on his relation to the person of the king, his princely position is that of the worst slave, entirely dependent on the whim of the favour of the King. The King holds the freedom and life of these “princes” in his hand as if they were — and indeed they are — his chattels. To him they are no princes, just a butler and a baker. He is their absolute master and at the slightest provocation they get kicked into the dungeon.

V. 3. במשמר. The place of detention of the מקושש (the desecrator of the Sabbath in Num. 15,32 I.L.) is also called משמר, only on remand. In the house of the prince of the cooks, there was a dungeon. They were given into his charge. He could keep them where he pleased. See above on V,20.

V. 5. Everything which is written beyond ויחלמו חלום שניהם seems entirely superfluous. “Each one dreamt his dream”, “the dream was like its explanation”, of course, for the explanation must go according to the dream. Finally “the butler etc.” why repeat, we know quite well who they were. But it seems we are told all these particulars of the dreams because it was just these that made them uneasy. In the dreams themselves there was nothing extraordinary. That the butler dreamt he was preparing wine and offering it to the King, which he had probably been doing for the last thirty years, and similarly the baker, what was there in that that it should require interpretation? But the definiteness of the dreams and the similarity of them both in one night, struck them. Both dreams seemed to be the same, each one engaged again in the old occupation. “Each one dreamt his dream in the same night, the two of them who were now imprisoned, saw themselves, the one as butler, the other as baker, to the King, and the dreams hardly seemed dreams but almost as the interpretation of a dream”, i.e. were so clear that they only seemed to lack one little point to make the meaning of the whole apparent and to require no interpreting. If, for example, instead of three vine branches, the butler had dreamt three days, everything would have been clear and understandable. But it was just this evasive clarity and the similarity of the dreams, and even the number three to seem stressed in both of them which made these dreams seem to have some relation to their impending fate, that caused them to grope uneasily for the meaning — פתר, (related to פטר, to open, not indeed a mechanical opening from outside, but an organic one out from inside, as פטר רחם and פטורי ציצים) is a nice word for the interpretation of a dream, or for every reasonable explanation. A perfectly rational person can explain a dream quite exactly without wishing in any way to insist that it need necessarily come true. The meaning should not be read into it from outside but must come out from the dream itself. Such an interpretation of a dream is a deep psychological task, just as the explanation of any symbol, the hermeneutic interpretation of any passage of Scripture should be פתרון, getting at the sense from within outwards. The veriest hodge-podge can always be placed into everything, but to seek out the meaning from within (hence also the term דרש) produces just the one, the right one. And just as at organic birth and at the unfolding of every bud, there is an inner point of force from which the whole development takes its course, so at every “closed” symbolism there is one kernel, one central idea which has only once to be grasped, for all the rest to be understood and follow naturally.

V. 6. זעף, related to צעף from which we get צעיף, the veil. צעיף, external veiling of the face, זעף, the veiling of the countenance from within. The appearance of a troubled face is as if something there was asleep, dead; the soul, the life is missing from it, its ordinary expression of liveliness is veiled.

V. 7. How many words are superfluous in the first half of this verse! Almost as many as there are words. The whole rigmarole of the two co-prisoners is repeated, וישאל אותם would have been quite sufficient. Their personalities are well enough known to us already. But, unless we are entirely mistaken, just here the mental genius, the חכמה of Joseph is shown to us. He noticed them worried, had no idea yet about what, so he enquired from the court officials of Pharaoh etc. The difference between the point of view with which an ordinary person looks at the world and things and of a Joseph is just this: — an ordinary person looks at things just in general, to a חכם every person or thing appears classified into its own speciality and individuality. The former speak to “merchants” “learned men” etc. The latter keeps in mind, all the time he speaks to anybody, all the individualities and special relationships of the person. Joseph never forgot who and what they were, for what purpose they were there, kept their whole situation in sharply defined lines in his mind. They were במשמר (and in that the Egyptian Pharaoh differed, to his advantage from his later jovial Persian colleague, inasmuch as, when angered, he did not immediately order “hang them up”), so that tomorrow they could be outside again. Finally they were אתו, together with him there. Joseph could have had a vague idea that, as they were only imprisoned on remand, there was a possibility of their having later on some favourable influence on his fate, and so might have had an idea that their being אתז together with him might be an act of Divine Providence. And just because he always kept in mind all the connections of persons, he listened to all their words and saw all that they did — their dreams too — always in connection with their individual personalities and also understood from that personality how to take them and how to value them.

V. 8. You have no one here to interpret? If dreams are worth interpreting, if they have a meaning, then God must have sent them and arranged for them to be understood. But God is here too, and can grant the understanding to be given through the mouth of anybody.
V. 11. על כף פרעה. Pharaoh stretched out his hand to receive the cup from me.

V. 14. כי, for surely God placed you here to have the dream, and me to interpret it, because He will restore you to favour as before, and because, even if you will only keep me in mind for a time, ultimately you will mention me to Pharaoh.

V. 15. It is remarkable that already here the land is called ארץ העברים. This family must already have been considered so important that the land where they were living was already known as their land.

V. 16. כי טוב פתר can not mean “meant something good”. If one does attach value and meaning to dreams, it can not be the good news it contains or the reverse, but its truth or probability which decides the worth of an interpretation. Moreover an opinion of the worth of an interpretation must be able to be formed already before, independently of, the actual happening. For Pharaoh, too, later on, acclaims Joseph as far-seeing and wise as soon as he hears the interpretation of his dreams, without waiting to see if it is correct, by the nature of the interpretation feels certain that it will come true. טוב פתר in any case means “well interpreted”, although we have very few examples of such adverbial use of טוב. If one thinks that through dreams or other symbolic signs that the One who sends the dream to the mind of a person wishes thereby to tell him something, the kind of symbol in the dream must be of such a nature that the receiver of it can explain it to himself; it must be clear and apparent. He who hears the explanation must, if it is a correct one, be able to say to himself: “I really ought to have thought that out myself”. The butler dreamt that he had a vine in front of him etc. All that Joseph added was that three tendrils which the vine had then to mature to blossoms and grapes, were three days which still had to pass. All the rest is then so clear that the butler could have said to himself “that is how I should have explained it to myself”. But if these dreams were surely sent by Providence, and so used the prevailing belief in dreams as a means to rescue Joseph, we can see here how הקב״ה speaks in pictures, and can learn from it how the explanation of His pictures must always be sought in the simplest and most apparent meanings, must never be read into them but always out of them; and we may only believe that טוב פתר, that we have hit on the right explanation when the explanation lies so closely and near to what has to be explained that one has to say to oneself “it can hardly mean anything different and comes naturally from the matter itself”.

אף אני בחלומי. “I too was in my dream”, probably means to say: “I, too, was the centre point, in the foreground of my dream”. I, too, dreamt about myself” — סלי חורי as חורים means, the free, noble ones, so סלי חורי can mean a superior, fine basket, no common one.

V. 17. All the food was worthy for a Pharaoh, and yet it was not he but the birds who ate it, and indeed they had the impudence to eat it away from me from the basket on my head. No bird would do that to a living person. It would be too afraid.

V. 20. יום הולדת את פרעה, literally, the day on which the mother was brought to bearing Pharaoh, in any case, a peculiar circumlocution. It does not suit the majesty of a Pharaoh to present himself as a new-born baby. The thought is therefore led away from him and on to the mother, so that every thought of a helpless swaddled baby is respectfully avoided. For הולדת, in any case, refers to the office of the midwife. Thus in Ezekiel (Ch. 16,4 & 5) where the birth of Israel is to be depicted as being in defiance of all natural circumstances, “all the conditions were unfavourable for thy birth, without a miracle thou would’st have weltered in thy blood”. There also it repeatedly says, נשא .נשא ראש .יום הולדת אותך also means: to take up the existence of something in the sphere of thought, hence to count. Counting people is expressed by “counting the heads”, probably because when a mass of people stand together, their bodies form a solid compact mass which can not be counted, and only the heads protrude separately and so can be counted. Both names were on the list of servitors, they had not yet been cashiered but were only remanded in custody.

V. 23. שכח, related to שגח ,שגע ,שגה. See above VIII,1. שבח means forgetting through being taken up by other matters. Related to שקה, saturated, שכח, mentally to be so full of something that there is no room for anything else. The butler was not concerned to keep the memory of Joseph constantly fresh in mind, he was so full of the present that he forgot him.

V. 1. קץ ,מקץ from קצץ related to גזז to cut off, separate, also to כסס to fix the number and measure from which we get כס, a vessel of a certain size. Cf. גזר ,כרת, to cut off, separate and to fix. Thus also קצץ, both. ויהי מקץ, it was just as one came to the end of two full years. — פרעה not his own name, but the title given to Kings of Egypt, similarly to Abimelech, as all Kings of Philistia were called. According to that the word is certainly of Egyptian origin. Were it to be Hebrew, or if the meaning is similar in both languages, it would be derived from פרע to be free, unbound, and would be most appropriate for the Kings in Egypt. There was no other state where all classes were so bound and unfree as in Egypt. The whole life of everybody there was clamped down and regulated by rules and caste. There was only one person who was free, the one who stood at the head, the King, and even he was only free in a way, for the lives of the Kings too were bound by strict laws of custom and etiquette. So it was no ordinary person who dreamt. This was the dream of a king. — עמד על, where this does not mean actually standing on something, it usually has the meaning not only of the place next to which somebody stands, but at the same time indicates that his mind and thoughts are directed towards it. Thus ויעמד העם על משה (Ex. 18,13) העומד על בני עמך (Dan. 12,1) See on Ch. 28,13. Accordingly “he was standing next to the river”, considering it. The river was what he was thinking about, the Nile, on the overflowing of which the whole fertility of Egypt was dependent.

V. 2. בריא, healthy, sound, fat. — אחו, meadow, from אחה to bind together, from which we get אח, brother. Grass is a “social plant” which as a rule never grows singly. Hence אחו, really, sociability. — The river produces seven times good cows and seven times bad ones. As the Nile dispenses its gifts only once a year, this would immediately say that the seven cows mean seven years, and this would also go for the seven ears of corn. For Pharaoh was standing considering the river, was thinking of it as the giver of the fertility of the country, accordingly Egypt’s riches in cattle and corn. Cows and corn are gifts of the river. Further, when the good cows came up of the river they found pasturage and went there to graze. But when the bad cows came up, the good ones were standing again at the bank of the river because they had evidently finished up all there was to graze on. The bad cows were not cannibals by nature. Hunger would not have made them eat up the others had these left them over food in the meadow. Hence the warning lies to hand in the dream not to eat up everything in the years of plenty. The whole meaning of the dream is simple and clear in the dream itself. Thus does God speak when He uses metaphor, and this interpretation of Joseph is the pattern and the criterion for every explanatory interpretation. דרש, not to read into, but to read out of.

V. 4. וייקץ פרעה, the appearance of the bad cows gave him such a shock that he woke up, but was not fully awake so he went to sleep again and went on dreaming. קוץ and יקץ, are synonymous, like טוב and יטב. קוץ to be surfeited, to have nausea. In sleep the body regenerates itself, and when it has had enough “is surfeited”, it awakes. Ordinary awaking is beautifully expressed in Hebrew as an active action הקיץ. In sleep, the mind retreats to the background, and allows the body to “suck” at the breast of sleep — “sleep, chief nourisher in life’s feast”; — when it has suckled sufficiently then the mind shakes it away from the breast of sleep: הקיץ.

V. 5.—6. שדף, a milder form of שטף, washed through, of the wind, blown through. He woke up and lo! it was a dream. Until then it had seemed to be actually real, and even when he woke up the impression was still so strong that only when he was really wide-awake he realised that it was only a dream.

שבלים, Ähren, von שבל. Die Begriffsbezeichnung der Kornähre durch שכל ist dunkel. שבל ist offenbar verwandt mit שפל und שול, niedrig und der untere Saum eines Gewandes. Merkwürdigerweise bezeichnet daßelbe Wort שִבלֶת Kornähre und Strudel im Strom. שבלת שטפתני (Ps. 69, 13). Strudel entstehen durch plötzliches Hineinstürzen des strömenden Wassers in eine Tiefe, und somit entfernt sich die Bedeutung Strudel nicht von der Bedeutung des ,"abwärts", die in שול und שפל liegt. Demgemäß wäre auch שביל nicht einfach Weg, sondern ein jählings abwärts führender Weg, im Gegensatz zu מסלה, von ללo, dem aufwärts führenden Pfad. Jirmija 18, 15 in dem Verse: כי שכחוני עמי לשוא יקטרו ויכשילום בדרכיהם שבילי עולם ללכת נתיבות דרך לא סלולה stehen vier verschiedene Bezeichnungen für "Weg" und liegt der Sinn des Satzes nur in der richtigen Würdigung der verschiedenen Nuancen des Begriffes. דרך ist die Bewegung eines Wesens zu einem Ziele überhaupt. אורח der soziale Weg, der den Menschen zum Menschen gesellt. (Daher Jes. 2, 3 ויורנו מדרכיו ונלכה באורחתיו: von den Wegen des jüdischen Individuums, zu denen auch עריות ,מאכלות אסורות usw. gehören, werden nur einige, die sozialen jüdischen Wege aber alle Gemeingut der Völker werden). שביל der abschüssige Weg, den man auch unfreiwillig geht. מסלה der aufwärts führende Pfad, den nur die freie Energie des sittlichen Menschen, nicht aber die Materie geht. נתיב, verwandt mit נרב, ein Pfad, den man aus freier Entschließung einschlägt. Rings um sich sieht der Mensch nur שבילים und zwar שבילי עולם, außer ihm stürzt die Materie jählings dem Ziele zu, folgt blind der Kraft, welche die Wesen führt, und stets und wandellos sieht er diese Gänge unfreier Gebundenheit. "Was hat mein Volk dazu gebracht, mich zu vergessen und dem Nichtigen Weihopfer zu streuen? Die Unfreiheit, die sie überall um sich gewahrten, brachte sie zum Straucheln in ihren Lebenswegen, so daß sie freiwillig den Weg einschlugen, der nicht aufwärts führt." Von Gottes Wegen heißt es: auch sie "führen mit unwiderstehlicher, jäher Kraft; allein sie führen hindurch durch die Fluten auf unsichtbarer Spur!" בים דרכך ושבילך במים רבים ועקבותיך לא נודעו (Ps. 77, 20). — Bezeichnet nun שבל einen jähen, plötzlichen Zusammensturz von Kräften, so kann vielleicht שבלת, wie Strudel, auch eine plötzliche Entwicklung von Kräften bedeuten, die bis dahin geschlossen zum Ziele strömten, wie dies in der Ähre der Monokotledonen erscheint. Ohne Ansatz und Anzeichen einer Fruchtentwicklung steigt der Halm einfach und einheitlich empor, und plötzlich bildet sich die Krone von allseitig sich entladenden Fruchtkörnern.

V. 8. ותפעם, literally, it was knocked, beaten. — חרטומי (from חרט) those who were versed in engraved hieroglyphics. These, constantly engaged in the meaning of symbols were the most suitable from whom the explanation of a dream could be expected. None could explain them to Pharaoh. Already by the fact that they did not take the two dreams to be the same, and by the arbitrariness of their interpretations, Pharaoh could find none of the various explanations which they gave which could satisfy him.

קצף, verwandt mit קצב, כזב. כזב: wider Erwarten zu Ende gehen, daher auch: täuschen. קצב: mit gewaltsamer Einwirkung Ende, Grenze und Ziel setzen, bestimmen. קצף: mit gewaltiger Erregung einer Sache entgegentreten und ihr ein Ende, oder doch Beschränkung bringen. כסף: sich nach einem Ende sehnen, streben, vergl. כלה כֶסֶף: die Vermittlung, um zu einem Zwecke zu gelangen, das alles vermittelnde Geld. —

V. 11.—12. The butler had had experience of a kind of interpretation which, as soon as it was given, struck one as being right. So he said: I can quite understand why none of the attempted explanations satisfy you. We were once in the same position.

V. 14. We should pay attention to all the little points which show up Joseph’s character. The court officials wanted to rush him to the King (יריצהו). It was a question of soothing the King and he was but a despised imprisoned slave. But he took his time; first shaved and put on respectable clothes (only once elsewhere do we find חלף שמלתיו in the Piel, viz. II Sam. 12,20, and there too it occurred under the protest, or at least the disapproval of those who stood about him). Also not וירץ, he did not run, ויבא, he “went in” to Pharaoh. He was quite conscious of his own personality, and of his mission. It was just this quality, as we said above, that made him into a חכם, that he understood how to grasp every circumstance, every person, every position in the whole acuteness of its special character.

V. 15. תשמע חלום not תדע. I have heard of you that you “listen to a dream in such a manner that you solve its meaning from its very contents”. It all depends on listening to it correctly. Out of ten people who listen to a speech or a story, often each one hears it differently and only one correctly.
V. 16. בלעדי “that is not up to me”. I am not nearly great enough to admit that such should be said of me.

V. 17. It is interesting to compare what Pharaoh says he dreamt with the description above of what the dream actually was. From that we shall, incidentally also see how the חרטומים, even if they had been חכמים were led on a false scent. Every story that is told, with the exception of the Torah, has a subjective colouring, namely the impression the event made on the narrator. When God wishes to tell somebody something in a dream He does not tease them by giving them a riddle to solve. His speech even when He speaks in metaphors is always clear. But Pharaoh left out essential details. In the dream itself Pharaoh was standing על היאר, thoughtfully at the river, and in this consideration of the importance and meaning of the Nile for Egypt lies the whole key to the dream. But in his description he is standing על שפת היאר, the river is mere scenery. In the dream the cows were יפות מראה ובריאות בשר, good to look at and healthy of flesh, both go together and describe them at once with reference to their value to men. Pharaoh calls them יפות תואר they were beautifully formed animals. But no butcher looks at beauty of form, he leaves that to painters and artists and poets. That was why the חרטומים could have guessed at all sorts of possibilities, seven daughters, seven provinces, etc. The same thing with the thin cows. Above they were רעות מראה ודקות בשר bad to look at giving prospect of very little meat. Here they are דלות, needy, miserable, רעות תואר, “badly-formed” lacking in beauty and רַק ,רַקות בשר is not רֵיק empty, but, as רק, only, is a limiting preposition, is accordingly, limited in flesh, all epithets which refer more to the nature of the animal itself than to its utility for human purposes. (רקק is related to רכך, soft, to be tender, hence also רק, saliva, the softening liquid) he also omits to relate that the bad cows first placed themselves next to the good ones on the bank of the river, from which can be derived that they only consumed the good ones because there was no pasturage left in the meadow. The impression made by the bad cows must have been a much stronger one than that made by the good ones. Pharaoh heaps up their bad qualities in order to describe sufficiently the impression they made on him, and stresses what the poor nature of the bad ears were to him by describing the good ones which preceded them in the masculine gender, אחריהם.

V. 33. Whereas, otherwise, as a rule חכמה comes before בינה, here it says significantly חכם .נבון וחכם is related to אגם: taking in what is before one. He who recognises things for what they are and what they should be is a חכם. Both are gifts, are nothing that people have to create for themselves. But the truest חכם is the one who takes the nature of what things are and what they are meant to be from the One Who made things what they are and fixed what they should be. Therefore חכמת התורה is the highest. — בין ,בינה, insight or better, distinguishing sight. True insight, the ability to get at the actual nature of things is something that no mortal can have, but distinguishing ability, i.e. to recognise the result out of at least two given factors, the deductive faculty, is the real operation which the human mind is to exercise with its given power, its intellect. Now it is remarkable that just that mental activity which seems to us more passive, חכמה, the intellect, the power of receptivity is expressed in the active form, חָכָם ,חכמתי in the Kal, while that operation of the mind in which our minds appear most active, using the deductive productive faculty is always expressed in the passive mood נבונתי ,נבון. This may give us two important reminders. To take in what is given in nature and Divine Revelation of the nature and purpose of things requires the exercise of the utmost energy of the mind, a complete concentration of mental powers, so that the whole and true actuality is grasped. Without exercising energy one thinks one sees, hears and understands things and has only seen falsely, heard half and understood quite superficially, and what one has grasped is soon lost. Conversely, ordinary people find more pleasure in תבונה, the deducing, concluding activity of the mind, they feel themselves more productive, more doing something of their own, and accordingly require more the warning not to be too quick in coming to conclusions, in making them keep themselves more passive than active, to keep the two premises revolving in the minds until the conclusion results by itself, otherwise the conclusion may be too clever and the premises not true. None run the danger to make false judgements more than sagacious people. Hence, too, the deep saying of our sages, אם אין בינה אין דעת ,אם אין דעת אין בינה. Without theoretical knowledge (בניה), empirical knowledge (דעת) is insufficient, for theoretical knowledge must to a big extent control and rectify the empirical, and teach to differentiate between illusion and reality. But still more does theoretical knowledge require the empirical. For, without a sound empirical basis all theory builds on air. So that it is quite clear why, ordinarily, חכמה is placed before תבונה. But here the given conditions were perfectly clear. But the question was, to conclude from the conditions what precautionary measures were to be taken. For that the נבון was primarily required. But that which was ascertained by בינה must then be carried out with חכמה i.e. with the correct estimation of the actual conditions. For the practical execution the חכם is more important than the נבון. The intellectual man easily takes things to be other than they really are and makes mistakes. Hence “let Pharaoh seek a man of insight and a wise one and set him over the land”. שות .וישיתהו is more than הפקיד. In הפקיד the one who is appointed is more dependent and subordinate, in שות he is more independent and on his own. The times would become so hard, and if left to itself, the land would lose the means of help granted by the years of plenty. Therefore it was necessary to provide the country with a “guardian”, an agrarian dictator, so that the consumption in those years should not remain unlimited.

V. 34. But what should come from Pharaoh himself should be the imposition of a tax of twenty per cent of all produce. Here again Joseph shows himself a חכם. By the imposition and collection of this tax the trustee to be appointed is to remain protected, to keep him free from all hatreds as it would be so necessary for him to have moral influence over the people. Every tax, even the most necessary and beneficial, appears oppressive. So this should be imposed by Pharaoh himself through his appointed tax officials. There would still remain quite enough for the other to do. This fifth would supply just the most necessary means of existence. Why just one fifth? Perhaps this may be the reason. Let us assume that in years of plenty one uses twice as much as in ordinary years, and, in contrast, in years of scarcity one makes do with half the ordinary quantity. Hence in a year of plenty one would use four times as much as in a famine year. If this is so then it is quite simple that in any case one fifth of what is produced in a year of superfluity must suffice to feed one famine year even if everything else, the remaining four fifths are completely consumed.

V. 35. But still more is to be done, not just the barest minimum is to be provided for. This rule, proposed to be instituted by the appointed Guardian of Egypt, is worked out in this verse. But there are difficulties in comprehending it. It says, ויקבצו את כל אוכל וגו׳ if, in the good years all the food is to be gathered in, then the people would starve before the famine started. It is possible that יקבץ, which certainly otherwise does mean gathered together here has more the meaning of kept to itself, a meaning which in itself is not so very far away from the other, and lies in its relationship with יבש ,גבש ,כבש ,גוץ ,כוץ ,קפץ all of which express compression. According to that, two proposals seem to be made (a) the tax, in the previous verse, and (b) here, a protective precaution of its disposal, i.e. a limitation in doing business with the grain, primarily of export. For in ancient times Egypt was the storehouse of corn for the rest of the world. So אוכל, food in its natural state was to be kept in the land and not exported. Therefore it is repeatedly called אוכל and not תבואה in which even money could be considered included in the return of the year. So that during the years of superfluity the export trade is to be stopped. Not even one city should be allowed to deal in grain with another city, so that no corn is to be converted into unfruitful money. If the producers want to sell it, they are to be able to do so exclusively to Pharaoh, and the grain thus bought should be kept under his seal. And so that the benevolent purpose of this control, which was after all very stringent, should be apparent to everybody, and so prevent resentment, the grain bought by the crown should not be stored in central granaries, but אכל בערים ושמרו but kept under seal of the State in the cities themselves where it had been bought up, and so, everywhere among the population it would be kept visibly before their eyes that they had by this provision of corn an insurance against future lack of food — אינו דומה מי שיש לו פת בסלו וגו׳. — The people would thus be convinced that the government were not intending to speculate on selling abroad this corn they were buying up and forbidding the people to export.

V. 40. על פיך ישק. We never find a kiss on the mouth being a sign of homage. We do find throwing kisses with the hand (Job. 31,27) but never kissing on the mouth. Hence it is definitely preferable to take the other meaning of נשק viz. to make preparations, equip oneself. The meaning here would be: “On your mouth, according to what you say all my people shall equip themselves against the coming enemy, hunger”. The expression is the more pertinent as we can see from Is. 22,8, that נשק means precisely a prepared assembly of arms. First he assigns him to the care for his, Pharaoh’s household, and then to make the regulations for the people to make provisions for themselves — כסא. As קצה and קצע, designate a forcible separation and cutting off, and כסה the complete withdrawal from sight and unapproachability to touch of an object so is כסא a base which raises the person who mounts it above and unreachable to all others. And moreover it is not a pedestal on which to stand temporarily but a high seat on which to sit. For to the true king the צאת הצבא, leading to battle, is only exceptional calling, his real vocation is peaceful internal administration, and his more correct designation is his elevated seat in the midst of his people: “the throne”.

V. 41.—43. Verses 41—43 belong together: Pharaoh said to Joseph: See I have set thee over the land “for the well-being of the whole land” (נתתי, lit. I have given you I.L.) and as a sign of it he drew his own ring from his finger. A ring (presumably a signet-ring I.L.) is a distinctive mark of a man’s activities, and at the same time, a crowning of the hand. By placing his signet-ring on Joseph’s finger, he made him his representative, made Joseph’s hand into Pharaoh’s hand. The signification of the בגדי שש in ancient Egypt is unknown to us. — רבד, in Yoma 43b. is a row of stones laid in the ground. מרבדים רבדתי ערשי (Prov. 7,16) as well as the similar רפדתי יצועי (Job. 16,13) refer to a bed or bedding (as does רפידתו זהב in Song of Songs I.L.). Perhaps there is some relation to רבץ which is also used for setting stones, מרביץ בפוך אבניך (Is. 54,11) “lay thy stones with lapislazuli”, and possibly רביד הזהב means a stone set in gold, a medallion. Anyway it does not say רביד זהב but רביד הזהב “the” golden emblem, probably the highest decoration. By the ring he made him his “משנה״, his “double” his “alter ego”, made him ride in the chariot reserved for such a vice-regent, and had it called out before him אברך! literally: I command that one kneels down. Before an Egyptian majesty one did not proclaim ברכו “on your knees”, but, אברך, “I — i.e. the majesty who is appearing amongst the people — command that ye kneel”. To a true king only spontaneous show of respect is an honour. To the dictator-king voluntary show of respect is too plebeian, and not servile enough. There the command comes: I order you to greet me with due respect! This calling out in Joseph’s name אברך, that he commands that people are to fall to their knees before him, presents him to the people as the complete second Pharaoh.
V. 44. Probably on his return from the public installation procession through the city.

V. 45. צפנת פענח.
