If one tries to find analogies for the meaning of this name which is apparently Egyptian, צפנת would be צפן, hidden, and for פענח one could find in Rabbinic Hebrew פנח (Yebamoth 115 לפנחיא שבקיה see Rashi thereon) so that the name could perhaps mean: “he, with whom the most secret things are kept”, who holds the key to the most hidden secrets. Part of Joseph’s installation was apparently supplying him with a wife. In ancient Egypt a man without a wife must have been considered only half a man, and for the post Joseph was to occupy, a complete man was required. Even today the public are somewhat shy of placing their complete confidence in a bachelor. Added to this, the task which was to be entrusted to Joseph would be furthered if he himself had a wife and family. If the people agreed to restrict themselves wisely during the seven years of plenty there could be enough for thirty-five years. If senseless squandering took place, death from famine would ensue. Joseph was to exercise this wholesome and necessary control. He would have the most beneficial influence if he, the first in the land, set the example of simple living in his house and family life. But for that a wife and family were necessary. A single man without wife and family is not felt to be so intimately together with the general public in times of stress and anxious worry, but with wife and children, even if he is prince or king he participates in the general trouble of the people.
V. 47. קמץ) לקמצים to take a handful), where ordinarily there was a single fruit now there were handfuls.

V. 48. אשר היו בארץ מצרים, because the extraordinary productivity was only in Egypt, the opportunity for export was so much greater and the necessity was all the greater to exercise control and prevent it.

V. 49. That the store of every city was bought up and stored as state property to be sold later in the time of need brought about a wise economy. People are economical with what they have to buy. With what they get for nothing they are extravagant. — כי אין מספר. Not that there was no number for it. True, there are people who like to ascribe to the people of ancient times, especially Biblical times, every conceivable childish lack of ability, amongst other fables that they were not able to count beyond a certain number. But this is simply absurd. As soon as one has names, for 1,100,1000, even for 10,000 one can make up any possible number right up to infinity. רבוא and רבבה are in no ways indefinite numbers, but an exact precise count, which, for an example, can be undeniably seen from שש רבאות ואלף (61,000) Ezra 2,69. If רבוא were an indefinite number, meaning an infinitely great number, there could neither be numbers of it, as here, six, nor as here, an additional one thousand. It is quite definitely 10,000, as can be seen from Judges 20,10 ולקחנו עשרה אנשים למאה, ומאה לאלף ואלף לרבבה, etc. If, nevertheless, it does say here כי אין מספר, one must remember that, after all to one’s imagination there is a limit. Between 3000,000,000 and 3,155,000,000 in our minds there is no difference. We could actually count them but we have no idea of them. The store of grain heaped up more and more until one ceased to say to oneself, exactly “so and so many measures now lie there” because to one’s idea the sum of what was added made no difference, already yesterday it was more than one could think of.

V. 50. A peculiar way of describing it: two children were born, to him, which Asnath had born unto him. Added to which ילד in the singular instead of יולדו. In a similar way it says later on in Ch. 46,20 ויולד ליוסף בארץ מצרים אשר ילדה לו אסנת וגו׳. It seems that here the birth is regarded in two aspects, from the standpoint of the mother and of that of the child. A mother can physically bear a child to its father, but it can remain a question whether the child remains born to its father after the birth, whether in its inner tendencies and outer influences it remains his child spiritually and morally. In ordinary circumstances it suffices to say ותלד לו, what the wife bears to her husband grows up under their combined influence to be like them. There is no necessity then to say further that ילד לו that the child had been born to the father. But here this is specially and significantly stressed. The mother was the daughter of a highly placed priestly family, accordingly, initiated and brought up in all the “mysteries” and ideas of Egypt, and Joseph was, after all, only a slave and a Hebrew raised by the grace of the king. A person can be the much-feared ruler of the people outside and at home the cringing slave of his haughty wife. How much was demanded for Asnath to be truly Joseph’s wife and to become the mother of his children. Asnath need only not to have entered into Joseph’s spiritual and moral outlook on life with all her heart and mind, if Joseph had not been just Joseph, and the danger would have lain to hand that she would indeed have born him children, but the children would not have been born to him. To that must be added the impersonal יֻלד, in which form, like ויוגד etc. an action or an effect is looked at quite by itself as the subject of the sentence, quite apart from the doer or the one who effects it. “It was told”, the telling was effected. “There were born”, the bearing was accomplished. Thereby the birth is looked at occurring by itself, under some special influence, here the Divine Protection and Blessing. And that was indeed required here. To be the only Jew in Egypt, to have the daughter of the priest of an idolatrous cult for a wife, and still to have children and bring them up to be such that up to this very day parents bless their children and know no higher wish for them than that God may make their children become like these, that is certainly a זכיה, a merit that deserves to be specially stressed, and therefor, later on too, when the families of the House of Jacob are reckoned up, is mentioned in a similar manner.

V. 51. נשני is usually translated: God hath made me forget all my misfortune and all my father’s house. Whose heart does not turn within him at this thought. Joseph calls his firstborn after the fact that God has allowed him to forget his old father and all his family. That certainly would solve the question in the easiest manner as to why Joseph had not bothered about his father for such a long time. Simply because Joseph had no heart. Fortunately, however, “to forget” is not the only meaning of נשה .נשה also means “to be a creditor” (see Ch. XXXI1,33) and נשני can just as well mean: God has made my misfortunes and my family into creditors. What had seemed to me hitherto misfortune and mishandling, God has made the means to my attaining the greatest joy, so that I am deeply indebted to my misforune and my family. The form נַשׁני instead of נִשׁני is equally difficult whichever way one takes it, and could only be explained by a root נשש which otherwise does not occur. — Incidentally, the word עמל as work, toil,, has been misused to give the idea that Jews are lazy, they call work trouble. Against this can be quoted, that we do not visualise even Paradise as a “dolce far niente”, for even in Paradise he was there “for work”, לעבדה ולשמרה. But עמל is not any kind of work, but only a toilsome work without any definite result.

V. 56.—57. שבר .וישבר, according to the fundamental meaning of the word, viz. to break, to split up, seems to mean to retail, to buy or sell in small quantities. He would only sell quantities required for the immediate requirements of each family. Only so could speculative buying and cornering be prevented. As our sages remark, people had to attend themselves, nothing was sold to slaves, otherwise a man could send fifty slaves, and each person was only allowed to bring one beast of burden with him. And everybody had to come to Joseph. He, himself, attended the sales, did not depend on subordinate officials, but personally came into direct contact with the hungry householders who came to buy. That is why indeed it says in the following Chapter in V.6: ויוסף הוא השליט הוא המשביר. Although he was the שליט, the ruler, he himself was the משביר, the retail-seller. But these methods of his, so necessary and so wise in the circumstances, brought about all that followed. Only so was it imperative for everybody to come himself, otherwise Jacob could have commissioned just one of his sons, or even a stranger, to do the business, on behalf of them all. And only so did it come about that Joseph himself came into contact with his brothers. The repeated remark how dire the famine became gives the motive for all these precautions.

V. 1. וירא. It seems that Jacob had greater comprehension than his sons. He had heard that in Egypt they would only sell in retail to individual householders. The sons did not believe this, and looked one at the other, waited for one of them to undertake the journey for all of them. But Jacob understood the probability of the truth of the rumour from the urgency of the conditions, and therefore said: What are you looking at each other for? You must all go down yourselves.

V. 4. קרא .פן יקראנו אסון related to קרח ,קרע ,קרה, a family of apparently very varied conceptions: — to call, to meet, to tear, frost and ice. Nevertheless they are all modifications of one fundamental idea: —
קרא, to call, to cause somebody to leave the direction he had in mind, voluntarily to leave it and come לקראתי, in my direction.

קרע to tear, to bring the parts of material out of their natural direction into the opposite one. Whereas קרא is merely the summons to leave the direction voluntarily, קרע does it forcibly. Forcibly overcoming the power of cohesion. Every particle is forcibly called out of its direction. We have already learnt that the letter ח׳ mostly indicates the reverse of ע; thus נח (rest) is נע (moving) come to rest. If קרע brings the particles of a material into opposition to the force of cohesion,

קרח, freezing, does the reverse. It brings the particles of a material that naturally have the opposite direction to cohesion, are liquid, closely together, stop their liquid movement, makes them cohesive, firm. קרע “calls” the particles away from each other, קרח “calls them together.

קרה to meet. All those influences, happy or the reverse, which call an object or person out of its natural or self-chosen direction and cause it to take another one, are called מקרה. We call all events which we had not reckoned on, which are not what we had expected: “chance”. But perhaps it is not considered as such by the One Who brings about all happenings. To us it is “chance”, “luck”, because we had not reckoned on its happening, but it may well be just what was reckoned on by the Great Master of Plans. In actual reality “chance” is something destined. .פן יקראנו, he will be going in one direction, but something can occur which will “call” him right out of that direction. But if מקרה ,קרי is a “call”, there must be “a caller”. Our term “it happens” is heathenish. Nothing happens by itself, everything is designed. Man, and Man alone in this world has the power of moral self-will and can decide his actions for himself.
אסון, some overpowering happening, a misfortune.

V. 5. Here they appear for the first time as בני ישראל. It was indeed a moment of no small import. The whole future hung on it. And they came, all unconscious of it, just בתוך הבאים (“amongst the crowd” (I.L.).
V. 6. See above in previous chapter V. 56 & 57.

V. 7. ויכירם ויתנכר וגו׳. Apparently two contradictory meanings of the one and same root נכר: to recognise and to be strange to. But only apparently. נכר in the Hiphil הכיר means really nothing else but “estranging”, treating as singular. “Recognising”, is “treating as singular”, strange. We only recognise an object by making it singular, separating it out from everything else. The more signs of difference we see in an object, the more specially do we recognise it. With every such sign we “estrange” it from all other spheres, all other species, all other kinds, and finally from all other things of the same kind, i.e. separate it away from everything else and recognise it. So הַכִּיר means to pick out an object from everything else by its speciality. According to that נכרי is not the unknown — we can know something for years and still it can be נכרי — but something which is different, which by its life or nature somehow does not belong, is not suitable for joining. So that התנכר means, as in גם במעלליו יתנכר גער (Prov. 20,11) to distinguish himself from all others, to show himself in his peculiarities, or, as here and in I Kings 14,5, to show oneself in a different peculiarity than how one really is. He showed himself to them other than he really was, inasmuch as he spoke harshly to them, and also as a נכרי spoke to them in a foreign language through an interpreter, thereby he succeeded that הם לא הכירוהו.

V. 9. We must try, from what we are told, to explain Joseph’s behaviour. We should have thought that if only for his father’s sake, he would have made himself known to them immediately, especially as he had already recognised the Hand of God in all that had happened, and had learnt to appreciate all his misfortunes, including his brothers’ crime against him, as the working of God for his greatest happiness and good fortune. A clever man like Joseph would also not think that he had to fulfil all the details of his dreams. If a dream has any meaning, one can leave its realisation to the One Who sends it. It could only be that considerations of urgent necessity caused him to adopt a behaviour which otherwise must appear as senseless and purposeless spitefulness. This, apart from Joseph’s character, his undeniable cleverness can not allow us to suppose to have been the motive. If we put ourselves completely in his position we could arrive at the following explanation. Had Joseph wished his attitude towards his father and his brothers to remain really as the Governor, and nothing but the Governor, did he not care whether or not he would re-enter the family circle as son and brother, he would not have required all these contrivances. But he, who, even as an Egyptian prince had brought up his children for the House of Jacob, and who also desired his bones ultimately to rest in the land of his fathers, felt it absolutely necessary for him to be convinced of two things: (a) that he himself can have a different opinion of his brothers, and above all (b) that his brothers have a different opinion of, and felt quite differently towards him. Their inner feelings towards one another must have become quite different to what they formerly were, otherwise an intimate relationship would never be able to be re-established, and even if outwardly the family were to be re-united, the family would be lost for him, and he for the family. That Joseph’s opinion of his brothers was not without bitterness, that their ruthlessness still lingered in his mind, how they had been deaf to his entreaties in the pit, how they had ignored the pain they would give their father, is no more than natural. That could only be purged from his mind by proof of their complete change of mentality. It was therefore a necessity for him to test them, to see whether they would still be capable — and this time with perhaps real cause — of depriving the father of a son. For lifelong imprisonment and families starving at home would certainly be more serious reasons than the imaginary danger of the threat of Joseph’s supposed ambition for rulership. This test was necessary for Joseph’s feelings, so that, if they withstood it, the last drops of bitterness would be eradicated from his heart. But the second and perhaps the more important was: — Joseph remembered his dreams, remembered how his dreams awoke in his brethren the idea of his seeking to become king, and of the danger this threat was to them and their mission, and how this suspicion grew to such conviction that they could feel themselves justified, in supposed self-defence, in committing the greatest crime. If this was the case when he ran about amongst them in his fur-trimmed coat, how much more must he now be looked on by them with fear and anxiety when he really was a “king”, and moreover had reason to hate them, and, in the way of ignoble natures, to take his revenge on them. It was therefore more than necessary that they shall learn to know him in his true character, and for that it was above all, necessary for them to be shown what his actual position in Egypt really was. Until then they had only known him as the משביר the officer in charge of the retail selling, perhaps the clerk of a subordinate official, he must show them that he was the שליט, the Ruler; they must be made to realise that he could do with them whatever he wished, and if then, instead of all that they feared, he turned out to be their greatest benefactor, and only used his power, to ensure their happiness, he could hope that thereby they would be cured from all their erroneous ideas about him. In a word, that, the moment he revealed himself to them as Joseph, the scales would fall from their eyes, and on both sides it would be possible to cross out the whole of the past. Only so could he hope to be really restored to his father and his sons as son and brother. Unless we are mistaken it must have been considerations such as these which kept Joseph back from sending information to his father during the years of his good fortune. What good would it have done his father to regain one son and lose ten others, to have had to think of his family circle being split into two camps in opposition and in a state of enmity towards each other? But to attain his great purpose all these contrivances were unavoidable, and — in our opinion — fully worthy of the wisdom of a Joseph.

V. 11 et seq. It has already been remarked long ago that Joseph took up the point that, although each one could only buy himself and his family they all came together, to pretend that he thought there must be something else behind it, and so declared them to be spies. If that is so and it is a fact that in general families did not come together, it would be a characteristic sign of the influence that such a universal calamity effects. One generally says that trouble draws people together. But how long does it last? Only for as long as one can help the other. But when this possibility ceases the direct common need islolates. Each one fears the other may get in front of him and the store may give out, so it is each for himself and his family. That the בני יעקב did stick together in this greatest terrible need is no unworthy sign of Jewish family feeling, where, even in the extremest need where none can any longer expect anything at all from anybody else, where everybody can only see a competitor in everybody else, the family holds together. No one pushes himself in front. They wanted to receive everything — although they could only get it separately and individually — all together and at the same time, — אנחנו ,נחנו is what they say. — In describing their social position they modestly use the term נחנו, but when their character is attacked, with full proud consciousness, אנחנו. Honesty and unblameableness are worth more than יחוס (purity of decent I.L.) — כן from כון, that which is as it should be, which allows no considerations or intentions to make it turn away from what is right, “we have never, in any circumstances, been spies”. It is not in our nature to spy.
V. 13. They explained that their coming all together was out of brotherliness, and gave particulars which he could eventually verify.
V. 14. Joseph reposted with just that point. “Yes, because your father knew you were on a dangerous errand, he would not allow the youngster to go with you.

V. 16.—17. He makes them wait three days in prison to enable them to realise the seriousness of their position and to allow the urgency of it to work its effect on them. They themselves were in danger, their families would starve, there was reason enough for one or the other to persuade or force the father to come to the decision to part from Benjamin. For Joseph knew well enough that his father would not do that readily.
V. 20. ויעשו כן, they had no choice, they could not do otherwise.

V. 21.—22. אבל always opposes a previous supposition, darkens (אפל ,אול ,אבל) what previously had seemed clear and definite. As the brothers say אבל here, previously up till now they must not have considered themselves guilty. Even now they only reproach themselves with cruelty and harshness, up till now they had not done even that, had considered their behaviour as self-defence in face of peril. But Reuben sees their guilt not merely in hardness of heart, from the beginning he had said to them: you are doing wrong, committing a sin, he looked on Joseph merely as a child, and on his plans, of which they were so afraid, as mere childishness. So he says to them: You have not to reproach yourselves just that you did not let kind feelings prevail over those of justice, but you sinned gravely against him. אשם and חטא. When roots start with א׳, that letter always individualises the concept expressed by the other two letters of the root. Thus אבד ,אכל ,אהב etc. So too שמם .אשם means to be an empty space, hence שם, the indication of a place which something occupies or should occupy. שממה, a space with nothing at all in it, a waste, a desert. Also the desert of the mind, where no thoughts dawn is called שמם, an emptiness of mind, without imagination or thoughts. According to that אשם would be to bear within oneself reason for desolation, reason for שממה. Somebody can be robbed of all his possessions without it being his fault, that would be a state of שממה without אשם. But if the person feels within himself a reason for withdrawing from all possessions and joy in life, the consciousness of that is אשם. So that אשם is the consciousness that one deserves to be desolate, to be deprived of all the goods and joys of life. חטא is, as we have seen, a “darkening” an obscuring of our moral self, a withdrawal of that which should be לחם אשה ה׳ (— fuel to keep godliness burning brightly in the world I.L.). So that חטא designates sin from the point of view of its origin, its cause within the one who commits it, and its effect on his inner self. חטא is the inevitable immediate occurring result of sin, our getting further away from godliness, while אשם designates the external result of sin which is expected to occur. אשם is the voice of the conscience which gives the חוטא, the sinner, the prospect of שממה. That אשם is in closer relation to the external than to the internal factor of sin can be seen from the offerings. אשם גזלות and אשם מעילות is connected by the sin itself with external possessions, the sin is committed against other people’s property. The איל, of which the offering has to be, is a symbolic representation of a wealthy, leading personality, and אשם is the only offering that must be of a fixed minimum value. חטאות and אשמות are especially brought for שגג (sins committed unintentionally through carelessness I.L.) and it constantly uses the term ואָשֵׁם “he deserves, has earned שממה״, and this is intimately connected with the conception (שכך) שגג really “carelessness”. שגגה arises out of carelessness and indifference to spiritual matters, and results in only a small degree of self-reproach one easily makes excuses to oneself about it. Whereas מזיד (wrong done consciously and intentionally I.L.) can also be punishable by the human law courts, שגגה is left to God’s educational methods, by יסורין, external troubles and pains, to rouse our dull and sleepy conscience to realise that something is wrong in our mode of life and needs altering. This awakening of our conscience and inciting self-reproach and resolve for betterment after sinning through carelessness is the purpose of the sin-offering, which thereby is to take the place of education by means of suffering and troubles. This מגין על היסורין is especially stressed in אשם תלוי שבא על הספק (the special offering which had to be brought in certain cases where one was in doubt as to whether one had committed a sin through carelessness, see Hirsch on Levit. V.17 I.L.) where the doubt as to whether we had committed the sin at all is most apt to allow our feeling of guilt to be quiescent, and requires serious awakening still more urgently than in ordinary שגגה. Thus here too: for twenty years they had argued and defended themselves to themselves, but now they are shattered by trouble, and אבל אשמים אנחנו comes to the fore: after all, an unatoned wrong rests on us that threatens us and ours with danger and ruin, שממה, desolation — the voice of conscience can not be suffocated, you can pour ashes over the coals, but even after fifty years the flame can burst brightly up — אבל! After all, all what we said to ourselves is not true. באה אלינו not עלינו punishing fate is still advancing to us, our present calamity is only the beginning.
אל תחטאו בילד. You are doing wrong in attacking the lad. It is no Divine fire that burns within you. Your pious indignation will only land you in sin.

V. 23. לוץ, interpreter, mediator, poem, mockery, all the conceptions expressed by the root לוץ, have, at base, the common idea of ingenious לוז, “the art of transposing or transferring”. The interpreter transmits thoughts and words, clothes them in such a “word-garment” that they can find entrance into the understanding of the hearer; the mediator presents facts in such a garb that they find entrance to the judgment of the hearer in the desired manner; the art of poetry is to place thoughts in a beautiful form that appeals to the feelings. All this is an ingenious transmission out of the natural state into something that serves a desired purpose at the time. But there is also a pernicious “art of transposing” and that is the art of using words to make things appear to be different to what they are, and indeed to make evil and base into beautiful and noble, to distort holy and reverent into ridiculous. This is the art of jeering mockery, the art of the לצים.
V. 24. סבב, to circumambulate about something. הִסוֹב, to turn about yourself, to turn right round.

V. 25. ויצו. The order to fill their sack with grain was just the ordinary routine, the ולהשיב וגו׳ was what was special. צידה is not food in general but food for some special time. It is not food to be consumed at once, eaten up (טרף) but to be “taken and secured” (צוד) to be consumed later on. We have already referred to the sad fact that human food, regarded as having to be obtained in a struggle with nature and society as a whole, is called טרף and צידה .לחם from צוד is analogous to this conception.

V. 27. The relation of שק to אמתחת is obscure. שק from שקק, probably having the same meaning as נסק, to ascend, a means of carrying, formed from the root raising up, like סל from אמתחת .סלל from מתח to extend, stretch, seems to mean a larger, stretchable container in which several sacks and bundles are kept. It is also improbable that the money was just laid in the sack of corn itself, in which it could easily have gone amongst and under the corn and would not have become visable immediately on opening the sack.

V. 28. His fright was the greater as he saw his own money again, so that there seemed to be that some personal accusation was intended. That Joseph prepared this further quandary for them was all part of the whole plan. He wanted to make them realise how completely he was the שליט, how completely they were in his power, how he could do with them just what he pleased……and then etc.

V. 33. בעל and בעל .אדון is the lord, the master, in any case, the superior. אדון looks on the lord from a totally different, nobler, aspect. It is related to אדן the foot, the base of a pillar, the bearer, not one who could also destroy the other, but the bearer. Thus is ה׳ contrasted to the בעלים. To the heathen mind, the attribute of the Deity is essentially power to be feared. The quality of granting, giving, is to it, a sign of weakness. To it, gods are אל) אל ,אלילים no, not I.L.) denying powers, who find their joy in destroying human happiness, who are inimical to Man, who must be appeased or bribed by offerings. In contrast, הבק״ה is מתחת זרועות עולם, מקומו של עולם, down to the lowest depth: the home and bearer of all beings. Only an אדון can really in truth have an עבד. Joseph’s position was in the noblest sense רעבון בתיכם — .אדני הארץ, that for which your houses hunger.

V. 36. You can not take it amiss that I will not let Benjamin go with you. I just can not. True, I do not know how Joseph is no longer there, Simeon’s loss, too, is inexplicable to me. There may indeed be no connection at all between those events, all I know is that עלי היו כולנה both have come to me, I am bereft of both of them. If things repeatedly happen to somebody in a similar way, and he can not see clearly why they should occur, he should not place himself in a position for it to happen again until he gets some insight as to the cause. He should take the repeated fact as a סימן, as a warning sign to be observed, and, until he is clear in the matter, guard himself against a similar repetition. That is the teaching of our sages: בית, תינוק, ואשה אעפ״י שאין ניחוש יש סימן (although we may not be superstitious, we can take notice of “signs” regarding houses, children and wives I.L.) Chulin 95b. “Joseph became lost when away from me amongst you, Simeon also, and now I am to risk it with Benjamin — I may not.
V. 37. It was well meant, but there was not the slightest reason in it to move Jacob to alter his decision.

V. 3. עוד .העד העיד, to last, העיד, to bring about that something endures, hence to be a witness, i.e. to take notice of something, keep it in mind, and at the fitting time give evidence and establish the matter, i.e. make something lasting which otherwise would be transient. Hence עד also for a memorial. This giving evidence is all that a non-Jewish witness has to do. Jewish witnesses have also, at the moment of the deed to make the one who is about to commit a crime realise the law that he is about to break, again making lasting something (the law) which otherwise would be transient, i.e. to warn. So that העיד ב- is either giving evidence against somebody after the deed, or warning him before the deed. Here it is the latter. And העד העיד implies that Joseph had warned them at the beginning and had reminded them again seriously when they left, that they were not to dare to return without Benjamin.
V. 5. Therewith the urgent necessity was clearly presented to Jacob.

V. 6. ויאמר ישראל. Until then, since the loss of Joseph, he is always referred to as יעקב. For יעקב designates the depressed state of mind in which one feels oneself dependent, sinking, and “limping behind” circumstances, unable to be master of them, and having to submit to being dragged along by them. But the true Jew only feels depressed when he does not know what he should do. Only two things depress the righteous Jew, (a) guilt, having done wrong, and (b) being in doubt as to what he ought to do, but not about what could happen. As long as Jacob was in doubt whether he ought to let Benjamin go with or not, for so long does he appear as יעקב. But from the moment when the pressing necessity was clear to his mind — Benjamin’s life would be in as great a danger if he stayed back and starved as it would be if he went with — he pulled himself together and was ישראל. As soon as a Jew knows it is beyond his human powers to help himself further, he is told גול על ה׳ וגו׳, (Ps. 37,5 I.L.), what is too difficult for you “roll over” to God. Just what is most difficult but must be done, does he do with fresh, raised courage, for just there where it is beyond man’s own power to direct matters, “God’s Direction” begins for him. Therefore he makes no further complaint but only reproaches them for having quite unnecessarily mentioned their youngest brother at all to the man in power.

V. 7. ה׳ השאלה ,הידוע נדע. The letter ה has a threefold modulation. Its own sound is an animated breath, it is accordingly the bearer of existence in הוה ,היה etc. Where the existence is dependent, has no real independence, then the ה׳ is quiet, can not be heard. Thus the ה denoting the feminine, so also the optative ה׳ as נרדה, the going down is not yet positively decided on, but only exists as a wish. For a positive actuality the ה is audible הַסֵפֶר ,הַ־. If the existence wavers between being and not being, the sound also wavers ? הֲסֵפֶר הזה ,הֲ־ is this a book!

V. 8. To this father “Israel” Judah spoke. As long as his father did not see the absolute necessity Judah would not speak, he saw his father’s point, he may not send him. What he said would also have been of no avail, for what his father believed he was not allowed to do, he would not be allowed to do depending on the honesty of somebody else.
V. 9. Then the wavering suspicion which now rests against all of us, shall, with regards to Benjamin rest concentrated solely on me.

V. 10. If only we had not hesitated, you could long ago have been out of this worrying uncertainty. The journey is not so long. לולא from לול, a spiral staircase, and לולאות, knots which hold together. Our hesitation and uncertainty were the לולאות, were what held us back, all our wrong and unhappiness was the התמהמה, the indecision, otherwise everything would have already have been happily settled.

התמהמה von מהה, rad von מה: was; das unentschiedene Sachliche. מי: das unentschiedene Persönliche, von מגג ,מיי usw. die ein ins Unbestimmte übergehendes Zerfließen bedeuten. Ebenso התמהמה ,מהה sich unentschieden, unentschlossen halten; zögern, sich in dem Zustand des מה halten, wo man noch nicht weiß, ob rechts oder links.

V. 11. What בטנים are is undecided. Why did Jacob send nothing of the שבעה מינים, the seven kinds of produce which really constituted the שבח הארץ, here called זמרת הארץ? Simply because nothing was growing. All the things he sent were things that keep for a long time and came from previous years. That is why the Midrash too, takes בטנים ושקדים to have been nut oil and almond oil rather than nuts and almonds, as the fruits themselves would long ago have been eaten up.

צרי von צרה, verwandt mit זרח ,זרע ,צרע, hinaussetzen, streuen usw. Das ausschwitzende Balsamharz, daßelbe wie זמרת — .נטף. Höchst eigentümlich ist es, daß unsere Sprache, Gesang und Rebe mit derselben Wurzel bezeichnet. Wir haben drei Ausdrücke in Beziehung auf Gesang und Lied, שיר — .זמר שיר ,נגן ist das Lied im Gedichte. נגן ist die Instrumentalmusik. Möglich, daß נגן gerade Instrument heißt. Im Midrasch heißt מנגיניך: deine Machinationen. Ebenso heißt die Maschinerie an Salomos Thron: תרג׳ שני) מנגנון zu Esther 1, 2). Man leitet dies gewöhnlich aus dem Griechischen ab. Es ist jedoch möglich, daß נגן zu Grunde liegt. זמרה heißt die Melodie, der natürliche Gesang ohne Worte. Ist dies wahr, wie denkt sich unsere Sprache das Verhältnis der Melodie zum Lied, wenn sie die Melodie: "Rebe" nennt? Daß überhaupt Erscheinungen des Gedankens und der Rede durch Pflanzenerscheinungen ihren Ausdruck finden, ist unserer Sprache nicht fremd. So סעיף: Zweig und Gedankenreihe. מלל: abpflücken und מלה: ein einzelnes Wort, sowie מַלל: einzelne Worte sprechen. Vergegenwärtigen wir uns die Verwandtschaft von זמר mit צמר ,שמר, so ergibt sich die Bedeutung für זמרה, Rebe, als derjenige Pflanzenteil am Weinstock, in welchem die im Stamme aufsteigenden Säfte bewahrt, zusammengehalten und geläutert werden, bis sie die Frucht des Weines zu erzeugen fähig sind. Es wächst nicht die Frucht unmittelbar am Stamme, in weiten, sich schlängelnden Ranken strömen erst die Säfte hin, bis sie sich in der Beere zur Frucht gestalten. Ganz in demselben Verhältnis steht der Gesang, die Melodie, zum Worte des Liedes. Gefühle und Empfindungen, die in des Menschen Geist noch nicht zur völligen Gedankenklarheit für den Wortausdruck gereift sind, gewinnen auf den Flügeln des Gesanges diese Klarheit und Reife, um dann auf der Höhe der Begeisterung das Wort zu finden. Der natürliche Mensch spricht für andere, singt für sich, und in der wahren, der Natur nicht entfremdeten Kunst wird die Melodie nur Trägerin des Wortes sein wollen, wird die Melodie um des Wortes willen, nicht umgekehrt — wie in den meisten Operntexten — das Wort um der Melodie willen da sein. Die Melodie ist die sanft sich hinwindende Rebe, die auf ihrem Tongewinde das begeisterte Wort als Frucht darreicht. Die Richtigkeit dieser Auffassung dürfte auch in weiteren Sprachformen eine nicht unwillkommene Bestätigung finden. Das begeisterte Wort, die Frucht des Gesanges heißt: שיר .שיר ist aber — wie bereits (zu Kapitel 9, 21) entwickelt — nur ein Glied der Familie שכר ,שקר ,שגר. Alle vier, ,שכר ,שגר שיר ,שקר bedeuten ein Produzieren von innen heraus. שגר: die tierische Geburt. שקר die logische, absichtliche Produzierung, der in der äußeren Wirklichkeit nichts entspricht: die Lüge. שכר, die unabsichtliche geistige Produzierung der Phantasie, welcher ebenso nichts in der äußeren Wirklichkeit entspricht: der Rausch. שיר ist die wahre edle Produzierung, die nicht die konkrete Wirklichkeit, sondern das derselben zu Grunde liegende, nur von des Menschen Innern wahrgenommene Unsichtbare zum Ausdruck bringt. Das wahre שיר besingt immer Gott in der konkreten Erscheinung der Natur und Geschichte. Nun ergibt sich die einfache Parallele: wie sich זְמרָה, die Rebe, zu שֵכָר, dem berauschenden Saft, verhält, also verhält sich זִמְרָה, der Gesang, zu שִיר, dem begeisterten Liedeswort.

מנחה, probably such a gift which is נחה to prepare the way for somebody to somebody else. If the root was מנח related to מנה it would designate a gift of quite another kind, namely one intended primarily for the benefit of the receiver, while מנחה means a gift rather for the interests of the giver. With great delicacy Jacob repeatedly stresses the מעט. To such a great lord it would be an offence to bring any large quantity, it is only to be a mark of homage.

V. 12. משנה, either, “take the money again”, i.e. apart from the money you brought back, take money again for your purchases; or, apart from the money you brought back take double as much for purchasing as you took the first time, provide yourself with double the amount that you need. שנה, to repeat. צנה ,סנה ,זנה all mean being different, a change but a contrasting change. But שנה is only being otherwise individually i.e. a repetition of the same idea, the same appearance repeated in another individuality. Thus the very word with which our sages designate their teachings of the law, viz. שנה expresses that they only hand it down, repeat what they themselves have learnt and received, hence also שמעתתא, that which has been heard, in contrast to אגדתא, that which is original, self-produced. But nevertheless שנה does occur for a contrasting change, to alter oneself. — משגה an error committed through a too intense concentration of the mind, in contrast to שגגה, an error committed through carelessness, too little concentration of the mind, (see Ch. 8,1). Something can be overlooked through too great pressure of business. The buyer can have thought that he gave the money in, and had placed it back in the money bag. But the reverse can also happen through this great pressure of business, that the seller can erroneously think he has not received the money which has in reality already been paid. So provide yourselves with double the amount of money that is really required.

V. 14. לפני האיש. Only go trusting in the All-limiting One, God Who sets a limit at the right time to all suffering and troubles; at the moment of danger, at the moment you find yourselves לפני איש, before the man, God will direct His mercy towards you. רחמים designates that sympathy of God which is the most general and most unlosable, and which equally is the fundamental trait which should characterise the relationship of His creatures one to the other. It is family love, the love of parents to children, and children to parents, the love of children to one another on account of the common רחם out of which they come. People are inclined to mix up רחמים with the popular רחמנות and to take it to mean pity. And yet pity is a far lower feeling, far far beneath that which true רחמים means. Which is rarer, which ennobles Man more, to be moved to pity at others’ sorrow, or to be moved to joy at their happiness? There are very few people who do not feel sympathy with the suffering of their fellow men. But it is not everybody, not by a long way, who feels sympathy with a poor man today and feels joy to a similar degree if he draws the first prize in the lottery overnight, and tomorrow he sees him pass him in the street riding with his family in a Rolls-Royce. רחמים, the feeling that we are to have inherited means more than pity. The word is derived from רחם by which is designated the most self-sacrificing energy of one being for the formation of another being to come into existence and be completed; רֶחֶם, the womb, is the hearth of the deepest devotion. And afterwards, too, when the new being is there, the רחם begets not only sympathy with its crying but even more intimate joy with its smiling. A smile from the baby on the lap makes up for years of worry and sleepless nights. From this רחם is רחמים formed and not only suffers when the other suffers, but knows no rest until he sees him happy — ואני, and I, in the meantime, I will prepare myself, so that, if I am to be bereft of my children by your going away, I shall be ready to bear it.

V. 16. The reason why Joseph did not make himself known then at once would be because when he saw Benjamin he did not know whether possibly he had not been kidnapped away from his father. He wanted to put the matter to the test by seeing their reaction when he threatened to keep Benjamin back.

צהר .צהרים peculiarily related to צער, to be small, limited. Perhaps צהר does not mean, shining, rays of light, but perhaps indicates that light in which objects appear most precisely in the exact, most limited outline of their form, where even the smallest being is visible in its own speciality. According to the variation of this ability of recognition of objects, the various times of the day are named צהרים .ערב ,בקר ,ליל is a better designation than חצות, midday. Midday is just a point in time. No man dines at mid-day. But until mid-day light overcomes night, from there onwards night progressively conquers light. צהרים is the hour, half of which is filled with the growing and the other half with the waning light.
V. 18. להתגלל עלינו “to turn himself against us” i.e. to oppress us once again, “to come down on us, to pounce” i.e. to take us as slaves and to confiscate our beasts of burden.
V. 19. “At the entrance of the house”, they were afraid to follow him in.

V. 20. בי is of doubtful derivation. It is usually a request for a hearing and pardoning in circumstances of distress and embarrassment. The root can be either בהה, analogous to נהי and ני from נהה complaint, lamentation, and then בי in accordance with the meaning of בהה, the root of בהו, would indicate an unclear, embarrassed condition, an uncertain, wavering feeling. Or it would come from the root ביה which only occurs in the related בקע ,בכה and would then be the expression of a feeling of distress.
V. 21. ונפתחה, quite innocently, without any idea of anything, we just happened to open our bags.
V. 23. In order to allay their fears completely, so that they could eat with their minds at rest, he the steward, took it on himself to bring Simeon out to them at once.
V. 26. הביתה, probably the innermost room where Joseph awaited them.

V. 27. השלום אביכם is much more than השלום לאביכם which only expresses the enquiry after the harmonious agreement with the external conditions, while internally, within himself there could be a possibility of being worried and harassed. The question העודנו חי coming after the question about his general well-being reveals the whole anxiety of his filial heart. In asking after his father’s well-being the horrible thought suddenly strikes him: God, perhaps in the meantime he has died, and quickly he adds “He is still alive isn’t he?”

V. 28. They could only answer שלום לאבינו, but not, as he had asked, that he was שלום, for he missed Joseph and Simeon and Benjamin — קדה .ויקדו וישתחוו, from קדד, the root of קדקוד, means bowing from the waist with the forehead touching the ground, a bending which we can hardly accomplish. But השתחויה means prostrating oneself completely flat on the ground and so express complete submissiveness and resignation. Also for a request one throws oneself down similarly, הכל בזכות השתחויה. But קידה is always used for thanks, and then השתחויה follows. In ancient times they paid attention also to such small expressive trifles. By the other one having shown us kindness we feel ourselves up-lifted, he has granted us an upright position, that is why we bow our heads standing, acknowledge our position as due to him, and then, by השתחויה promise to pay our debt of gratitude by complete devotion to him. At the beginning, in V.26, it only says וישתחוו, but now, when he had received them so amicably, and had shown such interest in asking after their father, it says זיקדו זישתחוו and here the וישתחו is written חסר, the feeling of relief expressed in their קידה had already overwhelmed them (see Sucka 53a).
V. 29. חנן ,יחנך is to make a stream of blessings flow down, related to ענן.

V. 30. נכמרו רחמיו, for he knew the ordeal which he intended to inflict on him, and in what a painful position, even if only temporarily he could not avoid placing him. כמר, deep emotion being excited, it is also the root of מכמרת, a net. כמד the pagan priest. In Rabbinic Hebrew כמר של זיתים, laying fruit on top of each other to keep them warm and become ripe and mellow, or to bury them in the earth for the same purpose by shutting them up. מכמר בשרא (Pessachim 58b) the beginning of meat becoming foul. ביב שהוא קמור, קמֹר תחת הבית a hidden drain. The fundamental meaning: to keep back something that really wants to set itself free, by shutting it up, and thus let it come to fermentation. Thus on the one hand, a net, and on the other, the process of fermentation. Transposed to the realm of feelings, it would be hidden feelings that one carries about within oneself, which, just by being repressed, “boil up” to such a degree that they can no longer be contained within one’s breast, cf. כי יתחמץ לבבי. Accordingly: being deeply affected by one’s feelings. Probably from the same idea, pagan priests are called כמרים in contrast to כהנים. The Jewish כהן does not depend so much on devoutness, feelings. Jewish Divine Service is not designed to excite dark mysterious feelings. The Jewish Sanctuary makes its appeal primarily to the mind, the intelligence rather than to feelings: התפלל, to rectify one’s judgements to get clear about one’s relationship to things in general, and of ones’ obligations. Feelings are very cheap. One can weep copiously before God in prayer, and get up and be no hair breadth betten than one was before. The כמר the pagan priest reckons on exciting feelings. But the כהן is to be כן to himself, and מכין to others, give them a firm clear basis on which to stand, a direction where to go. In heathenism feelings are worked on, thereby to enchain the intelligence. But feelings are a clock without hands, a “movement” which in itself knows not whence or whither, which one can use in any way one likes. Hell is made hot or the mind fanatic, it celebrates its triumph if נכמֹרו מעים, when the inwards of the believer are excited to a point of fermenation. גמר is also related, having the meaning of thoughts so matured that they can now be translated to words and deeds, גמר אומר and similar expressions. That which כמר is for feelings, גמֹר is for thoughts, גמר חסיד, he feels himself restrained, has nothing more to do here, must either go into a lunatic asylum or die. ויבקש לבכות he felt he had to weep. (פגש, to find something, בקש to seek for something, both conceptions lie in בוא — .(מצא has the basic meaning of going in somewhere.

V. 31. אפק ,ויתאפק, to hold firmly, used for the well or pit used to contain the gushing water of a spring. A picturesque description of restraining one’s feelings. When he went out his feelings overcame him afresh and a fresh effort was necessary.

V. 32. Joseph himself also did not eat with the Egyptians. So that even as prince he did not disown his Jewish origin. עברים was only the characteristic description of the descendants of Abraham. It is, accordingly, very significant that already at that time when they hardly consisted of seventy persons they were so characteristically prominent that they had a special national name, and Joseph, already earlier, could call the land of Canaan תועבה — .ארץ העברים. The root תעב is really very striking. It is apparently related to תאב and both have grown from דאב to have pain. Both have the meaning of a deep feeling of pain. תעב by the presence, תאב by the absence of the object concerned. Then, inasmuch as תעב to abhor, abominate only occurs in the Piel, and תאב, to languish, pine for, in the Kal (it does once occur in the Piel, מְתָאֵב אנכי את גאון יעקב (Amos 6,8) and then there too it means abhor), the whole matter can be explained by the changing effect of the meaning of the Piel, as גָאל and גָאֵל, but there געל in the Kal is also the opposite of גאל.
V. 33. תמה .ויתמהו, an idea about which we are not clear, to be astonished.

V. 34. חמש ידוח. In this Egyptian story we are struck with the number five occurring where in Jewish circles we expect seven, here, at the presentation of his brothers to Pharaoh, and at the imposition of the tax. This could possibly lie deep in the difference of the general point of view. Five is probably derived from ten, and ten, from a human point of view, is a whole. In the heathen point of view, the world, from its origin, is complete, a whole. According to the Jewish point of view it is not yet finished, it is only seven, on the way to ten. God goes on with its creation, if not in a physical sense, at least in a social one. The harp singing and proclaiming the “Welt anschauung”, our sages teach, had at first only seven strings, David brought the harmony up to eight, but only at the time of משיחּ (the Messiah I.L.) will it be fully strung with ten strings. — וישתו וישכרו עמו, “with him” they became intoxicated, surely they did not drink immoderately, they drank just ordinarily (וישתו) but were not used even to the small quantity. Even if they had not reproached themselves all the time still they were always grieved at what they had thought was their duty to do and probably, all the time that Joseph was away they had refrained from drinking wine. That possibly it was Joseph’s intention to make them a little intoxicated is also quite probable, otherwise they would hardly have allowed the money to be slipped into their sacks a second time.

V. 1.—2. גביע, goblet. גבע a hillock. Related to גבא, a collection of liquid, a pool. גבא to get money in, to collect. And similarly to a collection in the depth, a collection of solid matter in the heights: a hillock. גביע seems not to be a cup out of which one drinks but a larger vessel in which the wine is mixed. With Pharaoh too we do not find גביע but כוס in the hands of the butler. גביע would be something more like our word flask. In a stronger form it is קבעת and so we can understand the combination את קבעת כוס חמתי (Is. 51,22) Joseph’s steward must have been a good honest man. Above, where it was a friendly act that he was to do, he was ready to do it at once so that it says simply: (V,17) ויעש האיש כאשר אמר יוסף. But here where he was given the order to play a very dirty trick on an innocent man, he seems to have become startled, he probably thought that Joseph was really not in earnest, it required Joseph’s strict command before he did it, for here it says ויעש כדבר יוסף אשר דבר.

V. 5. He is not to mention the object concerned, is to take it for granted that as soon as they see that they have been pursued they must know quite well what it is about. נחש .אשר נחש ינחש בו related to נחץ to go after something with all precipitate haste, נחש, with ש to go for the goal without having to overcome the ordinary intermediate steps, to try to achieve your purpose directly without having to overcome the natural intermediate obstacles, either (a) to bring about something leaving out the ordinary links or (b) to recognise something without the natural intermediate links of cause and effect, for instance to get to know the unknown, the future by means other than by conclusion from natural premises, both are ניחוש. Perhaps that is why a snake is called נחש, it glides away from that which lies in the middle, or it goes about by an indirect course. Here, either, “he uses it for hidden magic arts”, “and so you ought to have been afraid”, but then as they had it now in their possession, there would be no reason for them to have been afraid on that account, so probably either, “my lord will use magic powers to find out the whereabouts of the goblet and who had stolen it”, or, and this seems the most probable: “the goblet has a special value to him, it is irreplaceable, for he is superstitious about it, has a ניחוש about it, that, apart from its actual loss, he will be unlucky without it.

In accordance with that we can understand Joseph saying later to them Did you not know, then, that a man like me is superstitious, has ניחוש. Not, of course, that all superstitious people can find a nice example in Joseph, but Joseph was addressing them in his role as an Egyptian lord, an Egyptian magnate, not as a son of the House of Abraham. The higher, the greater a man has become, the more marvellous his fortune has been, the more superstitious he becomes, the more he believes in ניחוש — one has only to think of Napoleon — he is surprised at his good luck. The ordinary man does, after all, have quite a lot to thank his fate for, but when we reach the stage of believing that we have not to thank our צדקות, our moral worth, for our good fortune, then we easily ascribe it to mysterious supernatural forces (my speculation turned out to be lucky because a black cat crossed my path as I left home I.L.) and it is because of the demoralising effect of ניחוש that it is forbidden. For as soon as we believe that we can do something to effect our fate other than by being good, have to be afraid of something else than of doing wrong, we are at once in danger of becoming bad, omitting being good on account of ניחוש, or doing bad trusting to ניחוש. Then we no longer weigh our actions on the scales of the Torah, cease to do that which we ought to do, because we believe we can do something else to obtain our objects.
V. 7. חלילה. We would consider it the death (חלל I.L.) of the whole of our spiritual and moral character, had we done such a thing.

V. 10. All what you have said is perfectly correct. You are quite right. It is quite impossible that a person who, of his own free will, without being asked for it, brings money back, should be a rogue. But there is one here who has not given that proof of his honesty. He knew, of course, that the goblet was in Benjamin’s pack.
V. 14. Now Judah comes to the fore, for now it was up to him to live up to his guarantee.

V. 16. He uses every form, אמר: what can we say to touch your heart and be accepted by you; דבר on what can we insist; נצטדק: or justify ourselves. One thing we can say: herein we are innocent, but at another place we must have made ourselves guilty and that sin God visits upon us now. For Joseph had placed them under suspicion and had appointed Benjamin to come as a proof of their integrity, and now the poof of their integrity himself is shown to be a thief. Hence they must have thought that they all fell again under the old suspicion of being spies and so were all doomed to slavery. It was only after Joseph had proclaimed otherwise and said that only Benjamin was to be considered punishable that Judah dared to make the proposition that follows.

V. 18. באזני אדני, a nice expression if one wants to give someone something to consider very deeply. I will not appeal to your feelings, but will direct myself to your mind and intelligence. — חרה .ואל יחר אפך probably does not mean to become glowing that is חרר. It seems rather to be related to ארה .הרה ,ערה ,ארה to take something up to oneself, hence plucking off and ארון, a container, which takes something in which is to be used. ערה, the condition in which one “takes in” every impression, nakedness. הרה, “taking in” a seed. חרה, the excited condition in which the least touch or external influence make an impression, nakedness still more naked, that something so excites a person that one may not even mention it. “May that which I want to say not excite your sensitiveness, for, see, you are as Pharaoh. I honour you as a Pharaoh, so if anything that I say does not please you, do not think that I do it from lack of honour, what I say to you I would also say to Pharaoh.
V. 21 et. seq. All this talk probably went on during the three days of their imprisonment (Ch. 42,17).
V. 31. As soon as he sees that the lad is not there, he will die on the spot, we shall not have even time to explain the matter to him and try to make him see it in a less serious light.
V. 1. Up till now he had been able to control his feelings in front of the large mass of people who stood about him in the sale room. He could stand it no longer.

V. 2. ויתן את קלו, gave it free rein, kept it back no longer. “Egypt heard it, the royal household heard it”. This, in itself, is a sign of his high position, the whole land, the whole court, participate in an event of which nothing further was yet known than that Joseph had broken out into loud weeping. Altogether in the whole story, tears appear to flow freely. Tears also need not be genuine but such an uncontrolled sobbing נתן קול is a proof of deep feeling, a proof of sincerity.
V. 3. העוד אבי חי, is my father really still alive.

V. 5. אל תעצבו. Do not let thoughts of the way and means through which I was brought here disturb the joy over the fact that I am here, which, after all, is great good fortune. For עצב is the feeling of enforced having to give things up, of renouncing. You can quietly give yourselves up to the happy feelings of good fortune. אל יחר בעיניכם elsewhere חרה is always construed with ל-, only occurs in this combination — חרה a condition of feelings, and עינים, judgment by intelligence — here and above Ch. 31,35, and in both cases expresses, negatively, that what is חרה to the feelings is to appear in a different light by the insight of the intelligence בעינים. I can not prevent your feelings of regret and sorrow for wrong is wrong, and your feelings are justified. But your minds should temper even this consciousness by teaching you “to look at the deed with other eyes”, as I have long ago come to look at it. It is also possible that the כי does not mean “that” but “for”: — “for it is hither that you have sold me”. After all you are the indirect cause of the great fortunate position in which I now find myself here.

V. 7. להחיות לכם לפלטה גדלה is a difficult sentence. The object of החיה is never expressed with a ל. Perhaps it means “to preserve the land” for you to your great salvation. You were the purpose of this great Divine contrivance. Perhaps?
V. 8. לאב, the fundamental meaning of אב, (root אבה, to want, to be willing), is the one who has the veto, without his agreement, somebody else may do nothing, accordingly here, counsellor.

V. 11. כלכל ,אכלכל, the doubled כלל, to contain, include, envelop. Related to גלל, to roll, to turn something about its centre point, hence, ball, cranium, wheel. From that כלל, to form the periphery around a centre point i.e. to allow an object to include the whole measure of its innate powers in all directions. Hence also כל the whole conception, all. Hence כלכל to embrace everything, to cope with something completely, in accordance with all it contains. מי יכלכל יום באו “Who can completely take in all that the day of his coming means”, or, “grant him his whole periphery” i.e. fix the whole extent of the effect of his coming. But also, as here, to take on oneself the whole extent of somebody’s affairs, or to grant somebody the surrounding of all that belongs to him i.e. provide for him.

Joseph repeatedly points out to his brothers, how this whole chain of events clearly stands out as Divine Management, and in fact, hardly any other story presents to our eyes to a similar extent the ways of Divine Providence. It is the most living commentary on that wonderful pronouncement of “Solomon’s wisdom: רב מחולל כל ושוכר כסיל ושוכר עוברים (Prov. 26,9) “The great Master of the World achieves everything from the smallest beginnings, as physical so also social, He lets everything come from the smallest seedling. He it is Who brings everything to service”. Without knowing it and without wishing it, folly and sin also are used to serve His ends”. In this particular story the threads are visible and lie to hand, in others they are not apparent, but from this one we can learn the ways of God.

“By the two oz. of silk” — as our sages put it — that Jacob spent on the embroidery of Joseph’s coat, the ברית בין הבתרים (Gen. 15,9 — 21 I.L.) came to be fulfilled. In Canaan the family of Jacob could hardly have developed into a nation. As they grew in numbers they would have been scattered amongst the inhabitants. To become a nation without intermingling, they had to come in the midst of a nation, who in principle as a nation were opposed to the whole nature of the Jews, and that was Egypt (who were calculatingly brought up to hate pastoral nations I.L.). In the same way the fanatic bigotry which built the ghettos was the most active means in God’s Hands to keep us afar from the lack of culture of the Middle Ages, and in confined circles to nurse the sense of family life and family happiness and the sense of communal life in us. To ensure us a separate province in Egypt as the soil for our development, a youthful scion of the family had to proceed and become “father” to Pharaoh and ruler of the land. And so that no Egyptian could reproach the Hebrew with “you have no business to be here, you were not born in these parts”, all Egyptians had to leave the soil on which their cradles had stood and themselves become strangers on the land they tilled.

In a similar way the remarkable stream of migratory nations — which, in any case was so pregnant of important consequences — had already peopled almost the whole of Europe with strangers when the tribes of Jacob began their great wandering in the dispersion amongst the European people. So that to the expulsions of Germanic intolerance “make the Jews go back to Palestine where they belong”, history can riposte with the inexorable question: — “did then the cradle of your ancestors stand here”.

And finally, the first as well as the last Galut arose out of קנאה and שנאת חנם (jealousy and causeless hatred I.L.) which was the reason for the fate of the harsh melting-pot which they all had to endure, and become purified in the school of the bitterest suffering to feelings of equality and brotherhood.

V. 16. That the servants of Pharaoh were pleased with Joseph’s joy and the news that now, by having his family with him again he would remain permanently in the country is a proof of the high reputation for morality and honesty that Joseph had attained, so that even in the circles of state service no jealousy had arisen.

V. 17. טען to lade with something. מטעני חרב (Is. XIV. 19) empaled on a sword. From which we get the term in rabbinic Hebrew טענה, charge, the assertion of the complainant. A stronger form is טחן, to be crushed by a burden, to grind.

בעור .בעירכם from בער which has the meanings, of burning, animal and folly. We have hardly as many names for wisdom as we have for folly, perhaps because folly is more multifarious and promiscuous, בער סכל ואויל ,כסיל. Of the various meanings of בער, burning is in any case, the original.

In what connection is an animal called בעיר? It is called חיה, inasmuch as it represents animal life as opposed to vegetable, בהמה as the kind of animal subordinating itself to mankind as a במה (root בהם :בום) as a “pedestal base” for man’s superiority, בעיר after its instinctive character. We have considered the concept חטא in its relation to חתה and accordingly believed חטא to be an unintentional careless falling out of the “fire of godliness”, as well as כפרה as being a restoration to the אשדת as לחם אשה ה׳ (fuel for keeping the fires of godliness burning on earth I.L.) (see on Ch. XXXIX. 9) If this is no dream, then the godly forces in man to which he is to devote himself of his own free will, and therefore must also be able to withdraw from, would present themselves as a “fire”. But there are also living creatures who can not withdraw themselves from Divine Will, in whom every impulse and every action is an involuntary product of the Divine Fire of Life which had given them life, whose whole lives are accordingly a “burning”, As long as this force of fire lives in them, they can not withdraw themselves from it, and בעיר would accordingly be the most pregnant description of an animal from its unfree instinctive nature. Thus in Ex. XXII. 4, every damage done to property by an animal just following its instinct, שן ורגל, regarding which it is מועד מתחלתו (must be expected naturally to do I.L.) so that its owner bears full responsibility for not taking the necessary care to prevent it, is designated characteristically by the term בער and the animal as בעיר.

Among the varigated characters of folly, פתי (from פתה to stand open) designates the guileless, simple inexperienced person who is open to every influence and illusion and deceit; אול) אויל from which we get אולי, related to אפל ,אבל, darkening of the physical or mental light) the one who has no fixed views at all, everything is unclear to him and he always wavers here and there in doubt; כסיל, related to גזל, who firmly fixes his mind on some unjustified point of view and insists on it. He is the fool who plants his feet firmly down and insists on his own opinion from which no teaching or argument can make him budge.

Peculiarly סכל clearly related to שכל is apparently the very opposite, both have the underlying concept of סגל, the closest appropriation. שכל is that mental power by which a person appropriates the world in his mind, who changes notions and retains them. It looks at the objective world and takes it in subjectively in its own way. The סכל has this subjective power, but it stays there, he forms his own subjective ideas and judgements without rectifying them with the reality. — Finally בער is that person who really has no talents, who lives an instinctive life and whose life is hardly above that of an animal.

V. 18. חֵלֶב related to חָלָב .חָלָב that which the organism has separated out of itself for reproduction of another being; חֵלֶב what it separates out of itself of temporarily surplus material for its own future reproduction. Accordingly it is not the fat organically grown in other tissues, but which, as תותב קרום ונקלף, is separated out as reserve capital, as the stock in hand of the animal for future necessity. Hence also used as the metaphorical expression for the best, the most valuable, as here.

V. 19. צות, a very fine touch on the part of the Egyptian ruler. For Joseph really had the power to command, but the greater a righteous man is, the more care he takes to avoid anything that might be taken as a misuse of his power.
V. 20. אל תחס. The Cholem points primarily to a root חסס, related to חשש in rabbinic Hebrew, to have consideration for something, to have scruples about something.
V. 24. רגז .אל תרגזו בדרך is overwhelmingly not an inner feeling of anger but of fear. Hence probably: Have a good journey and have no worry about the future.

V. 26. ויפג לבו. From the analogy of מאין הפוגות (Lament 3,49) “ceasing”, ויפג לבו is usually taken to mean “his heart stood still”, ceased beating, he fainted, naturally from joy, and confirmation of this way of taking it was found in the following ותחי רוח יעקב, which was explained to mean “he came to again”. In itself it would be quite natural for an old man to be overcome by such joy……if only it did not say: כי לא האמין להם. If he did not believe them, he could hardly have fainted from joy. So פוג must be taken to have a different meaning. פוג means, a movement which comes to rest, leaves off, ceases. ויפג לבו seems accordingly to mean “his mind was startled, taken aback”, his heart stood still in doubt, for he did not believe them, he could not so quickly get used to the wonderful news they brought him.

V. 27. But when they told him all in detail, how Joseph had behaved etc., and he also saw the royal wagons, then the spirit of their father Jacob revived, then he rose out of the twenty years state of sorrow and grief, then שרתה עליו שכינה (he felt the Spirit of God upon him again), and therefore at once

V. 28. He is again called ישראל, whereas up till now—with one single exception when he pulled himself together to make a decision and mastered his doubts—he was always referred to as יעקב. Thus, above in Ch. 35,20, when he was in pain and grief over the death of Rachel it says ויצב יעקב וגו׳, and then, after he had plucked up his heart and resumed courage, it at once, in V.22 says רב — ויסע ישראל “it is too much”! The glory, the exalted position in which he is to find his Joseph again is something given over and above what could be expected. It is quite enough that he is still alive at all.

V. 1. Then Israel journeyed forth with all that he had, in the happiest frame of mind in the radiance and at the zenith of his whole life, his life which had been tried in so many ways with bitter troubles and struggles.

They journeyed southwards and came to the last city on the border, Beer-Sheba, glorified by the memory of his fathers. There he offered up sacrifices, זבחים. We do not find again that our ancestors offered זבחים. They, like all Noachides only offered עולה .עולות expresses giving oneself up completely to God. זבח in itself is a family meal to be eaten by the בעלים, the owners, and consecrates the “family-house” and the family table to a temple and altar. For זבחים which as a rule are שלמים express the higher thought that “God comes to us”. They are, accordingly, brought from that happy consciousness that where a family circle lives united and faithful to duty, and feels that God is caring for it, אלקים בדור צדיק there God is present. That is why שלמים, “peace-offerings” of family life blessed by God, are so specifically Jewish. The idea of being absorbed in God, devoted to God dawns in non-Jewish feelings also. But that one’s ordinary day-by-day life can be so penetrated by the idea of God that one “eats and drinks and sees God thereat”, that all our ordinary living rooms become a temple, our dining-table an altar, our sons and daughters priests and priestesses, that through and through spiritualising of our ordinary private lives, that is a gift of Judaism. The reason that Jacob-Israel brought, not עולות but זבחים lay in the fact that now for the first time Jacob felt himself happy and joyful and “complete” (שלם I.L.) in his family circle. It was in this consciousness and feelings that he brought a “family-offering”, and it was in this feeling that he brought his offering with deep significance, not to אלקים in general, but, לאלקי אביו יצחק. In the song at the Red Sea Israel says: זה אלי ואנוהו אלקי אבי וארוממנהו: “In this salvation of me God hath shown Himself to me as the Almight that bears me (אלי I.L.) so that I accept Him and become a suitable home for Him, but this is the same God that my fathers taught me, Whom my fathers also served, and Who only wishes to achieve a still higher acknowledgment through me”. Is is the teaching and זכות (merit I.L.) of the Patriarchs that I have to thank for this salvation. Similarly here also: this blessed state of bliss which Jacob has just received he does not ascribe to his own merit but to the זכות אבות. Possibly it is also a glance back to the עקדה. Jacob’s life up till now had really been little else but an עקדה being realised concretely in actual every-day life. Now he feels he is approaching the moment when he is arising up from it.

V. 2. God says: “Fear not to go down to Egypt”. But Jacob was in the most joyful mood. So that something must have occurred which sent him into an anxious worrying mood, so that he needed reassurance. And verse two tells us exactly what this was. Firstly, the way the vision is described: מראות הלילה; a “vision of the night” already expresses the serious impression of the whole. Then the call: יעקב יעקב! not ישראל completely disappointed Jacob and made him think of the subsequent gravity of the meaning of this descent into Egypt. Hence then also Jacob’s response: הנני! “I am ready for anything that Thou decideth”. To which God replies: “thou needst have no fear, I am the God to Whom Thou didst just dedicate the happy family-offering and the ultimate object of this move is also happy greatness. There thou art to grow into the promised great nation. I, Myself will accompany thee (thy whole family circle) down there, and will lead thee (when thou wilt have become a nation) up again from there, and, as far as thou thyself are personally concerned, thou wilt not again be separated from Joseph” (cf. Ch. XV.1).

V. 5. When he started out in an undisturbed happy mood it does not say (v. 1.) ויקם, but now he needed an effort to pull himself together and get up to go on, hence ויקם. The change of names here is significant. The family were in the most joyful mood, they had no idea of the sad future that beckoned in the future which they were on their way to meet. But the father was filled with the seriousness of the expected Galut which had been indicated to him. That is why it says: the sons of “Israel” led their father “Jacob”.

V. 6. & 7. They were all with him, and at one with him, they were all his children. He did not have the grief which his fathers had to endure of one son being estranged, but they were all his sons and grandchildren and although they had already formed many families, they all grouped themselves about their Father Jacob; they hung on him, they went with him, he brought them all with him down to Egypt.

V. 8 et seq. Just as the Jewish nation is built up altogether on chaste pure family life, just as later the census was always reckoned after the paternal roofs and families, in the same way at the moment of their entry into Egypt they are all again mentioned in accordance with their genealogy — יעקב ובניו, they were united, so much so that Jacob himself is counted with them.

V. 10. ושאול בן הכנענית. If Dinah, whom Simeon married is to be understood by כנענית, then שאול may not have been a son of Simeon, but have been begotten by Schechem and a son born by Dinah, and then even this son had not become estranged from the House of Jacob. She is called כנענית because her son was physically a בן כנעני. Then already here the principle is shown that the child of a Jewish girl and a non-Jewish father is reckoned as belonging to the family of the mother and not of the father: הולד הולך אחר האם.

V. 12. ער ואונן. Whenever these two are mentioned it is always stressed וימת וגו׳. Belonging to the godly family is not without its conditions, it is associated with purity and morality. It does not suffice simply to be born of Jewish parents. That is why it does not fail to mention Er and Onan here as well.

V. 18. In this register of births it is indicated that, if Zilpah and Bilhah became wives of Jacob, this occurred only at the instigation of their “mistresses”. It is also indicated at Rachel that she was really the one wife of his choice.

V. 20 ויולד ליוסף. In the land of Egypt, surrounded by a completely strange way of life, nevertheless “children were born to Joseph”. He did not just beget them, but also after they were born they were “his” and even his wife, the daughter of an Egyptian priest, bore them and brought them up for him.

V. 26. כל נפש. Esau’s household consisted of only six souls, and of them it says (Gen. XXXVI. 6.) כל נפשות ביתו, so is remarked in מ״ר; Jacob’s household consisted of seventy souls, and all together they are designated as just one כל הנפש לבית יעקב :נפש Outside Jewish circles each son often strikes out in his own way. But where the Jewish spirit is kept in truth and faithfulness, there, there may be seventy souls and in all of them just one spirit and the one same feeling reigns.

V. 28. להורות לפניו, so that Joseph could give him the directions, before he came, for them to go to Goshen. He did not want it to appear that he moved there with all his family on his own account, although he was the “father of the prince”, or rather, just because he was that. Jacob knew his world, and knew how everyone would judge him by themselves, and would very likely suspect him of despotical and arrogant caprice which they would allow themselves were they in his position.

V. 29. Joseph wept, Jacob did not weep. Joseph could still weep, Jacob was finished with weeping, he had wept enough in his life. Joseph was still weeping (עוד) even after Jacob had already spoken to him — in such small points the actual truth is mirrored. Since he had missed Joseph, Jacob had had a dull monotonous life, had not ceased from weeping, his whole life of feelings had been spent in grief over Joseph. In the meantime Joseph had lived a life full of changes, had had no time to give himself up so much to the pain of separation, he was kept fully occupied with each of his different posts. Now when he fell round his father’s neck again, he felt all the more what the separation had really meant to him, and lived once again through the past twenty years. Jacob had already become Israel, Joseph still wept.
V. 30. Now let me die! He felt himself at the zenith of possible happiness, felt he could never more be any happier. At this zenith of happiness he would like his life to end.

V. 31. “To the house of his father”, they all still formed a household. He said it to all of them for they all were to realise the contrast to the rest of the inhabitants in which they would find themselves, and which they were not to lose. — אגידה (I would like to tell I.L.) אומרה (I would like to say I.L.). In the paternal home he is not מושל, only expresses his desire and intention. “I would indeed, I think it the right thing to do” etc. — אעלה Goschen must have been situated lower than the capital. At a later date when a Pharaoh wanted to persuade his people to oppress the Jews, he expresses the fear ועלה מן הארץ (they will come up from the province I.L.), so this fact may be the explanation of this otherwise difficult term “come up”. Our forefathers were to settle in Goschen because that province lay beyond the whole central life of Egypt. “If this goes on” says this later Pharaoh, “and they continue to increase like this, at the first opportunity they will come up out of their province in which they are now shut in, and we shall not be able to save ourselves from the Jews”. But according to that, the ויעל of V.29 must refer to the position of Egypt relative to Canaan from were Jacob was coming.
