Perhaps even the title אפרתמים is derived from it. פרת would then be an adjectival Pual form, and בן פרת would be, a noble son, one standing by himself, by his noble character apart from his brothers, בן פרת עלי עין, and moreover, not only now as Prime Minister ennobled by his position, but already as he was distinguished by his character, before he went away, when he was still at the homely source. This source, at which, and from which Joseph drew his nobility was surely his mother Rachel, the memory of whom, as remarked above, specially filled Jacob’s mind in his last days. “It was from his mother that he won this nobility”. בנות, vocative, “daughters” or “women”! (like Leah’s saying: אשרוני בנות) “she too who became the source of Joseph stepped over the wall”, i.e. was no ordinary woman.

שור, wall, from שור to see, and indeed, to see that which others do not see, to visualise in your mind the distant future, hence also שיר, the visionary word, the inspired song, and especially used for “seeing” the invisible ruling of God in actual occurrences. Hence שור, wall, that which sees what it hides from the view of others, which encloses and shuts in, the homely circle. That this is no sophistical subtle play of words is proved by the other name for wall, חמא ,חומה in Chaldean means: to see.

The management of women is usually not visible, it generally does not pass beyond the boundaries of the home. כל כבודה בת מלך פנימה, אשתך וגו׳ בירכתי ביתך an exceptional woman, without wishing to do so, draws the attention of the world to herself, over the usual limited boundaries of her home.

V. 23.—24. וימררהו, similar to וימררו את חייהם (Ex. I.14) רבו, a difficult grammatical form. The form of the word does not allow it to be derived from רבה in the meaning of bow shooting, and even the meaning of archer by רבה קשת is in no way justified as קשת itself means bowman and רבה קשת would rather be a teacher or master of archery. If it comes from רבב to increase, it would be an imperative form which would be quite out of place here, and the idea of increasing does not fit in with the context. According to Rashi it would be the Pual form from רוב to quarrel, like רומו from רום and then it would mean, as quarelling is intransitive: they accustomed themselves to quarrelling. No just cause was given them for it, but they brought themselves into such hostility towards him by erroneous ideas about Joseph’s intentions and plans. שטם, related to סתם, to close up, hence means to nurse a secret resentment, a deep-lying hate, similar to נטר to bear a grudge. But the object of נטר and so also of שטם is not the wrong suffered, but the suffering person, מטרה ,לא תטור את בני עמיך (the target) from נטר is also the goal, the distant point at which one shoots one’s arrows. לא תטור את accordingly means, you shall not aim at your fellow man in secret, not carry him about secretly in your heart, so that when the opportunity arises you shoot him with the arrows of revenge. שטם is hatred hidden still deeper in your heart. בעלי חצים is usually taken as another expression for archers, and the brothers are so called because they caught him with their treacherous arrows. We would take it otherwise. To these arrows we immediately get a bow: ותשב באיתן קשתו, and this bow is in Joseph’s hand. Also we never find the word בעל in connection with a weapon — such as בעל חרב etc. — to describe the one armed with that weapon. But rather בעלי חצים were those who had the arrows for the bow that was in Joseph’s hand. Joseph had the bow and out of their hands he could have received the arrows, which, had he so wished, he could have shot at them. —

But איתן .ותשב באיתן קשתו that, which from ancient times has proved itself strong, on which the present time rests. אדן is related to it, the foot of a pillar, the bearer on which something rests. From that, also אתון, the jenny-ass, the animal which was primarily used for riding, to sit on, whereas חמור, from חומד burden, served more as beast of burden. Hence: “but his bow remained in its old state of rest”, immoveable, he did not take his bow from his shoulder to destroy them with the arrows they themselves had reached to him, when already

פזו .ויפזו זרועי ידיו, on the one hand מפזז ומכרכר (II. Sam. VI.16) an extraordinary show of strength and energy, on the other hand ,כלי פז עטרת פז very valuable gold; the connection between these two meanings is obscure.

זרוע יד: the arm of the hand (זרע ,זרה, to strew, throw) the organ by which the hand is set in vigorous motion, in which really the power by which the hand is set in vigorous motion, in which really the power of the hand lies, accordingly: not even when the arms of his hands were endowed already princely decorated by the Almighty dispensations of God etc.

Accordingly: they had treated him most bitterly, had talked themselves forcibly into enmity against him, had set him up as the target to be destroyed by their hatred, they, the owners of the arrows they thus laid ready to his hand — they had even sold him to slavery in Egypt, and that very act which they themselves had perpetuated had resulted in making him master of their fate and placed them completely in his power. But he did not take his bow down from where it rested on his shoulder to destroy his brothers with the arrows they themselves had provided, not even when, through the Hand of God, he had attained such royal power — that showed his nobility, the nobility of his mind and feelings, which, through his birth and mother’s influence, was innate in him, which had made him to פרת עלי עין, which, from birth had raised him so high.

The Almighty Power of God, which arranged Joseph’s fate so wonderfully, Jacob calls אביר יעקב וגו׳. He recognises in Joseph’s fate a repetition of his own. Just as he himself wandered away from his father’s home, in poverty and distress, and, by אביר יעקב achieved a wealthy, blessed, family life, so, to an even higher degree, did it happen to Joseph. “The same elevating Power that raised me from the poor shepherd boy to a wealthy head of a family, raised you from being a slave, to which your own brothers had sold you, to the position of princely power”. “It is the same God Who — from Bethel onwards — “shepherded” i.e. watched over and led forward the stone which Jacob erected on that night”. From then on He arranged it and showered His Blessing on the most unlikely, not on the great ones of the world, but on the lonely ones, showed His Greatness not on the persecutors but on the persecuted.

V. 25. Not ברכת רחם ושדים, as one would have expected from the natural sequence, but ברכת שדים ורחם, no child will be born unto you without the mother, already at the birth, being blessed with the means and strength to nourish it.

V. 26. ברכת אביך גברו וגו׳. The ordinary way of taking this to mean: the blessings of your father outdo (have prevailed above) the blessings of my parents has no foundation in the words, and grate against us as expressing monstrous conceit. But גבר על need not by any means have the meaning to exceed, outdo, or surpass, we find, for example, גבר עלינו חסדו (Ps. CXVII.2) Where גבר על חסדו designates the place on which God’s Love raises itself so high, shows itself so strong. Or again ויגברו המים על הארץ (Gen. VII.24). “The waters rose on the earth”, not above (certainly not more than I.L.) the earth. So here: “the blessings which your father has to give to you, have also only grown out of the blessings which my parents gave me”. They are the cause why I have blessing to give, and they are the base from which my blessing now arises and has strength. Be not indifferent to the blessings which departing parents give their children, the fact that now, in my hoary old age, I can give you blessings, that זכות has its roots in the purity of my parents, in the moment to which this old man once had to thank for his existence; not אבתי but הורי (my begetters).

גבעות עולם, not actual hills, but in the sense that we find in Habakuk II.6: גבעות עולם “when the hills of time sink down”, which means, of course, when those great ones sink down, who in the course of the ages raise themselves up bearers of the conditions of the time. תאות גבעות עולם is, accordingly, the final goal towards which all the great ones of the ages strive. And in fact, in these sons standing about his bed, Jacob did not have only the beginning of the development of his nation, but just thereby he had the beginning of the ultimate completion of the development of the whole of mankind about him — ולו יקהת עמים — accordingly: “until the very last goal, to which the whole development of mankind moves”.

נזיר אחיו, probably not “the crowned one of his brethren”. For נזיר elsewhere never means the crowned, socially ennobled-person, but always the morally ennobled one. For the fact that נזר does occasionally mean crown is only due to the fundamental concept of נזר which is, separated, apart, inasmuch as a crown is a sign of separation, is symbolic of the one who wears the crown being somebody apart from the rest of the people, just as זֵר, a hoop, from הִנָזֵר .זור, to keep oneself apart, far from everything which is not votive. נזיר, one who exercises self-control, to keep himself far from everything ignoble, a character which Joseph so brilliantly vindicated in his whole history.

Judah and Joseph are strikingly the two central points on which Jacob’s prophetic sight rested, and indeed right up to יקהת עמים, to תאות גבעות עולם, until the most distant future. And in fact we always find Joseph too at the side of Judah. בית יוסף and בית יהודה in the mouth of the prophets, comprise the whole nation. And even for that distant future, tradition tells of a descendant of the House of Joseph as precursor and companion to the one from the “House of Judah”, משיח בן יוסף and משיח בן דוד. The actual relationship is not clear because it is not revealed. But it certainly is not without reason if Jacob stresses here that the hopes and blessings of that distant future rest also on the crown of Joseph’s head as they do on Judah’s head.

V. 27. It would be rather sad if here, at his youngest son, with whom he concludes he could find nothing better to say than to picture him as a ravening wolf. But it does not say זאב טורף ,זאב ערב, but זאב יטרף so that זאב can very well be the object. But if here at the end, Jacob thinks of a wolf, it is indeed the last glance that he gives over his “flock”. For twenty long years of his life he had had to fear the real wolf for his real sheep — and now he sees his children, has blessed them, has recognised and described them in their differences and in the importance of each one of them in the whole course of time, and his last glance into the future had just rested on the end of time, on the victory over the last world-force, the מלכות רביעית; he sees the Galut and the power of the Galut against which his descendants will have to fight, and he proclaims: it will be the smallest of them, the youngest of them, who will be the one that will drive the “wolf” (the external Amalek) from the flock of Jacob. Already at early morning, at the beginning of the national history he will have administered a “serious wounding”, but in the eve of time, he will completely destroy him. For it is a tradition, מסורת אגדה, that the arch enemy, Amalek, will not be overcome by Judah, but by the weakest might of the son of Rachel. אם לא יסחבום צעירי הצאן (Jer. XLIX.20) “the youngest of the flock” will drag them along as prey. עד from עדד (related to חתת to break up) a piece torn off.

V. 28. All these are the tribes of Israel; they are twelve, no more, no less, that possibly you might reckon Joseph as two, or leave Reuben out; and they are all שבטי ישראל, all belong to the whole, are all fundamental “props”, pillars that God had dug deep in the lap of Time, on which the structure of the nation is to build itself; and this — it is not the blessing that Jacob gave his children, for it is partly only description of their characteristics — but it is what their father said (דבר להם) about them, how he described each one in their special characteristics when he blessed them. But, “with a blessing in accordance with their specialities” did he thereupon bless them. After he had proclaimed the speciality of each one of them, he blessed him accordingly, that in his speciality, and by and with that speciality he should find blessing i.e. happiness and satisfaction. Even those who here did receive a blessing together with their designation, and perhaps especially those, still required this special blessing, that the external blessed position that was to be theirs, should be a real blessing to them. For, against his will, and without his co-operation, God can make no man happy. And the reverse also holds true, the true Jew changes the bitterest experience into a source of the richest blessing, עוברי בעמק הבכא מעיז ישיתוהו. — “Not” runs a saying of our sages “because he apportioned the strength of lions to Judah, the boldness of wolves to Benjamin, the speed of deer to Naphtali, should you think that all were not included in the blessing, that is why it says, each one according to his blessing, he blessed them, not him אותו, but all of them אותם “each one participated in a general blessing, and the special blessing of each one was for the benefit of all.

V. 29. אני נאסף וגו׳, our sages explain this, as meaning: אם זכיתם ונטפלתם בי ,ואם לאו אני נאסף אל עמי if you bury me or do not bury me, and wherever you do bury me, does not affect me, my true self, in the least, אני, I will be raised away to my people, to the sphere to which I belong, my real self will by that time have long been taken up to that height to which no human help can accompany the departing soul. But for you, it will be a necessity and a merit to occupy yourselves with my casing which I leave behind, carry it then to the land and the place where my ancestors rest, and lay me next to them.
V. 30. The district in which Abraham had lived and worked so long, and then also acquired the burying-place for his wife.

V. 31.—32. Jacob repeats to his sons quite exactly the place and the legal title of possession. For 200 years had passed since then. We see, how, already in those very ancient times, matters were kept in order, and rights of possession were securely kept.

V. 1. “He threw himself on his father’s face”. Literally “he fell”, that expresses the deep emotional action where one more or less unconsciously “falls”. He fell on his father’s face and let his tears flow freely, and when he could weep no more, he gave him a parting kiss.

V. 2. חנט, it is obscure why embalming is called חנט. It might conceivably be related to ענד to wrap up, because mummies are wound round with bandages. But this seems unlikely for the wrapping is not the essential part of the procedure, חנט otherwise designates a certain stage in the development of fruit trees: חנטה פגיה (Song of Songs II.13). In the Talmud חניטה is the time when fruit has reached the stage when the duty of מעשר becomes incumbent so that אכילת קבע is prohibited until tithe has been taken. חניטה is identical with עונת המעשרות. In the Jerusalemic Talmud this is explained as being the time when the fruit is so ripe that it or its seed or pip, if sound, would grow, accordingly when the essential materials are collected together in it to the essential degree of formation, accordingly when it is already penetrated by the aromatic essences which give the fruit its characteristic taste. Now embalming is nothing else but filling out and penetrating the arteries and veins and soft tissues of the body which have been emptied out, with aromatic materials, so perhaps therein lies the connection between the two uses of the word חנט.

Embalming shows a marked contrast in the idea which it expresses to Jewish ideas. Such contrasts, when they occur, are to be specially stressed, opposing that tendency which, denying the Divine source of the Torah, likes to make out that the whole “genius of Moses” having been matured in the schools of the priestly teachings of the Egyptians. What a diametric contrast is shown here! To the Egyptian the body was embalmed so that its individuality should persist. But the soul did not remain in its personal individuality, but wandered from body to body — even to animal bodies — in manifold metamorphosis. To the Jew the soul persists, the body wanders, once the soul has gone home to the circle where it belongs, the body has nothing more to do with the individual. But rather, it is a מצוה, as soon as possible to bring it in as close contact as possible to the dissolving earth. It becomes earth again, and can then go through all the possible changes and vicissitudes of earthly matter. The Egyptian believes in the wandering of the soul, and tries to protect the body from all possible wandering or change. The Jew believes in an eternal personal existence of the soul, and hands the body over to material earthly change. Possibly it was therefore that just in Egypt, Jacob stressed so strongly, אני נאסף אל עמי ,קברו אותי וגו׳, as remarked above. Perhaps it was just the lack of belief in Egypt of the permanent individuality of the soul, as well as the embalming of corpses which resulted in the colossal building of pyramids designed for dwellings for the dead. As one believed the soul to be wandering, one wanted at least to keep the body. Embalming was accordingly not Jewish, and Joseph here may only have made a concession to the Egyptian customs as they would have considered an omission as showing a great lack of piety. Perhaps also the reason for Jacob making Joseph swear not to bury him in Egypt was, as our sages remark, to avoid the Egyptian making an ע״ז out of his body, for at bottom, the preserving of mummies in Egypt usually resulted in making it into a god and praying to it. The physicians embalmed “Israel”, in accordance with his status. In true Jewish burials, thank God, one can not see whether it is a rich man or a poor one, but one can well notice whether he was נפטר בשם טוב (left a good name behind him) or בחייו קרוי מת (he was as good as dead while he was alive).

V. 3. In Jewish circles, mourning only begins after סתימת הגולל, after the prescribed duties of tending the body have all been completed. But there, where the burial has really no importance at all, as it makes no difference in the case of embalmed bodies, whether they are kept in the ground or above it, the mourning can begin already before the burial. But it is to be noticed that Jacob was mourned for, also by the Egyptians.

V. 4. et seq. It is remarkable that Joseph, in his exalted position which allowed him to be so near to Pharaoh took such an indirect cause to get his request granted. It seems that Joseph was not so sure that it would be granted and therefore preferred this indirect way. A refusal given and received through a third party can more easily be ignored on both sides. The matter could well be connected with the existing general antipathy to foreigners which could have made it much disliked to know that a foreigner was at head of the state, and especially one from Canaan. By this taking his father to be buried in Canaan, Joseph’s origin would again come freshly to the minds of the people.

“אם נא מצאתי״ and “וידבר״ a combination which shows the perfect statesman in dealing with Pharaoh’s court officials. וידבר expresses the decision, the peremptoriness, of the tone, אם נא וגו׳ the courtesy, the politeness of the form, of the speech. The form of speech which a higher statesman uses is extremely polite, it is in the tone that one can recognise his consciousness of his position. Similarly, in Abraham’s request to the sons of Heth. Stiff, stately, in tone, polite in form. He know quite well that they would not refuse him, on the contrary, be only too pleased to do a favour to a man in his position.
V. 7. זקני בית פרעה are the highest officials at the court. זקני ארץ מצרים, the highest officials in the government.

V. 10. ספד .מספד could be related to זבד, an apportioned part, at Ruth II.14 צבט, measured out, apportioned, like: ,שבט ,שפת ,שפט ,שפד שות, underlying meaning, to give somebody that which is due, is fit and proper, to him, or to place something in its fiting place. According to this ספד, is giving somebody, now, after he has gone away from us, that place in our memory which is due to him. Before the הספד, nobody can say of any man, what position he will take in our memory, he can have altered considerably in his last years for the better or worse, and it is only in הספד that he receives the permanent register in mankind.
V. 11. Accordingly, a place on the border of Canaan immortalised, by its name, the recognition which a Jewish patriarch found in a foreign country.

V. 12. So far the Egyptians accompanied them, but they did not cross over into Canaan. For that reason, and probably also to avoid the land of the Philistines, they took this round-about route to the Jordan. From there, the children alone took the body and buried it in accordance with their father’s wishes. The whole of the accompanying retinue waited on the other side of the Jordan, at the border, until they came back from the funeral, and then accompanied them back again home.

V. 15. As long as children live about a father, a mother, for so long do they find in their parents a force which holds them together. Even amongst the best of children there can be small differences but as long as the parents are alive, all discord vanishes in the common love and attachment to them. After the death of the parents the bond holding the children together becomes loosened, they do not meet so frequently and become more estranged from one another when father and mother no longer form the centre point. Now here, in this case, it was no more than natural. The brothers “saw”, felt that the father was no longer there. — לו from לוה, a postulate, assuming that, let us suppose that such is the case.

V. 17. They showed great delicacy in what they had him told in their father’s name and what in their own. The father speaks of both פשע and חטאה in their behaviour towards him. פשע, related to פצע to attack, to wound the person, to improperly lay hold of a person; פשע specially used for laying hands on something entrusted to your case, despicable misuse of a more or lesser intimate relationship. But the father excusingly also lets them speak of a hastiness, חטאה, an act of rashness, which allows the presumption that possibly Joeph could also perhaps not have been entirely without blame. But in their own name they only speak of פשע of direct wrong-doing “we know of no excuse”. Further, they say “שא נא לפשע״, but in the father’s name, “שא נא פשע״. Jacob says “lift up, do away with the crime of your brethren”, think no more of it, let it be as if it had never existed.” But they say “do away with that which pertains to the crime”, its results, its influence, לפשע. We remain guilty, we forget nothing of it, but let it have no consequences with you, (Similarly it does not say ואהבת את רעך כמוך “Love thy neighbour as thyself” but לרעך. With the different kind of human personalities the former could hardly be demanded. Nobody could love all the people he knows equally, to the same extent. There can be people whom one just can not stand. But לרעך, that which pertains to thy neighbour, his health, his well-being, his happiness and success, that you are to love and further as if it were your own, however unsympathetic the person himself might be to you. You are to be pleased with his success as if it were your own, further his happiness as if it were yours, and be as sad at his misfortune as if it had happened to you). Further, they do not call themselves אחיך, as the father does, they have forefeited the right to that title, they treated him most unbrotherly, but they say, we are still עבדי אלקי אביך, we participate in, and have the same mission and calling, are fellows of the same covenant.
V. 19. God can judge, the thoughts, the intentions. I, as a human being, have only to think of the result, and in that it is rather that I owe you deep gratitude.

V. 21. אנכי אכלכל אתכם. This is not to be taken as meaning that Joseph took his brothers’ chief worry to be about the possibility of their material support being withdrawn or reduced. Such a supposition is already refuted by וינחם אותם וידבר על לבם. What this verse means is rather: “Once again, have no fear that our father’s death will make the slightest difference in my feelings towards you. The proof will be in your hands every day that I am and will remain exactly the same as before”. וינחם אותם, for נחם is consolation and regret, both a complete change of feelings to the way one had felt towards something hitherto. Up till now one had considered something to be right had perhaps boasted about it, and then suddenly finds out that one has to be ashamed of it: regret, remorse. Similarly, real consolation is only such, that brings the conviction to one who has suffered pain and grief, that this too leads to ultimate good and everlasting happiness, not the “Babylonian idea of consolation” which says “what can one do, one must accept what can not be avoided” (Baba Kama 38a), but which awakes the consciousness that if one were able to see through and over all the conditions and results and consequences as God can and does, one would not alter what has happened even if one could. Thus Joseph here tries to show his brethren just the opposite point of view of what happened in the past. “God used you as the instrument to bring about my own and so many other people’s good fortune” etc. And then וידבר על לבם, not merely אל לבם, but that his words prevailed over their feelings. נחמה is directed not so much to the heart as to the intelligence, and then וידבר על לבם (Cf. XXXIV.3).
V. 22. ישב, generally means, quiet, unstrained (the reverse of יצב) care-free living.
V. 23. From Ephraim he had great-grandchildren, from Manasseh, grand-children, Ephraim developed faster.

V. 24. אנכי מת, not with the self-confidence of his father; נאסף פקד יפקד — .אל עמי, these two little words became the ray of light that kept the hopes of coming dawn awake for his descendants through the dark centuries that lay ahead. פקד, as already remarked, related to בגד. in one’s mind to invest somebody with the befitting conditions. Hence to appoint somebody to an office, to place him in a position where he can develop his personality. His official position is his spiritual garment; hence also the garment can be the symbolic expression of his office, and a כהן מחוסר בגדים does not appear in the required appearance for עבודה. Used, referring to God’s relation to Man as פקד את שרה it means the same: He invested Sarah with the “cloak of fate” that was due to her. Gave her the destiny that was befitting to her. A childless woman lacks the “garment”, the sphere in which she can best develop her activities. Referring to a nation — as here — it has again the same idea: intervening in the course of events to arrange for it to get the fate that is due to it, be it good or bad. So that here the House of Jacob was told: As the time will come when it will be necessary for God to יפקוד אתכם, you must expect that in the meantime He will not do so. This gives us altogether the conception of the Jewish Galut, both of the earlier and later times. As God chose a powerless יעקב-people; its Galut is no special fate. Not Israel’s fall requires a special act, as special והלכתי עמכם בקרי) השגחה I will just leave you to chance). Israel’s preservation is a נם. Left to itself it declines, and only if it gives itself up to the eagle’s wings of the Divine Guidance is it raised on high. A בית יעקב set as גרים in the midst of an עם לועז, in the midst of a “strange-tongued” people, of a people whose whole spiritual outlook is so diametrically opposite to its own, as Egypt was, must expect Galut in its bitterest form as the natural outcome. So that by the יפקד ה׳ אתכם they were prepared for the trouble that then came, but also for the delivery from it which was promised.

V. 25. He did not make them swear as his brothers, but as “בני ישראל״, accordingly to include the coming generations. There was no presumption in making them undertake this duty, for it was they who had brought him down there, it was a little atonement they could make, he was entitled to lay this duty on them. At the same time this duty and these bones on which they were to perform it, were a pledge for the confidence with which they were to await the return to Canaan.

V. 26. ויישם is an obscure form. Above, with Laban (Ch. XXIV.33) it is קרי and כתיב and we took that to indicate Laban’s vacillating behaviour. Perhaps here it points to the unusual procedure in the House of Jacob — which he himself had ordered for the reasons given above — of keeping a body unburied in a sarcophagus. “He had himself placed in a coffin in Egypt, literally: he placed (himself) in a coffin. The בארון במצרים could be (the מצרים seems superfluous I.L.) in contrast to his father’s burial. His father had himself brought to Canaan immediately after his death. Joseph was satisfied to be kept in a coffin to be brought up to Canaan in the future.

ארון is a nice word for coffin. It only occurs elsewhere as the container for the tablets of the Law, and for collecting-boxes for holy purposes (II King XII.10). Both are containers not for anything to be buried, but for something to be received and kept on behalf of somebody, the donation to the Temple for the Temple, the Law for Israel. According to that ארון as a coffin is also a container in which the casing left behind by a human being is — temporarily — kept.
Exodus: V. 1. With this second book the history of the Jews as a Nation starts. We are led out of the history of the individuals and families into that of the Nation by a list of those men who are already known to us as the “main stem” of the Jewish People. ואלה, and it is out of these men, with their different individualities and characteristics that the Jewish Nation developed. But there was one basic trait which they all had in common, and this formed the foundation of Jewish nationality את יעקב איש וביתו “each one with his household came with Jacob.” Later on, when the national body, dismembered by Pharaoh’s mishandling, appeared to lie helpless on the ground as a welcome feast to the vultures of history (as it had appeared to the prophetic vision of the ancestor), and, at the call of God, was to arise “in its blood” to immortal life, God began the building up of His people on the rock-like foundation of “homes”, — שה לבית אבות שה לבית — on the bond of children to parents, and parents to children. And here we are told that this basic foundation of the immortal People of God — even if it had been forcibly and violently crushed and disturbed at the time of the redemption — was implanted in them when the Children of Israel originally moved down into the Egyptian womb, out of which, through suffering and woe, they were to be born as a Nation. את יעקב איש וביתו, although each one of them constituted an independent and separate home they all hung firmly and intimately on Jacob. את יעקב implies a much more intimate connection than עם יעקב. All together on the old stem and yet each one an independent and separate branch, a separate independent centre, for a circle of their own; all children of Jacob, and yet, on the other hand, themselves fathers for their own children. This spirit of the family, with which each son builds his home only as a branch of his father’s house, which allows every father and grandfather to go on living in children and grandchildren, so that parents with their children, and children with their parents are ever intimately united — this it is wherein lies the root of Israel’s eternal blossoming, wherein lies the secret of the everlasting stem of Jewry.

V. 2. The grouping is characteristic. The first four are the sons originally destined for Leah, after Judah it says: ותעמד מלדת (Gen. 29,35). Issachar and Zebulun were granted to her as awards for her special efforts. Benjamin is attached to her as Rachel’s son (she would naturally have acted as a mother to him when Rachel died at his birth. I.L.), and in the following group the sons of the שפחות are placed together. If we look at Jacob’s proclamation on the importance of his sons for the future of the nation, we find there, too, (Gen. XLIX), Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun and Benjamin described as being the most important (not reckoning Joseph who was already in Egypt).

V. 5. The חכמים remark that when speaking of Jacob’s house, the Torah uses the expression נפש although there were seventy souls, whereas of Esau’s house, although it consisted, at the time, of only six souls it speaks of נפשות (Gen. 36,6), for in all the members of Jacob’s house, one spirit, the uniform soul of the same principle, prevails.
V. 6. דור, verwandt mit דבר, תפר: aneinanderreihen; alle gleichzeitig Lebenden, Zeitgenossen.

V. 7. We are told nothing more about this generation beyond the fact that they had already increased enormously וישרצו they were as prolific as insects — the smaller the animal the greater the number at each birth. With human beings, twins, triplets, quadruplets, etc., are usually weaker, and frequently do not live, so that such births do not really bring about an increase in the population, or, at best, only of weaklings. Here, however, it is specifically added, וירבו ויעצמו; their “ישרצו״, their multiple births lived and were strong; וירבו the parents reproduced themselves physically and spiritually (see Gen. 1,28) in their children. ותמלא הארץ not Egypt, but the province of Goshen in which Joseph had settled them because it lay in a remote corner of the country, and both the mental outlook and the occupation of the Jews were repugnant to Egyptian ideas.

ותמלא הארץ, nicht Ägypten, sondern die Provinz Goschen, die ihnen Josef um so lieber angewiesen hatte, weil sie ein entlegener Landstrich war und die Iwrim ihrem Geiste und ihrer Beschäftigung nach den Ägyptern zuwider waren.

V. 8. The first causes of the oldest רשעות, anti-semitism, can unfortunately not be definitely established from these first sentences. ויקם מלך חדש על by no means designates an ordinary lawful change of dynasty. קום על is always an overthrow by force. So it seems that the old dynasty was overthrown and Egypt fell under the power of an invading dynasty from outside, hence also אשר לא ידע את יוסף, to a fresh native dynasty Joseph would not be unknown. It is quite characteristic that the motive given for the whole subsequent enmity against the Jews is that the new King did not know about Joseph. The people did know of him and did not look askance at the Jewish province and at the Jewish people growing in it. They considered the Jews as benefactors and not as intruders, and did not feel their own security threatened by their growth.
V. 9. הנה עם בני ישראל the Children of Israel have become a nation.

רב ועצום ממנו can not very well mean more numerous and stronger than we are. The Egyptians were certainly more powerful and more numerous than the Jews living in Goshen. So it must have been that the conquering dynasty brought numbers of their own people to live in the land. The Egyptians were already subjugated, and it was to his own people that the King spoke: “We need not fear the Egyptians, they are already under our power, but in this outlying province, a race is growing that may become too strong for us, whom we may not be able to conquer so easily”. But more likely this ממנו is to be taken as in Gen. 26,16 לך מעמנו כי עצמת ממנו מאד, which can only mean, “you are much too strong for us, we can not look on complacently, that you, a single individual, are so powerful, more powerful than any single individual amongst us.” Exactly the same here: Egypt was divided into castes, consisted of different unrelated “עמים״, so the King could well say: See, these Jews who still hang together as one נפש, they will become too powerful for us, there is no single caste which is as numerous, which has such an amount of potential power as they have.

Note in general: (a) this first anti-semitism was not brought about by anything bad that the Jews had done. Pharaoh could not bring any accusation against them, otherwise he would not have been driven to act against them covertly, בחכמה (v.10); (b) this first רשעות was engineered from above, did not spring from the people. They were incited from above, Jew-hatred was a political measure which the new dynasty used to strengthen their own position of force and violence. There is little new under the sun and historical events at large are as old as history itself. Whenever a tyrant wished to oppress a people, he liked to give them a lower class whom they could oppress, and thus be indemnified for his own oppression. Many of the Jew-Laws of the Middle Ages and later have to thank this policy for their origin. Similar considerations may have guided this first instigator of the first Jew-Laws. He wanted to compensate the Egyptian people whom he held in oppressive subjection by creating for their benefit a caste of pariahs on which every other caste could look down with contempt and in comparison could imagine himself a free man. But the fact that Pharaoh could not reproach the Jews with anything beyond their rate of multiplication, and to justify his intended harshness had to take his stand on supposed motives of high state policy, is a brilliant testimony to the high standard of the social behaviour of the Jews. It is true that we can learn from Ezekiel (XX,8) that the same can not be said of their spiritual behaviour, that they did not retain their faithfulness towards God, but assimilated Egyptian evil ways and became familiar with things that should find no favour in the mind-eye of a Jew (שקוצי עיניו ibid.) and which the heart of a Jew should reject as unworthy (גלולי מצרים ibid.). Although no direct mention is made of this here, still the complete absence of any record of any positive public expression of the Jewish belief such as we repeatedly found in the lives of the Patriarchs, קרא בשם ה׳ and ויבן שם מזבח which were not so much external propaganda as expressions of the preservation of Jewish belief and ideals in the midst of a country of very contrary ideas, does lead us to the conclusion that there was, in Egypt, a lowering of the Abrahamitic spirit. Had Pharaoh had the populace on his side from the beginning it would have been superfluous to have stirred up jealousy so artificially, or to have roused such far-fetched fears in their minds.

V. 10. The meaning of this verse is obscure. If the accent אתנח stood under ירבה instead of under ועלה מן הארץ ,לו could have been taken simply to be the purpose, and the verse would say: We will restrict them to such an extent that they will take the first opportunity that offers to move out of the land, inasmuch as by attaching themselves to our enemies they will get land and rights of citizenship with them. But the accent is against this, and makes the עלה מן הארץ not to be taken as the purpose to be achieved by the new tax regulations but as part of פן וגו׳, as part of what is to be prevented by these regulations. But then it is difficult to understand why the departure of the Jews should be an event so much to be feared. They were not yet slaves. We must accordingly assume that the Jews had already made themselves so useful and of such importance to the country, that although one wished that there were not so many of them, one feared the effect of their complete departure, and considered their presence in limited numbers both useful and necessary. Then it seems more probable that the עלה מן הארץ is to be understood, not as going away from Egypt, but as coming up out of their allocated province lying right in a corner of Egypt, and spreading all over the country. But in that case the reason for a time of war being necessary for that, is not at all clear. Perhaps after all, there are two separate apprehensions. If anybody feels enmity towards someone, he usually attributes a similar feeling in that person towards himself. Pharaoh might say: “The Jews are our enemies and likely to be treacherous towards us. If they become numerous, and war breaks out, they will be on the side of our enemies; and, in any case, if we let them become numerous, Goshen will no longer contain them, and we shall have them spreading over the whole land.” The bad conscience of the nations towards their Jewish inhabitants in later times has similarly suspected them of holding with the Moors, the Turks, the French, etc. Also תקראנה a plural form, is difficult to apply to the nominative of מלחמה which is in the singular. Here, מלחמה is probably not the subject, but the object, and תקראנה — happenings, as in Isaiah 41,22. (and the traslation would read: When events are War, i.e. when occurrences bring war……I.L.).

V. 11. “They set over them fiscal officers to afflict them by their burdens” (מס — tax. I.L.). The Jews in general were declared to be an object for revenue, out of whom the State should try and extort as much money as possible. They were to be regarded as “foreigners who do not belong here”, and, as such, must pay any price demanded for the air they breathe. סבלתם סבל: is not primarily a burden which is imposed with the object of oppressing anybody, but simply a burden which is loaded on to be borne and looked after. The expression itself would not express anything specially malicious. So that סבלות were burdens which were applied in the form of tax demanded for the requirements of the State. But we are told that the real reason was nevertheless למען ענותו, — these Jews must not become too presumptuous, we must think out what legal form we can devise as means of extortion and vexation.

סכן .ערי מסכנות see Gen. 19,4, מסכנות: contrivances to provide for exigencies which may arise, storage-towns. Perhaps these were towns for storing the produce tax introduced by Joseph for the benefit of the State, by which possible “years of need”, “hunger-years” (מסכנות) were to be carefully provided for. If that were so, making the Jews build them would be a double-barrelled act of derision. For the building of a city a great variety of handicrafts are required, so that all of them would be employed. The cities they built were state buildings “for Pharaoh”.

V. 12. This labour-tax, imposed in the form of an “emergency-law”, did not achieve its object. The more they tried to weaken the Jews and limit their growth, the more numerous they became, and the more they spread, so that ויקצו literally “they were sick”, not of the Jews but they were sick of everything, because of the presence of the Jews. “If they went to the theatre it was full of Jews, if they went to the circus, again all Jews” (Yalkut). The cantillation on ויקצו is a זקף גדול (a separating one, a kind of comma, I.L.).

V. 13. Herewith the maltreatment of the Jews entered a second phase. Until now, as “foreigners”, burdens had been imposed upon them, which, outwardly at least, had the form of legally controlled measures. Now they were declared slaves, גרות was followed by פרך .בפרך — עבדות only occurs elsewhere in תנ״ך in פרכת the dividing curtain in the Temple in front of the Holy of Holies, and has the idea of dividing, shutting off. By declaring them slaves, they divided them off from the rest of the people, as being creatures without any rights whatsoever, they shut them right off from all the rest of the population who could claim legal rights. Slaves are declared to be a different order of beings to ordinary human beings. Ruthless harshness, ענוי, then follows automatically. We find פרך used in the Talmud meaning crushing, crumbling, נפרך בצפרן, and according to that it would read: “The Egyptians made the Children of Israel into slaves with the full weight of crushing harshness”.

V. 14. The first מסים they had to do or pay, as citizens. They still retained their rights, but had to pay for their right to protection by special levy of labour-tax. But no private Egyptian could order them about. After that, they were degraded to slaves, creatures without any right of appeal or redress for any wrongs committed against them. It no longer says, ויעביד פרעה but ויעבידו מצרים, the people received the right to treat them as slaves. Then a third degree was added וימררו וגו׳. One can even be a slave, have to work hard, but not have annoying spiteful treatment, refined, thought-out spite, to embitter every spark of life.

So were realised all the three phases גרות ,עבדות ,ענוי, which had been foretold to Abraham, and which were later retained in the carefully chosen לשונות של גאולה, the description of the Salvation, as well as in the laws of Chometz representing the conditions of slavery in Egypt, ,איסור אכילה הנאה ובל יראה וגו׳.

The root and beginning of this indescribable maltreatment was גרות, the supposed lack of rights of a foreigner, as such. That is why the laws of the Torah concerning the rights of foreigners offer the profoundest contrast to all other national laws up to this very day. Twenty-four times, whenever, and in every case, where the Torah lays down the law concerning rights of persons and things, the “stranger in the land” is placed under the special protection of the Law. The degree of justice in a land is measured, not so much by the rights accorded to the native-born inhabitants, to the rich, or people who have, at any rate, representatives or connections who look after their interests, but by what justice is meted out to the completely unprotected “stranger”. The absolute equality in the eyes of the Law between the native and the foreigner forms the very basic foundation of Jewish jurisdiction. In Jewish Law it is not nationality which gives man his rights but the rights of man give nationality! and the Torah knows no distinction between the rights of man and the rights of citizen. Everyone who acknowledged the moral laws of humanity — the שבע מצות ב״נ — could claim the right of domicile in Judea. This principle, this respect for human beings as such, apart from all chance of birth and fate, is proclaimed everywhere in the Torah by remembrance of what was experienced in Egypt. In Egypt, the cleverly calculated lowering of the rights of the Jews on the score of their being aliens came first, the harshness and cruelty followed by itself, as it always does and will, when the basic idea of Right has first been given a wrong conception.
V. 15—16. The King now tried to accomplish that which his indirect methods had failed to do, by shorter, more direct, but still secret ways.

אבנים. This is generally taken to refer to the stool on which women were placed when they were bearing children. But this word is never used elsewhere with this meaning. The usual expression for this is אבנים .משבר only occurs in the תנ״ך in one other place (Jer. 18,4) and there it very definitely means a potter’s wheel. In any case it is difficult to think it refers to a stool or table on which the delivery takes place. For once it is delivered one can usually already know whether the baby has been born alive or not. But from the whole story it seems evident that the King wanted to have the killing done secretly, so that not even the mother should know of it. Our חכמים, in Midrash Rabba, also do not think that this refers to the “bearing-stool” but rather to a part of the body of the mother. One of the explanations given there is מקום שהולד נפנה בו the place in which the child turns, clearly the womb, in which the child makes the movements towards birth. We get the same way of taking it from Sota 11b. אר״ח סימן גדול מסר להן בן פניו למטה וכוי cf. Nidda 31a. זו הופכת פנים וזה אינו הופך פניו from which it appears that Pharaoh told the midwives to note the movements the child is making, which differ just before actual birth in boy babies and girls, and if it is a boy to act quickly before the baby is born. This may be a hint to us that אבנים is not to be taken as a literal expression. For the potter is called יוצר, he forms things which take shape under his hand. In Jer. 18,4, it is quite clear that אבנים in the potter’s workshop is the place on which a mass receives a form. Probably it is a revolving disc which is there thought of, and so we think that what it says here is: “Keep an eye on the labouring womb”. Ascertain, as early as possible, whether it is a boy or a girl, and if the former, before birth actually takes place, grab it quickly and kill it. In any case, the root is אבן and the form ﭏבֶן hence אָבנים. Possibly the potter’s disc consisted of two stones. It is possible also that the word comes from the root בנה (with the prefix א, as אפן comes from פנה) which does not only mean to build, but also to form, to shape: תבנית.

V. 17. ותחיין. Not only did they not do what the King had ordered them to do, but they did everything possible to keep the babies alive. Everything that the King tried, turned out the very contrary of what he had wished. His demand to the midwives made them extra zealous in the opposite direction, so that no breath of suspicion should be attached to them, that, obeying the King’s orders, they had done something, or omitted to do something, by which the child’s life could be endangered. Henceforth they must do everything possible, work with all their art, go down on their knees and pray to God, that now no still-born child should be born, no child come into the world with any hurt.

V. 19. כי חיות הנה. There is more life in them, from נח ,חיי instead of דגש. As already remarked (Jeshurun VIII. P.436) חיי differentiated from חיה, designates the special physical activity of life, which as a matter of course, absorbs everything which is compatible, and rejects everything incompatible. Every tiny speck that feeds and supports itself is חי. “Our women are not like the Egyptians, they are full of vitality, they need nobody else. Just as animals are provided with the power of life, to accomplish the act of giving birth without assistance, so are our women”.
V. 20. וייטב ה׳ למילדות He allowed it to be well with them (see note on V.17).

V. 21. להם the people. When the King saw that with all his laws the people only became more numerous and stronger and founded more and more families, he became furious at last, and openly gave the cruel order for the extermination of the Jewish boys.

V. 22. לכל עמו to the whole of his people. He had seen how the Jewish women had made his order illusive. It is indeed questionable whether any King giving such a cruel order to a limited number of people could reckon on his mandate being carried out. The humane feelings of those commissioned to carry out the deed would be aroused, and, in any case, the murdering of infants would be marked by the disgust of the whole nation. But it is equally unlikely that in a whole nation of Egyptians there would not be inhuman monsters who would make use of the King’s wish, in order to use their devilish and sadistic lust on innocent babes. So the King made his proclamation to לכל עמו and so felt surer it might be carried out. No persons specially designated would thereby receive the odium.

V. 1. The name is not given, simply the description “a man and a woman from the house of Levi”. For we already know the meaning of the “house of Levi”. From the mouth of the dying Father we have learnt its faults, but also have been shown what deep spiritual worth can lie in these very faults. The Levite spirit which was to be the saving spirit in times of oppression, אחלקם ביעקב, (see note on Gen. 49,7) was the very one that was called for in just such times as were then ruling. According to tradition, the midwives themselves were also from “the house of Levi”. In such times courage was required to become a father or a mother. So it does not say: ויהי איש מבית לוי ויקח וגו׳ but וילך וגו׳ in this וילך lies the whole great resolution that was necessary for taking such a step. Note further, that it does not say: ויקח בת לוי but את בת לוי i.e. one who was already definitely known. In any case we know from the sequel that when this occurred, the couple had been married previously. A sister was already there and this sister had already a brother. All this tells us what our חכמים say viz. that this was not their first marriage, but that a man who had separated from his wife in consideration of the King’s cruel order, made up his mind to take her back again to oppose this order.

V. 2. טוב, this is usually taken to mean that he was “beautiful”. But nothing could be more unnatural than this idea. What mother does not find her baby beautiful? Moreover, if the baby had been less beautiful, would a mother, on that account, not have done her very utmost to snatch it from certain death. טוב means good. She saw that it was a good baby, one which did not cry for no reason, so that one only had to satisfy its requirements and it would keep quiet, and such a baby it would be possible to keep hidden.

ירחים is not the usual expression for months. חדש designates the month according to the striking, visible-to-all, return of the light of the moon after its regular disappearance. It is, therefore, the general name for a month as a period for reckoning time. But ירח designates the moon with reference to its physical cosmic, telluric influence, particularly on the maturing and development of fruit and vegetable life, ממגד גרש ירחים (Deut. 33,14). תספור ירחים תמלאנה (Job 39,2), so that here it is quite the pertinent word to be used. She could only keep the child hidden during the first three months of his development.

V. 3. הצפינו, Hiphil. Why could she no longer keep him hidden? Because she could no longer manage that other people would let him remain hidden. The child was now three months old, everybody wanted to play with him, and even if he did not cry, he would be brought to chuckling and gurgling and crowing etc. She could not prevent her own people having to do with the child, and so it could no longer be kept secret.

גמא from גמא to sip, quaff, a plant that drinks a lot of water, היגאה גמא בלא בצה. (Job 8,11). סוף reed-bank, that בסוֹף grows at the end of the dry land, where water and land meet. If this explanation is right, and we really have a plant designated by the place where it grows, it might give us a clue to an appellation which otherwise is puzzling. חציר is grass and חצר a courtyard, not a yard in our sense of the word, but the whole free space surrounding a building, related to עצר ,עזר etc. So, too, the עזרה in the מקדש corresponding to the חצר of the משכן, the space surrounding the whole of the Temple. Generally speaking the great plant-world, where it is still untouched by human hands, consists of two elements יער, forest, and חציר the land not occupied by trees, covered by grass; downs, prairies etc. We have already previously considered יער in its phonetic relation to יאור river, especially with the Nile being fed by the melted snow of the mountains. The underlying meaning of both would be, gathering up of water. Hence also the related קערה ,קער a dish for liquids. An essential importance of forests is their ability to collect moisture. All fruitfulness is dependent on the amount of rain, and that again is dependent on forests. So that יער is really the vegetable יאור and may be said to feed the חציר the surrounding lower growth, the grass. It is remarkable that סוף is connected with סופה the storm. Possibly סופה is simply that which has gone over the סוף beyond the boundary, as שוף is the sudden slipping out, and then סופה would be the sudden storming of the wind out of the limits within which it had hitherto kept, while סערה would describe the storm more as a whirlwind, related to סחר ,סהר.

V. 4. ותֵּתַצב should really be וַתִּתְיַצֵב. This is an unusual form, composed of joint Kal and Hispael. We find analogous composite forms, as e.g. הוּכַּבֵּס from the Hophal and Piel; הָתְפָּקְדוּ from the Hophal and Hispael; יִרַדוֹף from the Kal and Piel. תֵצַב points to the Kal (although ע״צ are generally חסרי י׳ as in אֶצָרך and וַיֵצֶר לוֹ etc.) and would mean “stood there”, simply; but תתיצב “she placed herself there with full intent, full energy”. That which is related by the Word of God differs sharply from that which is related by Man. The latter is very rarely kept purely objective, people are not satisfied to relate facts just as they did occur, they introduce the feelings, moods, etc. of their heroes, putting themselves in their place. And where can one find a better occasion than this, in which the narrator would not have failed to express the deep feelings of the people concerned, the despair, the fear, the heroic decision, the trembling heart at carrying it out, the agonising appeal to God while awaiting the result. The Word of God simply relates the bare fact for us to understand. What a Jochebed, a Miriam felt at such a moment, every feeling person can feel for themselves. But as far as it just affects the facts, the Torah paints for us the finest nuances. At such a moment one’s acts are only semi-conscious. One does know what one is doing and one’s own will does function; but at the same time the tragic possibilities of the moment are so overwhelming, that one is half following the directions of some higher forcing power. The sister knew that she went and stood waiting there, but she also suddenly stopped there as if placed there by some higher power ותֵּתַצב a mixture of considered and forced action. לְדֵעָה not לָדַעַה that would simply imply a motive of curiosity, but לְדֵעָה — a noun form — to obtain knowledge, implies the pre-conceived intention to use the knowledge obtained for every possibility of further rescue.

V. 5. על היאר (we should expect ביאר) at the side of the river where it is not too deep. Or possibly it means the Upper Nile, above the city, where it is not yet muddy with the dirt of the town. Perhaps the mother had intentionally placed the baby there because it was cleaner, and the place for bathing, perhaps even reserved for women, and a mother could expect more pity from mothers. Her attendants kept to the bank. We at once get a glimpse of the refined character of the Princess. She only takes a single maid with her into the bath and does not reckon that her ladies-in-waiting should find it such a high honour to be about the Princess when she is in her bath!

V. 6. She opened it and saw the child. Only when she had opened it, did she find out its contents. So the baby could not have been crying. What a “טוב״ child! In such circumstances! We can see already in these little traits the tendency to the future ענו מאוד, to the quiet, patient, modest, lack of pretention, which marked the great character of our great leader. And when she opened it ותראהו את הילד she saw him first as a baby, והנה and then he began to cry. A yelling infant is not beautiful and does not attract by its charm. It was the first impression of the child peacefully looking up at her that won the Princess’s heart. Then he yelled. The sight of a strange face makes a child cry, and especially here the physiognomy of an Egyptian woman was something he had hitherto never seen. In his hidden state he had, of course, only been used to the Semitic profiles of his parents and family.
V. 7. From the Hebrews. On account of the enmity against the Hebrews which Pharaoh had artificially engendered one could hardly have any confidence in entrusting the child to an Egyptian wet-nurse.

V. 9. הֵיליכי an unusual form of הַוֹליכי which could have the meaning of “lead”, and in a child of that age would be an unsuitable expression; we should have expected קחי. But הֵיליכי seems to be similar to the הַיְצֵא for הוציא used to Noah. Just as there it does not mean “lead out[[illegible]] but “let them go out”, and indicates the longing which creatures which had been shut in for such a long time, have, to get free, for whom one only has to open the door and they go out by themselves, so here the form היליכי seems to have the underlying thought: — see to it that the child gets out of its dangerous positon and place. If it could walk and realised its position it would hurry away by itself.

V. 10. משה related to מצה to draw something with effort out of of the water, to suck up a liquid. She did not call him משוי one drawn up from the water. Perhaps this gives us an indication of the whole tendency of the education which the Princess gave her foster-son, and the deep impression that was made from the very first on his character. By giving him this name she said to him: All his life, he is never to forget that he was thrown into the water and that I drew him out of it. Therefore all his life is he to have a soft heart for other people’s troubles and always be on the alert to be a משֶׁה a deliverer in times of distress. His Hebrew name always kept the consciousness of his origin awake within him. The Princess surely enquired from the mother what the Hebrew term was, to express this thought, otherwise she would have given him his name in Egyptian. In all this we can see the noble humane character of the saviour of Moses.

V. 11.—12. According to Jewish teaching the man who would stand up as a prophet in Israel, must be, even before he receives his call, outstanding as a חכם גבור and עשיר. God does not pick out weaklings, simpletons, nor those who are socially dependent on others, to be messengers of His Word, “Strong, wise and independent” must the man stand forth whom God is to send as His messenger. With this one sentence, Jewish prophecy is sharply differentiated from all which certain people so thoughtlessly like to associate with it. Of these standards of personality which are the necessary preliminaries for prophets, גבורה, healthy physical development, stands not undeservedly, in the front rank. To what an extent do they try to rob Jewish prophecy of its actual power to help and build up the world and mankind, by first stripping it of its clear godliness, and then relegating it to the dim realm of visions, hallucinations, magnetic clairvoyance etc., etc. But all these are phenomena which only occur in conditions of sickness, debility or morbidity. The very first demand which our prophecy makes on its bearers, is health and strength. Only in a healthy, unweakened body does the mind attain that clarity that can draw from the well of the Torah — which is open to all — that חכמה which forms the second preliminary condition, and also עושר, the self-confidence and independence which forms the third.

V. 12. ויפן כה וכה, he looked in all directions to be sure that he was unobserved and could dare to do the deed. That he would not have dared had there been witnesses is vouched for by אכן נודע הדבר in V.14. This trait in Moses’s character is of most decisive importance. He has a deep feeling of duty which makes him jump to the aid of any innocent person whom he sees mishandled. He justifies the name his adopted mother gave him. But he is far from that daring boldness which rushes without thinking into danger, so that he is far from that attractive and infective daring which would be necessary for a leader to put himself at the head of a great multitude, and to urge them along with him to the hazardous enterprise of breaking their chains, and, sword in hand, fighting their way to freedom from the tyrant and his power. A man who first “looks all around to make sure there are no witnesses”, to such a man it would not occur in a dream to become the saviour and leader of his people. Spontaneously, “out of himself”, the very first elements for such an historical “hero” were entirely lacking.

V. 13. מַצָה .נצים=strife. נצה related to נשה .נשה=of one’s own free will, or at least without resisting, to transfer into the power of somebody else, having given a part of one’s fortune into his hands, and so having some demand on him. נצה=to offer resistance to submission to somebody else, from which we naturally get — strife. When one of the striving ones gets his point, the נצה becomes נצח, the strife is at rest as is usually expressed by the sound ח. Hence also נסה, to bring out, in a peaceful manner somebody’s power of resistance and overcoming, to put him to the test, to try him. Transposing this procedure to chemical processes it becomes מצה. The chemical process of fermentation is nothing other than the particles of a mass coming into “strife”. If this “strife” has begun but is arrested, the result is מצה=arrested strife. Hence the Law. דברים הבאים לידי חימוץ אדם יוצא בהן ידי חובתו במצה.

V. 14. This מי שמך לאיש reveals, already early in our history, a trait which characterises us even today, and which lies at the root of all our national faults and — virtues. 600,000 adult men have not got the courage to defend their children against non-Jewish underlings, but to the authority of a Jew not one will submit. For such a people no human authority is of avail, anyone making the most justified reprimand must be prepared for it to be considered pure arrogance, denying the principle of the equality of all! This fault we have not completely lost even after we have been schooled in the Galut-school; what intractable stuff must we have been before we attended this school! God chose for Himself not the most tractable but the most intractable race of men — עז שבאומות — gave them His אשדת His His Torah was first to prove itself! Hard blows of Fate must hammer us so that we become hard as steel — AND yielding and flexible as steel. Towards God — flexible, but inflexible, unbendable, hard and firm against all human non-godly authority. This “stiff-neckedness”, this obstinacy, can also degenerate and mistake its object. But without it we should never have become the undying immortal People of the Law.

V. 15. The ויבקש להרוג shows a rather remarkable situation. Pharaoh was an absolute monarch and Moses had committed a murder. Also it does not say להמית the usual expression for capital punishment but להרוג (to slay, assassinate I.L.). It seems accordingly that, as the adopted son of the Princess, Moses must have occupied a very distinguished position, so that Pharaoh had to have consideration, of which an ordinary individual would not have had the benefit.

ויברח וישב He fled, and only came to rest, only quietly settled down, when he reached the land of Midian. Between his flight and his settling in Midian there must have passed a considerable length of time. At his return to Egypt he was 80 years old, and at most his second son, had just been born. It seems highly improbable that the event recorded in V.12 et seq. could have occurred much later in his life than the ויגדל משה of V.11.

V. 17. ויגרשום — ויושיען — צאנם Here the daughters are twice referred to with masculine terminations and once with feminine, such a change in genders is never without reason. Here the explanation is fairly obvious. The shepherds came and pushed them away, did not treat them as girls, but treated them roughly as if they were one of themselves, whereas in general, even amongst the roughest, the weaker sex is protected. Moses helped them because they were weaker (feminine), not necessarily because they were in the right, of which he, as a stranger, could not judge, but because they were roughly-handled girls. The watering of the sheep however, was not part of the rescue. But to tell us that Moses did not do this out of gallantry, but simply out of kindness, and that he would have done the same had they been men who had been frightened and hustled and exhausted, it says וישק את צאנם He took their part because they were women, and watered their sheep for them out of kindness towards distressed human beings.

V. 21. הואיל משה באר .ויואל משה (Deut. 1,5; Sam. I. 14,24; Isaiah 29,13) root יאל related to יעל .יחל יעל = to be useful, to be furthered, to prosper. יאל = the beginning of furthering a project, the first decision to an undertaking, the continuance of which can be expressed by יעל, so that ויואל = he made the decision. יחל, to pause in something which has started = to wait. Hence also הואיל, to cause somebody to make up his mind, or to cause such a decision to mature, to set about doing something. ויואל שאול accordingly need not come from אלה an oath (which would be an irregular derivation) but means “he brought the people to making the resolution”. נואל, the Niphal would then (just as ושנתו נהיתה עליו (Dan. 2,1) “his sleep was disturbed in its being; נוחלה אבדה תקותה (Ez. 19,5) “her expectations were lost”, where in every case the passive form is used to express being frustrated and hindered), express decisions being frustrated and restricted, perplexed not knowing how to decide. אשר נואלנו (Numb. 12,12) sins which we have committed without sufficient previous consideration, without real intention.

V. 22. גר הייתי בארץ נכריה is not very clear. Where else is one a גר but in a strange land? Moreover הייתי “I was”, when he gave the name he still was. It seems to imply that one can be a גר anywhere, but after a short time one becomes at home there, the land is no longer נכריה. In the name of his first-born Moses expresses that he does not yet belong to Midian. Although he is free and without worries and now a ‘paterfamilias’, his heart is still with his people in Mitzrayim. But as this is somewhat uncomplimentary to his surroundings we can understand why he says גר הייתי and not גר אני. In truth he still felt it, but out of his delicate consideration he puts it in the past tense. גֶר שׁוֹם not גר שָׁם so probably not from שָׁם there, but from שמם quite in accordance with the idea of ארץ נכריה.

V. 23. בימים הרבים ההם “in those many years” which had passed since Moses’s flight (cf. note on v.15). The connection between the death of the King and the “sighing” of the people is quite clear. As long as the originator of such a terrible inhuman act, as passing an edict enslaving the whole of a free and innocent people, as long as he is alive, the hope can always be present that his conscience will awake and lead him to make an alteration in the wrong he had so violently instituted. But once a state institution — with whatever crying injustice it may have been started — passes into other hands, with all the power of the state behind it, and it is received as an established fact and the origin may be unknown, then it is sanctioned as being the normal condition of things, and the new government even think it wrong to alter the old conditions which they take over. The new government assume the legality of what they find, and the free people who had been enslaved with such devilish violence are doomed to be pariahs for evermore. This is the curse of having old established wrongs in a state. The past cultivated a field with blood and tears, and the present gathers the harvest with their conscience completely undisturbed, on the grounds of a fait accompli, and has no longer any idea of the curse that hangs on each ear of corn it so joyfully carries home. As long as the King of Egypt lived, the children of Israel had hopes of a possible change in their fate. When the King died, they saw themselves condemned for ever to slavery, and groaned and cried up for help from this slavery. It states repeatedly that their groaning and their cry upwardss for divine justice were מן העבדה. Their groans and cries for help were not on account of their burdens and toil, they were strong and hefty, could bear a lot, and this treatment might be altered. But of עבדתם, over this state of slavery to which they now see themselves condemned for all time, over that, did their cry against injustice go up to God the Judge. זעק to cry out loudly (see Gen. 17,17). ,שועתם שעה — שוע to turn towards someone, שַׁוֵעַ to call to someone to turn towards us i.e. to help.

V. 24—25. Every way of paying attention which can be attributed to human beings, is here applied to God וישמע .וידע ,וירא ,ויזכר ,וישמע not זעקתם or שועתם but נאק .נאקתם occurs very seldom, it is related to נהק (Job 6,5; Ezekiel 34,12). In any case it designates the last despairing cry to which a hearer must say “that man is lost if I do not help him”. They cried out against the wrong that was being done to them, but they did not realise the real danger they were in, but God realised it, and heard the cry of their threatened moral future which they unconsciously uttered in their זעקה and He remembered the promise for their moral future which He had made to the אבות in the past. But inasmuch as God’s intervention here was brought about, not by the wrong that Israel suffered, but by consideration of the fact that otherwise they would have completely and irrevocably degenerated, and what He had promised as a ברית as something that would in all circumstances be absolutely fulfilled—would be broken. We see here indicated that which Ezekiel repeatedly refers to, viz., that Israel had NOT kept itself free from assimilating Egyptian abominations, and on their own account were not worthy of redemption. (See Ezekiel Ch. XX). The urgently threatened future and the distant past filed past God’s eye, and therefore וידע ,וירא He looked at the present, saw the actual condition of the Jews, וידע and recognised its moral effect on their characters, and accordingly extended to Israel His special care השגחה פרטית. That tells us that the time had arrived which had been proclaimed a couple of centuries previously by Joseph פקד יפקד ה׳ אתכם. Up till now God had not specially intervened, had allowed events to take their natural course. What had happened to them up till now was the simple consequence of their homeless and stateless condition and the degeneration and low state of morality of the country in whose midst they lived. Now God intervenes and therewith their salvation was assured.

V. 1. מדבר is not primarily a wilderness in the sense of a waste desolate desert, but rather the word itself etymologically indicates a place suitable for pasturage, grassy uncultivated steppe. Fundamental meaning of דבר (related to דור, a row of contemporaries, a generation, also to טור ,תור, a row, תפר, to sew together) is a combination of similar things. Hence also דוברות, raft; דבורה a swarm of bees, and especially ורעו כבשים כדברם דֹבֶר (Is. V.17). בעדר בתוך הַהָבְרוֹ (Micha 2,12) = assembling of the flock in the fold. So also assembling of the nation under one Lord, וַיַדְבֵּר עמים תחתי (Ps. 18,48). — Choreb is here already called the Mount of God; for at the time when this was written down the Revelation of the Torah had already taken place there. But it is deeply significant that the very commencement of the redemption started here at Choreb, at the future birthplace of the Torah. Thereby is made clear from the very beginning that the whole object of the redemption was only מתן תורה, to lead the people here, and here to constitute them into the “People of the Torah”.

V. 2. לבת from לבב like לב the innermost heart, the centre of the fire. The angel appeared in the centre of the fire, and the fire was in the centre of the thornbush, so that the thornbush was not surrounded by fire. The signification of the phenomenon accordingly was not that here was a bush standing in the fire without getting burnt, and so was not meant to signify: Israel will not perish in the Galut. Rather as our חכמים take it too, the fire reposed in the heart of the bush, and the angel in the fire (so also later שוכני סנה) (Deut. 33,16). As it says at מתן תורה (Ex. 19,18). והר סיני עשן כלו מפני אשר ירד עליו ה׳ באש and XXIV,17, ומראה כבוד ה׳ כאש אכלת בראש ההר Godliness, taking up its home down here on earth, and wishing to be found down here, always announces itself as Fire. The Torah itself is nothing but Fire taking the form of Law, אש דת (Deut. 33,3). As fire, it contains the powers of fire, and the purposes of fire, to penetrate us, to refine and purify us, to warm us, and to quicken and enliven us. We, on our part are to give up every phase of our lives to be לחם אשה ה׳ to be food, fuel for this Fire of God, to nourish and keep the fire of godliness burning here on Earth. So the lesson of the “burning bush” is: — applying it generally, that אין מקום פנוי בלא שכינה אפי׳ סנה the humblest home is not too humble to be a resting place for Godliness, everything and everybody here below, even the lowliest in the eyes of man, has the calling and the ability to become bearers of Godliness. (שמות רבה). Moreover, וסנה איננו אכל i.e., not being consumed, not being lost in the Godly, is the mission of each who offers himself to receive the Godly within himself, but only near and intimate contact with the Godly, (the idea of שכינה coming from שכן a neighbour, one who dwells next to you, not one by whom you are completely absorbed and lose all your own personality. I.L.). Or applying it nationally, the lesson would be (again from the Medrash Rabba) שותף אני בצערן ,עמו אנכי בצרה even in Israel’s thorny degradation I am with them, I share their troubles, am with them amongst the thorns.

V. 5. “Step not hither, but take thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place on which thou now standest is a holy place, is ground which has a holy destination”, has been chosen by God, that from it the deliverance of mankind shall go out, through the deliverance and choice of a People. Instead of trying to find out about the phenomenon that lies beyond and outside your sphere, understand the high destiny of the ground on which you already stand, and give yourself up entirely to that. Taking off one’s shoes expresses giving oneself up entirely to the meaning of a place, to let your personality get its standing and take up its position entirely and directly on it without any intermediary. So the כהנים in the מקדש had always to function barefooted, and nothing was allowed to be חוצץ, to intervene between their feet and the ground, or between their hands and the holy vessels used during the עבודה, or between the priestly garments and their body. Nothing in the Mikdosh was mere gaudy show, man-designed to impress and have effect on the eye of the beholder. Everything was to work back on the personality of the ministrant, and if one wished to act in the service of the Mikdosh one had to identify oneself directly with it, and become sanctified by it, and be a part of it, הרצפה מקדשת the floor sanctifies the priests (Zebachim 24a).

V. 6. אלקי אביך Whom your father taught you to know, אלקי אברהם וגו׳ Who showed Himself to be present already in the time of your ancestors, not only in the ever increasing prosperity of an Abraham, not only in the continuing and then waning prosperity of an Isaac, but also in the harder fate of a Jacob. אל האלקים to the Vision of God, which was being revealed to him.

V. 7. ה׳ The One who was shaping the new future. עני עמי אשר במצרים I have looked at the masses now being held in the deepest degradation in Egypt, in their destiny to become My People, i.e., as the future nation who are to be subject only to Me and to take their guidance solely from Me. I have considered their present degradation in connection with this, the great destiny that awaits them. ואת צעקתם שמעתי מפני נגשיו and also, apart from this future that awaits them, I have heard their cry, as the cry for help from human beings forcibly robbed of their human rights, and considered it in connection with the moral standard of their oppressors, כי ידעתי את מכאביו, for I have not remained ignorant of their personal individual sufferings. I have felt for them with every lash, with every pain, with every bitterness that they have endured.
