Here again we have reference to the three phases which characterised th Galuth Mitzraim .עני וגו׳ עמי אשר במצרים — גרות ,נגשיו — עבדות ,מכאביו — ענוי.

V. 8. The land is טובה, it is in accordance with the intended intellectual spiritual and moral development of the nation, and it is also רחבה roomy, so that it can also develop numerically therein. — זבת וגו׳ It is very characteristic that the description of abundance of produce by זוב only occurs in reference to Eretz Yisroel, is never used with this meaning elsewhere, but is the constant expression used of the Land of Israel. In תנ״ך the word זוב never means overflowing. It occurs mainly to describe a human pathological condition, and otherwise as a flowing forth caused by miraculous power (Ps. 78, 20) or by violence (Lamentations 6,9) הכה צור ויזובו מים, He struck the rock and water flowed forth; שהם יזובו מדוקרים stabbed, their blood gushed forth. Taking all this into consideration, ארץ זבת חלב ודבש does not seem to describe a land that develops this abundance in accordance with its natural fertility, but a land that only does this under special conditions. Palestine is a hard land (Gen. 26,3): הארצות האל. We saw it repeatedly visited by famine, and also after Israel left it, it lay barren. למטר השמים תשתה מים is said of it. A land which, unlike Egypt, does not offer its inhabitants simply to take advantage of its natural conditions of fertility, but which can only blossom and flourish “under the continuous special care of God for it, from one end of the year to the other.” When it gets water, it blossoms out luxuriously. But it only gets this water from above. It is a land that makes it necessary for its inhabitants to be good. For a hard people, as we were, a hard land is fitting. אל מקום הכנעני The present inhabitants have become degenerated by the luxury they enjoy there, and the land “spits them out”. Only if they keep themselves free from all Canaanitish abomination will Israel be able to keep its abundance for themselves.

V. 9. And now, you have only got to realise the one fact, that the people are crying for salvation and I am willing to save them. Therein lies sufficient incentive for you to offer yourself to be My implement.

V. 11. You set [[illegible]] two mighty tasks, I am to master Pharaoh and Israel, to overthrow Pharaoh and to lead Israel; for neither of them can I find the slightest vestige of ability or talent in myself. And well might a man weigh himself up again and again before undertaking such a mission. Were it only a matter of his own fate, perhaps he could risk it, but the weal or the woe of a whole people hung on the success of his undertaking. And so, a man, and especially a Moses who was ענו מאד מכל האדם אשר על פני האדמה a man of the most modest character, “the most modest of all men on earth”, who felt in himself no trace whatsoever of the stuff out of which successful agitators, national leaders, generals, heroes and rulers are made, well could such a man recoil in amazement before the thought of such an undertaking, even if the demand came from God Himself. Would not the whole undertaking come to grief through his insufficiency, his clumsiness, his timidity and weakness against Pharaoh, and he would then only heap misery upon misery on his unhappy brethren? Did he not have to deny that he had any of the imposing overpowering personality which would be necessary to form a People of God out of the downtrodden masses, brought up as slaves under the constant lash of the whip?

V. 12. “He spoke: Because I shall be with you! And just this will be for you the sign that I have sent you. When you etc.” Just that, in which you see your complete unsuitability for the work, makes you the most suitable for it. Just because you feel through and through how completely lacking you are in the ability even to undertake such a mission with your own powers — to say nothing of accomplishing it —, and because this inadequateness is so thoroughly apparent in your whole character, just because of this, you are the most fitting messenger for My mission. I require a man who is at the same time the greatest חכם and the greatest ענו. Your marked insufficiency will, for all time, stamp the works which I shall accomplish through you with the “sign” (האות) that what you do, could only be accomplished in My mission and by My powers. Your insufficiency is the guarantee that you are sent by God. Without it, the salvation in Egypt would fall into the category of world-historical events which glorify human greatness. And it is not hero worship nor yet a human dynasty that I would found through you and with you. When the salvation will have been accomplished, you are not to be a King, or ruler of the people. תעבדון (the plural). You, and the people, are to come to this mount as servants of God, you and the people are to enter the service of God on this mount; and only בהוציאך, only if a man like you will have brought the people out, will this object of the whole salvation be possible, will I then be able to say אנכי ה׳ א׳ אשר הוצאתיך מארץ נלצרים, for then you and the people will stand there in complete equality as My servants. And תעבדון את האלקים this same appearance of God which has become visible to you here, and which sent you to save the people, will then appear again on this same mount to all of you, and will complete the winning of the people to My service.

V. 13. The question, which name of God he shall proclaim to Israel is only understandable if we realise the motives of his mission. Names of God, ה׳ and שד׳, were known to them well enough from the time of the patriarchs. But from all that had passed hitherto it must have been quite clear to Moses that his mission was a double one. First to Pharaoh to accomplish the salvation, and then the real and incomparably more difficult one to Israel; to educate and prepare them for the great goal to become “the people of God”, as had been definitely expressed to him as the object of the whole redemption, in the בהוציאך. Had his mission been only redemption from slavery, he would for the present only have had to arrange his approach to Pharaoh. But Moses at once recognised that his mission to Israel was the real core of his task, to make them worthy to be saved, and thereby to lead them nearer towards their real great destiny. He was in no doubt as to what he would have to say to Pharaoh, but for his mission to Israel he wished further elucidation. Hence the question: “When I shall then come to the children of Israel and say to them, the God of your Fathers has sent me to you” — this sending assumes something fresh, some new relationship — “which Name shall I then tell them?” So the giving of this Name must give them the key to the new relationship which they are to have to God.

שֵׁם related to שָׁם; the intellectual “there”, the place, the category, wherein an object is to be registered. Every naming of an object is giving that object a place in the realm of our minds. It tells us where we understand that object to belong. Or also it comes from שמה (like בן from בנה) related to שמע the צמא of the intellect, spiritual thirst, like ראה related to רעה is the appeasing of spiritual hunger. Seeing, the eye brings the actual material object to the consciousness of the mind. Hearing, the ear brings to the perception the inner relations of what we see. What we hear are שמות, the inner truth of things. Our whole comprehension of God lies in the שמותיו של הקב״ה. Everything that we are to know of God, which God has revealed of Himself to us, is not for our eyes but for our ears and mind. And according to what name we give Him, according to that, have we an idea of His relation to us and our relation to Him. Hence the significant ויבטחו בך וידעי שמך ,אשגבהו כי ידע שמי ,דעת שם ה׳, According to this, the meaning in Ps. V.2 כי הגדלת על כל שמך אמרתך would be: That which thou hast promised for the future, transcends by far that which we already know of Thee. We only require “to know God’s Name” when we have to enter actively into relationship with Him. If we are only passively to allow ourselves to be saved and blessed by Him, we require just as little consciousness or knowledge of Him, as for our birth. It is only when we are actively, as עבדי ה׳, to act in the service of God that we require “a knowledge of a suitable Name”. With the knowledge of this Name we have to know what idea He wishes us to have of Him, and this knowledge is to guide us in our conduct towards Him, and to tell us on what thoughts of Him we are to base all our doings, or abstainings from doing. Moses’s question as to the Name he is to bring them in his mission to Israel is equivalent to the question: What idea is he to bring to the children of Israel which is to bring about a change in their ideas, and to bring them to decide by themselves to step from the service of Pharaoh into the service of God?

V. 14. If I am to express an idea of Myself which, if he comprehends it, and if he allows himself to be completely absorbed by it, will completely change a man, will raise him out of, and above all other creatures, and bring him into direct intimate relationship to Me, then I name Myself, I express Myself as: “I shall be that which I Will be”.

All other creatures are that which they have to be; with their coming into existence they are bound by the will of the One Who alone can say, not only “I am” but that “I shall be that which I wish to be”. This expresses the personal, absolute free nature of God. Inasmuch as God does not proclaim here “I am that which etc.” but “I shall be etc.”, He stresses, by using the future tense, that the future is completely unbound, completely dependent on His free will. This expresses the characteristic Jewish conception of God, and the fresh new knowledge of Him which was to be known to mankind by the redemption from Egypt — a knowledge which is to serve for the redemption of the whole world.

The conception of God in non-Jewish circles, is, at the most, as the origin of the world in its physical state since it came into existence, and even then, when this thought does raise itself from the denial of the existence of God into the vague, obscure, non-mundane existence of an actual God, it still relegates the work of God really to the past. At one single moment, they say God did stand in connection with the world, the moment in which the world came into existence by God’s power or will. Since then His work, the world, is self-contained. Everything, even the most distant future is simply the irrevocable result of the physical laws of nature given when the world came into existence.

To this point of view, everything in the world follows unalterable given laws, which, at the utmost, did once originate from the power of a higher One. To them it is actually only man with his — apparently — free powers of action, who could bring about an — apparently — new Future. God and the world are bound, and Man is free!!! Accordingly, in order to save their unfree, bound, God they have to declare that the freedom of Man is itself a delusion. Man is not free. What he imagines to be his own free decisions are but the products of unconscious influences arising out of his past, he is but a puppet dancing to the strings pulled by this past of his — and so from heaven to earth, in the whole realm of being, to them there is nothing at all that can say “I shall be”, because to them nothing can say “I will”. אהי׳ אשר אהי׳ comes crushingly against this delusion, which, with the denying of the freedom of God has to deny the free will of Man; and by declaring the absolute freedom of God, puts the future of Man in its true perspective. In the last words of the description of the Creation אשר ברא אלקים לעשות the work of God is declared not as finished, but as only beginning, as these words referring to our earth and its heaven imply that God called them into existence לעשות to go on working. This working is indicated as being the mission of the immediately preceding last creation of the Creation, Man, who had been placed as the free administrator and manager of God’s creation. Now these four words אשר ברא א׳ לעשות mark the transition from the completion of God’s creative work in Nature, to what then began and which reaches out to, and guides and forms and influences, the whole distant future — God’s creative work in the History of Man. ממלאכת עולמו שבת, ממלאכת הצדיקים והרשעים לא שבת, אלא פועל עם אלו ופועל עם אלו, מראה לאלו מעין דגמטרין שלהן ומראה לאלו מעין דגמטרין שלהן “From the creative work of the world He ceased, but not from work on the righteous and wicked, but He goes on working creatively with the one and with the other, makes the one (the righteous) experience an inkling of the ultimate future that awaits him. and lets the other (the wicked) also experience an inkling of the ultimate future that awaits him.” (Rabbi Pinchas in the name of Rabbi Oshiya in the Midrash on this verse). Up to this point we only find God proclaiming Himself as אלהים, the God of Nature, of the Laws of Cause and Effect, but from here onwards we find a new name added to אלקים, viz: the four-lettered name of God, as the God of the assured future of Mankind. In the same way here, at the beginning of the Geula from Egypt, where God first showed Pharaoh and the whole world His creative interference in the development of the History of Mankind, we find a new designation of Him, אהי׳ אשר אהי׳. This expresses with absolute certainty that basic truth, the very cornerstone of all Truth and of all Happiness, that the future goal of mankind is absolutely assured, and it is a call for Man to use his power to carve the immediate future, in God’s service, i.e., to make God’s will his will.

This word, אהי׳ אשר אהי׳ breaks the chains of every other power, sets Man upright and free in the service of God, — a co-worker in the Future which He desires. Under the free God, free Man rules the world for the Future which God’s free will desired. With every impression of Godliness which Man impresses on his own internal self, with every such impression that he stamps on the external world about him, Man works at the creation of this Future. The guarantee that this Future will ultimately be absolutely achieved lies in the very fact that God, with the power of His absolute free and unbound will, created this world for this Future, so that even the apparently most opposing conditions and events must be leading up to this one, great, sure goal. We express this confidence, in the ever-recurring Kaddish which we have interwoven into all our public divine services יתגדל ויתקדש ש׳ ר׳ “God’s great name shall come to ever greater and ever holier realisation בעלמא in the world די ברא which He has created כרעותה, according to His free Will”.

V. 15. There could be a difference between — כה תאמר ל and — כה תאמר אל The one — ל need only mean for Israel, for his instruction, not necessarily spoken directly to Israel but to the זקנים or instructors; the other — אל would be the speech to Israel. The אהי׳ אשר אהי׳ was said only to Moses. For the instruction of the masses אהי׳ would suffice in the teaching to look at the Future as being in God’s hands, without going into its being the result of the unique absolute freedom of God. And this idea which emanates from the thought of the personality of God as אהיה, “I shall be”, is in the first place, only to be spoken for Israel to their leaders and teachers. The message to Israel, instead of referring to the personality of God of the Future, refers to the effectual agency of the Future; instead of “I shall be”, “Who causes everything to become” (the four lettered Name). Even this, the Name given out to be the general Jewish conception of God, is kept only in their silent innermost consciousness. God is thought and spoken of, only in Hiss immediate relation to the fate of men and nations, by the שם אדנות “My Master”, the most essential idea that is to result from this whole consciousness of God, the Name which places Man in every moment of his being and doing in the service of this, Our Creator and Moulder of the Future. זה this, the four lettered Name, the שם הויה is My Name for the Future, וזה and this in its actual result for the people, is nothing else but זכרי, the שם אדנות, placing the people in My service, by which I am to be thought of by generation after generation.

V. 16. It is certainly not without deep significance that here, and everywhere else, when it has already said א׳ אבותיכם it adds specifically א׳ אברהם וגו׳. It is fairly obvious that it wants, thereby, us always to keep in mind that our relationship to God should be absolutely independent of our social success or non-success in life. Dissimilar as the external fortunes of our patriarchs are shown to be, flourishing and prosperous in the life of Abraham, at its zenith and decline in Isaac, and apparently submerged, in the life of Jacob, the nearness to God, and the bond with God, remains always the same; in every sphere of life, God reveals Himself, and everybody is assured of God’s grace.

אתכם ואת העשוי לכם, in both relations have I already “invested” the conditions with appropriate fates. “You”, inasmuch as your destiny demands an alteration in your state. “That which is being done to you”, inasmuch as it calls aloud on the Justice of God as the greatest crime against a whole nation.

V. 17. According to this have I decided to bring you out of your present wretchedness into the very opposite, to a land in which at present seven voluptuous nations wallow; a land in which it is entirely dependant on the moral behaviour of its inhabitants whether it blossoms for them in most luxurious abundance, or denies them its produce, or even spews forth its degenerate inhabitants.
V. 18. You are not to go alone, to appear before the King possibly as an individual enthusiast and zealot, he is to see that you have the whole people behind you.

העברִיִים. This is the first time that an address had been made to a King in the name of the Jewish People as such, and here we find a form עבריים, which never occurs again. Elsewhere it is always עברים. Possibly here the character which lies in the word עברי is quite specially emphasised, and insisted that it is not only the character that marks the people as a whole, but one which characterises every member of the people. Just as one single man sufficed for God, a man who like Abraham (according to ר׳ יהודה׳s explanation of עברי) had the courage to leave the whole world on one side, and to pass over alone with his God to the other side, so has each of his descendants inherited this courage and this strength of character. Moses is to make his demand to Pharaoh in the name of the “Ibriyim”, and thereby express the idea that in each single one of them, the whole nation is represented, each single one of them has the courage and the mission to stand alone against the whole world, and to represent and carry on the nation by himself. (In the mouths of the Prophets, other nations habitually are described by the picture of an animal, Israel is pictured preferably as a tree. An animal can be killed with a single pressure of the trigger-finger, or a single stab of the dagger. But a tree reproduces with every part, the possibility of the continuance of life of the whole. Even if the root is severed, a branch, a twig, a bud, a germ, is often sufficient to reinstate the destroyed plant, and to save its continued existence). “Not עברים but עבריים are we” is Moses to say. The spirit that moves me to speak lives also in the elders, lives in every individual of the people, down to the very last man. Our People does not let itself be destroyed. In each single individual is reproduced the spirit, the courage, the decision of the whole. It seems probable that this is the reason that this name is emphasized here in its full significance.

קרה ,נקרה, also even קרא to encounter, according to its basic meaning to call, always refers (as we have repeatedly remarked) to something outside ourselves having an influence over us. It is always some external power that forces us out of our intended or expected direction, into its desired direction. That is why “chance” for which the word is used, is only subjective, only from our point of view “chance”, but in itself can be just the opposite, can be the product of Divine Providence which by this מקרה, this “chance” calls us into the direction intended by it. Here, in the address to a heathen King, we find the expression used by God in exactly the same way as it is used later by Balaam of the mutual relationship between himself and God ואנכי אקרה כה, אולי יקרה ה׳ לקראתי and then the story takes up this point of view, and adopts the same idiom, ויקר ה׳ אל בלעם (Numbers 18,3, 4, 15). Balaam says “I will let myself be called” i.e., I will give myself up to a power which lies beyond me, will give myself up to “impulses from God”, so that He will lead me I know not whither. And he imagines it possible that in the same way some higher power can similarly influence his God, to make it “chance” that he and his God meet each other. To the heathen, neither in his relation to God, nor in that of his God to him, is there any real freedom, neither can, out of themselves, definitely decide anything. At rock bottom everything is fixed by physical necessity, where everything has power to act on something else, but not on itself. It is on this idea that the pretended or imagined power of קסם (charms), rests. Balak attributes to Balaam the power of being able to force down the anger of the gods on the people of his hate. Balaam admits the possibility, and says “I will give up my own personality and give myself up to that power that forces men and gods, perchance the gods will also be forced by it”. And the tale follows the delusion and adopts the expression ויקר ה׳ וגו׳ etc., Here, also, God, at first lets Moses enter quite into one point of view of heathenism. אלהי העבריים נקרה עלינו “Our God Who for centuries has not let us hear anything about Him has now (“forced by that necessitating Power that rules over gods as over men” נקרה) been called over us. That must have some important meaning. We must bring Him sacrifices, perhaps assuage His anger”, (compare Ch. V.3 פן יפגענו בדבר וגו׳). Nobody can do anything about it. It is a higher direction. The first demand is not at all שלח את עמי, but simply contains the request to allow an offering to be brought, and as this is not possible in Egypt, the request includes the granting of a six days leave of absence. And all quite in the language, and from the point of view of Pharaoh himself.

V. 19. But not even the simple natural request which at base is really entirely in his own interests — to prevent a wrathful God destroying his slaves — will Pharaoh grant, however forcibly (ביד חזקה) you put it to him. One almost has to believe that even in such an ancient time, in the high royal circles, in spite of the frequent imposing proclamations, and all the outward show of religion, at heart they had no real respect for the gods and priests, and only used it all for political power over the masses. Otherwise the fear of the gods would have swayed him to make this little concession. Where ninety gods are honoured there is surely place for a ninety-first, especially as here, where the application is made in the name of the higher power which rules all the gods.

V. 20. פלא .נפלאתי is that which occurs outside the natural sequence of cause and effect, and so reveals Him Whose will is not restrained by the ordinary laws which govern the world and nature, but show rather that His will and power, restrain and govern these laws of nature. By a miracle proclaimed and accomplished by God, the godliness of the ordinary course of events springs into our eyes. It shows us that the ordinary natural way of things have not only an originator, that not only their origin, but also their continuance, has its root in God. They do not exist and continue because they once came into existence by God, but because, and only as long as, God wills them to continue. To teach the godliness of ordinary natural things is the object of miracles.
V. 21. The hate of the mass of the nation against the Jews in Egypt did not exist originally, it was only artificially called into being and fostered from above by Pharaoh and the government.

V. 22. שאל ,ושאלה. This word has an unfortunate history. It occurs at least a few hundred times in תנ״ך and there it always has the meaning “to demand, to request, to obtain by entreaty”, never “to borrow”. In one single instance alone it is used for borrowing וכי ישאל איש מעם רעהו (Ex. 22,13) and this one single instance, because it just happens to describe a legal relationship and in consequence the word שאל has become current in all the laws referring to a borrower, and is of every-day use, has been the cause of people seeing in the expression שאלה here, at once the idea of “to borrow”. But they overlook completely the form of speech which is inevitably used. Always, everywhere where שאל means to demand, to request, i.e., where that which is demanded or asked for, is to completely leave all connection with its present owner, שאל is construed with מאת or with מ-, it is to come away from the person. But in the one case where it means borrow, it is used with מעִם. It is only to be taken away from being with the person, but it still belongs to him. Accordingly when Hannah entreats God for a child we find repeatedly that: שאלה מעמו, she wants to express that what she is begging God to give her, she will always consider as remaining belonging to God. In the same way what God demands of us does really only become our very own in our readiness to give or dedicate it to God, hence מה ה׳ שואל מעמך (Deut. X.12). But here it very definitely and expressly says ושאלה אשה משכנתה. Just as in Chap. 11,2 it says וישאלו איש מאת רעהו וגו׳. So that it quite definitely means to demand, to ask, and in no wise whatsoever to borrow.

נצל ,ונצלתם as נשל, to strip oneself of something, נצל to cause or bring about that somebody strips himself of something. You will be in such a position with regard to the Egyptians that they will grant your request in excess. They will hand over, more than you demand or expect, partly to get rid of you and partly through sympathetic feeling towards you.

V. 1. God has just told him that his coming before Pharaoh would at first not be attended by success. Naturally then Moses could assume that the failure of his mission would justifiably raise doubts in the minds of Israel as to the reliability of his statements: — the God whom you say appeared to you and sent you to us and to Pharaoh could not really have done so, otherwise you would have had success with Pharaoh.

For the original preparation and equipment of Moses no אות, no miracle was necessary. God pointed to the result, to success, to Moses and to us, for all time, כי אהיה עמך ו ז ה לך האות. The mere fact that we, with all our utter lack of power, but with the Torah in our arms, have been able to make such a world-historic path through the ages, is itsself the eternal completely convincing proof of the divine origin of the Torah, and of the veracity of the mission of Moses. But here, at the beginning where the successful issue was still lacking, where already beforehand repeated failures had been foretold, there was every reason for doubting the authenticity of Moses’ mission, and Moses was fully justified in presupposing such a doubt.

V. 2.—5. The metamorphosis, the fact that what is now a staff, at one’s will changes into a serpent, and at one’s will becomes a staff again, is in itself an אות, a means to accomplish the conviction that the man who comes equipped with such powers is a messenger of the One unique Power that reigns over the ordinary natural order of things, by Whose will alone, the laws of nature were made and continue to function. But going a little deeper into the matter, it can also become clear to us why God should have chosen just this sign and no other. First, God asks Moses to consider what he has in his hand. Just as to Jeremiah “What does thou see?” (The cutoff ה which hurries over the מה and concentrates the thoughts on the זה may nevertheless be meant to remind us, that God’s miraculous power could have shown itself equally well on any other object that might have been to hand). Anyway, “Consider what you have in your hand”. “A staff”. What is a staff? The most natural emblem of man’s mastery over nature. A stick, a staff has a double function, (which has a corresponding double meaning in the root נטה which means incline, to lean, and also to stretch over something). A staff is (a) an elongation of the hand by which a man supports himself on the ground and (b) an elongation and extention of the sphere of his power, and sign of his mastery. So the people are to be shown by Moses: that, on which man leans and supports himself, and by which he commands, will, if and when God wishes it, change to the very opposite, to a snake. All animals attach themselves more or less to Man, but the snake has איבה hidden within him towards Man, Man runs away from the serpent. Hence: that One has sent you, Who when He so wills, makes the very thing on which Man reckons he supports himself, and which sserves him as a means of his mastery, rise up against him; and the reverse: that which now stands against him as a fearsome enemy force, changes at His will to an accommodating support and to an obedient tool in his hand. But just this proclaims your Sender as ה׳, as that one on Whose will depends every coming moment, every moment of the Future. And, significantly, here it again repeats אלקי אבתיכם, אלקי אברהם וגו׳ to refer and point out how God, from your very origin showed Himself in an equal degree of care and management in the most diverse conditions of life: He is as much the God of Jacob as of Abraham, the fate of the servant comes from Him as much as that of the prince; if He wishes it, He will make Pharaoh the slave and you the ruler, change Pharaoh’s staff to a whip for his back, and Pharaoh’s whip to your staff.

V. 6. At the demand to throw the staff to the ground the entreating word נא is not there, but we find it here where Moses’ own hand is to become leprous, a demand which contains a request for personal unpleasantness. In such delicate nuances the authenticity of a written record is revealed.

V. 7. To place one’s hand in one’s bosom and thereby make it leprous, and to place it there again and thereby make it healthy, is by itself a sign that one is sent by God. It teaches, that not only the “staff”, but also the hand that holds and guides it, is in God’s power. More, it teaches, if God changes that which is accommodating to Man into something hostile, malignant, and the reverse, then if Man would withdraw entirely unto himself and depend entirely on himself, he simply could not be sure of himself. If God wills He throws discord into the very being of Man himself, He has no need to break the staff. In the concealing bosom of Man himself, God lets the hand die off, if He so wills, and revive again with fresh life when He wills it. But Ps. 74,11 teaches us that the phrase “to lay one’s hand in one’s bosom” in Hebrew, is an idiom, exactly as in German, for inactivity (in English we say “fold one’s arms” I.L.). So that this sign can have the further meaning for the people: Doing nothing, “laying one’s hands in one’s bosom” can, just as God wishes it, bring death, but it can also, if it is done at God’s behest — in שב ואל תעשה — bring salvation. Let them learn from this sign also to wait patiently, God knows the right time, for laying one’s hands in one’s bosom and when to take them out.

V. 9. If after these two signs they still have not gained complete confidence, then begin at once the עשר מכות before their eyes. Show them that you have been sent to lay hands on the Land itself, that the God Who sent you has indeed the power to break the staff of existence of this mighty state. The Nile is the whole support and personification of the might of Egypt.

V. 10. It repeatedly says in V.8: והאמינו, ישמעו לקול האות and this can not be just an expression for believing or disbelieving Moses, this is expressed in V.9 without the word קול. Rather קול must refer to the instructive and inspiring explanation of the signs which was to accompany their performances, and Moses could well say to himself that eloquence and impressive speech-making was required for this.

בי from בהה, confused, unclear, an interjection which expresses an anxious disturbed feeling “I am still uneasy, do not feel that I possess the ability to carry out the mission successfully”. — כבד-פה seems to be a defect of the organs of speech generally, כבד-לשון heaviness, clumsiness of the tongue in particular. “I have difficulty in starting to speak, and then when I do speak, I stumble and trip over my tongue”. It is a bad thing when an orator, and especially an orator addressing the whole nation, is laughed at. It requires a great deal of intelligence and understanding to overlook the lack of eloquence and faults of diction of a speaker, on account of the contents of his speech. Such judgment can hardly be expected from mass of the people with women and children.

V. 11. “Am I not ה׳?” Am not I the One who changes staff to serpent and serpent to staff? Can I not then make the stammerer into an orator, and the orator to a stammerer? Indeed a stammerer is the most fitting for this mission. Every word of this stuttering stammerer is itself an אות. If a man who ordinarily stammers speaks easily and flowingly in God’s mission, every single word brings its own credentials with it.

(אִלם from אלם to bind, tie up, tongue-tied. חרש from חרש to plough, the deaf have to “plough” their own fields of thought, for no seeds are planted in the soil of their brains from outside. מקח is a stronger form of בקע ,פקע, to split, open out, and is one who has an extraordinary open organ, specially wide-awake. עוֹר ,עור skin, עור to be awake and to be naked. The basic meaning of עור, to be made naked for external impressions, hence skin, the organ which makes the human body receptive to external impressions, the sense of touch. During sleep, receptivity is withdrawn from the outside. The deeper the sleep, the less is one in contact with the world outside through one’s skin. With awakening, preception through the skin returns. עִוֵר is a “skin-man”, a man of touch, a blind man whose perception of the external world depends solely on his sense of touch).

V. 12. הוריתיך not from ירה but from הרה to absorb a living germ within oneself (as הוליך from הלך). הוֹרֶה to lay an organic living germ in someone else. It is the noblest expression for teaching, that which is taught is to be laid, as an intellectual or spiritual germ, in the mind of the pupil, taken up by the latter and nursed to grow into an intellectual living organism, even as the germ grows in the mother’s womb.

V. 13. I do not feel myself to be sufficiently good and wise, or efficient enough, am not the right man for it; Your mission will, of course, be accomplished, but first of all it will be bungled by me, and You will then have to send someone who is better, more efficient than I am; rather send this other one straight away.

“So send, I pray you, through that one whom you will have to send”. This utter lack of confidence in himself and his ability, is in itself the most vivid proof of the divine origin of all that which was done and spoken by Moses, the most vivid proof that the Torah was indeed given through Moses, but not by, or out of Moses. Proof of the truth, the unquestionable truth of the fundamental sentence וידבר ה׳ אל משה. Further, in certain circles they like to relegate the prophecy of נביאי ה׳ on whose mission the whole of Judaism rests, into the sphere of ecstasy, of transport, where a man loses his own will, and sees, hears, speaks and does things of which he has no knowledge afterwards. Here, we see the complete opposite, how Moses not only keeps complete consciousness, but also keeps and expresses the fullest independence of his own will and his own ideas. Right up to the last moment he expresses his doubts and makes his request. This proves complete freedom of consciousness, reasoning, deliberation and decision; in a word, the clearest, most wide-awake condition of the mind and feelings of our prophet in the supreme moment of his life. Our sages have given us the important dictum מעולם לא ירדה שכינה למטה מעשרה and therein have probably meant to indicate the fact that the Godly never comes over into the sphere of the Human to such a degree that the human element in man is completely ‘possessed’ and becomes the passive instrument of the Godly without retaining a will of its own. The very name שכינה itself expresses this idea, it regards God’s Presence on earth as being a שכן (a neighbour) to humanity, coming down into the nearest proximity to Man, but in no wise completely absorbing him. It would be the height of presumption to try and state anything positively about what נבואה and רוח הקודש really are, nobody who has not himself experienced it as a נביא could do that, but one is justified, nay in duty bound, to give consideration to every attempt which can be made to deduce from the word of God, at least what נבואה, what true prophecy is not, so that the idea of this fundamental fact can be kept clear from all those morbid and extraneous ideas with which people like to mix it up, with the idea of thus “sweeping away all difficulties”.

V. 14. Here, for the first time, we come across the name “Levi” as a description of character. To be a “Levi” one must have strength, courage and decisiveness. Your brother has all these. I should not have to spend much time were I to ask him, he has the words already at the tip of his tongue. He, too, knows about it and rejoices that you have received such a mission.

V. 15. et seq. Here we see at the beginning of the spiritual and intellectual upbuilding of our people a peculiar arrangement which endured during the centuries, viz., the separation of teaching from oratory, eloquence. Moses had not thought of his poor power of speech until God’s demand mentioned repeatedly קול האותות, a mission of eloquence which he felt had been denied to him. The use of words in the service of the Divine Teaching is, of course, a dual one, (a) to give a true, complete and exact rendering of the Lesson, (b) to render the contents of the Lesson in such a way that it will be understood, appreciated and taken to heart by the people. We find these two services completely separated also by our sages, those true followers of our Moses and Aaron. On the one hand we find the חכם who had to render the דין, the הלכה, precisely true and pure in the most concise form compatible with the understanding of those who were able to grasp it, and on the other hand was the מתורגמן who had to bring the halachic content of the speech of the חכם to the people in an explanatory form, which would appeal to them, make them understand it, and bring it impressively home to them. This division of the service of words is most important in insuring a true handing-down of the Word of God, of the Torah. There is the same relationship between the שמעתתא the content of the Law given clearly and precisely for the intellect, and the אגדתא the popular lecture, making appeal to feelings and sentiments, so that the halachic message gets accepted and carried out. To win the feelings and love of the people for the truths of the Torah, it is not sufficient merely to develop the theme of the actual teaching, one has to take into consideration the level of the education of the people one wishes to attract and impress. One must start off from the opinions, the ideas, views, desires and efforts which they already have, and build up from these the truths one wishes them to absorb. This is the “job” of an Aaron, a מתורגמן. This demands the gift of eloquence, of rhetoric. Whereas mere speech only requires the clear and distinct presentation of the truth one wants to teach, convincing eloquence wants to grip the heart of the hearer with its words, and to bring the hearer not only to the knowledge of the particular teaching, but to its acknowledgment and acceptance. An orator easily runs into the danger, as he starts from the point of view of his public, of bringing over something of this point of view into the Teaching he is trying to implant, in order to make it more feasible to his listeners, and so of losing some of its exactness, and of clouding its clearness, by the introduction of ideas which are really estranged from it, and of obtaining its acceptance by concessions. An orator frequently runs the danger of producing a great number of words which contain very little! An age which so often takes speech-making as the whole test of man, would be saved from a good deal of misery, if in its choice of leaders, it would follow the example of our ancestors, and separate the gifts of eloquence and חכמה which are only seldom found together in equal degrees. Our congregations would then have only חכמים at their head even if they were כבד-פה וכבד-לשון.

V. 18. Deep and thoughtful is the remark of our sages, that all living wanderings in this world are only הליכה לשלום, only a way towards peace, an effort for us to find harmony and accord with, and in, all conditions of life, but, in this world, not an entry בשלום into actual peace and harmony.

V. 19. Moses, at first wanted to go alone, he was quite ready to risk himself amongst his enemies, but not his wife and children, the more so, as no family is so exposed as where the head and protector is engaged in public service. But God ordered him to move entirely to Egypt and give up his home in Midian, he need no longer fear danger from his enemies.

V. 20. It appears Moses was in possession of one single beast of burden on which he had intended to ride. But now he mounts his wife and children על החמר and he goes on foot with the staff in his hand.

V. 21. Up till now God had only given Moses three אותות, but had not ordered him to do any one of them before Pharaoh. But if we realise the sense of these signs, and think how they are to be the guarantee that Moses is the messenger of Him Who has the power to change the very support and power of a man into a danger to his life, more, to change that which is most dangerous to men into an obedient and useful support, and to an adaptable tool for his power; at will to kill and revive the very hand itself that wields the staff, then God had given him with these signs all that was necessary for Pharaoh too. All the further miracles were nothing else but God calling up the staff of the might of Egypt to rise threateningly against Egypt, and finally to kill the hand itself that commanded these signs of Egypt’s might.

אות is a sign which is directed in the first place to the intelligence, to impart some knowledge, but after all, whether a man takes notice of it or not, is left to him. But מופת (the Hiphil of יפת, same meaning as פתה to be open for, response to an impression or a teaching, and in the hiphil, to impress somebody with a teaching, to make him responsive, impressionable for teaching), מופת is a sign ad hominem, which lays hold of a man to force him to take notice of the teaching which the sign gives. If all the drinking water in Egypt turns to blood, if vermin crawl over the King from all directions, these are מופתים which force the King to give attention. But if any single one of such “signs” were to persist, its endurance would make life unendurable, and the King would have to give in, not from conviction, but from necessity, fear, and despair. “But this shall not happen, I will let him have the strength and courage to endure the plagues, so that finally he comes to the conviction that God is the צדיק and he and his people are רשעים (Ch. 9,27). But even then he will not let the people go until after you have announced the death of his son. So that until you get the order for that announcement, you need not worry if your mission remains unsuccessful; only after this punishment which touches him at his nearest and dearest will he let the people go.”

V. 22.—23. בכר .בני בכורי ישראל related to בקר ,בגר ,פקר which all have the idea of being free. הפקר (also הבקר) ownerless, בגרת the stage at which a girl ceases to be under the complete control of her father. בוקר the time which allows all things to emerge clearly from the obscuring of night (לול — ליל). בקר. That part of one’s livestock that lives in the open and is not confined in folds. Now בכור is not free one, on the contrary, he should be the first servant, and we find בכור of animals and plants. The form is an active one not a passive. בכור is not the one who has become free, but the one who makes free (just asסגור is not “the closed” but that which closes). The forces of the mother’s womb which up till now have been bound, closed, are freed, opened by him. He is פטר רחם. He is not בכור for himself, but for what follows him. With him, the mother enters her calling as “mother”, for the future. He breaks the ice. His קדושה lies therein, that through him, the home first gets children, through him the רחם becomes קדוש and everything that passes through this portal afterwards is “holy to God”. A firstborn only becomes קדוש when he is born, ביציאתו מרחם; and also of one’s property it says וכל מקנך תזכר פטר שור ושה. “Your whole possession of herds shall be thought of, in the firstborn of ox and lamb”. So that when God speaks of Israel as בני בכורי it expresses the idea that with Israel, the mother womb of humanity is opened, with Israel is commenced the list in which the names of all the nations should appear as My sons. So that in your own name and in the name of the whole of humanity I come to you. Israel is My first but not My only child, it is only the first nation that I have won as Mine. (In the same sense our sages have taken ואבדיל אתכם מן העמים (Levit. 20,26) to mean כאדם שבורר וחוזר ובורר). Not as בני בכורי but as בני (V.23), do I demand freedom for Israel, as I would for any nation that gave itself to Me as My son. Israel is not the first in rank, but the first in time.

V. 24. ויפגשהו ה׳. The same God who had just sent him out with such a great message and on Whose mission he was just occupied, suddenly came against him and preferred to let him die. From what follows it is evident that Moses had neglected to circumcise his son, and that this was the cause of his life becoming suddenly endangered. Was he not embarked on a mission to accomplish the salvation of a people who whole meaning and importance in the world rests on the idea of Mila, and should he, just he, bring in the midst of this people an uncircumcised child! Rather let him die than let him introduce his mission with such an example. This is how it seems ויבקש must be understood, a word which is doubly difficult if applied to God. God does not wish the death of any man, and he whom God wishes to kill is dead. But taken this way (He prefers) this word tells us the important fact that God’s plans are dependent on no man, הרבה שלוחים למקום. No man, — not even a Moses — is indispensable to God. It disposes of the erroneous idea into which we might have been led by the previous verses, by the insistence with which God pressed Moses to undertake the mission. We also see here how God does not overlook any fault in His Messengers, not even in a Moses. Quite the contrary: בקרובי אקדש. That point is here, right at the beginning, made very clear.

V. 25. חתן דמים אתה לי. Words, to which, like all obscure phrases, the most diverse meanings have been given. They are usually taken to refer to the child, who, on the day of Mila, is called a bridegroom. It seems from the Gemara (Nedarim 32a) that this appellation was quite usual and customary, and then it would probably have its origin from this verse. But apart from the fact that if these words refer to the child, it is extremely difficult to give them appropriate sense, any explanation which refers the אתה to the child necessarily assumes that in this whole incident Zipporah’s attention and concern was concentrated on the child and not on Moses. As a matter of fact, the opinion in the Gemara to which we have referred, does take it that it was not Moses but the child that was in danger of its life.

But if we consider that the sentence ותאמר כי וגו׳ must be the reason for her preceding action, and consider further that the words in the next verse חתן דמים למולת spoken after the danger had pasesd, only differ from those spoken before, in the change of לי to למולת so that the ל- as a prefix must have the same meaning in both, only that in the second sentence whatever was referred to by Zipporah in the first sentence now refers to מולת, and if we let ourselves be guided simply by the words of the text, we arrive at the meaning being as follows: — Zipporah sees Moses in danger of life, sees him brought to the edge of the grave by God, on the very road on which God had sent him. She recognises that there can be only one cause for this, quickly catches the child up and circumcises him, places the severed foreskin at the feet of her husband, struggling in the throes of death, and says: “I do this, because you have become the “betrothed of Death” (more literally blood-guilt) for my sake, on my account! i.e., it is my fault, it was I who kept you back from fulfilling this duty, you did not insist on it out of love for me, and so on my account you became the “betrothed of the death penalty”.

The words of our sages justify us in taking this interpretation of Zipporah’s words. There has always been discussion as to whether this child was the first one, Gershom, or the second, Eliezer. Most opinions incline towards the latter and think that Eliezer had just been born, the Mila having had to be postponed on account of the journey, the incident then occurring at an inn near the end of the journey, where the first and immediate duty should have been the Mila, and the danger to Moses arose on account of procrastination then. But this inn could not have been so near the end of the journey. It was after this that Aaron met Moses at Horeb, and that, we are told, was a three days’ journey from Egypt. In the Mechilta on פ׳ יתרו R. Eliezer Ha-Modai actually states that Jethro would only consent to give his daughter to Moses on the condition that her first son should be allowed to remain dedicated to idolatry, and that this was the reason for Gershom remaining uncircumcised, and that was why Moses’ life was in danger. (Moses is then supposed to have agreed, trusting to his influence afterwards.) R. Eliezer takes even the name גרשום and the given interpretation of it, in connection with these circumstances. And such an excuse could indeed well fit in. He was a stranger in a land which was שום a desert, bleak waste to him. If this was really a fact we could take the word חתן literally. “For my sake you have become a ‘bridegroom of blood-guilt’ ” i.e., for my sake, when you became a bridegroom, you took on yourself a capital crime. But it is not even necessary to go as far as this, we need only think that Zipporah, who, after all was not a daughter of Israel (and at the beginning had possibly not yet completely absorbed all the ideas of Moses) found it hard to allow her child to be circumcised. In the force of circumstances, Moses gave in to a postponement.

But not thus was Moses to come to Egypt, and not thus Zipporah. Not in Midian, but on the journey — free from all influence of parents and relatives, alone, thrown back entirely on herself, Zipporah is to soar to the heights of Jewish Womanhood. Like an offering she lays the Orla of her child at the feet of her husband struggling in the throes of death, and says “I know full well that it was for my sake that you took on yourself such a grave capital crime!” But when the danger passed away, וירף ממנו, and she saw that she had done the right thing, then she said, “It was not for my sake that you betrothed yourself to Death but for the sake of all future מילות.” As is the case in all atoned-for sins, the loss to the prestige of the Mila-idea by Moses’ procrastination was much more than made up for, by its reinstatement when atoned for, as is worked out at length both in the Mechilta and in the Mishna in Nedarim 31b. Moses’ life would have been at its end if his child had not been circumcised! By this fact Mila becomes securely assured for all times. If this could not be overlooked even in a Moses and even at such a momentous time, who, unless he has thrown off absolutely everything, would dare to neglect Mila out of any consideration whatsoever. “Now, it is not I who get the benefit from it, but our combined error will benefit all future circumcisions and ensure their being meticulously respected.” Hence מולת in the plural.

V.29. This is the first time that the זקנים appear, and the only time that they are called זקני בני ישראל Otherwise they are always called זקני ישראל, those who on account of their spiritual abilities and maturity are suitable to represent and bear the community, Israel. At the moment, however, there was not yet a community, and so not yet any זקני ישראל, so Moses gathered the זקנים out of the בני ישראל. Only when they went under Moses’ guidance to represent with him the whole of Israel did they become זקני ישראל, that is why above in giving the commission Ch. III, V. 16 & 18 they are already so designated.

V. 31. ויאמינו. Believe or belief does not adequately express or translate אמונה. To believe always presupposes some lack of conviction. One does not easily sacrifice one’s property or one’s life for that which one only believes. האמין is more, האמין is to acknowledge that which is told us, as אמן as the firm fixed point on which we can depend, and on to which we can hold; that is to be our אומן to guide and educate us. The Divinity to which Israel gives the אמונה is the firm fixed starting point for everything else in their lives. Something which is sure and reliable and beyond all doubt. It gives its belief to anything else only if and when and as far as this other belief agrees with this one criterion of the Truth. We are told here that the people accepted two things from Moses, (a) that God considered that the time had arrived to “invest” (פקד) Israel with the fate that had been promised them, and (b) that God had seen their misery, that is to say that even if the real salvation should not come immediately, they could at least expect that they would be protected under God’s eye from fresh new injustice. ויקדו shorter Niphal form of קדה .ויקדו remaining upright and bowing with the head towards the ground, probably the expression of submitting the head, the thoughts, the intellect, to a higher power. השתחויה throwing the whole body prostrate on the ground i.e., placing yourself with your whole existence at God’s disposal. They did both.

V. 1. ואחד באו. It does not say ויהי אחר הדברים האלה ויבאו which would be the normal way of describing the historical progress of the event. For with this first appearance of Moses and Aaron before Pharaoh, nothing at all was achieved towards the redemption. It was, rather, just a preliminary effort, important to demonstrate what could be accomplished from a Pharaoh by way of simply putting the case before him. The whole story shows us how important and necessary the subsequent method by miracles was for all those who participated here, for Pharaoh, for the people, and even for Moses. They approached him with a demand which, had Pharaoh already attained a right conscience, would have been immediately granted. They did not ask to be given complete freedom, only for permission to celebrate a festival. They asked this in the name of ה׳, of the God on Whose breath every coming moment of our future, and the future of all mankind, hangs; and of אלהי ישראל Who is specially Israel’s God, Who has chosen just this people, just in their absolute lack of power and independence to reveal Himself in their fate and endurance as the sole Conquering Force in the history of Man.

— ויחגו from חגג from which we get חג the Festival. As חגג and חוג have the basic meaning of forming a circle, one is inclined to take the idea of חג Festival as a day which always recurs in the cycle of the year. But then חגג must refer to the Festival and not to the celebrants. The Festival, not the celebrants, recurs with the cycle of the year. So that it seems more likely that a Festival is called חג because the celebrants form a circle round the centre to which God has gathered them as a community about Him. חגג means, to gather in a circle round about God, and round about the Torah which He has set to be the centre point of our lives, so that we represent ourselves as the People of God and His Torah. That is why only those festivals are really called חג which can also be called רגל because they invite each individual to communal gathering round about the Torah of God deposited in the Temple. So, שלח וגו׳ “Let My people go, so that they may gather together in a circle round Me; and I do not ask for it here where they have fallen under your power, but far from you in the wilderness where their belonging to Me can freely be shown, also because there, their celebrations will cause no offence to you.”

V. 2. The Pharaohs were as agile and fine in discussion as any politician of our time. “You come to me in the name of your God, whom I am to obey, and freely give away what belongs to me, I do not know of such a god, and if you speak in the name of your people, in the name of some future high mission which this god has given over to you, well that also is not sufficient to make me give up even for a short time, anything which is mine.”

V. 3. So they make a fresh proposal entirely from his point of view and way of looking at things. “If you do not know ה׳ at least you understand if we speak of ‘the God of the Hebrews’. We, too, like the Egyptians have our God, and if He, forced by that Higher Power that rules over gods and man (see נקרא Ch. 3,18) appears here, down in this world, that is, as you know, of portentous significance, and He must be pacified. Otherwise, pestilence and sword may overtake us, and then not only we, but you and your people would be involved. So, for your own sake — you, too, fear the wrath of the gods — grant us the festival!”.

V. 4. Up till now Pharaoh has spoken; now, as King of Egypt, he addresses Moses and Aaron personally: “I know your type of old men quite well! Sacred Festivals! Revelations of gods! You know quite well that I know, and I know quite well that you know, that all such nonsense is only for the masses. Between mature educated men like you and me, all religion and worship of gods is simply a matter of policy. You must know quite well that I quite understand that all this is only demanded להפריע וגו׳, for the purpose of loosening and easing off the pressure of the labour. Up till now the people know nothing other than that they exist under pressure of the law, that hard labour is the natural lot to which they are born. Why do you put other ideas into their heads, why suggest to them that there is also a time when they need not work? This is not worthy of you, such old, mature, intelligent men.” Pharaoh chooses his words with great nicety. He very carefully refrains from speaking of סבלות when referring to the people. While Moses and Aaron, the nobles, the elite, may have סבלות, the cares and responsibilities of their calling, while his Egyptians, as we shall see further on, have the burdens and cares of their various professions, the labour under which the Hebrew slaves pant is merely מעשיו their duly appointed tasks. לכו לסבלותיכם “get about your own true serious occupations.” This stirring up of a people is unworthy of you, becomes you not at all!

V. 5. When they still stood expectantly there, he came down close to them and told them confidentially, that which, as Pharaoh, i.e., as King, there was no need to impart to them, what his real reason was for refusing them. The עם הארץ have now increased to such numbers — עם הארץ are not the plebians, the mob, the expression originally had no such deprecatory implication. In Levit. 4,27, it is used to designate the whole nation with the sole exception of the princes. In Levit. 20,4, it is even used for the Sanhedrin, the supreme body of the nation entrusted with the responsibility of the guarding and carrying out the Torah by the nation. So here עם הארץ does not refer to the slave-caste, the Jews, but to the real inhabitants of the country, the Egyptians. Pharaoh says: See, the country has now become so populous that the State can only carry on, if every single individual pulls his weight and works hard and unceasingly at his job. The whole stability of the country rests on the Egyptian people, compared to whose intellectual and industrial efforts the mere mechanical work of the slaves is of little account. Now consider what bad policy and what danger to the state your demand really entails. You ask for a whole week’s holiday for the Jews. This will naturally give our hard-worked Egyptian population the idea of having their week, or even weeks of holiday. This would bring chaos to the whole of the industry of Egypt and might even lead to the ultimate downfall of the State. That I can and will never allow. — הן, Ha! You had not thought of that!

V. 6. נגשׁ ,נוגשׂי to approach something or somebody — a general term — whether with friendly or unfriendly intentions, נגשׂ only in an unfriendly sense, to approach somebody especially with a demand, hence a personal creditor, נֹגֵשֹ. Here, those who had to see that the demands of the state on the enslaved people were duly complied with, — the “collectors”. שוטרים were their subordinates, who enforced the delivery of these demands. So, later in the Jewish state, was the relation of the שופטים to the שוטרים The שופט expressed the demands of the Law, the שוטר saw that they were carried out. (Hence the “instrument”, the document by means of which a creditor established his claim and enforced his payment is called a שטר). So also in Job 38,33 the influence of the heaven on the earth is called משטר, the office of a שוטר, it is only the executive instrument of a Higher Officer, the שופט כל הארץ.

V. 7. לא תאספון for תוסיפון. This seems to contain a nasty hint for the נוגשים and the שוטרים. The people are to go and look for the straw. “See to it that there is no אוסף, that they do not find the straw gathered together anywhere, that no humane soul מאסף gathers the straw in heaps for them.” Pharaoh wants, not only to intensify the labour, but also to keep the people scattered, so that none have the opportunity of putting such impractical ideas as “fearing God”, “sacred festivals”, etc. into their heads. — קשש, from which we get קש, related to גזז ,קצץ, to cut close, to cut off, hence קש pieces of straw cut off, cut short, stubble, in contrast to the proper straw, תבן with which they had hitherto been supplied. תבן ומספוא (Gen. 24,25 & 32) where תבן next to מספוא would refer to straw for bedding the camels. But it could also fundamentally be related to גשש, to grope around, from which קשש would then mean, seeking something to pick up, and קש, that which is picked up, gleaned, as גוש, something graspable would also be connected with לבנים — .גשש, possibly the basic conception is from לבן, white-heat, incandescent light, hence לבנה brick, as being clay burnt hard in glowing fire. לבן white, the completely unbroken ray of light.

V. 8. מתכנת not מספר, another nasty stab, מתכנת is not the number, the total sum, but the relative quantity. As תקן is the relative quality, and so תַקֵן means putting things in their right relationship, in right order, תכן is the numerical proportion of each part of a whole sum or mass. So we find it in connection with שמן המשחה and קטרת. So also in Ezek. 18,25, and Sam. I. 2,3. So also תכן here. Pharaoh does not say, the Jews have hitherto delivered so many million bricks monthly or even daily and that total must be kept up. That would have enabled them to make it possible by dividing the labour, some seeking the straw while the others fire the furnaces, or by gathering the straw one week and firing the bricks the next, no, מתכנת of the bricks, the daily quantity which each man had delivered hitherto must be kept up, this was the inhuman cruel order, demanding the impossible.

V. 9. תכבד וגי׳. I am not doing this as a piece of barbarity, also not at all in my own interests. I must see that the Jews get trained, become practical, they must be kept hard at their work, so that they find in it their natural activity; they must learn to be productive, to manufacture: ויעשו בה be no longer dreamy, meditative, ואל ישעו not let their minds wander in metaphysics, in impractical, useless things, like “spiritual”, “God”, “religion”, “fear of God”, etc., things which render the Jews useless to the State.

V. 11. גרע .אין נגרע וגו׳, to make less in number; כרע to make less in height, to kneel; ,ירַע (from which we get יריעות curtains) to make less in space, to restrict; קרע, to make less in substance and cohesion.

V. 12.—13. ויפֶץ active. Pharaoh had demanded — as many of the later Jew-laws did — that which was quite impossible. He who is looking for straw can not be making bricks and vice versa. The people accordingly adopted the only way out, some went out to seek straw while the others made the bricks. But this was not what Pharaoh wanted. Officers must be appointed to see that each individual delivers the same quantity that he had done hitherto.

אוץ to push forward to a purpose, from which we get עץ a tree, a combination of fluids and forces which are driven up on high, there to give nourishment to the fruit. Intellectually: to combine the factors for a purpose, to make a plan, עצה ,עוץ.

V. 16. וחטאת 3rd person feminine of the עבר instead of וחטאה, literally your poor (hence feminine) people who flog us by your orders, sin against us, but it is not really their fault, it is by your command.

V. 18. עבד ,עבדו to use one’s strength for the purposes of someone else. Further, to work the soil i.e., to use one’s strength to bring soil to its appropriate cultivation. The עבד physically and morally is partially absorbed by the personality of his master, hence the word is related to אבד עבט to become indebted to somebody, hence העביט to make somebody indebted by a loan, and עבט a pledge. The same conception as the legal term in Talmudic Hebrew שעבוד.

V. 20. פגע ב- to meet somebody by chance. פגע את usually to go directly to somebody. Moses and Aaron stood outside and waited for them to come out from their audience with the King. They had probably gone there with their full knowledge and consent.

V. 21. One can not blame these men who took on their own backs the strokes intended for their brethren — and thereby became the prototypes of those noble men of the future centuries of Galut, who, as elders of the community went to the stake on behalf of their persecuted brethren — one can not blame them if they lost faith in the mission of Moses and Aaron. באש the sensation which anything foul arouses in us. God, has so implanted the joy of life and living in Man that he has a natural feeling of disgust of anything dead or decaying. Hence באש is a usual expression for anything arousing this disgust. If we are conscious of having done wrong to somebody, we feel that this person must consider us morally foul, and that we have become נבאש disgusting to him. Related to this is בוש, to be ashamed of oneself, to have this feeling of moral foulness in oneself. This is the feeling of disgust which God has implanted in us at our own foulness which gives us no rest until we have freed ourselves from it. So here הבאשתם את ריחנו (See Gen. 8,21). You have made the idea of our existence foul in the eyes of Pharaoh and of his people, i.e., Pharaoh and his underlings now consider us a people to be avoided. Up till now we have been ill-treated, but, thanks to the benefit they have derived from us, they have at least made our continued existence possible in their own interest. But now, through your having awakened the idea of freedom in us, we appear to them as people who are useless to the state, who seek to shirk their duties, to make holiday, and so you have placed a reason in their hands to achieve our annihilation.

V. 22.—23. וישב. He thought he had utterly failed in his mission, and returned to the One Who had entrusted him with it. למה וגו׳, Two questions למָה and לָמה (see note on Ch. 32,11, 12). To what purpose hast Thou dealt this people whom Thou wouldst save, fresh misery which certainly does not further their deliverance. And why, for what reason, didst Thou send me, just the most incapable, who, from the very beginning felt his utter incapability, which now I see so fully confirmed. And all לעם הזה — what have they done that Thou shouldst heap such wretchedness on their heads? Although God had prepared him beforehand that Pharaoh would at first not listen to him, the people had understood him — and justifiably so — that at least a stop would be made to their maltreatment, and that at very least, they would receive no addition, no fresh ill-treatment. Were they not told (Ch. 4,31), וישמע העם כי פקד וגו׳, that the time of the Geula had arrived and that, כי ראה את ענים, even if the Geula would not occur so immediately, God had taken up their wretchedness, so that He would protect them from further ill-treatment, and now, just the opposite had occurred! והצל לא הצלת, not even from fresh and additional hardships hast Thou saved Thy People! עמך Thine own people! In the first question Moses says לעם הזה, quite apart from any special relation to You, simply as human beings, as a people, they are no worse than others, certainly no worse than the Egyptians, so why must just they suffer such unnameable misery? And since I stood up in Your name, they have become Your people, Your name is associated with their fate, and if Your name is not to be dragged down, and people are not to form false ideas of You, Your name should have sufficed at least to protect them from fresh distress! — הרעתָה You have caused this new distress, have not only allowed it, but actually by sending me, provoked it!

Let us visualise the actual position at which Moses now stood. His mission had completely misfired. Pharaoh had only become harsher and added derision to oppression. The people looked on Moses and Aaron as deceivers, or at best, themselves deceived. Moses himself had lost all confidence in himself, he would not be Moses if his mistrust of his own ability was not deepened, if he did not think that probably he was to blame, that he had bungled his mission by handling it the wrong way. What man would not have to have doubts of himself when he sees 600,000 innocent men cruelly tortured and cast down in utter despair through him!

V. 1. עתה, This is just the moment for which I was waiting. This complete lack of power, this despair must first be made evident, it must first be made clear that by ordinary human means nothing can be accomplished with Pharaoh. In the presence of the representatives of the people, Moses and Aaron must stand there completely stumped, and their complete inability to do anything clearly demonstrated, before the deliverance can commence, as the sole work of God. עתה now, the very last trace of any natural means of help has disappeared, it is now apparent that Moses is only the instrument of God, and the deliverance is stamped as the work of God, and God only. יד חזקה the higher irresistable Hand of God is to be apparent, and that is why this moment of utter despair could not be forgone.

יגרשם ,ישלחם, two apparently contradictory terms, ישלחם, against his will, ינרשם, against Israel’s will; both are to be fulfilled. In the moment of deliverance, it shall be with the free will of neither Pharaoh nor of the people — לא יכלו להתמהמה. Just as, at the moment of birth, mother and child are both, having no will of their own, under the working of higher power, so Israel right up to the very last moment, is to remain a slave, and it is to be evident that he is a slave, so that the history of his deliverance shines forth for all time, completely and solely as the work of God alone.
V. 2. אני ה׳. These two words contain the whole answer to Moses’ despair. In the previous verse Moses’ doubts had already been quietened by the general statement which is now developed in detail.

אלהים is the invisible One Who governs and directs the visible (אלה). He is the One Who has directed all that has visibly happened up till now. All the despair, all the degradation, the wretchedness and misery sprang naturally from conditions which God had allowed to arise. They were the natural outcome of Egypt’s degeneration and might, and Israel’s impotency and weakness. But, henceforth אני ה׳ מהוה חדשות, the One Who exerts His Will quite independently of existing conditions, even completely in spite of, or against, them. With this moment man is to enter a completely new world, a world which is to be independent of all those conditions which hitherto had governed the events of world history.

V. 3. And this new revelation of God had been prepared from the very beginning of Jewish history. All its development led up to this moment. “I was already ה׳, even when I only appeared to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob as אל שדי and did not allow My intended rule, as ה׳, to be apparent to them in the experiences of their lives. You are surprised that up till now things have become worse and worse, that even your having been sent has, up till now, only been a means to push the misery of your position right to the extremest limit — do you not realise then that your whole history up till now has been on a continuously downward grade? Abraham the נשיא אלהים amongst the nations — and Jacob, the poor slaving servant who first “had to slave to get his wife and then had to slave for his wife!” I could equally well have led you on an upward path. Instead of letting Abraham get a son in his hundredth year, I could have caused a family to be raised by him by the time he had reached seventy, and allowed his descendants to flourish in happy favourable circumstances to a powerful nation on its own native soil. But then that nation would not have been just the People of God, not עם ה׳, the nation that reveals God as ה׳. Then this nation would be no different from all other nations, would have developed like them from ordinary natural causes, like them, stand on material visible firm ground, would find the source of power and greatness in material power and greatness, and only aspire to the spiritual and moral, as far as their materialism left space for it, and as far as it fitted in with their materialism. But, in contrast to the other nations, this nation is to get its land, and have its foundation, solely in God, and in, freely of its own will, carrying out God’s Will, and only to have material substance and its own land, from and for this God and this aspiration. Remember, that the idea of a free almighty God, and of the resultant conception of Mankind being free, had been entirely lost; that men and nations were theoretically and practically sunk in materialism, denying the pure conception of the complete freedom of Will of Man. By the entrance of the “Abrahamitic Nation”, the old ideas were to be reawakened, and Mankind saved from the depressing effects of this materialism and lack of true freedom of will. That is why this nation had to start where other nations finish. It had to lie stricken to the ground, weltering in its blood, with nothing but despair and loathing of itself — בגעל נפשך — and only rise up into a People through God’s creative call, so that the very existence of this People proclaims to the world: אני ה׳! (Ezekiel 16,5).

That is why the leading up to this moment in which the utter helplessness of the descendants of Abraham reached its climax, — so necessary for the revelation of God as ה׳ — was, from the beginning, God’s plan when He guided the history of the Patriarchs on a downward path, and only revealed Himself to them as אל שדי as the “All sufficient One”, at Whose hand one can come successfully through all the vicissitudes of life.

לא נודעתי להם. Of course, we do find the name ה׳ already in the history and on the lips of the Patriarchs. But here it is by no means a question of a simple knowledge of this Name. דעת שם ה׳ is something very much deeper. Perhaps it will only be at the end of all the happenings of history, that we shall attain this. Isaiah speaking of this ultimate Geula says לכן ידע עמי שמי (Is. 52,6). It really means: to understand God’s methods of planning and ordering which are implied in this Name. An understanding that can only be completely achieved out of the collective experience of all the ages, and the Patriarchs stood at the beginning of the ages! So ושמי ה׳ לא נודעתי להם, “As that One Whose name is ה׳, they had not come to know Me.”

V. 4. But I was ה׳, I could have immediately established them and their descendants as the free, independent beginning of a nation when I first set up My bond with them, to give them the land in which they remained foreigners for the duration of their lives.

V. 5. (וגם ,וגם) And this bond was also very much in My mind when I allowed their descendants to endure the inexpressible wretchedness, progressing until their very existence was threatened, yea it was for the fulfillment of this bond that I allowed this to occur.

V. 6. Therefore: אמר לבני ישראל say to them (not דבר), explain it to them, put it to them so that it appeals to their minds and to their hearts — and note, not אל בני וגו׳, not directly to them, but לבני וגו׳, for them, tell it to the זקנים so that they can bring it home to the minds and hearts of the people — that אני ה׳, only as ה׳, in opposition to all existing circumstances, וגאלתי וגו׳ ,והצלתי וגו׳ ,והוצאתי וגו׳, and then ולקחתי וגו׳.

ארבע לשונות של גאולה, four phases in which the work of deliverance is presented, and which must be appreciated for the understanding of all that follows. והוצאתי ,והצלתי ,וגאלתי, are the freeing from the existing Galuth, ולקחתי is the destiny which is then to be allocated to them, the object of the whole deliverance.

The existing Galuth is here described in three phases עבדות ,סבלות and — as גאולה is mentioned without mentioning from what — a lack of גואל, a necessity for גאולה. In the ברית בין הבתרים this Galuth was predicted to Abraham as עבדות ,גרות, and ענוי. All these phases have been fulfilled; in the ענזי tormenting, the degradation, the deprivation of all joy of life; in the סבלות, in the degrading, mocking harshness with which Egypt heaped on their tasks. One can be an עבד without being oppressed with סבלות. One can be overburdened with סבלות without being an עבד; the עבדות, the deprivation of liberty in עבדות מצרים, in the caste of slaves to which Egypt had relegated them. גרות in the lack of a גואל which is exactly the condition of גרות. Later on in the Torah (Numbers 5,8) “the stranger” is described as גואל .אין לאיש גואל is the relative who takes the need of his relation as his own, and stands up for him. The stranger in ordinary countries has no one to take such a place. In any wrong done to the very lowest inhabitant, every other inhabitant sees an injury done to his own rights. He sees in this wrong a threat to his own claim for justice, and to his own feelings of security.
