But the fact that at this point they were also given the order to allow the Egyptians to present them with vessels of gold and silver, and the time for this could extend at latest until midday of the 14th, makes us presume that this order must have been given not long after the ending of the darkness. According to all this, the events seem to be grouped as follows: —

On Nissan 1st, the month was already appointed as the month of redemption, and orders given for taking the Pascal lamb on the 10th, and sacrificing it on the afternoon of the 14th, and the death of the firstborn on the night of the 14th—15th announced. But the instructions regarding the demanding gold and silver vessels, as well as the precise time of the slaying of the firstborn, was not yet given. Both these were only given after the darkness had ended. The darkness waned on the evening of the 13th. After the intense darkness of the plague the Egyptians greeted the ordinary darkness of night as the dawn. It was at this point that God spoke what is recorded in Ch. XI, vv. 1—3, regarding the demand for vessels, as well as fixing the time for the death of the firstborn at midnight precisely. This latter is not mentioned in vv. 1—3, as we get to know it immediately from Moses’ reply to Pharaoh. On that same evening Moses handed on the instructions to the people, as well as the information as to the precise time of the ultimate Egyptian calamity, and then after midnight he was summoned to the presence of Pharaoh. So that when Moses came to Pharaoh he had already had his complete instructions from God. This grouping of the events also clarifies a sentence in the Gemora (Berachoth 14a) which otherwise would seem rather extraordinary. There the expression כחצות הלילה אני יוצא וגו׳ (V.4) is discussed. If the כ can not be taken as an adverbial phrase of comparison (i.e., just like) it would comprise an unseemly lack of precision in transmitting a message of God. According to ר׳ זירא Moses purposely used this indefinite expression (he takes the כ really to mean, “about”) to allow for the possibility of error in the calculation of the Egyptian astronomers as to the exact occurrence of midnight. But רב אשי says: “בפלגא אורתא דתליתר נגהי ארבסר הוי קאי והוי קאמד משה לישראל אמר הקב״ה למחר כחצות הלילה כי האידנא אני יוצא בתוך מצרים״ exactly at midnight of 13th—14th Moses said these words to Israel: — thus hath God spoken: “Tomorrow just at this same moment of midnight will I go forth into the land of Egypt.” The word ישראל would seem remarkable, as apparently these words in V. 4 were said to Pharaoh. But, as we have shown, before he had been summoned to Pharaoh, Moses had already given Israel this information, and Moses’ reply to Pharaoh (according to this interpretation) would run: — “You have spoken quite correctly, I shall not come before you again, for God has already said that when, as now, midnight occurs again, I shall go out in Egypt and all the firstborn sons will die”. The reason that R. Ashi prefers to take these words as a repetition of what Moses had said to Israel in preference to R. Zeira’s theory that Moses actually stood before Pharaoh at midnight exactly and said to Pharaoh “Tomorrow at this very time etc.” may well be, that after three days of such complete darkness when there was not the slightest differentiation between day and night, and this condition ending at night, the bewildered Egyptians would hardly know at what time of the day or night they really were. The Yalkut, however, has the rendering of R. Ashi’s dictum: — והכי קאמר להו משה and not לישראל, and according to that version, Moses did stand before Pharaoh at midnight exactly and announced to him, כחצות וגו׳ “Just at this very time tomorrow etc.”.

We can quite well understand why the first half of Ch. XII, as well as the first three verses of Ch. XI, are out of the chronological order. The whole run of the plagues with their result on Pharaoh is first related, and then the story switches over to Israel, to tell us of their preparations for the exodus. Hence Ch. XII, is of necessity retrogressive. But what is related in Verses 1—3 of Ch. XI, occurred practically at the same time as Moses was summoned to Pharaoh, it immediately preceded the summons and is interposed in the middle of Moses’ reply to Pharaoh in order to justify and vindicate his reply.

V. 1. ויאמר ה׳ אל משה. At the same time as Pharaoh had him called. See previous note. The contents of V.2 & 3 tell us that these words were not said (as might seem to be the case from the context) while he was before Pharaoh, as this instruction, as well as the opinion the Egyptian people had of Moses and the Jews, has absolutely nothing whatever to do with what Moses had to say to Pharaoh. — ישלח אתכם מזה does not mean “will let you go to serve your God” but clearly, “will send you away from here never to return”. That lies in the מזה, and to make it clearly definite is confirmed by the following כשלחו כלה. For שׁלח כָלָה means to send you away so that he is finished with you, has nothing more to do with you, that, as far as he is concerned, it is as if you no longer existed. Compare the expression in Jer. 5,18 et seq. אעשה אתכם כלה.

V. 2—3. The statement made in the preceding verse that Pharaoh will drive you out for ever is a further proof of the correctness of the meaning we gave above (Ch. 3,22) of שאל מאת (not מעם) being to ask for something as a gift, not as a loan. — נא ;דבר נא always implies a certain reluctance, some opposition on the part of the person addressed. See note on Gen. 12,13. אמרי נא etc. The people had just proved their sterling moral quality in the most brilliant manner. For three days long their oppressors, chained in blindness, were completely helpless in their power; for three days long all their treasures lay open in their houses, and no Jew took the opportunity to take the slightest advantage either against their persons or their possessions. At the moment when they recovered the use of their eyesight and found all their possessions untouched, God made this recognition of the moral nobility of the Jews at last overcome the Egyptians’ antipathy to the Jews. This moral greatness on the part of his people, more than all the miracles he performed, made the man Moses great in the eyes of the Egyptians. It must indeed have gone against the grain of Moses and the people to risk to some extent losing this moral victory by such requests. But it was the Will of God, that His people should not go out in poverty — we must remember that all the previous generations that had lived in slavery had been in no position to acquire even the smallest possessions for themselves. God wanted the first foundation stone of the prosperity of His people to be acquired and consecrated through the recognition of their moral greatness by those who had hitherto despised and looked down on them. Hence this נא. Added to this, time was pressing. There were but twelve hours to the next midday. Hence דבר נא באזני העם persuade them, urge them to take this step. So, at the very time that Moses was standing before Pharaoh, and Pharaoh was threatening him with death, outside, the people were already preparing for their departure, and Moses and the people were celebrating the great moral victory they had achieved over their masters and oppressors, who, by their ready and generous acquies cence to their requests seemed to be moved to make some slight atonement for their past behaviour. From this response of the Egyptians we learn the high moral meaning of the promise, ואחרי כן יצאו ברכוש גדול.

V. 4. אני יוצא; as, כי הנה ד׳ יוצא ממקומו לפקוד וגו׳ (Is. 26,21), or כי או יצא ה׳ לפניך להכות וגו׳ (Sam. II. V.24) et alia. It always designates a direct intervention by God for the destruction of an opponent. What had hitherto occurred in Egypt was brought about by His messengers, who were at the same time to be heralds to give the people some idea of God, and threateningly to announce His arrival; they were אותות ומופתים. Now He Himself comes forth in His opposition to Egypt, and that immediately spells the death of Egypt’s dearest and most prized class. אני, from אנה: spoken by anybody, always means that the speaker feels himself in opposition to the one addressed, whereas אנכי implies that the speaker ecompasses, carries the other with him.

V. 5. This was the moment announced right at the beginning in Ch. IV, vv. 22—23 בני בכרי ישראל וגו׳; שלח בני וגו׳; הנה אנכי הרג את בנך בכרך not out of hatred of your son, but to effect the salvation of My son. In the death of your son you will at last learn to estimate My feelings at the mishandling of My son.
V. 6. The centuries-long mishandling, the murder of the Jewish children, left them silent. Now there will be an outcry. — נהיתה: to be brought about by something.

V. 7. יחרץ. Right down to the animals, not only will nobody do any harm to Israel, but no inimical action — though perfectly harmless, like the barking of a dog — will be done against them. Right down to the animals all will be filled with silent respect for the Jewish people. Quite similarly — and there not referring merely to dogs — we find in Joshua 10,21: לא חרץ לבני ישראל לאיש את לשונו.
V. 8. צא. This expression, too, indicates a definite departure rather than a temporary excursion to the wilderness to celebrate a festival.

V. 9—10. These two verses bring the story back to the point at which the miracles of God had not yet accomplished their purpose and the beginning of the final salvation not yet announced. After completing the narrative of the whole series of signs and wonders which were to reveal God to the Egyptians, and have their effect on them and on Pharaoh, we are now taken over to the world of the Jews, and informed of the preparations which were being made there for the night of deliverance. The story goes back to the moment after the plague of locusts, before the commencement of the darkness. Pharaoh had at last felt himself compelled to the admission חטאתי לה׳ אלקיכם ולכם. But with the cessation of the plague this better tendency had also disappeared. Pharaoh remained in his old obduracy and did not let the people go.

V. 1—2. Then, i.e., while still in the land of Egypt, God gave Moses and Aaron a new mission to their own people, whose success was to be made more certain. Up till then, Moses and Aaron had been the messengers of God to Pharaoh, on Israel’s behalf. Henceforth, they are to be God’s messengers to Israel; and this mission is in close relation to their mission to Pharaoh. Up till now their vocation had been to perform אותות ומופתים in Egypt. These were to bring the Egyptian people back to what they had completely lost — a consciousness of man’s duty to God and to his fellow-man, and to try and bring about a change, a fresh start, a rebirth in Pharaoh. But erroneous ideas and depravity had held sway for too long over this heart for these means to work the change. Only by the influence of dread and terror could submission to the will of God be forced upon him. Released from this dread, his heart remained in its old hard unimpressionable state. God took this point up, and — so that erroneous ideas and depravity which even terror-bringing miracles would not be able to eradicate should never embed themselves in the hearts of what was to become His people — He began the construction of the inner life of His people by the institution of an אות. This regular, periodically recurring sign was always to draw the looks and the thoughts of the people afresh up to Him. It was to summon them to ever fresh rejuvenation out of the darkness of error and depravity, and so to ensure a constant rebirth to truth and purity that would for ever protect Israel from Egyptian spiritual and moral insensibility.

Just as God told Noah to turn his looks away from the earth which had just been regiven to Man, and direct them to heaven, and, showing him the rainbow, said זאת אות הברית, this is to be the sign, the guarantee, of My covenant with the new future which I promise to humanity, in the same way, in Egypt, at the threshold of the new Jewish future, He called Moses and Aaron into the open, showed them the silver crescent of the new moon, and said: “This renewal is to be to you a beginning of New-moons” (literally a beginning of renewals, of revivals), “and it, the month that is beginning with it, is to be for you the first of the months of the year!” There are two מצות contained in this verse, (a) קידוש החדש על פי ראית הלבנה בחידושה, fixing the beginning of the month with the new moon becoming visible, and (b) to make the order of the months of the year start with Nissan, the month of the Redemption.

ראש חדשים cannot mean the head, the first of the months. Firstly this would then be completely identical with the second half of the verse, i.e. ראשון הוא לכם, and there would be no reason at all for the repetition. Moreover, ראשי חדשים wherever it occurs elsewhere, never has the meaning of the first month, but always the first of, or beginning of, the month. So that, החדש הזה can not mean “this month” but “this renewal of the moon.” Actually the word חדש primarily has not the meaning of ‘month’ but “beginning of the month” e.g., חדש ושבת ,מחר חדש ,עולת חדש בחדשו etc. The meaning month is only a secondary, derived one. So that when God referred to the freshly-appearing light of the moon, and said החדש הזה לכם וגוי it meant what our tradition takes the words to mean: viz.: כזה ראה וקדש (Rosh-Hashana 20a). “Look out for this reappearance, and consecrate the beginning of your months.” As, however, the order does not begin: ויאמר וגו׳, דבר אל כל עדת בני ישראל וגו׳, but the command about the beginning of the month was given primarily specially to Moses and Aaron, and only the following commands about the Pesach offering, V. 3, are very markedly introduced with the words דברו אל כל עדת וגו׳, herewith is laid down in the written word the tradition that was given verbally, viz., that the fixing and consecrating of the beginnings of the months is placed only in the hands of the very highest authorities of the Torah who took over the position of Moses and Aaron, to whom had been said: החדש הזה לכם on which the Gemora (R. H. 22a 25b) says: עדות זו תהא מסורה לכם ,לכם.

From this fact, that it is commanded to fix the beginnings of the months according to the actual sight of the recurrence of the new light, מצוה לקדש על פי ראיה, those who do their utmost to lower the status of the old Jewish past in the opinion of the contemporary present, have made the absurd assertion that the Jews lacked the astronomical knowledge of the course of the moon, that it was only centuries later that they acquired this knowledge from the Greeks, and that until that time, they had to satisfy themselves with the crude emergency-method of watching for the appearance of the new moon each month. We call this an absurdity, because it is obvious that no definite reckoning of time could be based on actually seeing the new moon; in cloudy seasons many weeks would pass without such a sight being possible, moreover the mere waiting and watching for the occurrence implies a calculation of the time when the possibility of seeing it would occur. As a matter of fact the תורה שב״פ (Rosh-Hashana, 23, 24, 25) tells us that calculation was at the base of the fixation of the moment of the possibility of the new moon being visible, and that is was on the result of such calculation that the evidence of the witnesses had to be controlled; also that if no witnesses turned up on the 30th of the month, the 31st became the 1st of the next month without the new moon having been seen. Again, David could say to Jonathan, הנה חדש מחר, so that he knew the day before that the morrow would be the 1st of the month (Sam. I. 20,5). More, it is clear from ויהי ממחרת החדש השני (ibid. v. 27) that already in Saul’s time two days ראש חדש were kept, just as we do now, an institution that can only be based on the reckoning of the path of the moon, making the previous months alternate between מלא and חסר. It is impossible to take the שני there to refer to the 2nd of the month, for the whole arrangement depended on the fact that the King held a special banquet to celebrate ראש חדש at which David’s absence would be conspicuous. But it refers to the second day of “New Moon”, as יונתן translates it: והוה ביומא דבתרוהי דהוא עיבור ירחא תנינא, and similarly in V.34: ולא אכל ביום החדש השני, he translates it ביום עיבור ירחא תנינא. (It is striking that ת״י calls the thirty-first-day יום עבור, elsewhere this name is only given to the thirtieth day. See R.H. 19b & Rashi on ליל עבורו there & 25a).

Even without all this, a consideration of the laws and ordinances concerning “the consecration of the beginning of the month”, the ceremony of קידוש החדש, shows us that the meaning and object of this law must be something quite other, quite higher than an astronomically exact regulation of the reckoning of time; that, although indeed the most exact astronomical calculation does lie at the base of this rite, it is not the planetary occurrence that is to fix the beginning of our months, or to which the celebration of our ראש חדש refers.

Let us summarise some of the striking features: The whole procedure of the ritual of the קידוש החדש immediately raises it from an ovation to the planetary phenomena of Nature, and stamps it as pertaining to the realm of human social life. “משפט״ is the character of the procedure, and accordingly it can only be done in the daytime, and must even — in characteristic contrast to civil processes — be completed in daytime (R.H. 25b). It can only be performed by a bench of three competent judges, and again in comparison to civil processes, these three must possess a high degree of speciality. Further, whereas to establish any factual condition one witness is sufficient, עד א׳ נאמן באיסורים, here, as in all matters pertaining to persons, two witnesses are necessary (R.H.22a). But that it is not at all the planetary occurrence in the sky that fixes the beginning of the month, so that all that would be necessary would be for the law-officers to take note of such occurrence, is clearly evident from laws such as ראוהו ב״ד וכל ישראל נחקרו העדים ולא הספיקו לומר מקודש עד שחשכה הרי זה מעובר (ibid. 25b). This refers to the case where on the 30th, while yet daytime, the new moon is visible and has been seen by the judges, the court, and by all Israel; or of the case where the thorough examination of the witnesses who come and testify that they have seen it has been satisfactorily completed by day, but in either of these cases, if night has fallen before the judges have pronounced their מקודש “it is consecrated”, then the 30th is not the 1st of the month, in spite of the fact that the new moon has actually been seen by everybody, or alternatively has been vouched for, and completely confirmed and established, the new month only starts on the 31st. This is striking evidence that it is not the actual condition up above, but the consecrating declaration of the representatives of Israel that is the decisive factor on which the beginning of the month depends. This, the fact that the nation itself fixes the date of the beginning of the months is what the command refers to when it says: אלה מועדי ה׳ מקראי קדש אשר תקראו אתם במועדם (Levit. 23,4), and it seems to us that it is just the idea of מועד which lies at the root of all these ordinances. For ר״ח is also called מועד, more, as we shall see, it is just ראש חדש which has the broadest and most comprehensive idea of מועד, without having, like the other Moadim, at the same time reference to historical and seasonal events.

מועד. (from יעד, to call a meeting, related to יחד) means a place fixed for an assembly, (hence אהל מועד ,ונועדתי לך שם) or a time fixed for such an assembly. Here, the latter. מזעדים are times fixed for our meeting with God. This meeting, to speak in terms of human beings, is to be voluntary on both sides. It is not to be the master ordering the attendance of his servants, it is to be God, Who wishes His people to come to Him. He accordingly specifies the time, about which this “coming-to-Him” is to take place, but leaves the fixing of the exact day to His people, so that this “coming together” shall be a mutual arrangement. We emphasize this “mutual”, on both sides. Were the beginning of our months, and consequently, the dates of the Moadim to be fixed exactly by the astronomical phases of the planets, so that, for example, the phase of the moon automatically made ראש חדש and the Moadim, then we and our God too, would appear to be bound by the blind and unalterable laws of Nature, and our Moed of the New Moon above all would give an impetus to the idolatry of a Cult of Nature. But that is exactly what it should NOT be. This erroneous idea which could so easily be formed, is to be emphatically and energetically countered. It is not to be the conjunction of the moon with the sun; not the moon receiving the rays of illumination afresh, that is to induce the beginnings of our months, it is not that ,to which our celebration of New-Moon is to be dedicated. But each time the moon finds the sun again, each time it receives its rays of light afresh, God wants His people to find Him again and to be illuminated with fresh rays of His light, wherever and however, in running their course, they have had to pass through periods of darkness and obscurity. The moon, finding itseslf again in conjunction with the sun is only to be a model for our finding ourselves again with God, the rejuvenation of the moon a picture of, and an incentive to, our own rejuvenation. Moed is literally conjunction.

So that it is not the astronomical procedure nor astronomical calculation, but we ourselves, we have to make our “חדש״ and to fix the day of our “מועד״, our finding ourselves with our God. Hence the command מצוה לקדש ע״פ ראיה, that the objective astronomical certainty is not sufficient, but the subjective taking note of it is what is desired. This also makes the reason for the דין clear, that only אם נראה בזמנו is the positive declaration מקודש essential, i.e., that it is only when the consecration of the new moon coincides with its actually having been seen, that the consecration of Rosh Chodesh is dependent on the announcement of the representatives of the nation, for it is then primarily that our festival of the New Moon requires to be guarded against the appearance of Nature Cult. But when the month is מעובר, when the day of the actual appearance of the New Moon has already passed, this necessity is obviously not so urgent (ibid. 24b). Finally this also explains the whole deep idea underlying the sentence מעברין את החדש לצורך (ibid. 20a), that there was a possibility, which was often realised, of the representatives of the people simply shifting the day of Rosh Chodesh to the 31st — although the new moon had been seen on the 30th — for the convenience of the people e.g., so that י״כ and שבת should not fall on consecutive days. Above all, it explains the dicta and the דין (on the verse referred to above, Levit. 23,4) viz., אתם אפ׳ שוגגין ,אפ׳מוטעין ,אתם אפי׳ מזידין, if, by error or even intentionally, or misled by false witnesses (who are subsequently found out) the 1st of the month has been declared on the wrong day, nevertheless Yom Kippur and the other festivals are to be kept in accordance with this erroneous declaration; אין לי מועדות אלא אלו. God only recognises those “Moed-days” which have been fixed by the representatives of His people. חידוש הלבנה is to be nothing else but an incentive to our חדשים. Hence also the special essential meaning of י״ט שני just for times which are — unfortunately — בקי בקביעא דירחא. For only the most narrow-minded ignorance can find it a matter for jubilation that we are בקי בקביעא דירחא, that we have no longer any doubt as to the exact date of each ראש חדש. This certainty of ours is solely due to the sad fact that in our Galut we have no national representatives authorised by סמיכה, who, על פי ראיה are empowered to fix the ראש חדש by their consecration, on our behalf. But through this, our new moon festivals and our moadim would lack that essential character which makes them into our new moons, our Moadim, had not the wise foresight of our last national representation in the person of Hillel the Younger fixed the beginnings of all the months for the whole period of our dispersion until our future restoration, by the adventitious aid of intercalation of an occasional day in a month, and a month in a year. But just because during this time of Galut, the beginnings of our months, and hence the dates of our Moadim, being fixed beforehand, appear to be entirely dependend on an unalterable fixed calendar, our festivals would be in danger of entirely losing the imprint of free choice in the fixation of the festivals which should lie between God and His people, did not the second day of Yomtov keep alive the recollection of the original קידוש על פי ראיה, and the idea of the fixing of our festivals by the people. For these second days had their origin in those better times when we still had a national centre, and still had our national representatives for whose decision all outlying communities had to look and wait, before they could fix the date of their festivals. It was just in this looking and waiting, that these communities recognised themselves as members and part of a great whole, and could feel that their festivals were times arranged freely by themselves for the coming together of God and His people. Those communities where the messengers from the centre could not reach in time, and who were accordingly in doubt as to which day had been fixed, kept both days. And the members of our last representative assembly indeed knew well what they were doing, when at the time that they fixed the calendar for the whole of the future years of Galut, שלחו מתם they sent a message to all those communities who, hitherto, had had to keep the two days of Yomtov, saying to them: — הזהרו במנהג אבתיכם בידיכם “meticulously keep up the custom of keeping two days which you have taken over from your fathers” זמנין דגזרו המלכות גזרה ואתי לקלקולי, “in the stress of times of oppression and persecution, the true knowledge of the Torah and also of the way we are now fixing the calendar may become lost, you will then fix new moons and festivals according to dead reckoning or by the actual sight of the moon, no longer know that it is not astronomical calculations, nor the actual occurrence, but the consecrating fixation by the representatives of Israel that makes new moon and festival into Jewish Moadim”. It is therefore, a profound truth that for Israel in Galut, it is only the second day of Yomtov that ensures the first day its sacred Jewish character.

It is only after all this, that the words החדש הזה לכם ראש חדשים get their real meaning. “This renewal of the moon shall be a beginning of renewals for you.” i.e., noticing, realising, the fresh birth of the moon shall induce you to achieve a similar rejuvenation. You are to fix your moons, your periods of time by taking note of this ever fresh recurring rejuvenation. It does not say החדש הזה ראש חדשים, but לכם וגו׳, it is not a question of the actual months but of our months. That is also why, as ר׳ עובדי׳ remarks in his commentary on הל״ק ה״ח לרמב״ם we find new moons and festivals referred to as חדשיכם and מועדיכם whereas the definitely fixed seventh day is never called שבתכם. That is also why it does not say ראש החדשים, as immediately following it says חדשי השנה, but ראש חדשים; for it is new, fresh Jewish months that are to be made, whereas the Year, as we shall see, remains the old one.

So the Jewish consecration of the New Moon is an institution for the periodical fresh spiritual and moral rejuvenation of Israel by finding itself again in conjunction with its God. Our sages put the whole idea in pithy brevity in their explanation of החדש הזה לכם by דוגמה לכם, this renewal of the moon gives you “your model”; and they give the meaning of ראש חדש — which literally finds its expression in the קרבן מוסף — as being concentrated in what they explain to be the goal that the שעיר ר״ח attempts to attain, viz. לכפר על טומאת מקדש וקדשיו שאין בה ידיעה לא בתחלה ולא בסוף: to work against all our estrangement from all holiness and holy ideas into which we have unconsciously drifted, and which we ourselves would not notice. Without this regularly bringing ourselves back into communion with our God, without this regular monthly being radiated afresh by the light and warmth of His spirit, we should always slide farther and farther from Him, always be getting more and more estranged from Him; quite unconsciously and without our noticing it, our natures would become less and less responsive to the light of His spirit, our natures would become darker and darker until — like Pharaoh — our hearts would become so חזק and כבד that even the most startling אותות and the most affecting מופתים would not achieve the rebirth, the rejuvenation of our inner selves.

But the Jewish idea of כפרה comprises not only the spiritual and moral rebirth of our inner selves, but along with it a fresh arrangement of our external, our social and national conditions. The rebirth of our inner selves must come first, the other then results, both lie in one hand, the Hand of our God, and in our voluntary finding ourselves again with Him, both are assured.

So חדש proclaims salvation from sin and evil, and that is why this institution stands at the commencement of the building up of our nation. The truth which it teaches forms the foundation stone of our Jewishness, and it is this which differentiates it most sharply from all paganism. The heathen knows no חידוש, not in the world, not in humanity, not in his gods, nor in the powers he places above men and the world. To him everything is bound by cast-iron necessity. To him all todays are evolved from yesterdays, and every tomorrow must with absolute certainty follow from today. Just as he denies the יש מאין, the free creation by the free will of a creator, so for him there is also no יש מאין in the moral nature of Man, no יש מאין in the fate of Man. Guilt and evil must for ever and ever beget only guilt and evil. For him nothing of godlike freedom dwells in the human breast, for him no free God reigns in and over the world, everything swims down the stream of blind unalterable necessity, all freedom is but an illusion, everything new is only that which existed in the old!

Therefore, בארץ מצרים, in the land of the most consistent paganism, in the land in which this pagan immutability extended even into the state system of social life, and created the chains of caste, in Egypt, God called the future leader of His people out into the open, showed him the narrow crescent of the moon struggling out of complete darkness into new light, and spake “This is to be your model”. Just as it, bound by physical laws, rejuvenates itself, so are you, but of your own free will, to create your own rejuvenations. Whenever it occurs it is to remind you of your own possibilities of rejuvenation, and, inasmuch, as I rejuvenate you, and you rejuvenate yourselves, you are, moon-like, to pass across the night sky of the nations, and proclaim everywhere the teaching of “חידוש״, this teaching that God has given Man the possibility of always being able to start afresh, that his whole moral and physical fate is entirely in his own hands. This חידוש is, moreover, nothing else than the direct corollary of the 4-lettered name of ה׳, the God Who has the complete mastery to arrange every coming moment of the future, by which name the Jew silently within himself worships his God.

ראשון הוא לכם לחדשי השנה. This is a second separate command — to begin the sequence of the months with Nissan. שנה, Year, from שנה to repeat, such a cycle of days after which the same “day of the world” recurs, i.e., after which the earth again stands in the same position in the heavens, and in consequence the whole seasonal character of the earth repeats itself. With the passing of a month, it is only a similar phase of the moon that recurs, but the whole of the rest of the character of the days in each month is quite different from that of the preceding one. Here it does not say חדשי שנה as above it says ראשי חדשים, but חדשי השנה, not months of a year but months of the year. This implies that the old year of the world goes on, but that within it a new cycle of months is to begin. And actually thereby we do get a double cycle of time. A ‘world year’ beginning of Tishri — henceforth to be the seventh month — and a Jewish year which is henceforth to begin with Nissan, the month of the redemption from Egypt. The fact that, although the sequence of months begins with Nissan, the year is to begin and and at Tishri, is taught from the expression in Exodus 23,16: חג האסיף בצאת השנה, “The Harvest Festival at the outgoing of the year”, or from חג האסיף תקופת השנה, “The Harvest Festival at the change of the year” (Ex. 34,22). So we get two beginnings of the year, just as we know of two beginnings of the day. We have a year which begins with the Autumn, and although it knows Spring and Summer, ends again in Autumn; and we have a year which begins in Spring, and although it knows Autumn and Winter, always ends in Spring again. Similarly, we have a day which begins at night, and although it rises to Morn and Midday, ends again with Night, and we have a day that begins with Morn and although it sinks to Eve and Night, ends again with a fresh Morn. Outside the מקדש, the Sanctuary, the day begins and ends with Night, within the Sanctuary the day begins and ends with Morn. The year of the earth, its products, as well as all association and dealings with all goods of the earth — לשנים ,לשמיטין ,ליובלות ,לנטיעה ,לירקות ,למעשר בהמה — are reckoned from Autumn to Autumn. Israel’s years, the years of its festivals and its Princes, count from Spring to Spring. Here we have an exhortation on our double nature, worked into the log-book of our lives. Everything pertaining to the earth is born bare and without blossom out of the night, and even though it rises to the brightness of midday and riches of blossom and fruit, sinks bare and blossomless to the night of its grave. Everything holy and Jewish has its origin in Light and Life and even though it has to meet and contend, in running its course, with Night and Death, out of darkness and death it struggles back to Light and Life, and what was born out of morn and spring, ends again at dawn, rejuvenated to a new Spring.

V. 3—6. עדה) ,עדת from יעד to fix, to appoint) a society united by their common calling, a community. בית אבות the parental home which can comprise several families which are all united in attachment to a common ancestor. So בית אב can comprise a whole tribe (Numbers 17,17). בית an individual home. — ואם ימעט הבית מהיות משה. It is difficult to find an analogous phrase where היות מ- means to have part in anything or belong to anything. Added to which, no home can be too small to take part in a lamb, it can only be too small to have a lamb to itself. If that is what is meant here it should say מהיות לו שה. Besides this is already expressed by the preceding שה לבית אבות which implies that it is permitted for several families to unite in such cases. But היות מ- means, to be far from something rather than to belong to something, and ואם ימעט וגו׳ means if the household becomes too small מהיות משה by some of its members not wanting to join that lamb, and this expresses the Halacha בא הכתוב ללמדך שלעולם נמנין על הפסח ומושכין ידיהם ממנו עד שישחט (Mechilta on Pesachim 89a). “This verse comes to teach us that one can always join in, or withdraw from, the Paschal lamb until it is actually slaughtered”. That is also why it does not say: — ואם מעט הוא הבית וגו׳ but ואם ימעט וגו׳. It is nevertheless possible that the מ of משה is a productive one i.e., the house becomes too small to come from a lamb, in which case the offering is looked on from the point of view, that it, the offering, is the basic cause from which the home results, which, as we shall see, is completely in accordance with the meaning of the Pessach offering, especially the אכילת פסח, the eating thereof, about which it is primarily speaking here. [במכסת נפשות, as also במכסת הערכך (Levit. 27,23) and מֶכֶס לה׳ (Num. 31,18). As we do find the form מֶמֶר ליולדתו (Prov. 17,25) from מרר, and the תכֹסוּ which immediately follows definitely comes from כסס, then מֶכֶס and מִכְסָה could also very well come from כסס. But the meaning of this root is not simply to count, but to subtract and to add, i.e. by counting to take away from one sphere and add it to another sphere, hence levy, tax, tribute. The word is related to גזז and to קצץ so that it has a basic meaning of cutting off, of separating, the usual basic conception in Hebrew of allocating. From which we get also כוס, a vessel of an allocated quantity, in which the quantity allocated to each one is handed in contrast to גביע and קובעת which designate the larger drinking vessels and which relate to כוס as a bottle to a glass. So here: If, by withdrawal from participation in the lamb, the household becomes too small, let him and his neighbour join by adding of persons i.e., the neighbour gives over some of his people to make up the requisite household]. אשי לפי אכלו וגו׳ each, according to his eating capacity i.e., according to their ability to eat from the lamb, are you to reckon up to the number of persons partaking of any particular lamb. Only such persons as can and should eat from the lamb can take part in it, and only for such is it to be fixed beforehand. Hence the dictum: — שחטו שלא לאוכליו ושלא למנוייו פסול (Pesachim 61a).

ולקחתי אתכם לי לעם was what God had declared to be the positive object of the Geula from Egypt. Not a “congregational church”, in which to pray to Him, was what He wishes to create, but an עם, a people, a nation, a “social” community, a state, should arise from this redemption, whose whole “social” existence was to have its root in God, be built up by Him, rest on Him, be arranged and constituted by Him, and be dedicated to Him. With the קרבן פסח God laid the foundation stone of this edifice.
Let us see how God built up a state.

The people with which He build it were slaves; as such, they had no personality, no property, no family, ,עבד ,גופו קנוי לרבו ,עבד ,אין לו חיים עבד ,מה שקנה עבד קנה רבו by His dictum ויקחו להם איש, God gave them, in full sight of their masters (on the 10th of Nissan one day before the darkness commenced) Personality and Property. By the law that one was to “take” for several, and then also to “slaughter” for several, He established immediately the “equality” of all in the eyes of God and the Law, inasmuch as anyone can, in civil law (taking) and religious law (slaughtering) legally represent and act on behalf of anybody else. This idea is expressed in the legal code as שלוחו של אדם כמותו (Kidushin 41, 42). But, inasmuch as the word איש is used, it also implies that for the exercise of this right, maturity is required. איש זוכה ואין קטן זוכה (ibid. and תוספות).

These individuals, now raised to independent beings with some rights, were gathered by the state-building Word of God, first into families. This family bond was extended upwards, the bond of children to parents which unites even married children with their children, to grandfathers and great-grandfathers, to בית אבות, and downwards the bond of parents to children, which allows children again to found independent homes in which they live again with their children as their parents had done with them. But in this State, even this home-building bond upwards is to be entirely a matter of free-will, and no obligatory attachment is to be recognised, the possibility is at once provided for, אם ימעט הבית וגו׳, of homes forming their own groups according to their own free will and pleasure. אינו שוחט על ידי בנו ובתו הגדולים וע״י עבדו ושפחתו העברים, וע״י אשתו, אלא מדעתן (Pesachim 88a), “One may not slaughter the Pascal Lamb on behalf of his grown-up son or daughter or his Jewish slave or his wife without their agreement”.

The right which Man has to independence, to equality, to freedom and property, the bonds of blood and the free choice which gathers together and separates them into homes, this right is the basis of God’s State. But these rights are elements that tend to individualise, that stand men and homes firmly on their own feet, and prevent interference by others. What then is the cement, the medium that attaches one home to another, and which makes society, the community, emerge from the family in the Jewish State? Is it, as in other state-building systems, necessity, the requirements, the thought of the weakness of the individual, the necessity of mutual help and assistance which tears the individual out of his egoistic isolation, and is it this worry for his own self that suggests to him to worry about the well-being of his neighbour? It certainly is also a need, a necessity, but it is the necessity for an outlet for his super-abundance, it is the necessity for fulfilling his duty. אם ימעט הבית וגו׳ is what the Jewish state-building word says, it is not the poor that need the rich, the rich need the poor; “Whose home is too small for the blessing that God lends him, let him seek out a neighbour who can supply him with people to whom his overflow can be of use, who can help him to fulfil the exercise of his duty!” God can look after the poor without the rich. But the rich man can not carry out the task of his life without the poor man. It is not necessity, it is the consciousness of duty, מצוה, which, in this Jewish State of God’s, is to join house to house to form a national community. It is only out of this concrete national community, ensured by משפם, united by צדקה, that the formal national state emerges as ישראל — .קהל עדת ישראל, the Nation, — עדה, the independent members who bear the responsibility for the mission of the nation, the community, — קהל, the governing and leading head, the representative of the nation.

But each individual, each home, each family, the whole totality as a whole and as individuals, in this moment of their new fresh existence are to present themselves to God as a שה; everything is to be merged into the one idea of being צאן מרעיתו, to think of God as their Shepherd, as the רועה ישראל, and to place themselves under His guidance and leadership. This conception that makes us think of God as our shepherd, and us as His flock, was, from the moment when God undertook our “leadership”, to be the most general, most perpetual idea which we were to keep of our relation to God, and God’s relation to us. The כבש אחד בבקר and כבש אחד בין הערבים in which Israel was to present itself and give itself up to its God day by day at the rising and sinking rays of light, was nothing else but the continuation and repetition of this first moment in which Israel began its path through history as a שה, and left its leadership to God as the רועה ישראל, as the נוהג כצאן יוסף. But the Jewish “lamb” is not “the lamb carrying the troubles of the world”, treading meekly the path to the slaughterhouse, a meek and sad creature; שה תמים זכר בן שנה יהיה לכם, perfect, unblemished, manly, in the eternal freshness of youth, is it to express the idea of our nature, complete and independent, and yet forever young, never outgrowing the Godly guidance, such is the “flock” of God to be, whether we feel ourselves to be as כבש or עז in our social position, מן הכבשים ומן העזים תקחו. Within the species צאן, choice is given between sheep and goats. The latter, עז, bears the character of greater independence externally, towards others, and hence עז also means to offer opposition, to be obstinate. The goat shows his horns to every stranger, but to his shepherd he is as obedient and pliant as the sheep.

והיה לכם למשמרת. For four days, attention was to be riveted on this lamb, to guard it against any mutilation, to keep it in its תמים state, its absolute “completeness”; תמים .טעון ביקור לימים, the complete surrender of the whole of oneself in every direction and in every connection, is the first and basic essential of any and every קרבן, of any and every attempt to get nearer to God, just as the preliminary condition for the covenant of Abraham was התהלך לפני והיה תמים.

בין הערבים, between the two ערבים, between the two “mixtures of day and night”, the one, where night already mixes itself with day, the other where day is still mixed with the night; the one where the day begins to dwindle, the other where the last rays of daylight depart, i.e., between the moment when the sun has passed the zenith until the beginning of actual night, this is the whole afternoon of 14th Nissan. This was the point of separation between the 14th which still belonged to the state of slavery, and the 15th which really only began at nightfall, but which ‘dawned’ already in the previous afternoon — which was to bring salvation and freedom. Israel is to prepare itself for this moment in which externally, the salvation, the וגאלתי אתכם בזרוע וגו׳, and internally, the election, the ולקחתי אתכם לי לעם, were to begin, by presenting itself for such election as “the sheep of His flock” ready to follow God’s guidance, and to express by שחיטה its readiness completely to give up the life it had hitherto lived.

V. 7—8. But giving up to God one’s former life or the life one has hitherto lived, שחיטת קרבן, is never an act of destruction, of annihilation, it is always only the essential preliminary to achieving through God a higher state of existence. The blood that is shed is immediately taken up and received for this new higher life, קבלה. This idea, that nothing is given up by the idea of שחיטה is particularly evident in the Pessach offering which is from beforehand only to be slaughtered for the use and enjoyment of those persons who, in it, have presented themselves and given themselves up to God. In no other offering is the אכילה so essential, (see Pesachim 78b et seq.), only of the Pessach offering is it said שלא בא מתחלתו אלא לאכילה (Pesachim 76b). To be free and independent — is this aught but having the use and enjoyment of oneself! To be able to expend all one’s personality with all the use of all one’s organs and abilities, on oneself, is the very nature of independence. It establishes the ego in its full personal worth, and makes his bodily and spiritual self a domain over which he has the sole disposition. That is the reason, we imagine, why the Pessach offering being eaten by the same persons to whom it belongs, those, who, before it was sacrificed were fixed as being the personalities whom it was to represent, was so essential at just this offering. The Pessach offering is just the expression of obtaining free independence by giving oneself up to God, the regaining of one’s own self, which, up till then, had been absorbed and lost in the personality of the master of the slave. That is also the reason why here שלא למנוייו .שחיטה שלא למנוייו ושלא לאוכליו פסול would be, just slavery. And שלא לאוכליו would be, giving up, sacrificing, without the compensating regaining of one’s independent life.

But it is not free independent individuals which are to be the elements out of which God wishes to build up His people, it is, as we have seen, out of free independent houses, formed by the bonds of blood or by free choice. Only within the sphere of a freely-formed family is the individual to grow to the use and enjoyment of his own self. Hence, the blood which has been offered is taken up and placed on the מזוזות and the משקוף of the houses in which the lamb which has been offered is to come back to the use and enjoyment of those that had offered it, as it says על שתי המזוזות ועל המשקוף על הבתים וגו׳. The מזוזות and the משקוף represent the house, the home. The idea of a house is a double one, firstly to shut the inhabitants in, against the human elements, i.e., privacy, to protect them against intrusion; and secondly, shutting the inhabitants in against physical elements, protecting them against the intrusion of rain etc.; the one represented by the walls, the other by the roof. The two door posts, the מזוזת, represent shutting out the social element, the lintel, משקוף (from שקף to look down from above) represents the protection against the physical elements. The slaves when elevated to free human beings with full human rights over their own family life received משקוף and מזוזה, insurance by God of their protection against instrusion by the forces of man and nature. To achieve this, he was first to place his whole self at the disposition of God, giving up to God, as his Shepherd, every kind of existence he had hitherto lived. This is what was to be expressed by the placing of the blood of the slaughtered lamb on the doorposts and lintel of the houses in which the offering itself was to be eaten. It is not the walls that will protect him against the unfriendly forces of fellow man, nor the roof against the unfriendly forces of nature. Within the walls and under the roofs, it is God that protects those who are ready to give themselves to Him.

ואכלו את הבשר וגו׳. On this freedom-bringing night they themselves are to receive back the lives they were ready to sacrifice, but צלי אש ומצות וגו׳, but only roasted directly on fire, and with unleavened bread, and bitter herbs are they to enjoy them. The meaning of מצות and מרורים is clear. Just as, at the moment of the exodus their oppressors did not grant them time even to leaven the bread, and so they had to take it out with them as מצה, so, during the whole period of their slavery they did not get time even for leavening their bread, the whip of the overseer and the breathless rush of the overwhelming labour was always behind them and only permitted the quickest and easiest preparation of their food. So מצה is the real bread of slaves, and we still refer to it as “the bread of affliction which our forefathers ate in Egypt.” Hence it is definitely the symbol of עבדות. That מרורים represents the וימררו את חייהם, and so is the symbol of ענוי, ruthless tormenting, is equally clear. But if then in מצה and מרור we have two of our well-known three phases of the Egyptian Galut, it does not seem far fetched to suggest that in צלי אש we can see the missing third element, the גרות. Without standing, no firm ground under its feet, swinging to and fro, not צלי קדר, roasted in a pan, but תלוי בשפוד, hanging on a spit, thus, is the קרבן פסח to mature to a state fit for use. Without standing, driven to and fro, no right to the ground under their feet, is literally the condition of aliens, of גרים, in which this people, now rising to freedom and independence had to be matured for their ultimate goal. So, centuries later, when, once again, the fate of גרות, of exile, hung over the head of Judea, those who thought they could defy the threat used the same metaphor in the opposite way, and said, referring to Jerusalem היא הסיר ואנחנו הבשר, “it (Jerusalem) is the pot and we are the meat” (Ezekiel 11,3) i.e., in Jerusalem we have our natural permanent land which can not be taken away from us, and on which we shall reach the zenith of our greatness. And the Prophet replied, announcing the Galut: היא לא תהיה לכם לסיר (ibid.) “It will not be as a pot unto you”. According to this צלי אש ומצות על מרורים would mean: — remembering, at the moment of regained freedom, the three preceding stages of Egyptian oppression, גרות ,עבדות ,וענוי. This is to keep alive in our minds the fact that, right up to the moment of redemption, the pressure still lay heavily on us, we were still the same slaves in the power of the Egyptians, and it was God, and God alone Who granted us freedom, we ourselves had not the slightest hand in it.

V. 9. נא (from נוא: to be disturbed, to be interrupted in a movement which has been commenced) incomplete, half-cooked. The opposite is בשל מבושל במים to be thoroughly cooked by the addition of water or other liquid. You received freedom complete from the hands of God, and no human addition was required. And you received the freedom all at once כולו כאחד. (See Rashi Pesachim 74a, Mishna). All at once the chains fell off, from head and hand and foot, and from all the activities for nourishment and for life itself ראשו על כרעיו ועל קרבו. This ראשו וגו׳ is proof of the symbolic nature of the procedure.

V. 10. ולא תותירו: We have already remarked on V.2 that in the sphere of offerings, the day is reckoned from morn to morn; and also on V. 7—8 that שחיטה without אכילה would represent destruction of life without regaining it On a higher level. But equally so, אכילה separated from שחיטה would be independence, gained, not on the basis of a preceding giving oneself up to God. Accordingly, the eating of the offering must take place on the same day as the sacrifice was made, so that it remains in direct connection with it. With the dawn of the next day, the day of the sacrifice has passed. Leaving anything over beyond the day of sacrifice would express the possibility of independence without sacrifice, and this supposition must be denied. The denial is to be expressed by the burning of anything left over. שרפת פסולי מוקדשים in general is always meant to express a positive denial of those ideas which are not in accordance with the conceptions of the בית-המקדש which these objects (the פסולי מוקדשים) have managed to convey. The burning is accordingly a positive act of reasserting the correct ideas which the בית-המקדש preaches, and so itself falls into the category of the עבודות, the procedures of the בית-המקדש, and this is clearly indicated by the fact that the burning of נותר ופגול equally with שחיטה וזריקה may only be done by daytime. The repetition of עד בקר (which otherwise seems to be redundant I.L.) indicates that this burning may only take place on the morning of the second following day, the 16th, as שריפת קדשים אינה דוחה י״ט.

V. 11. וככה וגו׳: as an expression of your confidence that the moment for the exodus has now arrived. — חפז ,בחפזון (related to חפש, seek, חפץ to strive for something), always expresses a forced haste which is to escape from a danger rather than to reach a goal.

פסח related to פשׂע to step, and even, as it seems from Is. 27,4, to step out vigorously, Chaldean פסיעה ,פסע, simply to step, a pace. If then פסח is ‘to limp’ and פִּסֵחַ is ‘lame’, we seem to have here, as in נוע and ,נוח עלה and חלה etc., etc., another example of the ח indicating a restriction, a hindrance, of the idea which is expressed by the ע in the root. In any case, as פסה quite definitely means to limp, and פִּסֵחַ equally definitely means lame, פסח, is a restricted, slow, halting stepping along. פסח על would accordingly mean “to step haltingly over something.”

In Isaiah 31,5, four ways of God’s protection and salvation of Jerusalem are described: גנון והציל פסוח והמליט. Sometimes גנון “fencing in”, so that the danger can not get at it from any side; sometimes הציל, that the danger has already got at it, but God snatches it out of danger’s very hands; sometimes פסח, “passing over”, that it finds itself in the midst of danger, and, while all around everything succumbs to the danger, it alone remains untouched, the danger passing it over; and sometimes המליט “escaping”, had it remained where the danger was, it would have perished, but God helped it to flee. As גנון and פסוח are in the infinitive mood and הציל and המליט are in tempus finitum, the idea is expressed that the ordinary, constant care of God over Israel is of the nature of גנון and פסוח, and הציל and המליט become necessary on special occasions. Moreover as פסוח means a slow halting passing over of the danger, it tells us that at all times when “thousands fall on your right side and tens of thousands on your left” salvation pauses till the threatened-one has made itself worthy to be saved. And that is exactly what the Pessach was here. By what was expressed by the whole of the ritual connected with it, Israel was to make itself deserving that the destruction that befell the Egyptian houses should pass over their heads. Fully conscious of this, were they to eat and enjoy their Pessach offering. Fully conscious that it was only their adopting the “flock and shepherd” attitude to God, as expressed by the Pessach offering, which allowed them to enjoy the quiet confidence that the danger which hovered over their heads also, would not affect them. This feeling of tension, of having to avoid a threatening danger is exactly expressed by חפזון and we can understand the connection ואכלתם אותו בחפזון and פסח הוא לה׳, it was only slowly and haltingly that the danger passed away from over heads (פסח). So press on, delay not to make yourselves deserving for it to do so (חפזון).

When ר׳ עקיבא (Berachoth 9a) takes the חפזון to refer to the flurry of the exodus, which occured only in the morning, and thereon bases the dictum that the Pessach is allowed to be eaten till morning: עד שעת חפזון, he can hardly have meant that this חפזון only refers to the pressing hurry of the exodus, for it says בחפזון and not עד חפזון, and moreover one would then have to take it, that the Pessach was to be eaten only at the end of the night or even at the beginning of the morning. But probably what ר״ע wanted to say was only that the whole night, right up to daybreak, was a time of חפזון, and that when, after midnight, the חפזון of the danger of death had passed, the חפזון of the departure began, and so the whole night till morning was the time allowed for eating the Pessach. ראב״ע presumes that there was no flurry at all for Israel, for it says לא יחרץ כלב לשונו — on which sentence this view is based, in the מכילתא — and he takes the חפזון to refer solely to the alarmed confusion of the Egyptians at midnight, and the connection between the פסח and ואכלתם אתו בחפזון would be: while outside, confusion and alarm is raging for the Egyptians, you are quietly to eat your Pessach meal, for it is a meal of “the danger being directed away from you”. But still the ב remains difficult to understand, as it does not mean the limit of the time, but the duration of it.

V. 13. לכם לאת as a sign, a symbolic expression of what this blood was meant to imply, a complete rendering up of your self to God’s direction. — נגף למשחית as much as to say נגף להיות למשחית, a blow which becomes a destructive one.

V. 14. In Ch. 34,25, ולא ילין לבקר זבח חג הפסח, the 14th Nissan is definitely called חג. Even (Ch. 23,18). ולא ילין חלב חגי עד בקר is taken by some authorities to refer to the קרבן פסח (see מ׳ למלך on הל׳ קרבן פסח א׳ז׳). So היום הזה here can very well refer to the 14th Nissan. — חקת עולם. Just as לחם חקי ,חק לכהנים etc. designate that which is due to somebody, his requirement, that which is destined for him, so חק and חוקה in the Torah is always that which God has fixed for the care, upkeep and carrying out of an idea, etc., as being that which we are due to give to it.

V. 15. שבעת ימים מצות תאכלו can not be the command to eat מצות continuously for seven days. Where the number of days or years is not expressed with ב- (as e.g. בערב תאכלו) it obviously means that whatever is described in that time, goes on during the whole of that time. For instance when it says כי ששת ימים עשה ה׳ וגו׳ it does not want to tell us in how many days God worked at the creation, but that the creation went on uninterruptedly throughout six days and only reached its completion with the seventh day. Accordingly here, if we take it as a positive command, it would be a command to eat מצות unceasingly throughout seven days, which would be an absurdity. So that it can only be taken as meaning the negation, throughout seven days, when you want to eat bread, you may only eat it unleavened. Quite similarly we find בסכת תשבו שבעת ימים which can also only mean the negation, if or when, throughout these seven days, you want to “dwell”, you may only do so in סוכות, which does not exclude the permission to journey outside your succah. Taken positively it would mean that one would have to remain uninterruptedly in the סוכה throughout the seven days. It is to this that the אך refers, אך ביום הראשון.

The seven Mattzo-days following this first Pessach-day have only this negative conception with regard to מצה, but, on that 1st day, the Pessach-day the 14th, the positive command applies, תשביתו שאור וגו׳. In the same way it does not say כי כל אוכל חמץ מיום הראשן עד יום השביעי ונכרתה וגו׳, in which case one would only be חייב כרת if one ate חמץ uninterruptedly from the first till the seventh. But what it says is, that with each eating of חמץ one is חייב כרת from the first till the seventh day, i.e., one is חייב כרת על כל כזית וכזית. The אך is to be taken as being in parenthesis, and the כי כל אוכל וגו׳ then goes on to give the reason for the שבעת ימים. This clearly indicates the more negative way in which that command is to be understood. Then naturally the second יום הראשון refers to the first of those seven days, i.e., the 15th Nissan. Moreover, as here the אך is in contrast to the more negative command of תאכלו which is to be carried out in the whole of the seven days, it, the אך, introduces a positive command to be carried out on that 1st day, (the 14th as explained above) but the אך has a limiting power of חלק (Pessachim 5a) by which the command only applies to the second half of the day.

We have already understood מצה to be the expression of עבדות, of social dependence; חמץ is the opposite of חמץ ,מצה is accordingly the expression of social independence. The Pessach-day is to be לזכרון for us, is ever again to bring back afresh in our minds the moment in which we obtained freedom and independence, and never to let us forget the ways and means by which we achieved freedom and independence. That is why the day that brings back to us our arising to freedom and independence, introduces a whole cycle of days, not with the sign of freedom, but with abolishing the symbol of independence. שבעת ימים, for a complete cycle of days we are not to allow ourselves any bread of independence. More, on the day on which we achieve independent personalities and independent homes — ויקחו להם—איש—לבית — we are to clear out from all our homes — מבתיכם — the specific symbol of social independence, and then, throughout seven days we may not nourish ourselves with the bread of independence, but must remind ourselves, and thereby express the fact, that at the moment of our arising to freedom and independence, neither in our persons nor in our possessions was there the slightest trace of independence, or even of the ability to achieve independence (שאור); we were still in complete lack of freedom and utter lack of power, and it was only the free directing and commanding power of God which allowed us to arise to freedom and independence. Hence whosoever eats the smallest quantity which could make a difference in keeping himself alive, of the bread of independence (אוכל כזית חמץ) during these seven days of remembrance of our arising to freedom, denies thereby the Godly origin of our achieving freedom, is thereby looking on this arising as a human achievement, and thereby he exterminates himself from the future of Israel (כרת) inasmuch as he forsakes the basis of the past of Israel.
שאר may be related to שער a storm, and indicate the agent that causes a strong fermenting action.

V. 16. מקרא קדש as said above on קדוש החדש, the Moed-days are consecrated and dedicated to a renewed “meeting” with God by being fixed by the representatives of the community of Israel. By this fixing by the national community, each individual Jew is accordingly invited as a member of this community to the Sanctuary on these days, i.e., is called upon personally, or if this was not possible, at least in spirit, to join in with this gathering round about this central point of their common holy calling. This is the constantly recurring demand for the realisation of the real basic object of the redemption from Egypt, viz ולקחתי אתכם לי לעם והייתי לכם לאלהים. While on the Pessach and Mattzo Festival, the constitution of Israel to a nation through God is always freshly renewed by means of the Pessach offering and Mattzo, these periodically recurring calls to Israel to renew their bond with God and His Sanctuary are to act as positively furthering the mission of their lives והייתי לכם לאלהים, to let themselves be guided in every phase of their lives by God. So that all the Moed-days which have their origin in events in Jewish History are at the same time מקראי קדש. Finding themselves at one with God is the same as finding themselves at one with His Sanctuary. So on these days every individual Jew is an individual “invitee” (קרוא) to God in His Sanctuary, and this idea finds its material expression in a raised standard of living, in better clothes, better food, nicer surroundings. On such a day everyone is to feel that his own personality is really valuable, and he is to show this in his general appearance. (כבדהו במאכל ובמשתה ובכסות נקיה. Mechilta).

In the Jeshurun, we have shown that a cycle of seven days is always a period within which the attainment of a fresh higher level (or of a level that is to be renewed) is brought to its achievement. When a Moed is dedicated to such a cycle of seven days, the thoughts, ideas, feelings which the Moed is to refresh to new life, start on the first day and are to attain the summit of clarity and force on the seventh day, and then send us back in the state of elevation and vivacity which we have attained, to a fuller and more thoroughly lived daily life. That is why this “call to God and His Sanctuary” comes with full force on the first and seventh days. On the first, which calls us out of our ordinary daily life, and brings to us the idea which is to be revived and refreshed and strengthened, and on the seventh, which, with all its force is to give us this idea, completely assimilated, to take back with us for our daily life.

It is out of this מקרא קדש idea that the following double law of איסור מלאכת עבודה on י״ט and the היתר אוכל נפש comes. מלאכה (as has already been explained on Gen. 2,1 from מלאך a messenger, one charged with the carrying out of somebody else’s thoughts) means making any material into the bearer and executor of our thoughts, i.e., that it becomes henceforth a means for the realisation of some certain thought. So that מלאכה is not labour, but accomplished work. What מלאך is in person, מלאכה is in material. If the material is one, the use of which is for human food, and the work done on it is to render it fit for consumption, (which includes making fire), it is called מלאכת אוכל נפש. Every other kind of work which is made, not directly for the sustenance of a human being, but primarily in the service of that cultural mission with which Man has been entrusted — the reconstructing of the elements of this world — לעבדה ולשמרה — is called, in contrast to מלאכת עבודה ,מלאכת אוכל נפש. Accordingly, we find everywhere else with reference to the days of Moed, with the exception of כל מלאכת ,י״כ עבודה לא תעשו. Here this addition is obviously unnecessary, as here מלאכת אוכל נפש is expressly excluded from the prohibition. Now it does not say אך אשר יאכל לכם וגו׳ but אשר יאכל לכל נפש and thereby two things are expressed. Firstly that only דבר השוה לכל נפש i.e., it is only allowed to do work on such food which would be usual for the average man, but not such that would only appeal to very exalted classes and habits, that would only satisfy very artificial requirements (Ketuboth 7a). Further, the principle that is dealt with in Pesachim 46b, namely, that in judging the punishableness of a case, only the work in itself comes into consideration, i.e., whether at the moment of its being done, it could possibly be of use for food on the Moed for any person. (הואיל ומקלעי ליה אורחים). (Although the quantity he cooks is more than it is possible for him or his family to eat, it is always possible that guests or poor people might turn up I.L.).

The restrictions הוא לבדו and לכם limit this permission for work on food. It may only be done for fellow-Jews (לכם) and even then (הוא לבדו) only work on actual food, and only such accessory work (מכשירי אוכל נפש) which could not be done just as well before י״ט Accordingly, the prohibition to do מלאכה on the מקרא קדש days of the Moed has the following meaning: Man was set in this world with a twofold mission, to serve and develop his own personality, and to serve and develop the world (לעבדה). The Jew invited to the Sanctuary, is, by this invitation, called away from his duty to use the creative forces that God has granted him, in altering or improving the world. Invited to עבודת ה׳ he is released from עבודת הארץ. He is to come within the precincts of his holy centre from which the impulse for all his activities is to spring, and from there he is first to receive afresh inspiration and consecration of those forces he is thereafter to devote to the service and improvement of the world in general. But a higher consciousness of his Jewish personality is part of this renewed consecration, and preparation of nourishment for Jewish persons is accordingly included in the conditions of the מקרא קדש. And in this a “Jewish person” is thought of in his generality, דבר השוה לכל נפש, not extravagant tastes and luxurious conditions are implied in the invitation, and each Jew has not to consider himself as an individual invitee, but as being invited along with all his fellow Jews, so that preparation of any amount of food that could be used on the Moed-day by any other Jew is not forbidden (הואיל).

V. 17. Just as the קרבן פסח had to be למשמרת for four days before it was offered, and long before the festival itself, Jewish minds were to be directed to thoughts, that the expression of their giving themselves up to their Shepherd must be complete and whole in every direction and not lacking in the slightest degree anywhere (תמים), in the same way (ושמרתם) we are to meet the day of our exodus each time it recurs, with the presentation of carefully prepared unleavened bread, and we are carefully to keep it from leavening, with the idea that it was on this day that God led us out to freedom, and for that reason this day is to be met not with the bread of independence, but with the bread of our own dependence. This care which has to exercise our minds already before the festival is at the same time taking care that the day itself shall be kept, and ensures it against being forgotten or neglected (ושמרתם את היום).

V. 18. Whereas, as remarked on V.15, the eating of Mattzo on the other days is not obligatory, and only excludes the eating of leavened bread, which has been prevented from leavening for this special purpose, and with the thoughts in mind as explained in the previous verse (משתמרת לשם מצה) is to be eaten. (מצת is written חסר here, perhaps to indicate that it is sufficient if only כזית is eaten as a symbol.) The prohibition of leavened during the seven days of the Mattzo Festival is to do away with every thought of independent human assistance in the conception of our attaining our freedom. The positive eating of Mattzo at the beginning of the Festival of Salvation is to make us combine the thought of our having attained our social freedom through God, with the thought of our belonging to God, through which, and for which, we became free men. Towards God, Israel who has become free, always stands with Mattzo in his hands. Out of the servitude of man we have stepped into the service of God. All leavened was forever to be banned from the altar in the Sanctuary of God. (Levit. 2,11). By these sentences, the command for Mattzo, and the prohibition of chometz, even apart from the Pessach offering, is made a duty for all times.

V. 19—20. See commentary on V.15. מחמצת. Hiphil form of חמץ. As in Ps. 69,32, the Hiphil forms, מקרון מפריס denote the presentation of an object, “to show horns and claws” or האדים ,הלבין, to show the red or white colour, so here מחמצת means that which, while it is not תמץ itself, does offer חמץ in a recognisable form, anything that has חמץ mixed in it in sufficient quantity to be considered prominent. This is תערובת חמץ כזית בכדי אכילת פרס; such a mixture is liable to the same punishment — כרת — as pure unmixed כל מחצמת .חמץ extends the idea, and includes any mixture in which the contained chometz can only be recognised by its taste. תערובת חמץ טעמו ולא ממשו. It is just by such extension of the prohibition of חמץ that our conscientiousness is kept keenly awake during the whole of the Mattzo Festival, and thereby this basic symbol of our national existence being borne exclusively by God alone, is presented to our minds in the most impressive manner. But for the duration of our Redemption Festival חמץ is to be banned from our domain (לא ימצא), from our use (הנאה), and from our nourishment (אכילה), and here again are shown those three phases of the Egyptian Galut that made our existence, by גרות, without domain, by עבדות, powerless in the disposal of our forces and means, and by ענוי without pleasure in food. We had no independence (חמץ) with regards to our domain, our homes (לא ימצא), to the use of our possessions (הנאה) and to our food (בכל מושבתיכם .(אכילה, whereas, during the whole year it is only from the altar and from food coming from it that חמץ was banned, and only bread that was brought to it, or came from it that had to be מצה, on the Mattzo Festival this symbol was to be in evidence in all our dwelling places, in order to bring home to us, just in our ordinary home lives, our lack of independence towards God. This is why the מצה של מצוה on Pessach eve, had to be מצה הנאכלת בכל מושבות (see Pesachim 36a).

V. 21. משכו וקחו וגו׳. “Withdraw from all ideas of your past and of your future, and give yourselves up entirely to the idea of becoming that which is expressed by the offering (צאן) for your families.” By משכו and קחו you show the two things that comprise the idea of dedication and sanctification. הפסח evidently presupposes that this idea was already known to the people, so that they must have been already informed of the whole laws of Pessach and Mattzo. It is possible and probable that these words were said to the people on 10th Nissan, the day on which they were to carry out the command given to them on the 1st ויקחו להם וגו׳.

V. 22. Here, right at the very first Mitzva, we have a concrete example of תשב״פ (the spoken, traditional Torah). Here we have recorded in the “written Torah” that Moses gave additional details of the procedure to be carried out, which are not mentioned above in the “written” record of God’s commands. In the same way, at all the later laws, Moses had to receive and transmit more detailed explanations which were not given in the written record of God’s words, which only contain a general reference to the law, and leave these detailed explanations for verbal transmission.

אגודת אזוב, one can already hear by the sound אזב that it is a weaker form of עשב and it always designates a weak dependent growth in contrast to the strong high-reaching cedar. In any case we learn from Para, XI,9 that it is of the order of low shrubs. It is very doubtful if it is our hyssop, for, although hyssop is found growing along walls and would accordingly comply with אזוב אשר יצא בקיר, it grows fairly high and is strong enough to be used for hedges and borders of gardens. Anyway it always represents smallness and weakness. Perhaps the contrast מן הארז אשר בלבנון ועד האזוב אשר יצא בקיר (Kings I. 5,13) is to be sought also in its characteristics. “Hyssop” is a low plant, to be found on every wall, it requires no special soil for its growth, but cedars are only to be found on the heights of Lebanon. Smallness, weakness, humbleness, all these characteristics are in accordance with the use the Torah makes of אזוב, here, and also with טומאת מת and מצורע. The blood is to be placed on the houses by means of Hyssop. The “placer” himself is weak, unimportant, and only gains strength and a future by the blood of the Pessach. Whereas in the case of the פרה, having a “bundle” of hyssop is only a מצוה but a number is not essential, here it is מעבכ, essential, that the blood be placed with a “bundle” of three entwined hyssop stalks. The blood is to represent being placed by and belonging to, not a single individual but a חבורה, an אגודה, a company of personalities.

Above it says: ונתנו על שתי המזוזת ועל המשקוף, here והגעתם על המשקוף ועל שתי המזוזת to teach that אם הקדים זה לזה יצא (Mechilta), that the order did not matter, that both, the acknowledgment of our giving ourselves up absolutely to God in our social life and position (מזוזת) as well as in our physical life and position (משקוף), are equally important.

V. 24. את הדבר הזה, this word, that God will see the blood on the houses, and as a result will grant salvation. Thereby God establishes this first Mitzva to a most striking symbol, and the performance of the Mitzva to a definite speech in symbolic language between us and God, bringing about a positive act of salvation. This, at the same time, gives meaning and importance to all later similar mitzvoth. The change of person from plural to singular: לך — ושמרתם expresses: — either, “Keep this Word nationally as a nation so that it becomes a law unto each one of you individually and to your children for ever”; or, “Keep this Word in your masses, so that it becomes a law to your nation and to successive generations for ever.” For addressing in the singular is always directed to each separate individual or to the whole nation regarded as a unit. In any case the address here being made in both singular and plural avoids the possibility of error in both directions. The Torah is satisfied neither by being simply acknowledged and kept in private individual lives, nor by simply being acknowledged and kept nationally, such as by the appointment of public representatives to carry it out. The Torah wants to find its acknowledgment and realisation nationally in the nation as a whole, and in every individual Jewish home, in every individual Jewish breast.

V. 25. והיה כי תבאו וגו׳. When you will no longer be מעונים and no longer עבדים and no longer העבדה — .גרים, in a broad sense our whole life is “עבדת ה׳״, Divine Service, and to be עבד ה׳, to spend all his powers in every moment of his life in fulfilling God’s Will, is the highest possible goal to which Man can aspire. In a narrow sense we call those practices in which we place ourselves ever afresh in the service of God and equip ourselves for this service, i.e., sacrifices and prayer, specifically עבדה. In the תורה however, we do not find the appellation עבדה applied to any offering except to Pessach. The Pessach offering was that procedure by which first of all, Jewish men, Jewish homes and the Jewish State entered into the service of God, and it is the Pessach offering which is the procedure by which this entry is to be renewed afresh, again and again. Hence כי תבאו וגו׳ when the last trace of the Egyptian slavery will have disappeared, and you will be happy, free and settled, then you are scrupulously always to repeat this עבדה, always to put yourself back in the beginning of your national existence when you were without happiness, without freedom, without land, and, as you did then, always repeat afresh your entry into the service of God.
V. 26. This is the question asked by a generation which has become estranged from God, which places Man in the service of himself alone, and only places value in an action if it is of tangible use.
