V. 27. ואמרתם וגו׳ not ואמרתם להם, as later ואמרת אליו ,והגדת לבנך, but simply “ye shall say”. The Torah does not expect any result from direct teaching or preaching to a generation which is sunk in materialism and thus estranged from God, but it does from the example of Mitzvas earnestly carried out in understanding and conscious enthusiasm. Undisturbed by the derisive protests of a generation in which the spirit and meaning of the religious practices have been lost in the ossifying effects of materialism, you are to proclaim, let who will hear it, that it is still זבח פסח הוא לה׳, that it is still a meal that leads out of death to life, that, for Israel, Life and Freedom still depend on the same conditions that first brought them to Israel, so that this עבדה, this repeated symbolic entry into the service of God is a procedure of the highest value and most pregnant with results for all times. This is why — as this זבח פסח וגו׳ etc., is not a direct answer to the רשע — the Haggada can cloak his riposte to him in the sentence בעבור זה עשה ה׳ לי וגו׳ which contains the importance of these symbolic mitzvas we have to perform, and which refers to the duty of carrying out the Chometz and Mattzo mitzvas which we have to do at all times even when the Pessach — as at present — can not be brought.

V. 28. וילכו ויעשו וגו׳ ,כאשר וגו׳ ,כן עשו. Moses and Aaron remitted it faithfully and truly, Israel accepted and carried it out faithfully and truly, and so Israel’s act completely corresponded to God’s command. This shows incidentally, how, from the very beginning, the Law came to be kept solely on the base of verbal tradition. Out of the six hundred thousand men who had to bring the Pessach only the elders had the order direct from Moses, the others only got it through a whole series of intermediate transmitters, and neverthless the Torah tells us that the order was carried out completely in accordance with the command that God had in the first place given to Moses and Aaron.

V. 30. לילה, adverbial, at night, as גנובתי יום גנובתי לילה (Gen. 31,39) and elsewhere. Pharaoh shook himself up out of his sleep, and called up his servants and the whole of Egypt to wakeful activity.
V. 31. צאו מתוך עמי is a complete permanent going away. — ולכו עבדו, appease your God, carry out His wishes.

V. 32. וברכתם גם אותי as you thereby achieve blessing for yourself, at the same time bring about that I, too, get blessing again, that all the wounds that I and my land have suffered on your account become healed again.

V. 34. The seven days prohibition of chometz as given in V.15 et seq., only applied to the future festivals of remembrance of the salvation, as it clearly says in V.14. But פסח מצרים אין חמוצו נוהג אלא יום אחד on the day of salvation itself, the prohibition was at most for that day, the 15th Nissan (see Pesachim 96b and 28b and, moreover, as appears from there, לא יאכל חמץ היום אתם יוצאים the prohibition was only against eating chometz, but not against having it in one’s possession: see ר״ן on רי״ף on the Mishna ר״ג היה אומר וגו׳). Accordingly, they had both the necessity and the intention to prepare a sufficiency of bread for the journey, but the urgent hustle of the Egyptians did not permit them to do it (see V.39). [בצק, probably related to פסג, (from which we get פסגה, an elevation), to become high, and פשק to stretch, the dough looked on as rising, so also the foot רגלך לא בצקה, did not become swollen]. — על שכמם they had already packed all their belongings, and ladened them on the beasts of burden and were only occupied with baking bread. But sc pressing was the fear of the Egyptians, that they did not give them time even to load up the troughs with the dough on to the animals. They had to take them as they were on their shoulders and hurry out.

V. 36. Although above in Ch. 3,22 it says ונצלתם וגו׳, here, where וישאילום immediately precedes it, and the subject is the Egyptians, it can very well be that the subject of וינצלו is also the Egyptians. “And they (the Egyptians) stripped Egypt.” The honesty and magnanimity which the Jews displayed during the three days of darkness had so raised the opinion of the Egyptians towards Israel, that they pressed their possessions upon them before they asked, and stripped themselves of their treasures.

רגלִי, as this word remains unchanged in the plural, it seems to have a collective meaning, a number of people on foot; pedestrians. The women are not mentioned, so that under טף only boys seem to be understood. The verse would accordingly refer to the contemporary and future backbone of the nation.

V. 39. כי לא חמץ, they were hustled out so hurriedly, so uninterruptedly were they kept in active motion, that even on the journey the dough had not yet risen and become וחמץ. The facts that גרשו ממצרים and גם צדה לא עשו להם, that they were driven out of Egypt, that they could not even prepare the necessary bread for the journey, so that at the actual moment of the exodus, it was on their part an unwilling one, this fact impresses for ever on this exodus the stamp of its being exclusively the act of God, and makes the prohibition of מצה and חמץ into a symbol of still greater significance. Without this memorial, Israel’s descendants could have looked on the exodus as being a human achievement similar to so many others in history. We have just heard in the preceding verses that they were 600,000 sturdy men, so their liberation would be no wonder, the wonder would only be that they submitted for so long to such inhuman oppression. But then the Mattzo tells us that they were driven out of Egypt, so driven that they could not even prepare their bread properly, they would have liked to tarry for at least as long as מלוש בצק עד חומצתו, as it would take to finish the leavening of their bread, but this they could not do, the Egyptians would not allow it, so they were still, even in the moment of their exodus, completely, as before, in the power of their oppressors, and above both — as over the mother and the child at the moment of birth — it was God alone, who was directing matters in His All-mightiness!

V. 40. It does not say יִשלשים שנה וארבע מאות שנה ישבו בני ישראל במצרים but ומושב אשר ישבו וגו׳. Now מושב elsewhere is never used in connection with the duration of time of a living or settlement, but always referring to the locality of a living or settlement, the residence, seat. Once it refers to the manner of the seating. In Kings I. 10,5 the Queen of Sheba admires the מושב עבדיו ומעמד משרתיו the manner in which Solomon’s courtiers (the courtiers of a court are called עבדיו) were seated at his table and the placing of the attendants and waiters round about it. So we think we are justified in taking the meaning here also to be: The same manner of living in which Israel lived in Egypt had lasted four hundred and thirty years. Just before, we have been told of the last and most significant feature of the manner of their life; they were driven out of the land with the unfinished dough for their journey on their shoulders; in this one last moment is still concentrated the ענוי ,עבדות and גרות in its undiminished power. And then it goes on to say: This being considered as aliens in the land, which characterised their stay in Egypt, and begat all the atrocities, had really lasted 430 years. During all that time Israel had been aliens without any right of domicile in the world. This fate dates back to the moment when their ancestor Abraham, who himself lived, albeit in honour, as a stranger in a strange land, was informed of the fate of centuries of גרות for his descendants. From the birth of Isaac, the first זרע אברהם, 400 years had passed, from the day on which the fateful ידע תדע כי גר יהיה זרעך וגו׳ was pronounced, it was 430 years. From Jacob’s entry into Egypt it was 210 years. If — as a tradition says — the night of Abraham’s victory ויחלק עליהם לילה (Gen. 14,15) was the night of Nissan 14—15, then the doom pronounced in the ברית בין הבתרים can have been said on 15th Nissan, and that would be the explanation of בעצם היום הזה in the following verse 41.

V. 41. כל צבאות ה׳, (not צבא in singular), as has been already repeatedly remarked, Israel is considered as a number of tribes, diverse in character and characteristics but with all their differences, united and assembled around the One Lord and Leader.

V. 42. שמורים. This is the only place where this form of the word occurs. The Piel form denotes the intensive force, the plural form the quantitative strength of this “care or guarding”. Throughout centuries the most careful and most varied dispensations of God had been directed towards this night, caring for, and educating all His צבאות to prepare them to become a nation able to be the bearers of His intention for the whole of humanity. Henceforth this night is given over to this nation for God. They are to keep their most careful, most varied attention directed to it, to bring to realisation the mission they received in it, giving themselves completely up to it, throughout generation after generation. It had been a ליל שמורים לה׳ and now it is to be a ליל שמורים לכל בני ישראל לדורותם for the accomplishment of God’s goal for humanity: לה׳!

V. 43. V.38 informed us that a large number of various kinds of strangers attached themselves to the Jews at the exodus, on that follows this חקת פסח this law which the Pessach demands, concerning the personality of its participants.

In the Pessach offering the Jewish Nation asserts all its members, assembled in family groups, as being God’s flock and at His disposal, and then, in eating the same, it receives itself back, freed from physical and civic death. This is the bond between God and Israel, which has eternally to be renewed for Israel’s world-historic path through the ages. The basic condition for it is: — that only those may take part in it who belong to this Jewish bond with God both by nationality and conviction (the nationality may be either by birth, choice or attachment), and must have performed the sign of belonging to this bond, the Mila, on themselves and on those belonging to them, (i.e., sons and slaves). This excludes the מומר, the Jew, who by his way of life has estranged himself from the Jewish bond with God, שנתנכרו מעשיו לאביו בשמים, as well as תושב ושכיר, the non-Jew whose relation to Jewish circles is only through domicile or contract; ערל, the uncircumcised — even שמתו אחיו מחמת מילה, see Yebamoth 70a Rashi and Tosaphoth — and one who has not performed Mila on his sons or slaves. On the other hand, both proselyte and the slave who with Mila have become Jewish take part in the Pessach with complete equality with the native-born Jew.

בן נכר. נֵכָר is not like נָכְרִי an adjective, or adjectival noun. It is an abstract noun, and always denotes that which is un-Jewish, pagan; paganism rather than the pagan. So we find אלהי נכר הארץ, the gods of the heathenism of the land. בן נכר is one who, either by birth or by the principles of his life, belongs to heathenism. That here, this latter, the “unbelieving” Jew is included, can be deduced from the other named categories. If even the גר תושב is excluded by תושב ושכיר (V. 15) and every uncircumcised, by ערל, a heathen who has no relations at all with Jews or Judaism must certainly be excluded, so what else then can be referred to by כל בן נכר וגו׳? But it is characteristic that the Torah presupposes that the attachment of the ערב רב in the first place gives rise to the possibility that thereby a Jew too could come to fall away from Judaism.

V. 44. עבד איש מקנת כסף. The consideration of certain circumstances is necessary, correctly to understand the fact that the Torah presupposes and allows the possession and purchase of slaves from abroad to a nation itself just released from slavery. No Jew could make any other human being into a slave. He could only acquire by purchase, people who, by the then universally accepted international law, were already slaves. But this transference into the property of a Jew was the one and only salvation for anybody who, according to the prevailing laws of the nations, was stamped as a slave. The terribly sad experiences of even the last century (— Union, Jamaica 1865) teach us how completely unprotected and liable to the most inhuman treatment was the slave who in accordance with the national law was not emancipated, and even when emancipated, wherever he was, looked upon as still belonging to the slave class, or as a freed-slave. The home of a Jew was to them a home of freedom. There, he was protected by law against mishandling, the law courts were accessible to him, and — this can not be sufficiently valued — had the option if he wished (Yebamoth 48b) of joining, by מילה and טבילה, the Jewish bond with God in conjunction with the rest of the household. He would then become like the children, a member of the home, and take part, like the children, in the eating of the Pessach offering which constituted Israel into the People of God. More, according to the accepted Halacha nobody could place his home under the guiding protection of God, — i.e., could take part in the Pessach — who had in his possession a single slave who had not been accepted by מילה and טבילה as his equal in the bond with God. (That is also why the slaves in Abraham’s household are called חניכיו, initiated by him in the Abrahamitic bond with God. See note on Gen. 14,14 and 15). Exactly as מילת זכריו excludes him so does מילת עבדיו מעכבתו מלאכל בפסח! (Jebamoth 70b). This also explains the change of the person in this verse, and the emphasis with which the “thou” in ומלתָּה is emphasised. It does not say וכל עבד מקנת כספך ומלתה אותו אז וגו׳ but וכל עבד איש וגו׳ ,ומלתה וגו׳. So that the Torah is not speaking to the master, but of him. The Torah is addressing the Nation as a whole, whose representative, the father, and here the master, is to be considered in the Mitzva of Mila (see note on פרשת מילה in Gen.). The sentence accordingly runs: — “If anybody (איש) has a slave as his property, then thou, the Nation, must be able to reckon him as belonging to thee by ׳׳מילה״, Mila must first be performed on him for thee, then may he, the master, partake of the Pessach.

V. 45. תושב. In the Jewish state, every stranger could have right of domicile and claim to all the legal rights of citizenship, without becoming converted to Judaism, as long as he gave up idolatry and undertook to keep the general basic laws of humanity, the ז׳ מצות בני נח. Such a man was called a תושב, having rights of domicile. שכיר is one whose whole connection with a Jewish home is that of being a hired labourer.

V. 46. בבית אחד וגו׳. It strikes one as most peculiar that here, in the middle of the list of the persons who are to be allowed to partake of the Pessach, comes instructions as to the way and manner in which the Pessach is to be eaten. But just by placing it here, the Torah gives us the explanation of the meaning of these instructions. Right at the beginning, as we have seen, the Mitzva of Pessach was to be the foundation and consecration of the Jewish home. Not individuals nor yet the nation as a whole, but homes, persons united in family groups, form the basis on which God built up His Nation.

“Homes”, above all, are the object of His never-slumbering care and guidance, and as a member of a household is every individual son of Israel to enrol himself as “the flock tended and shepherded by Him”.

זאת חקת הפסח, this law of the Pessach gave the personal qualifications which are necessary for membership of a Jewish home. Its members must belong to the Jewish national bond with God, by calling and mode of life, and their bodies must be sealed with the sign which God has instituted as the sign of the Jewish national bond with God. For just as God wants to look on the Nation only in the homes, so He wants to see the homes only in the Nation. The home is not to be something isolated, belonging only to itself. Rather, every home is to be naught but the soil in which the spirit of national unity and the common national mission is to receive and achieve its care and fulfillment. Therefore, a home belongs only to one who belongs also to the nation. Now the national mission of the total nation is a very great one and of a very manifold nature. Each home has its own special characteristic, and is always a shade different from every other home, due to the character, tendencies, ability, position etc. etc., of its inmates. Each home can develop its specialised fraction of the nation’s mission only in the home, and so, by the working together of all such individualisation, the whole mission of the whole nation can best be accomplished.

By the ordinance בבית אחד יאכל and לא תוציא מן הבית מן הבשר חוצה every home in its own speciality receives the highest acknowledgment of its importance and sanctity. Whereas the preceding laws limit the household to such members as belong to the nation and the national mission, these phrases elevate each separate home into exactly the idea of a sanctuary. The national Sanctuary מקדש (in contrast to במה where יוצא is כשר) is ideologically considered as a self-contained living entity, which holds everything fast to itself that is dedicated to it. So long as it is dominated by the מקדש it achieves its mission, but torn away from it, it fades away and perishes כיון שיצא בשר חוץ למחיצתו נאסר. In the same way every house which represents the home of the group united in the Pessach offering, becomes a self-contained holy circle from which no member and no portion of the offering may become estranged. A Pessach may indeed be eaten by two separate companies הפסח נאכל בב׳ חבורות but each group forms for itself a separate closed circle (according to רמב״ם they must even divide off the groups by actual walls הל׳ ק״פ ט׳ג׳) and each person may only eat at the table of his own Pessach. אין האוכל אוכל בשני מקומות, בבית אחד יאכל; no portion of the meat of the offering may be brought outside the circle לא תוציא מן הבית מן הבשר חוצה, and everything which has been brought outside its circle became פסול just as every יוצא does outside its own assigned circumference of the Sanctuary (within the precincts of the Temple, within the walls of Jerusalem etc., as the case may be).

And just as here the Jewish Nation built itself up symbolically on the clear separation of homes, and definite assignment of every member to the place of his Pessach as representing his own family circle, so later on, at the real actual building up of the Nation we see again and again as the first essential basis, the counting of Israel למשפחתם לבית אבותם. The pride of Israel and the source of its immortality is its pure family life which forms groups by its chaste purity — יחוסין שלהם — (see מדרש אספה Yalkut ויהי אחרי המגפה Numb. 25,19), a pearl, the care of which is demanded first of all by the “sign of the covenant of Abraham” which is also here one of the necessary qualifications for the Pessach.

ועצם לא תשברו בו. The real offering consists primarily of the blood and the flesh (i.e., the muscles), that is to say the active part of the animal, ועשית עולתיך הבשר והדם, (Deut. 12,27 and Zebachim 86a) excluding the bones which only form the passive framework. An offering is essentially a giving up of oneself and of the activities prompted by one’s own will. In the Pessach offering one receives oneself back. This symbolic “enjoying of oneself again”, represents the gift of the return of one’s personality, i.e., regained freedom of will. This refers primarily only to בשר the active part of the personality (the muscles). With this בשר, this ממַשֵׂר of the נפש, there are the bones, the means placed at the service of the will, to enable the activity of the muscles to function, and to hold the whole together. They are not the creature itself but they are placed at the disposal of the creature and in conjunction with it, עצם שיש בו בשר, they represent, not indeed activity, but the means by which activity is achieved. As long as the בשר on them can represent the dedication by one’s own free will of one’s activities to God. i.e., as long as the בשר is טהור, the bones, as the means used by this free will for activities, themselves become important, and must be treated with respect, must be protected from fracture. Apart from their use in conjunction with the בשר in pure and holy uses, the means themselves are worthless. In conjunction with it, they take on the importance and meaning of our morally free personality. Hence the dictum: ,אין בו כזית בשר אין בו משום שבירת עצם ,בטמא אין בו משום שבירת עצם (see Pesachim 84). Taken together with the two preceding precepts the verse would express: No person is to be withdrawn from the home, no בשר from the person, and no עצם from the בשר; the consecrated idea of the home is to hold all and everything fast to itself.

V. 47. And although they are divided into such carefully separated and individualised homely groups, they are nevertheless to form one united עדה; all the many are together at the same time to bring the one and same offering, are to place themselves and all that belongs to them on one and the same footing, have one and the same calling, become thereby the one united עדת ישראל, inasmuch as they all perform the one and same procedure: יעשו אותו.

V. 48. Right at the beginning of the constitution of the nation of Israel, it was declared that this constitution had in mind not only the sons of Abraham who had been redeemed from Egypt, and their descendants. All that had occurred from Abraham until the redemption from Egypt had been for the whole of humanity. Every human being can make this past his own, and enter the circle of the redeemed ones. Neither descent nor the right of birth in the country are considerations for the right to enter this constitution; only that which man carries within himself, only that which is truly human in a human being weighs ought in this consideration. The native born Jew loses all value if he becomes בן נכר, estranged from Judaism. The born heathen receives full and complete equality of rank as soon as he enrols himself into the Jewish bond with God. This Torah State grants simple right of domicile with all the rights of private citizenship, as remarked above on V.45, to every human being, even if he does not become a Jew, as long as he recognises the duties which lie in the calling of every human being, and thus becomes a גר תושב. The proselyte, גר צדק can even bring the Pessach offering although his fathers did not go out of Egypt. It was for him as well, that our fathers suffered in Egypt and received their freedom from the hand of God. Moreover, as expressed in V.27, Pessach belongs henceforth not only to the past, is not merely a memorial festival of ancient days, but is an ever to be repeated, ever progressive, building up of every present and every future on the old basis that was made for all time by יציאת מצרים.

[זרח ,אזרח does not mean to beam, to shine, in general, but to shine up out of the depths. We have already come across the contrast between the ע roots and the ח roots. Here too, זרע means to sow down into the depths and זרח to radiate up out of the depths. Hence referring to the sun, to rise, and מזרח the place where the sun shines its rays up out of the depths, the place of the sunrise. אזרח, a creature which finds itself there where it has come up out of the darkness, from not being here into being here: of plants, those which are still in their indigenous soil; of men, those who are native born].

V. 50. Siehe V. 28. Wenn sich dieser Bericht treuer Ausführung des von Gott Gebotenen auf das noch in Mizrajim vollzogene Peßachopfer bezieht, so muss dieses Gesetz noch am 14. Nissan gegeben worden sein und wäre dann wohl seine Stellung hier nach dem bereits erfolgten Auszuge daraus erklärlich, weil durch den dabei hervorgetretenen Anschluss einer Masse Fremder die praktische Anwendung desselben hervorleuchtet. Möglich, daß dieser Anschluss sich bereits in der Nacht vom 13. zum 14. bemerkbar gemacht, wo die sittliche Würdigung des jüdischen Volkscharakters so siegreich die Achtung und Zuneigung der ägyptischen Bevölkerung errungen hatte. Es wäre dann schon bei diesem ersten Peßach die Gelegenheit zur Anwendung dieses Gesetzes reichlich gegeben gewesen.

V. 51. על צבאותם. As indicated in the first paragraph of the laws of Pessach in Ch. 12,3, 4, and more fully and precisely by the last laws V.43 et seq., all the masses of the Jewish people had crystallised by birth or choice into family groups. Each such home and group had received in these laws its holy consecrated meaning and importance in the midst of the nation. Accordingly not only every tribe, but each family, each household could in truth be described as a צבא, as a group forming itself about God, and it was צבאותם, in such groups forming themselves in bands about the common centre point, that the exodus was accomplished. Thereupon God gave the law of the consecration of the firstborn, through which, in each such family group, the idea that was to keep them united together and also united with the rest of the nation was to have its living representative.

V. 1. As above in Ch. 12,21 et seq., here at the second Law we are again given a striking example of the תשב״פ. Here again, as in that first instance, we are again given not only the words of God’s speech to Moses, but also the words in which Moses transmitted this law to the people. The sentence in which we are told God’s word to Moses contains just the short dictum קדש לי כל בכור וגו׳. But Moses’ transmission to the people contains a great deal more, with a whole lot of instructions etc., which are not mentioned at all in God’s recorded words to Moses. If, as is the case in all the further Mitzvahs in the Torah, we had here also not been told exactly how Moses transmitted God’s word to the people then we should have taken the simple general sentence קדש לי וגוי as being the “the written Teaching” and all that Moses explained to the people on this sentence, with details about the laws of Mattzo, the duty of Hagada, the mitzva of Tephillin as well as especially the more detailed laws about the carrying out of the קדש לי כל בכור law, all that is contained in V.11 et seq., would have remained as תשב״פ and only known to us by tradition. These first two laws are accordingly an instructive example of the way and manner that God, the Lawgiver of the תורה, wished to have the revelation of His Will transmitted to us.

V. 2. קדש לי כל בכור. In the immediately preceding verse Ch. 12,51 recapitulating what had been said previously, and introducing what was fresh, we had been told, how the same grouping in tribes, families and households in which the nation had gathered for the Pessach was continued for the exodus, how God lead them out על צבאותם in “these their groups”, telling us, how the nation remained divided in these groups. Perhaps that is also why it says in Hallel בצאת ישראל וגו׳ then היתה וגו׳ and ישראל ממשלותיו and not ממשלתו as we should expect. Israel presented itself to God, as a “number of Kingdoms”, an unlimited number of circles placing themselves under His guidance and direction as their Shepherd.

But in order that these individual, separate groups should not fall asunder, in order that the one thought of their common mission which unites them all about the One God should remain vivid and vital in all of them, God appointed living representatives of this thought within the families and homes. That is what He did when he spoke קדש לי וגו׳ “Make holy unto Me”, literally, “Make it the calling of every firstborn to be absolutely and exclusively ready for Me and My purpose; the opener of every womb amongst the Children of Israel in man and beast is Mine.” He thereby appointed, in the midst of the family, the firstborn son as His representative, to be the bearer, cultivator, and defender of His Will; and in the herd, the firstborn, as the expression of the family possessions belonging to, and being given up to, this Will. By the efficacy of the first born sons and by the consecration of all firstborn, the homes and families are to be kept conscious of the holy common mission of the nation, so that in every home and in every family it is only the great national calling that becomes developed in the whole manifold diversity of the characteristics of families and homes.

This consecration of the firstborn to the service of God is not identical with the preferential rights of the firstborn in the matter of inheritance. A son can be a בכור לכהן without being בכור לנחלה and vice versa (see Bechoroth 46a). Every firstborn child of its mother is appointed as the God-serving representative of the family, provided this first child is born in a natural way (excluding יוצא דופן) and is a son. He must be בכור לולדות ולרחמים and זכר as it is expressly mentioned here that he must be בכור and פטר רחם, and that the law only affects the male firstborn is distinctly expressed in Deut. 15,19.

From the fact that this priestly character of the first birth is attached to פטר רחם, so that, for example, הבא אחר נפלים (a child who is born after the mother has had a previous miscarriage I.L.) is not בכור לכהן, it is at once evident that the law in its deeper conception is a consecration of the mother’s womb. Inasmuch as this first child is born, not only for the home and family, but in the first place equally for God, this makes the woman’s womb, that by the birth of this child has become a mother’s womb, declared as being dedicated to God. This makes all the following children, all that pass through this womb, all births, all the houses and families that are being built up in Israel, as belonging to God. It is only in the רחם and through the רחם that the בכור becomes קדש. (In the case of animals this idea is definitely expressed by the דין that at the birth it is the רחם, possibly even only direct contact with the רחם that is the sine qua non for the בכור to be קדוש: see Chulin 70a). So that the קדושה of a firstborn does not lie in himself. It is rather the רחם, that is to say, the consecration and holy mission of the mother’s womb, which only comes to its realisation through him, which gives him himself קדושה. But that this consecration is only attached to male first births lies in the different vocation of the sexes. It is the male sex which is exclusively called upon for national representation. The male sex is, as is already expressed in its name זכר (from זכר preserving, remembrance) the Keeper of the national tradition.

בכור see above (Ch. 4,22). פטר to free, to let out, also to be let out. פטר רחם would seem primarily to refer to the child, and would be: “that which has been let out from the mother’s womb.” But then it would refer to every child. So it must be taken to refer to the mother’s womb and designate the opening of the hitherto closed space, similar to פטורי ציצים opened blossoms. רעם ,רחם, is a hefty commotion, thunder. רחם, according to the opposing meaning of the ח to the ע, is protection from every commotion, designates that maternal space that encloses the coming child from all commotion; hence רַחֵם mother-like care acting to protect against all harm. לי הוא they belong to Me, to represent My demands in the family and on the family.

V. 3—9. ויאמר משה. Nothing gives more cause for consideration than the manner and way in which Moses transmitted to the people the order given him in the preceding verse. We have already remarked how therein we have a striking example of תשב״פ before our eyes. But we still have to find out what the connection is between these apparently totally unrelated laws and ordinances and the matter he was given to transmit. The relation must be a very close and essential one, as it is clear that they are given as detailed expositions of this single command. קדש לי כל בכור “Sanctify unto Me every firstborn”, was what God had said to Moses; and Moses impressed on the people the remembrance of the exodus, and the prohibition of Chometz, reminded them that it was in the month of Aviv that they went out, and that in the future they should celebrate the Festival of Pessach and Mattzo, gave them the duty of Hagada, and of Tephillin and only then goes over to elaborate the command that had been given him to sanctify the firstborn!

But if we look for the underlying thought of all the dicta and ordinances which are brought here as introduction to the law of the firstborn — some of them reminders, others completely new — we can find no other than this: — The whole nation is called to the service of God on the basis of the redemption out of Egypt, and the education of all children (not only the בכורים) for such service. But then the intimate and essential connection between all these sentences and the law of the God-serving consecration of the firstborn becomes immediately apparent.

The sanctification of certain persons, things, times or places, can very easily result in the pernicious idea that holiness and sanctification is limited to these persons, things, times and places. With the giving over of these things to holiness, the tribute has been paid, and the demand of holiness for everything else has been bought off. All other persons and things, days and houses are thereby given over to the so-called lower interests of life. It is clear how such a delusion of the preferential consecration of certain phases can bring about the most demoralising lack of consecration of all the rest of one’s life.

When, therefore, the sanctification of the firstborn was to be introduced into the sphere of the Jewish nation, Moses had, first of all, to remind the people how the redemption from Egypt places them all on one level towards God. Egypt was for all of them a בית עבדים, there, they were all born slaves. The strong Hand of God alone saved them out of it. At the recurrence of the date of the day of deliverance, this fact was for ever to be brought to their minds by not eating the bread of independence.

Let them look around; it was in the month of Aviv that they went out to freedom. The same God that brings about Spring in nature, and calls the seeds, which have lain chained in darkness throughout the winter, up into the light and into freedom, it is that very same God who brought about their Spring. He it was Who called them up from being chained in the wintry darkness of the Egyptian grave, into Light and Freedom and development of life. But, just like Nature, they, too, are still yet in the month of Spring. They have yet to strive for the attainment of maturity and the bearing and ripening of fruit. They have, like the green stalks, “eagerly, greedily”, (see note on אביב Chap. 9,31) with fresh enthusiasm to drink up out of the soil of freedom and of belonging to God, all the forces and strength which this soil grants; and use it all to produce “fruit”, to the attainment of the full maturity which God calls on them to reach.

They are to come to a land where this freedom can be furthered, should be furthered, by the added independence which riches grant. It is a land that can be one of overflowing abundance, (see Ch. 3,8) but which, up to the present, has only resulted in producing nations degenerated through Canaanitish luxury and voluptuousness. Hence, when they will have come into this land, the first thing that they will have to do will be to place themselves in the service of God by celebrating this Festival of Remembrance in this month of Spring. Then, not merely one day, as now, but a whole complete cycle of seven days are to be given up to this nation-wide remembrance, and to the whole nation ranking themselves into the service of God. Then, not only the first day, but also the seventh day, which leads us over into our ordinary daily life again, will see us gathered round God in a festival circle (חג). Then, not for one day, as now, but for seven days will the bread of dependence be in our hands, for seven days no sign of independence will be seen in the whole Jewish national realm. Then, under the impression of such a festival, the education of all your children is to begin, to educate them for this national calling of the service of God. Hand and Eye, deeds and thoughts of all, are to be called into this service, and every mouth is to be made into a herald of the teachings of God.

It was only after these proclamations that the call for every man and the education of every child for the service of God, and for His teachings, on the basis of the redemption from Egypt, must be eternally renewed and taken to heart, that the proclamation of the first born followed. This could then have no other meaning, and be taken in no other way than that it is to be a means for ensuring the realisation of the call and education of all for the service and teachings of God. But this in truth is nothing else but the carrying out of that which, as we have seen, is already expressed in the term פטר רחם, inasmuch as this term has to be taken as defining the sanctification of the firstborn as the consecration of the mother’s womb, and thereby all the children that follow.

V. 3. זָכור וגו׳ Always to be kept in remembrance, hence the infinitive form rather than the imperative. — בית עבדים .מבית עבדים is a house in which the father and the mother, and in consequence the children too, are slaves. Such were their homes in Egypt. There they were born slaves. Here, where the equal calling of all children was to be proclaimed, this designation of their condition in Egypt occurs for the first time. They are reminded that without the redemption by the יד חזקה of God, they and their children would still be slaves, so that they all, in an equal degree, belong to God, with their freed personalities. — ולא יאכל חמץ, the איסור אכילת חמץ is the expression of the knowledge and the recognition of the fact that בחזק יד הוציא וגו׳. Incidentally the wording יַאָכֵל אל expresses the idea: “see to it that חמץ does not get eaten”, accordingly להזהיר גדולים על הקטנים the duty of parents, of adults in general, to see that children, whilst still in their minority, do not become used to transgressing Jewish laws, לעשות המאכיל כאוכל. (See Mechilta on this verse, and קרבן אהרן on ת״כ on Levit. 11,13). A warning that is quite in accordance with the whole contents of this chapter of Jewish education.

V. 4. בחדש האביב This reference to God being identical in nature and in history, as well as the similarity of the two, is a thought that runs through the whole of the Jewish teachings of Divinity. The fact that the Redemption from Egypt occurred in Aviv is so important for our remembrance of the event, that next to קידוש החדש, (Ch. 12,2) it forms the second factor in making our yearly calendar. While the consecration of the month is dependent on the course of the moon, the recurrence of the Spring depends on the course of the sun, hence, as according to Deut. 16,1 precautions have to be taken that the Day of Redemption, Nissan 15, should fall at the beginning of Spring, the institution of עיבור שנה is necessary to level up the difference between the lunar year and the solar one.

V. 5. אל ארץ הכנעני וגו׳ Only five of the seven nations inhabiting the land are mentioned here. According to מכילתא on this verse, and ספרי כי תבוא (see רמב״ן), only the land of the five mentioned here are suitable for really great fertility. Perhaps these nations were also the most luxurious and depraved. It would then be the more significant that, according to the ספרי quoted, it was only from the lands of these five nations that ביכורים could be brought. In ביכורים the blessings of the Land are laid at the feet of the Torah and thereby two things are expressed. Firstly that the blessings of the Land only come through submission to the Torah, and secondly the undertaking that these blessings shall be used in the faithful carrying out of the dictates of the Torah.

V. 6. שבעת ימים. Moses said this on 15th Nissan, the day of the exodus. This, as remarked above, was the only “Mattzo-day” on this first Pessach. On the future recurrence of this date, the “Mattzo-command” is to be kept for seven days, and then on the seventh day, also a חג לה׳ is to be kept. That is why here, there is no further mention of the first day of the חג.

V. 8. והגדת וגו׳. As already remarked at the beginning, here too, on mentioning the Festival of the building-up of Jewish homes ever afresh on the basis of the Redemption from Egypt, the duties of Jewish education are immediately indicated. Our children are not to be induced to the faithful observance of the Torah by habit alone, nor is it to be accomplished by mere preaching. We must show them the way by our own keen and enthusiastic example, and at the same time, by teaching them the meaning and sense of our doings, wake up their minds and their hearts so that they learn to do the Mitzvoth with understanding and enthusiasm, so that their zeal for their Jewish observances appeals to their minds as well as to their feelings. — בעבור זה because of these practices, because of all these things that you see me doing (eating Mattzo and מרור etc., see the Hagada). When I came out of slavery into freedom, the one and only thing I could do towards getting this freedom was the undertaking that for all time I would make it my duty to fulfil these commands. This undertaking was the only reason for, and its fulfilment the only object of, the whole redemption. Everything else God did for me. From this you can measure the inestimable value of these practices. Our whole existence, based on God and dependent on God rests, on them.

V. 9. This and the following verse may still belong to the teachings which the father is to give to his son. The remembrance of this redemption is not to be merely a matter of a Festival of Remembrance, this remembrance — the fact that your whole present free existence is entirely due to the יד חזקה of God, so that with your whole being you belong to Him — is to be a guide for all your acts (לאות על ידך) and the basis of all your thoughts (לזכרון בין עיניך). Then every word that you speak — and it is in words that Man formulates all his will and all his thoughts — will flow from the teachings of God, so that you become a herald of His Torah.

והיה לך לאות וגו׳ as above XII,13 והיה הדם לכם לאות על הבתים. Just as there, the blood is to be “a sign for yourselves”, i.e., an expression of our giving ourselves and our homes up to the mission we had undertaken, so the fact of the redemption is to be expressed in a sign on our hands, to symbolise both our remembering and realising the implications of the redemption and also our giving up our hands to the result of the redemption, our belonging to God. That our “hand” belongs to God, is the very first result of the redemption. We ourselves had no hand in this redemption. God’s Hand alone was strong on our behalf. It is this Hand alone that we have to thank for the re-attainment of our own “hand” which in Egypt was not our own. But we only received it back on the condition that henceforth we use this “hand” restored to us by God, exclusively in His service.

Tradition teaches that this sign is to be worn not on the hand but on the muscle of the arm that controls the whole upper limb. We could have deduced this, anyway, from the nature of the Mitzva. From Deuteronomy we know that the sign is to be constantly worn, and to be bound to the יד and this, of course, would be a considerable hindrance to the use of the hand. Apart from this, it is also indicated by the parallel with the sign to be worn on the head, which is similarly expressed as בין עיניך and nevertheless refers to the place on the forehead from where the eye receives directions for its use. Another indication lies in the direction that (in accordance with הצנע לכת לפני ה׳) the sign referring to our actions is only לנו and not (והיה לך לאות) ,לאחרים לאות not to the world in general, hence it should be worn on a part of the upper limb that is usually covered (Menachoth 36b). בין עיניך as ולא תשימו קרחה בין עיניכם למת (Deut. 14,1) where it is quite clear that it can only refer to the place where normally there is hair, above the forehead.

למען תהיה תורת ה׳ בפיך. It is the living word, not the dead letter, to which the teachings of God are entrusted, similarly בפיך ובלבבך לעשתו (Deut. 30,14) and ואשים דברי בפיך (Is. 59,21) or ודברי אשר שמתי בפיך (ibid. LI,16). Not only to teach others, but to learn ourselves are we directed not to the bare script, but to that which has been entrusted to our mouths. So, highly significantly, it says: לא ימוש ספר התורה הזה מפיך (Josh. 1,8). By the written word of the Torah you are immediately to call to your mind that which has been given over to your mouth. The Torah wants even a solitary scholar to actually speak the words he reads, and by the living word impress the teaching on himself. Everybody is first of all herald of the Torah to himself, and by words, through his mouth, is he first of all to find way to his real inner self. Hence also the dictum לא הכשירו למלאכת שמים אלא עור טהורה בלבד (Sab. 28a) so that ס״ת תפלין ומזוזת may only be written on parchment made from animals that we are permitted to eat. Even the material on which the teachings of God’s Torah are written shall say to us, as God said to the prophet (Ezek. 3,1) אכול את המגלה “Eat this scroll!” i.e., absorb its contents completely, let its contents become part of your very self.

V. 11. והיה כי יביאך וגו׳. As long as Israel was still journeying to the land of its independence, “the eagle wings” (כנפי נשרים Ex. 19,4) of the Divine Providence which alone bore them safe and sound through the wilderness were visible and evident. All that time the daily existence of each one of them alike hung directly on the power of the Almighty; for all that time the exodus from Egypt really continued. They were still in the process of the Redemption and neither the consciousness of all belonging together nor that of belonging to God, was in any danger of being lost. Only when the last trace of the Egyptian calamity had disappeared, when the land that promised them independence and prosperity had become theirs, and each one of them with his family found himself under his own vine and his own fig-tree, then the danger would arise that the individual family groups and homes would become absorbed in their own interests, and the consciousness of the whole of Israel belonging together in the one common Divine mission might become lost. Then, above all, would the practical importance of the institution of the dedication of the firstborn to the service of God begin. That is why here too this institution appears in connection with the entry and taking possession of the Land. According to one opinion in the Gemora (ריש לקיש Berachoth 4b) actually only those firstborn who were present at the Exodus, and those who were born in the first year immediately after the Mitzva was given, were to be consecrated. Then קדשו ופסקו, at all further births the consecration of the firstborn ceased until the actual entry into the Land. ר׳ יוחנן however, is of the opinion (ibid.) that the institution started in full force with the exodus, and continued uninterruptedly, קדשו ולא פסקו and then the sentence והעברת וגו׳, והיה כי יביאך וגו׳ would be taken to mean עשה מצוה זו שבשבילה תיכנס לארץ i.e., fulfil this command, as, for its sake, you come into the Land. We think this can not be taken to mean anything else but that here the והיה כי יביאך ,ביאה would be taken as the result of והעברת וגו׳ (the כי would be taken as “so that”). It seems that when we find כי יביאך וגו׳ in connection with Mitzvas which are not dependent on the possession of land such as בכור ,תפלין, the thought והיה כי יביאך וגו׳ is only to emphasise the importance of the command. The Mitzva is so important that its fulfilment belongs essentially to the object for which the Land was to be given. God gives you the Land, so that, and because, you, as owner of the Land, should and will carry out this Mitzva. Without this Mitzva the possession of the land would be lacking in its object, perhaps even pernicious for your mission.

V. 12. והעברת ל- literally, you shall cause to pass over to, you shall make every firstborn pass over every other consideration, and lead him to God i.e., rejecting every other relationship, dedicate him to God. So also: אתם נצבים וגו׳ לעברך בברית וגו׳ i.e., giving up all others, entering into the bond with God, so here: When you have become possessor of the Land and have become firmly established there, grouping yourselves in your homes, then shall you guide all the male firstborn of your family and of your possessions to God, breaking away from all private considerations, as an expression of all of you, and all of your possessions, belonging to God.
— אשר יהיה לך which belong to you. Only if both the mother and the young animal are exclusively Jewish property does the sanctification of the firstborn apply.

V. 13. We have already worked out on Gen. 49,11 how, in contrast to the horse, the ass is the animal of peaceful prosperity. Asses were the beasts of burden for moveable possessions. The three categories of the sanctification of the firstborn, בכור בהמה טהורה, בכור אדם and פטר חמור represent, accordingly, Man, his food, and his possessions, and the sanctification of the firstborn declares (a) the family as belonging to God, (b) the food of the family, and (c) the possessions of the family all belonging to God.

The firstborn sons are to have the status of priests, and are to officiate at offerings: עבודה בבכורות עד שלא הוקם המשכן (Zebachim 112b). They were the “young men of the Children of Israel” whom Moses sent, when Israel concluded the covenant of the Torah with God, as representatives of the national union of the families of Israel, to bring the offerings of devotion and joy. (EX. 24,5). They are to keep alive and foster in the family life, the consciousness of the national submission to God, and of the Divine Mission of the nation.

בכור בהמה טהורה was to be offered upon the altar of the national sanctuary — בכור אינו קרב בבמה (Bechoroth 4a) — as an offering for human consumption קדשים קלים (later on they were given over to the כהנים as their property, for this purpose Numbers 18,15). This was to keep alive in the minds of the of the people the idea that the nourishment of the family, the prosperity of thier flocks and herbs, was also to be used in the servire of the national mission, and that the food of the home should not be desecrated by selfishness (used solely for selfish purposes).

פטר חמור had to be redeemed by a שה, — since the Pesach offering the most general representation of an ordinary Jewish personality (see Bechoroth 12a). According to Bechoroth 11a, if a lamb was not available the redemption could be made by giving the monetary value of the firstling. As long as the redemption had not been made, every use of the animal is prohibited אסור בהנאה. If the redemption does not take place at all, it has to have its neck broken and must be buried. The lamb or alternatively the value of the firstrling, must be given to the כהנים (Numbers ibid.). If we consider these laws, we come across similar ideas to those we encountered in the laws of שבירת עצם בפסח (Ch. 12,46): Lifeless property — represented by the beast of burden — in itself has neither intrinsic value nor meaning. It only gets value and meaning when changed into something living which can be used for the Divine Sanctuary of the national mission. Only when this purpose has been recognised by redemption, is the animal allowed to be used. Thus the idea is impressed that furthering the Divine object in having a Jewish nation must be the ultimate goal of the use of possessions for private and individual purposes. But the private individual who imagines that he will increase his private property by witholding his possessions from the holy objects of the community will find that he has fallen into a grave error. אם לא תפדה וערפתו is inscribed over every Jewish fortune. He who selfishly intends to keep it for himself, is himself sentencing it to destruction. It was only under conditions that Israel received again the right to possessions. Keeping any possessions at all, is, for Israel, dependent on keeping the condition that they are to be used solely in the service of God.

וכל בכור אדם בבניך תפדה. Already here we find a redemption mentioned for first born sons, although according to the original destination — which they forfeited at the incident of the golden calf — they were to be dedicated to a priestly, God-serving vocation. Without this redemption they would apparently have had to belong exclusively to this priestly vocation and would thereby be separated from the circle of the family. But that is just what they are not to be. They were to be, like all the other sons, an integral and intimate part of the ordinary family life, and there, as a model, bear, represent and realise the general Jewish holy calling. For it is not indeed in the Temple, but in the home, where the calling is fulfilled in its truer ultimate reality. The redeeming of our firstborn sons accordingly expresses the thought that the true actual service of the holy mission of Israel is to be carried out by the whole ordinary life of our children.

V. 14. מחר from which we get מחיר, exchange, exchange value, מחר the day which takes the place of today, the morrow. But where it does not mean the actual to-morrow it means a time which is different from the present. So וענתה בי צדקתי ביום מחר “when I shall have left this service”. (Gen. 30,33), מחר יאמרו בניכם לבנינו (Josh. 22,24) “when the history of our time will have been forgotten”. So also here: “When the remains and effects of the slavery, and the redemption therefrom will have disappeared from being realised by personal experience”. — מה זאת. What does this preferential consecration of the firstborn mean? — בחזק יד: With force, against the will of, and breaking the power of, the master who was holding us fast. — הוציאנו We were all slaves, it was only through God that we became human beings again, and so we all belong in an equal degree to God.

V. 15. הקשה. Pharaoh denied God, refused what God demanded of him, called his own that which was through and through God’s. God punished the obstinacy with which the Egyptians denied this fact of belonging to Him, by killing their firstborn. I dedicate all my firstborn to God so that we should not forget how we and all we possess belong to God.

V. 16. ידכה on your hand also, although you are no בכור. This verse belongs to the speech of the father to his son. — טוטפות, forehead ornaments. The Gemora in Sabbath 57a explains המקפת מאזן לאזן “A band which stretches from ear to ear”, i.e., a diadem. The etymology is obscure.

The same fact which gives the reason for the consecration of your firstborn brother applies to to you and ennobles you too, as it does all of us. The consecration of your firstborn brother ensures your consecration for you. (For notes on תפלין see Deut. 11,18).

V. 17—18. The ideal mission of the people of God was indicated in the preceding institutions of the Pessach offering, the Mattzo Festival, the consecration of the firstborn, and the law of Tephillin. Now the story goes back to the actual reality of the people. They had only just been redeemed from slavery, they were just at the beginning of their mission. We are at once shown that the people were by no means near that ideal stage to which they were called. At the same time we see how completely and absolutely lacking they were in the slightest trace of that power and that courage which could have attained freedom for themselves by themselves, or kept it if it had been attained. Not only the attainment of freedom, but the keeping of it too, was through the work of God alone. By themselves, so we read, they would have returned to the old slavery, if, on the road to assured independence, they were threatened with having to fight; and yet “they went out of Egypt fully armed.” It was not the sword at their side that was lacking, but the heart underneath that failed. They had no courage to fight, and above all they lacked the spirit of trustfully putting themselves in God’s hands under any and all circumstances, of finding will and courage, power and enthusiasm in the consciousness of His guiding.

In this narrative the ordinary name of God, אלהים, is used, and only in V.21 where the extraordinary guidance of God became visible in the pillars of cloud and fire, does the name of this extraordinary guidance ה׳ recur, as it occurred in the description of the extraordinary miracles in Egypt. The object of the establishment of a Jewish nation was, that amongst the nations of the world who develop their national life unconsciously under the guidance of God, there should be a people who were fully conscious of God in their national life. But the Jews were not ripe for such a life. In such a life one has simply to use all one’s own powers to the fullest extent of human possibility to the ends which God sets, and leave the success of such efforts to the promised support of God. The Jews were first to be educated to the full consciousness and confidence that God’s direct care for those who faithfully obey Him will not only be exercised to save them from threatened destruction, but will also care for their existence day by day under all circumstances. This they were to learn from extraordinary experiences, and this education was the meaning and object of the wandering in the wilderness, the meaning of the detour which God now made them take.

ולא נחם. Whereas נהג indicates also, and perhaps primarily, the leading of creatures without will and sense, נחה is used exclusively for the guidance of creatures endowed with will and reason, to the goal desired by them. נחה is phonetically related to נאה, attractive, desirable. נהה to long for something painfully and in vain, hence נהי, lamentation. נחה to lead to a desired end. — כי קרוב הוא gives the reason why the way through the land of the Philistines would really be the natural one.

V. 19. One has to consider why this fact is mentioned here and not above at the first account of the departure from Rameses. Perhaps it wants to emphasize the contrast. Six hundred thousand armed men on their way to take possession of the land promised to them by God could not be trusted to have sufficient confidence in this promise to face human opposition, and fight, feeling secure that victory must be theirs by virture of this promise. Whereas the true Jew — like Joseph — looks with full assurance, even beyond his death, to the fulfilment of God’s promises, and finds his trust has not been misplaced. God is שומר אמונתו לישני עפר “He who keeps faith with them who sleep in the dust” also in this sense. Looked at from this point of view, the bones of Joseph carried at the head of the train preached a constant sermon to the people who had to be led this detour through the wilderness on account of their lack of spirit and fortitude.
V. 20. קצה is any extreme point of a place, hence ‘beginning’ as well as ‘end’.

V. 21. וה׳ הולך וגו׳ ,בעמוד וגו׳. The pillars of cloud and fire were the visible signs of God’s special guidance, and here they served also as the means of His guidance. — לנחותם the same as להנחותם: “To let them be guided by the pillars.”

V. 3. נבכים according to its form must come from נבך not from ביך otherwise it would have to be נבוכֹים, as נבך .נכונים as נבכי ים (Job 38,16) the depths of the sea, hence נבכים “to be sunk” to be immersed, “caught in the land”, they can not get out; on one side the sea which they can not cross, on the other Baal Typhon (see following note) will not let them pass, and that is why they have had to turn back. (Typhon was the Egyptian god of the sirocco, of death, evil, blight and barren wastes, hence the desert would be one of his domains).
V. 4. וחזקתי: See notes above on Ch. 7,3, X,1, XI,9 and 10. — ואכבדה: I wish to be recognised in the full weight of My Greatness and Power.

V. 5. כי ברח העם. For several reasons this cannot mean, “that the people have fled” i.e., have no intention of returning. As we saw above, Pharaoh had sent the people away from his country with the full idea of their not returning, and here, too, he reproaches himself with the fact that כי שלחנו ישראל מעבדנו. Moreover, their turning back is by no means evidence of flight, rather the reverse. Finally, the reason for Pharaoh’s change of mind towards the children of Israel is expressly given in V,3, as being the desperate plight of the people in having, as he supposed, their path to freedom cut off. So this ברח can very well refer to just this turning back which would be reported to Pharaoh as a flight from the might of Baal-Typhon before whom the people were driven back in terror from their intended entry into the desert. In this, Pharaoh saw a defeat of the power of God, Whose supposedly invincible might had driven him and his people to what he now thought to have been the over-hasty decision to let the people go entirely out of their servitude. He now, accordingly regretted this decision.
V. 6. He placed the whole battle line under his own direct command and led them on.

V. 7. בחור is the term always used to designate a picked champion or warrior. So Kings I. 12,21, מאה ושמנים אלף בחור and elsewhere. — וכל רכב מצרים the first were war-chariots, these were transport wagons. The most important thing was to get Israel back as soon as possible before they could be released from what he thought was their desperate position. That was why he tried every possible means to transport the whole army in wagons.

V. 8. As “King of Egypt,” he should have shown respect for the common rights of peoples. Israel was no longer the people who had come down from their forefathers as slaves. They had gone out ביד רמה free independent human beings, he himself had given them their freedom. He no longer had any rights over them, and if he now wanted forcibly to drag them back to slavery, this could only be judged by most universal consciences as an act of violent slave-raiding. הרים יד במלך (Kings I. 11,26) means to rebel, to rise against the King, so that יד רמה means complete independence, dependent on nobody. That was the legal status which Pharaoh had given the people at their departure. They were not sent away as slaves who had been granted a three-day’s leave. He had let them go completely, and their “hand was high” i.e., had become independent.

V. 9. That Israel’s journey out to the desert, their journey back to Pi-Hachiroth, the report to Pharaoh and the journey of Pharaoh’s army to Pi-Hachiroth could all take place within six days, becomes understandable when one remembers that, as it says in Ch. 13,21, the people journeyed day and night, so that, what was ordinarily a three day journey to the desert would have been accomplished in a much shorter period. Also Pharaoh’s army travelled for the most part on horseback or in chariots, and the people had come back to Pi-Hachiroth towards them. Wherever Pharaoh’s army is mentioned, horses are in the foreground. For it was just through their being mounted (Egypt was renowned for its chargers. I.L.) that they were such a danger to Israel, and flight into the desert was not to be thought of. Israel had only cattle and sheep and asses, animals of peaceful calling. Military chargers were lacking in Israel’s national make-up, and later on too, they were not to play an important part in Israel’s national greatness.

V. 10. נשא עין is, as already repeatedly remarked, an intentional looking out for something. They heard in the distance the noise of the approaching Egyptian army, which of course made them look in that direction. By the repetition of the subject בני ישראל here with ויצעקו וגו׳ any idea of disapproval of their crying out to God is removed. Their fear was a natural one and their cry of help to God, was in no way unworthy of their “Israel-character”.

V. 11. They were doubtful with regard to Moses’ mission. In their position, and from their standpoint, a very understandable doubt. How could they, how dared they, just quietly assume that God would help them in such an extraordinarily miraculous manner, for which there was absolutely no precedent, and which was so completely against all natural expectation. These continuous doubts form an important proof for the truth of Moses’ mission, as R. Jehuda Halevi remarks in the Kusri. Moses had to deal with a clear-minded people whose minds were not befogged by fantastic ideas, and who were not easily taken in, or convinced, by the first man who comes along. If then, ultimately, this very people have cheerfully given themselves up for centuries to fight the world, and to die for “the teachings of this Moses”, it is a proof that the sending of this Moses must have won them over to an unassailable conviction by the force of actual deeds and occurrences. — המבלי אין וגו׳. This sharp irony even in moments of deepest anxiety and despair is characteristic of the witty vein which is inherent in the Jewish race from their earliest beginnings.

V. 12. It seems that they, quite naturally, had feared that they would have to be exposed in the wilderness to both hunger and sword. They must necessarily have feared the sword of attacking hordes in their passage through the wilderness to be able to say: “Is not this, that which we told you already in Egypt?”. According to this, חמושים, mentioned above would be attributed to the people’s own precautionary measures. God had only prescribed a staff in their hands, but they thought that they were obliged and permitted to provide themselves with arms. The notes on V.17 of the previous chapter, by this idea, get a still greater confirmation.

V. 13. התיְצבו וראו probably in the same sense as ותתצב אחותו (Ch. 2,4) place yourselves expectantly there. And exactly as there, in the consciousness that you can do nothing further, but to wait and trustfully expect the rescuing Hand of God. The one and only activity that such a critical moment demands of us is an internal one, the ישב :יצב) התיצב with the harsher, more emphasized צ sound) to bring oneself to a state of calm and to the mood of quietly standing and waiting.

[ישועה must surely be differentiated from ישועה .תשועה comes from תשועה ,ישע from יֶשַׁע .שוע (related to ישה, the root of יש, the real, essential being in existence) designates the highest degree of the reality of “being” which God gives Man. And ישועה is salvation from an existence which is threatened. But שוע related to שבע ,שפע, designates more, an abundance of goods, hence also שׁוֹע the well-to-do. שׁועַ accordingly, refers more to the sphere, the periphery of a being than to the being itself. The opposite idea would be the conception of narrowness, limitation, need צרה, and תשועה would be the granting of an extended sphere, granting of power, freeing of domain. Hence תשועה is used primarily for granting victory in battle, where the enemy who threatens our domain is beaten back. Hence possibly שַׁוֵעַ (which above we tried to derive from שוע having the meaning of שעה to turn, for which however there is but one single example הָשַׁע) might mean to strive for תשועה, as התחנן means to strive for חן.].

V. 15. The word התיצבו in V.13 shows us what Moses’ opinion was of the nature of the expected salvation. He thought — as really happened later in our history to the army of Sennacherib — that God would destroy Pharaoh and his army without him or the people having to do anything at all. Accordingly, while calming the people, his soul cried up to God, praying that He would grant the promised aid. To that he received the reply מה תצעק אלי — דבר אל בני ישראל ויסעו. “Indeed the salvation is still dependent on the people, the first step must be taken by them, they must first show themselves deserving of salvation by a courageous, fearless act, cheerfully showing their trust in God. Let them break camp and unconcernedly march into the sea; then God will start His salvation.”

V. 16—17. “Not I alone, (says God) have to be active, the people too, must do their part by their trusting courage, you, as My messenger, by proving the event to be an act of God, by its occurrence at the waving of your staff, and finally I Myself, in arranging the event in such a manner that the Egyptians will have the daring to follow you into the sea.” — ואכבדה the ה here as well as in V.4, expresses the thought: Pharaoh’s destruction is not indispensable for Israel’s salvation. He could well be terrified by the phenomenal occurrence, turn back and give up the pursuit of Israel. But by the wickedness that lay in his whole undertaking he had earned his destruction, and God wanted to reveal the whole weight of His Greatness in the destruction of this mighty power. He would use the same element to destroy a human power united to do wickedness, that retired in awe to grant salvation to those that were helpless and innocent and looked for their help solely to God. — ברכבו וגו׳ “in spite of”, literally, with, as בחרי אף (Is. 7,4).

V. 18. This revelation of the whole weight of My Power should be a warning and instructive lesson for the Egyptian world, and for all those who, like Pharaoh, set the greatness, welfare and victory of nations on military power and force, without any consideration of moral values.
V. 19. The sea is not to retreat before the angel of God, but before human beings putting their trust in God.
V. 20. By the cloud taking up its position between the two camps, the Egyptian camp remained in darkness when the pillar of fire lit up the Jewish camp.

V. 21. The east wind whipped the water apart right down to the ground, so that the water towered up on either side and the exposed ground was dried by the wind. Thus a path was made from west to east and in that direction Israel passed through the sea.

V. 24. באשמרת also אשׁמורָה (Ps. 90,4), is a division of the night. Perhaps there were periods into which the night was divided for relieving the guards, each such “period of guard” was accordingly called an אשמרת. According to Berachoth 3b, the night was divided into four or three such “watches”. The morning watch was the last period of the night. — השקיף is always a looking-down from above. “Through” or “by means of a pillar of fire and cloud”; such a pillar was the messenger and servitor of His glance, it accomplished His Will. In Ps. 77,18 & 19, the passage through the sea is described as being accompanied by terrific earth-shaking storms, perhaps this is meant to express the bewildering, and, as is seen from V,23, the destructive effect of this pillar of cloud and fire. — ויהם “and brought into confusion” as we also find ויהם ה׳ את סיסרא ואת כל הרכב וגו׳ (Judges 4,15) and והמתי את כל העם (Ex. 23,27).

V. 27. איתן ;לאיתנו from אתן (with prolonged נח as קיטור from קטר) the root of אתון the beast of burden, and related to אדן the base or foot of a pillar, designates a firm unaltered ground pointing back to its aboriginal state. Against its nature, water had piled solidly upon water. Now it returns to its natural state in the ocean bed. — וינער. In the following “song at the sea”, the drowning of the Egyptians is repeatedly pictured as the sinking of stone or lead in water. This picture is apparently at variance with what is described here as happening. The Egyptians did not crash down from above into the sea. They were on the bed of the sea and the floods crashed down on them from above. The word וינער may, however, supply the clue. נער is essentially a shaking off, or a shaking out, in general, emptying. As we have observed above, the greater part of the army was in wagons or chariots. These chariots and wagons were lifted up by the water and overturned so that their contents were shot out into the water, and, stark with terror, not even making an effort to save themselves by swimming, sank like stones or lead into the depths.

V. 28. לכל חיל פרעה: “for the whole army etc.” If it simply wanted to enlarge on את הרכב ואת הפרשים it should say כל חיל or וכל חיל but the ל prefix to כל together with the repetition in verse 29, ובני ישראל וגו׳ of what has already been said in V.22, leads us to take these two verses together as pointing out how the contrasting effects of this one event reveal God in His Almighty Power. For the whole army of Egypt that followed hard on their heels, the waters crashed and engulfed them, and for the children of Israel just in front, the waters remained upright to the right and left and gave them dry passage. More, both events may have taken place at the same time. While on the east side Israel was completing its passage, behind their backs on the west, the waters were already crashing down upon the Egyptians! This is the יד גדולה, this was the Greatness of the Hand of God, which in this event showed the whole of the physical nature of the World in service of the justice of the free Master of Nature.
V. 30. The cantillation shows that על שפת הים refers to את מצרים and not to Israel. Accordingly the sea must have cast up the dead bodies onto the shore.

V. 31. יראה and אמונה, these are the two principal feelings which Israel is for ever to have towards God. There is only one whom we should fear and trust simultaneously, and that is God, the Unique One, Who is as full of love as of justice and equally united and all-powerful in the exercise of His love as of His justice. To reveal and teach all three, His justice, which is ever to be feared, His love which is ever to be confidently expected, and His exercising both at the same moment with complete freedom over every other power, such is the meaning for all time of this great moment of salvation which laid the Egyptian giant as a corpse at the feet of the slaves now freed for ever. But just as this moment was the proof of God’s Hand exercising His love and His justice with unlimited power, so was it also the proof for all time of the genuineness of Moses His servant. Moses’ hand was raised over the sea and thereby God led the Egyptians to death, and Israel to the path leading to life and freedom.

V. 1. The peculiarity that אז is frequently construed with the future tense, when it introduces an event which from the standpoint of the narrator is in the past, may be understood by the meaning of this adverb. אזי ,אז (from root אזה related to חזה seeing in your mind something invisible, far off) transposes the thoughts away from the present to make you see an event which occurred at some other period, past or future, actually in the process of happening. The tense is accordingly chosen, not which would be in accordance with the time of relating, but which is suitable for the period of the happening itself. At the moment at which our story has reached, the singing is regarded as just happening, hence the future tense. אז שר would mean, then, at that time they sang (they had sung). אז ישיר “then they began to sing” (they broke out into song). — Where אז is used with the verb in the past (and does not wish to imply the plu-perfect) so that the אז places the event in the moment of its happening, but the verb is used relating to the time of the narration, it is presumed that the event itself is known, and only the time of its happening is what is to be told. Thus אז הוחל לקרא וגו׳ the fact that “calling in the name of God” did once have a beginning is supposed to be known, but what is to be informed is, that it started in the time of Enoch. Also when אז is not used in the sense of “at that time”, but “thereupon”, and wants to continue the story, the past is used, as אז אמרה חתן וגו׳ (above Ch. 4,26) or אז אמר שלמה (Kings I. 8,12). Nevertheless, this requires somewhat deeper investigation (see V.15).

שיר (related to שקר ,שכר ,שגר) to express thoughts and feelings that have been called into existence within oneself. Generally, an inspired or rapturous expression of what some external event has revealed to the inner self, that which the physical eye can not see, but which has become clear to the mind’s eye. Hence, in the first instance, words singing of God in history (see Gen. 9,21).

— אשירה לה׳ i.e., “To God, to His glorification, to spead the knowledge of Him, would I sing, how infinitely high He has shown Himself in that which we have here experienced. סוס ורוכבו, that mighty army that we so dreaded, has He flung into the sea. He and He alone acted in the whole of this occurrence. אשירה I would sing, O’ that I could find words worthy of Him, words that would express the excitement I feel deep within me”. How similar, and yet how different this modest, full-of-God אשירה, to that proud, full of only his own glory: “Arma virumque cano” or “Je chante ce heros etc.” We find רמה used of shooting arrows רמה קשת and it seems to be used in that sense only (see V.4). [The רמת לחי of Samson can also have been said referring to the fact that he used the bone as weapon. It seems to be related to רמח, javelin].

V. 2. עזי from עוז ,עזז is the power of resistance, the invincibility. The fact that I remain unconquered — that Pharaoh and the sea have left me untouched, and זמרת, this singing in which I am engaged, both עזי וזמרת are the work of God. We have already on Gen. 43,10, indicated the relation of זמרה the melody, to שיר the words of the song. We thought that melody was the audible soaring of the spirit to the heights of rapture, and the mature outcome of thoughts that were working in the soul. This loftiest work of the human spirit in which his noblest energy unfolds itself, is, when it is inspired by thoughts of God, itself a work of God. It is, as the songster King of Israel says of himself, God’s spirit that speaks through him and it is His words that hover on his tongue. (Sam. II. 23,2, רוח ה׳ דבר בי ומלתו על לשוני). Hence in all these sentences referring to זמרה, the personal pronoun “my” was missing (here and in Ps. 118,14 & Is. 12,2), not זמרתי but זמרת. The singer wants to say expressly that it is not זמרתו!

The Name יה (related phonetically to כה and כח) is always used to designate a revelation of the Might of God, His working and ruling become visible and evident. Hence thereby is said here: Both my salvation and the rapture that this salvation has awakened in me, i.e., both my external fate and my internal life are a revelation of the presence of the power of God, showing itself working for, and in me. — ויהי לי לישועה and that was my salvation. God saved me, because in me, He saw a suitable instrument for revealing His government in the formation of nations and men. My external weakness, and my internal strenth and receptivity, have won for me the help and support of God. In הללויה this name of God is joined to the singing of the deeds of God in one conception. At the base of this form of expression may be this same idea in which the inspiration of the song, singing of the deeds of God, is itself considered an act of God. And this may well be the meaning of the saying of ר״י ב״ל in Psachim 117a: גדול מכולן (מכל מאמרות של שבח) הללויה שכולל שם ושבח בבת אחת.

זה אלי: Henceforth that will be my God. As here I see and understand that my fate and my inner life has been directed by Him alone, henceforth I will place the whole of my internal and external life at His disposal, and allow my whole ife to be directed and guided by Him (only then can one call God “my God”). He shall be אלי, literally “The Director of my movements”. ואנוהו, and so will I offer myself to be His home. My whole existence and life shall be a Temple of His Glorification, the “home” of His revelation; this is the natural consequence of נוה — .זה אלי (related to נוח) designates a place which offers itsself as a resting-place.
