That is why then we see just here at once in the chapter of the foundation of the Sabbath all the radical elements of the נולד ,מוקצה ,הכנה :שבותי דרבנן and also תחומין as far as it is דרבנן.

V. 31. בית ישראל. Israel as בית as a family, and the representatives of family life, the women, called it Manna, food apportioned-out by God! The oldest “seekers and explainers of the subtle niceties of the scripture” דורשי רשומות, already pointed out the significance of this, דורשי רשומות אמרו בית ישראל קראו את שמו מן (Mechilta). Getting and keeping the feeling of being happy and contented with moderation, trusting in God and His providing, is above all dependent on the women of the household accepting this spirit, and on their care of an adherence to this spirit of living. It is therefore significant that it was just the women who first recognised the Manna as the gift from God to each individual of his due sufficiency, and by giving it the name “Manna” fixed this idea so that it should constantly be taken to heart. — גד this name indicates small particles, from גדר, to cut up, divide into fine particles.

צפיחת. According to the commentators, a cake-dough: R. Eliezer explains it in the Mechilta כסולת זו שהיא צפה על גבי נפה, as the finest flour that remains suspended on the sieve. (so translate, as “the finest flour with honey”). The procedure of obtaining flour from corn is described in Menachoth 76b, that the shelled grains of corn were shaken in a fine sieve until all the coarser flour (קמח) fell through and was separated. This was carried on with finer and finer sieves until only the very finest amylon-containing grains remained, and this was then ground. This sieving was therefore called ריקוד, making the grains dance in the sieve.
דבש as a rule is not honey but fruit juice, and honey is probably only called by the same name because it is also the “juice” which the bees suck out of the blossoms.

V. 32. The command for this storage told the generation of the wilderness that this wandering in the wilderness would come to an end, and that they would ultimately be led into normal conditions, but that they and their descendants were to keep the spirit engendered by living on the Manna, even when living in normal conditions; and also that they were even then to look on their food, which the rest of the social and physical world consider as טרף ,לחם and צידה as obtained by fighting, competing and catching away from others, as מן as the “modest but sufficient” portion allotted by God. Therefore, also the צנצנת המן the “storage flask of Manna” was to be kept לפני העדות directly together with the tablets of stone which testified to the Torah being a gift from God. “God who had given the Torah also gives food to keep life alive for the keeping of this Torah. God who gives the food has also given the Torah to direct the life that is kept going by this food.” The consciousness of both these facts belongs together and each is complementary to the other.

V. 33. צנצנת from צנן a cooling flask. Warmth, as we know, was injurious to the consistency of the Manna. The vessel in which it was to remain intact for such a long time must be one which keeps out heat. Perhaps a stone vessel.
V. 34. As God had commanded Moses long before, at the first sending of the Manna, later on when the ark of the tablets of the covenant was in existence, Aaron laid the flask of Manna in front of it.

V. 35. First we are informed that the children of Israel were fed by the Manna for as long as this was necessary, i.e., as long as they were not in an inhabited country. Then, that they continued eating Manna until their actual entry into the Promised Land, so that they went directly over from being fed by Manna to enjoying the produce of the Land, so that the produce of this land which was only lent to them for the service of God, should remain “Manna” to them and they were only to continue enjoying it as מן, as food sent by God.

V. 36. עשירית האיפה was later the normal basic measure of all מנחות, accordingly a quantity representing the food of a person before God. So that this measure itself already carries the Manna-idea to our food which in the מנחה we beg God to remember. Perhaps even the word מנחה, if the מ is part of the root, which would then be מנח, would be related to מנה, the root of מן and then have the meaning of מָנָה.

V. 1. It does not say ואין מים לשתות, but ואין מים לשתות העם, they were not yet without water, but they looked at the country, and saw that there was not there sufficient water for such a number of people, and so, that they would be short of water.

V. 2. וירב is not תלונה as וילן in V.3, which we found (from the meaning of לון) to mean seeking relief from some privation or distress that one is beginning to feel, but וירב is chiefly used for establishing a supposed or real claim to something to which one has a right, as in the dispute over the wells (Gen. 26,20). Here, they were not yet making any reproaches, did not refer to their requirements, but, as a justified claim, demanded water. Where we camp, there must be water: תנו לנו וגו׳. As the ן in תריבון and תנסון stresses the 2nd person, the retort runs: you know quite well that it is not I but God who has led you hither, and surely you have by now had sufficient experience of God to quietly trust to Him, that here also He will not let you die of thirst. In ordinary circumstances your demand would be quite justified, but, you etc.

V. 5—6. From Rephidim to Horeb is but one station and from these verses seems to have been hardly a day’s journey. It seems that, had it not been for their untimely murmurings, God would have let them realise and feel the scarcity in Rephidim and then let them move on to Horeb, which was the real goal of their wandering in the wilderness, and then there at Horeb He would let water gush out of the rock for them. There, they were to receive the Torah and there they were to tarry for a long period. They had already on a previous occasion been three days without water and had not perished. So that they surely had a certain provision of water with them on their wanderings. This whole idea is strengthened by the tradition that after Horeb, water, as the so-called Well of Miriam, travelled with them, so that henceforth for every refreshing drink that they enjoyed in the wilderness, they had to thank, and were to thank, the rock on the Mountain of God where they received the Torah. This would also explain the expression במחקק במשענתם which occurs in the Song of the Well (Numbers 21,18). “The same style that wrote the Law for them, dug the well for them which kept them alive in the wilderness.” And as a matter of fact we do not find again that there was any lack of water from this provision of water in the first year until the death of Miriam in the fortieth year. It was only that their untimely murmurings brought it about that God, now already in Rephidim, provided them with water from Horeb. The words ויצאו ממנו מים ושתה העם, seem to indicate that the water flowed down from Horeb to the camp of the people in Rephidim. So also this incident is sung in Ps. 105,41. “They demanded and He let the quails come, and satiated them with the bread of Heaven, He opened a rock and water flowed and went as a stream through wildernesses.” According to this, עבור לפני העם, would mean “precede the people, pass on before the People, you go on to where the people are to come later. ומטך the staff with which you took away the drinking water from the Egyptians, shall now produce water for Israel to drink”.

V. 7. ריב :על ריב וגו׳ ועל נסתם וגו׳ against Moses, נסותם against God. From this, too, one can deduce that the necessity for water had not by any means yet reached the pitch of requiring urgent and immediate relief. God would have led them to Horeb in good time and there given the full requirements for the whole of their future wanderings. In Rephidim it was only doubting faintheatedness that wants to be sure of help before the danger is there, that asked היש ה׳ בקרבנו וגו׳, which was not so much a doubt of the Power of God, as the doubt whether He was also בקרבנו whether His wonderful Might was ever present also amongst human beings, and whether their wants and requirements were really near to Him. The general ideas on Nature, God and Man were so completely opposite to the Truths which were to be realised in Israel and through Israel; Nature and its Laws were thought to be so completely absolute and above any other power whatsoever; the gods themselves to be similarly bound by these laws; and Man to stand so powerless under the double ban of the blind powers of both Nature and gods, the step to Jewish conceptions of these matters was such a tremendous and overpowering contrast, that we really can not wonder if these basic ideas which lie at the root of all Jewish thought and actions only became firmly established in the minds of the first People of God very gradually, and that it required all the great and wonderful experiences of our history, which was then just at its commencement, to make these truths really and truly and safely fixed in our consciousness. For the very foundation of Jewish Teaching is based on recognising: (a) Nature as being a creation of a completely free, Almighty unique God, Who still retains completely free mastery over it, and is in no wise bound by it, or the laws He has made to govern it; (b) God, as the One, Personal, Free, Almighty Creator with completely unlimited powers of governing the world and (c) above all, Man as being created by this free Creator as a personality with complete free will of his own, to whom is given, again by the free Creator, the mission of raising himself above the forces of Nature which stand far below him, by, of his own free will, subjecting his own will to that of God, to become the first free servitor of God.

V. 8—16. All the experiences which Israel — destined to become the Nation of God — had hitherto made, since its entry into the wilderness, Mara, quails, Manna, Sabbath, water-from-the-rock, taught it to know its future relation to Nature, taught it what independence of the forces of Nature it was to gain, simply by subjecting itself to the Will of God. They still had one experience to make in these preparatory weeks for the reception of the Torah. It remained for them to learn what the position of the future People of God was to be, as a nation amongst the nations; its position in relation to human forces and for the future of human violence. This experience they were to have while still in Rephidim, the means of teaching was Amalek.

In the same way that the Spirit of Esau, in its night attack on Jacob who was on his peaceful way to his individual independence, made Jacob live through the whole struggle and fight that the descendants of Esau would impose on the descendants of Jacob throughout the night-centuries of world-history, and proclaimed the final ultimate victory of Jacob, so it was Esau’s grandson, Amalek, who was the first and only nation that, completely unprovoked and unthreatened, attacked Jacob’s grandson, Israel, on their way to national independence. However weak and tired out by their wanderings, עיף ויגע, this people with women and children seeking a homeland must have appeared, the Might of God which hovered over them protecting and guiding them, had become so imposingly evident, that the fear of it paralysed all the other nations, even those not immediately threatened. Philistia feared, Edom remained stunned, Moab trembled, Canaan was quite dumbfounded, it was only Amalek, completely unprovoked, who hurried out of his way to gain renown and take up arms against the Force which had laid even a Pharaoh low. He alone לא ירא אלהים, did not fear God. He alone, was the heir of that spirit which chose the sword as his lot, who sought to realise the seeking renown in laurels of blood and the נעשה לנו שם with which old Nimrod started the history of the world to the destruction of the happiness of nations and men. This seeking renown by the force of arms is the first and last enemy of the happiness of mankind and of the Kingdom of God on earth. The policy of the Pharaohs — using force ruthlessly to further their own interests, certainly has interest in keeping up slavery, but it can even be a friend of freedom, when freedom serves its interest. But Amalek’s renown-seeking sword knows no rest so long as one single pulse beats in freedom, and pays no homage to it, so long as any modest, quiet happiness exists which does not tremble before its might. Similar forces, armed to the teeth like himself, Amalek does not hate, but rather sees in such measures a sign of recognition and fear of his sword. He wages war against them of course, but honours opponents who acknowledge him and have similar principles to his own.

But in Israel he sees an object of mortal hate and complete disdain, where one dares to think the sword is dispensable, where one dares to trust in spiritual-moral powers, powers of which the sword has no idea, and which are beyond its reach. In the representative of the idea of the greatness which Man can attain by Peace, Amalek sees the utter scorn of all his principles, sees in it his one real enemy, and senses somehow his own ultimate collapse. ויבא עמלק וילחם וגו׳, “Amalek came and made war on Israel in Rephidim”. Perhaps if Israel’s faintheartedness had not caused Rephidim to be transferred from a passing station to a camping ground, Israel would long ago have already been led on to Horeb, and Amalek would not have caught them in Rephidim. But as it was, Israel had to endure this fresh anxious and worrying experience.

V. 9—12. Attacked by Amalek, Israel had to wage war, but it is not Israel’s sword but Moses’ staff that conquers Amalek; and it is not any magic power in the staff but the אמונה which is expressed and brought to the minds of the people by the uplifted hand, the giving oneself up with complete confidence to God that achieved the victory. אמונה, “so his hands remained as an expression of confidence until the sun set”.

אמונה used absolute like this, occurs as the description of the character or meaning of some subject-matter. כל מצותיך אמונה (Ps. 119,86), or again ואמונה עניתני (ibid 75). “That thou hast sent me troubles was אמונה on Thy part.” So also here. That which his hands meant was אמונה. Aaron and Hur were at the side of Moses as the representatives of the People. Not the confidence in God of the Leader, but the confidence in God of the People, which the Leader inspired, led to victory.

V. 13. חלש ויחלש, whereas חלץ means the loosing of a constricting band i.e., freeing, חלש is the loosing of the natural forces which hold one together, i.e., weakening. Joshua only weakened Amalek. His final defeat remains for the distant future. Israel itself is not yet mature. Until Israel attains maturity, the existence of Amalek as a contrast is necessary for the development of Israel’s education.

V. 14. בספר, in the book of the Teachings and the law, ושים וגו׳ and that which you have written down in general for remembrance, you are to enlarge, explain and develop for the mind of Joshua. Here we have an example of כתב and בעל-פה for an historical event just as we had it for the Laws. Compare ואלה המשפטים אשר תשים לפניהם (XXI,1).

את זכר עמלק. It is not Amalek who is so pernicious for the moral future of mankind but זכר עמלק, the glorifying of the memory of Amalek which is the danger. As long as the annals of humanity cover the memory of the heroes of the sword with glory, as long as those that throttle and murder the happiness of mankind are not buried in oblivion, so long will each successive generation look up in worship to these “great ones” of violence and force, and their memory will awaken the desire to emulate these heroes, and acquire equal glory by equal violence and force. Only when the divine laws of morals have become the sole criterion as to the worth of the greatest and smallest of men, and no longer in inverse proportion but in direct proportion to greatness and power do the demands of morality grow, and the greater and more powerful a man is, the less any lapse in the laws of morality is excused, then and then only will the reign of Amalek cease for ever in the world. That this is the final goal of God’s management and direction of the history of the world is expressed here after the first weakening of Amalek, “I will utterly obliterate the keeping up the remembrance of Amalek from as far as the heavens reach”. So also in Ps. 9,7, the thought is poignantly expressed, that only with the doing away with the remembrance of devastations and conquests will the perpetrators of these deeds disappear אבד זכרם המה!

V. 15. ויבן משה מזבח. Just as Jacob, after he had won the name Israel by his night-long fight with the genius of Amalek, built an “altar for remembrance” ויצב שם מזבח (Gen. 33,20 see notes there), and thereby immortalised the acclamation אל אלהי ישראל, so did Moses here build “an altar of remembrance” after the first victory over Amalek, and after the meaning of this victory had become clear to him. Amalek’s greatness lies in “destruction”. Israel’s mission is “building”, the peaceful human building up of everything earthly up to God. This building an altar, this final raising up of the whole earth to form an altar to God, is the antithesis of Amalek’s Sword. (Compare Ch. 20,22). This altar of Moses in the wilderness starts the war to be waged against Amalek, that is why he called it ה׳ נסי “God calls me to the fight and shows me where I am to fight”. נס is neither a weapon nor a defence. נס is the sign that is held aloft to give the fighter the direction and the place where the fight is to be fought. The work that God lets Moses start and found, has not got for its object simply the internal constitution of Israel. The object of the building up of the nation of Israel on the development of every humane feeling and ideal, is to fight and overcome everything ungodly and inhumane on earth. This development does not attack, but it is attacked, as by Amalek here, and in this defensive fight, Amalek gets defeated.

V. 16. ויאמר. He gave it this name and thereby expressed that etc.; or, He said this because etc., כס does not occur elsewhere. It is manifestly the incomplete כסא, just as יה is only a part of the Name of God. It is evident, as our sages say אין השם שלם ולא כסא שלם עד שיאבד זכרו של עמלק as long as the memory of Amalek is thought of as renown, neither God’s Throne nor His Name is complete. God then only rules in Nature, but not in the world of Mankind. At most God’s Mastery is recognised and acknowledged as being over Nature, but not as being over the world of Man, as long as Man does not subordinate his actions to God’s Will, as long as the ideal of Man’s greatness is fixed on might and power, and not on his showing his homage to God by completely carrying out His Law of Morality. So here Moses proclaims: The governing (or directing) (יד) power of the Throne of God — incomplete though the Throne may still be, and incompletely recognised though His Name may still be — is nothing else but a war for God, i.e., for His complete recognition, against Amalek from generation to generation. The underlying idea of God’s direction of history is naught but war against Amalek until the Goal of Time is reached.

V. 1. כי הוציא ה׳ that He brought Israel out of Egypt as ה׳, i.e., that He freed Israel by means of such miracles that showed Him to be ה׳, the One Who, with completely free uncontrolled and unlimited powers over the world and its contents, shapes the Future of Mankind. In contrast to Amalek, these extraordinary revelations of God’s doings attracted the thoughtful priest towards God, to which was associated also his special interest in these happenings, as Moses’ father-in-law.

V. 2. אחר שלוחיה. Probably in the pressure of his duties, in order to be able to give all his time and all his attention and life to carrying out the tremendous work which his mission entailed, Moses had sent his wife and children back from Egypt to his father-in-law. But this sending her home had not been misunderstood and had in no way spoiled their relation to each other. Jethro had remained חתן משה and Zipporah אשת משה. (This explains these words which otherwise are quite superfluous, we know who Jethro and Zipporah were.)

V. 3—4. The names of the children are repeated here with additional information, obviously to let us see that Moses had made it clear to his father-in-law from the beginning what his past had been and what were his relations to the enslaved people in Egypt. Both are expressed in the names he gave to his children. Eliezer was born shortly after his return to Egypt, the ויצילני וגו׳ obviously refers to the assurance which God gave him. Ch. 4,19 לך שוב וגו׳ ,כי מתו וגו׳. Hence it was only to his younger son that he could give the name Eliezer. As long as he had to live in banishment, the sword of Pharaoh was still hanging over his head.

V. 5. In V.2, where we are informed of Jethro’s decision, and in V.6, in the message with which he announces his arrival to Moses, the children are called בניה Zipporah’s children. Jethro wishes to be neither a burden nor a hindrance to Moses. Moses had sent his wife and children home to him. It could very well be that Moses was still not in a position to keep them with him. Accordingly, Jethro had the intention of still keeping his daughter and grandchildren with him. It was not to take them back to his son-in-law, but a longing to get a knowledge of God, and a longing to see his son-in-law, that led him to go with his daughter and grandchildren into the wilderness. But here in our verse 5, the objective fact is recorded of what they were to Moses, and of course the fact was, that they were Moses’ father-in-law, his sons and his wife. That is why here the sons are mentioned before the wife, who, in any case, as the father-in-law is mentioned first, comes last as being the dearest and nearest.

הר האלהים. If as רמב״ן already remarks, both the sequence of the story as well as the record of the deeds of God, which Jethro mentions in V.10 indicate that Jethro visited Moses in Rephidim before the giving of the Torah, then this הר האלהים can not refer to אשר הוא חנה שם. In any case, where the naming of a place occurs without a preposition, it indicates the place as the goal, the object of the journey rather than a stopping-place. So הר האלהים refers to חורב. As רמב״ן further remarks, Horeb was nearer to Midian than to Egypt. Moses used to feed Jethro’s flock on Horeb. So that Jethro would have to pass the Mount of God before he came to Rephidim. Also he had reason to presume that Moses would be at Horeb, as he could very well have known from Moses that this was the real goal of the wandering in the wilderness. This had been revealed to Moses before he left Midian to return to Egypt. So Jethro first came to Horeb and from there he sent the announcement to Moses (V.6).
V. 7. וישתחו, Although in the meantime he had become the divinely appointed ruler of a whole nation Moses still remained just Moses in all ways.
V. 8. תלאה from לאה see Ch. 7,18.

V. 9. ויחד from חדה related to עדה to be decorated. While the other expressions for joy שיש ,שמח designate the inner feelings of gladness, חדה seems to express the outward signs of joy, to show signs of joy rather than to feel them, from which one opinion in the Gemora (Sanhedrin 94a) finds in the choice of this word an indication of a feeling of sorrow for the downfall of Egypt, of which the Priest of Midian could not entirely free himself.
V. 10. אתכם Moses and Aaron.

V. 11. To understand בדבר we must enlarge on the ידעתי of the first part of the verse. Jethro had recognised the greatness of God, by deeds which showed how the One Who did them saw right through to the innermost thoughts of the Egyptians towards the Israelites. Jethro recognised how all the plagues which were sent over Egypt stood in the closest relation to the fundamental ideas of גרות ,עבדות and ענוי which the Egyptians had in mind to inflict on the Israelites אשר זדו עליהם (as we worked out in the explanation of the grouping of the plagues). So that these plagues revealed God to him not only as an All-Highest power, but as a God who sees the inner thoughts of men, nations and princes, and by His mode of government teaches and educates them. Not only the sublimity but the proximity of God — כי לה׳ הארץ ,כי אני ה׳ בקרב הארץ — is the most characteristic feature, is the greatness which differentiates God from all the gods, and it is just to that, that Jethro here calls special attention. That is also why he pronounces the momentous בריך which is naught but the immediate response to his becoming conscious of this proximity of a God who examines and weighs up human beings. For by uttering a ברוך a man expresses his giving up all his completely free powers of action to do solely that which will please and give satisfaction to God. (See on Gen. XIV.19). This particular character of God’s government, which Jethro recognises, is expressed by our sages as מדה במדה i.e., by making the punishment fit the crime, by the punishment showing up the real fundamental nature of the crime (See Tractate Sota 8b et seq.).
זוד related to צוד ;סוד (see on Gen. 10,9) means to form an evil design — על against somebody. As וכי יזד איש על רעהו להרגו (Ch. 21,14).

V. 12. Although it does not say לה׳ (which name of God is used exclusively in connection with all our Jewish sacrifices), the fact that Aaron and the elders took part in it is a guarantee that the offerings were dedicated to the One and Only God. עולה וזבחים an offering of giving oneself up to God, and offerings of joy.

שלמים=זבחים :לפני האלהים of which the greater part of the animal which has first been sacrificed to God comes back to be enjoyed by the bringer himself. This establishes the Truth, that worthwhile material enjoyment can itself become divine service; these offerings invite, as it were, the offerers to God’s table, משלחן גבוה קזכו and the meal is partaken לפני ה׳ in the Presence of God. Our sages remark — Aaron and the Elders sat down to table, but Moses, in whose tent the meal took place, as host waited upon his guests.

V. 13—15. From these and the following verses we can get some idea of the camp life of our forefathers during the forty years wandering in the wilderness. From the simple, easy and quickly accomplished provision of their daily food (the manna) and from the description which Moses gives in Deut. 8,4, XXIX,4,5, & II,7 as to the lack of the necessity to procure and make their other requirements, we must come to the conclusion that by far the greater part of their daily lives was entirely free from those activities which normally would have taken up most of their time. How then did they occupy their time? They came to Moses, or, as we shall now be informed, to the men whom he appointed to deputise for him, דרש אלהים .לדרש אלהים as has been worked out in Gen. 25,22, means “to seek teaching and help from God”. It comprises, accordingly, the relationship which every phase of our life and actions must have, and which we must keep, towards God, if God is to be our God. It is, accordingly, the most comprehensive of all the demands of God, which the prophet expresses in the words דרשוני וחיו (Amos 5,4) and to be called דורשי ה׳ is a title, to be worthy of which, is our mission, which begins with the first conscious breath that we take and only ends with the last breath that we draw. But as seeking teaching and help from God is expressed by the words “seeking God”, the blessed happy Truth is thereby declared, that, with the help and teaching that we seek from God, we find God Himself; we get God Himself for the small and even the smallest matters of our life, we introduce God, into the most material matters of our life, and our whole existence becomes godly, as God has said ועשו לי מקדש ושכנתי בתוכם. So that the time of their wandering in the wilderness was indeed the High School of the Jewish Nation. To spread the Torah, the Teachings of God through every stratum of society of the Jewish nation was to be their task for all the coming centuries; the people stood about Moses from morning till night, and V.15 declares their purpose to be in general: “They come to me לדרש אלהים״.

V. 16. Gives us details. First כי יהיה להם דבר בא אלי. When they have any matter about which they require instruction or help they come to me. Then ושפטתי וגו׳ I have to adjust their disputes. Both are cases of “seeking God” in special cases and for special cases. Finally והודעתי וגו׳ they come to me to get to know and to learn the Laws and Teachings of God. This latter is “seeking God” in general. God’s help itself is a necessity if we are to arrange our lives in accordance with His Will, and Knowledge of His Will a necessity for such arrangement. God’s Will for our external practical life is here summarised in חוקים which limit all our acts within the bounds of what is right and permissible. His Will for our inner life, for our minds and feelings, is comprised in תורותיו, His Teachings which fructify our inner selves with the life-seeds of Truths and Goodness. Even before the Lawgiving on Sinai they already had laws, the Noachian Law as well as Mila and Sabbath, which, e.g., דינין and עריות would require explicit explanation and teaching.

V. 18. נבל (related to נול ruins, נפל fallen) means a diminution, a wasting away of the forces of life; of plants, withering; of animals נבֵלָה the carcass; of mental forces נָבָל the mental degenerate, the fool; here a wasting away of powers of action, to be exhausted.

V. 19. ויהי אלהים עמל there is nothing in my advice which God would disapprove of, nothing, on which you could not reckon on God’s help. — היה וגו׳ literally “Be thou, for the People, opposite God” i.e., be the representative of the People to God, and when they seek instruction and help from God through you, you bring their difficulties to God. This is a function which nobody else can do for you. Equally: —

V. 20. והזהרתה. This is the only occasion where הזהיר occurs with a double accusative. It is used either by itself as והזהיר את העם (Ezek. 33,3) or as in להזהיר רשע מדרכו (XXXIII,8) and in both cases it clearly means “to warn”, just as in the Nifal הִזָהֵר ,נזהר it means to let oneself be warned. On the other hand זהר quite definitely means light, lustre, brightness and הזהיר to spread light, והמשכילים יזהירו כזהר הרקיע (Dan. 12,3). It is related to צהַר from which we get צָהֳרַיִם midday. So הזהיר must mean to light up an object for somebody which otherwise he would not have seen, would not have noticed. Hence also the double accusative, to cause an object to receive rays of light and to cause these rays to fall on the eyes of someone. So here it would mean: Cause the Law and the Teaching to shine clearly and brightly into their eyes and make them so important to them, that they guard themselves against transgressing them. והזהרתָּה, that you must do yourself, both imparting the warning of negative commands, and והודעת להם וגו׳ imparting the positive commands.

In ב״מ, 30b this verse is explained as follows: והודעת להם זה בית חייהם (פירש״י ללמוד להם אומנות להתפרנס בו) את הדרך, זו גמילות חסדים, אשר ילכו, זה ביקור חולים (אפי׳ לבן גילו), בה, זו קבורה (אפי׳ לזקן ואינו לפי כבודו), ואת המעשה, זה הדין, אשר יעשון, זו לפנים משורת הדין.

דרך is always the way to a goal, the endeavour to accomplish a purpose, and in the sphere of one’s life’s work, indicates as a rule one’s activities in earning and making profit, on the honesty and purity of which the purity of one’s morality depends. Here the teaching on this point is taken to be: Teach thou them that this activity for our own livelihood and well-being, which is usually so concentrated on ourselves, must not only include benevolent care for the well-being of our fellow-men, but that this benevolent care for others is quite specially the real purpose of our working for ourselves, that everybody is to live only for others; yea, they are to be so overflowing with this brotherly love, that they perform acts of love even at the risk of their own existence, (e.g., caring for people in illness even if there is great danger of infection ביקור חולים לבן גילו), and at the expense of their own prestige (e.g., attending to the dead and their interment, which otherwise, having regard to one’s position or to one’s age one would not do. קבורה לזקן, ואינו לפי כבודו). Left to himself, an unenlightened man takes the purpose of his דרך, his way through life, to be purely his own advantage, his own comfort and good living. But והודעת להם, when you enlighten them, they will look on their existence and their livelihood as being only for the benefit of others, will look for דרך of בית חייהם as being solely in the way of גמילות חסד, and ילכו in self-sacrificing pursuit of that, they will go בה exclusively on that path.

And equally so והודעת להם את המעשה אשר יעשון, enlighten them concerning their deeds, the way they are to behave and act, אשר יעשון, as between man and man. The ordinary standard by which a man measures his dealings with his fellow-man looks upon these dealings purely objectively in themselves, and, at best, measures them by the standard of strict justice and correct honesty, את המעשה זה הדין, but he forgets that something may be in itself strictly fair and correct, and the other party has no right whatsoever to demand anything else, nevertheless for his own sake, out of consideration of his own personal worth and the mission of selfsacrificing love which is attached to his own personality, more, much more, can he be bound to do: אשר יעשון זו לפנים משורת הדין, not holding to the letter of his rights. This is the teaching to bring גמילות חסד into דין, love into rights, which the judge may not demand, but which those who would be righteous are to dictate to themselves. Jethro thinks that this teaching concerning the very highest level of our moral social mission, too, must also come from Moses himself. If this event occurred, as we presume it did, before מתן תורה, it is all the more understandable that “the way they are to go” and “the deeds they are to do” are taken by the Gemora to refer primarily to general human behaviour and duties.

V. 21. חיל every accumulation of forces whether of possessions, power, moral or mental gifts is called חַיִל hence, fortune, army, goodness, virtue or valour. — בֶעַצ related to פצע to wound, an advantage gained at the expense of another. (cf. נשך). Hence also בַצֵעַ, accomplishment of something which can only be established through the destruction of that which is opposed to it.

The organisation suggested by Jethro and carried out by Moses requires searching consideration. If the שרי אלפים וגו׳ is to be taken to mean that six hundred judges were to be appointed, one over each thousand, six thousand over the hundreds, and so on, and all these judges to be of equal status and competence, then each individual of the people would be placed under four judges, his “ten” judge, his “fifty”, his “hundred” and his “thousand” judge, and in practice there would of necessity arise such a confusion and doubt as to who was the competent one, that would be far removed from the שלום the “peace” (v.22) that was to be the object of the innovation. It seems therefore that the suggestion was to introduce different ranks of competence and שר אלפים etc., to mean, not indeed one placed over a thousand, but rather one picked out of a thousand as the “best and most capable”. A שר אלף was one chosen out of a thousand, a שר מאה one chosen out of a hundred etc. It is evident that if one first gathers a nation together in groups of a thousand and extracts the best of each thousand, then in groups of a hundred and picks the best out of each group, and so on till groups of ten, there will be four groups of men, each group being superior in character and ability to the succeeding one. If we consider, as seems to be deduced from Deut. 1,13 that all these men who were to receive appointment were nominated by the people themselves, and only confirmed and appointed by Moses — there it says “choose, — literally give — for yourselves men of wisdom and insight, who are known to your tribes, them will I set at your head” — then this mode of choosing seems even more to the point. Each thousand had first to pick out the best and most efficient man and then each hundred and so on until the smallest voting groups of tens. So that four grades of efficiency and trustworthiness were formed, each one superior to the next. In the same way as here under Moses, four grades of judges were appointed, so later, in the Jewish State, there were four grades of courts of justice under the supreme Sanhedrin which took the place of Moses. A court of three judges in every community, one of twenty-three in every large city, two of twenty three at the foot of the Temple Mount and, at the entrance to the Temple, and as the supreme tribunal, the court of seventy one which sat in the Stone Hall of the Temple itself. Just as the first Jewish Judges here were elected from the people and by the people, so later on, one of the qualifications demanded for a judgeship was מומחה לרבים tested by the people. There could always be an appeal from the lower courts to the one above it, right up to the full Sanhedrin. But it was not the litigants who appealed, but in cases where it was in any doubt, the lower court itself went up to the one above it. Similarly to what it says here כל הדבר הגדול יביאו אליך, the judges themselves are to bring cases in which they are not confident of giving correct decisions, up to you, and this can very well imply that they were first to submit their case to the court immediately superior to them before they brought it to Moses (see Sanhedrin 88b).

The total number of judges may seem surprisingly large. The actual number appointed here would be 78,600 so that every seventh or eighth man in Israel was a judge (Sanhedrin 18a)! But every man who lived an honest life and who had some knowledge of the Law (the Torah) was called upon to be a judge in Israel. Actually every man in Israel is expected to live an honest life and not to be ignorant of the Law. And the whole nation, every individual of the nation, was considered a bearer and representative of the Law (the Torah) to such an extent that any three right-living men of the people could come together to form a court (Sanhedrin 5a תוספות ד״ה דן אפי׳) and could judge any denial of rights and enforce the observation of all rights. The benefit of such an institution can well be judged and estimated if we contrast it with the difficulties and expenses of obtaining legal rights in other spheres. Apart from this, these chosen men of the people were appointed not only for deciding legal processes, but they were also responsible for the teaching of the people. The Teachings which were revealed to Moses were transmitted by these men to the people, explained and elucidated to the people, and kept vividly alive in the minds of the people by them. So דמב״ם also takes the traditional order in which the Torah was transmitted (Introduction to Mishna referring to Erubin 54b) כיצד סדר משנה וכו׳: “First Moses gave it to Aaron, then in his presence to his sons, then in their combined presence, to the Elders, then in the presence of Aaron, his sons and the Elders, to the assembled nation, so that then by the השרים על כל ישראל by these elected officers of the Law (Torah), the people were taught until the Torah was completely understood and assimilated and carried out by the whole nation. וישוטו השריט על כל ישראל ולהגות עד שידעו בגרסה המצוה ההיא וירגילו לקרותה עכ״ל״.

V. 23. As it does not say אל מקומו יבא בשלום but על מקומו it seems that it does not want to express simply a peaceful home-coming but arriving at “the place and position to which they are really meant to come.” That really expresses the whole true work of a judge, viz. to direct everybody and everything to the standpoint and place it should occupy, to bring it or them there, and establish it or them securely on it. That is indeed why he is given the name (שפת שפד) שופט “Putting and keeping things in their place.”

V. 24. Nothing is so instructive for us, as this information regarding the first legal institution of the Jewish State, coming immediately before the chapter of the Law-giving. So little was Moses in himself a legislative genius, he had so little talent for organising, that he had to learn the very first elements of state organisation from his father-in-law. The man who tired himself out to utter exhaustion and to whom of himself did not occur to arrange this or some similar simple solution, equally beneficial to himself and his people; the man to whom it was necessary to have a Jethro to suggest this obvious device, that man could never have given the People constitution and laws out of his own head, that man was only, and indeed just because of this the best and most faithful instrument of God!

V. 26. ישפוטו an unusual form for יִשְׁפְּטוּ. It is comparable with the similar form לא תַעבוֹרִי מזה (Ruth 2,8) for לא תַעַברִי. We would suggest that ישפוטו may be a composite form made up of the singular and plural, of ישפוט and ישפטו, and then would express the idea that the decisions that they would make ישפטו would also really be the decisions of Moses ישפוט, they would be given in his spirit and in accordance with the principles and rules they had received from him. In the same way the לא תעבורי in Ruth may be a composite form made up from the masculine תעבור and the feminine תעברי and the expression intentionally wavers between the two genders just to dispel any suspicion of gallantry or sex in this general benevolence of Boaz. Compare the change of genders above in Ch. 2,17 in a similar occurrence.

V. 1—2. ביום הזה on the selfsame day on which they came to the wilderness of Sinai they immediately pitched their camp, and, as Israel, encamped opposite the Mount. Up till then, whenever they entered a fresh region of the wilderness, we always notice how they looked at the place with a critical eye to see whether it was suitable for encampment. But Sinai was really the goal of their wandering. They had been told that their salvation originated from here, here, they knew they were to enter the service of God. They were, after all, so much the sons of Abraham, had, after all already become so much “Israel”, and all that they had lived through had, after all, already had sufficient effect on them, that, when they arrived at their goal in front of Mount Sinai, all material considerations disappeared from their minds, and, as “Israel” they immediately encamped opposite the Mount. By this act they placed themselves at God’s disposal awaiting His further commands. This fact may well justify the opinion that the previous outbreaks of dissatisfaction and despondency had their roots rather in doubts of the mission of Moses and Aaron than in a real wavering in their trust in God. This also allows us indeed to understand the word of God which He sent them through Jeremiah. “Go and cry in the ears of Jerusalem saying: Thus saith God, I remember thee, the devotion of thy youth, the love of thy bridal state, how thou wentest after Me into the wilderness, in a land that was not sown.” (Jer. 2,2).

V. 3. While the people were encamping opposite the Mount, Moses, as their ambassador, went up to God, to express their readiness to carry out what had been destined for them: תעבדון את האלהים בהר הזה. But as he was ascending, God called down to him from the summit: כה תאמר וגו׳. This contains the fundamental ideas of what God understands עבודת אלהים to be. It is to בית יעקב, the family, and especially to the pillars of home life, the women, into whose minds this fundamental idea is to be impressed and explained; to the בני ישראל (where, as here, used in contrast to בית יעקב, this refers especially to the men) תגיד you are to make it completely realistic (from נגד) and put before them so that they never lose sight of it.

V. 4. אתם ראיתם, the basis of your knowledge of God and of yourself does not rest on belief, which can, after all, allow an element of doubt. It rests solidly on the evidence of your own senses, on what you have seen with your own eyes, have yourselves experienced. In exactly the same words Ch. 20,19 speaks of the fact of the revelation of the Torah ,כה תאמר וגו׳ אתם ראיתם כי מן השמים דברתי עמכם. The two fundamental truths on which the whole of Judaism rests, יציאת מצרים ומתן תורה, the exodus from Egypt and the Lawgiving on Sinai, stand firmly on the actual evidence of your senses, and as they were seen, heard, felt, and experienced simultaneously by so many hundreds of thousands of people, every possibility of deception is ruled out. Both these fundamental truths accordingly share the highest degree of certainty, are completely out of the realm of mere believing or thinking, are within the bounds of what we know with certainty, and are, accordingly, irrefutable facts which must serve as the starting-point of all our other knowledge with the same certainty as our own existence and the existence of the material world we see about us.

אתם ראיתם, you have seen what I did at one and the same time to Egypt and to you, how I overthrew the greatest human power on earth because they set themselves forcibly and actively in opposition to Me, and how I raised you up, you, the most helpless and downtrodden of humanity, because you trusted in Me and gave yourselves up to Me, raised you up high above the reach of all enemy power and brought you into direct relationship to Me. You have seen how I am the Only One Whom Man has to fear, and at the same time the Only One in Whom Man has to trust and have confidence. (Compare above Ch. 14,31).

V. 5. And now, — now you have come hither to the place to which I invited you to תעבדון את האלהים בהר הזה, to enter My service on this Mount. אם שמוע תשמעו וגוי, if this is what you really earnestly wish, to obey Me and to carry on the bond and relationship you have started with Me, then the fundamental condition I make is, that you become, more than all the other nations סגולה to Me. סגולה, from Koheleth 2,8. וסגלת, כנסתי לי וגוי מלכים זהמדינות as well as from Chron. I. 29,3, עוד וגו׳ יש לי סגולה זהב וכסף it follows that סגולה indicates a possession which is a special property of one sole owner, really the treasures of kings and countries, a unique treasure of gold and silver over which the owner alone has the disposition. Similarly in Baba Bathra 52a and Baba Kama 97b, קבל מן הקטן יעשה לו סגולה, החובל בבניו ובבנותיו של אחרים, גדולים יתן להם מיד, קטנים יעשה להם סגולה, where סגולה designates property which is to be made secure for a minor who is not yet old enough legally to hold property, and which is to be made safe that he, and he alone, is to be the sole permanent possessor. So that סגולה is a treasure, a possession over which nobody else has any rights, which has no relationship whatsoever to anybody else. So the use of this word for the fundamental condition which is demanded of us in our relationship to God indicates that we must become completely and exclusively His possession in every phase of our being, that our whole existence and all our desires be dependent on Him, that we give no place to aught but Him to have any influence on the direction of our lives and actions. כי לי כל הארץ: For this relationship you are to bear towards Me is really nothing exceptional, is nothing but the beginning of the return to the normal condition which the whole world should bear towards Me. The whole of humanity, every nation in the world really is destined to belong to Me and will be ultimately educated by Me up to Me.

V. 6. And it is just for this ultimate destiny of the whole world that you are to become a ממלכת כהנים and a גוי קדוש unto Me. ממלכת כהנים, each and every individual of you is to become a כהן, a priest, inasmuch as he is to allow all his actions to be “regulated” by Me, to take the עול מלכות שמים faithfully on his shoulders and become a true כהן who by his word and example spreads the knowledge of God and loyalty to Him, as Isaiah expresses it in LXI,6, “But ye shall be named the Priests of God, men shall call you the Ministers of our God”. And גוי קדוש, just as, individually you are to appear priestlike, so is the impression which Israel as a nation is to make on the world to be one of holiness to God. You are to be a unique nation amongst the nations, a nation which does not exist for its own fame, its own greatness, its own glory, but the foundation and glorification of the Kingdom of God on Earth, a nation which is not to seek its greatness in power and might but in the absolute rule of the Divine Law — the Torah — for that is what קדושה is. לא פחות ולא יותר :אלה הדברים, as our sages say, no less and no more, but אלה. Less would not be sufficient for your future and more is not required.

V. 7. וישם לפניהם, is more than a mere transmission of the words which God had spoken unto him. It implies at the same time, explaining and making clear the whole matter. Hence the reply of the nation could run: “Everything that God has spoken” etc. For the whole extensive and comprehensive meaning of the demand: סגולה, and of their mission to be ממלכת כהנים and גוי קדוש had been explained and made clear to them

V. 9. In dense cloud, in such a manner that the people will be able to bear. Just as they had been made certain by the evidence of their own senses of the absolute Might of God over all the powers of Man and Nature, so now they are to see and hear and experience for themselves with equal certainty the second fact which is to form the second cornerstone of their future, the fact that God can speak to Man and did speak to Moses.

ויגד. As we have already been told in V.8 that Moses had brought the reply of the people back to God, this ויגד here can only be a repetition of that reply. With this repetition of the words of the people Moses wanted to suggest, that, as the people had already completely and unanimously declared themselves ready to carry out everything that God would command them, and thereby also proclaimed their complete confidence in Moses as the transmitter of these commands, such an overwhelming revelation might possibly not be necessary to establish and ensure this confidence. Hence we have dared to translate this ויגד quite literally as, to hold out.

V. 10—13. But just this erroneous confidence of Moses himself in the people having already attained their spiritual and moral maturity may make the meaning and necessity for the preparations and precautions which now follow so much clearer. For if we really understand these latter correctly, they all had the object of making the people realise (and to establish for all time) the great gulf that existed between the spiritual and moral stage on which the people already stood, and the height to which the Law they were yet to receive was destined to elevate and educate them through the course of centuries, nay, thousands of years. Closely in connection with this would then be a second object, viz., to let it be established historically that throughout the whole occurrence, God, so as to speak, stood opposite the people and that His word came to the people, not that God, spoke in the people or out of the people, and that the Word of God did not come out of the people.

For the Jewish Law — the Torah — is the only one that did not emanate from the people whose constitution it was to form. Judaism is indeed the one “religion” that did not spring from the breasts of the men who find the spiritual basis of their lives in it. It is just this “objectivity” of the Jewish Torah, the Jewish “religion”, that makes it unique of its kind, that differentiates it sharply and specifically from everything other on earth, that is called Law and Religion, that allows it to be the one centre-point of culture which may be regarded as the lever and the culminating goal of every other advance and progress, but itself as the given absolute ideal to be above all ideas of progress. Because all other “religions” and laws only emanate from the minds of contemporary humanity, are nothing but the expression of what at a given time, a certain circle of human beings have arrived at as their conception and conviction of God, and of what the mission of Man is, what his relation to God and his fellow man should be; therefore all other religions and laws, like all other phases of culture, knowledge, art, morals and manners which emanate from the minds of contemporary man, must change, advance and progress with Time. By their nature and origin they are nothing but the adequate expression of the degree of human development reached at any particular time. But the Jewish “religion” and the Jewish Law did not emanate from the contemporary convictions of human beings, they do not contain the convictions of any certain people at any certain time of what God is and what Godly and human matters are; they are given by God, and contain that, which, according to the Will of God, should be Man’s conviction in all ages regarding God and Godly matters, and, above all, of men and human matters. Right from the beginning, the Law of God, found itself in opposition to the people in whose midst it was to find entrance. It had to exercise its power first of all on this people, who as עם קשה ערף, opposed it. This opposition on the part of the people in whose midst this Law found its first home on earth is the clearest proof of the divine origin of Law which did not come out of the people but to the people, and only won the people to be its bearers after centuries of struggle, and only then by the force of historical events.

To make known, as strikingly and definitely as possible, the nature and origin of this contrast which so markedly characterised the Law in its beginning, seems to be the object of these preparations and precautions. It comes to the people. Its arrival is awaited for three days. And even to be allowed to await its arrival the people must make themselves worthy by sanctifying their bodies and their garments and so bring to their consciousness symbolically the rebirth of their inner and outer lives which is to be brought about by this Law. Not as they already are, can they receive the Law. Only the decision, ultimately to become what and how it should be, makes the nation worthy to receive the Torah. The complete separation between the origin of the Law and the people is also to be apparent in actual space. The place from where the people get the Torah is completely, very specifically, separated from them, and raised to the realm of the extraterritorial. No man, not even an animal may be on the Mount or even touch it. Should one do so, it must be killed. Only after the Giving of the Law has been completed was the place restored to the domain of humanity, and men and animals are again allowed to tread there. The people themselves were to be directed back and kept back, within bounds, by a barrier. All this to impress the fact of the superhuman origin of the Torah.

בו ;לא תגע בו וגו׳ refers to the Mountain. או ירה יירה. The object of the verb ירה (to cast, usually of arrows) is always the thing or person who is cast, not the object at which something is cast, this latter is construed with לירות וגו׳ לישרי לב :ל- (Ps. 11,2) etc. Here too, according to Sanhedrin 45a.b. it does not mean “be shot with arrows”, but “cast down from a height” דחיה, the first and essential act of סקילה. He is to suffer the same death-penalty as for the sin of מגדף (blaspheming God) and עע״ז (idolatry). For these too, the actual death is דהיה, and actual killing by סקילה only takes place if the דחיה does not instantly kill. יבל .במשוך היובל means “to bring home” hence יבול (cf. תבואה) the produce of the fields (that which is brought home), יוֹבֵל the year of homecoming. Hence also probably the signal horn, which was blown as the sign of the occurrence of the “homecoming”, of the “freeing” of slaves, debts and lands held on leaseholds, was also known as the יוֹבֵל. So also at the procession encircling Jericho we read that יובלים were blown. The signals blown there were no warlike ones for it was just Israel’s sword that was not to conquer Jericho. It was rather a signal to the walls of the town, a demand that they “free” the city and give it back to what were henceforth to be its lawful owners. Here the יובל was the signal for “returning back”, for the discharge of the people, for the ending of the giving of the Law.

V. 16—19. The people saw the whole of Nature trembling at the approach of the Glory of God, they alone, Man alone, was to remain upright, and remained upright, expectantly awaiting his God, the God of the Universe. As soon as he consciously entered the service of God, he was taught the incomparable higher nobility of Man and his unique position in being directly near to God. Heaven and earth, the whole trembling universe lay behind his back and he stood upright before his God. The whole of Nature roared, thunder rolled, lightning flashed, mountains quaked, the air wafted calls of the trumpet, but Israel had ears only for the talk between God and Moses — “they heard Moses speaking and God answering him audibly!”

V. 20—25. פן יהרסו וגו׳ לראות וגם הכהנים וגו׳ יתקדשו. What they had to do was to hear, not to see, and indeed to hear with full clear consciousness, that the Word was objective, that it came to them from without, not from within themselves, that they stood opposite to God, and that God directed His Word to them. And the priests too — at that time still the firstborn (see above on Ch. 13,1) — who otherwise approached God at the sacrifices as the representatives of the family, are not to imagine themselves higher or holier or nearer to God than the rest of the people; are not, under such an illusion, to press themselves in front of the people, are rather to ponder on the fact that for them too, the task was, still להתקדש, to work themselves up to that stage of holiness i.e., of being absolutely and in all ways at the disposition of God, which would make them fit to be כהנים, leaders, directors, and models in front of the people. Nobody, including the priests, had yet reached the stage up to which the awaited Torah was to call them all, and up to which it would train and educate them. Hence the repeated warnings against pressing forward. And even Moses was to be down with the people at the moment when God, from the height, directed His Word to Israel. Moses went down to the people and spoke to them (V.25), then (XX,1) God spake all the words that follow. The Torah was to be directed not only through Moses, but to Moses as to the people.
Kap. 20. V. 1. Vergl. Jeschurun (III. Jahrgang S. 439).

V. 2. אנכי, we have already repeatedly drawn attention to the delicate difference between אנכי and אני, especially in God’s speeches. Whereas אני indicates the speaker rather in contrast to the one addressed, as the one from whom — אנה a speech emanates, אנכי proclaims the speaker as that person who is intimately near to the one addressed, who comprehends and bears and keeps him, through whose personality the one addressed really gets his personal existence and his standing. Nothing is more overwhelming than the thought of how, in the midst of all the commotion, and out of the turmoil of the universe quaking in its very foundations, God proclaims Himself as the אנכי of the universe, through Whom alone all other existence receives the possibility and the actuality of existing, and then immediately turns to each individual Jew and says: “I am your אנכי ה׳ אלהיך :אנכי״.

As this verse is not to be taken as a declaration, but as a מצוה, as one of the commandments, it does not mean “I, ה׳ am your God” but “I, ה׳ am to be (should be) your God”. This makes the foundation of our whole relation to God to be that demand which our sages express in the term קבלת עול מלכות שמים (taking on oneself the duties which are involved by considering God as one’s King).

The so-called “belief in the existence of God”, as ancient and modern theological philosophers like to express the idea of “the first commandment”, is miles away from what this fundamental verse of Jewish thought and Jewish existence demands from Jewish thought and Jewish life. Not the fact that there is a God, also not that there is only one God, but that this One, unique, true God, is to be my God, that He created and formed me, placed me where I am, and goes on creating and forming me, keeps me, watches over me, leads and guides me; not that my connection with Him should be through ten thousand intermediaries as a chance product of a universe which He brought into being aeons ago, but that every present breath that I draw and every coming moment of my existence is to be a direct gift of His Almight and Love, and that I have to live every present and future second of my life solely in His service — in a word, not the knowledge of the existence of God, but the acknowledgment of God, as my God, as the exclusive One in Whose hands is the disposal of all my fate, and as the exclusive One guide of all my acts, it is only with this, only with the acceptance of this Truth, that I can lay the foundation of a Jewish Life. To the demand אנכי ה׳ אלהיך there is but one corresponding reply אתה אלהי!

As the founding fact for this fundamental Truth, we are referred to the Deliverance from Egypt — a fact which we had experienced for ourselves. Moreover we are to realise it in two phases: ,אשר הוצאתיך מארץ ,מצרים and מבית עבדים, the first revealing God, as the Director of our Fate, the other as the basis for all our powers of action and all our energies belonging solely to Him.

ארץ מצרים. The state and the land that held us enchained, represented the pinnacle of statecraft based on violence and power, and on the use of the forces of Nature to serve such violence and power. As breaking the power of human violence, judging human perversity and Nature-worship, smashing tyranny, bringing fresh hope to, and saving and raising up down-trodden helpless innocent ones; in short, as directly intervening, arranging and directing human matters and human history, has God inscribed in our minds our salvation, our “being brought out of the Land of Egypt”. The One Who could say to us אשר הוצאתיך מארץ מצרים, we must for all time acknowledge as the sole guide and director of our fate.

מבית עבדים. We have already remarked on Ch. 13,3, that בית עבדים describes Egypt as a place in which we were born slaves, where, accordingly, the fact that we had been forcibly robbed of our freedom was completely forgotten, and slavery was regarded as our natural condition and status. Reminding us of this brings into our minds the thought of how complete our social degradation really was when God called us to freedom and independence. From this fact comes our complete and quite special “belonging to” God. It was only directly from God’s Hands that we have our heads, our hearts and hands, that we have our own personality, and the right to earn, to possess, and to dispose of our own property. That is why He, and He alone, has the right to dispose of our persons and our property, why we, with our selves, our powers and our property stand solely in His service, have to use our persons, our powers and our property solely in His service, have to recognise Him alone as the director of all our doings. It was only this complete giving ourselves up to God, that made us free from the servitude to Man, it was only under this condition that we obtained our freedom, that we have our freedom. Whereas other men and other nations are only beholden to God, for their actual creation, their physical existence, we are also for our historical and social existence. We passed directly over from עבדות פרעה to עבודת ה׳ and our national Hallel hymn sings: אני עבדך בן אמתך פתחת למוסרי, “I am Thy born slave for Thou loosened my bonds”.

V. 3. לא יהיה לך, is the first result of the fundamental V.2, אנכי, and it is a negative one. As expressly explained in V.5, the recognition of God excludes the idolatry of any other being. If God is God, then everything except Him is “no-god”, everything besides Him is only His creation, His servitor, every fibre of its being, every atom of its power is dependent on Him. The greatest and the tiniest achievement is entirely dependent on His sole free almighty Will. Before His Presence, — and this Presence comprises the whole universe, — there can be no other god, not the remotest idea of the possibility of any such other god shall be given space in our minds. This denies the conception of שתוף, that error which, without denying God, thinks that it can place another at His side, sharing His Deity, and forgets that the placing of another god at the side of God means doing away altogether with the real idea of God (See סמ״ג לאוין א׳).

The expression על פני occurs, however, as was remarked on Gen. 16,12, for an occurrence which takes place, against, or in opposition to, the other’s will. And here also it may express the idea that allowing the possibility of another god is called a crime against the true conception of God which we owe Him.

V. 4. The error becomes greater when the idea of the existence of another god is given more concrete expression by making some pictorial representation or image of it. פסל, although פסל by its basic etymological derivation, refers to sculpture, and seems to refer primarily to images carved out of wood or stone, nevertheless, places as Is. 40,19 הפסל נסך חרש, where the image is cast, teach us that the idea of פסל is independent of the method by which it is produced, and refers to any kind of representation in relief. But תמונה includes (as remarked on Gen. 1,11) any and every kind of representation of an idea. תמונה can accordingly also designate a painted picture or even simply any symbolic representation. Now it does not say: תמונת אשר וגו׳ but תמונה. So that it is not “an image or likeness of that which is in the heaven etc.”, but both are in the accusative: “Thou shalt not make for thyself that which is the heaven above etc. etc., not in an image in relief nor in any other representation.” This is important for what is said in the following verse לא תשתחוה להם וגו׳. If in V.4, פסל and תמונה alone are accusatives, then the להם etc., would also refer only to them, and in that case it would be really only image-worship which would be forbidden. But if — as is the case — אשר בשמים וגו׳, the objects existing or imagined in the heaven etc. are also in the accusative, then the להם in V.5 refers to both, the things themselves and their images, and the worship of God, forbids both. — מעל .ממעל would be the very highest space above us that we could possibly reach. ממעל starts from there and extends upwards to the utmost limit. “Everything which is close above us up till the infinite heights above”. And in the opposite direction מתחת from below our feet downwards.

V. 5. The crime becomes greater when divine worship is paid to anything created or to any representation of it. This active worship of another is here pronounced as השתחויה and עבודה. According to the Gemora (Sanhedrin 60a) there are two separate classes or forms of worship. (a) השתחויה, throwing oneself prostrate, although it does not belong to עבודות פנים, i.e., although it is not one of the prescribed procedures in the Mikdosh to show our allegiance to the One God, it is nevertheless a forbidden act to do before any other being or its representation, even if it is שלא כדרכו, i.e., does not belong to the special cult of this particular idol. (b) With עבודות other than השתחויה however, there is a difference, עבודות פנים i.e., those procedures which are ordered to be done as an expression of homage to God, in His Mikdosh such as זיבוח, וקיטור, ונסוך are forbidden to be done to, or before, any other being without exception, but any other act of worship is only forbidden if it is כדרכו, if it is the ordinary cult of this particular god (throwing a stone on a cairn before the god Margolies, would be a capital crime, because that was the way he was worshipped, but throwing a stone before Venus would not I.L.). If we consider the meaning of the symbolic act of complete prostration before someone else, and also the meaning of the idea of עבודה, and the acts which serve to express them, then השתחויה appears to be the rendering up of your complete passive life, while עבודה is the expression of rendering up your active life, your actions, to the disposition of this person. השתחויה is the recognition of, and homage to, another as the sole master of our fate, עבודה literally, giving oneself up to the service of another, is the recognition of, and homage to, this other as the master of our actions. The two together form the complete idea of what we have already found to be the whole content of our acknowledgment of God. It is characteristic that, in the Temple of the One God, it is עבודה above all, not השתחויה, that is demanded. His Temple is the sanctuary of His Law, the Torah, His Holy of Holies is called דביר, the Place of the Word, and it is the Ark of the Law over which His cherubim spread their wings to be the bearers of His שכינה. It is not acknowledging God as the sole master of our fate, but acknowledging Him as the sole Lawgiver for our lives, that makes us into Jews, and this, of course implicitly presupposes the former. But it is the erroneous idea that there is, or can be, something else besides the One God that can have some influence on our fate or fortune, it is this, above all, that entices us to a pagan falling away from God. That is why השתחויה, before anything else, or anybody else, is such a falling away from the One, Only God. Needless to state, then, that the surrendering of our whole power of living, of all our activities and all the enjoyment of our lives to the service of anything else, in the way that we dedicate them to the service of God, by זיבוח and קיטור and ניסוך must indicate a falling away from God, as must also, behaving in the particular way which heathen ideas imagine to be the wish of any particular god or godess. The demoralising effect which עבודה זרה (idolatry) exerted on men’s lives and acts is understandable when we consider how it presents the forces of Nature as divine ideals which are served by giving oneself up to one’s natural instincts and passions, so that crimes and bestialities could be raised into the realm of divine service, as acts showing honour to the gods. The burning desire to sensual lust was itself considered as inspired by the gods and עבודה זרה and גלוי עריות (promiscuity) always went, as our sages point out, hand in hand.

Hence: Allow no other god to have any influence on your fate or your actions for קַנֵא .כי וגו׳ אל קנא (related to קנה, to have something for your own) means to demand something as your right, or to stand up for your own or somebody else’s rights which have been violated. Now here it does not say מקַנֵא “I demand My rights on you”. “I do not relinquish you or the tiniest part of any of your due relations to Me,” but “I am ”אל קנא that is what I am, I should not be Who I am, if I were not אל קנא, this “קנא״ is a specific distinguishing mark which differentiates Me from all that which men call gods. You can not think of Me without realising that I am אנכי .קנא: as the Personality Who bears you and the whole universe, as ה׳ on Whose sole Will every future moment of the world depends, as אלהיך Who took you out to arrange and guide your whole future history, and your whole life and actions, I am אל קנא, I exclude all else and demand the whole of yourself, with all your present and all your future.

פקד עון אבות. Who is able to gauge the depth of true justice and the loving seriousness of His educative judgment which God reveals to our mortal eyes with these words? Who would dare to try and draw the limits within which the idea, expressed by these simple words, extends?

פקד — related to בית ,בגד — means to invest something with what is befitting to it; mentally, with the qualities which are due to it, practically, with the due position, vocation, circumstances, condition etc. Used of the Divine Rule — decreeing what is appropriate or deserved, for anybody or anything. ערן from עוה to be crooked, to take a “crooked” direction, hence, the conscious departure from the straight prescribed path. It is the most appropriate expression for consciously giving ourselves up to a purpose which is not in accordance with our mission in life, hence, an expressive word for consciously departing from what we know to be right.

It is clear that this “measure” of God’s rule is only applied “לשנאי״. It is expressly stated to apply only there and then, where successive generations are all שונאי ה׳, who hate the way of life which God has indicated for them, who look on it as “thorn-like” (שונא related to סנה), and reject it as a misery, as a disturbance and danger to their happiness, or to their efforts at happiness.

And now, פוקד עון אבות על בנים וגו׳ ,לשנאי. Does it mean that God remembers the sins of the parents when children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren hate Him? That when children, grandchildren and even great-grandchildren continue on the path of sin, God thinks back to the first step which the parents took, considers that the sin has not yet become embedded throughout many generations, that return is still possible, and He tries, by educating them in the school of suffering, to lead the children, the grandchildren or even the great-grandchildren back again to Him; but if return is not achieved until into the fourth generation, further generations perish in their sin? Does it mean that He visits the sins of the fathers on the children if the children hate him? Do the sins of the fathers go on working in children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren who continue on the downward path in sin and misery, chastised because of their sins, children who were set on this path by the example of their parents, are these children from their very cradles given sin and wretchedness as companions through their lives? Does it mean that God punishes parents by the wretchedness which they heap on the lives of their children by the sins which they let these children inherit from them? Does it mean that God carries over the sins of the fathers to children, grand and great-grandchildren? That instead of destroying the parents on account of their sins, God waits till the fourth generation, perhaps grandchildren or great-grandchildren will rectify the guilt of the parents, and only then, if there is no betterment, does He allow the generation to perish in their continued guilt?

Whatever the real truth of this measure of God’s Rule may be, two certainties are expressed by it for our most earnest reflection. Inasmuch as it is the same One God, Who wishes to be guide of our actions, Who is the Law-giver for our lives, it is this same God Who grants and maintains our lives for the fulfilling of His Law, it is certain that we ourselves build up or drag down our lives according to whether we adhere to, or fall away from, His Law. There lives a God Who judges men according to their deeds, Whom nobody can evade and Who allows nobody to evade Him.

And it is certain that parents build their children’s weal or woe with adherence to, or falling away from God’s Law. Children are indeed, fruit on the tree of the life and fate of their parents. For our children’s sake we should keep ourselves healthy, for our children’s sake keep ourselves moral and good, for our children’s sake keep ourselves mentally keen and alert. As certain as it is that God sends each and every child into this world with a perfectly pure soul, equally certain is it that dark and troubled propensities and predispositions, weaknesses and sins which parents be-queath to their children with their physical existence make life a hard task for them. Their pure little souls have to test and prove their godlike power in overcoming their tendencies. The unhappiness, the shallowness, the example of moral degeneration with which the sins of the parents line the cradles of their infants, prepare a hard steep path of traits, on which these little world-citizens have to struggle to win the triumph of moral probity and integrity.

But God be thanked, and God be thanked ten thousand times more, we are also given the certainty עושה חסד לאלפים לאהבי ולשומרי מצותי that God lets the happiness of the children blossom out of “the loving devotion and loyalty to duty” of the parents throughout thousands of generations. The goodness, the mental and moral purity and excellence of the parents, from a rich firm soil, which with each succeeding faithful generation becomes richer and firmer, out of which the generations blossom happily and readily to mental and moral goodness. Even when they diverge from the straight path, the way back is easy for them to find, and God’s love and God’s clemency never forsakes them.
Both are the methods of the rule of One Unique God Who alone reckons the deeds of men, and Who alone fixes their fate.

V. 7. נשא שם :השם seems to be an understandable phrase of השבע. We have already worked out (Gen 21,23) the idea of השבע as being the placing of the whole of our visible existence under the power of the invisible One in the event of something that we have said not being in accordance with the truth, or of our failing to do that which we have said we would do. In exactly the same way נשא שם ה׳ means taking the name of God upon oneself, i.e., placing oneself under the Name of God; submitting oneself to the power and might of the God who intervenes in earthly affairs, as His Name (the 4-lettered one) expresses it; calling it down on oneself in the event of one’s spoken word not being true, or of not carrying it out. It is clear that, in an oath, the two phases of our acknowledgment of God are jointly expressed — his watching over all our deeds (and our words esentially belong to our deeds) and His power of ordering cur fate. An oath in the name of God implies both, and by the actual submission of our whole future under God’s power of deciding our fate, wishes to prove the truth of our statements and the honesty of our actions. Hence, conversely, a false oath is the most direct denial of God in the most contemptuous manner.

Here it is not speaking primarily of a false oath but of a useless oath, a שוא .שבועת שוא related to שוה to be even, level. In a remarkable manner, Jewish thought — as expressed in the Hebrew language — connects the idea of similarity, of being the same, with the idea of nullity, of non-existence. נדמה may mean either “it has become”, or is, similar to — — or “it has been destroyed”. And in a still higher degree שוה means to be alike, and שוא, not existing, or futile. It seems that it is considered an essential sign of true existence to have individuality. Everything which really exists must have something characteristic which differentiates it from all others. Everything real is individual. What is absolutely שוה i.e., which is absolutely like everything else, which has nothing of its own to show, is שוא, does not exist. So לשוא means “to nothing”, without any purpose, without any result, and שבועה לשוא is a purposeless, useless oath, an oath which has not, and can not have, any effect. The Law reckons four kinds of such oaths.
