(1) נשבע לשנות את הידוע, an oath that denies a self-evident fact, that black is white, stone is gold etc. (2) לקיים את הידוע, that affirms a self-evident fact, “I swear by the Name of God, that two is two”. (3) שאי אפשר לו, who swears to do something that is physically impossible for him to do e.g., to fast for a week, to jump over the moon etc. (4) לבטל את המצות who swears to do something that is morally impossible for him to do, e.g., not to lay Tephillin, to take revenge on somebody etc. In all these cases the oath is either useless, superfluous or without object or effect. Here the sin occurs even in the promissory oaths at the moment the oath is taken, the swearer is immediately punishable, but the vow has no effect. Swearing (in God’s Name, of course) useless, superfluous oaths, or oaths without object or effect, is simply playing with the most solemn of all solemn acts of man, with the submission of his words and deeds to the judgment of the God Who decides and fixes his future and his fate.

כי לא ינקה ה׳. This declaration of God, makes every oath taken in His name an actual factual pledging of the whole earthly fate of the swearer for the truth of, or the carrying out of, his spoken word. כל העולם כולו נזדעזע, the whole world shuddered, our sages say in Shebuoth 39a, when God uttered His לא ינקה on Sinai. For with this לא ינקה the whole world was called into service to accomplish the sentence of God on the words of the man who breaks an oath.

V. 8. אנכי demands our positive recognition of God as the ruler of our fate and the guide for out actions; לא יהיה לך expresses the negative consequence of this recognition, the exclusion of any other allegiance; לא תשא makes this recognition the basis of all intercourse between man and man, inasmuch as the whole social structure of human society finds its final security in the positive solemnity of this recognition as it appears in the oath, that appeal to the presence and government of God in human affairs. לא תשא then warns against frivolous playing with this most solemn idea. זכור now reminds us of the ancient memorial which God established right at the beginning, when He first set up Man to be His representative as “servitor and guardian” (לעבדה ולשמרה) of the world. It was to ensure this recognition, the forgetting of which had been the sole cause of the downward path along which the development of human history was leading the world, and the consequent necessity for the election of Israel to be God’s herald in leading it upward again.

Hence the Sabbath is not introduced here as a new institution, the existence of Sabbath is presumed. It was there already, had been there since Man first existed in this world, and Israel is only commanded “not to forget” the Sabbath in the way that humanity that had gone before, as well as his contemporary fellow-men, had forgotten it, and were forgetting it. Even the “sanctification”, which the “Sabbath of God”, was to receive by Israel keeping the “Sabbath of Man”, was no longer a new thing. Its general principle, and in reference to certain human activities, it had already been conveyed to Israel by the stopping of their activities in getting their food in Mara and with the manna. There, the beginning of the “Sabbath of Man” being a practical and actual sanctification of the “Sabbath of God” had already been introduced. Here Israel was only “reminded” not to forget this sanctification. So that שמור את יום השבת לקדשו כאשר צוך ה׳ אלהיך (Deut. 5,12) is just a literal elucidation of our זכור את יום השבת לקדשו. If we remember how it was first in Mara that the seventh day, by the cessation of human activities, may have received the name “Sabbath”, then זכור את יום השבת is nothing else but שמור את יום השבת לקדשו כאשר צוך ה׳ אלהיך.

But this identification of זכירה and שמירה (which, according to tradition were spoken and heard simultaneously at the Lawgiving on Sinai, and so are justified in being considered in mental and practical observation as one inseparable unity) is the most emphatic protest against that misconceived attempt to relegate the Jewish Sabbath solely and entirely to a “spiritual commemoration”, applying solely to the mind, to the זכירה, and rob it of its essential component, the שמירה, the refraining from all constructive work, the שביתה from which it derives its name and nature. In the פסיקתא (פ׳ כ״ג), we find the significant sentence: ,אמר ר׳ יודן: זכור נתן לאומות העולם שמר נתן לישראל, and this says exactly the same as we have explained above (Ch. 16, 23) on the Sabbath of the Manna. The first institution of Sabbath for mankind, only established it as a spiritual commemoration for “remembrance”, to “keep it in mind”. But as such it became entirely lost to mankind. To bring the Sabbath back and to preserve it, Israel was given the command of שמירה, the concrete, physically noticeable keeping of the Sabbath as a symbol of its spiritual content. It is just this שמירה, rather than the זכירה which latter should already have been the common possession of all mankind, which is the specific Jewish Law of Sabbath. Accordingly, he who takes away the שמירה from our Sabbath and imagines he can satisfy himself with the זכירה is denying the whole Jewish Sabbath, and is destroying the whole institution which God has established in Israel for the purpose of ensuring Sabbath for the whole of mankind.

But as the mission not to forget the Sabbath is expressed as a positive command, זכור “remember”, a positive activity is thereby implied, which is to make us realise the day and its meaning. Moreover, as this command is not expressed in the imperative זְכוֹר but in the aoristic tense (indefinite in point of time. I.L.), it is not limited just to the duration of the day itself but extends beyond it, yea, even to all times. Hence, first of all the order זכרהו על היין בכניסתו (Pesachim 106a) “declare the great, the sanctifying meaning of the Day at its entry by קידוש״. That this has to be done over a cup of wine and as introduction to the meal at home is the prescription of our sages. They have placed a כוס — in Jewish scripture the symbol of the lot or fate that God apportions each man — in our hands whenever we are to take to heart the fact that the conditions of the moment are Divine ordinances, ordained by God. They specially wanted the introduction of Sabbath to take place in the homely circle because it is there that its sanctification is really meant to be realised, it is there that it is meant to bring its real blessing.

Hence further in the Mechilta: מכאן שמוסיפין מחול על הקדש, that we are to let the sanctity of the Sabbath at its beginning reach over into the weekday, to cease work before the entry of the Sabbath, so that we come to meet the Sabbath day in the Sabbath spirit. Equally so, from the same principle, to let Sabbath at its expiry reach over into the weekday, and to again proclaim the meaning of Sabbath as an institution which is to raise and sanctify our whole life, by הבדלה, so that we take the Sabbath spirit with us over into the working life of the week.

Hence finally in the Mechilta: לא תהא מונה כדרך שאחרים מונין אלא מונה לשם שבת; not to call the days of the week as others do — as being dedicated, each one to a special god, or being under a special planet — but to count every day from the standpoint of Sabbath, as leading up to Sabbath. The thought of Sabbath is thus spread over all your days. Thus we make Sabbath the goal and prize for all our work, and learn to consider the object of all our work to be, to lay the results of our efforts, acknowledgingly at the feet of our Lord and Master.

V. 9. תעבוד; Not as self-glorification, but as “service” shalt thou consider thy powers of construction and thy mastery over the materials of this world. As service performed in the Kingdom of God, as service to thy God, and as performed at His bidding, for His world. It was לעבדה ולשמרה to serve it and to keep it that he placed you in it; to raise it, by appropriating its materials, changing and transforming them out of the sphere of blind physical existence into the realm of human purposes, to serve and further God’s aim for the world. In this spirit ועשית כל מלאכתך art thou to accomplish all thy work. We have already defined the idea of מלאכה (Gen. 2,2). Just as מלאך is a personal creature who carries out the will and message of someone else, so is מלאכה any material or thing that is made of service to carry out the will or order of anybody’s mind. עשית מלאכה is the transformation of thing or of some material into being our מלאך i.e., to impress on something or material such a permanent state or condition, that henceforth it is qualified to serve the purpose that we desire it to have — we make it serve our will and our purpose. Every עשית מלאכה is exercising our mastery over the matter of this world. And this mastery of ours we are to exercise only as “service” תעבוד.

V. 10. ששת ימים וגו׳ ,ויום השביעי וגו׳, “Six days shalt thou do thy work, serving God and His world, and the seventh day is “cessation of work” שבת to thy God ’לה״. On this seventh day you cease your work, to pay homage ever anew to God, as ה׳ אלהיך ,to express ever anew that every future breath you draw, as well as every future swing of the pendulum of the world’s clock belongs to God, Who is your God, from Whom you get every particle of the world that you obtain, and Who expects every ounce of your powers to be used in His service. You are to do no work on Sabbath, just to make you look on the work that you do all the week, in the light of “service” to God. On Sabbath you strip yourself of your glorious mastery over the matter of the world, and lay yourself and your world, acknowledgingly at the feet of ה׳ אלכיך.

Mechilta: ששת ימים תעבוד וגו׳, וכי אפשר לו לאדם לעשות כל מלאכתו בששת ימים אלא שבות, כאלו מלאכתך עשויה; דבר אחר, שבות ממחשבת עבודה, “Six days shalt thou serve and do all thy work, is it then possible for any man to have done all his work in six days, but it means, “שבות״ cease work, make Sabbath, and consider all your work as completed”. The value of your work is not measured by having accomplished any fixed end that you have set yourself, but by honest efforts to achieve an end that is pleasing to God. And just as it is certain that the faithful worker in God’s world has completed his work on the day God calls him away from this world—however little he may actually have accomplished, as long as what he did do, or even only commenced to do was the whole of what his powers and abilities enabled him to do — so each one of us has completed his work with the entry of each Sabbath. It is the Master who then says “enough!” and if what we have done is enough for Him, it is enough for ourselves! Another explanation of the Mechilta on these words runs: “And do all thy work” means “Be done with all thy work”, i.e., Let your mind also cease from thoughts of your work, do not think of your business on Sabbath!

לא תעשה כל מלאכה. The whole idea of Sabbath has been distorted and the whole laws of Sabbath undermined by the translation “thou shalt not do any work”. When Jews began to be disloyal to the oath they took at Sinai, which swore “to bring life into line with the Torah” and altered it to “bring the Torah into line with Life”, then the great Law of Sabbath, that basis on which the whole Jewish life is built, had to receive a new interpretation to make it harmonise with the demands and requirements of life. Without having the slightest concern whether there was any foundation for it in the Torah, or whether such an interpretation was even permitted by the Torah, Sabbath was proclaimed as a day of bodily rest so that the mind might be freer to devote itself to God and spiritual matters. Prohibited מלאכה was then accordingly defined as labour, hard physical work. Only hard physical work they said is prohibited on Sabbath, but easy, non-strenuous work, or work undertaken for spiritual activities is allowed, and so “the adjustment of the Law to the requirements of Life” was accomplished. But nowhere in the Torah is there the slightest suggestion that the cessation of all מלאכה is not in itself the realisation of the essential nature of Sabbath, that this שביתה should simply serve as a means. Everywhere by שביתה ממלאכה and in it, is שבת kept, everywhere in the Torah by עשית מלאכה and in it, is Sabbath desecrated. The Torah says כל העושה בה מלאכה. Not, who did not attend Divine service on Sabbath, who did not listen to the sermon etc., but who had performed a מלאכה on Sabbath כל העשה ;ונכרתה וגוי מלאכה ביום השבת מות יומת! Those who brought the gatherer of sticks before the court did not first enquire whether he had not perhaps already been to service and heard the sermon, and so had paid Sabbath its dues, or whether perhaps he wanted to use the twigs for the preparation of the Sabbath meal. He had gathered twigs, he had gathered together the products of nature from their natural source and taken them into human possession to become human property for human purposes, or he had picked them up in the רשות הרבים and had carried them ארבע אמות further on, in a word, he bad performed a מלאכה, that sufficed to find him guilty of death. And equally so the idea מלאכה in no wise necessarily entails the idea of strenuous physical labour. It occurs nearly two hundred times in the scriptures, and in no single instance does the word itself indicate strenuous work, just as the slave-work in Egypt is never called מלאכה. But everywhere the essential idea of the word מלאכה seems to be — as indeed its etymological derivation from מלאך has told us — not the greater or lesser amount of bodily fatigue but the intelligent carrying out of an intention. So that, even if we knew nothing of the oral traditional explanation, simply from the actual meaning of the word, and from the hundred-fold evidence of the way it is used in the Bible we should say that לא תעשה כל מלאכה means “thou shalt not perform any constructive work”. Thou shalt not carry out thy intention on any thing, make no thing the bearer of thy purpose, thy ideas; in general, thou shalt not produce, not construct! More, without the explanatory teaching of the Oral Law, we might perhaps have been induced to have taken the idea to extend farther and to be more comprehensive, and to have taken it to include every carrying out of our intention on things, and it is just the Oral Law that teaches us to apply the idea, precisely and literally only to עשית מלאכה, to constructive work, to using material for מלאכה, to be an actual bearer of our intention and purpose, to exercising our power of constructing, altering, and using the material of the world for our own purposes. Actually, this idea of constructive work is the essential mark of the איסור מלאכה on Sabbath in the הלכה. Prohibited work on Sabbath must be productive, constructive, not destructive, כל המקלקלין פטורין. But if the קלקול, the destructive process is itself part of the constructive (e.g., pulling a house down to rebuild it I.L.), then it is a מלאכה. The work must be intentional not דבר שאין מתכוין, more, the actual result of the activity that produces it, must be what was in the mind of the doer e.g., digging a hole is only a real מלאכה if it is the hole that you want, but not if it is the earth that you take out that you want, it must not be a מלאכה שאינה צריכה לגופה. It must also be done in the ordinary way of human skill, not done כלאחר יד, so that it shows the application of full human intelligence. In all cases it is the achieving of the purpose, and never the greater or lesser amount of bodily fatigue, which makes the decisive point. Certainly bodily labour, workday exertion etc., is equally forbidden on Sabbath, but this comes under quite a different idea, and is not prohibited on account of איסור מלאכה.

גדולים :אתה ובנך ובתך, Children who have reached their religious majority are included in the אתה, to them the Torah, the Law is directly addressed. So here it must refer to the little ones who are not themselves responsible. Grown-ups may not encourage these little ones to break the Sabbath, more, they are guilty if their little ones do violate Sabbath with their silent acquiescence. (Sabbath 121a, Jebamoth 114a). עבד ואמה if they have completely entered Judaism by מילה וטבילה, are, of course, bound to keep Sabbath on their own account, like any other Jew or Jewess, if they have not entered Judaism, then, with regards to Sabbath they have the character of a גר תושב whom we may not cause to do any work for us which we are forbidden to do ourselves (Shulchan Orach 304). אתה וגו׳ ובהמתך, this is the prohibition of לאו דמחמר, to cause any animal to do any work for us that we may not do ourselves. This is quite apart from שביתת בהמה the command to keep your own animals free from all work on Sabbath which is expressed in למען ינוח שורך וחמורך (Ch. 23,12). וגרך אשר בשעריך, although גר אשר בשעריך as a rule it taken to refer to a גר תושב, here the Mechilta explains it as a גר צדק as the law regarding the גר תושב is given in Ch. 23,12 by והגר. But there seems generally to be a difference between גר and גרך, and everywhere by גרך, a גר צדק, one who belongs completely to you, is to be understood. (cf. places like Deut. 31,12; XXIV,14; XXIX,10). In Deut. 5,14, בהמתך is explained by giving as examples .שורך וחמורך שור is the animal of work (ploughing etc.) חמור the beast of burden. So that the two categories of מלאכות are indicated, real productive work and הוצאה carrying (see on Ch. 35,1).

V. 11. So: “Six days shalt thou exercise in the service of God, the power He has lent thee of mastery of the things of thy world”, bring them into the service of thine own purposes, and for such purposes; creator-like, change and transform them, make them all bearers of the evidence of thy power. But the seventh day brings a cessation of such activities, “שבת״, to acknowledge “’ה״ as thy God.

לה׳ אלהיך. Thou art to step back, to allow God’s rule over the world to come to the fore… how so? By neither directly, nor by means of any living force that obeys thy command, exercising thy mastery over the matter and creatures of thy world וינח וגו׳ ,כי ששת ימים וגו׳, for, even if God’s creative work does rest now, has rested since the first seven days, even if it is Sabbath in Creation, no new creations appear in the heaven, earth and sea that encompass thee, in heaven, earth and sea, thou seest everything being formed only in accordance with existing forces and laws, and at most only through thyself, Man, canst thou see new combinations and new creations being produced, nevertheless a world-creation did precede this world-sabbath, a תנועה did precede the מנוחה, a מלאכה the שביתה. It is only since the seventh day that God’s Creation rests, until that seventh day, God, by His Creation, made heaven, earth and sea proceed to more and more completion. And because He has rested since these first seven days, and is not apparent to Man as Creator — and yet the whole future happiness of the world and mankind is dependent on Man’s recognition of Him as Creator and Master of the world — therefore ברך ה׳ את יום השבת ויקדשהו, therefore did God bless the Sabbath inasmuch as He made it holy; therefore the cessation which keeping it holy brings to Man’s activities is no restriction but a blessing. Yea, all the future of the development of mankind in general, and each individual in particular lies in keeping it holy. The recognition of God as the Master of the world which He created which Sabbath ensures, the stepping-back of Man’s mastery of the world in face of this recognition, the laying of himself and his creative powers at the feet of God, is the necessary condition for solving the problem of how to bring about the ultimate happiness of humanity. Therefore doth God say unto thee: זכור את יום השבת לקדשו. “Keep thou in mind the Sabbath which the rest of mankind has forgotten, keep it holy by the cessation of work, even as thou hast been commanded!”

In Deut. 5,14, is mentioned a further consequence for the general social life which this ever-recurrent acknowledgment of God by keeping the Sabbath brings in its train. This is למען ינוח עבדך ואמתך כמוך. Sincere and faithful homage to God makes all men equal. Sabbath makes the slave free and places him in line with his master before God. Above, at the institution of the Pessach we have already drawn attention to the position of slaves in Jewish households and in Jewish Law, and what was said there is confirmed by this stressed effect of Sabbath.

There, in the next verse it states further: וזכרת כי עבד היית בארץ מצרים ויצאך ה׳ אלהיך משם ביד חזקה ובזרע נטויה, על כן צוך ה׳ אלהיך לעשות את יום השבת. “Remember that you were slaves in the land of Egypt when God, your God, brought you out of there with a strong Hand and outstretched Arm, therefore did God, your God, command you to celebrate the day of Sabbath in deed”. The יד, the active force, and the זרוע the power behind the force, that brought you out of Egypt were those of God. You yourselves had lost both, were slaves, and only through God’s “Hand and Arm” did you regain both. God only gave you both again, the power and might of independence, for you to use and expend both solely in His service. While all mankind owe their actual physical existence to God, as the Creator of the world and are invited by the Sabbath to acknowledge their Creator, Israel in addition owes its social existence to God as the Creator of its national existence as a nation amongst the nations. Therefore, when God wished to form bearers of the Sabbath who were to keep it by direct acts of homage, and so proclaim it before the eyes of the world, He picked you out of the midst of mankind because your “hand and arm” belonged to Him more than those of all other men; because your independence, your free “power and might” are the historical proof, memorial and evidence, of His mastery over the world of Nature and Human History. That is why He ordered you, by laying down your “Hand and your Arm”, by inhibiting your “power and might” on every Sabbath to be a striking testimony to the whole world of “שבת״. The whole history of Israel from Abraham to Moses is simply God’s creation of a nation to be the bearer of Sabbath, and so the Jewish Sabbath is both זכר למעשה בראשית and also זכר ליציאת מצרים (see also on Ch. 35,1) (also Hirsch’s articles on The Jewish Sabbath).

V. 12. The knowledge and acknowledgment of God, which אנכי demands from us, which לא יהיה expresses as its negative result, and which לא תשא proclaims as the solid basis for all intercourse between man and man, and which זכר wishes to be recognised by an act of homage in our activities, this knowledge and acknowledgment rests essentially on יציאת מצרים (as is expressed at once by the addition of אשר הוצאתיך in the אנכי verse, and also in Deut. as we have just seen on the explanation of זכור). Not on the results of our research into Nature, but on the actual events in the history of our people by which God became revealed to us, and made His Will revealed to us, did God found our Jewish Knowledge and acknowledgment of Him, as the One Who directs our fate, and Who is to be the guide of all our acts. Heaven and Earth had spoken in vain to mankind, worse, the sermon that they really preached had been twisted into polytheistic conceptions; and it was only the historical revelations of God in the history of the Jewish people, which brought back the monotheistic idea to mankind for their understanding of nature and history. יציאת מצרים and מתן תורה these two basic facts in the history of the Jewish People which constitute the basis for our submission to God, as the Guide and Director of our history and our lives, these facts are actual historical truths. But the knowledge and acknowledgment of historical facts depends solely on tradition, and tradition depends solely on the faithful transmission by parents to children and on the willing acceptance by children from the hands of their parents. So that the continuance of God’s whole great institution of Judaism rests entirely on the theoretical and practical obedience of children to parents, and כבוד אב ואם is the basic condition for the eternal existence of the Jewish Nation. Through father and mother, God gives the child not only physical existence, they are the actual bond that joins the child to the Jewish past, that allow it to be a Jew or a Jewess, and they are those who are to hand over to them the Jewish mission in knowledge, morals and education. The child is to receive history and the Law from their hands so that ultimately he can transmit both to his children. In the same way that it looks up to its parent, are its children some day to look up to it. Without this bond the chain of generations is broken, the Jewish past is lost for the future, and the Jewish nation ceases to exist. That it is worthy to have its place in the Ten Commandments indicates this importance of parents, and allows the Torah to say: כבד את אביך ואת אמך למען יאריכון ימיך על האדֹמה אשר ה׳ אלהיך נותן לך!

We have already elsewhere indicated the meaning of כבוד as being the expression of the spiritual and moral worth of a being, from its relation to כַּבֵד heavy, weight, mass. We could say that כבוד is the spiritual and moral weight of a being. So that כַּבֵּד would mean “showing up your estimation of the value” and כבד את אביך ואת אמך demands of us that we demonstrate in every way, and in our whole behaviour to our parents, how thoroughly we are permeated by the great importance, that God has given to our parents with regard to ourselves. This comprises complete obdience to, and courteous anticipatory carrying out of all their wishes. The only limit to this is, if these wishes should be contradictory to the wishes of God (Levit. 19,3). Parents are, of course, meant to be the heralds of God’s wishes, and it is the transmission of these that gives them their great importance. It is this mission of parents, and not the greater or lesser amount of self-sacrifice and care which they have given their children which lies at the root of this “כבוד אב ואם״; an “honouring” which only grows greater with the maturity and age of the children, extends beyond the death of the parents, and in its unconditional egregious demands, transcends by far what would be the outcome of ordinary so-called “natural” feelings of gratitude, (see Kiddushin 30b, 31, 32).

By not saying כבד אביך ואמך but את אביך ואת אמך the Torah includes not only the persons of father and mother, but also those who represent the personality of the father or mother. The “honouring” of the father must extend to his wife, the stepmother, and of the mother to her husband, the stepfather. (See Gen. I. on את השמים וגו׳). The elder brother is also included.

In Deut. 30,17-18 it says ואם יפנה לבבך וגו׳, הגדתי לכם היום כי אבוד תאבדון, לא תאריכון ימים על האדמה אשר אתה עובר את הירדן וגו׳ and also in IV,26, לא תאריכון ימים עליה כי השמד תשמדון. In accordance with these verses, the למען יאריכון ימיך על האדמה וגו׳ here also would refer in the first instance to the national continuance of existence on the land which is lent to them by God. Only if the knowledge of God which the first generation had obtained by the direct revelation of Him, and the bond which this first generation had thereupon contracted with God is transmitted by כבוד אב ואם to children and children’s children, and thereby the very last generation feels with the same fresh enthusiasm the same direct relationship to God and His Torah that the first generation did, then and only then, is the continued existence of the nation on the land that is to be lent to them, guaranteed. כבוד אב ואם is, as already remarked, the necessary condition for the everlasting continuance of the nation. But as the command כבד את אביך וגו׳ in its form and content, is no national, but an individual one, to be carried out by each individual, our sages (at end of Chulin) see in למען יאריכון expressed, the continued existence of the individual in the next world as well as the national immortality in this world. In Deut. 5,16 the words כאשר צוך ה׳ אלהיך are added in explanation to כבוד אב ואם just as they are to שבת, and thereby is indicated that just as the sanctification of the Sabbath was already ordered in Mara, so was the duty of honouring our parents. שבת and כבוד אב ואם belong together. They form the two great educational institutions to which God has entrusted the future of His People. By the addition of ולמען ייטב לך there in Deut., it is explained that not only אריכות ימים the unbroken continuous existence for all future time, but also true happiness in every present time is conditional on כבוד אב ואם.

V. 13. The first five commandments, in אנכי and לא יהיה לך proclaim the knowledge and acknowledgment of God as the One Who is responsible for our fate and the guide of all our acts, in their positive and negative signification respectively; in לא תשא this knowledge and acknowledgment is set as the whole basis of our individual and social life; in זכר homage to this idea is ensured by the ever-recurring act of cessation of work; and in כבד את אביך ואת אמך its continuous transmission through the ages is ensured by the influence of the home. Now the following five commandments proclaim the result of this knowledge and acknowledgment in our social life. If God is the One Who is solely responsible for your fate in life and is to be the Guide of all your actions, then every one of your fellow-men must be considered as standing equally under His care, and every one of your actions towards him comes under His observation. Every man at your side is placed where he is by God’s Direction and, equally with yourself, has all human rights granted by Him, so that all his possessions, his life, his wife, his freedom, his happiness, his honour, and his property must all be considered as sacred to him. Thou shalt not take his life, nor break up his marriage, nor rob him of his freedom, nor smirch his honour and his happiness by false evidence, more, thou shalt not even allow thyself to covet anything which makes the home of thy fellow-man, and that includes everything which he can call his own!

רצח .לא תרצח is the highest degree of רצה .רשע: justified willing, רשע: unjustified, law-breaking, willing; unlawful exercise of free will. (רצע materially boring through, רצח the highest degree of law-breaking, — murder). Whereas הרג and המית also occur in connection with legal killing, רצח always refers to murder. Only in reference to the death which has to be meted out to the murderer does רצח occur twice in Numbers 35,27 & 30. There it seems to be used from the standpoint of the murderer himself. He feels the same blade drawn against him that he used against his fellow-man. Perhaps even in these two cases it only refers to the killing by the גואל הדם. That would depend on whether — at it certainly seems to do — the ירצח את הרוצח in V.30 does refer to the גואל הדם. Every shortening of life and even if it is only hastening death by one minute, is considered as שפיכות דמים (Sabbath 151b).

Under לא תנאף is also understood the prohibition of procuration (Shebuoth 47b), and also the prohibition of immorality of any kind in the widest sense (Nidda 13b). לא תגנוב is taken to refer to stealing human beings, i.e., forcible enslavery by abduction, which, equally with murder and adultery, is a capital crime.

ענה .לא תענה ברעך is always a speech which is brought about by somebody or something else. Hence, generally an answer, a response. Even where it is used for an original speech which is not in response to another speech, it always refers to a speech which was provoked by an incident to explain it. The declaration of a witness always presupposes that it was called into being by his actually having witnessed the occurrence to which it refers. Hence ענה ב-, to make a declaration against somebody which is in accordance with what actually happened; to testify against somebody. עד שקר cf. עד שקר העד (Deut. 19,18) hence, not false testimony (it does not say עדות) but a false witness. So that here also, the עד שקר can only be taken as being in opposition to the subject implied in לא תענה “thou, as a false witness, shalt not testify against thy fellow-man”. Jewish Jurisprudence differentiates between עד מוכחש and עד זומם, between actual and personal falsity of witnesses, the one when the witness was actually present at the occurrence but gives false testimony about it, the other when he was not present at all at the occurrence, so that he really is not qualified to give evidence at all. The one is false testimony and the other a false witness. עד שקר includes both, false testimony and false witnesses. Just because it wants also to include at the same time אזהרה לעד זומם (Makoth 4b) it does not say לא תענה ברעך דבר שקר which would express “thou shalt not give false testimony against thy neighbour”, but עד שקר “thou shalt not testify as a false witness against thy neighbour”, so that the falsity can apply equally to the person as to the matter. In Deut. 5,17 the עד שקר is further explained as עד שוא and that just stresses the one phase, the false witness, the עד זומם. The testimony given by such a one is in itself “nothing” שוא, even if the facts are perfectly true, he can not give evidence on them as he was not present. This incidentally gives the warning not to give evidence as a witness, however positive one may feel of the certainty of the truth of a crime, by circumstantial evidence, or through being told of it by thoroughly reliable persons. A witness can, and may, only testify to what he himself has seen. Only that which he has actually seen makes him into an עד, as mentally retaining that which his own senses have perceived, gives עוד, gives “endurance” in the human mind of what would otherwise be only transitory. (See on Gen. 21,30).

V. 14. לא תחמוד. The Mechilta differentiates between חמדה and תאוה; whereas the latter indicates only inner longing, lust, the former includes longing which proceeds to action, as לא תחמוד כסף וזהב עליהם ולקחת לך (Deut. 7,25). So also ולא יחמד איש את ארצך (Ex. 34,24) which certainly can not mean, “nobody will covet your land” but “nobody, out of covetousness of your land, will use the opportunity of your being away from it, to raid your land”. Hence also the רמב״ם (Hilch. Gesela 1, 9), “He who lusts after any acquirable possession of his neighbour, and pesters him by incessant importunity through friends or by other means, until he gets it from him, even if he pays him a high price for it, transgresses the injunction לא תחמוד. That even paying well for it does not rectify the transgression of this injunction is clear from the Gemorah (Baba Metzia 6b) which declares that ולא תחמוד לאינשי בלא דמים משמע להו that the idea that לא חתמוד only applies if you do not pay for the object, is a popular fallacy. (This opinion, however, is not quite universally held, see תוספות on Sanhedrin 25b). So that obtaining a coveted object by means of pressure, even if it is then obtained perfectly legally by purchase or otherwise, is prohibited by לא תחמוד. In connection with אשת רעך this would be the case if one persuaded somebody to divorce his wife or otherwise induced him to do so, so that one could marry the wife afterwards. In Deut. 5,18, this prohibition is further extended by the term לא תתאוה and thereby prohibiting even allowing the feeling of coveting anything belonging to another to arise within oneself. The wording there is ולא תחמוד אשת דעך ולא תתאוה בית רעך שדהו וגו׳. Significantly it does not say there תתאוה in connection with אשת רעך but לא תחמוד. Regarding all other possessions the תאוה in itself is not yet a sin, but leads to sin. But regarding the wife of your neighbour, the תאוה itself is already חמדה, thinking lustfully about the wife of another is already considered an immoral act — your neighbour’s wife is מחמד עיניו (Ezek. 24,16). In this case תאוה and חמדה are considered identical and so do not occur in separate categories. (This explanation may solve the difficulty of the סמ״ג 158).

In general the Torah must prohibit specifically both חמדה and .תאוה חמדה so that you do not think that, provided the intention is to acquire the object legally, you may covet an object, and תאוה so that you do not think that the sin only starts with the deed. He who wishes not to come to sin, must stifle the lust at its inception, for even the desire is a sin before God, is a crime against your own self, your own mentality which should be kept clear, solely for pure, justified efforts.

In the text of Deut. (which, of course, is more explanatory, elucidating) שדהו is added to the examples, so that one should not think that תאוה is only forbidden with regard to property that could be stolen, מטלטלין, where covetousness could so easily lead to crime; and then finally there, all the social prohibitions are joined to make one sentence by the לא תנאף וגו׳ ולא תחמד, on the one hand to make all the property of others sacred and to forbid every kind of crime against it in one and the same utterance of God, and on the other, and this perhaps more specially, to stress the whole importance of the last as referring to all of them, “thou shalt not murder and not commit adultery and not steal, and not give evidence as a false winess, and not lustfully desire anything, and therefore thou shalt not allow the desire for everything that is not pertaining to thee to arise in thy breast.”

It is just this לא תחמד and לא תתאוה, which sets the seal of God on the Decalogue. A mortal lawgiver could also have decreed, “thou shalt not murder etc.” But “thou shalt not covet”, only God can forbid. He alone can test the heart and kidneys. Before Him, not only deeds but thoughts and inclinations are manifest. Men can only forbid crimes, and where necessary, bring committed crimes before their tribunals. But the hearth, the real breeding place and birthplace of crimes, keeps beyond their cognition. But once it has matured there, it is seldom that it is deterred from being carried out by fear of the punishing arm of human justice. That is why all human building up of states remain incomplete and vain and vulnerable efforts as long as they are to be borne and carried on by the fear and majesty of human beings, as long as, even if they do lay the first foundation stone “with God”, they think they can carry it on without God, do not subordinate ordinary human power to the State, the State to the Law and the Law to God, but on the contrary only nurse and encourage religion and homage to God, as a means of getting support for faltering homage to Man. Only when God will become “King over the whole world” and thereby His Will will become the Law for mankind, only then can prisons be closed and wretchedness disappear from the world.

In other respects, however, the “Ten Commandments” have in no wise any greater holiness or greater importance than any other commandment in the Torah. They are neither the whole Law nor are they holier laws than all the rest. God clearly and expressly proclaimed them as being merely a preparatory introduction to the whole following, real giving of the Law, “I come to thee”, God has said in Ch. 19,9 “so that the people may hear that I do speak unto thee and so have belief in thee for ever.” Thereby this revelation on Sinai is expressly stated to have for its object solely the preparation of the people for the whole of the rest of the lawgiving which was to be transmitted to them by Moses; and to prove to them beyond all possibility of doubt, by their own experience, that “God does speak to Man” (as it says later), so that they would receive all the following Torah that Moses was to bring to them, with unshatterable belief and trust as “the word of God”.
But nevertheless they are fundamental laws, general headings of chapters to which the whole of the rest of the lawgiving are really the ways and means of carrying them out.

If we consider the order in which these fundamental laws were given, they may express yet one further idea which may be not unessential for the whole conception of the Divine Institution of the Torah. The first half begins with אנכי and finishes with כבד, the second half begins with לא תרצח and finishes with לא תחמד. The demand for the recognition of God begins with a demand for the mind. (אנכי, לא יהיה לך) but it is not satisfied with mere spirit; it demands the expression of this spirit in letter, in control of word (לא תשא), of activities (זכור) and of the family (כבד). The social laws begin with a demand for letter, for control of deeds and words (,לא תרצח תנאף ,תגנוב ,לא תענה), but are not satisfied with letter only, but demand control of spirit and feeling (לא תחמד).

This expresses the important idea: All: “religion”, all so-called “honouring God in Spirit” is worthless, if the thought, the idea of God, is not strong enough to exercise its power practically in the control of our words and doings, of our family and social life. Our deeds, our way of life must first prove that our “religion”, our “honouring of God” is genuine. And on the other hand all social virtue is worthless and crumbles at the first test, as long as it only aims at letter, at outward correctness, is satisfied with being considered righteous and honest in the eyes of fellow-men, but refuses inner loyalty, does not depend on the conscientiousness of that pure inner conscience that only God sees and God judges, and which has its root and finds its nourishment only in quiet but constant looking up to God. All Spirit must be developed into Letter, into Act. All Letter, all Acts, must have their source in Spirit, that is the inspiration that hovers over these fundamental ideas of God’s Torah and fuses the two tablets, the “religious” and “the social”, into one inseparable whole.

V. 15. In V.19 it says “you have seen that I have spoken to you from Heaven.” The conviction that a word has been spoken by any special person can only be accomplished by the simultaneous realisation of eye and ear. With closed eyes we can fix the general direction from which a sound proceeds but we can not fix the exact point from which a sound that reaches our ear emanates. So here too, the people saw the sounds addressed to them simultaneously with the flash of lightning. They saw that the words came to them from where the lightning flashed, and so also saw the notes of the Shofar. This (verse 15) is literally: אתם ראיתם כי מן השמים דברתי עמכם. And they saw how the mount went up in smoke, how the most solid of earthly matter could not bear this proximity of the Godly. וירא העם, this, what it saw, the Words flashing with lightning, setting the mountain on fire — so to speak — אשדת — דבריו שמעת מתוך האש, — as it is accordingly combinedly called later — this made them tremble, and involuntarily they stepped backwards.

לפד ,לפיד, verwandt mit לפת: zwei Dinge mit Gewalt zu einander bringen, auch: seinen Körper mit Kraft zusammenziehen, daher überhaupt: mit einander und in einander verschlungen machen, und לפיד: mit einander verbundene Feuerbrände: Fackel. So auch rabbinisch: לבד, eine engere Verbindung, daher auch: Filz.

V. 16. ואל ידבר עמנו אלהים ,דבר אתה עמנו. Here they state that God spoke to them as man speaks to man. That they should experience this fact themselves, was the essential object of this event which God had arranged for them. This firmly established the fact of God’s speaking to Man, by the personal experience of the whole nation, and thereby the “revelation” the וידבר ה׳ אל משה לאמר, which stands at the head of every part of the Torah was firmly ensured against every twist by which people try to change the revelation to man, to a revelation out of man, the revelation to Moses, to a revelation by or out of Moses i.e., the revelation to a non-revelation.

V. 17. בעבור .לבעבור נסות in the transition to something, in the intention to achieve something. לבעבור for this intention: נסות אתכם so that you prove to yourselves whether you are able to receive God’s Torah directly from Him, and inasmuch as you yourselves feel the necessity for an intermediary, you will all the more give the God-sent intermediary your full confidence, and also ובעבור וגו׳ so that the impression of this direct communication should remain with you for all time. God contracted the bond of His Torah with you directly, He spoke to each one of you personally: אנכי ה׳ אלהיך, and each one of you personally and directly acknowledged Him and His Torah. To no man but directly to your God, did you swear to be faithful to Him. This direct personal relationship which you have entered into will hold you true to your mission and protect you from indifference and sin.

V. 19—23. These five verses contain the most important and farthest-reaching consequences of the fact of the absolute directness of our relationship to God, which by the revelation on Sinai had been personally experienced by the whole nation and every single individual in it.

They had seen that God had spoken directly to each and all of them, so that no intermediary and nothing intermediary is necessary for God to come to us. This should for all time do away for us every attempt to place anything whatsoever — and even if it is to represent God Himself to us — at His side. When God wants to make Himself and His special Presence with us apparent, it will be through His blessing which we are to enjoy by His special Nearness to us, by His constant dwelling in our midst. Not by any representation of Him, but in His work, in the effect of His Presence in our lives, are we to see God, and to be certain of His Presence.

We are indeed to have symbols in our midst, symbolic representations, symbolic objects, hymbolic acts, but — herein lies the striking difference of all Jewish symbolism — our symbols are not to be of what Man requires to realise Divinity, but of what God requires from man, to realise what God demands of a true human being.

V. 20. לא תעשון אתי. Thou shalt make nothing at all next to Me! Whatever you make out of your own ideas to represent, to bring to your minds the supernatural, will always become אלהי כסף וגו׳, will always become idols. Men represent Divinity to themselves in symbols; you are not to do so. Even figures that I have ordered you to make, you may only make as I have commanded and for that purpose only, so that only according to My express command must you, and may you, form the Cherubim I allow to represent human traits; left to your own caprice, you would represent Godly ones, and your symbol would become an idol שלא תאמר הואיל ונתנה תורה רשות לעשות בבית המקדש הריני עושה בבתי כנסיות ובבתי מדרשות ת״ל לא תעשו לכם: לפי שהוא אומר ועשית שני כרובים אומר הריני עושה ארבע ת״ל אלהי כסף וגו׳ אם or הוספת על שנים הרי הם כאלהי זהב (Mechilta). That which you make לכם for yourselves will always be a symbol of God, an אלהי כסף. Even the halls of the Temple in their architectural dimensions or the vessels of the Temple in their prescribed patterns and size may not be copied. (Rosh Hasha. 24a and b).

V. 21. You shall not make images, shall not form the likeness of the sun or moon or anything that is with Me: but I do allow you to form for yourselves things that are with you; what you are to do, is not to bring heavenly things down to you on earth, but to elevate all earthly things up to Me. When you wish to come to Me, you have not to represent to yourselves things that you imagine are with Me in heaven, but rather to ponder on how I wish things to be carried on by you on earth. It is the earth not heaven that concerns you if and when you wish to come near to Me. The altar that you build up to Me should represent the earth raised up to God by Men’s deeds, Men’s action. “An altar of earth” מזבח אדמה: direct and immediately from the earth is to arise (Zebachim 58a). מחובר מאדמה ,שלא יבננו על גבי מחילות ולא על גבי כיפין, even an intervening space of a hand-breadth would make the altar ר״ש שם ט״ו ,תוספתא פ״ט אהלות) פסול). The temporary altar of the Mishkon was itself a freshly erected heap of earth, which was then enclosed in hollow box — נבוב לוחות.

וזבחת עליו, not on it, but by it, referring to it, to perform the עבודות דם and to burn the אימורים or the איברים as the case may be, on and about it is the שחיטה of the sacrificial animals to be done. The שחיטה is not to represent death, destruction, but is to have the positive active object of being given over to that which the מזבח represents i.e., the elevation of everything earthly, material, up to the spiritual, to God. This meaning of the שחיטה is so essential that if at the time of the שחיטה the altar was in the slightest degree imperfect (although it was rectified before any of the ritual which was actually to be performed on it was done) the whole offering was ,פסול כל הקדשים שנשחטו שם פסולין — (Zebachim 59b). Similarly retrospectively, nothing may be eaten of any offering if meanwhile the altar had become imperfect: מזבח שנפגם אין אוכלין בגינו שירי מנחה קדשי קדשים, קדשים קלים (ibid. 60a). In any case, as we have already remarked on Gen. 8,20, the term זבח itself denotes not so much the negative idea of slaughtering, but rather the positive one of preparing food for a meal, and מזבח is not so much the place of slaughter, but the place of meals, where the offering becomes לחם אשי ה׳.

Hence, it is not heaven, but the earth, raised up towards God, which is to be in our minds when we wish to step near to God. It is on it, a מזבח אדמה, that we have to dedicate in עולות our active life, and in שלמים our “enjoying”, our passive life to the endeavour to get nearer up to God, whether we feel our position in life to be the most modest one of צאן, or in the consciousness of the most free independence as בקר (see Levit. Ch. I and III).

אזכיר את שמי. Where I wish My Name to be recognised i.e., where I wish to announce My special Presence so that people will say ה׳ שמה “God is there! ” there you will not have to look for Me in images but will recognise Me in the blessing that I will dispense to you. Cf. the expressions ושמו את שמי על בני ישראל ואני אברכם, שם ה׳ נקרא עליך, להיות שמי שם, לשכן שמו שם, המקום אשר יבחר ה׳ לשום את שמו שם, etc., etc.

V. 22. ואם וגו׳. And when you will have finished your wanderings and entered into your permanent State, and then will have also to change your “wandering” altar into a permanent one of stone, then every stone of your altar is to preach to you the holiness and dedication to God of the whole of your national life. No steel may have touched a stone out of which you wish to build your altar, no steel may touch any stone out of which you have built your altar. The stone over which you have swung your steel becomes desecrated thereby for the altar of God (רמב״ם הל׳ בית הבחירה א׳). Not destruction, not sacrifice, nor giving up life, is the meaning and purpose of the altar, and the sword, the instrument of force and violence can not get any consecration at the Jewish altar, right and humanity must build the altar, and the realm of rights and humaneness, not the mastery of the sword, is to spread from it. In the “Hall of Stone” adjoining the altar of stone, Jewish Right had its permanent citadel (the Sanhedrin was housed there. I.L.) and not the sword, the altar is the symbol of Jewish Justice.

V. 23. And just as the altar is to be a preacher of right and humaneness, those twin spirits of society striving upwards to God, so is it to be a preacher of modest decency, that fundamental trait of godliness in humanity without which justice and humaneness will be sought for in vain in human society. With גלוי ערוה the heights of the altar will never be mounted! ותשחת הארץ לפני האלהים ותמלא הארץ חמס (Gen. 6,12) is the oldest and the most serious experience of the history of Man. (“The world became morally corrupt before God, then the whole world became full of injustice and inhumanity.” I.L.).

To summarise this epilogue to the “Ten Commandments”:- the three main sins which undermine our relation to God are countered, and to banish them, to expel the very last trace of them from our midst is the object of the Divine Lawgiving. These are שפיכות המים ,עבודה זרה and גלוי עריות, the culmination of sin against God, of sin against one’s fellow-man, and of sin against oneself. V.20 and 21 ע״ז, V.22 ש״ד, and V.23 ג״ע. God, society and the human being are the subjects of the Divine Torah, and this epilogue announces that just as our relation to these form the contents of the Lawgiving, so it, and it alone, is to form the subject of the symbolism of the Sanctuary, as a whole, and of all its parts. The altar and the Torah itself have solely human beings as their subject matter and meaning as well as the godly building up and extending of all that true humanity should be.

V. 1. ואלה: Immediately preceding, in the construction of the altar, the symbolic expression of the fundamental basic principle was given, viz., that our whole relationship to God is to be taken as one through which justice and humaneness for building up human society and morality and decency for the work of each individual on himself, are to be gained and formed, on a firm unshatterable basis. To that principle the ו adds the Mishpatim, the legal laws by which the building up of Jewish society on the basis of justice and humaneness is first of all ordered. חרב, the “sword”, force and harshness are thereby to be banned from the Jewish State, only then can they be worthy to erect an altar to God in their midst. That is why these Mishpatim come before the building of the Mishkon. The laws which then are dedicated to the banning of גלוי ערוה in its wider sense, the controlling and restraining of the animal in Man, which hinders and checks the “way up to the heights of the altar”, i.e., perfecting the individuals by the principles of morality and decency, then follow in the 3rd book.

But it says אשר תשים לפניהם not אשר תדבר אליהם or אשר תצוה אותם or otherwise. We only find שום לפני, — apart from the transmission of God’s Laws to Israel through Moses, — used in one specific connection exclusively, viz., as the special expression for serving prepared food to a guest. So ויושם לפניו לאכול (Gen. 24,33) and וישם לפני שאול (Sam. I. 9,24). So also Sam. I. 28,22 et alia. So that, used for the transmission of laws, it means nothing but a clear and comprehensive transmission which is placed before the people in a clear and understandable manner which they can completely understand and carry out. The explanation of the Mechilta: כשולחן ערוך ומוכן לאכול לפני האדם “like a table laid and prepared for a meal before somebody”, is accordingly the literal sense of the expression. So that in the heading, in the introduction of these laws the fact is stated that the following written notes contain only short naked sentences whose precise application and complete exposition is left to verbal tradition and transmission. So that in these following verses of Mishpatim in the תורה שבכתב we do not see the Law in its completeness, but can only take the whole total Law from the תורה שבעל פה.

V. 2. כי תקנה עבד עברי. To the unprejudiced mind, nothing can show so strikingly the truth of the traditional oral-law as the first two paragraphs, V. 2—6 and 7—11, with which this “Mosaic Lawgiving” starts. The civil and criminal laws of the Nation are to be given, the fundamental basis and the ordinances of justice and humaneness are to be laid down, which are to govern the relationship and behaviour of man to his fellow-man in the state; the first matter to be dealt with, quite naturally deals with the rights of man, and this starts with the sentences: “When a man sells another man”, and “when a man sells his daughter!” What an unthinkable enormity if actually this “written word” of the “book of Law of the Jewish Nation” should really be the one and only sole source of the Jewish conception of “Rights”. What a mass of laws and principles of jurisprudence must have already been said and fixed, considered, laid down and explained, before the Book of Law could reach these, or even speak of these, which, after all, are only quite exceptional cases. And it is with these sentences, the contents of which deny and limit the very holiest personal right of man, the right to personal freedom, that the Law begins.

But it is quite a different matter if the written word, the “Book” is not the real source of the Jewish conception of Rights, if this source is the traditional law, which was entrusted to the living word to which this “book” is only to be an aid to memory and reference, when doubts arise; if, as indeed is stated in the “book” itself, the total and complete Law had been given over to the people in its complete form, and had been impressed upon them, and explained to them and lived by them for full forty years, before Moses, just before his death, was to hand them this written book. Then we can well understand that it is just the exceptional cases which principally come to be described, so that just from them, the normal general principles of justice and humanity may be more strikingly realised. Then we can understand how it is that general principles of justice are altogether not so much given in this “book”, but preferably single concrete cases, and these are described in the “book” in such an instructive manner that the principles which underly them, and which had been entrusted to the living minds and living practice of the people, can easily be seen from them. Then we can understand how the language used in this “book” is so skillfully chosen that often by the use of a striking expression, an unusual or altered construction, the position of a word, a letter etc., a whole train of ideas of justice and human rights is indicated. After all, it was not out of this book that the law was to have been acquired. This book was to be given into the hands of those who were already well informed in the Law, simply as a means of retaining and of reviving ever afresh this knowledge which had been entrusted to their memories; and also to the teachers of Law as a means of teaching to which the students can go for references to the traditional actual laws, so that the written sentences lying before them would make it easy for them to recall to their minds the knowledge they had received orally.

The תורה שבכתב is to be to the תורה שבעל פה in the relation of short notes on a full and extensive lecture on any scientific subject. For the student who has heard the whole lecture, short notes are quite sufficient to bring back afresh to his mind at any time the whole subject of the lecture. For him, a word, an added mark of interrogation, or exclamation, a dot, the underlining of a word etc. etc., is often quite sufficient to recall to his mind a whole series of thoughts, a remark etc. For those who had not heard the lecture from the Master, such notes would be completely useless. If they were to try to reconstruct the scientific contents of the lecture literally from such notes they would of necessity make many errors. Words, marks, etc., which serve those scholars who had heard the lecture as instructive guiding stars to the wisdom that had been taught and learnt, stare at the uninitiated as unmeaning sphinxes. The wisdom, the truths, which the initiated reproduce from them (but do not produce out of them) are sneered at by the uninitiated, as being merely a clever or witty play of words and empty dreams without any real foundation.

When the word of God wants us to realise what are the principles of rights and humaneness which it demands for the respect of the human being, it starts off with the criminal. And it takes for its example the criminal against property, that criminal who, in all other states, is threatened with the direst punishment to body and freedom, and it shows us what is the treatment that God’s idea of Rights in His State, dictates. Let us read this law:-

כי תקנה עבד עברי. The oral tradition teaches us that the case dealt with here is that described in Ch. 22,2, that a thief who can not restore the value of his theft to his victim is sold to help him make this restoration, אם אין לו ונמכר בגנבתו. Such a sale can only be made to make up the value of the actual theft itself, but not to bring it up to the double value where this is imposed as a fine (V.3 ibid.). Such a sale is only imposed on male thieves, not on females. The written note on this Halacha is, that there it does not say in a general term אם אין לו ונמכר which would be sufficient, but adds the word בגנבתו (which as we know, the דין tells us just for the theft but not for the fine. I.L.); and also it does not say בגנבה (for the theft, which would suffice.) but בגנבתו, his theft and not her theft, excluding female thieves. The case where a man sells himself out of dire poverty is provided for elsewhere וכי ימוך ונמכר לך (Levit. 25,39). That is why it says only here כי תקנה עבד עברי he is already an עבד before you buy him, has been declared one by the court, and it is from the court only, that you can buy him. Nevetheless, as the Mechilta remarks, to you he must remain an עברי your fellow-national, it is only that the court has no option but to call him עבד. יכול תקראנו עבד לשום בזיון ת״ל כי תקנה עבד עברי, התורה קראתו עבד בעל כרחה.

שש שנים יעבד. It does not say ועבדך שש שנים, so his obligation to service extends beyond your personality — if the master dies he has to serve the son — but, on the other hand, in Deut. 15,12 it does actually say ועבדך שש שנים, so the extension of his service is limited to the nearest representative only — the son, but does not extend to any other heir if there is no son (Kidushin 17b).

שש שנים יעבד ובשביעית יצא, were it to say שש שנים יעבד ואחרי כן יצא the regaining of his freedom would depend absolutely on his doing six years service, and omissions through illness would have to be made up at the end; were it to say שש שנים יהיה עמך ובשביעית יצא the seventh year would unconditionally in all cases bring freedom; the way the sentence is worded is to remind us that both service and seventh year are factors that may necessitate some adjustment to the terms of his service. The Halacha is, that he goes free automatically in the seventh year unless he had been completely incapacitated from work for the greater part of his years of service; in this latter case he would have to make the time up (ibid 17 a).

The idea of the nature of the work he has to do is fixed by the command כשכיר כתושב יהיה עמד (Levit. 25,40). No other kind of work can be demanded from him than that which has been his usual occupation up till now (אי אתה רשאי לשנותו מאומנותו), (e.g. if he had been a bootmaker, you can only make him work for you at bootmaking. I.L.) According to the further sentence לא תעבוד בו עבודת עבד (ibid 30) you may not demand from him personal service even such that a son or pupil would gladly, and of his own free will, perform for his father or teacher (Mechilta).
חנם. without any reparation at all, even if the master has been put to considerable expense on his account e.g., to cure an illness.

V. 3. גף from גפף the body (related to גב from גבב the back). If he entered service simply with his own person as a single man, then his master may not impose on him the relationship described in V.4 But as it says “if he entered by himself alone” it indicates that if he were married he would enter slavery together with his wife. This is indicated even more clearly in ויצאה אשתו עמו. So that if he is a married man it is evident that the wife must enter the service with him. But the status of the wife can be in no wise that of a slave or servant. As stated above, even for her own theft, no woman is sold into slavery, so she certainly can not be made to suffer in this way for the crime of another. On the contrary; what the Halacha teaches is, that the wife may not be separated from her husband, and that during the time of service, when the husband can not look after and maintain his wife and children, the master has to provide board and lodging for them. רמב״ם and רמב״ן are of different opinion on the question as to whether, as compensation for the maintenance he is forced to supply, the master is entitled to such of any possible earnings of the wife that normally the husband is entitled to take. רמב״ם says “No”. But רמב״ן argues, that as the master takes over the responsibilities of the husband he takes over this right with it. A single man can also, if he wishes, and obtains permission from his master, marry during his period of service, and the master is then also bound to provide for the wife.

V. 4. As the master is called אדניה “her master” it can only be speaking here of a non-Jewish slave, a שפחה כנענית (as indeed the Halacha teaches). For a Jewish woman there can be no question of such a relationship. In the one and only case, described in V. 7 of an אמה עבריה, she could only marry the master himself or his son. Now, generally, no marriage at all is allowed with a שפחה כנענית. This is the one exceptional case where it is allowed, and here indeed only if the man is already married. The expression יתן לו אשה moreover, demands that, for the duration of the period of service, the relationship must be kept to that of a formal marriage, לו אשה המיוחדת לו, שלא תהא כשפחת הפקר (Mechilta).

האשה וילדיה תהיה לאדניה. In all cases where there is no true spiritual marriage, but where the parties can only be regarded as living together physically, the rule is, that the children take the status of the mother (Kiddushin 66b).

V. 5. אם אמר יאמר (“If the slave repeatedly says”). The decision which fixes his fate for such a long time must be repeatedly stated by the slave, and moreover, לא אצא ,ואם וגוי ,העבד וגו׳, this decision must be stated כשהוא עבד and בשעת יציאה, at a moment when he is still under the vivid impression of both the conditions between which he has to decide, בתחלת פרוטה אחרונה ובסוף פרוטה אחרונה, i.e. in the very last minute of his duty of service. אהבתי את אדני וגו׳ and similarly in Deut. 15,16. כי אהבך ואת ביתך ,כי טוב לו עמך (“I love my master” and “For I love you and your household, for it has been well with him with you,”) all the conditions which are implied in these expressions, must be present, if his decision to remain is to take permanent effect. Both he and the master must have a wife and children (ואת ביתך — את אשתי וגו׳), both must be in good health (טוב לו עמך) and the affection and attachment must be on both sides (ואח ביתך — אהבך) (Kiddushin 22a). If we imagine any one of these conditions to be lacking on either side, the decision may very well have been a too hasty one. If the master is single now, and later on a wife and children come into the home, or if the slave is now single and he gets a wife and children later on, the conditions could easily become intolerable. If either of the two is ailing, the decision could have been made out of a feeling of weakness and dependence which would pass when he is well again, or if the master is ailing at the time, out of a feeling of self sacrifice, which decision later on, when good health returns, and it is too late, could easily be regretted. If the feeling of affection is on one side only, the decision is considered as being altogether unnatural and indicative of an unnaturally emotional mood to which such a far reaching result should not be accorded. In the case where both are ailing, the question as to whether the decision is effective, is left undecided (ibid). But in this טוב לו עמך is also contained the most important norm for the treatment of a slave in the home of his master. It demands complete equality of the slave with his master and the rest of the household, in food, clothing and bedding, so much so that it became a popular saying “who buys a Jewish slave for himself has bought himself a master.” The moral responsibility is great on both sides את נוהג בו באחוה, והוא נוהג בעצמו בעבדות, “the master must treat him as a brother, but he (the slave) must treat himself and behave as a slave.” (Kiddushin 22a).

V. 6. For the meaning of האלהים as judge see Gen. 1,1. Judges who are designated by the name אלהים must be מומחין and סמוכין i.e., their knowledge of the Law must be proved and recognised, and their permission to declare and decide what the Law is can only be conferred on them by one who himself is a מומחה and who has סמיכה. This induction (סמיכה) by transferring one’s own right and powers to a successor, must reach back to the very first representative of the Torah — to Moses himself — and can only take place in the land of Israel, on the soil of the Land of the Torah (see Rambam, IV הל׳ סנהדרין).

As והגישו is repeated, it is evident that bringing the slave to the court must have a purpose of its own (in addition to the piercing of his ear). In the Mechilta this purpose is explained to be שימלך במוכריו “to talk the matter over with those who had sold him.” It is doubtful whether the master or the slave is the subject of this sentence in the Mechilta. The slave, so that the judges should try to dissuade him from his decision, or the master, so that the further retention of the slave and the רציעה should only be done with the authorisation of the court. Rashi adds the words שמכרוהו לו and so evidently thinks it refers to the master.

From Deut. 15,17 ונתת באזנו ובדלת, we know that the piercing has to be done to the door itself and not to the doorposts, from ורצע אדניו את אזנו here, that the ear has to be pierced only up to (not into) the door (Mechilta, Kiddushin 22b).

ועבדו. Here it does not say ועבד as in V.2 but ועבדו. The עבד נרצע has only to serve the master, but not the son after the master’s death. Moreover, the ועבדו לעולם can only have the meaning, “as far as he is concerned he has to continue for ever in service”. He has lost the possibility of himself achieving his freedom. Up till now the time of his duty of service was definitely limited. In no case could it exceed six years, and even during this period he could at any time acquire his freedom by paying off the proportionate value of the remaining period of his service. (This reduction of the purchase price which is referred to in connection with the law of אמה עבריה which follows this law, in the word (גירעון כסף) והפדה, applies to a man also). But henceforth he has no power at all to free himself. “He has to go on serving him for ever,” and can only regain his freedom by the death of his master, or by the advent of the “Home-bringing Year”, the “יובל״ which leads everyone back again to his heritage, and everyone back to his own hearth. ושבתם איש אל אחזתו ואיש אל משפחתו תשובו (Levit. 25,10).

If we consider this Law, which the Word of God has placed at the head of His precepts of the Rights of Man, we shall find that there is hardly another one which would be as eminently suited to give us an insight into the underlying ideas and conceptions of the Torah’s system of Jurisprudence and its institutions of Law and Human Rights, and their very fundamentally different character to all other systems of Law. This is the one and only case in which the Torah orders a deprivation of freedom as a punishment (we shall see that even this case is not to be looked at as a punishment); and how does it order it? It orders the criminal to be brought into the life of a family as we might order a refractory child to be brought under the influence of Jewish family life; and with what precautions does it surround this undertaking! How careful it is that the self-confidence of the criminal should not be broken, that, in spite of the degradation he has brought on himself, he should still feel himself considered and treated as a brother, capable of being loved and giving love! How it insists that he may not be separated from his wife and family, and what care does it take that his family should not be left in distress through his crime and its result. In depriving him of his liberty, and thereby of the means to provide for his dependents, the Torah puts the responsibility of caring for them, on those who, for the duration of his lack of freedom, have the benefit of his labours.

Punishments of imprisonment, with all the attendant despair and moral degeneration that dwell behind prison bars, with all the worry and distress that it entails for wife and child, are unknown in Torah jurisprudence. Where its power holds sway, prison for criminals does not exist. It only knows of remand in custody, and even this, according to the whole prescribed legal procedure, and especially through the absolute rejection of all circumstantial evidence, can only be of the shortest duration.

But even this one single case in which the Torah ordains loss of freedom as a result of crime, can not be regarded as “punishment”. For as the thief can be condemned to a maximum period of six years’ slavery only for the repayment of the actual amount of the theft, but not to bring the amount up to the fine which is imposed for the theft (כפל), (payment of double the value), the motive for this sentence can not possibly be punishment. It is obviously nothing but the simple consequence of the crime demanding repayment. Now repayment is not punishment, it is merely doing away with the effects of the crime, which last as long as the illegal or criminal damage or loss to the property of another is not made good again. Whosoever lays hands on somebody else’s property, whether condemned by the court or not, at the moment of the deed, becomes automatically responsible to pay for it out of his own pocket, and if the pocket be empty, out of his powers of filling it i.e., with the work of his hands. We should perhaps rather be inclined to ask, why it is only in the case of direct theft that the Law estimates the value of a man’s earning capacity, and, where necessary, sells the criminal for this amount, and why not in all cases where the Law demands repayment, and the means are lacking wherewith to make it. Perhaps the reason may lie in the fact that theft shows the most direct contempt of the idea of the rights of property, and is exercised just at the time when the owner entrusts his property to the sense of honesty and respect for the Law of his fellow-men (see on V.37). Man’s whole position in human society begins with the idea of personal possessions, and men prove their right to civilised social life by their respect for the idea of personal possessions. We can understand that it is just in the case of theft only, that the whole personality of the thief is used for the repayment of the theft.

This condemnation to slavery is so very much the result of the duty to repay, the Law is so very far from wishing to inflict punishment by it, and personal freedom is regarded by it so much as a holy treasure, that it is only in cases where the value of the theft equals or exceeds the estimated value of six years’ work that the Court may proceed to sell the thief. If the value of his work exceeds the amount of his theft, the Court impounds his labours for the repayment of the amount of the theft, but does not deprive him of his freedom. (Kiddushin 18a). Besides, according to the Mechilta, the victim can renounce altogether his right to repayment by the sale of the malefactor, and content himself with a signed promise to pay as soon as the circumstances of the thief improve.

In his whole period of slavery, there is only one condition in which this man, who has been sold to make reparation for his act of contempt of property, is really brought to feel his degradation. This is the Law that his master may give him a slave-girl as a wife for the duration of his service, whose children then remain in the possession of the master. Such a union is prohibited to a free Jew, and as this marriage altogether bears only a physical character and not a spiritual one (— אין קידושין תופסין —) and the wife who is given him, although she must be מיוחדת לו, may only remain with him for the years of his service, it seems to have the purpose of bringing home to him how morally low he has sunk, how he has forfeited the moral height on which a Jew should stand, and has sunk back halfway into the degree of a mere physical existence. This may also well be the reason for the fixing of the service to just six years, and for giving the seventh its power of bringing freedom. By his crime he has relapsed into the realm of the “six” — the purely material physical world. He has not allowed the thought of the “seventh”, of the invisible, but ever-present “One”, to restrain him from grasping at the visible material. He has lost the “fear of God”, and thereby has sinned against his own “godlike nobility”, which is the heritage of Man. He has, accordingly, to achieve the restitution of what he has lost by this sin, by investing the whole of his own material physical existence in subordinating his “six” to work himself up again to “seven”. As a result of his crime, he is a slave for six years, the seventh brings his freedom. Throughout the rest of his life he will be accompanied by the warning — “Six”, enslaves you, “Seven”, makes you a free man. Giving ourselves up to the sway of passions and inclinations makes us into slaves, giving ourselves up to the dictates of God, makes us free men, and unites our “six” with the One to make us “seven”. By bringing God and His Law into our physical material life, each and every phase of that life is raised into the sphere of spiritual, free, godlike nobility, in which every human life should be lived.

The slave who prefers the security and carefree comfort that is assured to him in the state of bondage to his own independent family life with all its worries and cares, is taken by his master to the door or doorposts of a home and his ear is there pierced with an awl by the master to the door. not to the doorposts. מזוזות, the posts, are representative of an independent home. As such they occurred in the moment of Redemption in which God raised the Egyptian slaves to free men, and gave them once again the right, and thereby the duty, of founding their own independent homes. Placing the blood of the Pascal Lamb — to which each “soul” (מכסת נפשות) had to be reckoned — on the “posts” of the homes, gave thereby each Jewish soul the high call to take part in building up homes of free men for God. But דלת the door, the swinging means of entrance and exit for the members of the home, represents not the home, but belonging to the home. The Jew who belittles the dignity of being “doorposts”, independently to bear on his own shoulders the burden of a home, and sells his freedom for the ease of “belonging” to some one and who has no ear for the call of God to freedom and independence, his ear is bored to a door, in the presence of a “doorpost” and thereby the stamp of “belonging to a home” impressed on him. (cf. Kiddushin 22b) מה נשתנה דלת ומזוזה מכל הכלים שבבית, אמר הקב״ה דלת ומזוזה שהיו עדי במצרים בשעה שפסחתי על המשקוף ועל שתי המזוזות ואמרתי לי בני ישראל עבדים ולא עבדים לעבדים והוצאתים מעבדות לחירות, והלך זה וקנה אדון לעצמו ירצע בפניהם.

But just as it is to the slave, so is the freemaking power of the seventh year a warning to the master too, and for all masters, whose brethren have been brought into a state of dependence on them, to keep clear in mind the invisible, sole, one and unique Master; to consider Him as One above masters and slaves, and not to abuse their higher position based on money and position to keep their brethren who have come to be dependent on them in illegal bondage.
