Right at the very last stage of the Jewish State, Jeremiah had still to proclaim the disregard of the principle which is expressed by the freemaking power of the seventh year as the final cause of the fall of the State (Jer. 34,13 et seq.). According to Jerushalmi Rosh Hash. 3b, פשרת שילוח עבדים was the very first Law which Moses and Aaron had to bring the Jews (above Ch. 6,13, ויצום אל בני ישראל) as the basic condition for their redemption. We said that Jeremiah pointed to disregard of the principle expressed by the law, not to disregard of the application of the law itself. For according to the accepted Halacha of Kiddushin 14b, the service of one who sells himself out of dire destitution is not limited to six years but has to last the full term of the contract, which can only be shortened by the death of the master or of his son, or by the advent of the Youvel. According to that, we must take Jeremiah’s reproach to be:— “Even one who has been sold by the court for a theft should get his freedom in the seventh year, how much more then must you not keep in bondage beyond the term of his contract or after the entry of the Youvel Year, one who out of dire necessity has of his own free will sold himself to you”. According to the ריטב״א, Rashi takes the sentence in the .ברייתא המוכר עצמו נמכר לשש ויתר על שש to mean, that, implicitly, one who sells himself, only does so for six years and does go free in the seventh, and only by a special contract does the service extend for a longer period. According to that Jeremiah would refer to the application of the Law in normal cases and the wording in that chapter certainly indicates Rashi’s interpretation. Moreover, the Gemora in ערכין 33a takes the מקץ שבע שנים תשלחו to mean: after the end of seven shemita years i.e., at the entering יובל.

V. 7. From V.8 we know that the condition of ייעוד must be connected with this sale, i.e., the intention of eventually marrying the girl, in which case the money given to the father is considered as the betrothal gift, מעות ראשונות לקידושין נתנו (see Kiddushin 18b). From both the possible eventual effects of this sale, it is quite evident that this sale can only be made during the age in which the earnings of a child belong legally to the father, and in which the father has the legal authority to dispose of the hand of his child, i.e., to contract a marriage which is legally binding on the man, and to receive the marriage gift in her stead. In other words, during the period of her immature minority. In respect of both these rights (her earnings and disposal in marriage) the period extends to mature puberty i.e., to six months after the advent of puberty, generally taken to be at 12 years, and to be mature six months later i.e., at years of age, after which the girl becomes בוגרת “independent” (Ketuvoth 46b). But nevertheless, the authority for this sale is only valid from the period of complete childhood קטנות until with the advent of puberty the girl reaches the stage of becoming a נערה, usually taken to be with the completion of the twelfth year. We can already see from this limitation that the intended eventuality of marriage is the predominant idea of the “sale”. The girl only remains in service while she is not yet of marriageable age. As soon as she becomes marriageable the master must either marry her or let her go free without further ado (see V.11).

Further, all the consideration which we have to observe according to the Scriptures regarding the exalted position of Jewish women, regarding the relation of parents to children, as well as the care and considerations which parents must have in the suitable marriage of their children, force us immediately to the conclusion that the case כי ימכור איש את בתו לאמה “when in this way a Jewish man sells his little immature daughter to be a servant for her to be eventually married”, can only be, that the extremest bitterest necessity can have brought him to it. And according to the Halacha really he must first have sold his house, home and land, even have sold his last shirt before he may decide to take this step (Kiddushin 20a, Rambam Hilch. Abadim 4,2).

But in general, a father should not make use even of his legal authority to give his little daughter in marriage during her minority. In normal circumstances it is actually called אסור, it says אסור לאדם שיקדש את בתו כשהיא קטנה עד שתגדל ותאמר בפלוני אני רוצה, “It is forbidden for a man to give his daughter in marriage while she is a child, until she has grown up and declares: “That is the man I want to marry”. This not only declares any forced marriage as sinful, but even the only too common practice of persuading a daughter into a marriage as equally so (Kiddushin 41a). A union that necessitates the closest intimacy can only thrive if it emanates from the most complete free will without any persuasion being necessary. The Law gives the father the legal power to do it, for it knows it can depend on Jewish fathers to make use of it only in cases of urgency, when such a disposition over the future of the child serves as the means of its salvation and well being. For such cases, the fact of this and similar modes of action having legal force and sanction can be of the greatest value, and they have proved their worth time and again in the varied and eventful history of our people (see תוספות ibid) (and especially in the Middle Ages. I.L.). The Torah could boldly make it possible for practical use to be made of such theoretical ideas of rights. It knew that all the rest of its laws and institutions would create and nurture such feelings in its adherents, that possibilities could quite safely be given into their hands without any fear of their being abused or misused. The Torah itself in V.8 calls the behaviour of the father from the child’s standpoint בגידה a betrayal, something contrary to what a child can usually expect from its father, and this shows, clearly enough, that the case is to be regarded only as an exceptional one.

לא תצא כצאת העבדים, apart from the fact that עבדים עברים, Jewish slaves are not referred to simply as העבדים, without any adjective, it can here only refer to עבדים כנענים because from כי ימכר לך אחיך העברי וגו׳, ואף לאמתך תעשה כן, (Deut. 15,12 17), we know that all free-making incidents, the seventh year, the Youvel, and the death of the master, are equally effective to male and female Jewish slaves. So that the reference here can only be, as indeed the Halacha teaches, to עבדים כנענים non-Jewish slaves, who, according to V.20 get their freedom by bodily injuries יוצאים בראשי איברים. A Jewish maidservant (and so also through the above-quoted equality of sexes, a Jewish man-slave) does not go free as a result of such injuries. They are not real slaves, and letting them off the few years of their service would be no equivalent for bodily injuries. They have to receive full compensation for their loss as every other Jewish person would, their condition of service continues, and a Jewish girl would expect, without consideration of the crippling she has suffered, or just because of it with greater confidence, that the master would marry her, in accordance with the conditional promise which he had originally entered into.

V. 8. יעד .אשר לו יעדה (related to יחד) is used predominantly to designate a personal union; הִוָעֵד, mutually to agree to come together, to fix a coming together; מועד the time or place for such a meeting. Here, the fixing or arranging for a marriage union. In accordance with the underlying idea of the word יעד, although in general cases the father has the right to accept the betrothal gift and bind his little daughter to marriage without asking her consent here in this case, the consent of the maid is required, אין יעוד אלא מדעת דידה (Kiddushin 19a). The word itself which the Torah uses implies the idea of a mutual decision. Rambam Hilch. Avadim 4,8 also takes it this way as the Halacha. Nevertheless, תוספות (ibid 5a) takes it, that here also the consent of the girl need not be obtained. — יעדה is past tense and so refers back to the act of purchase, and indeed, according to the קרי which is לו can not be taken otherwise, as now he does not want to marry her. He had, as remarked above on V.7, right at the beginning in handing over the money to her father “designed her to be his bride.” But this decision was not an absolute one, it was to be dependent on his declaration later on, it was only a conditional one. Hence the כתיב which is לא. He had decided to marry her and now he has decided not to marry her. But as the קרי is לו and the כתיב is לא and not the other way round, and in all cases of קרי and כתיב it is the קרי which is predominant and the כתיב is only meant to bring a modification to it, it is evident from the wording too that מצות יעוד קודמת, that in the first place his duty is that of marriage, and that this is expected from him.

והפדה, as the subject of the following לא ימשל as we shall show, can only be the father, so the subject of והפדה is likewise the father. If the master afterwards declares that he does not want to marry her then he, the father, has to achieve her redemption. If he has meanwhile acquired the means, the court forces him to redeem her; or, in the event of his still being without means, the family is made responsible to do so (Kiddushin 18a). But the master has to help in this matter too, inasmuch as he has to allow a deduction to be made in the return of the money he paid proportionate to the amount of service the girl had already given מגדע פדיונה ויוצאה (ibid 16a).

לעם נכרי לא ימשל וגו׳, can not possibly refer to the master, he has no right whatsoever to re-sell her at all, not even to anybody who could not come under the designation of עם נכרי. Here also the subject is the father. עם נכרי, we have already repeatedly had occasion to remark that עם does not by any means only mean a nation in its entirety. We have pointed out how the Jewish Nation is considered as consisting of a number of circles (sailors, soldiers, merchants, students, teachers, etc., etc., each one of which is an עם I.L.) hence the common expressions in the plural ,בעל בעמיו ,עמיך ,עמיו הכרת מעמיה ,רכיל בעמיך etc. etc. Each family circle is עם and עם נכרי is a family circle which would be permanently “strange” to her. Cf. נכריות נחשבנו לו (Gen. 31,15) and נכרי לבני אמי (Ps. 69,29). He, the father, has not the right to sell her into a circle which must, or should, remain srange to her (i.e., in which she must remain an outsider I.L.). He may only sell her to a man to whose family circle — or that of his son (V.9) — she can, and eventually should become a member by marriage. אין מוכרה לקרובים (Kiddushin 18b). He may not sell her to such blood-relations with whom a marriage would be forbidden. He may also not sell her על מנת שלא ליעדה with the express condition that marriage shall not take place, and therefore too, he has to achieve her redemption as soon as the master declares he does not want to marry her.

בגד ב- .בבגדו בה to prove oneself as being merely a cloak towards someone. By putting on a garment, by clothing ourselves, we give any and everybody who meets us, the right to find a real human being in us, and to expect only that which is worthy of human beings from us. If we fail to justify this trust that is given us, then we are simply “an empty garment” a בגד which lacks the real man within it. Similarly מעל and מעיל the priestly garment. מעילה is deception in holy matters (such as using for ordinary purposes that which has been dedicated to קודש I.L.). We were trusted to behave in a priestly manner and we proved ourselves to be simply “an empty priestly cloak.” The father has behaved in an unfatherly manner towards his child, other than what a child is entitled to expect from a father. (So that now to translate the whole verse it would run: “If she is displeasing in the eyes of her master who had conditionally (לו and לא) designed her to become his wife, then he (the father) must see to it that she gets redeemed, he has no right to sell her into a family circle to which she will remain an outsider, inasmuch as he has behaved in an unfatherly manner towards her.” I.L.).

V. 9. כמשפט הבנות וגו׳. According to Rambam this refers to the master, he, the master, has to fit her out for the marriage, as if she were his own daughter, similar to the הענקה (Deut. 15,14), the fitting out and setting-up which the Torah makes it incumbent on a master to provide, when any Jewish slave or maidservant leaves his service. But this special duty of providing a bridal outfit if a master marries his Jewish maidservant to his son is nowhere mentioned in the Halacha. Therefore, the משפט הבנות seems rather to refer — as Rashi, and equally so, the Mechilta take it — to the rights which a wife can legally demand from her husband and which are mentioned in the following verse. Our verse would then read: “He, (the son) has to treat her in exactly the same way as other wives who are given in marriage as “daughters” בנות, and not as slaves, have the right to demand.” But the reason why this is mentioned only here, and not already above in the case of the father himself (to whom of course it applies equally) may well be, because in the case of the son there is more reason to fear that he might treat her with less respect than in the case of the father, and it is the concise way of the Torah always to quote only the extreme example for its laws where we could least expect them to apply. The father had received her while she was still a free girl, the son marries her as a slave, and after she has been rejected by his father. And in the following verse an even more striking example is given where the possibility of her being treated with disrespect is even more likely, in the supposition that the son takes a free woman as another wife beside her.

V. 10. This is the only place where the Torah speaks of the duties of a man towards his wife. When it wants to lay down the משפט בנות, the elementary rights of the daughters of its people, it picks out for its example a woman of the very lowest social grade, the child of a beggar, of a man who has had to sell the very shirt off his back, and then, to save his child and himself from starvation has to sell her as a slave! This maid, disdainfully refused by the master (V.8), perhaps mishandled and disfigured by him (V.7) now becomes the wife of the son. Then the Torah takes this wife, and sets her beside an ordinary bride, a girl married out of a free rich family, and proclaims the great maxim: “Not by one hairbreadth may the treatment of the one differ from that given to the other.” The normal משפט בנות, the rights of married women are enumerated here in this chosen special case which preaches to us such a profound lesson. Through this, that great principle which pronounces the respect for the rights of our Women, became the norm in Israel: עולה עמו ואינה יורדת עמו “A wife can rise in station on her marriage but need not fall”: without the slightest consideration as to whether she brought a dowry of a hundred thousand pounds or came to him as the tattered naked child of a beggar, she has the right to be treated in accordance with the husband’s station in life. But where the usual standard of her life at home was of a higher standard than of the man she marries, unless she has definitely agreed beforehand to give it up, she has the right to demand to continue to live in the manner to which she had always been accustomed — “with marriage a woman rises to his station in life, but does not fall from hers”.

The רמב״ן, the רב המגיד, the ר״ן and others do not take שאר here to mean the duty of providing food, and take מזונות as a legal obligation, to be only תקנת חכמים. If this were to be the case it would give us an even more striking proof of the height at which the respect of Woman stood in the Jewish Nation. For then the Torah would have found it no more necessary to make a husband’s duty towards his wife into a right which she can legally claim, than it does for the duty of a father to provide food for his children. The legal claim of children to be fed is also only תקנת חכמים! And just as the Torah, with full confidence, entrusts the fate of children to the natural paternal feeling of Jewish fathers, so equally quietly it entrusts the fate of wives to the love and respect of Jewish husbands.

V. 11. ואם שלש אלה can not possibly refer to the immediately preceding three marriage duties of a husband, the end of the verse ויצאה חנם וגו׳ very definitely proves that. Once she is his wife, she can only leave him by גט and, moreover, the חנם אין כסף could then have no meaning, as she is no longer under any duty of service from which money could conceivably free her. The שלש אלה refers to the three eventualities which have been mentioned which could bring her term of service to an end, viz., that the master marries her, the son marries her, or that she gets bought out. ואם שלש אלה, if none of these happen, then at the time of the conclusion of her service she simply goes free without any further ado. As already remarked on V.7, she could only be sold during her childhood, as קטנה, and in any case her period of service could only extend to complete maturity, בוגרות (taken usually to be years of age) as the father’s legal rights both to her earnings and to the disposition in marriage, only extend to that time, and he obviously can not hand over the master a greater or longer-lasting claim than he himself possesses.

ויצאה חנם would then indicate that it was self understood that her period of service must end with the end of her father’s legal jurisdiction over her, i.e., on her attaining ימי בוגרות (usually years, I.L.). For a longer period the father could in no case give over rights of mastership, as he himself has none beyond that time. But our verse adds אין כסף, there is to be no compensation. So the period of her service must evidently end at a time over which we could think he still had rights and could be entitled to compensation, otherwise there would be no occasion for the text to say אין כסף, no compensation is to be paid. Obviously then, the service to the master must end at a time prior to that at which the father’s rights end. This time is, at the beginning of her puberty (taken generally to be at 12 years old I.L.). Hence the sentence in Kiddushin 4a ,ויצאה חנם אלו ימי בוגרות אין כסף אלו ימי נערות. She leaves service at the entry of the ימי נערות and although the father still has rights over his daughter till ימי בוגרות (6 months later) which could conceivably have been taken to be included in the sale, and therefore a claim for some compensation could have been thought justified, the Torah takes away the right to any such claim by the words אין כסף. As soon as she becomes a נערה she goes free and the master gets no compensation.

At the same time another law is indicated by this verse. As the Torah does mention ויצאה חנם, which we say refers to going free at בוגרות there must be some possible case where this occurs. This is actually the case in the condition known as אילונית where, on account of physical immaturity, נערות does not come at all, and the girl attains her legal majority בוגרות simply by attaining a specified age, and she passes directly from a state of קטנות to that of בוגרות.

Crime and poverty, these are the two factors which, in ordinary social life are inclined to bring the respect due to every human being down to the very lowest level, right down to zero. The Torah takes the criminal, and the child of extremest penury, and places them at the head, in its laws of human rights. It shows us thereby what it’s ideas of the respect due to a human being are, and how it insists that this respect must be shown, right down to the very lowest classes of society.

Now from V.12—32 follow laws referring to human rights; from 12—17 crimes against life, and conditions that are placed on par with life itself, V. 18-26 crimes against bodily well-being — wounds and injuries to body and health, — 27-32 fatal and other injuries caused by animals.

V. 12. Life itself as the condition which, above all, is necessary for all possessions and everything else connected with existence on earth, stands at the head. Our sentence מכה איש ומת is complemented by another verse איש כי יכה כל נפש אדם (Levit. 24,17). It is only by taking them together that we get the full legal idea of murder, both as regards the doer and the victim. Our מכה here, with a completely general subject (“whosoever” smiteth I.L.) receives its limitation by איש there, which implies ability to understand the nature and consequences of his act, and excludes קטנים; and the limitation to the male sex, which might be read into איש there, is removed by our מכה, and women murderers are included. The possibility that the victims could be limited to the male sex by the איש of our verse is negatived by the נפש אדם of the other, which includes women and children, and the איש only makes the limitation to the possibility of living, and excludes a נפל etc. Finally, the too wide application of the act which could be implied by כי יכה, is modified by ומת to an absolutely fatal blow. But it does not say הורג איש, but the blow and the result are separated, because it is not necessary for death to follow immediately on the blow, but if it is judged that the blow was of such a nature that death must inevitably follow, the death penalty has to be inflicted.

V. 13. צדה to take your direction towards something, to take aim at something. Now it says here אשר לא צדה “he had no intention of throwing (or shooting) in that direction,” which is explained in Baba Kama 26b, פרט לנתכוין לזרוק שתים וזרק ארבע to exclude the case where he did aim in that direction at an object two yards away, and the stone or shot went four yards and killed somebody. Here, as well as in Numbers XXXV and Deut. XIX, where more details on unintentional manslaughter are gone into, and explained, and especially from the specified example given in Deut. 19,5, the conditions in which this punishment of exile to a city of refuge is to be imposed are very precisely indicated in both directions. The act must be equally far from sheer carelessness as from unforseeable accident. It must not be קרוב למזיד nor קרוב לאונס. In the former the guilt is too great for it to be atoned for by simply having to live in a City of Refuge, and in the latter, the guilt is too small to require such atonement. If, for example, someone threw a heavy stone in the direction of a man standing four yards away and he had the intention to throw it only two yards, but the stone flew on the two yards further than he had intended, and killed the man, this would be a careless lack of precaution which can not be atoned for by גלות. It is קרוב למזיד. Such a case is excluded by אשר לא צדה here. But if he intended to throw it in quite another direction, and by some unexpected chance, the stone flew towards the man and killed him, מתכוין לצד זה והלכה לה לצד אחר, again he is not חייב גלות, it was קרוב לאונס the guilt is too small. This case is excluded by בלא צדיה (Numbers 35,22) (Makkoth 7b). גלות is only imposed when it is only the intention itself that is lacking, but conscientious consideration must have been able to foresee the possibility, even if not the probability, of the accident. For instance, the special example given, the flying off of the axehead from the handle when felling trees. According to this, the precise expression here והאלהים אנה לידו seems here, too, to express the limitation of the idea on the other side. It does not say והאלהים אנה אותו that God had brought it about, that would involve complete innocence on the man’s part, would be אונס or קרוב לאונס. But אנה לידו, his יד, his activity was a prime factor in causing the accident, only it was not the sole factor. The possibility of the accident lay in his act, and God arranged matters so that it became an actuality. So that אשר לא צדה excludes קרוב למזיד and האלהים אנה לידו excludes קרוב לאונס also.
The similarity of the punishment for careless manslaughter to the fate נע ונד which hung over the first murderer, is commented on in Gen. 4,12.

V. 14. וכי יזד איש וגו׳ is complete מויד (see on V.18). Between it and the שוגג punishable with גלות of the previous verse lies קרוב למזיד, criminal negligence, where the only thing lacking from the complete crime is the ערמה the intention to kill, and where, accordingly, the death penalty is not to be imposed, but on the other hand, can not be atoned for by גלות.

מעם מזבחי וגו׳. The Jewish altar grants no protection to the criminal. In Jewry there are not two principles which mutually control and modify each other, like Church and State, Justice and Mercy etc.; right next to the “sword-hating” altar was the chamber of the highest Court of Justice. It was one and the same principle which was to be taught by the altar, and which the Sanhedrin had to see was carried out in the practical life of the people. The whole idea of the right to grant clemency or mercy was entirely absent in the Jewish Code of Law. Justice and judgment is the perogative of God not of Man. When the very precisely defined Law of God, — giving Man no scope for his own judgment or arbitary discretion — ordains death for a criminal, the carrying out of this sentence is not an act of harshness to be commuted for any consideration whatsoever, it is itself the most considerate atonement, atonement for the community, atonement for the land, atonement for the criminal, atonement in quite the same way as that brought about by the altar. And if the priest was actually officiating at the altar, and even if he was the one and only priest available, and the accusation of murder was brought against him, away from the altar must you drag him to the court, to satisfy the Law of Justice.

V. 15. As הכאה to designate killing requires the addition of ;ומת הכאה by itself is evidently not killing. But the Halacha teaches that, nevertheless, at least a wound must have been inflicted for capital punishment to follow. In connection with V.12, accordingly, the Law would read: מכה״ איש ומת וגו׳. Whosoever striketh a man so that he dies, is guilty of death, but ומכה אביו וגו׳, if he strikes his father or mother, even if the wound is not fatal, he is equally guilty of death.”

V. 16. Just as in the previous verse, the partial killing i.e., the wounding of a father or mother is raised into the category of complete killing, and made into a capital crime, so the Torah teaches that freedom is a treasure, the robbing of which is social murder and equally to be punished by death. But kidnappers are only to receive capital punishment if נמצא בידו and also, as added in Deut. 24,7. והתעמר בו and then ומכרו, i.e., if he has made the man feel that he is being treated just as an object, a thing. This is implied by: נמצא בידו “that he is found to be in his power”, i.e., that it is declared by witnesses that שהכניסו ברשותו that he forced him into his premises, התעמר בו, i.e., השתמש בו, that he made him serve him in some way as a slave, and then ומכרו sold him (Sanhedrin 85b).

V. 17. Stealing human beings is actual destruction of the dignity of a human being. Towards father and mother one does not have to go so far, even expressing the desire for their ruin, קללה, incurs capital punishment, and even cursing them after they are no longer alive.

Although the legal death penalty for these four crimes is expressed by the general term מות יומת, the Halacha teaches, and it is indicated elsewhere in the Torah itself, that the mode of execution is not the same in each case. Murder is punished by execution, סייף, wounding parents, and slave raiding by חנק, cursing parents by סקילה. The different methods of inflicting capital punishment (there are four) are in a very profound relationship to the nature of the crime committed. But this can only be considered when taken all together, so must be left till we come P.G. to Levit. XX on the פרשת עריות.

V. 18. וכי יריבן. It does not simply say וכי יכה איש את רעהו וגו׳, but וכי יריבן וגו׳ to tell us that the duty of compensation which is here laid down, is quite independent of provocation or intent. Not only if someone deliberately goes out with the intention of striking somebody else, but also if the blow was quite unpremeditated, and came about as a result of a dispute or argument, the law applies. For ריב primarily means a fight with words in contrast to וכי ינצו וגוי of V.22, which refers primarily to an actual fight. It is only in cases where corporal punishment rather than compensation is involved that the question of ill-will, or criminal intention comes into consideration. The act must then be done, not only במזיד (V.14) but also בערמה with the full consciousness of the criminal nature of the action i.e., with התראה. But all the cases in the Torah where monetary payments have to be made (with the exception of the few cases which bear the character of קנס) are in no wise fines. They are simply the duty of restoration, of compensation (which comes purely as the just consequence of the damage done), and have nothing to do with the greater or lesser degree of wrong-doing of the act. The one who has done the damage has the duty to make it good, even if no court condemns him to it, or even if, through lack of witnesses, no court could condemn him to it. It is only with regard to the nature and extent of the compensation to be made i.e., whether just for the actual damage done (נזק) or also for the further consequences of it (,צער רפוי, שבת, בשת) that the degree of consciousness and intent with which the deed was done, makes any difference. With regard to replacement or paying compensation for the actual damage done, a man is in all cases responsible אדם מועד לעולם בין שוגג בין מזיד בין ער בין ישן סימא את עין חבירו שיבר את הכלים משלם נזק שלם, “A man is always responsible, whether the damage was done intentionally or accidentally, whether he was awake or asleep (in the latter case only if the object damaged was within his reach before he went to sleep) — if a man blinds his fellow-man or does damage to his property, he is always bound to pay the full value of the damage done.” (B.K. 26a). The further effects of the damage, — pain, doctor’s bill, loss of work, — demand a certain amount of consciousness of the danger of his act; insult, shame, requires actual intention, because doing anything unintentionally does away with any idea of insult (see B.K. 26b and 27a). Accordingly it says here וכי יריבן (and inded with the ן which makes it more pronounced), they were occupied only with a discussion, had no intention of doing each other any injury. The blow may have occurred in a moment of aggravation. This in no way lessens the duty of compensation, the object of which is not punishment but simply making good again, as far as possible, the damage done. This is why (since monetary payments are not fines for wrong done, but compensation for the damage done) in bodily injuries where the compensation can never be really adequate, and the pain can never be taken away by the compensation paid, even after full compensation has been paid, it is considered that the guilt remains in the eyes of God, and can only be wiped away by the injured person giving his full forgiveness. (B. K. 92a Rambam הל׳ חובל ומזיק V.9 and חושן משפט, 422,1 but others take this point to refer only to בשת).

גרף .באבן או באגרוף to keep close together, to hold together, hence אגרף the closed hand, the fist. But inasmuch as the Torah names the means by which the injury is done and does not simply say והכה את רעהו ולא ימות וגו׳, we learn that not only the result, but also the means by which it was achieved, must come into consideration by the court. It mentions אבן as an object by which injury and death can be accomplished, and the fist, which is ידוע i.e., which can not be missing when the case is before the court, is מסור לעדה ולעדים (B.K. 91a). This is to remind us of the דין that a man is only responsible for such injury which would normally result from the use of such an implement. Results that normally could not be expected to ensue from such a blow with such an instrument, must come from other conditions, for which the attacker is not to be made responsible. Accordingly, the court has expertly to estimate the blow as well as the implement used, in relation to the effect produced, יש אומד לנזקין (B.K. ibid).

V. 19. על משענתו can not possibly mean a stick or a crutch. If the victim could previously walk without any such assistance, and now, through the assault, is lame, he can obviously not be considered compensated simply by the payment of his medical expenses and loss of work. Equally obvious is it, that it can not refer to the period of his weakness during convalescence, for as long as the results of the injury continue, ונקה המכה can not be said. Also it would then say על משענת if it referred to a support which he is now obliged to use in consequence of his injury. But משענתו means his ordinary normal means of support, and designates על בוריו, his complete recovery. He goes about again in the same way as he did before receiving the injury.

ונקה המכה can not mean free from the death penalty, it is unnecessary for the Torah specially to tell us this, as the victim is still alive and has not been killed. It means freed from remand in custody, and refers to the case where אמדוהו למיתה the court had judged the blow to be of sufficient violence for a fatal result to follow, and had sentenced the man accordingly, in which case, he has to be kept in custody to await events. Now, our ונקה המכה reminds us of the דין that אמדוהו למיתה וחי פטור ממיתה וחייב בה׳ דברים (Sanh. 78b). It is in consideration of this verse that the Halacha applies the preceding verse, in which the words ולא ימות seem quite superfluous, to the opposite case, where the blow, in the estimation of the court was ולא ימות, should not have fatal result, and sentence was passed accordingly. In such a case, even if the victim does die, the aggressor is free from the death penalty or the גלות penalty; אמדוהו לחיים ומת פטור ממיתה וחייב בה׳ דברים (ibid). But on the other hand אמדוהו למיתה והיקל ממה שהיה ולאחר מכאן הכביד ומת חייב (ibid).

רק שבתו יתן וגו׳. Here only the expenses incurred by his being confined to bed are mentioned (following ונפל למשכב) (and also incidentally, as the Mechilta points out, the דין, that in the case of a blow which is judged to be of a fatal nature, and a fatal result does follow, no payments of expenses are to be made). The duty of paying compensation which is incurred immediately the blow is struck, נזק ,צער ,בשת is stated in V.24. רק שבתו וגו׳ (not ושבתו but רק שבתו I.L.). This רק limits the compensation to be paid to the loss of work and expenses which are incurred and necessitated by the actual injury itself, and excludes cases of malingering or where the patient lengthens the period of illness by not carrying out the doctor’s instructions עבר על דברי רופא (B.K. 85a).

ורפא ירפא. By the insistence expressed by the double wording, the Torah uses the opportunity incidentally to oppose the erroneous idea that having resource to human medical aid shows some lack of the trust and confidence one should have in the Divine assistance, מכאן שנתנה רשות לרופא לרפאות (B.K. 85a). The Torah takes it for granted that medical aid is used, and actually demands it here, and as תוספות remarks (ibid.) not only here in the case of wounding but in all ordinary cases of illness.

V. 20. That here it is talking of an עבד כנעני is proved by כי כספו הוא in the following verse. בשבט an instrument of correction. Only if an instrument legally permitted for correction is used, and only if it is used for the purpose of correction, does the concession in V.21 apply. (Rambam Hilch. Rozaiach. 2,14).

נקום ינקם designates execution by beheading, as in והבאתי עליכם חרב נוקמת (Levit. 26,2). This death by חרב is the method of exacting the death penalty for murder. That the punishment for murdering a slave is expressed by the term נקמה seems profoundly significant. From Gen. 9,1-6 it seems that murder is to be looked upon as a scornful denial of the צלם אלהים-nature of a human being. So that murdering anybody, is an attack on the godly nature of the whole of the human race, and in particular, that of the circle to which the victim belonged. Hence, in an ordinary case, the nearest relative takes the matter up, as גואל הדם as “Taker-up of the matter, champion of the spilt blood.” A slave has no relative to take up his cause, to be a גואל. He is to find this גואל in the Community of Israel. It — the Community — has to come forward as the avenger of the godly dignity of a human being which has been dragged in the dust in his case.

V. 21. יום או יומים, according to the Halacha, designates a period of twenty four hours. It must fix a quite definite time, and if the concession applies after one day, there is no point in mentioning the second one. As, in the Temple, the day begins with the morning and outside the Temple, in civil life, with the evening, any period of twenty four hours will contain one day or two days according to the one or the other reckoning; יום שהוא כיומים וימים שהוא כיום (Mechilta).

כי כספו הוא. This reason given can not be taken to mean that he is in some way of a lower degree of humanity than an ordinary free man. For it only applies to the master, to everybodf else the full ordinary law of murder applies. The reason can only lie in the relationship of the master to his personal property. This relationship is so sharply dependent on the reason given, כי כספו הוא, that the concession only applies if the slave was כספו המיוחד לו his own personal property, so that if, for example, he belonged to two people, the concession would not be made to either of them (B.K. 90a). The idea of this reason is difficult to find. Death which follows later on, might allow us to consider it as not necessarily being the absolute result of the blows, and this possibility, combined with the right of chastisement which the master possesses, so that the beating in itself is no wrong (see above) may possibly be the reason for this concession. Just as in the case of unintentional manslaughter, the penalty of Galut is imposed only if death follows so immediately that no “lying in a draught” or “violent movement” etc., could have hastened the oncoming of death (Gittin 71a).

V. 22—23. We have already remarked that נצה in contrast to ריב primarily denotes a quarrel accompanied by acts, a fight. So also in Deut. 35,11, כי ינצו אנשים וגו׳, להציל וגו׳, מיד מכה, it clearly describes a fight. Here too, the case is of a proper fight, and if V.23 can visualise the death penalty imposed if a fatality occurs, it must refer to a fight where the intention was to kill, a fight to the death במצות שבמיתה הכתוב מדבר (Sanhedrin 74a). Hence in this complicated problem, very important fundamental principles of law are laid down.

First we have the principle of נתכוין להרוג את זה והרג את זה he intended to kill his opponent but his blow caught the woman. The Halacha in this case is not quite decisive. According to the הכמים he incurs the death penalty, according to ר׳ שמעון he does not. (Sanhedrin 79a). Rambam decides like the latter (Hilch. Rozaiach 4,2) but see כ״מ on it. According to the view of the חכמים, V.23, where it speaks of a fatal result, would refer to the accidental killing of the woman, but according to רבי שמעון it must speak of the intentional killing, either of the opponent or of the woman — as the Halacha accepts the view of the תנא דבי חזקי׳ that in no case of killing is there any monetary fine, the נפש תחת נפש can not be taken (as רבי ibid.) would have it) to refer — like the immediate folowing עין תחת עין — to ממון. Then we have to consider the case where causing the death of the יולדות entails monetary compensation to the father.

The sentence אם לא יהי׳ אסון ענוש יענש, which immediately implies also the opposite הא אם יהי׳ אסון לא יענש, gives us the great principle in law that חייבי מיתה שוגגין פטורין מתשלומין, in cases of crimes incurring capital punishment, even where no death sentence is to be inflicted, no monetary payments or fines are to be made. This principle is made more explicit and complete by the saying of the תנא דבי חזקי׳, which runs: — מכה אדם ומכה בהמה, מה מכה בהמה לא חלקת בו בין בשוגג בין במזיד, בין מתכוין לשאין מתכוין, בין דרך ירידה לדרך עלייה לפוטרו ממון אלא לחייבו ממון אף מכה אדם לא תחלוק בו בין בשוגג בין במזיד בין מתכוין לשאין מתכוין בין דרך ירידה לדרך עליה לחייבו ממון אלא לפוטרו ממון (כתובות ל״ה א׳) “In Levit. 24,21, the Torah puts the monetary compensation for the killing of an animal and the death penalty for the killing of a human being in the same verse, and thereby indicates to us the rule: — That just as in the case of killing an animal in every case, monetary compensation has to be paid without consideration of the greater or lesser amount of consciousness or intention of the act, or of the amount of negligence, in the same way in the case of killing a human being no difference is made, but in all cases no monetary compensation is to be made.” But just in this contrasting juxtaposition of man and animal may be indicated the reason for this principle which evolves from the higher dignity of a human being, which must be upheld in all circumstances. For the life of an animal there can be compensation in money, but never for a human life לא תקחו כופר לנפש רוצח. At the moment when anybody’s life is forefeit to God’s justice — and that is the case even when the crime itself is of such a nature that it should be avenged by human justice, but the circumstances are such that it can not legally be carried out — from that moment, no monetary obligations can be imposed on him. The gravity of the crime, and the unparalleled dignity of his own human life which he has risked and forfeited, do not tolerate any question to be raised of money. Just imagine if one were to demand from a murderer, in addition to his life —or even from a murderer who for some reason or other has had to be let off — the paltry price for repairing the hole in the coat that his dagger had made! The Law is so sensitive in keeping up this principle that it applies it even to ממון אחר i.e., even to some other monetary liability which occurs simultaneously with the capital crime; and, for example, did not impose compensation for any property that had been destroyed by the missile discharged at the murdered victim. According to ר״ת even in our own problem here, we have an example of such ממון אחר. Compensation (in the event of the loss of the babes) has to be paid to the husband, the death penalty has to be paid on account of the wife מיתה לזה ותשלומין לזה and still compensation has only to be paid if the woman was not killed. More, even if a murder had not been accomplished, but only attempted, the criminal was only a רודף, a “pursuer”, and on his “path to murder” he had destroyed somebody’s property, he is not called on to pay compensation for the damaged property רודף שהיה רודף אחר חברו ושיבר את הכלים בין של נרדף ובין של כל אדם פטור (Sanhedrin 74a). On his way to murder, his life was at the disposal of anybody who, if no other means were possible, could, and must, prevent the crime by killing him. And it is logically proved (ibid.) from our problem here, too, that if anybody saves a threatened victim from being murdered by killing the murderer, when he could have prevented the crime by merely wounding him, he is guilty of murder, and himself incurs the death penalty. (יכול להצילו באחד מאיבריו ולא הציל (אלא בנפשו) נהרג; להרמב״ם חייב מיתה לשמים אבל אין ב״ד ממיתין אותו). If this were not so, if everybody who was setting about murder was in every case to be kept from murder by being killed, then our רודף, even if אם לא יהי׳ אסון, would not have to pay compensation for the babes, for, at the moment he did the damage to the ולדות his life would be at the disposal of everybody. — This principle, that חייבי מיתות אפי׳ שוגגין פטורין מתשלומין, is applied to all crimes, which, if they had been done במזיד ובהתראה would be punishable by death. It is usually referred to by the formula קים ליה בדרבא מניה. “It is enough that he gets the highest form of punishment.”

ונתתה נפש תחת נפש, Previously it says ונתן בפלילים he, the damager, has to pay compensation. Here, at the death penalty, it says ונתתה, and with the person stressed by the ה׳, thou, the Jewish community, is to give life for life. The fine, money, had to be paid by the guilty one, it was up to him to pay it as compensation, even if no court had sentenced him to do so. The court only tells him how much it is his duty to pay, ונתן, and he has to pay it. Not so with one who has to pay with his life. He has not to give up his life. Indeed, it is not his to give. His death at his own hands would only be a second crime. More, no assistance to his condemnation even, is expected from him, the Law has made it impossible for him to do so. According to Jewish Law no criminal can accuse himself. His confession has absolutely no bearing on the judgment to be passed on him. It is only before the carrying out of the death sentence, that he is admonished to confess for the sake of his own atonement. The disposal of his life lies solely in the hands of God, and in certain cases in the hands of the community which is delegated by Him for these cases. But as it says ונתתה and not ולקחת, as the carrying out of the death sentence is regarded as a “giving up” of a life, rather than as a “taking” of it, all attempts to look on the death penalty as taking revenge on the criminal, as a deterrent, or even only as a repayment, are opposed. If any of these were the case it would indubitably have had to say ולקחת, that the forfeited life has to be taken from the murderer. ונתתה makes us look on the punishment as “restitution” making good again the damage done by the murder, whether to justice, to the Law, to the idea of the value and dignity of a human life, or to all of these, which overlap each other. The community has to give up the life of the criminal to these ideas, which have been destroyed by the crime. With this word ונתתה is also incidentally expressed the idea that each individual life belongs to God and to the community, and that with every death, even with that of a murderer, the community suffers a loss.

V. 24. The cases mentioned in this verse are all cases of mutilation, cutting off, or maiming a limb or organ, and the representatives of the most varied activities are named. The eye, the organ of perception; tooth, of bodily maintenance (digestion) also of speech; hand, of productive activity; foot, of movement. The loss of an eye or of a tooth does not entirely destroy the function concerned, but only weakens it, whereas the loss of a foot or a hand usually does away with the activity that was previously possible. The permanent loss which is caused by such mutilations comes under the legal term נזק, loss.

V. 25. The cases mentioned in this verse are wounds without permanent mutilation. כויה a burn, is taken as an example of simple pain צער (B.K. 84b). “Burning” is chosen because it is possible to imagine it causing pain without inflicting any actual wound, as for instance if a glowing piece of iron is passed over the finger nail. פצע (related to פצח ,פצה opening) is the open wound. הבורה (from חבר to be joined) indicates a closed wound. But it occurs in connection with פצע (Prov. 20,30) חברות פצע תמרוק ברע and according to that, it seems to be the more far-reaching effects of a wound, inflammation, or, more in accordance with the literal meaning of the word, swelling. The verse in Proverbs would mean: “Not the open wound but the חבורה, the inflamed swelling caused by it, is where the evil penetrates dangerously”, (מרק means to penetrate deeply). According to this we should have wounding in its three successive effects: — pain, the cut, and the inflammation.

עין תחת עין וגו׳. It is already pointed out in B.K. 83b et seq., how the taking of this legal canon literally, in the sense of an eye for an eye, would be morally impossible for any idea of equity; how for instance, if a one-eyed man were to put out an eye of an ordinary two-eyed man, or how the criminal could easily die from the effects of the punishment (at the time of the Gemora of course, death from septic poisoning would be a common sequence from such an “operation” I.L.) whereas he had only caused the loss of an organ etc. etc. It has also been pointed out how the law, mentioned above in V.18 and 19 that injuries which entail staying in bed and medical attention, have to receive compensation for these items, how this law itself refutes taking עין תחת עין וגו׳, פצע תחת פצע וגו׳, as jus talionis, for inflicting a similar wound to the criminal would make him equally bedridden and requiring medical assistance himself. But in addition to these factual considerations which lead us to the conclusion that the only meaning which would be in accordance with the whole spirit of the text is what the traditional Halacha teaches, viz., that here it is only speaking of monetary compensation for the injury inflicted, in addition, a closer consideration of the word תחת on which really the whole idea rests will show us that the explanation of the Halacha is also in accordance with the literal meaning of the wording of the text.

The basic meaning of תחת is below, beneath (adv.) and under (prep.) it can accordingly only express the idea “for”, in the sense of “instead of”, and is accordingly the proper expression for compensation. It primarily describes the place which anything occupies, hence (Habakuk 3,16) ותחתי ארגז “I am stuck to where I am, do not care to move from my place, and tremble”. If anything is taken away from its place, an empty space is left. When something else is “put into the place” this is literally a “replacement”. So ויקח אחת מצלצתיו ויסגר בשר תחתנה (Gen. 2,26). (Similarly שכר, reward, wages, is nothing else but סכר ,סגד filling up a space). Hence also תחת הנהשת אביא זהב (Is. 60,17) etc. etc., and many other places where something coming “in the place of” something else is expressed. Hence also, the quite usual expression for compensation, i.e., for that payment with which one has to refill the “empty space” one has brought about in somebody else’s condition. In the verse immediately following לחפשי ישלחנו תחת עינו, and again in V.36 שלם ישלם שור תחת השור, and in V.37 חמשה בקר ישלם תחת השור; or Deut. 22,29, תחת אשר ענה. Hence also in Numbers 25,13 תחת אשר קנא לאלהיו, “as compensation, as reward for his devotion”. תחת can hardly ever be taken in the sense of punishment, chastisement for anything, in the way in which כי ,יען etc., occur. תחת אשר לא עבדת וגו׳, Deut. 28,18, is not a punishment for… but describes the completely opposite condition which has taken the place of the earlier one. Not “for that” “in return for” in the sense of “on that account”, “because”; but “instead of”; in place of the happiness and abundance in which you refused to serve God, now you must serve men in misery and need. — התחת זאת לא ימות שמעי (Sam. II. 19,22), seems at first sight to refute this view, but in reality, is a confirmation of it. Shimei had fallen at the feet of David, had acknowledged his wrong, and had drawn attention to the fact that he had been the first of his tribe to come and pay homage to David. On this Abishai asks: — התחת זאת, “and as a reward for this voluntary self-abasement to which he had been driven by necessity shall Shimei be let off punishment for his previous crime?”

In any case תחת, in the vast majority of cases, indicates compensation, rather than penalty or punishment, and עין תחת עין etc., means nothing else but, he has to restore an eye for an eye, he has to give the one whose eye he has put out, another eye. But by putting out the eye of the ‘doer’, the victim in no wise gets his eye back. But as no man can restore an eye in nature, the law can mean nothing else but “full compensation for the eye”.

So also in the Gemora B.K. 84a, after a whole list of explanations showing how this Halacha (of monetary reparation) is derived from the text itself, R. Ashi quite simply says: אתיא תחת תחת משור, כתיב הכא עין תחת עין וכתיב התם שלם ישלם שור תחת השור מה להלן ממון אף כאן ממון.

It is only in the case of murder נפש תחת נפש, where the crime has destroyed a concrete personality which really would have to be compensated for, that the punishment is carried out on the person of the murderer. Even this punishment, as we have seen, is expressed quite definitely as restitution by the use of ונתתה וגו׳. It is only that, in this case, personified Justice, and the extreme value of human life, take the place of the actual victim, who normally would be the one who is primarily entitled to claim restitution. But in cases of mutilation or wounding, where the one who is primarily entitled to demand compensation is actually there, it would be simple folly to allow him to go quite uncompensated, and wish to satisfy the idea of restoring the broken ideal of Justice and Right, by actual mutilation or wounding of the perpetrator of the deed. Rather by inflicting full compensation for the eye both the person and the idea get restitution.

The ב- also with which the Law is laid down at עדים זוממים (Deut. 19,26) עין בעין שן בשן וגו׳ denotes compensation. So we find Gen. 29,18, אעבדך וגו׳ ברחל בתך הקטנה and V.20 ibid. ויעבד יעקב ברחל; and 25 ibid. הלא ברחל עבדתי; ibid. XIII,16 שכרתיך בדודאי בני; ibid. 26 עבדתי אתך בהן etc. etc.

We have mentioned this legal canon in our commentary on Gen. 9,6 and understood it in the sense that it expresses the fundamental idea that everybody has a right to anything only as long as he respects a similar right in his fellow-man, so that he would lose the right to his own eye by putting out the eye of his neighbour. Compensation for the lost eye would then be a means of atonement for keeping his own eye. This way of looking at it is commendable, because according to ר׳ אליעזר in B.K. 84a, it is not the value of the lost eye, but that of the perpetrator, which has to be valued for the compensation. But that would not be in accordance with the definite meaning of תחת, restitution. Reb. Eliezer’s view is not accepted as the Halacha. In any case the actual words of the text give the simple duty of compensating to the fullest possible amount for the bodily damage done. And this damage is estimated in all its direct and indirect consequences. V.24 speaks of compensation for mutilation, compensation for the permanent disability which the loss of an organ involves. נזק, absolute loss, also called שבת גדול complete disability. V.25 in כויה and חבורה refers to צער, compensation for pain endured, and in כויה, pain brought about by the instrument used, mechanically, as well as in חבורה, the pain caused pathologically by the disturbed organic parts, (see B.K. 84b).

If the way we have taken it is correct, that in חבורה ,פצע ,כויה, the process of wound in its three successive phases, pain, cut, inflammation, is indicated, then it is clear that, after the permanent damage has been fixed for compensation by עין תחת עין etc., and the transitory pain by כויה וחבורה, no direct object of compensation remains which could be described by פצע תחת פצע. So we find in B.K. 85a that in פצע תחת פצע nothing really further is indicated, but the idea of the duty of compensation is extended in two directions. Firstly ליתן צער במקום נזק and then לרבות שוגג כמזיד ואונס פצע .כרצון is the actual wounding, when there are any permanent results — after the passing away of the phases indicated by כויה and חבורה — payment for these is already indicated by עין תחת עין. So פצע תחת פצע is taken to mean, firstly: “Wounding in all its phases must be compensated for”, so that כויה וחבורה i.e., צער (together with the indirect results indicated above שבת ורפוי) is to be paid also in cases where the permanent damage נזק has to be paid. And further פצע תחת פצע “wounding has to be paid for” i.e., for the permanent injury caused, the נזק has to be paid in any and every wounding without any consideration of any greater or lesser intention with which the act was done. For absolute פצע the actual result is the only thing that comes into question without any consideration of the subjective nature of the act, whereas the other direct and indirect results only receive compensation if there is at least a certain degree of intention or carelessness מזיר or קרוב למזיד.

Accordingly פצע תחת פצע is firstly to be taken by itself: פצע for every פצע, and secondly in connection with כויה and חבורה which also have to be compensated even when פצע is paid for פצע. That is why פצע תחת פצע is placed in the middle. At a real permanent injury, פצע ,כויה and חבורה receive compensation.

Apart from the indirect results mentioned in V.19, שבת, the transitory inability to work caused by being confined to bed (שבת קטן as opposed to שבת גדול the absolute permanent disability which is understood by נזק), רפוי, the medical expenses, and the direct results mentioned here, נזק and צער, the Law recognises another direct result of wounding which is entitled to compensation. This is בשת, the shame endured by the blow itself, or by the bodily disfigurement caused. This is referred to in the Written Law in the problem discussed in Deut. 25,11. It is not far fetched to assume that this is also referred to in our text here under the heading of חבורה as swellings and inflammation are generally causes of bodily disfigurement (black eye etc. I.L.).

V. 26—27. When עבד and אמה occur in the Torah without any particularization it always refers to עבד כנעני to Canaanite slaves. שן ועין are merely examples, and by the repetition of לחפשי ישלחנו, are to be taken as רבוי, and to be comprehensive to the widest extent (see on XXII,6). They only exclude mutilations which are not like the “eye” but grow again, or are not visible, as both eye and tooth are. They include כל מומין שבגלוי ואינן חוזרין. The tooth has to be mentioned as well as the eye, because it is an organ which is not visible at birth, and so might be thought not to be so essential. (Kiddushin 24b). As the Torah mentions ושחתה the destruction of the eye even as the result of כי יכה, of a blow (it does not say directly if a man knocks the eye of his slave out I.L.), it clearly means that there need be no intention on the part of the master. The Halacha is, that the slave gets his freedom if the mutilation can be attributed in the very least degree to carelessness on the part of the master. In all cases where נזק would be imposed in an ordinary case, the slave gets his freedom, even if it is due to clumsiness in an act done with the very best of intention e.g., שהיה רבו רופא ואמר לו לחתור שנו והפילו, “if the master was a dentist and he intended scaling the teeth and he knocked one out.” (B.K. 26b and Kiddushin 24b). But as the Torah in this freedom-giving, fixes a compensation which in general is far higher than the value of the damage done, and further, as this compensation is fixed equally in all cases, without any consideration on the different values of the organ which is destroyed (no difference between an eye or a tooth), דבר קצוב, it is clear that this obligation to give freedom which is expressed as “compensation” is to be considered, not as תשלומין as compensation, but as קנס, a punishment, a preventative measure to induce equanimity, mildness, and an even greater degree of care and consideration in the handling of slaves than one has to exercise with free men.

V. 28. Here it does not say שור איש as it does in V.35, for here the sentence is pronounced on the animal itself. All animals are included in this law, just as שורך וחמורך in the Decalogue (Deut. V.14) are only mentioned as examples and are explained to be such by וכל בהמתך (Mechilta and B.K. 54b). But, as execution is decreed for the animal even if it is ownerless, this fate can not be taken as a procedure against the owner. It seems to be the Divine Judgment, מיד כל חיה אדרשנו (Gen. 9,5) which God delegates human justice to carry out, just as, in the case of a murder, the capital punishment carried out by human justice is to be regarded in a similar manner, as a partial delegation of the sentence ומיד האדם מיד איש אחיו אדרש את נפש האדם (ibid.). The motive in both cases — as can be deduced from the context of the verses in Genesis — is to keep the godlike dignity of the earthly life of a human being vividly conscious in the human mind.

סקול יסקל השור ולא יאכל את בשרו. As soon as the fact that the ox has killed a man is proved by the evidence of witnesses, it has to be killed by stoning, and may not be killed for food instead. Even if it had been killed by correct שחיטה, so that it is now בשר “meat” which otherwise is permissible to be eaten, nevertheless its flesh may not be eaten, שחטו אחר שנגמר דינו אסור. More, its death is to serve a higher, moral, purpose, it is dedicated to that, and so withdrawn from any other use whatsoever; with the pronouncement of the sentence it becomes אסור בהנאה (according to ר״ת only at its death, see תוספות B.K. 24a and Zebachim 71a). According to the opinion of ר׳ אבהו אמד ר׳ אלעזר, which is accepted as Halacha, in general, wherever the Torah forbids use with the term לא ,לא תאכל ,לא תֵאָכֵל :אכילה יאכל, it implies also all use, הנאה, unless the Torah itself elsewhere allows some use other than eating e.g., selling or giving as food to animals, (Deut. 14,21 & XXII,30), in which case such use is permitted. Here where את is added, it does not say ובשרו לא יאכל or לא יאכל ובשרו but את בשרו (see on Gen. 1,1) the בשר is to be understood in its furthest extension, and even עורו, the skin is prohibited (B.K. 41a & b).

נקי. As it is not the normal nature of oxen to attack men (B.K. 41a), and the case here is speaking of such a normal animal (תם), where such an abnormal action could not be anticipated or expected, the owner of the animal is not to be considered guilty in any way of neglecting to keep it under stricter guard. At the same time it is not superfluous for the Torah to tell us so. In V.35, in the case where an animal (תם) does abnormal damage to property, a fine of half the damage done (חצי נזק) is imposed as a preventative measure (קנס). So one might easily have thought that in our case here, too, perhaps חצי כופר, half the amount of the atonement-money of V.30 would have to be paid. So that it was necessary to say, that in our case here, the owner is completely נקי, no payment at all is to be imposed. The necessity for telling us this, may also lie in the fact that actually, the owner does have to pay his share for the damage inasmuch as he loses the total value of his animal. So that what is said by נקי may be, that, beyond this loss, he has nothing more to pay.

V. 29. נַגָח a noun form (an ox who is a “gorer”) as חַטָא ,גַנָב, which designates the character, a peculiarity which has become the nature of its possessor. So here too, an ox to whom goring has become natural. This abnormal peculiarity is declared to be the “firmly” formed nature of the animal (חזקה) if it occurs three times on separate days. In B.K. 41a various possibilities as to how this could happen, as the ox has to be killed the first time it kills a man, are shown, e.g., it could run away and escape etc. etc. If רבא (B.K. 23b) is not in conflict with the accepted Halacha that the character of נגח is given after three killings, and only after the fourth is the owner called to account and takes this to be תמול מתמול חד שלשום תרי ולא ישמרנו האידנא חייב, but then raises the difficulty for himself to find the fourth stroke indicated in our text, then perhaps רבא may take the ואם שור נגח הוא, of V.29, in connection with the case of V.28, as follows: — but if the ox which has just gored shows itself thereby to be a שור נגח, as it had already gored yesterday and the day before, i.e., had gored twice before the present goring, and henceforth the owner does not keep it under guard, then at the next goring the owner is responsible. It is in this sense too that we have translated it. And V.36 too would be understood in רבא׳s sense.

והועד בבעליו. The meaning of העיד (from עוד, duration, lasting) as both to give evidence as witness, and to warn, has already been explained on Gen. 8,22. Here it has both meanings. As the owner had been informed by witnesses of the thrice repeated goring, and the character which his animal had thereby acquired, he was thereby automatically warned, i.e., it was made clear to him that it was his duty to guard it accordingly. The Gemora leaves it in doubt (B.K. 24a) שלשה ימים דקתני לייעודי תורא או לייעודי גברא, whether it is sufficient for the owner to be warned once that his animal has killed three times, or whether he has to be warned three times. We are inclined to the former, and translate והועד בבעליו “and this has duly been testified to its owner.” According to the other opinion it would read “and this has been testified (on each occasion) to the owner”.

השור יסקל וגם בעליו יומת. The two together have brought about the death of a human being; the owner, as the controlling intelligence, who is as responsible for watching over the live and lifeless possessions in his power as he is over his own actions. Hence כמיתת הבעלים כך מיתת השור, the judging and sentencing of the animal has to have the same procedure as would be necessary for the execution of the master. (B.K. 44b). The animal has only to be condemned to death if the killing was done under conditions similar to which a man would be condemned. Also, as in the case of a man, the death sentence can only be pronounced on an animal by full court of 23 judges (Sanhedrin 2a). But nevertheless, sentence can be pronounced and carried out even if the animal is ownerless. The whole underlying motive of this judicial killing of the animal seems definitely to be rather the upkeeping of the moral idea indicated above, than a police safety regulation to prevent further mischief.
יומת, he has forfeited his life, before the Court of God he merits death, but the human court has only, as expressed in the following verse, to impose a fine as “atonement-money”.

V. 30. אם כפר. If this verse were written in the indicative mood, the duty of paying atonement-money would only apply to the case of the preceding verse, in which the animal has to be killed, and would read “but nevertheless only a fine of atonement-money shall be imposed on him etc.” But as it is put in the conditional, this duty applies beyond this particular case to every case “when” or “whenever” the Court has to impose atonement-money, even in cases where the animal does not get killed, e.g., where the animal was attacking another animal and happened to gore a man to death. (B.K.43b).

V. 32. A profound reason probably lies behind this law that the amount of the atonement-money to be paid for the killing of a slave is a fixed amount of thirty shekels, whereas in the case of a free man, it varies according to the greater or lesser value of the victim. The value of any human life can not be expressed in pounds, shillings and pence. But כפר, atonement-money has to be paid in certain cases. This “atonement-money” the token value of his own life, in the case of a free man, is estimated at the amount he would fetch if sold in the market as a slave. There is no other way of fixing the value of a human life in terms of hard cash. This is also the way which has to be employed to find the damage to be paid for mutilations. For a free man this is no degradation, as he is a free man the application of this valuation loses all idea that it can really be the actual value of his life. But to value the life of a slave according to his market value, would bring the matter into the sphere of real actualities, and so would be in direct opposition to the very idea which this law is meant to uphold, viz., the godlike value of every human life. That is why the Torah prefers to have a fixed amount in the case of slaves, and it fixes it at the highest amount of redemption-money to be paid for the self-dedication of a Jewish woman (ערך) (Levit. 27,4), whose position with regard to not being bound by מצות עשה שהזמן גרמה is also shared by עבד ואמה.

V. 33. As the Torah speaks of both actions פתיחה and כריה, and does not find it sufficient to say “if anybody has a pit and leaves it uncovered”, it is not speaking here primarily of the owner of a pit, not of a בור שיש לו בעלים. In such a case there could be no question of כריה after mentioning פתיחה. If the legal responsibility rests on the duty of every owner to safeguard the public against any danger arising from his property, it is perfectly immaterial in what way the dangerous property came into his possession, whether, for instance, the owner dug the pit on his own land, or whether it was there when the land came into his possession. There would also then be no reason to suggest that the Torah must expressly mention “digging” to tell us that the responsibility is no greater in that case (as actually רב יוסף wanted to say to explain a view of ר׳ עקיבא in B.K. 50a), or tell us that increasing the depth of an existing pit is equivalent to digging it (as, in truth, is the reason given on 51a ibid.), as in all these cases the duty of an owner to look after his dangerous property is in no wise altered or affected. But in mentioning the two ways in which the defendant may be connected with the pit, it is quite evident that it is not as possessor but as causer of the danger that he is to be made responsible, as רבה (ibid. 49b) proves: — אמר קרא כי יפתח וכי יכרה. אם על פתיחה חייב על כרייה לא כל שכן אלא שעל עסקי פתיחה ועל עסקי כרייה באה לו. So that our case here speaks primarily of בור ברה״ר, of the uncovering or digging of a hole in the public thoroughfare i.e., of the responsibility for contriving a danger to the public, and the originator of the danger is called also בעל הבור ,בעל התקלה (V.34), as the originator or causer of the danger. But at the same time this also declares responsibility for בור ברה״י for any of one’s property which may be dangerous to the public e.g., if anybody gives the public the right of access to a well in his private domain,הפקיר רשותו ולא הפקיר בורו, where the responsibility lies on him as the actual בעל בור. In the first case dealing with responsibility as “causer”, both כריה and פתיחה are necessary to be mentioned. Either to tell us that even for פתיחה the duty of covering is immediately incumbent, and even for כריה the placing of an efficient cover suffices to remove responsibility which one might think remained, unless he filled the hole in again; or to teach us at the same time the law laid down in B.K. 51a להביא כורה אחר כורה שסילק מעשה ראשון, that if somebody deepens an existing hole and thereby increases the danger, he has to share a proportionate responsibility with the originator, but if, by his deepening, the whole nature of the danger of the pit is altered, e.g., if previously it was only בור לנזקין, of sufficient depth, only to threaten injury, and he deepens it sufficiently to make it a בור למיתה, a danger to life of man or beast, then סילק מעשה ראשון, the whole responsibility, whether for life or limb, rests exclusively on the second one.

For just as כי יפתח speaks of an existing pit, so does כי יכרה, and that is indeed why the term is chosen and not חפר; whereas חפר only means “to dig”, כרה means, not only “to dig”, but also “to prepare”, to “arrange”, and so would be the exact expression to designate the alteration of the nature of a pit which had already been dug. The repetition of איש here expresses just the סילק מעשה ראשון, that, although the originators of the pit may be several, if the nature of the danger is altered, the responsibility for compensation lies exclusively with the last one who made the alteration. According to this כי יפתח איש בור could speak of a בור לנזקין and כי יכרה איש בור of a בור למיתה. For both could speak of one and the same pit, of a בור ט׳ a hole only nine טפחים deep, which is not yet a danger to life. If anybody opens such a pit, and does not cover it up, he is responsible for all injury done to animals. If now somebody digs it deeper and makes it a danger to life, he takes over the whole responsibility for the whole pit both for injury or death (B.K. 10a).

וכי יפתח איש בור, ולא שור בור. The owner of an animal is not responsible for damage done by a pit or hole which his animal makes in somebody else’s property. He has, of course, to pay for the actual damage done to the field or garden, but the responsibility for the due protection of the pit falls on the owner of the property.

ולא יכסנו. A cover sufficiently strong to stand up to ordinary conditions, suffices to remove responsibility. The legal term for such normal care is שמירה פחותה, ordinary care. Protection against unusual conditions is called שמירה מעולה, extraordinary care. Normal care, שמירה פחותה, is all that is demanded to remove responsibility for all damage done by our possessions, with the exception of the case of שור תם (V.35) where as a preventative measure שמירה מעולה (קנס) is imposed.

ונפל שמה, not בו, which could equally well mean “through it” or “thereby” as “in it”. If the hole had only brought about a fall, the animal had not fallen into it, but stumbled over it נפל לאחורי בור חוץ לבור (B.K. 53a) the owner, or causer of the danger, is not held responsible. He has only to pay for damage which his property or contrivance, itself directly inflicts, but not which it only indirectly causes. Here the animal injured itself on קרקע עולם. The object which actually injured or killed the animal was not put there by him. The ground at the bottom of the pit, although equally קרקע עולם, only received its dangerous properties through him, and so is considered his contrivance. In the same way falling down from a heap which has unlawfully been piled up in the public thoroughfare, תל ברה״ר, is considered as the responsibility of the maker and not as קרקע עולם.

Here we have the far-reaching idea of גרמא, indirect causation, in the Jewish laws of compensation. It is divided into גרמא בנזקין in more indirect “causing”, and דיני דגרמי in nearer, more direct causing. But the difference is purely with regard to legal responsibility. Morally, even where the law has not to impose any compensation, every גרמא בנזקין anything that we do, by which somebody else receives damage or loss, is a grave crime for which we will be held responsible by God. (B.K. 56a).

Es kommt übrigens bei der Grube nicht nur der durch die Fallhöhe bewirkte Stoß des Bodens in Betracht. Auch wo dieser weich wäre, kann die in einer Grube gesperrte Luft (הבלא) durch Betäubung den vornüber Hineinfallenden schädigen, und ירבs (nicht rezipierte) Ansicht beschränkt sogar, wo der Boden der Grube nicht Eigentum des Urhebers ist, den Anteil desselben an der Verantwortung zunächst auf diese Betäubung — בור שחייבה עליו תורה להבלו ולא לחבטו — B. K. 50b. Nach dieser Ansicht dürfte dann die durch Betäubung und Stoß erfolgte Schädigung des in die Grube gefallenen Tieres als eine in "Gemeinschaft" vom Urheber der Grube und dem Boden als קרקע עולם — bewirkte Schädigung zu beurteilen sein, der Ersatz aber dem Urheber der Grube voll und allein obliegen, nach dem Grundsatz des כל היכי :ר׳ נתן דלא אפשר לאשתלומי מהאי משתלם מהאי, d.h. insofern einer in Gemeinschaft mit einer andern, nicht verantwortlichen Potenz einen Schaden anrichtet, hat er die Verantwortung allein zu tragen (B. K. 53a). (שטה מקובצת zu B. K. 50b gibt eine andere Motivierung dieses Schadenersatzes nach רב).

שור וחמור. The Halacha teaches (B.K. 53b), שור ולא אדם ,חמור ולא כלים, that the duty to pay compensation in this case applies only to animals which get killed but not to human beings who get killed. In any case, for human beings, it would be a question of כופר, atonement-money (V.30 and 31) and not of compensation. But here, by the limitation to animals by שור this, too, is not to be imposed. Further, that the duty for compensation only applies to the חמור to the damaged animal of burden, but not to its damaged burden, כלים. If we consider the law in view of this Halacha, the underlying principle of equity (which is also expressed in the following (Ch. 22,4) law) would seem to be: — the owner or perpetrator of a danger-bringing object is only responsible for the damage of such property as is directly threatened by the dangerous nature of his property or his contrivance. By an “inanimate object at rest”, of which בור is the classical example, only living creatures, animals and men, are directly threatened, not lifeless objects (for the victim must go to the danger, the danger does not come to the victim I.L.). Further, it is only a question of replaceable goods. So שור וחמור represents all living replaceable property, which would include all animals and in the first rank, the human body in a sound condition. Hence בור brings responsibility for the death or injury of animals and, for injury to persons. Human life does not come in the category of replaceable or compensatory goods. A human life destroyed by somebody’s property being insufficiently protected casts a deeper guilt on the one who brought it about. And if, in the case where a person has been killed by בור, no atonement-money is imposed as it is in the case of שור, this need by no means be taken as an indication of a lesser crime. It can very well be just the reverse. In the case of living property, שור whose actions after all, are spontaneous, and so do not reflect the personality of the owner to the same degree as dangerous inanimate objects which תחלת עשיתו לנזק are a constant and immediate threat to all living creatures, in their case the Torah prescribes כופר as פדיון נפשו, but in the case of בור the moral guilt of the perpetrator can not so easily be atoned-for, but remains before the Presence of God. It comes under that general warning cry of the Torah ולא תשים דמים בביתך, “harbour no blood-guilt in thy home!” (Deut. 22,8) which makes us responsible before God for every danger to life in our midst which is due to our lack of care. It is true, nevertheless, that in B.K. 9b כופר בשור is treated as a חומרא, and from that stand-point the fact that no כופר is imposed in בור may be explained by the consideration that, on the other hand, accidents caused by בור can only occur through the active participation of the victim, whereas in the case of שור the victim is entirely passive, and the aggression is entirely caused by the killer, whose owner has to consider himself to a certain extent responsible.

V. 34. בעל הבור, the owner, or the perpetrator, בעל התקלה, from whom the threat of danger originated. Similarly, we find Prov. 18,9 גם מתרפה במלאכתו אח הוא לבעל משחית, “carelessness is equal to (lit, the brother of) originating destruction.”

כסף ישיב לבעליו, as it has already said ישלם that he is bound to replace the dead animal by paying compensation, the addition of these words can only be meant to tell us more about the way in which this compensation is to be made. If the Torah wanted to prescribe, that here compensation must be made expressly only in actual cash, it would have said ישלם כסף לבעליו. But כסף ישיב לבעליו tells us that “the value”, (which the preceding ישלם has already expressed) “has to be restored to the owner” i.e., he need not give actual money, but any means by which the money can be obtained to get back his lost property.
