Hence, B.K. 10b, ישיב לרבות שוה כסף. The compensation can be made, not only in money, but in value. That is already implied by the use of ישיב instead of יתן. He did not make him lose money, but the value of money, so the term ישיב can not really mean he shall restore money, but he can restore what he has caused to be lost viz., money-value. Under the term money-value is understood any transportable goods (מטלטלין) however cheap they may be, even “bran” as the expression ואפי׳ סובין runs. It is only when reparation has to be made in land קרקע, in non-transportable property that a difference is made in the quality which he has to render, and in those cases the compensation has to be made in עדית ,מיטב, the very best that he has, according to the Law מיטב שדהו וגו׳ ישלם (XXII,4); מיטב שדהו של מזיק (B.K. 7a). Non-transportable property must attract buyers by its quality, if it is to be easily converted to cash. Transportable goods of any quality can be taken to a market where such goods are in demand, hence of them it is said: כל מילי מיטב (B.K. 7b). Nevertheless the repayment of a loan has to be made in cash, and only if the borrower has none at all can he satisfy the lender with goods. Wages for day-workers and payment for work done, must always be paid in cash; if necessary, the payer himself must convert his goods into cash (B.K. 9a; תוספות ד״ה ר׳ הונא)
לבעליו. By not saying לבעל השור והחמור the Torah reminds us of the Halacha that שור וחמור are merely given as examples and it refers to כל דאית ליה בעלים and only כלים are excluded (B.K. 54a).

והמת יהיה לו. Inasmuch as the incident in V.33 which makes compensation enforced, is described in general terms ונפל שמה וגו׳, and the result of the fall is not expressly specified, compensation is not restricted to the case where the animal is killed, but applies equally to injuries, and here only one of the two possibilities, בור שיש בו מיתה, is given prominence.

The “לו״ can not refer to the מזיק, to the one who has to pay. For לא כך היה, that would be self-understood. If he has to pay the whole value of the animal killed, the carcass by that very fact belongs to him. It, accordingly, definitely refers to the ניזק, the owner of the dead animal. But the Torah can not simply want to tell us that he can deduct the value of the carcass and has only then to make good the actual amount lost. That also is self evident, especially as immediately preceding it, has told us that כסף ישיב he can pay the value in any kind of transportable goods. He could actually pay the whole amount in dead carcasses, and naturally can reckon in the value of the dead animal lying before him. But what the Torah is referring to, is the principle (B.K. 10b & 11a) שהבעלים מטפלין בנבלה ופחת נבלה דניזק “That the killed animal lies there at the risk of the owner.” The defendant has only to haul the animal out of the pit and estimate its value there and then. If the owner neglects to have it taken away and sold, and it deteriorates and loses value, that is his loss. The same expression (והמת יהיה לו) is used in V.36 in the case of an animal killed by a “goring ox”, and is there taken to be used for the express purpose of referring to this law. That it is used here, is taken to want to indicate the law that the responsibility for damage by בור only applies to such animals as are completely and entirely profane property, which finally as מת are לו, at his entire disposal, for any purpose he may desire, but does not apply to שור של פסולי מוקדשין, which even after פדיון is only מותר לאכילה becomes profane property only for the purpose of human consumption, but while alive may not be used לגיזה ועבודה וְחָלב, and when dead may not be used לאכילת כלבים for animal food, (B.K. 53b). The exclusion of שור פסולי מוקדשין from compensation for damage by בור is intimately a part of the great legal principle which excludes the מקדש, to the most far-reaching extent, from any right to demand compensation for damage — נזקין להדיוט ואין נזקין להקדש — which principle we shall have to consider in greater detail in V.35. קדשים ,פסולי מקודשין which, have become unfit for the purpose to which they have been dedicated, as remarked above, do not altogether lose their connection with the מקדש even after they have been redeemed, although they then become profane property, the profane use that may be made of them is very restricted. The idea of הקדש in them, does not completely disappear. They appear rather to be objects of dual ownership, הדיוט והקדש. This condition is also very strikingly apparent in other directions (see Makkoth 22a). All other possessions which are dangerous in motion as שור and אש differ from בור that they דרכן לילך ולהזיק, they go and do the damage. The victim of the aggrestion and its owner are completely passive when the damage gets done, and it is entirely the sole act of the aggressor. Hence, in these cases the consideration of the duty of an owner to look after his dangerous property outweighs the consideration of the הקדש part which still exists in the damaged פסולי מוקדשין, and compensation has to be paid. But in the case of בור where אין דרכו לילך ולהזיק, no damage can be done without the co-operation of the victim, it must come to the בור and fail to notice it. This indeed is also the reason why, for inanimate objects, as not being directly threatened by בור no compensation need be paid. Nevertheless as בור is תחלת עשיתו לנזק, is by its very nature a danger to living creatures, the Torah does impose compensation for all damage to living property of such owners who are to be protected by Law against damage, but in the case of property which, in addition to the fact that it itself has contributed to the occurrence of the damage, belongs, to a considerable extent, to an abstract owner, הקדש, whom the Torah does not wish to protect by laws of compensation, there the two factors together, outweigh the partial claim which exists, and the rule, אין נזקין להקדש is stretched to apply even to פסולי מוקדשין. According to this we can quite well understand the answer which the Gemora gives in B.K. 53b to the question: מאי חזית וגו׳. For the Gemora there says: It mentions twice in the Torah והמת יהיה לו (here and in V.35) and we take it, that here it is for the purpose of excluding פסולי מוקדשין and in the case of שור in V.35 פסולי מוקדשין are not excluded and והמת יהיה לו is to tell us that בעלים מטפלין בנבלה and then the Gemora asks מאי חזית. How do you know it is not the other way round? And then it gives the answer that we go to the underlying motive: מסתברא פטור גבי בור הואיל ופטר בו את הכלים. The same reason that lies at the base of the פטור for כלים works for the פטור of פסולי מוקדשין.

בור is the classic example (אב) for responsibility for all inanimate property which causes injury while it is at rest. (i.e., not in motion, either actual ownership, or causing the object to become dangerous, even if it is not in one’s actual possession). A piece of glass, a sharp piece of broken china etc., where it can injure man or beast comes under this heading, is a תולדה דבור. But it does not even have to be thrown directly into the street; if it is placed in such a position where under ordinary conditions, it could be expected to roll or be blown into the street, and when at rest in the street, causes injury, the same responsibility is incurred, e.g., אבנו סכינו ומשאו שהניחן בראש הגג ונפלו ברוח מצויה והזיקו בתר דנייח, “a stone, a knife, anything placed on the roof and blown into the street by an ordinary, everyday wind etc.” (B.K. 3b). If it does damage as it falls, before it comes to rest, it would come under the heading of אש (Ch. 22,5). Compensation for damage caused by בור is only enforceable for such living creatures, as are directly threatened by it, i.e., for such as, in general do not walk with their eyes on the ground שאין דרכן להתבונן בדרכים and do not usually notice what lies on the ground before them, e.g., men and young animals, or old ones after dark.

It is an essential trait of Jewish piety, one of the necessary characteristics of a true Chassid, to be careful not to throw broken needles, banana skins, or anything which could possibly inflict injury, anywhere where they would be menace to passers-by. B.K. 30a, האי מאן דבעי למהוי חסידא לקיים מילי דנזיקין.

V. 35. נגף .וכי יגף is the designation of a blow according to its injurious or destructive action, hence מַגֵפָה sudden death. But נגח, the stronger form of נגע, is only the designation of the act of the blow, and when applied to animals, primarily a blow with the horn. From או נודע כי שור נגח הוא, V.36, it can be seen that here too, נגיחה, goring with horns, is meant, but it refers to it here as נגיפה to refer to its fatal effect. In the case where a man is attacked (V.28) the blow is only called נגיחה, for, as is explained in B.K. 2b אדם אית ליה מזלא. Man is under special heavenly protection, and in spite of what would normally be a fatal goring, death need not necessarily follow the blow. Hence the rule: מועד לבהמה לא הוי מועד לאדם but, of course, the reverse rules. So that an ox has killed three other animals does not yet bear the character of a “goring ox” towards men, until he has killed three men. Goring is only the classic example, but any injury inflicted by the vicious, unprovoked attack of any, ordinary inoffensive animal, comes under the heading of קרן as תולדה קרן (B.K. 39a).
שור איש in contrast to וכי יגח שור of V.28; here it speaks only of an animal which is the property of a responsible person.

ומכרו. The Halacha teaches תם משלם חצי נזק מגופו that, for the abnormal vicious, unprovoked damage done by a normally inoffensive animal belonging to a responsible owner (i.e., קרן), only half the value of the damage done need be paid. And even this half must be obtained from the value of the offending animal. The owner of the injured or killed animal really only holds a claim on the offending animal itself. The rest of the property of the defendant is not considered as security אינו משלם מן העליה, whereas in all other cases of damage (not קרן, as explained above) the very best goods of the defendant are considered as held in security for the damage done נזקין שמין מן העידית, במעולה שבנכסיו (B.K. 15b). Immediately after the attack, the plaintiff attains a right in the attacking animal up to the value of half the damage done to his animal הוחלט השוד. If the value of the offending animal exceeds this half, the two parties are to be considered as partners in the ownership of it שותפי נינהו (B.K. 33a). Further according to the accepted Halacha this half-compensation is not actual compensation (ממונא) but a preventative measure to ensure that owners look after their oxen properly. פלגא נזקא קנסא כי היכי דלנטריה לתוריה (B.K. 15a & b). Finally we learn from the accepted Halacha that the case speaks primarily of the incident occurring on completely neutral ground, in a place where plaintiff and defendant have equal right to have their animals there e.g., a public thoroughfare, the open country, or a yard which they own jointly etc. etc. But it is also made to apply to ברשות הניזק to a place belonging to the plaintiff where the attacking animal has no right to enter at all, and even in that case the indemnity does not exceed half the value (B.K. 14a, 24b).
All these details of the Halacha are indicated with characteristic brevity in the text itself, and we can deduce from it the underlying idea and reason of this law.

In the text there is no reference anywhere to a personal obligation to make restitution, as it does in V.36. It does not say חצי השור ישלם תחת השור, but only lays down what is to be done with the living and the dead animal. The way in which the case is presented indicates that the plaintiff has in no wise a claim on the defendant himself but has to go to the animal, מגופו משתלם. It lays down that they have to divide both the living and the killed animal. This naturally can only speak of a case where both animals are of the same value, otherwise the defendant could even make a profit. But, in the case indicated, his living ox takes the place of the killed one, and as they divide both the animals, each of them bears half of the damage done. If each ox was worth two hundred, and the carcass of the dead one was worth 50, so that the loss was 150, each of them would get 125 and each would lose 75. This gives us the general rule:- out of the value of the living ox the plaintiff can reimburse himself up to half the amount of his loss. Now, as the text does not say ומכר but ומכרו the conversion of the animal into money is not the business of the defendant alone, but of the two of them together, it thereby indicates their position as joint owners, as שותפין. Immediately, with the blow, the ox belongs to the plaintiff up to half the value of the damage. This would have practical legal consequences, if, for instance, the plaintiff disposes of his share, הקדישו ניזק. (There is another opinion expressed in the Gemora which is not accepted as Halacha, that the plaintiff is not a partner, but that the living ox is held as a surety for his claim, יושם השור בב״ד, בעל חוב הוא (B.K. 33a). Finally, the text makes no mention whatsoever of the locality of the incident, while in the case where the animal does damage by eating (שן) in (Ch. 22,4), the incident there is restricted to being on the premises of the plaintiff שדה אחר. This indicates to us that in our case of קרן the owner is responsible also on neutral territory, in רשות הרבים, in the public thoroughfare; and, in stressing the person by the “Nun paragogicum” in יחצון, it is indicated that the whole law is dependent solely on the persons of the plaintiff and defendant, and quite independent of the locality. It is accordingly laid down that even in רשות הניזק, on the premises of the plaintiff, he can not claim more than half of his loss, but that he can claim this half, even in אמר קרא יחצון אין חצי נזק חלוק לא ברשות הרבים .רשות הרבים ולא ברשות היחיד (B.K. 26a). Only if the incident occurred ברשות המזיק, on the premises of the defendant where the plaintiff had no right to allow his animal to enter, only in that case is no payment to be made (B.K. 14a).

According to the rule, that, wherever the amount of damage to be paid is not the value of the damage done, but either more or less, the case is not one of the duty of compensation, but is a preventative measure (with the single exception of חצי נזק צרורות which we shall go into on Ch. 22,4), we have here too, in our case of goring, קרן, to take חצי נזק as קנס (B.K. 15a & b). As soon as anyone obtains possession of any animate or inanimate object, he becomes responsible for that which his property does. The property of a person is fundamentally only an extension of his own body; and just as any man with intelligence is responsible for the actions of his own body, so when he takes possession of any unreasoning property he becomes its guardian, and is responsible for any damage it may do, as we have already learnt with regard to inanimate property, in V. 33 & 34 under the heading of בור. But he is only responsible for such acts of his property which from their known nature he could reasonably expect to happen, and accordingly should take care to prevent their happening. “Goring” קרן i.e., intentional damage through pure viciousness, is not in the normal nature of oxen. In this respect they are “תם״ or as the expression in B.K. 15a runs, סתם שורים בחזקת שימור קיימי, in this respect they require no care or guarding. So that if nevertheless an ox does do damage in this manner, no claim for compensation really lies against the owner. Nevertheless, in the interest of safeguarding public traffic, the Torah threatens the owner of an animal with a monetary fine in such a case כי היכי דלנטריה, so that on the public highway he should take care and watch over his animal even for acts which normally are not to be expected. Now if the Torah had imposed full compensation, it might even have increased the danger of public traffic. It might have encouraged owners to drive their animals through the streets without any care whatsoever, even to try and have them injured, knowing that they were fully insured for complete compensation. But, by the Torah in these cases, making both of them suffer loss, it makes both of the owners take such care of their animals that alone can ensure safe public traffic. It places any two animals which meet in the street under the combined care of the two owners, and establishes a temporary common interest which altogether forms the basis of the rights of open traffic. That is why in the text too they appear as common owners שותפין, both animals together paying for the loss for which both owners are made responsible. And that too, is why the claim of the plaintiff does not extend beyond the actual animal of the defendant. The idea of the preventative measure is nothing else but to consider the common interest of all owners of animals, both in the attacking and the attacked, to prevent any possible accident. The reason why, even in the רשות הניזק too, the compensation does not exceed half the damage, is because this preventative fine seems really only necessary to be imposed for considerations of public traffic; for the rare exceptional cases of the unauthorised entry into strange premises, the Torah would normally have held to the strict law, would not have made a special law to ensure security, just as the similar גזרות דרבנן are not concerned with a מלתא דלא שכיחא. But as such a preventative fine was to be imposed for the public thoroughfare, the Torah made it general, even for that seldom-occurring case, and did not raise it above the amount of the ordinary fine. Raising it to the full amount of the loss in the רשות ניזק is rejected (B.K. 25a) in accordance with the general rule for derived cases דיו לבא מן הדין להיות כנדון, “a law which is derived from another is limited, and must not go beyond the scope of the law from which it is derived”.

V. 36. See notes on V.29 — ולא ישמרנו בעליו, this condition is not mentioned in V.35 in the case of a שור תם. So that, there, the preventative measure is imposed unconditionally. Just normal ordinary care שמירה פחותה, does not absolve one from having to pay, it is specially imposed just to bring about שמירה מעולה, taking care to control animals against unusual conditions שאינם מצוים. The responsibility for שור המועד, to whom goring has become part of its nature, and hence an action to be expected, is a real legal responsibility. It is only incurred through neglect of :שמירה ולא ישמרנו בעליו. If this were to mean extraordinary care, שמירה מעולה, as in the case of תם, the text would not mention it at all and the compensation for מועד would then be as unconditional as it is for תם. The express mention ולא ישמרנו can accordingly only be meant to put מועד on the strict legal basis which only demands taking precautions against ordinary circumstances which are to be expected, שמירה פחותה, and only, in the absence of such ordinary care is compensation enforceable. ולא ישמרנו implies no שמירה at all. In B.K. 45b, the question is discussed whether the צד תמות במקומה עומדת i.e., whether the blow of a normally-looked-after מועד for which no compensation need be paid, should nevertheless have to pay the statutory fine of half-damages which even a תם has to pay. תוספות and the רא״ש take the view of ר׳ אדא בר אהבה, that this half-damage fine has to be paid in the case of שמירה פחותה of a מועד as it has to be in the case of a תם. But רמב״ם adopts the view of רב that as long as it is given שמירה פחותה a מועד is completely free from having to pay anything at all. The surprising fact that according to this latter view the Torah would treat מועד more leniently than תם can be understood if we consider that the payment of the “half-damage” is not strictly equity but only a preventative measure קנס, and as such, only concerns מלתא דשכיחא, normal occurrences, and the מועד condition itself is a seldom-occurring exceptional case. And further, that מועד where the duty of compensation is a matter of pure justice, requires no fine as a preventative measure. The legal consequences, that he has to pay the whole of the damage as a just duty which need not be based on the evidence of witnesses is a much more efficient and stronger spur for the owner to keep his goring ox under efficient control than the imposition of a preventative fine of half damages would be, which he is only bound to pay if the claim is legally based on denunciation by witnesses (see note on Ch. 22,8).

From the words of the text: וכי יגף שור איש את שור רעהו, tradition teaches the important principle שור רעהו ולא של הקדש (B.K. 6b) and תוספות works out that, not only for damage done to הקדש through neglecting to guard animals or other dangerous property, but even for direct damage done by the man himself, no compensation in any form is imposed, נזקין להדיוט ואין נזקין לגבוה “compensation is to be paid for damage done to profane property but not that done to property dedicated to God”. Whether the idea is that one who does such damage is to be told: “in doing this destruction you do not hurt God but yourself”; or, that God does not wish any human hand to be raised to represent Him with regard to His property; or, that making actual material restitution would do away with the real nature of the crime, which is, spoiling the idea which the destroyed object represented, in any case the fact is certain that under the regime of this Law anybody could break the holy Ark of the Covenant, tear the holy Veil, destroy the vessels of the Temple, demolish the whole treasure of the Temple without finding any judge in the world who would be empowered to make him pay one penny for damages. This fact is surely quite unique amongst all the legal systems of the world, and we can not refrain from remarking how even this one, single, unique fact is a striking proof that in dealing with this Torah system of Law we have before our eyes the work of no human brains, and that most certainly it is not the product of a priestly hierarchy to which people are so inclined to relegate the Jewish Law. Priests, hierarchs, would certainly have stamped the perpetrators of such sacrilege with the mark of Cain as criminals of the worst type, and would have appointed the secular arm to make it their first duty to protect and avenge their sacred treasures. It is only for the profane use of קדשים (and there indeed to a higher degree where it is due to a mistake and not wilful) מעילה, where compensation has to be paid, which we shall בע״ה go thoroughly into when we come to the Law concerning it (Levit. 5,16).

Damaging the altar or any part of the building of the Temple — נותץ אבן אחד מן ההיכל ומן המזבח ומן העזרות — is simply forbidden by a לאו and as such, is punishable by (ספרי פ׳ ראה) מלקות. Involuntary, unintentional — or even wanton and mischievous, if it lacks the necessary legal warning — damage is not punishable at all, whereas unintentional damage to private buildings is unconditionally liable for full compensation. In other directions too, in civil law קדשים are not protected, with regard to אונאה, overcharging, שומרין, the responsibility for custody, or תשלומי כפל וארבעה וחמשה fines inflicted for theft. (B.M. 57a).

V. 37. From 22,3 & 6 we know that for every inanimate (movable) thing that is stolen (with the exception of things that are קודש as remarked on the preceding verse, and I.O.Us., which are not considered as being property in themselves), כפל the double has to be repaid. Here, we learn that in the case of oxen or sheep, if they have been slaughtered or sold, the repayment has to be five or fourfold. From express repetition of שור and תחת השה ,תחת השור :שה (instead of merely תחתיו) we learn that this magnified “double-payment” is limited exclusively to oxen and sheep. According to the rule which was mentioned above on V.35 we know that this payment, as it exceeds the actual value of what has to be replaced, is to be considered not as compensation, but as a fine, as punishment. Finally we know that this fine or punishment is only imposed for theft גנבה, but not for robbery גזלה. Property that has been robbed has simply to be restored (itself or its actual value). והשיב את הגזלה אשר גזל (Levit. V.23). If we realise the relative ideas of theft and robbery, and the characteristics of oxen and sheep in reference to these ideas, the reason for these laws becomes clear. Robbery is taking property away from its possessor by force; theft, taking it away stealthily. The robber seizes an object which is under the personal guardianship of its owner. The thief finds the object left under the guardianship of the public respect for honesty and law. So that robbery is a simple crime against the individual whose rights of possession have been violated. Theft is a double crime, a crime against the individual rights of possession, and a crime against the general idea of respect for rights of property, under the protection of which, the owner had left his property. This idea forms the basic principle on which the whole of civilised communal life rests. Without the presumption that the general public has respect for rights of property, no man could leave any movable property out of his sight for one moment. The thief accordingly has to pay the value of the theft, as restitution to the owner; and then again an equal sum for his contempt of the principle of general honesty against which he has offended. As a member of the general public, the object had been placed under his protection, and instead of justifying the trust, he had betrayed it. This is also why the fine can only be imposed by the representatives of the public, the court — the owner himself, on the grounds of the crime committed against him, has no claim to it. In the case of a self-confessed theft, the fine is not imposed, it is considered that the act shows restitution of respect for the principle, and so the fine is unnecessary.

But this public respect for the rights of possession has to be trusted to, in a greater degree, for cattle and sheep, — animals which have to be put out to graze, — than for all other property which is kept indoors. Moreover this trust in the general honesty of the public has to be greater in the case of cattle, which are left entirely in the open, than for sheep which are at least penned at night. This higher degree of trust may well be the motive for the higher degree of the fine, where it is betrayed, and in accordance with their peculiarities, greater for cattle than for sheep. These ideas of the difference between robbery and theft, and of the difference between שור and שה and all other property, and between themselves, lead us to consider also that there is much more opportunity for theft than for robbery, for the theft of cattle and sheep than for other property, and finally for the theft of cattle than for that of sheep .גנבה is more שכיח than גניבת שור ושה ,גזל more than other property, גניבת שור more than גניבת שה. As has already been remarked גזרות דרבנן similarly to קנסות דאורייתא, have primarily in mind things which are שכיח, which are to be expected under ordinary circumstances, but not the exceptional, seldom-occurring cases. The Torah takes more preventative and deterrent measures against theft than against robbery (which latter accordingly remains on the basis of simple equity), against theft of cattle and sheep than of other articles, against theft of cattle than theft of sheep.

This idea of the underlying reason also explains the otherwise surprising interpolation of this law regarding theft in the middle of the sequence of אבות נזיקין. The inner connection is the idea of קנס. At base it is the same idea, which in the case of שור תם ברה״ר makes the ניזק and the מזיק as שותפין with regard to dangers to be avoided (both animals are placed under the responsible care of both parties to ensure the safety of the public traffic) and that threatens the thief with כפל and the cattle or sheep stealer with enhanced כפל.

But ארבעה וחמשה is only imposed after טביחה או מכירה. In B.K. 68a, two views are expressed as the reason for this. The one is because נשתרש בחטא, i.e., אהנו מעשיו, it is only by selling or slaughtering that his crime has permanent results; the other is because שנה בחטא because he repeats his crime. Either objectively with regard to the crime, or subjectively with regard to the criminal. For as long as the object remains unaltered in the possession of the thief, the owner has not lost the claim on the object itself, even if, as a result of knowing that the object has been stolen, he has given up expectation of recovering it, יאוש (and סתם גניבה יאוש בעלים in all cases when theft is discovered the presumption is that the owners had considered the article as irretrievably lost). The real duty of a thief is to return the property itself in natura. But if the article has undergone some permanent change while in the possession of the thief שנוי שאינו חוזר לברייתו, has become something else (as by טביחה, or even if a stolen lamb has grown into a sheep, or a calf to an ox), or if after יאוש there is שנוי רשות, it has passed into the possession of a third party, then the owner has lost the right to his former possession, and can only claim compensation for its value. According to the first view אהנו מעשו ,נשתרש בחטא the higher fine is only to be imposed when, by מכירה or טביחה the crime itself has become complete i.e., the object has been taken away from its owner for good. That would only be the case if the sale took place after יאוש and as יאוש is presumed to take place at every theft, the case of מכירה in our text is of יאוש ושנוי רשות. Then, by the theft, the thief has made the owner lose actual possession of the article, but by the slaughter or sale he has made him lose the ownership of the article. But according to the second view, שנה בחטא — which is the view accepted as Halacha — no weight is placed on the actual effect of the second act, it is sufficient that שנה בחטא that he, the criminal, repeated his crime. This seems to mean, that, as far as it lies in his power, he takes a second action which can have the effect of preventing the owner from having a claim on the object itself. This would only take place if, — and he can not possibly know if it is the case — יאוש has actually already taken place, or, according to another opinion, if it takes place even after שנוי רשות (ח״מ 353, 3, but see the ש״ך on it). — This effect of יאוש and שנוי on the status of property, in doing away with the rights of the owner, must be considered as a result of the two basic factors on which the idea of property is founded, viz., the spiritual abstract will of the owner (i.e., the sense of ownership) and the material actual power of possession. These two factors also come into play at every קנין, at the act of acquiring any moveable possession (see note on Levit. 25,4).

This question of טביחה ומכירה is also connected with the teaching of an important basic principle. For, together with שליחות יד and מעילה it is the exception to the great law אין שליח לדבר עברה, “no man sins at the bidding of another” i.e., every one is himself responsible for the sins he commits. If somebody does commit a crime by order of somebody else, then, legally it is not the employer or the one who gives the order who is responsible, but the one who carries it out. (But in any case, morally, before God לצאת ידי שמים, the one who gives the order is also responsible until the sin is atoned for, see ש״ך on ח״מ 32,2).

We have already remarked on Ch. XII, et seq. how, immediately the Jewish National Body was constituted by the קרבן פסח, the idea of the absolute equality of one and all before God resulted in the justification of the principle of שלוחו של אדם כמותו i.e., that in all acts pertaining to divine service, or civil law, one person can act for another. Of course this only applies to acts which have to be performed objectively, but not to such things which have subjectively to be carried out by the person himself who is to be affected. For instance, while somebody can very well slaughter the Pessach offering on behalf of somebody else, and then the act which had to be performed on the animal is considered exactly as if the person had done it himself, no one, at the bidding of another, and in his place, can eat of the offering, or lay Tephillin on behalf of someone else. The act could in any case be reckoned to the account of the one who ordered it to be done, but the person who is to be affected remains himself, and only himself, and it would be the same as if the one who gave the order had bound the Tephillin on the arm and head of the one who carries the order out, but all the same his own head and his own arm would remain without Tephillin etc. etc. (see קצות החשן on ח״מ 182).

This agency, this representation of one person by another is limited to acts which are permissible. No man may, and hence no man can, place himself at another’s disposal to do something which is forbidden — אין שליח לדבר עברה, no crime in civil law can be considered as being done at another’s bidding, and in civil law, only the actual perpetrator can be called to account, for דברי הרב ודברי התלמיד דברי מי שומעים, “if the word of the pupil is contradictory to the word of the master, whose word is to be obeyed?” i.e., no human authority can demand, or expect obedience for something that God has forbidden (Kiddushin 52b). According to תוספות (B.K. 79a ד״ה נתנו לבכורות) the rule only applies where the one who carries out the order knows of the illegality of the act, and according to that, if somebody took an animal out of a stall in the belief that it belonged to the man who told him to do so for him, the man who gave the order would be responsible for compensation, (but see the ש״ך on ח״מ 348 ס״ק ו׳, who adopts the opposite view of the נ״י).

There are three exceptions to this general rule that אין שליח לדבר עברה viz., שליחות יד ,מעילה and our own case here of טביחה ומכירה so that the thief himself is liable for the four or five fold compensation even if he has the animal killed by someone else who knows that the animal is a stolen one. But the reason for these three exceptions can be understood. The reason is perfectly simple, for the fact that if A by mistake gets B to use an object belonging to הקדש for profane purposes on his — A’s — behalf, A is responsible for מעילה if B knows the הקדש nature of the object. For the whole idea of מעילה (as we shall see when בע״ה we come to investigate it in due course) lies in the profaning of הקדש by mistake. Hence שליח שעשה שליחותו, בעל הבית מעל אפי׳ נזכר השליח (Kiddushin 42b תוספות) and the converse נזכר הב״ב ושגג שליח השליח מעל. The reason seems also quite clear for the fact that if a שומר exercises שליחות יד על ידי אחר i.e., gets somebody on his behalf to take up in his hand an object which has been entrusted to his care, even for a momentary use, the שומר himself, and not the other one, is immediately considered as a גזלן in relation to the object, and, as such is חייב באונסין (i.e., has to pay the full amount in compensation, even for the unavoidable and blameless loss of the entrusted object, such as the natural death of an animal). For this responsibility comes solely from the character of שומר and not simply from the unjustified taking up of another’s property with the intention of using it. True, a non-שומר — and that is what the other one is — does become a גזלן in respect to any object of which he makes unauthorised use — שואל שלא מדעת. But that is only if he actually uses it, if he merely takes it up with the intention of using it and then immediately puts it back again, he has no further responsibility towards it. But the שומר, as soon as he picks up the property entrusted to his care, with the intention of using it, even if he does not carry out this intention, but puts it back in its place without using it, by his action is considered a permanent גזלן in relation to it, and is responsible for complete compensation to the owner for anything at all that may happen to it afterwards. Now, whether he takes the property up himself, or causes somebody else to take it up for him, in both cases he has sinned equally against his duty as a שומר and has to bear the consequences. It is an essential part of his duty as a שומר just to see that nobody else does touch it (see notes on XXII,7). In quite the same way one can understand the law that if a thief gets somebody else to kill a sheep or ox for him that he has stolen, it is not the latter, but the thief himself who is responsible for the four or fivefold payment (even though the other knew that the animal was a stolen one). For this fine only results from the continuation or the consummation of the theft (נשתרש בחטא, שנה בחטא) and can accordingly only be applied to the one who committed the theft.

Diese traditionelle Bestimmung der טביחה ע׳׳י אחר wird (B. K. 71a) zunächst an der Zusammenstellung des וטבחו und מכרו des Textes gelehrt: מה מכירה ע"י אחר ,sowie Verkauf notwendig durch Mitwirkung eines andern geschieht, אף טביחה ע׳׳י אחר so habe auch das Schlachten die im Texte ausgesprochene Folge, selbst wenn es durch einen andern geschieht". Es wird ferner dort auf das "או", hingewiesen, או לרבות את השליח, וטבחו או מכרו — von andern auf das wiederholte "תחת לרבות את ,"תחת ל תחת השור, תחת השה, השליח. Der Begriff der disjunktiven Partikel או, wo sie nicht eben zur Bezeichnung der Disjunktion notwendig ist, או לחלק, wird häufig als רבוי, als eine Erweiterung des Begriffes gefasst. Wie das Wort או an sich, von אוה, wählen, schon eine "Auswahl", somit eine extensive Erweiterung bezeichnet, so ist ja auch an sich eine jede Disjunktion "oder" ein erweitertes Raumgeben. A "oder" B lässt die auszusprechende Bestimmung nicht auf A allein beschränkt sein, sondern gibt Raum auch dem davon jedenfalls verschiedenen, vielleicht auch ganz gegensätzlichen B. Hier gibt es einem ganzen, formalen und realen Gegensatze Raum, erweitert somit die Anwendung der Bestimmung ישלם über den nackten Begriff וטבחו hinaus auf den ganzen durch מכרו gegebenen Gegensatz. וטבחו an sich ist formal und real in Vergleich zu מכרו beschränkt. Die Handlung geschieht durch den Dieb selbst allein, und der gestohlene Gegenstand selbst wird zum Verbrauch zugerichtet. מכירה ist in beiden Beziehungen ein Gegensatz. Der Gegenstand wird gegen einen andern vertauscht und die Handlung geschieht unter Mitwirkung eines andern. Es bleibt also in beiden Beziehungen die Bestimmung nicht auf das real und formal durch טבחו allein Gegebene beschränkt, und die formale Erweiterung des או, auf וטבחו übertragen, ist buchstäblich: לרבות את השליה. — Ebenso die Wiederholung des "תחת": Indem damit die vervielfachte Zahlung wiederholt als auf das gestohlene, geschlachtete oder verkaufte Objekt bezogen wird, so wird damit die subjektive Art des an ihm Geschehenen in den Hintergrund gestellt. Es genügt, daß es, nachdem es gestohlen, auch noch geschlachtet oder verkauft worden. Wie diese beiden letzteren Handlungen, aus welchen die erhöhte Pön resultiert, geschehen, ob unmittelbar oder mittelbar, ist gleichgültig, und: תחת לרבות את השליה. (Vergl. oben: . (לרבות שוגג כמזיד וכו׳ :פצע תחת פצע
The term טביחה is always taken to imply שחיטה, killing according to the prescribed ritual to render it permissible to be eaten.

V. 1—2. מחתרת, breaking in, from חתר the specific expression for penetrating closed spaces by breaking in חתר בחשך בתים (Job 24,16) etc., is the exact opposite to the cattle and sheep stealing of the previous verse. These were completely accessible, entrusted to the honesty of the public, for deriding of which trust, the enhanced fine resulted. מחתרת presumes the property to be shut in, primarily against such an hour when the protective eye of the public representative of the Law does not function, and so a condition for helping oneself arises, which, were it not that the community does protect Law and order, would be the universal one. This hour is the period of night. Hence in the verse quoted above, Job asks, why God allows the complete darkness of night which is so favourable to burglary. Just a little light of dawn would prevent most burglaries. Then we have the same word referring to the thief — התר בחשך בתים יומם חתמו למו לא ידעו אור, “in the darkness he breaks into houses, during the daytime they are sealed up to him, light is not his friend”. Hence we find in Sanhedrin 72a הבא במחתרת נידון על שם סופו, “the housebreaker by night is met by what he ultimately would do.” He knows that the owner, thrown entirely on his own means of protection, will defend his property if necessary with lethal weapons, so one can presume that he too is ready and prepared for eventual murder, and the owner is accordingly, on the grounds of self-defence, allowed to forestall the thief by killing him, for אם בא להרגך השכם להרגו.

But in daylight, as a rule, one can not presume that a thief has necessarily any thought of murder. See ראב״ד on רמב״ם ה׳ גנבה פ״ח. Hence as a rule, by night אין לו דמים; by day דמים לו. But as it does not say in our verse ואם זרחה השמש but ואם זרחה השמש עליו, we get the additional law:- even if it is not yet day in general, but it is day only for him, — the thief — that is to say, if the circumstances are of such a nature that one could confidently presume that even this nightly intruder has only “day” thoughts and no thought of murder (e.g., if his personal relations to the owner are of such a nature) then דמים לו the owner is blood-guilty if he kills him before he is threatened. So in the Mechilta: ,אם זרחה השמש עליו וכי השמש עליו בלבד זרחה והלא על כל העולם כלו זרחה, אלא מה שמש שלום בעולם אף זו אם ידוע הוא שבשלום עמו והרגו חייב. And in Sanhedrin 72a אם ברור לך כשמש שיש לו שלום עמך אל תהרגהו ואם לאו הרגהו.

שלם ישלם. The thief-by-day does not incur the loss of his life, but he has to pay back all that he has stolen, and his whole personality is surety for such repayment so that אם אין לו, if he has not got the where-withal to repay he must let himself be sold, and slave to earn the value of what he had stolen. (see on Ch. 21,2 et seq.).

V. 3. אם המצא תמצא. In verse 8 ואשר ירשיעון אלהים ישלם שנים לרעהו, the law is laid down that the fine of double repayment has only to be paid following a verdict of the court, but that מודה בקנס פטור, in a case of self-accusation, or of free admission in a claim made to the court, but un-supported by witnesses, simple repayment only, but not double value is to be paid. It has already been remarked how in the case of self-accusation or free admission, we can see in such, acknowledgment of the power of general law and order, an atonement which renders a fine to be imposed by the court unnecessary. Now by our אם המצא תמצא this law receives a substantial complement. מציאת הגנבה ביד הגנב, obviously excludes self accusation or free admission. The stolen artciles are found in his hand by others, he had kept them secret and denied it. The basis on which judgment can be given on such a “find” can only rest on witnesses. By the double expression המצא תמצא the condition that this fine can only be imposed if the “finding” is supported by the evidence of witnesses is intensified, as being a necessary condition. “Only if he is legally found to be a thief by witnesses has he to pay double”, the whole procedure from its beginning must rest on witnesses’ evidence: — אם המצא בעדים תמצא בדיינים. If he had come to the court on his own initiative, or had confessed to the court before the witnesses arrived to give evidence against him, he does not have to pay double מודה בקנס ואחר באו עדים פטור.

The double expression המצא תמצא also extends the law in another direction, namely to extend the idea יד, hand, into the idea of possession, which includes anywhere in his possession e.g., חצר etc. Whether he actually took it with his hands, or if the animal had run into his courtyard and he had shut it in, and kept it, אם המצא תמצא however, or wherever it is found as a theft in his possession he has to pay double, שנים ישלם.

In V.2 the duty is expressed which he has to carry out even without there being any witnesses or any sentence by the court, תשלומי קרן the simple but full compensation for the value of what he had stolen. This value, the קרן, is there called גנבה. (Hence also the law ונמכר בגנבתו ולא בכפלו, see note on Ch. XXI verse 2 et seq.). Now in V.3 it says: “but if he is found to be the thief of the stolen property by the evidence of witnesses, he has to pay double.” This קרן, the value of the theft, called גנבה in the text, is here designated חי and as it refers to animals as examples, חיים. This can not be meant to tell us that the animals are found alive in his possession, i.e., not slaughtered or sold, to tell us that only then, if they are alive, only twofold has to be paid, and not fourfold or fivefold as in V.37 and 21, for the examples given include חמור, and for an ass, as for every other object except cattle and sheep, even if they are sold or slaughtered, only double value has to be paid. The epithet חי only designates the way and manner in which the גנבה, the value of the stolen property, the קרן has to be paid, that it has to be paid חי, compensation must be full at the whole value it had at the time of the גנבה irrespective of any lowering (or raising) of the market price at the time it comes to court, אחייה לקרן כעין שגנב, whereas in the cases of fines whether double or four or five fold, the value is taken as at the time judgment is given, כשעת העמדה בדין. Fines only become encumbent on the thief by the process of the court, so that it is the moment when judgment is pronounced that is to be considered for fixing their value; while קרן, to restore the actual property or its value is his duty from the very moment he committed the theft (B.K. 65a).

V. 4. This verse comes back, and carries on with the laws concerning responsibility for damage done through insufficient care being taken of one’s dangerous belongings, which were interrupted by V.37 of the preceding chapter. These laws dealt primarily with matters referring to living property. V.35 and 36 dealt with קרן, with the responsibility for abnormal damages which were not to be expected from the ordinary nature of the animal. Here it treats of such damages which the owner must expect to occur from the ordinary nature of his animal, with regard to which the animal is מועד מתחלתו is called normally מועד, in contrast to damage by goring (נגח) where the animal only becomes מועד by repeated fatal gorings. These “to-be-expected” damages are רגל and שן, damage which an animal does in the course of its ordinary proceeding on its way, by tramping, and by following its natural trend to feeding. From this idea of מועד מתחלתו, exercising its powers in accordance with its nature, we can understand the thrice repeated expression בער with which the text here characterises both the animal itself and the damage it does. There are three expressions for an animal: — חיה, inasmuch as it develops an independent individual animal life, בהמה inasmuch as it subjugates itself to human beings as במה, as a base for their rule, and finally בעיר, an unreasoning lack of free will, it instinctively follows solely the urges of its nature, it is בַעַר (see Gen. 1,24).
It is especially with regard to these innate tendencies of the nature of an animal as בער that a man takes over responsibility at the moment any living creature becomes his property. He has to place the manifestations of power, regarding which the animal is בער, under the care of his intelligence, to guard the rights of property of his neighbour from damage. On acquiring an animal, the owner becomes the guardian to prevent the animal from following that which he would otherwise do, his natural urges, to the detriment of other people’s property. That is probably also the reason why here, where he has not kept the “manly” authoritative guard over his animal, the masculine suffix referring to the property, is written in the feminine בעירה. So that כי יבער איש שדה וגו׳ would mean literally: — “If anybody lets a field or vineyard be affected by the natural actions of an animal, — he either allows the animal to run about uncontrolled in somebody else’s field, or allows it to feed just as it likes in somebody else’s field — then he has to give in compensation the best of his own field and the best of his own vineyard.” Just as the consuming power of fire is called by the same name as consumption by living creatures אכילה, so is the consuming power of the animal feeding in the natural manner called בער (burning).

ושִׁלַח וּבִעֵר. As it expresses as directly inciting what is after all only a lack of preventing, the law is thereby indicated that he is only responsible if his neglect is really equivalent to incitement עד דעביד כעין ושלח וכעין ובער i.e., if he had not taken any care at all to prevent his animal tramping down or eating the produce of the field, not even שמירה פחותה, not even just ordinary precautions. But as long as he did take sufficient precautionary measures which would suffice for ordinary circumstances, he is free from responsibility, and here, as is the general rule for נזיקין in cases where the Law is based on equity as for בור and מועד, no שמירה מעולה is required. (B.K. 55b).

ברשות הניזק :בשדה אחר. Responsibility for damage done by an animal following his natural propensities is only incurred when the animal has no right to go there, and the damaged goods have the right to be there viz., in the premises of the plaintiff. Where the animal has the right to be, e.g., in the public highway, its owner is not responsible for damage which is inseparable from the natural urges and movements of the animal. There it is rather up to the owner of fruit, fragile goods etc. etc., to keep such goods out of the way of animals who would be likely to eat them or trample on them. שן ורגל are accordingly פטורים בר״ה, and if an animal eats somebody else’s fruit in the ר״ה (public street) the owner of the animal has not to pay the full value of the fruit, but only the actual value of what he saves himself in fodder משלמת מה שנהנית. (B.K. 19b). Finally, it does not say ובער שדה אחר he causes the field of somebody else to be eaten, as it says כי יבער איש שדה but ובער בשדה אחר he causes crops to be eaten in the field of somebody else, so that the damage is considered not so much in itself but as damage to a part of a field. This is a reference to the Halacha that it is not the actual amount of the damage done which has to be valued for compensation, but only its relative value to the whole field, or the whole acre. The court has to estimate how much less the whole field or the whole acre would fetch on account of the damage done, and that is all that need be paid שמין בית סאה באותה שדה כמה היתה יפה וכמה היא יפה, (see רש״י and תוספות there).

There is a striking declaration of אביי in B.K. 23b, according to which the responsibility here laid down for damage done by an animal following the normal course of its nature is only incurred if the owner of the field had properly fenced his field and the animal had broken through, or the fencing had fallen down during the night. But if the animal ran into an unfenced field the owner of the animal need pay no compensation. According to this opinion, every owner would have to fence his field in, a condition which in general is not the case, and apparently never was the case (see B.B. 2a). So that our text would speak of a case which seldom occurs, almost of an exceptional one. ב״י ,רמב״ם ,רי״ף ,תוספות, all take the oposite view, that of ר׳ יוסף, according to which the responsibility for שן ורגל applies also in cases of unfenced fields. But בה״ג and ר״ח, and following them the ש״כ on ח״מ 397 do adopt the opinion of אביי and make a difference between houses in a town where the owners are not obliged to keep the doors shut in daytime, and where accordingly שן ורגל apply even where doors are left open, and the doings of animals in the open country where one can not prevent an animal running into an open field.

Perhaps this would explain the opening words of our text: כי יבער איש שדה או כרם which otherwise seem quite superfluous. It would have sufficed to say כי ישלח איש את בעירו ובער בשדה אחר for it seems that שדה and כרם differ in the case in question here. שדה is, as a rule an open unfenced field, but כרם a protected one. This is clear from many instances, but is particulary apparent in Numb. 22,23 & 24. Bileam’s ass turns aside from the road in V.23 and goes into a field. But in V.24 the path goes through a vineyard and it is closed in on either side. According to this the opening words of our verse would say: “If a person does damage by his animal to an open or to an enclosed vineyard”, and this would agree with the view taken by רי״ף ,תוספות and רמב״ם. The other view takes כרם to express the condition which must exist also for שדה, viz., that it must be enclosed: שדה דומיא דכרם.

V. 5. כי תצא אש. If an existing fire goes over into the premises of another, i.e., it spreads by itself, שלם ישלם המבעיר את הבערה, the one who started the fire is responsible for compensation. Fire is here clearly regarded with reference to the duty of being kept under control in a double character, firstly as ממונו, as dangerous property which an owner has to guard against damaging his neighbours’ property, and then as חציו as a dangerous missile which he has set in motion and whose effects are to be considered as his actions. The Halacha also expresses itself on this matter in this double character. For everything which at the time the fire is lit, would, under normal conditions, be threatened by the fire, it has the character of an arrow in the hand of the one who lit it, and then he is responsible, not only for compensation for damage to property, but also for compensation and punishment for injury or death of human beings, in exactly the same degree as by direct wounding or killing.

But where כלו חציו, “his arrows come to an end”, where the action of the fire can no longer be considered as the direct personal act of the one who lit it, where the fire continues doing its damage through circumstances which arise subsequently e.g., a wall breaks down (not due to the fire) and had he immediately re-erected it, it would have prevented the fire spreading, or where the fire started by itself in a place where the owner had not taken sufficient precautions against the possibility of a fire speading to his neighbour’s territory; in all such cases the damage has to be considered not as חציו as the direct action of the owner, but only as ממונו, as the result of his not having taken sufficient precautions to guard his potentially dangerous property. Then the owner, as in שור and בור, in injury to persons, has only to pay נזק, but not צער רפוי שבת ובשת, and in damage to property the responsibility is lessened and limited in accordance with the fire being regarded from the standpoint of ממונו. That is to say, that, just as in the case of בור, compensation has only to be made for objects directly threatened by it, but no compensation need be paid for כלים (these being inanimate and immobile and can only be brought to the danger by others, and hence can not be considered as directly threatened by the בור see notes above on בור), so in case of damage by fire, where the fire is regarded as ממונו, as property insufficiently guarded against doing damage, only for objects directly threatened by it, i.e., object lying exposed בגלוי, but not for hidden objects טמון does compensation have to be paid. The objects given as examples in the text, thorns, corn ricks, standing corn, and the field itself, include movable and immobile goods, valuable or not valuable, inflammable or non-inflammable as being liable for compensation, and only exclude טמון, concealed goods. But this exclusion of טמון does not apply where the lighting of the fire itself is done where one has no real right to do so e.g., on somebody else’s property, or where it is to be considered from the standpoint of חציו, as the effect of a personal act (see B.K. 22a & 60a et seq).

אש, fire, is the example given, and the legal term, for all damage done by inanimate property which is set in motion by ordinary natural forces and which does the damage while in motion. This would include e.g. אבנו, סכינו, ומשאו שהניחן בראש גגו ונפלו ברוח מצויה והזיקו בהדי דקא אזלי a stone, a knife or anything that one has left on the roof, and which is blown down by an ordinary every-day wind, and which does damage as it falls. If the damage or injury is caused בתר דנייחי, after the object has come to rest on the ground, it comes under the heading of בור (B.K. 6a).

With אש the ארבעה אבות נזיקין the four categories of dangerous property, שן ורגל ,אש ,קרן ,בור, or as the Mishna calls them השור, והבור המבעה, וההבער are concluded. They are summarised in their common quality: הצד השוה שבהן שדרכן להזיק ושמירתן עליך וכשהזיק חב המזיק לשלם תשלומי נזק במיטב הארץ. They are all dangerous property, the guarding of them is the owner’s duty, and if damage is done by any of them, the owner has to pay compensation with the very best of his own property (B.K. 2a). They differ in their own characteristics; in the case of קרן there is a difference whether it is תם or מועד; in שן ורגל no compensation has to be made if the damage is done ברה״ר; in בור no compensation for כלים or מיתת האדם; and in אש, on the hand, no compensation for טמון, but on the other, compensation has to be paid for damage done even to goods which can not be burnt (ibid. 5b).

V. 6-14 deal with the responsibilities which are incurred in the case of duties which are voluntarily undertaken. These cases are divided into שומר חנם, שומר שכר, שואל and שוכר, the unpaid custodian of the property of another, the paid custodian, the borrower and the hirer. In working out the different responsibilities incurred, and in the laws laid down regarding them, many general basic laws of civil law and justice are incidentally laid down, laws which have far-reaching application.

As is clear from the text, V.6—8 deal with a custodian who is not responsible if the object left in his charge is stolen from him פטור בגנבה; V. 9—12 with one who has to pay compensation in such a case, חייב בגנבה, and who is only free from responsibility if the property is lost in a manner which could not possibly have been prevented, פטור באונסין, he is free in cases of “overwhelming force”, if, for instance, an animal dies a natural death, מת, or is taken from him by overpowering violence נשבה. The Halacha teaches us that the first case speaks of a שומר חנם an unpaid custodian, the latter of a שומר שכר a paid one. A non-paid custodian in accepting custody, implicitly undertakes to give the entrusted goods the same care that he normally gives to his own property e.g., that at night time he places them in a securely closed place. But a paid custodian (unless of course, special conditions are agreed) implicitly accepts the duties of a watchman, so that if he leaves it out of his personal surveillance he would be responsible even if it were stolen by thieves breaking in to properly closed premises (B.K. 57a תוספות ד״ה כגון שטענו; B.M. 93b להכי יהבי לד ח״מ 313,2; אגרא לנטורי לי נטירותא יתירתא). The circumstances described, and the words in the text, are completely in accordance with these laws. In the case of the שומר חנם the text speaks of “money or vessels” as the examples of the goods entrusted; these are goods of such a nature that one does not usually keep constantly under one’s personal surveillance, but is satisfied to deposit in a safely secured place. The custodian only offers his “house” for them. (cf. תוספות B.K. 41b ד״ה לומר) Hence also וגנב מבית האיש and ונקרב בעל הבית וגו׳. But in the case of the שומר שכר it speaks of חמור או שור וגו׳ i.e., such objects as are normally protected by the personal presence of a shepherd or herdsman. Hence also ואם גנב יגנב מעמו the entrusted property was to be guarded not merely by his “house” but by himself.

וגֻנַב not as in V.11. גנב יִגָנֵב in the Niphal, by which the theft is established as a fact, but in the Pual a construction which leaves the origin and cause of the absence of the object quite undetermined, a בנין שלא נזכר שם פועלו as it is called in Hebrew Grammar. This expresses merely the assertion of the custodian טוען טענת גנב.

אם ימצא הגנב. In B.K. 43b one opinion takes this to refer to the גנב עצמו, to a case where the thief is really found; and takes the case of טוען טענת גנב, where the custodian declares and takes an oath that the object has been stolen from him, and then it is discovered that he himself is the thief, to be referred to only in V.7 & 8. Another opinion is, that already here in our verse 6, it speaks of this case where טוען טענת גנב ונמצא שהוא עצמו גנבו and then our אם ימצא הגנב would be translated “if he is found to be the thief, then he, the custodian found to be the thief, has to pay double the value.” Then V.7 & 8 would give the further explanation that this compensation in double has only to be paid after a false oath of denial has been sworn.

V. 7. ונקרב בעל הבית אל האלהים is an expression for the oath of denial corresponding to the שבעת ה׳ תהיה בין שניהם of v.10. (B.K. 63b). The root קרב only occurs in the Niphal in one other place (Josh. 7,14) ונקרבתם בבקר לשבטיכם in the story of Achan, and there too, it refers to coming before the judgment of God to clear oneself of the charge of appropriating some of the spoil of Jerico which Israel had vowed not to touch. It has already been explained on Gen. 21,3, that the idea on an oath is הִשָׁבֵעַ, is “a placing of one’s visible means of existence under the punishing power of the Invisible one.” This “placing oneself before God,” seems to be expressed here, by הִקָרֵב. So that although the אלהים here is חול, and so refers primarily to the human judge, it does nevertheless seem that this particular appellation of a judge does designate the judge quite specially as the representative of the justice and judgment of God, and we accordingly translate this phrase “he, as the master of the house, has to place himself in the proximity of God.” The property had been entrusted to his care as בעל הבית for him to keep safe “in his house” as if it were his own property. He declares that it has been stolen from him. There are no witnesses for this, then ונקרב בעל הבית וגו׳ he, as “the master of the house” has to place himself and the further existence of his “house” under the judgment of God in the oath of denial. The “existence of his whole house” means the whole of all his possession and his own personality as owner. This he has to declare forfeit if his spoken word be untrue and the missing property is still in his possession.

אם לא שלח ידו במלאכת רעהו. Strangely enough, this sentence, as well as V.10, is usually taken to be the context of the oath he has to take, without giving consideration to the fact (as has already been remarked and explained on Gen. 21,33) that in the form the Jewish oath takes, אם denies, and אם לא asserts. Accordingly שבועה אם לא שלח וגו׳ would mean that he swears that he has stretched forth his hand to the property of his neighbour, and if he wanted to deny it, he would have to say שבועה אם שלח וגו׳. So that אם לא שלח ידו וגו׳ can not possibly be the context of the oath he has to swear, and is definitely to be taken as the conditional mood: “If he has not (i.e., provided he has not) stretched forth his hand etc.” This is also how the Gemora takes it in B.K. 107b. The whole sentence reads:- אם לא ימצא הגנב “if the thief is not legally found, that is, if the asserted theft can not be confirmed by witnesses, ונקרב בעל הבית אל האלהים then the master of the house, then he, as master of the house, must place himself near to God, i.e., he, as master of the house, has to clear himself by an oath before the court with regard to his whole behaviour towards the property entrusted to his house, and then he is free from having to pay any compensation, provided of course, אם לא שלח וגו׳, that he has not already stretched out his hand towards the goods entrusted to him. i.e., had not previously on any occasion been about to use it.” For even if he had only stretched out his hand with the intention to make some use of the property for himself, at that moment he forefeits his relation to the object, as a שומר, and becomes a גזלן towards it. As such, he becomes responsible for repayment to the owner for whatever happens to it, even if it gets stolen from him.

The oath of denial which the court has to impose on him comprises all the phases of his relations to the object. ג׳ שבועות משביעין אותו he has to swear three oaths, (a) that he has not been instrumental to the theft by neglect of normal precautions, in which case he would have to pay the actual value of the object (not the double.) שבועה שלא פשעתי בה (b) that he had never taken it in his hand with the idea of using it for himself, in which case he would also, as mentioned above, only be responsible for the actual value. שבועה שלא שלחתי בה יד, (c) that he has not still got it in his possession. Should it afterwards be found that the presumed stolen article is really still in his possession, then he, as thief, would have to pay double the value in accordance with V.8. שבועה שאינה ברשותי.

שליחות יד בפקדון is the term applied to anyone who takes in his hand any object that has been entrusted to his keeping, either with the intention of keeping it entirely, לגוזלו, or to use it in any way that would lessen its value, even if he does not carry out his intention. As soon as his intention has begun to be translated into action, i.e., as soon as he takes it in his hand with such an idea in his mind, he becomes חייב באונסין and has to pay full compensation for whatever happens to it, even if he puts it back immediately, for שליחות יד אינה צריכה חסרון, in the case of שומר the damaging intention need not necessarily be carried out. But however if the intended use of the object would cause no damage, loss, or lessening of value to it, then the mere intention is not sufficient but he has actually to use it, as שואל שלא מדעת, before he is considered in the light of גזלן towards it, and, as such would be liable for compensation for whatever happens to it. (B.K. 31a; CH. M. 292). (See above on XXI,37) אם לא שלח ידו ב- is used here exactly in the same sense as the intention of Haman which was not carried out (Esther VIII) על אשר שלח ידו וגו׳.

With extreme delicacy here in the case of שליחות יד the property of a neighbour is described as מלאכת רעהו, a term very seldom used. This literally means: Something which stands at the disposal of his neighbour, which is “like a messenger” for his neighbour (from מלאך a messenger). Here it is dealing with what is, after all, only a momentary unlawful use of another’s property, and so the term מלאכת רעהו very neatly expresses just where the sinful nature of the action lies. Although entrusted to him, the disposition of the article, the decision what use to make of it, is not at his, but his neighbour’s discretion; it is מלאכת רעהו.

V. 8. על כל דבר פשע we follow here the view — which is the one accepted as Halacha — of רב חייא בר יוסף (B.K. 107a) that עירוב פרשיות כתוב כאן, כי הוא זה, אמלוה הוא דכתיב and also the explanation of the ריב״א (תוספות thereon) which is also adopted by the רא״ש and the later authorities. According to this view from על כל till שניהם is in parenthesis, and the law here laid down regarding the oath, refers, not just to the custodian’s oath, but universally to every process in civil law e.g., for all the cases referring to loans which V.24 deals with, and accordingly would only be applicable to our cases of custody where these are regarded from the common general aspect of loaned property, but not to cases where the claim rests on the special and specific relationship of a custodian. This taking the text to refer to general claims under civil law, and in consequence limiting its application in cases of “custody”, in connection with which it is actually stated, solely to where such cases can be regarded as being in principle the same as general cases, is called עירוב פרשיות; such “mixing together headings of law cases” makes the law enforcing an oath to be taken to apply to every case in civil law where the claim is regarded from a similar aspect. The words in the sentence in the Gemora ,כי הוא זה אמלוה הוא לכתיב, would accordingly mean בטענה דשייכא במלוה “with reference to a plea which is also usually put in a claim for a loan.”

This generalisation of the text referring to an oath imposed by the court, may also be found in the words על כל דבר פשע וגו׳. In V.7 in ונקרב בעל וגו׳ the oath was mentioned for the custodian who declares that the entrusted object had been stolen from him. Thereupon the Torah mentions in parenthesis על כל דבר פשע וגו׳ אשר יאמר כי הוא זה ער האלהים יבא דבר שניהם, “at every accusation (claim) where he (the accused) says “it is this” the words of the two of them have to come to God i.e., by an oath, the decision is to be placed in God’s Hands. So that whenever the accused says כי הוא זה an oath is to be imposed. He says כי הוא “that it is so”, but זה “this is how it is.” He does not deny the whole matter, is not כופר בכל, but he says כי הוא the charge has some foundation, but זה, it is limited to “this”, not to the extent that the plaintiff claims, but he is מודה במקצת הטענה he admits part of the charge. In כי הוא lies the הודאה he admits the charge in principle, and he must do this ממין הטענה, he must admit, not only the charge in general but must agree to the exact nature of the charge, not for instance if the charge is concerning wheat and he admits to barley, טענו הטין והודה לו בשעורים. In זה lies the כפירה, the denial of the extent of the charge. The charge is two measures of wheat, he admits that he owes one measure. (Shebuoth 39b). This lays down the law that שבועה דאורייתא that the judicial oath ordained by the Torah is only to be imposed where מודה במקצת, where there is a limited agreement to the charge, but not where כופר בכל, where the whole charge is completely denied. From the dictum in v.10 ולקה בעליו ולא ישלם we learn that the oath is imposed only on the accused, (Shebuoth 44b) it says כל הנשבעין שבתורה נשבעין ולא משלמין “every oath which the Torah imposes is only for the protection of claimed property; to refute, never to confirm a charge.” Originally there was no נשבע ונוטל, no acquisitive but only a defensive oath.

According to the interpretation given above, that עירוב פרשיות כתוב כאן, this general rule of כי הוא זה i.e., that the oath is only imposed in cases of partial admission but not of complete denial, would then apply to cases the four kinds of שומרין; and in cases brought for “custody” too, the oath would only be imposed for cases which conform to this rule. Just as, for instance, in claims for loans: מנה לי בידך אין לך בידי כלום ,פטור but אין לך בידי אלא חמשים זוז חייב “you owe me a pound. I don’t owe you anything”, no oath is imposed, but “I only owe you ten shillings”, he must take an oath; so in the case of our custodian “I gave you two sheep to look after. You did not give me any sheep.” He need not take an oath; but “you only gave me one sheep” he must take the oath.

But in claims that arise from the special and particular relationship of a custodian to the object entrusted to his care, such as טענת גנבה, the plea of theft, in the case of שומר חנם, of an unpaid custodian, or טענת נאנסה the plea of unpreventable loss in the case of a שומר שכר, of a paid custodian, the oath is imposed in all cases, even if there is no partial admission (i.e., we do not require cases such as “yes, I must give you back one of your sheep but the other one died”).

So we have here two classes of disputed claims in which the defendant has to take an oath: מודה במקצת cases of partial admission, and שבועת שומרין the oath of denial of a custodian, as שלא פשעתי בה etc. Now there is a third kind which completes the total of cases of judicial oaths which the Torah imposes, this is עד אחד, a claim which is supported by a single witness. In all cases where, had there been two witnesses to the transaction, the defendant would have to pay, he must take an oath to refute the charge if it is supported by the evidence of a single witness (Shebuoth 40a).

If we realise the whole idea of what an oath really means, and especially the judicial oath, and then look for the common characteristic of these three kinds of accusations, we shall be able to understand the reason why the Torah confines the judicial oath to just these three categories.

שבועה, an oath, is placing the whole of one’s visible existence as forfeit to the judgment of God if one’s asserted word is untrue, or if one does not fulfill one’s promised word. If one’s word refers — as it does in the judicial oath — to some possession or piece of property, then the oath puts the whole of one’s property and possessions in the first place as forfeited in the event of one’s right of possession to the particular object in dispute being an illegal one. We can understand that a judicial oath can only be taken as a protection for the disputed ownership of the article. He sets off the whole of his possessions as a protection for the attacked portion of his property. But we can also understand that in two cases of the judicial oath, this placing of the decision before God, this עד האלהים יבא דבר שניהם as our text puts it, can not take place. Both in the case where the claim is fully substantiated, and where it is not substantiated at all. In the first case, an oath is impossible, as the truth of the contrary to that which he would swear is already completely established for the court by the testimony of witnesses, or by the admission of the defendant, so that the accusation stands fully justified and the court is bound to give the verdict accordingly. In the second case an oath is quite unnecessary, the possession of the defendant is not really attacked at all, a totally unsupported claim, or accusation, has to be considered by the court as not having been made. So that a judicial oath can only be imposed where the accusation is not fully substantiated, but at the same time not fully denied, so that the attack on the right of possession must be considered as being made, i.e., as being incompletely established, so that, where there is insufficient proof to the contrary, the attacked possession can only be protected by an appeal to the Justice of God, by taking an oath. ’וכן פי הריטב״א.

If we consider the three categories שבועת שומרין ,מודה במקצת and עד אחד, they all come under the common idea of a possession incompletely attacked. In מודה במקצת the attack with regard to the object, in שבועת שומרין with regard to the cause, in עד אחד with regard to the proof, is insufficiently established legally. The מודה במקצת acknowledges and admits the demand made to him regarding part of it; — the plea of the שומר that the object has been stolen or lost through circumstances which he could not possibly have prevented admits thereby the main basis of the demand that he had received an object to take care of, and had not returned it to its owner, he only affirms that for some reason or other he need not return it; — finally by עד אחד the proof for the justice of the claim is half established, so that all three categories can really be considered as הודאה במקצת in its wider conception. In all three categories the possession of the defendant is attacked by, in one way or the other, incomplete proof, and he can only protect his possession against the presumption of the complete truth of the half-proved claim by an oath.

If we then think we can see the understandable similarity of these three categories, including שבועת שומרין with הודאה במקצת inasmuch as they all three can be regarded as coming under the formula אשר יאמר כי הוא זה i.e., the incompletely proven charge, then the transition from the denial oath of the custodian to the canon or doctrine of הודאה במקצת by the generalising term על כל דבר פשע seems all the more apt. It is, as if the verse says: “In general, at every accusation which is not entirely refuted but partially admitted, the דבר שניהם, the charge and the plea are to be brought from the human court to God, i.e., to be placed before God by an oath.”

Although by order of the Torah no oath is imposed in cases where there is no evidence to prove the claim, and the claim is completely refuted by the defendant, nevertheless, in the times of th Amoraim, even in cases of complete denial of the charge לא היו דברים מעולם an oath שבועת היסת was ordered, to provoke an admission. This oath differed from a proper שבועה דאורײתא inasmuch, as, amongst other differences, the defendant can refer it back to the accuser, and say “you swear” מיפך שבועה which he can not do in a שבועה דאורײתא (41b).

In accordance with the objects given as examples, ’שור, חמור, שה, וגו the oath is only imposed in cases dealing with claims for דבר המטלטל וגופו ממון, transportable goods which have, intrinsic value. This excludes קרקעות landed or immovable property, עבדים slaves, who are legally regarded in the same category as immovable, and שטרות I.O.Us, cheques etc., which are only drafts for value, but have no actual intrinsic value in themselves. (Shebuoth 42b). If oaths taken before the court really mean submitting the claimed property in the first place, and all one’s property following, under the penalty of being destroyed by God’s punishing justice if it is not legally and justifiably in the possession of the present owner, and if it can perhaps be assumed that such submission always refers primarily to the kind of objects to which the object in question belongs, then perhaps we can understand that the oath can only refer to such objects that (a) are real objects of property themselves, and not documents whose destruction would not be a loss of property itself, but only the proof of the right to property. In addition (b) objects whose existence and meaning do not extend beyond the personality of the one who takes the oath, but which are part and parcel of the person who has them, whose existence can be considered as dependent on the will — and hence also on the worthiness — of their owners, and which if they are destroyed, are lost to the owner only. But such property, considered entirely as part and parcel of the personality of its owner consists solely of מטלטלין of movable goods. They are entirely absorbed by the personality of their owner, are completely dependent on him, he can dispose of them as he wishes, even destroy them, and if they are lost, they are really only lost to him personally. The idea of immobile property in Jewish Law is diametrically the reverse. Immobile property is not absorbed by the personality of the owner, he does not hold it, but האחז is the expression for possessing landed property, the owner is held and borne by the land, each owner is only the temporary user, generations pass over the same piece of land, and every owner has to leave the land to the future possessor of it. But one can only offer as a pledge before God, for one’s truth and one’s honesty, that which is in truth “one’s own”, and which is completely covered by one’s own personality. An oath taken for קרקע would be calling down destruction if the oath were false, on something which reaches far beyond the personality of the one who was swearing falsely. And the same applies to an even higher degree to עבדים, slaves.
