An עבד, a slave, has a moral independent place and meaning and importance before God, and in no wise can be considered as a mere piece of property entirely absorbed by the personality of his owner. Just think of the crazy horribleness of an oath referring to עבדים. Such an oath would mean: “I call on God to exercise His punishing destruction on this slave and on all my slaves, if the claim regarding a slave in my possession is true and if what I swear regarding the slave is a false oath!” In this case the senseless immorality of such an oath strikes one immediately, inasmuch as the punishing stroke is invoked on the head of some other quite innocent person. It seems to us that such considerations as we have attempted, may really be the underlying motive of these specific regulations regarding the oath in Jewish jurisdiction.

’אשר ירשיעון אלהים וגו. Up to these words the verse is in parenthesis. As it is dealing with the judicial oath of denial which the custodian has to take, the Torah takes the opportunity incidentally to mention the general rule concerning judicial oaths. Then ’אשר ירשיעון אלהים וגו, continues with our case where the custodian asserts that the entrusted article has been stolen from him. — If then after he has denied his responsibility to return the article and has taken the required oath, the court finds he is a רשע i.e., witnesses testify that he still has the article claimed in his possession, then he, as a thief, has to pay double the value to the owner. It is only when טוען טענת גנב בפקדון, when he has tried to free himself by falsely swearing that it has been stolen from him, that the fine of double pay is imposed, but not if he has falsely sworn to some other plea e.g., that he has lost it, or that it has died etc. (B.C. 63b טוען טענת אבדה בפקדון פטור מכפל). For by טוען טענת גנב he has been guilty of showing the greatest disdain of the basic principle of general respect for the Law (to atone for which the fine is imposed) inasmuch as he has declared on oath his pretended upkeeping of this principle at a time when he himself has committed the greatest crime against the rights of property! In טוען טענת גנב he has misused the principle of respect for the Law, to mock at the Law, similarly to a thief, whose theft only becomes possible through the trust with which the owner left his property to the protection of this general respect for the law. This is not the case to such an extent, when he makes any other plea. But if a man finds an object, and when the owner claims it from him, declares falsely that it has been stolen from him טוען טענת גנב באבדה he, too, would have to pay the double fine, for an אבדה is also a פקדון and the finder thereof is a שומר, and is even given the responsibility of a שומר שכר.

It has already been remarked on V.3 that, incidentally in this verse, the general rule of מודה בקנס פטור is expressed, that is also very likely why it does not say אשר ירשיעון האלהים (as we would expect) where it would then refer only to the case in question and to the previously mentioned court, but אשר ירשיעון אלהים i.e., “provided that his guilt has been established by a court and not by his own free confession”.

Regarding the laws concerning theft, it must further be mentioned, that from the expression in V.6, וגנב מבית האיש, the law is deduced ולא מבית הגנב a thief who steals a stolen object from the house of a thief does not have to pay the double value: אין הגונב אחר הגנב משלם תשלומי כפל. This clause affords a welcome confirmation of our way of looking at this fine of כפל. One who has obtained possession of an article by mocking at, and disregarding the principle of the protective power of the general recognition of the rights of property, such a person can not place that article under the protection of that principle.

In the words with which this case is introduced, ’כי יתן איש אל רעהו כסף או כלים וגו, certain rules affecting the nature of the parties concerned, as well as of the objects of the charge, are laid down. ’כי יתן איש וגו makes it necessary for the charge to be made by one who is legally considered mature, an adult, אין נתינת קטן כלום hence the law אין נשבעין על טענת חרש שוטה וקטן (Shebuoth 38b, see Ch. 1000,96,1).

By the combined description of the objects of the charge as כסף או כלים, where כלים in the plural requires at least two, and to be called כלים must be objects of a definite value, דבר חשוב (the smallest object e.g., a pin, whose actual value is practically nil, is considered of definite value because it is a כלי and is of definite use, is a דבר חשוב), and by applying these qualities of כלים to כסף, we get the following rule: — Although in general by the term כסף is to be understood even the smallest copper coin, a פרוטה, a farthing, — and such value would in general suffice for an object to be the subject of a lawsuit, here, where the imposition of an oath comes into question, the object of the charge must be a minimum of two כלים, or if the charge is for money or goods other than כלים, it must refer to a value of two of the smallest silver coins i.e., two Geras (גרה see Ex. 20,13) or expressed in Chaldean coinage a Moah (מעה). According to the opinion of רב — which is the accepted one — the actual value about which he swears must be at least two Moah, כפירת טענה שתי כסף, so that in the case where the oath is imposed on account of הודאה במקצת (partial admission) the least possible value of the object of the charge must be שתי כסף ופרוטה, so that the admission could be regarding the שוה פרוטה and the oath would be imposed for שתי כסף, hence the sentence in the Mishna (Shebuoth 38a and 39b) הטענה שתי כסף וההודאה בשוה פרוטה. But nevertheless in cases of loans where there is only a single witness טענת מלוה והעדאת עד אחד and the oath is imposed by the demand of the plaintiff being supported by the single witness, then the value of the charge need not exceed one Peruta (1/64 of the two Moahs) (Shebuoth 40a). The reason for this distinction may be the following: — In ordinary cases of litigation the minimum value of the subject of the litigation must be one Peruta. That in cases where an oath has to be imposed the value must be greater can be attributed to the sanctity of an oath taken in God’s Name. If the object is too petty it may border on a שבועת שוא, where the plaintiff insists on an oath and the defendant would then prefer to pay the trifling amount in question sooner than undergo the solemnity of an oath. In the case of partial admission מודה במקצת and equally so in the case of the oath of a custodian שבועת שומרין there is absolutely nothing at all against the truth of what the defendant declares and to which he has to swear. The presumption of the truth of that which the defendant denies in the former and of what he asserts in the latter is completely in the balance. The court does not satisfy itself with his mere declaration, because in the first case, regarding the object of the claim, and in the second, regarding the basis on which the claim is made, the claim has some degree of substance. But with regard to what the defendant has to take an oath about, there is absolutely nothing whatever to tilt the scales against him. Hence in these two cases, the מודה במקצת and the שבועת שומרין, the pertinence of the disputed object comes into question. But when a single witness testifies to the untruthfulness of the declaration of the defendant, then what he has to swear about, is the direct opposition to this evidence. An independent and disinterested witness (as all witnesses have to be) is an attack on the truthfulness and honesty of the defendant. This attack on his character makes the value of the object in dispute absolutely immaterial. So long as it has some value that can be legally recognised at all (פרוטה) the evidence of a single witness is sufficiently important for the defendant to have to clear his impugned character by an appeal to the decision of God, by taking an oath.

There is an opinion, and this is accepted by the רמב״ם and ב״י, according to which שבועת שומרין is also imposed even if the object in question has only the value of a Peruta, and the value of two Moahs is only required in cases of מודה במקצת. For this opinion too, the reason could be the same as that worked out above. Even if, in the case of a custodian, the character of the defendant is not compromised to the extent to which it is in the case of the single witness, nevertheless at all events, it is to a much greater degree than in cases of partial admission. While in partial admisssion there is nothing at all against the denied part to which the oath refers, in the case of custodians, it is proved, either by admission or evidence, that the defendant had, in any case, accepted a responsibility towards the object about which the oath is taken, and that this responsibility had not been fulfilled. He had received the object to look after and return, and he had not returned it. This undisputed fact does at least compromise the character of the custodian to a degree which makes the value of the object itself quite immaterial, and would make him have to take an oath concerning the conditions which he avers to dispense him from the responsibility of returning the object, and so clearing his character (provided of course that the claim is about something that has at least the smallest value that can have legal recognition). Here also the personal consideration can make up for the little importance that the intrinsic value of the object gives the case.

V. 9. We have already remarked on V.6 that Vv 9—12 deal with the paid custodian. He is paid to give his constant personal guard to the object in his care. Hence he is responsible for compensation for גנבה ואבדה if the animal is stolen in his absence or runs away, cases which normally would have been prevented by his presence. He is only free for מיתה if the animal dies a natural death, or for some other similar loss which by no means in his power he could have prevented, אונסין. We also drew attention there to how this relation of custodianship (paid watcher) was indicated in the text by the objects named as examples, and by using מעמו in contrast to the מבית האיש of the שומר חנם.

Here only three cases of accident are mentioned (a) מת ,נשבר ,נשבה (V.9) all definitely cases of force majeure, unavoidable events for which in no case is he responsible for compensation; (b) גנבה ואבדה for which he must pay (V.11) in all cases; and (c) טרפה (V.12) that, being of a doubtful nature, lies between the two, and the onus is upon him to prove that he could not have saved the animal.

מת או נשבר או נשבה. In the Mechilta it takes נשבר to be ששברתו חיה wounded or killed by a wild beast. But one can ask against this, that this case would then fall under the heading of טרפה which is dealt with separately in V.12, and which even according to the explanation of the Mechilta itself, forms a separate category, owing to the doubtful nature of the event. It seems more probable that נשבר would mean a broken leg or other fracture caused by a fall (as עורת או שבור, Levit. 22,22) and הנשברת (Ezekiel 30,22—34 & IV,17); it is true that in Kings I. 13,26 שבר is used for being torn by a wild beast, and again there in XXVIII. In any case נשבר and נשבה equally with מת refer to אונסין גמורין accidents which were completely unavoidable on the part of the custodian. נשבה is the forcible carrying off by לסטים מזוײן armed bandits.

אין רואה, the oath of denial prescribed in the following verse is only permitted if the accident occurred in a place where no witnesses can be presumed to have been present. But if the place is such that witnesses can be presumed to have been there, the custodian has to bring witnesses to prove his declaration, and then can not get out of having to pay compensation by taking an oath אין רואה שבועת ה׳ תהיה בין שניהם, הא יש רואה יביא ראיה ויפטר (B.M. 83a).

V. 10. שבועת ה׳ תהיה בין שניהם. He has to take the three oaths of denial already mentioned on V.7: — שאינה ,שלא שלח בה יד ,שלא פשע בה ברשותו, the last, of course, only if he pleads נשבה. In ordering the oath with the words שבועת ה׳ תהיה בין שניהם other important laws in general to judicial oaths are laid down: — (1) שבועת ה׳ תהיה בין שניהם this teaches that מלמד שהשבועה חלה על שניהם (Shebuoth 39b) “the gravamen of the oath rests on both of them.” Rashi explains this to mean that the responsibility for a false oath rests also on the plaintiff, inasmuch as he had been careless in having dealings with a dishonest person, and so indirectly had caused the Name of God to be desecrated by a false oath, “that he had not taken sufficient care to entrust his money to a trustworthy man”, and so באו לידי חילול השם. (According to סמ״ע Ch. M.87 & 20,61 in the moment that he sees his opponent ready to commit perjury, he should come to terms with him). And similarly in the case of a true oath, according to the view of R. Chananel quoted by הל׳ שבועות) הגהות מײמוניות Ch. 11,6), the sin of שבועת שוא rests not only on the plaintiff who provokes this unnecessary oath, but also on the defendant, for having had anything to do with such a man. This is how R. Chananel is quoted by the הגהות מײמוניות, but חגהות מײמוניות himself is not of the opinion that in such a case the one who swears truthfully bears any responsibility, and it seems so equally from the Gemora Temura 3b. In the Jerushalmi Talmud (Shebuoth 6,5) the בין שניהם is taken to indicate that wherever a judicial oath is taken, in any case, one party is not free from guilt; if the oath is false, the swearer; if true, the opponent. Incidentally the Gemora there finishes the whole matter up with the admonition not to decide lightly to take even a true oath: בין זכאי בין חײב לשבועה לא תיעול.

(2) שלא ישביענו הדײן בעל כרחו :בין שניהם. (Mechilta): The oath lies entirely between the two parties, the court itself need not insist on it. If the defendant prefers to pay rather than to swear, or if the plaintiff is willing to let him off, the court need not impose the oath. (3) ולא בין היורשין :בין שניהם: “The oath lies only between the first two parties but not between their heirs” i.e., the plea of ignorance (of not knowing the particulars) can protect the heirs from having to take an oath. If, for instance, an heir is sued for a debt of his late father, and he agrees that part of it is owing, but says he knows nothing about the rest of it, — the charge is מנה לי ביד אביך and the defence is חמשין ידענא חמשין לא ידענא — he can naturally not swear that the rest is not owing, but then the inability to take the oath does not have the consequences which it would have had for the father. For if he, the father, the debtor himself, admits part of the claim, he can only counter the claim for the remainder by an oath, as he is מודה במקצת. But if he can not take this oath, if he pleads לא ידענא, then he has to pay the whole amount claimed according to the rule laid down here כל המחויב שבועה ואינו יכול לישבע משלם. But the plea of ignorance on the part of an heir, protects him from having to pay, as an heir need not necessarily know anything of the obligations of his father, and the onus of proving the whole debt is entirely on the plaintiff (Shebuoth 47a).
אם לא שלח ידו. See note on V.7.

ולקח בעליו ולא ישלם. This addition, which seems unnecessary and quite self-understood, gives us the general fundamental rule for all judicial oaths: מי שעליו לשלם לו שבועה: כל הנשבעין שבתורה נשבעין ולא משלמין (Shebuoth 45a) that by an oath, a claim can only be refuted, נשבע ונפטר, but never a claim substantiated נשבע ונוטל. It says here בעליו, the oath is for an object pertaining to a claim, not a means for a claim, the plaintiff “gets” an oath, but he can never get anything by taking an oath himself. ולקח בעליו ולא ישלם, the oath takes the place of payment, it has to satisfy the demand, it can never demand payment. This main canon concerning judicial oaths is founded deep in the very nature of an oath, and has its roots deep in the ground on which our whole Jewish Jurisdiction rests. An oath is a direct appeal to the justice of God Himself, it places the case under His decision, when the matter in question can not be made clear enough for man’s decision, and if guilty, calls on God’s Justice to enforce punishment. It is only an absolving supplement to the plea of the defendant, that an oath is used to call for the decision, and if necessary, the intervention of God’s Justice; human justice is to retire before Divine Justice. But to use it as a supplement to the plaintiff’s cause, to impose payment, would make it force human justice to decide, and intervene and enforce the defendant to pay, the very opposite to the nature of an oath to leave the decision and enforcement of payment to God. Our whole criminal and civil jurisdiction, moreover, rests on the great fundamental principle, that the (חזקה) presumption must be, that every man is innocent, that every piece of property held, is lawfully held, until and unless the contrary is proved. In civil law this principle is reduced to the formula: המוציא מחברו עליו הראיה, the onus of proof is on the claimant. Every claimant demands an alteration in the status quo, and it is the court that is to make this change, it is to be an act of jurisdiction by the court. Every moral procedure, which of course would include a lawsuit, must be preceded by the conviction of its legality. So that the illegality of the status of the property claimed, and the legality of the change demanded, must be evident to the court before it causes the change to be made. In civil law such evidence can only be assured by the admission of the defendant, or by the evidence (personally or by signature on a document) of two witnesses, in rare cases also by certain circumstantial evidence (e.g. B.M. 5b) חזקה אין אדם פורע תוך זמנו, or where, in exceptional cases, the claim has some inner, innate justification (מגו) מגו להוציא, or in cases of ברי ושמא where the defendant has said איני יודע אם החזרתיו לך (B.K. 118). So where the charge is not completely substantiated — and we have seen that all the three cases in which an oath is imposed עד אחד, מודה במקצת and שבועת שומרים are in this category — it is only the defendant who can be called upon to justify, by an appeal to God, as his witness and judge, his right of possession which has been challenged; and although certainly the supposition of guilt has not been proved, it has also not been completely refuted. But the plaintiff can not make his attack, which is insufficiently backed by facts, complete, by adding confirmation of the righteousness of his character. Hence, also, even in מודה במקצת in cases where the presumption of guilt is counterbalanced by reason of inherent circumstances as well as in משיב אבדה (Gittin 51a & b, see רשב״א thereon), or, according to some opinions, also when the accused has one witness to support him — ’עד א מסײעו — (Ch. M. 75,2), no oath is to be imposed on the accused.

Accordingly מן התורה there is no נשבע ונוטל. But nevertheless in later times, out of consideration of general usefulness, the Rabbis imposed an oath on the plaintiff in five cases viz., השכיר, והנגזל, והנחבל, ושכנגדו חשוד על השבועה and חנוני על פנקסו (see Shebuoth 44b).

V. 11. ואם גנב יגנב. This doubling of the idea includes אבדה if the animal has run away, לרבות אבדה. We find the term התגנב used for hiding oneself, to secretly put oneself out of the sight of someone (Sam. II. 19,4). Here, in connection with a custodian, this meaning lies all the more in the expression גנב, as with this word it wants to express all those accidents, which, as a rule, would be prevented by his personal presence, and to prevent which, he is primarily appointed. Every accident which occurs during his absence (or during his sleep) which comes under the idea of “theft”, i.e., which is usually only undertaken unseen, which would also include house-breaking, even if it is done with such forces that, if he had been there, he could not have coped with it, and so would be free from responsibility as an אונס, makes the custodian responsible, as it is assumed that the entry would not have been undertaken if the watchman had been present and awake. This absolute responsibility for everything that can be included under the idea גנבה may be likewise expressed in the extending of the idea by ואם גנב יגנב in contrast to the following ’אם טרף יטרף וגו: “If it is purloined from him in anyway, he has to pay for it, but if it is torn to pieces in any way, he has to bring witnesses to the court as to how it happened, but if it is decided definitely as torn to pieces, he has not to pay”.

V. 12. טרפה is in the middle between מיתה and מיתה .גנבה is always beyond his control, it is גנבה .אונס גמור is always preventable by his presence. טרפה is of doubtful nature, there are cases of wild animals with whom a watchman can cope, where even his mere presence could keep them away, but there are also cases which must be considered as completely אונס. Hence יביאהו עד (cf. above XVIII, 19, ’והבאת אתה את הדברים וגו and 22 והיה כל הדבר הגדול יביאו אליך, also Sam. I. 27,11 להביא גת), he has to present it, the whole occurrence, to the court through witnesses, so that it can decide whether it would have been possible for him to have saved the animal. If it is quite clear that it was really the prey of a wild animal, and in fact beyond his power to rescue it, then he is free from having to pay compensation (יביא עדים שנטרפה באונס Mechilta and also B.K. 10a). In a similar way, if other goods get lost or spoilt in the hands of custodians, e.g., porters, המעביר ממקום למקום, the court has to ascertain if the accident has to be considered as innocent, אונס, or as culpable carelessness. (B.M. 82b). But our Rabbis teach us there, as דרך טובים and אורחות צדיקים, that even if legally entitled to compensation, one should not only, not impose any payment from poor porters, but should even pay them their wages for the porterage.

A hirer has the same responsibility as a paid custodian. The use of the object is considered as equivalent to the charge for hiring and for the care and watch which has to be kept over it. שוכר כשומר שכר. This Halacha is contrary to another opinion expressed in the Gemora, which considers the use of the article is what is paid for, and the guarding of it, as service given freely without getting anything for it. (B.K. 80b).

V. 13. שואל, a borrower, of whom this verse treats, is the exact opposite of a שומר חנם. The unpaid custodian gives everything, the borrower gets everything. Accordingly, the former has the least responsibility towards his charge, has only to pay in cases of פשיעה, of gross negligence. The latter on the contrary, as is here stated, has to pay even if שבורה ומתה, even for completely unpreventable accidents, is חײב באונסין; he is only free from payment when מתה מחמת מלאכה if the object borrowed suffers or gets spoilt by using it for the purpose for which it was lent.

’בעליו אין עמו וגו. The Halacha teaches that this עמו does not refer to the borrowed object but to the person of the borrower, and hence means: Only if the lender at the time of the loan, is in no wise in the service of the borrower, is the latter responsible for compensation for whatever happens to the object. But if the lender, at the time of the loan, was in the paid or unpaid service of the borrower, the latter accepts no responsibility at all for the object, and even in cases of negligence need not pay, שאילה בבעלים פטור even פשיעה בבעלים פטור היה עמו בשעת שאילה אין צריך להיות עמו בשעת שבורה ומתה, היה עמו בשעת שבורה ומתה צריך להיות עמו בשעת שאילה (B.M. 95b). This law is mentioned here in connection with a שואל, but according to the Halacha (ibid. a) is equally applicable to all the four cases of custodians. This law is perhaps the most difficult of all the laws of Jewish Civil Law to comprehend. The simple literal rendering of the words of the text seems, in contrast, so plain, that, at first thought, it seems that hardly anywhere else can we find such a great contrast between the wording of the text and the interpretation which the Halacha actually gives to it. What is more natural than to take בעליו אין עמו and אם בעליו עמו to mean: If the owner was not present when the accident happened, the borrower has to pay, but (V.14) if the owner was present then he need not pay! And on the other hand, what is more incomprehensible than the law: If anybody borrows, hires or takes into his care, anything from somebody who is in his service (עמו במלאכה), he is free from having to pay compensation for anything that happens to it. The 223 שו״ת חות יאיר at end already points out how striking this Halacha is, and how simple the literal wording of the text is, and says it is an unsolved problem which he has vainly taxed his brains to make sense of, and to find the reason for. (Sect. 223 to end).

But, if we consider the case more closely, we find that what we thought was such a simple and plain way of taking the meaning of the text, would entail such an absurdity that it can not possibly be the real meaning of the words. According to that way of taking it, a שואל is only responsible for damages if the owner of the animal was not present when the accident occurred. But if the owner himself was present he could have looked after his property himself, and so the שואל should go free. Now, apart from the fact that if one has given any of one’s property into another’s charge, by that very act, one is relieving oneself from the duty of looking after it, and the full responsibility for looking after it, lies entirely with the custodian, and one can not think of any possible legal grounds why this duty should be any less if the owner happens to be present, apart from this, one must bear in mind that here in this case שבורה ומתה are mentioned, which are occurrences — such as death from natural causes — which can not be prevented by the presence of any human being at all, this, indeed, is the very essence of the idea אונסין גמורין, and regarding these, the presence or absence of the owner, or anybody else, can not make the slightest difference. So that it is quite impossible for the Law to mean, that if the animal dies a natural death in the presence of the owner, the custodian is free from payment, but if the animal dies a natural death without the owner being present, the custodian must pay compensation. This would be completely absurd, and it can not be supported that this is the meaning of the text. It is true that רב המנונא (B.M. 95b) does suggest such an interpretation of our text, but the Gemora quite definitely rejects it. If, on the other hand, in accordance with the Halacha, the modification בעליו עמו applies to all cases of custodians, we can quite well understand why the text mentions it only now, in connection with a שואל. Because just in that case, compensation has to be paid even for שבורה ומתה for אונסין גמורין in connection with which, the בעליו אין עמו can not be misunderstood to refer to the presence of the owner, and so that erroneous interpretation is obviated. That may also be why the case of נשבה is not mentioned, here, because in the case of armed robbery, the question of defence and repulse can be thought of, and it does not bear the character of אונס גמור so definitely.

So that nothing remains but to take the text as the Halacha applies it, as Rab. Ashi explains it in B.K. 96a. If somebody borrows something from, מעם רעהו, his fellow-man, but not at the same time, his fellow-man himself, — this is then made clear by adding בעליו אין עמו, — that the owner of the borrowed property is not himself at the time in the service of the borrower (that the borrower has not the use of the lender himself also). According to this, the בעליו אין עמו, as well as אם בעליו עמו can be the continued extension of the object of וכי ישאל: If anybody borrows something from his neighbour, but not his neighbour himself etc. etc., in exactly the same way as the Mishna B.K. 94a, ’השואל את הפרה ושאל בעליה עמה וכו. In any case, the Law itself is perfectly sure and definite, that; if the owner of any property handed over to the care of a custodian, is, at the time, in any relation whatsoever in service to the custodian, by accepting the property in his care, the custodian accepts none of the various responsibilities stipulated for the different kinds of custodians, and is not liable to pay compensation, even in cases of obvious carelessness, פשיעה בבעלים.
It only remains to try and find some insight into the reason and motive of this peculiar law. Perhaps the following deliberations may not be entirely unqualified to assist in gaining such insight.

If we consider the various responsibilities for which the payment of amounts to be paid are quite out of proportion to the benefits the custodian gets out of the property concerned, and on the other hand the responsibilities are of such a nature that, apart from cases of custodians, no compensation would be imposed. Compare the fees usually paid for custody, to the liability of the possibility of having to pay the whole value of the entrusted object; the free use of an animal for a day, to the liability of having to replace it, even if it dies a perfectly natural death in the house of the borrower; the responsibility of the paid custodian even for the theft by night out of properly locked premises, etc. etc. And even פשיעה, gross carelessness, apart from cases of custodians, does not entail legal responsibility for compensation (although moral responsibility is certainly there כדי לצאת ידי שמים). All the occurrences for which custodians are responsible are not cases of direct damage, but only indirect causation, only גרמא which מן התורה are outside the normal jurisdiction of the Law. For example הפורץ גדר בפני בהמת חברו, if somebody mischievously breaks down the wall or door of a stall, he is legally only responsible for the actual damage done to the wall, but for the escaped animal, he is פטור בדיני אדם וחײב בדיני שמים (B.K. 55b), and similar cases. It seems, accordingly, that in laying down the laws concerning the “four custodians”, the Torah wants to indicate the very definite idea of the responsibilities which anybody who enters into any such relationship must — in the absence of any specific agreement — implicitly accept as being inherent in such relationship. The שומר-relationship belongs after all, to those so-called voluntary jurisdictions whose responsibilities depend on free mutual agreement. The Law of the ארבעה שומרים is particularly the principle foundation for all social inter-relation. In a wider sense, all social inter-relation right up to the King, comes under the idea of שומר. It is all a matter of trust and confidence and service rendered. To the conscientious mind that would deal justly, the Torah shows here the whole severity of the obligations and responsibilities implicitly undertaken even in a service which is undertaken quite voluntarily and without pay e.g. in שומר חנם. It leaves it to the necessity for making a definite positive agreement when the service is undertaken, if anybody wishes to limit any of these responsibilities, as in B.K. 94a מתנה שומר חנם להיות פטור משבועה, ושואל להיות פטור מלשלם וכו׳. This does not come under the heading of מתנה על מה שכתוב בתורה, making a condition which is against something that is prescribed in the Torah, which condition would have no legal standing at all. For, firstly, there is a rule, that, in matters which are purely monetary, any stipulation may be made, כל מתנה וכו׳ בדבר שבממון תנאו קײם; and here, as the Gemora puts it מעיקרא לא שעבד נפשיה there was no real obligation on him to accept the service in the first instance.

Now the Torah seems to assume that if anybody has placed himself at the disposal of another, and then hands him over some object, he implicitly imposes no greater responsibility for the object than is borne towards himself. If a man engages another to work for him, and the workman, while in his service, suffers injury to his person, the former is not legally bound to pay compensation. So that if he takes into his care anything from his workman, he implicitly undertakes no greater responsibility for the object. So that on the other hand a positive definite arrangement must be made for greater responsibility.

There is one single case in which the responsibilities of custodians are imposed even in the case of בעלים (employers), and this seems to confirm the probability that our interpretation is correct. This is the case of שליחות יד, that if the custodian has simply laid his hand on the entrusted property with the intention illegally to use it for himself, he immediately loses the status of a custodian and acquires that of a גזלן and is חײב באונסין (B.K. 41b 346, 1, קצות החשן). Now שליחות יד is a direct laying of hands on the object which can not implicitly be excluded from compensation by comparison to the responsibilities held with regard to the person, as any laying of hands on the person of the workman, unconditionally entails legal liability. So that, in this exception we can find a very illuminating confirmation of the theory we ventured to give for the underlying principle of שאילה בבעלים.

אם שכיר הוא בא בשכרו. If the animal is a hired one, the hirer has acquired the duty of a custodian by paying for its use. The advantage is not one-sided, כל הנאה is not שלו as it is in the case of שואל but it is נהנה ומהנה, the advantage is mutual as in the case of שומר שכר so that the responsibilities are similar to those of a שומר שכר; he is חײב בגנבה ואבדה and פטור באונסין (Mechilta).

V. 15—16. From the condition mentioned in V.16 that the marriage of the maid is dependent on the disposition of the father, it is clear that it deals with a girl who is still at the disposition of her father, i.e., one who has not yet reached sexual maturity. This is also clear from the complemental case discussed in Deut. 22,28, where the girl is described as נערה, a designation which, as we have already explained on Gen. 24,16, always includes קטנה and excludes בוגרת. We have, accordingly, the case of the seducing of a young girl, not yet of age, still under the protection of her father. The fine imposed in V.16 is to be paid to the father, as it is expressly stated in the parallel case quoted above ונתן וגו׳ לאבי הנערה חמשים כסף (Deut. 22,29). The whole case can accordingly come under the idea of גנבה theft. Just as the general respect for the Law should be such, that, trusting to it, people need not keep their property directly under their eyes, and the thief who takes mocking advantage of this trust, has to make amends for it by paying a fine (in addition to repaying the theft), קנס, in the same way fathers are not to have to guard the innocence of their daughters by lock and bolt, they are to be able to trust to the general respect for morality; and anyone taking advantage of this trust and misusing it, to rob a child of her innocence, has to make amends for the theft by paying a fine, if the father will not allow him to marry the girl and right the wrong he has done her.

אשר לא אורשה. The idea of ארוסין does not exist in non-Jewish marriage laws, so we have no word in English for it. “Engagement” is not the same thing. An engagement is only the solemn promise of the intention to marry, but it does not yet constitute any foundation of an actual married state. Sin with an engaged person is no adultery. But an ארוסה does belong exclusively to the man, she is betrothed to him by קידושין but not yet married to him, the sin of a נערה מאורסה is considered even more serious adultery; all that is still lacking is the going over into the house of a husband which will be accomplished by נשואין.

מהר ימהרנה; as the root of מַהֵר to hasten, also related to מחר from which we get מחִיר the means of purchase, barter or exchange (and מָחָר the day which will come in the place of the departing day, the morrow). מהר, in the Kal, seems to mean, to eagerly strive for something, and specifically to get most intimate possession of somebody, to endeavour to get married to somebody. (We find it used in Psalms (XVI,4) with reference to deities אחר מהרו, those that have striven to attach themselves to another god). Hence מׂהַר that which a man settles on the woman for her marriage to him, the marriage settlement; that which, according to Jewish marriage laws, the husband assigns to his wife in the כתובה. Even according to the generally accepted view that כתובה דרבנן it seems that what later on became the prescribed law תנאי ב״ד, had originally been the accepted and general custom which was only later raised to an absolute binding law. In both cases, here and in Deut. 22,18, the fine (here stated to be reckoned by the amount of the מהר) is imposed in lieu of the marriage which really should have taken place; and the fine only consists in paying that the which ordinarily—whether according to custom or law — is paid at the breaking-up of a marriage by death or divorce, here has to be paid instead of entering into the marriage. In the case quoted in Deut. the fine is fixed at fifty shekels. In the laws laid down in Pea 8,8, ’מי שיש לו מאתים זוז לא יטול לקט וגו, “he who has two hundred Zuzim (which equal fifty shekels of the currency of the time, סלע מדינה which is only one eighth of the value of the Tyrian currency כסף אורי in which all the silver coins mentioned in the Torah are reckoned) in his possession may not avail himself of the municipal distribution of charity”. According to this Mishna, then, the fifty shekels of the Torah would suffice to provide the bare necessities in food and clothing for one person for eight years. So that such a sum would ensure the existence of a person for some years, without earning anything at all, living on capital. Used as capital for doing business, it could be considered as sufficient for a whole life, as the Mishna quoted above, goes on to say, that a business capital of fifty Zuzim i.e., a quarter of the amount, is considered sufficient for earning one’s living מי שיש לו חמשים זוז והוא נושא ונותן בהם הרי זה לא יטול. We can assume that a girl must be about twenty years old before she could invest such a capital in some business where she could earn an independent living. Then, from the time when, according to the legal normal age for a girl to leave the narrow close confines of her father’s care, and to rely more on herself, viz., 2½ years of age, she would be able to live on her capital for seven years, and still have enough in hand to start herself in business. So that with the whole sum, a father could assure the whole future of his child for life.

V. 17—19. כשף .מכשפה seems to be related to ישב and קשב on the one hand, and to כזב on the other. The מכשף wants to מישב and מקשב the forces of Nature “to soothe and enchant them” and “to make them obedient to his orders”, but he is מכזב with it all, “only practices deception with all of it”.

לא תחיה. Here, and in V.18 and 19, the sentence of death is expressed in three different terms: יחרם, מות יומת, לא תחיה and this may be to characterise three kinds of motives which can bring about the sentence of death. לא תחיה, the crime, considered isolated and in itself, and committed in isolation, may not in itself be deserving of death, but you, the Nation, in its representative, the court, may not let the criminal live. He must die out of consideration for the pernicious effect of his crime on the community. מות יומת, the criminal has forfeited his life by his crime, without any consideration of its influence on the community. יחרם by his crime, the criminal has forfeited the right to live in human society. חרם literally a net. (Habakuk 1,16).

So החרים literally, to put into a net, to bring completely out of all contact with all other existence i.e., to cut off by death. If we consider the three crimes which are here given as types for these three categories, we can see how, from their innermost nature, they comply with what we have assumed to be the reason for the differentiation. כישוף according to our way of understanding it (adopting it from Maimonides) כזב, nothing but deception, nothing but an assumed mastery of God’s Laws of Nature, would be rather a folly to be smiled at, or a madness to be pitied, than a crime to be punished, were it not that it exercises such a deep demoralising influence on the community. כישוף has always been practiced only in the service of immorality and crime. For matters which were in accord with the Deity one could trust to the intervention of Divine Providence. Only for matters where one knew that one was in opposition to the Divine Will was one driven to try to find a by-way, some indirect means by which to gain one’s end without the assistance of, and against the Laws of a benign Providence. It was in response to this demand that the wizard, the מכשף, worked. The Gemora (Sanhedrin 67b) aptly explains the word מכשף as an abbreviation of שמכחישין בפמליא של מעלה which can equally well mean: “They deny that all the forces of Nature are under the control of a higher power, the Divine Will”, or “they allege that they can paralyze the forces of Nature which are controlled by God alone, and which fulfil His Will alone”. It is to show how ridiculous in itself such a procedure is, that here, the only time in the scriptures, מכשף is written in the feminine מכשפה, whereas elsewhere in the תנ״ך it always occurs in the masculine. The מכשף — whose supposed art is quite usually practiced by any old woman, and this also shows the absurdity of its pretensions — as such does not deserve death, so it does not say מות יומת, but nevertheless לא תחיה, because of the erroneous ideas which he spreads, and the devastating effect he has on morality.
שוכב עם בהמה, is the very opposite. Society in general is in no ways affected by this crime. Nevertheless the crime in itself touches the vilest depths of degradation, hence מות יומת.

זבח לאלהים. We have the general rule which is applied throughout the Torah: — דבר שיצא מן הכלל ללמד ,ללמד על הכלל כלו יצא. When any general rule is expressed by one special example of it, this example is to be taken merely as an example, and the rule is to apply generally. So זביחה here is meant to be an example of all procedures that are prescribed to take place with offerings that are brought to the One True God. It refers to all עבודות פנים (all the sacrificial procedures of the Temple I.L.) i.e., המקטר ,המזבח, המנסך, under which הזורק is also included (Sanhedrin 60b). If anyone does any of these particular acts, which are prescribed for showing allegiance to the One God, (or השתחויה which in this respect is considered equivalent) to any other god or deity whatsoever, even if this particular service is not usually paid to this particular god, אפילו שלא כדרכה, and even if he does not wish to deny thereby the service due to God Himself, but only to attribute some divine power beside Him, שיתוף (yea, even, according to the Mechilta, if he has no real intention of honouring the ע״ז, as long as he does any עבודות פנים to anything else) he is thereby actually denying the very fundamental principle in which the whole of Jewry has its roots. Hence יחרם he is condemned to be excluded from this Jewry by the annihilation of his existence. The actual mode by which the death penalty is exacted is the same for all these three crimes viz., סקילה (the reason for this will be apparent when we come to consider, and go into, the question of the four different methods of inflicting the death penalty in Jewish Jurisdiction). — That the idea of שיתוף, that not only a complete denial of God, but that even a belittlement of the conception of His unique Oneness which must exclude everything else, by giving divine attributes to anything besides Him, is equally forbidden and equivalent to denying Him, is here expressed by the addition of the words בלתי לה׳ לבדו.

V. 20. ’וגר לא תונה וגו, is in close connection with the preceding verse. There we were told that even a native-born Jew of the purest descent loses his right of existence in the Jewish Community the moment he departs in the least degree from the purity of the basic principle of the Jewish conception of God. And in contrast, a heathen born and bred, as soon as he attaches himself to Judaism by simply acknowledging the Jewish principle of the conception of God, can demand the fullest equality and the full equal rights in Law with any Jew. By the juxtaposition of these two verses, the great, oft-repeated in the Torah, basic law is laid down, that it is not race, not descent, not birth or country or property, altogether nothing external or due to chance, but simply and purely the inner spiritual and moral worth of a human being, which gives him all the rights of a man and of a citizen. This basic principle is further ensured against neglect by the additional motive כי גרים הײתם בארץ מצרים. It seems that this has not exactly the same meaning as the ’ואתם ידעתם את נפש הגר וגו, of V.9, of the following chapter. Here it says simply and absolutely ’כי גרים הײתם וגו, your whole misfortune in Egypt was that you were גרים “foreigners”, “aliens”, there, as such, according to the views of other nations, you had no right to be there, had no claim to rights of settlement, home, or property. Accordingly, you had no equal rights in appeal against unfair or unjust treatment. As aliens you were without any rights in Egypt, out of that grew all your עבדות and ענוי, your slavery and wretchedness. Therefore beware, so runs the warning, from making rights in your own State conditional on anything other than on that simple humanity which every human being as such bears within him. With any limitation of these human rights the gate is opened to the whole horror of Egyptian mishandling of human beings.

ינה .לא תונה (phonetically related to כנע, to humble, to humiliate, כנה to call something not by its right name, גנה in rabbinic Hebrew, to villify) means to be illegally deprived of material or spiritual possessions, hence (a) in business matters, in sale or purchase to be overcharged, אונאת ממון (Levit. 25,14) וכי תמכרו ממכר וגו׳ אל תונו איש את אחיו; (b) in social intercourse, אונאת דברים to be hurt by words. Accordingly the complete implication of וגר לא תונה would be:- Neither by words nor by deeds shall you hurt an alien. In B.M. 58b it is taken to refer primarily to hurting his feelings by words אונאת דברים. We shall have to draw attention on V.21 & 22 which are closely connected with our V.20, to the change from the singular to the plural in the person addressed. We believe that when the singular is used it addresses either the individual as such, or the nation as a whole, also the representatives of the nation as a whole, whereas the plural form addresses the nation in all its individual members, has the social, rather than the national unity in mind. (Compare Numbers X, where a single trumpet call was used to summon the leaders of the nation, but two were used to call the whole community in all its members). Accordingly here the admonition against differentiating against strangers, is directed primarily to the State as such.

It — the Jewish State — is not to practice any אונאה against foreigners, because they are aliens, it is not to impose heavier taxes or grant lesser rights than it does to the native-born; ולא תלחצנו and in no ways is it to restrict them in the free exercise of any means of gaining their livelihood. From Numbers 22,25 and Kings II. 6,32, we know that לחץ primarily means a restricting of space, a restriction. Hence, literally “you shall not restrict him”.

V. 21. אלמנה from אלם to be dumb; יתום from יתם phonetically related to the rabbinic term גדם mutilated hand, קטם to break off. The widow has lost her mouth in her husband, has nobody to speak for her any longer, the orphan has lost his hand in his father, he has no longer anybody to depend on, or to lead him. ענה (see Gen. 16,6) to make somebody feel his עוני, his dependent position, to misuse his weakness and lack of protection. It says ’כל אלמנה וגו not only poor, even rich widows and orphans are easier to be taken advantage of and misused, than other people. — לא תענון, whereas the hampering and reducing the rights of aliens is quite legal in most countries, and on this account the address in the previous verse was in the singular, to warn the Jewish State, there is hardly any law to be found anywhere which sanctions any reducing of the general rights in the case of widows and orphans. But in society, amongst people, in the intercourse of man and man, they are bereft of anybody to stand up for them, to protect them, guide and advise them, and so are exposed to being wronged and humiliated. Hence in their case the Torah addresses primarily the members of the community לא תענון in the plural, “thou shalt not misuse their weakness, or make them feel the weakness of their position”.

V. 22—23. אותו !אם ענה תענה אותו primarily referring to the orphan, but in its meaning also including אלמנה. Woe if thou too, the State, misuse them, let them feel that they have lost the one who stands up for them and looks after them! Woe, if widows and orphans suffer amongst the people, and do not even get support, and their rights upheld, by the official protectors of the public rights, as Isaiah so bitterly reproaches (I,13), יתום לא ישפטו וריב אלמנה לא יבא אליהם. Woe, if they finally have to cry up to Me, for I will surely give ear unto them, and I shall make the State and the community pay dearly for it, if their weak and unprotected ones have to appeal to Me before they can find justice.

The dialogue between Rabbi Ishmael and Rabbi Simeon as they were being led out to suffer martyrdom teaches us what Jewish judges and Jewish consciences took this warning to mean. רבי לבי יוצא said R. Simeon to R. Ishmael on the way “Rabbi my heart fails me” שאיני יודע על מה אני נהרג “for I can not think what I can have done to deserve death”. On which R. Ishmael answered מימיך בא אדם אצלך לדין או לשאלה “think, has it never occurred that somebody came to you, to decide what was right or to ask a שאלה ,ועכבתו עד שתהא שותה כוסך ונוטל סנדלך או עוטף טליתך, and you kept them waiting until you had finished your drink or changed your shoes or thrown your best robe over your shoulders, אמרה תורה אם ענה תענה, אחד ענוי מרובה ואחד עינוי מועט. The Torah says ענה תענה doubly, to teach that in making people feel their dependent position, it makes no difference whether it is in great matters or little things, in all cases it is forbidden, אמר לו נחמתני רבי “You have comforted me” (now I can take my punishment gladly.) answered Rabbi Simeon (Mechilta).

V. 24. ’אם כסף תלוה וגו. If we compare the places where לוה occurs, not referring to loans, in the overwhelming majority of cases it is convincingly clear that it refers to the attachment of one person to another which furthers the welfare of that person. So in Gen. 29,34 of the attachment of the loving husband to his wife, of the attachment of the Levites to the Priests in taking part in the service of the Temple, the attachment of proselytes and of the other nations to Israel and to God (Isaiah 14,1 and LVI,3,6, and Esther 9,27). According to this הַלוֶה in the Hiphil would mean to attach somebody to oneself to further his interests, to attach someone to oneself so that he gets the benefit of your personality, not so that he loses his own independence by this attachment, but that it is to make him more independent. כסף through money, inasmuch as you give him the use of some of your money. The real direct object of the לוה is not כסף but העני ,עמי, which accordingly is construed with כסף .את is the means, through, or by means of, money, as חרב תאכלו, Isaiah 1,20 etc. So that the sentence runs literally: “If, by money you draw My people — the poor who are part of you — nearer to you”, etc. ’ואת עמי וגו the words את העני are clearly in apposition to את עמי. You are actually lending to the poor, but in lending to the poor you are lending to “My People”. In the עני עמך in the poor who are nationally joined to you, who are to rely on your support and assistance, you are always to think of “עמי״, My social community. Realising the implication of עם) עם means living one with the other, from עם — with I.L.) you are merely doing your duty in giving loans (cf. מלוה ה׳ חונן דל Prov. 19,16). The original basic calling of Israel was ולקחתי אתכם לי לעם, to become a social community of God. Not the service in the Temple, but the social life they were to build up under the rule of the Torah, was to stamp them as “the People of God”, to reveal to the world the glory of a life lived under God’s Rule. The most natural outcome of this calling, the most direct result, which is both the basis and the acknowledgment of the calling to be ’עם ה, is this whole law of הלואה. It is not the abstract theory of fair dealing that it stresses, but it brings into concrete practice the idea of building up our Jewish community on the thought that everything that we possess really belongs to God. It is not משפט but צדקה, the idea of doing one’s duty.

First of all, לא תהיה לו כנשה. We have already worked out on Gen. 32,33, that נשה means causing a loss to somebody, a loss either of power or forces, or of rights, or of possessions. Hence, anyone who comes to a person and demands restitution for having suffered such a loss is called -נשה ב. Now inasmuch as it does not say here לא תהיה ב ו כנשה but ל ו כנשה the Torah here demands not only, that (a) a creditor shall not proceed against the debtor to the utmost extent that the strict application of the law would entitle him, but that (b) apart from legal proceedings, he is not to show that he is a creditor of this debtor, that, in general it may not be apparent from his demeanor towards the debtor that he has an unsettled claim against him. Hence, the prohibition to take legal proceedings against, or otherwise to bring pressure on, a debtor who is without means, or who is temporarily unable to meet his obligations. Hence, the instruction, even for the court itself, not to exact the very last penny which is legally due, but to leave the debtor the means for his daily existence, and for his clothing, bedding, and tools for his work. The Torah in Levit. 27,8 takes a similar attitude to the Sanctuary (the treasurer of the Mikdosh) accepting the full value of a vow, where the payment of it would entail the מך, the ruin of the person, ואם מך הוא מערכך but enough must be left, here too, for a sufficiency in the above-mentioned necessities of life, (see Ch. M. 97, 2,23 et seq.) מסדרין לבעל חוב. And finally, hence the great teaching of Rabbi Dimi: — כי אתא רב דימי אמר מנין לנשה בחברו מנה ויודע שאין לו, שאסור לעבור לפניו, ת״ל לא תהיה לו כנושה, רבי אמי ורבי אסי דאמרי תרוײהו כאילו דנו בשני דינים, שנאמר הרכבת אנוש לראשנו באנו באש ובמים. “If anybody has a claim on a person, and knows that this latter is not in a position to meet it, he must go out of the way of that person, to avoid arousing the feeling of shame in his mind, for the Torah says לא תהיה לו כנושה ‘thou shalt not appear unto him as one demanding the payment of a debt’. Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi added: — ‘Were he to do so, it would be as if he had killed him twice over, as if he had drowned him and burnt him, as it says (in Ps. 66,12), ‘thou hast delivered us into the power of Man, into fire and water are we come’.” So that whereas in non-Jewish circles the debtor carefully keeps out of the way of his creditor, the Torah teaches the other way round, to spare the feelings of the poorer man.

לא תשימון עליו נשך. The first half of the verse, addressed to the lender, who usually is an individual, is in the singular person, here the address is made to the community, to all the members of the community, looking on them as עם, and this idea is still further stressed by the paragogic ן. Thou, the Jewish Community, as such, being such, shalt not impose any interest on borrowers. From this, one can see at once that Jewish Law does not consider this law of interest from the point of view that there is anything intrinsically wrong in interest itself. It is not antagonistic to the idea of right, but it is definitely against the principle on which Jewish Communal life is to be founded. If the Jewish lender were to be allowed to consider himself purely as נשה, as one who, completely out of his own good will, places the use of his money for a certain time, at the disposal of somebody else, he should be allowed to take payment for the temporary loss of his money, or the use of it. But this is exactly what he may not do. It is neither entirely his own money that he is lending, nor is the decision to lend it entirely a matter of his own goodwill. His money is to be regarded as belonging also to God, to lend it is a duty, and the borrower is not simply an individual, he is עמי, an integral member of the community of God, of the community which God wants to be built up by the magic power of “duty”. When God first restored the Egyptian slaves to the status of human beings, and invested them with the right to own property, he cemented them together into a community, not by the force of necessity but by the command to attend to duty. It is not the relatively poor man who has to search for a rich man, but the richer man who has to look around for a neighbour who can make use of his surplus wealth, and much more, and in a much higher sense does the rich man need the poor man, than the poor man needs the rich one. The poor man only finds the rich man a support for his material necessity, but the rich man finds in him the means for carrying out his highest spiritual and moral calling, to render to God, the tribute of acknowledging that every halfpenny of our possession is lent to us by God. When God raised us into the position of being able to possess property of our own, He kept back for Himself the right of the disposition of our property, and in the first place, He placed עמו, the community to be founded by the spirit of His Torah, as the beneficiaries. This is the spirit of Zedaka, the Jewish idea of duty which right up to today, has created the miracle of the existence of the Jewish people; and the highest form of this Zedaka is הלואה, the duty to lend (see notes on Deut. 15,8). But this is also the spirit which makes the right to interest disappear.

So the duty of lending money without interest is one of the rocks of that granite base on which Jewish social life rests. Carrying out this duty is at the same time one of those great acts of acknowledgment by which God wants our allegiance to Him to be sealed by acts of sacrifice in daily life. The less the law against interest clashes with the dictates of our natural sense of what is right, the more the simple idea of fairness justifies it, the less actual wrong there is in demanding interest, the more does the prohibition of interest join the ranks of those laws which, like Sabbath, Schemita and Jobel are to be evidence and reminders that it is God Who rules over the world and over Israel. Just as the giving up of work on Sabbath, agriculture and the demand for payment of debts in Schemita Year, the title to bought property and persons in Yobel Year, all proclaim God as the real Master and Owner of the world, so the giving up of the perfectly justified demand for interest on loans is ordained, to show that we are to consider God as the real Owner and Master of our movable property too. Hence also the more detailed laws of loans free of interest (Levit. 25,38) conclude with the words אני ה׳ אלהיכם אשר הוצאתי אתכם מארץ מצרים לתת לכם את ארץ כנען להיות לכם לאלהים, where express reference is made to our submission to God’s Will as expressed in His Torah as the condition on which, and the object for which, He gave us our freedom and independent possession of property.

Hence also the saying of Rab. Jose. “See how blind are they that lend on interest. If otherwise one is called godless one is cut to the quick, but these people bring pen and ink, scribes and witnesses and have a document written, signed and witnessed stating: So and so has denied the God of Israel, כפר באלהי ישראל! (B.M. 71a).

The fact that the prohibition against interest on loans is not to be looked at simply from the concrete effect it has on social conditions, but that it really is to be looked at from the point of view of an act of acknowledgment of God, seems evident from the fact that not only is it forbidden to take interest, but in quite equal degree the Torah expressly prohibits the payment of it. (Deut. 23,20 & 21). Nevertheless, the whole effect which the prohibition of interest has on the whole structure of social life is incalculable. The preceding laws work against all the inequality of rights which birth and fate tend to bring, in ordinary social life. This law takes away the worst effect of the power of money, that most potent factor in causing social inequality. It breaks the too great power of capital. If this prohibition is strictly kept, all capital is in itself dead and unproductive, and can only be of use by wedding it to labour. It raises labour to the primary and essential factor of social well-being. Capital is forced to recognise the equality of labour. The rich man must either bring his otherwise dead capital to production by his own powers of work, or he must associate himself with the power of labour of the poor man, share profit and loss with him, and in his own interests further the interests of labour. Every crisis of labour becomes to an even higher degree a crisis of capital, and capital can never make profit from the ruin of labour. The possibility of that shocking contrast, where the wretchedness of the labouring class is rampant right next to the most luxurious opulence, has the ground cut away from under its feet by this law.

We have already remarked that Jewish Law in no way denies the natural justification of interest in itself, and only positively forbids it out of the principle of Jewish social united life. One could argue, that, in the modern way of looking at it, money may be considered as a utility object, and so one could bring interest on loans under the heading of “hiring” (שכירות), payment for the temporary use of which — as rent for a house, the use of a car etc. — is allowed under Jewish Law. But this argument overlooks the fact that in the case of a hired object, it remains all the time the acual property of the owner, the hirer uses the property itself, and pays for the wear and tear, whereas money lent, immediately becomes the property of the borrower, מלוה להוצאה נתנה for which he really only owes the lender the actual value of it, and the lender is only making use or profit out of an object which is his own property (cf. ב״מ 69b).

But, if the Torah raises interest-free loans to the highest duty of social brotherhood, and protects the borrower against harsh treatment or even embarrassment, on the other hand, Jewish Law makes the punctual and regular repayment of debts an absolute duty for the debtor, forbids any careless or speculative use of borrowed money, and advises everybody rather to refuse to lend anything to a frivolous borrower than to place himself in the position of becoming a pressing creditor (Ch. M. 97,4).

V. 25. More precise details of the laws regarding pledges are laid down in Deut. 24,6, 10 et seq. They are dictated by the utmost consideration for the rights of person and home. Here it says אם חבל תחבל, which the Gemora (B.M. 31b) takes to mean, “in whatever way the pledge has come into your possession”, even if in a perfectly legal and correct manner, it makes no difference, these laws apply. (B.M. 31b). The idea expressed in the word חבל does imply some interposition on the part of the creditor, who, by this act wants to “bind” (חבל a rope, a string), the object or the debtor, to himself. Accordingly, this law only applies to a pledge which is taken after the loan is already existing, a משכון שלא בשעת הלואה, but if the debtor hands over something as a pledge at the time the loan is made, משכון בשעת הלואה, the creditor is not bound to the temporary return here ordered.

’עד בא השמש וגו. It is of course assumed that חבל תחבל, as a legal proceeding, usually took place by day. Hence: If you have taken the garment of your debtor as a pledge in daytime, you are to give it back to him again till sunset, and only take it away in the night. It is clear that it is speaking of כסות יום day wear. Apart from this, if we compare the places where שלמה occurs, we find there is not a single one which can refer to anything else than a garment. This is also indicated by the word’s relationship to צלם, the figure, so that שלמה would mean cloth adapted to the human figure, whereas שמלה is used, referring also to a garment, but also quite definitely to a rug or cloth with which to cover or envelop oneself, to bed-clothes, i.e. coverings generally, see Gen. 9,23, Deut. 22,17; Judges 8,25; Sam. I. 21,10; Prov. 30,4. Hence the Mechilta explains the שמלתו לעורו of the next verse to mean “shirt”. So that if, in the parallel case in Deut. 24,13, it says ושכב בשלמתו and not שמלתו it must mean his nightshirt and not his bedcoverings, and that would make it obligatory to return nightclothes for the night, although the necessity for this does not appear so pressing, as one could always wear a day garment for the night in a case of necessity. כסות and שמלה describe the two purposes of wearing clothes, protective covering and veiling “the animal body”.

V.26. במה ישכב. As the preceding part of the verse speaks of day-clothes, this question must refer to a different class of objects, to the requirements of his sleeping-place, מצע his bedding or blankets, as the Mechilta takes it. So that with this question a fresh train of thought must be introduced, something like, “besides, on what shall he sleep?” You have to ask yourself this, too, and act accordingly. That which he requires for the day you must give him back for the day, and the requirements of the night for the night.

We have already referred on V.24 to the law, that even when the court is called on to enforce the repayment of loans, it has to leave an impoverished debtor the necessities of life in bedding, clothing etc. etc. So that there, the question of having to return these things does not arise at all. But here it is speaking of a pledge, which does not constitute payment, but is only to ensure payment. The pledge is not taken as repayment but only as security. Nevertheless the creditor does at once acquire a right in the pledge, inasmuch as if he holds a pledge, the debt is not automatically cancelled in the “Schemita”, and on the death of the debtor the pledge does not pass over to his heirs, but remains a possible means for the eventual repayment of the debt. (Ch. M. 97,16). — כסותה with ה feminine, “feel his weakness”.

This return of a pledge at every time of necessity is a tiresome duty which makes its conscientious fulfilment all the more significant and important. Hence the man who faithfully carries out his duties is pictured by Ezekiel (XVIII,7) by the words חבלתו חוב ישיב “he returns his pledge with the punctuality of a debt he has to pay”.

V. 27. קלל .לא תאור ,תקלל the opposite of כבד, weight and honour, would refer primarily to the “weight” i.e., to the influence and external position a man occupies, literally, to wish that somebody should become “light”, lose his “weight”. ארר on the other hand, related to ערר, to be lonely, unfruitful, dried-up, and to חרר, to be consumed by fire, is to wish adversity, ruin, to the person. In a judge, it is not so much the person as the position, the office which stands in one’s way, whereas in a נשיא it is the superiority in wealth and personal dignity that is a thorn in one’s side. Hence the curse that is directed to a judge is expressed by קללה, to a נשיא by מארה. The curse in the one case is incited by defiance, in the other by envy. — נשיא בעמך, בעושה מעשה עמך (Sanhedrin 85a), provided the prince does not behave as if he was something other than of the people, but behaves as being one of the people and subordinates himself, as the people have to, to the dictates of the Torah.

V. 28. מלאתך ודמעך. In Temura, 4a, מלאתך is explained as בכורים and דמעך as תרומה and the prohibition לא תאחר taken to mean that בכורים (מלאה) are not to be given after דמע) .(דמע) תרומה, a tear, metaphorically used of that of olives and grapes, i.e., wine and must, cf. Greek, Dakruon tone Dendrone (Theophr); arborum lacrimae Plin. 11,6 I.L.), that in general, the prescribed sequence for the dues to be paid to the כהן, the לוי, or to be reserved for consumption in Jerusalem are to be strictly kept.

מעשר שני is not to be given before מעשר ראשון ,מעשר ראשון not before תרומה and תרומה not before ביכורים .ביכורים are called מלאה, because the duty to separate them falls already במלאה when the fields are “full”, when the ripe produce fills the fields, already before the harvest (cf. פן תוקדש המלאה). Why תרומה is called דמע is unexplained. Rashi’s explanation because תרומה מדמעת, is refuted by תוספות (Temura 4a) as being untenable, as this characteristic of תרומה is only דרבנן. Apart from this, this expression would then hardly be used to differentiate it from בכורים as a mixture of ביכורים in חולין has also the same effect. תוספות does give another explanation, that תרומה is called דמע because תרומה can also be given in a liquid form, e.g., wine, while ביכורים must only be given as fruit in natura, as grapes. But this also seems quite a secondary matter and hardly to be used as a specific differentiation between them. Perhaps the following might be a possible explanation. The characteristic difference between ביכורים and תרומה is, that the obligation to give ביכורים arises as soon as the fruit ripens on its stalk or on the tree, whereas תרומה only falls due when the human work on the fruit is completed, at גמר מלאכה. (In Temura 4a there seems to be a printer’s error both in Rashi and in תוספות. Rashi explains ולהכי קרי לביכורים מלאה משום דלאלתר שנתמלאת התבואה ונגמרת מלאכתה הוקבעה לביכורים. The word מלאכתה should surely be omitted. It is not the completion of the human work, but of Nature’s work that brings the obligation of ביכורים. Rashi himself mentions this in his commentary on the Torah: — חובה המוטלת עליך כשתתמלא תבואתך להתבשל, והם ביכורים). So that the duty of giving ביכורים is incurred when Nature, that of תרומה when Man, has completed the work on the fruit. Hence ביכורים are called מלאה, after the time when the fruit still untouched by the hand of man, still “fills” the fields. מלאה means the whole produce-abundance of the fields (Deut. 22,9, where מלאה is explained as הזרע אשר תזרע ותבואת הכרם). But תרומה is דמע. As the juice of grapes is called דם ענבים “grape blood”, so here is it descriptively called “grape-tears”. There is probably no other fruit which is so “mishandled” by man, as grapes are. They are “trodden” and “pressed”. (Possibly wine gets its name ײן from יון having the same meaning as ינה, pressing out, extortion). To represent the idea of גמר מלאכה, the completed human work on the fruit, as opposed to מלאה the untouched fruit on a tree or stalk, a better representative than wine could hardly be found, or a more pertinent description than: דמע, a tear.

בכור בניך. This law has already been given above (Ex. XIII) and is further supplemented (Numb. 18,15 et seq.) by the law of redemption on the thirtieth day. Taken in connection with the preceding מלאתך ודמעך and the succeeding ’כן תעשה וגו it seems that here, it has reference to that law. Just as the duty to give ביכורים and תרומה only occurs when the status of ripeness and maturity is reached, so the dedication of the firstborn, which the act of redemption expresses, is only to take place on the thirtieth day, when the child has passed the first period of maturity of his life. The thirtieth day is always taken as the decisive symptom of the ability to live in all cases where it is doubtful if a child can live. On the thirtieth day of its life a child is also externally proved to be a בן קײמא. To this then follows: —

V. 29. ’כן תעשה וגו, the law that similarly the giving over of first-born animals to a כהן has to take place only after a suitable period. This is fixed at fifty days for a שור and thirty for a צאן (Bechoroth 26b). This difference in the period also explains the disjointed כן תעשה לשורך לצאנך without the conjunction ו. Until this time, the owner of a בכור has to feed and look after it, חײב ליטפל בו. Nevertheless if the animal is fit for sacrifice, and the כהן wishes to offer it earlier, it may be handed over to him during this period. Hence the law that follows: שבעת ימים. Just as thirty days, for human beings, so does seven days form the first period of life, and decide in cases of doubt, whether the animal is considered as able to live or not. Also, in cases where there is no doubt, it is only after attaining this period of life, that the ability to continue to live can be visibly recognised. So that this may be the reason for the law that the human firstborn may not be redeemed before thirty days after birth, and an animal may not be brought as an offering before seven days. It is mentioned here with reference to בכור and in Levit. 22,27 regarding all offerings. Before the lapse of the seven days, the animal as far as its fitness for sacrifice is concerned, is called מחוסר זמן (See משנה למלך ה׳ איסורי מזבח 3, 8).

V. 30. It does not say אנשים קדושים but אנשי קדש, men of an holy calling; a man is not yet קדוש if he does not eat טרפה, but he can then more easily become so. מאכל טרפה gets in the way of our accomplishing our holy calling. It is more difficult for one who eats טרפה to climb to that spiritual moral height which we all should reach. This reason ’אנשי קדש וגו with which the prohibition of טרפה — the first dietary law of the Torah after Sinai — is introduced, immediately refutes all the theories which have been — and are being — put forward, of dietic, climatic, and contemporary reasons for the dietary laws. (With the idea, of course, of abrogating them).

It is not our bodily health, but our spiritual and moral purity and capability, our קדושה, our being ready, our becoming ready, our remaining ready, for everything which is godly and pure, which is the expressed object of the Lawgiver of these laws.
This is clearly mentioned here, as well as in Levit. Chap. XI, Chap. 20,25 et seq., and in Deut. 14,21 — everywhere expressly impressed where details of these laws are given.

טרפה. That טרסה does not mean a “torn animal” is evident from Levit. 7,24 וחלב נבלה וחלב טרפה and Levit. 17,15 and XXII,8 נבלה טרפה. as “torn” comes under the heading of נבלה (see Kings I. 13,24 et seq.). The use of טִרֶף for food, and הטריף as nourishing or supplying with nourishment, also the general use of the root טרף for the legal seizing of goods from the possession of a buyer if the goods had been pledged, טורף לקוחות, and the quick snatching up of lots out of a box טרף בקלפי (Yoma 4,1), all go to show that טרף does not designate so much the actual destructive act, as the final result and physiological importance which wounding has on a living creature. Accordingly, it does not mean so much tearing to pieces, as snatching to oneself, seizing something for food, and that is the idea of טרפה (See Rashi B.M. 41a). As long as a living creature is unwounded, every part of it belongs to itself, all parts of it are there to serve the whole. A fatal wound snatches the body away from its purpose of serving the individual animal, and changes its purpose to that of serving as nourishment for its original elements, the earth, or for other animals. So that a טרפה animal is one which is already taken over to be nourishment for another sphere. As such it belongs to the שדה, as physical and chemical nourishment for Nature, and is forbidden as nourishment for human beings, who belong to a holy morally free calling, who are אנשי קדש, whose act of feeding — an act which on the surface is quite on par for them with all other living creatures — itself should be a morally free-willed act. Human beings who are אנשי קדש are not to sit at the same table with that which belongs to the animal world, or the “bound” unfree world of Nature. Hence the characteristic of טרפה is אינה חיה, that the wound is a fatal one, and the animal normally will not live for twelve months longer. Tradition gives us eight kinds of wounding by which an animal becomes טרפה viz. קרועה ,נטולה ,הסרה ,נקובה ,דרוסה, פסוקה ,נפולה, and שבורה, blow with the paw or foot, being pierced (a hole made), organic incompleteness, mutilation, a tear, a fall, splitting and fracture, and these are memnotechnically recorded by the words דן חנק נפש. It gives us likewise eighteen organic defects שמנה עשר טרפות e.g., ’נקובת הושט, פסוקת הגרגרת וכו׳ וכו, a hole in the oesophagus, a split in the trachea, etc. etc., by which the various cases of טרפה-woundings can be established.

We have already remarked that the basic meaning of טרף is not tearing to pieces, but snatching, and טרפה does not mean torn to pieces, but torn away. Conforming to this meaning of the word, we find the idea of טרפה extended to include all meat which has been taken away from where it organically belongs: — בשר שיצא חוץ למחיצתו. This legal term includes also בשר מן החי flesh which has been taken or fallen off from a living creature; הוציא עובר את ידו, a limb of an unborn animal which is stretched out of its pregnant mother before the שחיטה of the latter; the flesh of sacrifices which has been brought outside the prescribed area of the Temple, i.e. בשר קדשי קדשים שיצא outside the עזרה, or קדשים קלים outside the walls of Jerusalem. In this last instance the Temple of the Torah is symbolically considered as a living organism to whose soul, the Torah, all parts of the offerings belong. Taking them out of its areas is symbolically separating them from this living organism to which they belong, severing the connection in which alone their meaning and dedication has its roots. (See תוספות מכות 18a ד״ִה ולילקי משום בשר).

To a cursory glance the laws in this paragraph V.27—30 may seem very disconnected. But a closer consideration shows them all to be the realisation of one single idea which gets realised in various different aspects. V. 20—26 gives the Torah basis for ensuring the complete equality of all citizens in the eyes of the Law, and in their social treatment. Neither birth nor origin, nor fate nor fortune shall be allowed to make any difference in our duties regarding the rights and humane treatment of our fellow men. עני ,אלמנה ,יתום ,גר, may in no ways suffer any disadvantages. Then, within this national community built up on complete equality regarding all humane and civic rights, V.27 et seq. demands nevertheless respect and recognition of that organisation which God has instituted in His People by the higher and lower calling to service for the efficacy of the Law and of the Temple of the Torah. Such institutions appear as Judge and Prince (V.27), Temple, Priest and Levite (V.28). Regarding these, the demand is made, not only for respect in general, but recognition of the different degrees of rank, by keeping the right order in which the required gifts are paid. Then it goes on to indicate how, even within the family itself, even in the flocks and herds, there is a similar distinction made by the institution of the firstborn (V.28 and 29), and how the whole Jewish nation in all its members is itself (תהיון) to be exalted to a holy calling over the rest of humanity, but for the rest of humanity (V.30).
