This exalted calling is to be expressed in the food which they eat being raised above the “unfree” sphere of the physical and animal world, which simply has to obey the calls and laws of Nature, לכלב תשליכון אותו.

V. 1. The whole contents of verses 1 and 2 show that the first sentence: ’לא תשא וגו too, is primarily directed to the court, the judge, the representative of the community. The rules laid down in these two verses make it incumbent on the court to adopt such procedure that will ensure it as far as possible from giving wrong decisions. They deal accordingly with the processes of the law in all its stages:- Noting the facts of a case by the declaration of the parties or of witnesses (V.1); arriving at and pronouncing the verdict (V.2).

נשא .לא תשא שמע שוא in a concrete sense, to take something up, transposed to the abstract sense of the inner life, to take something up in one’s mind for consideration. Hence also, the expression נשא ראש for counting; and used in connection with the court of justice נשא פנים, to take the face, i.e., the personality of the parties into one’s mind and consideration, to take notice of personalities and not simply of the matter itself, by itself. נשא שמע to take what one hears, a declaration, into one’s mind, to get information by a declaration. In civil cases where there are no witnesses, the facts of the case can be accepted by the declaration of the parties, and the case proceeded with. But in criminal cases the facts of the case can only be taken into consideration by the testimony of witnesses. Now our first verse makes it the duty of the judge, in the case of the declarations of the parties themselves (i.e., where there are no witnesses) to take every posible precaution to protect himself from accepting a wrong presentation of the case. So we find our verse taken to be אזהרה לבית הין שלא ישמע דברי בעל דין קודם שיבא בעל דין חברו, a warning to the judges, not to listen to one party before the arrival of the other, opposing party (Sanhedrin 7b), so that no one-sided, partial impression of the facts of the case be formed beforehand. By implication, this is also a warning by the Torah for the parties themselves, that no party may present their case without their opponents being present אזהרה לבעל דין שלא יטעים דבריו לדײן קודם שיבא בעל דין חברו (Although this prohibition refers primarily to the judges taking care in how they listen to the report of a case on which they have to give a judicial decision, it is applied also to forming one’s opinion of one’s fellow-men socially, and is taken as a warning against מקבל לשון הרע equally to מספר לשון הרע as a warning not to listen to any derogatory talk about a fellow-man and, of course, how much more, not to originate it. (Makkoth 23a). The Gemora there, connecting this sentence with the preceding ’לכלב וגו declares that anybody who misuses speech, that precious mark of human superiority, has deprived himself of human superiority, and has sunk deep below the standard of an animal!).

’אל תשת ידך עם רשע וגו. Testimony and verdict, i.e., witness and judge together form the factor of a process at law, and indeed the witness is the principle factor, he instituted the proceedings, and especially in criminal cases, is the sole basis for establishing the facts of the case. Hence the judge is not to join his “hand”, i.e., the power of judgment with which he is entrusted, with a רשע, not to allow this power to be misused by such a man, so that an outrageous wrong (חמס) might be committed against somebody. This sentence proclaims the incapacity (פסול) of a רשע to give evidence as a witness (פסול מחמת עברה). By רשע is understood generally, one who transgresses the Law. According to Rambam (Hil. Eduth 10) — whose interpretation here is accepted by most authorities including the Ch. M. — the term רשע here is limited to one who transgresses any law that is punishable by מלקות, or one who sins from self-interest (חמוד ממון — חמס, love of wealth).

This prohibition is also taken as a warning against appearing in the court as a witness together with a רשע, even if you are convinced of the objective truth of the testimony to be given. (Mechilta. The Gemora, Shebuoth 30b brings this warning for the individual witness under the heading of מדבר שקר תרחק, V.7).

V. 2. רעות .לא תהיה אחרי רבים לרעות here can hardly be taken in the sense of evil, morally bad. All these laws give instructions and special precautions to the judges, and it would be remarkable if now the judges were to be specially forbidden to do anything bad or wrong. Apart from this, the fact is, that — as is apparent from the end of the verse — the verdict has to go according to the opinion of the majority of the tribunal, and this opinion has to be accepted as representing true justice. If it is taken to mean to be an instruction for the expression of the opinion of any individual member of the tribunal, it would make even less sense. Not only לרעות where something wrong seems about to be decided, but in any and every case, even in cases of doubt, where the opinions of the judges are divided as to what is “right”, no member of the tribunal many ever express anything but what is his own true opinion of the matter, whether it agrees or differs from any or all of the others. So it is clear that here לרעות must be taken in the sense of להרע או להטיב (Levit. 5,4) of נשבע להרע ולא ימיר (Ps. 15,4), in the sense of injury, misfortune, the ills of life, as the word רעות occurs just as often for troubles and misfortunes as for evils. By רעות, here, is meant — as tradition indeed teaches (Sanhedrin 2a) — verdicts for the death penalty, which are not to be carried out by a simple majority.
Whereas for a verdict of “not guilty” a simple majority of one vote is sufficient, for the reverse, a clear majority of at least two is required.

ולא תענה על רב לנטת. If ריב here is to be taken to mean a case at law to which a verdict has to be given, then, especially having regard to the importance of this law, the expression would be much too specific, as it would limit it to only one category of cases. For ריב could only apply to civil cases, in which two parties oppose each other, whereas in criminal cases according to the Jewish idea, there is only one party before the court, the accused, the accusers in the case, are completely impartial and disinterested witnesses. So that ריב seems to be used in the sense of דברי ריבות בשעריך (Deut. 17,8) where it means a difference of opinion between the judges, and ענה would be, giving expression to one’s opinion, giving the vote. נטה means to turn aside from that which one has perceived to be right. Now if it were to mean, “record no vote which deviates from your conviction of what is right”, it would say לא תענה לנטות ,לא תטה לענות means rather, do not vote in such a way that the decision may be given against people’s own convictions. According to that, the sense of the law would be: — If the views of the judges are divided in any case before the court, so that the decision has to be made by voting, this voting must be done in such a manner that nobody is induced to give his vote against his own opinion. Halacha, tradition, teaches that דיני נפשות מתחילין מן הצד that the voting in capital cases (over the death penalty, or even מלקות) must start from the younger members of the court. Were it to begin from the top, from the oldest and most authoritative member, the younger members might object to differ from him in such a serious matter, and might vote, not in accordance with their own views. It is always advised to start with the youngest even in civil cases. This Halacha is based on our verse here, and it is remarked that it is even indicated in the exceptional way of spelling ריב without the י which occurs nowhere else and so could also be read as לא תענה עַל רַב. We have shown that לא תענה עַל רַב is the immediate practical effect of לא תענה עַל ריב לנטות, (see נמוקי יוסף on Sanhedrin 36a).

אחרי רבים להטות, is the reason for, the object of, the preceding sentence. It declares absolutely that all views must finally incline to that of the majority. Once the opinion of every member has been given, the vote of the majority becomes law and verdict, and the minority who differ have to accept the opinion of the majority as being true. This law, that judgment must rest on the majority, and not on the minority, is then the reason for the preceding prescribed care in the manner of voting and that accounts for the cantillation joining it closely to ’לא תענה וגו. If one were to start with the oldest, the younger members would easily come to vote with him out of respect, so that finally the judgment might come to rest on the opinion of this single person, whereas it should rest solely and truly on the opinion of the majority. לא תענה על ריב לנטות because, or so that אחרי רבים להטות.

This canon אחרי רבים להטות, according to which the view of the minority is completely absorbed by that of the majority, and the vote of the majority becomes the vote of the whole court, finds manifold application as “the rule of the majority” אזלינן בתר רובא, in all sorts of directions in the law.

Just as the decisions of a majority of judges become the decision of the whole court, so for the legal judgment in all sorts of cases, does the whole bear the character of the majority of its parts, the special qualities of the minority vanish in the whole, and every and any individual part of the whole is considered to have the qualities of the majority. And this is not only the case where, like here at the Sanhedrin, the majority is actually there before us, רובא דאיתא קמן, but even in cases where the majority can only be presumed on the strength of knowledge and experience, רובא דליתא קמן. (Chulin 11a). We have tried to work out in the חורב (p. 462—467) how deeply this canon is based on the nature of the human faculty of perception.

V. 3. ודל. We have three expressions for the poor: אביון; ,עני ,דל דל (from דלל related to טלל from which we get תֵל debris) is one who has come down in the world. עני (from ענה to answer, to respond to) one whose existence is dependent on others. אביון (from אבה to be willing, to acquiesce in) one whose will is dependent on others. הדר is the outward show of honour and respect (cf. Levit. 19,32). Nothing is more pleasing to one who has been rich and has now come down in the world, than to feel himself treated with the old signs of respect, nothing is more in accordance with the spirit of this Torah than to show that the estimation of, and respect for, a man does not rise and fall with the condition of his fortune. Outside the court of law, nothing could be a greater Mitzva than להדר דל. But בריבו, when he stands before you in a lawsuit with an opponent, even in mere outward show, both must be treated exactly alike. Not even in mere outward show, not even from the most humane consideration, may you show one more attention than the other.
V. 4—5. כי תפגע, but outside the law-court you must save and help the possessions of even your enemy and hater.

איב ,אויב designates hatred which shows itself in acts, deeds, while שנא is more an inner enmity, hatred. Hence in the case of the שור תועה, where there would be an actual concrete loss, it says אויבך even if the owner has done you real harm, you should still save him from loss. But חמור רובץ תחת משאו, is at the moment only a difficulty in which he finds himself, there it says שונאך, the owner is one who does not wish you well, he would be pleased to see you in similar straits; in you too, you feel something of malicious joy, but, וחדלת, you may not let it continue. You must cease, you must leave all considerations which would keep you from helping him, and jump to help him. עזוב תעזוב עמו, it is true that we do find the root having the meaning “fixing”, “fastening”, i.e., to set something up “so that it can remain left to itself”, ויעזבו ירושלים עד החומה (Nehem. 3,8). But as here it is not speaking of loading up, טעינה, but of unloading the burden under which the animal is lying, פריקה, the way the Targum takes it is indicated, “you must leave all ideas of enmity and help him”.

The Halacha takes the two expressions פגיעה V.4 and ראיה V.5 together, and teaches that the duty of assisting to unload the animal is not only incurred if one actually meets it or passes by (פגיעה) and on the other hand, if you see it in the far distance (ראיה) you need not go right out of your way to it, but you are bound to go to its assistance if there is ראיה שיש בה פגיעה, i.e., you see it fairly near to you. The distance is fixed at 266 ells. After one has rendered the necessary assistance one should accompany the animal for some distance to be quite sure that it can now proceed without difficulty מדדה עמו עד פרסה, but for this one can accept compensation.

Moreover, the Halacha sees in his unloading of the animal not only a duty you have to carry out towards your fellow-men in difficulty, but also towards the suffering animal, that צער בעלי חײם is דאורײתא. To help his fellow-man he would only be obliged עמו if the man himself is doing all he can himself. But for the animal’s sake, he must render assistance even if the master wrongfully and lazily stands there doing nothing, and leaves the whole of the work to him. But in that case he can demand payment from the owner. (B.K. 32b). — אוהב לפרוק ושונא לטעון, מצוה בשונא כדי לכוף את יצרו. Although פריקה, rendering help in unloading, should usually take precedence over טעינה rendering assistance in loading (Deut. 22,4), as the former is duty towards both man and beast, while the latter is only towards one’s fellow-man, nevertheless one has to help loading the ass of an enemy, before helping in the unloading of the ass of a friend, because the duty of self-conquest is still higher (ibid.).

V. 6. Verses 4 & 5 gave us in parenthesis the duty of being well disposed and ready to help in ordinary every day life, outside the law-courts, although inside, the dictates of strict justice alone must prevail. Now V.6 comes back and continues the rules for legal procedure in the courts. The Jerushalmi at end of Pea IV gives the following interpretation of this verse: The stress is to be laid on — בריבו: “In his legal contests you may not incline the scales of justice in favour of your poor man, but outside the court where there is any doubt as to the rights of the claims of the poor e.g., as to whether an ear of corn is לקט, a sheaf שכחה etc., the poor must be given the benefit of the doubt. ספק לקט לקט, ספק שכחה שכחה. This is quite in keeping with the expression אביונך it is your poor man, as a poor man he is incumbent on you, and as an אביון he feels he is bound to conform his will to the decision of the rich man upon whom he is dependent, so that it is up to you to give him every advantage, and not try to stand on your rights when giving him the care and provision on which he has to reckon. Nevertheless, בריבו when he stands before you in a legal contest in the court, not by a single hairbreadth may you deviate justice in his favour.

V. 7. מדבר שקר תרחק, this is the most comprehensive and far reaching sentence for the duties of a judge. It makes it his duty in general meticulously to avoid any and every thing by which there is the slightest possibility of the veracity of the judgment being affected. Hence לדײן שלא יעשה סניגרון לדבריו that the judge should not become his own lawyer, to insist that the opinion he has expressed must be correct, but that he should always be ready to retract what he has said, as soon as he feels the slightest doubt of its being right; hence שלא ישב תלמיד בור לפניו, that in any case at law, he should not appoint for consultation on any point, one who is not absolutely master of the subject; hence לדײן שיודע בחברו שהוא גזלן שלא יצטרף עמו that he should not undertake a civil case in conjunction with a colleague whose character he knows to be unreliable for a judge; hence לדײן שיודע בדין ,שהוא מרומה שלא יאמר הואיל ועדים מעידים לפני אחתכנו ויהא קולר תלוי בצואר העדים that a judge who feels convinced that the case on which he has to give judgment is based on a fraud, but has no definite proof of it, may not give a verdict contrary to his conviction on the strength of the testimony of the witnesses brought, and quieten his conscience by saying that the responsibility for his judgment rests on the witnesses. In such a case the judge must withdraw from the case; hence לשנים שבאו לדין, אחד לבוש סמרטוט ,ואחד לבוש איצטלית בת מאה מנה שאומר לו לבוש כמותו או הלבישהו כמותך that the judge shall insist on both parties appearing before him completely equal even in their attire, and shall not allow one to be dressed in luxurious clothing and the other in rags etc. etc. And just as for the judge, so for the parties and witnesses, most important duties are drawn from this verse (see ibid.). (Shebuoth 31a & b).

נקי .ונקי וצדיק אל תהרוג is one who is actually innocent, צדיק shows itself from the following כי לא אצדיק רשע to mean, one who is pronounced “not guilty” by the Court. The meaning of the sentence is:- If, after sentence has been pronounced, some fresh ground for defence is produced, the carrying out of the sentence has to be stopped, and the defence gone into so that no נקי should be killed. On the other hand, once the court has declared someone innocent (צדיק) even if afterwards his guilt is made evident, he is not to be brought to judgment again, כי לא אצדיק רשע in that case we can safely leave him to God, the real Judge, המשפט לאלהים הוא. The human judge has only to carry out what God has delegated him to do. If in accordance with those means of proof which are before him, he has had to declare a guilty man innocent, God, in His Court will know how to deal with the guilty one.

V. 8. שחד related to שחט and שחת. From this relationship we get the basic idea of its meaning “to bring about the destruction of the spiritual and moral force of life of somebody”. Bribery kills the intellectual and moral force of the one who receives it. The intellectual force which makes a man fit to be a judge is called פקח, a clear open sight for the right way to look at the facts, and the laws which apply to them. The moral force is called צדק righteousness, which only recognises what is right, and which wishes to express nothing that is not right. Bribery blinds the sight of one who otherwise sees clearly, unconsciously prejudices his way of looking at the case and ’יסלף וגו. If we compare the meanings of the roots זלף ,שלף, צלב (Chaldean) and perhaps also the rabbinic כמצליף of Yoma 53b, סלף would mean, not so much crooked and turned the wrong way, as shaking, faltering, instability. Bribery would make even an honest judge, who wishes nothing but what is right and just, not as clear and firm and decisive as he should be in giving expression to what is right. His sight becomes clouded, his word faltering. He becomes as רבא pithily puts it חד one-sided, “bribery is called שחד because it identifies the judge with one of the parties”. But the idea of bribery in the spirit of Jewish law is given the widest extension. Not only money or goods but the smallest most unimportant favour, service or attention, the brushing off of specks of dust from the coat, the kicking away of a piece of dirt which happens to lie in front of the foot of the judge etc. etc., has caused Jewish judges to declare “I have become unfit to be your judge”. A Jewish judge must be conscious of absolute absence of any bias whatsoever, otherwise he may not judge (see Ketuboth 105, 106 and Ch. M. 9). Jewish administration of justice was completely free, and was not allowed to be paid for. The principle was categorically applied הנוטל שכר לדון דיניו בטלין, he who takes pay for administering justice, his decisions are void and have no legal or binding force (ibid.). If the judges had no other means of livelihood and had to devote all their time to the courts, it was permitted to give them an annual salary from public funds, but litigants were charged no fees and were not allowed to pay any (see ibid.). Only if litigants fetched somebody who was versed in the law away from the occupation by which he gained his living, for him to give a decision in some dispute, was he allowed to be reimbursed by them for an amount which could be publicly and clearly recognised as his actual loss, בטילא דמוכחא (ibid.). Only the secretaries (scribes who had to make records of all cases) and beadles of the court had to be paid by the litigants, and the judge was bitterly blamed and accused of self-interest who was מרבה שכר סופרים וחזניהם, who did not keep even these expenses down to the very lowest limit in his court. (see Tur Ch. M. 9).

V. 9. This verse clearly refers back to V.20 of the previous chapter, and resumes the train of thought, in order to develop a fresh series of laws out of it. V.20 introduced a basic sanction for the two fundamental principles on which the Jewish State was to be founded:- Complete equality of all before the law, and the highest degree of consideration and kindness for all those who required help. All the laws from that V.20 to our V.9 contain nothing else but the result of the application of these principles for the procedures in the courts, on the insistence of the equality of all, and for the formation of general social life on the principle of love and consideration of one’s fellow-man. V.9 now once again places these principles of equality and benevolence at the top, particularising how aliens are to be treated in the Jewish State with completely unrestricted enjoyment of the laws and rights of the inhabitants, and with the greatest consideration in every respect. (The treatment meted out to strangers is always the surest standard by which to measure the respect for human rights, and the humanitarianism which prevails in any state). With this it introduces a series of institutions which here are only mentioned in general terms, but all of them, apart from the special lesson which each of them has to teach, have this in common, that they all, as a result of their innermost nature, keep alive this spirit of equality and humanitarianism, as they all get the people in the way of considering themselves as being only aliens in the land and on the earth, which is not really their own but belongs to God. This idea leads them away from placing too much value on wealth and material property which is the source of all inequality of rights, and of all harshness and lack of brotherhood in this world. This underlying idea of all these institutions leads the nation to a more just, i.e., a higher appreciation of all spiritual, intellectual and moral values which demand and beget equality of all men, and universal love of fellow-man as being that which is essentially humane in humanity. Sabbath-of-the- Years (Shemita) Sabbath-of-the-days, the Festivals of Spring, Summer and Autumn (Pessach, Shevuoth and Succoth), Chometz and Nausar, Bikurim and Bosor-bechalab are sketchily mentioned here, all from this one point of view. By this we are shown at the end of the fundamental laws of this “social Lawgiving”, Mishpotim, not only that significance these so-called specific “religious” institutions too, have for general social life, but how social life has its real soul in just these institutions, and how they form the never-failing source out of which it can draw ever fresh nourishment for its spirit and life-force. They, and they only, have the power to achieve the realisation of a national life which is truly based on justice and humanitarianism which will be true and lasting, as it will flow from the inner conviction of the people. All the external, superficial institutions of state and law, without these institutions, strive mostly in vain, and always only clumsily, to establish such a national life.

ואתם ידעתם — לא תלחצנו, the granting of unrestricted rights (of living, working, earning a livelihood etc., I.L.) to aliens is demanded from the community or nation as such (hence the singular), the most considerate personal treatment from every member of the community, (hence the plural).

V. 10—11. שמיטה. For six years you are to treat your land as your own property, but during each seventh year, תשמטנה, literally, you must let it go, may not plough it, nor sow it; ונטשתה, and what does grow on it, you must leave to itself, may not treat it as your own property; undisturbed, and without asking your permission, the poor of your people, who at all other times are dependent on your good will, are to enjoy it, and what they leave, the beasts of the field are to have. This law is given in fuller detail in Levit. XXV, and from there we know that the owner himself may eat of the produce of his own fields and orchards during the seventh year in company with the poor and the animals, but he may only do this, as long as some of the particular kind of produce he is using, still remains in the fields for the animals; כלה לחיה מן השדה once there is no more of any particular kind left in the fields, no man may keep any of that kind in his house. This time is called the time of ביעור, and even during the time when its use is allowed to be enjoyed, there are restrictions in the manner in which it may be used.

This Sabbath-year is the greatest act, on the part of a whole nation, of recognition that God is the sole, one and real Owner and Master of their country, inasmuch as in that year they lay it in homage at His feet, and refrain from exercising their rights of ownership on their lands. But by this, they acknowledge themselves as גרים ותושבים as “aliens”, and “dwellers only by the tolerance of the Owner” in their own land. This feeling does away with the arrogance, which, priding itself on standing on its own soil, tends to become unsympathetic and harsh in dealing with the poor and landless ones. Moreover, it engenders that frame of mind which lovingly includes the stranger, the poor and also the animals, as creatures of God, who have the right to live in a land which belongs to God, which all are to share in common.

כן תעשה לכרמך לזיתך. The omission of a conjunction (ו) between the two nouns indicates a difference in the application of this law to each one of them. Both regarding the period reckoned for fruit formation (חנטה, עונת המעשרות) which decides to which year the fruit belongs (the 6th or 7th) as well as to the time they remain on the trees which decides the time of ביעור, the laws referring to כרם and זתים differ. (See Pessachim 53b Rambam Shemita 7,11 the כ״מ on this paragraph and the Mechilta on this verse).

V. 12. And what the Sabbath year is for the relation of the Nation to the Land, that, the Sabbath Day is, for the individual to the World. By observing it, Man acknowledges God as the Creator and Master of the World and of himself. Every seventh day he acknowledgingly lays himself and his world at the feet of God, and refrains from exercising his own mastery over any of God’s creations. But this again automatically makes the Sabbath into a school for teaching the recognition of every other creature besides oneself as being equally a child and object of the same Creator, and this freeing all creatures from the mastery of Man is one of the objects of Sabbath, this day of acknowledging God, למען “so that the beasts of work and beasts of burden should have rest from working for Man”, and also that the “son of your slave” and the “stranger in your midst”, should come into their own personalities, become conscious of the worth of their own self, be their own masters (ינפש). The Mechilta deduces from למען ינוח שורך וחמורך, the further duty, that not only must one leave one’s animals at rest on Sabbath but must turn them out and allow them to graze undisturbed, הוסיף לו הכתוב  נײח אחר להיות תולש ואוכל מן הקרקע,
בן אמתך והגר (see Ch. 20,10). —

V. 13. ’ובכל אשר אמרתי וגו, this can not mean: “Guard yourself against transgressing all that I have prohibited you to do”, for it would then have to say ’מכל אשר וגו. The sense of ’בכל אשר וגו is clearly: In all the commands and prohibitions that I have given you, you are to guard yourselves, i.e., place yourselves under your own guard, make for yourselves such laws, take such precautions, that you do not come to transgress My word. What is right and what is wrong, what your duty is and what your task, My Law — the Torah — will tell you. To take such precautions that My commands get carried out and My prohibitions not transgressed, is the work I expect from your conscientiousness. Herewith is given the great command of “Fencing around the Laws and finding means to ensure the carrying out of the Laws” סײגים ,גדרים) גזרות) and תקנות. It is to the conscientious observing of these alone that we owe the fact that the Torah itself has been kept alive. It is significant that before and after this command, all the commands are given in the singular person addressed to the community, to the nation as such, but this is in the plural, addressed to all the individual members of the nation. Thereby this task is made the duty for the conscientiousness of each individual Jew as such. If this task of protecting the Law was in practice carried out by the עיני העדה, by “the far-seeing leaders” of the nation, they instituted nothing but that which each individual in the nation would have been bound to fix in accordance with his own discerning conscientiousness. And even these commands of the Rabbonim were not dictatorially forced on the nation, but only recommended as the result of their judgment, and their ratification made dependent on the free acceptance and observance on the part of the people. The Mechilta also takes this sentence in this meaning אין לי אלא דברים שהן משום מלאכה, דברים שהן משום שבות מנין ת״ל ובכל אשר אמרתי אליכם תשמרו.

The Torah then immediately explains the idea of this “placing a fence” round the Law, by giving an example, and uses for it the first prohibition of the Decalogue, the prohibition of idolatry. The sin itself is idolatry. To utter the name of an idol, and certainly, simply to cause such a name to be uttered by somebody else, is by no means idolatry. Nevertheless our verse says we are to abstain from this, as well as from idolatry itself, clearly by this extended self control, to protect oneself from coming to the real sin. We have here in the Torah the most precise example of avoiding not only the evil itself, but everything that merely touches it, or that could possibly lead to it.

ושם אלהים אחרים לא תזכירו, not even for the purpose of fixing a meeting-place שלא יאמר אדם לחברו שמר לי בצד ע״א פלונית, — a man may not say to a friend “meet me beside such and such an idol” — ולא ישמע על פיך, you may not cause even a non-Jew to take an oath by the name of an idol ולא יגרום לאחרים שידרו ויקײמו בשמו (Sanhedrin 60b). With one single exception — ותשא בריתי עלי פיך (Ps. 50,16). — על פי is never used for speaking a word — בפי means that — but it always means (unless of course it refers to a definite place such as על פי הבאר) at the command of, by means of. The prohibition of even mentioning the name of an idol, does not apply to names which in any case occur in the Scriptures (Sanhedrin ibid.). The prohibition is, according to ’הגהו׳ מײמוני on הל׳ ע״ז V.9 limited to those names that involve the granting of divine attributes to the idol, assuming, of course, that they are not mentioned in any way that might seem to acknowledge them — ד״מ) בלשון חשיבות on י״ד 153). This also explains — as ’הגהו׳ מײמוני remarks — the occurrence of various ע״ז names in the Talmud.

V. 14. רגלים. We have no actual proof for רגל having the meaning “time” in the same sense as פעם. Apart from here, we only find it used in that sense in the story of Bileam (Numb. 22,28, 32, 33). If we compare the words רגל and רגל ,פעם, apart from its general meaning of foot seems preferably to be used for the foot in motion, the raised foot, whereas פעם indicates the foot set down, striking the ground. Hence we get לרגל הילדים, לרגל המלאכה “according to the pace” (Gen. 33,14) and רַגַל to scout, to spy. But פעם seems essentially to have the meaning of “knocking against”, of striking down on something. Hence also פעם, the anvil, פעמון, the bell, also mentally of הִפָּעֵם :רוח[[illegible]] literally, knocking on his feelings i.e., mental unrest. It seems, accordingly that רגלים here does not mean three “times” but pilgrimages, and similarly the שלוש רגלים in Numb, means the three “wanderings” which the animal had made from the ever-narrowing path, for which it had been beaten. So the Gemora (Chagiga 3a) takes רגלים to refer to walking, and to free the חיגר, a lame man, from the duty of ראיה, of appearing at the Mikdosh on the Festivals, but takes the change of expression to פעמים in V.17 to free בעלי קבין, people with wooden legs who can not place the foot on the ground at all.

רגלים — pilgrim festivals (from רגל the progressing foot). The root חגג has already been explained on Ch. 5,1 to have the basic meaning of “forming a circle” and its application to a festival חג, as the expression for the nation gathering together around their spiritual centre, around God and the Temple of His Torah.

שלש רגלים תחוג לי בשנה would accordingly mean literally “Three pilgrimages shall you undertake to form a circle around Me each year”. The Festival is called רגל from the duty of every male, adult, sane, healthy and strong Jew to trek up to the forecourt, the עזרה of the Temple of the Torah; is called חג because of the general, universal, simultaneous nature of this duty by which the whole nation finds itself gathered together about its common sanctuary, and thereby each individual feels himself a member of this huge circle. Inasmuch — as the Torah goes on to point out — as these pilgrim Festivals occur just at the times of the most important agricultural activities, the forsaking of one’s fields at such a time to present oneself at the Temple of the Torah, as a son and servant of the Torah, this leaving of one’s home in the time of the most pressing material needs, is for each person a great sacrificing act of acknowledgment of God, which must tend to break the icy bonds of materialism in the breast of every Jew. And inasmuch as when he gets there he learns to look on himself as only a member of a great circle, all bearing a common mission, it is just in these times which normally call him most pressingly to look after his own personal welfare, that the feeling of national unity is awakened in him; and it is this feeling combined with his innate powers of enthusiasm which banishes the curse of selfishness and egotism from the Jewish character.

V. 15. The first of these Festivals is the Festival of Mazzos, on which the whole free, independent nation spends a cycle of seven days in the surroundings of the Temple, with the reminders of slavery constantly with them. They are thereby completely to impregnate themselves with the consciousness of belonging to the service of God, in carrying out His Will as revealed in the Torah, on the grounds of their origin (עבדות פרעה) and of their calling (’עבודת ה) (see above Ch. XII & XIII). תשמור The nation has to see to it that this Festival does fall in the חדש האביב in the month of the first standing grain (see on Deut. 16,1 שמור את חדש האביב). As historically and understandably the month of Spring is in the deepest connection with the Festival of Redemption (see Ch. 13,4 et seq.), that itself gives the nation the task of arranging that this Festival, and in consequence the two other Pilgrim Festivals, fall just at the time of the most important agricultural activities. This willing act of acknowledgment of God, which entails so much sacrifice, is considerably enhanced by this free fixing of the date by the nation itself which gives these Festivals the character of voluntary self-sacrifice cheerfully undertaken.

ולא יראו פני ריקם, and when you appear in My Presence “you shall not come with empty hands”. When you leave your home and hearth to present yourself before My Presence you are not to fall into the fatal error of thinking that the Temple is something apart from home and hearth, that the Temple is reserved for spiritual and heavenly matters, and the home, for material and earthly matters only, that you provide “food” for “spirit and fine feelings” in the Temple, so that you can the more definitely care for material and sensual affairs in the home, that you visit the Temple only so that you can more quietly keep your house and hearth dedicated to material egotism and the most egoistic materialism. Not so! When we appear before God, we are to appear with our possessions, our material possessions; are to appear with זבח ונסכים with עולה ומנחה (see Levit. 23,37), our whole selves with what we possess for food (סלת) of health (שמן) and for enjoyment (ײן), all to be included in that which we place at the disposal of God, to receive its dedication and consecration in the Temple. The three Festival-offerings, which everybody has to bring, correspond to the threefold nature of the Festivals themselves. For the idea of רגל, presenting oneself in the Temple of the Torah one has to bring עולת ראיה; for חג finding oneself at one with all one’s fellow nationals one brings שלמי חגיגה; and for מועד finding oneself at one with God (see above Ch. 12,14) one has to bring שלמי שמחה. These latter pertain to the joyful consciousness of the Presence of God in the family circle, which raises the home to a Temple, the family table to an altar, and the members of the household to priests and priestesses in the holy service of living their ordinary home lives in carrying out the mission of God.

V. 16. חג הקציר בכורי מעשיך, we have to repeat the word חג as an addition before בכורי, the Festival of the “Cutting”, the Festival of the First Fruits. This is the second of the pilgrim Festivals, שבועות, on which the offering of the שתי לחם of the new wheat opens the summer season for the bringing of the מנחות of the year’s produce (Levit. 23,17) and generally introduces the bringing of the בכורים (V.19 and Deut. 26,1 et seq.). חג האסף is סוכת (Levit. 23,39). באספך את מעשיך — מעשיך אשר תזרע, a man “sows his activity”, his power which he exercises with judgment and circumspection into the lap of the earth, there he must leave it to await the blessing of God, if he is to garner a harvest in autumn.

V. 17. פעם means definitely “time”. We have remarked above on V.14 that the word primarily designates the foot placed down, the course partially completed, an integrating part. So that here, it can refer to the three parts of the course of the year in which the year in its progressive course puts down its foot, has completed one step. “With every fresh progress in the course of the year, at the commencement of the Spring, of the Summer and the Autumn shall all your… etc…” — זכורך. The form זָכוֹר — which only occurs here and in Deut. 16,16 in this connection, and apart from this, in Deut. 20,13, in which last case it also does not describe merely the sex, male, but at the same time the maturity of independence (see Sifri) the grown-up male — seems to be the passive form of the present participle. As remarked on Gen. 1,17, we believe that the use of the word זכר to describe the male sex, is meant to convey the idea that the special function of that sex is זוֹכֵר, to form the chain of tradition of the human race, by which the achievements of each age are handed down from generation to generation. זָכָר is an active form like זָכוֹר חָכָם passive, would accordingly be, those who are “thought of” as being already in this “chain of ages”, who have already taken up an integrating position in their age, by their acts already made their mark in the Book of Time, i.e., the grown-ups, manly ones. And in fact it is only the grown-up, mentally mature, free, healthy, young and strong of the male sex who are bound to appear in the Temple on the three pilgrim Festivals. People of weak intellect, juniors, women, slaves, deaf or dumb, lame, blind, ill, aged, delicate, are free from this duty (Chagiga 2a). This is one of the laws of the Jewish gathering in the Temple which so markedly contrast the Jewish ideas of the Temple to other non-Jewish institutions which outwardly appear to be similar. The Jewish Temple is no place of “wonder-working grace” to which it is, above all, the diseased, the suffering, the aged, the blind, the lame, the weak and the women who make the pilgrimage; that suffering, downtrodden pitiful contingent of humanity who tramp up from the “vale of troubles” to seek miraculous comfort and healing for the multifold troubles of this earthly life. The Temple of the living God, the Sanctuary of His Torah, does not fall in line with the hospitals, the hostels, the houses of refuge for shipwrecked lives. It is the elite of the nation, the vigorous and virile, the very backbone of the people, in whom all action of the present, and all hope of the future rests, that the Living God expects and awaits in the Sanctuary of His Torah. Out of the busiest activities for the present and the future are they called, to equip themselves for His service before God, the Master, in the sanctuary of His Torah, so that the active working power of the nation should remain His; so that this living power sees the strength of its present existence and the hopes of its future, not in its own might, but in the use it makes of it to carry out His Will; so that, in the Temple of His Torah they may find the equipment to make their whole life, pulsating with freshness and energy, full of success and achievement, a hymn to the Glory of God. האדון, the One Who is to be served with every beat of one’s pulse, the Master, ’ה the One Who considers and provides for every future moment.

יֵרָאֶה. The explanation which our Rabbis have given on this expression is indeed a deep one: — יִראֶה יֵרָאֶה, כדרך שבא לראות כך בא ליראות, מה לראות בשתי עיניו אף ליראות בשתי עיניו (Chagiga 2, 2). They take the form יֵרָאֶה not to be only a passive form “to be seen by God”, but also to be reflexive “to see oneself looked at by God”. The real purpose of every attendance in the Temple of God is not to be seen by God, but to see oneself before the Presence of God, to bring to your mind that you are looked at by God. In the text of the Torah too, we find the ראיה expressed as referring to both these ways: ראית פנים “seeing” (i.e., being conscious of the Presence of God (V.15) and ראית כל זכור “those who attend being seen”. Accordingly, first לִראוֹת and then לֵרָאוֹת which could do away with ר״ת׳s objection to Rashi’s explanation in Chagiga 2a. Accordingly, they add: — “In the measure that you come up to the Temple to see, in that measure shall you come to be seen”. As you keep conscious and realise the full extent of God’s seeing, and wish to be seen in the full extent of His seeing, so must you also be seen by Him, “seeing to your full extent”; you must be fully conscious with the whole power of your mental eye if He is to “see”, to look down on you personally with the full extent of “His regard”. His “seeing” depends on your “seeing”, not just a passive letting yourself be seen, but your appearing before God, must be a mental act of the highest energy, a most positive, the most positive, act of your conscious mind. Hence, applied to the concrete, a blind man or a one-eyed man is free from the duty of appearing in the Temple.

V. 18. Three characteristic verses bring this chapter of the Festivals to a conclusion, and with them, at the same time these basic foundations of the social laws, משפטים. They are closely related to the three pilgrim festivals and guard their spirit. לא תזבח and closely connected with it (see below) לא תלין related to ראשית בכורי וגו ;פסח to שבועות and לא תבשל גדי to סוכת.

לא תזבח על חמץ. The meaning of חמץ, leavened dough, as a symbol of civic independence, as well as its presence in the possession of Jews as being a forbidden expression of independence towards God, and of not submitting our possessions to God’s Will, has already been indicated above (Ch. 12,8 & 18 et seq.) from the historic importance of חמץ during the slavery in Egypt and the redemption from it. Now here the prohibition is given to bring the Pessach offering on the afternoon of the 14th Nissan if any one of the participants, viz., either, one of the officiating priests who performed the הקטרה ,זריקה ,שחיטה, or אחד מבני חבורה, one of the company to whom the offering belonged, still had any Chometz in his possession. This implies the duty of having to remove all Chometz from our possession already before midday of the 14th Nissan. The Pessach offering is, as was worked out above (Ch. XII) essentially a dedication of Jewish homes. As is the case in no other offering, the אכילה, the eating it in one’s homely family circle is the expressed and whole meaning of this offering, and is the object for which it is brought שלא בא מתחלתו אלא לאכילה. Hence it is significantly here called זבח and its being brought זבוח, for זבח is essentially a family meal, and זבוח its preparation. זבחי is accordingly a family meal dedicated to God. To bring such an offering in the Temple, and at the same time to have Chometz at home expresses at the most, that one considered the people themselves, the members of the family, as belonging to, and dedicated to God, but their lot in life, the material means of their living as being not dependent on God, neither thanks to Him, nor dedicated to Him. This would be the most pernicious cleft and separation between home and Temple, and it is just the home which is meant to be offered and dedicated in this offering.

ולא ילין חלב חגי. The idea which איסור חמץ impresses on the mind of the nation in a negative way on פסח (the festival of the birth of our civic independence) is expressed in a positive way at all offerings (except the עולה which is given over to the fire in its entirety) by using the חלב and the אימורים (the parts that had to be burnt on the altar) as fuel for the fire on the altar. חֵלֶב, — whose etymology and meaning has already been given in Gen. 4,4 — is the reserve capital of the animal organism kept for future use. It, together with כליות, the kidneys, forms the part of the offering that is given over to the אשדת of the altar. The כליות, the kidneys, in accordance with the etymology (from כלה to long for, to pine away, to languish) and from its constant use in conjunction with כליות ולב ,לב) are taken to be the organs of the lower inclinations and desires. Whereas in זריקה and נתינה, the דם the נפש, the whole individuality, the spiritual and mental personality, is given its direction as a never-ceasing striving upwards to the “altar-heights” of the Jewish calling, הקטרת חלב וכליות expresses the truth that also the striving for the enjoyment of the promised possessions, that wealth, and the satisfying of physical desires, are not excluded from the divine heights up to which every person is to strive; that just these lower and material matters can be, and should be, changed over into fuel or food for the “godly fire”, for keeping godliness alive on earth, and as a means of “giving satisfaction to God”. More, that this giving just the חלב וכליות over to the fire of the Torah is the most important and most necessary result of, and condition for, the giving up of the soul, the דם, to the height it is meant to attain. The giving over of the חלב and the כליות (usually, as here too, simply called חלב or חלבים as being the object of the desires which are represented by the כליות) must accordingly remain in close connection with the דם=נפש so that it must be done on the same day (the day reckoned from dawn to dawn, see Ch. 12,2). Any postponement would express the idea that our behaviour towards our wealth and the material enjoyments of life is a matter of indifference to the spiritual heights to which we should devote our energies. And it is just the purification and consecration of these material matters which is to be the blossom and fruit of our spiritual soaring. Hence לא ילין חלב חגי עד בקר.

But that which is the regular rule for all offerings is here quite specially emphasised for the חגיגה offering, with which every individual fits himself into the circle of the whole community and helps to form the national circle about God in His Temple of the Torah. For if the admonition to moral sanctity in one’s efforts towards material possessions, and one’s enjoyment and use of them, is important for private life, it is even more important for the national life. Are not states and nations enmeshed with the erroneous opinion that the codex of the laws of morality only apply to private life, and that national interest sanctifies breaking the holiest of the laws of morality if thereby power or possessions for the nation are acquired? The Law of God knows no such distinction. It says חלב חגי “the material possessions and efforts of a national circle that calls itself ‘My Circle’, of a Nation that bears My Name, may be just as little separated from the personal giving oneself up to God and His Laws, as is the case with the individual. משפטים apply just as much to the rights of nations as to the rights of individuals.

V. 19. ראשית, the first fruits of your fields and trees, which announce the success of your work, תביא are you to bring, not as תבואה, as “that which is to come home to you” not to your home, but — starting from the Festival of the Lawgiving — to the House that God, as your God, had built to His Torah. It is for it, for this Torah, that every ear of corn fills itself, every fruit ripens, everything is its תבואה, everything which the combination of the rays of the sun and your handiwork bring to completion, is its harvest. It is not the physical sun of your world to whom you owe thanks for the blessing, it is God Whom you thank for the blessing, it is He Whom you acknowledge as your God. Every tiny grain of corn which ripens for you grows as a blessing for fulfilling His Torah, and for this Torah you build a Home on Earth. Therefore take thou the first fruits of this blessing and bring them as a mark of homage and acknowledgment and of dedication in this Home of His Torah.

לא תבשל גדי. That גדי does not only refer to a kid, a young goat, is proved, as is remarked in Chullin 113b, by the description of young goats as גדי עזים but גדי by itself is a term for the cub or young of any בהמה טהורה. So also רעי את גדיותיך (Song of Songs 1,8) כשסע הגדי (Judges 14,6) also probably ונמר עם גדי ירבץ (Is. 11,6) in all of which places it is hardly just the young of goats which is meant. The word גדי itself — root is גדה, to separate, to part, related to גדע to cut off, to cut through — designates the young, according to its former, now separated, connection with the body of the mother, similar to גוזל the young bird, from גזל, snatched away, from a similar, now ceased, relationship to the mother bird. The young bird as such was never joined to the body of its mother so that its present condition could be expressed by גדה a cutting through. The mother bird had hatched it out of the egg. It is a product, not a part of the mother bird. Its belonging to the mother is in the nature of property, and when it is hatched and independent and soon does not even know the mother bird whose property it is, it takes itself away, it robs the mother bird, who has the greatest right to it, of itself, it becomes גוזל. And nevertheless the bird still hovers on the wings of motherlove over the young who really still require her care, small though the thanks she will get for it may be, על גוזליו ירחף (Deut. 32,11) a picture which will appear more significant and pithy according to what is indicated by the word גוזל.

The Halacha teaches that these words forbid the cooking of the flesh of any בהמה טהורה i.e., beef, mutton or goat-flesh, with the milk of a בהמה טהורה i.e., with the milk of cows, sheep or goats. But חיה ,בהמה טמאה and עוף are not included in this prohibition. We can accordingly understand why the text chooses גדי and חלב אמו to sharply define the objects affected by this prohibition. It would be difficult to express בשר בהמה טהורה in חלב בהמה טהורה, with equal brevity and precision, otherwise. בשר and חלב alone would be too comprehensive, and would include meat and milk of any kind, including venison and fowl etc. Even adding בהמה and saying again בשר בהמה טהורה would not suffice, as we find quite clearly that under the term בהמה (e.g. in Deut. 14,4 & 5). חיה too is included, and here חיה must be excluded. If, as is remarked in Chullin 113b, the word גדי used by itself includes the young of פרה and רחל (cow and sheep) there is hardly any other word that on the one hand includes the species בקר וצאן and on the other excludes all other species, and no shorter expression to limit the milk too, to that of these species, than חלב אמו. If, however גדי and חלב אמו may still seem insufficient, as it could be taken to restrict the prohibition to the flesh of a young animal in its own mother’s milk, that idea is countered by the consideration that the Torah gives us the extreme example — even this flesh and this milk, which after all were so intimately connected together are to be kept apart in cooking! Not even גדי בחלב אמו may you cook together! When we have gone into the meaning and spirit of this rule, the choice of just these words will become even more significant.

The underlying reason for the other dietary laws seems to be the avoidance of the exciting or depressing effect of certain foodstuffs on one’s temperament and feelings as the warning words with which they are accompanied clearly indicate: ואל תטמאו את נפשתיכם ,אל תשקצו את נפשתיכם, etc. etc. But in בשר בחלב no such dietic influence on character can be thought of. For with בשר בחלב even the simple preparation of such a mixture by cooking, is prohibited, similarly to the כלאים mixing of two organically differing plants, or cross-breeding two different species of animals, of using two organically differing animals together for human work, or of mixing wool and linen in human clothing (— in this latter case, it is true, that it is only the wearing, not the preparation of such mixture which is forbidden —). In all these cases there can be no question of any direct effect on the human organism. Furthermore, a mixture of בשר בחלב is not only prohibited to be eaten — in which case one could think of some such effect — but is אסור בהנאה is prohibited from having any use at all made of it, similar to a mixture of כלאי כרם. Just as this latter has to be prevented from being used at all, by burning, so does בשר בחלב have to be treated by burying, and even if one were to burn it, any use of the ashes would be prohibited according to the rule. כל הנקברין אפרן אסור, והנשרפין אפרן מותר (Temura 33a 34b). That not only eating, but even preparing such a mixture is prohibited, is expressed by the wording of the text ’לא תבשל וגו. That such a mixture may not only, not be eaten, but not sold or given as a gift to a non-Jew, or made use of in any way, is indicated at the repetition of the law (Deut. 14,21) where it is placed in direct contrast to the permission to use נבלה. That, you may give away or sell, but בשר בחלב you may not even cook! Hence the threefold repetition of this law, here, in Ch. 34,26, and Deut. 14,21, is explained (Chullin 115b) as referring to the threefold prohibition: — אסור אכילה, אסור הנאה, ואסור בישול. But preparing the mixture by cooking, must constitute the very essence of this law, as all three prohibitions occur under the term לא תבשל.

If then this prohibition can be attributed neither to any direct dietic effect, nor to any temperamental moral effect, it can only be of a symbolic nature, as we have already had symbolic meaning in the dietary laws forbidding the eating of גיד הנשה and in the אסור חמץ.

As a law of this nature, it immediately takes its place in the ranks of those laws of forbidden “mixtures” which are regarded as a forcible interference and violation of the great “Law of Species”, such as כלאי אילן and כלאי בהמה, the propping or cross-breeding of different species of plants or animals (which are כלואים “barricaded” against each other). This great Law of למינהו proclaimed at the creation of each living organism (see Gen. I) keeps every one of the tiniest and the greatest of the millions of organic creatures throughout all the ages during which the world has existed and will exist, within the prescribed form and power and material of its species. Or better — as בשר בחלב does not actually bring about any actual interference with the laws of Nature as laid down by the Creator — it ranks with laws like כלאי זרעים ,כלאי בגדים ,לא תחרוש בשור וחמור and כלאי כרם, which are to remind Man in all the activities with which he masters, and uses for his own purposes, the forces of the organic world, which are laid at his feet — in agriculture, in labour, in his clothing and now here, in his food — to remind him in the manner and in the materials which he uses, of the Great Giver of the Laws of Nature. To remind him of the One Whose למינו-order rules all created life into the very core of their existence, Who has prescribed for each one the Law governing its special existence, and its development in accordance therewith, and to Whom all living animal and vegetable creatures give faithful eternal obedience, in order that he too, as Man and Jew, should remain faithful and obedient to the Law. To the Law with which the same Giver of the Laws of Nature has indicated to him as his למינו, and thereby informed him of His Will, how he is to understand the special nature of his mission as Man in the sphere of creation and as Jew in the sphere of humanity, as has already been explained on Gen. 1,11.

Amongst all these warnings and reminders for the faithful carrying out of the Law (Torah) “as the sole solution of our מין-mission as Man and Jew”, the בשר בחלב law heads the list. It comes to us, this reminder of the Divine Law given to all creatures, and to us of our Jewish human calling, just at the moment when we are about to assimilate into the fibres of our being animal matter from animals which the Creator has designated as fit for consumption, — בהמה טהורה. It is at this juncture, more than ever, that the warning comes home to us, still to remain conscious of our higher מין-calling in face of assimilating even permitted animal matter into our systems, and to remember that our mission is to raise the animal parts of our bodies up to the heights at which even the human material body is meant to be kept, and never to allow the human body to sink to the instinct-bound level of animals, although we do reproduce the tissues of our body from the animal world.

So, even considered from this general point of view, the אסור בשר בחלב appears as the most impressive and direct ad-hominem-speaking warning to keep the Law holy; as the reminder that the ruling of the Divine Law (of למינו) does not begin with being a Jew, but that the ruling of this law is everywhere present in every fibre of all organic life, and that the Torah, our Law is naught but the precise specification of God’s למינו world-law as to what a human Jewish life is to be. We understand the interweaving of this “Law of Non-intermixing of Species” into the whole sphere of our domestic life, and if none of the dietary laws rules the Jewish kitchens and Jewish tables so much as the keeping apart of “milk and meat”, no other has so much the mission of being the herald of God, and to keep us conscious, every moment of our lives of God’s Law, of the duties of Jewish human beings, and the dignity and high status of being a human being.

We also understand how this law comes to appear three times, each as the conclusion and seal of a great chapter of laws; above all, how significantly it can come, we would add, must come, as the conclusion and seal, above all, of “Mishpatim”. By far the greater number of these social laws, all built up on the principles of human rights and brotherly love, do not come within the scope of, and can not depend on, legal enforcement. It was to the inner conscientiousness, the God-fearing respect for His Law of His citizens, that God wished to entrust the keeping of His dictates of social rights and behaviour. Not legality, mere outward conformity to the law, but loyalty, faithful adhesion to the underlying principles of the law, is to form the character of Jewish citizens. God did not appoint policemen or court officials who can only get at the citizens out in the open, to be the watchmen and guardians of His Law, but spiritual and mental heralds of what is right, who accompany each Jewish citizen into the innermost sphere of his home life, who let the little Jewish children already grow up under the dictates of “מותר״ ,“אסור״, “allowed”, “forbidden”! These visualise God, the Maker of the Laws of Nature that govern the world, as being in the same way the Maker of the Laws that are to govern the lives of Jewish human beings, and permeate the whole life of the Jew with the spirit of lawfulness. We have seen how the בשר בחלב law proclaims itself as one of the first and most successful of these heralds of the Torah. It is the most fruitful educational institution for the “loyalty” of Jewish social life, and it is not for nothing that it stands as the final bulwark of the social lawgiving, Mishpatim.

Its importance as a reminder for adhesion to law i.e., for the voluntary submission of the whole of human life to Divine Law, hence for keeping the למינו-Law for human beings, for the idea and meaning of human life, is greatly enhanced if we realise the physiological meaning of these two materials which are to be kept apart in Jewish diet.

Nourishment and reproduction mark the type of the lowest stage of organic life, plant life, whose whole existence consists in passively carrying out these two functions. When the organism loses its passivity, and receives, for the functions of nourishment and reproduction, the addition of a body with powers of locomotion and thought, it becomes a animal. Actually in the higher animals, these two joint systems, the animal and the vegetable appear in two separate parts. The diaphragm separates the body of the animal into a vegetable realm of alimentation and reproduction, and a purely animal realm of movement and thought, but in an animal, thought and movement are entirely in the service of the vegetative side. The vegetative objects of food and reproduction are the sole objects which occupy the thoughts of the animal, and for which the muscles of movement are employed. The animal is nothing more than a moving and living plant. Now the material in which the vegetative side of animal life is most clearly characterised is — milk. It is the specific food for carrying on the species — whereas meat — the muscles etc. — represent the specific animal side. Animal and animal-vegetable in intimate intermixture, as presented by בשר מבושל בחלב, is the animal world. It is thought and action being under the control and government of the objects and allurements of food and sexual life. The physiological meaning of the two materials explain even more lucidly the choice of expressing them as גדי and חלב אמו.

Man is different. In him also the two systems appear. He too is endowed with the alimentary and sexual objects of the plant, and the thought and movement of the animal. His inner organism, too, is divided into a vegetative and an animal sphere. But to him a third system has been granted, which is what characterises him as a human being. He was endowed with the breath of God, which raises his animal power of thought into an understanding and discerning spirit, and the animal power of action into free untrammelled power of exercising his will, and which is able to, and meant to rule, as a human being, over both the vegetable and animal nature of his being. In Man, thought and action are not to fall under the domination of alimentation and sexual life.

Just as in his upright position (in contrast to the horizontal position of animals) the animal part of Man is above the vegetative, and above both, the human part, the head, rises heavenwards, so, in Man, his animal forces are not to sink to the vegetative objects of life and vegetative allurements. In him, the vegetative is to submit itself to the animal, and both to the human intellect, which is called upon to rule and master them and him, with godlike free energy, in the service of the One Free God, up to Whose Glory his head raises itself, and Whose Will he has the ability to understand and perceive. So that both the animal (meat) and the animal-vegetative are to have quite a different relationship to each other and to the human organism when they are to be absorbed into the latter, than the relationship they had, when they were part of, and belonged to, an animal organism. Now, their function is no longer to mutually intermix and serve each other, but both to subordinate themselves to the “human”, and to let themselves be penetrated and led by the spiritual-moral human creature. So that to join together meat and milk which are fit to be absorbed in the human organism בשר בהמה טהורה and חלב בהמה טהורה by cooking, would accordingly express the very reverse of what is the true function of human beings. It would be the derision and mockery of the למינו-Law for human beings, inasmuch as such a mixture lowers the morally free human creature down to the level of the unfree animal. Such a mixture must, accordingly not only, not be made, אסור בישול, but must have no place whatsoever for human food or use, אסור אכילה והנאה.

If now we further consider the אסור בשר בחלב in connection with the preceding verse ’ראשית ביכורי אדמתך תביא וגו, the law looked at in this connection would be:- Everything which ripens for the food and enjoyment of Man in field and orchard is to find its function and dedication in submitting to, and giving itself up to, the Torah, but not the reverse. Man is not to give himself up to the enjoyment of food as his aim and goal of life. Everything on earth that ripens for Man’s enjoyment is to be raised to the divine part of the human being, but the divine part of the human being is never to be allowed to sink to animal enjoyment of the senses. A warning, that finally may be considered in intimate relation to חג האסיף the Harvest Festival, the third of the pilgrim Festivals. Not for that has God ordered the cycle of the seasons, and now pours His blessings into the lap of expectant Man, that now the enjoyment of this blessing should drag him down to animal-like enjoyment, but so that what has ripened under the sun of the physical world should now enter the sphere of human life, should leave the unfree physical world, and be elevated up into the sphere of morally-free human activity. If גדי representing animal life produced by the blessings of Nature, were again to be מבושל בחלב אמו in the hands of Man, again to find its whole function and end in the vegetative purposes of life — nourishment and reproduction, — the whole cycle of the seasons would be robbed of its purpose, the whole of life on earth would begin and end in an unfree physical cycle, and it is meant, like the top of the altar and the ladder of Jacob, to blossom out of the earthly basis up into the free heights of moral human perfection!

V. 20 et seq. In various ways the following is in relation to the preceding. The last part of Mishpatim from V.20 of the preceding chapter to the end, deals primarily with the equal rights of every inhabitant, and their mutual duties to one another in the future State, by reason of considering the land as belonging to God. The Sabbath of the week and of the years, as well as the pilgrim Festivals at the time of the spring, summer and autumn progress of the year, are mentioned, as furthering and fostering this consciousness of everything belonging to God, as well as the spirit of equality and brotherhood.
To that is appended the following: —

(1) The fact that Israel did not owe the soil of this State to their own valour, but that it was entrusted to them by God, solely and only as a result of their obediently placing themselves under the direction of the Divine Will.

(2) That this faithful obedience to the Divine Torah is also the sole means of ensuring their remaining in the land (as this is constantly to be expressed nationally and individually by the pilgrimage in spring, summer and autumn, and by the laying of the first fruits at the feet of this Torah).

(3) That, accordingly, it does not allow itself, by contact with the present inhabitants of the land who are only gradually to be evacuated, to be deluded into the heathen error of thinking that the physical fact of remaining in the land has nothing to do with the keeping of laws of morality, and in accordance with this view idolises the physical powers of Nature as being the power that grants the possibility of remaining in, and retaining the land.

(4) That no trace of such heathen, erroneous ideas of the gods be tolerated on the soil of this State; and even if the social laws based on the Torah insist above all on the equal rights of domicile and complete equality in the eyes of the law of the “stranger”, this is to be on the express condition, that he ceases to worship idols.

הנה אנכי שלח מלאך. We have already remarked on המלאך הגואל (Gen. 48,16) that the term מלאך does not necessarily imply an individual, a human or superhuman creature, but may also be used for any contrivance which God arranges for some special purpose. One could have been able to take it here to mean “angel” or in the general meaning “Fate, Providence”, literally “something sent”, if V.21 & 22 did not speak of the obedience which is to be given to this מלאך and the instructions and orders of God which he has to transmit. We do not find that God sent His instructions and orders through an angel, and so we must, even if we do take it in that general sense, take it that Moses is specially to be understood by the term, who, in any case, belonged, in no small or unimportant degree, to those measures and means which God used to fulfil the fate of Israel. Bearing in mind the verse in Numbers XX, where, by the term מלאך Moses is specifically to be understood (וישלח מלאך ויוציאנו ממצרים) we think it is not far-fetched to take the “messenger of God” sent before Israel, of our verse here, too, to refer specially to Moses. In any case, it states here, that, just as their protection in the wandering through the wilderness was quite clearly, solely the direct work of the almighty power of God, so the taking possession of the Promised Land, אשר הכנתי which God had prepared quite specially as the land for the people of His Torah, was to be purely the work of the same Divine Power and not the achievement of human swords. — הכנתי the characteristics of the soil of Palestine, and the climate and physical properties which were accorded to the land, are all in accordance with the mission that the life of the nation based on the spirit of God and His Torah, was meant to develop. (cf. Deut. 11,10—12 and in conjunction with it, 13 et seq.; Jonah 1,3 and expressions such as אוירא דא״י מחכים etc.).

V. 21. תַמֵר the Hiphil of מרר i.e., to cause bitterness, see that there arises no dissatisfaction with his leadership, no murmurings against him. — לא ישא לפשעכם he can not give your disobedience any indulgence. It is significant that here פשע is in the singular, and כם in the plural, regarding the nation in its individual members, whereas in the whole of the rest of the address even in the words immediately preceding in the same verse, אל תמר בו the whole nation is considered as one unit. The nation is not to tolerate disobedience or revolt even in single individuals of its members. Such toleration would transfer private, individual guilt into public, national guilt, and the whole nation would then have to pay for the disobedience and revolt of the individuals — as indeed repeatedly happened in the course of history. כי שמי בקרבו for he bears My name within him, is My representative, speaks and orders only in My name. It is not his own will, his own authority, for which he has to demand respect and acceptation, and disregard for which he could overlook. He, himself, is only a שליח, only a מלאך, has only to see that the Will and Authority of his Sender is respected and effective. He has no power to forgive his Master’s affairs.

V. 23. והכחדתיו, one by one, מעט מעט “little by little” as the reason for it is given in V.29 & 30. This gradual disappearance of the old inhabitants will result in longer contact with them and the consequent danger of accepting and copying their ideas and ways. Hence the warning in the following verse. — כחד related to יחד. We have already remarked in considering the roots דמה ,שוא the special way of looking at things which underlies the expressions in Hebrew for being destroyed, coming to nothing, and being nothing, and which leads to the same words and roots being used for “being similar to”, “being equal to” and being null, void, vain, perished. Here we have the same idea, יחד to join together, to become one, and כחד to cease existing.

V. 24. לאלהיהם, the gods, on whose grace they believed their own prosperity and that of their country depended. ’לא תשתחוה וגו, you are neither to think that your future is dependent on the supposed physical powers of these gods, nor that you owe them anything for your past and present (השתחויה ועבודה) and so you are not to allow their delusions to have any influence on your doings. הרס to pull down from a height; their emblems, which they proclaim as the Lord of their fate and prosperity, you are to pull down, and מצבתיהם the memorials, which gratitude for supposed benefits received has erected to them, you are to destroy.

V. 25—26. Only to ’ה to your God, are you to think that you owe anything, and to His service, i.e., to carrying out His Will are you to dedicate yourselves; and note, not ועבדת, not merely the nation in its national representation, but ועבדתם, the Torah must be carried out by every individual member of the nation, וברך את לחמך and then the physical prosperity of the land, which the nations expect from their worship of the supposed powers of Nature, will be blessed by Him. והסרתי, the transition to the first person seems to express the following idea: — That which the others expect from their worship of Nature, you will receive from serving the Law of your God. But more than that. I will grant this blesing in a manner, and to a degree, which far exceeds the blessing expected by others. The natural illnesses and weaknesses which, under the regime of Nature, are considered indispensable from human life, will, under the regime of My Torah, not manifest themselves in your lives. Illness, childlessness and early deaths will be unknown in your land. Not only the land, the inhabitants themselves will be blessed.

V. 27 et seq. It is significant that V.26, which, by its sense is closely connected to the preceding verse, is allocated by the “Parsha-division” to the following Parsha which starts with verse 27. Just as the rich blessings of health and strength will show themselves as the direct acts of God, so will this same power of God effect the weakening and destruction of the inhabitants who are to disappear from the land in your favour. For both, your healthy rise, and their decline and fall, you have only to thank your moral submission to the dictates of God’s Will. It seems, that if Israel, right from the beginning, had kept up to the heights of their calling, and had not, by repeated disobedience shown that they required an educative guidance and management, and hence one full of trials, they would not have had to wage any wars to conquer their land. The inhabitants of the land destined for Israel, who, by their degeneration were doomed to destruction, would have vanished from the land by means that God would have used, and Israel, the People of God’s Law, would simply have taken root in the land.

V. 33. כי יהיה לך למוקש, it, the fact of their remaining in the land without giving up idolatry will become a snare unto you. Do not depend on the heights of purity that you have attained, do not trust yourselves, not to have to be afraid of the proximity of impurity and false ideas, that living together with these people full of their false ideas, you will be able to raise them up to your own true ideals, and not on the other hand let them drag you down to their false ones. It is only in isolation that you can grow strong and firm enough for your ultimate spiritual conquest of the nations of the world. Until that time is reached יהיה לך למוקש being with them will only be a snare for you.

V. 1. The first act of the Lawgiving was finished, it formed the four chapters 20—23. It concluded with the warning against too much self-confidence in the spiritual and moral maturity already attained. This leads back, in Ch. XXIV, to the presence of the people gathered about Sinai to receive the Torah, and connects directly up again with the end of Ch. 19,24. There, we were told of the people being kept fenced off, away from the Mount, the warning had repeatedly been given not to surge up to the manifestation of the appearance of God. Only Moses and Aaron were to be allowed to go up. While the first ten commandments were being given, even Moses was down below with the people, and only at the giving of the succeeding laws — from Ch. 20,19 and onwards, had Moses approached nearer than the people to the clouds which surrounded the Divine Manifestation, but the people remained in the distance. To this, our verse now refers with the words: — ’ואל משה אמר עלה וגו, where, as usual, the past perfect tense implies the pluperfect (i.e., But to Moses He had said) and here it completes that which Ch. 19,24 had told us, by adding that the two sons of Aaron and seventy elders of the people were also to go up with them. Here, too, we are told that even after the conclusion of this first portion of the revelation of the Torah, the people were again kept far from the Mount itself, and only Moses and Aaron and the chosen seventy of the people were allowed up on the Mount, and even there the difference had to be made, that Moses alone had to betake himself right up to the top, his companions, however, after expressing their submission to God by prostrating themselves together with him, had to remain at a distance from the summit, while Moses alone was to go right up to the immediate proximity of God. So that the nation was to present itself in three separate groups; the people completely isolated from the Mount, Aaron and a selected elite of the people, half way up, and Moses at the summit.

Above, on Ch. 19,10—13, it has already been worked out, how by this fixing the limits of the situation of the people for the reception of the Torah, two facts which specifically differentiate this system of Laws from all others, were meant to be expressed: — The superhuman, supernatural origin of this Law, and at the time of this origin the spiritual and moral distance of the people who received it from the height to which in the course of time it was to be raised by this Law, it was the Israel of the future for whom the contemporary generation received the Torah from the hand of God.

With this idea underlying the people’s distance from the Mount, and even of their chosen ones from the summit, our chapter (XXIV) connects itself with the immediately preceding warning which is based on the still immature state of the people.
