The result of living together with the heathen nations, and the allurements of their rites, unfortunately proved only too clearly the distance between the people and the moral and spiritual height, the attainment of which the receipt of the Torah made their mission in life. And just this fact that the People of God were only expected to attain the full height of their calling in the future, seems to be one of the leading ideas of the following verses (see on V.4).

But that Aaron and the picked ones of the people did to a certain extent, accompany Moses up the Mount, does, on the other hand, demonstrate the fact that between the height of Moses and the people no specific dividing cleft lay, that there is no idea that Moses should have had some superhuman nature which accounted for the degree of nearness to God which he attained. The graduation rather goes to show that Moses was simply a man like all other men, it was not the kind of godliness, but the degree of it, that was more highly developed in him than in others; and everybody is called upon, as being able to try and reach his greatness.

V. 3. ויבא משה, away from the ערפל (Ch. 20,18) where he had received the laws up to then. He was to bring these over to the people, and then, in accordance with his directions, again to go up the Mount with Aaron and an elite of the people. — ויספר is not the ordinary expression used for transmitting orders or commands, but is rather describing events. Used for the Torah, it can only designate something more than just a literal repetition of the words of the commands, comprises accordingly, the actual formula of the Law with all the explanatory meaning for its practice, i.e., תשב״כ and תשב״פ the written Law and its verbal explanation.

V. 4. ויכתב משה that which we have before us viz., from ’ויאמר וגו׳ אתם ראיתם וגו Ch. 20,19 till כי יהיה לך למוקש Ch. 23,33. — מזבח תחת ההר on which was to be expressed the devotion of the people to hearing and accepting the Law, and their happy consciousness of their having achieved thereby a bond of nearness to their God — ושתים עשרה מצבה לשנים עשר שבטי ישראל, these twelve tribes were all actually present, so there was no reason to represent them symbolically. So that it was not the twelve tribes that were actually there at the time, but the whole future Israel, the eternal Israel, it was it and it alone of which these memorial stones were to serve as representation, את אשר ישנו פה ואת אשר איננו פה as it says in Deut. 29,14. Far beyond the narrow sphere of his contemporaries did the view of our Moses roam, when he erected the altar and memorial stones to the Law he had brought over. Just as the oath of the covenant for the Torah כל הדברים אשר דבר ה׳ נעשה was taken on behalf of all the coming generations, and all their souls were stamped thereby with the seal of their mission that can never be lost, so were all these souls present in the mind of Moses when he erected the altar; to the tribes of Israel who were present he added symbolically all the future ones in the twelve memorial stones. So did Elijah too, take twelve stones when he re-erected the altar on Carmel to the One Unique God (Kings I. 18,31) “according to the number of the tribes of the children of Jacob to whom God had given the name and the mission “Israel”. This Israel, this one unique people, bearers of the banner of the One Unique God, was no longer there. Torn assunder in their unity, the minority were wavering, and the majority who stood about him were entirely under the political and religious sway of the Baal priesthood. “Israel” in whose name he erected the altar to the One, Only God, that Israel did not stand about him. Only in spirit, in the idea, were they present to him. Only symbolically could he call them around him, and his twelve stones expressed equally the degeneration of his contemporary generation and his confidence in the everlasting continuance of the People of God, even beyond such times. Just like Moses, he raised his view over and beyond the limited and limiting present, and built the stones to the immortal Israel of the future.
That was why Moses sent: —

V. 5. נערי בני ישראל, the young men, the youth, the immediate bearers of the future. They brought עולות — the offering of complete surrender (really “elevating” offerings, offerings denoting climbing upwards to the heights, hence זריקת דם למטה מחוט הסיקרא see on Levit. Ch. I) and זבחי שלמים offerings of “meals of peace”, the offering of the happy blessed consciousness of the bond of being near to God in the midst of worldly life (— of being a guest at the table of God on earth —). They brought these elevating and peace offerings in פרים, oxen, the expression for “workers in the service of God” (see ibid.) in which service they had just entered by accepting the Torah. (In the Gemora Chagiga 7b doubt is expressed whether the פרים refer to עולות also or only to שלמים. If the latter, then they would first have expressed themselves in עולות by כבש as צאן מרעיתו, to their Shepherd, as the nation to be led by God, and then, in שלמים by פרים as having entered His service to express their happiness and joy before their “Master”).

V. 6. אגן und עגן bedeuten beide eine anderes umschlingende, festhaltende Biegung, daher auch chaldäisch עכנא: die Schlange. Hier אגן ein Becken, und zwar vielleicht mit völlig rundgebogenem Boden, בלי שולים (Peßachim 64a) ohne Basis, so daß man es nicht ruhig hinstellen konnte, um das Gerinnen des zum Sprengen bestimmten Blutes zu verhindern.

V. 7. ספר הברית, the Law written down, as mentioned in V.4 which V.3 tells us had been fully transmitted verbally and which their vow of acceptance, נעשה, rendered into a ברית (a bond which must absolutely be kept in any and every circumstance I.L.) — נעשה ונשמע, above in V.3 on receiving the verbal transmission, it was sufficient to vow נעשה. The Law had been fully explained to them in all its details and meaning. To that, all they had to promise was “to carry it out”, to “do it”. But the written Law contained the Law only in its short basic formula, as we have the Torah before us to-day, the detailed meaning and explanation remained for verbal teaching, and that entails applying one’s mind by listening. The vow נעשה to the written, readable Torah, would only refer to the literal Word, quite incomplete without the verbal tradition. Hence here they added “נשמע״ and thereby declared: Everything which God has spoken, not merely these basic principles which have been read to us here, will we carry out, and to accomplish this end we will also “listen”, i.e., by getting to know and to keep that which has remained verbal, we will get ourselves in the condition of being able to carry out the will of God really and completely.

V. 8. ויזרק על העם. From Yebamoth 56b and Kerithoth 9a it is clear that this was a sprinkling towards the people, and not as Onkelos translated it, a throwing on the Altar as an atonement for the people, וזרק על מדבחא לכפרא על עמא. The one half of the blood had already been thrown on to the Altar (V.6) and now Moses threw the other half towards the nation. This would express the idea, that every drop of blood, every ounce of our forces, that we give up to carry out God’s will on earth, is given back to us in the full measure that we give it to God. We receive it back from God, and we only really have true possession of ourselves if we offer ourselves to God. This would be the response to their part of the bond, their נעשה ונשמע, and would make the covenant a mutual one, and so we can understand the words which Moses used when he made this gesture: ’הנה דם הברית וגו. The ספר הברית contains the demands that God makes of us, the דם הברית received back (after having been directed to the Altar of the Torah) expresses the grants that we can expect from God, if we do give ourselves up to the ספר הברית.

V. 10. Who would be presumptuous enough to try to specify what it was that they saw! But taking the literal words of the Torah we would dare to remark:- As it says very definitely in Ch. 33,20 “thou art not able to see My presence for no man can see Me and live”, and equally definitely in Deut. Ch. 4,12 & 15 referring to this revelation on Sinai, it repeatedly states that no material form whatsoever was seen when God spoke to us out of the fire on Horeb, the ויראו אלהי ישראל, can only refer, not to God himself, but to the phenomenon by which God announces His presence. Or, and this seems to us the more likely meaning of the words, it is to be construed in a similar way to ראיתי את העם הזה והנה עם קשה ערף הוא (Ch. 32,9) or ראיתי את הארץ והנה תהו ובהו ואל השמים ואין אורם (Jer. 4,23) “I saw” the people and behold they are an obstinate people”, or “I saw” the earth and behold it is empty and waste, the heavens, and their light has disappeared”. Where it is not really the people, or the earth, or the heavens, which is the object that is seen, but the condition in which the people or the earth or the heavens are in, and the meaning of course is “I saw that the people are obstinate, that the earth was waste, that the light had disappeared from the heavens”. In the same way, possibly ’ויראו את אלהי ישראל ותחת רגליו וגו may mean “they saw that at the Feet of the God of Israel was like the formulation of a sapphire brick, etc.”.

אלהי ישראל, a term which occurs so frequently in the books of the prophets, occurs very seldom in the Pentateuch, and when it does, it is always on a special occasion, and with emphasis. Used by itself, and not as an attribute to ’ה, it occurs only three times (a) here, (b) in Gen. 33,20, when Jacob — for the first time an independent head of a family on his native soil — built himself a house and erected an “altar as a memorial” proclaimed thereby God, as “the God of Israel”, ויקרא לו אל אלהי ישראל; and (c) in Numb. 16,9, where Moses reminded Korach and his supporters, ’המעט מכם כי הבדיל אלהי ישראל אתכם וגו, that He to Whom Israel as a whole belongs as the instrument and servant for His purposes, He alone is entitled to choose within this nation that belongs to Him, the special instruments and servitors for His will. Here it is quite similar. It was only now, just after they had concluded the “covenant-relationship” to God, that God had truly become אלהי ישראל and now they saw “at His Feet” כמעשה לבנת הספיר. For several reasons לבנת כספיר can not mean the “whiteness” of sapphire. The colour white does not occur elsewhere in the feminine, but as לָבָן e.g., מחשף הלבן (Gen. 30,37), so that we should expect לְבֶן הספיר Then מעשה in describing things never refer to the colour, but to the nature of the work, or the shape or form given to the object: מעשה רשת ,כמעשה אופן מעשה חשב ,מעשה שושן, etc. Finally, sapphire is not white, but blue, sky blue, רקיע דומה לאבן ספיר (Chulin 89a). According לבנת can quite well be the stat. constr. of a brick. The preparation of bricks is expressed by the term עשה Ex. 5,16. כמעשה לבנת הספיר .ולבנים אומרים לנו עשו would accordingly mean, either like the preparation of, or like the shape of, a sapphire brick. “At His Feet” i.e., for the building of His Throne, they saw that a brick had been laid with their covenant. Just as when they were עבדי פרעה they had to prepare bricks in the service of Pharaoh to build up the might of the Pharaohs, so now, as ’עבדי ה in the service of God, they make “bricks” for building up the Kingdom of God on earth, and their נעשה ונשמע was the first brick for this covenant. But they saw that such a brick is “sapphire”. Everything material, earthly, which is brought in faithful service to this building joins itself to the heavenly, becomes permeated with the heavenly, becomes heavenly (sapphire) and “is in no wise behind ‘the heavenly’ itself in purity” וכעצם השמים לטהר.

V. 11. To raise an unfriendly hand against somebody is usually expressed by -שלח יד ב (it is true that in two single instances in the תנ״ך we do find שלח יד אל used with this meaning, Gen. 22,12 and Job 1,12). It would be difficult to think that here we are told that God did not raise His Hand against the chosen ones of Israel mentioned in V.9, although they had gone up towards the Appearance at the top of the Mount. There could be no cause for Him to do so, as it was at His express command that they had gone up. We find ’יד ה also used for the power of the spirit of God, which seizes a prophet and raises him up into the realm of prophecy. (Ezekiel and elsewhere). — אצל from which we get אֵצֶל next to, means primarily divided by space, and in Isaiah 41,9 where אצילים once again occurs ומאציליה קראתיך it seems to be synonymous with the preceding אשר החזקתיך מקצות הארץ, and means those who are separated by space, at a distance. We suggest that here too, the אצילי בני ישראל refers to those standing at a distance, those, kept back from proximity to the Mount and the Divine Appearance, i.e., to the people kept behind the barriers. Those called up to be near to the presence of God, on the Mount (V.9) were gripped by the ’יד ה, and accordingly ויראו they saw את אלהי ישראל etc. (a very high degree of prophecy). But to the masses standing afar, God did not send this ’יד ה but ויחזו (in comparison to ראה the more concrete and closer seeing, חזה (from which we get חָזֶה the breast) denotes an inner vision, or seeing from a distance) “they saw God in their minds” or perhaps “they looked up to the distant manifestation of God”, ויאכלו וישתו without being raised above the ordinary, normal, everyday standpoint, limited by their senses. Those seized by the prophetic spirit were raised up to God Himself, the Children of Israel who were not raised to this eminence, nevertheless, sitting at the sacrificial meal, felt the nearness of God within them (V.5). They enjoyed the bliss of feeling the proximity of God, in the midst of material, earthly life, that highest normal result of Jewish Torah life. The reference in Deut. 27,7 to the national covenant with the Torah concluded at Sinai similarly runs וזבחת שלמים ואכלת שם ושמחת לפני ה׳ אלהיך, (compare verses 5—7 there with V.4 & 5 of our chapter here). In Megilla 9a אצילי בני ישראל is taken to refer not to the whole nation but to the נערי בני ישראל (V.5), the firstborn sons, who being consecrated to represent the families at every Divine Service, are called אצילים “those separated out”. In that case too, לא שלח ידו and the ’ויחזו וגו could be understood in the sense which we have indicated.

V. 12. As Moses, together with Aaron and the elders, was already on the Mount (V.9) this command can only refer to a further mounting right up to the summit. אשר כתבתי, in accordance with what we are told in Ch. 31,18, at the end of Moses’ stay on the Mount: ויתן וגו׳, ככלתו וגו׳ :אשר כתבתי להורתם — שני לחת העדת וגו׳ כתובים וגו׳: The written Law is only an instructor’s text book, by reference to which the real teaching — which is to be retained for verbal tuition — is to be kept intact, and ensured.

V. 14. שבו לנו, a similar construction to ימים רבים תשבי לי (Hosea 3,3). בזה here in the vicinity of the Mount, do not journey on in the meantime. ’בעל דברים :מי בעל דברים וגו literally, the owner of words, in contrast to the owner of things, i.e., whoever raises a claim against anything which is in the possession of somebody else, יגש he has to come אלהם, to court, not the other one. Herein lies the general principle המוציא מחברו עליו הראיה it is up to the one who claims anything in somebody else’s possession to prove his case. So long as no such proof is brought, the possessor is in no way bound to justify his actual possession.

V. 2. ויקחו לי. Nothing is to be given directly to God, but the gifts of each individual are to be given to the community, for the Divine purposes. This implies that it is not the individual, but the community, who has to erect the institutions for God’s purposes, and it is not for single givers but for the community that these arrangements have to be established. תרומה from רום to be raised above something, hence “lifted up out of” i.e., to be separated for some higher purpose. נדב ,ידבנו (related to נטף, to flow out from within) to incite to make a gift. It denotes the most complete freedom of will. תקחו, includes Moses himself in the general community.

V. 8. ’ועשו לי מקדש וגו. In our treatise in the Jeshurun (reprinted in the Gesammelten Schriften vol. 3) entitled “Grundlinien einer Judischen Symbolik”, we have worked out very thoroughly and proved the symbolic nature of the Tabernacle as a whole, and of the materials used for it in detail. With regard to the explanations which follow here, we would refer our readers to that article, which discusses thoroughly the question as to whether all these things really are symbolic, inasmuch as here we are taking as the basis for our explanations of the text, the results we obtained there.

It only requires a glance at Ch. XXVI, in Leviticus which concludes the laws regarding the consecrating of the Temple and of our lives, which come after the instructions for the building of the Temple which begin here in Exodus, ’אם בחקתי תלכו וגו and finish up with ’ונתתי משכני בתוככם וגו to be able to say to oneself with the utmost certainty, (a) that the ושכנתי בתוככם of our verse extends far beyond the mere presence of God in the Temple, but that it means the proximity of God in our midst, showing itself in accordance with the covenant, in the whole happiness and prosperity of our private and national life under His protection and blessing. But also that (b) this blessing and protecting Schechina — proximity of God — is not brought about by the mere correct erection and upkeeping of the Sanctuary, but can only be won by consecrating and giving up our whole private and public lives to carrying out the Divine Torah. A fact that is not only proved historically by the destruction of the Sanctuary, once in Shilo and twice in Jerusalem, but which is distinctly stressed as a warning, not only in the Torah itself, particularly at the cardinal principles of the whole of the Torah ג״ע ,ע״ז and ש״ד Levit. 20,3, Numb. 35,34, Levit. 15,31, Deut. 23,10 & 15, but also immediately at the foundation and building of the Solomon’s Temple (Kings I. 6,9 & 12) and on almost every page of the books of the prophets e.g. Jer. VII.

If then our text does nevertheless promise ושכנתי בתוכם as a result of ועשו לי מקדש, then evidently the meaning of the מקדש can be nothing else but the expression of all that is required of us to bring about the promised Schechina-Presence in Israel. With ועשו לי מקדש ושכנתי בתוכם two ideas are given to us, and the whole building of the Tabernacle and its furniture is to symbolise these two ideas. The idea of מקדש and the idea of משכן. The one, מקדש, the whole of the task we have to do for God, and the other, משכן, the promises God has given us if we do it. The task ועשו לי מקדש consists of our giving up the whole of our private and public life to the fulfilment of the Torah. The promise ושכנתי בתוכם, the protecting and blessing-giving presence of God in our midst, manifesting itself in the happiness of our private and national lives. The Tabernacle is to be מקדש the Home of Consecration, and משכן the Home of God’s Proximity to us. From this home we are to get inspiration for our own consecration and to gain the resulting reward. So that the sphere within which we have to try and find the meaning of the Tabernacle as a whole, and its component parts in detail, is simply mutual covenant-relationship between God and Israel, brought about by the giving and acceptance of the Torah. It is just because of this meaning of the Tabernacle that this chapter of the building follows immediately on the preceding fundamental principles of the Torah and the resulting ברית that was concluded thereupon.

Looked at from this point of view, the materials which were to be donated for the building of the משכן—מקדש indicate those of its qualities by means of which that “קדושה״ is to be obtained, as well as this “שוכן״, this proximity of God to us is proclaimed. For, had we not first received these objects of our gifts from God, and in donating them to the Sanctuary do we no t receive them back ourselves in doubly enhanced value, even as Jacob expressed it when he laid the first foundation stone for the very first House of God (Gen. 28,22) וכל אשר תתן לי ,עשר אעשרנו לך; or as David expressed it even more poignantly at the preparation for the building of the first Temple כי ממך הכל ומידך נתנו לך (Chron. I. 29,14) “everything comes from Thee, and what we give unto Thee comes from Thy Hand”; or, what was brought here to us in still more comprehensive brevity in the throwing of half of the blood of the ברית towards the Altar and towards the people, which had just been done (above XXIV,6 & 8).

In our discussion in Jeshurun V. p. 232 et seq., we have proved that in the תנ״ך, metals in general, in accordance with their physical property of hardness, are used as a metaphor for firmness and strength (e.g., Jer. I.15, Job 6,12, Isaiah 48,4) and in accordance with their being valuable, as a metaphor for valuing spiritual values (e.g., Prov. 2,10, Ps. 19,11, Job XXVIII), but quite specially in accordance with their metallurgical properties as the most suitable metaphor for all goodness and truth in every stage of admixture with evil and the untrue, and also for all the processes of tests and purifying and refining applied to morality and truth (e.g., Job 23,10; Zacch. 13,9; Mal. 3,3; Is. 48,10; Prov. 25,4, 10, 20 & XXVI,23; Jer. 6,29 & 30; Ps. 119,119; Ez. 22,18; Is. 1,22; Dan. 2,32 & 33). In all these places metals are used to designate the various degrees of moral purity and truth. Whereas copper represents an ignoble nature, one not yet refined; silver describes the stage of still requiring purification, but of being able and fit to be refined; gold, which is usually found pure, and unmixed, and also resists the strongest tests, is the picture of the purest, most sterling, moral nobility and of true, real permanence and constancy.

As metals combine the highest degree of adaptiveness with the highest degree of firmness and stability; under heat and hammer can be adapted to any desired form, but once they have received that form, retain it with a persistence that can only be destroyed by violence, they represent by these properties just those very characteristics that we should have towards our duty in general, and especially towards the will of God, as revealed to us by His Word. His Word is described, too, as “Hammer” and “Fire” (Jer. 23,29). So that metals offer themselves more than anything else for allegorical expressions of our moral relations to our calling.

So that, according to their metallurgical characteristics as indicated:- Copper would represent the ignoble nature, Silver, the one who is ready to be ennobled by purification, Gold, the original and test-resisting, the most complete purity and goodness.

In our articles in the Jeshurun we have discussed at length and in detail, and proved, that human clothing generally serves as the picture of human nature and character. We worked out how human nature has a vegetative side — absorbing nourishment and sexual life, with all the accompanying allurements and impulses, efforts and enjoyments, and also an animal side — life, with all its living powers of knowledge, will and effort — and we showed how also in the Laws of Tzitzis and Shatnes, wool as material for clothes represents the animal side of human beings, and flax, linen, the vegetative side.

For use in the Sanctuary here, the cloth materials to be given were again only wool and flax:- תכלת ארגמן ותולעת שני, wool; שש, flax, and these are further specialised by their colours, white, blue and red in two shades.

שש linen, flax, representative of the vegetative, is white, and white, as explained there, is the colour of purity. Moral purity in the Torah refers principally to the powers of our vegetative life. Degeneration in sexual life and in matter of food is the deepest stain on the purity of a human being. Purity is the character which just for the vegetative aspect of a human being, forms the degree of nobility which God demands.

Wool, representative of the animal aspect, is itself of animal origin, and so too, are the dyes, the colours here mentioned, blue, purple and scarlet, of animal origin. Of the two reds (as proved in the Jeshurun article) שני is the paler, ארגמן the nobler, so that if red in general, as the colour of the blood, represents Life, שני is the lower, the animal stage of Life, ארגמן the higher, the human stage of Life. תכלת, skyblue, the colour which, at the limit of our horizon seems to point to a realm beyond human sight, represents the godliness which is revealed to us, the colour of God’s bond with Man, the sign of spirituality, of godliness, which permeates and directs the whole life of a pure human being.
עזים, goats’ hair, only used for sacks and mourning and penitence clothes, is a material giving protection and defence.
Concerning ערת אילים מאדמים ,ערת תחשים see Ch. 26,14.

עץ .עצי שטים, tree; wood, in general, is the picture of progressive growth and development (see Jeshurun VI, p. 86) to which in ארז the cedar tree (one of the ten varieties of which is שטה) is added the special characteristic of strength and size. So that עצי שטים, used for the Tabernacle and its contents, is the symbol of a strong, enduring ever-fresh progressive development.

The material mentioned in verses 3—5 are all joined by a copul. ו. They all belong together as being the material out of which the actual building and its contents were to be made. V.7 mentions precious stones which were required for the outfit of the priests. So that priests and their garments are included as an essential part of the Sanctuary itself. They are part of the כלי מקדש as רמב״ם too classifies them in a spiritual sense in the יד חזקה, and as we shall have to realise when we come to study the laws regarding the sacrifices. (We shall see how the priests themselves — especially the High Priest — and their garments serve symbolically, in quite a similar way, to the Temple itself for the minds of the people. Surprisingly, in V.6, oil for the lights, and spices for the anointing-oil and for the incense are also mentioned. Now שמן המשחה does not really belong in its real sense to the מקדש, but as it is essential for the consecration of it and its contents, and as they are really only inducted into the character which they represent by being anointed with it, we can understand its being included amongst the rest of the constituent materials. But oil for lighting and incense, seem only to belong to the category of materials necessary for the service in the Sanctuary, like flour for the showbread, wood for the fire on the Altar, lambs for the daily offerings etc., and their being reckoned amongst the materials to be subscribed for the building of the Tabernacle is striking. Nevertheless, if, as we shall have to show, the spiritual life we are to lead, inspired by, and directed to, the Torah, finds its expression in the Sanctuary in the burning of the lights, and the achieved ideal of all sacrifice to God — the complete sublimation of self to be pleasing to God — is the meaning of the burning of incense, then the mention of these immediately with the gifts for the building, tells us that the establishment of this building is to achieve the two highest aims of human existence, viz., clear true enlightenment, the goal for one’s mind, and being pleasing to God, the goal for one’s acts.

’אבני שהם וגו (see Ch. 28,9—17). וכן תעשו. It does not say כן תעשו but וכן תעשו so that it is not just the conclusion of the preceding, but a fresh command: “And so are ye always to do”. The Gemora (Sanhedrin 16b) takes it that by this is to be understood, that, just as here, the Tabernacle could only be erected and arranged under the direction and authority of Moses, so, in the future too, every matter that concerns the Temple could only be done by the authority of, and under the direction of, the Sanhedrin, the official representation of the nation.

V. 10. The orders start with the furnishings, for they are the essentials. The Tabernacle is there for the furnishings, not the furnishings for the Tabernacle. It is the furnishings, the כלים, the מזבח ,מנורה ,שלחן ,ארון, which constitute the מקדש. It is they, that are to make us see the sanctification and devotion, the elevation of all mundane matters to God; the building itself, the משכן, represents the result of this devotion, the fulfilment of the promise ושכנתי בתוכם as a result of the ועשו לי מקדש.

ועשו ארון. The first and only כלי of which even the wording in which the command to make it is couched shows that it is something which is expected from the whole nation, is the ארון, the Ark of the Testimony. Just as it says immediately above ועשו לי מקדש so here ועשו ארון, and so also of the symbolic forms of cherubim that crowned the Ark, V.19, it says מן הכפרת תעשו את הכרובים. Of everything else the command is in the second person ועשית ,וצפית, etc. It almost seems that the whole task ועשו לי מקדש lies concentrated in the ועשו ארון עצי שטים, and everything further is merely a wider extension of the ארון .ארון (from ארה to pick off for eating, (Song of Songs V.2 and Ps. 80,13) related to הרה to absorb a seed of life, the root of תורה) designates a container in which that which it receives is accepted there permanently. So in Gen. 50,26, of a coffin, and Kings II. 12,10 and Chron. II. 24,8 of boxes for donations for the expenses of the Temple. The Ark receives the Torah for Israel or rather, by the Ark, or with the Ark, Israel accepts the Torah.

ארון עצי שטים. Israel receives the Torah with its, Israel’s, eternally fresh ability for development and progress (see above) and for this progressive development. The Torah is given complete, concluded, the Tablets are stone ones. The two together, form a complete cube of stone. Each Tablet is six טפחים long, six ’ט wide, and three ’ט thick, so that together they form a solid cube of six cubic טפחים, a cubic ell, (amma) the largest unit in cubes (Baba Bathra 14a). Not the Torah, we are the tree, we can, and we should develop and ennoble ourselves in unending progress through the Torah. Israel receives the Torah to become thereupon ’עץ שתול על פלגי מים וגו (Ps. 1,3).

’אמתים וחצי וגו. The dimensions of the Ark are governed by the size of the Tablets. The measurements of length and breadth given here are external. The walls were half a טפח thick, reckoning the ell at six טפחים — in accordance with רבי מאיר — the internal space would be fourteen ’ט long and eight ’ט wide. The two Tablets lying side by side would occupy a length of twelve ’ט and a breadth of six. In the space next to them lay the copy of the Torah completed by Moses (Deut. 31,26). According to רבי יהודה, all the measurements given for the furnishing of the Tabernacle were of the “smaller ell” of five טפחים; so there would have been no room in the ארון for the ס״ת, and he accordingly says that the ס״ת lay outside the Ark on a kind of bracket which was attached to the Ark for that purpose (See B.B. 14a).

V. 11. וצפית. With the qualities of susceptibility and living ability of development, must at the same time be associated, firmness, stubborn persistance, and immutability for all that is noble and good, true and genuine; to the wood, metal; to the tree, gold. The Divine Torah demands both the ability to develop and at the same time firmness in those that receive it, and this noble firmness has to hold good both internally towards itself, and externally to outside influences, מבית ומחוץ תצפנו. The Ark consisted of three containers, an inner and outer one of gold, and between these, the one of shittim wood. In inner and outer life, sterling and firm, noble and genuine, free from all dross, resisting all alteration and deterioration, these are the conditions, these are the golden limits within which, life from the Torah is to progresively develop like a tree. Inaccessible to all evil, ready for all good, זהב and מצות לא תעשה — עץ and מצות עשה — such is the dual nature of the character which makes Israel fit and able to be the containers of the Divine Torah.

ועשית עליו זר זהב סביב. The Ark is to be surrounded by an upward projecting circlet. This circlet was formed by the edge of the outer golden wall of the Ark being extended above the cover of the Ark. זר, a circlet, a ring, (from זור to be strange, by reason of one’s inner nature, to be separated from others), seems, both by its form and its name, to represent, on the appurtenances of the Sanctuary, the quality of holiness and of unapproachability, and in this respect to be related both in word and in fact with נזר, a crown, a diadem. Inasmuch as here in the case of the Ark, the זר was not a separate piece, but was formed by a projecting part of the Ark itself, it seems to mean: — If Israel will only give itself up to keep and use its strength and firmness in sterling purity in its inner and outer life, then by itself it becomes unassailable also from outside forces: וראו כל עמי הארץ כי שם ה׳ נקרא עליך ויראו ממך (Deut. 28,10).

V. 12—15. בדים, carrying-poles. These were not simply means for transport, which would be only necessary when carrying the Ark from one place to another, they were never to be allowed to be separated from the Ark. לא יסורו ממנו ,והמסיר בדי ארון לוקה (Yoma 72a). They belonged essentially to that which the Ark represented symbolically. So much so, that according to the words of our text, they had to be on the Ark even before the Tablets were placed in the Ark, and the cover placed over it. תוספות ibid even supposed that the Ark had to have two pairs of these poles. One pair that always remained on the Ark, and which were never allowed to be taken out of it, but which were not actually used for carrying, and so were a purely symbolic appendage, and a second pair that were only inserted at the time of, and for the purpose of, transport. The wording of our verse 12 and of Numbers 4,6 would favour this supposition but V.14 here would seem against it. In any case the essential importance of the poles for the Ark is ensured by the command that they may never be separated from the Ark, in contrast to the poles for the other appurtenances of the Sanctuary. From Kings I. 8,8, we learn that the front ends of these poles pushed the curtain outwards, and so, although covered, were visible. To anyone in the Sanctuary they were the sole visible evidence of the existence of the Ark of the Covenant behind the curtain.

The בדים, the means of carrying the Ark, symbolically represent the command and the mission to carry the Ark and its contents, if it becomes necessary, away from the precincts of its present position. The command that these means of transport may never be lacking is to emphasise in our minds the fact that from the very beginning it must be made clear that this Torah and its mission is in no way bound or confined to the place or existence at any time of the Temple and Sanctuary.

This meaning of the constant presence of the בדים, as proof of the independence of the Torah of any place, receives further emphasis when it is contrasted to the other appurtenances of the Sanctuary, especially to the Table and Menora, both of which had to be supplied with בדים, but the poles did not have to be permanently in place, but only inserted when actually to be used. The thought immediately jumps to one’s mind:- Israel’s Table and Israel’s Menora — its material life in its full completeness, and its spiritual and intellectual life in complete clarity and brightness — are bound to the soil of the Holy Land. Israel’s Torah is not.

In Yoma 72a, attention is drawn to the apparent contradiction between V.15 בטבעות הארון יהיו הבדים לא יסורו ממנו and the previous verse ’והבאת את הבדים וגו׳ ,לשאת וגו which seems parallel to והובא את בדיו בטבעות referring to the Altar (Ch. 27,7) (See תוספות ibid.) and the explanation is given as lying in the construction of the poles. מתפרקין ואין משמטין (ibid.) i.e., they can be forcibly taken out, but do not slip out by themselves. They were, as Rashi explains, thicker at the ends than in the middle. The prohibition לא יסורו ממנו and המסיר בדי ארון לוקה in itself obviously presupposes the possibility of their being taken out. The bearers should never be lacking, but they can be lacking, can be forcibly wrenched away from the Ark. But the Ark itself remains uninjured in that case, and waits — for new bearers!

פעם פעמתיו as a corner, only occurs here, and again in Ch. 33,3 with reference to the ארון, and once again in Kings I. 7,30 in reference to the ים של שלמה. As פעם really means a step, רמב״ן thinks it refers to the bottom corner. Perhaps it also wants to indicate that the rings were to be fixed in the “direction of the stride”, i.e., to be so placed that the poles would go through them in the direction in which the Ark was to be caried. For the Ark stood in the Sanctuary (along the west wall) from north to south, the poles stretched from west to east, with ells of the length of the Ark between them, so that there was room in front and behind for two bearers on each side, who carried the Ark along broad side forward. (Menachoth 98a & b).

V. 16. ונתת אל הארון את העדות. The Torah is entrusted to the people who are prepared, in “gold-like” purity and firmness, and in “tree-like” ever fresh development, to carry it with them for ever. The Torah is represented by the עדות-Tablets, the very presence of which prove to all successive generations the fact of the revelation of the Torah by God, and hence are called עדות “the Evidence”, or Testimony. So that right from the beginning God reckoned on people denying His Torah, and to teach and warn them He deposited the “Evidence”. Evidence is, after all, only necessary for doubters and deniers.

V. 17—20. כפורת. All the other uses of the root כפר, pitch, a surround, village, the leader of the lions, atonement, all have the basic idea of covering, protecting, guarding. כפורת, accordingly means nothing else but a cover for protection. Out of the cover two cherubim arose. These cherubim were not added to the cover, they were קשה) מקשה related to ישה from which we get יש and ישע both of which designate an intensity of existing, describes a high degree of material coherence, (hard, massive) hence מקשה solid, not joined together from several pieces but worked from one single piece). The cherubim were made with the cover, of one piece of gold, משני קצות הכפורת the two ends of the cover ended as cherubim, the cover itself at its two extremities became cherubim.

We have understood the ארון to represent the acceptance of God’s Torah by Israel, and carrying it out with the resistance of pure gold against all evil, and with the constant development of trees for all good. To this keeping of the Torah, the כפורת adds the משמרת, the protection, the care, the שמירה of the מצות, which, together with the doing of the actual Mitzva — ושמרתם ועשיתם —comprises the whole of that which God expects of Israel for His Torah. But just as the cherubim have פניהם אל הכפרת their mental attention concentrated on the כפרת as well as סוככים בכנפיהם על הכפרת actually protecting it with their wings, so do our sages see in the שמירה which these כרובים direct us to give to the Torah, a dual task, (a) to concentrate our mental powers on it, תלמוד to grasp its meaning, to carry out its precepts with intelligence, and (b) the actual protection of the מצות by the making of סיגים ותקנות, the “fences” which Israel is to set up for itself as a משמרת, a protection about the Torah and institutions which it is to establish, to act as spurs to urge itself towards the keeping of all the mitzvos of the Torah.
So that ארון and כפורת point to our receiving the Torah from the Hand of God, and devoting all the powers of our intelligence and action to guarding it and living it.

But the cherubim to which the ends of the כפורת form themselves, show the results which this guarding and living the Torah bring to Israel. We find כרובים in the Holy Scriptures having two definite meanings: — (a) as watchers and protectors and (b) as bearers of the Glory of God.

As watchers and protectors of the way to the Tree of Life כרובים were appointed (Gen. 3,24). אַת כרוב “thou art a cherub, ממשח הסוכך, appointed as protector by anointment” runs the message of Ezekiel (XXVIII,14 et seq.) to the Tyrian power of empire, and this mighty power is then immediately described as “a protecting or guardian cherub”. The meaning of cherubim as watchers and protectors is, thereby indubitably established. With no less uncertainty do we find their meaning bearers of the Glory of God. Borne by a cherub, God hurries, world-shatteringly to the rescue of His servant David. (Ps. 18,11). In Ezekiel IX & X, cherubim are described as the bearers of God’s Glory. But it is especially the stereotyped attribute of God, יושב הכרובים, (Ps. 80,2; Ps. 99,1; Sam. I. 4,4; Sam. II. 6,2; Kings II. 19,15; Chron. I. 13,6; Is. 37,16) that proves this meaning of the cherubim. Moreover, as it does not say יושב בכרובים or על הכרובים but וישב הכרובים, the meaning is — as can be deduced from the analogy to the expressions יושב בארץ and יושב הארץ, as well as everywhere where יושב occurs with or without a preposition — not a temporary or transient Presence, but a permanent one, a residing, and accordingly the הכרובים can well refer solely to the cherubim in the Sanctuary.

Here, too, the cherubim appear quite clearly in this double function of protectors and bearers. The very description of the attitude they are to be given, implies this. “The cherubim are to have their wings spread upwards (למעלה upwards, not מלמעלה above, over) covering סוככים with their wings over the cover, their faces directed one to the other; towards the cover are the faces of the cherubim to be directed”. The function of protecting and guarding is quite explicit. Both the סוככים with their wings, and keeping their faces directed downwards onto the cover, clearly express this. But the other function too, the bearing of the Glory of God, seems to be expressed in the פורשים כנפים למעלה. Their wings are to be spread upwards to bear Something from above. The wings spread סוככים protecting above the cover and also upwards פורשים למעלה fulfilled simultaneously the double function. They protected the cover, and bore the Glory of God. True, the protecting and guarding character seems the prominent one, both the protectors and the object to be protected are visible. The second function can only be expressed by the position of the wings being arranged as if to bear Something resting above. The bearers and the act of bearing are visible but That which they are to bear is invisible. For That is the Glory of God to which no shape can be given.

Now the cherubim are not described as being direct guardians and protectors of the Tablets themselves but of the סוככים בכנפיהם על הכפרת, וכפרת אל הכפרת יהיו פני הכרובים both their mental concentration (פני אל) and their actual material protection (סוככים) are directed to the כפרת. But, on the other hand, as the cherubim are nothing separate from the כפרת but are part of the cover itself, which, after it has completed the actual protection of the Tablets — משני קצות הכפרת — rises up above itself, and becomes its own cherubim which protect itself and become bearers of the Glory of God, the following idea is strikingly expressed:-

With every effort Israel makes to carry out and protect God’s Torah, it achieves only its own preservation, and furthers its own well being and happiness, and prepares itself to be the home of the Glory of God on earth. Israel using its powers of intelligence and conscientiousness in the fulfilment of the Torah becomes cherubim — כרובים משני קצות הכפרת — who protect and keep itself, and allow the Glory of God to rest on Israel. The complete appearance of the golden cover, ending up in golden guarding and bearing cherubim, protecting the “Ark of the Evidence” which enclosed the Torah in its golden and wooden walls, preached the words which God spoke to Joshua the leader of Israel: — רק חזק ואמץ מאד לשמור לעשות ככל התורה אשר צוך משה עבדי, אל תסור ממנו ימין ושמאל למען תשכיל בכל אשר תלך. לא ימוש ספר התורה הזה מפיך והגית בו יומם ולילה למען תשמור לעשות ככל הכתוב בו. כי אז תצליח את דרכך ואז תשכיל הלא צויתיך חזק ואמץ אל תערץ ואל תחת כי עמך ה׳ אלהיך בכל אשר תלך. (Josh. 1,7—10).

Here the gold-like qualities of strength and firmness which have to be kept and exercised in carrying out the Torah by continuous and unceasing study of, and occupying the mind with the Torah, are emphasised, and also the resulting sensible and rational and happy mode of life, and the then ever present proximity of God (Schechina) manifesting itself in help and blessing throughout life.

The Ark and its cover also express that which God promises our whole nation as a result of their guarding and keeping the whole of His Torah. והיה עקב תשמעון את המשפטים האלה ושמרתם ועשיתם אותם. ושמר ה׳ אלהיך לך .את הברית ואת החסד אשר נשבע לאבתיך. ואהבך וברכך והרבך וגו׳ וגו׳ וגו׳ (Deut. 7,12).

And finally, what the Torah itself declares on every page, that by taking care and precautions and keeping the Torah, Israel is only founding its own preservation and its own happiness, and keeping up the bond of the blessing-giving proximity of God.
So that ארון וכפרת are the representation of the task ועשו לי מקדש, and the כרובים the representation of the result that ensues therefrom ושכנתי בתוכם.

All that now remains is to consider the question: Why שני כרובים why two cherubim? The כפורת which at its end rises to cherubim, i.e., the care of the Torah, which God has entrusted to them, becomes its own cherub and the cherub of God’s presence on earth, all this is one single idea, and one single cherub would represent it. Why then two cherubim? This question is the more necessary as the answer to it is essential for the understanding of one other point which has not yet been considered. The cherubim have to have their faces directed not only downwards towards the כפורת but also, as expressly mentioned, each towards the other ופניהם איש אל אחיו, so that their attitude must represent two ideas. While they conjointly accomplish the guard of the כפורת, the guard of the guardians of the Torah, they mutually consider each other, and have each other in view, or rather, the other way about, in mutually considering and having each other in view, they conjointly accomplish the guard of those that guard the Torah. For the order of the verse runs: — והיו הכרובים פרשי כנפים וגו׳, ופניהם איש אל אחיו אל הכפרת יהיו פני הכרובים.

The ארון, as well as its contents, and the ideas they are meant to bring to us, all offer divers points from which an answer to our question could be worked out. Everywhere we find a dualism present. The “Testimony”, the object of the care, consisted of two tablets. The Ark, the “receiver” of the Tablets, accepting dedication to carrying out the Torah, consisted of two materials, require two qualities. The “care” itself, as we have seen, required two factors, the theoretical, mental care, and the practical, actual care. Each of the three components which made up the idea and meaning of the Ark — the Tablets, their acceptance and the special measures necessary to ensure their being carried out, consisted accordingly of two factors, both essential, each complementing the other, both having to keep the other in mind. So that the protection necessary for the Torah could well be represented by two cherubim with their faces directed towards each other and both together downwards towards the כפורת, as we have tried to work out in greater detail as a solution to our question, in Jeshurun VI, p. 246 et seq. (the article referred to above and re-presented in Gesammelte Schriften and now translated into English I.L.).

In the general basic rules laid down in our article “Grundlinien einer Judischen Symbolik” the meaning of any symbol in the Torah may not be stretched beyond that which is directly expressed in the description given of it. Also, where several explanations fit, the one which is least farfetched, and which seems naturally to conform to the general train of thought which the symbol seems to wish to indicate, is the one recommended to be adopted. Accordingly, of the various ways in which this duality of the cherubim can be taken (see above, and again see article) two only should be retained. These two, moreover, in their innermost meaning can be shown to have exactly the same idea underlying them.

To refer the duality of the cherubim to the duality of the Tablets which from the main contents and the whole raison d’etre of the Ark, would at first seem to offer the most natural explanation. They (the Tablets) represent the most comprehensive and general idea which Israel is constantly to bear in mind, and they are the objects to which, one can suppose, contemplation of the cherubim on the Ark would most readily direct one’s thoughts. The two Tablets, as remarked above on V.10, lay side by side, so that, if one stands in front of the Ark and thinks of the cover in two halves right and left, each half covers one Tablet, so that if each half on the cover rises to become one cherub that cherub is evolved from the guard of one Tablet. Now the two Tablets were of exactly the same size, — לחת כתיב שני לחת העדות, — they proclaimed themselves to be one unit. If one Tablet did contain preferably the basic principles of our relations to God, מצות שבין אדם למקום, and the other that of our social relation to our fellowmen, they are still in their value before God and in all influence in ensuring our happiness, completely equal to each other, neither can do without the other, neither can take the place of the other, neither may lose sight of the other. If the guard which Israel keeps over the Torah is to become their own guardian, and end up in their becoming the bearers of the Glory of God on earth, then this guard must be given to both Tablets in equal measure, each completing the other, each keeping the other constantly in mind; this guard, to be complete, must not erect itself as one cherub, but a pair of cherubim, which mutually consider each other and have regard for each other, and in together completing the guard of the guardians of the Torah offer themselves thereby as a home for the Glory of God on earth: — משני קצות הכפרת שנים כרובים פניהם איש אל אחיו — סככים בכנפיהם על הכפרת ואל הכפרת פניהם — פרשי כנפים למעלה.

But, to understand the duality of the cherubim, it is not even necessary to go back to the contents of the Ark, which, after all, are hidden from the eye. The כפירת itself, representing the direct “guard of the Torah” offers the motive for this duality. If the cherubim-cover represents “the guardians of the Torah”, by that guard becoming guardians of themselves, of their own happiness, and at the same time bearers of the Glory of God on earth, then this guard is simply Israel, who, by the ארון, symbolically accept the Torah to carry it out with all their powers of action and firmness, and by the כפרת accomplish this guard with protecting firmness. But then the pair of cherubim, which in its ends the כפורת becomes, can represent the picture of Israel, and show them how they are to emerge, as a consequence of their accomplishing this keeping of the Torah.

But, as we shall see when we come to consider the public or national offerings, the Torah uses two forms to represent the whole nation, either as one unit, or as a duality. Just as in words it uses two expressions for the nation, the one, גוי, regarding the nation as a single body (גו), regarded externally as one closed unit, the other עם, regarding the nation internally as a large number of individuals joined together socially (עם ,עמם), so, in the Sanctuary the nation is represented in a twofold manner, as one single united whole by the number One, and as a large number of members belonging together, by the number Two, the minimum symbol of plurality. Accordingly, here, too, the whole nation of Israel is represented not by one cherub but by two, by a pair of cherubs, and the wooden-golden Ark with the golden cherubim-cover would express: —

Wenn Israel mit goldener Festigkeit die tatkräftige und pflichtgetreue Erfüllung des ganzen ihm übergebenen Gesetzes bis zur Vollendung hütet, dann gestaltet es durch diese Hut in ihrer Vollendung sich nicht nur in seiner einheitlichen Gesamtheit zum גוי קדוש, sondern in allen seinen Gliedern zum ממלכת כהנים, zu einer Gesamtheit, deren jegliches Glied die dreifache Bestimmung erfüllt: des Nächsten Heil fördert, das Gesamtheil schirmt und Mitträger ist der göttlichen Herrlichkeit auf Erden — dann wird Israel zu Cherubimpaaren, die, in gegenseitiger Achtung und Beachtung einander friedlich zugewandt, einer für den andern da sind, einer für den andern Bürge, einer dem andern anvertraut, — in brüderlichem Gesamtwirken die Gesetz hütende Gesamtheit schirmen, — und sich zusammen zu einem Throne der göttlichen Herrlichkeit auf Erden vollenden, — dann wird Israel zu שנים כרובים משני סוככים בכנפיהם על הכפרת — פניהם איש אל אחיו — קצות הכפרת — אל הכפרת פניהם - פורשי כנפים למעלה —; dann wird יושב הכרובים identisch mit יושב תהלות ישראל! (Ps. 22, 4.)

If here we have considered Israel itself as a cherub, it may not be superfluous to remind ourselves that even the Kingdom of Tyre is explicitly described as a protecting cherub (Ezek. 28,14). If Tyre was a “cherub” into whose protection the culture of the nations was given over, then with greater justification Israel can appear as a “cherub” to whom God’s Laws for humanity are entrusted, who has been appointed in the world לשמור דרך עץ החײם and to whom God said:- ועשו לי מקדש ושכנתי בתוכם.

In their real inner depth both these ways of looking at the duality of the cherubim can be absolutely identical. For do the Two Tablets of the Testimony contain aught other than just that very same double reference which is shown both in the direction of their glance and the spread of the wings of the cherubim? Are the מצות שבין אדם לחברו of the one Tablet anything other than the looks of the cherubim directed one to the other, and the nation guarding the Torah, other than the wings of the cherubim covering it? And the מצות שבין אדם למקום of the other Tablet, are they anything else than the glance of the cherubim directed downwards towards the protection of the Torah, and the spread of the wings of the cherubim to receive the Glory of God from above? And, accordingly, is the Ark with its cherubim-cover anything else but the representation of the complete meaning of the Divine Torah guarded in the Ark, being kept in all its purity and entirety?

V. 21. The Torah forms the real essence of the Ark, it is only by its “Testimony” that the Ark has meaning, and the cherubim-cover, with its rich symbolism, has reference only to the Torah being received and accepted as the contents of the Ark. The ארון must become the ארון העדות before the כפרת is placed on it. By that act the Sanctuary is erected to the Torah, and that, which in the life outside is to be the highest and most comprehensive mastering factor, is also that, which, within the Temple, is to be guarded as the all-holiest. The Jewish State and the Jewish Temple are not two separate categories. Conjointly they serve one and the same purpose, the realisation of the Torah which is to form the one and only principle of the Jewish nation.

V. 22. ונועדתי from יעד related to יחד, place and time fixed for a meeting. It is not as a result of some personal relationship of Moses to God, that He will speak to him but מעל הכפרת מבין שני הכרובים אשר על ארון העדות, as a result of His proximity to Israel in accordance with the Brith, as a result of the presence of God in the midst of the nation that keeps His Torah. How very much the revelation to Moses was conditional on the deserts of the nation is shown in the Mechilta (at the beginning of בא on the word לאמר) and equally so in Sifra (on the first לאמר) by the fact, that, during the thirty eight years in which God was unfavourable (from the sin of the מרגלים) till the fortieth year no Word of God came to Moses, in the direct manner as described in Numb. 12,8 “mouth to mouth”, ומראה, as it says “when the whole generation had died, God spake unto me etc. etc.” (Deut. 2,18) כל ל״ח שנה שהיה כועס על ישראל לא היה מדבר עמו שני ויהי כאשר (תמו כל אנשי המלחמה למות וידבר הי אלי (דברים ב׳ י״ח. (So also the Gemora in B.B. 121a & b where the 15th Ab is explained as the day fixed for joyful remembrance of the return of the spoken Word of God to Moses).

V. 23. שולחן. Table in the Scriptures, is not an article on which work is done, a work table or bench, but primarily — as the name שלחן from שלח to send, to present, indicates — a domestic piece of furniture which offers us things to use and to eat. It is used almost exclusively to designate a dining table, as indeed in our language too, we associate “table” primarily with this idea. It is therefore symbolically used for nourishment, food, material abundance, and well-being, wealth, comfort (e.g., Ps. 78,19 and XXIII,5; Is. 65,11; Job 36,16). The שלחן (V.30) was for the purpose of bearing the לחם הפנים prescribed in detail in Levit. 24,5 et seq. i.e., “Bread and Incense”. That “bread” represents nourishment, food in general, needs no proof. Equally easily we can see that “smell” generally expresses the satisfaction or dissatisfaction one finds in anything (in English e.g., that smells good to me, that transaction smells fishy, the odour of sanctity etc. I.L.). One has only to think of הבאשתם את ריחנו (Ex. 5,21). So that, perfume, sweet odour, would indicate a feeling of comfort and ease, the satisfaction that one finds in something. And inasmuch as לבונה frankincense, is, relative to קטורת the compounded, made-up incense (frankincense was one of the eleven spices of which the incense was made up), as a simple natural thing is to an artificially compounded one, frankincense, and especially לבונה זכה pure frankincense, would represent, pure, simple, natural feeling of comfort, or ease and satisfaction.

But if it is nourishment and comfort which the Table bears or rather offers i.e., that which we call the makings of a comfortable existence, then we can only regard the Table itself as that which grants this comfortable existence i.e., that phase of national life which creates a comfortable standard of living; the development of the material aspect of the national life.

Hence the Table was made principally of wood עצי שטים ,עץ, ever fresh progressively developing, without other limits than it set itself, such as were necessary to ensure its own “blossoming”; the מסגרת (V.25) the enclosing rim, or the strips that held it together, was also of עץ. The Table retained this עץ character, although its top was covered with gold, the symbol of firmness and strength. This metal disappeared in the general character of the meaning of the Table, שאני שלחן דרחמנא קרײה עץ; just as in the general appearance of the Table the gold was not conspicuous, it was צפוי שאינו עומד (see Menachoth 96b & 97a).

V. 24—25. But if the activity which creates a comfortable standard of living finds its expression in ever-green, growing and expanding “wood”, it has nevertheless to make a “pure solid base” for such comfort. It must offer this comfortable standard of living on a pure gold, solid, sterling foundation, on צפוי זהב טהור — and ועשית לו זר זהב סביב. The position of this golden band is given more precisely in the next verse, where it says ועשתי זר זהב למסגרתו סביב. This reiterated reminder of the golden band around the Table and the different position it had to the one around the Ark, indicates a special importance for it with regard to the Table.

In V.11 we have already recognised in זר, both from its form and name, the sign of keeping away everything that is not in harmony with the idea of the object enclosed by the circlet, the sign of its holiness and inviolability. The זר of the Ark surmounted it, it rested, as it were, on it, ועשית עליו זר זהב סביב ran the instructions. It did not surround the Ark but stood as a continuation emanating from, and surmounting its golden cover. We accordingly thought, in the case of the Ark, that this sign of holiness and inviolability must be taken to refer to its relationship with the outside world.

But here it is the Table itself — which moreover, excepting a thin covering of gold to its top, consisted entirely of wood — which is surrounded by this golden band. We accordingly think that the band must be taken to refer to the Table itself, and to mean the sanctification, i.e., the keeping away of everything unrefined and unholy from the activities and purposes which the Table represents.

The band of the Table was given its special position as being around the מסגרת. There is some doubt as to the exact meaning of this מסגרת. According to Menachoth 96a, it was either an upstanding rim to the top surface of the Table, or a long strip of wood holding the legs of the Table together. In the first case it would be (according to Sukka 5) merely a הכשר כלי, an adjunct to the top of the Table, and have no separate meaning of its own. In the second case, it would be a separate part of the Table and have its own independent meaning. A זר around the מסגרת in the first case, as a band of gold around the rim of the Table top, would represent holiness as the special stipulation for the basis on which one is to get material comfort in life, and — being round the מסגרת — especially for the protected maintenance of it. But in the second case, as a band of gold around the strip that enables the feet to bear the Table, it makes this holiness the stipulation for all one’s efforts and activities to set up a comfortable standard of living. The essential nature of “one’s activities to set up a comfortable standard of living” is fresh progressive development of power — as we recognised by the material of which the Table predominately consisted, שטים wood. All the more was it then necessary repeatedly to insist that holiness and purity are the fundamental stipulations for one’s efforts in material matters. Just because it is in the material and sensual side of life that the greater danger of lack of purity and holiness lurks, was it necessary repeatedly to warn us to limit our efforts in this direction by the זר זהב טהור, by the golden band of pure sanctifying consecration. Altogether, we do not find purity in its various nuances נקי ,זך ,טהור as מנקיות ,זהב טהור ,לבונה זכה — so insisted on, in the case of any other of the appurtenances of the Sanctuary, as it is with reference to the Table. Although the “pure gold” only appeared as a covering to the Table-top and as a band around the Table, this gold-like purity was so much the basic condition for the “Table of Jewish comfortable standard of life”, on which bread was to be laid out before God, that the whole idea of the Table is summed up in Levit. 24,6 by the term השלחן הטהור “the pure Table”. Only as a pure table does our “table”, our material life, as well as our spiritual one, stand before God, ’השלחן הטהור לפני ה. And only זר, purity, makes our מסגרת into a מסגרת, gives power to our efforts, and permanence to our achievements.
V. 26. ארבע הפאות אשר לארבע רגליו, the four corners of the Table ended in the four feet.

V. 27—28. A comparison between these verses and V. 14 and 15, shows the essential fundamental difference of the carrying-poles of the Ark and the Table. These latter were only ונשא בם את השלחן ,לשאת את השלחן, merely for the concrete purpose of transport, and were only inserted in the Table at the time of transport, so were accordingly entirely without symbolic meaning.

V. 29. Just as צפוי זהב טהור sterling purity, forms the basis on which Jewish well-being has to be offered, so must the means for keeping and enjoying the fruit of well-being — the fixed shapes and forms, the supports and means of ventilation, and keeping fresh and clean — כפתיו ,קשותיו, קערתיו ,מנקיותיו — all had to be of pure gold.

קערתיו אלו הדפוסים :קערתיו (Menachoth 97a). The dishes were forms to keep the loaves in the prescribed shape until the time for arranging them on the Table. The loaves representing the “Jewish comfortable standard of living” were baked in prescribed metal moulds, and to keep this shape, were kept in golden forms until they were arranged and stacked on the Table. This shape, according to רבי חנינא, whose tradition has the most to be said for it (see Menachoth 94b and תוספות ibid.) was a flat surface with both ends turned upwards כמין תיבה פרוצה, and the length of the two upstanding walls together, equalled — or according to ר״מ nearly equalled — the length of the base. This shape made each loaf offer as much — or nearly as much — for the purpose of bearing the next loaf (they were ranged on the Table in two stacks of six loaves each) as it used for its own base! Does this express anything else than, putting all selfishness aside, the giving oneself up to the interests of one’s brother-man as being the condition demanded for a comfortable standard of living? That every man acquires and holds as much for others as for himself, grants as much, or nearly as much, of the abundance of his table to his neighbour as to his own table. (More, according to the other tradition כמין ספינה רוקדת each loaf only gave one fortieth of its length to a narrow base, and with all the rest of it stretched gradually up to support the next loaf lying on it). This brotherliness stands out so strikingly in everything to do with the loaves, that we are forced to take it as the fundamental stipulation for that which these loaves represent, i.e., according to the way we understand it, as the fundamental condition for material comfort. From the very beginning each loaf had to be made from two עשרונים of flour (Levit. 24,5). But one עשרון is the measure for the daily requirement of one individual, in accordance with the עומר לגולגלת, of the Manna sent from heaven. So that two tenths are, right from the beginning, a double portion, for oneself and at the same time for one’s fellow-man. Further, they had to be baked not only in the prescribed form, but only in pairs נאפות שתים שתים ובדפוס (ibid. 94a). Finally, twelve loaves were baked (corresponding to the twelve tribes of Israel) which were arranged on the Table in two equal stacks, side by side, in pairs. So that in material, in shape, in the preparation, and in the set-out, the character of brotherliness was distinctly impressed.

From Menachoth 96a we learn, that from the ends of the flat surfaces of the loaves four upright pieces extended upwards קרנות similar to those of the Altar. These “horns” however, were bent horizontally to serve as supporting points for the next loaf, קרנות לגוויה דלחם כײף להו ולחם עלײהו נח ליה. If קרנות signify — as we shall explain more fully when we come to consider the Altar — striving upwards towards God, then, having these on the “bread of Jewish comfort”, would signify:- Apart from one’s fellowmen, Jewish wealth is to be directed to God. But directing one’s wealth to God is again only to be achieved by using it for the support of one’s fellowmen.

By this direction to God, brotherliness becomes duty, the calls of love become the calls of duty, חסד becomes צדקה. That which one’s fellowmen could only hope for, God has the right to demand, and He does demand it for one’s fellow men.

כפתיו אלו בזיכין :כפתיו. The incense lay ready in בזיכין sacrificial bowls (Tamid 5,4 VI,3 says that בזך was also the prescribed vessel for the daily קטרת). If incense signifies satisfaction and content — which is just that which transforms bread into well-being, wealth, — then, having the incense, the expression of one’s own satisfaction, in sacred vessels, בזיכין, ready to be used on the Altar to God, i.e., as an expression of achieving God’s satisfaction, would express the thought:- One’s own feeling of satisfaction and content, has to be entirely dependent on God’s satisfaction and content, that we can only find content and happiness in wealth and well-being, if this happiness and content brings “happiness and content” to God also. Our own comfort and well-being must be ready in “pure offering-bowls” to offer satisfaction to God. The בזיכין were also two, and this duality is essential, and similarly to the stacks, מעכבין זה את זה (Menachoth 27a). If, accordingly, the shape and the coupling of the loaves and the incense, set brotherliness as one of the first conditions for our prosperity and welfare, the בזיכין, the offering-bowls in which the incense stood ready for offering, set God’s being satisfied and pleased as a second condition.

קשותיו אלו סניפין, ומנקותיו אלו קנים אשר יוסך בהן שמסככין בהן את הלחם (ibid.). From the Mishna on 94b and 96a, we learn that each stack of loaves had two golden stands to support it (סניפין, called קשות in our text). These were fitted with little projections (פיצולין) on which open tubes (i.e. gutters) קנים (called מנקיות in our text) rested. These golden gulleys ran between the loaves to allow the air to circulate between them, and prevent them from getting mouldy. The fact that these stands are elsewhere (Numb. 4,7) called קשות הנסך the supports of the covering, shows that these stands really belong to these tubes, אשר יוסך בהן by which the loaves are “over-spread”, the stands were there for the tubes. This definitely supports the view of Rashi (ibid.), whereas, according to תוספות, the stands only supported the bottom loaves, which, as they rested directly on the Table, were the ones which least required support. It is difficult to see what meaning the expression קשות הנסך could have according to תוספות. 94b tells us that the purpose of the סניפין was to support the loaves, סמכי ליה ללחם, to prevent the weight of the upper loaves breaking the lower ones אגב יוקרא דלחם תלח. But they (the stands) could only accomplish this by means of the tubes which rested on them. If, according to תוספות, the tubes merely rested on the loaves (and not on the stands as well) they would increase the weight without taking any of the strain of the weight. But on the other hand the tubes did not bear the loaves by themselves, but only in conjunction with the loaves which they covered. The upstanding ends of the loaves were grooved and into these grooves the tubes were sunk to such a level that they were kept by the supports just slightly above the top of the walls of the loaves, and so imperceptibly kept the loaves from touching one another, שקועי משקע להו ומגבה להו פורתא (ibid. 96a).

Accordingly, we regard the stands and the tubes, קשות and מנקיות as being parts of one and the same apparatus. These open tubes, (or perhaps better described as gutters), which, supported by the golden stands, kept the loaves apart, served the double purpose (a) אגב יוקרא דלחם תלח, of preventing the weight of the upper loaves crushing and breaking the shape of the lower ones, and (b) משום איעפושי, to prevent them from becoming mouldy by remaining in too close contact. Whereas the קערות gave that shape to the loaves and kept them in that prescribed form that enabled them to represent each bearing the other, and so be the symbol of communal brotherhood, the קשות הנסך brought about such separation of the one from the other as was necessary for the preservation of the uninjured and undisturbed existence of each single one. The former brought about, that, in spite of each being a separate unit, each one bore and was borne by the other. The latter, that in spite of all joining together, none injured or spoilt the other, but each retained its own independence and its own atmosphere.

Transcribing this to the sphere of the conditions necessary for the national well-being, in which the shape of the loaves seemed to us to represent brotherly love, we have to look for the idea which both keeps the well-to-do apart, with their individuality uninjured and undisturbed, and also joins them together in brotherhood, for mutual support. The idea which immediately jumps to one’s mind is Law, Right. The principles of Law are the golden unalterable firm pillars which bear the golden unalterable firm lines of demarkation between fusing all personalities together into one whole of brotherly love, and protecting the independence of each individual against injury and disturbance by his neighbour. The fundamental principles of the Law are the קשות הנסך, are the קשות and מנקיות, are the supporting and clear-keeping elements, which alone make possible and feasible the reign of brotherly love. Without the Law of Rights which balances the joining and the separating, humanity degenerates into an impersonal, unfree mass, crushed and stunted by Man’s violence and corruption. It is only the Law of Right which creates personalities of independent property, who, through brotherly love, which this Law of God has made into a duty, freely use it for the maintenance of their fellow-men. It would be difficult to represent this Law of Rights more exhaustively than was done by the סניפים and קנים in all their finest nuances.

So that to the idea of brotherliness which is so emphatically impressed on the bread of Jewish wealth by its material, shape, preparation and layout, is associated the idea of Rights and Law, by which alone the whole is assured of the possibility of existing and enduring.

Taking everything together which the Table represents, it preaches to us: — Bound only by the limitations of holiness and purity, freely developing industry creates a firm, golden basis for a comfortable standard of Jewish life — שלחן עצי שטים וזר זהב סביב ועליו צפוי זהב טהור.
The principle on which it is formed is Brotherhood: דמות לחם הפנים כמין תיבה פרוצה.
The pillars which hold it, are the Laws of Right: קשותיו ומנקיותיו.
That which gives it happiness, is God’s satisfaction with it: בזיכי לבונה.
So that all the ruling principles of the Torah for our lives are outlined, viz.
The limitations imposed for purity and holiness: חקים,
Brotherly love: מצות,
Law and Rights: משפטים,
Giving satisfaction to God: עבודה,
and only for a Table built up on, and for, such lines, does it say: —

V. 30. ’ונתת וגו “and on this Table place ‘Presence-bread’ before My Presence always”. Only on such a Table, and for such a Table, does bread become “Presence-bread”, gained and used in God’s presence, granted, protected and blessed by God’s presence.

V. 31—32. The directions that the Lamp had to be מקשה solidly worked from one single piece, as well as the prescribed cups, knobs and flowers, were only indispensable when it was made out of gold (Menachoth 28a). But it was never allowed to be made out of scrap-metal (גרוטאות) and in all cases it had to be of metal (ibid.), and also the other parts, base, shaft and arms were indispensable (ibid.). That, if the conditions were such that gold could not be provided — as occurred in the earliest days of the Maccabean Restoration — the Lamp could be allowed to be made of less precious metal, is indicated in the text by the repetition of תיעשה (the Lamp is to be made in all circumstances I.L.) after it has already said ’ועשית וגו. By this repetition the sentence takes the form of כלל ופרט וכלל and makes the זהב not exclusive but used exemplarily, כעין הפרט i.e., metal generally (ibid. 28b). This might also explain the unusual form in which תיעשה is written. It makes the passive form visible even without vocalisation, stresses it to be specially noted, and thereby orders the Lamp to be made “in all circumstances”; תיעשה, it is to be made!

ירך is the base, the foot, קנה the shaft. The base and shaft formed the real מנורה by which term the central shaft is always to be understood, as distinct from the side arms, e.g., in V.34 & 37 and in Numb. 6,2. — גביעים are cups in the shape of Alexandrian goblets longish and narrow (Rashi), כמין כוסות אלכסנדרײם (Menachoth); כפתורים are apple-shaped knobs כמין תפוחי הכרתײם “like Cretan apples”; פרחים, blossoms, “like the forms of blossoms on pillars” כמין פרחי העמודים (Menachoth ibid.). These decorations on the Lamp are described in more detail in V.34. The Lamp was eighteen טפחים high (handbreadths, measured with closed fist). Directly on the base was one “flower” פרח out of which the stem or shaft arose. The base and flower together occupied three טפחים. On this shaft rose two טפחים without any ornamentation. The 6th טפח was filled by a cup, a knob and a flower. The shaft rose again for two טפחים unadorned, the 9th טפח consisted of a knob, out of which, as described in V.32 and 35, two arms arose, one on each side, reaching up to the height of the top of the Lamp (i.e., up to 18 ’ט perpendicular height from the ground) the 10th ’ט was plain, the 11th again consisted of a knob out of which two arms, right and left, reached up to the top of the Lamp, the 12th ’ט was plain again, the 13th was filled by a third knob with two arms, the 14th and 15th were plain again, the 16th, 17th and 18th were filled by three cups, one knob and one flower. Then, on the top of the shaft the actual lamp rested. From the central shaft, of which the Menora really consisted, on either side were the קנים, the arms, three on each side. These arms extended to the same height as the middle shaft, had lamps on their tops, so that seven lamps burned in a row on the top of the Menora.

V. 33. On each of the six arms (at the height from the ground of 15 to 18) were three cups, one knob and one flower. The cups are described as being משוקדים which can mean “almond-shaped” or “like almonds”. According to Yoma 52a & b, it is doubtful whether this משוקדים does not extend to the knobs and flowers as well (at least to those on the central shaft, see הל׳ ,מל״מ בית הבחירה III,2). The separating accent on משוקדים in V.34 seems to favour this view.

V. 34. ובמנורה on the central shaft, the real Menora, four cups one in the 6th, and three in the 15—18 ’ט (see rough sketch). — כפתורים, there were two knobs on the central shaft in addition to the three described in the following verse as being under the three pairs of arms, five altogether. — פרחים, there were three on the central shaft, one directly on the base, one in the 6th ’ט and one at the top (see sketch).

V. 35. Altogether there were 22 cups, 11 knobs and 9 flowers, and we are told in Menachoth 28, that these parts were so essential that the lack of any one of these would make the whole Lamp unusable, all are מעכב זה את זה.

V. 36. The suffix זקנתם is striking. It can only refer to the arms and is difficult to say “the arms of the arms”. We should have expected קניה וכפתריהם. The arms are parts of the Menora, and the knobs, parts of the arms. But it seems that there is a difference between קנים and קנים .קנות are arms in general. But the arms consisted of knobs, כפתורים, and of smooth parts, which latter are as the stalk to the fruit, and hence are called קנות, they are the bearers of the כפתורים.

V. 37. As already remarked above on V.32, the arms came out of the sides of the central shaft, and rose to the same height. With the light on the central shaft there were seven lamps in a row. Now here it is arranged that the lamps resting on the six arms are to turn their lights towards the central light, so that the three lamps on the right side turn leftwards and the corresponding ones on the left, turn to the right. This order is repeated again in Numb. 8,2, אל מול פני המנורה יאירו שבעת הנרות and Menachoth 98b, remarks thereon, מלמד שהיו מצדדין פניהם כלפי נר אמצעי.
