V. 38. The tongs and pans were for the daily service of the Menora, they were required for the הטבה, the daily cleaning of the lamps, and preparation of the oil and wicks.

V. 39. The accessories mentioned in the previous verse were not included in the kikar. Out of this, only that which was of one piece with the Menora was hammered, viz., the Menora itself, and all the arms, cups, knobs, flowers, and also the seven lamps at the top, which, according to Menachoth 88b, were also beaten out of the one block of gold solidly with the Lamp. These ornamentations, arms and lamps are here termed the כלים.

If we now ask, what is the significance of the Menora in the Sanctuary of God’s Torah, the reply seems, at first glance, perfectly simple. The lighted Lamp, radiating light, we would suppose, is symbolic of light, and Light, we would suppose, equally simply represents knowledge, understanding; and we would find nothing simpler than to take it, that the Lamp, especially remembering its position, opposite the Table, and in front of the Ark of the Covenant of the Torah, represents spiritual, intellectual understanding, which, together with the Table, representing material well being, would then show the results of a Jewish national life based on God’s Torah, and dedicated to keeping it, as being material well-being and intellectual clarity.

But carefully testing this reply to our question with the Holy Scriptures does nevertheless justify us in having some doubts as to whether this simple explanation is really the whole meaning of the Menora.

It is true that in the Scriptures too, נר and אור, Lamp and Light are not unusual metaphors used for the source and dispenser of spiritual intellectual knowledge; and האיר to light; for giving spiritual light, enlightment and insight. “The Word of God is a lamp for our feet and light for our path”. (Ps. 119,105). “For the Command (מצוה) is a lamp, and the Teaching is light”. (Prov. 6,23). “God’s Command is clear, enlightens one’s eyes” (Ps. 19,9). “Even the commencement of His Word illuminates, gives insight to the most inexperienced”. (Ps. 119,130). And God has called Israel “in righteousness hath taken him by the hand, hath kept him and destined him to be a covenant unto the nations, to be a light unto the nations, to be a light unto the peoples” (Is. 42,6). “For teaching cometh from Him and for His Justice doth He create a quiet and peaceful home, that it may be a light to illuminate the nations”. (Is. 51,4). “Up, let us wander in the Light of God” (Is. 2,5). “For see, darkness covers the earth and deep darkness the nations, but God radiates over Israel, and His Glory shines above them, and nations walk by His light and kings by the rays of His dawn”. (ibid. LX,2). But where humanity goes to wrack and ruin in murder and pain, this happens because “they rise up against the Light, would never recognise the ways of God, and never sought rest in His paths (Job 24,13).

But with equal certainty, and with far greater frequency we find נר and אור, Lamp and Light, used as the metaphor for the source of continued existence and life, of development and blossoming, of undisturbed progress and happiness, of cheerfulness and joy. “Who”, complains Job, “will give me back the months of the past, the days when God protected me. When His Lamp shone above my head and I walked through the darkness by His light” (Job, XXIX,2). “There, will I make the horn of David flourish, there have I prepared a lamp for My anointed”, says God, of Zion (Ps. 132,17). “But for how long does it last, the lamp of the wicked becomes extinguished and misfortune overtakes them” (Job, XXI,17). Similarly we find the “extinguishing of the Lamp” as an expression of the cessation of happiness (Prov. 13,9; XX,20; XXIV,20). On the other hand “Light is sown for the righteous, and for the upright ones, joy” (Ps. 97,11). “The light of the righteous is joyful, whereas the Lamp is extinguished for the wicked” (Prov. 13,9). “The light of the eyes rejoiceth the heart” (Prov. 15,30). “Light is sweet” (Eccl. 11,7). Job, “hoped for good, and evil came, for light, and darkness came” (Job 30,26; Is. 59,9; Jer. 13,16). “To the Jews came light and joy, bliss and honour” (Esther 8,16). “God redeems the one who turns towards betterment from the way to the grave, so that his soul yet sees the light, that he still becomes illuminated by the light of life”. (Job 33,28,30). “Awake and rejoice, ye that sleep in the dust! For the dew of light is thy dew” (Is. 26,19) etc., etc., etc.

So that if we take all the facts together which lie to our hand in numerous examples of the meaning of Light in the Jewish conception, then “knowledge and understanding” would be only half, and only one aspect of what “Light” represents in the Holy Scriptures. “Movement” is the other great effect which Light has, and it is only “movement” together with “perception” that is the full and complete meaning of Light. Movement, not, of course, in the mechanical sense of change of place, but movement in that organic meaning which forms the idea of what must be the forerunner of all development and progress, whether organic living or spiritual. Light illuminates and also awakens Life, these two effects of Light make it simultaneously the metaphor for perception and for the joy of living. For joy is nothing but the feeling, the consciousness of growing life (cf. ציץ=שיש ,צמה=שמח). Now, if we go into the sphere in which the thoughts of Jewish symbolism in general, and of the Temple in particular, generally move — in the sphere of individual or national spiritual and moral life — and seek there that which is the cause of both perception and action, which both illuminates and causes “movement” — which accordingly would find its most suitable symbolic expression in Light — we find only one thing, and that is רוח, the Spirit. רוח is that which simultaneously gives knowledge, perception, insight, and wisdom, and gives the impetus to the willing and accomplishing of moral good.

Joseph, gifted with clearer insight and perception, is a man in whom is the spirit of God. (Gen. 41,38). Bezalel is filled with רוח חכמה, the spirit of wisdom, with ’רוח ה, the spirit of God. (Ex. 35,31). The spirit of God came upon Biliam (Numb. 24,2). Moses is to appoint Joshua as his successor for he is a man who has רוח בו, spirit in him (Numb. 27,18), he is full of the רוח חכמה, of the spirit of wisdom (Deut. 34,9). Spirit came upon the chosen elders of Israel (Numb. 11,16 et seq.), and, “O that”, Moses wishes, “the whole nation were prophets, that God would send His spirit on them” (ibid. 29). “The spirit of God spoke through David and His word was upon his tongue” (Sam. II. 23,2). “The spirit of God rests on Israel and the word of God is in its mouth” (Is. 59,21). God pours His spirit upon our children, (Is. 44,3) and ultimately on all flesh (Joel 3,1). “The prophet becomes a fool, the man of spirit, idiotic” (Hosea 9,7). In all these and in many other places (as in Ps. 77,7), and “my spirit began to mediate, it is the spirit in man and the breath of God in them which understands the experiences of the years” (Job 32,8), in all of them, spirit is that which perceives and recognises and which gives perception.

On the other hand, in places like: — “Because Caleb had a different spirit and he followed Me completely” (Numb. 14,24). “Everyone came whose heart urged him to it, and everyone whose spirit moved him to it, brought the ‘heave offering’ (gifts) for God” (Ex. 35,21). “God let Sichon’s spirit be hard and his heart daring, so as to deliver him into Israel’s hand” (Deut. 2,30). “The bad spirit between Abimelech and the lords of Schechem” (Judges 9,23). “The spirit of God which came over Jephtah” (ibid. XI,29) “which moved Samson” (ibid. XIII,25) “which clothed itself in Gidon and Abischar” (ibid. VI,34 and Chron. I. 12,18). “The spirit which moved the King of Assyria to repentance” (Kings II. 19,7). “The spirit of Cyrus which God awakened, to allow Israel to return” (Ezra 1,1). “The spirit of unfaithfulness which leads astray” (Hosea 4,12 & V,4). “The spirit of impurity which God will remove from the world” (Zac. 13,2). “The strong spirit”, “the free spirit”, for the renewal of which David begs (Ps. 51,12,14). “The new spirit” which God promises Israel (Ezekiel 11,19; XVIII,31; XXXVI,26; XXVII,14). In all these cases, spirit is not which has knowledge, perception, but that which moves the willpower to good or bad deeds. Even in the places where, as in Gen. 26,35, Rebecca’s daughters-in-law were a “bitterness of spirit to her”, in Sam. I. 1,15 Hannah’s spirit was depressed”; “God is near to those broken in spirit” (Ps. 34,19); “loneliness of spirit,” “high spirit” (Prov. 16,18 & 19), and frequently elsewhere, spirit represents that side of our “soul-life” that we call “feelings”; even then, it is just a description of how that phase of our relation to objects about us finds its expression, how our inclination for, or against anything, our feeling for, or against anything, expresses itself. So that it is the description of exactly that moment which forms the birthplace of our decisions for good or for bad.

Accordingly, we feel justified in taking the Light in the Sanctuary as the symbolic representation of spirit in its double relationship, the theoretical and the practical, understanding and the will to do things, knowledge and action.
Luckily in the Bible itself we have found unmistakable confirmation and support of our explanation.

To Zachariah, the bearer of God’s message to Zerubabel the national leader, who has to lay the foundation stone of a new Jewish national life on the ruins of the destroyed Jewish State, and thereby accomplish a work, to which at every step “the adversary and hindrances stood”, to Zachariah, was shown the Lamp with its seven lights. When he asked the angel who brought him the word of God for an explanation of the meaning of this apparition, the angel replied “do you then not know the meaning of these lamps?” and he had replied, “No, my Lord”, the angel said to him: — “This is the word of God to be transmitted to Zerubabel:- Not by means of the strength of an army, not by physical strength, but by My spirit,” sayeth ה׳ צבאות (Zach. 4,6). Here we have proof that spirit, and indeed God’s spirit, is that which is represented by the Lamp bearing the seven lights. And indeed this symbolic meaning must be such a natural evident one, that the counter question of the angel “do you then not know what this represents?” sounds somewhat of a reproach that the prophet should require further elucidation of this symbolic apparition. Note also, that if it is here indicated to Zerubabel that it is the spirit of God, by which he will accomplish his mission, here again spirit appears not merely as a mental medium, but also as the practical means of action. For the Word was sent to Zerubabel, the Leader, not to the Teacher. He did not have to teach what the will of God was, but to recognise and understand it, and carry it out; to him was entrusted the laying of a foundation stone on which, and on the edifice that was to be finished on it, “the whole of the Divine Providence” was directed.

Apart from this, in other places, the word of God itself has expressed what the nature and content of the spirit is, that God calls “His spirit”. In Isaiah, XI,2, speaking of the branch that was to grow from the stem of Jesse, it says ’ונחה עליו רוח ה, and this spirit of God is then immediately, more precisely, explained as ’רוח חכמה ובינה, רוח עצה וגבורה, רוח דעת ויראת ה, as the spirit of wisdom and perception, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of understanding and fear of God. So that again it is quite unmistakably confirmed, that the spirit which God calls His spirit, and which as Zachariah teaches us is represented by the Lamp, is not a spirit of mere theoretical knowledge and understanding, but is the means of both understanding and action.
מנורה
But, if the Light that the Menora bears, represents the spirit that God gives us of understanding and doing, what then is the meaning of the Menora in relation to the Light it bears?

If we picture its whole appearance, with its flowery base, its stem and arms, with their almond-shaped cups, knobs and flowers ירכה ופרחה, קנה קנים עם גביעים כפתורים ופרחים, the whole appearance strikes one as a tree, which blossoming upwards from its root, develops as bearer of this Light.

If we moreover consider that it was the only piece in the Sanctuary that was made entirely of gold, we at once get the idea that with its material, representing firmness endurance and unchangeableness, and with its shape, development and progression, the whole would represent the development and growth of firmness, endurance and eternal unchangeableness. So that in its appearance it offered a complete contrast to the Table. This latter, according to the nature of its material, is predominantly wood, representing constant growth and development. It only gets limitations, strength, firmness and endurance, by its accessories. It has for its object, material life, which is subject to all transformations and changes of growth, blossoming, maturity and…death, and only in the Sanctuary of God, by the spirit of the Torah and its ordinances, does it gain firmness and endurance and meaning for eternity. The Lamp, on the other hand, was through and through of gold; by its material, accordingly, proclaiming unaltering firmness and eternity. It is only, as expressed by its form, in the Sanctuary of God, by the spirit of the divine Torah, that it is to blossom and develop. But there is nothing firm, unalterable, and eternal in Man other than the innate godly in him, of which we are conscious by perception of what is true, and by the will to do good. This perception and will in Man, as well as the objects of his activity, that which is true and good, are in themselves eternal and unalterable, are subject neither to diminution nor change. Although the conscious developed godliness in the breast of the mature Man may seem inexpressibly richer than the slumbering godliness in the breast of a child, nevertheless this slumbering, godliness in the child’s breast is, in itself, fully equal in quality and purity to that which has come to full development in the mature Man. It is only the external conditions which give the appearance of a difference of degree. In the same way, the simplest truths, and the commonest, most everyday acts of goodness are not one whit less true or good, than the highest, most sublime truths, or the highest, rarest act of goodness. Everything which is really good or true, is just good and true, there can be no question of more or less. In the development of the material, every degree can only be built at the cost of the lower one. Lower forms die off, so that higher, more complete ones, arise. Every thing higher, more completely developed, is a denial of the preceding lower, less completely developed form; a grave is the cradle of all life, and phoenix-like, all life arises out of the ashes of past forms and generations. But in the spiritual sphere of truth and goodness, at no stage and for no stage do they lose their meaning, validity or justification. What is once good and true, remains for all time, good and true. Every higher and more sublime truth and goodness is no negation of, but a realisation of everything which was good and true that had preceded it. The most mature old man can not dispense with the virtues of his childhood, more, his most mature virtues are nothing but the realisation of the very same virtues in a more developed and more comprehensive condition of life. The most complicated system of the highest most far-reaching truth can not dispense with the simplest truth that served it as a starting point; more, it is just in the firm, unassailable stand of those most simple truths from which it developed, that the whole existence of its furthest reaching truths has its roots.

So the Tree of Knowledge and the full development of what is true and good, is a golden Tree, gold from root to blossom, in every part and at every stage of growth and development, gold; — in every tiny part and at every stage, equally pure gold and solidly true and good —; and in the fullest and highest development from root to blossom all of one piece, inseparable, not added to, bit by bit, but from the very beginning endowed for the whole conception of its highest and fullest completion, in short, it is a tree as is pictured for us in the מנורת זהב טהור which מקשה תיעשה and whose ירכה וקנה ,גביעיה כפתריה ופרחיה ממנה יהיו, in the solid pure gold Menora, worked out of one solid block of gold, together with its base, shaft, arms, cups, knobs and blossoms, all pure gold and all worked out of the one piece.

If we now consider the separate parts: first of all the seven lamps tell us that the spirit, which is to be nurtured, is no narrow one-sided one (which would be represented by a single lamp) but that this spirit is to be applied to a diversity of ideas. Moreover, taking what we have found to be universally the symbolic meaning of the number seven (see article on “Milah” in Jeshurun & English translation), we at once recognise that it is not merely a diversity of ideas, but a complete totality of all spiritual knowledge and its practical moral application (the exercise of one’s will in the right way). Considering the lamps more closely, we find that to this character of diversity is added at the same time the idea of the most harmonious unison. We see the centre lamp having its light burning straight upwards or straight in front of it (see further on), but right and left, on either side, the lamps having their lights directed towards this centre light in such a way that the three right hand ones turn left, the left ones right, so that they all turn towards this centre light, in the direction of whose light all seven are accordingly united. So that the aim and object to which the centre light strives, is the common goal of all the lights of the Menora. Further, these lights themselves are carried by seven arms. But not that each one of them has its own separate base and separate stem. They all stand on one base, one root, one stem bears them all. Further, a more precise examination shows, as also the directions of the Torah indicate, that the stem on which the centre light rests, and which rises straight upwards from the root, is the real main stem, out of which, only after it has grown half way up, the remaning six arms branch off in pairs. The Torah repeatedly draws our attention to the fact that these six arms “come forth” from the central stem. So that the centre light is not only the common goal but also the common starting-point of all the lights. They all come from the one central stem and they all strive together to the same ultimate goal. So that we have to understand the seven lights, not simply as seven, but as one and six, as one out of which six come, and into which the six finally re-unite. Now our research into Milah and Tzitzis (referred to above) has shown that the number “six” is the sign of the material created world and, in conjunction with it, the number “one”, the seventh, as the sign of the One, non-material, standing outside the physical world but in connection with it, the One only God. According to this, we have to regard the one central stem with its one central light as the spirit of knowledge and will to act, striving upwards to God, as the spirit of striving to the knowledge and service of God, and the six arms with their six lights, as the spiritual efforts of our minds and acts directed to the physical world. But, it is the central stem itself which branches out in these six arms, the six side arms come out of the one central stem, and with their six side lights turn again in the direction of the one central light. This teaches that the spirit of knowledge and service of God, which is to be cultivated in the Temple of the Torah, is no abstract, isolating, turning away from knowledge of the world and worldly efforts, but rather that it is just in such knowledge and directing one’s mind to building up the world, that it finds its full activity. So that all the efforts of the mind and spirit which are directed to the knowledge of this world, and the fulfilment of its demands, cease to have to be considered as being estranged from, or departed from God, or from knowledge of God, or from His service. On the contrary, just these worldly matters in being directed towards a knowledge of God, and a fulfilment of His will, find therein their real starting point and goal, the whole base of their justification and consecration; all science and all moral activity have their starting-point in God, and their goal and ultimate culmination in God. All true knowledge and all true morality has only one base, one root, one goal; God is its beginning, God its end, ’תחלת חכמה יראת ה the beginning of wisdom is the fear of God, and ’ראשתי חכמה יראת ה, the first fruit of wisdom is the fear of God.

Whereas in the wording of the Torah, first of all, this differentiation of the one central shaft from its six side arms is definitely stressed ועשית מנורת זהב, and וששה קנים יוצאים מצדיה, on the other hand these side arms themselves are repeatedly themselves differentiated in pairs “three arms of the Menora from its one side, and three arms of the Menora out of its second side”; and this difference is further detailed by the fact that two arms are always to project together from the same place on the Menora, over one and the same knob, “’וכפתר תחת שני הקנים ממנה וגו״. So that the central light directed solely to God, (the 7th), in its branching out to direct and illuminate the physical world (six), is presented in a dual, contrasting manner. In the light directed to the concrete world it separates into two contrasting differences, which, however, strive to unite again in the centre point of their origin. Now we have already found above how spirit, which is what the light of the Temple Menora represents, is understood as getting or granting perception, and getting or granting action. In human beings it shows itself in perception, understanding and in the human will; mental clarity and the will to act morally are two phases in which the presence of spirit is demonstrated, and from this fact alone we should already feel justified in seeing in the two different sides of the Menora this contrast of the spiritual, mental, and the moral, (of theory and practice I.L.). Both are in their origin and in their actuality indeed so inseparably one, that each, of necessity, presupposes the other. The truly moral, i.e., the doing of good deeds which one recognises as being good of one’s own free will, presupposes the mental activity, otherwise it would be an unconscious act in the realm of instinct rather than in that of morality. But equally so, the mere act of perceiving, of recognising the good, presupposes the will to translate it into action, for it demands that the powers of the human free will be directed towards the object which it recognises as good. And every conscious direction of one’s powers to achieve some desired end, is already a translation into action of one’s moral will. So that the living spirit in the human being is essentially both theoretical (exercise of one’s mentality, perception) and practical (exercise of one’s bodily powers) at the same time. It is only the abstract way in which we take it, according to the predominating objects of any activity of the spirit, whether the object of the endeavour is mental perception or actual deed, that makes us call the one, theoretical perception, the other, practical application of one’s will. This difference lies in the result, not in the source. At their root they are one, and they tend to come together again in their goal. All perception of what is true has only value, if it is directed to, and serves for, the accomplishment of good, if it ultimately conduces to the doing of good. And all actual doing of good must always remain conscious of the understanding of that which is truth, and can only draw its motive and the guarantee of its real true value from the well of the perception and understanding of the truth. Exactly as the two side arms come out from the same point of the central stem, and when they have attained the same height up above, they turn their lights towards each other again and thereby at the same time to the common central point. But if now, as is here the case, this central point is the “seventh”, the spirit of striving upwards to God, the spirit that is to be kept and fostered in the Sanctuary of His Torah, we understand all the more, how, in this central point, all perception and understanding and all will translated into action come from one common root and are united to one common good. For we are able to recognise this root and stem of our spiritual life struggling upwards to God, as nothing other than that all-embracing spirit which in our Holy Scriptures is called ’יראת ה. The fear of God, which Scripture calls ’יראת ה is that highest degree of knowledge and understanding which immediately begets the highest degree of morality, is that spirit in which perception of the highest truths pairs with the doing of the greatest good. (This may seem to read somewhat wordy and complicated but the idea is really quite simple. Hirsch, of course only speaks of truth and morality because the Menora in the Temple preaches morality and good, but the same idea applies to immorality and evil, and is here perhaps simpler and clearer. For example: — I ask you to do an immoral act. I know of a perfectly safe and undetectable way in which you can steal £100 from your neighbour. You reply that you cannot steal. Why not? Because your spirit of honesty will not allow your will to direct your feet and hands to go and do the immoral deed. It requires your mind to direct and your body to do it. If you can imagine stealing it while you were sleep-walking it would still be stolen, but you would not have committed an immoral act. For a truly evil act we require the two processes, will and action, but although we seperate them into two processes in reality they both spring from the same source and the final result is the same. Similarly, knowing a thing is wrong, and willing not to do it are two different things, but only when the knowing and the willing work together can we say that the person is completely moral. — I.L.)

In Menachoth 98b, the tradition as to the exact position of the Menora in the Sanctuary is doubtful. In any case it is sure that it was on the south side, opposite the Table. The doubt is only as to which direction is stood with regard to its arms, whether these were placed from east to west or north to south. If the former, the central light rose straight upwards, continuing the direction of the central shaft, and the side lights were on the one side directed from west to east, and on the other from east to west. In the latter case the central light was directed forwards to the west, towards the Holy-of-Holies, and the side lights had their direction on the one side from south to north, and on the other side from north to south. Later on we shall have to give the meaning of the various sides of the Sanctuary special and thorough consideration, as these, especially in the ritual of the sacrifices, have a very essential importance. Here we anticipate that investigation with the remark that the sides of the Sanctuary get their meaning from the particular appurtenance allotted to that side. In the west, the Ark of the Law stood with its cherubim-cover; in the north, the Table with the shew-bread; in the south, the Lamp with its lights; the east was turned towards the people, on that side was the entrance, and there, one behind the other in two different places, stood the Altars which invited the people to happy self-sacrificing giving themselves up to the Divine Torah awaiting them in the west. We believe that we are not in error if we take the west side to represent the Torah and the presence of God that it, and it alone, brings about; the north side, the material life; the south, the spiritual; and the east, the concrete nation, the people of Israel invited to self-sacrificing dedication to God and His Torah. If the Menora was placed between north and south, the centre light was turned westwards, forward towards the Ark of the Covenant resting in the Holy-of-Holies. This would more precisely specify the spirit that is to be nurtured in the Sanctuary, as that spirit which God wants to be found in the Torah He has revealed, and in the Bris-relationship which He established for this Torah with Israel (both of which we found the Ark of the Covenant to represent). This spirit is then shown by the three south lights being turned northwards to be of such a nature, that theoretical and intellectual spirituality must be directed towards practical material matters, and by the three north lights being turned southwards that practical material life must be directed towards spiritual ends, and that both together must always return afresh to their source in the centre point to God and His Torah and His Bris. In this case (i.e., the Menora standing N. — S.), the centre light would be that נר מערבי, that נר תמיד, the light that was never to be extinguished, to be kept eternally burning שממנה מדליק ובה היה מסײם, “from which all the other lights get kindled and with which the tending of, and solicitude for the lights, always ended”. The fact that this light never went out (although it received only the same amount of oil as the others and had to burn so much longer. I.L.) was to be taken as evidence עדות היא שהשכינה שורה בישראל, that the presence of God rested in Israel, so that it was in all ways consistent with that which we had already found to be impressed on the whole construction of the central shaft. (See שבת 22b).

If the Lamp was placed between east and west, the centre light simply burned straight upwards. The lights turned from the west to the east would mean that the knowledge and understanding obtained from the Torah is what produces Israel’s historical. bond with God (the east, representing the life of the people based on the Torah. I.L.). Those turning from east to west, would designate the practical actual life of Israel directed towards the spirit coming from the Holy-of-Holies of the Torah and the Bris, which consecrates and raises it. Both together, the spirit of the Torah, and the practical life of Israel, are brought to their common root and their common goal — the spirit striving upwards to God. The Torah seeks its realisation in Israel, Israel seeks its moulding in the Torah, and both Torah and Israel לימוד ומעשה have value only if they are לשם שמים, dedicated to reaching the one common goal, to strive upwards to God. But, if the Menora had this position, the נר מערבי did not coincide with the central light, but was the middle light of the three east side lights turned westwards, and accordingly the culminating point of the caring for and fostering the spirit — הטבה והדלקה — is not to be sought at the place, where, according to the construction and position of the Menora, the origin and goal of the spirit lies. If the נר מערבי, that ’תמיד לפני ה and that ממנה מדליק ובה מסײם, was the middle light of the three east to west lights, it would indicate that the care and fostering of the spirit would constantly find its starting point in that tendency to incline towards God and His Law which is innate and never entirely extinguished in Israel. It would show, that it was just this fact, that this spark is never extinguished in Israel, that Israel always remains inclined towards God, always remains the people of His Torah, always turns towards the Schechina resting above the Torah, it is just this fact which is the עדות, the evidence that the Schechina is enthroned in Israel. It is diffcult to decide from the traditional sources which of these two opinions is the correct one. רמב״ם in הל׳ בית הבחירה פ״ג adopts the first view, that the position of the Lamp was from North to South. Rashi, Raavad and most other authorities decide in favour of the second opinion, that the Lamp stood with its lights running from east to west, and we adopt this opinion for the position of the Chanuka-Menora in our Synagogues (See Menachoth 97b; Sabbath 22b; Rashi ibid.; כסף משנה to Rambam; מזרחי Numb. 8,2).

Above, by the information that Zachariah (IV,6) gives as to the meaning of the Menora as the symbol of ’רוח ה we were led to the more precise meaning of this ’רוח ה which Isaiah gives. There, in Is. 11,2, in which the spirit of God in its highest degree is pictured as resting on a human being, even at first glance, it is evident that this spirit is of a two-sided nature. On the one hand it is proclaimed to us as the spirit of חכמה, עצה ,דעת, and on the other as גבורה ,בינה יראה, i.e., as the spirit of both theory and practice, of knowledge and accomplishment. This confirms that which we have already recognised as the meaning of “spirit” in the Holy Scriptures. If we now consider this verse in Isaiah more closely, we get a surprising agreement with all which we have found in the scheme of the construction of the Menora, and this agreement is so striking, that one can hardly refrain from thinking, that in fact, this verse in Isaiah is nothing but an expression in words of the symbolism of the Menora.

“’ונחה עליו רוח ה׳, רוח חכמה ובינה, רוח עצה וגבורה, רוח דעת ויראת ה״. Here the spirit is described in its totality as being a single thing ’רוח ה, which expands into six members. These six members form three pairs, each pair has one common bearer, for it does not say ’רוח חכמה ורוח בינה וגו, but ’רוח חכמה ובינה וגו.

This is the complete מנורת זהב ,ששה קנים יוצאים מצדיה ,שלשה מעדה האחד ושלשה מצדה השני וכפתר תחת שני הקנים ממנה וכפתר תחת שני הקנים ממנה לששת הקנים היוצאים מן המנרה. More, it goes on to say ’והריחו ביראת ה and “הריחו״ by all etymological analogy can mean nothing but “to permeate somebody with spirit”, to fill him with spirit, to inspire him. So that according to this, after having described the spirit of God coming to rest on the shoot of Jesse in all its sevenfold completion, one of these seven “parts” is emphasized as being the root and medium of this whole permeation and inspiration Exactly as among the seven lights of the Menora there was one light from which the lighting of all the other lights began, and to which the tending of the lights always came back ממנה מדליק ובה מסײם! More, to make the comparison complete, the bearer of this seven-rayed spirit of God comes forth as a shoot from a rooted stem, and on him rests the one spirit of God, with its six branched developments. So that if we look at this place in Isaiah in the whole of its context we could see a picture of the Menora expressing its thoughts (see sketch above).

Up till now we have only considered that structure of the Menora which is prescribed unconditionally for all circumstances, and which has to be adhered to, even when the Menora can not be made of gold and has to be made of other metal. In that case the additional restriction was imposed that it may never be made מן הגרוטאות out of scrap metal. This restriction would express the idea that those capabilities of the human character which are to be developed into bearing the spirit of God, are original gifts with which human beings are endowed from their origin, and not something derived from other gifts and built up from them. This also expresses the fact that for this spiritual development everybody is called upon, not only those specially gifted just as the Menora need not necessarily be made of gold, the noblest of metals, but if that is lacking, is also to be made from other metals, and in that case, if necessary, need not indispensably be beaten out of one solid block. When we remember that the spiritual development which is meant to be expressed here, is not a sterile, one-sided, merely theoretical one, which has only intellectual value, but is that spirit that begets the complete good man, then we can very well understand the thought that to become a bearer of the light that the Menora represents, everybody, according to his natural abilities, is called upon, and everybody has to work for such development. Everybody, in his own sphere and with his own particular abilities, can reach the highest degree of moral and spiritual perfection commensurate with his sphere and abilities, and thereby climb to the height of his calling; everybody can participate in the ’רוח ה in the ’רוח חכמה ובינה עצה וגבורה דעת ויראת ה, in proportion to his gifts. And just as for the individual, so it is for the Jewish State. It is not only in “golden times”, in an age like that of David or Solomon, but, quite independent of favourable or unfavourable conditions, even in “brazen” or “iron” times, Israel is called upon to strive upwards to the spirit of God, and work itself up to the height of its mission. But, on the other hand, of course, the spiritual and moral goal which the Menora represents, is the very brightest degree of spiritual and moral perfection that a human being, as such, can attain and, where available, makes a demand for the very noblest and most valuable forces. The very best and most valuable in Man for the highest! But where this spiritual and moral development can and does take place in conditions of purest gold, then it is not only from beginning to end מקשה, worked with master craftsmanship out of one piece, but certain special forms of this development are shown, which we now have to investigate.

If the Menora was made out of gold, then there had to be on the base, shaft, and arms גביעים כפתורים ופרחים “cups, knobs and flowers”, the position and numbers precisely ordained, and were so indispensable, that the omission of any single one of them, rendered the whole Menora unfit for use מעכבין זה את זה.

Of these three ornamentations, the meaning of the פרחים is the most definitely clear. פרח is the most general term for blossoming. Hence when we come across פרחים as symbolic shapes, we are not primarily justified in thinking of a more complicated meaning than “blossoms and blossomings”, and that, then, would give us the clue from where to seek the meaning of the other mouldings which we find set in association with them, here the גביעים and the כפתורים.

גביע also has a quite unquestionable meaning — cup, goblet. From Jeremiah 35,3, we can further deduce that גביע does not really mean the vessel out of which one drinks, גביע seems rather to be the larger vessel in which the wine was brought in, and which was then drunk out of כוסות. It says that גביעים מלאים ײן וכוסות were placed. This would also be in accordance with the meaning of the roots כוס and גבע. Whereas כוס in the co-related כסס gets the meaning, to allot to apportion, and so would radically mean a vessel in which his appointed measure is handed to a person, (from which it then often occurs as a metaphor for all the fate God apportions and sends to people), גביע in all related roots and derivatives גבע ,גבעה ,גבא ,גבה ,גבה, etc., refers to a collection, an accumulation of matter. So that גביע would be the container in which the whole amount of the liquid to be drunk is placed and kept, כוס the vessel into which the apportioned amount for each drinker is poured for him. So that גביע, according to its basic meaning would form a contrast to פרח. For whereas, as we have seen, in גביע the idea of a gathering together of matter is innate, פרח in all related roots and derivatives: אפרח ,פרא ,פרע, the Chaldean and Rabbinic פרח to fly, has the meaning, to become free.

But for כפתור there is no analogy to be found in speech or script. So we have to fall back solely on tradition, which teaches us, Menachoth 28b, that it was in the shape of Cretan apples, כמין תפוחי הכרתײם. The כפתורים were, accordingly, knobs on the shaft and arms in the shape of fruit, of apples.

If we consider these parts of the Menora as belonging together and in the order in which they invariably occur, כפתור ,גביע and פרח, they appear to us as component parts all belonging to one system. The very definite meaning of פרח as blossom or flower, as well as the explanation of כפתורים as being shapes of fruit, lead us to seek this system in the sphere of botany. We are further led in this direction by the expression משוקדים almond-like, or almond shaped, which is added to the closer description of these mouldings, which, apart from this point, will prove to be highly important for the whole meaning, but which, in any case, can only lead us again to the idea of plant life.

Luckily we have not to go far into botanic research to find in plant structure a system which corresponds exactly to such a formation as we are seeking. פרח itself, the blossom, gives us the data for the understanding of the meaning of these shapes. For every normal blossom consists essentially of three parts (a) an external, usually green leafy sheath, the cup or capsule which harbours the seed or sperm, and which receives the fructifying pollen by means of the pistil, (b) the fruit-knot (the future fruit) and (c) the crowning flower which surrounds the stamens or filaments of the pollen. These correspond exactly to our three shapes on the Menora, cup, knob and flower. We would then, first of all, have to consider these mouldings as a general symbol for fruit-developing blossoming. We would then also understand why these ornamentations are only indispensable when the Lamp was מקשה זהב made out of gold in one piece; in complete purity. Just then would the sign be necessary to emphasize that, although the whole light-bearing tree stood there in one solid piece, complete and perfect, it nevertheless did not represent a finished barren existence, but rather, essentially an eternally fruit-producing blossoming of Life.

We have capsules, fruit-knots and blossom, can it be that the stamens, the filaments with the fructifying dust, the element that gives life to the whole, can they be missing? We know from Menachoth 28b that cups, knobs and blossoms filled up the last three טפחים at the top of the shaft, so that the shaft ended with the blossom, the פרח on which the נר with its light-bearing wick, rested. From Kelim 11,7, we know that פרח was also the name generally given to the depression on a lamp which was designed to receive the light itself. If then our Lamp reached its summit in cups, knobs and the final crown of blossom, and out of this blossom the light burned on the wick, it was just this burning wick which was the pollen-bearing filament, it was the light itself, the spirit, the spirit of God, which was the fructifying element, which, coming to the Tree of Light quickens the awaiting fruit seed into life, development, and perfection, and brings it to its completion of ripe mature fruit.

Wir haben somit: Kelch, Fruchtknoten, Blumenkrone und Licht, das befruchtende Element am Staubfaden. Sollten sich uns Kelch, Fruchtknoten und Blume nicht ebenso in Begriffen aussprechen, wie sich uns von selbst die Staubfäden mit ihrem befruchtenden Pollen, als das befruchtende und belebende Element des Lichtes und Geistes dargestellt?

Scripture itself has expressed the light of the Menora as the spirit of God, and this spirit again in a sixfold radiation. Closer consideration again shows these six phases of spiritual development to be only three, as the six are paired into three: —
חכמה ובינה
עצה וגבורה
’דעת ויראת ה

Do not these three phases of spiritual development, stand in the same relation to רוח הי, their source and summit, as כפתור ,גביע and פרח, as capsule, fruit-knot and blossom stand to the נר, to the pollen filament with its exciting, moving, life-bringing element?

גביע, the goblet, both by its actual and etymological meaning, has given us its meaning as “collector, accumulator”. And in fact, the actual function of the capsule of the blossom is that at that point the forces and sap of the tree go no farther in making the twig grow longer but gather these forces in it to form a new formation. Where a blossom develops, the twig ends, growth of the twig comes to an end. The saps and forces of the tree are collected here to produce fruit, the highest goal of plant development, and the first vessel to hold this collection together is the capsule.

כפתור, in the fruit-knot the whole wealth of sap, material and forces of the plant forms itself into germs of fresh plant formation. Whereas everything, which, up to this point, had grown on the plant, stem, branch, twig and leaf, was dependent on, and part of, the plant itself, the formation of fruit-knots has the purpose of ultimately separating themselves from the parent plant to begin their own independent development of life. A quite original future with an infinite abundance of powers of formation slumbers in the tiny seed germs which the fruit-knot hides. But these germs of the future are asleep in the fruit-knots. They are awaiting their awakening to the freedom of their own lives. And the power for this awakening and freeing to life does not lie in the fruit-knot itself. In the fruit-knot itself they lie bound, awaiting freedom. This awakening and release to freedom can only be brought to them by the fructifying pollen which פרח, the crowning flower, the blossom, produces and matures on its stamens, the pollen filaments.

פרח are the “wings of freedom” of the plant which strive upwards to acquire the pollen the “dust of life” on their filaments to bring awakening and form, life and maturity, release and freedom, to the seed germs of the fruit-bud.

Let us then consider the three above mentioned pairs of phases of spiritual development leading up to ’רוח ה in comparison with what we have now worked out, as the meaning of our three mouldings on the Menora.

חכמה ובינה both are activities of recognising that which is true and good. All truth — and truth includes both what is true and what is good, one the truth of what is, and the other the truth of what should be — all truth is something which is objectively there, which is given, and every recognition of it is not creative but an acceptance and admission of something unalterably given. Nevertheless חכמה describes more the receptive activity of the spirit and mind, and בינה the productive, חכמה occupying itself more with grasping, perceiving, understanding and retaining truths of knowledge which lie before one, בינה showing itself in מבין דבר מתוך דבר in combining and deducing truths, so that בינה really seems to be productive and create something new. But it only seems to do this. In reality the new truth is only subjectively new. It is only new in so far as, up to then, it had not been realised. What בינה does, is only to survey every given truth, not only in itself, but at the same time with all the deductions and consequences which are implied in it. Any new truth that claims to be more than a phase which had not yet been recognised of, or a deduction from, an old existing truth, ceases to be a truth, and enters the realm of phantasy and illusion. In the world and in revelation, God has laid down all the facts, all the truths that human minds can recognize. The sum of all truths which the human brain can recognize is there and closed. חכמה ובינה have solely the task to get at, gather, continue and complete and develop to their furthest deductions and finest implications these given treasures, and to clarify the knowledge obtained, and retain it. חכמה and בינה are the capsule or cup for collecting and keeping all truths which exist for human knowledge.

The spirit of mind becomes really productive only in עצה וגבורה, in making decisions for advice, and power for action, by which the knowledge obtained by חכמה ובינה forms itself into resolution for action. By means of עצה וגבורה the individual, who up till now has been merely a thinking person, is prepared to step beyond himself and actively take part in the world of happenings, and in that world of events which are brought about by preceding causes and actions, to use his powers of free action as effective seeds to bear the future. עצה וגבורה are the fruit-knots which form resolutions and decisions, as germ seeds of the future, and keep them ready to mature into deeds.

But for these resolutions to mature into deeds, good deeds, real deeds, i.e., deeds that have real lasting value, for that — even as the capsule expands into the blossom for the seed-germ of the fruit-knot to attain the fructifying element of the pollen — flower, the noblest development of the mind, viz.: —

’דעת ה׳ ויראת ה, the knowledge and understanding of God, and the fear of God, must strive upwards to attain in רוח הי the one right spirit that alone produces resolutions for, and gives the power for true right actions and deeds. If all the study and knowledge of the world does not lead to seeing God in the world, and to understand the world as coming from Him; if the knowledge of the revelations of science does not lead to the fear of God, to a knowledge and recognition of one’s own relation to God, to the desire to be nothing else in the world but a servitor of God, then the germs of deeds which can build the world and eternity slumber in vain and have no ability to make free decisions or the power to do things that matter. The seeds dry up, the noblest and most godly qualities in Man remain unborn, because all knowledge and all power lack that life-giving and guiding breath of God, which only descends where all knowledge culminates in the knowledge of God, and all power in the fear of God; and the knowledge of God, and the fear of God, make the spirit of God, accessible to fructify the resolutions and powers of Man. ’דעת הי ויראת ה are the crowning flower and blossom, which grant the seeds of action which lie in human resolutions and powers, the fructifying and life-giving spirit of God.
Hence we venture the grouping: —

That the structure, whose meaning we are considering, stands before us in its outward appearance as parts of a plant, and in its meaning as spiritual or mental activities — the activities of the mind in the stages of its most eminent development, is further indicated with great decisiveness by the use of an expression to which we have already referred. The cups of the Menora are repeatedly characterised as משוקדים, almond shaped or almond-like; and, as we mentioned above, tradition is doubtful whether this משוקדים in XXV,34 — as the accent shows — does not apply to the general shape of the כפתורים and פרחים as well. Now שקד both linguistically as a verb, and actually as an almond, is, when used symbolically, the specific expression for the most intensive concentration of the mind on an object or a purpose. Just as the almond tree is the earliest to blossom, and has blossoms before it has leaves, so is its name שקד the general expression for eager, untiring, getting quickly to its goal, zealous and assiduous, working of the mind. “If God doth not guard the city, in vain doth the watchman שקד watch” (Ps. CXXVII.1). “Happy is the Man” says Prov. 8,34 “who listens to Me, לשקוד, eagerly watching at My doors day by day”. “Even as שקדתי עליהם, I zealously watched over them, unceasingly to crush and destroy, so אשקד עליהם לבנות ולנטוע, will I increasingly and zealously watch over them, to build up and to plant” (Jer. 31,28). “What dost thou see?” was Jeremiah asked, at his first call, “מקל שקד, an almond rod do I see” was his answer. “Thou hast seen well” answered God, “for שקד אני על דברי לעשתו, I am acting zealously to carry out My word” (Jer. 1,11). In Numb. 17,16 et seq. that prince of the tribe is to be shown as the chosen one of God, whose staff breaks into blossom, and this staff is then to be kept before the Ark as an eternal memorial. Then Aaron’s staff, the blossoming of which was to prove the tribe of Levi, and in that tribe, the family of Aaron, to be chosen for the priesthood ויצא פרח ויצץ ציץ ויגמל שקדים, “broke out into flower, produced pollen stamens and ripened into almond”. So we see here “שקד״ the earnest, unceasing, eager devotion to one’s calling, applied to the character which shows the tribe of Aaron to be fit to be chosen for the highest spiritual calling of the Jewish priesthood. We think we can take this as no small confirmation of the way we have taken the meaning of the almond-like shape of the blossom-mouldings on the Menora. The shaft and arms of the Lamp bear those same symbols which characterise the rod of Aaron resting in front of the Ark of Evidence, as being the “stem” of the priest! Here, as there, blossoms ripening into almonds! We translated ציץ as pollen-stamens. We think that ציצת in Ezek. 8,3, strands of hair, and ציצת the fringes on garments, bear out this interpretation.

It is further significant that this שקד character, this character of restless zeal, hurrying to accomplish its purpose, seems to be impressed particularly on the גביעים, the cups that collect and absorb knowledge, חכמה and בינה. In any case, apart from this, the mental activity expressed by these cups is placed very much in the foreground by the fact that the one כפתור and the one פרח are always preceded by a threefold cup שלשה גביעים משקדים; so that the גביעים activity is stressed extensively (שלשה) and intensively (משקדים) more than the others. This mental גביעים-activity, this gathering, absorbing, and keeping the knowledge of truth, is no other than that which we call “למוד״, “learning”, and this again is just that activity which demands our constant application יומם ולילה day and night. The גביעים משקדים on our Menora call out to us הוי שקוד ללמוד תורה! And the שלשה גביעים משקדים, out of which the one כפתור and the one פרח come teach us גדול לימוד שמביא לידי מעשה!

If the identifications which we have dared to make between the cups and חכמה ובינה, between the knobs and עצה וגבורה, and the flowers and ’דעת ויראת ה, be not altogether wrong, then we would have in the three pairs of arms, at the side of the Menora, cause to see before us these same manifestations of the “spirit; only that here they appear to be independently developed while on the stem they appear as only the developing progress on the way towards ’רוח ה׳ = נר ה. Inasmuch, now, that these same cups, knobs and flowers appear on the side branches too, we would be given the thought: — If ’חכמה ובינה, עצה וגבורה, דעת ויראת ה, develop in the human to such a degree that they obtain ’רוח ה, then enriched through this ’רוח ה, each one of them will blossom out by itself into a separate marked manifestation of the power such inspiration gives. Each one will attain the height of perfection in full concurrence with all the other energies of the mind and spirit. חכמה as well as בינה ,עצה as much as דעת ה׳,גבורה as ’יראת ה, each one of these separate rays of the one spiritual-mental life, requires, if it is to attain the highest degree of perfection, the almond cup-like energetic work of real truth, the formative and effective power of method, and the animation of the life-giving spirit of God, through seeking the knowledge of, and having the fear of God.

Hence for each one of these branch-manifestations of the spirit of God, the bearer of it, the central shaft, furnishes a fruit-knob כפתור תחת שני הקנים ממנה; for עצה וגבורה, mind and strength — the mind consciously working for practical purposes, עצה; the power to overpower and conquer difficulties, גבורה; require כפתור, require it in more concentrated power, raised to a greater degree, to bring each one of these manifestations of the spirit to actual reality in godly purity and perfection.
Now, in a most significant manner parts of this fruit-blossom structure on two places on the central shaft, still draw our attention.

ירך, the foot, the root of the stem, out of which the whole Tree of Light arises, just below where the stem steps forth out of it, bears a פרח, a flower without a capsule and without a fruit-knot. After a space of two טפחים, in the third טפח, the sixth of the total height from the bottom, there is a complete arrangement of capsule, fruit-knot and blossom, but only on a reduced scale, in miniature. For whereas the blossom arrangement at the top of the shaft occupies three טפחים, as each part of it fills one טפח, in this miniature arrangement, cup, knot and blossom are concentrated into the space of one טפח (see תוספות Menachoth), also it has one single capsule, whereas the others have three capsules. If we picture the Menora to ourselves, we see the blossoms in four different stages, each advancing to greater completion:— (a) פרח on the ירך; (b) גביע כפתור and פרח in the sixth טפח; (c) ’כפתור תחת שני הקנים ממנה וגו. (in 9th, 11th and 13th טפחים) and (d) כפתור, שלשה גביעים and פרח in the last three טפחים at the top of the shaft. It at once strikes us that this development of blossom begins at the lowest stage with that, with which it ends at its highest completion at the summit. פרח the crown of blossom is the last sprout at the summit of the shaft, and פרח, a blossom, designates the beginning of a blossom sprout at its earliest stage. Agreed that this latter is a blossom which is neither preceded by a cup, nor which has fruit for getting the quickening element. It is just a blossom by which the whole stem rises out of the root. We have recognised this growing blossom on the Tree of the Mind, as representing the knowledge of God and the fear of God, ’דעת הי ,ויראת ה. And in very truth are not the knowledge of God, and the fear of God, even as they form the noblest and highest blossoms that human beings can develop from their own spiritual intellectual lives, and which are necessary at the highest stage if the spirit of God is to be attained, and the human mind is to be perfected to be a bearer of the spirit of God, are they not in very truth the very same factors with which, in earliest childhood, the first development of spiritual life has to begin? Are they not, in very truth, in a double sense ראשית דעת the earliest beginning and the highest ultimate blossom of human knowledge? And is not the deep unassailable truth laid down here in the Sanctuary of God, on the symbolic tree of human spiritual development that:-If, later in life, in mature manhood, the knowledge of God, and the fear of God is to develop to the highest degree, then at the very root of spiritual life, in earliest childhood, this knowledge of God, and this fear of God, must be nurtured, and it must be made the underlying base for all other spiritual and intellectual development. Of course, at that age, it is a blossom without capsule and fruit-knot. At that stage is a ’דעת ויראת ה a knowledge of God, and a fear of God, which neither yet comes from the “cups” created by חכמה ובינה nor which is yet directed towards ripening into the “fruit” of action, עצה וגבורה. It is rather a flower of knowing God, and fearing God, which is given directly with the root and stock of the human mind ירכה ופרחה. Out of this deep and innermost seed, without theoretical preparation—without a capsule—the mind can be awakened and taught and educated, מפי עוללים ויונקים יסדת עוז. And, at this earliest stage, this childish ’דעת ויראת ה has net yet to occupy itself in maturing and ripening the fruit seed of עצה וגבורה—this seed of עצה וגבורה which produces acts and deeds is altogether not yet present. This childish ’דעת ויראת ה has only to occupy itself with the rather unconscious, but ready and willing giving itself up to, and growing up to, the path to the Light, so as then, in childhood, to form the beginnings of those three manifestations of spiritual life, the capacity for the attainment of חכמה ובינה, the capacity for עצה וגבורה, the capacity for ’דעת ויראת ה, so as first to get the talent for all these, to practice and to develop on a small scale גביע כפתור ופרח. Then in adolescence, first use all energy of resolution and power to the specialised cultivation of each of these three manifestations וכפתור תחת שני קנים ממנה וכפתור תחת שני הקנים ממנה, וכפתור תחת שני הקנים ממנה, and then finally, fully mature and grown up, to direct all these branches back again to the one centre point, and out of the flowing well of חכמה ובינה to develop a ’דעת ויראת ה which, bringing life and maturity to all עצה וגבורה knows how to draw light and spirit — clarity and understanding — from above, in the ’נר ה, the Spirit of God:
’שלשה גביעים משוקדים כפתור ופרח ועליה נר ה

V. 1. יריעת, from etymological derivation, tapestry, tent-fabric, which serves to surround and enclose a space. ירע ;יריעת related to כרע גרע, according to its fundamental meaning designates a depreciation, a lessening, גרע in value, כרע in height, ירע in circumstances, as אל ירע בעיניך, and so in the meaning of יריעה as here, in space, confining, surrounding with a barrier. So that יריעה does not mean curtain in general but quite specially tent-cloth, material used to surround and enclose a space.

שש, as already remarked on Ch. 25,4, are the threads of fine linen. Tradition teaches (Yoma 71b) that, as the name שש implies, each thread consisted of six strands, and the woollen threads too, the ארגמן ,תכלת and תולעת שני were simply six-ply שזר ,משזר .חוטן כפול ששה we find also as the root of שזרא synonymous with שדרא, the vertebral column, backbone, (אונקלס translates לעמת העצה by לקביל שזרתא. The Aruch has the rendering in many places in the Talmud שזרא in place of שדרא). The meaning of שזר accordingly seems to be a linked chain, a jointed pillar, a jointed stick, and here also “a thread of strands”. This was obtained by twisting several strands together. Each twist or coil formed one thread. So that משזר means twisted. משזר is only mentioned together with שש, but in accordance with the tradition in the Gemora and with what seems indicated in the text by the repetition of the שש (Ch. 39,27, 28) that each of the four threads (linen, purple wool, scarlet wool, sky-blue wool) was first twisted into 6 ply and then the four 6 ply threads were twisted together to form a twenty-four strand thread, not as Rashi seems to take the text, that one strand of each of the four materials was first taken and these four threads twisted together and then six of the resulting threads taken and joined. Both according to the text and to the way it is taken in the Gemora Yoma it does not seem to have been six four-ply, but four six-ply threads that were used. The סמײג (law 173) also seems to take it this way. Also see הלי כלי ,מל״מ מקדש VIII, at end of 3.

כרובים מעשה חשב תעשה אותם. In Yoma 72b it says: רוקם מעשה מחט לפיכך פרצוף אחד, חושב מעשה אורג לפיכך שני פרצופות: “the רקימה mentioned in V.35 denotes needlework, embroidery, hence the figure are only on one side, but the חושב mentioned here was woven work, so that the figures were on both sides of the material.” By רקם, needlework, the figure was embroidered on an underlying background so that it appeared on one side only. But by חושב is meant a weaving of such a nature that the whole texture of the fabric consisted of the figures which were completely visible on both sides (see Rambam ibid. 15). Further, as it says כרובים תעשה אותם they did not consist of material on which cherubim were embroidered, but the curtains consisted of cherubim woven together, they were “cherubim-curtains”. The word רקם seems related to רגם to throw stones, the figures seemed to be thrown on to the material. But חשב has the basic conception of combining, joining, (hence also the חֵשֶׁב האפד the connecting piece) so that they were complete figures which were joined together by weaving. The חושב wove figures complete figures, right through the material, clear on both sides, and joined them together. There is no techincal word which rightly translates this. Weaving, as we perforce have translated it, does not really suffice.

V. 2. Die Ausdrucksweise ארבע באמה ,עשרים באמה. usw. bedarf noch einer Erklärung. Sie kommt in einem Satze mit der gewöhnlichen präpositionslosen abwechselnd vor, z. B. Kön. I. 6, 3: עשרים אמה ארכו על פני רחב הבית עשר באמה רחבו על פני הבית. Es ist gewiss ein fein nuancierter Unterschied, dessen Aufklärung erwünscht wäre.

V. 4. לול .לולאות bezeichnet ein Ineinanderverschlungensein. Daher לול: eine Wendeltreppe, לַיִל: die Zeit, in welcher die Umrisse der Gegenstände ununterscheidbar ineinanderfallen, die Nacht. לולאה, eine Schleife.

V. 5. קָבָל עם ,מקבילות (Kön. II. 15, 10) so viel wie נגד העם, dem Volke gegenüber, in Gegenwart, קַבֵּל, entgegennehmen, empfangen. הַקְבִיל sich zum Empfange darbieten, einem andern in gerader Richtung zugewandt sein, hier noch vollständiger, von mit einander zu verbindenden Schleifen: jede der andern zu deren Empfange zugewandt.

V. 6. קרס ,קרסים Jesaia 46, 1 u. 2 קרסו כרעו ,קרס נבו sich krümmen. Die Verwandtschaft mit גרס ,גרז ,קרץ, die alle ein gewaltsames Schneiden, Trennen und Brechen bedeuten, lässt vermuten, daß קרס eine starke Biegung fast bis zum Bruche bezeichne. Daher קרסים, stark gebogene Spangen, die die in deren Krümmung gebrachten Schleifen sehr festhalten.

V. 6. והיה המשכן אחד. From the size of the boards over which the curtains (or tapestry), were hung (17—25) it can be deduced that the inner space of the Sanctuary was 30 cubits in length, 10 cubits in breadth and 10 cubits in height. The length of each curtain was 28 cubits, and the total breadth of the ten curtains was 40 cubits. The curtains were hung with their length across the breadth of the Sanctuary so that (taking internal measurements) it would require a length of 30 cubits to completely cover it, 10 up and 10 down the boards at the sides, and 10 across the top. Leaving out the thickness of the boards which were one cubit thick — according to the view of רבי יהודה (see Sabbath 98b) they were tapered at the top to just a finger-breadth — the curtains would only reach down to 9 cubits on each side and the silver feet (V.9) under the boards would be uncovered and visible. According to רבי נחמיה (ibid.) the thickness of the boards would have to be deducted and the curtains would only hang down eight cubits on either side, and two cubits up from the ground would be uncovered. The 40 cubits of the breadth of the curtains had to cover the 30 cubits of the length of the roof, 10 cubits the height of the back wall, and add again one cubit for the thickness of the boards so that there would be only 9 cubits down the back wall and the silver feet would be exposed. But according to רבי יהודה these were also covered (see ibid.).

V. 9. ’וכפלת וגו. The breadth of the eleven goats’-hair curtains which formed the “tent” over the “dwelling” measured a total of 44 cubits, 4 cubits, the breadth of one whole curtain, more than the cherubim-curtains. Of this one curtain-breadth, according to the directions of the text, half, i.e., 2 cubits, was to be thrown in front over the entrance (כפלת, doubled over or divided equally).

V. 11—13. The goats’-hair curtains were hung in a similar way, their length over the breadth of the building, their breadth over the length. They were 2 cubits longer than the cherubim-curtains, so that right and left they reached down one cubit longer than the latter (V.13). Their total breadth was 4 cubits more, of which two cubits were thrown over the front (V.9). So that at the back they stretched 2 cubits lower than the cherubim-curtain. According to ר׳ יהודה, these 2 cubits trailed out along the ground behind the structure. According to ר׳ נחמיה, who held that the boards were not tapered at the top so that one cubit has to be deducted for the breadth of the boards, this “train” was only one cubit long. According to both of them “the משכן was like a stately lady walking along the street with the train of her skirt trailing behind her”, לאשה שמהלכת בשוק ושיפוליה מהלכין אחריה (Sabbath ibid.).

V. 14. The covering of skins formed the roof of the tent. According to the interpretation of ר׳ יהודה (Sabbath 28a) there were, in accordance with the literal words of the text, two covers, that of rams’ skins below, and that of tachash-skins above. According to רי נחמיה (ibid.) there was only one covering of skins consisting half of rams’ and half of tachash-skins. Then the מלמעלה of the text would have to refer to the whole, the covering was מלמעלה לאהל. On 28b (ibid.) we are told that תחש was an animal that was only accessible to Moses, and that it was doubtful whether it was a species of בהמה or whether it was a wild חיה. In any case it was certain that it was טהורה, a “pure” animal and it seems to have been a unicorn, having a single horn on its forehead. The name תחש might indicate that it was an animal characterised by special speed, from חוש, to speed, as in Job 31,5 ותַחֵשׁ על מרמה רגלי.

V. 15. קרש ;הקרשים related to ירש ,גרש seems not to mean “boards” generally, but specially “wall-boards” which by “driving-away” those who have no right, keep a place “reserved” for those who have a right to it. עצי שטים עומדים. According to Yoma 72a, this indicates עומדים, שעומדים דרך גדילתן, they had to be put up in the way they naturally grow, the root ends below, the top ends above. So that even as boards they had to retain their “tree” nature. דבר אחר שמעמידין את צפוין, they are those which bear the golden overlays, i.e., although overlaid with gold, their nature as boards, wood, is to remain the predominant idea (תוספות ibid.) similar to the top of the Table (see above). ,דבר אחר, עומדים, שמא תאמר אבד סברן ובטל סכוײן, ת״ל עומדים שעומדים לעולם ולעולמים, they remain “standing, existing”, even if and when their hope and outlook seems quite lost”. (room, space for a “sanctuary” in our lives is always there. I.L.).

V. 17. שלב .משלבות (probably related to שלף to pull out) to extend something, like the rungs of a ladder. The boards were cut out at the bottom into two tenons, fitted for insertion into corresponding cavities for them in the silver feet.

V. 18. The south side is called נגב, probably because the rays of the sun coming down perpendicularly hit the head “piercingly”, (related to תימן .(נקב from ימין the right, also a name for the south, as being on the right when facing the rising sun. Perhaps this designation is added here because the “face” of the Sanctuary is to be considered facing the east so that the south is on the right. (As the service on the Day of Atonement so clearly shows, the “Mishkon” starts in the west in the Ark of the Torah and its influence is directed always outwards towards the people. I.L.).

V. 24. תמים ,תואמים. According to ר׳ יהודה (Sabbath 98b) the boards were one cubit thick at the bottom and gradually tapered upward so that at the top they were merely a finger breadth thick. This is here expressed for the corner boards, that below they were תואמים, that they joined up levelly with the boards of the side and back walls, and above were תמים tapered down to the required size to fit the rings. The width of the structure was ten cubits, the six boards of the rear wall measured nine cubits so that there was a space of half a cubit on each side. The corner boards had to close this space and also to extend across the thickness of the boards of the side walls. As the corner-boards were, like all the other boards, cubits wide and all the boards were one cubit thick at the bottom, the cubits of the corner boards fitted exactly, at the bottom, the half cubit empty space, and the 1 cubit of the thickness of the boards of the side walls. But this thickness tapered upwards to a fingerbreadth, and, accordingly, the breadth of the corner-boards had to be planed down correspondingly to fit. דשפי להו כי תורין their finished shape was “like a hill that was perpendicularly steep up one side and a gradual slope on the other”. According to this, the תמים of the corner-boards would express a double thinning in breadth and in thickness. But according to רבי נחמיה, the boards were left the same thickness all the way up, and the תמים would not mean “coming to an end”, but would be the demand for the boards to be תמים boards, “complete”, all of one piece, not made up of two or more pieces joined together. — טבעת, it is not sure whether it was only the corner-boards which were held together with the side-boards on each side by means of a ring, or whether this joining by a ring applied to all boards.

V. 28—29. תיכון ;והבריח התיכון usually means the middle, not the inner e.g., Judges 7,19, האשמורת התיכונה, hence the addition בתוך הקרשים. The other four bolts on either side ran along the surface of the boards through rings of gold and under a gold covering. But this centre bolt ran invisibly inside the boards, which were bored through for this purpose, and while the other bolts only reached on either side as far as the centre, two above and two below, the middle interior bolt מן הקצה אל הקצה went right through from one end of the wall to the other, through all ten boards. More, according to Sabbath 98b, there was only one central interior bolt which miraculously extended in one piece right through both side walls and the back wall, and so truly held the whole Mishkon together as one single piece.
V. 30. והקמת וגוי. See note on V.6.

V. 31. פרך ,פרכת (related to פרק, to separate, from which פרק a part, a limb, a member) means likewise to break. Hence פרכת, separation, separating curtains, a curtain by which spaces are divided off, “formed into parts”, but, at the same time, are kept as parts of a whole, remain in connection with each other. This purpose as הבדלה dividing, separating, is expressly mentioned in V.33. In Ch. 39,34 it is also called פרכת המסך, so also in Ch. 40,3, וסכת על הארן את הפרכת, and in V.21 וישם את פרכת המסך ויסך על ארון העדות, so that the dividing curtains had also at the same time a “covering” a protecting purpose. Hence, (Succa 7b) the instruction that the פרכת had דניכוף ביה פורתא דמחזי כספך, not only to hang straight down to form a dividing wall but also at the top had to extend a little horizontally inwards and, so appear also as a protecting roof for the inner space, the space for the Ark of Evidence.

V. 33. תחת הקרסים. The ten curtains of cherubim-tapestry were, as described above in V.3—6, joined together into two sets, each of five curtains. These two were joined together by hooks and loops. The tent of cherubim-tapestry consisted accordingly of two halves joined together, each half being 20 cubits wide. The back, western half, had to cover, according to ר׳ יהודה the 10 cubits of the back wall (according to ר׳ נחמיה nine cubits of the wall and one cubit of the thickness of the boards at the top) and 10 cubits of the western part of the building. Along the border line of these 10 cubits were the קרסים and as the פרכת hung down from these clasps it divided the structure into an inner western room of 10 cubits long, 10 cubits wide and 10 cubits high, (this was the קדש הקדשים) and an outer room lying eastwards of it, 20 cubits long, 10 cubits wide and 10 cubits high — the קדש. Significantly it says והבדילה הפרכת לכם, which indicates that the division is not so much an absolute one but rather as one that is there for us to note, and to be kept as far as we are concerned. Further, it must not be overlooked that

V. 34. the hanging of this dividing curtain is mentioned before the laying of the cherubim-cover on the Ark of Evidence, thereby making this division a condition for our whole conception and understanding of the significance and meaning of the כפרת (as worked out at length in previous chapters. I.L.). When the work was actually carried out, Ch. 40,20 & 21, the Ark with the כפרת already on it, was first brought into the משכן and then the dividing and covering curtain drawn.

V. 35. By the use which was to be made of it, the space of the קדש in front of the פרכת, 20 cubits long by 10 cubits wide, also fell into two spaces of 10 cubits each. Within the western space (10 × 10) the Table and the Lamp were placed. The Table was on the north side, cubits from the side wall and within the front five cubits, and similarly on the south side the Lamp stood opposite it. Between the two, in the centre foreground, on the rear (i.e., western) border line of the front ten cubits, stood the golden Incense Altar, the erection of which is only prescribed in Ch. XXX. (See Yoma 33a and Yalkut פקודי).

V. 36. Whereas the פרכת, like the cherubim-tapestry, was מעשה חשב ,כרובים, the curtain before the entrance, although of the same colours and materials was not כרובים but was only מעשה רקם (see note on V.1).
THE משכן

Let us now picture the Mishkon according to the instructions given in this chapter, erected for the “contents” described in the preceding chapter. Standing before the entrance in the east we should see in the western background, the Holy-of-Holies, the Ark of Evidence; in front of it, in the “Holy”, the Table on the north side and the Lamp on the south שולחן ארון מנורה, all three surrounded by upright shittim-boards which are gold-clad and resting on silver feet and united by visible and invisible shittim-wood-golden bolts. They — the “contents” — are covered and surrounded by white, double red, and blue cherubim-tapestry, which, in the north, the west and the south, flows down out of sight behind the shittim walls and which is visible to us only as forming the roof above and as a curtain in front of the Ark, protecting it and separating it from the Table and the Lamp.
Now what does all this express in the light of what we have already found to be the meaning of the “contents”?

First of all, these “contents” themselves, the ושלחן ,ארון and מנורה, what is their relation to each other in view of the relative positions allocated to them. It is the ארון at the base, which appoints the Lamp with its right hand and the Table with its left. It is the Law of God, which, when received and accepted as “תורה״ (from הרה) as “the Seed of Life”, with eternally progressing growth (wood. I.L.) and everlasting firmness (gold) to be guarded and kept and fulfilled, it is this Torah which produces with its right hand i.e., in the first instance, the everlasting Tree of Light of the mind and spirit, but at the same time with its left hand lays the Table of material well-being with all the reservations for wealth and well-being that the Table requires — (honesty, purity, sharing the wealth, brotherhood, and love. See preceding chapter. I.L.) ארך ימים בימינה, בשמאלה עשר וכבוד.

But where human beings give up all which exists in human nature of “wood” and “gold”, of the capacity for progress, and of the ability to be firm, to become an ארון for the תורה, to take up the Divine Law as the guide for what men and nations should be, to absorb the will of God as the fructifying seed of life within them; — where they decide to use all their ability for progress, and all their powers of firmness and resistance, to bring this seed to fruition and maturity, and from it, and from it alone, to develop the “Tree” of their mind to blossom up to God, and from it, and from it alone, to build up their “Table” of well-being with all its attendant happiness-bringing and happiness-spreading genii of purity, honesty and love; — where they are willing to combine all their human abilities for progress and firmness to form a מקדש, a home for godliness and eternity on earth; there God lets the cherubim of His שכינה come down to surround protectingly and helpingly (יריעות) that group of human beings that wishes to form itself into a מקדש to Him, so that this special help can manifest His special proximity to them (משכן). (If they will make a Mikdosh, He promises Mishkon. I.L.).
