As the אהל had no other vessels than those mentioned in V.8, V.8 can only be taken as the explanation of this concluding phase of V.7, and the ו of the ואת השלחן וגו׳ as a ו copulative, “the Table, as well as” etc. This also would then explain why here in referring to the שלחן it only says כליו and not כל כליו as it does of the מנורה. The appurtenances of the Table, with the exception of the קערות, belong intrinsically to it, and always remain on or about it. They are part of, and included in כל כלי האהל. But the כלי המנורה are only instruments for the service of the Lamps, are not an intrinsic part of it, and have no permanent place at all in the אהל (actually in the בית המקדש there was a special room for storing all these כלים I.L.), so that they would have to be specially indicated by the כל.

V. 10. שרד .ואת בגדי השרד phonetically related to שרט to cut into, has the basic meaning of separating, keeping apart, hence the word שָׂרִיד בגדי השרד have been taken to mean the protective overalls, the covers which had to be made to fit over the holy appurtenances of the Sanctuary during the journeys in the years of wandering. (Numbers IV). The ו in the following ואת בגדי השרד, by which the בגדי השרד are indicated as being something other than the בגדי הקדש, would speak for this meaning. But in Ch. 35,19, and again in XXXIX, 1, and in XXXIX,41 the purpose of these בגדי שרד is given as לשרת בקדש, and this can hardly be taken to refer to the packing up for the journeys. In addition it would be most striking, if it were to refer to them here, that these covers are not mentioned at all above when the instructions for making the בגדים etc. were given, and they must be considered as of such secondary importance that there is no mention of them at all until they actually had to be used. So that it does not seem possible to take the words בגדי שרד to be anything else than a description of the priestly garments, and to take the ו of ואת בגדי הקדש in exactly the same way as ואת השלחן in V.8, following ואת כלי האהל is to be understood (see above). Then שרד would be taken as meaning singled out, selected, distinguished, and it is also understandable why this attribute of the sanctity of the priestly garments should be specially prominently stressed just at the making and delivery of them out of the hands of the artists. For it is with these garments that those who are appointed to the priestly office are to be separated and distinguished out of the common communal life which they had hitherto shared with the artists and the whole nation. It is the nation itself, that, through its artists, makes these garments of distinction by means of which henceforth for all time, one family is to be separated from all others, and raised above all others. This שרד was certainly present in the minds of the skilled workers and of the nation in whose name they worked, and the work was carried out freely and cheerfully. Onkelos always translates בגדי השרד by לבושי שמשא which would be equivalent to בגדי השרת.

V. 12. ויאמר. No new law is introduced here. The Law of Sabbath had already been given. Here it receives new explanatory phases, and with special reference to the preceding order to work at building the Sanctuary. That seems to be the reason why it starts ויאמר ה׳ and not, as by other pronouncements of permanent laws, with וידבר. With reference to the work of building the Sanctuary which He had ordained, God explains how the Sabbath is to be kept in this respect.
V. 13. ואתה דבר וגו׳. That which God had said to Moses merely as explanatory remarks, he should nevertheless teach in the sharp decisive manner of a pronouncement of a Law.

אך את שבתתי תשמרו, these words place שמירת שבת above the command of building the Sanctuary. Before שבת, even the מלאכת המשכן has to retire. This is the first time that the duty of keeping Sabbath is brought under the conception of the word שמירה, and three times in this Sabbath-chapter is this idea repeated (V.13, 14 and 16) so that it proclaims itself as the real purport of this chapter. But this conception teaches us to look on שבת as a precious object entrusted to our care, to which all the duties of שומרים apply. We must accordingly not be פושע with it, not be a שולח יד on it, never allow it out of our sight, not allow ourselves to use it according to our ideas or requirements, and, with anxious conscientiousness, keep away and fend off, everything that might possibly damage this sacred treasure which has been entrusted to our care (שמירה I.L.). With such intensity, this idea of שמירה only occurs elsewhere referring to the Torah as a whole, but to any individual Mitzva perhaps only with regards to the laws of Pessach: את חג המצות תשמר, ושמרתם את המצות, שמר את חדש האביב, ושמרת את החקה הזאת למועדה, and even there only in scattered places when the occasion arises to refer to Pessach again, but not as here thrice repeated in the same paragraph. And moreover it is not the Sabbath in general, but “שבתותי״, each individual actual Sabbath that occurs in all Time, is recommended to our “care” (שמירה), each actual Sabbath-day demands our dutiful attention afresh, demands afresh our whole duty of “guarding” it. (ימים שבנתים הוו ידיעה לחלק אעפ״י שלא ידע Sab. 67b תוספות there, and according to ר׳ נחמן בר אבוה also 69b). And it is not in connection with some private, profane, business or professional enterprise, it is the מלאכת המשכן, a piece of work dedicated to the highest national and godly purposes, it is the building of a Temple to achieve nearness to God against which Sabbath is to be protected, and thereby the keeping of the Sabbath that is demanded of us in connection with all other, less holy purposes, is impressed with double force upon us.

כי אות היא. As the word Sabbaths in this verse is in the plural,שבתותי, the היא can not refer to the Sabbath day, but can only refer to the שמירה, and this raises the abstinence from work on Sabbath, שביתת מלאכה to an אות a symbol, and the signification of this symbol is a mutual one, ביני וביניכם, by this sign, God recognises us, acknowledges us, and by means of this sign we acknowledge God, according to the purport which this sign expresses. This purport is given here and is introduced by the word .לדעת דעת is the purpose of every sign, of every אות, a symbol is an אות just because it is a means of making something known, and the knowledge to be made known by שמירת שבת is כי אני ה׳ מקדשכם that God makes us holy, i.e., separates us out of all others and places us “at the ready” for His service. By שמירת שבת i.e., refraining from carrying out any constructive work, we lay ourselves, our world and the powers God has given us of mastering it, in homage at God’s Feet, and acknowledge ourselves, our world and our productive powers as being holy to God, i.e., as belonging exclusively to Him for the fulfilment of His will. As long as Man existed, Sabbath also existed, to make Man holy (as remarked on Ex. 16,23). But it (the שבת of בראשית I.L.) was only an abstract idea, any visible expression of it, anything tangible, anything that could be appreciated by our senses was entirely lacking, it lacked an אות, a symbol and therefore it dwindled and disappeared as mankind went astray. When God chose Israel to be His instrument for His Kingdom on earth, i.e., for His being acknowledged as Creator and Director of mankind, which is nothing else but realisation of “שבת״, He then made Sabbath in Israel something tangible, something more than a mere abstract idea, by giving it the concrete symbol of prohibition of work, and God’s Sabbath became Man’s Sabbath. Henceforth the “keeping of Sabbath” is a sign of God’s relation to Israel and Israel’s to God, the distinguishing sign that God had made and does make us holy unto Him.

V. 14. ושמרתם את השבת וגו׳, the שבת in contrast to שבתות of the preceding verse; therefore guard, esteem, keep, protect, watch over the Sabbath, the whole institution of Sabbath, for it is a Sanctuary for you, i.e., your godliness flows out of it, and it keeps up and renews the holiness of your whole personality. מחלליה מות יומת ,כי כל העשה וגו׳, the כי seems difficult to understand, it makes כל העשה וגו׳ the reason for מחלליה וגו׳. As מחלליה is plural and מות יומת singular, מחלליה can not be the subject of יומת but is the object of it, and מות יומת is a verbum impersonale, “one shall judicially put to death the Sabbath-desecrator”. So that this verse is not speaking so much of the capital gravity of the one who desecrates the Sabbath as of the duty of the community to bring him to justice. Now חילול שבת literally “the killing of Sabbath” i.e., destroying the living and life-giving idea of the Sabbath, can in its real sense only be done by breaking it in the presence of others, thereby weakening or killing the power of this Sanctuary in the minds and feelings of others. So our sentence here speaks of the desecration of Sabbath in the presence of witnesses who are always taken as representing the whole nation. A desecration of Sabbath before witnesses would accordingly be: - in front of the nation, killing that institution on the base of which the whole nation with its calling and mission rests, and the nation has the duty of destroying the existence of the Sabbath-desecrator and thereby restoring the holiness of the institution again in its midst. The killing or keeping alive of the idea of Sabbath in the minds of the people is such an essential part of the purposes for which Sabbath was established, that, as is the case in no other law except the understandable related one of חילול השם, the idea of בפרהסיא exercises such an important influence, that the sin of desecrating Sabbath בפרהסיא, i.e., if done in the presence of the whole nation — i.e., ten adult members of the nation, always taken as representing the nation — מחלל שבת בפרהסיא is considered on par with עובד עבודה זרה, and, as having broken with the whole of Judaism מומר לכל התורה כולה. Now the concluding phrase כי וגו׳ fits in with the context in the following sense: - If the desecration of the Sabbath is done before witnesses, human justice is to take the life of the criminal, for, before God, every one who does a מלאכה on Sabbath, even if unseen by a fellow-man has forfeited his existence and his future.

V. 15. Here, too, יֵצָשֶה is verb. impers. and מלאכה is the object. One shall carry out the work ordered for the building of the Sanctuary in six weekdays but the seventh day remains, even towards the building of the Sanctuary, a day to celebrate God’s sanctity in its unassailable holiness, by complete cessation of constructive work (see above Ch. 16,23); anybody who performs a מלאכה on the Sabbath day, even if it is for the establishment of the Sanctuary, has forfeited his life.

V. 16. ושמרו. So, all the more certain is it, that in all other general affairs, the Children of Israel have to keep the Sabbath, and by the earnestness and conscientiousness of this care transmit it to their future generations for all time as a ברית עולם, as an institution of God, given in unconditional, complete absoluteness for all time. (See Gen. 6,18).

V. 17. Above (V.13) the שמירה, the abstaining from work was designated an אות, here it is the day itself. The day in itself is the memorial of God’s free creation of the world; our refraining from work on this day is the memorial of our recognition of the Creator as our Master, and of our being called by Him to His service. נפש :וינפש is the individuality, the individual personal creature (see on Gen. 1,20 and Jeshurun VIII, P.435) so that הִנָפֵשׁ would mean to withdraw into one’s own personality, in contrast to working at something external to one’s self, so that it also means resting from an exertion, literally coming to oneself (Ex. 23,12., Sam. II. 16,14). Here it has the original meaning. Nowadays we see God nowhere in His creative activity, וינפש, He has withdrawn to Himself, it is Sabbath in the Creation. But the Sabbath-day is the memorial that a free creative activity preceded this retirement, this Sabbath; that God formed heaven and earth for six days and then with the seventh day He ceased creating when He withdrew into the present state where we can not perceive His work. (See on Gen. 2,1—3).

Sabbath is the memorial for our relation to God; the Temple, the memorial for our relation to His Torah. It is understandable that the building of the Temple must give way to the Sabbath. The Temple itself presupposes the Sabbath. To פקוח כפש, to save life, Sabbath gives way. פקוח נפש דוחה שבת as in general, in regard to other commands, it says אשר יעשה אותם האדם וחי בהם (Levit. 18,5) ולא שימות בהם, or specifically referring to Sabbath כי קדש היא לכם ,היא מסורה בידכם ולא אתם מסורים בידה (V.14), the object of the giving of the Sabbath is your sanctification, hence keeping it may not be a threat to your life, or (V.16) ושמרו בני ישראל את שבת, חלל עליו שׂבת אחת, כדי שישמור שבתות הרבה, the Sabbath requires “keepers”, in the midst of Mankind; so break one Sabbath on account of one whose life is in danger so that he shall be able to keep many Sabbaths (Yoma 85b). In keeping alive the “keeper” you are keeping Sabbath itself alive, just as in the endangered life of the keeper, the life of Sabbath itself is considered endangered.

V. 18. ויתן אל משה, the subject in this sentence, God, is not mentioned, it is meant to be deduced from all the preceding, so that this verse is joined on to the immediately preceding verses. Hence the giving of the Tablets is no separate act on its own, but it is just that which brings all that went before it to its conclusion. All that went before it served as the necessary preparations, the necessary conditions for its occurrence. If God spoke in Ch. 20,21 the words מזבח אדמה תעשה לי and then, before this building of the Altar was allowed to be proceeded with, the building up of the nation on the basis of Justice, Humanity and Morality had to be established in משפטים and then in תצוה, תרומה and כי תשא up to now, the building of His Sanctuary ordered and arranged, then the meaning of the whole of this building — as indeed is expressed by it as a whole and in every detail of it — can be nothing else than to be the home of the Divine Torah. The Torah, the carrying out of which is the condition for the special presence of God; doing homage to which, is the way we are to do homage to God, and as witness proclaiming the Divine origin of which, these Tablets are to be brought in as the visible inhabitants of the Sanctuary. It was for these “witnesses” that the whole structure was to be erected. The means for their accommodation is the very first instruction which God issued when He gave instructions for the holy furnishing of the Sanctuary (Ch. 25,21). Human hands are to build the dwelling, but the inhabitants — not as in other temples, some representation of something godly made by Man’s hands, but the realisation of what humanity should be as drawn by the Hand of God, no human image of God, but a Divine ideal for Man and Nation — the inhabitants are given by God.

לדבר אתו: at first all God’s speeches giving out the laws were דבור אל משה. Moses’ attitude to the Word of God imparting the laws was only passive, receiving and absorbing. But ככלתו, before the Lawgiving was finished, Moses had absorbed the teachings to such a degree that to use the simile of ריש לקיש in רבה, “as a well-instructed pupil at the end of the course goes over the whole matter again, actively discussing it with the master”, the Torah uses the word אתו here, לדבר אתו and not .לדבר אליו שני לחת העדת —. We have already remarked on Gen. 1,14 that writing the feminine plural חסר wishes the plurality of the objects to be considered in the singular, that is to say as one common single idea which finds its realisation in the combination of more than one object. So here, too, the form לחת in which the Tablets are presented in writing teaches that the two Tablets of stone are to be considered as a mutually complementary single whole; לא זו גדולה מזו each one exactly the same size, the Tablet of the duties towards God, and the one of the duties towards one’s fellow-man, both of the same size, both of the same weight (ש״ר), only both together, in equal importance constituting the one Divine Law. (see above on XX 14). Placed together, too, they formed one complete finished cube of which each composed the half (see on Ch. 25,10). — לחת אבן, whereas the Ark that was to receive it was made from “tree” material, the Tablet of the Law is of stone. The given Law is unchangeable, we its receivers and observers, are to develop ourselves on it, and about it and through it in constant progress. כתבים באצבע אלהיט: as directly the work of God Himself as “the heavens, the work of His Fingers” (Ps. 8,4), as clearly bearing witness to God, as the miracles in Egypt pointed to “the Finger of God” (Ch. 8,15).

V. 1. While above, in the heights, the revelation of the Law, was brought to that conclusion — by the instructions for making the Sanctuary of the Torah and by the handing over of the “evidence of the Torah” — through which the Torah henceforth was to have its home in their midst as the soul of the nation, to permeate the nation as a whole, and each individual of it, with the spirit of their mission, and by carrying out its injunctions to obtain the assured presence of God in the nation as promised ועשו לי מקדש ושכנתי בתוכם, — below, on earth, events were proceeding which proved only too realistically, that the fact which, at the preparation for receiving the Torah, had been so earnestly and emphatically brought home to the people symbolically by the injunctions, לך אל העם וקדשתם וגו, וגם הכהנים וגו׳ יתקדשו, והגבלת את העם וגו׳ (Ch. 19,10, 12, and 22) was indeed a very real and present factor in the life of the nation. We refer of course, to the fact of the distance that yawned between the actual contemporary state of the people and the ideal heights of the Torah which they were to receive, which we indicated above (on Ch. 19,10 et seq.) with all the fundamental consequences which this fact entailed. The people who could not overcome the absence of their Moses for forty days; who, still under the impression of the accompanying flaming lightning which showed them with elemental clarity לא תעשה לך פסל, could make for themselves the “golden calf”, that people were still such a distance away from the truths and demands of this Torah, that it is quite impossible to think that this Torah could have been produced, as other laws and other religions have been, by the people living at that time, as a product in accordance with the ideas of that age. Also the event shows us, both how absolutely finite and unyielding God had made His Torah, and the absolute certainty with which He had decided that it should achieve its aim of winning a home for itself and becoming effective on this earth. Right at the beginning of its first entry into this world, forced by the unworthiness of the people who had been prepared to be its first acceptors, into the alternative of giving up the Torah or the whole of the contemporary members of that people, the decision did not waver for one minute to give up the whole of that generation, create a new generation for the acceptance of this Torah and…wait. The words אכלם ואעשה אותך לגוי גדול, to make an end of the nation that had been made ready to receive the Torah, and to ensure Moses and the Torah a different future, expresses right from the beginning the completely absolute destiny which this Torah will have, guaranteed and looked after by God Himself. Never, and at no time, has this Torah to accommodate itself to any age, but every age has only as much right and justification for its present and future as it orders its life in accordance with this Torah. The Torah is the absolute highest aim for the Jewish-nation, and the generation of that time were still at an infinite distance from achieving that aim. And even if nevertheless this Torah with its unalterable ideal demands was allowed to enter the contemporary nation of that time, the purpose clearly was not to allow it to be always altered by this nation to suit convenience and demands of each age, but to make the nation, its bearers, undergo changes for so long, until it had worked itself up to spiritual intellectual and moral heights of this Torah. In short, by this occurrence, the first and immediate work that this Torah, which was to enter the nation as its ruler, had to accomplish was:- to use its Divine power in educating the people up to allegiance to its ideals, and the first and immediate work which its Sanctuary had to accomplish was one of כפרה, that is, to be dedicated as a place of never-tiring education for a purer better future.
Before the Sanctuary of the Torah was to be erected, the people and the priests were first to be made conscious of their necessity for כפרה.

We dare to say “were to be”. For the importance of this whole occurrence, after what has been indicated above, in general, and still more after we have gone into the details, is so great for the objective nature of the Torah, and for the meaning of its Sanctuary, and for the relation of the nation to both, that we seem justified in supposing that this forty days absence of Moses was meant to be a test for the people. From it, by way of actual historic experience, before the real entry of the Torah and its Sanctuary into their lives, the people would acquire that understanding of them both which is so essentially necessary for the working of both of them on us to be successful.

בשש .וירא העם כי בשש משה the Piel of בוש, originally “to find oneself disappointed in an expectation.” (see on Gen. 11,25) hence ויחילו עד בוש (Judges 3,25) “they waited until they saw themselves disappointed in their expectations” i.e., they waited outside the door so long until they came to the conclusion that they could no longer expect their expectation to be fulfilled. Hence, not to fulfil the expectations of somebody else, to such a degree that he gives up the expectation. Moses stayed away so long that they doubted whether he would return at all. הִקָהֵל על :ויקהלו העם על אהרן to gather in masses against somebody, to overpower somebody by a mass gathering. The expression occurs twice; in Numbers 16,3 and XX, 2, the first against Moses, the second against Moses and Aaron, and in both cases Moses and Aaron offered no opposition even in words. At Korach’s uprising, Moses at once “cast himself on his face”, and only opposed him after he had received the suggestion from God. In the second instance, Moses and Aaron saved themselves from the crowd by going to the entrance of the Tabernacle (V.6 ibid.). In any case the expression הקהל על expresses using force, or offering violence, and the same thing is indicated by the final verse in the description of the occurrence (V.35) על אשר עשו את העגל אשר עשה אהרן where clearly the people are shown to be the originators of the deed that Aaron did, and the people as ordering and Aaron as being forced to obey. We find exactly the same mode of expressing this in Gen. 39,22, ואת כל אשר עשים שם הוא היה עושה. Inasmuch as it says there “the governor of the prison committed into Joseph’s hands all the prisoners that were in the prison” and then adds “and whatever they did there, he was the doer of it”, it is clearly said that everything occurred under Joseph’s orders, they all had to obey him, he was the directing intelligence and the will, and all the others simply the tools, so that what they did was really his doing. So here too, what Aaron did was the work of the people.

עשה לנו אלהים אשר ילכו לפנינו כי זה משה האיש אשר העלנו וגוי. The purpose אשר ילכו לפנינו and the reason כי זה משה האיש show clearly that here it is not a case of idolatry in the usual sense, not a turning away from God. That which Aaron was to make was not to take the place of God, but of Moses. They presumed that Moses had had an accident and was dead, and so they wanted Aaron to give them a “Moses” whom they could not lose. But that they had the idea at all, that for them to have an assured future had to be linked with the presence of a “Moses”, and the erroneous idea that Man can make, may make, must make a “Moses” for himself, these are just the conceptions which are diametrically opposite to the fundamental Jewish idea of God, and of the relationship between God and Man, and Man and God, which had been made clear to them already immediately after the Revelation on Sinai with the warning words אתם ראיתם וגו׳, לא !תעשון אתי וגו (XX, 19) (see note there).

מזבח אדמה תעשה לי — לא תעשון אחי these two complementary sentences of that admonishing, enlightening address form the fundamental parting of the ways between the Jewish and the heathen non-Jewish view of the relationship of Man to God. That Man can make gods for himself, i.e., that he can put up an image, an article, a power, an institution, a man, as his highest ideal, and then think that this object which he has chosen to worship would become invested with godliness also by the All-Highest world-directing Godhead, and so become the bearer of his fate; and that Man is to make gods for himself, i.e., that, to ensure his future, he has to put up such objects of his own choosing and making, to represent the highest idea he can form of that All-Highest, world-directing Being of Whom he has a vague perception, thereby to show his homage to the All-Highest, to win His grace and to acknowledge his dependence on Him; and that altogether it is in matters of one’s lot and fortune, in the passive receiving phase of life, that Man has to occupy himself with his dependence on God, on trying to understand God, and what God is to him — these are the delusions which from time immemorial have dominated the non-Jewish world, and which have engendered both crude and spiritual fetishism.

That Man can make no gods for himself, need make no gods, may make no gods; that he has not, by representing the godly by a corporeal form, to bring God near to him, but, by making the whole of his own being spiritual and moral, and by subordinating all his activities to the dictates of God, to bring himself nearer to God in every phase of his life; that, altogether, it is not God, but himself that he has to influence, to achieve nearness to God and to be sure of God and of His protection and guidance; that above all, it is not so much what his lot is going to be, but what his deeds are going to be, that is to be his chief concern, and that his doings and goings being in harmony with the will of God, are the only things that could possibly have any influence on his fate and fortune; but, before everything, that God is in no wise whatsoever of a physical nature on which, by any procedure according to one’s own ideas, any restrictive influence could be exercised and made submissive to one’s own will, but that He ב״ה is the most absolute Personality, free of will and almighty in direction, Who has established His will as the absolute measure for all things, and the absolute norm for the free will of Man, to which Man must choose cheerfully to give up his own free will if he wishes his success and happiness to be arranged for by the Divine direction of the world; that this free-willed obedience is always and everywhere all that is necessary for Man’s happiness and well-being, and that nothing, absolutely nothing, can take its place: such is the Truth which Judaism teaches on which all the delusions of heathen subjectivity founder.

Any subjectivity in this direction is heathenism and idolatry. It is the delusion of being able to exercise, according to one’s own subjective desire, a controlling influence on the arrangement of the future, which is equivalent to saying, on the will of the Supreme Deity. It is placing the ego on par with, yea, in opposition to, the Divine will. That was expressed by the pertinent words of Samuel to Saul: “see, to obey is better than sacrifice, paying attention than the fat of rams; for disobedience is the sin of witchcraft, obstinacy and oracle-working are all self-willed procedures” (Sam. I. 15,23).

It was caught in this heathen delusion of subjectivism, that they spoke to Aaron: “Up, make us gods that shall go before us, for this man Moses, who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we know not what has become of him.”

They saw in Moses, not the instrument of God’s will, chosen and sent by the completely free initiative of God, but a human being who, by himself, had surpassed ordinary human nature and become godlike. They thought his influence decided the will of God, and that it was his presence that ensured for them the protection of the Godhead. For them, it was not God Who had brought them out of Egypt by means of Moses, but it was Moses who had been the means of making God accomplish that work of redemption. For them, it was not the Divine Torah which they had obtained through Moses, not the “Rules for Life”, the Mishpotim which they had obtained through Moses, all of which remained with them even when the temporary transmitter had departed, not in these did they see the safe bond between them and God, and the safe pledge of God’s protection, as well as the given way for each one of them personally to get into the proximity of, and approach to, God; but to them it was the demigod nature of the man Moses which was the necessary link for their connection with God, and his presence the pledge for the Divine protection. As then, they saw the initiative for the relation of Moses to God, in Moses, and not in God, they thought that even after the supposed departure of Moses, they would be able to exercise some similar compelling influence on the Godhead by means of some object which they would put in his place. And if this could be done, it must be done.

They had not yet completely and clearly absorbed the Jewish conception that Man has free access directly to God, without the necessity of any intermediary, and that the one and only necessary condition is acting in obedience to the behests of God, or their belief in this idea had become weakened by the anxious thoughts of wandering henceforth in the wilderness without a leader.

V. 2—4. That Aaron acted under the pressure of an overwhelming force of the people, as expressed in the words of the text in V.1 and V.35, has already been remarked above. That he did not act correctly but extremely the reverse, is expressed in Deut. 9,20 (להשמידו ובאהרן התאנף ה׳ מאד). He should have been ready to risk his life by opposing it by word and deed. But, and this is how his procedure has always been taken, he considered it was in the interests of the people themselves, to do as he did, and so that to be the right thing to do. He could have thought that over his dead body the people — after all one misses Hur, who had been left at his side to assist him (Ch. 24,14), from which one assumes that he had already paid for his opposition with his life — over his dead body the people would only have given themselves up to their folly with still greater unrestrained licence, and so he could believe that by keeping the matter in his hands he would be able to draw it out, and put it off, till Moses’s return, and, in any case keep the aberration within the closest limits possible. All the details of the story indicate this. He demands the jewellery of their wives and children which he expected they would not so easily or quickly allow themselves to be deprived of. Hence the expression פרק which everywhere expresses a separation only to be accomplished with considerable effort. Hence also V.4 ויצר אותו בחרט וגו׳, instead of casting it directly into a mould which of course, would be the quickest immediate way to do it, he melted all the gold into one mass — ואשליכהו באש V.24 — and then carved it, and so, slowly, produced the shape which would have been quickly obtained by casting. חֶרֶט related to חרת definitely means a writing graver, a style — חֶרֶט אנוש (Is. 8,1) which for this purpose would be the weakest instrument which would do the work in the slowest possible manner.

The question is worth considering why Aaron, who was given a completely free hand in the choice of the form, should have just chosen that of a calf. It has been suggested that it was meant to reproduce the Egyptian Apis. But the Apis of Egypt was no idol-figure but a real living bull, and only a bull of very definite form and markings (it had to have a white forehead mark upon a black hide symbolising the second life of Ptah. I.L.). How should Aaron have picked out just the form which in the land where the people had hitherto lived was worshipped with the highest idolatrous rites. The very fact that Aaron did choose this form is the best reason for assuming that here an Apis, or anything in the shape of an Apis, is not to be thought of. But we have already had the opportunity on several occasions to remark — and when we consider the offerings it becomes practically a certainty — that cattle, בקר, שור, פר, being serving assistants in carrying out the work of human beings, represent, in sacrificial symbolism, the using of one’s powers and strength to work in the service of a higher being. So that what Aaron was about, was, on the one hand to satisfy the demands of the people who were asking not for another god but for another “Moses”, and on the other hand by doing this to keep the error within the bounds of this semi-defection; and for this purpose no more suitable form could be found than that of cattle, which represented no directing force but a serving one. And in choosing a calf and not an ox, Aaron expressed even this force in its weakest aspect.

ויאמרו אלה וגו׳ אשר העלוך וגו׳. These words have to be carefully considered so that one can put oneself into the train of thought out of which they were spoken. As רמב״ן already remarked on this verse, nothing shows up the mental aspect of the heathen deluded way of thinking than the words אשר העלוך, in the past tense. אשר ילכו לפנינו of V.1 permits the assumption merely of crass fetishism. But the belief that the calf which had just been made by Aaron’s hands could have accomplished the Redemption which took place before its existence, assumes utter senselessness and stupidity. Of necessity we must take these words to go above and beyond the concrete actuality of this animal form which had just been produced, and to see in it a higher power which existed, or was believed to have existed, before its production, and the symbol of which, or the carrier-on of which, the animal form just made was to be. If we consider, that it was produced through the request to receive another “Moses”, then the animal-image just made would primarily be regarded as being in the same relation to the Godhead as that which, in their opinion, Moses stood.

We have already found that, to their idea, this was not that of a messenger sent by God of His own free will, but had to be that of some being who was essential to them for influencing God to look after them and protect them. So that this calf was a reborn “Moses”, a reborn “intermediary”, and inasmuch as they placed it in direct conjunction with God, by saying in the plural, “here, O Israel, you have again the gods that brought you up from Egypt”, they revealed their illusion that the efficacy of God Himself required the partnership of this “intermediary” (cf. the Trinity idea. I.L.). They were משתף שם שמים ודבר אחר as our sages call it (see note on XXII,19). It would have been the same sin had they greeted Moses himself with the welcoming cry אלה אלהיך ישראל אשר העלוך מארץ מצרים.

V. 5. וירא: He saw how they had already passed across the narrow bridge from the notion of a divine intermediary to that of a real god, and he wanted to put up a barrier in opposition to this, by an act of positive allegiance to God, the One Only One. At the same time he wanted to gain time by fixing the celebration of the Altar for the next day. — לפניו, before himself (in front of his tent probably, I.L.) not before the calf, the repetition of the name “Aaron” expresses that he did this act in opposition to the utterance of the people and in the full energy of his own personality.

V. 6. From V.8 it is evident that Aaron’s intention was frustrated, and the offering was brought not to God, but to the calf. As העם, the people, is brought in as a fresh nominative to וישב we see that the people as a whole did not take part in the offering. It was the leaders in word and deed, who went to this extreme, but the people did join in the feasting and merrymaking. This merrymaking is characteristically termed צַחַק. In צַחַק there is always the idea of a denial of the object which is met with צחוק, a feeling of superiority over something important, great, high, noble (see on Gen. 17,17). Offerings brought to the One God, and His Torah, in obedience to His Laws, make the bringer submit himself and give himself up to the dictates of His holy laws of morality. It involves homage to something which is higher than Man, something high, great, noble, which invites Man up to its own height. Heathen offerings brought to a god made by oneself, as they spring from the depth of subjectivism, inspire the individual who brings them to the most audacious subjectiveness. After all he does not vow by his offering to offer himself up. With his offering he conjures what he supposes to be the master of his fate into the service of whatever his subjective desire happens to be; with his offering he thinks he can overcome the anger or indifference of his god; with his offering he intends to enchain not his own subjective desires, but his god. We can understand how — quite apart from the demoralising idealisation of sensual Nature which lies at the base of the gods of the heathens and their sacrifices — the complete reversal of the Jewish idea of sacrifices, debauchery and licentiousness which are simply the unchaining of the individual, could arise directly in the train of heathen offerings. צחק here too, is an unchaining of sensuality, and, as the word implies, not debauchery out of desire or passion, but more of deliberate debauchery to demonstrate the freedom from moral chains, a mockery of the laws of morality by a canonization of immorality.

So, at the very time that the Divine Law of Morality was to have found a home and Sanctuary on earth in the midst of the Jewish people, they experienced the fact, for themselves and for all future time, that the slightest aberration from the idea of acknowledging God as the One and Only One, brings in its train the heathen cult in every form, inevitably denying His Law of Morality. And the one who was designed to be the first High Priest of the Jewish people experienced for himself and for all future time, that Jewish priests may not try to be “clever”, that God’s Truths are not his own, with which, and for which he may make concessions, of which he may give up a part to save the rest. The Divine Evidence is inscribed on granite. One can acknowledge it, one can deny it, but no priest can alter the tiniest bit of it.

V. 7. שחת .כי שחת referring to moral corruption always occurs in the Hiphil, השחית כל בשר את דרכו (Gen. 6,12), והשחיתו מאבתם (Judges 2,19). שחת in the Piel always means a real, actual spoiling ruin. We have already remarked (on Gen. 6,11) that שחת really means “to dig a grave for one who is engaged in auspicious progress.” So here too: “Go down”, your staying here has lost its purpose, your people have destroyed the relationship (to Me I.L.) which had begun, have made the carrying out of it impossible.

עמך אשר העלית is spoken in the sense of the erring people, and expresses the very root of their error, which had its origin in their not considering themselves purely God’s people, but also Moses’ people, and considering that Moses had been a necessary and indispensable agent for the Redemption.

V. 8. מסכה has an אתנח, so that the sentence עשו להם וגו׳ is separated from the following one, and forms one consecutive thought with the preceding one. They have already departed from the path prescribed by לא תעשון אתי by having made an עגל מסכה, even by thinking that with it they would only be able to create another Moses for themselves. But they have gone further still, by השתחויה and זביחה they have paid it the tribute given to a god, and by that have shown the degree of depravity they meant by their אלה אלהיך וגו׳.

V. 9. Where, as here, ויאמר is repeated without there being any intervening speech, a reply had been expected, and only when this is not forthcoming and because it is not forthcoming, the speech is resumed. Cf. Gen. 16,8—11. Here too, a pause shows that either an answer was expected or the immediate compliance with the order to go down. Moses’ consternation prevented the one or the other, and the further speech of God, by making clear to him what the immediate fate of the nation — without his intervention — would be, brought home to him that a crisis had arrived which demanded his intervention, and also indicated what the nature of his intervention should be. Hence, whereas above, in V.7 God’s speech was introduced by וידבר, the term used for absolute command and judgment, here it continues with ויאמר, the term used for explanatory speech appealing to the intellect and feelings. — קשה ערף assumes that a demand is opposed by adherence to ideas to which one had previously been accustomed. In this extremely harsh epithet lies at the same time an indication of a reason for mildness. It implies that the aberration of the people was not so much a new surprising transgression, but sprang from a point of view due to habits of thought of their life hitherto, which had not yet been completely overcome. The attitude of mind out of which the demand עשה לנו אלהים וגו׳ emanated, was not surprising in people who had been cradled in Egypt, and referring to this circumstance too, Moses begins his intercession in the following verses.

V. 10. הניחה לי; if this meant, “leave me, do not hinder me” it would be הניחה אותי. But הניח ל- means “to leave something to somebody”, hence it can also mean “to permit something to somebody”. Here the object is missing, it is either the people or the whole circumstances. Here the צווי is not absolute but hypothetical like הוכח לחכם ויאהבך (Prov. 9,8) תן לחכם ויחכם וגו׳ (ibid. 9) etc.

So the meaning is: if you were to leave it to me, i.e., if you do not intervene and intercede, if the people are left to themselves, if nothing comes forward out of the people, and in the people, to mitigate and help them over the apostasy, there is no alternative but that they will be destroyed. But My purpose and My promise that it will be realised through Isarel will not be lost; for you still remain and you will I make into a second Abraham, and the “great nation” that I promised him will I raise afresh from you, who are also Abraham’s seed.

V. 11. חלה .ויחל משה means to be ill, so חַלֵה is “to cause illness” from which חלה פנים is taken to mean, “to weaken anger”, i.e., to pacify, to appease. But חלה פנים occurs in passages where anger is not to be thought of, e.g., פניך יחלו עשירי עם (Ps. 45,13); רבים יחלו פני נדיב (Prov. 19,6); וחלו פניך רבים (Job 11,19). In all these places it clearly refers not to appeasing somebody’s anger but to the effort to gain the favour and goodwill of a superior. So the fundamental derivation of this word must be looked at from a different angle. In Gen. 22,2 and XLVIII,1 we have already pointed out that חלה with the ח-sound has the opposing hindering meaning to עלה with the צ-sound. The secondary meaning of עלה is, continued or ascending development (hence עלה the leaf); חלה means retarded, hindered development, illness, and תעלה, restored development, convalescence, recovery. Now if חלה is the contrast to עלה in its secondary meaning, it can very well be so also to its primary meaning, upward direction, and חלה would primarily mean to interrupt an upward movement and direct it downwards. חלה would then be, the effort to bring something directed upwards to be directed downwards. חלה פנים would accordingly be literally, to bring a face, which, in accordance with its nature, its position or the present circumstances, would only be looking upwards, to look downwards to something lower. But this is nothing else but to endeavour to get a superior being to condescend to good-will to a lower, or to endeavour to get an angry being to forgivingly descend again to a lower. We have used the usual translation for ויחל “then Moses supplicated before God, his God” as this comes near to this idea. A better and more correct translation would be: “Then Moses endeavoured to gain the condescending good-will of God, his God”, and this would be fundamentally connected with his request contained in Ch. 33,12 and 13.

אלהיו: Who had placed him in quite special relationship to Him, and had appointed him to be the messenger of His will (hence his God). It was from the standing of this appointment and from the purpose which lay at the root of this appointment that Moses spoke all the following.

מלרע :למה and רפה and in the next verse (12) מלעיל and דגוש. We imagine, this is not without meaning. In the first case the accent and stress is on מה, the unknown, sought-for object, and -ל has its ordinary meaning, i.e., to, so that the whole word means “to what”, i.e., “what purpose?” The reason for it may be quite apparent but the object to be achieved by it can not be grasped. In the second case the stress is on the -ל, on the whole pertinence of the matter. To the questioner the matter seems quite without relevance to anything, to be without reason. It is the question for the reason: Why? The reason for anger here was quite clear. They had been warned: זבח לאלהים יחרם בלתי לה׳ לבדו (XXII,19) and לא תעשה לך פסל וגו׳, לא תשתחוה וגו׳, כי אנכי ה׳ אלקיך וגו׳ (XX,4 and 5), and anyway, to question the justification for God’s anger would be blasphemy. But Moses asks to be shown what purpose is to be achieved by it, and stresses the fact that this attitude would perforce work against that which, as he goes on to say, must be supposed to have been God’s purpose in choosing this people. In V.12 (see note thereon) the result is quite clear, but the reason is sought for allowing such a result to occur, which could be the very reverse of the original purpose. Quite in the same way above Ch. 5,22 למָה הרעתהִ לעם הזה למָה זה שלחתני, to what purpose hast Thou brought this fresh trouble to this people, this trouble serves no purpose which can help Thine intention of saving them, and as my inability to be of use for Thy mission is immediately apparent by this result, why didst Thou entrust just me with this mission, who already beforehand had felt my incompetence for it? And also Numbers 11,11: לָמה הרעת לעבדך לָמה לא מצאתי חן בעיניך לשום וגו׳ To what purpose hast Thou laid upon me this troublesome burden, does not the ever recurring sinning of the people prove the complete failure of my labours, the incompetence I felt from beforehand, the utter purposelessness of sending me, and why hast Thou refused me the special grace I asked for to exempt me from a task so far beyond my powers. In order to fully establish this hypothesis it would be necessary to make sure that it would apply in every case where it occurs in the Scriptures.

בעמך אשר הוצאת וגו׳. The people that Thou hast taken from out of the false views of the nations, and established as a nation, and of whom Thou hast said to me — mortal that I am, in the language of human beings — that Thou hast now seen that they are stiff-necked, this people is Thy people. It was Thou — not short-sighted I, but Thou — the All knowing, Thou, Who plucked them forth from the mass of nations expressly with the calling to be Thy people. They were known to Thee with all their faults also with their most prominent one, their stiff-neckedness when Thou didst lead them out of Egypt with that great revelation of Thy powers of miracle, and with the application of Thy mighty strength overpowering all human power. It did not happen in accordance with the natural course of events. Nature and historical precedence were all against their very existence. Thou overcameth both with force and strength for the very purpose of establishing this people, in spite of their stiff-neckedness as Thy people, Thou couldst not possibly have expected that they would show themselves immediately in unbroken faithfulness, obedient to Thy behests. Thou couldst not possibly have had the intention to destroy them at the first evidence of their unyielding disposition. Otherwise Thou wouldst have chosen a more tractable race of men for the revelation of Thy power and strength over the forces of Nature and men. As Thou didst choose just this most obstinate race for Thy purposes, Thou must surely have had in mind some other way than immediate destruction at the first disobedience. Perhaps it was just as much the idea of the wondrous overcoming of the obstinacy of the most obstinate of human races, which in view of Man’s free will could only be accomplished in the course of time, as the utter lack of the power of resistance to the overpowering dominion of their cruel masters, which led Thee to pick out just them for the revelation of Thy power and strength against all the forces of Nature and men. So to what purpose wilt Thou, then, since it must certainly be against Thine original intention, now immediately destroy, in Thy certainly justifiable anger “Thy people, that Thou didst lead out of Egypt with such great power and such tremendous force”? This can not be Thine intention.

V. 12. למה יאמרו מצרים. Moreover, it was not only educating this people to be Thy people, the enlightenment and instruction of the other nations was essentially one of the objects of this whole miraculous redemption. According to Thine own words, Pharaoh and Egypt were to learn כי אני ה׳, כי לה׳ הארץ, כי אני ה׳ בקרב הארץ that there is a personal, absolutely free God, Who, as Lord and Master, directs the world with Almighty power in justice and love. Who recognises even the most despised and mishandled slave as His child, yea, His firstborn child, and Who sends to the mighty tyrant of His child the message: “Set thy slaves free that they may serve Me, as My children, as My people.” Why, then, for what reason, shouldst Thou, now, wish to reverse the intended effect of Thy redemption to the very opposite by the destruction of those whom Thou hadst redeemed? Instead of teaching them to know better; it would only strengthen the Egyptians in their fallacy of denying the directing power of a just and loving merciful God, and worshipping force and tyranny. In the ignominious fall of their previous slaves, they will only see an extenuating confirmation of their own treatment of a human race, which evidently “was worth no better fate”. In the exodus they would see, not the liberating work of an Almighty God, acting in justice and love, but the malicious work of a Providence enticing the people to their ruin. For what reason canst Thou now desire such a reversing frustration of Thine original purpose?

In explaining this verse we have allowed ourselves to be guided by the assumption that there is an understandable difference between [[illegible]] and [[illegible]]. The רד״ק in שער המלים makes the accent, and the presence or absence of the Dagesh simply grammatically dependent on the initial sound of the succeeding word. Before the letters א׳ ה׳ ע׳ it is מלרע and רפה. The only snag however is that the large number of exceptions which he quotes makes the rule itself seem doubtful.
רעה :ברעה as in להעביר את רעת המן (Esther 8,3) the intended evil.
והנחם, see note on Gen. 6,6.

V. 13. This reference to the Patriarchs, and reminder of the assuring oath given to them, may not be taken to mean that the intended destruction of the people would be in opposition to this promise. For the indication given at the same time of the intention to build up a great nation from the descendants of Moses would be equally a fulfilment of the promise. The descendants of Moses are also descendants of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. But this reminder seems to be in intimate connection with the whole attitude in which Moses had hitherto been trying to have the incident taken, and on which he was basing his prayer, so that this reminder follows as the final support for his prayer. First, by mentioning Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, remembrance is asked for the noble germ from which this now “hard-necked” people sprung. This original germ must have been so potent with nobility that Abraham was followed by an equally noble Isaac, and Isaac by an equally noble Jacob, and this would surely not have disappeared without leaving a trace in the nation which descended from them. In the course of time this germ would surely work itself through and produce men of similar character to their origin. Further, by bringing the oath that God swore to them into remembrance the thought is brought into prominence that the certainty of this trait of worthiness persisting or at least the capacity for becoming worthy, must have been in mind when the promise was given, otherwise the promise could not have been ensured by an oath that the descendants would have an eternal claim to the land.

What would be if they all become degenerate and not even one Moses was to be found amongst them? This oath itself must assume that the descendants of Abraham can never in their totality become so degenerate that they could not be brought back to a better state by the educational guidance of God. On this, on the possibility of their being educated up to something better which must have been aassumed when Israel was chosen, Moses bases his appeal to ward off the impending disaster.

V. 14. וינחם ה׳. See note on Gen. 6,6. The whole object of God’s second speech (V.9 and 10) was obviously only to make Moses conscious of the grave necessity for decisions being made; and to make him find out for himself the possible motives of the further decisions of God, as well as what action the situation demanded of himself. And this object was achieved. In the fact Moses saw a means of salvation from the threatened destruction of the contemporary nation, in an appeal on the grounds that they could be won over to a better future, the guidance to such a better future had already found somebody suitable to undertake it, and that was Moses himself; and with this, the otherwise inevitable destruction of the nation was avoided. All Moses’ reflections had the one tendency, to make it perfectly clear to himself that, from the beginning, God must have had in mind some way of dealing with such a situation other than immediate annihilation; and, that He would adopt that alternative was the object of his prayer. But by this, Moses had implicitly taken upon himself to do his part in taking up the cudgels for the Divine Creed, which had been betrayed, as we can see from what followed: and it is quite in keeping with Moses’ modest character, to undertake to do this with all his energy without making a lot of talk beforehand of what he intended to do. Of Phineas too, God says later on in Numbers 25,11, השיב את חמתי מעל בני ישראל בקנאו את קנאתי בתוכם ולא בליתי את בני ישראל בקנאתי. If God’s Law finds no representative on earth amongst men, then He has to intervene with His dread punishment to rescue the Law itself. One Phineas in the nation, by rescuing the Law, at the same time rescues the nation. So here too, does Moses. By its becoming apparent that Moses realised full well what would have to be done in the nation to save the Divine Creed, God would be given cause not to allow the destruction which otherwise He had ordained to happen.

V. 15—16. After the developments described in the preceding verses Moses went down with the mission he had himself recognised, but which had been sanctified, nay induced, by God, to take such steps against the treachery which had been practised against the Divine Creed which would serve to save the future for the nation. He went down to fight for a home for the Torah to be still established in the midst of the nation, hence שני לחת העדת בידו. He went down, Phineas-like, as מקנא לה׳ and what he subsequently did, was done, not following special instructions from God, but according to his own feelings as to what was required by God.

כתבים משני עבריהם וגו׳: exactly what this means regarding the writing on the Tablets is not quite certain. In any case it seems that by the two phrases כתבים משני עבריהם and מזה ומזה הם כתבים two definite things are told us. Firstly that the writing went right through both sides of the stone and was not engraved merely to a certain depth; and secondly that in spite of this, the words appeared correctly written from both sides, and that, for instance נבוב did not appear on the reverse side, as it normally would, as בובנ with the words running backwards. The writing penetrated right through and nevertheless could be read from both sides. If it merely wanted to tell us that the Tablets were written on both sides, one of the phrases would have been quite sufficient and the other completely superfluous. This also makes us believe that what רב חסדא says in the Gemora (Sabbath 104a) כתב שבלוחות נקרא מבפנים ונקרא מבחוץ כגון נבוב בובנ רהב בהר סרו ורס only wants to explain the one phrase כתובים משני עבריהם, and wants to make us understand that the letter did go right through the stone, and so give the reason for what he goes on to say, that מם וסמך שבלוחות בנס היו עומדין for the inside of a ם or a ס if bored right through the stone could only stay in place by a miracle, in the ordinary course of Nature it would inevitably fall out. But not that the Tablets would actually seem to us on the reverse side in so-called “mirror-writing”. For this would be against what the verse goes on to say viz: מזה ומזה דם כתובים, they presented on both sides writing in proper legible letters both in formation and order. We imagine that this too was the reason why ר׳ חסדא chose those words to illustrate his meaning which did not occur in the Ten Commandments; for he could not say that אנכי appeared otherwise than אנכי on both sides of the Tablets. נבוב בובנ was only used to explain what כתובים משני עבריהם would mean without the further addition of מזה ומזה הם כתובים.

We are further informed that not only the writing, but the actual Tablets themselves were a direct work of God’s Hands. They were intended to be עדות, evidence of the direct Godly origin of the Torah.

Finally, this nature of the writing is summarised for us in the words: חרות על הלחת. The root חרת does not occur again. One would first of all associate it with the phonetically related חרט, which, not actually as a verb, but as a noun חֶרֶט means an instrument for engraving writing — a graver. Now even if one accepts the meaning of חרת as “engraving” here, it still can not mean ordinary engraved writing. After we have already been told that they were כתובים משני עבריהם מזה ומזה הם כתובים that the writing penetrated right through the stone, חרות and especially חרות על הלחות can not mean engraved on the Tablets, which would indicate merely an engraving on the outer surfaces. But it seems much more likely that the relation of חרת to חרט is similar to that of מות to מוט and to indicate the complete boring through of the stone. Then חרות על הלחות would express the special miraculous nature of the writing. It was חרות bored right through, and still על הלחות and still it appeared engraved on whichever side of the Tablet it was looked at. Still it is not imposible that חרות is not derived from חרט at all but comes from חור with ת servile, as זלות ,פרות. Now חור means white, free and open, from which we get the meaning of opening and hole. The basic meaning seems to be “unhindered”. Hence: free, open, and the unhindered i.e., unbroken, rays of light: white. So that חרות could also mean “opening” in the sense of the stone being bored clean through, or actually “freedom”, and in this sense חרות על הלחות would mean “in free mastery over the Tablets” and thereby express that ’ם וס׳ שבלוחות בנס היו עומדים. The Tablets did not bear the writing but the writing bore and held the Tablets. Then the sentence in Aboth 6,2 אל תקריחָרוּת אלא חֵרוּת, that the Torah makes “free”, would be a literal fact, brought home to one’s mind by a glance at the writing of the Tablets. Just as the writing of the Divine Evidence was not only independent of the material but raises the material serving it to its own level of freedom above the ordinary laws of Nature which govern matter, in the same way human beings, who take upon themselves the spirit of this writing and make themselves the representatives of this spirit, are raised, borne and held by this very spirit itself, above the blind force of “you must”, the lack of free will which clings to all matter, i.e., they become “free”.

As these special characteristics of the making of the Tablets and of the writing are told just here, and not as might have been expected, above in Ch. 31,18, they must be in close connection with what was happening at this time.

If a Law is to be promulgated and the tablet on which it is brought is written on one side only, the one who is to publish it is placed in a definitely dictatorial position towards the massed people to whom he proclaims it. He alone has the written Law in front of him, and the masses must accept from him what he reads out to them. He is the definitely indispensable intermediary between the people and the Law. But if the same Law, and especially here where it came to the people in the same directness from God as it had come to Moses, is visible on both sides, if the Law presents itself all the time equally to Moses and the people, then the Law comes down directly to the nation and to every member of the nation, and Moses disappears entirely from this transmission, becomes simply one of the people, the people can read the Law to Moses as well as he can read it to them. So that even if “this man Moses” disappears, the people do not require a Moses; the Torah presents itself at all time directly from God to every individual.

Looked at from this point of view, one can understand the various opinions expressed in Shekalim 6,1, according to one of which all the ten Commandments were written on each of the two Tablets, to another, twice ten, or to another opinion, even four times ten, on the front, back and each side. So that there were from the beginning two copies of the Law, and each Tablet written on all sides. This would be to demonstrate the spreading of the Torah on all sides amongst the people, and from the very inception, by the Evidence of the Torah itself, to do away with the idea of there being any exclusive or excluding position of a Moses to the Torah.

V. 17. From Ch. XXIV, V.13 and 14, it is evident that Moses and Joshua had gone away from the people, and Aaron and the elders were to await their return. But from V.15 it is clear that Moses went up to the summit of the Mount by himself. From this we gather that Joshua remained on the Mount away from both Moses and the people, so that it was only now, when he came down from the summit that Moses met Joshua.

רוע ,ברֵעה, primarily meaning “to break”, hence רע, morally broken, evil, is also used to express voices which reach the ear only in repeated intermission and thereby excite and affect the hearer strongly, hence תרועה, a loud alarm and the consequent inner shock and emotion, and הריע, to excite such emotion by producing such a sound. But רֵצַ as a noun means noise, as למה תריעי רֵצַ, “Why dost thou wail so loud?” (Micha 4,9). But here it says רֵעה instead of רֵעו to designate the people in the moral weakness of their wantonness.

V. 18. קול ענות גבורה and חלושה, a sound which proclaims victory or defeat, which is brought about by conquering or by being defeated. קול ענות, a sound of humiliation, impotence, a sound that renders us powerless. Not that which brings about such a sound, but the sound itself and what it implies — the same as what was indicated in the ה of רֵעה, the moral wantonness, is what strikes us down. It could also be ענות, rape and violation in a sexual sense, as in נשים בציון ענו (Lament. V.11). There is an old tradition that the women took no part in the apostasy. Then this would say that the women were dragged forcibly into this bacchanalia and were made to pay for their opposition.

V. 19. So long as pagan ideas in any form have their origin merely in mental error and remain restricted to the mind and thoughts, there is always hope that they can be overcome by teaching the truth, and a return to better and truer conception of things may easily be accomplished. But when heathen erroneous ideas pass over from theoretical errors to the sphere of the practical poisoning of morals, and unleashed moral excesses become sanctified acts at the Altar of Error, then sensuality clings to the source which offers it such welcome food, and just as it is easy to teach people right who have merely been led astray in theories, so is it hard to improve people whose morals have been corrupted, and to teach them what is right. As long as Moses only knew of the calf and its worship he hoped that he would still be able to make a pure home amongst the people for the Torah, and he took the Testimony of the Torah down with him. But when he saw the calf and the dances around it, then he realised how the pagan erroneous theories had borne their usual fruit, the shaking off the restraining yoke of morality, and unchaining sensuality, then he saw that a nation would first have to be entirely re-established for this Torah, and without any hesitation, with joined hands — יָדָו the plural in the singular — he cast the Tablets into pieces and thereby expressed in no uncertain manner, the unworthiness, the unfitness of the nation, as it then was, for this Torah. תחת ההר is below, at the bottom of the Mount, when he had seen the demoralizing effect of the worship of the calf.

V. 20. His first action was to vividly show up to the people their supposed god in its complete nothingness. He not only destroyed the idol, but every individual of the people had, with his own bodily person, to help in completely exterminating his god, without leaving a trace of it. The people had to drink up their god. That in which they had placed their trust to ensure their material bodily future, had to find the quick end to its short existence, in their very bodies. That in which their bodily sensual purity had already begun to find its grave, must find its grave in their very bodies. With such suggestive pithiness does a Moses teach and educate. But the fact that no hand was raised to save their god from the hands of the man Moses, that no mouth refused to drink the dust of its god, was the first sign of repentance, and also perhaps showed how a more energetic opposition in the first place might have succeeded in holding the people back from going astray.
על פני המים; in Deut. 9,21, אל הנחל הירד מן ההר i.e., in a stream that flowed down the mountain.

V. 21. The first and most urgent thing to be done was to prove the futility of the object of their worship by its concrete destruction. That prepared the way for coming back again to a more sane state of mind. Only then did Moses turn to Aaron. The lack of all opposition to his treatment of the calf — their god — showed what energetic action could accomplish, so that now the question to Aaron was all the more forcible: “What force had the people used against you that you had to allow them to persist in their error?” הבאת can not mean “you brought the sin on them”, that would indicate some positive action on Aaron’s part at the committing of the sin, and of that, of course, Moses could not yet have known anything. The הפעיל here, can, accordingly only have the meaning of allowing to occur, as ולא תותירו ממנו (XII,10) or ולא תורד שיבתו וגו׳ (Kings I. 2,6).

V. 22—24. How great Aaron shows himself in this reply! Not a word to justify himself, does not mention the circumstances of which we know, which would serve to modify his guilt. Nothing of the overwhelming threatening mob — ויקהל העם על — nothing of his attempt to use the vanity of the women as a means of delay — nothing of his laborious work at engraving and modelling to postpone the completion of the work as long as possible — nothing of all this. He will not adduce any reason for the mitigation of his own guilt which would increase the guilt of the people. He takes practically the whole guilt on his own shoulders, accuses himself of the most listless weakness. “You know what the people are like when they are in a bad mood,” is his whole excuse, “You know how energetic and impetuous they are when they are under the influence of some passion. That is why I did not try to oppose them, but acceded at once to their request (compare the ויקהל העם על אהרן ויאמרו אליו קום עשה לנו וגוי of the actual happening, with Aaron’s mild report, !ויאמרו לי עשה לנו וגוי). I threw their gold into the fire (to melt it, but he says nothing of his further long drawn-out work), and in this way, through my yielding weakness ויצא העגל הזה this calf originated”.

V. 25. From this report, Moses recognised that the voice of truth and duty had completely disappeared from the nation. It had become פרוע (related to ברח, פרח, פרא etc.) free, unchained, completely uncontrolled by lawfulness or conscience, but that it had only reached this state of lack of control, because Aaron had failed to bring into play this voice of truth and duty with virile energy amongst them. This voice, which should have been the controlling and restraining rein on their will and deed had not been adopted by Aaron who had left the people completely to themselves. But this “themselves” of the nation is described as being only morally weak, פרעה, not פרעו (weakness and yielding to passion is expressed here in feminine gender I.L.). For, while on the side of the Law, no influence at all had been brought to bear, on the other side a very strong factor was active, to which the people, left to themselves, yielded without resistance, and this factor was קמים .קמיהם always refers to those who revolt against those in power and rise to destroy them. So, against the choice of David for King (Ps. 18,40 and 49), against the power and might of Israel (Deut. 28,7), against the influence of the prophecy of Jeremiah (Lament. 3,62), against God (Ex. 15,7; Ps. 74,23; Jeremiah 51,1, where Babylon is called לב קמי, “the heart of those who revolt against Me”) Now, at this time Israel had hardly reached a position of power, that their enemies could be described as קמים. We therefore take קמיהם to mean קמים אשר בתוכם i.e., those who were to be found in their midst who were against God and His Law. There was a minority amongst them, perhaps all the riff-raff, the ערב רב, the camp-followers, the אספסוף אשר בקרבו (Numbers 11,4), who had gone out of Egypt with them, who bore the yoke of the Torah very heavily and only with reluctance, who took every demand of the Torah as encroachment on their personal liberty, who preferred the pagan licence and freedom from restraint, who were always קמים, rising against God and His Law, always ready to stand up against God and His Law. As long as the spirit of the Torah had its representative, and the spirit of lawfulness joined the majority of the people to the Torah, these people did not dare to come to the fore, and at least their influence was paralysed by the respect for the Torah which the representatives of the Law nursed amongst the people. But when Moses was absent, Aaron, more than simply silent, and the deserted people caught by the circumstances in the toils of a misconception that would lead them far away from God and His Torah, then it was easy for these קמים, these enemies of the power of the Torah to draw the unsupported people in their moral weakness (ברעה I.L.) over to their way of thinking; and under these קמים Aaron allowed the people to become שמצה .לשמצה is usually taken to mean a blot, a disgrace. The root שמץ occurs here, and only twice elsewhere, in Job 4,12 and XXVI, 14: ותקח אזני שמץ מנהו; and ומה שמץ דבר נשמע בו. But in both these places nothing is further from the meaning than the idea of abuse or denunciation. Quite clearly in both cases שמץ expresses just a slight trace of what is really there. In the first sentence Eliphaz is describing a revelation which came to him in a vision of the night. “Something, a word, was secretly brought to me, and mine ear retained a trace (שמץ) thereof”. The second sentence concludes a beautiful description of the greatness of God in nature with the words: “See, these are, after all, but a part of His ways, שמץ דבר, and what a tiny part of the whole is thereby brought to our understanding? The thunder of His Allmight, who can dare to understand that?” Even in Talmudic and Mishnaic language, where the word is frequently used in conjunction with שמץ פסול ;פסול, the idea of defect defect is not sure but that there is only a presumption for it, and this weakening of the certainty of the existence of the פסול lies in the word שמץ. So in Avoda Zara 30b, תמרא משום שמצא, שיכרא משום שמצא דשמצא, where שמצא דשמצא is in the sense of גזרה לגזרה. In חמרא itself there is only a supposition that there may be יין נסך and in שיכרא only the supposition that it might lead to חמרא. The context in every case indicates that the meaning of the root שמץ is something half-way between existing and not existing i.e., an irresolute wavering uncertainty of being. A study of the phonetic relation to other roots brings us to exactly the same basic idea of complete lack of independent existence. Accordingly we do not think we are mistaken in taking שמצה בקמיהם to mean the complete lack of independence, the lack of any determined self-will, completely under the influence of the enemies of the Torah in their midst. The majority had become the moral minority.

V. 26. The immediate necessity, accordingly, was to establish again out of the midst of the people respect for the Law, and representatives of the Law who would stand up for it against the קמים, the minority who were enemies of the Law; who would be ready to see that the Torah ruled and to oppose that minority. That is what the Levites became.

V. 27. כה אמר ה׳ וגו׳: they had been warned: זובח לאלהים יתרם (XXII, 19). They had all been doomed to destruction, which by direct or indirect participation they had incurred (V.10) and God Himself had incited and approved the intervention of Moses to save the whole nation (see 10—19).

V. 29. After they had completed the deed for the salvation of the Torah, Moses said to the Levites: “Remain what you have started to be this day! Establish yourselves as ‘enthusiasts’ and representatives of the Divine Torah”. No special appointment, no special assignment is required for that. When the Torah is treated with scorn, every single individual is called upon as representative and saviour of the Torah. The duty and responsibility which rests on each individual invests him with this commission, and the less office and appointment stamps his act with officialism, the more effective and significant is his act of salvation, and the deeper it impresses everybody with the lesson of what spirit should be alive in all of them.

כי איש בבנו ובאחיו. But only he can stand up for the Torah against the community, who does so against his nearest and dearest too. Only that which he refuses to overlook in his own children and relatives, can he insist on in others. The כי איש וגו׳ is in parenthesis: because of that, because you did not spare your own, you need have no scruples in coming forward publicly. The ולתת וגו׳ is the continuation of מלאו etc. The assumption of power you can take on yourselves (מלאו ידכם I.L.), appointment you need not wait for from God, but the ברכה the support and the happiness-bringing results of your having taken up the cudgels for God on your own initiative, that you can expect from Him.

V. 30. By the execution of the guilty — (according to Yoma 66b the 3,000 men killed were those who had committed the sin בעדים והתראה, after formal warning, or at least only those who had actually זבח וקטר, actually sacrificed to the golden calf, but not those who had merely participated in the general worship of it) — the authority of the Law was again established and thereby the continuation of the nation as a nation was rescued. But then it was up to Moses to attempt to win back its continuance, or rather its re-establishment as God’s nation i.e., as the bearer of His Law, and as a memorial of His domination of this world. So he said to the people: “Although the most guilty were executed yesterday, the consequences of your great sin still rest on you, and you all have a share in this sin, all who participated to a greater or lesser degree in it, all who approved of it, or even who only silently and passively allowed it”. אולי אכפרה בעד חטאתכם. We have already repeatedly drawn attention to the idea of כפרה being:- obtaining protection from the consequences or results of sin, and also shown that the objects of the כפרה can be either the person or the sin itself. כפר, literally to cover, protects the person against the effects of the sin, or “covers” the sin, so that it has no effect on the person. Quite in the same way, it is sometimes construed with בעד referring to the person: וכפר בעדו ובעד ביתו (Levit. 16,6) or as here referring to the sin. The optative אכפרה combined with the אולי must mean: perhaps I can achieve כפרה, as I long to do.

V. 32. ועתה אם תשא חטאתם — the conclusion is missing, but that perhaps is indicated in ועתה .ועתה directs consideration to the time which is now to be expected. This “now”, everything which could occur henceforth, the whole future from “now”, Moses can only think of, it only exists for Moses if God will grant forgiveness to the people. Without this pardon, for him there is no more future, his existence is at an end, there is no further “now”, no עתה! This would also explain the converse: ואם אין מחני נא מספרך אשר כתבת. This ספרד can not refer to the ספר of the תורה, even if one refers the past tense to that part which had been already written down as ספר הברית (Ch. 24,7). For then the same expression which occurs in the following verse מי אשר חטא לי אמחנו מספרי would have no meaning, for in any case their names have no special mention anywhere at all in the whole תורה.
