That they only wish to find their homes where God indicates and are ready to give them up and move on to where His Mouth calls them. How they had to learn and act in accordance with this devoted following God, is just what is shown in the following.

וביום הקים. As soon as the Sanctuary was erected the cloud, by which God announced His guiding Presence in the people (Ex. 13,21, 22) descended upon it; and just thereby testified that the משכן was the place of God about which the people were to encamp as their common centrepoint. — לאהל העדות. Ch. 17,21, 22 designates אהל העדות as being the place of the Holy of Holies in which the ארון העדות stood. In Gen. 49,13. לחוף ימים ישכון the ל׳ designates the direction of a position — towards — so here too לאהל העדות could designate the direction of the כסה הענן. The cloud covered the tent of the place of the Evidence, it rested with its base on the אהל העדות, the most Western part of the structure, and announced thereby that it is just the presence of the תורה which is the condition for the Presence of God in the nation.

V. 16—23. But the cloud was the Shepherd’s crook by means of which God, the רועה ישראל, announced His Will to the People He was leading, where and when they were to encamp, where and when to break camp. And, as is here described, the will and the intention of this direction was absolutely unpredictable. Sometimes a long rest, sometimes just a few days. Sometimes only a night or a day and a night, or two days, a day, a year, and, as רמב״ן remarks, as there was nothing to indicate the duration of the stay, the people must often have received the sign to stop, have made all the arrangements to encamp and then perhaps just after a few hours to pack up again, break camp and follow the cloud onwards again. Such was the school of the wandering through the wilderness, which was to teach us for all time to follow God devoutly and trustfully, to have complete confidence in Him, however little His Guidance may seem comprehensible to us. Though He tells us, now to leave the place where we have only just made ourselves comfortable, then to stay patiently in the most cheerless conditions, still always to do what He directs, always to feel cheerful under the crook of God’s guidance, and always to be ready to defer the plan of our life to God, and to follow His Guidance even on most incomprehensible paths with enduring patience and with never failing courage.

But if we look more closely at the report given in V.17-22 of the testing exercises with which God wished to educate His People for all time, it is not so much the strain of lengthy wanderings as the patient endurance of the lengthy stops which seem to be stressed as the real task of the tests. Nothing is mentioned of the wanderings and their duration, but very definitely and repeatedly we are told of standing fast in long rests. Already in V.17, it says ואחרי כן יסעו וגו׳, that they only broke camp after, and not before, the cloud rose up, and in V.18, after it had already said: על פי ה׳ יסעו ועל פי ה׳ יחנו it repeats again כל ימי אשר ישכן הענן וגו׳ יחנו. Finally in V.19, the fact that לא יסעו that they did not break camp even when the cloud rested on the Sanctuary for a long time, is recorded as שמירת משמרת ה׳ as a special observance of God’s command, as a special proof of obedience. Clearly then their exercising enduring patience is specially stressed. This is the more understandable when one thinks of the inhospitality of the desert, and remembers that the people knew quite well that the wilderness was not the end of their wanderings, but that their goal lay beyond, and that every tarrying anywhere in the wilderness only held them back from the Promised Land. These were exercises in that virtue of quiet and cheerful devoted and confident enduring patience which the “People of God’s guidance” require more than any other in their Galut-wanderings through the “wilderness of the nations”, as the Prophet calls it, during so many centuries of the future, and which the word of the Prophet so significantly renders as, אם יתמהמה חכה לו (Habak. 2,3).

V. 23. על פי ה׳ ביד משה. Their encamping and their journeying forth took place according to the orders of God, as shown by the position of the cloud, but through Moses’s mediation. Moses had each time to effect the carrying out of the demand of God which had been made to the people by the cloud, as is immediately described in detail in the following chapter.

V. 2. חצוצרות. The root is obviously חצר with the second radical letter doubled instead of a dageth to strengthen it: חצורה. Thus II. Chron. 5,13. מחצצרים for מחצרים. As can be seen from our notes on Gen. 2,18 and Ex. 27,9. חצר is an accessory surrounding to a central principal phase, a court-yard in the real meaning of the word. חצר as a verb, would be: to make a “court” round about oneself. Transposed to bugle-sounds חצר would be, to let a signal be sounded, and חצוצרות the instrument for producing such sounds, the bugle. For every signal calls those to whom it is directed, either actually in person, or as a direction for their attention, to the one from whom the signal emanates. Accordingly it makes this latter into the centre point of a circle who are attached to him. It is a “court-forming” sign and its instrument is שתי חצוצרות, שיחו שוות .חצוצרות במראה בקומה ובנוי (ספרי) as always in the Torah when only two objects are prescribed and the number two is given as well as the plural (which by itself would designate the lowest plural number, as מיעוט רבים שנים I.L.) the complete similarity of the two objects is demanded. (See Levit. 16,5). V.4 orders that blowing with one trumpet gives the signal for calling the representatives of the nation, the heads of the thousands, together as a national unit, but with two, the whole nation with all its individuals So there were two reasons for the complete similarity of the two instruments, viz., to show the heads and the people in completely equal worth and to show the numbers of the nation in complete equality of all its members. — כסף is the noble חצר-metal (See Ex. 27,19). — מקשה, hammered out of one piece, representing the unity and quality of the caller and the called. Nevertheless מקשה is not מעכב (not absolutely essential. I.L.) at the חצוצרות (Menachoth 28a) — עשה לך ויהיו לך: כל הכלים שעשה משה כשרים לו וכשרים לדורות חצוצרות כשרים לו ופסולים לדורות. All the things which were made through Moses could be used also after his death except the חצוצרות hence the repeated לך. Probably the difference between Moses and all those that came after him was kept in the minds of those that followed him just by this. The ולא קם נביא עוד בישראל כמשה was most strikingly expressed thereby. The trumpets which had called leaders and people to Moses were not allowed to be set to the mouth of anybody else after his death. — מסע ,ולמסע את וגו׳ here is a verb, to cause to break camp, hence את המחנות. Thus the שתהא מזמן העדה ומסיע את המחנות :ספרי.

V. 3—7. ותקעו וגו׳. From V.7 it is evident that תקע designates a different note to that of הריע, and if then in V.5 it says ותקעתם תרועה and not והרעותם analogous to the verb תריעו of V.7, it can mean nothing else but a combination of the two notes — (“ye shall tekiah a teruah” I.L.) that you shall introduce a תרועה by a תקיעה, and according to that the תרועה יתקעו of V.6, would then prescribe the תרועה to be finished by a תקיעה. And in fact that is exactly what the Halacha orders (Rosh Hashana 34a). תקע originally means to ram or drive something in, a nail into the wall, a stake or peg into the ground, or the hand of one who makes a promise into the hand of the one who receives the promise. This latter is symbolically with all your energy devoting your hand, the means by which you do things, or rather, as it is usually called תקע כף and not יד, the means that you possess, to the use of the other person. The hand of the one who promises thereby enters the service of the other. Transferred to the sphere of music it designates the forceful and prolonged blowing of a column of air into a wind instrument or the strong prolonged note produced thereby penetrating the ear. תקיעה therefore, is פשוטה the plain continuous unbroken note of a wind instrument. — רוע and רעע to break, תרועם בשבט ברזל (Ps. 2,9) in music designates the broken, trembling note, consisting of several small short blasts, the תרועה. In V.2 the immediate purpose of the חצוצרות is given as being מקרא העדה and מסע המחנות for signalling the nation to assemble or the camp to break up. In verses 3, 4 and 7, תקיעה the plain unbroken calling note is given as the signal for assembly and in 5 and 6 תרועה, the broken agitated alarm note as the signal for breaking camp. Moreover, ותקעתם תרועה introduced by a תקיעה and תרועה יתקעו followed by one. To call the nation together as a unit, i.e. by its representatives, “the princes and heads of the thousands of Israel”, the call was given on a single bugle, corresponding to the conception of unity (V.4). But if the nation is to assemble in all its numbers then, in accordance with the idea of plurality, the signal is given through two bugles. The signal to break camp was, as already remarked, תרועה which was preceded and followed by תקיעה. Now as תקיעה is the “call” signal, תרועה the “alarm” signal, the meaning of the combined signal would be:- the first תקיעה alerts the whole camp to direct them to the presence of the head commander. If no תרועה follows immediately then the order is: repair to the head commanding officer to receive orders or communications from him. But if a תרועה does follow immediately it gives the order at once to set everybody and everything in motion, to pack up, break camp, and prepare to march on. The final תקיעה orders them, after packing up and breaking camp, to follow thither where the further orders of the leader directs. This would be the meaning of תרועה יתקעו למסעיהם, a תקיעה is to follow the תרועה and give thereby the direction to journey on

According to the wording of the text (V.5 & 6) the breaking-up signal was repeated only for the breaking camp of the second, the south camp, the west and the north camps followed on without any further signal. As a matter of fact if we consider the manner of the breaking camp as described in V.14 there was only need for a signal for the breaking of the first and second camp. For while the first camp, that of Judah was decamping, the contents of the Sanctuary had first to be covered in their prescribed covers to be handed over to the Kohathides and the Tent of the Temple and the courtyard to be taken down and loaded on to the transport-wagons by the Gersonides and Merariides. See verse 17 and Ch. 4,4 and 15. It was necessary that this dismantling etc., of the Temple had been completed and the Gersonides and Merariides had followed on and joined the camp of Judah, before the second camp set itself in motion, and this second camp which together with the Kohathides had stood ready with the holy contents of the Sanctuary since the breaking up of the first camp, followed on and attached themselves behind the first camp. This arrangement was necessary so that, as is expressly stated in V.21, when the new encampment was made, the Gersonides and Merariides could have already arrived and set up the Tabernacle and the courtyard ready to receive all the holy contents when they arrived with the second camp. So that it was essential that the second camp did not move before the dismantling etc., of the Temple was fully completed and for that had to wait for the second signal. The other camps who by then were already quite ready to move off, followed automatically in due order. Nevertheless according to the ספרי a third signal was given for the decampment of the two last camps, and takes it that this was commanded by תרועה יתקעו למסעיהם. According to another opinion quoted there were four signals blown, one for the departure of each camp.

V. 8. ובני אהרן הכהנים. It is highly singnificant that the signals had to be given by כהנים and indeed, according to ר״ע in the ספרי by כהנים תמימים, priests who were fit for עבודה as the term בני אהרן הכהנים always makes essential (Levit. 1,5). The people who, in the name of the Torah, in the Sanctuary of the Torah have to receive and arrange the symbolic actions of the devotion of the nation to the Torah, they are the same who, in the name of the leader of the nation, call the people, or their heads, to learn what is to be done in the name of the Law of God. Here as there they were the heralds of the Law to the nation, and if the paramount chief of the nation makes his call through the נהנים, the thought lies just therein, that it is not on the strength of his own personality, but on the strength of his position to the Torah that he is convening them. — והיו לכם להקת עולם Apart from the temporary use just ordained, which applied only to the time of the wandering in the wilderness, the חצוצרות receive in the following a permanent import for the future, and there too they are to be used only by the כהנים.

V. 9. וכי תבאו מלחמה. Throughout we find the general expression for going to war: יצא למלחמה. The expression בוא למלחמה occurs only rarely. We find it again in Ch. 32,6 in Moses’s speech to the children of Gad and Reuben האחיכם יבאו למלחמה. Whereas יצא למלחמה has the idea of going to war vigorously, also voluntarily, stirring up war outside one’s own territory, בא למלחמה, and still more our בא מלחמה designates submitting oneself to the dangers of war, to become involved in war. Unprovoked, war has come, so one must join up. Hence Moses’s question האהיכם יבאו למלחמה and in contrast to that ואתם תשבו פה (shall your brethren go into the war and ye remain here? I.L.). Your brothers would certainly much prefer to have reached their goal already, as much as you. But the war is a necessity, it is there, your brothers must go in to it, and you want to get out of your duty?! Also in Ch. 31,21, אנשי הצבא הבאים למלחמה it is dealing with the איסור טומאה results which their participation in the war has effected and which now, at the conclusion of the battle, they are to get rid of. They have resulted, not because they יצאו למלחמה but because they באו למלחמה, because, through the war they came into contact with dead bodies and acquired booty of איסור-utensils. Apart from this, according to the ספרי on V.5, there, taking part in that war, which had been designated beforehand as the last act in the life of Moses, had the stamp of unwillingness impressed upon it. (refer to it). In our verse, the וכי תבאו למלחמה speaks of unprovoked, forced war of defence. For it is בארצכם. It is no war of conquest outside your country, the enemy is in the land. He has invaded your country and presses hard on you in your own land. He is צר הצרר אתכם, you are in trouble. In such distress: והרעתם בחצצרת (“ye shall blow Teruah on the bugles”). The immediate purpose of this is given as ונזכרתם and ונושעתם which clearly indicates this Teruah to be a cry for help directed to God. In the preceding verses the note was a signal from the leader making a demand to the nation, here it is the nation, which by the same note, has its call sounded up to God. And as again it is the כהנים who raise this call, who are the servitors of the Sanctuary of the Torah which forms the bond between the nation and God, it is to the Torah to which they look for their hopes to be heard. And as the Teruah is the signal of the demand to strike camp, to become vigorously active, so also is the Teruah directed to God in times of need, naught but the cry: קומה והושיעה נא (arise and save we beseech Thee! I.L.) or as it says in V.35: קומה ה׳ ויפצו אויביך וגו׳ (Arise O’God and let thine enemies be scattered I.L.). But it does not simply say: והרעתם וגו׳ ונושעתם וגו׳ but ונזכרתם ונושעתם וגו׳. But ונזכרתם assumes that the זכירה has been lacking hitherto. God had forsaken them, had left them to the ordinary natural course of events, had withdrawn His special care for them so that the natural weakness of Israel compared to the superior strength of the enemy had brought about their trouble. So that the first thought of their urgent cry to God is: “turn to us again, direct Thy special care towards us again, help us again”, and the help for which they entreat is then only the immediate result of this Presence of God turned again towards the nation. If, as the Halacha teaches, each Teruah had to be preceded by a Tekiah and this Teruah of the call for help had also to be introduced by a Tekiah, then, similarly to the introductory Tekiah of the Teruah for the camp to be struck calling the attention of the people to the leader, so here too, this Tekiah would be the cry to God to turn His attention to us again, naught but the imploring cry: זכרנו! Then the final Tekiah concluding this Teruah would express the prayer: Remain with us also after Thou hast helped us, forsake us not again wander Thou with us!

V. 10. וביום שמחתכם. From סוכה 53b we learn that the חצוצרות were blown daily at the morning and evening תמיד and also at the מוספים on Sabbath and all the festivals; and there the only question is raised (54a et seq.) whether, when a day has the character of a combined festival, and accordingly two or three מוספים were brought, e.g. Sabbath and New Moon, or Sabbath and New Year, or when three מוספים were brought, one for Sabbath, one for New Year and one for New Moon, whether the Tekioth were blown separately for each, or whether the different מוספין were altogether accompanied by just one Tekiah, and the Halacha decides for the latter. But it is difficult to know how to reconcile our text with this report. Our text mentions expressly the festivals and new moons and apart from them, “the day of our Simcho”. On the one hand we have the question just what is meant by “the day of our Simcho” a concept that in any case must designate something other than the festivals, as it is mentioned in addition to them; and on the other hand, under which heading do שבת and תמיד come in. In ספרי there are two opinions. The one explains: וביום שמחתכם אלו שבתות (Sabbath is the day of your Simcho) but leaves the question, under which heading does תמיד come, unsolved. The other understands תמידים to be what the Torah calls יום שמחתכם but does not discuss under which designation שבתות are to be included.

Let us remark first of all that שמחה — Simcho, joy — by no means necessarily designates an exuberant joy brought about by some special occasion, but can very well be used to designate that cheerful mood, that feeling of inner happiness which should really form the keynote of our whole life. Places like Ps. 90,14; IV,8; XCVII,11; C,2; and CIV,34; Eccl. 9,7 111, 12; and XI,9; Prov. 5,18; XXIII,24 & 25, and XIII,9, can be sufficient proof of that. And now when it is speaking, as here, of the Nation as such, which is immortal, knows no death and no impoverishment, אין צבור מת ואין צבור עני and at the Divine place of the Sanctuary of the Torah, at the threshold of which death and mourning must stand back, where under the rays of light of the Presence of God, only שמחה של מצוה (the quiet tranquil joy of doing what is right I.L.) flourishes, where the thought שהשמחה במעונו (that joy is in its true abode I.L.) becomes a reality, where everybody receives the call עבדו את ה׳ בשמחה, there every ordinary day could well be designated as יונו שמחה; and this designation is used here in contrast to the preceding יום צרה where, through God having forsaken them, trouble and oppression has befallen the nation. So that יום שמחתכם can well refer to the daily תמידים-offerings, and שבתות be included under מועדיכם. After all, especially with regards to the special offering of the day, שבת is included in the concept מועד, as, according to Pessachim 77a, the final sentence (in Numb. 29,39) אלה תעשו לה׳ במועדיכם does refer to all the קרבנות צבור (the national offerings I.L.) which have a fixed day on which they are to be brought, so that the מוספי שבת would be included. (see above on IX,2).

But if every ordinary normal day of our life which is not saddened by some special trouble or grief is a יום שמחה by the consciousness of God which accompanies every moment of it, the day which is specially dedicated to this thought of God, as Sabbath is, which is given up exclusively to the thought which, accompanying all the busy activities and endeavours of the other days interweaves the breath of שמחה into them, surely that day can pre-eminently and quite specially be considered as “the day of our joy”, יום שמחתנו. In whatever mood the Sabbath may strike one, be it on the full note of complete harmony of life, עלי עשר, (the ten-stringed instrument, symbolic of a Paradisal life, Arochin 13b I.L.), or on a note of a tired, worn-out condition, עלי נבל (נבל , an instrument whose notes correspond to the condition of נבל, to be withered, worn out I.L.), or on a thoughtful note, considering the solution of the problems of life, עלי הגיון בכנור (the notes of the harp soothe the mind upset by worries and induce quiet consideration I.L.), the thought of living and striving in God’s world, amongst the creatures and creations of His Hands, as is awakened by the Sabbath will always force its way to our consciousness: שמחתני ה׳ בפעלך במעשי ידיד ארנן “for Thou hast given me joy with Thy Work, with that which Thy Hands have made do I loudly exult”. (Ps. XCII), or, as our Prayer-book puts it ישמחו במלכותך שומרי שבת “they that keep the Sabbath have joy in Thy Government and call it a delight.” So that by יום שמחתכם, Sabbath can well be meant, and תמירים would then come under the heading of מועדיכם as indeed regarding the very significant דחית הטומאה they do come under the concept of מועד (see above on Ch. 9,2).

So the Torah tells us:- When, on days of joyful consciousness of our God, at times when certain memories specially invite us to union with our God, days which incite us to self-rejuvenation, we then give expression to this consciousness, to this striving to union with God, this self-rejuvenation, by seeking “to get near God” (קרבן I.L.) by dedicating our actions and the joy of life to Him in the עולות of the תמידים and מוספים and the שלמי צבור of the כבשי עצרת we are then to “call up to God”, (by Tekiah on the bugles), to look on our attempts to get near to Him which we express in the vows these occasions stir us up to make (all sacrifices are in the nature of vows for future behaviour I.L.) and come near to us even as we (listening to His Voice, see below I.L.) are striving to get near to Him. The Tekiah on the bugles blown at the national offerings is, accordingly, again the cry of Israel up to God for Him to come to us. It expresses exactly the real thought of קרבן; and in our striving upwards to God and calling on Him to come down to us we make these moments of offering into שבתות — מועדים and תמידים are also מועדים-offerings, see above on IX,3 — to moments of the union of Israel with its God.

According to the Halacha this Tekiah blown at the offerings was not a single note but a Tekiah, Teruah, Tekiah similar to the cry for help in the preceding verse, and the fact that nevertheless there it says והרעתם and here ותקעתם is explained by the רמב״ן that there the meaning of the Teruah is to be stressed, here that of the Tekiah. There it is a Teruah accompanied by Tekiah, here a Tekiah accompanied by Teruah. There the purpose of the blowing is the intervention of God, and the proximity of God the means for it; here, the proximity of God is the purpose and His intervention the means. For the proximity of God, the continuance of it is dependent on an intervention of His Almighty Power by a miracle of His Divine loving kindness, by כפרה, by the complete covering over and doing away with everything in our past that would stand in the way of our efforts to be worthy of getting near to God, and makes us as reborn, fit to give ourselves up to a new pure future. (For in the natural law of cause and effect, having sinned once makes it much easier to sin a second time, but in addition to סליחה, forgiveness, God has promised us He will overcome this law of nature for us, and grant us כפרה, render us as new born and as if we had never sinned, and the past have no effect; though indeed we, on our own part, may never forget what we have done in the past and be ever on our guard. I.L.). The Tekiah, Teruah, Tekiah at the offerings accordingly calls God to us (Tekiah) to effect כפרה (Teruah) and to remain further near to us to guide us through life (the final Tekiah).

It is not impossible that the different meaning of the Tekiah-Teruah-Tekiah when blown as a call for help or as a call at the offerings was indicated in the manner in which the notes were blown, and in the former the Teruah was more prolonged and blown louder, while in the latter it was the Tekiah which was stressed. This would be similar to the prescriptions for the difference in blowing the combined fanfare on the Shofar and the bugles on fast days and on New Year respectively (Rosh Hashana, 26b; and see below).

והיו לכם לזכרון לפני אלקיכם. In places like והיה היום הזה לכם לזכרון (Ex. 12,14), also referring to the names on the Ephod and the חשן (ibid. XXVIII,12 & 29), and also to the Tephillin: ולזכרון בין עיניך the זכרון does not seem to designate the means of remembrance but the means of bringing the recollection which is to be kept in mind. Here, too, the subject of the verb והיו seems to be not חצוצרות, the bugles, but עולות וזבחי שלמים the offerings which, through the Tekiahs are to be brought to the remembrance, kept in recollection before God for us. The Tekiahs are a call up to God: May He take note of what we are now doing down here and keep in His recollection the vows and intentions of devotion which we are expressing by our procedures. The והיו לכם promises on His part the granting of the prayer we are sending up to Him, and at the same time אני ה׳ אלקיכם proclaims the result of it, the realisation of the promise of the continuous relationship of our bond with God. Looked at more closely, the three sentences, ותקעתם ,והיו לכם לזכרון ,אני ה׳ אלקיכם correspond to the Tekiah-Teruah-Tekiah. ותקעתם is the call and appeal to God; זכרון is the prayer in Teruah that He may consider our offerings worthy of bringing כפרה; and אני ה׳ אלקיכם the prayer, prayed for in the final Tekiah, for the proximity attached to the Covenant accompanying the nation throughout its existence.

(Cf. the remarks made on the Tekiahs blown on a Shofar on New Year and Jubilee Year on Levit. 23,24). In Rosh Hashana 26b and 27a we are told that in the Temple Shofar and bugles were always blown simultaneously. On New Year on either side of the Shofar notes on the bugles were blown, the notes on the Shofar more prolonged as the real Mitzva of the day was Shofar. On adys of national trouble, fast days, תעניות, the two bugles were in the middle and an accompanying Shofar on either side, the notes on the bugles longer, those on the Shofar shorter, as the Mitzva of the day was bugles. This combination of bugles and Shofar in the Temple is expressed in the exhortation: בחצוצרות וקול שופר הריעו לפני המלך ה׳ (Ps. 98,6). If we consider that Shofar represents God’s voice to us, and the bugles our cry to Him, their combination in the Sanctuary, the abode of the Torah of God and His promises to us, would express the Truth: — Shofar is accompanied by the bugles, the bugles must be accompanied by the Shofar, i.e. if we listen to God’s call to us (Shofar) then we can confidently expect our call to him (bugles) to be heard; and we can only send our calls up to God in times of stress (bugles) if at the same time we are ready and undertake to listen to His Voice directed to us. (Shofar).

The Tekiahs at the offerings translated into words are found in the ברכת עבודה in רצה of our daily שמנה עשרה, (which corresponds to the תמידים), but especially in the interpolation of יעלה ויבא on days of מועד and ר״ח.

V. 11. מעל משכן העדות ,ויהי בשנה וגו׳ (see on Ch. 9,15). The cloud rested on the Sanctuary because it was the abode of the “Evidence”. It rested really on the Evidence because it was just that, the evidence of the Torah being of Divine origin (the tablets of stone and the continuous miracle which the nature of the writing displayed I.L.) the obedience to which, was the condition for the continuance of the Presence of God in the midst of the people — בחדש השני בעשרים וגו׳. It was only after those who had been prevented in Nissan and so had celebrated פסח שני on the 14th of this month, and thereby had the mission of Israel as the People of the Guidance of God brought home to them again, that now, after encamping at Sinai for nearly twelve months Israel was to journey on towards entering the promised land of the Torah.

V. 12. נסע .ויסעו וגו׳ למסעיהם (related to ויסחך מאהל ,נסח (Ps. 52,7). “pluck thee out of thy tent I.L.) really means to raise oneself out of the resting place one has hitherto occupied, hence, to break camp, to set oneself in motion. Then it also means continuous breaking up, remaining in motion, to journey. This concept is used principally of the setting forth of a mass of people whom it is difficult to set in motion, as here, of a whole large camp and also of Abraham with the whole of his household and possessions where each forward move is really a continuous act of “moving house”. In our chapter it accordingly occurs with both meanings: striking camp and journeying forth. Here:- they struck camp to start the journey which lay before them till the entry into the Promised Land. — ויסעו וגו׳ ממדבר סיני וישכן הענן במדבר פארן. For the present it was just a move from one wilderness into another.

V. 13. ויסעו בראשנה על פי ה׳ ביד משה. From Egypt to Sinai they had also journeyed under Divine guidance through the agency of Moses. But to journey in the way that was now prescibed for them, viz, as the People of God’s Torah, in orderly organised groups around the Sanctuary of His Torah, directed to rest or journey on according to the cloud resting on, or rising from the Evidence of the Torah, and led by the Ark of the Covenant in the van, in that way they had never yet wandered.

V. 14. לצבאתם: in orderly organised groups. Presumably the families of each tribe were grouped together within the tribal camp, and this repeated designation לצבאתם in each of the four camps refers to this. It would be more likely to refer to the three hosts of tribes that were assigned to each standard if it had said לצבאתיו which could refer to דגל or מחנה. But the plural clearly refers to the preceding בני יהודה so that it makes us assume that within the בני יהודה itself there must have been several צבאות, organised groups.
V. 17. והורד המשכן, and in V.21, ונסעו הקהתים see notes on V.6.

V. 25. מאסף כל המחנות. The underlying concept of the root אסף is to absorb something into oneself or altogether to take it up, for some special different purpose. It is, (like to many other words prefixed with א, like אכל (from כלה I.L.) אבד etc.) סף the end with the prefixed individualising א, ending, ceasing, so as to become given to another purpose (cf. Gen. 49,1). Hence אסף is also used simply for taking away without giving any other use or purpose of the object, as אסף ה׳ את חרפתי (Gen. 30,23). (God has removed, taken away, made an end of my shame I.L.). In an army column marching to war the leading head of the column is called החלוץ, literally a “detachment”, it is the body of troops detached from the rest, sent ahead as the most “vigorous” who contact the enemy first and generally used for pioneers who have to overcome the first difficulties. The rear part of the column is called “מאסף״ who form the end of the column of troops, make the troop into a closed unit and keep it together as a rear-guard, a description in which the associated idea of אסף as defensive protection is expressed (see Joshua 6,9 et seq.). In the Jerusalmi (Erubin V.1) there are two opinions as to the formation in which the camps moved on the journeys. The one view puts it that they marched in a square formation כמין תיבה in the same way that they encamped, Judah in the van, Reuben to the right, Dan to the left and Ephraim in the rear, for it says כאשר יחנו כן יסעו (Ch. 2,17). The other opinion concludes from the wording of our verse מאסף לכל המחנות that they journeyed כקורה in a straight drawn-out line, Judah leading, Reuben, Ephraim and Dan following so that the latter in the truest sense was מאסף, closed the ranks. But, if we consider that according to V.14-21 there is no doubt that the Kohathides followed the camp of Reuben so that the Gersonides and Merarirides who followed the camp of Judah could have the משכן set up when the Kohathides arrived with the ark and the other appurtenances, and also that the camp of Dan only set itself in motion after the camp of Ephraim according to the order of the march given here, and Ch. 2,31 definitely states לאחרונה יסעו, the opinion כמין תיבה can hardly have the meaning that they actually kept the form of a closed square while on the march, but this opinion can only be taken to mean that even on the march they kept the relative positions they occupied when in camp, viz. Judah to the fore, then, not directly behind, but keeping to the right, Reuben followed, then in a line straight behind Judah, Ephraim moved on, and finally to the left behind Ephraim, Dan brought up the rear, so that when the time came to halt, each camp was in the right position for encampment.
V. 28. אלה מסעי, this was altogether the general order adopted for all the striking camp and forming up for all their further moves, ויסעו, and now, thus they moved on.

V. 29. ויאמר משה. In Judges 4,11, Chobab is named as the father-in-law of Moses, so that חתן משה here must refer to חבב and not to Reuel, and if in Ex. 2,18 Reuel is called the father of Zipporah and her sisters it must be understood as the grandfather, comparable to אלקי אבי אברהם (Gen. 32,10) and other places, as Rambam points out there. His real names seem to have been יתר and יתרו, Ex. 3,1 and IV,18 and so also in Ex. XVIII. According to Ramban (ibid.). Jethro received the name Chobab after his conversion to Judaism and hence after that he is called by that name. See also the ספרי thereon. The root חבב, quite common in Rabbinic Hebrew, as an expression of love and estimation, only occurs once in תנ״ך, in Deut. 33,3, אף חובב עמים כל קדושיו בידך. The root seems related to חוב, indebtedness, a word which is likewise quite common in Rabbinic Hebrew and only occurs once in תנ״ך viz.: חבולתו חוב ישיב “he returneth a pledge with all the obligation of a debt”. (Exekiel 18,7), and חבב could be a love that one is bound to give, and a love out of feelings of duty. Perhaps the אף חובב עמים in Deut. would say: Also, when Thou wouldst lay the nations under obligation by giving them highest gifts. Thou takest all his, (Israel’s) holy ones in Thy hand (כל קדשיו בידך) והם תכו לרגלך וגו׳, and they (the nations) will be led to Thy feet, by he (Israel) bringing some of Thy saying towards them (ישא מדברותיך). If perhaps this is the meaning of that sentence, then חבב would be the greatest loving act of God’s Management to place the nations of the world under obligations to Him, by bringing them to a knowledge of God and obedience to Him through Israel’s teaching and example. Then חבב (cf. the forms עולל ,שולל ,שובב all having passive meaning) would be one who feels himself in duty bound under obligations to God through such highests acts of His Love, a name which is highly befitting to Jethro who so understandingly came over to Judaism from heathenism. What serious consciousness of duty Jethro handed down to his descendants, and how brilliantly they came to perform it, we shall have occasion to remark on V.31 and 32.

נסעים אנחנו. This striking camp was done in the presumption that they would now immediately proceed to enter the Promised Land. The Lawgiving was over, so what lay next was for them to take possession of the land on which the Law, the Torah, was to find its complete realisation.

V. 31—32. ויאמר אל נא וגו׳. The request in the previous verse appeared to be made from the standpoint of Jethro’s own interests: לכה אתנו והטבנו לך. That, he had rejected: לא אלך וגו׳ not for any advantage it might be to me would I forsake my fatherland. Moses accordingly repeats his request and explains it more precisely: אל נא תעזב אתנו, your remaining with us is something that we need, your going away would be “forsaking” us, כי על כן וגו׳: for not in your interest, but the reason that I have asked you (see Gen. 18,5) ידעת וגו׳, you possess the knowledge necessary for our encamping in the wilderness, you know every district there, and wherever we shall be directed by God to pitch our camp, you know all the possible advantages to be had from that particular spot that we could use. והיית לנו לעינים, you can serve us there as a pair of eyes, can let us have the benefit of your knowledge of the locality, and when I said והטבנו לך I was not thinking of any actual material recompense but just in general הטוב ההוא וגו׳ ,הטבנו לך, we would see that you would find with us compensation for the home and fatherland you gave up for our sake. By the sacrifice you make for us, and the great use you would be to us, you would well have acquired the right to have, and we the duty to give you land and establishment. We will give you a share in the land which God gives us (that is the טוב in Moses’ first speech in V.29). Inasmuch as this giving is expressed in the same term which is used for Israel being given the land: אשר ייטיב ה׳ עמנו והטבנו לך what is delicately implied is: You need not be shy of accepting this, as if it were a gracious gift we would be giving you, we ourselves are receiving the land equally only as gracious gift from the Hand of God, and that which for us is purely a gift טובה עמנו, for you is טובה לך (not עמך) something that you thoroughly deserve. From the fact that Judges 1,16 tells us that descendants of Moses’ father-in-law inhabited עיר התמרים the Date City, according to II. Chron. 28,15. Jerico יריחו עיר התמרים, we know that Chobab acceded to Moses’ request and journeyed to the land with Israel. According to that he must have rejoined Moses in the wilderness after his first return to his home recorded in Ex. 18,27. There in Judges I. 16, Moses’ father-in-law is called קיני and by this name his descendants seem to be designated. In any case the בני קיני descend from חובב the father-in-law of Moses. For in Judges 4,11, it states quite definitely וחבר הקיני נפרד מקין מבני חובב חתן משה (“Now Heber the Kenite who was one of the descendants of Chobab the father-in-law of Moses had severed himself from the Kenites”). And when Saul went out to fight the Amalakites (I. Sau. XV) and found a branch of the Kenites living amongst the Amalakite population he told them to move out of there to avoid suffering in the defeat of the city, and gave as his reason, ואתה עשיתה חסד עם בני ישראל בעלותם ממצרים (V.6 ibid.) “for ye shewed kindness to all the children of Israel when they came up out of Egypt”. Thus Israel remained grateful to the memory of the service rendered by Moses’ father-in-law. The most fruitful district around Jerico, דושנה של יריחו was, according to the ספרי, allotted to the descendants of Jethro who inhabited it for 440 years until the building of the Temple. But his descendants also inherited his חובב-serious attention to the important matters of life. They, the קינים הבאים מחמת אבי בית רכב not only formed משפחות סופרים the families of scribes, who, by nurturing study and learning were the most brilliant families of Israel, but were also the יושבי יעבץ, who left their rich fields and orchards around Jerico to attach themselves as disciples to the illustrious spiritual company under the mastership of Jabetz in the wilderness of Judah. (I. Chron. 2,55 and IV,9 & 10, as well as Judges I. 16, ספרי thereon). They were also the בית רכב, the Rechabites as is evident from the quotations above, who, faithful to the dictates of their great ancestor Jehonadab, recognised early and avoided the depravity of the cities and the government by renouncing living in houses, planting vineyards or drinking wine, vowed to live a nomadic life in tents to save liberty and moral purity for themselves and their descendants. And perhaps they have kept themselves true to their principles to this day in the Rechabites of the Arabian desert, kept by the Divine Promise לא יכרת איש ליונדב בן רכב עמד לפני כל הימים (Jer. 35,2-19). (The English missionary Dr. Wolff found the Rechabites living near Mecca in Arabia in 1828. He credits them with the observance of the pure Mosaic Law, the תשב״כ. They speak Arabic and a little Hebrew. They number about 60,000. I.L.).

But this request which Moses made and recorded that his father-in-law should remain with them to help them with his knowledge of the terrain and his perspicacity is a fact of no small importance for a true and just estimation of the “mission of Moses”. As the organising advice of just this father-in-law (Ex. 18,13-27) proves for all time how little talent for organising — that very first qualification for a state-building legislator — was innate in Moses, so does the fact which is told us here completely refute all the nonsense that is circulated of Moses having knowledge of all the plans and their specialities in the desert, with the object of reducing the Divine element in our wanderings in the wilderness to the lower level of a clever and cunning leadership. The man who required the advice of his father-in-law for the most elementary organisation and arrangments of the camp, and wrote both down for the everlasting memory of his people, he could only have accomplished lawgiving and leadership as the instrument of God, and was the very last man to wish to surround himself with the halo of more than human insight and miraculous powers.

V. 33—34. ויסעו וגו׳. As it does not say ויסעו שלשת ימים but דרך שלשת ימים it probably wishes to express the hardship and strain caused by such a three days journey. But ארון ברית ה׳ נסע לפניהם דרך שלשת ימים they had the Ark of God’s covenant before their eyes during the whole of the three days trek looking out for a suitable place for them to rest, and this constant view could well keep them in the fresh and cheerful mood of knowing that God was leading them, as well as ענן ה׳ עליהם the cloud of God which remained constantly with them and made them feel assured on all their wanderings that they had God’s Protection accompanying them.

V. 35—36. ויהי בנסע הארון. We have already remarked in our introduction to Ch. VIII, that in this section, the history of the development of the Jewish Nation, which had been broken off to relate the sin of the golden calf and the final fresh renewal of the “covenant” relationship between God and Israel in Ch. XXXIV of Exodus, is now taken up again and continued. Had Israel already reached the height which a true realisation of the Lawgiving on the Mount of God assumes, the further course of its history would have taken a different and simpler path. The way from the Mount of God would have led immediately to the Land of God. A really true realisation of this Torah in the land, would have elevated the Jewish Sanctuary of the Torah and the Jewish People of the Torah to a Light of God radiating far afield into the sphere of the nations of the world — a fate which now only beckons as the goal of Time — and, like Israel’s history, the history of mankind would have been a different one.

But the people did not stand yet on the heights of their calling. Immediately in the very next verse we are taken down into the midst of their camp, and thereby introduced to a series of faults which finally stamped that whole generation as being unfit and unworthy to enter the Land of the Torah. They showed that the promised permanent possession of the land would have to be postponed for centuries, a time that would have to extend far into the history of the education of Israel up to its calling. And even the beginning of this life of education in the land would have to await the dying off of that whole generation and for a new generation to grow up. So that the preceding V.34 forms a most definite cleavage, a true parting of the ways. So much so that this V.34 is considered as the end of a book, and the following Ch. XI as the beginning of a new one, and the two verses 35 and 36 standing between as ספר חשוב בפני עצמו as an important book on its own and hence also it is placed in inverted commas, סימוניות מלמעלה ולמטה, so that really there are not five books of Moses, but seven (Sabbath 115b & 116a and Yadayim 111).
Let us try to get at the meaning of “this important book”.

It says: בנסע הארן ויאמר משה קומה וגו׳ and ובנחה יאמר שובה ה׳ וגו׳, when the Ark set forth, Moses ordered it to start, and when it came to rest, Moses ordered it to do so. But indeed neither starting nor coming to rest occurred at Moses’ orders, and yet Moses accompanied both by his demands, as though what had already happened was now to do so. Clearly this expresses the fullest, most complete, most joyous acquiescence in the Will of God, which greets every decision of God as if it were one’s own decision, the highest degree of complying with Gamliel’s injunction: עשה רצונו כרצונך (Aboth 2,4) (“Make His Will as if ‘twere thy will”.). The Sifri says similarly: ויאמר משה קומה ה׳ וכתוב אחר אומר על פי ה׳ יסעו וכו׳ משל למלך שאמר לעבדו הנראה שהעמידני בשביל שאני הולך ליתן ירושה לבני wherein the completely working together of the directing of Moses’ will to that of God, is found. But this selfless submitting to, and agreeing with the Will of God by Moses is the most complete contrast to the suller, mood and disloyal feelings of his contemporary generation, as the incident which follows immediately, proclaims. It is just that height of being spiritually and morally completely penetrated with the consciousness of God which, as a national characteristic, only beckons as the goal of the ages the path to which is to be paved by Israel through its Torah. But it was just the lack of it that brought about the great parting of the ways if Israel’s history which makes these words of Moses being considered as at intervention between two books of Jewish history.

And it is הארן, with the moving forth and coming to rest of the Ark of the Torah he had brought over to the nation that Moses greeted with the request for God to move forth and to come to rest. So that it was with the “moves”, the progress of His Torah that Moses saw the “moves” of God on earth. Where this Torah finds no home, there is no home for the Presence of God, and where a home is prepared for this Torah, there a home is made ready for the Presence of God on earth.

And Moses recognised that this Torah from its very entry into the world would have to expect אויבים, opponents, and משנאים, that people would hate it. It’s demands for justice and love are so very much in opposition to the dictates of force and selfishness the curse of which is felt so keenly by the weak and needy. The upkeep of these dictates against the laws of justice and love guarantees the coalition of all the people in power who form a tacitly united front in the world, of אויבים, opponents to the Torah who form a barrier to the entry of its influence into the world in general.

And its demands for self-control and sanctification of morals are so much in contrast to the allures of ignoble passion that one finds in the breast of the ignoble masses in all classes, not only שונאים but משנאים, not only hatred but persecution and still Moses recognised the final victory of his Torah in the world. Just because the course and progress his Torah has made and makes in the history of the world means the ingress and progressive move of God in society in general and in the feelings of mankind, therefore the enemies and haters of His Torah are the enemies and haters of the Kingdom of God on earth. That is why when he saw the Ark of God’s Torah setting forth he expressed his confidence that when his Torah had completed its course on earth, its penetrating entry would make the coalition of its enemies disperse and the persecuting hate take to flight before it. The Sifri also takes it in the same way: קומה ה׳ ויפוצו אויביך אלו המכונסים, וינוסו משנאיך אלו הרודפים, מפניך הם נסים ואין אנו כלום לפניהם וכו׳ (the מכונסים and רודפים are taken from the contrast ויפוצו and וינוסו, the former implying that they joined together, a coalition, etc.). And שַׂנֵא in the Piel is a propaganda of hatred.

ובנחה, (written feminine but read masculine I.L.) and when the Ark of the Torah came to rest Moses visualised that time and that sphere of humanity where the Torah would no longer stand in virile strong contrast to an opposing world of mankind, where it, still in its undiminished virility, nevertheless feels itself the מאורסה, the “betrothed” of individual man and mankind in general, borne by mankind in all its endeavours, and that will be the time where the thousands of Israel will be changed to myriads, the time of which one of the last successors of Moses says: ונלוו גוים רבים אל ה׳ ביום ההוא והיו לי לעם ושכנתי בתוכך (“and many nations will be attached to God in that day, and I will dwell in the midst of thee” I.L.) Zac. 2,15. So that when the Ark came “gently” (נחה not נחו I.L.) to rest, Moses said: “Come home again, O God, to the myriads of the thousands of Israel”. רבבות אלפי ישראל cannot mean ten thousand times a thousand or even twice ten thousand thousands. For then the smaller number would come first, it would say אלפי רבבות like אחותנו את היי לאלפי רבבה (Gen. 24,60). In any case, in Moses’ time Israel reached at most 1/2 millions whereas רבבות אלפי ישראל would be twenty million. We therefore think we many take it to refer not to Moses’s own time, but as “the myriads of the thousands of Israel”, i.e. the myriads that would ensue from the thousands of Jews, by descending from them and by attachment to them. In any case אלפי ישראל does not designate strictly “thousands”. It refers to the closed masses within the nation and the tribes, cf. ראשי אלפי ישראל (ch. I,16 etc.), אלפי הדל במנשה (Judges 6,15).

If our way of taking them be not entirely erroneous, these two verses would comprise a compendium of the whole history of Israel and the world introduced by Moses’s divine mission, and well can these two verses form a book on their own. We believe we can find a commentary on them in Ps. LXVIII, the contents of which sing the history of the victorious Kingdom of God on earth which was started by Israel and the Torah. Even in the wording, this Psalm proclaims itself as an echo of our two verses. Compare V.2 (יפוצו אויביו וינוסו משנאיו מפניו I.L.) and V.18 with them. This latter רכב אלקים רבתים אלפי שנאן אדני בם סיני בקדש “Two myriads of thousands of blessed high beings (angels I.L.) were hitherto the bearers of God’s Glory, now God is amongst them (אדנ׳ בם, amongst men who are worthy to be in His service, and by whom He allows Himself to be called my Master I.L.) and His Sinai is in the Sanctuary (see Ex Ch. 27,8 p.496 in English version); is equally a paraphrased explanation of our שובה ה׳ רבבות אלפי ישראל (the רבבות אלפי ישראל are now what until then were רבתים אלפי שנאן) just as V.2 literally repeats the words of our verse.

V. 1. While Moses greeted the guidance of God, even when it led through wildernesses and deserts, now and for all future time, with complete disinterested devotion, in happily being-at-one with the Will of God, and thereby proclaimed the point of view in life and the feelings which should be the common possession of every member of the whole nation, the people were far away from such spiritual perfection. The “people” — in contrast to Moses — were כמתאננים (see on Gen. XXXV.18). The people were as if mourning over themselves. They looked on themselves as already dead, and mourned over their very selves! The cloud of God over them and the Ark of His Covenant with them only made them feel cut off from the rest of the world and its requirements for living. The whole unique connection with God which they received in its place, the proximity of God, the Sanctuary of God in their midst, their mission, their God-promised destiny, all offered them no compensation, remained worthless and without meaning in their eyes, had not yet become to them a higher, fuller, happier life — they felt themselves buried alive and mourned over themselves. They were “bad”, they were far off from, and in just the opposite feeling to, the feelings which would have corresponded to what God had destined them to have. And they were not רע בעיני ה׳, they were באזני ה׳, they were conscious that God was aware of what was in their hearts and they set themselves against Him and complained that He had made their lives worthless and without meaning. ותבער בם וגו׳, the actual death that threatened them made them realise that not only were they still alive but that they valued their lives. They had no right yet to mourn over themselves. בקצה המתנה, the fire did not break out in the middle of the camp, nor in several places but it began definitely at one end of the camp and threatened to progress right through the camp and destroy it completely.
V. 2. ותשקע האש, it sank down, there where it was burning and did not spread.

V. 4. והאספסוף like וְהָאֲספסוף the ערב רב whom they had gathered, absorbed in their midst when they came out of Egypt. The א being quiescent gives the nuance of meaning that the absorption was more of an external nature, that those who were “gathered in” did not really enter into the real national being of the nation. It was more of a ספף than an אסף. Israel was more of a סף, a container, a vessel, and a “threshold” to them, they were “contained” in Israel but never really became an integral part of it התאוו תאוה. It was not a longing which awoke in them willy-nilly by external causes, but one which they gladly provoked by themselves. וישבו ויבכו the התאונן of V.1 was also an internal weeping so that the term וישבו ויבכו “they started weeping again” is quite apt. If the way we have taken the meaning of רבבות אלפי ישראל above be not erroneous this leading astray of the people by האספסוף אשר בקרבו would also be in the sharpest contrast to the ideal destiny to which Israel was to mature that was expressed there Israel in its numerical smallness should be, and one day will be, the spiritual nucleus to which the myriads of the nations ultimately returning to God will attach themselves — and here it itself falls under the demoralising influence of an ignoble minority of strangers who are staying in its midst!
את הקשאים usw. Wir folgen in der Übersetzung der herkömmlichen Auffassung dieser Pflanzennamen, ohne dafür eine etymologische Begründung geben zu können.

V. 6. נפשנו יבשה; cf. יבש כחרש כחי Ps. 22,16. It is not nourishment that we lack — all the vegetables mentioned in the previous verse are not exactly nourishing food — what we lack are the tasty stimulating foods that excite the appetite. We miss the change of diet so necessary for health בלתי אל המן עינינו, the complete monotony, the unvarying sameness of our food makes it unbearable.

V. 7—8. והמן וגו׳. Against this apparently justified complaint the text tells us the specialities of the manna which could show up the shallowness of the grumble. It was כזרע גד appealed to the eye (see Ex. 16,31) according to Yoma 95a. עגול כגידה ולבן כמרגלית round and pearl white. If we compare the places where elsewhere עין designates the impression which the colour of an object makes on the eye we find it used throughout referring to shining articles. כעין הקרח הנורא, כעין תרשיש, כעין נחשת קלל (Ezek. I & X) and if בדלח, according to Rashi, is crystal, its transparency could be designated thereby (see on Ex. 16,14) — שטו העם. The people could not use the manna entirely without any work at all on their part, it was to be enjoyed as the result of their own efforts as שטו roaming in various directions to collect it etc. round the different camps, וטחנו ברחים etc., ground fine, pounded coarse, cooked or baked, all gave sufficient change in obtaining and presenting the manna and provided mental spice to it. — לשד only occurs elsewhere in תנ״ך in Ps. 32,4 נהפך לשדי “my moisture is turned to the drought of summer”, where it refers to the moisture, the juices of the body. According to that, here it would indicate the richness of oil, melted oil. In Ex. 16,31 the taste of the manna is described as כצפיחית בדבש as the finest wheat flour with honey. Here it does not say וטעמו וגו׳ but והיה טעמו and this, according to רשב״ם explanation would be its taste after cooking or baking, whereas there it gives its taste in its raw condition.

V. 9. וברדת הטל וגו׳ (see on Ex. 16,13-14). To all this was added that the way and manner in which the manna fell showed the quite special care with which it was presented to them so that it lay there each day as מן, as the special gift granted by God, a fact which more than anything else should have made it sweet and valuable to people of even minor intelligence.

למשפחתיו: it was no open rebellion, they did not gather in groups or crowds, they wept and complained at home. But they stood at the entrances of their tents and wailed and the wailing and complaining was general.

ובעיני משה רע. Moses judged this as being something that announced the complete failure of his mission. He was to have won the people to the highest ideals of human spiritual and moral perfection — and the people are wailing at missing leek and onions!

V. 11. למה הרעת. My mission, for which from the very beginning I felt myself unqualified, is my misfortune. I would gladly bear it if I could see any good for other people resulting from it. But through my lack of ability the people are going to ruin and my suffering is useless. למה לא מצתי וגו׳,. As מצתי is written without an א there could lie in the word a suggestion of מצה, sucking, drawing with intense longing to the very last drop (cf. Ps. 63,10, and LXXV,9 etc.) I have prayed so imploringly to be granted the grace not to be entrusted with this lofty mission just because I did not feel myself competent for it. Should not this doubt of my own ability have been sufficient reason for my request to have been granted? Is not self-confidence the very first necessity for the mission to be a leader of a nation, and was not my mistrust of my own abilities the proof of my real unfitness for it? Why didst Thou refuse to grant my request? The ולמה לא מצתי חן בעיניך is either in parenthesis, and לשום וגו׳ continues directly the sense of למה הרעת וגו׳, or one can take למה לא מצתי וגו׳ to mean: why hast Thou found me so little worthy of being granted my request, that Thou placed etc. Perhaps לשום וגו׳ is an elliptical sentence on its own: To lay the burden of this whole nation on me! i.e. who could understand that!

V. 12. האנכי הריתי. Am I its mother? אם אנכי ילדתיהו or its father, as in Gen. 4,18 & X,8 et seq. If father and mother fail in their task of educating their children it certainly is a misfortune for the parents as well as for the children. But in that case it is something natural that goes with the birth of children. It belongs, as so much else does to the various conditions of life in which people are born and which makes the great diversity of individual lives and problems to be solved. Moreover there are other factors which effect the scale of the balance to no little degree, the natural relationship of love, respect and the confidence which children have in their parents, all of which considerably lighten the task of education. But I am not their natural educator. It was You Who chose me to be their educator, and You just picked on a man who lacks entirely the power of eloquence, is no speaker, is no imposing personality, lacks all the factors that should belong to one who is to win the respect of, and have influence on a whole nation.

V. 13. מאין לי בשר וגו׳: They know quite well that they are demanding something from me which is quite beyond my power to give them. And as, having the completely sufficing and satisfying food in the manna, what they are asking for is something dispensable and superfluous. Their demand is nothing but plaguing tormenting of the man in whom they see the leader of their fate. And had he been the right man he would long ago have won their love and respect which would never have allowed such vexatious desires to arise.
Just because the demand was for something quite dispensable and superfluous neither Moses nor the people could expect that God would grant it in some miraculous manner.

V. 14. לא אוכל וגו׳. I cannot carry out the task You set me all by myself. I have not sufficient influence on the people and not the ability to acquire it. For this task I am only one half of the right man. I can receive Your Torah and transmit it and teach it, but I cannot form a nation for this Torah for You. I cannot exercise the educative and formative mastery over the minds and feelings of the people which would lead them to such a goal. (cf. Ex. 3,11).

V. 15. ואם ככה את וגו׳. The feminine form את here evidently refers to some holding back of the Power of God, and what is implied by its use here would be: If You leave me to my own weakness of which I am fully conscious, and if You do not wish to come to my help by changing my nature as indeed You would have the power to do — that is probably what Moses meant by אנכי לבדי, I, by myself of the previous verse — then I beg of You to let me die now, before my time, so that I do not live to see my misfortune, i.e. the complete failure of my mission, in the complete deterioration of the People. Similarly, right at the beginning of his mission (Ex. 4,10), Moses had expected that as soon as God sent him, He would equip him with the necessary power and force of eloquence and when he found that God had not done so — גם מאז דברך אל עבדך (ibid.) — he recognised all the more his unfitness and unworthiness for his mission. Of course he had no idea that just this weakness of his, combined with the extreme modesty of his character, would remain for ever the warranty of the Divine origin of his mission. This is perhaps also what our sages mean when they explain the feminine appellation here by השש כחו של משה כנקבה (see Rashi), Moses expressed the feeling of his own weakness by God having refrained from having used His great virile power to assist him.

V. 16. אספה לי שבעים איש. Just as, in the later centuries of the decline and fall of the Jewish State, the appearance of such a glorious list of inspired prophets shows how, after all, a large spiritually and morally pure circle of families must have existed in the midst of the people, out of whose bosom such men could have come; so does this order to pick out of Israel’s elders seventy men who were to be deemed worthy of taking part in the godly work and filling the people with the spirit of God — and at a time when the people have been shown in such a poor light — show us how the knowledge of God and devotion to Him and His intentions for Israel must have struck deep roots in quite a large circle in the midst of the masses who were yet to be educated up to a similar height.

מזקני ישראל. Up till now, and even before the historical beginning of the nation, “זקנים״, “elders”, had been there, and had taken a prominent authoritative position among the people (see Ex. 3,16, and the following chapter, as well as Levit. 9,1); yea, as we shall hear at once, they had an official activity, they were שוטריו, the overseers who watched over the duties which the people should perform in their life. Out of these elders who already had influence on the people brought about in a free national manner by the confidence the people had in them, and who accordingly had the kind of parental relation to them which Moses complained that he lacked (V.12), seventy are to be called to work together with Moses in the education of the people, and this calling is to be publicly conferred on them by God.

אספה לי not אספה in general, not אספה לך to satisfy the personal feeling of requiring assistance which has come to you but אספה לי, a permanent institution for the realisation of My purpose is to be founded in the nation. This was the institution of the supreme national tribune, the Sanhedrin, which was to consist of seventy members together with a Presiding Elder — as here the seventy elders with Moses. They have to consider themselves, for all future time, as only the co-helpers under Moses for seeing that the task transmitted by Moses becomes accomplished by and in the nation.

V. 17. אצלתי,וירדתי ודברתי עמך ואצלתי: by its fundamental meaning אצל designates something which is left free from something else, not absorbed by it, hence, in space “next”, the point where the space occupied by something comes to an end. Hence also אצילי ידים where the arms border on the body, the shoulder; the space which remains outside a sphere or province (Is. 41,9); and people who do likewise (Ex. 24,11). If we compare the places, Gen. 27,36 הלא אצלת לי ברכה and Eccl. 2,10, לא אצלתי מהם, in which אצל occurs as a verb, in both cases it obviously does not mean to take something away from a somebody which is in his possession, but not to let something come into somebody’s possession, to keep something back from somebody (to keep it “next” to him, outside him), which could have very well come to him. And so here it would not mean: “I shall take some of the spirit that is in you and lay it on them”, but, “I will keep back some of the spirit which comes upon you (when I speak to you) and lay it on them. When I speak to you I will let some of the spirit that otherwise comes over you alone, come over them too. Thereby they will become a spiritual part of your personality, will belong spiritually most intimately to you.

מן הרוח אשר עליך. The term used for imparting the spirit of prophecy is sharply differentiated from those used referring to every other kind of spirit which God grants. The spirit of God is in Joseph. (Gen. 41,38). God filled Bezalel with spirit of God (i.e. inspired I.L.) Ex. 31,8 and XXXV,31). Joshua was full of the spirit of wisdom (Deut. 34,9). God planted His holy spirit in the people, through Moses. (Is. LXIII.11). The spirit of God which armed Gideon with courage (Judges 6,34). Similarly in Ezek. 2,2 and III,24) and in Chron. 24,20 and in II Chron. 12,18, “in”, is used. All such gifts of spirit from God were an increase of the spiritual capacity of the recipients. What resulted from such special spiritual gifts and inspiration did not exceed the normal measure of human capacity. It remained human words and human acts, borne and elevated by special gifts and inspiration from God. But the spirit of prophecy does not proceed from within, הרוח אשר על, it comes onto a person, over him, rests on him. Thus of the spirit of prophecy which came over Saul, (I. Sam. 10,6 and 10), over his messengers (ibid. XIX,20), over Azariah (II. Chron. 15,1), over Ezekiel (Ezek. 11,5), over Isaiah (LXI,1), over the servant of God, over Israel, over all mankind (Is. 42,1; XLIV,3 and LIX,21) as well as Joel 3,1. It is a power of God, a Hand of God, יד ה׳ which comes over a person (Ezek. 1,2; III,21 & XXXVII,1) it is something Divine of which a man becomes the bearer, bringer and herald, something that comes to him from without, from above to him, on him, which raises him above the level surface of normal human beings and which makes his humanity into a step of the Divine on earth. What he says and what he does is God’s Word and God’s doing and the man is merely His conveyer and His agent. Thus the acts of strength of Samson were also accomplished by the spirit of God coming over him (Judges 14,6 and 19 and XV,14), and just by that denomination designated as supernatural.

V. 18. התקדשו וגו׳. We have already repeatedly had occasion to remark that the fundamental meaning of קדש is being ready for a purpose in general, so that קָדֵשׁ designates the complete giving oneself up even to the grossest depravity. So that התקדשו here can mean just quite generally “hold yourselves prepared”. But as, nevertheless, התקדש elsewhere always has the meaning of holding oneself ready for a serious solemn moment, here, too, the use of this expression could have the underlying idea that the enjoyment of a treasure long withheld from us, and finally granted to us by God, is always a serious moment worthy of earnest thought. When God denies a request or desire it is never from lack of power or of good will. What He denies us is always denied for our own good, and if finally it is granted to us at our unseemly persistent pressure, we can well consider whether the granting will really prove more beneficial for us than the previous denial was. So Rashi also takes it הזמינו עצמכם לפורענות.

V. 19—20. לא יום וגו׳. It will be given you in such quantity that you will not only satisfy your momentary lustful longing, but you will be able to eat for a whole month until you are replete and sick of it. יצא מאפכם is a hyperbolical expression for super-repletion. You will be so full of it that it will seek all possible means of egress. זרא as זרה means, to throw away, cf. תזרם כמו דוד, צא תאמר לו (Is. 30,22), “Cast them away as a menstruous cloth: get thee hence, shalt thou say unto it”, it is not far-fetched to say that זרא means “to vomit”. — יען כי מאסתם את ה׳ אשר בקרבכם the intimate spiritual relationship to God, which your isolation has given you, and which should more than compensate you for any deprivations, if indeed there be any, has lost all value for you, and לפניו, in full view of His Presence which should indeed well bring to your minds what you have gained. You weepingly ask למה זה .למה זה יצאנו וגו׳: we see nothing in our present circumstances which could be a reason for our exodus from Egypt.

V. 21—22. ויאמר משה וגו׳. Inasmuch as God answered Moses’s complaint in the urgency of the moment, simply by the charge to pick out the elders and attached the injunction thereto to tell the people they would receive satisfaction on the next day, he could well take it that the appointment of the elders was itself the means to give that satisfaction, and that he, with the assistance of the new executive board, was to attend to the feeding of the people. He could believe that this feeding of the people was the first task to which the seventy men were to render him assistance. The immediate urgency was to satisfy the people, the lack of assistance of which Moses complained was a matter for the future and if it had no connection with satisfying the immediate outcry then he would have expected the provision of meat to be seen to first, and then the election of the elders. So that Moses must have assumed that this provision was expected to lie within the sphere of the ordinary duties for him and the elders to attend to from the natural sources at their disposition, and hence his amazed cry ואתה אמרת בשר אתן — !שש מאות וגו׳, is not an actual quotation of what God said, but the implication contained in it. “Thou sayest, I should etc.”. Similarly to אלקים דבר בקדשו אעלזה אחלקה שכם: “God spake in His Sanctuary, I shall be happy, I shall divide Schechem”. (Ps. 60,8) — צאן — .הצאן וגו׳ and בקר require שחיטה but for fish simple אסיפה suffices (Chulin, 27b).

V. 23. היד ה׳ תקצר. It does not say here, as it does in Gen. 18,14 היפלא מה׳ דבר, for Moses quite correctly recognised that here there was no question of a miracle to occur, in which case there would not have been the slightest doubt of its result, in his mind. But he imagined that he was directed to the sphere of the national sources at his disposition and therefore asked for a solution of the apparent impossibility. To which he was given the reply that, without resorting to miracles, God’s Power was quite sufficient to be able to bring about what was demanded by His words out of the sphere of the quite natural existing conditions. היקרך (see on Gen. 24,12): whether My Word, although it seems quite beyond what you can expect, will not actually come to pass. This יקרך exactly designates the coming event as being something which certainly does lie quite out of human reckoning or expectation, but nevertheless occurs by quite natural means, from causes which are directed by God to accomplish the intended result.

When we consider that by the election of the seventy elders to help Moses in the directing of the nation, the institution of the Sanhedrin was founded (Sanhedrin 2a and 16b) which throughout all the coming centuries, directed its people in the most varied conditions to which God led them, and which was to be the messenger of the Word of God even in times when Moses had long departed this world, and no public miracles would occur to support the realisation of God’s word: then the whole character of this event — its improbability even in the eyes of Moses at the moment when he had to deliver God’s message to the people; its being fulfilled within the realm of natural existing conditions, only these conditions being directed by God to accomplish His purpose — can be understood in its deep relationship to this election of elders. This also gives us the reason why the election had to precede the event, which, after all, had the purpose of satisfying a temporary requirement of the people. Well could, and can, all future זקנים of the Jewish people, whenever they had, and have to stand up for the Word of God in times when, according to all human reckoning, the conditions seem to offer no support to the realisation of the Word they have to represent, well could, and can, they always look back to this first moment of the election of the first Jewish זקנים and imbibe confidence, and feel assured that, as long as the Word they bring and represent is truly the Word of God, they can quietly trust to the invisible management of God which even without heaven and earth collapsing, quite within the sphere of natural causes, though completely beyond the reckoning of human shortsightedness, knows how to arrange circumstances favourably to bring about the realisation of their words. The first event in which they had to assist gave our זקנים the grounds for confidence for the whole of their future work.

V. 24. ויצא משה. “Moses went out” from the place where God had spoken to him perhaps the אהל משה, into the public sphere of the people. He went into their midst and transmitted to them the words of God as recorded in V.18-20 which could well have brought the thinking part of the nation to come to their senses.

V. 25. וירד וגו׳ וידבר אליו, the text does not tell us what it was that God said to Moses. Is it to bring home to the minds of all future Sanhedrins that date from this moment, the fact that not everything that God said to Moses is recorded in the written script of the Torah? Is it to indicate to them that the oral Word of God, the תשב״פ (the Torah that was to remain unwritten but to be transmitted traditionally by word of mouth I.L.) was to be the basis of the activity for which they were just being elected? — וַיָאצֶל, an unusual form, as קל of אצל it would be ויֹאצל. The form וַיַצֵל in which the word occurs would indicate a הפעיל from צול, the root of מצולה related to צלל, the conception of the dark depths. Perhaps the intention in using this form was to indicate the disparity between the degree of the Spirit that was given to the elders and that granted to Moses. It was only a deep shadow of his spirit. — נבא ,ויתנבאו (see on Gen. 20,7). If נבא (related to נבע) means the gushing forth of the Word of God, so that הִנָבֵא, the passive form, would mean: to be brought into a vessel through which the Word of God gushes forth, to be an organ of the Word of God, then הִתְנַבֵּא would mean to offer oneself to be a vessel of the spring, to be an organ of the Word of God. The Hithpael form is predominently used for a lower stage of the prophetic word, a preliminary stage or an isolated case of it (cf. I. Sam. 10,5, 6, 10 and XIX,23 & 24). The expression used for serious words of prophecy is always in the Niphal form: ולא יספו — .הנבא and never again. Only in this moment of their being chosen were they granted the honour of participating in the Spirit of God that descended on Moses as a proof of their being called henceforth to be at one with Moses, and to consider every Word of God given to Moses as being given likewise to them to see that it is carried out.

V. 26. וישארו וגו׳. Seventy elders were gathered by Moses about the Tent. As is evident from this verse, Eldad and Madad should also have gone out with them to the Tent, they were amongst those who had been marked by Moses for that purpose. בכתובים. But as only seventy in all were to be elected, we can take it, that, to show no preference, Moses had picked out seventy-two, two from each tribe, and left it for God to decide which two weer not to be elected, as being the least worthy to be accorded the spirit of God. Out of modesty Eldad and Madad on their own account remained behind. They were convinced that they were the least worthy of all those worthy men, and just because of this modesty, although they remained in the camp amongst the people, the spirit of prophecy descended on them too. This is in accordance with one opinion in Sanhedrin 17a. According to another opinion, there, Moses cast lots for the seventy-two, and these two drew blanks.

V. 28. אדני משה כלאם. Joshua took the attitude of Eldad and Madad to be an infringement on Moses’s authority, a violation of his prerogative. The chosen elders were granted a participation in the spirit of prophecy only as sharing Moses’s spirit, but Eldad and Madad appeared on the scene by their own independent election.
V. 29. המקנא אתה לי. Are you standing up for my rights? Do you find Eldad and Madad’s conduct an infringement on my rights, and think that you have to stand up for them? (see on Ch. 5,14).

This behaviour of Eldad and Madad at the moment when the elders were called to form the first Sanhedrin, and Moses’s remarks thereon are of the deepest importance for all the successors of this Jewish “Institute of Elders” for all time. It proclaims that by the appointment of the highest intellectual and spiritual authority in Israel, no monopoly in intellectuality or spirituality is to be formed, that the spiritual gifts of God are in no way dependent on office or profession, and that the lowest in the nation could be considered as equally worthy of the spirit of God as the first official in the highest office. But Moses’s answer to Joshua remains for all teachers and leaders as the brilliant example they should keep before their eyes as the highest ideal aim of their work, viz., to make themselves superfluous, that the people of all classes and ranks reach such a spiritual level that they no longer require teachers and leaders. And indeed the successors of these “elders” have well inherited the spirit of their Moses, have recognised their highest mission to be להרביץ תורה בישראל to make the knowledge of the Torah the broadest foundation of life in the people, and have proclaimed והעמידו תלמידים הרבה (“establish many “learners”), many pupils” I.L.) as the first maxim for all spiritual leaders of their people. With his “המקנא אתה לי״, “are you jealous for me”? our Moses has broken down the dividing wall between “intellectuals” and the “lower classes”, between clergy and laity, for ever in Israel. In Sanhedrin 17a, various opnions are given as to what the prophecy of Eldad and Madad proclaimed. According to one it was concerning the coming event of the quails.
