That there could have been a doubt as to the mode of execution although the dictum מחלליה מות יומת had already been made, and, unless more precisely specialised, סתם מיתה is בחנק (see Levit. on XX,10) is explained by תוספות (Sanhedrin 78b and Baba Bathra 119a) as being due to the similarity in the concept of חילול שבת בפרהסיא and ע״ז which made Moses suppose that the punishments of both might also be similar and here again we would have the close connection between this פרשת מקשש and the immediately preceding פרשת ע״ז.

(On the introductory words ויהיו בני ישראל במדבר the Sifri has the sentence:- בגנות ישראל הכתוב מדבר שלא שמרו אלא שבת ראשונה ושניה היללו. If one considers that מחלליה מות יומת was in any case said only after מתן תורה, the Sifri can not be referring with this שבת ראשונה to the command of שבת given at the time of the manna but can only refer to the Sabbath after מתן תורה where first of all the comprehensive command לא תעשה כל מלאכה was given. It could even be questionable whether תולש and מעמר were altogether forbidden before מתן תורה and whether the prohibition extended beyond הוצאה (carrying I.L.) and אפיה ובישול (cooking I.L.). Several of the difficulties raised by Mizrachi on V.32 could perhaps be solved by this remark).

V. 35—36. מחוץ למחנה, כל העדה, רגום אותו וגו׳, ויאמר וגו׳ (see on Levit. 20,2, and on XXIV,13, 14, 16 & 23). ויאמר וגו׳. At the מקלל Levit. 24,13 in the quite similar case it says: וידבר ה׳ וגו׳, there a quit[[illegible]]new legal decision was pronounced, the death penalty had not yet be[[illegible]] declared for blasphemy, hence וידבר ה׳. Here it was only an explanation of the מות יומת which had already been ordained, hence ויאמר ה׳.

V. 37. ויאמר ה׳. It is extremely seldom that actual laws are introduced by ויאמר. Where it does occur it is usually explanations of laws already given, such as: ויאמר וגו׳ זאת הקת הפסח (Ex. 12,43), ויאמר וגו׳ אך את שבתתי וגו׳ (ibid. XXXI,12), ויאמר וגו׳ in V.35 just before, or where it is the consequence of an ordinance previously made, as וידבר וגו׳ אחרי מות וגו׳ ויאמר וגו׳ (Levit; XVI, 1), or where the law that follows is attached to some event which preceded it, as ויאמר אל אהרן וגו׳ (Numb. 18,1), or, finally where the very first law was given to Moses: ויאמר וגו׳, החדש הזה וגו׳ which the law given is declared as the goal of all the preceding events and God’s guidance of them (concerning Levit. 21,1, refer to commentary thereon). Here the ויאמר וגו׳ not only attaches the law introduced by it to the event immediately preceding it, but, as we shall see, it presents itself altogether as the summing-up of all the events and laws contained in this שלח לך chapter.

V. 38. דבר וגו׳ ,ואמרת וגו׳ ועשו להם וגו׳. As we have already remarked in Jeshurun V, p.313 (and reproduced in the Gesammelte Schriften in the article on symbolism I.L.), had this been a clearly irrefutable apodictic command it would have been worded ועשו .דכר וגו׳ ,ויעשו להם וגו׳ pronounces the fulfilling of the command as being the result of the explanation and teaching which Moses was to give them, the ואמרת אליהם, more as a result expected to have come by itself. “Explain to them, bring all the preceding and all the consequences that are attached to it so home to them that they will gladly make “fringes” on their garments as I bid you”. Menachoth 42b, learns from the wording דבר וגו׳ ,אל בני ישראל ,ועשו וגו׳ that the ציצית have to be put on by a ישראל, that ציצית בנכרי פסולה and also Sukka 9a that ציצית גזולה פסולה for ועשו להם ,משלהם. Also from גדילים תעשה לך (Deut. 22,12) that בעינן טויה ועשיה לשמה, that the whole preparation of the fringes, the spinning as well as attaching them to the garments must be done for the purpose of the Mitzva.

ציצית from צוץ (related to סוס ,שוש ,זוז) a movement pressing outwards from inside, hence ציץ, sprouting, blossoming, from the stem and branches of plants, and as a noun a shoot, a blossom; on animal bodies, wings and ציצית curls, then also ציץ, the protruding band on the forehead of the high-priest, and in rabbinic Hebrew זיז a projection. הציץ piercingly peering through a lattice. Here, according to the Halacha, threads “issuing forth out of garments אין ציצית אלא יוצא״, the word ציצית only means something that comes out from something else” (Menachoth 41b) אין ציצית אלא ענף, “Tzitzis designates threads sprouting,” as in Ezek. 8,3 יקחני בציצת ראשי it denotes “a lock of my head” (ibid. 42a).

על כנפי בגדיהם not על בגדיהם, anywhere on their garments, but על כנפי, there where the garment ends are the ציצת to begin, they are to be that which “sprouts forth” from the garments. They are accordingly to be fastened on the corners of the garments not above three thumb-breadths and not below a קשר גודל — the length of the upper joint of the thumb — from the edge. They are to come out על כנפי וגו׳ above the end of the garment before where the garment ends, נוטפת על הקרן “flowing down” out of and on the corner, (ibid. 42a).

בגדיהם. We have repeatedly had occasion to remark — at the בגדי כהונה (Ex. Ch. XXVIII, נגעים Levit. 13,41), כלאים (ibid. XIX,19) — that in the Torah wool and linen are taken as the real materials used for clothes, and hence by בגדים סתם as a rule only woollen and linen garments are to be understood. In accordance with that there is one opinion (Menachoth 39b) that holds that the duty of tzitzis מדאוריתא only applies to garments of wool or linen, and if made of other materials the mitzva would be only דרבנן. Rambam adopts this view as halacha. But according to another view expressed there in the Gemora the duty of tzitzis applies to garments made of any material whatsoever, (see below). בגדיהם, even דשותסות, a garment for common use of more than one owner also has to have tzitzis. But, on the other hand, טלית שאולה, a borrowed garment need not have tzitzis, it must be, as it says in Deut. 22,12, כסותך, thy garment (Chulin, 36a). ונתנו על ציצית הכנף וגו׳, as here הכנף is used by itself and not limited by the addition כנף הבגד, another opinion sees in this the extention of the duty of tzitzis beyond that which is implied by the word בגד i.e., wool and linen, to materials of any sort, and then is also taught regarding the material out of which the tzitzis itself is made, :ציצית הכנף מין הכנף; the corner of a garment is presumably of the same material as the garment itself, and taken in conjunction with the idea that the meaning of צמר ופשתים applies also to the tzitzis-command from the juxtaposition of verses 11 & 12 in Deut. XXII, (refer to it), the following canon results: צמר ופשתים, פוטרין בין במינן בין שלא במינן, שאר מינין במינן פוטרין שלא במינן אין פוטרין i.e. tzitzis made out of wool or linen, as the general material for clothing are valid for garments made out of any material, but if made out of other materials are only valid for garments made out of that same material (see רשב״א on Sab. 27b), (e.g. silk tzitzis would be no good on a woollen talis, but could be used on a silk one I.L.).

ועשו וגו׳ ונתנו וגו׳. These two terms are mutually complementary. ועשו could be taken to mean that the tzitzis could be made with the garment, when it is woven the threads are left loose hanging at the ends of each corner. Against that ונתנו על indicates that the tzitzis were separate and then brought to the corners of the garment, but only in such a manner that ועשו וגו׳ that they are firmly attached to them. From the two terms together the prescription emerges that they must be fastened to the corners of the garment by a firm knot (ספרי). In Menachoth 39a it takes it that it is also indicated therefrom that קשר עליון דאוריתא that this joining the tzitzis to the garment by a firm knot is the way prescribed; by the Torah, and that it required a special explanation to allow סדין בציצית, a linen garment to be provided with tzitzis even if it meant doing away with the prohibition of כלאים (Deut. 22,11 & 12), so that the Torah assumes a firm joining of the tzitzis with the garment. However סדין בציצית (woollen tzitzis on a linen garment I.L.) is not allowed מדרבנן as a guard against lessening the importance of “schatnis” in general (Menachoth 40a and b).

The tzitzis-command contains two prescriptions: ועשו להם ציצית and ונתנו על ציצת, (a) to make fringes on the corners of garments, and (b) on these fringes to put a thread of תכלת-coloured wool. The former, the ציצת הכנף have no prescribed special colour. As fringes of the garment ציצת הכנף they are presumed to be מין הכנף similar to the garment also in colour, and as garments were predominantly white, they are referred to in general terms as לבן, white. But the colour white is entirely immaterial and לבן only means: not תכלת (Menachoth 38a). To the fringes of the garment one thread of תכלת is to be added. But לבן and תכלת are not absolutely essential to one another, התכלת אינה מעכבת את הלבן, והלבן אינו מעכב את התכלת, in the absence of the one, the duty is fulfilled by the other alone (ibid. 38a). The number of the threads, and the proportion of תכלת to לבן is not quite certain, the most generally accepted tradition is eight threads, that is to say four threads doubled over in the middle and passed through a hole in the corner of the garment and knotted together so that eight ends hang down, and according to רמב״ם half of one thread was dyed תכלת so that there were seven לבן and one תכלת (Menachoth 41b; רמב״ם, Tzitzis 1,6).

The tzitzis-command given here is essentially complemented by what is said in Deut. 22,12: גדלים תעשה לך על ארבע כנפות כסותך אשר תכסה בה. What here is called ציצת and פתיל, free threads hanging down (ענף like ציצת ראשי see V.37) is called there גדיל ;גדלים, cord (a thread “enlarged” in circumference by tightly joining together several threads). (Thus גדלים מעשה שרשרות Kings I. 7,17 מעשה עבות in Ex. 28,14 is translated by Onkelos as עובד גדילו, and in rabbinic Hebrew גודל is not the great finger but the “thick” one the thumb). So that tzitzis is גדיל as well as ענף, i.e. after the threads have been knotted on to the garment they are wound round by one of the eight threads into a tight cord, גדיל, for part of their length and then the rest allowed to hang free, ענף. It should be one third גדיל and two thirds נויי תכלת שליש גדיל ושני .ענף שלישי ענף, (Menachoth 39a). From this complementing verse it follows that it is only a four-cornered garment that has to have tzitzis on its corners; if it has only three, it requires no tzitzis, and if it has five, still only four have to be provided with tzitzis (ibid. 43b). But the four tzitzis form a mutually essential unit so that if on one corner the tzitzis are lacking or unfit in any way, the Mitzva has not been done at all. ארבע ציציות מעכבות זו את זו שארבעתם מצוה אהת (ibid. 37b).

תכלת is the special shade of sky-blue colour that formed the basic colour of the Sanctuary of the Torah (see Ex. on XXV,8 and XXVIII,43). No other shade of blue may be substituted for it, not any of the thousand similar קלא אילן colours. If the תכלת is not available the Mitzva is fulfilled by the לבן threads as already remarked.

V. 39. והיה לכם לציצת. After it has already said: ,ועשו להם ציצית ונתנו על ציצת וגו׳, if the Torah then goes on והיה לכם לציצת וגו׳ it must want to say that this is the purpose of the concept of “Tzitzis”, as well as of the external mode in which it is to be presented, and that this purpose is to be accomplished by וראיתם אתו etc. — וראיתם אתו sets daytime the time when one recognises things by one’s sense of sight as the time when the duty of tzitzis applies, פרט לכסות לילה (Menachoth 43a). Hence the tzitzis-command is one which is limited to a certain time, מצות עשה שהזמן גרמא, so that women are not bound to this duty (referring to this exclusion of women from certain of these mitzvas and their inclusion in others of the same nature see on Levit. 23,43, p.711 in my translation. I.L.). Opinions differ as to the application of this limitation of the mitzva of tzitzis to the day and excluding the night. According to רש״י and רמב״ם the time is the decisive factor, in daytime one would be bound to put tzitzis even if one wore night clothes, at night one would be free from the duty even if one wore day clothes. According to ר״ת and רא״ש the garment is the deciding factor, a night-garment is free from the tzitzesduty even if worn in the daytime, and a day-garment would have to have tzitzis even if worn at night (see Tur א״ח 18). According to the accepted Halacha tzitzis is חובת גברא and not חובת טלית i.e., the duty is only incumbent when a four-cornered garment is worn but כלי קופסא, a garment in the cupboard need not have tzitzis. On the other hand כסית סומא garments of a blind man have to have tzitzis. וראיתם אתו only fixes the time of ראיה in general, only designates day time in general, when things can be seen even if any particular individual is deprived of the possibility of seeing. ישנה בראיה אצל אחרים as the Gemora puts it in Menachoth 43a. But the mitzva of tzitzis is no irrefutable one. The Torah does not order that a garment with four corners must be worn. The duty in the Torah assumes that we will wear such a garment and expects us to impose this duty on ourselves. (Menachoth 41a; see on V.38).

וראיתם וגו׳. By this the fringes achieve the purpose which was expressed in the preceding והיה לכם לציצת. Looking at them is to act as a reminder of all God’s commandments, and thus to incite the resolution to observe them. ראיה מביאה לידי זכירה זכירה מביאה לידי מעשה, “Looking brings one to remembering, and remembering brings one to doing”. Menachoth 43b).

ולא תתורו וגו׳. On Ch. 13,2 we have already shown that תור, used with a subjective purpose designates an effort to get to know things as to how they can be of use and help to us. The mental activity designated by תור seeks to find out what is good or not good for us. לבב, one’s innermost heart forms wishes, עינים, the eyes seek the means to satisfy these wishes. And indeed, left to itself, it is only one’s ego, with all its requirements, urges and desires, which forms the motive of this “wishing heart”, and the eyes only recognise the material relationships of the material world. In the service of this “wishing heart” and recognising eye”, the judgment of one’s mind התר אחרי הלב והעין, will call everything “good” which is in accordance with one’s own sensuous nature; will call everything “bad” which does not offer satisfaction to it, or which even stands in the way of yielding such satisfaction. And also to achieve what is desirable and to avoid what stands in the way of being so, the mind which only “investigates and spies out” (לתור I.L.) things through the spectacles of the heart and eyes would only measure and value things according to their relationship to its own sphere, and fear or hope according to the result of that verdict. But where what is wished for and what is avoided, fear and hope are only formed by the dictates of a mind which forms its judgment from what “the heart and eye” direct, there, no place is left for God and His Law, no room for thoughts of God as the Director of our actions and of our fate, no room for God to have influence on what we desire or what we avoid, on our fears and hopes. Serving heart and eye does not agree with serving God, אחרי לבבכם ואחרי עיניכם אשר אתם זנים, following the dictates of your heart and your eye, you break faith with God.

But it is quite a different matter if God and His Torah form the fundamental basis of all our acts, the starting-point of all our considerations, thoughts and judgments; if we look on our whole being, with heart and eye, in the service of a Higher One, subordinate the wishes and dislikes of our own hearts to His wishes and dislikes. Then we feel at one with God, and we no longer feel that power and greatness lie in satisfying our senses or the dictates of our minds, but in the exertion of our moral will, which will we have absorbed into the Will of God. And with God we feel our own strength and power over our own world, while without Him the most gigantic force in our world shrinks to pygmy-like nothingness. And just as our wishes and dislikes, so also are our fears and hopes completely transformed when in place of being in the service of our hearts and eyes we enter the service of God.

Our verse is also thus explained in Berachoth 12b:- אחרי לבבכם זו מינות וכה״א אמר נבל בלבו אין אלקים, אחרי עיניכם זו הרהור עבירה שנאמר אותה קח לי כי היא ישרה בעיני, אתם זונים זו הרהור ע״ז וכה״א ויזנו אחרי בעלים and that lays down the profound truth that מינות, the denial of God, is not, as it ostensibly boasts to be, the father of a heart wishing to be free from the laws of morality, but is the child thereof. The נבל “the morally faded, withered one” tries to quieten his conscience by denying the existence of God. And מינות, denying God, degenerates into ע״ז, polytheism. Only the consciousness of God makes us spiritually free. He who, in order to escape the mastery of One Power, in a trice denies Its existence only throws himself under the yoke of בעלים, a host of blind forces of nature forcing him hither and thither without reason like a toy balloon in the wind. We make one further remark. We have frequently remarked on the fact that עולה (the elevating offering I.L.) is מכפר on עשה and at the same time on הרהור הלב and we took it that having sinful and empty vain thoughts was not so much a positive active giving oneself up to sin and evil and illusion (חטא I.L.) as neglect of occupying the mind with thoughts of godness and truth (an עשה I.L.). Where the mental energy fails to be directed to thoughts of goodness and truth, thoughts of sin and vain imaginations start by themselves. Here too the לא תתורו אחרי לבבכם וגו׳ is only the effect of the ראיה and זכירה directed to the עשית כל מצות ה׳.

V. 40. למען תזכרו וגו׳. V.39 spoke of the remembering God and of His Commandments which we are to keep which are to be brought to our minds by looking at the tzitzis. But the purpose of this remembering is למען תזכרו וגו׳ that in general, that without having to use this reminder, by ourselves we keep God’s commandments constantly in mind and fulfil them. In V.39 the tzitzis-symbol is there in front of our eyes and brings God’s commandments to our minds at a moment when we have allowed them to escape our attention, hence they are referred to as מצות ה׳ and not as מצותי. But V.40 declares the goal to be that it is not the symbol that we are to have in mind, but God Himself in His special relation to us — אלקיכם ,מצותי — and let that so constantly and completely fill our minds that we go through life always conscious of our duty, so that we do truly belong to our God with the whole of our existence, which is what is meant by being “holy” unto Him. V.39 ensures us the stage to be reached as human beings, V.40 raises us to the calling of Jews.

V. 41. אני ה׳ אלקיכם וגו׳. And as the source of our being conscious of God as the Director and Manager of our fate and Ordainer of our actions, and of our calling as Man and Jew, the tzitzis-symbol directs our minds to the fact of the יציאת מצרים; the exodus from Egypt, where God let us experience personally His relation to us as our Liberator, Saviour and Lawgiver — הוצאתי וגו׳ להיות וגו׳. That experience forms the basis for all time of this consciousness of ours, and gives us, for all eternity the guiding principle for all our thoughts and all our desires, the all-embracing Word of God אני ה׳ אלקיכם.

If we consider how the Torah itself expresses the meaning and purpose of these tzitzis threads on our garments (verses 39-41), there can be absolutely no doubt in the matter. Quite clearly they are to be reminders, by calling to mind the Divine Torah and our duty to it, to guard us against wrong ideas which would lead us to defection from God and our duty; and to keep us faithful, pure and holy to our mission on earth as human beings and Jews. The question only remains as to the connection between this means which the Torah has chosen and the ideas it is to remind us of. Then, first of all we think we can say that just as the Mila on the body, the Tephillin on arm and head, the Mezuzah on the door of the home have the purpose of sanctifying the body, the arm, the head, the home to which they are placed as symbols, by devoting them to their godly purpose, so also the tzitzis on our garments are to announce the sanctification of human clothing by devoting it to the purpose which God has indicated for it. To find the meaning of tzitzis on clothes we must start with the meaning of clothes for the moral calling of man. We must do this all the more as the name tzitzis as “shoots” (see on V.38 I.L.) does not only designate the external appearance as threads “growing out” of the garment, but also their symbolic purpose והיה לכם לציצת (V.39 — cf. ועליו יציץ נזרו Ps. 132,18) and thereby clearly expresses:- by them human clothes are to “sprout”, i.e. achieve the blossom and fruit which lie in them as the purpose of their existence; and ציצת הכנף says to us:- let your clothes not be unfruitful, do not cover yourselves in vain and without thought in human garments, let clothes fulfil the purpose on you for which they were given to you!

But, according to its historical origin (refer to Gen. 3,7 & 21) the relation of clothing to our moral human calling is such an intimate one, and the going astray which preceded it, and against which it is designed to protect, is not only related and similar to that which is mentioned in our V.39 here, but is so identically similar to it, that it seems to us that the association of ideas could hardly be more striking. One has only to bring to mind the words ותרא האשה כי טוב העץ למאכל וכי תאוה הוא לעינים ונהמד העץ להשכיל (ibid. 6). “and the woman saw that the tree was good for food and that it was tempting to the sight, and appealing to the understanding” to say to oneself: Men came to disregard the command of God because they were תרים אחרי לבבם ועיניהם “went astray after their own hearts and eyes” and called that “טוב good”, which according to their lustful eyes and their minds seeking out the satisfaction of their senses, promised such satisfaction. And if, such placing themselves under the dictates of their hearts and eyes, they sank to the level of animal-wisdom which indeed is directed to place its judgment of what to desire and what to avoid on its own heart and eyes; and if they then learnt to cover their animal nakedness by the feeling of “shame”, that voice of God deep within the human breast, and then had this teaching confirmed and consecrated by the garments with which God provided them when He sent them out of Paradise for them to keep constantly in mind that the human calling is something different and higher than that of animals, and that he is directed to submit his power of judgment as to what is “good or bad” to the dictates of a Higher Being; then the admonishment of clothes, translated into words, could not run otherwise or more strikingly than:- וזכרתם את כל מצות ה׳ ועשיתם אתם ולא תתורו אחרי לבבכם ואחרי עיניכם אשר אתם זנים אחריהם (“and ye shall remember all the commandments of God and do them and ye shall not go astray after your hearts and after your eyes following which ye become unfaithful to Me”)! And so the tzitzis as “sprouts from garments” express already by themselves, the demand to obey this admonishment, the meaning innate in human clothing.

But, after the most generally accepted tradition, the number of tzitzis threads is eight. Of these, seven, as ציצת הכנף, as sprouts coming out from the garment, are לבן, have the colour of the garment, and represent the idea already contained by the garment itself. To these, as an eighth, the פתיל תכלת the sky-blue thread is to be added. After they have all been firmly attached to the corners of the garment by tight knots, the seven “white” and the eighth תכלת threads are wound together to make a cord of a third of their length, and this firm third made permanent by tight knots, and the remaining two thirds left to hang freely down.

All this teaches the firm energy we have to use to live up to the “admonition of clothing”. “Six”, “seven”, “eight”. [The symbolism of the number seven: Elsewhere Hirsch has shown, from its occurrence in general in the Torah — apart from actual laws — that it expresses completion, consummation. The origin of this meaning is to be found in the work of the Creation. The visible material world created in six days received with the seventh day a day of remembrance of, and bond with its invisible Lord and Creator, and thereby its completed consummation. Similarly the symbolism of the number seven in the Menora, in the Temple, in the Mussaf offerings, in the sprinklings of the blood on Yom Kippur, in the Festivals of Pessach and Succoth, in Sabbath, Schmita, Tumma etc. etc. The symbolism of the number eight: starting afresh on a higher level, an octave higher. The eighth day for Mila, Schmini Azereth and Israel as the eighth of God’s Creations. With the creation of Israel God laid the foundation for a fresh, higher mankind and a fresh higher world, for that שמים חדשים and that ארץ חדשה for which Israel and its mission is to be the beginning and instrument (Is. 65,17).] So that there are three elements in us. (a) our material sensuous bodies, like the rest of the created visible world = 6; (b) the breath of free-will, invisible, coming from the Invisible One = 7; (c) the calling of Jew, coming from the historical choice of Israel = 8. I.L.); these are the three elements out of which the tzitzis threads show us to be woven. All these three elements are given to us, all three are woven into our being and are to be realised in completing our calling. But in these three energies two are to be the directing and ruling ones; the “six” in us is to subordinate itself to the seventh and eighth which are also given as part of us, and is to allow itself to be overcome, wound round, by the firm restraining bonds of duty. This being “wound round by”, this bringing ourselves under the control of duty is the first indispensable condition for our carrying out our calling as human beings to which clothing admonishes us. It is that, the exercise of our own power of freedom in moral matters, that first makes us into human beings, makes us worthy of wearing clothing, keeps the animal element in us in the background, and of its own free will subordinate itself to the human element in us. But this subordination is no subversion, this overpowering no destruction. Once the bodily sensuality has submitted itself to the bonds of duty through the Divine and Jewish elements, it becomes completely equal to its brother-energies, and like them, is to expand in free development within the limits of Jewish human duty. Yea the freedom it then obtains is greater than the repression (two thirds to one third I.L.) and not only the seventh and eighth but also the six all flow out together in completely equal free development.

But the eighth thread, representing the power of Judaism is to be dipped in תכלת, in sky-blue dye, the colour of the horizon, which in its nature and name (coming from כלה the end I.L.) indicates the limit of human perception with which Man can enter the realm of the supernatural, and brings to our minds the revelation of God which we could see in the Lawgiving and in the events of our history, (which was also why it was the prime-colour of the Sanctuary of the Torah). This פתיל תכלת, sanctified to be a symbol of the Torah, by its presence — as well as by its absence being so strongly prohibited to be replaced by anything else however similar — preaches how it is only by the one Torah of God, once given and never able to be abrogated or replaced by anything else, that we are able to accomplish our Jewish mission for mankind and therein to find the bond and covenant of God with us. The eighth thread of the tzitzis — whether waiting for the תכלת colour or having it — stamps us all as אנשי קדש as men of a holy calling as members of the ממלכת כהנים וגוי קדוש!

But the tzitzis-command, like most of the other mitzvas reminding us of God and our duty, is confined to the day-time or to a day-garment representing day-time activity. It is not only when human activity goes to rest that acknowledging the sovereignty of God begins for us. It is in the midst of Man’s day-time activity in using his power of mastering the world that God’s Torah plants the standards of its symbols. The upright, active, working man is, in his greatness and with his greatness, to be acknowledgingly near to God. Not our passive enduring, our active working life is to be the tribute on the altar of God’s Torah. In life, in active working life does God’s Torah expect to be realised by us, וראיתם אתו וזכרתם את כל מצות ה׳ ועשיתם אתם ולא תתורו וגו׳.
Confining it to day-time makes tzitzis into a מצות עשה שהזמן גרמא which only the masculine sex have to observe, (see Levit. 23,43, p.711).

But clothes have two meanings. They are “בגד״, by covering the animal phase on the human body, to bring to mind the moral character of human beings. But they are also כסות, protective covering against the inclemencies of the weather. At the same moment that his moral weakness made clothing necessary to remind Man of his moral calling, at that same moment God’s educative Love drove him out of the agreeable mild comfortable charm of Nature’s Paradise into the raw antagonism of a world presenting “thorns and thistles”, and protective clothing became necessary, and he had to carry on the mission of humanity under conditions of the most changeable diversity of weather and temperature. So that just as the tzitzis-command for clothes as בגד, as covering for the sensuous body, runs ועשו להם ציצית על כנפי בגדיהם לדרתם, and thereby expresses our carrying out our Jewish mission for humanity for all time, independently of all changes in the times, לדרתם, in the same way the same command for clothes as כסות, as protective covering is expressed thus: גדלים תעשה לך על ארבע כנפות כסותך and thereby makes our carrying out our Jewish mission for humanity unconditionally applicable to every place in the wide world, and independent of all changes of climate or conditions. Wherever, and in whatever isolation thou mayest have to set thy wandering foot down, everywhere, in ארבע כנפות, in every direction, be it to the south or north, east or west, thou art to bear the same admonishment with thee, to carry out the one same task wherever thou mayest be. Firmly tied is the גדיל to be which reminds thee of thy mission to humanity in the ideal of thy Jewish calling and which demands the cheerful self-controlling subjection of all thy mental gifts and endeavours to the restraining cords of God’s Torah. No time and no place can loosen a single thread of this cord of thy duty, לדרתם and בארבע כנפות in every age and in every place is thy human existence to be absorbed by thy Jewish calling.

But just as God’s educative love gave Man the first garments only after the feeling of shame had by itself awakened in him the necessity to cover his nakedness, so does He leave His command for tzitzis to be fulfilled by the free impulse of our feeling of the necessity to be educated. It is only after we have, of our own free-will, clad ourself with a four-cornered garment that the command of tzitzis applies to us at all. (V.38). The sanctification of our lives to be brought about by tzitzis presupposes our own consciousness of our requiring such a means of attaining holiness.

We have presented the mitzva of tzitzis more fully and worked out the symbolism etc., in greater detail in the Yeshurun 5th year (now reproduced in the Gesammelte Schriften Vol.3, under the heading of Grundlinien einer judischen Symbolik, a truly wonderful article I.L.) and would refer our readers to it.

If now we look back on the whole of this section שלח לך of which the tzitzis command forms the conclusion, this latter at once appears in the closest connection with the מרגלים episode, just as we saw that the whole group of mitzvas which followed viz. שגגת ע״ז ומגדף ,חלה ,נסכים with the attached מקושש all came from it. The מרגלים were sent out לתור את הארץ as their task was repeatedly called. By failing in this תרים-mission they came to open defection from God and dragged the nation in with them in the fateful sin. And now at the end the institution of tzitzis comes and daily and hourly warns us: לא תתורו אחרי לבבכם ואחרי עיניכם אשר אתם זנים אחריהם — is this anything other than a daily and hourly warning against the same error into which the תרים את הארץ fell? It was only אחרי לבבכם, only in service of their own heart’s desires, and אחרי עיניכם on what appeared to their eyes to be likely to achieve those desires that they based the judgment of their minds and reported on the characteristics of the land and drew their conclusions thereon. But they forgot that it was not אחרי לבבכם but אחרי ה׳ as Caleb did, that they were to go; that they stood in the service of God; that they were to enter the Land in His service and for His service, so that God and the fulfilment of His Will, and to be worthy or not of His hoped-for support was the only yardstick by which they had to measure themselves and the Land and its inhabitants in their relation to each other for the future that lay before them. It was only that they were תרים אחרי לבבם ואחרי עיניהם that they completely lost the thought of God as the Leader of their actions and Decider of their fate, and in spite of their spiritual relation to God, shrunk in their own minds to the size of grasshoppers without any power, and the Land and its inhabitants, in spite of their moral depravity, grew to gigantic proportions quite imposible to conquer. In their eyes that which God rejected became “good” and what was promised by God was in their eyes “bad”, and in face of this reversal of judgment the gates of the revived Paradise which had been promised them clanged to before them, just as once the same reversal of judgment had lost Paradise to the first human beings.
There we would have a further and final trait which makes the parallel of the cases complete.

By תור אחרי הלב והעינים Man lost Paradise, and as a warning against future similar errors and as an educational means of reminder of consciousness of duty in the future he was given: clothes. By תור אחרי הלב והעינים Israel in the wilderness lost the regaining of Paradise which was meant to begin with the ארץ זבת חלב ודבש, and as warning against future similar errors and as an educational means of reminder of consciousness of duty in the future they were given: tzitzis on their garments.

The former was a denial of God as being the Guide to our actions, the latter denial of His being the Decider of our fate. פרשת ציצית takes them both together, and, referring to יציאת מצרים declares the fact that guarantees us both (Ex. 3,12) and proclaims אני ה׳ אלקיכם אשר הוצאתי .אתכם מארץ מצרים להיות לכם לאלקים אני ה׳ אלקיכם

V. 1. שלח לך was the section of the rebellion against God. קרח is the section of the rebellion against Moses. ויקח קרח without any object. Similarly in II. Sam. 18,18 ויצב לו בחייו את מצבת וגו׳. Grammatically the whole following events is the object of the verb, the לקיחה, logically both instances designate an unjustified procedure in their own interests. Absolum “took”, assumed the right to himself, had the presumption to have a monument erected to himself during his lifetime. Korach assumed the right to himself, had the presumption to question Moses and Aaron regarding their position in the nation. But as this is expressed by the term לקיחה it tells us at the same time that the motive for his procedure was a selfish one, what he did was for himself and the form in which he posed as being entirely in the interests of the public was just only a form, pure camouflage.

V. 2. ויקמו לפני משה וגו׳. The peculiar order of succession in which the participants in the uprising are introduced probably shows the degree of their participation. Korach appears as the instigator of the whole affair, hence ויקח קרח. Dathan, Abiram and On attached themselves to him as additional agitators for the rebellion. These four presented themselves before Moses, ויקמו וגו׳ after they had won over two hundred and fifty men from the people who supported their stand as agitators of the masses, ויקהלו על וגו׳.

V. 3. ויקהלו וגו׳ ויאמרו וגו׳. Korach, Dathan and Abiram presented themselves before Moses, and after they had collected two hundred and fifty men whom they had incited to support their reproaches and demands, spoke as representing the masses: רב לכם etc. Now as by כי the declaration כל העדה וגו׳ is given as the basis of the preceding assertion רב לכם, and the following question also is not adduced by מדוע but by ומדוע as a further question, it seems that they approached Moses with two separate assertions, or rather with an assertion and a reproach. First the assertion: כל העדה etc. and therefore רב לכם, the whole community, and indeed not כלה as a unit, but כולם in all its individual members, is holy and God is present in their midst: every individual of the six hundred thousand is holy and therefore near to God and so no priests are required to bring God near to them by expressing their thoughts and feelings in offerings on their behalf; and it is just to these six hundred thousand and not to any one person that God had promised His Presence, so that He requires no prophets to make His Word reach these six hundred thousand. Hence רב לכם, God is near to all of them and they are all near to Him therefore no Aaron and no Moses are required, hence the whole position of Moses and Aaron is a pretentious arrogance based on a false foundation. And further, if individuals are required at the head of the nation for national affairs in relation to God, why just Aaron and Moses, why not leave it to the nation to choose their leaders, what right have Aaron and Moses to place themselves (תתנשאו I.L.) at the head of the nation?

V. 4. וישמע משה וגו׳. Moses heard, or rather understood, the motive of these assertions and accusations raised against him. It was a denial of the Divine origin of his mission, and not indeed out of any erroneous conception which could be corrected, but out of honour-seeking jealousy, which, under the cloak of representing the public interests, only sought satisfaction of his own selfish interests, and for this purpose was trying to oust Moses and Aaron from their positions by flattering the self-complacency of the people with dazzling sophisms. For the premises on which Korach based his revolt were false and the deductions in their application to the circumstances to which he referred them, no less false. כל העדה כולם were by no means קדושים already, they were אנשי קדש (Ex. 22,30) men of a holy calling, קדושים יהיו (Levit. 17,1) they have the calling to become holy, and just by this calling are קדושים לאלקיהם (Numb. 15,40), are an ,עם קדוש לה׳ (Deut. 7,6) are men hallowed to God, a nation hallowed to God, belong with every fibre of their individual and national life exclusively to God; but קדושים “holy”, that they are not yet. And just so that they always work themselves indefatigably up to their holy calling, so that they do not mix up what they are with what they should be, do not imagine themselves already holy because they are hallowed to a holy calling, but that they should rather keep this holy calling of theirs always before them as the goal set by God for all their endeavours, just for that their holy calling was given a symbolic representation of its ideal realisation in the Sanctuary enclosing their “evidence of God”, which just for that reason nobody was allowed to consider himself worthy to approach without further ado, to which even an Aaron was only allowed to approach by God’s express command and even then not as his individual self but only clad in the garments symbolising his service. And just for that reason was it proclaimed for the people and priests alike: והזר הקרב יומת, because they would be placing what they actually are in place of what their calling is to be, and thereby kill the whole effectiveness of the Sanctuary. The whole ranking of the nation into לוים ,כהנים and ישראלים, and the Sanctuary fenced off in the centre, preaches to all קדושים תהיו but not yet: קדושים אתם. And even if there were already כולם קדושים in which case it would certainly be up to them themselves to choose the best and most able amongst them as leaders and public officers to attend to the public requirements, just as they already had from the nation itself their נשיאי עדה and קריאי מועד, of which the two hundred and fifty traitors were the living examples — and thus incidentally contradicted the first part of their accusation inasmuch as they themselves showed that even when the absolute equality of all was undisputed it was still necessary to have representatives for them —; still for matters which did not arise from within the nation, where the initiative in no wise lay with the people, altogether not in any human sphere, for that which was to come not out of the people, but to the people, for God’s messages to the people where is the man, where the nation who would be bold enough to say to God: Why didst Thou choose this one and no other to be Thy messenger? The true and genuine messenger of God — and none more so than a Moses — is surely the first and most ready to admit his unworthiness and to beg God to choose a better, more worthy and more able person to be His herald. But if then God still sends him and no other as the most worthy and most suitable to be His messenger who can come up to him and say: מדוע תתנשא על קהל ה׳? This תתנשא (raised yourself I.L.) is the denial that God had sent him, makes Moses into a cheat and the fact of his mission into a lie, therefore:

וישמע משה ויפל על פניו. The truth of a fact can only be proved by a fact, not by reasons or reasoning. Reasons and reasoning can establish its probability or its necessity but can never prove its actuality. The veracity of a messenger can only be proved by his sender, the sending of Moses only by God Himself. That is why no word of an answer from Moses himself could refute the accusation of Korach. If God would not consider it right to confirm the veracity of his being commissioned by God, in face of this denial of it, then his mission was at its end — ויפל על פניו.

But Aaron, although, as comes to light in the sequel, it was really his priestly position which had excited Korach’s envy, and he only sought to destroy Moses’ authority in order thereby to make an end to Aaron’s privileged position which that authority upheld, Aaron remained passive at this whole matter. He only held office and honour at Moses’ behest. Office and honour were to him also no personal question. For them he would break no lance, would give no word in defence. The genuineness of his brother was the sole deciding factor. And to establish that anew for the people was a matter that God alone could do.

V. 5. בקר .וידבר וגו׳ בקר וגו׳ not מחר, in the morning, not to-morrow i.e., let to-day and the night pass. As the decision could only be shown by the destruction of the rebels, they should have time to come to their senses, especially in the quiet and retirement of the night when everyone is relegated more to the company of his own family and his own self and removed from the influence of friends who would lead him astray. Also Moses wanted to use the time to make warning admonitions to the rebels as is shown in the sequel. And, as a matter of fact, On is missing at the deciding moment, for, according to tradition, his wife kept him back from taking further part in the rebellion, and similarly at the time of the catastrophe the sons of Korach plucked up courage to allow their better feelings to gain control and were saved from the fate that overtook the others. — ויודע ה׳ את אשר לו, God will make known who is His i.e., who is His instrument, His messenger and servitor, this is Moses’ attestation; ואת הקדוש והקריב אליו, and who, if not absolutely holy is still the holy one, i.e. is so holy that God finds him worthy of the calling to be allowed and have the duty to come near to Him in representation of the people. This is Aaron’s attestation. The former is the refutation of the false deduction from the true premise that בתוכם ה׳. The latter the refutation of the false deduction from the false premise that כל העדה כולם קדושים.

ואת אשר יבחר בו וגו׳, expresses the way and manner by which this decision will be made evident. God will choose the one and designate him as the one who may and should come near to Him, and thereby the whole matter will be decided in every direction. He will decide whether everybody, or only one designated by Him as כהן may and should come near to God. And if this one is the same as Moses had already in the name of God announced as chosen for the priesthood, then at the same time the veracity of Moses’ mission coming from God will be confirmed. And this decision will be shown in this way viz., the chosen one will be the one whom God allows to approach Him, whose approach He tolerates. This makes the direct implication and gives the warning that God will not tolerate the approach of anybody else and that the proof of their rejection could very likely be fatal for them.

V. 6—7. Moses had seen through Korach. Nothing but jealousy of the priestly honour conferred on the tribe of Aaron, placing the rest of the Levite families in the background, had brought him to rebellion. To do away with this distinction — perhaps that the popular vote might even confer it on him and his descendants, — he had declared the equal right of everybody to have this honour, to be the motive of his uprising and raised doubts as to the authority of Aaron being raised to that dignity being directed by God. Very well then, if they are really convinced of the truth of their assertions let them dare to put them to the test, and in accordance with what they asserted let them approach God with a high-priestly function. The highest point of the high priestly office is the offering of קטרת, in the action symbolising the highest degree of giving oneself up completely, without any reservation whatsoever, (the incense is completely sublimated leaving no residue I.L.) to giving satisfaction to God. In accordance with their assertion that they are all worthy to be priests, let them then approach God by offering incense and stand ready for God to decide. But, he warned them, not only for all the rest of the tribes who were represented by the two hundred and fifty men, but even for the Levites who stood after all quite near to the Sanctuary, as whose representative Korach wished to be regarded, it was a fateful arrogant presumption, hence: רב לכם בני לוי!

V. 8—11. After his speech pointing out the seriousness of what was to happen on the morrow if they insisted on their assertions and placed themselves under the decision of God, Moses did not fail to try persuasive remonstrances and spent the rest of the day doing so. ויאמר אל, explaining, trying to persuade, not וידבר as in V.5. As Moses approached Korach, and Dathan and Abiram separately it appears that the rising formed itself into two groups with different aims. Although the rising was against Moses and Aaron conjointly, still Korach had one thing in mind, and Dathan and Abiram another. Korach, the Levite, conducted himself as being really the champion of the rights of his tribe, insulted by the preference given to Aaron. He, the pretended representative of equal rights for all, quite liked the privileges which he and his tribe were accorded. Instead of stripping himself of them, which would be consistent with his charge, he was not satisfied with them, and, under the cloak of equal rights of all, sought for the dignity of the priesthood to satisfy his ambition. Dathan and Abiram, on the other hand, seemed not to have cared much for the priestly office or priestly dignity. We miss them also among the incense-bringers in V.17. Only the two hundred and fifty men and Korach and Aaron are expressly mentioned there. But it seems to have been the political position of Moses to which they objected, and they probably only joined Korach in the supposition that once the belief in Moses’ mission coming from God was undermined, his position in the nation could have altogether have the ground cut from under him.

המעט מכם, is it too little for you, i.e. is it less then you imagine what is due to you. — לעבד עבדת ה׳ ולעמד לפני העדה לשרתם (cf. on Ch. 3,6-8) עבדת משכן ה׳ is the service of erecting, looking after, protecting and transporting the Sanctuary and its contents. This service is one which is rendered also in service of the nation, לפני העדה (see on V.6 ibid.). לשרתם to do that which really is the task of the whole nation. This “service of the community”, according to the Jewish idea, constitutes the worth and dignity of all public service. It is no being set above the community but in its service, no שררות but עבדות (Horioth 10a). The idea of the worthiness of such public “service” lies in the fact that it must be considered service, that the honorary officers etc., are to fill their minds with the concept and purposes of the community, and from the point of view and in the spirit of the public have to look after the purposes of the community.

לכן וגו׳. By your ומדוע תתנשאו על קהל ה׳ (why have ye raised yourselves over God’s community?) you have accused me and Aaron of the greatest sin against God, the usurpation and misuse of His authority and His Name for our own ambitious selfish purposes so that our whole position would be at least a lawless going beyond and so against the Will of God. This accusation recoils with double weight on you yourself and your co-traitors. They are not satisfied with being the holy people of God, you are not satisfied with being a servitor of God’s Sanctuary and His Name but you want to be priests in the Sanctuary and for that you rebel against law and order which affects not us but God. You are the נועדים על ה׳ who have gathered together to express resentment against God. הִוָעד always has the meaning of gathering together for a common purpose about something that has occurred or which it is desired should occur. Hence also מועד (see Ex. Ch. 12,2 p.24, and Ch. 25,22). עדה also comes from the same root, a community formed by a common mission and united by it. Hence also here, Korach’s faction joined by their feelings and purpose, an עדה. What was wrong about it does not lie in הועד and עדה but in ,ואהרן וגו׳ — .על ה׳ but that you drag Aaron in as an object of your resentment, that indeed is completely without reason. In any case it is not he who deserves your hostility. The position which he occupies, he assumed on my orders which I transmitted to him in God’s Name. If anybody is to blame it is solely myself. תלינו, see Ex. on XVI,7. The תלונו :כתיב and the תלינו :קרי says that in reality they had only their own interests in view, were נלונים, but would not let that fact appear and incited general discontent, they were מלינים with which to cover their selfish תלונה.

V. 12. וישלח וגו׳. We have already remarked that Dathan and Abiram seem to have formed their own party in this rebellion of Korach. Korach’s rising was primarily against Aaron’s position as priest, and only indirectly, as its cause and support against the authority of Moses. But Dathan and Abiram were directed against Moses, and their aim was to put an end to the political leadership of Moses. The hostility to Moses — direct or indirect — was the factor that united the two factions. That was why Moses wished to speak to Dathan and Abiram by themselves, separately from Korach, but they replied לא נעלה. In just this expression they compressed, in biting sarcasm, the whole hatred of their feelings. — שלח לקרא ל- in no wise involves a dictatorial “order” coming from a superior. But rather it is used to designate a friendly invitation (cf. XXII,5, 20 and 27; Ex. 2,20 and XXXIV,16; I Sam. 16,3; I. Kings 1,19, et alia). But עלה is not only going up to a higher place, but also going up to one who occupies a higher, more important position, going to a superior, and is especially used for going to a court of law, ועלתה יבמתו השערה (Deut. 25,7); ובועז עלה השער (Ruth 4,1). Moses, in the most friendly way, had asked them to come to him. But they took the invitation as a “summons”, and answered “We are not coming up to “my lord”, i.e. we do not take orders from him, it is a presumption on his part to order us about from above to come to him, “we do not “go up” to him”.

V. 13. המעט. Have you not done us enough harm already in bringing us up from such a glorious land as Egypt (“up” i.e. under the promise to bring us to a still better one, or referring to the higher position of Palestine) only now, according to the latest fate you have proclaimed for us, that we are to find our graves here in the wilderness, that you also want to השתרר וגו׳. We have three expressions for ruling: שרר ,שור ,שרה, they sound very much alike but are different in their meanings. שרה designates ruling by superior power, שור leading by moral influence (cee Gen. 17,15) but שרר (related to סרר the most intractable disobedience) designates capricious tyranny which allows no laws to bind it. This is what they reproach Moses with, and even find a proof of it that he allows himself to call them to him to which he has absolutely no right whatsoever!

V. 14. אף לא וגו׳ can not refer, as להמיתנו במדבר of the previous verse does, to the fact that the whole of the generation that came out of Egypt was now doomed to die in the wilderness without entering the Promised Land, for that had already been said, and in any case could not be introduced by אף, “furthermore” as it would only say the same thing again. So we believe we can take it to mean as follows: To us, the older generation which came out of Egypt you have already brought misfortune and broken your word. We have left that lovely land and now we are to die in the wilderness. But we do not even believe at all in your further promise that our children will come to possess the land. That is by no means so certain however glibly you speak to us of possessing fields and vineyards, and even give us laws and regulations concerning them (for instance immediately after proclaiming the fate of having to die in the wilderness Ch. XV,II & 18). How glibly you gave us also, נחלת שדה וכרם “gave” us (ותתן לנו) with words but still have by no means brought us into the Land. Your promises regarding the children will end in the same way in disappointment as your promises to their fathers did — העיני וגו׳, do you think you can make us blind, not to see things as they are? Sforno explains ותתן לנו וגו׳ in a similar way in his commentary.

V. 15. ויחר וגו׳: really, “this burnt Moses very much”. That he should be reproached, that any one would dare to suggest that he had misused his position to arbitrary actions hurt him deeply. — ,אל תפן אל מנחתם, the understanding of the meaning of this sentence offers considerable difficulty. It can not refer to the incense which was to be brought on the next day by the rebels who were associated with Korach. For, as we have already remarked, Dathan and Abiram took no part in that. So just because of that fact we think that perhaps it could be explained as follows:- the uprising of Korach and the two hundred and fifty men was a direct rebellion against God and His orders regarding the procedure of offerings in His Sanctuary to be carried out by Aaron. The conceit with which they were ready, in their overestimation of themselves, to offer God the incense of their own choice dissociated itself from these offerings which were in truth rendering homage to God. In this priestly factor of the rebellion Dathan and Abiram took no part. With their Mincha they remained on the normal basis of the whole nation; with the symbolic expression of their homage to God they were satisfied to include themselves in the national public Mincha offerings brought daily on behalf of the public in the Sanctuary; they sought to perform no priestly functions on their own behalf. And still Moses prays to God אל תפן אל מנחתם “Turn not to their offering of homage”. For even if they did not actually infringe on the laws concerning the symbolic expression of homage to God their concrete behaviour was a much deeper infringement on the homage due to God. For inasmuch as they accused Moses concerning their denied entry into the Promised Land and mockingly cast doubts on such entry in the future, and saw in it all only the inaptitude of Moses who was masking his dilemma under a supposed sin of the nation; and inasmuch as they thus presented Moses as the unscrupulous deceiver of his nation; and at the same time accused him of the basest attempts at dictatorship and tyranny, they had declared the whole mission of Moses to be a low deceit, and thereby denied the whole Divine origin of his mission as well as the whole special relation of God to Israel which indeed had become a fact just through and in this mission. But by this they declare as far as they are concerned, the utter worthlessness of the whole basis on which a testimony brought by Moses for a Law of God revealed to Moses and brought by Moses and a Sanctuary erected to that Law rests and so a system of offerings dedicated to the teachings of that Sanctuary of God’s Law can have no meaning whatsoever for them. So that Dathan and Abiram did not abstain from attending with their censers among the two hundred and fifty because they wished to recognise and be included in the normal lawful procedures of the sacrifices in the Sanctuary, but because they held themselves aloof from all such practices. Therefore אל תפן אל מנחתם! Perhaps this way of taking it is what is meant in the explanation which the Midrash Rabba gives on this sentences: כך אמר משה לפני הקב״ה רבונו של עולם יודע אני שיש מאלו חלק באותה מנחה שהקריבו, מלבד עולת התמיד ומנחתה, והיתה של כל ישראל קריבה, הואיל ופירשו אלו מבניך אל תסתכל בחלקם תניחנו האש ואל תאכלנה, (“This is what Moses said unto God: O Lord of the Universe, I know that these men are included in the public allegiance-offering which is brought on behalf of the nation, as well as in the daily elevation-offering and its accompanying allegiance-offering, but have no regard to their portion of it, let the fire on the altar disregard it and not consume it, for they have separated themselves apart from Thy children” I.L.).

לא חמור אחד נשאתי וגו׳: had my character been stained by the very slightest personal advantage I took of my position, or by any despotic domineering attitude I assumed, they would have the right not only to doubt but to deny the authenticity of my God-given mission. The character of Thy messengers must be unsmirched. Thou sendest none whose characters have even a trace of a tendency towards improbity or tyranny. Purity of character is the first of the credentials of Thy messengers. The reproach that confidence in my mission was shattered by wilful tyranny, that I do not deserve. Not only did I never ask a single person of the people to carry my load for me but I never even placed it on, or used one of their asses for that purpose, and no single person did I consciously hurt of my own free will.

It is doubtful in which sense the נשאתי here is to be understood. נשא does occur several times as simply taking away: ונשא שה מהעדה (Sam. I. 17,34) נושא את פת בגם (Daniel 1,16). But as מַשְׂאת means a gift, and indeed mostly a gift to show honour (Gen. 43,34; Jer. 40,5 and Esther 2,18) and also a tax or due to be given to a superior in a similar sense to תרומה or the shekel gift for the Temple: משאת משה עבד ה׳ (II. Chron. 24,69), so here, too, נשא could mean taken up as a due. “I have not even laid claim to the use of an ass for myself as being my due”. Onkelos takes it in the same way: .לא חמרא דהד מנהון שחרית
לא חמור אֶחָד מהם not the ass of any one of them. ולא הרעתי את אַחַד מהם, nor have I hurt any particular one amongst them, one, who by his behaviour would have deserved it (See on Gen. 3,22).

V. 16. ויאמר וגו׳. Verses 6 and 7 were only spoken hypothetically, what they were to do if they persisted and wished to put the decision regarding their accusing statements to God Himself; now here they are repeated as directions. After Moses’ attempts had achieved no results in any direction, he said to Korach: as you are not susceptible to human representations היו לפני ה׳ then be before God, i.e. place yourself with your demands before God, dare to make your demands to God that He shall decide between your demands and Aaron.

V. 17. By offering קטרת they would make their claim to the priesthood valid before God. Here Aaron is also named and the two hundred and fifty are grouped by themselves but Korach placed with Aaron. For there were two assertions about which judgment was to be given, (a) the equal right and the equal worthiness of the whole nation to the priesthood, an assertion which was to be proved by the two hundred and fifty מקריבי קטרת (offerers of incense); but also (b) that if the community was to be represented before God by a single individual, this need not necessarily be just Aaron, but could possibly be even Korach, an assertion which was to be put to proof by Korach standing at Aaron’s side and both functioning as high priests. (See on V.3).

ונתתם עליהם קטרת: in a striking manner here as well as in V.18 and also above V.7, accordingly, in the whole of this event, the incense is referred to as being placed on the censers and not on the fire, whereas in the case of Nadab and Abihu (Levit. X,l) and similarly at the normal bringing on י״כ (ibid. XVI,12) the קטרת was placed on the fire. There it says ויקחו וגו׳ איש מחתתו ויתנו בהן אש וישמו עליה קטרת and similarly ולקח מלא המחתה גחלי אש וגו׳ ונתן את הקטרת על האש but here, קחו איש מחתתו ונתתם עליהם קטרת and קחו לכם מחתות וגו׳ ותנו בהם אש ושימו עליהן קטרת ויקחו איש מחתתו ויתנו עליהם אש וישימו עליהם קטרת. Here clearly the מחתות are in the foreground and are representative of the persons who brought them. In the case of Nadab and Abihu the persons were entitled to officiate, hence also their כלי the מחתה. But the offering was an unlawful one, it was אש זרה because it was אשר לא צוה אותם, it was devised subjectively by themselves. But here the unlawfulness did not lie in the offering. It was identical with what Aaron brought. It is possible that it was the ordinary incense-offering which the high-priest had to bring daily on the מזבח הזהב. In any case the unlawfulness lay in the persons themselves that they stepped forth with their מחתות presenting themselves as priests justified to perform priestly functions. Hence the stress on the מחתות: dare to offer the קטרת before God in your own self-manipulated vessels that is your test. That then too would be why, at the moment of their actually carrying it out the מחתות are described abnormally in the masculine three times: וישימו עליהם ,ויתנו עליהם ,ונתתם עליהם to stress the defiance and the presumption which lay in their use. Hence also even referring to the fire it does not say, as in Levit. and above בהן, but עליהם, the censers always regarded not as containers for the fire but as the base on which the offering was dared to be brought. Hence also instead of the number of men it mentions the number of censers, חמשים ומאתים מחתות. Therein lies the idea: so many men, so many כהנים, the most poignant way of expressing the asserted equality of right to the priesthood.

V. 19. ויקהל וגו׳. Korach must have felt himself so sure, he must have so convinced himself, so have talked himself into the full belief of the truth of the relationships to God which were here in question, that even for the moment of so fateful a decision he called the whole nation to participate in his conflict and to witness his triumph. It must then have been his intention, without waiting for the intervention of God, to enforce his will and achieve his purpose by sheer force of numbers, by the weight of the masses. In any case this flocking together of the people was directed against (ויקהל על- I.L.) Moses and Aaron and those that came were accordingly on Korach’s side.

V. 21. הבדלו וגו׳. As remarked on V.19, by their coming they had placed themselves on Korach’s side, and thereby had not kept themselves free from participation in his guilt. Their flocking together is described as ויקהל עליהם i.e. against Moses and Aaron.

V. 22. אל אלקי הרוחות וגו׳ .ויפלו וגו׳. Thou knowest how easily the “spirits” the minds of the masses can be swayed to wrong ideas by the influence exerted by the superior intellect of one who hitherto had enjoyed uninfringed confidence and who places dazzling prospects and highly coloured assertions before them. When the masses rise to commit crime, as a rule the true guilt lies with a few superior agitators. Then, at human intervention all too often it is the lesser guilty masses who have been led astray who bleed and suffer while the real guilty ones go free. But Thou אל אלקי הרוחות לכל בשר, as אל, Almighty, canst reach those whom Thou recognizeth as the guilty ones, and as אלקי הרוחות לכל בשר knoweth how to measure the real guilt of each one. האיש אחד וגו׳. After all it is only Korach who is the guilty one, and the people, as being only led astray by him, could well enjoy Thy clemency. We have repeatedly had occasion to remark at similar events, how, by evoking his entreaties, God awoke in Moses an insight into the motives of His Rule, and elevated his mind into thinking along the lines of the Divine Rule.
V. 24. העלו וגו׳. by this action they were to dissociate themselves from belonging to the rebels, and atone for their הקהל על משה ואהרן (having gathered against Moses and Aaron I.L.).
V. 25. ויקם וגו׳. Dathan and Abiram were the ones who had most directly insulted Moses, and we see him, at the very last moment, trying to save them by making them come to a better frame of mind.
V. 27. נצבים, standing boldly upright.

V. 28. את כל המעשים האלה, probably refers to all his previous activities, not just specially to his having elevated Aaron to the priesthood and the recent declaration of the elder generation having to die in the wilderness.

V. 29. מות כל אדם .אם כמות וגו׳ is dying a natural death in the course of Man’s innate mortality. פקדת כל האדם is dying a “natural” death as the result of some accident or event which brings an earlier death to a person, such as בחרב ,במים ,באש ,ברעב etc., events which occur also in accordance with the existing laws of nature which God has also ordained. It results from God’s allowing a person to meet the effect of these dangerous natural causes or keeping him from them. Such a death is also פקדת כל האדם, an event which does not lie beyond the sphere of happenings to which other men, too, are liable in the ordinary course of things. As sure as all so-called natural events, everything that occurs according to the existing natural laws of the world, only occurs as a result of God’s Will, for He Himself had made these laws and they only work as long as it is His Will that they should do so; further, sure though it is that Man, with all the happenings that determine his life and death, prosperity and ruin, is still under a special Providence of God, and nothing small or great, even in the “ordinary run of things”, happens to him which God’s Will has not directed; nevertheless, it is certain that if כמות כל האדם ימותון אלה and פקודת כל האדם יפקד עליהם they had died ordinary deaths and met with ordinary fatal accidents which would be no less the fulfilment of God’s pronouncement, still such death and such a fate could not serve as a proof of the mission of Moses being at God’s behest. For that mission was based on the intervention of God which was accomplished in a manner beyond the natural order of things, by which God wished to show Himself just as ה׳, as standing in free power over and beyond the laws of nature, as the One from Whom these laws originated, by Whose Will they act; they are bound by Him, but He is not bound by them. It was to reveal Him not only as He Who once created and ordered the world as אלקים, but Who, as ה׳, has the power at any minute to introduce a completely new future not dependent on the past, and Who is ready to use this power for the benefit of human beings whom He has gifted with a breath of His Own free-willed freedom of will, and thereby created them in likeness to His Own free-willed Personality to creatures who, in normal matters, can raise themselves above the force of the powers of nature, and who, recognising the Will of God, are to serve Him, not instinct-bound as animals, but of their own free choice. With this mission of Moses God wished to begin the educating and re-elevating mankind up to Him, and to the exercising of his free-willed moral powers (see on Ex. 6,3). After all the mission of Moses itself, as is every Word of God sent to Man, an act of the most free-willed Personality, which can only find its credentials in convincing אות ומופת from that free-willed Personality. Hence אם כמות כל האדם וגו׳ לא ה׳ שלחני (if these men die as all men die etc., then it is not God Who hath sent me I.L.) But:

V. 30. ואם בריאה וגו׳, but if their downfall is brought about by something new that just proclaims God as ה׳, in Whose Name I acted, וידעתם כי נאצו האנשים האלה את ה׳, then you will know that these people in denying that I was carrying out God’s commission, altogether denied the free-willed Rule of God and His work.

V.32. ואת כל האדם אשר לקרח. As according to verses 17-19 Korach was with those who were offering incense at the entrance of the Sanctuary, it would seem from this verse that he was not included among those who met their death in this particular manner. But nevertheless it says in Ch. 26,10: ותפתח הארץ וגו׳ ותבלע אתם ואח קרח, according to which Korach did die in this manner. Hence in Sanhedrin 110a there is doubt as to in which catastrophe he met his end, whether with the בלועים or the שרופים and there one opinion is expressed that he, as the originator of the whole misfortune, was forced to endure both of them.
V. 33. ותכם וגו׳ ויאבדו וגו׳. The earth closed in over them in such a manner that no trace of their downfall remained visible and they had thus completely disappeared from amongst the people.

V. 35. ואש יצאה וגו׳ at the same time. While those in the camp suffered being buried alive, the מקריבי הקטרת were killed by the fire by אש מאת ה׳. The fire which otherwise consumed the offerings on this occasion consumed the offerers.

V. 1—3. כי קדשו. One could have taken it that the מקריבי הקטרת (those that offered the incense) had first of all dedicated the censers in general to be כלי שרת (to be given as permanent property of the Sanctuary I.L.) and this קדושה would not be lost by their wrongful use. But from the reason adduced in the following verse כי הקריבם לפני ה׳ ויקדשו it seems ordinary sense. Perhaps it could be taken in this way:- קדשו, they remained as an unlawful act could hardly be considered to confer קדושה in the ordinary sense. Perhaps it could be taken in this way:- קדשו, they remained hallowed by the purpose to which they were dedicated. הקריבום לפני ה׳, they had brought them before God to bring about a decision from Him over the true and real priesthood which He desired. They achieved this purpose although at the cost of the lives of those who had sought it thereby, and through it had become חטאים בנפשתם. But achieving this purpose was such a holy important fact for the Sanctuary of God and its future, the realisation of which is such an indispensable condition for the whole sanctifying effect which this Sanctuary and its offering-procedures are to have on the whole life of the people, that these censers which served to achieve this purpose are to remain dedicated to the maintenance of what had been achieved, so that they had become “hallowed” in a double sense! They remained dedicated to their original purpose, to prove what the true priesthood is, and, as through this lasting decision they belonged permanently to the most holy purposes of the Sanctuary they themselves became holy, as did everything that belonged to the service in the Sanctuary.
ואת האש זרה הלאה, the fire that was brought on them remained abandoned, and just for an eternal reminder that what was offered on them was rejected, the censers were to be kept.

את מחתות. It puts the object before the predicate to lay special stress on it, and to bring out its character by which it was to remain an אות a sign of teaching and warning. With these מחתות the offerers became sinners against themselves. They sinned against themselves and brought about their own ruin! In the connection in which the sinning against themselves is expressed here with the ordering of the censers for an overlay for the altar, את מחתות החטאים וגו׳ ,ועשו אתם וגו׳, the thought could well lie:- their running after honour had sought to break the laws of God regarding the service of the altar, this endeavour had only resulted in their ruin, and that ruin had only served to strengthen the altar with all its God-ordained laws, (see Hirsch’s Commentary on Ps. 42,1).

V. 5. להקטיר קטרת; By קטרת here may well not be meant just incense, but be an expression for everything that is מוקטר לפני ה׳, for everything that is given over to the fire of the altar. Thus קטרת אילים (Ps. 66,15). קטרה itself was never offered on the מזבח הנחשת so that a warning sign on that altar would least of all refer to it. — כאשר דבר וגו׳, the words recorded in Ch. 16,5-7 which Moses addressed to Korach he had said at God’s behest. For a man like Korach the warning lay in them, not to place the question of a non-authorised person officiating in the Sanctuary for God’s decision which in any case would be of a fateful nature. Just as the decision was shown on him in such a disastrous manner, so would it be shown on any unauthorised person who would dare to approach the altar as a priest without his being authorised to do so as being a descendant of Aaron. A warning which was fulfilled also on King Uzziah. (Chron. II. 20,6).

V. 6. אתם המתם וגו׳. From V.17 it seems that they were not yet convinced by the death of the two hundred and fifty that the election of Aaron to exclusive priesthood rested purely on a decree of God to ensure the nature of His Sanctuary and of the offerings brought therein, against people who might not stand so near to Him. They still imagined, so it seems, that the election of Aaron, admittedly at God’s behest, nevertheless rested more as a personal distinction conferred on the brother of Moses. So that they took the sin of the two hundred and fifty as being punished by God for the personal insult to Moses and Aaron, which they thought could have been averted by Moses and Aaron forgiving the insult, and so they could — and should — have prevented the death of such a considerable number of fathers of families. They did not grasp the true reality of the event, which in no wise could have been settled by such a pardon, but rather demanded an imperious decision by God, if His Work — towards which Moses and Aaron dwindled as mere unimportant instruments — was to be saved and maintained for its eternal goal.

V. 10—11. הרמו וגו׳ This accusation was certainly a purely personal reproach, as a result of which God said to Moses: If you wish it, get yourselves up out of them and I will immediately make an end of these masses that rise up against you. But they did not move, on the contrary, threw themselves down on their faces before God; and instead of going away from the people — instead of demanding the death of their offenders as a penalty, like the deaths which the accusing masses fathered on them, calling them “bringers of death to the people of God” — Aaron had to rush into the midst of the nation condemned to death, and with the קטרת rising up to God, the symbol of the most complete giving oneself up to God, place himself between the dying and the living, making atonement for them and proving himself and his mission, contrary to their accusation, the redeeming conqueror of Death.

V. 17. דבר וגו׳. We worked out on Ch. 1,2, how, in accordance with their branching out from one common stem, the tribes of the Jewish people are called מטות, branches, so that we find here “מטות״ the most appropriate name. Nevertheless as each tribe inherited and transmitted to its members some characteristic speciality within the common general characteristics of the nation, each formed a special בית אב within the one common בני ישראל, So that as מטות they are considered in their similarity, as בתי אבות in their different specialities. So that as here, the twelve בתי אבות of the Jewish nation are to be represented by twelve מטות, scope is given to the thought, that it has to be decided whether, in spite of their difference, because of their characteristic similarity they could perhaps be worthy to be considered all equal in the matter to be decided here, or whether, in spite of their common similarity, the characteristic tribal differences would be against such equality.

V. 18. ואת שם אהרן וגו׳. We have already worked out on Levit. 22,9 that Jewish priests do not cease to be Levites, that the priesthood is only to be considered as Levitism in its highest degree of perfection, so that the tribe of Levi has to see in the “cohanim” only the elite of its undivisable totality, and the priests to consider their mission only as the highest development of the task of the Levites. Hence Aaron is nought but ראש לבית לוי, and his staff is the staff of Levi, מטה לוי.

V. 19. והנחתם. By the “staff” and in it the “stem”, the tribe, being laid down in front of the עדות אשר אועד לכם שמה, the question is placed for the עדות to decide, and brought to be settled from its standpoint. By this the people are told that here it is not dealing with a question of “personal” preference, as was erroneously supposed in V.6, but it concerns an institution with which the “עדות״ and the associated Presence of God in the midst of the people is associated in the very first place. It concerns the מטה, the branch on the tree of the Jewish nation as being the one chosen by God to show that, by reason of its special characteristics it is one which is most suitable to represent this “evidence of the Torah coming from God”, and to nurture the service of the Torah among the people.

V. 20. והיה וגו׳. He whose מטה blossoms is shown by God’s judgment to have innate in his מטה (tribe I.L.) the germ for the future flowering and bearing fruit of the עדות, the “Evidence”, in the people. At the same time the owner of that staff is marked as the right representative of that chosen tribe. שכך .והשכתי וגו׳ is the precise expression for calming something raging and roaring and bringing it to rest (cf. Gen. 8,1 and Esther 2,1). Up till now the distinction given to Aaron had aroused the passions of the people against you, but really against Me, as this distinction is not really your doing but Mine. So that every fit of passion against you really reflected back on Me. All that will now cease, as Aaron’s priesthood will be shown to be purely an act of God’s choice and its motives free from every personal favour of the chosen one, and the evidence thereof to be kept for all time. (V.25 I.L.).
V. 21. ומטה אהרן וגו׳, externally Aaron’s staff differed in no way from the others, it was just a staff like the others.
V. 22. לפני ה׳: for the decision of God.
V. 23. מטה אהרן לבית ליי, thereby at the same time the tribe of Levi is chosen out of the other tribes, and Aaron out of the other Levites (see [[illegible]] V.18).
