But every other person, and even a single witness, who, as a single one, is not considered a witness at all, (and someone can have been present at a case which has been brought to court and duly attested by two other witnesses, without his being able to join those two witnesses, (see Makkoth 6b) every other person, accordingly, who as a single person can give no evidence but can only express an opinion, has indeed to be heard by the court if he wishes to bring forward anything which could tend to the accused being set free, דיני נפשות הכל מלמדין זכות ואין הכל מלמדין חובה, that is what it says עד אחד לא למות ,יענה בנפש למות, apart from the board of judges, the opinion of no individual person may be heard to further the prosecution of the accused, but לזכות, for the defence anybody and everybody may well be heard. This provision, that a criminal court gives ear to anybody who can give an opinion in favour of the accused, but to nobody who would speak against him, except, of course, amongst its own members of the bench, is deeply characteristic of the whole of Jewish criminal jurisprudence which has to guard itself less against setting a guilty person free than against sentencing an innocent one (see Ex. 23,7).

V. 31. אשר הוא רשע למות .ולא תקחו כפר וגו׳, but if, according to the evidence of the witnesses and the laws of justice he is to be sentenced to death, in no ways whatsoever does it lie in your power to remit the sentence, for instance by paying a heavy fine. Justice is not your ordinance, which, as men have ordered it so can they grant dispensation from it. Justice is God’s Law, you are only instruments who have to carry it out by His orders.

V. 32. ולא תקחו כפר לנוס וגו׳. It is difficult to take נוס as being anything other than the infinitive of a verb. Even if one wanted to take it, as Rashi does as a noun נוס, similar form to שובי מלחמה in Miccha 2,9 or מולים היו (Josh. 5,5) it would still have to be לַנוּס. It must mean: You may not take ransom for having to flee to a reception-city, not even only to return home before the death of the high-priest.

V. 33. חנף .ולא תחניפו וגו׳, as is definitely clear in its use in Job and Proverbs means: to play the hypocrite, to put on an air of piety; to present an appearance externally which by no means corresponds to the inner reality. So that he who makes a man into a hypocrite takes away the inner kernel leaving the outer appearance unchanged. Whereas ענף the twig, the branch, and ענב the grape designate the most faithful and most complete visible coming out of the inner being, חנף is — as one so often finds in the ע and ח roots — a negation of ענף and ענב, it is the outer appearance of a branch, but the branch brings forth no blossom and no fruit, it is the outer appearance of the fruit, but the fruit contains nothing of the noble sap of a richly blessed interior. Now if a country becomes a “hypocrite”, this is literally a “חנופה״. It is still the same land which is meant to produce the richest abundance of fruit under the blessing-giving rays of God’s sunshine and His dew; but the land, the dew, the sunshine deceive, no inner blessed germ sprouts out to life and to give joy to mankind, and what does sprout forth is again deceiving, there is no blessing in the pith and saps of the germinating powers of the young shoots and plants. Now it says: ולא תחניפו את הארץ, if you tolerate intentional murder and careless manslaughter, then you make the land אשר אתם בה in which you are (not merely אשר אתם יושבים בה as in V.34), in which your earthly existence has its roots, which is to see its noblest product in you, you make the land into a “hypocrite”. It deceives the expectation which otherwise you are justified in entertaining from it, it keeps back the blessing that should flow out from it, “כי הוא יחניף את הארץ״, for blood, human blood is the noblest juice that the land matures, and innocent blood spilt makes the land into a “hypocrite”. In Man called to near-divine freedom of will, the purpose of all earthly development and forces reaches the summit of its goal. In every living drop of human blood which bears the נפש of a human being, and is the means of its existence here below, heaven and earth touch each other, the earthly is mated to the heavenly; a human society to which every drop of the blood of its members is not holy, which does not take up the cudgels for innocent human blood which has been spilt, denies the purpose for which the forces of the earth work, breaks the condition upon which the soil of its land belongs to it, deceives the expectations in which the earth offers its forces, becomes a “hypocrite” to its country and makes its country into a “hypocrite” towards it. ולארץ לא יכפר לדם אשר שפך בה כי אם בדם שפכו: this חנופה of the land is only purged when the innocent blood which has been spilt, and the human being whose existence down here has been brought to an end thereby, finds a champion, amongst the human society which goes on living after it, to take up its cause, and the murderer atones for his existence down here which was forfeited by the murder by being killed by that champion of the murder. For by shedding the blood of his brother-man, his own blood has lost its justification, he himself had forfeited the right to go on living; and tolerating the further continuing living on of one who has deliberately and with foresight murdered a fellow-man, is an insult to and derision of the higher dignity of the conception of Man being near God, is a breach of the contract under which God gave the earth to Man, under which God had given the land to Israel.

At the moment when God allowed Noah and his sons to tread again the re-gifted earth and handed over to them the vegetable and animal life on it at their free disposition He proclaimed with the words ואך את דמכם לנפשותיכם אדרש וגו׳ שופך דם האדם באדם דמו ישפך כי בצלם אלקים עשה את האדם, the validity of the inviolable higher dignity of the likeness of God in Man as the fundamental condition for the use of this gift and this free right of disposal. At the moment when God handed over to Israel the land as the base for their richly blessed development for making His Torah a reality, with the words ולארץ לא יכפר לדם אשר שפך בה כי אם בדם שפכו He renewed the same proclamation for Israel as the fundamental condition for the blessed possession and blessed enjoyment and use of that land, and extended it further by the atoning institution for unpremeditated manslaughter.

V. 34. אשר אתם יושבים בה אשר אני שוכן בתוכה is a different relation of the land to its inhabitants than that depicted in V.33 by אשר אתם בה. There the land is looked on as the basis of human existence. The land refused to grant the inhabitants such existence if the destruction of the existence of a man by a man leaves them indifferent. Here the land is looked on as the basis of ישיבה and שכינה, of the national social life and the Presence of God on earth. Both, the national social well-being of the life of the people to be built up on devotion to God and His Torah, as well as the Presence of God promised to such an elevation of communal social life up to God (Ex. 25,8), clearly rest on the recognition and consciousness of the higher dignity and value of human life, of the recognition and consciousness of human beings being in the likeness of their Creator. If the whole of God’s Torah rests on the three fundamental bases of justice, Love of fellow man and Moral sanctification of one’s own life, then the whole Torah stands or falls with the recognition and consciousness or the denial and repudiation of the higher dignity and value of human beings being in the likeness of God! Justice rests on the recognition of one’s brother men being in the likeness of God, sanctification of morals and love rest on the recognition of one’s own self being in that likeness. If Man is only in the likeness of animal, purely a physical being like all living creatures around him in the Creation, then force, and selfishness and satisfying animal urges are for him also the sole activating forces of his life, there can be no talk of Justice and Love and sanctification of morals; then טומאה “physical lack of freedom”, “necessity” with all its consequences of force and depravity is the exclusive stamp of the earth and human life, then it is the animal-ideal to which the tribute of worship is paid in home and state, of individual and national life, then for God, the One to be recognised and acknowledged in Justice, Love and Morality, for Him there is no place on earth.

But the Torah recognises indifference of the community towards the shedding of innocent human blood as the most open denial of the fundamental basic law of the godliness of the nature of Man, as the factual proclamation of טומאה as the principle of private and national life. Therefore it says, to the state of Israel (in the singular I.L.) לא תטמא את הארץ אשר אתם ישבים בה: “Do not proclaim the principle of טומאה as the principle which rules the land — the land which has you for its inhabitants in whose midst God announced His Presence — by your indifference to human blood”; כי אני ה׳ שכן בתוך בני ישראל, for, it has just said :י אני שוכן בתוכה that God is present in the midst of the land, it is not the land as such, it is the people, the nation, the children of Israel, and the life they develop therein through which conditions on earth are made worthy for the promised Presence of God in the land. And if this Presence of God is to become known as being in the midst of the nation, then, however far from the goal of its perfection the lives of individuals may be, however much the imperfections pertaining to טומאה may still cling to individuals, the guiding banner of the idea of the godliness of the nature of human beings and the consequent value of their lives in the eye of God having regard to their ultimate perfection under His educative Love, must ever be held aloft, so that in opposition to the appearances of טומאה the principle of טהרה receives its devoted acknowledgment and the spirit of the nation remains worthy of the promise given to it אני ה׳ שכן בתוך בני ישראל (cf. on Levit. 18,25 et seq. and XV,31).

It is only by these concluding sentences that the institution of רוצח and ערי מקלט — the materialisation of which was to be the first national duty on obtaining possession of the land, and which Moses himself instituted before that for the land taken into possession on the Transjordan side — can be seen in its clearest light. It is respecting the holiness and the incalculable value of every drop of blood of even the lowest of its citizens, with the proclamation of which the People of God are to take possession of their land. To this State the life of its inhabitants is to be considered as the holiest and most precious of all the earthly treasures in its possession, and the public are made responsible for every minute of shortened life of its members. The “likeness to God” of human beings which lies at the root of, and is expressed by, this respect for the holiness of human blood is to be the first factor, to which “God” is at once to attach itself as the second, and both together, God and the likeness to God of human beings, with all the logical consequences of these conceptions are to form the spiritual and moral bases, and be the fruit of life of this State and of the private and social lives of its adherents. Every one of its inhabitants is guaranteed existence and possession of land only on the condition that he respects the “being in the likeness of God” and the consequent inviolability of life of every one of his co-inhabitants, and that this respect begets due conscious care and circumspection in all his doings. The מקלט-cities set at equal distances throughout the land, all only coming into effect at the same time (V.13) proclaim this principle factually applying without exception to the whole land and to all its inhabitants. The authorisation of the גואל הדם by the court — or where necessary the appointment of one by it — is not made only in the name of the victim or his near relative but in the name of the principle of the State which has been violated by the slaying of one of his adherents.

The legal regulations for intentional murder present themselves only as carrying out the declaration already given in the Noachian laws, viz. שופך דם האדם באדם דמו ישפך (Gen. 9,6). These cases receive, primarily the characteristic, as well as all the rest of the limitations which belong to the whole of Jewish criminal law. Cases must be based on עדים והתראה i.e. on the crime being declared by two eye witnesses who were present and warned the criminal and put to him the exact nature of the punishment which he would incur if he committed the threatened deed (see hereon the notes on Ex. 21,14 and XVIII,5 as well as Deut. 17,6). Further, there must be no possible doubt that death resulted as the direct effect of the deed, as the tendency altogether must be overwhelmingly to bring a verdict of not guilty and capital punishment could only follow on the most rare cases of the most complete evidence to which no loophole could possibly be found. But when that did occur there was no authority whatsoever to reprieve or remit the sentence. (see on Verses 31 & 32).

In Gen. 4,14 we have already referred to the similarity of the treatment of the first murderer to the fate of exile meted out to the unpremediated but careless manslayer. This banishment from home, this exclusion from the whole national soil and being relegated to one single city which receives him and keeps him confined within its boundaries, any capricious going beyond them being taken as a gesture of contempt of the gravity of his misdeed and justifies the champion of the blood using his blade against him — all this is only a modified suffering of what his brother-man was caused by his hand, whom he sent away from his home, his country and his whole existence on earth. And this being snatched away from the whole sphere of the life he had been living hitherto, and out of a free contact with all that to which a man’s feelings are attached in his homely cricle, as well as the constant care he has to exercise to avoid the dagger of the retaliation which he knows is pointed at his life may well be calculated to bring home to him and make him learn to value the whole worth of the precious treasures which his criminal thoughtlessness has made a fellow-creature lose. But the whole character which is stamped on this banishment to a מקלט-city is not that of punishment but כפרה expiation, that he should be freed from the serious consequences of the guilt which bears heavily on him (Makkoth 26, 11b, ד״ה מידי גלות ,תוספות). This character is also shown in the loving provision for all the material and spiritual welfare of the banished people which the community has to provide for them in the places to which they are banned (see on V.11).

But one still has to consider what the connection can be between the כהן גדול and the banishment of a manslayer to a Miklot-city. The sentence of banishment runs: “until the death of the highpriest”, and it must be one who is functioning at the time when the verdict is pronounced. This cannot possibly be just to give a term to the period of the sentence, but must rather have such an intimate connection with the crime and the verdict that if the highpriest dies after the verdict, but before the accused had gone to the place of his banishment the sin is considered to have attained its atonement and he is free from having to be banished. On the other hand, if there is no high-priest in office at the time the verdict was given, the accused must remain in a Miklot-city until the end of his life. And, as a matter of fact, the Gemora in Makkoth 11b does take the death of the כה״ג as the concluding כפרה, the final atonement of the sin: מידי גלות קא מכפרה מיתת כהן הוא דמכפרא (see תוספות there) and on 41a, there, it ascribes to the כה״ג some possible participation in the guilt which could be atoned for by his death. There it designates as a possible participation in the guilt the fact that perhaps he may have shown some indifference towards the well-being and freedom from guilt of his contemporaries and failed to offer up prayers for them, שהיה להם לבקש רחמים על דורן. Or, as it puts it — there on 11b, regarding a high-priest who had just been elected between the occurrence and the sentence on it, that possibly he had been indifferent to the fate of banishment which threatened the accused and possibly may have omitted to pray that if there were any extenuating circumstances which would result in a verdict of not guilty, these may not escape the recognition of the judges היה לו לבקש רחמים שיגמר דינו לזכות ולא בקש. (We believe that both these sentences must be taken in this hypothetical sense. For neither the misfortune itself nor the sentence pronounced on it is any positive proof that the contemporary highpriests were actually neglectful in failing to offer the prayers which one expects from them although the sentences do say ולא בקשו I.L.). For only God could know that. And the second prayer שיגמור דינו לזכות must surely be taken completely as hypothetical. For otherwise it would be a prayer for a false, or anyway an erroneous verdict. This sympathy of the priest, his sharing with the offence and the fate of banishment of the unintentional manslayer was so vivid in the minds of the populace that, according to Makkoth 11a, the mothers of the highpriests used to look after those banished and supply them with food and clothing so that they should not pray for the death of their sons; אמותיהן של כהנים מספקות להן מחיה וכסות כדי שלא יתפללו על בניהן שימותו (see ibid.). In Sifri the following reason is given for the relationship between the highpriests and those sentenced to banishment: ר׳ מאיר אומר רוצח מקצר ימיו של אדם וכהן גדול מאריך ימיו של אדם אין דין שישב המקצר לפני המאריך, ר׳ אומר רוצח מטמא את הארץ ומסלק את השכינה וכהן גדול גורם שהשכינה תשרה על הארץ אין בדין שיהא מי שמטמא את הארץ לפני מי שגורם להשרות את השכינה בארץ i.e. the murderer shortens life, the highpriest lengthens it, it is not right that the shortener of life should live in the presence of him that lengthens it; or the murderer brings טומאה over the land and drives the Presence of God away, the highpriest brings the Presence of God over the land; it is not right that he who brings טומאה over the land should live in front of him that brings the Presence of God over the land.

If we take all these remarks together, the underlying thought seems to be, that the unpremeditated killing of a man is an event which is a contradiction to the mission of the highpriest and that a certain amount of responsibility for it could be ascribed to the high-priest.

When we consider that the banishment is really a banishment to the cities of the Levites, or more correctly to a city of the Levites, so that the manslayer is completely handed over to the influence of the “Levites”, the “assistants of the office of priests”, this fact would bring the connection with the whole mission of the Levites and the priesthood into closer consideration.

The highlight of the whole profession of Priest and Levite, the highest representative of which is the highpriest, lies in the conception: “teacher and expiation”, expiation in the Sanctuary, teaching, outside the Sanctuary, two elements that touch each other most intimately.  The expiation, the atonement which the priest has to attend to in the Sanctuary deals preferably, almost exclusively with שגגה with unintentional aberration from the right path. זדון, the wilful intentional doing wrong, the defiance of keeping the Torah is something not to be treated by the influence of the priest but comes under the authorities of right and law of the courts. But to spread the spirit of considering, and the seriousness of making resolutions for right living which places the whole of our life under the regime of the Torah, and makes us carefully weigh every step and every action with that consideration and precaution which precludes every carelessness and gives no room for punishable thoughtlessness, to nuture that seriousness in life which protects one even from שגגות, that indeed is quite essentially the purpose of the priesthood among the people. And just as, when, in sins against God — שבין אדם למקום — a punishable thoughtlessness has led to שגגות in capital sins, שיש בהן כרת, the כפרה is effected by priests in the Sanctuary (—and well may the importance of אכילת בשר חטאת which we have stressed elsewhere, be associated also with the admonition to the priests who eat it, to work against the spirit of שגגה amongst the people —) in the same way, when, in the realm of sins against fellow-man — שבין אדם לחברו, punishable thoughtlessness, שגגה has led to the capital sin of killing a man, reproach and admonition to the priests and their highest representative, the highpriest in whose time of office the judgment was given, comes in a double relation to the verdict. The banishment is taken as a banishment out of his presence, and at the same time his life is lived in sympathetic suffering with the condemned to the extent that his subsequent death is considered as a concluding atonement for what had happened. The Priesthood, and its higher bearer, the highpriest, has to awaken and nurture that life of duty which lives under the guidance of God, and ever afresh regenerates the following of that guidance, which allows one’s own life to run to the limit of its appointed course and never intervenes in the run of life of others. Thereby at the same time he has to awaken and nurture that spirit of conscious moral freedom of will which keeps the whole life away from the sphere of טומאה, the realm of blind physical lack of freedom and forms the morally free human life into a bearer and agent for the Presence of God on earth (an old version of the Sifri runs: גורם שתשרה שכינה על האדם בארץ). To both of these duties of the mission of the priesthood, the death of a man as the result of a human act which should have been controlled by conscious human intelligence, but was left to the play of blind physical mechanical forces, is the most crying contrast. אין בדין, say our sages, it is not consonant with what is right, it does not fall in with that principle of Jewish life which is to be kept clear from all doubt and mistake which the highpriest has to represent and nurture, that the מקצר ימים and מסלק שכינה should go about under the eyes of him who has to teach and foster the spirit which is to מאריך ימים and משרה שכינה. If there is a כה״ג there at the moment when the verdict is declared, the verdict is to be understood as a banishment from the circle of the כהן גדול, and thereby the judgment on what had happened placed in the light of the standpoint of the highpriest, which he, as the representative of the priesthood, represents, and the spirit of which is to be nurtured and fostered amongst the people by him and his fellow-priests. But at the same time with the limitation עד מות הכ״ג, accordingly with the proviso that, if the highpriest dies before he does, that death concludes the כפרה of the happening which the verdict of banishment had started. The continuance of the banishment is to be lifted, inasmuch as just in this death the sign is to be found that on the part of the priesthood the welfare of the people had been kept in their hearts with the intensity to instil in the minds of the people that seriousness of life which would have prevented the שגגה happening of such capital consequences. If, at the moment of the pronouncement of the verdict there is no highpriest in office so that the priesthood and the nation have no ideal representative, the banishment purports “out of the sphere of the nation” which — as a nation does not die — naturally reaches to the death of the one who banished, so that if he dies outside the Miklot-city his body is buried within it, also as his sentence is taken as a banishment out of the proximity of the highpriest, if he had died before the highpriest, when this latter dies, his remains may be reinterred in the graveyard of his home.
See the continuation of רוצח בשוגג in Deut. 19,1-10, also Deut. 21,1-9.

V. 1. As already remarked before, the concept משפחה is taken in a narrower and wider sense. As is evident from Ch. 26,30 et seq., the grandfather of Zelophehad had six sons, each one formed the head of a family. In a wider sense these six families together were considered as one family, one משפחה, as the משפחה of the Gileadites, and the heads of these six branches of the Gileadite family, the great-uncles of the daughters of Zelophehad approached Moses and the princes with their remonstrance.

V. 2. ויאמרו וגו׳. As we shall have to remark on V.6, the regulation which was made here at the plea of the heads of the Gileadite family only applied to the contemporary generation amongst whom the land was divided for the first time. The application itself indicates such a limitation. Above in Ch. 27,3 the application of the daughters was made in general terms, it referred quite personally to the relation of the daughters to their father and their concern at a father’s name becoming lost if there was no right of inheritance for daughters when there were no sons. There, there was not a word about the impending division of the land. That is why the decision given there applied for all time and in all circumstances. But here the application was provoked quite specially by the impending division of the land and refers to the consequences which the decision given there would have for this division. So that already from that fact it is easy to understand that the resulting decision here would only be for the generation living at the time of the division of the land. If the application and the settlement of it went beyond that time then the first sentence of the application את אדוני צוה ה׳ etc., would be entirely superfluous. It would have sufficed to have said אדני צוה בה׳ לתת וגו׳, then it would deal with doing away with the consideration that all future legacies given by the right of heritage through a daughter were to be set aside. ואדני צֻוה בה׳ — את אדני צוה ה׳, at the first order the initiative came from God, the second was the result of a representation by Moses. לתת את הארץ בנחלה וגו׳, they reminded them, that by the first order the land was to be divided בנחלה in the manner of a “stream” that “flows downwards in its appointed bed”, for that is the real conception of the right of inheritance being “a נחל״. The fundamental conception is that it should stay within the assigned province of the property of the home, the family, the tribe, the more so as it was at the same time assigned בגורל, as is explained on Ch. 26,55 with the co-operation of the אורים ותומים, accordingly every assignment of any portion of possession of the land had to be made as being an order from God, e.g. if a portion of the land was handed over to Judah it was not to be taken into possession by another tribe. ואדני צוה בה׳ וגו׳, but the second order which gave the daughters of Zelophehad the right of receiving the portion of land which they would inherit through their father at the division of the land would be in opposition to this tendency which was to be stamped on the whole division of the land by this mode of assignment. For

V. 3. והיו וגו׳, the right of daughters to inherit given them in Ch. 27,8, contains also the law that an inheritance they received through there being no brothers, or descendants of brothers after their death, goes to their sons (or according to one opinion also to their husbands, see V.11 ibid.) So that, if the husband, and so the children begotten by him, belonged to a different tribe, the inheritance would pass over from the possession of one tribe into the domain of another one, (which is also why the right of inheritance granted to daughters in general is called העברה — see ibid.). Now if the daughters of Zelophehad were to marry outside their tribe and the above mentioned rights of inheritance with all the consequences thereof be applied to them too, then immediately at the division of the land which was to be made according to tribes such an העברה would occur. More, it could happen, if the daughters of Zelophehad married now outside the tribe and died before the division leaving descendants (or perhaps their husbands), that at the division of the land, a piece of land assigned in accordance with the Divine decision, to the tribe of Menasseh would have to be assigned to some other tribe.

V. 4. ואם יהיה היובל וגו׳, and the direct apportionment by lot would make no difference to this assignment, it would be no temporary one, as if it would have been if accomplished by sale, but would be a permanent withdrawal from, and loss to the landed property which really fell to the tribe of Menasseh, as ירושה does not revert even in Youvel. (The heads of the families of Gileadites speak of a loss to the inheritance of their fathers, they say מנחלת אבותינו and not מנחלתנו. This seems to be spoken in the sense of the fact which lay at the base of the mode of the division of the land, that the land was apportioned to the באי הארץ only as the heirs of the יוצאי מצרים, — see Ch. 26,55).

V. 6—7. זה הדבר וגו׳ (see on Ch. 30,2). The laws introduced by the words זה הדבר are, as a rule, only temporary ordinances, applying just at the time. And as already remarked on V.2 the following limitation given here to the marriages of heiresses in their own rights only applies to the contemporary generation of those who participated in the division of the land. More, according to Baba Bathra, 120a, the אך למשפחת מטה אביהם תהײנה לנשים said to the daughters of Zelophehad was no dictatorial limitation to their rights of marrying whomsoever they liked but only עצה טובה, a piece of good advice which indicated their marrying within their own tribe as being highly desirable. By לטוב בעיניהם תהײנה לנשים their rights remained perfectly unlimited, as in fact appears to be conceded to them by והעברת את נחלת אביהן להן (Ch. 27,7), unless one wants to take the term העברה used there for the rights of inheritance of the daughters of Zelephehad as not to be taken in its literal meaning there, but only used in conformation with the general pertinent term for the rights of inheritance of daughters. The limitation of marriage of heiresses to within their own tribe would only apply to all other heiresses of their time.

The ולא תסב נחלה וגו׳ can altogether not be meant in absolute exactness. Such a transfer of inherited land from tribe to tribe would irrevocably occur in every case where all the brothers die after the marriage of the daughter to a member of another tribe. So that it can only in itself be intended to prevent as much as possible the alienation of hereditary landed property from its original tribe. By the legal establishment of the העברת נחלה at granting conditional rights of inheritance to daughters amongst the general laws of inheritance (Ch. 27), as well as by the introductory words זה הדבר אשר צוה ה׳ this possible prevention of the alienation of inherited property is only for the duration of that generation and we would only have to try to find what interest was served by all the legal attention which had to be given to this short-lived temporary measure.

Already at considering the Youvel institution in Levit. 25,10, we deliberated on the great value which the Torah lays on keeping the borders of the provinces of the tribes intact, and for the separate tribes continuing living apart from each other in their own allocated territories. By that means, we thought that the greatest furtherance was rendered for carrying out the one common calling of the nation in all the various conditions of life which the different professions and occupation in which the various tribes specialised, imposed on their members. And it was of great importance that these differences should be maintained traditionally and developed to the fullest extent in each tribe. (refer again to our notes on Levit. 25,10, where it was worked out at length the extreme importance of stressing the fact that the full Torah-life was not to be thought of as applying or appealing to any one class of thinkers, students or professors, but was exactly the same for soldier, sailor (Judah, Zebulun) thinker, tailor, rabbi, teacher, husbandman, field-worker, merchant (the other tribes as specialised prophetically already by the Father of the Tribes on his deathbed, see Gen. XLIX, etc. etc. I.L.). That, from this point of view, it was above all, most important at the beginning of and the time immediately following, the conquest and division of the land, to hand over the province, sharply marked off for the respective tribes in its completeness and to take every possible precaution to avoid any mixing up by the rights of inheritance, of the land allotted to each tribe, is, we think self evident. The less, in all future time, any legal hindrance is to be placed on the mutual intercourse and intermarriage between the tribes but rather the whole nation is to be united by meeting together three times a year about their one national Sanctuary, all the more would it be necessary at the beginning for each section of the country to be stamped with the speciality of its particular inhabitants so that they make themselves thoroughly at home and conversant with their tribal speciality (which to a large extent is influenced by the nature and position of their territory I.L.) which thus becomes traditional for that section of the country and the intended individual development of the tribes receives its assured place in the land. We believe that from this point of view both limiting the marriage of heiresses to members of their own tribe, as well as making this apply only to the first generation of those that came to take possession of the land, is quite understandable.
ידבקו, to attach oneself, as ודבק באשתו (Gen. 2,24) ותדבק בנערות בועז (Ruth 2,23).

V. 8. וכל בת ירשת נחלה ממטות וגו׳. From the term בת ירשת נחלה ממטות בני ישראל (which ממטות is in the plural I.L.) whereby a daughter is designated as an heiress receiving a legacy from two tribes, the Gemora (Baba Bathra 111a) teaches the law that at property left by a mother, her children have quite the same right of heritage as at property left by a father. Accordingly, a daughter whose father and mother belong to different tribes, at their death can receive a legacy from two tribes. Then the question is discussed (ibid. 112a) whether, at the marriage of such a double heiress, consideration has to be given to the tribal alienation of the maternal legacy also, so that a bridegroom has to be chosen who belongs both on his maternal and paternal side to the same tribe as the bride, or whether consideration for the maternal legacy need not be made at the marriage שכבר הוסבה, as an alienation of the same has already taken place by its having fallen to the daughter who legally belongs to the tribe of the father. From this problem also it is evident that absolute prevention of tribal alienation of inherited property cannot have been in mind at this law of the Torah.

V. 9. תסב נחלה וגו׳. The portions of the land allotted to any one tribe are not, right from the beginning, to be assigned in any part to any other tribe, כי איש בנחלתו ידבקו מטות בני ישראל for every tribe with all its members are primarily to be attached to the province allotted to it. Every part of the land is primarily to be kept as much as possible stamped with the special tendency of the tribe to which it is assigned, and every tribe is to keep the speciality of that tribe as the mode of life of its members as much as possible, without exception. (see on verses 6 and 7).

V. 10—12. כאשר צוה וגו׳. This definite information that all the daughters of Zelophehad married according to what they had been told, within their paternal tribe would endorse the opinion given on V.6, that this had been told them only as “a piece of good advice”, so that they could have acted differently without any detriment or having acted against the law. All the more must it be reckoned to their credit that all of them acted in accordance with what had been pointed out to them was in the best national interests.

The day on which the last member of that generation, which entered the land and took possession of it, died, and consequently the lifting of the ban on heiresses of landed property intermarrying between the tribes was promulgated by the national legal authorities, יום שהותרו שבטים לבא זה בזה, the fifteenth of Av. חמשה עשר באב retained permanently the character of a general national popular holiday. (Baba Bathra 121a).

V. 13. אלה המצות וגו׳. The commandments and regulations given from Ch. XXII until here:- the fresh census of the people, the regulations for the division of the land, the appointment of Joshuah, the national offerings, the rights of voluntary law-making (regarding the making and remission of vows, I.L.), the treatment for use for food of vessels taken over from non-Jewish possession, the rights and duties of the tribes who received their land in the Trans-jordan area, the cleansing of the land from polytheistic matters, fixing the borders of the land, the miklot-cities, the temporary measures at the marriage of heiresses of land property, all these laws and regulations are more or less in connection with the imminent taking possession of the land, hence were given at the border and in view of the land .בערבות מואב על ירדן ירחו
Deuteronomy: V. 1. אלה הדברים, “these are the words”, refers to the whole of the contents of this fifth book. Just as the last chapter of the fourth book reported the orders and regulations which God had given through Moses regarding the taking possession of the land which was now imminent, so in this fifth book is laid down all that Moses had still to tell the people. He was about to depart out of their midst and they would have to carry out their task in taking possession of the land without his guidance. The detailed description of the exact locality which follows here, seems to wish to fix with precision the place where Moses lived the last weeks of his life down here. The place where the people last saw their leader in their midst, where they last heard the living words of their Moses. The more every word of these last speeches of our God-sent leader bears the stamp of the whole depth of feeling with which his heart clung to his people and their future happiness, the more the deep longing is expressed therein to give his whole spirit and soul to his people for the future so full of trials and tests which awaited them, and the less this spot in the wilderness is recognisable by any speciality of its own, all the more is the wish understandable to keep it in memory by the knowledge of its exact location. For our Moses departs from us, and no monument, no commemorative column, no earthly commemorative token is left behind him. The whole earthly personality of our Moses disappears with his death. Only the place on earth where the last of his faithful words were heard by his people is handed down with the most possible precision so that if a later descendant of his people comes to this place; it may bring to him an echo of the Word of Moses and inspire him to be a faithful follower in his people and for his people.

מול סוף, it does not seem probable that here סוף is to be taken as referring to ים סוף, which indeed does not occur anywhere else without the ים. It appears rather to be the name of a place. תפל and לבן also do not occur elsewhere. If, according to an opinion in the Sifri, all these places are reminders of sins of which the people had been guilty on their long wanderings through the wilderness (such as lack of faith at the ים סוף I.L.) then it is not impossible that Moses and the people gave these names to certain places round about the plain where Moses used the last weeks of his life to make instructive and admonishing addresses to the people. These names, testifying to national lapses, by bringing to mind these errors of the past were to awaken firm resolutions for a purer, more loyal future.
V. 2 אחד עשר יום. The place described is reached from Horeb by a twelve day’s journey towards the mountains of Seir.

V. 3 ויהי וגו׳ דבר משה וגו׳ ככל וגו׳, not כל אשר וגו׳ but ככל אשר צוה ה׳ אותו אלהם (see on Numb. 30,1.); he repeated again not only everything that but as God had commanded everything. He gave out once again the short precise sentences of the Torah, and, at full length the details of “how” the commandments were to be carried out, the ככל, the “how” of all the laws. It is the same as the באר of V.5., the explanation of the Torah. This repetition and explanation of the Torah is not placed before us in this fifth book. Neither repetition nor explanation of the written laws laid down in the preceding books form the principal character of this fifth book. Of the just over a hundred laws which are contained in this book more than seventy are completely new, are not contained at all in the previous ones שמע, לא תתחתן, אסור הנאה של ע״ז, ברכת המזון, והיה אם שמוע, ברכות וקללות על הר גריזים ועיבל, לא תעשון כן לה׳, שמה תביאו, איסור במה, לא תוכל לאכול בשעריך, שחיטה, מעשר עני, ועשית עלתיך הבשר והדם, לא תוסיף ולא תגרע, נביא שקר, מסית, עיר הנדחת, זקן ממרא, שמטת כספים, צדקה, סנהדרין, אשרה, יחיד שעבד ע״ז, עדות, מצות המלך, חזרה מערכי המלחמה, ראשית הגז, משמרות כהונה, נביא אמת, הסגת גבול, עדים זוממים, קריאת שלום במלחמה, לא תשחית, עגלה ערופה, יפת תואר, בכורה, בן סורר, לא תלין, כלי גבר על אשה, שלוח הקן, מעקה, חרישה בשור וחמור, מוציא שם רע, אשת איש, נערה מאורסה, אונס, לא יקח אשת אביו, פצוע דכה, ממזר, עמוני ומואבי, אדומי, מצרי, קדוש מחנה, הסגרת עבד, קדשה, אתנן ומחיר, פועל בכרם, גט, מחזיר גרושתו, נקי לביתו, משכון, אבות על בנים, מלקות, לא תחסום, יבום, זכירת עמלק, בכורים, are all laws of the Torah ודוי מעשר, כתיבת התורה על אבנים, הקהל, כתיבת ס״ת, which are in no wise presented as mere repetition or explanations of what had already been given in the preceding books.

On the other hand מצות הדיינים, עשית פסל, עשרת הדברות, איבוד ע״ז, ליראה ולאהבה את ה׳, עבודה זרה, בשר תאוה, איסור דם, אבר מן החי, לא תתגודדו, מאכלות אסורות, קרחה, מעשר שני, בכור, פסח, שבועות, סוכת, מצבה, בעל מום, מולך, נחש וכשוף, תמים תהיה, רוצח בשוגג, השבת אבידה, שעטנז, ציצית, רבית, נדר, גנב נפש צרעת, השבת עבוט, עשק שכיר, מטה משפט, חבול בגד, שכחה, פאה, עוללת, צדק משקלות appear as repetition of laws already contained in the earlier books. To appreciate the tendency of this fifth book one must find out why those new laws were reserved to be given only here at the end, and why, out of the whole Torah which Moses repeated to the people just those were again picked out to be again fixed in the written text.

Perhaps consideration of one of these groups of laws some of which present themselves as repetition, will give us the key with which to answer this question. In Ch. 16,1-17 the laws of celebrating the Festivals are repeated. But, at the very first glance it strikes one that here, in this repetition only שבועות ,פסח and סוכת are mentioned, whereas a comparison with the chapter on the festivals (Levit. XXIII), makes one miss mention of י״כ ,ר״ה ,שבת and שמיני עצרת. Now these four which are not mentioned have this in common, that, according to their essential meaning they originate purely from our relationship of the individual to God. So that their most essential realisation would have been able to have been made in the wilderness too, and their being kept would hardly have been touched by the impending settling down in the land. It is a different matter with סוכת ,שבועות ,פסח. The one aspect of their meaning, the relation to the soil and its seasonal development would really only come into consideration henceforth; yea the סוכת-festival, even with the historical reference to the “living in huts” in the wilderness would only have meaning after that life had been given up to living in houses and cities, as also it may have been difficult to carry out its מצות לולב in the wilderness. Finally for all three, the important duty of the whole nation pilgrimizing up to meet together to form a national circle to make the Sanctuary of the Torah the national centre-point, would naturally only start with the decentralisation of the nation in the land, whereas in the wilderness, the nation was always united about the centre-point. It seems therefore highly probable that, at the repetition and explanation of the whole of the Torah during the last weeks before the entry into the land, not י״כ ,ר״ה ,שבת and ש״ע but שבועות ,פסח and סוכת were inserted for a second time in the written text in view of the influence that the circumstances which would now arise with the possession of the land, would be likely to have on their being carried out. Corresponding to this would also be the fact that just the two factors which are predominantly stressed at these repeated commands in the written text are:- the relation to the seasons of the year and the resulting regulation of the whole calendar: ,שמור את חדש האביב ,באספך מגרנך ומיקבך ,מהחל חרמש בקמה; and the concentration of all the festival celebrations in the centre-point chosen by God וזבחת פסח וגו׳ במקום אשר יבחר וגו׳, לא תוכל לזבח את הפסח באחד שערך וגו׳, כי אם אל המקום וגו׳ ובשלת ואכלת וגו׳, ושמחת לפני ה׳ אלקיך במקום וגו׳, שבעת ימים תחוג וגו׳ במקום וגו׳, שלש פעמים יראה וגו׳.

If we now consider the whole of the rest of the laws contained in this book from the same point of view, first, the repeated admonishments and its associated evils and errors are, of course, on account ע״ז against of the contact with the polytheistic inhabitants of Canaan which would only begin with the entry into the land, thus:—עיר נדחת, מסית, איסור הנאה של ע״ז, לא תתחתן, אשרה, יחיד שעבד ע״ז, נחש וכשוף, מולך, לא תתגודדו, איבוד ע״ז עשית פסל, מצבה.

Further, the same idea applies to the national leadership, and the jurisdiction which had to be organised throughout the land from the highest central court of justice after the departure of Moses:- סנהדרין, נביא שקר, מלקות, צדק and מלך, עדים זוממים, עדים, זקן ממרא, שופטים, נביא אמת משקלות, לא תהיה קדשה.

That the laws touching on conducting war, as קריאת משיח מלחמה, נקי לביתו, קדוש מחנה, יפת תאר, לא תשחית, שלום and the laws prescribed to be carried out at once after the first treading on the soil of the land, the כתיבת התורה על האבנים, ברכות וקללות על הר גרזים ועיבל presented themeselves just then to be specially noted speaks for itself. Also the permission for בשר תאוה which started with the imminent decentralisation of the people all over the land, by which the שחיטה and the observation of all the dietary laws were entrusted to the conscientiousness of every individual of the people, sufficiently explains the writing down or respectively the repeated writing down of the מצות שחיטה, of אבר מן החי ,איסור דם and the chapter on מאכלות אסורות, as well as the laws preserving and keeping alive the attachment to the central Sanctuary:- ודוי מעשר, מעשר שני, בכורים, לא תוכל לאכול בשעריך, שמה תביאו, איסור במה. But with the transition from the direct guidance of God, and being provided for by Him in the wilderness to the ordinary normal human conditions in the land, such different changes also in the social life of the people before them, that the writing down for the first time or the repeated written stressing of a whole series of social laws is amply explained. So, for instance, the whole detailed law of צדקה, the law of מעשר עני, שמטת כספים, פועל בכרם, which appear in the text for the first time in this book, as well as the repetition of the laws regarding the duties imposed towards the poor and needy, as שכחה, פאה, עוללת, רבית, חבל בגד, עשק שכיר, השבת עבוט. During the whole period of the wandering in the wilderness where God provided for shelter over one’s head, clothing and all the requirements of life there were no poor, perhaps not even a daily help to be paid. It was only with the entry of normal conditions where people’s livelihood was handed over to the production and intercourse of men that differences of fortune and people having to depend on and wait for aid from fellow-men arose. In the wilderness where everybody had everything and only what was really necessary, there was no necessity and no possibility of צדקה. So, further it was only with the transition from being entirely provided for directly from the Hand of God to the normal conditions of life that the man really became the man, became the provider of the civic existence of his wife and home. In the wilderness this essential phase of marriage was missing. It was only in the land that marriage received its full importance regarding the basis of social rights and legal positions. Hence, whereas in the earlier books laws regarding the conditions and regulations governing the physiological and ethical written determination of the laws governing the entering and dissolving of the marriage state פצוע דכה, גירושין, קידושין, מצרי, עמוני ומואבי, ממזר, as well as the מצות יבום and משפט בכורה closely connected with the legal civic rights aspect of family life was reserved for the repetition of the whole of the Torah just before the entry into the land. As it appears to us, this point of view makes the appearance of these groups of laws in this fifth book perfectly clear and natural; and these laws picked out for general discussion are so much in the majority, that we think we are justified in thinking that we may expect a closer consideration of the other laws will show us a similar reason for their insertion in this fifth book.

But whereas, at the whole repetition of the Lawgiving looked at from this point of view, certain groups of laws were repeated or given for the first time just at this particular time, the introduction with which Moses הואיל באר את התורה, began the repetition of the explanation of the whole Torah is given to us in its entirety. For just these first eleven chapters which contain the comprehensive introductory speeches of Moses wish to lay down the fundamental points of view, the thoughts, and the general mitzvas towards God and His Torah to be borne by looking back at all the God-revealing experiences which were now coming to an end. These speeches coming from Moses’s mouth, and laid down for all time are meant to be taken to heart ever afresh by Jewish minds and Jewish feelings, that thereby they may be elevated to become enthusiastic faithful sons of the Covenant of God in that covenant. They are the feelings of יראת ה׳ and אהבת ה׳ and דבקות בה׳ borne by the fundamental thought of אחדות ה׳ in theoretical and practical consciousness. It is the duty of למוד התורה for every man of the nation, and that of ושננתם לבניך for every Jewish father towards his children, as well as the indivisability and immutability of the traditional Torah in לא תוסיף ולא תגרע. At the same time, in the introductory speeches to the Torah which form the real testament of Moses to his people, those commands are incorporated which accompany every Jewish person however isolated he may have to live, which are still to-day our constant reminding teachers for God and our duties, as קריאת שמע, והיה אם שמוע, תפלין, מזוזה, ברכת המזון, and later, in the “Festival Chapter”, זכירת יציאת מצרים daily as well as ציצית and שעטנז appear again in the written Torah. For the people are going out of the hitherto influence of the central guidance into an individual life where more than ever the Jew needs constant admonition to his calling and even his garments are to become to him a preacher of the duties of a Jew and the moral nobility of human beings.

If we take all this together we believe we are not in error if we see in this fifth book a compendium of those laws which were necessary for the authorities as well as for every individual of the people to realise just now at the imminent transition from the wilderness into the land, their being committed to writing having been reserved for this compendium, or their written repetition appearing necessary for this purpose. If therefore this book is casually referred to by the name משנה תורה and thereby taken to be a “repetition of the Torah”, this cannot be taken to mean that it is actually a repetition of the laws already contained in the previous four books. We have seen that the far greater number of laws which appear in this book are given for the first time. But rather this appellation of “repetition” can only be fitting insomuch as this book gives us the information of the verbal repetition and explanation of the whole of the Torah with which Moses concluded his activities on earth for his people, out of which certain laws which this book contains, partly new ones, partly repetitions of laws already given in previous books, were written down.

V. 5. הואיל משה באר וגו׳ (see on V.3.) הואיל often takes the infiniive after it is as כי הואיל הלך (Hosea V.II), ולו הואלנו ונשב (Josh. 7,7), הואל קח (Kings, II. V.23) and elsewhere. As already remarked on V.3, the first eleven chapters of this book contain the “introductory speeches” with which Moses introduced the repetition and explanation of the whole Torah. The first part of these speeches (Ch. 1,6 till III, 22) have the tendency to impress on the people as fundamental thoughts, the conviction, drawn from their own experiences, that what was required for overpowering the nations and taking possession of their land was not strength of arms or being good at warfare but complete devotion to God in fulfilling His Will. And that such obedience to God, which in peace forms our sole calling, is also in war by itself sufficient to overcome all forces which oppose us. With obedience to God we can accomplish everything, without it, nothing. Not as a powerful nation, master of the art of war, but as the People of God’s Laws of Morality is Israel to enter its path in the history of nations. On this path Israel’s victories and defeats are alike proof of this fact in contrast to the development of all other nations.

V. 6. בחרב, the whole district round about Sinai is called “Horeb”. Thus ויבא אל הר האלקים חרבה (Ex. 3,1), רב לכם שבת בהר הזה. Cf. ויפגשהו בהר האלקים (Ex. 4,27). Moreover הר does not only designate mountain in the narrow sense of the word but the whole mountainous district of which the mountain itself forms the highest point. Hence הר is used also for highland in contrast to שפלה the lowland (V. 7). So that בהר הזה means quite simply:- in the surroundings of this mountain, in this mountainous district. רב לכם וגו׳, the purpose for which you were first led to this mountain on your way from Egypt to the Promised Land, and were to tarry there awhile (Ex. 3,12) is already sufficiently accomplished. Here you received the Torah by the acceptance and adoption of which you entered the “service of God”, and you have made yourself sufficiently conversant with it, and have erected a Sanctuary to it in your midst, so that now nothing further is lacking for you to move into the land which has no other purpose than to become the base for the realisation of this Torah.

V. 7. פנו וגו׳. When we consider that בערבה בהר ובשפלה בנגב ובחוף הים is clearly a topographical description of the land of Canaan according to the different nature of the various parts of its territory, as then it is summarised as ארץ הכנעני etc; but that this topographical description בערבה etc. equally clearly refers back to the preceding הר האמרי ואל כל שבניו; then it is evident that הר האמרי וכל שכניו designates the whole of the country into which they are to go. And in fact, just as כנעני in its narrow sense only designates one of the nations that inhabited Palestine, but in a wider sense of the word the whole land is called ארץ כנען, so do we also find אמרי, although in itself only one of the inhabited nations, used as representing them all and the land called ארץ האמרי (see Amos 2,9,10 and also here in verses 20 & 27). The Amorites were the first Palestinian nation on which the Israelites stumbled on their way from the wilderness, so that the whole land could well be understood by them as הר האמרי ושכניו and also called simply בערבה .ארץ האמרי. From Ch. 3,17 & XI,30 it is evident that both sides of the Jordan, the surroundings of the Dead Sea —which itself is called ים הערבה is understood by the name ערבה. Similarly the surroundings of Jericho are called ערבות ירחו (Jos. 5,10 and elsewhere). Altogether it is not easy to determine the exact meaning of ערבה. Whereas in the books of the Prophets it clearly designates an idea synonymous with “desert”, e.g. in Jerimiah 6,6: - המוליך אותנו במדבר בארץ ערבה ושוחה וגו׳ nevertheless it occurs next to מדבר and ישימון as the name of a special place. Sam. I, XXIII,24: במדבר מעון בערבה אל ימין הישימון. In the Sifri ערבה is explained as מישור של יער, a wooded plain. — שפלה is the lowland, the deep-lying district at the side of a mountain. Thus Jos. 11,16 הר ישראל ושפלתה.

By חוף הים ,נגב ,שפלה ,הר ,ערבה the whole land seems to be described according to its different topographical parts; ערבה: the plain of the Jordan, הר: the highland, stretching in the middle from north to south, שפלה: the lowland on either side, נגב: the lowlying land in the south, חוף הים the sea coast in the west. Similarly in Josh. 11,16 the land conquered by Joshuah is described as:- ההר ואת כל הנגב ואת כל ארץ הגשן ואת השפלה ואת הר ישראל ושפלתה (cf. the same in XII,8 ibid). There חוף הים is missing, the Mediterranean district occupied by the Philistines which was then still unconquered by Joshuah.—In the Sifri, by שכניו the Amorites, Ammon and Moab and the mountains of Seir are understood. Then, as the commentator זרע אברהם remarks hereon, the exclusion of the domains of Ammon and Moab and Edom from Israel’s possession was only fixed after the sin of the spies and as a result from it, but originally these lands too were destined to be part of the land of Israel. This would well agree with the Midrath Rabboth on Gen. 15,19, where the three nations whose lands were promised to Abraham, the קיני, קנזי וקדמני, amongst the ten nations who inhabited the Promised Land, but whose territories were reserved to be given to Israel in the future, are taken to be Ammon, Moab and Edom, whose lands were to be incorporated in the Land of Israel at the future restoration. Thus Isaiah in XI.14:—אדום ומואב משלוח ידם ובני ארץ כנעני .עמון משמעתם is used to embrace all these parts in one. והלבנון: the Israeli mountainous range is itself really the southern extension of the Lebanon mountains. Here the whole of Lebanon right up to the Euphrates is reckoned in with the land originally promised. (see Gen. XV.18).

V. 8. ראה נתתי לפניכם וגו׳ באו ורשו, without one stroke of a sword, אין אתם צריכין לכלי זיין, were Israel to have taken possession of the land, had they only lived up to the ideals of their calling (ספרי; see Ex. 23,27 et seq.).

V. 9. ואמר אלכם בעת ההיא. Similarly also in V. 18: ואצוה אתכם בעת בעת ההיא .ההיא: “at that time”, at the time in which you were to go to take possession of a land inhabited by powerful inhabitants well versed and experienced in warfare, I did not drill you in the use of weapons, did not make you study plans of war and strategy, did not perfect you in armour and arms, did not appoint military officers and generals; even at the moment of imminent conquest of nations and countries, one thing and one thing only was to concern you, to know the most faithful and most conscientious realisation of God’s Torah being practiced in your inner circles. Keeping the Divine Laws of morality suffices to conquer the world. Let Israel only correspond to the ideal of its Divine calling and leave its external position in the world to—God. בעת ההיא: at the time mentioned in verse 16, when they were still in Horeb. לא אוכל לבדי שאת אתכם, (cf. Ex. 11,11 & 14), this includes carrying out the whole task of all that results from Moses being given the leadership of the people and which is referred to in its various aspects in V. 12.

V. 10. ככוכבי וגו׳. Just as when one looks at the starry heaven one only gets an impression of countless numbers and does not think of counting the individual stars, so do you give the same impression when one looks at you in your totality. After all, history does not offer many opportunities of looking at an assemblage of the whole of a nation at one time, six hundred thousand able men, at least two and a half million people, gathered together. Looking at the uncounted mass of the people and comparing them to the uncounted mass of the stars could also at the same time be to counter the erroneous way of considering them in their totality as just an uncounted mass amongst whom individuals lose their importance. But they are like the uncounted stars amongst the mass of which each individual one nevertheless retains its independent importance, is a “world on its own”, has its own value as a sign of God’s management and rule of the universe (see on Gen. 15,5).

V. 12. טרח .טרחכם ומשאכם וריבכם used commonly in the Talmud for wearisome trouble; in היו עלי לטרח ,תנ״ך (Is. 1,14) and Job. XXXVII:11 אף ברי יטריח עב where it means the forcing apart of a heavy cloud by the rays of light, where what stood there as a thick mass of dark cloud is broken up and spread around as little clouds of vapour edged by light, יפץ ענן אורו. In rabbinic Hebrew טרח also has the meaning of setting something heavy in motion, shattering. טריח (Baba Bathra 18a, and Chulin 45b.). Here טרח is activity which is strenuous, משא the irritating enduring, the bearing of things which demands patience (cf. specially Numb. 11,11 & 14) both of which require unremittingly the leadership and teaching of the people, which Moses had to attend to. When ריבכם, the individual personal quarrels were added to the list which Moses by himself had to settle, it became more than the strength of even a Moses could bear. In טרחכם, ספרי and משאכם are referred to the difficulties which the office of judge and leader has to suffer from the different peculiarities of character which specialised the people, and טרחכם to the quarrelsome sense of the litigants who came to court, and משאכם to the tendency to ironic witticisms on the personal doings and omissions of the leader, which would tend not a little to undermine his authority were they not met by being completely ignored by Moses’ ענוה.

V. 13. הבו לכם וגו׳: you give, or: bring forth for yourselves, i.e. choose and out of your midst, name to me, חכמים, men who know the given laws, ונבונים who have the ability to draw the right conclusions and decisions from the facts given to them in the case before them (see on Gen. 41,33 and Ex. on מנורה p. 471) וידעים לשבטיכם whose characters are known to you. Their חכמה and בינה I can find out by myself, by testing, but their character can only be known by their lives, that is only known to those who have associated with them. In this ידועים לשבטיכם all the demands of the moral character which Jethro specialised as יראי אלקים אנשי אמת שנאי בצע (Ex. 18,21) are contained, whereas the חכמה ובינה mentioned here come under the virtues demanded there by אנשי חיל. It is characteristic that Jethro in his proposition to Moses places righteousness of character in the foreground. Moses in his demand to the people to choose men for judges puts intellectual qualities first. This could establish the fact that in truth, accordingly in the opinion of a Moses and Jethro, excellence of character, fearing God, loving truth, hating self-interest are necessary to a much higher degree for giving correct judgements than depth of learning and sharpness of mind. But public opinion looks above all for a learned and clever man to be a judge. As a matter of fact, in the later practice of Jewish law, in ordinary civil matters, any three simple honest men out of the people, שלשה הדיוטות, are considered competent to settle cases, and knowledge of the Law, the Torah was sufficiently spread amongst the people to make the assumption possible that amongst any three of them אי אפשר דלית בהו חד דגמיר at least one of them would be sufficiently versed in the knowledge of the law. (Sanhedrin 3a,). ואשימם בראשיכם: once I have appointed them, at your own proposal, to be over you, then certainly the matter is taken out of your hands, and their authority is “set” fixed by me. Then their authority is like the Law itself אשר ”שם״ משה לפני בני ישראל (Ch. 4,44). In the respect you give to those “set above you” you are showing respect to the authority which “set them there”, and to yourselves out of whose midst they proceeded.

V. 15. ואקח את ראשי שבטיכם וגו׳ ואתן אותם ראשים עליכם, the men, by their personalities already enjoyed general respect and confidence, by which they had already become the “heads of the tribes”, the first, the most influential men in the people. Now they have become ראשים ”עליכם״, they receive the official position of a superior appointed by Moses, “given” an authority to be respected by the people. This fact that only ראשי השבטים were appointed by Moses as ראשים על שבטים would be at the root of what was continued as the general normal procedure long after in Jewish legal practice:—full legal authority ever dependent on two conditions, מומחה לרבים and נטילת רשות, the preceding “having been tested by the public” which rests on the recognition of the conscientiousness and general excellence of character, and then upon authorisation being conferred by the highest national representative, the ריש גלותא in בבל or the נשיא in ארץ ישראל (see Sanhedrin 9a,),—שרי אלפים, see on Ex. 18,21.

V. 16. ואצוה את שפטיכם. Here ואצוה has entirely its fundamental meaning connected with צבה: to direct somebody to his post, to give him his duty. So in Ch. 3,28, וצו את יהושע וחזקהו. Or Sam. II, VI,21, לצוות אותי נגיד (see Gen. 2,1 at end). Accordingly it goes beyond the following sentences which only stress some special factors of the general duties of that post. Thus Sanhedrin 7,b: ואצוה ,כנגד מקל ורצועה תהא זריז, according to תוספות there: שלא להטיל אימה על הציבור לרדותם יותר מדאי, not to misuse the judicial powers of punishment given to them so that they become unduly feared by the public, and further on the next page there אזהרה לדיין שיסבול את הצבור, warning the judges of the tiresomeness of their office and the necessity for their having patience even with outrageous conduct of the public, to know that a judge is appointed to train the public and patience is expected from him. כאשר ישא האומן את היונק, “even as the nurse bears with the baby”, Quite similarly the ספרי on our verse: אמרתי להם הוו מתונים בדין שאם בא דין לפניך פעם אחת שנים ושלש אל תאמר כבר בא דין זה לפני ושניתין ושלשתיו אלא מתונים בדין takes it to be an exhortation to be careful and thoughtful in pronouncing judgment, not to be quick in giving it, to give each case individual repeated consideration even if it is quite similar to cases which have previously come before you on several occasions. Altogether not to consider the office as giving rights of superiority but as one entirely of service, yourself as a servant, not a master, of the community לשעבד הייתם עומדים ברשות עצמכם עכשיו הרי אתם משועבדים לציבור “formerly you were your own masters, now that you are in office, you are the servants of the community”.

שמע בין אחיכם, not ושמע איש ואחיו וגו׳ the judge may not listen to one party by itself, but always only in the presence of the other party, his position is always to be solely בין אחיכם, and no party may try to get the ear of the judge first and put his case before the opponents are also there. No preliminary opinion of the case may be formed by the judge. אזהרה לבית דין שלא ישמע דברי בעל דין קודם שיבא בעל דין חברו ואזהרה לבעל דין שלא יטעים דבריו לדיין קודם שיבא בעל דין חברו. That the hearing must only be made in the presence of the two parties is an admonition made equally to the judges and to the parties themselves.

צדק .ושפטתם צדק is the conception of right, of justice: משפט, putting the conditions of the people and the matter of the case in order according to this conception, the realisation of justice and right in due order, hence צדק את הדין ואח״כ חתכהו :ושפטתם צדק (Sanhedrin 7,b) דין is the result for the special case derived from the general laws of justice and right. First be absolutely sure in your own mind of the outcome of the case in question in accordance with, and out of the general source of justice and right, and then proclaim it in precise words. Thus משפט becomes naught but realised צדקה in a concrete case.

בין איש ובין אחיו ובין גרו: it is to be quite the same to you whether the case on which you have to give your decisions is between two of your native-born countrymen or between one of them and a stranger who has come from outside to live amongst you. With his entry into your contry the גר, the stranger, becomes גרו, is made the equal of every native. (see Levit. 24,22, and Ex. on XX,10). In Yebamoth 46,b, the teaching is further taught on this verse, that attaining the character of a גר i.e. legal entry into Judaism can only be obtained through a ב״ד (a court of justice I.L.): גר צריך ג׳ משפט כתיב בי׳ (see תסופות there and 4a). In Sanhedrin 7,b גרו is taken to refer to a tenant in the same house and the whole passage בין איש ובין אחיו ובין גרו is explained as, for instance, אפילו בין בית לעלייה, אפילו בין תנור לכיריים, even a petty dispute between the respective rights of the tenants of the ground floor and the one above, or how far the oven or fireplace must be from the wall etc., on which the ערוך remarks: no matter may be considered too petty for the judge to give it serious consideration. He must acquaint himself with all the necessary details to bring justice and equity in all cases of dispute or quarrel.

V. 17. לא תכירו פנים—see on Levit. 19,15,—כקטן כגדול. After in לא תכירו פנים all personal considerations of the contending parties in the case is forbidden to the judge, and it is demanded that he should “not know them at all” in forming judgement, as, according to Jewish conception of justice the most correct pronouncement of judgement results when the parties are really personally unknown to the judge (see ibid), the words כקטן כגדול cannot refer further to the social position of the persons, and Sanhedrin 8a, refers it to the greater or lesser importance of the matter in dispute: שיהא חביב עליך דין של פרוטה כדין של מאה מנה, (that a case involving only shillings or pence must be of equal importance in your eyes to one of hundreds of pounds I.L.), and indeed not only that the smallest matter in dispute must receive the same care and conscientiousness in forming and pronouncing the verdict, לעיוני ביה ולמפסקיה as the most important one, which would be self-understood, but לאקדומיה, that the smallest least important case which had been reported first must be given precedence to the most important case which had only been reported later.

לא תגורו מפני איש, really: you have not to fall back on account of anybody (see Gen. on XIII,4). Sanhedrin 6,b. teaches from this מנין לתלמיד שיושב לפני רבו וראה זכות לעני וחובה לעשיר מנין שלא ישתוק שנאמר לא תגורו מפני איש לא תכניס דבריך מפני איש, that even a law-student, sitting at a case where his teacher has to decide between a poor man and a rich one, and knows of something which might favour the decision for the poor man may not refrain from interfering and keeping it back out of awe of his master and fear of the rich man. There, on 7a, the meaning of גור is taken to be keeping something to oneself, holding something back to oneself, לישנא דכנושי, referring it to ויין וגו׳ ולא תאגור (XXVIII,39), אגר בקציר מאכלה (Prov. 6,8), אגר בקיץ (ibid X,5), in which places all אגר mean a gathering-in of fruits to store them. We have repeatedly had occasion to draw attention to the meaning of the roots פ״א at which, as a rule, the conception which lies in the two last letters is so individualised by the preceding א that the א indicates the idea of the purpose and aim of the activity which is expressed by the two following letters. If the idea of landlessness lies in the word גר—as we believe it does, somebody being taken out of his real soil and place of development, then the א placed before it gives the word the meaning of something being taken away from its soil, for oneself. So that the concept גר lies at the root of אגר and can give us the explanation of it. This meaning is clearly evident in the word מגורה, barn, the place for storing the grain which has been gathered in. And in גר also, there is not only the concept of being separated from one’s homeland, but at the same time, of being taken up, accepted in another place, he is indeed one who has become at home with us out of foreign parts. One who stores up in his own mind and keeps to himself, an opinion, a view which has grown and matured in the soil of due consideration can then very aptly be expressed by גור, and that is not to be done by one who is there to give his opinion in judgement, out of consideration of any man whatsoever, ;לא תגורו מפני איש כי המשפט לאלקים הוא, in giving judgement you are doing the work of God. It is not your affair which you can decide in accordance with your own ideas, it is God’s Justice which is to be made actual through you. Therefore you are not to keep back your just judgement out of the slightest fear of any man, as, doing His work, you can safely depend on His protection and support. כל דיין “every judge” is says in Sabbath 10,a, כל דיין שדן דין אמת לאמתו מעלה עליו הכתוב כאלו נעשה שותף להקב״ה במעשה בראשית “every judge who, by his verdict makes true justice into an actual accomplished Truth is considered as if he had participated in God’s work of creation. For through him human conditions receive that form which was the intention of the Creator when He set human beings in the world with the ability of their own free will to make His laws of justice something real and actual. So much is the pronouncement of a just judgement considered a work of God to be made in His Name that in Sanhedrin 8,a we find on the sentence כי המשפט לאלקים הוא the explanation given: אמר הקב״ה לא דיין לרשעים שנוטלין ממון מזה ונותנים לזה שלא כדין, אלא שמטריחין אותי להחזיר ממון לבעליו that just as a false verdict is a sin against man so is it also one against God, Who makes it His business to rectify the wrong done which has been done in His Name.

והדבר וגו׳ תקריבון אלי ושמעתיו, Sanhedrin 7,a remarks: Moses, in his modesty does not say ואשמיעכם “I will let you hear what is right”, but ושמעתיו “I will consider the matter” אי גמירנא גמירנא ואי לא אזלינא וגמירנא, “if I can decide from what I have already been taught, I will give you a decision, but if not, I will seek the necessary instruction”.

V. 18. ואצוה אתכם וגו׳, refers, according to the context, to the nation who בעת ההוא (V. 9. I.L.) during their stay at Horeb had been taught by Moses the whole law for all the activities of their lives. In ספרי it is specially referred to the ten differences given in Sanhedrin 32,a, in which civil law differs from criminal law.

V. 19. ונסע וגו׳ את כל המדבר הגדול והנורא ההוא אשר ראיתם. This is the Wilderness of Paran (see Numb. 13,3 & 26) אשר ראיתם, they had learnt to know it for the second time at the end of the forty years on their second move to Kadesh. המדבר הגדול והנורא ההוא, if it still required a proof of trust and confidence in God’s protection, this journey through this terrible desert must have established it, a journey in which everybody down to the smallest child must have experienced the special protection of the Almight of God.

V. 21. חתת .ואל תחת (phonetically related to אתת from which we get אתותם cutting or digging implements, עט ,עטט, stylus, חדד sharp, עדים עד עדד to snatch away, to tear, really to be broken קשת גבורים חתים (Sam. I. 2,4) “the bow of the mighty ones lies in pieces”. החת broken, to lose courage, to be afraid.
V. 22. & 23. וייטב וגו׳ ותקרבון וגו׳, see on Ch. XIII.2.

V. 24. וירגלו אתה, literally, they went through it step by step. Whereas הלך looks to the goal at the end of the journey, מרגל has a goal at every step, as he wants to learn to know the land through which he is wandering.

V. 25. ויאמרו טובה הארץ וגו׳. As far as the excellence of the land they were all agreed, and indeed they brought proof of it in the fruits they brought. Everything else was only the subjective personal impression which the gigantic appearance of the inhabitants of the country had made on their timid souls. Had the people been filled with the right spirit they would only have accepted the report of the excellence of the country and everything else would have left them quite untouched.
V. 26. אבה .ולא אביתם וגו׳ ותמרו, to give in to the will of another (see Ex. 10,27 and Deut. 18,8 et seq). מרה, to oppose the will of another (see Gen. 26,35). המרה, to act against somebody.

V. 27. ותרגנו באהליכם וגו׳. The etymology of רגן is obscure. Its use in Prov. 16,28 ונרגן מפריד אלוף and באפס עצים תכבה אש ובאין נרגן ישתק מדון (ibid. 20) prove that רגן designates causing and maintaining a quarrel. It seems to mean to irritate, and הֵרָגֵן mutually to irritate one another, and נרגן which after all is also a niphal form, such an agitator, who, under the appearance of looking after himself and to be upset by what he himself has to endure, or to feel the wrong done to others as if it were being done to himself, stirs others up to dissatisfaction and disloyalty. Hence the sentence in Prov. 26,22: דברי נרגן כמתלהמים והם ירדו חדרי בטן, “the words of an agitator sound as if it was their own quarrel they were taking up but still sink deep into the innermost feelings of others”. In his mild manner Moses only refers to what they spoke about amongst themselves in their tents (Numb. XIV.1.) and passes over the agitation and open revolt against himself and God (ibid II.4).

V. 29. ערץ .לא תערצון has the peculiarity, which must be explained, that it means both getting a fright and giving a fright, so that the root ערץ is used both for passively being frightened, as transitively giving a fright. אולי תערוצי (Is. 47,12) can hardly have any other meaning than: “Perhaps Thou wilt spread terror, show Thyself fearful”, and hence לערוץ הארץ (ibid. II, 19 & 21) surely has only the meaning “put the world in terror”. Perhaps the meaning of “concentrating all one’s forces” lies in the root ערץ. So that it means: to strike terror into somebody with all the force of one’s might, “to impress him”, as well as: to have such an opinion of somebody that one has the feeling that one has to collect all one’s forces to oppose him, i.e. to let onself be deeply impressed by someone”.
V. 36. מלא אחרי ה׳. See on Numb. 14,24.

V. 37. & 38. These verses 37 and 38 are in brackets. The speech is continued in V. 39. As in V. 36 Moses only thought of Caleb as the one spy who would enter the land, it was necessary to mention Joshuah as well, who was indeed Caleb’s comrade in the mission of the spies and who was likewise to enter the Land. It seems that Joshuah’s faithfulness and loyalty at this mission was so very much self-understood, he being the immediate disciple of Moses, that it did not need to be as specially stressed as did that of Caleb.
