What Jewish witnesses have to do is:—to admonish and warn before the criminal act is committed, and to accuse the criminals before the court and be responsible for due punishment to be inflicted after it has been perpetrated; and God makes heaven and earth to be His admonishers and warners, and finally His executors of punishment on you if you exchange the service which is His exclusive due for the service of anything which heaven and earth include. The world, heaven and earth, will not smile on you if you stake your giving satisfaction to God against courting their favour. ושברתי את גאון עזכם ונתתי את שמיכם כברזל etc. (“And I will break the pride of your power and will make your heaven as iron and your earth as brass, and your strength will be spent in vain for your land shall not yield its increase, neither shall the trees of the land yield their fruits”. Levit. 26,19 and 20) runs the warning of the punishment. And ונתתי מטר ארצכם בעתו וגו׳, וחרה אף ה׳ ועצר את השמים וגו׳ (“And I will give the rain of your land in its proper season etc. etc; then the anger of God will glow against you, will hold back the heaven and no rain will come and the earth will not yield its produce etc. etc.” Ch. 11,14 et seq.), so runs the alternative which we have daily to place before ourselves and our children to choose from.

כי אבד תאבדון מהר מעל הארץ וגו׳, by the addition of the words מעל הארץ וגו׳ the meaning of complete annihilation is taken away from the concept אבד and gives it the meaning of only a relative passing away, being completely removed out of the Land. So also ואבדתם מהרה מעל הארץ הטובה in Ch. 11,17. Here they are told that if their defection should reach the height depicted in the previous verse, they will then rapidly be removed from the Land, לא תאריכון ימים עליה כי השמד תשמדון. Compared with the limited תאבדון מעל הארץ וגו׳, the absolute השמד תשמדון clearly designates complete destruction which indeed anyway is innate in the basic meaning of שמד. So Amos. in Ch. 9,8, הנה עיני ה׳ בממלכה החטאה והשמדתי אתה מעל פני האדמה אפס כי לא השמיד אשמיד את בית יעקב נאם ה׳. So that כי השמד תשמדון of our verse gives the reason for quickly removing Israel from the Land as soon as their defection should have reached a certain stage. They are no longer to be left in the land, for were they to stay there it would mean their having to be entirely annihilated.

Their speedy removal from the Land is their spiritual and moral salvation. They must lose their own country and national independence so that they do not fall into the same degree of degeneration which brought about the destruction of the Canaanite inhabitants before them. Thereby the same thing is said that our sages said when they attached significant meaning to the numerical value of the disastrous word “ונושנתם״. The numerical value of the letters of the word add up to 852. But we only stayed in the land 850 years, 440 till the Temple was built (480 years after the exodus from Egypt, i.e. 440 after entry into the Land), Kings I, VI,1, and 410 years that the Temple existed. So that their fate of being driven out of the Land overtook them two years before the space of time indicated by צדקה עשה הקב״ה עם ישראל להקדים שתי שנים לונושנתם :ונושנתם (Gittin 88,a) “and this quick getting the people out of the land was a benevolent act of God for their salvation.” The State and Temple went to ruin, but the people, with a remnant of their spiritual heritage that was still left in their hearts, went out to meet the solution of their great mission in the Dispersion.

V. 27. והפיץ וגו׳. You will become scattered and spread amongst the nations. You will not remain together in exile, some of you will come amongst every nation. There could be a double purpose in this scattering Israel amongst the nations. Nowhere would they form a compact numerically large mass, and would remain protected from the political errors amongst which they would find themselves in their future social lives; and they will be seeds of God, strewn about in the world, and בעמים, in the midst of the social life of the nations will awake and nurture the idea of a different way of looking at the world and life and a different way of living one’s life. For הפיץ is not exclusively used for a destructive scattering but also for strewing seed, to spread by scattering, והפיץ קצח (Is. 28,25), and יזרעאל “the seed of God” was the name given to Israel in Exile (Hosea 2,2) when they had accomplished this purpose.

ונשארתם מתי מספר וגו׳, although small in number you will still remain a separate גוי amongst the גוים, a separate nationality amongst the nations. When one considers that, as far as is known, there are at most four or five million Jews, at most double the number that went out of Egypt, and one considers the fact that this number was reached, yea exceeded, already in David’s time, considers that, in spite of the loss of the ten tribes, at the time of the second Temple (according to Pessachim 64,b) the number was reckoned at over twelve million, and that, according to Josephus during the siege of Jerusalem over a million died there alone, so that one cannot be far wrong in assuming that at the fall of the Jewish State through the Romans there were at least four million Jews in the world, then it does really seem that, in spite of the much talked of Jewish fecundity, their numbers remain more or less stationary during the long centuries of the exile, and that by special Divine providence what is here pronounced ונשארתם מתי מספר בגוים וגו׳, “you remain few in number”, has been uninterruptedly realised.

V. 28. ועבדתם שם אלהים, there you will be subservient to the heathen gods who seemed to you so attractive with their allurements, and will get to know what kind of influence they exert, will get to know by painful experience what men become when the divinities they worship are מעשה ידי אדם gods which they make for themselves, עץ ואבן etc. Here heathenism is pictured in its concrete manifestation. But what it says applies equally to the popular exoteric conception of idols which prays to its god as being actually innate in the manufactured image, as to the esoteric, the way the educated and initiated look at it, who honour in the idol the symbolic representation of the forces of nature which rule the world. The former was, according to the books of the prophets, the general widespread belief of the people. To it applies in the most literal sense מעשה ידי אדם עץ ואבן וגו׳. But also the educated heathen who sees in his images of gods the symbolic presentation of the personified forces of nature, in truth is honouring gods אשר לא יראון ולא ישמעון ולא יאכלון ולא יריחון “who neither see nor hear nor eat nor smell”. For the forces which they deify are only physical powers “without objective intelligence and without subjective consciousness”. They see not and they hear not; they lack objective perception. They taste not and they smell not: they lack subjective consciousness. Neither what things are in themselves, nor what things are to them do they perceive, they have neither mind nor will, so that they stand in their purely physical blind lack of freedom deep below not only mankind but even below all organic life, where, even at the lowest stage the beginning of some perceiving and willing consciousness dawns. But where a human being casts himself down and prays to purely physical forces, places his fate and what he does or refrains from doing under the powers of blind necessity, powers that are entirely without any self-will at all he strips himself of his spiritual height and his honouring his gods only works demoralisingly upon him, כמוהם יהיו עשיהם כל אשר בוטח בהם (Ps. 215,8). The blind lack of freedom of his idol becomes his ideal, ועבדתם שם אלהים וגו׳, and you, subjected to the heathen world, will learn to feel the whole weight of this demoralising idolatry.

V.29. ובקשתם משם. From this contrast, the elevating, free-making nearness of the One Unique truly living God Who had become Israel’s portion in the world as ה׳ אלקיו will then flash up all the more in your hearts, “ye will seek Him and ye will find Him”. Even as helots of a heathen world you will be aware of His illuminating, elevating, free-making Nearness which ennobles you and brings happiness, if you תדרשנו בכל לבבך ובכל נפשך will ask only Him for what is right and good, and go to Him only, for help. Both are called דרש את ה׳. The whole history of Israel in exile with its victorious endurance and continuous existence externally, and its happiness-bringing efforts towards inspiration, understanding and ennoblement internally is a continuous revelation of the living God in contrast to the dead and deadening heathenism.

V. 30. בצר לך וגו׳. It seems that this contrast will ultimately provoke a final struggle, and באחרית הימים a final oppression awaits Israel. From this final trouble, and purified and steeled by all the experiences it lived through, Israel, at the ultimate end, will come back to complete, and then unbroken obedience to God.

With ה׳ אלקיך in V. 29 the address changes from the plural to the singular. The fate of trouble falls on every individual in the dispersion, nobody is exempt from it. And the purifying effect of this trouble must also prove true in the whole multitude of all the single individuals. But in the midst of all this scattering of the individuals of the nation, it still remains a single spiritual and moral unit. In this final effect of all to return to the One God, this union of the Jewish multitudes is felt, and holds the scattered multitudes, without any visible external bond, together as a “single” unit spiritually united about their One God. ובקשתם משם (in the plural I.L.) את ה׳ אלקיך (in the singular I.L.) ומצאת וגו׳.

V. 31. כי אל רחום (see on Ex. 33,19. For God will not forsake you because He has already done so much for you, because you are the product of His quite special caring rule. For רחמים (from רחם, the womb, as we have worked out in Ex. I.L.) is the love of a creator for his creation because it is his creation. Hence the prayer in Ps. 25,6 זכר רחמיך ה׳ וחסדיך כי מעולם המה can remind God of all the benefits which He has already bestowed on us, to be also confident of His further love.—:לא ירפך הרפה את— means to let something go that one has held fast, אחזתיו ולא ארפנו, “I held him and would not let him go” (Song of Songs 3,4); בצדקה החזקתי ולא ארפה “I hold fast to my righteousness and will not let it go” (Job. 27,6). God will not give you up. God originally picked you out for His special purposes, and for the task you were to accomplish, did great things for you. He holds you fast for these purposes of His, however much you may have sinned against Him hitherto. ולא ישחיתך, that is why He does not let you perish, you remain kept for the future of your mission. ולא ישכח וגו׳, this fact that your mission can never be lost rests on the ברית אבתיך, was established with the covenant made with your ancestors. Everything that rests on a ברית, that has been declared as a ברית, does become realised with absolute certainty, however much adverse circumstances may seem to make it unlikely, (see on Gen. 6,18).

V. 32. כי שאל נא לימים וגו׳ למן וגו׳ ולמקצה וגו׳. When שאל is construed with -ל, the -ל does not refer to the person or object to whom or which the question is posed, but the object about which the question is asked. Thus: למה זה תשאל לשמי “Wherefore is it that thou dost ask concerning my name” (Gen. 32,30, and Judges 13,18). In the frequently occurring שאל לו לשלום, “he asked him about his welfare” (Gen. 43,27 and elsewhere) both the person and the matter is designated by -ל. Here too it does not say: ask the whole past and the whole world, but “find out from the whole of the past and from the present condition of the whole world. Which is why the Gemora (Chagiga, 12,a) takes our text to say also that the sphere for human research is limited both in time, למן היום אשר ברא אדם על הארץ, to after the Creation, and in space למקצה השמים ועד קצה השמים, from one end of the heaven to the other end of the heaven. We are denied knowledge of, and it is useless to try and probe to find out what was before the Creation, or what lies beyond the created material world (which comprises the world itself, the heavens above and around it, the sun, moon, stars etc. as described as having been created in the seven days of the creation I.L.), nor to try and search out מה למעלה מה למטה מה לפנים מה לאחור (see תוספות ibid). But to obtain knowledge of Nature and History which is open to our research within these limits is not only something permitted but something which is eminently desirable to the fullest possible extent, for only a mind armed with such a wide panoramic view on all matters can draw the right conclusions of the Jewish position in the world in the whole of its speciality.

V. 33 & 34. השמע וגו׳ או הנסה וגו׳. From such an extensive enquiry it will follow that you are the one people in the world to whom God has come out of His Invisibility to make Himself known to you in the certainty of your having perceived Him with your own senses, and revealed Himself by proclaiming His rule directly to you. You are the only people who do not believe in God and His rule, but know it. You are the sole trustee for mankind of the revelation of God, of His rule, and His Will. Therein lies the eternity of your mission and the historical immortality of your wanderings in the midst of the nations. Therein lies the explanation to, the solution of, לא ירפך ולא ישחיתך etc. כי שאל נא וגו׳.

השמע עם וגו׳ ויחי. This hearing the Voice of God is in itself nothing beyond natural human capabilities. To the first human beings in their original pure condition, God was near on earth, and they heard the words God directed to them quite naturally. And also certain select individuals of their descendants, a Noah, an Abraham, his son and grandson with whom God introduced His return to the earth, were able to hear the speech of God and become worthy of it. But still never before had a nation in its totality been elevated to that stage, and added thereto in such direct personal contact that normally could be reckoned to sever the soul that was raised to such proximity to God from its bond with its body. For by this revelation the foundation was to be laid for a path in life continuing in the proximity of God just in the material life of our bodily senses.

V. 34. או הנסה וגו׳. It is not impossible that this נסה, and equally so הנסה דבר אליך תלאה (Job. 4,2) is not Piel but Niphal. Here it would then be used with a reflexive meaning:- “hath indeed a God ever proved Himself, shown the loftiness of His Might and Glory, לבוא to come into the midst of earthly conditions, לקחת לו וגו׳ to take a nation for His special purposes and His exclusive guidance, מקרב וגו׳, that had fallen completely under the power of another nation and was completely hemmed in by another nationality, במסות with deeds which proclaimed His Power, באתת with signs which proved His Presence, ובמופתים, with instructive deeds which force minds and feelings, ובמלחמות, with open war against those who refuse obedience, ביד חזקה, with a power which proves itself stronger than that which has been regarded as the strongest, ובזרוע נטויה, and with a mastering arm which stretches far above all earthly grandeur and realms of mastery, ובמוראים גדולים and with results which make the awesomeness of His Will and His Might perceived in its whole greatness, ככל אשר עשה etc. comparable to that which God did unto you in Egypt: לעיניך before your very eyes, to all of you together at the same time, so that it is raised beyond any possibility of doubt.

V. 35. אתה הראת לדעת. Your consciousness of God is no belief but a knowledge, and your knowledge rests on no report, nor on any conclusions which your minds come to, your knowledge of God rests on the certainty of the actual experience of all of you together simultaneously having had the direct actual evidence of your own senses. אתה הראת לדעת: your own eyes were given enough to see for you to know that God, Who was revealed to you under that Name (the four-lettered Name of the God of Love I.L.) is the one real God Whom the rest of mankind seek and believe in under such manifold delusive images: אין עוד מלבדו, and that apart from Him alone, there is nothing that has existence on itself alone. He alone is the absolute Existing One, every other existence is dependent on Him.

V. 36. מן השמים. He revealed Himself to you as filling heaven and earth at the same time, and His universal Presence penetrating into your innermost being; you heard His voice from heaven, saw His fire on earth, and became aware of His words out of the fire.

V. 37. ותחת כי אהב. This knowledge of God which you had through יציאת מצרים and מתן תורה, forms the characteristic speciality of your world-historic nature and calling. It only carries on in you the ברית founded when your forefathers were chosen, which was already referred to in V. 31.—ויבחר בזרעו אחריו. The ו, the suffix in the singular can only refer to God, and זרעו אחריו would be the descendants begotten by the ancestors for Him, and brought up to follow Him, in the sense of וימלא אחרי (Numbers. 14,24), מוכיח אדם אחרי (Prov. 28,23). — בפניו with His direct guidance (cf. Ex. 33,14 and 15).

V. 39. וידעת היום: Out of all the experiences you have had hitherto you must now have the most certain conviction—והשבת אל לבבך, and if at any time it should have slipped out of your innermost heart, or threatens to do so, bring it back again and again into your heart on the strength of these facts that you yourself experienced—that ה׳ הוא האלקים (that, whether He appears to us as ה׳, the four-lettered name of the God of Love, Who loooks at every passing moment of the present with an eye to the future ultimate happiness of mankind, or as אלקים, the God of Nature, the strict Judge Who allows effects to follow causes naturally, it is all ה׳, the One and Only God of Love I.L.) ממעל—מתחת. God is God in heaven, upwards above you in the whole unmeasured space of heights, and on earth, downwards below you in the whole unmeasured space of depths. By the addition of ממעל and מתחת to heaven and earth the conception is expressed of unbounded infinity.

V. 40 ושמרת את חקיו וגו׳. But this, all your knowledge of God, is to have the one effect, that, in this God-filled world in which His rule governs everywhere and everything serves His Will, you only know His Proximity, conscientiously fulfil His חקים and מצות with which He has set “limits” to all your desires and “tasks” for all your activities, אשר יטב לך by which alone you and your children can get happiness. ולמען תאריך and which is the sole condition for your remaining in the land which God gives you for all time, which remains the land of your calling for all time, but which you will only possess for as long as you prove yourself faithful to that calling.

V. 41. אז יבדיל. Moses informs us that, after he had brought home to the minds of the people their relation to God and His Torah, and how their having possession of the Land was dependent on their fulfilling that Torah, he also made due arrangements concerning the law which they were to carry out immediately at the division of the Land (Numb. 35,10), as far as it could partially be carried out in the Transjordan country. Although, as remarked on v,13 there, the three Transjordan cities which he appointed to be cities of refuge did not actually function as such until the other three in the Land had also been appointed. There, in Numbers, we tried to work out the deep fundamental significance of this law of the refuge cities, and in view of what we remarked there, the arrangements recorded here, in connection with the preceding exhortations to faithful fulfilment of the whole Torah, appears in a still clearer light. For, is not the appointment of the ערי מקלט at the division of the Land at the same time a topographical public expression of the fundamental principle of the dignity of human beings in the likeness of God. And does not this fundamental principle, next to the principle worked out in the immediately preceding verses of the One and Unique and metaphysical Personality of God, and together with it form the rock-like foundation of the whole of Judaism.
אז יבדיל (see Ex. 15,1.).
V. 42. לנוס שמה וגו׳. Here the Law is only touched on in general terms. For the details see Numb. 35,9 et seq. and Deut. XIX.

V. 44. התורה. The true conception of “God” which they obtained from יציאת מצרים (the exodus from Egypt I.L.) and מתן תורה (the revelation on Sinai I.L.) and the true conception of “Man” proclaimed by the ערי מקלט (the cities of refuge, see above I.L.) are the foundations of the Jewish national life, and this book in which Moses wrote them down is the “Law” the teaching, the Torah in which he laid down in writing as the inviolable norm for the children of Israel for all their behaviour.

V. 45. אלה העדות, and these are the same עדות for cultivating our minds and הקים ומשפטים for our moral and social behaviour which Moses taught the whole nation “verbally” (דבר, I.L.) on the whole journey from Egypt through the wilderness, and finally again in the conquered Transjordan district in view of the Promised Land.

V. 1. With this fifth chapter the third part of the preliminary speech, with which Moses introduced the repetition and explanation of the Torah, begins. The first part, Ch. 1,6 till III,22, tended to bring home to the people, from the experiences they themselves had lived through, the conviction that for taking possession of the land also, their remaining faithful to God was the indispensable condition, and that that in itself was adequately sufficient to ensure it. The second part, Ch. 3,23 till IV,49 is primarily dedicated to the rightful estimation of the Torah by Israel and above all, of God, in the true sublimity of its and His quite unique nature. With this fifth chapter the third part begins. This interweaves the general fundamental feelings of fear of God and love of God into those laws, the fulfilling of which was to accompany the people everywhere in the greater isolation which now awaited them, as the constant incitement to, and promoter of those feelings.

But this deeper going into the laws begins with once again looking back at the historic event of the revelation on Sinai. Above in Ch. 4,10 et seq. and 33 et seq. that experience was again brought to their minds to teach them therefrom the full and pure purport of our consciousness of God. Here it was repeated as being the foundation of the task of our lives, and for that, too, the Ten Commandments were also repeated as the fundamental principles of the whole Lawgiving.

ויקרא משה. With this chapter Moses’ speech approached more closely his real purpose, the repetition and explanation of the Torah, hence this introductory call, שמע את, “listen to”, not “obey”. הקים ומשפטים, the norms for our moral and social behaviour, comprise the whole Torah in a broad sense. דבר in the Kal refers chiefly to the contents of the thoughts which the words present (דובר מישרים דובר צדק etc. I.L.) see on Numb. 27,7. את החקים ואת המשפטים אשר אנכי דבר באזניכם היום, the laws governing your moral and social behaviour which I present to you this day according to their contents for you to apprehend and understand them. למוד :שמירה and עשיה, that is the sum of all that the Torah demands from us. למוד to appropriate that which we are told, by studying to really understand it; שמירה, conscientiously to keep it present in our mind, and only to act under the dictates of such conscientiousness; and עשיה, carrying it out, which is of course, the purpose, indeed the basis of the whole of it. Mere theoretical knowledge without practical fulfilment has no value, it does not even attain the right knowledge, if it is only striven for as an intellectual game and not with the serious intention of carrying it out:- כל האומר אין לי אלא תורה אפילו תורה אין לו, מאי טעמא, אמר רב פפא אמר קרא ולמדתם אתם ושמרתם לעשותם כל שישנו בעשיה ישנו בלמידה כל שאינו בעשיה אינו בלמידה (Yebamoth 109,a).

V. 2. ד׳ אלקינו וגו׳. God made a covenant with us at Horeb. The revelation of the Torah was no mere theoretical information which was left to our later consideration whether to pay attention to it and fulfil it or not. The revelation was an act of binding us to duty, and of our undertaking responsibility, the revelation tied an inextinguishable bond between God and us.

V. 3. לא את אבותינו וגו׳. A very large part of those still living—all those who were not over twenty years of age at the exodus from Egypt—had themselves experienced the revelation on Sinai, and the others had been born so shortly after the great event that what their parents had actually lived through and experienced was as sure and certain to them as if they themselves had been there. So that אבתינו is most likely to be taken in its wider sense, “our forefathers”.

ה׳ אלק׳ כרת עמנו וגו׳ כי אתנו אנחנו וגו׳. When he refers to the Torah given by God and the duties imposed thereby, Moses retires completely into the midst of the people (and speaks of “us” and not of “you” as in the rest of his address I.L.). In the giving of the Law and in the responsibilities incurred he had no greater and no lesser part than anybody else of the people.

V. 4. פנים בפנים seems to express a still greater directness, without any intermediary, than the more usual פנים אל פנים (Gen. 32,30; Ex. 33,11, and Deut. 34,10). The Presence is not only turned one to the other, but it penetrates into the other; through the Presence, the Mind of the one communes with the mind of the other. So also עין בעין (Numb. 14,14).

V. 5. אנכי עמד וגו׳. My position between you and God at the time of the Lawgiving lacked any trace of a lawgiver, was solely that of a transmitter of the Law. God, the Lawgiver, was apparent to you, and as He directed His Word to each one of you, so did each one of you also hear His Word directed to him personally. And if, at this great event, and altogether בעת ההוא, during the time of the rest of the lawgiving, I took up a nearer position to God than you did, stood between God and you to transmit His Word to you, that was because you were afraid and did not dare to approach as near as you were permitted to come to hear even the whole of the first ten fundamental verses—ולא עליתם בהר לאמר, you did not dare to come nearer up to the mount for the proclamation of the עשרת הדברות (the Ten Commandments), see Ex. 20,15-18.

V. 6-18. We have already considered in detail these fundamental principles of the Torah, and the fixing of the duties of Jewish life given by them, on Ex. 20,1-14, and deliberated there at the same time on the added explanations which the verses on לא תענה ,כבוד אב ואם and לא תחמוד receive here when Moses repeated them. We would refer our readers to there, and here only add a few further remarks:-

In verse 8 it does not say פסל וכל תמונה but פסל כל תמונה. Thereby the reprehensibleness of making any kind of image—the prohibition of which was quite specially important through their entry amongst the polytheistic inhabitants, and had formed the principle tendency of all the introductory admonitions hitherto—was stressed still more poignantly by making it an additional apposition to פסל. On the other hand it says in V. 9. ועל שלשים instead of על שלשים. When we consider that in the generations he had standing before him, not only children but grandchildren, accordingly the third generation of the יוצאי מצרים who had died in the wilderness as “sinners”, we can well understand that Moses’s thoughts and feelings did not pause at בנים and allow him to consider שלשים as a fresh thought, but that he preferred to combine children, grandchildren and greatgrandchildren together as one conception to a certain degree by the copulative ו.

In V. 10, מצותי is written מצותו and read as מצותי Accordingly it says to the generation now going over to the normal conditions of God’s guidance being invisible:- even if in future God no longer goes before you invisible guidance and you only think of Him as someone absent, He shall still remain always present with you in His commandments, and you shall fulfil His commandments, מצותו as being the commandments of someone present מצותי.

In verse 12 זכור is changed to שמור. For, in the change to having to live for oneself in the impending decentralisation, and the consequent activities of wresting one’s independence from nature and human competition, the Sabbath was to be impressed above all in its שמירה aspect, in its twenty-four hour sacrifice of ceasing work in acknowledging homage to God. So that those who henceforth would feel relegated to their own יד and their own זרוע, their own “strength and power”, should not forget the truth that every ounce of strength and every grain of power, and all that they might come to think was their own production, comes from God and belongs to God; the God Who showed them His strength and His power in the midst of the “might and power” of the great Egyptian state on the “slaves” who had been bereft of all strength and power, and it is He Who has given them the strength and power they now enjoy and call their own, and Who expects them to acknowledge this fact with the twenty-four hour Sabbath sacrifice of שביתת מלאכה והוצאה, ceasing exercising their “creative” power and control and regulation of things (see Ex. 20,11, and XXXV,2). That is also why the whole sphere of the power and strength of a man’s personality is still more completely described by ושורך וחמורך וכל וגו׳ (see on V. 10 ibid), and on the other hand, all the members of this sphere of man’s power are joined to him by the copulative ו in complete equality with his own personality to place themselves with him at the feet of God on Sabbath—. ועבדך, not עבדך, and that is why here למען ינוח עבדך ואמתך כמוך is stressed as a special visible consequence of the God-acknowledging festival of Sabbath when Man calls a halt to the exercise of his “strength and powers” (see on Ex. 23,12).

—In verse 16 the addition of ולמען ייטב לך in the fifth commandment says to every coming generation in the land, that their present wellbeing in the land has only to thank their faithful and devoted connection with the past and that every contemporary generation in Israel only receives happiness and prosperity if it takes over with honouring obedience the tradition of its history and laws from the hands of its parents as a heritage to be carried on for ever (see on Ex. 20,12).

Verses 17 and 18. We have already remarked on Ex. 20,14, that here, when Moses repeats the Decalogue, all the prohibitions of sinning against the life, the marriage, the property, the happiness, and the honour of one’s fellow-men, as well as the mere lusting after what is forbidden, are all taken collectively together as one thought by the copulative ו. And we pointed out, how, the last one, hankering, coveting, was stressed, to tell us that not only the actual criminal deed, but already the criminal thought, yea simply the longing for that which is forbidden, the breeding place of all sinful thoughts and acts, is brought by God before His judgement-seat; and that thereby the one real security for social life against crime—not to be attained by any human tribunal—is guaranteed by the loyalty of the feelings of its citizens nurtured by the fear of God. According to that, one can very well understand that this extension of לא תחמוד into לא תתאוה, and the all-comprising culmination of all social prohibitions in this latter, is duly stressed in this repetition of the Decalogue before the transition to taking possession of the Land. For they were just about to be transferred from the control of a central supervision to being scattered individually over the whole of a country, and thereby left still more to controlling themselves from their own inner selves. In that moment of removal from the proximity of the Sanctuary of God’s Torah, and the highest human jurisdiction living next to it, it was all the more necessary to bring the thought home to each one of the people of God’s examining the heart and mind so that they place even their mere desiring before His judging Eye. Quite in accordance with this prospect of their actually possessing property is then the inventory of their possessions supplemented here by שדהו, (see Ex. ibid; in the wilderness their houses too come under the heading of mobile possessions, they had no real estate at all). Perhaps that is also why עד שקר is changed here to עד שוא in which we believed the עד זומם to be rather indicated. And it is just at the entry into the Land, when there is a greater danger of social criminal lawlessness, that the warning comes against this highest form of criminal evidence. And moreover here in this place it would come in close relationship to לא תתאוה, as just in this case the criminal intention and not the actual act, כאשר זמם ולא כאשר עשה is punishable even by human jurisdiction (see on Ch. 19,19.).

V. 19. קול גדול ולא יסף. There is no real foundation for taking the meaning of יסף to be ceasing, that יסף and סוף should be identical, as יטב and טוב are. But everywhere else it means, increasing, going further, Thus also in V. 22. We imagine that here too it means going on, going further on: the Voice was a great one and still did not reach further, did not go beyond the Jewish circle, was not audible beyond that. It was only heard by those to whom it was directed, and just this limitation proved it to be the free-willed personal word of God, and raised it above all connection with any physical acoustic physical phenomenon. Thus similarly the ת״כ on Levit. 1,1 says of God’s speeches to Moses in general: וידבר ה׳ אליו מאהל מועד מלמד שהיה הקול נפסק ולא היה יוצא חוץ מאהל מועד, יכול מפני שהיה נמוך ת״ל וישמע את הקול וכו׳ הקול המתפרש בכתובים קול ה׳ בכח וגו׳ א״כ למה נאמר מאהל מועד מלמד שהיה הקול נפסק ולא היה יוצא חוץ לאהל.

V. 20. מתוך החשך, it has said repeatedly that the Voice came מתוך האש. So that it is probably to be understood thus:- “from out of the darkness and the mount blazing in fire” i.e. the mount was surrounded by darkness and blazed with fire, and out from that, accordingly out of the darkness and the mount standing in it in fire, the Word spoke to them. Perhaps also מתוך החשך does not refer to את הקול but to כשמעכם. They stood in the darkness with mount blazing in fire in front of them, and out of their darkness they become aware of the Voice to them out of the fire.

V. 24. ואת. You will hold yourself towards the words of God, woman-like, i.e. purely passive. We have complete confidence in you, that you will only transmit to us that which you have received from God. You will be nothing but a faithful instrument. Hence also that the mission of “hearing” is expressed by the more significantly stressed שַׁמע instead of שְׁמע.

V. 25. את קול דברי וגו׳ ,את קול דבריכם. There could well be a difference between שמע דברים and שמע קול דברים. Whereas the former only hears the words spoken, the latter also takes note of the voice, the tone in which the words are spoken, the sentiment of the speech which is expressed in that tone. This only occurs similarly once elsewhere, above in Ch. 1,34, וישמע ה׳ את קול דבריכם, and there too, what was reprehensible was not only in what the people said, but principally in the tone in which they said it, in which the whole of their doubting and despairing faintheartedness and discontented attitude towards God made itself evident. Here on the contrary it was the feeling of being penetrated with the whole of God’s overwhelming greatness and the certainty of the conviction of His personal revelation that was expressed in the tone of their words, and which was more apparent to God than it was to Moses; hence also God says to Moses היטיבו אשר דברו “all that they have said springs from the best of feelings”, and מי יתן etc: But inasmuch as God expresses the perseverance of our good feelings and the continuance for ever of our well-being which is consequent to it as a “wish”, that shows that He has adjudicated to the human breast the Godlike noble quality of freedom of will and our virtue and our happiness is laid in our own hands.

V. 27. שובו לכם לאהליכם: go back again to your ordinary family-life. They had been witheld from that (Ex. 19,15) by order of God for three days in preparation for the revelation, and it required the express remission of that order before they were allowed to resume their old relationships. In the Gemora, Beitza 5a, this is quoted as the example for the dogma that כל דבר שבמנין צריך מנין אחר להתירו, that a special law imposed by a reliable authority does not automatically cease to be in force when the reason for its imposition no longer exists, but requires the express remission by reliable authorities. (see תוספות there and Sanhedrin 59,b).

V. 28. ואתה פה עמד עמדי, but for Moses who was to abide for the revelation of the Torah, the פרישה מן האהל was not remitted, he was not to return to conjugal life, and this gave rise to the criticising remarks of his sister and brother (Numb. 12,1 and 2, see there and Sabbath 87,a תוספות there).

מצוה :את כל המצוה והחקים והמשפטים here probably looks on the whole Torah as obligation, liability to duty, it is no mere theory, every dictum in it imposes a duty on our inner and external life; directs us to the post in life to which God has appointed us, tells us what we have to do and what to refrain from doing (see Gen. on II,7). חקים and משפטים are the two principle categories under which the various parts of the Torah, here called מצוה, are collectively presented: the laws for our individual moral lives and those for our social life of equity. They are those which in the very first place are the conditions for the prospering of our individual and social lives and to which the other laws and teachings serve to nurture, educate and form.
ועשו בארץ, they only receive the Land for the purpose of bringing this Torah to complete realisation.

V. 29 and 30. ושמרתם לעשות וגו׳ is now Moses’s speech to the people and draws the conclusions from all the preceding. First ושמרתם, the duty of faithfully fulfilling the Torah as a duty towards God, and then בכל הדרך וגו׳, as being the one way to living a happy life in the present and to perpetuate our happiness for all time.
V. 1-3. Now it goes over to the repetition of the laws which God gave to Moses to transmit to the people after the revelation of the עשרת הדברות.

למען תירא וגו׳. Where, as here in verses 1-3 the numbers change about in an address, the plural always looks on the nation in its plurality of individuals and the singular as one united mass of people. The duty to the Torah affects each individual member of the nation, accordingly the nation in its plurality. The Torah is to be kept by each one and that cannot be done by representatives. A nation, a community which officially acknowledges the Torah in its official representation but in the individual lives of its members denies it does not exist as such in God’s Truth. On the other hand the well-being and happiness that blossoms from keeping the Torah is only promised in full measure to the nation as a whole and single individuals only participate in it when all their contemporaries pay conscientious tribute to the dictates of the Torah. The community, the nation as a whole only receives its moral character through the faithful lives lived by all the individuals, and the individual only receives his full measure of well-being and happiness in his participation in the general well-being. In this the principle: כל ישראל ערבים זה לזה stands out in bold relief in its significant consequences.

That is why it says here:- What concerns our obligations, the laws of morals and the regulations for our social life which God had commanded, must be learnt by every individual and kept by every individual (v.1.), so that thereby the nation as a whole attains the character of fearing God and conscientiously keeping the Torah for itself and for its successors and so achieving the duration of the nation as such for all time (v.2). And that is also why the nation as such is to have no national worry nearer to its heart than the care for the Torah to be kept, so that the highest national prosperity and the greatest blessing for its inhabitants be achieved as God had promised it would be through the land which was so able to blossom out to the highest degree (v.3). Prosperity and an ever-increasing population are the external signs of a happy nation. But, as here the increase is put in the plural, accordingly spoken of the nation in its individual members, it stresses the real spiritual and moral value which lies in this blessing of increasing population. It is the individual who multiplies himself in the blessing of having children, increases his spiritual and moral likenesses in bringing up children (see Gen. 1,28). The size of the population is a national blessing not because with the increase of the population the national military force grows but because with every additional infant soul the sum of true humanity to be brought to realisation in the nation grows, the treasure of humanity becomes richer in the nation.

V. 4. שמע. At once, the first sentence of the compendium of the Torah which Moses wrote down out of his recapitulation of the Torah for the guidance of the people in the decentralisation (see XXI,5) is the sentence which, up to the present day, for every Jew—even if he finds himself in the most solitary isolation—keeps his consciousness of being a Jew still alive; the sentence that the little Jewish child first learns to lisp at its mother’s knee and which is the last that his friends call after every Jewish soul as a farewell greeting at his departure from this world; the sentence which Jews have carried and carry through the world as the Standard of God for His reconquest of mankind, the sentence which is the last that a son of Israel who is sinking away from Judaism casts away from him; the sentence which expresses the Jewish consciousness of the “oneness of God” (i.e. of ה׳ the God of Love and אלה׳ the God Who dispenses justice as the Judge being all one and the same ה׳, all and only the God of Love, see below I.L.). And as a result of this consciousness, sentences are added which, wherever the Jew may live, educate his child, live his private and public life, when he lies down and gets up, prepares his hand for deeds, his mind for thoughts, build his house, fixes his doors, they bring to his mind the mission of his life, the purpose of his education, the purpose of his homely and public efforts, the principles behind his deeds, the axioms for his thoughts and the dedication of the whole of his private and public life, and which sentences he accordingly has to repeat daily, early and late.

Our knowledge of God does not rest on שמיעה but on ראיה; it was obtained by the evidence of the actual senses of the whole of our nation. Moses could say to his people: אתה הראת לדעת כי ה׳ הוא האלקים אין עוד. (Thou hast been brought to know by seeing that God (ה) alone is God, there is none else beside Him, (Ch. 4,35). But this revelation of Himself, making Himself perceptable on earth, God only did once, when laying the foundation for the creation of His People, so that it could be a means of conviction from generation to generation, from community to community, and remain by direct tradition the indisputable basis on which, for all eternity, every son of Israel has to build up all his thinking and doing. Henceforth it does not say ראה ישראל but שמע ישראל. Not out of the phenomena of nature and history is it that each one of us has to come to a conclusion in his mind as to the exsistence or non-existence of God. Far beyond the convictions which are arrived at from such speculative inferences and deductions, God demonstrated His Existence, yea His existence down here in the midst of all earthly conditions, to every one of our fathers by experiences which settled any possible doubt, for them to testify to their children who came after these events. They saw God with their own eyes breaking their chains in Egypt leading and feeding them through the wilderness and bringing them to the Promised Land. They heard Him with their own ears when He imparted the words of His Law to them at Sinai. Our knowledge of God rests on the evidence of this; testified by the whole assembly of the whole of our nation. Not from nature and history have we to deduce a belief in God, but, with the knowledge of God which we have been given in our hands, we are to look into nature and history and try to get an understanding of the phenomena of nature and the events of history. And then, with our eyes awakened by God to see Him in nature, with our ears opened to hear Him in history, everything, the greatest and smallest in nature, the greatest and smallest event in history proclaims itself as His work, His governing. Then in the world of nature and history of our own times we shall still see the ruling of the God of our fathers, and, like them, we will wander through this world with God, and of Jewish minds and hearts it will eternally say: “They did once see Thy ways O God, even the ways of my God, my King in holiness”, ראו הליכותיך אלקים הליכות אלי מלכי בקדש (Ps. 68,25).
Therefore: “שמע ישראל״.—

But here, the knowledge of God based on our common observation, proclaimed above in Ch. 4,35 in אתה הראת לדעת כי ה׳ הוא האלקים אין עוד מלבדו וידעת היום והשבת אל לבבך כי ה׳ הוא האלקים בשמים ממעל ועל הארץ מתחת אין עוד is condensed into the one word אחד. For what is laid down here as the very first fundamental truth of our knowledge for us ever to take to heart, the אחדות of our God is nothing but the positive denial of all ancient and modern polytheistic ideas and false opinions. In the midst of all the greatest contradictory appearance of the manifold presentations of nature, history and our own inner selves, a contradictory variety which, more than anything else begat—and begets—the polytheistic erroneous conception, this אחד expresses the fact, the truth:- of the whole of this apparent antagonism—heaven to earth, personal to universal, what one pursues to what one avoids, endures and conquers, constructive forces and materials to destructive ones, all the changes of day and night, of becoming and reverting, of blooming and withering, of living and dying, of having and losing, of eating and starving, of rising and falling, loving and hating, of joy and sorrow, the contrasts of freedom and subjection, of spiritual and material, of heavenly and earthly, out of which human beings feel themselves woven—it is One single One, God alone Who created and holds all these contrasts, arranges them and guides them, Who formed all these contrasts about us and in us, from Whom all our joy and all our sorrow comes, our spirit and our body, He created our bodies and invested them with spirit from His Spirit, and personality from His own, and freedom of will from His Free-will.

Polytheistic thinkers who looked at all the occurrences of the world subjectively from their relations to mankind grouped the whole of these contradictory appearances into two opposing factors, those that were in agreement with the wishes and desires of men and those that were opposed to them, and the whole of the variety of the rest of the world of gods came under the sway of two high godly powers who fought each other for the mastery of the world and men and it was just out of this irreconcilable struggle that the whole contradictory manifestations in the external and internal world of men resulted. For them there was a benign power of goodness to which light and life and good belonged and a power of evil which to them was the god of night and death and evil. This was the view of the dual nature of the world taken by the old Parseeism (of which Cyrus was the head I.L.) to which Isaiah in Ch. 45,6 had to bring the Word of God that “from the rising of the sun to the setting thereof they may know that there is nothing that occurs without Me, I am God, and there is none else. It is I that form the light and create darkness; I make peace and create badness, I God do all this”. יוצר אור וברא חשך עשה שלום וברא רע אני ה׳ עשה כל אלה.

But the full Jewish Truth which our saying שמע brings home to our minds declares that God’s “Oneness” does not merely mean that what the polytheistic conception regards as the spheres of two opposing god-heads are really both of them the ways of the One and only God, Whose Love governs every coming breath we draw (ה׳ I.L.), and Whose Judgement watches over every past breath we have drawn (איק׳ I.L.), but that His Rule only appears to our shortsightedness as dual, and in reality it is one only. His judgement when it denies or punishes us is itself only a manifestation of His Love. Not only ה׳ אלקינו אחד, but ה׳ אלקינו ה׳ אחד, even as אלקים He is ה׳!

Our חז״ל too have taught the אחדות expressed in שמע in a similar sense. Thus in רבות on our verse: אמר הקב״ה לישראל בני כל מה שבראתי בראתי זוגות, שמים וארץ זוגות חמה ולבנה זוגות אדם וחוה זוגות העולם הזה והעולם הבא זוגות אבל כבודי אחד ומיוחד בעולם מנין ממה שקרינו בענין שמע ישראל ה׳ אלהינו ה׳ אחד. And in אלה הדברים זוטא (see Yalkut on our verse) מי שאמר והיה העולם אינו כן האכיל אותנו אין לנו אלא הוא הרעיב אותנו אין לנו אלא הוא ה׳ אלהינו ה׳ אחד וכן איוב אומר ה׳ נתן ה׳ לקח יהי שם ה׳ מבורך. “The Knowledge of God ever to be refreshingly strengthened by שמע״, say our sages, “is accomplished as long as we acknowledge thereby His sole Rule over everything in the universe, in heaven and on earth.” כיון דאמליכתיה למעלה ולמטה ולארבע רוחות שמים תו לא צריכת (Berachoth, 13b). And קבלת עול מלכת שמים (accepting the hardships of life as being part of God’s government of love I.L.) placing ourselves entirely with the whole of our world under the sole Rule of God is what they designate as the meaning of saying שמע (ibid 15 a. et seq.).

But if speculative thinkers believe they can take the אחד of the שמע to vouchsafe some information, or throw some light on the nature of God’s being, by changing the title “One” to that of “one of them”, thereby to find some vague transcendental ladder by means of which to scale some insight into the nature of God Himself; for that, as far as we know, there has been no predecessor in the national sages of our people. Altogether, they are pursuing an effort which would leave the אחדות ה׳, that fundamental basis of all our thinking quite useless and unfruitful for our lives; and moreover, in our opinion, would very much lose sight of the limitations which are set to the extent of human knowledge.

אחד is written with a large ד, probably to prevent it being changed for a ר which would make it read אחר, just as in לא תשתחוה לאל אחר (Ex. 34,14) the ר is written large to prevent it being taken for a ד. The ר of the polytheistic thought is accomodatingly round. The ד of the Jewish truth is sharply angular. With the loss of this little sharpness the אחד becomes אחר. The reason for the large ע in שמע is not so evident. Perhaps it is to indicate that it should be distinctly stressed not to sound like שמא, “perhaps” the particle of doubt in Chaldean. The two large letters together form the word עד, testimony and witness. The contents of שמע ישראל is an attested testimony from Israel to Israel, and everybody who utters it stands forth thereby as a witness of God to himself and to the world. Perhaps it is not altogether too daring to venture to think עין, the eye was עד the witness for that which שמע ישראל expresses. שמע hands down the tradition אתה הראת לדעת.

V. 5. ואהבת is the direct consequence of ה׳ אחד. The uniform trend of life from the uniform ways of God. אהב as already repeatedly remarked, the פ״א roots indicate the conception given by the two last letters of tire word either being reflexively referring back to the person by the prefixed א as in אמר “exchanging oneself (probably from the root מור or מר as in תמורה I.L.) to exchange one’s ideas, i.e. to talk to someone; or referring to the object, as in כלה) אכל, destruction, with prefixed א, meaning making an end of something but not destroying but for assimilating with one’s own individuality I.L.). In אהב both meanings are contained, הב to give and to bring; איהב to give oneself and to bring to oneself. It is the feeling of striving to get the closest attachment to the other by completely giving oneself up to him and endeavouring to make him attached to you i.e. Love, the most intimate bond between two beings. ואהבת את ה׳ אלקיך בכל לבבך ובכל נפשך ובכל מאדך accordingly means:- “seek to get near to God by devoting the whole of your heart, the whole of your soul and the whole of your fortune”. Everything that you think and feel, everything that you strive for and desire and everything that you possess, shall be unto you only the means, only have value to you, for getting near to God, for bringing God near to you. But not the other way round, do not seek God to obtain and to keep what you think of, wish for, and have or would like to have. The nearness to God is to be for you the greatest good, the “good” in itself. As David expresses the Love of God:- ואני קרבת אלקים לי טוב (Ps. 73,28). (“But for me the nearness of God is what is good I.L.); מי לי בשמים ועמך לא חפצתי בארץ כלה שארי ולבבי צור לבבי וחלקי אלקים לעולם (ibid v. 25 and 26). (“Whom have I in heaven but Thee, and beside Thee have I no further desire upon earth. My flesh and my heart faileth but God eternally remaineth the rock of my heart and my portion”. I.L.).

In שמע ישראל God is called אלקינו (in the plural I.L.), it is God as He proclaims Himself ה׳ to the nation. ואהבת turns to each individual and shows God to him as “his” God, ה׳ אלקיך how He looks after him individually in the whole course of his life and would guide him in all his actions. Every individual person is a special object of God’s Love and guidance and it is just as “your” God that you have to think of Him, what He was and is and will be to “you” if you truly conceive love for Him.

לבב is the heart of hearts, the innermost centre of the human organic body (see on Gen. 20,5). נפש: the living and striving personality (see ibid I,20). מאד: the whole sum of means and forces, the “fortune” (see ibid on I,31). To Jewish teachings it is not true that God only wishes to be honoured spiritually, by our minds and feelings. The demand on us runs בכל לבבך ובכל נפשך ובכל מאדך. We have to prove our honouring God in spirit and feelings, our love for Him, by investing the whole of our existence, including our bodily existence, our desires, and our fortune. A love that is not prepared to make the sacrifice of even the smallest physical desires is a vain pretence. Yea, true love feels the necessity to prove itself by sacrificing even the dearest desires. But the stress in our sentence lies in the כל. If ה׳ אלקינו ה׳ אחד, if everything which we are, which we desire, and have, our mind, our body and our possessions comes from the one dispensing and accepting Love of the One God and only from it, then we, with every phase of our being belong to Him, are His בכל לבב ובכל נפש, ובכל מאד, with all that we think or feel and desire and have. Every thought, every feeling, every power that we have, everything that we possess is a bond that joins us to Him, that we possess as a pledge of His Love, and dedicate to Him as an offering of our love. The consciousness of the “Oneness” of God also unites the whole of our being with all the diversity of the apparent disparities of body and soul and conditions of fortune and fate to one single unity of what we are and what we desire. Always and with everything we are the same, have the same goal always and with everything, the same mission, the one same desire viz. in the whole diversity of our lives to “love” our God, to fulfil not our own but His wishes, to be worthy to remain near to Him, to make ourselves ever more and more worthy for His proximity. Man gives himself up entirely to the One Only God and this complete resignation makes him harmoniously at one with whatever occurs in his life.

Hence the saying of our sages in Berachoth 57a, חייב אדם לברך על הרעה כשם שמברך על הטובה שנאמר ואהבת את ה׳ אלקיך בכל לבבך ובכל נפשך ובכל מאודך, בכל לבבך בשני יצריך ביצר טוב וביצר רע בכל נפשך אפילו הוא נוטל את נפשך ובכל מאודך בכל ממונך, דבר אחר בכל מדה ומדה שהוא מודד לך הוי מודה לו i.e. Man has to pledge allegiance to God in ברכה for misfortune as much as for good fortune, for it says “thou shalt love God, thy God with the whole of your heart and with the whole of your soul and with the whole of your fortune”. With the whole of your heart: with both your inclinations, your propensity to good and your propensity to evil; with the whole of your soul: even if He takes your soul; with the whole of your fortune: with all your possessions, or, with every measure that He deals out to you, thank Him.

To love God בכל לבבך, i.e. ביצר טוב וביצר רע is the most important and farthest-reaching result of the consciousness of the “Oneness” of God (i.e. that even as אלקים He is ה׳ the God of Love I.L.). The attraction which evil, lowness, the ignoble and sensuality have for us from which the יצר הרע, the inclination to evil, arises, is given to us by the same God as is the יצר הטוב the attraction which goodness, nobility, the spiritual and moral has for us, it is the one and same love of the One Only God which has interwoven the former as well as the latter in our tendencies. And it is by no means a lesser expression of His Love that He has endowed us also with the susceptibility for the allurement of evil, yea, the final seal of His Love lies in this allurement of vice for us, our whole nobility, the whole height of our moral worth, lies in this allurement. Without it we would not be human beings, there would be no morality, no virtue, everything in us would be mere animal-like physical desires and accomplishments, For what we call instinct in animals is only the one-sided nature of animal-life. For animals have only one inclination, and only that has attraction for them which is in accordance with what they are meant to be and do, everything else leaves them cold or is repugnant to them. Hence the intensiveness and constancy of the manifestations of animal life (e.g. their pursuit of food and reproduction I.L.). Had what is sensually low and bad no allure for us, did it leave us cold or be repugnant to us as something opposed to our nature, and did what is good and right attract us with irresistable alluring force, were there no sacrifice and self-control also attached to the good and right certainly we should do no evil, but also nothing good; the good that we did do would not be our own doing, no morally free-willed human act, we should merely be following the physical necessitites of our natures which would be irresistably fixed by the alluring effect they have on us. With the absence of the יצר הרע our whole moral worth would be buried. (see Gen. on Ch. 3,1; IV,7; VI,5; VIII,21). Yea, in truth, none of our inclinations are in themselves good or bad. All of them, the most sensuous of the sensuous ones, the most spiritual of the spiritual ones become good or bad according to whether or not they are used within the limits and for the purpose which God has allotted to each one of them, or misused, going beyond the limits, neglecting the purposes, or changing them for other purposes than those which God has set for them. So that to love God with the whole of our heart means:- to keep our whole mind—with all inclinations and in every direction—dedicated exclusively to accomplishing the Will of God, and to use every one of our efforts in His service that such mastery and use of them brings us nearer and nearer to Him.

This loving God with all our heart at once entails the supposition that we are ready at any moment cheerfully to forego the dearest wishes of our hearts for the sake of this love, as soon as they are not in accordance with the Will of God, as well as to bear the denial of our dearest wishes bravely and cheerfully in the deep conviction that it is the same Love of God which is shown us in such refusal as we would have honoured in their being granted.

אפילו נוטל את נפשך :בכל נפשך. To love God with the whole of our living selves, with all the spiritual and physical phases of our personality, with every moment of our life, again means nothing else but to try to get near to God with our whole existence by fulfilling His Will, only to value our existence as being in His proximity, and not to think that this remaining in His proximity would be bought at too high a price by giving up the whole existence here below for it. He who loves his God בכל נפשו breathes every moment of his life in the loving service of His God, and prefers giving up his life to breaking faith with Him, אפילו נוטל את נפשך. It is Rabbi Akiva who taught the explanation of בכל נפשך as being אפילו נוטל את נפשך (Berachoth 61,b). And he was thought worthy by his God to seal with his last breath what he had been preaching all his life. The foreign tyranny had forbidden learning or teaching Torah at peril of life, nevertheless Rabbi Akiva did not allow himself to be disturbed in his office of teacher. He carried on teaching the Torah in public. Papus found him at it and asked him: “Akiva hast thou no fear of the government?”. “I will tell you a tale” was R. Akiva’s reply. “A fox walked at the river’s edge and saw the fish darting from place to place. What are you afraid of then? Of the nets of the fishermen. Well come up to me on the land and we will live together safely as our forefathers did. Are you he whom people call the cleverest of animals? What folly you talk, if here in our own element we go in fear of our lives, what would it be if we came out of our own element! So are we O Papus. Now, when we are engaged in God’s teachings of which it is said “it is thy life and the prolongation of thy days and we go about in fear of our lives, what can we expect if we forsake that!” It did not take long before R. Akiva was arrested and cast into prison. But Papus too, in spite of his heedfulness fell foul of the favour of the government and found himself in chains next to him. “Happy thou Akiba” sighed Papus, “who art in prison on account of preaching God’s Teachings; woe unto Papus who am caught on account of vain matters!”. It was the time for קריאת שמע when Rabbi Akiba was taken to the place of execution. They tortured him with iron implements. But he quietly and composedly recited the acknowledgment of God in שמע. “Even still now?” asked his disciples. “All my life I longed to fulfil the words בכל אפילו נוטל את נפשך ,נפשך, and now, when I have the opportunity shall I let it slip”, was R. Akiba’s reply. He held on to the word אחד till he breathed his last. (ibid).

But the Torah itself, by its other proclamation וחי בהם (Levit. 18,5,—refer to it) has given fixed rules for this giving up one’s life rather than transgress the laws of God’s Torah. Only against forces which aim at the annihilation of the Torah may life not be bought by the transgression of even the smallest law of the Torah. Even on account of ערקתא דמסאני, “even on account of an un-Jewish alteration of a shoe-lace”, יהרג ואל יעבור “you must let yourself be killed rather than transgress”, so runs the canon for such times. In normal times it is only the laws regarding עבודה זרה גלוי עריות ושפיכות דמים (idol-worship, sexual immorality and murder I.L.) that one may not transgress even to save one’s life. Concerning other laws, the חי בהם ascribes such value to keeping a life down here for faithful fulfilment of duty that where there is a danger threatened to life it is to be prevented even by trangressing a prescription of the Torah, יעבור ואל יהרג (see Levit. there). In cases of illness one has to discriminate between חולה שיש בו סכנה and אין בו סכנה whether the condition is one of danger to life or not, further whether the material to be used is prohibited דאורייתא or דרבנן, whether it is כדרך הנאתו or שלא כדרך הנאתו, whether it is to be used in the ordinary way of enjoying eating it or not (see Yoreh Deah 155,3).

בכל ממונך :ובכל מאודך. Loving God with all one’s fortune has to be shown both by using all one’s means in the service of God, as well as in renouncing every gain or acquisition which can only be obtained or kept through transgression of God’s laws. And indeed, regarding sacrificing money the law applies in exceptionally inviolable force. One has to sacrifice even the whole of one’s fortune if it can only be kept by the violation of even one of the Divine prohibitions. To fulfil a positive command one is not called on to make such a great sacrifice (see Yoreh Deah 157 and O. Ch. 656).

The explanation of בכל מאודך by בכל מדה ומדה שהוא מודד לך הוי מודה לו could be—in accordance with the phonetic similarity of מדד and מודה with אמד—not far removed from the actual concept of the word. One only has to transfer the meaning of כל from “all” to “every”, and take בכל מאודך to mean “in every condition of fortune”. Then the demand is made to acknowledge God lovingly in every position of fortune which He may allot to us. For מאוד is not really only one’s wealth of money but altogether the complex of all means for accomplishing anything and so comprises everything which the management of God’s Love measures out to us.

But the explanation of מאד by מדד is the more justified as the changing of a radical letter of the ע״פ words to א is not without precedent. Thus we find ימאסו in Ps. 68,8, for ימססו, and בזאו in Is. 18,2 for בזזו. More, it is not impossible that מאוד has altogether the meaning of measure, and בכל מאדך means, with the whole measure, or with every measure which you have and מאוד as an adverb would indicate the size of a quality or quantity in the greatest measure. Similarly to אנשי מדות (Numb. 13,32), בתי מדות (Jer. 22,14) very tall people, very large house, also איש מדה (Chron. I. 11,23 and XX,6) a man of great stature a giant.

V. 6. הדברים האלה, these, הדברים האלה are the object to which the predicates וכתבתם ,וקשרתם ,ושננתם of the following verse refer. Clearly the text of the verses וכתבתם and וקשרתם can only be the object of שמע ואהבת. On the other hand ושננתם and ודברת בם (not ודברת אותם—see V. 7) allow one to refer the whole teachings of the Torah as being the subject for teaching of the young and for the expressing of the thoughts of the adults. So that actually הדברים האלה אשר אנכי מצוך היום, include both. They refer to the words ואהבת וגו׳ וגו׳ ,שמע וגו׳ and also to the whole contents of the Torah given thereby. For the whole Torah is really in truth nothing but the revelation of how we have to prove our love for God, in our actions בכל לבבך ובכל נפשך ובכל מאדך. The אהבת ה׳ בכל לב teaches us the תורות, the teachings which make our minds and hearts free from illusions and passions, fill them with truths and noble thoughts; אהבת ה׳ בכל נפש teaches us the הקים, the laws which limit and sanctify the development of our bodily physical being within the bounds of morality drawn by God; אהבת ה׳ בכל מאד teaches us the משפטים and מצות, the laws of justice and equity and commandments which build up our social life on the principles of justice and duty; and אהבת ה׳ בכל לב ובכל נפש ובכל מאד teaches us the עדות, the evidence of these truths and tasks represented by symbolic acts of recognition, and עבודה, our dedication to all this by the procedures of the offerings which symbolise our seeking nearness to God by the service of our life and embrace the whole of our existence in every phase of it.

(ספרי) שלא יהיו בעיניך כדיוטגמא ישנה שאין אדם סופנה :אשר אנכי מצוך היום, The Torah of God shall never be to you like some ancient institution about which nobody takes much interest any more. היום, Fresh like the light of dawn that greets you, fresh like the deep breath of pure air that you draw in is the Word of God to remain for you; every day given to you just “to-day”, every day brought home afresh to you, and its contents to bring afresh to your mind the task of your life that new day. There is no greater enemy to our fulfilling the tasks of our lives than becoming blase in carrying them out, than losing the freshness of recognising them and enthusiasm in performing them.

על לב .על לבבך, where this term occurs elsewhere referring to words or their contents it expresses the idea that the words should not only reach the minds of the hearers but should have a certain weight, exert some influence, be taken to heart. Thus דבר על לב (Gen. 34,3 & L. 21; Is. 40,2; Judges 19,3 et alia); שם על לב (Is. 57,1; Jer. 12,11; Dan 1,8 et alia). Accordingly the demand here is, that the words spoken here as being our duty are to be kept present in our minds and exert a permanent influence on our hearts, accordingly on our feelings and thoughts. We are to place our hearts under the weight of these words, allow our thoughts and feelings to be mastered by them. So also the ספרי on our verse:- צריך להשביע את יצרו, one must bind one’s inner inclinations by oath to duty.

V. 7. שנן .ושננתם לבנך does not occur elsewhere meaning to teach. But nevertheless we believe that וכליותי אשתונן (Ps. 73,21) could also mean: “When my heart feels itself bubbling over with excitement and let myself be taught by my kidneys (the organ symbolising the lower sensuous desires and urges, see Levit. I.L.) then I am an irrational being and am like an animal towards you.” Everywhere else שנן means “to sharpen”. אם שנתי ברק חרבי (Deut. 32,41); חציו שנונים (Is. 5,28). Hence שן, tooth. But it also occurs as characterising the sharpness of a word or a speech: שננו כחרב לשונם (Ps. 64,4; and again in CXL,4) and an impressive example is called a שנינה, (Deut. 28,37) למשל ולשנינה, et alia. So that -שנן ל means to teach something in short sharp and easily remembered sentences.—דבר ב- ,ודברת בם does not mean just to say something but the ב- at דבר designates either the person to whom or through whom it is said: Numb. 12,2; אך במשה דבר ה׳ הלא גם בנו דבר and elsewhere very frequently of prophets, or to the object to which the speech refers, of which it is spoken תשב באחיך תדבר (Ps. 50,20), וידבר יהונתן בדוד טוב (Sam. I. 19,4) וישלח דוד וידבר באביגיל (ibid XXV,39), נכבדות מדובר בך (Ps. 87,3), ביום שידבר בה, Song of Songs 8,8), ואדברה בעדתיך (Ps. 119,46). So that ודברת בם does not mean “and speak to them”, but, speak about them, explain them, and if we take the two tasks together: ושננתם ודברת בם then the instruction is given regarding the teaching of the Torah, first to imprint it in short, sharp, concise sentences and then impress it by conversing and debating on it: תשב״כ and תשב״פ and similarly משנה and גמרא.

Thereby the saying of our sages mnemonically to substitute the similarly sounding ושניתם for ושננתם could be explained: מאי דכתיב ושננתם לבניך אל תקרי ושננתם אלא ושלשתם לעולם ישלש אדם שנותיו שליש במקרא שליש במשנה שליש בגמרא (Kidushin 20,2). Originally the study of the Torah was in two parts ושננתם, the concise sentences of the תשב״כ, and ודברת בם, the explanatory treatment of it תשב״פ. After this had been written down in the concise sentences of the Mishna, of which the explanation was again relegated to oral teaching, for us the study had increased to three parts: - the מקרא, the משנה and the גמרא, so we have to divide the time at our disposal also into three parts. There, in the Gemora, the demand is attached to the expression ושננתם, that we are to make ourselves definitely clear in our knowledge of the Torah so that we ourselves are sure and firm in our understanding, and those who come to seek instruction, receive no weak, wavering, doubtful explanation. ת״ר ושננתם שיהיו דברי תורה מחודדים בפיך שאם ישאל לך אדם דבר אל תגמגם לו אלא אמור לו מיד. From that we can also draw the admonition for us, when we transmit the knowledge of the Torah, to our children, ושננתם לבניך, to implant in them their obligation to keep the Mitzvas of the Torah with the whole sharpness of their definite orders, and not let them be weakend by compromising for so-called necessary considerations of the times we live in and subjective expediences.

עשה אותם עיקר ואל תעשם טפילה שלא יהא משאך ומתנך אלא :ודברת בם בהם שלא תערב בהם דברים אחרים שלא תאמר למדתי חכמת ישראל אלך ואלמוד חכמת הכנענים (ספרי), “they, the teachings of the Torah are to form the real subjects of our mental occupation, we are not to cultivate them as a side-issue, nor from the standpoint or for the standpoint of other scientific study, and equally indeed take care not to introduce into the sphere of our Torah-studies foreign matter and ideas which have grown on the soil of other scientific hypotheses. We are altogether always to bear in mind the specific higher level of our knowledge which differs from all other scientific knowledge through its Divine origin and not place it on the same level as the other sciences, as if it, too, rested on the basis of human knowledge. We have already worked out on Levit. 18,5 how these sentences of the Sifri quite clearly do not demand completely ignoring all scientific knowledge gained in other spheres, on the contrary, they rather presuppose having knowledge of them, but they give us the only correct standpoint from which our occupying ourselves with them can be beneficial to us, and they warn us of the danger the neglecting such a standpoint would bring to our mental life of study for true knowledge. (see p. 479 ibid.)

בשבתך בביתך וגוי. The renewal of our consciousness of the Oneness of God (שמע), and the resulting oneness of the task of our life (ואהבת), the placing of our thinking and wishing under the fundamental truths, as well as under their consequences, the laws revealed by God in His Torah (והיו), and the mission therefrom of educating our children by teaching them and ourselves these fundamental truths and these laws (ושננתם ודברת בם), is what we are to give our minds to always and everywhere, at home and abroad, start our night’s rest and our day’s work with them: ובשכבך ובקומך .בשבתך בביתך ובלכתך בדרך ובשכבך ובקומך should not be taken as continuation of בשבתך וגו׳ but refers back to it. We are to lie down and get up with שמע and דברי תורה whether we are at home or abroad.

There is difference of opinion in Berachoth 21,a as to whether קריאת שמע the duty to read שמע every evening and morning is דאוריתא or דרבנן. The accepted Halacha is that קריאת שמע דאוריתא. Still, even according to this opinion the most generally accepted view is that only the first verse שמע etc. is דאוריתא (ibid 13,b). According to ר׳ יונה on the רי״ף, even if ק״ש דרבנן, the בשכבך ובקומך has to be taken strictly, but referring to דברי תורה, as אביי (there 21,a) taking the view that ק״ש דרבנן explains the demand בשכבך ובקומך as ההוא בדברי תורה כתיב and then the duty to read דברי תורה evening and morning would be even דאוריתא, whereas if ק״ש דאוריתא it would be specially the reading of שמע which is demanded (see ’שאגת ארי 1.).

But it seems to us as if, even if, as the Halacha is, ק״ש is דאוריתא nevertheless at least ושננתם לבניך ודברת בם speaks also of דברי תורה in general. For therein, everybody, without exception, agrees, the duty of learning oneself and teaching one’s children is contained (see Kedushin 30,a; Rashi and ר״ן on Nedarim 8,a). More, in Yoma 19,b, ודברת בם is taken to refer to both ק״ש and ת״ר ודברת בם :בם (פי׳ רש״י יש .דברי תורה לך להשמיע מה שאתה מוצא מפיך) ולא בתפלה (פי׳ רש״י שהתפלה בלחש); ודברת בם, בם (פי׳ רש״י בדברי תורה) יש לך רשות לדבר ולא בדברים אחרים (פי׳ רש״י שיחת (הילדים וקלות ראש. According to that our text would have to be taken as containing two commands: —

(1) שמע ישראל וגו׳, i.e. “hear, O Israel”, make yourself hear it, say it to your ears or at least with understanding, הקורא את שמע צריך שישמיע לאזנו שנאמר שמע ישראל וגו׳ הקורא את שמע ולא השמיע לאזנו יצא (Berachoth 15,a & b). Accordingly the duty is to say שמע and indeed only the first line פסוק ראשון so that ואהבת וגו׳ is only added as the consciousness of the “oneness” of God expressed in שמע resulting in the consciousness of the “oneness” of the whole of Man’s existence and desires. והיו הדברים האלה וגו׳ goes on to explain the command of שמע and then הדברים האלה refers to the text of the sentence שמע and makes the demand that while the words are said they are to be taken to heart, על לבבך, bringing their meaning to the bottom of one’s heart והיו שלא יקרא למפרע, הדברים האלה על לבבך עד כאן צריכה כונה, and hence עד כאן צריכה בעמידה, if one says the שמע while walking one has to stand still for the actual שמע, the first line (according to other opinions until ראב״ד ,על לבבך and בה״ג in opposition to רי״ף and רמב״ם see ב״ח 63 א״ח (Berachoth 13,a and b.).

(2) ושננתם לבניך ודברת בם: the duty of learning and teaching the Torah. The object of the שנון and דבור which is here commanded can be taken to extend beyond the mere repetition of the שמע-sentence all the more as the consequence of that sentence affecting the whole of the task of our lives has already been expressed by ואהבת, and the knowledge of what that task really means can only be obtained from learning the Torah. בשבתך בביתך ובלכתך בדרך ובשכבך ובקומך would then refer to both duties, to the duty of קריאת שמע and that of למוד דברי תורה and expresses both duties having to be fulfilled in all conditions of life, whether at home or abroad, at the beginning of the day and at the end of it. According to that we would have the duty actually מן התורה to say the sentence of שמע and to learn some דברי תורה every morning and evening. And if in accordance with the direction of our sages we do not say only the פסוק ראשון but the whole פרשה and also פרשת והיה אם שמוע then we fulfil the command of שמע וגו׳ והיו הדברים האלה וגו׳ of קבלת עול מלכות שמים with the first sentence, the command of ושננתם ודברת בם with the rest of קריאת שמע which מן התורה we could do with any other paragraphs of the Torah.

As far as we can see there is nothing in the discussion in the Gemora which would be in opposition to this way of taking it, and it seems to us that by בשכבך ובקומך coming after ישננתם ודברת בם it can hardly be taken otherwise. And it would then completely agree with the dictum of רב in Nedarim 8,a אמר רב גידל אמר רב האומר אשכים ואשנה פרק זה אשנה מסכתא זו נדר גדול נדר לאלהי ישראל והלא מושבע ועומד הוא (פי׳ רש״י דכתיב ושננתם ל״א דכתיב לא ימוש וגו׳) ואין שבועה חל על שבועה כיון דאי בעי פטר נפשיה רב .בקריאת שמע שחרית וערבית משום הכי חייל שבועה עליה can very well teach this in the view that ק״ש i.e. the first sentence is דאוריתא, but that, with the rest of קריאת שמע the command of ושננתם would be fulfilled. Then that could also be the reason why Rav intentionally doubled the case in his oath-problem: אשכים ואשנה פרק זה and אשנה מסכתא זו and, the first with regard to the duty of learning תורה every morning and the second with reference to the general duty of occupying ourselves with the Torah given by לא ימוש. And Rav teaches us that מן התורה by reading the whole קריאת שמע morning and evening we should be fulfilling both commands, also that of ימוש if prevented from doing more, and therefore חייל שבועה עליה (his vow “to learn tomorrow” must be carried out) and נדר גדול נדר לאלקי ישראל (cf. Menachoth 99,a).

בשבתך בביתך ובלכתך בדרך. From this command in Berachoth 11,a and Succah 25,a it is taught that העוסק במצוה פטור מן המצוה i.e. who is engaged in carrying out a Mitzva need not interrupt doing so in order to fulfil another Mitzva if the time for doing that other one has arrived and it is not possible to do both of them at the same time.
