We are not to expose ourselves to the danger of allowing the purity of our conception of God and our relationship to God to be disturbed by them כי תועבת ה׳ א׳ הוא, for the heathen aberration represented by an idol, by its glorification by men, by its offerings and gifts, and by the implements of its rites, is in such contrast to the spiritual moral height for which God, Who first singled you out of this aberration, and to which all human beings by virtue of their designation are summoned, that everything engendered from this aberration is in the highest degree contrary to the Will of your God.

V. 26. ולא תביא וגו׳: your house, your home, the sphere of your human life must be free from any such trace of heathenism. It is חרם, falls under the ban of destruction, והיית חרם כמהו, and whatever phase of your existence and desires you place in connection with it, however distant the connection with it may be, would forfeit your own right to existence, and it would fall under the same ban. ,כל שאתה מהיה ממנו הרי הוא כמוה, anything which brings its existence to your mind is as obnoxious as it itself. ע״ז is תופס דמיו and, according to רמב״ם even חליפי חליפין אסורים (Avouda Zara 54,b—see on Levit. 25,5).

שקץ וגו׳. Just as it is to your God, so is everything connected with ע״ז to be to you, viz, the denial to the highest degree of everything on which your spiritual and moral state of being a human being rests, and in the crassest contrast to it. In this feeling you must keep it far away from you כי ”חרם״ הוא, literally “caught in a net” and a “landing-net” (see Levit. 27,28). It is under an interdict, shut out of the whole sphere of existence of true mankind, and drags everything that is connected with it down into the sphere of that excommunication.

V. 1. The end of the previous chapter dealt with the complete nullity of the heathen gods, and their complete removal, and the removal of anything that is in any way connected with them, from the whole domain of Jews. In contrast to that, this chapter stresses the positiveness of God, as Israel had come to know from experience, and demands their keeping constantly in mind what they had experienced, from which alone the faithful carrying-out of the Torah and the resulting founding of our permanent happiness can follow.

כל המצוה. Nothing in heathenism can contribute in the slightest to our happiness, and only the slightest connection with it drags us with it into its ban of nullity and destruction. For the overcoming of all heathenism is the aim of God’s government of the world, and of the mission of Israel among the nations. But our happiness and well-being is not founded merely on the denial of heathenism, but on the complete positive devotion to carrying out of the Will of God which His Torah reveals to us. The Jewish house, kept clear of everything heathen, (Ch. 7,26), must be a home of fulfilling the Torah if it is to be the place where our true lives and prosperity are to be planted. The place of that which, in the delusion of the nations, an idol is to the home, is taken for us by the mitzvas of the Torah.

למען תחיון ורביתם ובאתם וירשתם: keeping the mitzvas grants us personal life and prosperity shown by the blessing of children as well as independence and a flourishing condition of our country. Individual life, family blessings, and national prosperity are guaranteed to us solely by keeping the mitzvas, in caring for them we accomplish the care for our happiness.

V. 2. וזכרת את כל הדרך. Accordingly, this firm conviction, excluding everything else, of our duty faithfully to fulfil God’s commanments as the one and only means of keeping our connection with God, and as the one and only sufficing foundation for our happiness, forms the basis of our vocation for which God had wished to educate us during the forty years wandering in the wilderness, so that we did acquire this firm conviction.

Hence we are always to keep in mind the wandering in the wilderness under God’s direct protection.—למען ענתך, literally to make you completely poor, to make you lose all independence. לנסתך to test you, לדעת וגו׳, so that you learn to know yourself, learn to know how much of that moral strength you possess which is necessary for unswerving faithfulness to the Divine Torah. Complete devotion to the guidance of God, a trust in God which make us free from all other worries than the worry to do our duty, that is the fundamental feeling on which alone our obedience to God’s commands can rest. To be ready, if needs be, to go out into the wilderness with wife and child, to remain true and obedient to go, that is the question we all must put to ourselves to get the measure of our moral strength.

V. 3. ויענך וגו׳. He fed you in a way for which you can find no analogy in your own experience nor in that of your forefathers. למען הודיעך וגו׳, so that you could gain the conviction, by your own forty years experience, that “not by bread alone etc.”. לחם is the food “wrested” from Nature and the competition of your fellow men. “Bread” is the product of human intelligence mastering Nature and the world. So that “bread” represents human intelligence creating the continuance of its existence by mastering nature in social co-operation. Now the illusive idea that this creative power of Man is the sole condition for his existence on earth, and forgets God’s Ruling being the first factor of the provision of Man’s food, although His providing care is shown by every tiny piece of bread by which we sustain one minute of our existence, this illusive idea is the most dangerous rock on which our faithful attention to duty founders. “The worry to provide bread for wife and child” is, in itself such a justified incentive for our activities, that it easily tends to drive all other considerations out of sight, as soon as we believe that we, and we alone, have to provide for the existence of ourselves and those dependent on us. As soon as we believe that every acquisition that we wrest from Nature and our contemporaries ensures our and their existence no matter how that acquisition had been obtained, whether thereby we had cared for the laws of God and kept to the paths He had indicated, or whether only by clever deft handling we had secured the “bread” without giving a thought as to whether God would agree with these means. And where this looking on one’s own human powers alone having to provide “bread” does not lead us away from the path of what is right and where our duty lies, it is still inclined to make us think of providing beyond the immediate necessities towards an ever-widening future. We think we have never done enough to satisfy our imagined duty, and talk ourselves into believing we have not discharged it unless we have acquired beforehand the means of existence for the whole of the future and for that of our children and grandchildren, and so we make the “worry of providing bread” into an unlimited breathless chase after income which denies any time for interest in purely spiritual and intellectual matters.

That is why God led us into the great school of a forty-years wandering in the wilderness where all the factors were lacking which otherwise grant men their bread out of nature and human powers, and made the one factor which, in normal conditions tends to become pushed more and more into the background, and so easily forgotten, viz the Divine Providential Solicitude, made that factor come visibly into the foreground. Instead of “bread”, bearing the stamp of human achievement, He fed us with “manna”, He made this “food allotted by God” come to us day by day in such a manner modified for each soul in our huts that it demonstrated in the most striking clarity the most specific care of God for each soul, and each tiny soul, individually. And in this preparatory school for the course of our lives we learnt:- that not on bread alone not on what bread represents of the support of man and Nature, is man directed to seek means for his existence, but on everything that God ordains—bread too, that man makes by his own skill, is naught but such a one—can man live. He can be quite sure that he will not be lost, if, in order to keep faithful to God’s commands, he has to give up what normally he would get from Nature and man, and in the midst of the richest abundance of the gifts of Nature and man, it is only the most special care of God that will feed him. (see on Ex. Ch. XVI).

-חיה על, cf. ועל חרבך תחיה (Gen. 27,40), where the sword is indicated as the means by which Esau will obtain his livelihood. Similarly in Ezekiel 33,19: ובשוב רשע מרשעתו ועשה משפט וצדקה עליהם הוא יחיה, “doing right and duty to which a wicked man returns form a basis on which he can again find his living, the right to which he had forfeited by his wickedness.

מוצא פי ה׳ (cf. Is. 55,11), כן יהיה דברי אשר יצא מפי, where every ordinance which God gives is designated thereby. So also referring to men, the word which he expresses as a vow or promise or wish to be carried out, is called מוצא שפתיו (Deut. 23,24, and Jer. 17,16). So also of God referring to His pronounced destiny of the dynasty of David: ומוצא שפתי לא אשנה (Ps. 89,35).

V. 4. שמלתך, more, on your very selves you experienced the miraculous power of God, how He considered and provided for all the exigencies which the position in which you were, required. He gave your clothes and your skin such powers of endurance that your garments did not wear out, and your feet did not blister or swell on the long march.

V. 5. וידעת וגו׳. Places like יוסר לץ לוקח לו קלון (Prov. 9,6), הוסרו שופטי ארץ (Ps. 2,10), בדברים לא יוסר עבד (Prov. 29,19), ויסרני מלכת בדרך העם (Is. 8,12) אשר יסרתו אמו (Prov. 31,1.) as well as the conception of the noun מוסר all prove sufficiently clearly that the root neither in the Kal nor in the Piel, has the essential meaning of chastisement, punishment. Its relationship with יצר and ישר as well as with כשר and קשר makes us recognise the fundamental underlying conception to be:- exerting such an influence by which a variety of forces are brought into the same direction towards a purpose or goal, whether this impression is made by direct external means or internally by appealing to the mind. Teaching and culture, spiritual and moral education is, accordingly the underlying concept of יסר. The forty years wandering in the wilderness was nothing other than such an instructive and formative education; teaching of God’s ever-present, near and providing Presence; formative practice in trusting, cheerful giving oneself up to that guidance; both together founded the conviction that for us to attain moral perfection by learning and practising was a matter with which God’s Government was deeply interested in, by which it arranged our fate in accordance with the requirements of our spiritual education, and by the experiences which it makes us have in our lives does teach us and educate us in practising. Of this conviction that God with His management is like a father to us, and all the joy and trouble He sends to us aim at nothing else than our betterment and moral ennoblement, of this conviction it says: .וידעת עם לבבך

עם לבבך would in no wise be synonymous with בלבבך so that לבב would be the organ of perception or thought. But rather עם לבב must be taken in a similar way to Josh. 14,7, כאשר עם לבבי where it means “being in agreement with the opinion in my heart” to which Caleb remained faithful, although thereby he contradicted the opinion of his comrades; or, as it is used in Kings I. 8,17,18 and Chron. I. 22,7 et alia ,ויהי עם לבב דוד אבי וגו׳, the perpetual harbouring of a thought or wish that one carries about “with oneself”. Also את כל אשר היה עם לבבה (Kings I,X,3) cannot possibly mean “she told him all that she thought of in her heart”. What she wanted was to test his renowned acumen by her riddles, if he could guess the thoughts she presented to him in the form of conundrums. And on that it says ויגד לה שלמה את כל דבריה. But rather את כל אשר היה עם לבבה can only refer to those questions which she had thought out for that purpose and which she had taken along “with her” on her journey to Solomon. Similarly in Deut 15,9 דבר עם לבבך בליעל is not unworthy as a thought that one once allows to arise in one’s heart, but is a feeling that one carries about with one as a guiding principle. So that וידעת עם לבבך here would be the demand to take the knowledge we had gained by our past experiences of the fatherly education which God had made all that had occurred to us give to us, to take this with us in all future time as the guiding conviction of our lives.

V. 6. ושמרת וגו׳. This conviction will evoke the other conviction, viz, that we can only influence the benign moulding of our fate by an exclusive and complete devotion to fulfilling our duties. The degree of our moral perfection is the one thing that is completely in our own hands, but with this one thing, our fate too lies in our own hands. For it is just this moral perfection which is the goal up to which God wishes to educate us by all the happenings of our life. But this moral perfection of ours is nothing other than ושמרת את מצות וגו׳, than the most conscientious attention to the commands of God, ללכת בדרכיו to walk in the ways He takes and which He wishes us to take,—both are expressed by דרכיו — וליראה אותו and to keep Him constantly before our eyes.

V. 7. כי ה׳ אלקיך וגו׳. For the school of the wandering in the wilderness has come to an end. You are about to enter the future for which that whole exceptional condition on earth was to be a preparation. And now you have to prove and confirm, in a normal condition of men and nations, what you were to learn in that wonderful preparatory school, and may not unlearn it in the altered, happy conditions, if these, the happy future now beginning is to endure. ארץ נחלי מים וגו׳. First of all the nature of the country is shown in the sharp contrast to that of the wilderness by the abundance of water, and that itself is the preliminary condition for the richness of the products of fields and trees which is then described. נחל designates any large or small flowing water from a natural source, whether it is the union of springs flowing along as a stream or brook or the union of brooks as a river. נחל, related to נהל has altogether the meaning of leading on, flowing down, and so is the expressive designation of the movement of possessions as heritage from parents to children. עינות are the “eyes” of the earth, through which the internal contents of the earth come to light, i.e. springs or wells. תהומות from המם, billows, are great masses of water which form lakes in the midst of the land.

V. 8. ארץ חטה וגו׳. It requires considering why the description of the riches of the land should be given in two groups, clearly separated by the repetition of ארץ. Unless we are mistaken, the seven kinds of fruit belong in the order in which they are given, to increasingly warmer climates, and indeed date-palms דבש (see Levit. 2,11) belong quite definitely to hotter zones whereas vines flourish only in temperate ones. Perhaps the verse wishes to say: it is a land of wheat, barley, wine, figs and pomegranates, in which not only olives and date-palms occur, but is a land quite specially of olive trees and date-palms, in which they thrive equally to corn and vines. That would also explain the hyphen between ארץ and זית which joins the olive tree to the land still more pointedly as a characteristic speciality of the land and attaches it to become one conception with it. According to Oken 3,2, 1116 (a professor of Nature-research at Jena and then at Munich 1807-1851, I.L.) Palestine was the original home of the olive-tree, and it was from there that it was transplanted to Greece and elsewhere. So this land has the happy advantage that it bears a richness of the most select fruit of all zones. That the second ארץ introduces a second speciality of the land which is of equal excellence to those introduced by the first ארץ can also be deduced from the Gemora in Berachoth 41,b, according to which the Beracha to be said before eating dates has precedence over that of pomegranates, because the former is named in second place after ארץ while the latter is only in the fifth, זה שני לארץ וזה חמישי לארץ. On the preceding page there it says: כל הפסוק כולו לשיעורין נאמר, all the fruit mentioned in the verse are used for measures, e.g. המוציא אוכלין כגרוגרת ,עצם כשעורה מטמא וגו׳ (גרוגרת = a dried fig), כותבת) ,ככותבת הגסה ביה״כ ,אכילת חלב וכו׳ בכזית ,כלי בעלי בתים שיעורן כרמונים a date). The author of a work on the Halachic laws of measures once showed me the first printed sheets of his writings in which he showed me his remarks on this verse which seem to me to be worth noting. He points out how fruit, as barleycorns, olives, etc. were used for units of weights and measures, also outside Jewish circles in olden times. Then naturally in international transactions, for such measures the fruit of some definite country must be taken as the standard. Now the fruit of Palestine was so recognised in international business as being the very best, that they were quoted as the standard units for measures of length and weight. One did not quote just so many barleycorns, olives in general but so many Palestinian barleycorns, Palestinian olives etc. The שבח ארץ ישראל, the pre-eminence of the products of Palestine was shown accordingly in the fact that they must have been the best known, and passed in general as units of measures. To my regret the name of the author has escaped my memory, and I also do not know whether the work was completed and published.

V. 9. סכן ,מסכנות .ארץ וגו׳: to pay careful attention to something, from which סוכן the name of the keeper of the king’s treasury. Also מסכן, the miser, and he who has to be stingy from necessity. מסכנות, parsimony (see on Gen. 19,4.). לא תחסר כל בו it even offers you also that which is not a necessity but only raises the comforts of life. אשר אבניה ברזל וגו׳. From Chron. I, XXII,3, it is clear that mining operations in iron and copper were carried on in Palestine. חצב really to excavate, the fitting expression for digging the ore of rocks. Accordingly it is land that, by the nature of its soil offers the most suitable opportunities for agriculture and industry.

V. 10. אכל .ואכלת ושבעת וגו׳, to consume for the purpose of self-reproduction; שבע related to ספה ,שפע ,שבע ,צבה, all of which express a fullness, a satisfying. ברך את ה׳ “to bless God” means: to further God’s purposes and wishes for which the free-willed acts of human beings are responsible, or to vow, to promise to do so (see Ex. 18,10). (Man, the only creature given freedom of will, has the power to “bless” God, i.e. to further His purposes and wishes, or to thwart and retard them I.L.). As often as you strengthen yourself with that with which God has granted you, and satisfied the requirements of your bodily existence, then, in the consciousness that it is God, and God alone to Whom you owe every restoration of your strength, and all satsifying of the requirements for continuing living, you are to dedicate the whole of your being to His service, to fulfil His purposes and to the realisation of His Will on earth. And this promise of dedication you are to pronounce in the words of ברכה, of blessing Him. This is the command for ברכת המזון, the Beracha to be said after eating bread, by which the absolute conviction—gained by the miraculous feeding with the manna—of the direct care of God for each separate individual is nurtured and kept firmly retained in the midst of the normal conditions of man-supplied food. It makes every little piece of bread looked on as being as much the direct gift from God as was the manna dropped from heaven to the wanderers in the wilderness. The accepted Halacha in Berachoth 44,a, refers the command ואכלת ושבעת back to לחם in the preceding verse 9 and not to the fruits mentioned in V. 8, as with V. 9 starts afresh with ארץ and the land is characterised as being such whose inhabitants will not have to eat their bread in straightened circumstances but in circumstances surrounded with all the requirements of comfort. But the real object remains לחם and to this the ואכלת וגו׳ refers. According to that ברכת המזון would be commanded מן התורה only after eating bread, and thereby the significant truth laid down viz, not, as one would think, that, at the most, we owe things that we get but could do without, to God but rather that not even the barest necessities of life, not even “bread” is within Man’s power alone to supply, but that the simplest means of existence is a direct gift of God’s providing (see on verses 17 and 18); it is all מוצא פי ה׳, every breath we draw depends on the “mouth of God”.—By לחם, only “bread” made out of the five kinds of grain is understood חטה ושעורה וכוסמין שבולת שועל ושיפון,wheat, barley, oats, rye and spelt. These five kinds of grain are all included in the term חטה ושעורה. But there is nevertheless an opinion that the Beracha to be said after eating any of the seven kinds of fruit mentioned in V. 8 is also דאוריתא (see טור א״ח ר״ט and ב״י there).

The whole connection in which the mitzva of ברכת המזון stands with the preceding and succeeding verses, as well as the concept “Beracha” itself already teaches, proclaims that the Jewish “grace after meals” as it is called, is no mere formal giving thanks for the meal we have eaten. But it is rather, at the same time, together with the consciousness of the fact that it is God, and God alone, that we have to thank for our existence, to stimulate and keep awake the consciousness of all the consequences for the whole conduct and mission of our lives, which are attached to this fact. Hence our ברכת המזון consists of four Berachoth, which together comprise all the factors out of which the concept “Jew” forms itself under God’s general guidance of the world and His special guidance of Jewish history, and so makes it clear to every Jewish contemporary time what its mission and its task is.

What—through the manna—has become the unloseable convinced certainty of every Jew, that God,—as indeed His four-lettered Name “the Grantor of the Future” assures every human being—allows every person and the requirements for his continued existence to be an object of His providing care, and hence every piece of bread eaten is to be regarded as given by His Goodness (בטובו I.L.), whether, according to the deserts of the recipient, it manifests itself as “grace” (חן I.L.), or “love”, (חסד I.L.) or the never-failing “pity” (רחמים I.L.), that is what we express in ברכת הזן, the first Beracha, and solemnly promise the service of our life to the “Giver of Food to all” (הזן את הכל I.L.).

But though the fate and the mission of the life of every human being is near to God, the fate and the mission of the Jewish people is still in special relationship to Him and His rule of the world, a relationship which He has proved by promising and giving the Land of Israel to the Jews for all time. This Jewish land in its prosperity and in its ruin is the pledge of the special historical position of Israel on earth. To it the second Beracha ברכת הארץ is dedicated. But its conditions and its purpose are to be taken to heart. The whole Jewish historical position of the “Promised Land” rests on the ברית אברהם (Gen. 17,7 and 8) which places the whole body in the service of God, and its purpose is for the faithful fulfilment of the Torah, ויתן להם ארצות גוים וגו׳ בעבור ישמרו חוקיו ותורותיו ינצרו (Ps. 105,44 and 45). The land promised by God is accordingly only to be thought of in connection with ברית and תורה, and only to carrying on this ברית בבשרנו and faithful devotion to the dictates of the תורה do we have to thank the sustaining provision of the Divine ordinances “daily and hourly through all time”.

This Jewish national calling of belonging exclusively to the realisation of the Torah received its permanent expression in the Sanctuary of the Torah at Zion, and its permanent bearer in the dynasty of David, of the man who fought for and obtained the political independence of his people and at the same time bequeathed to them the strains of his harp which he had elevated to the spiritual heights of his vocation. To them the third Beracha is appointed. Jerusalem,—at the foot of Mount Zion, the summit of which formed the place of the Sanctuary of the Torah—represents the People of God congregated about God’s Torah as their ruling and instructing centre. The dynasty of David, their noblest stock, is always associated with the ultimate achievement of the Jewish loftiest goal. The Gemora in Berachoth 48,b, finds a reference to this character of its spiritual calling stamped topographically on the whole land by Jerusalem-Zion in the addition here of הארץ הטובה, as indeed above in Ch. 3,25, the spiritual calling of the whole country concentrated in Mt. Zion is similarly expressed by הארץ הטובה וגו׳ ,ההר הטוב וגו׳ (refer to it there).

The prayer in the third Beracha for the granting and continuance of personal existence and independence only in connection with the supplication for the granting and continuance of the national material and spiritual well-being had accordingly to be expressed during the duration of David’s dominion and the existence of the Temple in a prayer for the preservation of that bearer of the national future; but since the destruction and the exile this prayer formed itself into a prayer for the rebuilding of the old Jerusalem, בונה ירושלים.

Thereby the considerations to be taken to heart in ברכת מזון דאורייתא are completed. When the rebellion led by Bar-Kochba proved to be a fatal error and the need arose to make the Jews keep the warning constantly in mind not to make the attempt again to restore the Jewish State by their own force of arms but to leave that national future entirely to God’s management, then the sages, sitting in council in Javneh wrote a fourth Beracha: הטוב והמטיב. It was at the time when the downtrodden nation began to breathe again, and even the permission received at last to be allowed to bury the hundreds of thousands who fell around Bethar (Dio Cassius put the number of Jews who fell in the battles at 580,000, though not all at Bethar I.L.) was greeted as the beginning of a better time. These sages decreed that this fourth Beracha was to be said in the daily prayer after meals of their people, that the memory of the (then I.L.) unparalleled slaughter at Bethar should be perpetuated in the thanks that even the preservation of the dead bodies and then their burial could be considered as extremest grace, הטוב שלא הסריחו והמטיב שנתנו לקבורה (Berachoth 48,b), and for all future time our eyes be directed away from all human help and turned solely to God, exclusively to Him הוא הטיב וכו׳ הוא יטיב לנו, הוא יגמלנו וכו׳ הוא ימלך וכו׳ הוא ישבור וכו׳.

There seems to be a deep ethical significance innate in the Halacha which stresses the good fellowship of eating in company with others by the law that when three or more mature adults, בני מצוה, sit down together to a meal, breaking bread together, they are to hold fast to this fellowship also in the Beracha, and, by one of them inviting the others to pronounce a Beracha together, he, as well as they, take to heart the fact that One Provider of food, and the Goodness of One Being has fed them all; נברך שאכלנו משלו, ברוך שאכלנו וגו׳ (“let us bless Him from Whose bounty we have eaten and by Whose Goodness we live” etc. I.L.); and then one says the Beracha for all of them, which by saying אמן they agree to make it their beracha too. If nothing tends more to throw men back on to their own selves, and is liable to make each man a competitor to his neighbour than the struggle for food, then this fellowship in eating and in saying the Beracha should, so it seems to us, bring about freeing such feelings of selfish thoughts by calling to mind thoughts of the Goodness of God being directed to all at the same time simultaneously in the same way. Hence ברכת הזמון (this invitation to “bensh” together I.L.) is referred essentially to ברכת הזן (Berachoth 46,a, תוספות).

This וברכת את ה׳ אלקיך וגו׳ of the Torah has become the pattern and the basic type of the great institution of Berachoth with which the sages, forming the Jewish spirit of the people, have interwoven the whole of our lives. Just as here the Torah makes enjoying the fruits of the land an opportunity for turning our minds away from the fruit to the One Who gives it, and therefrom to make the decisions for our actions in the spirit which is comprised in the conception of ברכה, “blessing” of God, so has the wisdom of our sages made the whole of our life with all its happenings into such teachers preaching to us of God and our duty to Him. These Berachoth teach us ever afresh to look up to Him, and to renew our vow of devoting our lives to give Him satisfaction with them as expressed in the words ברוך אתה וגו׳ (Be Thou blessed I.L.). Every time we eat anything, every phenomenon of Nature that strikes us, every fragrant aroma we enjoy, every important event that occurs in our lives, every occasion to fulfil the mitzvas, the ברכות הנהנין, the ברכות הראיה והשמיעה, the ברכות המצות all place the vowing words ברוך אתה ה׳ in our mouths, makes us gain the true relation of our position to God, “our” God by everything and with everything.

Yea, the core and vital highpoint of the whole of our “Divine Service” (our fixed daily prayers I.L.) the whole of the עבודה שבלב (see on Ch. 11,13), of our dutiful “work on our inner selves” is quite specially this dedication of our lives to active fulfilment of God’s Will on earth expressed in “ברכה״. (the eighteen, or rather nineteen Berachoth of the Amida I.L.). That which the idea of the עולה is in the offering-service to God—it preaches the constant progress of struggling ever upwards towards the ideal height of our life’s calling—is translated in the word-service to God by ברכה. And actually, in the concept of our blessing God, ברוך אתה ה׳, the sum of all the Truths, the facts that form the basis of our spiritual life, are concentrated:- the special relationship of God to each individual person, each individual standing in the service of God, the moral freedom of will, by the granting of which God has made the fulfilling of His will, the achievement of His purposes on earth, “the blessing of His Work” dependent on the free-willed decision of His human beings, accordingly that Man dedicating himself to His service has the capability through such dedication to “bless” God, to say ברוך ה׳.

Our Berachoth very thoughtfully add the idea of מלך העולם ,מלכות to the ה׳ אלקיך :שם given in our text, and the Gemora (Berachoth 40,b) teaches that this is essential, כל ברכה שאין בה שם ומלכות אינה ברכה. For our Berachoth are to lead us over from matters which come to us in the passing temporal world over to the Ruler of all time right up to the hidden future (מלך העולם I.L.) so that we recognise in matters which proclaim to us our temporal nature He Who is ה׳ אלקינו. Equally thoughtfully the second half of our Berachoth speak of God in the third person, whereas the first half is addresed to Him in the second person. For the second half as a rule expresses the matter which refers to the One to Whom we have approached in the first half with the expression of our homage. The eating, the phenomenon, the mitzva refers us to Him, הזן את העולם כולו, or שכחו וגבורתו מלא עולם, or אשר קדשנו במצותיו etc. and to Him we approach with our ברוך אתה vow to live for the fulfilment of His wish with the strength which is the purpose obtained, or to be obtained by eating the food, in the world filled with His Almight, with the deeds done according to His commandments etc. etc.

Equally with the ברכות which our sages have composed for us to say after eating, based on our text and so saying them is דאוריתא, so is, in many opinions, a Beracha to be said beforehand, the one to be said before למוד התורה (Berachoth 21a) also דאוריתא (see רמב״ן in his postcript to מצוה טו׳ ,מצות עשה ,ספר המצות and פר״ח on א״ח 47; see on Ch. 32,3). These two Berachoth would accordingly be the pattern of all the Berachoth which our sages have instituted to be said. Those to be said before eating anything—the vowing intention to use the additional strength or energy gained by the food eaten, in the service of God—are first to make us worthy of having been granted the food and כל הנהנה מן העולם הזה בלא ברכה מעל is a saying of our sages “who enjoys anything of the world without a Beracha has behaved treacherously towards something which is really one of God’s things”; before the Beracha everything belongs to God, and only with the Beracha does one get any right to the good things of the world (Berachoth 35,a).

Equally so when we say a Beracha before doing a mitzva, it is designed to make us concentrate our mind to the right conception in which the Mitzva should be fulfilled, that the procedure to be undertaken is to be considered as a “mitzva”, as a command of God for the purpose of rendering us “holy”: אשר קדשנו במצותיו. A Beracha is accordingly only to be pronounced before such Mitzvoth which are designed to effect a sanctifying influence on us, to rectify, adjust and enrich our minds and our will, such as ציצית ,מגלה ,שופר etc., but not where only some concrete result is intended such as השבת עבוט ,השבת גזלה ,צדקה etc. at the performing of which, the frame of mind and feelings do not essentially or necessarily take part.

We believe that here we have found a key to the system of the ברכות מצוה. The only Beracha which would not conform to this would be the Beracha before fixing a מעקה (Deut. 22,8;- see Avudraham Ch. III), see חורב p. 678, (recently translated into English by Dayan Grunfeld I.L.).

V. 11. השמר לו. By ברכת המזון the mind is to be kept consciously awake to the fact of Whom we have to thank for the land and its blessings, under which conditions and for what purposes we receive it, that we only remain worthy of the blessings which we receive as long as we remain mindful afresh with each fresh blessing received from God of our duty to become “a blessing ourselves”, to fulfil what God has declared to be His Will for us on earth (והיה ברכה Gen. 12,2, I.L.). Just the very abundance of what we receive from God could make us forgetful of Him.

Significantly, מצות are placed first here and then משפטים and חוקות. For it is primarily to counter the feelings of selfish egotism which are so easily engendered by possessions and enjoyments that the admonition is to come with every possession obtained or food enjoyed to use such possessions and enjoyments only in the service of Him Who has “posted us” in His realm and granted us these things as means with which to fulfil His orders. This “employment of one’s forces and means for God’s Purposes” is exactly what the מצות are, and משפטים and חוקים express the demands of justice and equity and morality as the boundaries for our efforts to obtain possessions and enjoyments.

V. 12 and 13. פן תאכל ושבעת etc. While products of the soil bring the blessings of God to mind more than the work of Man’s hands, it is buildings and moveable riches which, above all give the self-satisfied feelings of one’s own creative powers. Hence, apart from the satiation granted by the land, these are specially stressed.

V. 14-17. ורם לבבך ושכחת. The Gemora in Sota 5,a, takes the general warning against pride and arrogance אזהרה לגסי רוח to be attached to these words, which show pride and ע״ז, pride and כפירה בעיקר bordering so close to one another. In actual fact arrogance does not just lead to forgetting God, it is itself the beginning of forgetfulness of God, for where the thought “God” lives, there is no place for “pride and arrogance” it says there כל אדם שיש בו גסות הרוח אמר הקב״ה אין אני והוא יכולין לדור בעולם “of the proud man God says: I and he cannot live together in the world”.

המוציאך. In your independence and the abundance you enjoy, you will quite forget how you were a slave in Egypt, and in what a helpless state you were in the wilderness, and that it is solely God Whom you have to thank for your independence and present abundance, and that your present state of having plenty to eat by means of the ordinary course of nature, is quite as much the work of God, and His Gift as was the miraculous feeding in the wilderness.
כחי is the strength to make things: עצם ידי the power to overcome difficulties and opposition. חיל is every assembly of forces and means standing at a person’s command (See Ex. 18,21).

V. 18. כח .וזכרת וגו׳, everything, all that makes your creative personality and your capacity to earn, the intelligence, the skill, the considering foresight, the physical and mental health, every factor of your existence, of what you wish for, and are able to accomplish, is not the result of the food you eat but as given to you directly from God. And so also the combination of external circumstances which bring about the possibility and the success of your work and endeavours, is dependent on Him and Him alone. He gives you the כח, the power to “make” your fortune. The very smallest part of your good fortune can be ascribed to your own merit. And you cannot even ascribe this blessing of God’s satisfaction with you to your own moral deserts, for it is not for your own merit, but for the sake of your fathers, whose virtues He rewards with the good fortune of their descendants. למען הקים וגו׳, that all this is being given to you.

V. 19. והיה. Constant reminders of God are necessary by such institutions of the Torah as ברכת המזון and others. One does not turn one’s back to God suddenly all at once, one only gets estranged from Him gradually and in no circumstances more so than in those where one has everything one wants. Hence the remark of our sages כל מקום שאתה מוצא אכילה ושביעה שם אתה מוצא אזהרה (“wherever you find references in the Torah to eating and being satisfied with life, there you will also find warnings given” I.L.).

V. 20. עקב וגו׳, just as the results, though often delayed, yet with certainty, follow obedience with blessing and prosperity (Ch. 7,12), so does the resulting ruin, though often delayed yet with certainty follow disobedience. Both come only gradually and late otherwise obedience would be no virtue and disobedience sheer madness. Hence the latter quite specially requires the העדה, as it says in the previous verse העדתי, the “conjuring up in the mind” of that which, as it is not immediately apparent, one does not think of (העד ,עוד see Gen. 43,3).

V. 1. In the previous chapter, the danger to their good fortune was pointed out to them which would arise out of their good fortune if, in it, they forgot the duty which only becomes greater the greater the good fortune becomes; the duty to become more faithful, more richly enabled servitors and accomplishers of the Will of God; if finally they came to forget it was God Who was the founder and giver of that good fortune, and imagine they could find the source and reason for their good fortune in their own powers and strength, and in the favour of the forces of Nature which they wooed and worshipped. In the moment that they ceased to be the People of God’s Torah they would also lose the land of God’s Torah, and would come to the same end to which the nations had come because of their culpable neglect of God’s laws of morality.

These thoughts are now followed up in this chapter, and first—in verses 1-6—the fall of the nations is brought home to them to be a double lesson for them. In spite of their tremendous strength the nations come to their ruin on their moral degeneration, as soon as the “measure of their iniquity was full” (Gen. 15,16). It was not the bravery and superior strength of the victors—the victors were weaker and fewer in number than the vanquished—it was God Who was the “consuming fire” before Whom the depraved ones melted away. The conquerors are only God’s tools, they only conquer what God had already doomed to destruction. And further:- just as little as Israel’s bravery had any great part in the downfall of the nations, so had the merit which their moral rectitude had already gained any great part in God’s decision to allow them to become the heirs and successors of the destroyed nations. Israel is not complacently to imagine that as the measure of their faithfulness to their duty which they had already proved sufficient to allow them to gain the possession of the lands of the conquered nations, it would also suffice to allow them to retain that possession. If they are not as bad as the nations, they are still by a long way not as good as the realisation of the demands to which the possession of this land is attached. Not their own merit, the merit of their forefathers and the promise made to them which is now being fulfilled to them, is what has brought them into the land. This merit of their forefathers and that promise was sufficient to give them the land. But they will only retain it through their own merit which they have first to acquire, for up till now they are still an עם קשה עורף. (a stiffnecked people I.L.).

שמע ישראל. That which is to be brought to their minds is just the opposite of what one would judge by the external appearance of events to be the case. The external appearance of the events would speak for Israel’s bravery and the moral greatness which they had already achieved. God’s Truth denied both, hence בא ,לבא—!שמע really to come home, to reach there where one belongs.

ירש .לרשת גוים וגו׳ ערים וגו׳ according to its actual basic meaning related to גרש, to drive or force somebody out of his possession; to become the successor in having the possession, is nevertheless used equally referring to the possessor and to the object possessed, to inherit and to the legacy. Thus here, לרשת גוים and ובצרת .לרשת ערים (see Gen. 11,6) made inaccessible, בשמים, so that they seemed to be removed from the earth.

V. 2. עם גדול ורם. It is doubtful whether גדול refers to physical size or to the large number of its inhabitants. As it is mentioned next to and in addition to רם, it would appear the latter (see Numb. 13,22). The whole of the inhabitants of Canaan seem to have been descendants of the Anakites. Thus we find in Amos 2,9 also as descriptive of all the inhabitants of Canaan ואנכי השמדתי את האמרי מפניהם אשר כגבה ארזים גבהו וגו׳.

V. 3. אש אכלה. Cf. Ch. 4,24. הוא ישמידם והוא יכניעם לפניך, because they had already been condemned to destruction before the Judgement of God, He bowed them down before you, made them lose their giant’s might and defiance before you so that you conquered them.

V. 4. הדף .בהדף, to thrust, push (Numb. 35,20), with מ to push away (Is. 22,19). בצדקתי, and in the following verse צדקה is used as the contrast to צדקה .רשעה is the dutiful faithfulness paid to God’s Laws. רשעה, literally, free will, arbitrary action, disobedience to the law, related to רשא ,רשה.

V. 5. ישר לבב is one’s innermost feelings directed solely to matters which are in accordance with what is right. צדקה is the legality of our behaviour and actions, ישר לבב the loyalty of our feelings. One can quite well imagine the one without the other. Only the two together make the truly moral person. You cannot be sufficiently proud of possessing the one or the other.—כי ברשעת וגו׳. Only two factors were operative in bringing about your victorious entry into the land. The full measure of guilt of the inhabiting nations determined their destruction and the oath sworn to your forefathers allowed you to step into their place .
V. 6. ידעת, you must know this by yourselves, for your קשה עורף—character, of which you still give proof, is diametrically opposite to the demands of the צדק-character.

V. 7-29. Ch. 10,1-11. This consciousness of the still persistent inadequacy for their great mission is now supported by a retrospective glance at their sins during the wandering in the wilderness. The sin of the Golden Calf formed the centre point of this retrospection, the others grouped themselves around it more as lapses. For nothing showed as much as this sin of the calf what an abyss still yawned between the people as they were, and the stage at which the Torah, which had been given to them with the whole revelation on Sinai, could have expected them to have reached and to keep. It showed how the Torah would first of all have to conquer the people themselves who were to be its bearers throughout the ages and who were to keep it themselves at all times. Hence from the beginning it had to look beyond the Israel of the moment to the Israel of the future. But there is one factor which quite specially comes to the fore in this retrospective review. The people had just been told that they had indeed conquered the Promised Land without really having sufficient merit to have deserved it, but that they would not be allowed to keep it without obtaining such a sufficiency of merit. (Ch. 9,1-6, and VIII, 19 and 20). This retrospection shows them clearly how little they can sit back quietly and give themselves up to any moral lapses and feel secure in the promise given to their forefathers. The promise given to their forefathers, that a great nation would be formed out of their descendants through which “all families of the earth would attain true happiness”, would be fulfilled even if at any time a whole generation of this nation would go to ruin and even one single righteous person remained faithful who would be able to carry on the great moral destiny of the covenant of the forefathers (V. 14). Altogether no nation, no community, no individual, however important their mission might be for God’s Work on earth, can imagine that they are indispensable for God’s Work on earth, and in that conceit, give themselves over to sin. The בקרבי אקדש takes effect on the nation as it did on individuals of the nation. The government of God goes on to achieve its goal passing over the destruction of any contemporary generation of the nation and any contemporary members of the nation, however great they may be. Even an Aaron was called forth out of his time to find his grave at the summit of the mountain whereas below in the valley the nation quietly proceeded on its way to its further goals (Ch. 10,6 and 7). And at this memory of his brother, Moses could well be thinking of his own imminent departure to his everlasting home, which indeed proclaimed the admonition to every future man in Israel: Forget not that even a Moses was not indispensable for the continuation of God’s purposes. Moses, too, died at the summit of a mountain and the nation proceeded uninterruptedly on towards its future!

V. 7. זכר אל תשכח, think of it always so that you do not come to forget it.—קצף .הקצפת is the most general term for anger. Just as כעס, related to כחש, is the feeling of pain at injury to the sincerity or veracity of something, i.e. the feeling of regret brought about by remonstrance at the idea of something not being what it should be, so is קצף, related to כזב, the feeling of indignation brought about by behaviour which is not in accordance with what one expects.

מרה .ממרים הייתם עם ה׳ elsewhere is always construed with the accusative or with—ב (against I.L.). ממרים הייתם עם ה׳ accordingly cannot mean: “you were disobedient against God”, but “you were disobedient with God”, i.e. you were never entirely with God, there was always some phase in which you refused obedience to God. Of course there is a good point implied in that also, viz. that these grumblings never meant complete denial of obedience to God, that even as ממרים they were עם ה׳ just as עם ה׳ they were still always ממרים.

V. 8. ובחרב. Already in Horeb, at once at the first founding of your national destination. ויתאנף וגו׳. Whereas קצף is the immediate feeling of indignation caused by the objectionable behaviour of somebody, התאנף is “getting yourself into a rage” against somebody deliberately and after thought. That is why it is used in connection with decreeing punishment and says that it is not to be considered as given in a moment of passionate rage but with self-controlled consideration. Thus here and in I. 37; IV, 21 and IX, 20. Also the התקצף in Is. 8,21 is such a becoming angry with his king and his gods after due consideration, he talks himself into a rage.

The relationship to ענף, a twig branching forth, could make אנף designate an inner feeling pressing to come out and to show somebody by word and deed what he deserves, what is really due to him. Yea the same idea as עברה, the highest degree of rage, formed from the point of view of coming out of oneself, passing beyond oneself, and שרו עבר, in Job. 21,10, means: to lay a seed-bud internally that presses to become external, to render pregnant.

V. 9. לוחות האבנים. The tablets are repeatedly mentioned with the addition of the material of which they consisted, אבנים. The words of the Law are graven in stone, they are unalterable, absolute, as stone, hence ברית and כרת (Gen. 1,18).

ארבעים יום וגו׳. The forty days and nights which Moses spent three times with God without eating or drinking, are repeatedly stressed in this retrospective review, here, in XI, 18 and 25, and in X, 10. They occurred before the giving of the first Tablets of the Law, again after the event of the Golden Calf, and then again before the giving of the second Tablets. These equal number of days of preparation before the giving and the regiving of the Tablets of the Law, as well as before regaining the full Grace of God in the intervening time between the two gifts, must have some deep inner meaning and significance. What influence such a forty-days entire separation from everything earthly and still having his whole being directed intensely to the highest earthly relations, in the Presence of God may have had on Moses’s innerself, now especially that middle period leading up to the loftiest revelation of God’s ways of governing the world (Ex. 33,12 et seq) may have elevated his spirit to a spiritual height appropriate to such a revelation, is beyond any attempt to get even an inkling of. But the effect which these preparatory periods of the absence of their leader must have had on the expectant nation waiting below is a subject which indeed offers itself for our consideration. And there, then, these periods of waiting, just by the forty days they were kept waiting, must have brought home to the minds and feelings of all the people, and made a deep impression on their hearts, both of the high importance of the nature of the goal they were to attain through Moses, the particulars of which they were waiting to receive, as well as the depth of the still imperfect conditions out of which they had to wait to receive such a goal.

Between מתן תורה and קבלת הלוחות there was a considerable interval. The former brought to them their duty to the Torah, but the latter, by handing over the Tablets of the Torah, wished to appoint the nation itself as the keepers, representatives and bearers of the Divine Torah for all time. The Law of God for them and for mankind was to be entrusted to them. That presupposes first of all they themselves standing most faithfully on the basis of the Torah. We can understand that the forty-days awaiting was to have the result of every one of the people working on himself, getting his whole self penetrated with all that he had experienced at Sinai, consolidating his נעשה ונשמע undertaking, and thereby should have achieved at least in intention the spirit that would be commensurate with the קבלת הלוחת-stage. We can understand how just the absence of Moses should have called on every man in the nation to become himself a representative of the Torah of God he had heard, so that we understand all the more the שבירת הלוחת לעיניהם, the “smashing the tablets before their eyes”, after they had stood this first test so wretchedly. It was not their duty to the Torah which this breaking demonstrated as broken or altered. It was their unworthiness to be the depository of this Torah which was shown them thereby.

By the destruction of the Golden Calf, by the resolute action of the tribe of Levi, by the execution of the guilty, and by the awakening of self-judging consciousness of their wrong-doing as evidenced by their own act of taking of their “Horeb-decorations”, the extermination to which the nation had made themselves due was averted and the way was opened up for a return to a pure relation to God and to the great mission of their future. But this consciousness must ripen to conviction, and conviction to serious resolution to the way of their lives in future to faithfully adhere to their duty. Never, never has mere momentary expression of repentance the power to expunge great or small guilt. It requires work on oneself to a complete rebirth of the pure condition of grace to accomplish that, and to attain the victory of the atoning miracle of a כפרה which buries the guilty past. To this achievement, the attainment of such a great goal a period of forty days was granted, which, as we surmised in Ex. 33,9-11, was spent by Moses before God, not on the Mount, but outside the camp, in his tent.

And Moses was promised “fresh Tablets of the Law, besides the broken ones”, the reattachment of a complete relation of God to the people, and the re-entry of the people to their future destiny on the basis of a past guilt atoned for. And again it was forty days during which the people were to stand the test of being separated from Moses, and to accomplish working themselves up to the height of the destiny which again awaited them, to become the depositary of God’s Torah for the future of their generations and for the future of mankind.Whether the period of just forty-days corresponds to the first period of the development of a human embryo and so is chosen as a symbol of “becoming a human being”, we only dare to suggest as a question.

V. 10. ככל .ועליהם ככל הדברים וגו׳, at once at the very first beginning of the revelation of the Law, at the direct Word of God and the direct Writing of God, the Word went farther than the Writing, the concise text of the Writing only indicated (ככל I.L.) the full rich contents of the spoken word. Cf, Megilla 19,b:- מאי דכתיב ככל הדברים וגו׳ מלמד שהראהו הקב״ה למשה דקדוקי תורה ודקדוקי סופרים ומה שהסופרים עתידין להדש בין כל דבור ודבור דקדוקיה ואותיותיה של תורה.
ביום הקהל. The people were gathered directly before God, and even Moses had retired towards the people (see Ex. 19,25).
V. 11-14. See on Ex. 32,1 et seq.—ויהי מקץ see on V. 9.

V. 15. וההר בער באש, the fire on the mount proclaimed God’s Presence still there—על שתי ידי, they rested on my two hands, I did not grasp them, did not hold them, I was only their bearer, the one who brought them. That differs from what it says in Ch. 10,3 of the second tablets, the material of which was the work of human hands.

V. 17. ואתפש Up till then I simply bore them on my hands, I was only the bearer and bringer of a treasure entrusted to me. But at the sight of your sin I gripped them, I handled them out of my own impulse, on my own decision, I saw that my mission had come to an end, that it would be acting treacherously to the treasure entrusted to me were I to hand it over to you and make you its depository, ואשלכם מעל שתי ידי, and threw to the ground that which I had been entrusted to bring to you.

V. 18. ואתנפל וגו׳ (see on V. 9). כראשנה probably does not refer to ואתנפל but to ארבעים יום. Of the first, it says above ואשב בהר וגו׳ (I abode on the mount etc. I.L.) and similarly of the last, in Ch. 10,10. Only for the middle period of forty days when he was pleading for כפרה for the great sin is the expression ואתנפל לפני ה׳ appropriate.—על כל הטאתכם, for the sin comprised various degrees, from those who instigated it, those who consciously and unconsciously participated, were drawn into the dancing etc. down to those who took no part in it, but abstained from actively objecting to it, and from defending the case of God.—להכעיסו would probably not refer to לעשות, but to הרע וגו׳, to do that which is so bad in the eyes of God that, where it is done it causes God, humanly speaking, grief and sorrow. One would then have to make it refer to the instigators, the ערב רב who certainly had the intention of a defection from God, and the whole nation were reproached that they, actively or without objecting, participated in something that in its first intention had a revolt against God in mind.

V. 19. יגר .כי יגרתי has a similar meaning to גור, as יטב and טוב. It seems that אף and חמה mean internal and external rage whereas קצף, as remarked above, means the disappointment and anger provoked immediately. Your sin was of such a nature that it would have deserved your immediate destruction, as indeed was immediately pronounced in Ex. 32,10, and even if, at Moses’s immediate petition, this was not immediately carried out, still until the inner change in the people’s mind and feelings had taken place, there was plenty of reason for אף and חמה. The liability to be annihilated which the nation had incurred and which still hung over the people, was what made Moses so afraid. To get כפרה for them, and for the people to become worthy of כפרה, was the designation of these middle forty days as already indicated above on V. 9.

וישמע ה׳ אלי גם בפעם ההיא. God had already, at once before he went down from the Mount, answered and granted his prayer not to annihilate the people there and then (Ex. 32,14). God also answered his prayers now, after the forty days, to grant Israel complete כפרה and to allow them to start afresh on their world-historic mission with the Law of God, the Torah in their arms. For the immediate purpose of this retrospection it was, above all, important to bring home to the people how extremely close they had been to being annihilated on account of their defection, so that they could never give themselves up to forgetfulness of their duties towards the Laws of God depending on the promise God had given to their forefathers.

V. 20. ובאהרן וגו׳. For even Aaron would have shared the same fate, had it not been for Moses’s prayers on his behalf, as a result of his behaviour—which fell short of one’s expectations—towards the sinful demands of the people. But that which the priest is to the people, Israel is to the other nations. Both are not only unprotected from the consequences of their sins by the position God has allotted to them, but their position makes them more gravely responsible for them.

V. 21. ואת חטאתכם. That complete destruction and powdering up of the calf took place before the forty days. It is nevertheless still mentioned incidentally as a postscript, probably to take the opportunity to press home to their minds the palpable manifest irrational absurdity of such an erroneous idea that something which could be utterly destroyed and scattered to the four winds of heaven could be imagined to possess the slightest trace of superhuman divine powers.

V. 22. ובתבערה וגו׳. V. 21 was more in parenthesis and our verse 22 continues with the train of thought started with the sin of the Golden Calf. Just as the calf, so in תבערה and מסה they fell to a defection of mounting confusion in their confidence in the Guidance of God. תבערה was a dissatisfaction with the Divine Guidance, מסה a doubt of it, and whereas the defection at the Golden Calf took place openly and in public, both תבערה and מסה remained more private and were primarily feelings which were only revealed to God. And the permanent reminder of them gives warning of the fact that even mere thoughts, thoughts that at most are expressed in words are revealed to God, and every single individual stands before the judgement of God with his thought, feelings and words (see Numb. 11,1, and Ex. 17,7). But as inner private rebellion, similar to the public defection at the Calf, is worse than inner doubts, so תבערה is mentioned before מסה although in time the latter preceded the former. To these mental lapses the sin arising from lusting sensuality in קברות התאוה is then added. (Numb. 11,4 et seq.).

V. 23. ובשלח וגו׳, finally the reminder of the מרגלים rebellion which was so fateful for the whole generation of the wilderness, and reached its high point in the open seditious נתנה ראש ונשובה מצרימה (Numb. 14,4), to which probably the ותמרו את פי ה׳ א׳ refers, out of lack of “confidence” in God’s assurance (not האמנתם בו but לו) you did not “believe” God in what He assured you in contradiction to the assertion of the astrologers, ולא שמעתם בקלו and you had not the courage to carry out what He commanded you; you lacked that eternally fresh courage and strength of obedience to God which, just out of obedience to God, and in that obedience creates and finds courage and confidence to accomplish anything and everything.
V. 24. ממרים וגו׳ is the summarizing whole judgment on the whole of their past (see on V. 7).

V. 25. ואתנפל וגו׳. This retrospective glance over the sinful past of the people, in which the sin of the Golden Calf stands prominently forth as the worst, closes with the information of the prayer with which Moses strove for and succeeded in obtaining during those middle forty days כפרה, and from that כפרה a renewal of the state of the attachment of Israel to its God by the old covenant. This was to indicate to his people and to all their future generations the motive which the Guidance of God, unhindered by such great and repeated sins of the people, could decide to allow the nation to continue for the future, and to lead them towards the fulfilment of their great world-historic mission amongst the nations of the world.—אשר התנפלתי—which have already been mentioned above (V. 18).

V. 26. ואתפלל (see on Gen. 20,7)—אדני וגו׳ (see on Ch. 3,24); The first Name he uses looks on God as his Master, and himself as God’s servitor, as being a tool worthy to be used in His service. It expresses his complete submission to every decision of God equally as he does when he touches on the factor that he dares to pray might influence and alter that decision. For that factor is no other than the work itself, which is the mission in the execution of which he stands. The second Name expresses the whole depth of God’s way of government. Its justice, yea its very punishing justice is only another form of God’s everlasting Love which always remains the same, and even the bitterest fate of the extermination of a whole generation is decreed only for the purpose of allowing a purer life of the future to blossom out.

אל תשחת עמך וגו׳: They are עמך, after all they are the only body of people in the world whose belonging to you and their obligations to you form the sole means of keeping them together and of forming them into a social united community; ונחלתך, and at the same time they are the “inheritance” which has come back to “You” out of the heathen erroneous conception of gods; אל תשחת: “so let them not go suddenly to their ruin when they are half-way to the goal which You have in mind for them” that is exactly the meaning of שחת (the conception of ruin rather than destruction, it is the overthrowing of a good condition, stopping the advancement of something and reversing the prospering intended for it, I.L.; see Gen. 6,11).

אשר פדית בגדלך, You redeemed them in a quite extraordinary manner, with the insertion of Your “greatness” ie. using Your Personality and Might so specifically superior to all other personalities and powers, אשר הוצאת וגו׳, they had fallen under the power of human hands but You freed them with the power of still greater overpowering power (ביד חזקה I.L.). Can You possibly wish to have expended all this extraordinary power in vain? Was not the nature of this people, the spiritual and moral stage at which they were, apparent when You picked them, and just them, out of the rest of the nations of the world to reveal Your Greatness and Your Might? You must have certainly known the deepest, most intimate nature of their being when You chose them for Your purposes—should not the reasons which decided their being chosen speak also in favour of their continued existence?

V. 27. זכר וגו׳. Are they not the children of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, whom You knew to be so fully worthy of being called Your servitors, who were and remained so pure and untouched in the most varied conditions of tests—should no trace of the high and lofty character of these ancestors be inherited by their descendants, should not some germ of that noble race be slumbering still in their descendants that in the future could and would develop into an equally noble perfection, so that out of the root of such a stem, at some future day, descendants may arise in a rich harvest of similar servitors eager in Your service? Remember what the ancestors were, what the descendants could become, and turn away, do not look at the —momentary, passing—unworthiness of their contemporary generation! Turn away, do not look at the “stubborness”, the “unbridled state”, the “thoughtlesness” of the present generation, and remember the willing obedience, the faithful adherence to duty, the seriousness with which their forefathers proved so truly to be Your “servants”.

V. 28. פן יאמרו וגו׳. Moreover You did not do what You did do for them solely for their own sakes, and for the sake of their forefathers, enlightenment and instruction for the rest of the world was at least to an equal degree the object You had in mind at all the amazing deeds that You performed for this people. And if now You do not lead them to the goal You decided for them, if You let them die out in the wilderness, the effect will be the very opposite of what Your purpose was. Powerless against some higher fate, inimically disposed towards mankind as the heathen gods were in the imagination of their votaries would God also appear in the opinion of the nations who were meant to get some idea of the free-willed Almight of God and the greatness of His Love for humanity just from His guidance of the fate of Israel.

V. 29. והם עמך וגו׳, and they are still, and will still always remain in the eyes of the world and compared to the other nations, Your People עמך ונחלתך. However low they have sunk, and however far off they are from their lofty goal, they are still nearer to You than all the others, they still bear Your Name, by their vocation are still עמך ונחלתך, by their very national origin are those whom You led out into freedom with the revelation of Your Almighty Power and Your Mastery of great nations.

Filled with all these facts, התפלל, Moses let his whole inner self be penetrated (פלל I.L.), and held up by them he dared to petition God אל תשחת! And it has already been said above in V. 19 וישמע ה׳ אלי גם בפעם ההיא that God promised him a re-attachment of His relations to Israel.
It was to this renewed choice of Israel for its mission that the third forty days were dedicated, to which period the following retrospection refers.

V. 1. בעת ההיא. At the end of those middle forty days during which Moses begged for a resumption of the special Divine relations of government of Israel (see Ex. 33,12 et seq. and XXXIV,1 et seq.)—ועשית לך וגו׳, thereby the indication was given beforehand that they were not to be broken again, which implies the assurance that, regardless of the imperfections and lapses of the people still to be overcome, their final calling to be bearers and keepers of the Divine Torah would last throughout with them.

V. 2. ואכתב וגו׳. God does not alter His Law to accommodate the lapses of Man. There is always only the alternative of defection from the Torah or faithful return to it. Not reform of the Torah, our reform to the Torah remains for all times the one task. God will only write on the new tablets exactly what was on the old ones. The Torah is something fixed and unalterable, something given and fixed by God, and waits over seceding generations for descendants who will be faithful to their duty.

אשר שברת. See on Ex. 34,1.—ושמתם בארון. According to Baba Bathra 14,b, לוחות ושברי לוחות מונחין בארון, the broken pieces of the first tablets were placed together with the new ones in the Ark in the Holy of Holies in the Sanctuary; a double memorial for all time, firstly, that the Tablets of the Law had already once lain in ruins on our account and every contemporary age of ours only stands on their atoning re-establishment, and then that any such atonement can be nothing but return to the old Torah.
V. 5. ויהיו שם כאשר צוני ה׳, they remain as the pledge and witness of the re-established bond with God.

V. 6 & 7. ובני ישראל וגו׳. Israel journeys on. The destiny of Israel and the mission of Israel is not dependent on any man, however great and indispensable he may seem. Unchecked by Aaron’s death the people move on to their future. Aaron departs from their midst and dies on the height of the mountain, his son takes his place in the nation and the people journey on towards their destined national calling. (see above in the introduction to Ch. 9,7).

הר ההר ,קדש ,עציון גבר ,עברן ,יטבה ,הגדגד ,בני יעקן ,מסרות and there on הר ההר Aaron died. Ramban suggests that Hor was a mountain ridge stretching from מסרה to קדש and that these places were situated at no great distance from each other along the pass or valley below the ridge. Aaron climbed up to the ridge in Kadesh and died up there opposite Mt. Mosera, thereupon the people returned again back to Mosera to keep the thirty days mourning in the proximity of Aaron’s grave, hence the journey back mentioned here: מבארת בני יעקן מוסרה. After the thirty days they then journeyed back again to גדגד and יטבה. It is possible, according to that the בארת בני יעקן (the springs or brooks of Bnei-Yaakan I.L.) the return from which is recorded here, lay in the district of יטבה which is described as ארץ נחלי מים.

V. 8 & 9. בעת ההיא וגו׳. The choice of the tribe of Levi also dates from that time of the re-establishment of the bond with God. By their proven faithfulness and devotion during the crises of sin and its atonement they had made themselves worthy of the permanent culture and representation of God’s Torah among the people. This separation of one whole tribe, who, with renunciation of participating in having any possession of land, were to find their whole calling in the service of the Divine Torah and its Sanctuary, belonged essentially to the ensurance of the future, for the continuance of the bond with God depended on His Torah being made into a reality in the nation. Just as the tribe of Levi had to be the bearers of the Ark of the Covenant, as its family of Aaronides had to carry out the symbolic service of devotion to the Fire of the Torah in the Sanctuary before God and to express the national blessing with the Name of God, so did the whole life of the whole tribe stand in the service of His Torah. They were to teach and guard the Torah, to stir up the minds and feelings of the people for devotion to the Torah, to make the whole nation worthy of being called “the People of God” as they are called, and thereby to achieve the blessing that lies in the Torah. The symbolic expression of the conditions and aims of the renewed bond with God (the Tablets of stone I.L.) was entrusted to the hands of the Levites, to be active in its concrete realisation was to be the occupation of their lives.—But by this הבדיל ה׳, by this separating out of the tribe of Levi from the rest of the nation to be born bearers and guardians of the symbolic Sanctuary of the Torah, the still actual concrete imperfection of the general community was constantly brought home to them.

V. 10. ואנכי וגו׳. And this distance of the contemporary nation from the height of their destined calling, which was only to be completely bridged in the future, as well as the task for each individual to work himself upwards towards that height was shown them by this third period of waiting forty days before they received the re-established Tablets of the Law. At the same time, similarly to the period before they were to receive the first Tablets, the people—who, with the Tablets of the Law were to be made responsible for the mission of preserving and representing the Torah—were again given an opportunity of proving themselves faithful to God and His Torah when left to themselves without their leader.

וישמע וגו׳. This refers to the granting of the greatest revelation of God’s ways in His Government of human beings (Ex. Ch. XXXIV), on the strength of which Moses dared to beg God for that all-comprising promise for the whole succeeding history and development of his people viz: אם נא מצאתי חן בעיניך אדני ילך נא א׳ בקרבנו כי עם קשה עורף הוא וסלחת לעוננו ולחטאתנו ונחלתנו (refer to it there), with the granting of which the atonement for the sin of the Golden Calf which Moses had been striving to obtain came to its conclusion.

גם בפעם ההיא, also this third time. The first favourable response was:- וינחם ה׳ על הרעה וגו׳ (Ex. 32,14), the second: ועתה לך נחה את העם וגו׳ (ibid V. 34). and the third: הנה אנכי כרת ברית וגו׳ (Ex. 34,10).

לא אבה ה׳ השחיתך cannot want to describe the third response, for not to destroy the nation was granted by the first and second responses. Also it does not continue the preceding phase and say ולא אבה השחיתך, but it forms an independent sentence unconnected by the copulative ו and with a fresh subject, the ה׳ repeated. It can accordingly only be taken as the summarising conclusion of the whole. By adhering to strict justice you had deserved extermination. But at the revelation to me of the ways of God in dealing with men I had learnt that God in His Love, educating people and mankind up to the future He designs for them, right from the beginning did not wish to accede to the demands of pure justice regarding you. (אבה has quite specially the meaning: to give in to a demand made to us, see Gen. 24,5). The pronouncement of destruction (Ex. 32,10) was only to effect the consciousness in the minds of Moses and the people of the enormity of the guilt incurred and to bring about a progressive recognition of it and an alteration in the mental attitude of the people which would make possible the setting aside of the demands of justice, a continued maintenance of the nation, and finally a complete renewal of the bond with it. But the fact that the people had really deserved destruction was to remain in the minds of the people and go with them in the new future which they were now about to start. That is the tendency which the whole retrospective review from Ch. 9,4 till here was to induce and that is why it concludes with this thought.
V.11. ויאמר וגו׳, and I received the direction to lead you to the Promised Land, taking possession of which is now before you.

V. 12. ועתה ישראל, and now since all that has happened up till now must have made it clear to you that all happiness in your future only depends on your faithfully carrying out all that God demands of you, what is it then that He does demand of you?

שואל מעמך: see on Ex. 3,22. מה — כי אם: what other than.—According to the cantillation ללכת ,ליראה and לאהבה are not three separate demands, but ללכת and לאהבה are the consequence of ליראה, to fear God in such a manner that it leads to our going in all the paths of God, which, in its turn, leads to the love of God. For ירא את ה׳ means: to keep God in His Greatness and Loftiness ever in one’s mind. (see Gen. on II, 19 at end of notes,) ללכת בכל דרכיו: and thereby be induced to strive for all the goals, the way to which He has taught us. And this developing all our forces, in the Presence of God, to the goals He has set before us in the ways which He has taught us to take, brings us happiness; these goals and these ways run so much in line with our true nature, the paths He indicates are such pleasant ones — דרכיה דרכי נועם — and the feeling of living under His Eye and achieving what He meant us to accomplish is such a happy feeling of beatitude that this God-fearing treading His paths itself begets the love of God, אהבת ה׳, that knows no higher delight than אוהב ה׳ to give oneself up entirely to God and to know that one is near to Him; ,ולעבד את ה׳, and out of this love to let all one’s thoughts and feelings of the heart and all spiritual and material forces of one’s life rise to the service of God, to accomplish His purposes on earth.

This יראת ה׳ is permanently the one root of all our living and acting in the Presence of God. It is the one thing that God has laid entirely in our own hands הכל בידי שמים חוץ מיראת שמים (“everything is in God’s Hands except the fear of God” I.L.). It is the one thing that is עמך so that God can demand it מעמך. It is the one thing out of all that He gives us, and with all that He gives us that He expects back from us to Him. אין לו להקב״ה בבתי גנזיו אלא אוצר של יראת שמים, (Berachoth 33,b). (“the only thing God has in His treasury is the store of ‘Fear of God’ ” I.L.). It is the key to all knowledge and having it completely is the aim of all knowledge. כל אדם שיש בו תורה ואין בו יראת שמים רומה לגזבר שמסרו לו מפתחות הפנימיות ומפתחות החיצונות לא מסרו לו בהי עייל ? “Every man who has knowledge of Torah but has no “fear of God” is like a treasurer who has been handed the keys of the inner chamber of the treasury but not the keys to the outer one, how shall he get in to the treasure”? (Sabbat 31,b), and חבל על דלית לי׳ דרתא ותרעא לדרתא עביד (How absurd for man to make a gate-way for his court when he has no court i.e. the Torah is only a gate for the “fear of God”, what folly to get the “gate” without having what the gate is to lead into, I.L.).

V. 13. לשמר וגו׳. This יראה and this אהבה, this God-fearing walking in God’s paths and this loving service of God with all one’s heart and all one’s soul can only be made into something concrete and real by conscientiously keeping the commands of God given in His Torah transmitted from Him through Moses, מצות the positive commands and חקות the moral limits within which we have to strive to accomplish them.

V. 14-16. הן וגו׳. The very thought of the unique position God has given us towards Himself should by itself be sufficient to awaken in us this love begotten of יראה. The whole universe, heaven, and the heaven of the heavens, the earth and everything on it is His, and still He has not come as near to any being as He has to you! Out of all men on earth He found your forefathers worthy of His special loving relationship. And you, as זרעם אחריהם, as their descendants following after them should show yourselves equally worthy of the special bond with God, you has He chosen from out of all the nations to serve His special purpose for mankind. The consciousness of this fact should bring you to do away with anything which is in opposition to such a position, should bring you to:-

ומלתם וגו׳, to make your heart “obedient to yourself and to your God”. ומלתם את ערלת לבבכם (see Gen. 17,10 et seq. and Levit. on XIX,23), literally: do away with the intractibility, the insubordination of your heart, bring your heart with its feelings and desires under your mastery, make your heart obedient to yourself; וערפכם לא תקשו עוד, be no longer obstinate, submit yourselves to God; free yourself from all stubborness and self-will. Taken together: Place yourself with all your mind and will in the service of God, and do not allow yourselves to be detracted from the service by any uncontrolled thinking or willing and by no stubbornness and self-willed obstinacy.
עוד: up till now it is that on which more than anything else that you have broken down, get rid of that defect.
שמי השמים, the universe, towards which the whole of our visible heaven shrinks to a point similar to the extent of the earth towards the whole of our skies.
