Although the לו of our text clearly refers to the son, still, as just before, by אשר ימצא לו ולא לה and ראשית אנו ולא אנה, regarding the inheritance to which the legal preferential right of the firstborn applies, both the inheritance itself and the one who leaves it are both strictly confined to לו, to the father, so when it once again repeats לו משפט הבכורה it tells us that altogether משפט הבכורה is only לו, only applies to the previously designated בכור on the father’s side, and only to the heritage left by the father, so that even a firstborn from both sides can only exercise his right as a firstborn on the legacy from the father (see לחם משנה on רמב״ם הל׳ נחלות ב׳, ח׳).

If we consider this whole institution of the בכור לנחלה, the two characteristic laws, the בן שנולד לאחר מיתת האב אינו ממעט בחלק בכורה that a posthumous son does not come into the reckoning of the firstborn’s portion, and that אין בכור נוטל בראוי כבמוחזק, this extra portion only applies to what is actually there at the time of death but not to other claims which are paid subsequently may give us a clue to the whole underlying idea of this institution. It could want to arrange that, immediately on the departure of a father, somebody should be appointed provided with the right of taking possession of the larger part of the family’s fortune to carry on the personality and responsibility of the departed head of the house, and thus, through this agreed and acknowledged leader, the family might be somewhat spared from suffering such a sudden disruption. As they did hitherto, about the father, the family and the household group themselves around the firstborn son. One further fact seems worth deep consideration, viz, that just as כהונה (priesthood I.L.) and מלכות (kingship I.L.) form two separate powers for the whole of the Jewish state, so also in the smaller sphere of Jewish homes the spiritual בכור לכהן ,בכורה, and the material בכורה, the בכור לנחלה are divided into two separate institutions (see Gen. 4,3-6, p. 100).

We remarked above on V. 16 that by ביום הנחילו את בניו, the testator is conceded the right to divide his heritage unequally among his heirs. In Baba Bathra 131,a, the question remains unanswered whether this right is allowed to be exercised already when he is in full health, as בריא, or only when he is dangerously ill, as שכיב מרע, which, if taken strictly יום הנחילו might indicate. In practice the latter applies.

The limitations which are set for making legacies do not apply to מתנות, gifts, and here too Jewish law makes a difference between the necessary form for the legal validity of gifts made when the giver believed he was dying, and those made when he was in full health.

Although an unequal division of one’s heritage is possible, yea, one can even arrange for someone who is not entitled to inherit, to have some of it, by giving it as a present, not a legacy, such procedures, though legal, are not approved of: אין רוח חכמים נוחה הימנו (Baba Bathra 133,b), and the Tur on Ch. M. 282 takes the opportunity warningly to repeat the admonition of our sages שלא ישנה אדם לבן בין הבנים אפילו בדבר מועט שלא יבא לידי קנאה, not to give any one child any advantage even in the smallest degree over the others, to avoid causing jealousy.

The reason for this addition to the regulations for legacies already given in Numb. 27,6 et seq. being kept for this compendium for the settling down in the Land is self evident. Only with that settlement in the Land did fortunes and differences in fortune begin to have any meaning, whereas during the Divine Guidance through the wilderness where every requirement was provided they would have made scarcely any difference.

V. 18. כי יהיה לאיש בן. To the institution of בכור לנחלה which places in the foreground the importance of a son as carrying on the personality of his father in pecuniary matters for the family and household now comes a law concerning a son who is a complete failure, בן סורר ומורה for whom the Torah makes the parents themselves demand an early death at the hands of the law as the only means to save him from complete ruin. In the eighth volume of the Jeshurun we went very thoroughly into this chapter of the son who turned out so badly. There we pointed out how, according to an interpretation in the Gemora (Sanhedrin 71a) this chapter deals with a problem which לא היה ולא עתיד להיות, which in the whole of the past and in all future time was and will remain only a theoretical “problem”, for it could never come to a concrete case considering all the factors which would be necessary to establish it. But nevertheless, or rather just on that account, it forms a rich source of pedagogic truths and teachings, studying which, דרוש וקבל שכר, will richly repay parents for their business of bringing up children.

This law which pronounces the death-sentence over a youthful delinquent as being “incurable”, and declares his early death to be the one means of salvation from later complete degeneration — בן סורר ומורה נידון על שם סופו ימות זכאי ואל ימות חײב (ibid 17b) — fixes that sentence on quite sharply defined factors of age and behaviour; but quite specially on the relations of the parents to each other and to the son. Only if the parents work harmoniously together and completely hand in hand can the parental task of educating their children be achieved and the fault to lie in the incorrigible nature of the son. But just thereby is given the most significant indication of those factors which every successful bringing-up of children must start with. We went, at great length, very deeply into those factors in the article referred to above. Here we will limit ourselves to describing those factors only as far as they arise out of the explanation of the text.

כי יהיה לאיש בן. (“if a man has a son”,) it does not say כי יהיה בן סורר מורה וגו׳ (if there is a disobedient and rebellious son I.L.), nor כי יהיה לאב בן like בן הײתי לאבי (Prov. 4,3) in both of which cases the son would be designated quite generally as the son of his parents, but כי יהיה לאיש בן quite similarly to the preceding כי תהײן לאיש שתי נשים, and thereby the son is considered in his relation to his father as a man, as a child in whom the איש, the father should be justified in already seeing a future successor and carrier-on of his virile personality, a “brick and builder” (one who continues the building I.L.) of his house, as the word בן really expresses. A thought which stands out in sharper relief by the contrast which this disobedient and rebellious son offers to the son discussed in the previous verse who is described as ראשית אנו. There the dying father sees in his son the one who, in pecuniary matters will be the carrier-on of his manly efforts to keep the family. He sees in the “glutton and drunkard” the future squanderer of the paternal fortune שסוף מגמר נכסי אביו (Sanhedrin 72a). So that while בן in itself would include a son also in childhood, כי יהיה לאיש בן designates the son at that age in which the father recognises in him the future man, who is already moved nearer to him, the כי יהיה לאיש בן, בן הסמוך לגבורתו של איש ,איש (ibid 68b). According to the Halacha this is the first three months after attaining puberty, after thirteen years of age. כל ימיו של בן ס׳ ומ׳ אינן אלא ג׳ חדשים בלבד (the whole period to which the law of the disobedient and rebellious son” is applicable is no more than three months I.L. ibid 69,a).

With this limitation we think the Torah gives a very important hint to all those educators who are seriously concerned with the moral future of their pupils. It is in the first three months after attaining Barmitzva that the Torah sees the critical time for the decision over the moral future of a boy. Just in the time when, according to the usual opinion, with the awakening sensuality, the “evil” in Man becomes roused to activity, the Torah expects the decisive breaking through of the “good”, which just in fighting against sensuality לגבורתו של איש works itself up to the virile moral strength of a man. The Creator of Man, Who gave to youths the time of the struggle, made that same time to be an awakener of the spirit, a time that glows with enthusiasm for everything noble and great, and turns aside with indignant disgust from everything common and low. And above all Jewish youths when their parents have done their duty to them, and have let them grow up “on the knees of the Torah and Duty” of תורה and מצוה, so that now as בר מצוה as a “son of the duties commanded by God” they can be responsible for the further educative power of this consciousness of duty. Of them it says to a yet higher degree בראתי יצר הרע ובראתי לו תורה תבלין (Kiddushin 30,b) (“I have created the inclination to evil, but I have created the Torah as a sweet prophylactic medicine against it” I.L.). By the obedience which the boy, now matured to a youth, pays to his parents in this first period of the nobility of youth, by the degree with which in that period he keeps himself afar from what is low and sensual and turns towards what is spiritual and lofty, the Torah recognises the power which the feeling of the spirit of “Mitzva” has over him, “Mitzva” under whose flag he is now to have enrolled himself with manly seriousness and youthful joy. It seems to us that it is not far-fetched to think that this is also in the mind of the Mishna (Sanhedrin 68,a) which does not say בן ולא איש, קטן פטור שלא בא לכלל עונשין but קטן פטור שלא בא לכלל מצות, for it is not so much from the fear of punishment as from the power of the urge of the joyful spirit of Mitzvas that the Torah expects the moral and generally elevating influence to have its effect on the youth. Hence also the Gemora explaining the Mishna takes בא לכלל מצות and בא לכלל עונשין as two different ages (ibid).

סורר ומורה, whereas סרר, like סור designates a stubborn turning away from a directed path not agreeing to it, thus פרה סוררה (Hosea 4,16) an obstinate intractable animal, in מורה there is the idea of positive acting in contravention (see Gen. 26,35). Thus also the Sifri: ומורה, שמורה לעצמו דרך אחרת and סורר על דברי אביו ומורה על דברי אמו סורר על דברי תורה ומורה על דברי הדײנים (according to the version in Yalkut). “He does not obey his father and acts in contravention to his mother, equally so he does not do what God has commanded, and does just the reverse of that which men demand.

איננו שומע בקול אביו ובקול אמו: only if the boy has a father and a mother, and only if both father and mother exercise their educative influence on him, and only if, as it says in V. 20 איננו שומע בקולנו, the father and mother have one voice, both treat him with the same seriousness, both stand over him in equal authority, in equal dignity, and above all, in the same agreed ideas and wishes, only then can they say to themselves that it is not their fault if their son is a failure. If any one of these factors is missing, where, above all, there is not complete agreement between the parents in bringing up their children, then the failure of the child is no proof of the moral badness of his nature. Under a truly better system of education on the part of father and mother, the child might perhaps have been different, and where the parents failed, life and experience may succeed in bettering.
This complete agreement between father and mother as being the irremissable preliminary factor in bringing up children is also stamped on all the following laws, thus:-

V. 19. היה אביו רוצה ואמו אינה רוצה, אביו אינו :ותפסו בו אביו ואמו רוצה ואמו רוצה אינו נעשה בן סו׳ ומ׳ עד שיהיו שניהם רוצין (ibid 71,a); (“if the father wishes the court to act and the mother does not, or vice versa, the court may not act I.L.). More, the opinion, quoted above, that sees in this law only a richly instructive theoretical problem, makes the pronouncement of the sentence dependent even on the equality of the parents in the impression which their physical appearance makes. אם לא היתה אמו שוה לאביו בקול ובמראה ובקומה אינו נעשה בן סורר ומורה מ״ט דאמר קרא איננו שומע בקולנו מדקול בעינן שוין מראה וקומה נמי בעינן שוין (ibid). (“If the mother’s voice was not as powerful as the father’s, if she was not as tall, if her appearance was less imposing, or vice versa, again the court may not act, the Torah implies the voices must be similar, so complete equality is required in all directions” I.L.). And in fact, the personal impression made by physical appearances is surely not without weight in affecting the susceptibilities of the child of our problem, and any inequality, e.g. in the greater or lesser imposing height, voice or weight of the father or mother would also tend to make the moral impression on the feelings of the child to be unequal. Also physical infirmities of the parents could have weakened the educative influence in the same way. At least human justice, to which after all, only external circumstances are primarily available, would have to refrain from passing judgment in such cases. The Halacha takes up all that is said of the parents in our text: ותפשו ,והוציאו ,ואמרו ,בננו זה ,בקולנו and teaches therefrom that it does not apply if there is blindness or deafness or dumbness or if one of the parents is a cripple.

זלל :זולל וסובא is the specific term for the ravenous eating of meat, just as סובא is for the guzzling of wine. Thus Prov. 23,20: אל תהי זלל .בסבאי ײן בזללי בשר למו כי סבא וזולל יורש וקרעים תלביש נומה (related to צלל, to sink into the depths) designates the highest degree of degradation in contrast to יקר, thus Jer. 15,19; ואם תוציא יקר מזולל כפי תהיה “If thou understandest to produce precious from vile, thy mouth will have God-like power”. So זולל is a man who has become like a beast and a זולל בשר knows no higher bliss than a large juicy steak. סבא (related to צבא to swell up and to שבע to be satiated) to fill oneself with drink, to guzzle. The disobedient and rebellious son only incurs the sentence of the court if he shows it in animal-like gorging with meat and drink, and as this is against the will of his parents and as a thirteen year old boy presumably has no fortune of his own, he, as the Gemora says, steals the money from his parents and squanders it in feasting with his similar good-for-nothing friends (Sanhedrin 71,a). As the Torah picks out from all the possible bad deeds to be a criterion of hopeless degeneration, just the case where, at the time a Jewish boy matures to youth and should turn with enthusiasm to the ideals of spirituality and morality, he shows himself surrendered to “gorging and guzzling”, there lies therein an important hint for fathers and mothers, altogether for the whole tenor of the home in which young human souls are to mature towards their spiritual moral future, not to allow “good eating and drinking” to be a predominantly “important” item of the home. Only where spiritual and moral matters are given incomparably higher value is the atmosphere created in which young people are protected from sinking into brutish pandering to the senses.

On the declaration of the parents: איננו שומע בקולנו the Gemora says that sentence may not be pronounced on the basis of the excessive gorging at occasions where eating is a Mitzva, but also not if the food consumed consisted of prohibited foods, as pork or shrimps or treifa meat etc., for the accusation is “he would not listen to our voice”, and this is not listening to God’s Voice. (ibid 70,b). We have explained this striking law—a law which for the experiences of our present day, and through them, is so very instructive for us—fully and at length in the article in the Jeshurun mentioned above, and would refer our readers to it.
V. 21. וכל ישראל ישמעו ויראו. See on Ch. 17,13.

V. 22. וכי יהיה באיש וגו׳. The previous law of the בן סו׳ ומ׳ concluded with the instruction וכל ישראל ישמעו ויראו and thereby the matter treated there is added to the other three cases where the punishment has to be widely published as a warning to all and sundry. That is now followed by the prohibition of allowing the bodies of those criminals for whom it is prescribed to be hanged on a gallows after execution to remain hanging there, with some similar idea of its acting as a warning and deterrent. But rather they must immediately be taken down again, and, like every other dead, be buried before sun-down on the same day. For, allowing the corpse to swing on the gallows for one minute has quite a different purpose to that of deterrent and is done in no wise with the intention of making an intimidatory spectacle.

The whole of this verse 22 is the protasis, the introductory clause of the sentence of which לא תלין וגו׳ is the apodosis, the concluding clause. For in no wise is the body of every executed criminal to be subsequently hanged. For two crimes only, מגדף and ע״ז (blasphemy and idol-worship I.L.) was the command given to hang the bodies after סקילה. In Levit. (XX,2, p. 569, 570) we have tried to work out the meaning of this, as well as this hanging being the supplementary completion of the thought דמיו בו which is realised in סקילה. Here only the law follows that even at these criminals the general prohibition and command לא תלין (thou shalt not hang) and קבר תקברנו (thou shalt surely bury) are to be kept in mind. Hence קבר תקברנו.

ת״ר אילו נאמר כי יהיה באיש חטא משפט מות ותלית הײתי :והומת ותלית אומר תולין אותו ואחר כך ממיתין אותו כדרך שהמלכות עושה ת׳׳ל והומת ותלית ממיתין אותו ואחר כך תוליו אותו (Sanhedrin 46,b). The wording of our text clearly indicates (by saying “he shall be killed and hanged I.L.) that he is not to be killed by being hanged, but that is a procedure to be undertaken after he is killed. Moreover, as the Gemora remarks there, the pronouncement of the verdict and the execution were held over, at such crimes where hanging was demanded, until the latter part of the day, and then after the sentence had been carried out, the body was hanged on a gallows, taken down again immediately and buried.

V. 23. לא תלין כי קבר תקברנו וגו׳. We have already remarked on the previous verse that this prohibition and command apply in general. כל המלין את מתו עובר בלאו (ibid) (everybody who leaves his dead unburied overnight transgresses a prohibition I.L.). Here, the opportunity is taken to lay down this law in connection with an executed criminal who has then to be hanged, in order to say that even here this law must be obeyed.
קבר וגו׳, the gallows on which the hanging was carried out had also to be buried.

כי קללת אלקים תלוי (see Levit. p. 569-70.) The hanging is not for the purpose of serving as a warning to others, but in the cases of blasphemy and idolatry it is the supplementary mitzva of the preceding סקילה. That mitzva is completed by the hanging, and the corpse is accordingly immediately to be taken down and brought to its grave.
ולא תטמא. We have repeatedly remarked how, by conjuring up the erroneous thought of Man’s lack of freewill, a human corpse is the very fundamental fount of all טומאה.

אדמתך: Your “human” ground—the ground that is given you to be the stage for the realisation of the moral, freewilled, God-like activities of Man—has no space for the bodily casing out of which a human being has departed, and which has now fallen under the power of physical unfree-willed necessity. It is to be taken away from this stage, the upper surface of this “human ground” and given over to the earth to which it now belongs and from which it came, כי עפר אתה ואל עפר תשוב (Gen. 3,19). וישב העפר על הארץ כשהיה והרוח תשוב אל האלקים אשר נתנה (“then shall the dust return to the earth as it was, and the spirit shall return unto God Who gave it”, Eccl. 12,7), let your “adama” remain pure for the living—and in life free-willed—“Adam”, ולא תטמא את אדמתך אשר ה׳ אלקיך נתן לך נחלה.

But the duty of burying a corpse is looked on as a duty towards the human brother who has departed to his home whose personality is to be present to us in the casing in which he lived which must be treated with all respect, and protected from any degrading appearance, as indeed this duty is expressed היתר טומאה לקרובים for the priests (Levit. 30,2-3); and also the Halacha teaches that although כל המלין את מתו עובר בלאו (if one does not bury one’s dead on the day of death, one transgresses a prohibition I.L.) still הלינהו לכבודו להביא לו ארון תכריכין אינו עובר עליו; if one postpones the burial for the honour of the deceased, one has not transgressed the law (Sanhedrin 46,a and b). The burial of a body which lies uncared for, a מת מצוה, is considered such a high duty of love that all the highest positive mitzvas have to be neglected to attend to it. Even the טומאה prohibition for a High-priest and a Nazir has to be disregarded, and even if the mitzvas were to be cumulative e.g. הרי שהיה כה״ג ונזיר והלך לשחוט את פסחו ולמול את בנו מטמא למת מצוה, even a High-priest who was also a Nazir and is about to fulfil the duties of bringing his Pessach-offering and circumcising his son must neglect these and attend to the burying of such a case (Berachoth 18,b, תוספות there, see Levit. 21,11 and Numb. 6,11). Yea, an unburied corpse is to be considered as a disgrace and degradation to all living people בזיונא דכלהו חײ, whose conception of the true worth of all human beings (being granted complete moral freedom of will I.L.) suffers at the sight of a dead body. (see לחם משנה on הל׳ אבל י״ב ,א׳).

וצע״ע דמאי קמבעי ליה בסנהדרין אי קבורה משום בזיונא או משום כפרה הא בברכות י״ט ב׳ סברת הש״ס בפשיטות דמת מצוה איכא משום כבוד הבריות וגם כמו שכתבתי בפנים הא דמותר להלין לכבודו מוכיח דקבורה משום בזיונא, וצ״ע. ולולי דמסתפינא הײתי אומר דהאבעי׳ הוא דוקא אי קבורת קרקע משום בזיונא או משום כפרה דהא רק ע״י קרקע הויא כפרה ע״ש, וצ׳׳ע).

V. 1. This chapter begins with a group of laws (1-5) in which three fundamental principles are laid down for the general civic and business life which is now really only beginning for the people, under the influence of which alone the social life can be formed in accordance with their calling. These three principles are: fraternal solidarity of all for the protection of each person’s possessions (v. 1-3); fraternal solidarity of all for the furthering of each person’s undertakings (v. 4.); upholding the natural differences of the sexes regarding occupations and ways of life, (v. 5). As usual, these principles are made known to us through actual problems and examples, of which the first is specially instructive at the same time for knowledge of the law in various ways.

This first problem of השבת אבדה (returning lost property I.L.) could come naturally in connection with the preceding duty of attending to the burial of human bodies. A corpse is nothing else but an אבדה (lost property), the fallen-off, left-behind casing of a human brother. The same feeling of duty which sees in the corpse the personality of the human being to whom it belonged, and something left to the responsibility of the care of all his brother-men, makes the personality of its owner seen in every lost property and makes the care of it the brotherly responsibility of every fellow man.

לא תראה וגו׳. The duty imposed here of caring for and returning an animal whose owner had lost it, or, as the law is extended in v. 3, any other lost property, only applies if, as it says here in the case of animals נדחים (straying I.L.) if the conditions make it quite clear, that the animal or the article is lost. But if it seems that it was placed there, where it is found, even if there is some doubt about it, it may not be moved. But if one had taken it away and kept it so that in the meantime the owner would have had time to come and fetch it, one may not then simply place it back, but must keep it carefully, and, if it is of such a nature that proof of identification is possible, public notices of its having been found must be made (v. 3). כל ספק הינוח לכתחלה לא יטול ואם נטל לא יחזור (Baba Kama 25b; see תוספות and more detailed laws Ch.M. 260,10).

On the sentence והתעלמת מהם the Halacha teaches פעמים שאתה מתעלם ופעמים שאי אתה מתעלם (ibid 30,a) (it could mean either “you withdrew yourself from it”, or “you would withdraw yourself from it” I.L.) that the law in v. 3 לא תוכל להתעלם is not an absolute prohibition, but depends on the nature of the object found and the personality of the finder, that, for instance זקן ואינו לפי כבודו, a respected Rabbi, or other similar person, who would not drive his own donkey home through the streets, or carry his own sack of potatoes home is not bound to do so to some lost property of that nature. In such cases the והתעלמת seems to be disconnected from its syntatic attachment to לא תראה and taken to be separate phrase. More closely considered, one might arrive at the following: כי תראה וגו׳ לא תתעלם מהם in which case תתעלם would certainly be an absolute prohibition and it would be forbidden to withdraw oneself from helping. But is says לא תראה וגו׳ והתעלמת whereby the התעלם is made into a modification of the ראיה and as such is forbidden; you may not see it with a “making-yourself-not-seeing-it” look, may not then “look the other way”, consider yourself as not having seen it, as if it did not concern you at all. From that it at once follows, you have to behave as if it was yours, do everything to it that you would do to your own, as indeed the canon runs: כל שבשלו מחזיר בשל חברו נמי מחזיר וכל שבשלו פורק וטוען בשל חברו נמי פורק וטוען “that which, were it his own, he would take home, unload and load up, that must you also do to the property of your neighbour (ibid 30,b). But nevertheless it is expected (ibid) that a man of character, when it comes to saving the property of his fellow-man will not hold himself strictly to the letter of the law, but לפנים משורת הדין, would do that for somebody else’s good which he would not do even for himself, and this doing more than what you are strictly bound by law to do for your neighbour is considered such a serious demand for equity and good will in social life, that there the significant pronouncement is made: לא חרבה ירושלים אלא שהעמידו דבריהם על דין תורה ולא עבדו לפנים משורת הדין, “Jerusalem only went to ruin because in their mutual relations one to the other they only allowed the principles of the strict justice of the letter of the law to govern matters and not equity and the happy give-and-take arrangements to prevail”. (see also תוספות on 24,b, ibid.; see also Ex. 18,20).

השב תשיבם לאחיך, even repeatedly החזירה וברחה החזירה וברחה אפי׳ ד׳ וה׳ פעמים חײב להחזירה (Baba Mezia 30,b) (“if he returned it and it ran away, however many times it happened, he is still bound to catch it and return it to its owner” I.L.); and indeed, on 31,a, there, it finds this unlimited repetition already expressed in the aoristic use of השב in the infinitive. The addition of the word תשיבם only extends the concept of the השבה, that it is sufficient if the animal is brought back to any enclosed place belonging to the owner, and he is not in duty bound to inform the owner, a duty which is incumbent in the case of returning a stolen object or something which had been entrusted to his care: הכל צריכין דעת בעלים חוץ מהשבת אבדה שהתורה רבתה השבות הרבה (ibid 31,a). By simply returning it, the thief or the guardian is still responsible for it until the owner is informed, so that he can take proper care of it (and in the case of living animals this is required even if the owner had no knowledge of its being lost, because meanwhile the animal had become used to other places, הואיל ואינקטי נגרי ברײתא (Baba Kama 118,b) literally “because it had become used to take steps outside).

V. 2. והיה עמך .ואם לא קרוב וגו׳ etc. This task of keeping it safely is modified by the task of והשבתו לו (giving it back to him I.L.) in which the duty is implied to lie, to see to it that the lost property does remain to be given back to the owner, that, in the case of an animal that the cost of feeding it, which can naturally be claimed to be refunded, does not amount up to the whole worth of the animal. Hence the sentence in the Gemora כל שעושה ואוכל יעשה ויאכל ודבר שאין עושה ואוכל ימכר שנאמר והשבתו לו ראה האיך תשיבנו לו, (“everything that earns its keep, let it earn and keep it, but what earns or produces nothing, but has to be fed is to be sold, for it says “and return it to him”, see to it that you do return it to him, i.e. where possible the object itself, but where not, the value of it, שם דמיהן ומניחן.

עד דרש אחיך אתו, it is your duty to keep it with you, not only until somebody demands it from you, but until you are convinced that it is אחיך the one who is so designated in V. 1, and until it is אתו, that very thing itself that he demands from you. Your “brother” proves his claim by אתו, by his detailed description of the object. This law, it seems to us, lies in the wording of the text. It could have used general terms עד אשר ידרש מעמך והשבת אתו. The Halacha gives a fresh interpretation to the words דרש אחיך (ibid 28,a) to have the meaning עד שתדרש אחיך i.e. דרשהו אם רמאי הוא, “Keep it until you have examined your brother”, make sure his demand is genuine and that he is no swindler. This proving his claim can be made either through עדים, witnesses who testify that the object is his, or by סימנין, giving distinctive details. These details vary in their worth as proof of identification. There are three categories: סימנין מובהקין ביותר, specially characteristic signs, e.g. a hole, a tear, or other imperfection on a definitely described place, which it is hardly to be assumed would be found on a similar article; סימנין מובהקים אמצעין, identifying signs of medium speciality, such as e.g. exact size of length, weight, number, also the place where it was found; finally סימנין גרועין, signs which are not specially convincing, such as a general description of size and colour such as, large, small, white, red etc. The question remains undecided whether proof by giving details has the validity of being original Torah authority or can only be granted Rabbinic authority, whether סימנין דאוריתא or דרבנן. Identifying marks of the first category are in any case adequate even דאוריתא, those of the last, by themselves not accepted at all. There is only a question in the case of the middle class which is usually taken as sufficient proof of identification. If that proof is regarding the case or container in which the articles are found, or, as if on the saddle which is on the animal found, then the question arises אי חײשינן לשאלה, if we do not have to consider whether the owner of the articles or the animal had not borrowed the case or the saddle, so that the identification of the container is no real proof of ownership of the valuables themselves, and also the consideration that certain articles are not usually lent to other people דלא מושלי אינשי, etc. (Baba Mezia 27b; Gittin 27b; Yebamoth 120b).
All these factors are also of great importance in deciding the identity of unknown corpses which are found.

A much higher degree of reliability is given to טביעות עין, the recognition and description of an article which does not depend on one special mark but on the whole of the thing itself. A means of recognition which indeed is not objectively conclusive proof and can only be relied upon to return the lost property in cases where there is every reason to assume the honesty and reliability of the claimant (Baba Mezia 23,b, and Chulin 96a).
Anyone who finds an article which he has to look after must facilitate its being claimed by publicising the fact that such article or animal has been found. (see on V. 3).

V. 3. וכן תעשה לחמרו. In this verse more details are given of the duty of caring for and returning lost property. The text is not satisfied with saying merely וכן תעשה לכל אבדת אחיך but complements the examples given in V.1., ox or sheep, by ass and garment on which Baba Mezia 27,a, teaches that חמור wishes to teach that an ass must be returned not only by evidence of the ownership of the animal itself but also by the evidence of witnesses or proofs of identification of the ownership of the saddle etc. (see on V.2). “Ox or sheep” teaches that the wool taken from the sheep or the hair from the tails of the oxen must also be returned. It is the complete ox, the complete sheep that must be kept for the owner. “Garment” teaches that the finder has only to look after and return such objects which, like garments, usually have recognisable signs on them and can be taken to have claimants. But objects which in no ways have any recognisable marks on them and it can be presumed that the owners have no hope of reclaiming them, יאוש, (such as loose coins etc. I.L.) belong to the finder, but only if it can be presumed that at the time when they are found the owner had already noticed his loss and given them up. But if the nature of the find is such that one cannot make this assumption, although it is sure that when he does become aware of it he will have no hope of getting it back, so that באיסורא בא לידו, at the moment they came into the hands of the finder, the right of ownership was still attached to the loser, the subsequent יאוש does not suffice to complete the right of ownership to the finder. Such a subsequent יאוש, anticipated by the finder is called יאוש שלא מדעת and the legal canon runs: יאוש שלא מדעת לא הוי יאוש (see Baba Mezia 21,a and b et seq.). For the whole idea of the right of possession arising from somebody else consciously giving up his rights to it, and also from acts showing actual possession, see Levit. 25,24.

There are objects to which owners can be presumed to have given up their rights of possession already beforehand e.g. תמרי דויקי, fruit blown by the wind on to the public highway from neighbouring trees, such, as a general rule, may be taken by the finder on the assumption that the owner מעיקרא מיאש. But if the trees were the property of under-age orphans, יתמי, who have no legal right to dispose of their possessions, such fruit is prohibited to be taken. (Baba Mezia 22,b).
On these principles the laws given in Baba Mezia 21,a et seq. are founded:- אלו מציאות שלו ואלו חײב להכריז (these “findings” he may keep but these he must publicise”) (see ibid).

לכל אבדת אחיך :וכן תעשה לכל אבדת אחיך makes it the duty of everybody to keep off any danger which threatens his neighbour’s property including landed property e.g. ראה מים ששוטפין ובאין הרי זה גודר בפניהם, to prevent a field from being flooded with which it is being threatened.

אשר תאבד ממנו ומצאתה (“which he has lost and everybody can find” I.L.). מי שאבודה הימנו ומצויה אצל כל אדם יצאת אבדה ששטפה נהר שאבודה ממנו ואינה מצויה אצל כל אדם (B.M. 22,b). Lost property which has to be kept carefully and returned is only such which is lost to the owner himself but is available for everybody else to find, of such the Torah says that the right of possession of the owner is still attached to it until he gives it up by יאוש, and in such cases, as remarked above, יאוש שלא מדעת לא הוי יאוש. But something which is taken right out of everybody’s reach, as e.g. if it was swept away by a river, of such, all rights of possession are objectively automatically removed and even before the owner knows what has happened. (B.M. 22b, ש״מ thereon).

לא תוכל להתעלם. By the way this prohibition is worded we think we can already see that similarly to V.1. the prohibition is not absolute, but that exceptions are permitted. If it was meant to be absolute, it would say לא תתעלם. But לא תוכל להתעלם says, it is not within your power to avoid this task, you cannot dispense yourself from having to do it. But it implies that the Torah itself grants dispensation in certain cases. (Cf. לא תוכל לאכל בשעריך Ch. 12,17).

Whether שומר אבידה has the reponsibilities of a שומר שכר (a paid guardian of an object I.L.) or a שומר חנם (a gratuitous one I.L.) and is responsible or not for theft or loss (Ex. 22,6-14) is a matter which is discussed in Baba Kama 56b, and is finally left undecided. (See Ch.M. 267,16 and ש״ך thereon). For the care of looking after lost property for its owner, and the trouble or work expended thereon, no payment in any way may be taken. Even according to the view that considers a שומר אבדה a “paid guardian”, the mitzva, the command to look after one’s neighbour’s property is looked on as payment in itself, and considers that, although doing the Mitzva itself cannot be considered as any material advantage, as מצות לאו ליהנות ניתנו still as, in accordance with the principle that העוסק במצוה פטור מן המצוה (See Ch. 6,6) still doing this Mitzva could exonerate him from having to do another Mitzva which would entail pecuniary expense, פרוטה דרב יוסף, or, as another opinion (ibid) explains it: כיון דרחמנא שעבדיה בעל כורחיה, הילכך כשומר שכר דמי, as the caring for lost property is not taken on out of his own goodwill but is a duty imposed on him by the Torah, it must be considered as being imposed with the full responsibilities of caretakers. That which payment imposes on a שומר שכר the dictate of the Torah effects here.

For returning lost property, as remarked above, no payment may be taken. For it is a duty which the Torah commands him to perform. But if the finder is just occupied with work which brings him payment, he is not bound to leave that without being recompensed for his loss. This permission is worded (B.M. 31,b): נותן לו שכרו כפועל בטל and indeed, as the explanation is worded כפועל בטל של אותה מלאכה דבטל מנה. This law is taken in different ways. They differ essentially as to whether being occupied with the lost property is to be reckoned as trouble, labour and שכר כפועל בטל של אותה מלאכה דבטל מינה would be reckoned by how much he would take to leave the paying work he is engaged on to do the less laborious work of looking after the lost property, or whether being occupied with the lost property being a duty does not come into the reckoning at all, and פועל בטל etc. is reckoned on how much he would take to give up the paying work to be idle. The question is whether פועל בטל means a workman giving up work altogether or only relatively so in comparison with a less laborious task. The ש״ך in ח״מ 265,1 decides for the former. If the work on the lost property could really claim a higher wage, than what he was engaged on, then in any case he can only claim the wage he is giving up as השבת אבדה in itself must be done gratuitously. According to the way the ר״ח ,רי״ף and other authorities take it, the occupation with the lost property does not come into consideration at all, and פועל בטל designates solely the price of the work he has to give up for the sake of the lost property. This price is not to be reckoned at the rate when labour is scarce and has to be paid at a high rate, but reckoned at the rates paid when the workers in that particular branch of labour are unemployed בטל and there are more applicants for labour than labour offered (see מ״מ on הל׳ גזלה 12,4). The wording כפועל בטל של אותה מלאכה and not מאותה מלאכה would certainly speak for this way of taking it.

V. 4. דרמו אינהו וטעונײהו באורחא :נופלים בדרך .לא תראה וגו׳ it and its load are lying on the road and it is difficult for the driver to get it loaded up again (B.M. 32a). It is accordingly speaking here of טעינה of helping to load up, whereas in Ex. 23,5 it was of פריקה of helping to unload. There (verses 4 and 5) השבת אבדה and פריקה are treated altogether more in reference to אויב and שונא, to help to be given even to someone with whom you are at enmity and on bad terms, and also with regards to צער בעלי חײם to the duty of kindness to animals. But here the duty of saving the possessions and helping others is given as a general command regulating general social intercourse. Baba Mezia teaches the law that פריקה בחנם, טעינה בשכר, that for unloading, just as for returning lost property no compensation may be taken, but for loading up payment is allowed to be taken. At lost property and at unloading, the threatened loss which is to be prevented is there, imminent, at the loading up, it is only furthering your neighbour’s plans. Therein could lie the reason for this legal difference. But the legal fact that rendering help at loading is a duty for which payment may be demanded, that the duty of gratuitous care for the restoration of lost property only applies to unemployed people, but that the Torah does not demand anybody to leave off earning his own living without compensation, seems deeply characteristic of the Jewish Law for social duties. The Jewish Law is far from considering that exaggerated superabundance of the milk of human kindness which demands completely losing sight of your own self and complete self-forgetting sacrifice, as being the general normal principle of social life, and only concedes virtue to begin where self-sacrificing blind devotion is prominently to the fore. Such a point of view could never become the general maxim, and were it to be realised would make an end of all social intercourse. Just because of its exaggerated exuberance it appears as an impractical ideal and would leave “practical” people room for naught but the barest egoism. Jewish general principles of the duties of social life grant the care for one’s own existence and independence the fullest importance, but peremptorily demand at the same time, with equal seriousness, next to this care for oneself, the helpful participation in the upkeep of the property, and the furthering of the undertakings, of one’s fellow-men. Jewish Teaching which, as we worked out on Levit. 19,17 make one’s endeavours for one’s own self stripped of every trace of selfishness through the point of view of its being a God-ordained duty, it alone could in truth seal its “Love thy neighbour as thyself” with the seal of God: אני ה׳. Hence also the Mishna could teach (B.M. 33a) from the standpoint of general duty: If it is a question of saving your own property or that of your neighbour שלו קודם, the Torah does not demand that you neglect your own, and רב יהודה אמר רב explains this by finding support in the sentence in Ch. 15,4, אפס כי לא יהיה בך אביון, so that שלך קודם לשל כל אדם (for you, your own need must come first I.L.). (This using this sentence to support this theory may not be so far off from the actual real meaning of the verse. A theory which would wish to place one’s own interests absolutely on par with the interests of everybody else would, if kept to its logical conclusion finally do away in a communistic manner with the whole conception of legal ownership of property and make the State to a proletarian one).

Nevertheless the same רב יהודה אמר רב adds the admonishing warning: כל המקײם בעצמו כך סוף בא לידי כך “he who makes this the guiding principle of his life (myself first!) will finally come to the very need from which he reckoned to save himself by it”! For the same Torah which drew for us the שורת הדין, the line of justice for all our behaviour, stepping across which, wrongdoing immediately begins, the same Torah expects the nobility of our feelings to make ourselves keep well inside that line לפנים משורת הדין and, for the benefit of others to give up that which is strict justice we could claim to keep for ourselves, and to do that which in consideration of the circumstances seems to be הישר והטוב בעיני ה׳, “what is right and good in the eyes of God” (see Ch. 6,18). The two complementary sayings of רב יהודה אמר רב places Rashi’s explanation in its true light when Rashi says:- לא יהיה בך אביון הזהר מן העניות, the duty to look after your own first only applies if it is to save yourself from poverty. But כל המקײם בעצמו כך וכו׳ אף על פי שלא הטילו עליו הכתוב יש לאדם ליכנס לפנים משורת הדין ולא לדקדק שלי קודם אם לא בהפסד מוכיח, ואם תמיד מדקדק פורק מעליו עול גמילות חסדים וצדקה וסוף שיצטרך לבריות; “although the law does not oblige him to do so, still nobody should hold himself strictly to the letter of the law, and only let his own interests come first when it it is apparent that otherwise his loss would be really important. If somebody were always to reckon exactly and consider his own interests first then he would dispense altogether with the other duties which are incumbent on him, the duties of brotherly love, charity and good deeds, and here it promises him that instead of achieving independence wellbeing and happiness with his selfishness, he will end up by having to be dependent on others.”

עמו (with him I.L.) and similarly in Ex. 23,5, The duty of rendering help only falls on him if the one who needs the help works with him. But if he—unless of course he is weak or ill—just sits idly by, and says: the Torah gives you the mitzva the command to load or unload, as the case may be, so go ahead with your mitzva, the other one is not bound to do anything; except in the case of unloading (in Ex.) he must do it out of consideration for the poor suffering animal; but then he can claim payment for his work (B.M. 32a and b).

V. 5. לא יהיה וגו׳. In the Gemora (Nazir 59,a) these prohibitions are taken in different ways. According to one opinion, here the changing of the clothes of the sexes is only forbidden if done for immoral purposes. But according to the teaching of ר׳ אליעזר בן יעקב which is accepted as Halacha, the first prohibition לא יהיה כלי גבר על אשה says that שלא תצא אשה בכלי זײן למלחמה, that a woman is not to go to war equipped with arms, and לא ילבש גבר שמלת אשה, that a man is not to prink and prank himself in an effeminate manner. It seems to us that it is clear that, according to this way of taking it the prohibition is not so much disguising one’s sex by dressing in female clothes as forbidding each sex that which is more specifically pertaining to the nature of the opposite one. A man is just as little to get himself up with powder and paint and lipstick etc. which is all quite in order for women to do, and is in accordance with feminine nature, as a woman is to appear in a profession which belongs to the nature of men (for it does not say שלא תצא אשה בכלי זײן but בכלי זײן למלחמה). As a matter of fact, it is forbidden by the לא ילבש גבר שמלת אשה for a man to pay more attention than is seemly for a man to the care of his skin, hair, curls, cosmetics, to have too much love for the mirror etc. etc. as well as to wear female clothes. (Nazir 59,a; Makkoth 20b; Avouda Zara 29a, תוספות there).

V. 6. כי יקרא וגו׳. The preceding laws (verses 1-5) proclaimed the fundamental principles for the foundation and development of the impending social life of the people. The great principles of solidarity and fraternity in looking after the property, and furthering the undertakings of others, as well as the preservation of the separate professions and ways of life of the sexes. The former form the fundamental pillars of social intercourse, as the latter serve the foundation of the “homes” which indeed are the granite base for all national well-being. In v. 5. already Woman was placed in the foreground in this respect. On that, that לא יהיה כלי גבר על אשה, which conceives Woman in the loftiness and worthiness of her profession as “Mother of the Home”, and in the “limitation” is to stand in the nation, highly respecting herself and being highly respected, protected and unassailable, on that, more than on anything else, the prosperity and the constant progress of the life of the people, is dependent. The degree in which the calling of Woman is held in high honour on all sides is an important yardstick by which the moral standard of a nation can be measured.

So that when now the Torah goes over to laws which predominately deal with the constitution of family life, it places an institution at the head which brings home to everyone in the nation the high importance which the Torah assigns to the homely activity of a female creature, inasmuch as it follows this activity even into the sphere of animal life, and assures immunity to a mother-bird while she is engaged in her activities of motherhood, and demands practical proof of such appreciation of a female creature in her profession from everyone to whom an opportunity occurs.

כי יקרא וגו׳. See Gen 24,6. Up till now you had no connection at all with the nest, only now do you meet it; פרט למזומן, the Torah only speaks of a wild bird, but not of one which belongs to human property (Chulin 139b) קן (from קנן related to גנן to protect) designates primarily the habitation of a bird for protection especially the place for the protection of the young—a bird’s nest. But by transition it is also used to designate the young birds living in the nest. Thus כנשר יעיר קנו (“as the eagle awakens its nestlings” I.L.) in Ch. 32,11.—צפור: only birds which are “pure” (ibid., see Gen. 7,14 and XV, 10, p. 281), it only speaks of birds which are permitted for food, at which accordingly, the inducement to take them is very natural.

אפרחים או ביצים, not only if there are several nestlings or several eggs, even one young, or one egg is called קן (ibid 140,b). Just as פרח is the flower bursting out of the bud, so is the young that comes out of the egg called אפרח.

והאם. The Torah only speaks of the female bird but not of the male, even if one was engaged in brooding or caring for the young the law would not apply (ibid). על האפרחים to keep them warm, protect them from cold. על הביצים, to hatch them. As על האפרחים או על ביצים is repeated and it does not say shortly עליהם, it is taught therefrom (ibid) לאקושי אפרחים לביצים וביצים לאפרחים that the nestling and the eggs are compared to each other; just as the eggs require the mother-bird, so must the nestlings צריכין לאמן require the mother and not be able to fly yet, and just as the nestlings are able to go on living בני קײמא so must the eggs also not be already gone bad. Also from תקח לך (v. 7) it is deduced that the young may not be טרפה fatally wounded, לך ולא לכלביך (140a). The care of the mother must still have a purpose and not be useless.

V. 7. שלח תשלח וגו׳. If then such a “pure” and ownerless mother-bird is found engaged with her maternal duties on nestlings or eggs, so that you have the opportunity of taking both, you are commanded to take up the mother-bird—so that you see that you could take it—but to let it fly away into freedom. The fact that it is exercising its function of motherhood protects its independence and freedom.
ואת הבנים תקח לך, this is not a command, but you are at liberty to do so, in contrast to האם, the mother.

למען ײטב לך והארכת ימים, do this in the consciousness that on the spirit of the Mitzva which you thereby fulfil, on the deep respect for motherhood which you express thereby, the happiness of the present and all the future depends. Compare the similar promise given at the command for the actual honouring of parents (Ex. 20,12 and Deut. V.16)—a parallel which could well confirm the way we have taken the meaning of this command to be.

In Chulin 141,a, it is taught: הנוטל אם על בנים משלח ואינו לוקה, if a person has appropriated the mother-bird from on the young, if he subsequently does let it fly away he is free from the punishment which he had incurred. This relationship of the prohibition לא תקח האם על בנים to the positive command שלח תשלח את האם, that after trangressing the prohibition, the punishment incurred thereby need not be suffered if the command is subsequently carried out, is taken to come under the concept of לאו הניתק לעשה that a prohibition to which a command is attached does not pay the penalty for the transgression if the command is carried out, the rule runs: כל מצות לא תעשה שיש בה קום עשה אין לוקין עליו (Chulin 141,a). Other examples of such prohibitions with a command attached to them are: לא תותירו וגו׳ והנותר וגו׳ באש תשרפו; לא תכלה פאת וגו׳ לעני ולגר תעזוב אותם; לא תגזול והשיב את הגזילה; ולו תהיה לאשה וגו׳ לא יוכל שלחה כל ימיו. In Makkoth 15,b, the relation of the prohibition to the associated command is taken in various ways. According to one way of looking at it, the transgression with the attached penalty has only then been committed if the command has been rendered impossible to be fulfilled, if, for instance, he had taken the mother-bird from off the nestlings and had killed it. This opinion says: ביטל עשה שבה חײב לא ביטל פטור. According to the other idea, the transgression with the attached penalty has been committed as soon as the act has been done. He has at once incurred the penalty, but he can have it remitted by fulfilling the command—and indeed according to Rashi on Chulin 141a, this must be done immediately he has been warned that he has done wrong, תוך כדי דבור של התראה, or, according to Rashi on Makkoth 15,b, immediately after the court’s summons, (see תוספות there). This view says: קײם עשה שבה פטור לא קײם חײב. In the first case the transgression depends on the impossibility of fulfilling the command. In the second the liability to punishment depends on the non-fulfilment of the command. There, in the Gemora, this difference is explained to be in connection with another difference of opinion, namely whether התראת ספק שמה התראה or לאו שמה התראה, whether the warning which has to be given before a transgression is made if judical punishment is to be imposed (Ex. 21,14; Levit. 20,67; Numb. 15,32), is effective only if there is no doubt that the act which the person is warned against doing is with certainty a transgression or if it is effective even if it is doubtful whether it need necessarily be so. If, e.g. according to the opinion that it depends on ביטלו or לא ביטלו, that the liability for punishment only arises if the possibility of performing the command of שלח תשלח has been done away with, so that at the moment of the prohibition being transgressed it is doubtful whether this will be the case or not, then the warning given at that moment is an התראת ספק; but if, in accordance with the other way of taking it קײמו or לא קײמו, the liability to punishment arises immediately the transgression is done—whether the punishment is remitted afterwards by the performance of the command or not—then the warning given has the character of an התראת ודאי. Here we have only noted the general outline of these legal conceptions according to רש״י and רי״ף .תוספות and רמב״ם have a somewhat different way of taking them, partly depending on a different version (see כ״מ on הל׳ סנהדרין 16,4).

V. 8. כי תבנה. The previous law taught the importance of the home and the mother’s work in it, and to show appreciation of its value even in a bird’s nest and a mother-bird. Now with the group of laws beginning with this verse, the higher importance of human homes and human activities in them is brought to mind. Here, as everywhere, the demand of the laws of morality is paired with the efforts shown as the driving force for activity already in animal life by the building of nests and the care for the young. The bird builds its nest for itself and its own immediate ones, and it is still egoism and the urge for self-preservation with all its powerful drive which guides it undeviatingly thereby. But Man is to build his house from the beginning with consideration for all his contemporary and future fellow-men. In the whole sphere of his home he may allow nothing which might be dangerous for anybody (v. 8). At all his agricultural work to produce food, at all his activities to master Nature, and in his human outer appearance he is to keep the Great Lawgiver of the World in his mind, Whose creative Will has created him with free will to obey His laws just as He formed animals and plants without free will, instinctively to give obedience to those laws (verse 9, 10 & 11), above all Man is constantly to admonish himself that, wherever his calling may take him it is only by self-conquering faithfulness to God’s laws that he has to prove his virile strength and human worth. (V.12). These are all laws which have already been expressed in the previous books (Ex. 21,28-34; Levit. 19,19; Numb. 15,37-41), in their social legal consequences, in their importance for sanctifying life, in their seriousness for fostering clear-headed circumspection, but are incorporated in this compendium for those now about to move into the Land, partly supplemented, but especially for the activities in the home and on the fields which are only now really to begin.

מעקה, the root עקה does not occur elsewhere. By the relationship of דום to בוז ,דמה to צוד ,בזה to צדה and others עקה could well be related to עוק to press, to confine. In any case מעקה means fencing in, a railing, a balustrade, and, according to the halacha it must be at least ten hand-breadths high.

ולא תשים דמים. Whereas דם in the singular designates blood in its unique importance as bearer of the life of an organism, דמים is just blood looked on as parts of that life stream separated from the main current, “spilt blood”. שום דמים, accordingly means causing such spilt blood to be a threat to the life of a person, and לא תשים דמים בביתך is the general legal warning against having anything dangerous to life in any place where we are responsible for it. Hence the sentence: מנין שלא יגדל אדם כלב רע בתוך ביתו ולא יעמיד סולם רעוע בתוך ביתו תלמוד לומר לא תשים דמים בביתך (בבא קמא ט״ו ב׳) “to have a vicious dog, a shaky ladder in one’s house is forbidden by these words, and also for the local civil authorities to intervene to have anything at all which might be dangerous removed, לסלק הזיקא, even there where the civil law would not have to impose compensation for damages” (ibid). Thus e.g. the Jewish courts outside Palestine who were not fully authorised by סמיכה (see Ex. 21,6) were restricted to such cases which arose out of the happenings of ordinary traffic or charges and claims referring to money or property, מילתא דשכיחא ויש בו חסרון כיס. Only for such cases were these courts authorised as delegates of the central national Sanhedrin as עבדינן שליחותײהו, but not for the exceptional, seldom-occurring cases or for such cases as כפל (having to repay double the amount) at גניבה (Ex. 22,3) or חצי נזק at שור תם (Ex. 21,35) which are purely קנס, penalties and not restitution (see B.K. 84b). A regulation which is usually referred to as the canon: אין דנין דיני קנסות בבבל. Nevertheless on the basis of our text, such courts could intervene and force the removal of any property which was a threat to safety.

כי יפל הנפל ממנו, from the fact that the unfortunate one who falls is called here, already before he has fallen, הנפל, “the falling one”, the Gemora in Sabbath 32,a, teaches the important lesson: ראוי זה ליפול מו׳ ימי בראשית שהרי לא נפל והכתוב קראו נופל אלא שמגלגלין זכות ע״י זכאי וחובה על ידי חײב “the unfortunate one had been destined to have such a fatal accident long ago, for the Torah calls him “the falling one” before he falls. But deserved good fortune is brought about to good people through good people, and the deserved misfortune to guilty ones through guilty ones. In all weal and woe that happens to men through men two factors are active together, the fate which God has destined for the one affected whether it is good fortune or the reverse, reward or punishment, and the free-willed good or bad deed of the people who bring it about. In accordance with our deserts God hands us over, or leaves us over, to the good or bad acts of our fellow-men on earth; and this too agrees with the great saying of the wisdom of Solomon: רב מחולל כל ושוכר כסיל ושוכר עוברים “the Great Master of the world brings everything to fruition and hires fools in His Service, and hires transgressors in His Service”. (Prov. 26,10). This is probably the same Truth which is expressed in the words והאלקים אנה לידו (Ex. 21,13), and which the Gemora in Makkoth 10b, finds expressed in the מרשעים יצא רשע ”משל הקדמוני״ (Sam. I. 14).

V. 9. לא תזרע כרמך. Just as at the founding of your home, you are at once not to think only of yourself, but at the same time of the care you must take of avoiding any danger to the well-being of your neighbour, so also when you plant your fields for your food and enjoyment at once remind yourself of the World’s Lawgiver Who reveals Himself in the whole organic world; Who, by His למינו-law, knows how to develop the existence and lives of all the various species and kinds of creatures in the prescribed paths of their exclusive differences, and you too, by His Torah has made you in duty bound to the calling of Jewish human beings, so that also with your efforts for food and enjoyment you are to remain a Man and a Jew. These כלאים-laws have already been given for animal breeding, orchard and field cultivation in Levit. 19,19, and there we have fully considered them, as well as incidentally at the בשר בחלב law (Ex. 23,18) which is related to them. Here, these laws are supplemented by the כלאי כרם law, a law which rests on the fundamental depths of the sanctification of the Jewish Land as the soil of God’s Torah, and on that account would offer itself, above all to be incorporated in this compendium for those about to move into that Land. We remarked already in Leviticus how the mere sight of this land cultivated under the regime of the כלאים laws must have called out to every passer-by “Put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the ground whereon thou standest is holy unto the Law of God. Man, whom this soil feeds and bears, must pay respect to the laws of God!”

Now there is one plant that one could imagine should not be allowed at all to be planted and cultivated on this soil of the Divine laws of morality because the enjoyment of the product which matures on this plant entices men, more than anything else, to demoralising excesses and lapses unworthy of human beings. On the soil dedicated to God’s laws of morality, the vine, one could well think, should find no place. But the Torah not only allows wine-growing in the Jewish Land, but uses the enjoyment of wine to be symbolic in offerings of—as it is used in inspired songs of praise of God to be expressive of—the loftiest feelings of joy before God: בקדש הסך נסך שכר לה׳! Hence the Torah surrounds the cultivation of the vine in the Jewish Land with a still greater increase of כלאים laws, only allows the vine to be cultivated under quite special conditions of keeping afar any possible mixture of species, and if any vine should have been planted without due respect to the laws, all its seed and produce has to be completely destroyed. All this expresses the great thought so characteristic of Jewish Law:- God’s Torah not only allows but sanctifies, even the highest material enjoyment of food, provided the eater keeps his enjoyment controlled by its laws, and does not exceed the limits drawn by the Torah for the Jewish “species” of human beings. Wine obtained from vines planted under the regime of God’s Law of “species” even comes into the Sanctuary to be used as offerings to symbolise the loftiest joys of life. Wine obtained from vines planted otherwise has no justified place even in ordinary life, and burning all such plants expresses the denial of enjoying food obtained without having regard to the Torah, and just thereby the sanctity of enjoying “morally” pure food. That is why this burning of כלאי כרם is called תקדש in our text. It is a negative expression of the positive holiness of material enjoyment which the Torah ascribes to it. (ואין זה מה שאמר רב אשי פן יהיה קדש ודחי הש״ס קידושין נ״ו ,ב׳ ע״ש). Compare the burning of פסולי המוקדשים which had to be done in the במקום קדש ,עזרה and in the case of פגול ונותר has even to be done in the daytime.

We have already remarked in Leviticus on these laws, that by the כלאים laws respecting breeding of animals and propping trees a real interference with the Law of Species is countered, but that at כלאי זרעים the כלאים law only effects a mental acknowledgment of the Great World Lawgiver Who reveals Himself in the Law of Species which is so wonderfully kept even in the world of vegetable life, as only a mere visible separation of the various kinds is demanded which would not effect a real separation of the species, just planting the seeds at a distance apart that leaves each kind room to draw its nourishment from the soil; שיעור יניקה, or alternatively it is sufficient if some visible division of the different kinds is effected above ground: מראית העין. For כלאי כרם too, similar laws hold good. The law differentiates between single vines גפן יחידית and groups of vines which are considered as כרם, as a vineyard; five vines which are planted in two rows of two in each, and the fifth standing in front in the middle line already constitutes כרם. A distance of six handbreadths is sufficient to be kept clear in the case of single vines, whereas four cubits on all sides is demanded for a vineyard the space required for working a vineyard, עבודת הכרם. But if there was a dividing wall, ten handbreadths high between the vineyard and the other plantations, one may plant close to the wall on either side. (See Kilaiyim IV).

פן תקדש המלאה. The use of the term קדוש for the איסור הנאה (the prohibition to have any use at all I.L.) of כלאי כרם, has already been explained by us. From here the legal term for this איסור הנאה effect has remained in the Halacha:- קידוש. Thus e.g. הנוטע ירק בכרם או מקײם הרי זה מקדש ארבעים וחמשה גפנים אימתי שהיו נטועות על ארבע ארבע או על חמש חמש היו נטועות על שש שש או על שבע שבע הרי זה מקדש ט״ז אמה לכל רוח עגולות ולא מרובעות (Kilaiyim 5,5). Tradition teaches that this term “תקדש״, “become holy”, or “fallen to the Sanctuary” of the כלאי כרם makes them אסור בהנאה so that they have to be burnt, and the Gemora in Kiddushin 56b, finds this able to be heard in the similarly sounding words פן תקדש, פן תוקד אש, and moreover this alliteration is there explained not to be superfluous as the concept קדש does not exclude the possibility of redemption (but כלאי כרם cannot be redeemed I.L.) כלאי כרם belongs to those איסורי הנאה which have to be destroyed, they have to be burnt. There are others whose use has to be prevented by burying them, and the law applies:- כל הנקברין לא ישרפו וכל הנשרפין לא יקברו הנשרפין אפרן מותר ונקברין אפרן אסור (Temura 34,a — see תוספות there) (“All that has to be buried may not be burnt, and what has to be burnt may not be buried, the ashes of what has to be burnt may be used, but the ashes of what has to be buried may not be used I.L.).

המלאה .פן תקדש המלאה הזרע וגו׳: the fullness, that which grows in the vineyard after sowing and planting, and הזרע אשר תזרע, by the accent this is in apposition to המלאה, what is sown and planted. Hence the sentence in Chulin 116,a תרי קראי כתיבי כתיב פן תקדש המלאה וכתיב הזרע אשר תזרע הא כיצד זרוע מעיקרא בהשרשה זרוע ובא הוסיף אין לא הוסיף לא. “the juxtaposition teaches that sometimes what is actually sown, sometimes the additional growths that grow from the original growth and all that grows up from what was sown and planted, all becomes אסור בהנאה. If something was sown wrongfully, sown באיסור e.g. the vine and other seeds or plants put into the ground together, then all is אסור as soon as it takes root. But if something was planted or sown בהיתר, and afterwards other plants or seeds are wrongfully planted there, זרוע ובא, then what was originally planted or sown remains allowed to be used and only the additional subsequent growth is prohibited, and moreover only if such additional growth is at least a two-hundredth part of the existing permitted growth, הוסיף מאתים אין לא הוסיף לא. So that sometimes the המלאה, sometimes also הזרע אשר תזרע is prohibited. If then the text goes on to say ותבואת הכרם, the המלאה הזרע וגו׳ would refer only to the other seeds which bring כלאים into the vineyard, and the sense of the whole sentence would be: so that the further additional growth or even the seed which you sow and the produce of the vineyard do not fall into the state of “prohibited sanctity” (i.e. prohibition to be used in any way I.L.).

כלאי כרם are, similarly to מן התורה ,כלאי זרעים only prohibited in Israel, the Land of the Torah. מדרבנן the prohibition applies everywhere but only in the strict sense i.e. if two seeds of a different kind are sown together with a vine. חטה שעורה וחרצן במפולת יד (Kiddushin 39a).

V. 10. לא תחרש. Just as when you build your house, you have to remember your duty to your neighbour, when working your vineyard, the general law of morals, so when you yoke the animals, over whom you have the mastery, into your service, you are to admonish yourself concerning the Mastery of the One Whose Law of Species meets you also in animal life, under Whose mastery you also are to stand just as the animal does. By your doing away with your power to exercise your own will in your work, and not yoking together for your service animals which God has kept apart, you remind yourself that for your own working life too, His למינו Call comes, and in all your work and doings you are to prove yourself “a Jew” (for that is the מין to which you have been allotted I.L.) in service of your Master.

שור וחמור of our text are only given as examples, being those usually at hand, דבר הכתוב בהווה, just as at the prohibition of work on Sabbath (Deut. 5,14) to שור וחמור the words וכל בהמתך are added, so we deduce that wherever שור וחמור occur in the Torah they are only meant to be examples, יליף שור שור משבת. Equally so חרישה is only an example of work carried out with the aid of animals, and driving carts, waggons etc. with animals of different species is equally prohibited. And even driving such animals along by voice alone, הנהגה בקול, comes under this prohibition. (Kilaiyim 8,2,3; B.M. 90b).

V. 11. לא תלבש שעטנז. Finally, let your garments in the whole appearance in which your human character appears be an admonition for the difference in the higher living animal and lower vegetable urges which are both in your nature, not to give the former over to the latter but rather the latter to the former, and both under God, as the fundamental condition of the calling to which God has directed you, and to not clothe yourself in “Shaatneis”, in a “muddled garment” in which animal material, wool, and vegetable material, linen are joined together. We have already considered this law in detail at length on Levit. 19,18 (refer to it there, pages 533-537). The two places in the Torah, as we have already pointed out there, mutually supplement each other. Here שעטנז is given in detail as referring to עמר ופשתים (wool and linen I.L.) and there the concept לבישה is extended to העלאה (see there).

V. 12. גדלים תעשה לך. The three preceding laws have interwoven the thought of our specific Jewish calling into all our doings and clothes by observing the negative command of כלאים and especially the last one of abstaining from having any prohibited mixtures of materials in the clothes we wear. Now the Torah adds to that the positive command of Tzitzis, by which, wherever we go, we are positively to keep our eyes and thoughts directed to God and our specifically Jewish calling. If, by the שעטנז-law, every thread of our clothing says to us “Be no animal”, the Tzitzis-command on our garment says to us “Be a Man and a Jew!” This Tzitzis command is given fully in Numb. 15,37-41, and our verse only brings a short supplement to it. There, in Numbers, we have considered this command, including our supplementary text, at length, and here will limit ourselves to merely stressing how characteristically this supplement has been kept back for this compendium, and how it fits with the purpose of this compendium. Of all the factors which we thought we recognised there, the two-fold meaning of human clothes, viz. בגד, as covering for the purposes of veiling and כסות as covering for the purposes of protection, and also the two parts of the Tzitzis, the ענף, the freely hanging ends of the threads, symbolising the free development of all the elements of human nature, the sensual, the human and the divine, and the גדיל, these firmly bound threads constricted into a cord, symbolising the submission of all that is sensual to all that is human and Jewish; and finally the unlimited application of the Tzitzis-admonition to time: לדרתם and place: ארבע כנפות, of this, just the factors גדיל ,כסות and ארבע כנפות have been reserved for this compendium for the impending decentralisation. For it is just these three factors which say to every Jew moving into the Land: however far away from the centre of the Sanctuary of the Torah and its immediate influence, to the east or west, to the north or south, your settling may bring you, whatever struggles against Nature and its elementary forces that settlement may entail at any time, everywhere and always be your own watchman, everywhere gird up your bodily sensuality in the strong bond of what is divine and human and Jewish in yourself, everywhere take the admonition of the תכלת thread, your priestly Jewish human calling, to make the divine human element in you firmly and strongly bind the sensuality which is part of the nature with which you have been created and never tear asunder the knots which bind you as a Man to God and the Sanctuary of His Torah.

This placing of the law of Shaatnis in juxtoposition to that of Tzitzis—the concepts of which we believe also belong together—סמוכים—is taken in Yebamoth 4 to be an indication of the legal fact that the observation of the negative law of the prohibition of Shaatnis has to be relegated to the background before the fulfilment of the positive command of Tzitzis. The woollen threads of the תכלת prescribed in Numb. 15,38, have to be used whether the garment is a woollen or a linen one, as indeed the term בגד as a rule is applied only to garments of either linen or wool. This היתר כלאים בציצית is a classical example of the sentence that עשה דוחה לא תעשה, that the Torah allows a prohibition to be disregarded for the fulfilment of a positive command, or, as this canon is expressed in Sabbath 133,a:- כל מקום שאתה מוצא עשה ולא תעשה אם אתה יכול לקײם שניהם מוטב ואם לאו יבא עשה וידחה לא תעשה “where a command and a prohibition clash, if by any means the command can be fulfilled without transgressing the prohibition, then both must be respected, but if the command cannot possibly be fulfilled without transgressing the prohibition, the prohibition must be neglected”. But the application of this rule is subject to essential further conditions, thus (ibid 132,b), בעידנא, the simultaneousness, that בעידנא דמעקר לאו קא מוקים עשה, the fulfilment of the command is accomplished at the moment the prohibition is transgressed as e.g. כלאים בציצית or מילה בצרעת, but where the command is not yet fulfilled when the prohibition is transgressed as e.g. to remove a נגע from a priest so that he can perform an עבודה would not be allowed, where בעידנא דמתעקר לאו לא קא מוקים עשה, then the prohibition may not be transgressed and the fulfilment of the command must be neglected (but see also תוספות on Pessachim 59a, ד״ה אתי עשה).

Just as at Tzitzis the law of shaatnes has to be abrogated, so does it have to be at the priestly vestments, and we have already considered both cases on Levit. 19,19 at end of notes (refer to it there).

V. 13. כי יקח איש אשה. The contents of the previous group of laws (verses 5-12) contained in the one thought, that of bringing home to themselves and to everybody the high and fundamental importance of the activities of the two sexes, divided between husband and wife, the common task of human homes, and the high importance of the female sex is placed foremost in them. These laws, more of a typical nature, form the introduction to the group of laws which now follows, which deals with the concrete actual building up of homes and society on the foundations expressed by those introductory laws. In them too, the importance of the female sex is again in the foreground.

Already on Ex. 21,7, we have noted the three stages, the ages of בוגרת ,נערה ,קטנה in which a woman attains her sexual maturity. Of these נערה is the stage of the arrival of maturity which however only attains complete independence at בוגרת. We have also already indicated (ibid XXII,11) that the Jewish institution of marriage is accomplished in two separate stages, (קידושין) אירוסין and נשואין (see Ch. 24,1). (קידושין) אירוסין forms the basis of Jewish marriage. It is the personal adoption of a woman to be a wife. Although sexual approach is not yet permitted and the ארוסה does not yet belong to the home of the husband, the personal matrimonial bond is concluded and any sexual intercourse with another man is adultery (cf. the relationship of ארס to ערס in Numb. on XV,20). Jewish Law, the Torah looks with specially serious consideration on נערות, that first stage of a maiden’s sexual maturity, and with an equally specially serious consideration on אירוסין, on that first stage of the matrimonial bond attained by purely personal acceptance. The respect which has to be shown to the sanctity of this stage proves the holiness and inviolability of a purely mental and spiritual expression of will on which the whole institution of marriage rests, yea, which altogether makes marriage into marriage. Hence the Torah knows no sexually higher feminine being than נערה בתולה מאורשה לאיש, a virgin, having already reached and still being in the first stage of sexual maturity and still only bound to a man by the simple act of personal acceptance. It is with the problem of the aspersion of a husband of such a virgin against her virgin unsullied innocence that the group of laws which follow here begins. Thereby it demonstrates the Truth:- the nation has no greater treasure than the virgin purity of its daughters, the home no higher pride than the virgin purity of its children; any attack against the innocence of its virgins is an attack on the honour of the house that brought them up, as well as on the nation whose name they bear.
כי יקח is the act of קידושין mentioned above.

V. 14. ושם לה עלילת דברים. From verses 20 and 21 it is evident that, on the part of the man, a legal charge has been preferred, and indeed such an accusation, which had it been found to be verified, would have resulted in a verdict of death by סקילה. He must have accused her of a definite crime on which a death-sentence of סקילה would have to be passed. But this is none other than an accusation of adultery during the period in which she was in the ארוסה stage as discussed in verses 23 and 24 and is further qualified in v. 21 by לזנות בית אביה. But, according to Ch. 19,15 et seq. it is established that a charge can only be made on the basis of the declaration of two witnesses who had given due warning to the accused at the moment of the crime being about to be committed, and pointing out the nature of the legal penalty it would entail עדים והתראה. This bringing a legal charge to the court is called here:- שם לה עלילת דברים. We know the term דברים for a legal charge from Ex. 24,14. Also from דבר as used above in Ch. XIX. 15. עלילה from עלל (from which we get עולל, the child looked on as being still in the developing state, and עול, the means of yoking forces for a continuous progressive activity, a yoke) does not designate a single action, but a series of deeds striving towards a goal, hence also used predominantly to describe God’s ways to accomplish His ultimate purpose. עלילת דברים accordingly designate the proceedings belonging to establishing a charge, the appearance of witnesses and their making their declarations before the court. We have accordingly translated it by “the process of a charge”. That is what שם לה what he has arranged for her, he has brought the witnesses before the court. לא אמר לעדים בואו והעידוני והן באו מאליהן הוא אינו לוקה ואינו נותן מאה סלעים (Kethuboth 46a) (If he did not say to the witnesses “come and testify for me”, but they came by themselves he does not get מלקות and does not have to pay the fifty selahs).). According to one way of taking it (ibid) ושם even implies hiring witnesses.

V. 15-17. ולקח אבי הנערה ואמה.
