Placing it together with לענה (bitter wormwood I.L.) points to its noxious bitter taste whereas ראש פתנים אכזר makes one presume a fatal material. Perhaps it designates a kind of poison which can come from both from vegetable and animal sources.

V. 18. שרירות .והיה וגו׳: the root שרר occurs in לא כרת שרך (Ezek. 16,4)! שררך אגן הסהר (Song of Songs 7,3) with the meaning of navel, similarly in ואונו בשרירי בטנו (Job. 40,16) in which latter quotation it designates the place where the strength of the animal is concentrated. In Rabbinic Hebrew שריר expresses firmness, legality הכל שריר וקים. It is phonetically related to צרר, to bind together, to press together which also corresponds to the concept compactness, firmness. Taken in the sense of the Rabbinic שרירות לב ,שריר וקים would be the confirmation, authorisation of his own heart. He only goes in the paths, which are ratified, not by God, but by his own heart, which his heart recognises as ספות—.שריר וקים from ספה, the root of מספא, fodder, related to שבע ,סבא etc., in Rabbinic Hebrew the quite common expression for “giving to eat”. אספי ליה כתורא (Baba Bathra 21a), דלא ליספו להו בידים (Yebamoth 1114a etc.). The meaning would be; he thinks to himself that the pronouncement of blessing and curse have only in mind that which is judged to be the behaviour of the majority, and if the nation had deserved and obtained the promised blessing, then he imagines, individuals, even if they do not deserve it, cannot be debarred from participating in the general prosperity. In the same way as when rain fall on a field, the weeds, which really should not be watered, do participate in the fructifying rain. That which is watered for its goodness is the רוה, the weeds which really should remain thirsty is the צמאה. Compare phrases like והיית כגן רוה (“and thou shalt be like a well-watered garden”, I.L.) (Is. 68,11), אצק מים על צמא (ibid. XLIV,3) הנה בעדי ישתו ואתם תצמאו (ibid. LXV,13). Here too then, the relationship with ספח which we already mentioned on Gen. 18,24 would be apparent, inasmuch as here, too, the unworthy would be included with the worthy, just as there the reverse is suggested.

V. 19. לא יאבה וגו׳. God will not accede to his request, not respond to his expectations. (See Gen. 24,5.) אלה .כל האלה has by no menas in the first instance the meaning of a curse but an oath. והיית נקי מאלתי (Gen. 24,41); תהי נא אלה בינותינו (ibid.) XXVI,28); ושמעה קול אלה (Levit. 5,1). It is—just as the idea lies in השבע (see on Ex. 20,7)—placing oneself under God and His jurisdiction in the event of what you swear to being untrue or if you fail to do that which you swear to do. Hence also נשא שם, and אלה is the root of the conception of God. But as nevertheless the Power of God called on in an oath is primarily to show itself in the punishing ruin of the one who makes a false oath, the term designates specially this ruin-bringing aspect of an oath, the curse which the one who swears a false oath bring down upon himself. Thus in Numb. 5,21 in the case of סוטה where אלה is mentioned next to שבועה.

V. 20. והבדילו וגו׳. God’s quite special judgment will fall upon him, which, by no means only watches over and judges masses but in quite individual השגחה פרטית watches every single person in what he personally does and refrains from doing.

V. 21-27. ואמר הדור וגו׳. With verse 20, the facts and explanations—which were interpolated to give the right estimation of, and the right way of taking the proclamation of the alternatives of blessing or curse in the future—come to an end, and this verse 21 now continues the announcement of the future which was interrupted by V.69 of the previous chapter. ואמר הדור וגו׳ follows immediately after V. 68 of the previous chapter. Both for your descendants as well as for the world in general, the catastrophe which is depicted as overtaking you and your land, and the lasting condition of suffering for both, taken in conjunction with the announcement made so very long ago and written down in this book, will serve for the most convincing, notorious, world-historic proof of God and His Rule (cf. above V. 46).
אשר יקומו מאחריכם; not אחריכם who come immediately after you, but מאחריכם also those generations which arise from those that come after you, accordingly, also the most distant generations.
אלהים אשר לא ידעתם, of whom they have not learnt to know by experience as they have learnt to know God, the God of their fathers. ולא חלק להם: see on Ch. 4,19.

הכתובה בספר הזה, the Land, the People and this book, those are the three factors belonging together, mutually explaining each other, which to this day are the everlasting testimonials of God in the eyes of the world.

“וישלכם״, that is the word which proclaims itself with a large ל for them and for the consciousness of the nations over the dispersion of this nation. Wherever they are that is not their original homeland, and whereever they may find themselves, they are not there just by chance. The God of the history of men and nations has “cast” them there. וישלכם, as a “great Lamed”, as a great “instructive” sign for the history of the development of the nations, perhaps also with the ל overshadowing the ש to be taken as ויליכם: He “led” them there, in being scattered out of their own land, there too, in the dispersion, to serve amongst the nations His Purposes for mankind.

V. 28. הנסתרת. Conditions and the state of affairs looking far ahead, looking into the future of the most distant times, are connected with the meaning of Israel in exile proving the existence of God and His Ruling of the world. But these, as נסתרת, we can leave to God, the future is hidden and belongs to Him. But what is revealed to us, what always and for all times is clear and known, and undoubted, that is:- that whatever the future has in store for us, whatever times we may have to live through, our task and that of our children remains for ever unchanged and that is, in exile or in our own land, faithfully to fulfil the Torah of God.

In Sanhedrin 43b, the נסתרת and נגלות are taken to refer to the responsibility which lies on the state and on every individual Jew for the Torah being kept. According to the solidarity imposed by the covenant of the Torah and which was renewed by the לנו ולבנינו עד עולם לעשות וגו׳ which made each individual responsible not only to keep the Torah himself but for the Torah to be made a reality in Jewry. This duty of solidarity, ערבות, that כל ישראל ערבין זה לזה, is here limited to the נגלות, to what is openly done or omitted to be done in public, the responsibility for which is shared by every one whose influence might have prevented the sin of commission or omission being done, and he had not tried to use such influence, שהיה בידן למחות ולא מחו. But נסתרות, sins against the Torah committed in secret remain לה׳ אלקינו, solely to God and His Government. Moreover according to the explanations which are deduced there from the eleven limiting dots over the letters of לנו ולבנינו and the ע of עד, corresponding to the eleven letters of the preceding ה׳ אלקינו, they tell us that even for the נגלות, the solidarity only begins after the crossing of the Jordan and hearing the proclamation of the covenant on Gerisim and Ebal (especially verse 26 in Ch. XXVII I.L.). But until then the נגלות also, like the נסחרות, were לה׳ אלקינו (see תוספות there ד״ה א״ל ר׳ נחמי׳, according to Rashi’s way of taking it). According to that, all belonging morally together which in the solidarity of all for all obtains such serious consequences, only gets its real actuality and importance with the settling down in the land, and the isolation which then began. And the motive for it could well be found in the consideration that it was just only in the ordinary civic life of business intercourse brought about by the normal efforts for livelihood and possessions that individual personalities get that importance which is necessary for them to have moral influence.
V. 1 & 2. והיה וגו׳. Now follows the great goal to which the whole sequence of the dark centuries of Jewish sufferings, so full of trials, will ultimately lead.

והשבת וגו׳. Above, on וידעת היום והשבת אל לבבך וגו׳ (Ch. 4,39) we believed השב אל לב to mean, to bring something back to your mind and take it to heart, if it had escaped your mind, or was about to do so. But places like the one here, and so also ולא ישב על לבו (Is. 44,19), זאת אשיב אל לבי (Lament 3,21) nevertheless seem to speak for another way of taking it. It seems, that noticing events which occur round about us, is considered as an activity of the mind used in an outward direction, from inwards outwards. But the working of the mind in then bringing such matters back to itself for judging consideration, is regarded as an activity of the brain working in the opposite direction from outwards inwards to bring back to itself what it has observed in the outer world, for which השב אל לב is the most suitable expression. A similar idea lies at the base of the expression “reflection” (thoughtful continued consideration, the action of the mind by which it takes cognizance of its own operations I.L.). In the quotation above from Lament. חסדי ה׳ כי לא תמנו etc. are facts which have occurred in his experience which he brings back to his mind to deduce consolation from them. Also the וידעת וגו׳ והשבת גו׳ quoted above, is the exhortation to direct your mind to the historical events which have just been recalled to you, (וידעת) and then bring them back before the forum of your considering and judging mind and make your decisions accordingly (והשבת אל לבבך).

So here too: Only after all that has been said in this Book of the Law thousands of years beforehand concerning the state of blessing and curse which will form your future, will have actually occurred, will you then bring back to your mind the sum of the thousands of years of experience of your external fate and deliberate on it, and the result will be that you will come back with your whole heart and soul to your God and His Torah; and will win your children to equal faithfulness to Him and His Torah. For your experience of these thousands of years will finally have convinced you for ever of your “God” and the “Divine origin of your Torah”.

בכל הגוים וגו׳, amongst all the nations whither God has scattered you, you remain, in spite of all changes, right to the end of the thousands of years the “People of God with His Torah in your hands”, and that makes possible, and together with the fulfilment of your fate, brings about your ultimate conversion, uplift and return for ever to God and His Torah.

ושבת עד וגו׳, not ושבת אל which could mean just a return, “towards” God and obedience to His dictates, but “right up to”, you will not remain half way—make compromises—but your return will be so complete that you will come again right up to God.

V. 3. ושב וגו׳. Sentences like this ושב וגו׳ את שבותך, and so frequently occurring in the Prophets and Psalms בשוב ה׳ שבות עמו (Ps. 14,7), ושבתי את שבות עמי (Jer. 30,3) שב שבות אהלי יעקב (Jer. 30,18) ושבתי את שבות מצרים (Ezek. 29,14) etc. make it seem that in such places שוב is used in a transitive sense and has the meaning of השיב “to bring back”. But apart from the fact that, except for this way of taking it, there is no example of a transitive meaning of the root שוב, even our passage here itself would speak against such a way of taking it. Clearly ושב וגו׳ and ורחמך are acts which precede the leading of Israel back to their homeland, the ושב וקבצך etc. Now here, and in most places where it is construed with ושב את שבותך ,את could well mean: God comes back with your exiles i.e. in the same degree and as soon as you go back to God in your exile, He also comes back to you. But places where it is construed without את, as בשוב ה׳ שבות עמו etc. there would be no explanation. So we rather believe that we can think of the quite normal way in which other intransitive verbs, and quite especially those that designate a movement, have the aim of the movement in the accusative after them. This we find also with שוב:- לך שוב מצרים (Ex. 4,19), שובה ה׳ רבבות אלפי ישראל (Numb. 10,36) בשוב ה׳ ציון (Is. 52,8), ויואב שב ירושלים (Sam. II, XX,22). Or take יצא:- וצא השדה (Gen. 27,3), צאו ההר (Nehem. 8,15), בצאתי שער (Job. 29,7). Also with את where then the accusative designates the object which one has in mind when leaving:- יצאו את העיר (Gen. 44,4), כצאתי את העיר (Ex. 9,26); and so also בני יצאוני ואינם (Jer. 10,20). Also the verb נגש:- ויגש דוד את העם (Sam. I, XXX,21). Also הלך with את (Judges 19,18).

It is most striking in the root בוא with the pronominal suffix of the accusative: אל תבואני רגל גאוה (Ps. 36,12) and many many other places e.g. Job, XX,22, Ps. 44,18; Is. 28,15, Prov. 28,22, Job. 15,21, Ezek. 32,11, Prov. 10,24; ibid XI,27, Ps. 35,8, Ps. 109,11. In all these places the suffix in no ways stands for the dative or for the preposition אל by which a mere reaching someone would be expressed, but it is a pure accusative and designates the object aimed at and achieved. There are very many more examples of the accusative being used with intransitive verbs (such as ויבך אותו אביו etc. etc. etc.) all of which bear the same explanation. Also the construing of ירא with את. For ירא is really intransitive. In all these cases the accusative designates the object which forms the aim, cause or relationship of an external or internal activity; and indeed this relationship is expressed as being of a much more intimate nature than would be expressed if it was construed with a preposition (e.g. ויבך אותו אביו is much more intense than ויבך עליו אביו would be, and so all of them I.L.).

Ganz in derselben Weise, glauben wir, sei die Konstruktion שוב mit dem Akkusativ aufzufassen, sei es mit Suffixum wie שובנו אלקי ישענו (Ps. 85, 5), mit את wie in unserer Stelle, oder ohne בשוב ד׳ שבות עמו :את u.s. Der Akkusativ bezeichnet den Gegenstand, der mit der rückkehrenden Bewegung aufgesucht wird, der das Motiv und Ziel derselben bildet, und drückt diese Konstruktion mit dem Akkusativ eine viel innigere Beziehung des Zurückkehrenden und seiner Bewegung zu dem mit derselben aufzusuchenden Gegenstande aus, als die Konstruktion mit ושב אל שבותך ,שוב אלינו ,אל ausdrücken würde. Dieses letztere könnte auch eine zufällige, gelegentliche, widerwillige und gezwungene Rückkehr sein, wie die Rückkehr der Taube zu Noach (Bereschit 8, 9) שוב את macht aber die Wiedervereinigung mit dem aufzusuchenden Gegenstand zum Motiv und Ziel der Rückkehr und lässt vielmehr die vorangegangene Entfernung als das Unfreiwillige erscheinen. Es steht dem nicht entgegen, daß der Ausdruck auch bei der Restauration anderer Völker: Moab, Sedom, Mizrajim (Jirm. 48, 46 sowie Ezechiel 16, 53 und 29. 14) vorkommt; denn auch dort ist das Aufblühen der Nation auf dem Boden des Heimatlandes die eigentliche Absicht der göttlichen Waltung, und war der zeitweilige Untergang eine nur infolge nationaler Ausschreitung mit Schmerz verhängte Katastrophe, wie dies namentlich bei Moab (daselbst) zum Ausdruck kommt.

So that what it says here is: a time will come when the hard times through which you have passed, and the Book explaining them which you have in your hands, will have had their effect on you, and in exile amongst all the nations, you will at last turn back to God and His Torah with all your heart and all your soul. And this return to Him will result in His turning to you again to “look you up” in exile, to be near to you as in former times.

ורחמך, and take you up again with His רחמים (His Parental Love I.L.) in the never-failing way of “God’s Goodness” (Ex. 34,7) (p. 647), as the result of His creative historic rule of the world, as פעלו בקרב שנים, as His accomplishment of “His work in the midst of the ages” (Habak. 3,2), as נצר מטעיו מעשה ידיו (Is. 60,21) as the long guarded flower-bed of His repeated plantings, as the work of His Hands that now at last has matured for its ultimate glory of flowering.
ושב וקבצך וגו׳, and gathers thee up again out of all the nations amongst whom He had scattered thee to be again a united nation.

V. 4. נדח ,נדחך (a stronger form of נדה, to place at a distance) to banish. וקבצך, He gathers you all together, even the most isolated, driven to the utmost distance of your dispersion, and יקחך, takes you again to your original destiny of being a nation exclusively His, as He declared His Purpose at your first redemption and being chosen: ולקחתי אתכם לי לעם (“And I took you to be a People unto Me” I.L. Ex. 6,7).

V. 5. והביאך וגו׳, and bring you home to the land which you have twice had in your possession, once through your forefathers under Moses and Joshuah, which was lost under the Babylonian conquest, and then as the people of exile under Ezra, but now never to be lost again. (See on Numb. 15,18).

V. 6. ומל וגו׳, and by everything that you have lived through in the past times of trial, and by what God now lets you live through in this final גאולה, at last every ערלה, everything “intractable” (see Gen. 17,10, p. 300) will be removed from your heart and from your childrens’ hearts for ever, so that henceforth “God” and “your life” are identical for you, and just as your breath is an indispensable part of your life, so will the consciousness of God, the consciousness and feeling of the nearness of His bond of the Torah to you, and your nearness to it will be so much a part of your “living”, that with the whole of your heart and soul, you will be absorbed in love of Him.

V. 7. ונתן וגו׳, a similar expression to ונתת את הברכה וגו׳ (Ch. 11,29). Thenceforth the same oath will apply to the nations with their love and their hate. That which God promised Abraham at his first entry into the history of the world will be fulfilled (Gen. 12,2; refer to it).

V. 8-10. ואתה תשוב וגו׳. Above in V.2 the return to faithfully carrying out God’s Torah as far as it can be done in exile is foretold. But now here follows the ultimate complete realisation of the whole of the commands of the Torah (את כל מצותי I.L.) to which the promise of the most complete blessing in every direction is promised, and then will become a reality, and without having to fear the repetition of the danger of back-sliding which prosperity had always brought in the past (see on Ch. 31,20).

V. 10. הכתובה refers to קול. The whole ספר התורה הזה is nothing other than the Voice of God fixed in writing. God’s Voice speaks to us out of it in all ages, and teaches us the “tasks and limits” מצותיו וחקותיו for our whole life on earth, in the observation of which our return to “God” our God with all our heart and soul will take place. This keeping of the Torah—not the extraordinary blessing attached to it—will be the exclusive aim of our whole existence, that is why just this Torah of God as a complete reality is again repeated here at the end. (קול to which הכתובה can solely refer is otherwise generally masculine. But it does also occur in the feminine in Kings 1,1,41 and XIV,6, as well as in Jer. 10,22). (According to the normal way of construing).

But with these clear and unambiguous sentences (1-10) the unshatterable granite base is laid down on which, still to-day and for all future time, Judaism rests. There clear and in no ambiguous terms is the קבוץ גליות proclaimed, the regathering out of the dispersion to the return of us all to the Promised Land which we are still awaiting, and equally clear and unambiguous, the נצחיות התורה, the unaltered lasting power of the Torah, as transmitted to us by Moses, to succeed in binding us to the observance of our duty. Only a complete return to inviolable unswerving loyalty towards this Torah in all the dispersion amongst the nations will end this dispersion, and only completely making this Torah into a reality on the soil of the land which belongs to it is the purpose of the future regathering of Jewry in it. These clear and unambiguous declarations of God, confounds everything which may be taught of the out-of-date condition of Israel and its Torah, to mislead the minds and intellect of people. Both belong, not to a decaying past but to the most living present and a future full of hope. And it is only by a clear recognition and estimation of this fact, and an unrestrained joyful giving oneself up to its conception that in every age we find what is right and pleasing to God, and the road to happiness to which we are directed by Him. הנסתרות לה׳ אלקינו והנגלות לנו ולבנינו עד עולם לעשות את כל דברי התורה הזאת (“the hidden matters we can leave to God, but what is revealed to us and our descendants is, for all time, to fulfil all the words of the Torah” I.L.) that was told us at the end of the previous chapter, to give us our bearings for the period of our exile, and the revelation of the future that awaits us which follows thereon in the commentary to it.

V. 11. כי המצוה וגו׳. In the foregoing, the fulfilling of the Divine Torah transmitted to us through Moses is pronounced as the permanent sole basis of our destiny at any time, and of all our hopes for the future, and the assurance is at the same time given that in spite of all the changes of fate it will never be lost to us or we to it, but that ultimately we will return to it, with all our heart and soul. As a reason for this confidence, the real meaning of the contents of this Torah, which has been traditionally handed down to us is pointed out as being so near and so understandable to the human intelect. לא נפלאת היא ממך, it contains no secret metaphysical references to anything beyond the grasp of ordinary human mind ולא רחוקה היא “and it is not far away from you”, to understand and keep it does not assume anything but the ordinary conditions of life of those who are in duty bound to observe it.

V. 12. לא בשמים היא: The teachings and actions which it has in view do not move in the sphere of the supernatural or the heavens, and nothing which was necessary for its being understood and accomplished remained in heaven in the Divine Revelation, that you could say: where can we find a mind superhumanly enlightened that it penetrate into the secrets of heaven for us, or bring us a new revelation from heaven, which we still lack, that will complement our present knowledge, then we could keep the Torah in accordance with the Will of God.

V. 13. ולא מעבר לים היא: And the teachings and actions which it has in view are not referring to somewhere else on earth far away from you, given for conditions other than yours, that you could say: “the Torah may be quite alright for other parts of the world where the climate and conditions of life are quite different to those here where I live, places which are oceans away, and not knowing them hinders me from even understanding these laws which I am supposed to keep; somebody must first cross the sea and study the basis of the laws on the spot, and bring us back the information that we lack so that we can learn to understand them correctly, before we keep them”.
There is nothing of all this.

V. 14. כי קרוב אליך הדבר מאד, for what the Torah is about, its contents, lie right next to you, what it is about is you yourself, and its contents concern your own life here on earth. To understand them you have only to delve down into your innermost self, and to look at your material human conditions with open eyes. And for what you require to understand beyond the mere words of the Book of Laws which has been given over to you you have not to go to heaven and not to the other side of the ocean to find, that is given to you בפיך, that you have in the tradition which is to be taught and learnt from mouth to mouth (cf. שימה בפיהם Ch. 31,19; על פי הדברים האלה (Ex. 34,27; לא ימוש ספר התורה הזה מפיך, Josh. 1,8; ודברי אשר שמתי בפיך, Is. 59,21), that you must learn, ובלבבך and to understand and grasp it with your mind and heart לעשתו to fulfil it. To “learn” with your intelligence and heart the Torah in the way of the oral tradition, for the purpose of knowing and understanding and doing its commandments, is the only way—and everywhere and at all times it lies near to everybody—to understand God’s Torah and from it to understand our eternal mission on earth.

That is why, because the subject of this Torah is our own whole life and the means of understanding it lie so near to hand, it will accompany us through all our wanderings through the ages, and after all our going astray and all our trials we shall find our way back again to everlasting faithfulness to it.

These three words “לא בשמים היא״ are the most effective means of protection and defence against the pretentious claim to supernatural enlightenment or even supporting itself on some Divine revelation to influence the Law and Teachings in Israel. Only חכמה not נבואה, only erudition, scholarship derived from the text and tradition, not some higher inspiration or prompting can lay claim to any validity regarding the teachings and keeping the commandments of the Torah since its conclusion by Moses. לא תאמרו, explains דברים רבה on our verse לא תאמרו משה אחר עומד ומביא לנו אחרת מן השמים לא נשתייר ממנה בשמים. “It is not in heaven”: you are not to say: another Moses has arisen and brings us another Teaching from heaven. Nothing of the Torah was left in heaven. And ר׳ חנינא adds היא וכל כלי אומנתה ניתנה, it was given together with all the moral traits of character demanded for its study, ענוותה צדקתה וישרותה ומתן שכרה, modesty, rightiousness, honesty, and all its promised reward. Who occupies himself with studying it in the right way obtains from it all the intellectual and moral qualities which are necessary for really truly knowing it, and these qualities grow with every step forward he advances in its knowledge. So it itself trains its disciples and bearers, and with its unreservedly being handed over to Israel guarantees by itself its everlastingly blossoming out again and again. It is, as Zacharia envisioned it, the golden candelabra, the מנורה, which bears the source of the oil and the olive tree on itself with which its lights are fed. (Zac. 4,2,3) — (See also on XVIII,15 et seq.).

V. 15. ראה וגו׳ is an epilogue directed to the generation then present. By everything which I have announced to you in the name of God in the preceding, and after all that you yourselves have experienced of God’s power of ruling the world and reliability, you must say to yourselves that your weal and your woe henceforth lie entirely in your own hands. חיים, here and in the following, does not mean merely actual physical life. It is the healthy combined unrolling of the physical, spiritual and moral personality of an individual or national life in accordance with what it was meant to be. The opposite of that is מות, death in all these aspects. טוב is the undisturbed happiness which results from such a life, and רע is the unhappiness which is the lot of מות of the death of all what one was meant to be.

V. 16. אשר אנכי וגו׳ is the alternative of blessings, the choice for which is placed before you, and explains the נתתי לפניך. I have laid life and what is good in your hands inasmuch as I have given you the commandments this day to love etc. and thereby attain life, success and prosperity. ללכת בדרכיו is the end in view of לאהבה את ה׳ א׳. You are expected to love God, and this love is to show itself by your striving for, and only for, such aims that lie in the paths pointed out to you by God, and that you only try to achieve these aims in those paths. In those paths you remain near to God, and get nearer and nearer to Him, and this being near to Him is what love seeks (see Ch. 6,5). וחיית ורבית is the וברכך ,חיים is the טוב.

V. 17 & 18. ואם יפנה וגו׳ is the antithesis, the opposite side, the disobedience which ends with complete defection, and the resulting ruin, the ואם יפנה לבבך .רע, according to Succah 46b: “but if your heart remains ‘cleared out’ of the love of God”. (Cf. Levit. on XIX,4).

V. 19. העדתי וגו׳. In the preceding announcement of blessing and curse, heaven and earth are appointed witnesses of God’s covenant with us and to represent it against us. Just as witnesses have to warn offenders against the attempted crime, and if the warning is ignored have to bring about the punishing for it, yea, in the first place are responsible for inflicting it, יד העדים תהיה בו בראשנה (Ch. 17,7), so the whole תוכחה shows how God sends the warning first by means of heaven and earth, and if no notice be taken, uses them as His instruments for the ruin of the guilty ones, even as they are the agents of His blessings when we have made ourselves deserving of them by devotion to our duty.
ובחרת בחיים למען תחיה וגו׳, not without our serious efforts, not without thought and will, not just by chance is “life” won. You must choose life if you wish to “live”.

V. 20. לאהבה וגו׳, and once again Moses summarises the conception of this “living” in loving God, which wishes for nothing else but to obey Him and in joy and sorrow, in life and death, close and intimately to remain bound to Him. This “loving God” forms our life and our happiness, כי הוא חייך וארך ימיך וגו׳. This love, finding its satisfaction in loving is expressed in Nedarim 62a, in the practical manifestation of it, thus:- עשה דברים לשם פועלם ודבר בהם לשמם אל תעשם עטרה להתגדל בם ואל תעשם קורדום לעדור בו “Do all the tasks of your life for the sake of Him Who sends them, speak about them for their own sakes, do not do them for self-aggrandizement, nor use them for a spade wherewith to dig”.

V. 1. וילך וגו׳. With the proclamation of the blessing and curse and the epilogue following it, that which Moses had to tell the people in the name of God had come to an end. He could consider his mission closed and turned to do what now remained for him to do before his departure. This was:- to say farewell to his people (verses 1-6), to present his successor to them and say a few words of encouragement to him (verses 7,8) and finally to write down the Torah up to this point (which he then thought was completed), and to hand it over to the priests and elders, with the instruction to read out of it after every seventh year, in the place of the Sanctuary of the Torah of God, at the assembly of the whole nation for the Festival. (verses 9-13).

Accordingly he did not call all the people to him as he was wont to do (by having the bugles sounded for a national assembly, as expressed by the term ויקהל I.L.) when he had to address them in the name of God, but וילך he went to the assembled people, in the simplest manner, quite in the way which characterised the most modest of men, to bid farewell to them.

V. 2. לא אוכל עוד לצאת ולבא .ויאמר וגו׳. Although it says of Moses in Ch. 34,7 that לא כהתה עינו ולא נס לחה, in spite of his hundred and twenty years his physical forces had not waned, this was a special gift from God for the time of his effectiveness. Now that this was to be concluded, he could henceforth expect only the natural state consonant to his age. So that he was perfectly justified in saying that he could not complain if he, at one hundred and twenty years of age could not reckon on having the strength to continue his public activity. וה׳ אמר אלי וגו׳. And just as in the ordinary natural course of things his strength had come to an end, the expressed Will of God had set an end to it.
לצאת ולבא is the general term used for the public efficient activity of national leadership (see on Numb. 27,17).

V. 3-5. ה׳ אלקיך וגו׳, you will not miss me, it is God not me that is really your leader and Who will also lead you in the new future that lies before you, and in my place He has appointed Joshua. How God gave you the victory over Sichon and Og, you have already experienced, and He will treat the nations in front of you in the same way. Only behave towards them entirely in the manner which I have ordered for your warfare to be conducted. (Ch. 20,10 et seq.).
V. 6. חזקו וגו׳, be firm in resistence and strong in overcoming (see Ch. 3,28). אמץ: perhaps (מצ(ה) ,מצ(א with prefixed א, to attain something for oneself.

אל תיראו ואל תערצו, see Ch. 1,29. — רפה .לא ירפך means to be weak, worn out, and לא ירפך could mean, “He will not let you become weak”. רפה is the opposite of חזק (Numb. 13,18), and the לא ירפך would come to support the demand חזקו and לא יעזבך to support the demand אמצו. But in all places where הרפה occurs with the accusative suffix it means to let something loose, to let it go, not to hold it fast any longer, i.e. not to use your power of holding something fast. Thus אחזתיו ולא ארפנו (Song of Songs 3,4); בצדקתי החזקתי ולא ארפה (Job. 27,6); אל תרפני עד בלעי רוקי (ibid VII,19). So indeed הדפו הרף as in Deut. 9,14 and Sam.I, XV,16 etc. So we think that here, too, it must have that meaning: “He will not let you go, hold you fast, not let you fall, not be wrenched away from Him. It is then equally a support for the exhortation חזקו, remain firm, do not let yourselves be overpowered for it is the Hand of God that holds you fast; if you hold faithfully on to Him, they must overpower His Hand if they want to overpower you.

V. 7. חזק ואמץ .ויקרא וגו׳, the admonishment addressed to the people חזקו ואמצו in accordance with the context referred primarily to the firmness and strength to be exercised in the fight against the inhabitants of the land. But the address חזק ואמץ to Joshua comprised his whole task as leader of the people. Thus repeatedly to Joshua (Jos. I. 6, 7, 9) רק חזק ואמץ מאד לשמר לעשות ,הלא צויתיך חזק ואמץ ,חזק ואמץ כי אתה תנחיל וגו׳ ככל התורה וגו׳ and this is explained separatingly in Berachoth 32b, חזק בחורה ואמץ במעשים טובים, remain firm in taking the knowledge of your tasks from the Torah and be strong in overcoming all obstacles in carrying them out. Firm in principles and strong in carrying them out are the first demands made on the leader.

V. 9. ויכתב משה וגו׳. Already in Ex. 24,7 and XXXIV,27 we hear that Moses had written down part of the Torah. But now, after he had written down all that followed after that and he considered the writing of the Torah finished he handed it over to the priests with the order he attached to it of reading out of it every seven years before the national assembly for the Festival. The commission for the שירה and the command to add that to the written Torah and thereby to conclude the Torah was only given to him later, v.14 et seq. — הכהנים בני לוי הנשאים. The Ark of the Covenant was ordinarily carried by the Levites of the family of Kehath (Numb. 3,31) and here also in V. 25 the Levites are called הלוים נשאי ארון וגו׳. But exceptionally on specially important occasions it was carried by the priests. Thus at the passage through the Jordan (Josh. 3,3 et. seq.), at the circumambulation of Jerico (ibid. VI,6), and at the final bringing the Ark into the Holy of Holies of the Temple built by Solomon (Kings I. 8,3; see Sota 33b). And it seems that the moment of the handing over of the first scroll of the written Torah by Moses to the priests and elders was such an occasion for which the priests had to appear with the ארון ברית ה׳, and this the more so as instructions were attached to it, the carrying out of which was to be done at a time when the Ark of the Covenant and with it this scroll written by Moses (V.26) had already a place chosen by God where it was under the care of the priests and no longer in the hands of the Levites. This would also explain the difference in the terms used. Here it says:- הכהנים בני לוי הנשאים וגו׳ to the priests “who were carrying” etc. at the moment they were carrying the Ark. But in V. 25 it calls the Levites נשאי ארון וגו׳ “the bearers of the Ark”, they were the regular carriers of it. That this occasion was not mentioned with the three others in Sota 33b, could be explained by the fact that here the appearance of the priests with the Ark was only just for the moment and was no carrying it from place to place which really belonged to the prerogative of the Levites.

V. 10. מקץ שבע שנים .ויצו וגו׳ is more precisely fixed by שנת שמטה as במועד is by חג הסכת. “At the expiration of seven years” and not seven years after now, but at the expiration of every Schmita period; “at a Moed time”, and not on Rosh Hashona Moed the first one of the eighth year, beginning the new Schmita period, but on the Moed of Succoth, and moreover בבוא כל ישראל etc. i.e. באתחלתא דמועד when the people come, i.e. at the beginning of the festival. Taken together then: במוצאי י״ט הראשון של חג בשמינית במוצאי שביעית, at the close of the 1st day of the Festival of Succoth of the eighth year following the conclusion of the seventh. (Sota 41a). These separately stressed fixed times would be what מקץ שבע שנים במועד would say: - at the end of each run of seven years, at a certain fixed time. This reading out of the Torah prescribed here is not meant to be a means of the people getting to know the Law, that, of course, should be nurtured daily in the ordinary life at home, for that it says ודברת בם בשבתך בביתך ובלכתך בדרך (Ch. 6,7) ולמדתם אתם את בניכם לדבר בם (Ch. 11,19), but it is something extraordinary which recurs from seventh year to seventh year for a quite special purpose. And moreover במועד, at a time which invites every Jewish soul to a meeting with God: שנת השמטה at every restart of a period of agriculture and business which had been interrupted by the year of relief and remission; בחג הסכות when the festival assembles the national circle all together in remembrance of the time when it was not agriculture or business, but where the miraculous grace of God provided for everybody and for wife and child under the protection of His cloud and guidance in the wilderness, and prepared and practised everybody in the right approach to the coming year of agriculture and business: בבוא כל ישראל וגו׳ when the whole People of God had responded to God’s call thither where—not God, He is to be found everywhere—where the pledge of His Presence everywhere amongst the people, where the Sanctuary of the evidence of the Divine Origin of His Torah stands, and everybody has already with his עולת ראיה, with his elevating offering appeared to be seen by the Presence of his God at the home of the Sanctuary of His Torah, there תקרא, immediately at the expiration of the first day of this “appearing before God” the nation, through its highest representative shall read out of this Torah to the whole assembled nation. So that with every entry of a period of agriculture and business, the consciousness proclaims itself ever afresh that the way to God only lies in the way of His Torah, the bond with God is the bond with His Torah, the Torah is necessary for the union of the nation and for the protection of the Nation, and the nation under whose care the evidence of the Torah rests, represents and guarantees the authenticity and Divine origin of the Torah.

את התורה הזאת, probably out of this very copy of the Torah written by the hand of Moses, given over to the priests and elders. See Baba Bathra 14b, Rashi there ד״ה ספר העזרה. This Sefer-Torah bore the name ספר עזרה from the fact, according to Rashi, that it was from it that the King read at the assembly and the High Priest on the Day of Atonement in the עזרה. According to the context there, this was the same one that was placed in the Ark next to the tablets of the Law (V.26) and one must then assume that although entering the Holy of Holies שלא לצורך עבודה was prohibited (Levit. 16,2, refer to it), this public reading out of the Torah on the seven-yearly day of הקהל must have been considered as צורך עבודה, and for this purpose entering the Holy of Holies was permitted. In any case it seems to us that, according to דברים רבה on this verse, such exceptions to the rule must be assumed. For there it says: אמר ר׳ ינאי משה כתב י״ג תורות י״ב לי״ב שבטים ואחת הניח בארון שאם יבקש לזייף דבר שיהו מוציאין אותה שבארון, Moses wrote thirteen copies of the Torah, one for each of the twelve tribes and one he had placed in the Ark so that whenever it was necessary to check a mistake in a Sefer Torah the one in the Ark was brought out for that purpose. So that access to the Ark of the Covenant must be permitted. In Baba Bathra also on 14a such a possible permission to take out the ס״ת is indicated. It is also possible that one could deduce such permission already from V.26 where the purpose of depositing the copy written by Moses is expressly given as והיה שם בך לעד. But תוספות there ד״ה שלא יהא (B.B. 14a) is of a different opinion and says that entering the ק״ק for such purposes was not allowed. It would however be quite possible that the ס״ת handed over to כהנים בני לוי of V.9. out of which, as we believe, the public reading was made was not the same one which, according to V.25 was laid down next to the Ark of the Covenant, but was the one, as quoted above, given to the tribe of Levi, whereby the aforementioned difficulty would disappear. Then the ספר עזרה referred to on B.B. 14b, mentioned above, could well be the copy of the tribe of Levi kept in the עזרה for the public readings which were given there, and from its nature לתחלתו הוא נגלל that of the similar one which was in the ארון was deduced.

In Moed Katan 18b, too, according to the version of the Jerusalmi in the Mishna, a ספר העזרה is mentioned, and Rashi explains ספר מוגה היה בעזרה שממנו היו מגיהין כל ספרי גולה. Another version there calls it ספר עזרא (Ezra’s Sefer). In any case during the time of the first Temple the copy written by Moses’ own hand kept in the עזרה could well have been used for the same purpose. So also in Jerusalmi Sanhedrin 2,4:- ומגיהין אותו מספר עזרה ע״פ ב״ד של ע״א. See on Ch. 17,18.

In the time of the kings it was the highest representative of the people, the King himself who read to the assembled nation, and, according to Sota 41a, what he read was:- from Deut. I,VI,3, from אלה הדברים עד שמע; Ch. 6,4-9, שמע, Ch. 11,13-21, והיה אם שמע; Ch. 14,22-29, XXVI,12-16; עשר תעשר and כי תכלה לעשר (both probably with an eye to the tithe-period starting again); Ch. 17,14-20, פרשת המלך; and ברכות וקללות עד שגומר כל הפרשה, probably Ch. 27,1-26 and Ch. 28,1-69.
V. 12. הקהל is one of the מצות עשה שהזמן גרמא which apply also to women (see Levit. 23,43, p. 711). וגרך אשר בשעריך see Ex. 20,10, p. 272.

למען ישמעו. Here they hear, in the most general assembly of the nation, the Divinity of the Torah and being in duty bound to it, proclaimed and guaranteed ever afresh by the nation itself through its highest representative, of the Torah which each one has in his home, however isolated and distant they may be. So that this consciousness renewed in the union of the whole nation may bring them to (למען ילמדו) למוד that the ever progressive study of the Torah becomes an enhanced demand; and together, this הקהל here and that וילמדו at home, by, in this great national union, taking God to heart as the common One leader of their actions and fate, may fortify and increase their fear of God (ויראו I.L.) towards ושמרו לעשות etc. fulfilling the whole Torah faithfully and conscientiously. This שמירה שמירה) לעשות as always consisting of learning and making גזרות I.L.) is the culminating aim of all the institutions of the Torah. Regarding the relation of women to למוד התורה see on Ch. 11,19.

V. 13. ובניהם וגו׳, the children who have not yet the understanding to be brought to the study and carrying out of the Torah by what they hear there read out of the Torah are nevertheless impressed by their parents and the great concourse of people all listening attentively to the king in the pulpit, and this working on their childish minds and feelings brings them to the fear of God. To them שמיעה למרד ויראה are not three separate factors (as with adults in V. 12. I.L.) but ישמעו ולמדו ליראה (the ו is changed to a ל I.L.) by hearing alone they learn the fear of God, but שמור ועשיה are still beyond them.

According to הא״ג ,מהרש״א on Chagiga 3a. בניהם אשר לא ידעו here are קטנים שהגיעו לחינוך, children of an age who can already be given an understanding of the Torah but are still too young to be entrusted with the duty of carrying it out, which would indeed be why here it does speak of למוד and יראה but not yet of שמירה לעשות. But the concept טף in the previous verse comprises children still in an earlier stage (infants I.L.) which is why the question could be put there in Chagiga טף למה באין to which the answer runs ליתן שכר למביאיהן. At bringing such very young children the merit lies primarily with the parents who bring them with them, and thereby gather themselves before God with their most precious pledges about His Torah to which they will later win their children, and thereby are to, and wish to, ensure the imperishableness of the Torah in Jewish circles. In מס׳ סופרים 18b. it adds to והן לקבל ,כדי ליתן שכר למביאיהן שכר, that the impression made by this great assembly of the whole nation to listen to the Torah being read was not without value for their future lives even for these tiny tots. See the commentator נחלת יעקב, ibid.

V. 14. ויאמר וגו׳. Whereas Moses considered his activities finished, and had already said his words of farewell to the people, and had already directed Joshua as being appointed by God (Numb. 27,18) to be his successor, and had already also handed over the written Torah to the priests and elders, Joshuah was still to be confirmed as being authenticated by God as Moses’ successor in a way that was visible to the whole nation. At the same time Moses was given yet the further mission to leave a שירה to the nation at his departure “a poem depicting the events of history coming from God, and God Himself within the events of history”. A poem which, added to the written Torah and handed traditionally down verbally to the people (שימה בפיהם I.L.) was to ensure Israel that its consciousness of its position and mission in the history of the world, and its special fate in consequence thereof would always lead it back to God.

הן: Your feeling was correct and what you did was quite the right thing to have done, your time to die has arrived; still, first call Joshua והתיצבו, and both of you place yourselves at My disposal. Cf. Ex. 33,21. XXXIV,2; Numb. 11,16; Ex. 2,4, and elsewhere. ואצונו. This commission to Joshua follows in V. 23. All God’s speech from V. 16 to V. 23 to Moses was said in the presence of Joshua. Compare this whole procedure with the similar appointment of the elders to be assistants to Moses. Numb. 11,16, 17, especially וירדתי ודברתי עמך שם ואצלתי מן הדוח אשר עליך ושמתי עליהם (refer to it there). — באהל מועד, there, where the Torah found its expression, and our devotion to the Torah and the protecting and blessing-giving Presence of God in our midst which is dependant on both, where accordingly, everything was expressed to which Moses’s mission had been dedicated up to now, and which now was to be given over to the further care of his successor.

V. 15. וירא ה׳—elsewhere only כבוד ה׳—probably designates the great importance of the moment. על פתח האהל, there can be some doubt whether this does not mean above the entrance, as at the entrance is usually expressed without a preposition. But nevertheless there are also examples ועל פתחינו כל מגדים (Song of Songs 7,14) לשקוד על דלתותי (Prov. 8,35) which would justify our taking it as “at” the entrance. ויעמד הענן על פתח האהל (“and the pillar of cloud stood at the entrance of the Tent”), that made all the people see that Moses and Joshua were receiving a speech from God inside the Tent. Compare Ex. 33,9 and 10.

V. 16. וקם .ויאמר וגו׳: there will be nothing secret about it, as doing something to be avoided or fight shy of. They will find it something quite justified, that they can do quite openly without any qualms of conscience. נכר .אחרי אלהי נכר הארץ: see on Gen. 35,2. They considered the gods honoured by the inhabitants of the land as belonging to the land, as such that nobody living in that land could neglect to honour if he wished to have protection and prosperity there. But in reality they are monstrosities which the Land, as the Jewish land, as the Land of the Torah should not tolerate, should keep as something foreign to it. בקרבו, as ארץ as a rule is feminine, בקרבו can only refer to נכר. He imagines that in this land to which he has come he finds himself in the midst of the regime of the local gods. Therefore he inclines himself towards these gods without at first formally breaking the bond with God to Whom he still brings offerings in the Sanctuary and also indeed still keeps prescriptions of His Torah, but at the same time serves the gods of the land on the hills. But in truth ועזבני, thereby he forsakes God. והפר את בריתי and finally he breaks his connection with the Torah to which he is bound by his covenant with God, on the fulfilment of which, before his entry into the land God had made His support and His blessing in the land dependent. (Ch. 28,69, and XXIX,8.).

V. 17 & 18. ועזבתים .וחרה וגו׳: I just leave them to themselves. והסתרתי וגו׳, and withdraw My special care of them, והיה לאכל, and then by itself it falls a prey to the other nations. Israel’s national collapse is the natural consequence of its weakness when left to itself. Israel’s historical existence and prosperity is the work of the miraculous power of God.

אין אלקי בקרבי .ואמר ביום ההוא וגו׳, cf. Ch. 7,21, לא תערץ מפניהם כי ה׳ אלקיך בקרבך אל גדול ונורא (“Be not terrified before them for God, thy God is in thy midst, a great and awesome God” I.L.). He does not say: “It is because God has forsaken me because I have done that which is evil in His Eyes”, but “it is because God is not in my midst that these misfortunes have overtaken me”. Not in his own behaviour, in God’s behaviour he finds the cause of his misfortune. God, Whom in spite of his sins he still thinks he can call “his” God, and Who had promised him protection and support against the nations, no longer keeps His promise, otherwise such sufferings would not befall him. He thinks he can blame God, and forgets to blame himself, forgets to go back to the causes why God no longer behaves to him as “his” God, forgets that

ואנכי הסתיר אסתיר פני וגו׳, forgets that God withdraws His special care at this time because of all the misdeeds that he practises על כל הרעה אשר עשה, because he has turned to heathenism כי פנה אל אלהים אחרים! He has forsaken God that is why he is foresaken by God. God is only Israel’s God as long as Israel is God’s People, as long as it places itself with all its existence and all its endeavours exclusively under God to fulfil His Will. And God’s special relation to it depends—more than with any other nation—on its special complete devotion to God in obedience and faithfulness (cf. remarks on Ex. 33,5). (The reference there to XXXI,34 should be XXXII,34). The whole accusation is wrong. God is בקרבו (in its midst I.L.) never ceases His special relation to Israel. But just because He is בקרבו no sin escapes His punishing attention, and misfortune follows sins, by which it sinks to—but not under—the moral level of the other nations. רק אתכם ידעתי מכל משפחות האדמה על כן אפקד עליכם את כל עונתיכם (Amos 3,2).

V. 19. ועתה וגו׳. And now, so that the answer to such a charge should always be at hand, so that, when troubles befall Israel and make it miss the special protective management of matters by God which it had previously enjoyed, and make it say: הלא על כי אין אלקי בקרבי מצאוני הרעות האלה “Is it not because my God is not longer in my midst that these misfortunes happen to me” that God’s answer be not lacking which will lead it back to the real cause of its troubles. For that, כתבו לכם את השירה הזאת (“write this poem for yourselves I.L.) so that this שירה could come and oppose every such charge and be the witness for God with His counter charge, למען תהיה לי השירה הזאת לעד בבני ישראל. This whole שירה is nought but the answer to the complaint arising from a time of distress, על כי אין אלקי בקרבי. (In Gen. on Ch. 9,21. Hirsch gives definitions of שיר and שירה. He says that שיר is the inspired expression of Truths which are visualised in the mind but which are not, or not yet, actually present. שירה sings of the invisible Hand of God in the events of the present, or which have actually occurred, שיר the future not yet perceptible in the present. Both speak of that which is not visible to the eye, although it is there, perhaps more true and more real than that which the actual eye takes to be true and real. I.L.).

In Nedarim 38a. the addition of the purpose of the poem given in our verse למען תהיה לי השירה הזאת לעד בבני ישראל is taken as proof that the command כתבו לכם השירה הזאת goes beyond the שירה itself and extends to the whole Torah, the closing epilogue of which is formed by the שירה. For as explained there אי שירה לבדה קאמר מאי סהדותא איכו, if the command refers only to the שירה, what sort of a witness would that be! For the שירה only ensures the consciousness in general that our weal and woe is dependent on our fulfilling the task which God has set for us, but what this task really consists of can only be found from a knowledge of the whole Torah. After all, what is said here of the שירה is also said in V. 26 of the whole written Torah: לקח ספר התורה הזה וגו׳ והיה שם בך לעד (“to take this Sefer Torah etc., and there it will serve as a witness against you” I.L.). And actually in Sanhedrin 21b, it is on the command ועתה כתבו לכם את השירה the positive command for every individual Jew to have a correct Sefer Torah written, is taught.—אעפ״י שהניחו לו אבותיו לאדם ס״ת מצוה לכתוב משלו שנא׳ ועתה כתבו לכם. Rambam (הל׳ ס״ת VII,1) gives the reason for the whole Torah being taken as comprehended in what according to the actual wording refers only to the שירה as being לפי שאין כותבין התורה פרשיות פרשיות, because it is not allowed to write the תורה disconnectedly (see on V. 26.—But concerning this reason see שאגת ארי׳ סי׳ ל׳ד and תשובה מאהבה on י״ד 270.).
The chief prescriptions for writing a Sefer Torah we have already considered in connection with Tephillin and Mezuzza on Ch. 6,9.

V. 20, 21. כי אביאנו וגו׳ והיה וגו׳ Verses 20 and 21 form one sentence. That there was a prospect of the defection and its consequences was declared in verses 16-18. Now here it is said what effect the שירה could have for such an eventuality. If then, when this foreseen future, the defection and the distress occurred, וענתה וגו׳. But with ואכל ושבע ודשן (eats, is satiated, and becomes corpulent), the conditions are revealed out of which—in spite of the תורה and שירה—the defection will come so that תורה and שירה will indeed heal, but not prevent, the defection, and this condition is:- the luxury which comes from the general abundance of all good things. The spiritual moral regime with which the Torah sanctifyingly surrounds also the material life of our senses does not go with a superluxurious life of the senses. That is much more attracted by heathenism, the unrestrained cult of gods which worships licentiousness, against which the serene moral happiness of life to be found in the bond with God loses its value. (ונאצוני, see Numb. 14,11), and so the bond with God becomes broken. With this ואכל ושבע ודשן ופנה the rock is described on which again and again Israel’s faithfulness and thereby Israel’s happiness becomes wrecked. Here, in faithfulness to God and His Torah to be exercised in happiness and wealth and abundance lies the task, the final real accomplishment of which still to-day belongs to the future, which then will have matured to its ultimate achievement, never to be lost again. Only then will good fortune come to us without its being a danger to our duty to God and His Torah, then our position of being richly blessed with worldly possessions will only be an incentive to a fuller carrying out of the tasks set by God’s Torah unhindered and untrammelled by any restrictions. That is why above in Ch. 30,8-10, in the promise of this ultimate future (V.9) after the return to faithfulness to the Torah (V.8) the return to such faithfulness in a still higher and more perfect measure (V.10) is repeated as an achievement which will not be endangered by the restored good fortune but rather will reach everlasting complete development.

והיה כי תמצאן אתו, then, in trouble, when as a result of its defection, many evil misfortunes have struck it, misfortunes which force a man back into himself (for that is the literal meaning of the word צרות which drive all thought of excesses away, צרות here according to the accentuation is really adjectival qualifying רעות) then the teaching which the שירה bears will have its effect on the people, then through the influence of this שירה, it will no longer accuse “its God” for its fate, then the contents of this שירה will always again step before it, in the name of God, as its accuser and lead it back to a true estimation of the cause of its fate and thereby back to God and its duty.

כי לא תשכח מפי זרעו, if ואכל ושבע ודשן ופנה אל אלהים אחרים (“and he eats and is satiated and waxeth fat” I.L.) shows us the shady side of Israel’s appearance in the world and the rock on which its national prosperity foundered, these words כי לא תשכח מפי זרעו show us the secret of its national immortality and of its ultimately fulfilling its mission. However deep its fall may be, and however far away its sin may take it, one thing remains to it throughout all the changes of its existence, one thing accompanies it throughout the darkest paths of its sufferings, and that is:- the Torah. And even if it should at any time turn its back on the whole Torah, the שירה of the Torah, testifying to its calling and its mission, and the Word of God out of it explaining its fate, will remain to the nation. And this spiritual spark of God, which cannot be lost, will suffice ever again to turn its mind to the Torah and warn its susceptibilities again to its teachings and tasks, and thereby keep the soul of life awake which never allows this nation to die, which makes it strong to endure all external oppression, and under all external misfortune, makes it keep a clear outlook, and a happy disposition and a warm heart and an open hand. כי לא תשכח מפי זרעו, this promise ensures that Israel will never come to the complete loss of its calling, never completely forget its mission, that it will remain to the end of time “the People of the Bible”, and in it there will always be the God protected spiritual principle from which it can always achieve its spiritual revival.

In Sanhedrin 90b, the word וקם is to be read also as attached “upwards” i.e. to the preceding words, and taken as הנך שכב עם אבתיך וקם (“see thou liest with thy fathers and will arise” I.L.) a reference to the resurrection of the dead, תחית המתים. According to Yoma 52b, this would be one of the five places where it is undecided (leaving out the question of, and taking no notice of the accentuation, ריטב״א ibid.) whether a word should be read “upwards”, with the preceding words, or “downwards” with the succeeding ones, המש מקראות בתורה שאין להן הכרע, namely ,שאת וקם ,משוקדים ,מחר ,ארור, (Gen. 4,7; ibid. XLIX,7; Ex. 17,9; ibid. XXV,34; Deut. 31,16), and according to תוספות there, the question is only raised which way they are to be read, upwards or downwards, but not, as e.g. in Levit. 25,37 (refer to it) the word to be interpreted as belonging both ways, to the preceding and to the succeeding. This way of taking it, repeatedly given by תוספות offers considerable difficulties, as also even apart from the accentuation, only the two places, viz Ex. 17,9 and XXV,34 could such a “one or the other” way of taking it be possible. But in Gen. 4,17 one could not possibly separate the word from the preceding, just as little as in XLIX,7 or in our verse from the succeeding words. If we read וקם in our verse solely with the preceding “upwards”, the words העם הזה would be entirely without a predicate. One is therefore constrained to understand the אין להם הכרע to mean that the question was whether the word in question could only be interpreted as belonging to the one sentence or perhaps it might be taken to be read with both, whether, in our case, it could only be read וקם העם הזה or whether one could also read it as הנך שכב עם אבותיך וקם וקם העם הזה. And in fact ר׳ יהושע and רבי שמעון בן יוחאי in Sanhedrin 90b, also seem to interpret the וקם as belonging to הנך שכב and to מנין שהקב״ה מחיה מתים ויודע מה שעתיד :העם הזה תורת חיים .להיות שנא׳ הנך שכב עם אבותיך וקם העם הזה וזנה and חדוא״ג מהרש״א explain the passage differently from תוספות (Apart from this, we allow ourselves to remark that ר׳ יהושע and equally so ר׳ אלעזר המודעי, regarding the passage in Ex. XVII, also do not agree with the opinion of איסי בן יהודה, see מכילתא thereon, so that it is quite possible they do not agree with him in the other passages also, and that would answer the difficulty of תוס׳ ישנים in Yoma 52b, ד״ה וקם.

If we consider the whole context, beginning with V.16, revealing the more immediate as well as the distant future of Israel, the reference included in these introductory words of the resurrection of the dead would offer a profound connection with this context. Just as the bodily dying of a human person is no eternal death, but rather, in the apparently dead-for-ever body there remains a “something” out of which the future Call of God forms the resurrection, so all the ways to the grave of the Jewish People are only apparently leading to their national death. אני ישנה ולבי ער “it seems to be sleeping the sleep of death but its heart within it remains awake”. Even if it flies away like dust to complete termination, even if, for a time it dies right away from its high calling, it still retains possession of a spiritual element that it cannot lose, אשר לא תשכח מפי זרעו, the “Book of Books” remains its everlasting original possession, and the spirit which speaks to it out of it becomes its traveller’s song wherever it tarries in its wanderings through the ages, זמירות היו לי חקיך בבית מגורי, it sings to it in the night of its exile-sufferings, ובלילה שירה עמי, until at last with its awakening power of song, it leads all the slumbering spirits, all dying feelings back to the old Truth with fresh courage to live, and out of the grave of its past the “People of the Bible” rise up to rejuvenated life. וענתה השירה הזאת לפניו לעד כי לא תשכח מפי זרעו.

יצר .כי ידעתי את יצרו וגו׳: that which a man forms within himself of his own free will of thoughts, ideas and wishes, which then becomes the direction of his actions and behaviour. See on Gen. 8,21. What this direction can be expected to be, the people had already shown in their forty years wandering in the wilderness, both for good and bad. They are difficult to be won permanently to the good, and even in the deepest defection they keep in connection with the good, from which fact their rising upwards again can be expected. Both the פנה אל אלהים אחרים and the לא תשכח מפי זרעו lie clearly already in their characters. Hence the purpose and establishment of the שירה.

V. 22. ויכתב וגו׳, probably with assistance, in any case in the presence of Joshua. According to the position of this sentence, this writing and teaching formed an integral part of the induction of Joshua. We have already pointed out how the induction of the זקנים was made by an address of God to Moses made in their presence, Numb. 11,16,17. But the address to Moses here in verses 16-21 contain important factors for his successor to take to heart.

They showed him the moral dangers to which his people would be exposed, to work against which would be a demand even more serious than the conquest and division of the land, as conquest and land would be futile if Israel became faltering in their faithfulness to God.

They showed him “learning”, the study which nurtures the knowledge and understanding of the Torah amongst the people, as the most important, yea, the one means of keeping Israel to faithfulness, and to bring them back from every lapse; and indeed not only just the knowledge of the Mitzvas but also the nurturing the knowledge of the spirit behind the letter of the Mitzvas, nurturing the knowledge of the lively consciousness of the unique, wonderful position and mission of Israel in the midst of the world with these Mitzvas; and that the care of this spiritual and intellectual means, the winning and educating all classes of the people up to the knowledge and understanding must be the very first thing he must aim at.

They showed him the indispensable demand which, in the very first place is made to every Jewish leader, not to be deterred or frightened away at any time by the general lack of faith towards God and the deviations from His Torah. At all times he must remain quiet, staunch and firm, consciously and seriously holding aloft the standard of the Torah entrusted to him by God, knowing that it can never be his task to adjust God’s Torah to accommodate the weakness of the aberration of judgement of any time; that beyond the time of aberration the Torah awaits the arrival of a future generation which will return with more devoted faithfulness to God and His Torah, for which in all times the leaders have to keep the Torah intact, and for how many or how few minds it will be so kept for the future trust to the promise כי לא תשכח מפי זרעו.

ויכתב משה וגו׳ וילמדה וגו׳. The Torah, the laws which Moses had to transmit to the people, were, as is evident from Ex. 24,3,4 as well as XXXIV,31,32, first given verbally to the people before they were committed to writing, with them, the full explanation, the oral tradition is the focal point and on Ex. 21,1, we have already tried to indicate the relation of the written to oral tradition (of the nature of notes for reference and remembrance to a given lecture I.L.). But שירה, the contents of the poem visualising God, is given in its completeness in the written words. With it the writing came first before the oral teaching to correctly understand it.

V. 23. ויצו וגו׳. All the preceding was said to Moses in the presence of Joshua and constituted the completion of Moses’s induction of Joshua and was followed by the direct command of God personally to Joshua. כי אתה תביא את העם, as is remarked in Sanhedrin 8a, Moses, in his speech to Joshua (V.7) said כי אתה תבוא את העם (“for thou shalt come with the people” I.L.) and thereby had only made Joshua thought of together with the people and the elders, but God’s address אתה תביא וגו׳ (“thou shalt bring the people” I.L.) gives him the direct command to bring the people etc. and stresses the principle that the supreme command at any time must be in the hands of one single leader דבר אחר לדור ואין שני דברין לדור “there must be only one supreme speaker for any contemporary time”, hence אתה תביא.
V. 24. עד תמם by adding the שירה also to it.
V. 25. ויצו משה וגו׳, see on V. 9.

V. 26. לקח וגו׳. We have already mentioned on V. 10 that, according to דברים רבה, that besides this copy of the Torah written by his own hand and deposited in the Holy of Holies, Moses had written twelve other copies and given one to every tribe. We have pointed out elsewhere how thereby it is clear that the Torah was made completely known to the people by oral teaching during the forty years wandering before it was handed over to them in any written form. The question dealt with in Gittin 60a, in connection with this verse 26 as to whether תורה מגלה מגלה נתנה or חתומה ניתנה does not affect in any way this fact which we have stressed. The whole discussion there, and the way the commentators take it, is not the question as to how the written Torah was given over to the people, but as to how it was made by Moses, whether מגלה מגלה piecemeal, written down at once as soon as any law was revealed to him, or חתומה when the whole Torah was connectedly completed. See תוספות and the super-commentaries thereon. (Only on the שמנה פרשיות does Rashi mention נאמרו ונכתבו ונמסרו),

According to that, the term could refer to the depositing of the copy of the written Torah which was placed in, or next to, the Ark in the Holy of Holies. See Jerusalmi Sota 8,3 at the end ד״ה על דעתיה דר״מ, the commentary ועוד אפשר וזה נלע״ד עיקר .מראה הפנים שלשון נתינה כאן אינו מיד משה לישראל אלא מהקב״ה למשה דומיא דלשון מתן תורה ולפי שמשה לא כתב התורה מפי עצמו אלא מפי הקב״ה יקרא אליו והוא כותב על ספר בדיו על כן כתיבה כזו נתינה קרו לה כלומר נתינת התורה בכתב, תדע דרק מכתיבה מיירי התם דאי לא כן אלא נתינה דווקא קאמר אדבעי אליבא דמאן דאמר חתומה ניתנה או דלמא כיון דלא אפשר כתבינן דלא הוי אלא היתר דרבנן משום עת לעשות וגו׳ לימא או דלמא כיון דרק ניתנה חתומה והכתיבה היתה מגלה מגלה כתבינן דהוי היתר אפי׳ דאורי׳. וכן היכא מוכח מקרא במגילת ספר כתב עלי דמגלה מגלה ניתנה דלמא משום הכי נקראת תורה מגלה כיון דנכתבה מגלה מגלה אעפ״י דניתנה חתומה אלא ודאי כל נתינה .בסוגיא זו כתיבה היא כנ״ל

מצד ארון וגו׳. According to ר״מ in Baba Bathra 14a inside the Ark at the side of the tablets, and then, according to the quoted place in Sota, the ס״ת is understood under the עדות mentioned in Ex. 25,21, and then indeed here too the purpose of the ס״ת deposited there is pronounced to be an עד. But according to ר״י there, more in accordance with the wording of the text, the ס״ת was not placed in the Ark, but on a ledge projecting at the side of it.

V. 27. ממרים הייתם עם ה׳. So also in Ch. 9,7 and 24. As remarked there, to be disobedient to someone is called -מרה ב or -את. But עם ה׳ does not designate opposition to, but connection with God, and ממרים הייתם עם ה׳ expresses just the double side of their character which the people had already shown under the whole of Moses’s leadership. They were never definitely faithful and their defection was never really complete—as is expressed above by ופנה וגו׳ and עם ה׳ .—כי לא תשכח וגו׳ they were always ממרים in some way, and as ממרים they still remained in one way עם ה׳. In that, as remarked above, lies all the trouble and also all the consoling comfort for Israel’s wanderings through the ages.
V. 28. ואעירה בם וגו׳. See on Ch. 30,19.

V. 29. כי ידעתי וגו׳. As soon as I have passed away from you the corruption will begin with you and you will begin to deviate from the path of your duty and then in later times when your fate overtakes you, misfortune will befall you because you will have gone as far as to behave in principle in opposition to the Will of God.

Nothing could serve to prove the Divine origin of the mission of Moses as much as the retrospective avowal and consciousness of conditions contained in these verses 27 to 29. If the “Law of Moses” were indeed only laws of Moses, the world could show no greater fool than just “this man Moses”! What greater folly could there be, than to give laws which are so completely opposed to the ideas and inclinations of the people for whom they are meant, that the lawgiver himself is fully aware that for centuries to come the people would not have made themselves at one with the Law, not have accepted the Law, nor the Law accept the people. And for the final achievement of the intended aim, to appoint no other guarantors than heaven and earth, and no other means than the Book of the Law and its teachings which in spite of all will not be lost to their children and their childrens’ children כי לא תשכח מפי זרעו!

And if now, after thousands of years we look back at these past thousands of years of this People and this “Book of Moses”, and consider how everything there has really happened in the course of time, how finally and just in times of the worst sufferings, this People has attached itself so deeply to this Torah, that for its sake it has endured an unparalleled world-historic martyrdom, and this Torah has become the “eagle wings” on which God’s Rule has carried it above all its trials in the midst of a world which offered it only enmity and scorn, misunderstanding and bitterness, out into ever fresh powers of rejuvenated spirit and life; how it has become the source of Life and Truth out of which the nations amongst whom God had scattered them have drunk—and drink; and how still today it is the Tree of Life, the seeds of which, seeds of knowledge and life, have been carried, consciously and unconsciously, by its scattered children, into the fields of the nations where they grow up for the good of mankind and for the common salvation of the world, so that Israel has in truth become a “Jezreel of the Exile” Hosea 1,4, (and II,2. ישראל becomes יזרע אל I.L.), and the cue for Jewish history ויתערבו בגוים וילמדו ממעשיהם has become fulfilled in both senses; so that, looking back, the thought lies indeed very near, that just on account of its dual nature, the ממרים הייתם עם ה׳, the ופנה אל אלהים אחרים and לא תשכח מפי זרעו, the Jewish People have proved the most suitable instrument for God’s purposes for the whole human race, for whose defections they have after all brought little sparks of fire and little seeds which can spread and grow, and so have been not the most ineffective agents for God—what thinking man, when he reads the final avowal of Moses in verses 27-29, and then allows his mind to pass over the history of this People and this Book can refrain from acknowledging that this Torah is not thy work “Man Moses” but is the Law of God Whose messenger only thou wast, so that the People and the Torah are and remain אצבע אלקים, the directing finger of God to mankind.

V. 1. This is the appointment of heaven and earth, declared in the previous chapter V. 28, to be witnesses and guarantors of the covenant of God made with Israel, and of what was to be said regarding the future which would result from this relationship (see there and Ch. 30,19). האזין, “to incline one’s ear” expresses a greater readiness to listen to what is being said than שמע .שמע, something can be heard even without the hearer wishing to listen, not so האזין. The carrying out of the expected representation of the covenant of God by heaven and earth, comes in the first place from heaven, only indirectly is it then consummated by the earth. The heaven is primarily active, the earth, more passive, for all blessing and the reverse, of the physical development of the earth and as far as they are dependent on that, also human social conditions are dependent on extraterritorial cosmic conditions which exist in what we call “the heavens”. What is to develop on earth must begin with the actions of the heavens. Hence the direct demand to השמים, and indeed האזינו השמים to accept and take over the words to be said ותשמע הארץ, not ושמעי הארץ, is more an indirect result of האזינו השמים.

The ספרי compares this introduction of the speech of Moses to the שמעו שמים והאזיני ארץ of Isaiah (Ch. 1,2) and remarks לפי שהיה משה קרוב לשמים לפיכך אמר האזינו השמים ולפי שהיה רחוק מן הארץ אמר ותשמע הארץ אמרי פי בא ישעי׳ וסמך לדבר ואמר שמעו שמים שהיה רחוק מן השמים והאזיני ארץ שהיה קרוב לארץ. Moses stood nearer to heaven and farther from the earth and therefore he demanded the heavens to האזנה and the earth to שמיעה. But Isaiah was farther from the heavens and nearer to the earth hence he said שמעו to the heaven and האזיני to the earth. What we said above of the relationship of the heavens and the earth could also be the underlying reason for these verses of the Sifri. In the service of the purposes of God’s Rule the heavens are the active factor, the giver, but the earth more the passive receiver. Moses, in his mission, could consider himself as being near to the active, dispensing activities of the heavens. For was he not sent to bring the seeds of light and warmth, of Truth and of Life to the fields of the development of mankind! Does not verse 2 at once compare the effects to be expected from his teachings and his promises to the fertility and prosperity which the gifts of the heavens effect on the earth! So that Moses could feel himself קרוב לשמים (akin to the heavens I.L.) and addresses his words directly to the ears of the heavens בא ישעיה וסמך לדבר. Isaiah, taking his cue from the master who stood so high above him, felt himself in his mission only akin to the passive earth—does he not refrain from saying כי אדברה (for I would fain speak) but says כי ה׳ דבר (for it is God Who is speaking I.L.), hence only שמעו שמים and והאזיני ארץ. And apart from that, when Moses had to speak the words of his mission, what he had to say referred to destiny which was still a matter for heaven, the earth on which and the time in which it was to be realised was still far away. But Isaiah stood in the time of the realisation and he was quite specially a transmitting messenger of it. His words accordingly were in the proximity of the earth. Hence too the term ואדברה when his word is addressed to the heavens, they are still only דברים declared destinies, the realisation of which could still lie in the distance, only when they touch the earth are they considered as consummated, (Cf. Gen. I. 22).
ואדברה, I would speak, I have something to say. This is the demand directed to the heavens. Moses will only speak when the heaven has placed its ear ready to receive his words.

V. 2. ערף .יערף the neck joint, the most responsive, most mobile joint in the body, the movement of which is quickest to obey direction of the will, and its opposite is קשה ערף (stiff neckedness, obstinacy I.L.). Hence the loosening of the hard surface of the ground by the droplets of the loosening rain is called ערף. Perhaps חרף is also related to it, the time of the year when the earth is subject to the loosening influences of the elements.

לקח ,לקחי is the term for teachings from the point of view of the pupils, teachings which are, or are to be, taken up.—נשל .נזל (to slip off, to fall off I.L.) to lose the hold it has hitherto had, נצל, the forcible separating something from its hold, נזל, the natural weak coherence of particles, designates the flow, the movement of liquids. Hence, the surprising contrast נצבו כמו נד נוזלים (Ex. 15,8).—אמרה ,אמרתי the common expression of God’s promises. (Cf. Numb. 23,19).

סער ,שער .כשעירים and סערה שערה: storm. שער disgust, horrible, שער hair שעיר the rough hairy animal, he-goat. The underlying meaning seems to be: a strong movement from within outwards; in space; storm; in feeling; disgust; physiological; strong outgrowth from the bodies of animals or plants; hair. Here it refers to space, storm, and moreover in a passive form like שעיר, the hairy-covered animal, so of a shower of rain driven by a storm, thus Onkelos translates it רביב ,וכרביבים—.כרוחי מטרא from רבב the root of רב, a big downfall of rain, perhaps also begetting a rich growth as רבבה כצמח השדה נתתיך (Ezek. 16,7).

The mission of Moses consisted of two factors, teachings and promises. He expected from the co-operation of heaven and earth in forming the future of his people that neither of these factors would be lost, that both would ultimately reach their aim, expected that the heavens and the earth appointed by God to be witnesses and guarantors of His covenant would not rest until his teachings, his Torah, has become לקח, taken into and to the hearts of his people, and the soil of their minds and hearts which had so long remained hard had become softened and loosened, so that the seeds of light and warmth, of knowledge and life could come up and shoot forth, and that his promises, refreshing like the dew would always revive the courage of his people and keep them upright in the hard times that lay before them, that both—the Torah and the Promises—would prove themselves purifying like storm-showers on the meadows and finally fructifying like a rich and plentiful fall of rain on vegetation.

V. 3. כי שם ה׳ וגו׳, for it is not his word that he has to speak, it is not he in whose name that he exhorts heaven and earth, it is God, Whose Name, Whose ways of ruling the world, as far as they are accessible to the human mind, (cf.
